[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 1 (part 1 of 3)]

﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾

Exegetes (mufassirun) have been perplexed about the status (mahall) of these letters that occur at the beginning of this surah and at the openings of a number of other surahs, totalling twenty-nine surahs, most of which are Meccan. Some of them occur at the beginning of the second surah revealed, which is Nun, wal-Qalam (surah 68). These letters are fitting to be a source of bewilderment, a cause of many differing opinions and extensive investigations. The total of the letters of the alphabet that occur as openings of surahs is fourteen letters, which is half of the letters of the alphabet. Most of the surahs in which these letters occur are Meccan, except al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran. The letters that occur in the surahs are: alif, ha', ra', sin, sad, ta', 'ayn, qaf, kaf, lam, mim, nun, ha', ya'. Some of them are repeated in surahs and some are not repeated. They are undoubtedly part of the Qur'an, and among the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses in terms of their interpretation (ta'wil).

There is no disagreement that these openings, when the reciter pronounces them, are the names (asma') of the letters of spelling (al-huruf al-tahajji), which in speech are pronounced by their referents (musammayat). Their referents are the sounds shaped in particular modes that arise at the articulation points (makharij) of the letters. For this reason, the reciter says, for example, (Alif Lam Mim) and does not say (Alam). They wrote them in the mushafs with the forms of the letters by which one spells in speech, whose written shape stands in place of what is pronounced in speech. They did not write them with signs indicating how they are read in the Qur'an, because the intention is spelling with them, and letters of spelling are written with their forms, not with their names.

It has been said that it is because the orthography of the mushaf is a sunnah that is not to be analogized upon. This (view) is preferable, as it is more comprehensive of the opinions that fall under it. Up to this point it has become clear that the most probable of those opinions are three: that these letters are there (1) to rebuke the obstinate opponents and to record their inability to produce a counterpart (mu'arada), or (2) that they are names for the surahs in which they occur, or (3) that they are oaths sworn by them to honour the status of writing and to alert the Arabs, who were unlettered (ummiyyun), to the benefits of writing, in order to bring them out of the state of illiteracy. The most probable of these three opinions is the first, for the second, seventh, eighth, twelfth, fifteenth and sixteenth opinions are refuted by the fact that if these letters were abbreviated from names or words, it would be necessary that they be pronounced by their referents and not by their names, because the orthography of the mushaf is a sunnah that is not to be analogized upon. This (first) view is preferable because it is more comprehensive of the opinions.

Their being nouns (ismiyyah) is known from two indicators. One is the acceptance of the states that nouns take on them, such as definiteness, as when you say "al-alif" and "al-ba'", and such as plurality, as when you say "al-jimat" (the jim's), and such as description, as when you say "alif mamduda" (an extended alif). The second is what Sibawayh transmitted in his book: al-Khalil said one day, and he asked his companions: "How do you pronounce the kaf that is in (laka) and the ba' that is in (darb)?" They said: "We say: kaf. ba'." He said: "You have only brought the noun and not pronounced the letter." And he said: "I say kih, and bih," meaning with a ha' that occurs at the end of the pronunciation, so that the tongue may rest upon it when pronouncing, if the letter remains on a single letter that does not appear in pronunciation when pronounced alone.

What is extracted from the opinions of the scholars, after removing their overlaps and uniting their similar ones, reduces to twenty-one opinions. Because the meaning of these letters is so obscure, I found it necessary to investigate the opinions completely. However, we can organize their spread by classifying them into three types.

The first type refers to the view that they are symbols abbreviated from words or sentences, so they are secrets whose locks are opened by the keys of the people of knowledge. Under this type fall eight opinions.

The first: that they are knowledge which (God, exalted is He) kept exclusively to Himself. This has been attributed to the four Caliphs in weak narrations, though they may establish that God informed His Messenger ﷺ of their intended meaning. It was said by al-Sha'bi and Sufyan.

The second: that they are letters abbreviated from names and attributes of God, exalted is He, whose openings are with letters similar to these disconnected letters. It was transmitted by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and said by Muhammad ibn al-Qurazi or al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Thus (Alif Lam Mim), for example: the alif is an indication of Ahad (the One) or Awwal (the First) or Azali (the Eternal), the lam an indication of Latif (the Subtle), and the mim an indication of Malik (the King) or Majid (the Glorious), and the like. According to this, their explanation would require a revelation (tawqif), and how could they have it?

The third: that they are symbols for the names of God, exalted is He, and the names of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the angels. Thus (Alif Lam Mim), for example: the alif is from Allah, the lam from Jibril (Gabriel), and the mim from Muhammad. This was said by al-Dahhak. There must be revelation for each opening among them, and perhaps we will point out that in its places.

The fourth: Shaykh Muhyi al-Din affirmed in the 198th chapter, section 27 of his book al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya, that these disconnected letters at the beginnings of surahs are names of the angels, and that when they are recited they are like a call to their angels, so the bearers of those names listen to what the reciter says after pronouncing them. They then say: "You have spoken truly," if what follows is a report, and they say: "This is a believer, truly he has spoken the truth and reported the truth," and so they ask forgiveness for him. This has not been said by anyone other than him, and it is a claim.

The fifth: that they are all symbols for the names and attributes of the Prophet ﷺ specifically. This was said by Shaykh Muhammad ibn Salih, known as Ibn Mulukah al-Tunisi, in a treatise of his. He said that every letter of the alphabet at the openings of surahs is a kinaya (allusion) for a group of his noble names and specific attributes. Thus the alif is an allusion to the totality of his names that begin with alif, such as Ahmad and Abu al-Qasim; the lam is an allusion to his attributes, such as Lubb al-Wujud (the Essence of Existence); and the mim is an allusion to Muhammad and the like, such as Mubashshir (Bringer of Good News) and Mundhir (Warner). So all of them are addressed with a vocative particle that is implied (muqaddar), by evidence of the appearance of that particle in Ya Sin. He did not attribute this view to anyone. His student Shaykh al-Islam Muhammad Mu'awiya wrote a commentary (ta'liqa) on this treatise, in which he added a great deal of enumeration, but it is not what satisfies the heart in its investigations. That commentary and its original are present in the storeroom of the Zaytuna Mosque in Tunis, number 514. This view is refuted by the obligatory deletion of the vocative particle, and his claim that it appears in Ya Sin is based on the view of those who said that Ya Sin means "O Master," which is weak, because the ya' in it is a letter of the alphabet. Moreover, the Shaykh himself counted Ya Sin, after that, among the letters that indicate names, referring to something like the ya' in Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad.

The sixth: that they are symbols for the duration of this Ummah's continuance, by the reckoning of abjad numerals (hisab al-jummal). This was said by Abu al-'Aliya, relying on a story transmitted by Ibn Ishaq from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Wathhab, who said: "Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab and Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf came and asked the Messenger of God about Alif Lam Mim, and they said: 'This is the term of this Ummah in years, seventy-one years.' The Messenger of God laughed and said to them: 'Sad' and 'Alif Lam Mim Ra'.' They said: 'The matter has become confused for us, so we do not know whether we should take the little or the much.'" End of quotation.

The Messenger of God's answer to them with a number of other letters from these disconnected letters at the beginnings of surahs is not an affirmation that they are symbols for the numbers of the duration of this Ummah. Rather, he intended to refute what they understood, by refuting that it could be beneficial to their claim, in the manner of the method called naqd (refutation by counter-example) in disputation (jadal), whose reference is to prohibition and the one who prohibits, and has no school of its own.

As for his ﷺ laughter, it was an expression of wonder at their ignorance.

The seventh: that they are symbols, each letter standing for a word. Thus (Alif Lam Mim) means: Ana Allahu A'lam (I am God, most knowing); and (Alif Lam Mim Ra') means: Ana Allahu Ara (I am God, the Seer); and (Alif Lam Mim Sad) means: Ana Allahu A'lam wa Afsil (I am God, most knowing and decisive).

It was transmitted by Abu al-Duha from Ibn 'Abbas. It is weakened by the fact that it has no governing principle, for he once matched the letter with the first letter of a word, and once matched it with a letter from the middle or end of a word.

They have compared it to the fact that the Arabs sometimes speak with disconnected letters instead of words composed of those letters, in both verse and prose. Among that is the verse of Zuhayr:

"With goodness, good things; and if evil, then fa (strike)
And I do not desire evil except that you ta (wish)."

He meant: "wa-in sharra fa-sharrin" (and if evil, then evil), and he meant: "illa an tasha" (except that you wish), so he came with one letter from each phrase.

Another said, a Qurtubi (of Cordoba):

"He called them: 'Alla tarkabuna' (Will you not ride?) ... alla ta!
They all said together: 'Alla fa' (Then ride!) ..."

He meant by the first letter "alla tarkabuna" and by the second "alla farkabu."

Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, the governor of 'Uthman, said addressing 'Adi ibn Hatim:

"I said to her: 'Stop for us,' she said: 'qaf' (I stopped),
Do not think I have forgotten the hurrying."

He meant: "qalat waqaftu" (she said: I stopped).

In a hadith: "Whoever helps in the killing of a Muslim with half a word." Shaqiq said: "It is that he says 'uq' in place of 'uqtul' (kill)." And in another hadith: "The sword is sufficient as shá" meaning "shahidan" (as a witness).

In al-Kamil of al-Mubarrad, from a qasida by 'Ali ibn 'Isa al-Qummi, who is a muwallad (later poet):

"And the wearing of the dust-cloud and the khafiqat (the hastening ones)
Shows you the manaa (deaths) on the tips of the lances."

He meant: "tureeka al-manaya" (shows you the deaths).

In Taleh (a term in the Sihah of al-Jawhari), Labid said:

"The manaa (dwellings) were effaced in the mata'lia, then became clear,
Then they grew old at al-Habs and al-Suban."

He meant: "daras al-manazil" (the dwellings were effaced).

'Alqama al-Fahl said, in Khasa'is, p. 82:

"As if their ewer is a gazelle on a height,
Scented with the sabaa of flax, perfumed."

He meant: "bi-sabaib al-kattan" (with the strands of flax).

The rajiz (rajaz poet) said:

"When she dropped her load at Quba,
And the killing continued in 'Abd al-Ashal."

That is, "'Abd al-Ashhal."

And the saying of Abu Du'ad:

"They drive hindal, a bewildered one, to its south,
As if its hooves were kindled with the hubaa."

He meant "al-hubahib."

And al-Akhtal said:

"Their manaa became in a land where the one with a troubled heart
Cannot reach it except the swift she-camel, the Ujud."

He meant "manazilaha" (its dwellings).

There occurred in (Tiraz al-Majalis - al-Majlis) for the later writers much of this, along with double meaning (tawriya), such as the saying of Ibn Makanis:

"I have not forgotten Badr, who visited me one night,
Restless, showing an opening for the dangerous one (khatar)."

"He did not stand except for the duration of what
I said to him: 'Ahlan wa sahlan wa mar'."

He meant part of the word "marhaban" (welcome). I have multiplied its evidences extensively to broaden the places of this strange usage. I do not intend by this to correct the bearing of the disconnected letters at the beginnings of surahs on that, because it is not fitting to derive the Qur'an upon it, and there is nothing with them indicating it, along with the double meaning by making "marr" from "al-muruur" (passing by).

The eighth: that they are allusions to states of purification of the heart. In the Futuhat, in the second chapter, he (Muhyi al-Din) considered them to be an indication of the branches of faith (shu'ab al-iman). The essence of this is that the total of the letters occurring at the beginnings of the surahs of the Qur'an, counting repetitions of letters, is seventy-eight letters, and "eight" here is the reality of "bid'" (a few). It was obtained for him by unveiling (kashf), so the number of letters is seventy-eight. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Faith is seventy-odd branches." So these letters are the branches of faith, and no one attains the secrets of faith until he knows the realities of these letters in their surahs.

How can someone claim that they are used with unknown meanings, when it is established that the listeners received them with acceptance, believer and opponent alike? Had they not understood from them a known meaning indicated by contextual evidences, the questioners would have asked and the opponents would have hesitated. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "Had the Arabs not known a meaning for them circulating among them, they would have been the first to deny that to the Prophet ﷺ. Rather, he recited to them Ha Mim (Fussilat) and Sad and others, and they did not deny that, despite their eagerness for a stumble and their desire for a slip."

I say: They have indeed asked about something clearer than this, when they said: "And what is al-Rahman?" As for what they cited from the verse of Zuhayr and others, it is from the rarities of Arabic speech, and is among what is produced in the manner of riddles and wordplay, and that is not suitable to the status of the glorious Book.

The second type gathers the opinions that refer to these letters being established in those forms as nouns or verbs. Within it there are four opinions.

The ninth opinion, among those listed about their meaning, is held by a group of scholars and theologians, and al-Fakhr (al-Razi) preferred it: that they are names of the surahs in which they occur. Zayd ibn Aslam said this. It is also attributed to Sibawayh in his book, in the chapter on the names of surahs among the sections of diptotes, or to al-Khalil. The author of al-Kashshaf attributed it to the majority. It is reinforced by the fact that these letters occur at the beginnings of surahs, so these letters have been made names, serving as markers for those surahs, and the surahs were named after them, just as we say "the booklet B" and "the bundle C." Al-Qaffal compared this to the way the Arabs named things after the letters of the alphabet: they named Lam, the father of Harithah al-Ta'i, and they named gold "ayn," clouds "ghayn," the fish "nun," and the mountain "qaf." I say: "Ha" is also a tribe from Madhhij. Shurayh ibn Awfa al-'Anasi or al-'Absi said:

*It reminds me of Ha Mim, while the spear is clashing;*
*why did he not recite Ha Mim before the advance?*

He means the Ha Mim and 'Ayn Sin Qaf [al-Shura: 1–2], in which is the verse: ﴿Say: I do not ask of you any reward for it except affection for relatives﴾ [al-Shura: 23]. This opinion is very far-fetched, since it is not the case that a name is not included in what it names. We have found these letters read together with the surahs by the consensus of the Muslims. Moreover, this opinion is refuted by the repetition of these same letters across several surahs, such as Alif Lam Mim, Alif Lam Ra, and Ha Mim, and because the names of the other surahs were not placed at their beginnings.

The tenth opinion: a group said that they are names for the Qur'an, agreed upon as such. This was said by al-Kalbi, al-Suddi and Qatada. It is refuted by the fact that after some of them there occurs what would not fit if they were names for the Qur'an, such as: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ [al-Rum: 1] ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum: 2], and ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1] ﴿Do people think﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2].

The eleventh opinion: every combination of these letters is a name of God. They related from 'Ali that he used to say: "Ya Kaf Ha Ya' 'Ayn Sad; Ya Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf," and he was silent about the single letters, which are then referred back to whatever fits them among the opinions above. It is refuted by the lack of connection between some of them and what follows them, since they could not be a statement or the like about the name of God, such as: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿This is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1–2], and ﴿Alif Lam Mim Sad﴾ [al-A'raf: 1] ﴿A Book revealed to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 2].

The twelfth opinion: al-Mawardi said they are verbs. The letters of ﴿Alif Lam Mim Sad﴾ [al-A'raf: 1] ﴿Book﴾ [al-A'raf: 2] are a verb, alama, meaning "descended." So the meaning of ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿This is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1–2] is: it was sent down upon you. This statement is refuted by the fact that they are not read in verbal forms, and moreover this cannot apply to all of them, such as "Kaf Ha Ya' 'Ayn Sad," "Alif Lam Mim Sad," and "Alif Lam Ra." Were it not for the strangeness of this opinion, it would be appropriate to disregard it.

The third category: it includes the opinions which trace back to the view that these letters are letters of spelling, intended by their names, for purposes that call for this. Among the opinions in this category:

The thirteenth opinion: that God Most High swore by these letters, just as He swore by the pen, to honour them, because their referents are combined to form the names of God Most High and the foundations of speech and knowledge. This was said by al-Akhfash. This opinion has been weakened by the fact that if they were sworn by, the particle of oath would have been mentioned, since according to the Basrans it is omitted only with the Name of God. It is also weakened by the fact that in some places an oath follows them, such as ﴿Nun. By the pen﴾ [al-Qalam: 1] and ﴿Ha Mim﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 1] ﴿By the clear Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 2]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "They have found it objectionable to combine two oaths on a single sworn object, to the point that al-Khalil said, regarding the verse ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl: 1] ﴿and the day when it appears﴾ [al-Layl: 2], that the second wa' is the one that joins nouns to nouns, that is, the conjunctive wa'." The answer to this is that the omission of the particle with other than the Name of God is a matter of disagreement, and that the dislike of combining two oaths is avoided by taking the wa' that follows these openings as the conjunctive wa', since they did in fact combine two oaths. Al-Nabigha said:

*By God, by God, Harith is the finest young man,*
*neither base nor obscure.*

The fourteenth opinion: they were brought in the manner of spelling, recited in sequence in the pattern of enumeration in spelling, as a rebuke to the polytheists and an awakening of their attention to the fact that this Book recited to them, which they were challenged to match with a surah like it, is a speech composed of the very same letters as their speech. It is as if it urges them to attempt a counter-challenge, and it encourages them to begin that attempt themselves by spelling out the letters (tahajji) and working at pronunciation, in a way that mocks them by treating them as people who do not know the forms of the language. So it teaches them, like the spelling of children at the start of their learning with the writing tablet, so that their inability to match it after this attempt is an inability for which they have no excuse. This view was held by al-Mubarrad, Qutrub and al-Farra'. Al-Kashshaf said: "This opinion has a strength and a soundness deserving of acceptance." I say: this is the one we choose, and the appropriateness is evident in their occurring at the beginnings of surahs: every surah is aimed at inimitability, since God Most High says: ﴿then bring a surah like it﴾. So it is appropriate to open with what carries the inimitability, as a preparation for the attempt to match it. This opinion is supported by the fact that spelling is evident for this purpose, which is why they did not ask about it, given how plain the matter was. Also, spelling was familiar to them for teaching purposes. So when the letters of spelling are mentioned in that familiar manner of teaching, in a context unsuited to teaching, the listeners recognize that they are being treated as learners, because their state is like his in inability to produce eloquent speech. This aspect is reinforced by the fact that these letters are, for the most part, followed by a mention of the Qur'an, its sending down, or its writing, except in ﴿Kaf Ha Ya' 'Ayn Sad﴾ [Maryam: 1], ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1] ﴿Do people think﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2], and ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ [al-Rum: 1] ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum: 2]. As for the reason for singling out some of these letters for spelling rather than others, and for the repetition of some of them, we do not know the reason; perhaps it is for the sake of the eloquence of the speech. This is supported by the fact that most occurrences of these letters are at the beginnings of Meccan surahs, except al-Baqarah according to those who regard all of them as Medinan, and Al 'Imran. Perhaps this is because those two were revealed close to the time of the Hijrah from Mecca, and because the purpose of challenge in the Qur'an revealed in Mecca is more fitting. It is also supported by the letters whose names end in a long alif, such as ya', ha', ra', ta' and ha', which are read at the beginnings of surahs as intended spelling, in the way children spell them in the writing tablet, seeking ease, as will come shortly at the end of this section, in the commentary on Alif Lam Mim.

The fifteenth opinion: they are a teaching of the separate letters, so that when they come to them afterwards in combined form, they will already know them, just as children learn the separate letters and then learn them combined. This was said by 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya, meaning: since there was no one among them who was skilled at writing except in some cities, such as the people of al-Hira, some of Tayy, some of Quraysh and Kinanah from the people of Mecca. The conditions of the Arabs regarding reading and writing have varied in diverse ways across different eras. At first they were a people of writing, because they migrated into the Arab lands from Iraq after the confusion of tongues, and Iraq is the cradle of reading and writing. History has established that Dakhm ibn Irim was the first to teach the Arabs writing, and he set out the twenty-nine letters of the alphabet. Then, when the Arabs became bedouin, that is, they settled in the desert, the tribes of the desert forgot reading and writing over the long passage of time, and their situation kept them from receiving the foundations of the sciences. So writing remained in the settled places, such as the settled areas of Yemen and the Hijaz. Then, when they dispersed after the flood of al-'Arim, they carried writing to the lands in which they settled. Tayy in Najd knew reading and writing, and they were the only group of the Qahtanites in the land of Najd. For this reason, the people of the Hijaz and Najd say that the ones who invented writing were three men from the Banu Bulan of Tayy. By "invented" they mean that they taught it to the 'Adnanites in Najd. The people of al-Hira used to teach writing, and so the Arabs of the Hijaz claim that they learned the script from the people of al-Anbar and al-Hira. The story of al-Mutalammis in the books of literature reminds us of this, since the one who read the letter to him was a boy from the young lads of al-Hira.

The Aws and Khazraj, although they were among the displaced Qahtanites, had also abandoned writing, since they were people of farming, horsemanship and wars. It is reported in the biographies that none of the Ansar in Medina knew how to write, and among the polytheist captives at the Battle of Badr there were some who knew how. Whoever among the captives had no wealth was ransomed by teaching ten boys of the people of Medina to write. Zayd ibn Thabit learned it in a group. And al-Shifa' bint 'Abd Allah of Quraysh knew how to write, and she taught it to Hafsah, the Mother of the Believers.

There is in the legends of the Arabs what suggests that the people of the Hijaz learned writing from the people of Madyan who lived near them. They mention a story that al-Mahd ibn Jandal, from the people of Madyan, was a king who had six sons: Abjad, Hawwaz, Huttiy, Kalaman, Sa'fas and Qarashat. He made his sons kings over the land of Madyan and its surroundings. He made Abjad rule Mecca, made Hawwaz and Huttiy rule al-Ta'if and Najd, and made the remaining three rule Madyan. They said that Kalaman was in the time of Shu'ayb, and that he was among those seized by the punishment of the Day of the Shade. They said: so the letters of spelling were the names of these kings. Then they added to them Thakhadh and Dhaghaz. This suggests that the story was fabricated to teach children the letters of the alphabet in an easy way suited to their minds, and that the letters Thakhadh and Dhaghadh were not in the alphabet of the people of Madyan, so the people of the Hijaz added them. Indeed, these are among the letters that are not frequently used and are not found in every language. However, this opinion is undermined by the fact that not all the letters occur at the beginnings of surahs. Rather, only half of them occur, as will be explained later from the words of al-Kashshaf.

The sixteenth opinion: they are letters intended to alert the listener, like a call used for alerting, as when you say "O youth" to rouse the listener's mind. This was said by Tha'lab, al-Akhfash and Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is like what is said in reciting the most famous poems: la wa-bal la." Al-Fakhr said in his commentary on the surah al-'Ankabut: when the wise speaker addresses someone who is inattentive or preoccupied, he places before the intended speech something to draw the addressee's attention through that preface, and then he begins the intended matter. That preface may be speech, such as a call or particles of opening, or it may be a sound, such as someone clapping to make the listener turn to him. So the Wise One chose for alerting letters from the letters of spelling, so that their indication of the purpose of alerting would be determined, since they have no meaning of their own. Thus they were devoted purely to alerting to an important matter.

The seventeenth opinion: they are a miracle in action, namely, that the unlettered Prophet, who did not read, pronounced the foundations of reading just as the skilled scribes pronounce them, so that the pronouncing of them is a miracle. This is clearly false, since for the unlettered it is not difficult to pronounce letters.

The eighteenth opinion: the disbelievers used to turn away from listening to the Qur'an, and they said: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it﴾ [Fussilat: 26]. So these letters were presented to them so that they would turn to seeking to understand their meaning, and then what follows them would reach them without intent. This was said by Qutrub, and it is close to the sixteenth opinion.

The nineteenth opinion: they are a sign for the People of the Book, who had been promised by their prophets that the Qur'an would open with separate letters.

**[Twentieth opinion]** Al-Tabrizi said: God knew that a people would later claim that the Qur'an is eternal (qadim), so He showed them that it is composed of letters like the letters of speech. This is an error, because the composition of speech from the sounds of words is a far stronger indication of its being created (muhdath) than the indication of the disjointed letters, since their sounds are few.

**[Twenty-first opinion]** It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that they are a praise (thana') with which God praised Himself. This returns to the first or the second opinion.

**[Summary of the opinions]** There is no doubt that all Muslims recite them by the names of the letters of the alphabet, such as *alif. lam. mim* (Alif, Lam, Mim), and not as *alam* (alam). Their written form, in the shape of letters, invalidates all the opinions of the first type and specifies that one should limit oneself, in general, to the second and third types. However, what falls under these two types varies in degrees of acceptability. The second, seventh, eighth, twelfth, fifteenth and sixteenth opinions are refuted by the fact that if these letters were abbreviations of names or words, the correct thing would be to pronounce them according to what they stand for (*samiyyat*, their referents), not according to their names (*asma'*, the names of the letters).

Once these two types are established and we discard the weak opinions falling under them, the most probable of those opinions are three: that these letters are for rebuking the obstinate and recording their inability to produce a counterpart; or that they are the names of the surahs in which they occur; or that they are oaths sworn by God to honour the status of writing and to alert the Arab unlettered people (*al-Arab al-Ummiyyin*) to the benefits of writing, to bring them out of the state of illiteracy. The most probable of these three opinions is the first.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: What occurs in these openings of the names of letters is half of the names of the letters of the alphabet, since they are fourteen: *alif, lam, mim, sad, ra', kaf, ha', ya', 'ayn, ta', sin, ha', qaf, nun*. They occur in twenty-nine surahs, according to the number of the letters of the alphabet. These fourteen include halves of the categories of the attributes of letters. Among the *mahmusa* (voiceless) letters, half are: *sad, kaf, ha', sin, ha'*. Among the *majhura* (voiced) letters, half are: *alif, lam, mim, ra', 'ayn, ta', qaf, ya', nun*. Among the *shadida* (plosive) letters, half are: *alif, kaf, ta', qaf*. Among the *rakhwa* (fricative) letters, half are: *lam, mim, ra', sad, ha', 'ayn, sin, ha', ya', nun*. Among the *mutbaqa* (emphatic) letters, half are: *sad, ta'*.

Among the *munfatiha* (open) letters, half are: *alif, lam, mim, ra', kaf, ha', 'ayn, sin, qaf, ya', nun*. Among the *musta'liya* (raised) letters, half are: *qaf, sad, ta'*. Among the *mustafila* (lowered) letters, half are: *alif, lam, mim, ra', kaf, ha', ya', 'ayn, sin, ha', nun*. Among the *qalqala* (echoing) letters, half are: *qaf, ta'*.

Then, the letters whose mention was omitted are overwhelmed by those mentioned. Glory be to Him, in whose every thing His wisdom is subtle. End of quotation.

Al-Baydawi added other categories of the attributes of letters, which we will not elaborate on here; whoever wishes may refer to them.

The essence of their statements is that the mention of the letters that were mentioned has been decided upon, and the omission of the mention of those that were omitted is, by way of representation of the types of attributes, through mentioning half, and leaving half is by way of *wa-liqis ma lam yuqal* (let him measure what has not been said), since the purpose is achieved, which is to indicate concern with writing, and the principle of brevity in speech.

Therefore, the mention of all these openings in the surahs of the Qur'an is among the scientific miracles (*al-mu'jizat al-'ilmiyya*). These are mentioned in the third aspect of the aspects of inimitability (*i'jaz*) that preceded in the tenth introduction of the introductions to this commentary.

As for the manner of pronunciation, they are pronounced in pause (*mawquffa*), without inflectional marks (*'alamat i'rab*), according to the rule of enumerated names, since they were not governed by any governing factors (*'awamil*). Their status is like the status of enumerated numbers when you say: *thalatha, arba'a, khamsa* (three, four, five).

**[Page 217]**

And like the status of names of things that are dictated to a writer for him, when you say, for example: *thawb, bisat, sayf* (garment, carpet, sword), without inflection. Whoever inflects them is mistaken.

For this reason, the reciters pronounced them unvowelled (*sakinatan*), with the quiescence of the one at which one pauses. What ends in a sound consonant is pronounced unvowelled, such as *alif, lam, mim* (Alif, Lam, Mim). What is among the names of letters with an extended final vowel is pronounced at the beginning of surahs as a shortened *alif* (*alifan maqsuran*), because they are used in the manner of spelling out (*mutahajjan bi-ha*), and in the state of spelling they are shortened for the sake of lightness, because spelling is generally for teaching the beginner, and their use in spelling is more frequent. So they occur at the openings of surahs in shortened form, because they are of the pattern of enumeration or derived from it.

However, people may make the opening of one of the surahs like its name, so they say: "I recited *Kaf, Ha', Ya', 'Ayn, Sad* (﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ [Maryam: 1])," just as they make the first word of a poem the name of the poem, so they say: "I recited *Qifa nabki* (Halt, let us weep), and *Banat Su'ad* (Su'ad has departed)." In that case, the sequence of letters in that opening may be treated as a single word, so that the inflections that apply to similar patterns of names apply to it. Thus *Ha-Mim* is not declined, as Shurayh ibn Awfa al-'Ansi, mentioned earlier, said:

*It reminds me of Ha-Mim while the spear is in contact, / so why did he not recite Ha-Mim before the advance?*

And as al-Kumayt said:

*We recited to you in the family of Ha-Mim a verse / which a jurist among us interpreted, and a grammarian.*

*Kaf, Ha', Ya', 'Ayn, Sad* (﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ [Maryam: 1]) is not inflected, since it has no parallel among names, either singly or in compound form.

As for *Ta-Sin-Mim* (﴿Ta, Sin, Mim﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 1]), it is inflected like a compound of the *mazji* (blended compound) type, such as *Hadramawt* and *Darabjird*. Sibawayh said: If you make *Hud* the name of the surah, you do not decline it, so you say: "I recited *Hud*," for the status of being a proper name and the feminine form, and he said, because it becomes like a woman you named *'Amr*.

For all of these, you may bring it in its inflection as it stands, in the manner of quotation (*al-hikaya*), and the position of these openings with what follows them in terms of inflection. If you make them letters for spelling, as an allusion to the polytheists and a rebuke to them, then it is clear that they are in that case quoted and do not accept inflection, because in that case they are like sound-names (*asma' al-aswat*), where only their utterance is intended. Their significance resembles the rational significance: they indicate that the speaker prepares the hearer for what follows them, like the enumeration of arithmetic numbers to one who is to add their sum, or subtract, or divide. So there is no inflection for them with what follows them. There is no sense in estimating (*taqdir*) a composition from these letters, since that informing is not intended, being evident. Rather, what is intended is what arises from enumerating them, namely allusion, because one who spells out letters to one whose state precludes that he be intended for teaching must, from the context, be intended for allusion.

**[Page 218]**

If you estimate them as names of the surahs, or of the Qur'an, or of God Most High as swearing by them, then it is said that they have rulings together with what follows them of inflection, some of which require extensive estimation. So leave aside prolonging discussion of them, for time is short.

These openings are Qur'an without doubt, but it has been disputed whether they are independent verses. The more evident view is that they are not independent verses, but are parts of the verses that follow them, according to the preferred doctrine of the majority of reciters.

It is narrated from the reciters of Kufa that some of them they counted as independent verses, and some of them they did not count, and made them part of the verse together with what follows them. The basis for this distinction has not become clear, until the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: This has no connection with analogy. The correct view from the Kufans is that all of them are verses, and this is most fitting for the adherents of this view, since distinction is arbitrary, because the proof is lacking.

In my view, they are verses, because they have a representational, allusive significance (*dalala ta'ridiyya kinaiyya*), since the intention is to make manifest their inability or something similar. Thus they correspond to the requirement of the situation together with what follows them of speech. It is not required, for the significance of speech on a figurative meaning, that it have an explicit meaning. Rather, the significance of correspondence (*dalalat al-mutabaqa*) in these letters is considered as implicit (*taqdiriyya*), if we say that correspondence significance must be accompanied by implication significance (*dalalat al-iltizam*).

What supports the early generations' application to these openings of the rulings of parts of verses is that they recite them when they recite the verse connected to them. For in the *Jami'* of al-Tirmidhi, in the book of *Tafsir*, in mentioning the occasion of revelation of Surat al-Rum: "Then it was revealed: *Alif, Lam, Mim* (﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-Rum: 1]), *The Romans have been defeated* (﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum: 2])." And in it also: "Then Abu Bakr al-Siddiq went out shouting in the regions of Mecca: *Alif, Lam, Mim* (﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-Rum: 1]), *The Romans have been defeated* (﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum: 2])." And in the *Sira* of Ibn Ishaq, from the narration of Ibn Hisham from him: "The Messenger of God recited to 'Utba ibn Rabi'a: *Ha-Mim* (﴿Ha, Mim﴾ [Fussilat: 1]), *A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate* (﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [Fussilat: 2]), until he reached His saying: *So say, I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud* (﴿So say, I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Fussilat: 13])," the hadith.

Upon this difference, there is a disagreement regarding whether reciting them counts in prayer, according to those who are satisfied, in reciting a surah together with al-Fatiha, with one verse, such as the companions of Abu Hanifa.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 2 (part 1 of 3):

Page 219
﴿That is the Book⁠﴾
This is the beginning of a statement that has no grammatical connection with the letters alif-lam-mim, as you have learned from what preceded, under all the possibilities, as is the most apparent view.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) has allowed, under the possibility that the letters alif-lam-mim are placed in the manner of spelling-out (al-tahajji) to show the inability of the polytheists to produce anything like part of the Qur'an, that the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara) may refer to alif-lam-mim considered as a letter intended for challenge (al-ta'jiz), meaning: "that meaning which results from the spelling-out," i.e., "those letters, considered as being of the same kind as your letters, are the Book," that is, its compositions are made of them. So what prevents you from opposing it? In this case, alif-lam-mim is an independent sentence placed for indirect reproach (al-ta'ridh), the demonstrative noun is the subject, and "the Book" is the predicate.

According to the more apparent view, the reference is to the Qur'an known to them on that day. The demonstrative noun is the subject, "the Book" is an apposition (badal), and its predicate is what follows. Thus the reference is to the Book that had actually been revealed, namely the sūrahs preceding Sūrat al-Baqarah, because everything of the Qur'an that has been revealed is what is called "the Qur'an," and what is later added to it joins it. Accordingly, "the Book" in this view is used literally for what had been written in fact. The word "the Book" in this view is a predicate of the demonstrative noun.

It is also permissible that the reference is to the whole Qur'an, both what has been revealed and what will be revealed, since its revelation is awaited and it is thus present in minds, so it is likened to what is present before the eyes. The definiteness is then for a conventional (taqdiri) previous mention, and the demonstrative is for a conventional presence. In this case, "the Book" is an apposition or explanation of that, and the predicate is "there is no doubt in it."

It is permissible in such a context to use the demonstrative for the near and the demonstrative for the far. Al-Radi said: The demonstrative noun was set for presence and nearness, because it refers to what is sensibly pointed at; then it is correct to point with it to an absent thing, so it is correct to use the far form, because the one spoken about is absent. It is rare to mention it with the near, present form. You may say: "A man came to me, so I said to that man," and "I said to this man." Likewise, in speech heard recently, you may point to it with the form of absence and distance, as you say: "By God, that is a great oath," because the utterance has passed away from hearing, so it becomes like the absent. But most commonly in this case, the pointing is with the form of presence, so you say: "This is a great oath." End of quote. That is, the more common usage in such a case is to use the far demonstrative, and the near one is rarer; the reverse applies to pointing at speech.

Ibn Malik in al-Tashil equated the use of near and far in pointing to a previously mentioned speech, when he said: "They may alternate," i.e., the near and far demonstrative nouns are pointed with to what they follow, meaning of the speech. His commentator illustrated this with the saying of the Exalted after the story of Jesus: ﴿That We recite to you of the signs and the wise reminder⁠﴾ [Al 'Imran: 58], then He said: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative⁠﴾ [Al 'Imran: 62]. He pointed once with the far and once with the near, while the referent is one. Ibn Malik's statement is more in accord with usage, since what occurs of both usages can hardly be counted. Al-Radi's claim that the near form is rarely used with a present-tense word is an unsupported claim.

If this is so, the ruling for pointing to an absent thing that is not speech is like pointing to speech in permitting both forms, because both are very common. In the Qur'an: ﴿He found in it two men fighting, one from his own party and the other from his enemy⁠﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]. When the two forms are equal, that usage becomes a field in which eloquent speakers compete and observe the requirements of situations. We have seen them choose, in the positions of using the demonstrative, what is most suitable to that context, which shows that they know their addressees by aims for which there is no means of recognition unless the usage is equal in the basic language, so that preference goes to one of the two usages, not in a sense such as added emphasis in the far demonstrative, as here. As Khufaf ibn Nadbah said:

I say to him while the spear bends its shaft: "Consider Khufaf, for I am that one!"

The near form is sometimes used to show little concern, as in the words of Qays ibn al-Khatim in the Hamasah:

When this death comes, it will not find a need
of my soul except that I have fulfilled its fulfilment.

Hence, there is no doubt that in the verse the demonstrative is the far form, to show the elevated rank of this Qur'an by making it far in station.

It has become common in eloquent speech to depict a noble matter as an elevated thing, difficult to reach, because a precious thing is dear to its people, so it is customary to place it in high places to keep it from wear and from being handled by many hands and from common use. Thus "the Book" here, when mentioned in a context of challenge to oppose it with what the letters of spelling in alif-lam-mim indicate, was like a precious thing difficult to reach in regard to their attempting to oppose it. Or because of the truth of its meanings and the benefit of its guidance, it is far from one who approaches it with idle talk, such as their saying "he forged it" and their saying "tales of the ancients" [al-An'am: 25]. This is not contradicted by His saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down⁠﴾ [al-An'am: 92], for that is pointing to a book set before its people, to encourage them to devote themselves to it and to take admonition from its commands and prohibitions.

Perhaps the author of al-Kashshaf built on the same basis as al-Radi, so he did not count "that is the Book" as an indication of exaltation or dignity. How excellent is the author of al-Miftah, who did not overlook this, for he said regarding the requirements of defining the subject by demonstrative: "or that by its distance he intends to exalt it, as you say in the context of exalting: 'that excellent man and those great scholars,' and as in the saying of the Mighty and Exalted: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1], ﴿That is the Book⁠﴾, going to its distance in rank."

His saying "al-Kitab" may be an apposition of the demonstrative, for the purpose of explaining the referent since it is not seen; the definiteness then is for previous reference, and the predicate is the clause "there is no doubt in it." It may also be that "al-Kitab" is the predicate of the demonstrative, and the definiteness is definiteness of the genus, so the clause conveys restriction of the true reality of the Book to the Qur'an by means of the definiteness of both parts; this is then a restriction by claim, meaning: "That is the Book that comprises the qualities of perfection among the class of books," on the basis that other books, when attributed to it, are as if missing from it in terms of being a book, since they do not complete all the perfections of books. This definition is sometimes expressed by grammarians when listing the meanings of the article al-, as indicating perfection. So it is not objected that how can the Book be restricted to being alif-lam-mim or to the sūrah or the like, since this is not a context of restriction but only of definition. The purpose of the definiteness and the demonstrative is apparent, and none of that is idle in any way, even if some doubts have occurred to some over others.

Al-kitab is a pattern (fi'al) meaning "the written," either as a verbal noun of kataba, formed for intensity in writing, since the verbal noun comes in the sense of the object, like "creation" (al-khalq); or as fi'al in the sense of maf'ul, like libas meaning "what is worn" and 'imad meaning "that which is supported."

Its derivation is from kataba meaning "to gather and join," because the book's pages and letters are gathered. The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that everything of revelation be written down, and he made for revelation a book. Naming the Qur'an "a book" is an indication of the obligation to write it down for its preservation.

Writing the Qur'an is a communal obligation (fard kifayah) upon the Muslims.

﴿There is no doubt in it, a guidance for the God-fearing⁠﴾
This is a state (hal) of "the Book," or a first or second predicate, according to what has passed shortly.

Al-rayb is doubt. The root of rayb is unease and agitation of the soul. "The rayb of time" and "the rayb of fate" are its calamities. God the Exalted said: ﴿We await for him the calamities of fate⁠﴾ [al-Tur: 30]. Since doubt necessarily entails agitation and unease of the soul, rayb came to dominate it and became a conventional meaning. One says "rabahu al-shay'" when the thing causes him doubt, i.e., by making what caused doubt in his condition, so it is transitive; and one says "arabahu" likewise, since the hamzah did not add an extra transitivity, so it is like laḥiqa and alḥaqa, and zalaqa and azlaqa. It has been said that arab is weaker than rab, arab meaning "close to doubting," as said by Abu Zayd. In accordance with distinguishing between them, Bashshar said:

Your brother, if you cast doubt on him, says, "You have only cast doubt"; and if you rebuke him, his side becomes soft.

In the hadith: "Leave what makes you doubtful for what does not make you doubtful," i.e., leave the act that brings you close to doubt about prohibition for another act in whose doing no doubt enters that it is permitted.

The readers in the mutawatir transmission did not differ on the fatha of "la rayb" as a negation of the genus by explicit wording, and this is its most eloquent form, because if it were raf', it would allow the negation of an individual instead of the genus. If the demonstrative in "that" refers to the letters gathered in alif-lam-mim, intending indirect reproach to the challengers, and "the Book" is a predicate of the demonstrative as previously mentioned, then "la rayb" is negation of a specific doubt, namely the doubt that arises about this Book being composed of the letters of their speech, so how did they fail to produce its like? And the negation of the genus in it would be real, not by claim. So the sentence "la rayb" is treated as emphasis for what the demonstrative in "that is the Book" conveys. In this view, the prepositional phrase "fihi" may be attached to "rayb" as an idle adverbial, so the pause is on "fihi," which is the preference of the majority, like His saying: ﴿and warn of the Day of Gathering, there is no doubt in it⁠﴾ [al-Shura: 7] and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of people for a Day there is no doubt in it⁠﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9]. It may also be that His saying "fihi" is a settled adverbial predicate of the following "guidance for the God-fearing," and the meaning of "fi" is the conventional figurative sense of containment, likening the indication of the word to the containing of a vessel. This would then be a correction of those who turned away from listening to the Qur'an and said ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an⁠﴾ [Fussilat: 26], seeking to lure down their bird of aversion, as if it were said: "This Book contains something of guidance, so listen to it." For this reason "guidance" is indefinite, i.e.,

there is in it some guidance, after the manner of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Abu Dhar: "You are a man in whom there is jahiliyyah." It may be that the predicate of "la" is omitted because it is evident, i.e., "la rayb mawjud" (there is no doubt existing). The omission of the predicate is used frequently in such expressions, as in "qalu la darr" and the Arab saying "la ba's," and the verse of Sa'd ibn Malik:

Whoever turns away from its fires, then I am the son of Qays, there is no escape.

i.e., there is no survival in that. This is a figurative usage. Then the pause is on "la rayb."

In al-Kashshaf, Nafi' and 'Asim paused on "rayb." If the demonstrative in "that" refers to the Book in terms of its being like a present, witnessed thing, and "the Book" is an apposition of the demonstrative for explaining it, then the preposition "fihi" is an idle adverbial attached to "rayb," and the predicate of "la" is omitted, in the common manner with such, and the pause is on "fihi." "Fihi" in this case carries the sense of negating the occurrence of doubt in the Book, meaning, in this view, negating doubt that it is sent down from God the Exalted, because the intended address is to those who doubt the truth of its attribution to God the Exalted. Their address will come with His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a sūrah like it⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23]. So their doubt is an established, well-known fact, but their doubt was treated as though it did not exist, because in the indications of the situations there is what, if they reflected upon it, their doubt would disappear. So that doubt, together with the proofs of its falsehood, was placed in the position of non-existence.

The author of al-Miftah said: "They reverse the proposition with the denier when there is with him what, if he reflected upon it, would restrain him. So they say to the denier of Islam: 'Islam is true.' The saying of the Mighty and Majestic regarding the Qur'an: ﴿There is no doubt in it⁠﴾, and how many a wretched doubter in it there is." This is according to this view. So the compound that indicates emphatic negation of doubt is used to mean disregarding the doubt, because the state of the doubter in the weakness of his doubt resembles the state of one who is not a doubter at all, by way of figurative depiction.

[Page 224]

Among the exegetes is one who explained His words ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ to mean that there is nothing in it that would necessitate doubt about its authenticity. That is, there is no disorder in it and no discrepancy. In this reading, "doubt" is a *majaz* (figurative usage) for its cause, and the prepositional phrase is a *ẓarf mustaqarr* (a stable adverbial phrase) serving as the predicate of *lā* (the negation particle). He points to His words ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisa': 82]. The meaning is that the Qur'an does not include speech that would cause doubt that it is from the Real, the Lord of the Worlds: speech in which some parts contradict others, or speech that departs from truth and virtue, or that commands evil and corruption, or that turns people away from noble character. The absence of these from it requires that whatever the Qur'an contains, when the reflecting person reflects upon it, he finds it producing certainty that it is from God. The verse here can bear both meanings, so let us take both as intended, according to the principle we established in the ninth introduction.

This negation involves no claim and no *tanzil* (treating something as if it were something else). This aspect therefore dispenses with treating what exists as if it did not exist, and it conveys an allusion to the books that the People of the Book had in their hands at that time, whose statements had become confused and contradictory because of the distortion that had befallen them. This is because making a declaration about negating doubt from the Qur'an, when no one holds doubt about what it contains (that is, doubt based on a cause that calls for suspicion, since the most they said about it were vague remarks such as "this is sorcery" and "these are the fables of the ancients), indicates that the purpose is allusion. This is especially so after His words ﴿That is the Book﴾, as when you say to someone who speaks after people who have been talking in a gathering while you remained silent: "This speech is correct," alluding to others.

By this aspect, the meaning also becomes unified whether one pauses at "fihi" or at "rayb." If one considers the adverbial phrase not to be the predicate, and the predicate is omitted, then this phrase can be dispensed with in this sentence. *al-Kashshaf* mentioned that the adverbial phrase, namely "fihi," was not placed before the subject, which is "rayb." That is, it is not placed before the subject on the assumption that it is a predicate of a noun of *lā*, unlike the placement of the adverbial phrase in His words ﴿There is no ghoul in it﴾ [al-Saffat: 47]. For if the adverbial phrase were placed first here, it would intend that another book contains doubt. End of quotation.

That is, because fronting in such a construction conveys restriction (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), it would indicate that the negation of doubt is restricted to this Book, and that other books contain doubt. This is not what is intended here. The restriction in His words "there is no doubt in it" is not intended, because the context addresses the Arabs who were challenged to produce something like the Qur'an, and they are not People of the Book who would need to be answered. What is intended is that they have no excuse for denying that it is from God, since they were called to counter it and were unable to do so. Yes, from it an allusion may be drawn to the People of the Book who backed the polytheists and encouraged them to deny it: that the Qur'an, because of its lofty status among its peers among books, contains nothing that calls for doubt that it was sent down from God. It stirs them to reflect on it: do they find in it anything that necessitates doubt? This stirs up their crouching admiration for their own book, the altered and distorted one, for doubt about realities is the precursor of their becoming manifest. The dawn heralded by spreading light before the sunrise is a herald of its unveiling.

He built his speech on the premise that a sentence qualified by restriction in affirmative form, if negation enters upon it, conveys the restriction of the negation and not the negation of the restriction. The examples of the author of *al-Miftah* (al-Sakkaki) regarding fronting the predicate for restriction treated equally what came in affirmative form and what came in negative form.

In my view there is an issue with this, which I will mention at His words ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾. The ruling on the movement or the stillness of the pronoun's *hā'* is established in the field of the readings in its foundational section.

As for His words ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾: *al-Hudā* is the *ism al-maṣdar* (a verbal noun form, a noun used in place of the infinitive). It has no parallel in the Arabic language except *surā*, *tuqā*, *bukā*, and *lughā* (the verbal noun of *laghā* in a less common dialect). Its verb, *hadā yahdī hadyan*, takes a second object with *ilā*, and sometimes takes it directly, by the broadened method of ellipsis, as in His words ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6].

In its precise sense, *al-hudā* is the indication that is capable of bringing one to the desired goal. This is the apparent meaning, because the basic principle is that synonyms are not assumed, so *hadā* is not synonymous with *dalla* (to indicate). Also, what is understood from *al-hudā* is the complete indication, and this matches the meaning to which *al-hudā* was transferred in the Sharia usage. It is also more consistent with the principles of al-Ash'ari, for *tawfīq* (divine enablement), which is the bringing to the goal according to al-Ash'ari, is a creation of God in the heart of the one who is enabled. Thus it suits interpreting guidance in a way that fits it, so that the one who guides conveys the legal guidance. The Qur'an is therefore *hudā*, and describing it with the verbal noun is for emphasis, meaning that it is a guide.

Legal *hudā* is the directing to what contains the welfare of the immediate life that does not undermine the welfare of the afterlife. Its effect is *ihtidā'* (being guided). Thus the God-fearing are guided by its guidance, while the stubborn are not guided, because they do not reflect. This is a meaning on which there is no disagreement. Rather, the theologians differed about the source of the attainment of guidance, but this question is not needed for understanding the verse. The details of the types of guidance were covered under His words ﴿Guide us to the path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6].

If the place of *hudā* is the beginning of a sentence, it should be the predicate of an omitted subject, the pronoun referring to the Book. The meaning would then be an announcement about the Book that it is the guidance. This carries, in the attainment of guidance through it, the emphasis that the use of the verbal noun implies, to indicate that it has reached the ultimate point in guiding people, so that it is itself the very essence of guidance. This alerts to the superiority of its guidance over the guidance of the books before it.

If the pause is at His words "no doubt," and the adverbial phrase is the beginning of the following sentence, and "*hudā*" is the subject whose predicate is the adverbial phrase preceding it, then it is an announcement that guidance is in it. The adverbial form indicates that guidance is firmly established in it. This therefore equals, in indicating firm establishment, the earlier aspect, which is the announcement that it is the very essence of guidance.

[Page 225]

The God-fearing (*al-muttaqī*) is one who has the quality of *ittiqā'*, which is seeking protection. *Wiqāyah* is safeguarding and preserving from what is disliked. The God-fearing person is therefore the cautious one who seeks to be saved from something harmful and disliked. What is intended here by "the God-fearing" is those who fear His wrath, who prepare themselves to seek His pleasure and to respond to His call. When the Qur'an is recited to them, they listen to it and reflect on what it calls them to, and so they are guided.

Sharia piety is the carrying out of commands and avoiding prohibitions, including the major sins, and not persisting in minor sins, outwardly and inwardly. That is, guarding against what God has made the transgression of which is a cause of His anger and punishment. All the major sins carry a warning of punishment for their doer, except for *al-lamam* (minor lapses).

The intended meaning of "guidance" and "God-fearing" in the verse is their linguistic meaning. The intention is that the Qur'an, by its nature, leads to the good goals, and that those prepared to reach them through it are the God-fearing. That is, they are those who have freed themselves from obstinacy, purified themselves from the lowliness of blindly following misguiders, feared the consequence, and protected themselves from the danger of God's anger. This is the apparent meaning. The God-fearing here are the believers who believed in God and Muhammad and received the Qur'an with strength and determination to act upon it, as the following attributes will reveal in His words ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] down to His words ﴿before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4].

In explaining that the Qur'an is guidance and how the God-fearing person is described, there are three meanings:

The first is that the Qur'an is guidance in the present time, because describing with the verbal noun substitutes for describing with the active participle, and the present is the basic tense of the active participle, with the intended sense being the moment of speech. The God-fearing are also the God-fearing in the present, because the active participle truly refers to the present, as we have said. That is, every person who purifies himself and prepares himself to receive perfection is guided by this Book, or it increases his guidance, as in His words ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

The second is that it was guidance in the past, that is, guidance was achieved through it, meaning through what was sent down of the Book. The God-fearing are then those whose mark was piety, that is, the guidance had its effect on them so that they became God-fearing. On this reading, it is praise for the Book by witnessing its guidance and a commendation of the believers who were guided by it. The application of "the God-fearing" to those who were characterized by piety in the past, although this is not the usual use of the active participle, is an application supported by the context of praising the Book.

The third is that it is guidance in the future for those who will be God-fearing in the future. The verbal-noun description here is specified by evidence, since the verbal noun does not indicate a specific time.

Describing the Book with the verbal noun yields a richness of meanings that would not be obtained if it were described with the active participle, so that it was said "a guide for the God-fearing." This is praise of the Qur'an and an honouring of it, and a transition to praise the believers who benefited from its guidance. The Qur'an has not ceased and will not cease to be guidance for the God-fearing, for all kinds of its guidance benefit the God-fearing in all degrees of piety, in all times and in their times, according to the extent of their eagerness, the reach of their knowledge, and the variety of their aims. Some benefit from its guidance in religion; some benefit in politics and the management of the affairs of the community; some benefit in morals and virtues; and some benefit in legislation and the understanding of religion. All of these are among the God-fearing, and their benefit from it is according to the extent of their piety. The scholars of the foundations of jurisprudence have made *ijtihād* (independent legal reasoning) in jurisprudence a form of piety, and they used as evidence for the obligation of *ijtihād* His words ﴿So fear God as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]. If one's effort falls short of full benefit from the Book, that is due to a deficiency in him, not in the guidance. The people of knowledge and righteousness continue to compete in acquiring, to the fullest of their ability, the guidance of the Qur'an.

The four sentences fit together in perfect harmony. The sentence "*Alif Lām Mīm*" is a demonstration of the inimitability of the Qur'an and a rebuke to the polytheists in general for their inability to produce its like, though it is composed of the letters of their own speech. This alone is sufficient as a call to their obstinacy.

The sentence "That is the Book" is a commendation of its status and that it has reached the peak of perfection among the conditions of books. It is directed to the elite of the intelligent, to say to them: this is a book composed of the letters of your speech, and it has reached the peak of perfection among books. This is what should spur you to follow it and to take pride that it was granted to you. You consider yourselves the best of nations, so how can you not hasten to follow a book that was sent down to you and is the best of books? The sense of this is like His words ﴿Lest you say: the Book was only sent down to two groups before us﴾ [al-An'am: 156] down to His words "and a mercy." It is also directed to the People of the Book, awakening them to the fact that it is superior to what was given to them.

The sentence "There is no doubt" (*lā rayb*): if the pause is at "There is no doubt," it is an allusion to all those among the polytheists and the People of the Book who harbor doubt about it. That is, doubt about this Book arose from obstinacy, and "there is no doubt" because it is the perfect Book. If the pause is at "in it," it is an allusion to the People of the Book in their attachment to the distorted version of their two books, along with what those two books contain of the causes of doubt and suspicion, namely the clear confusion that indicates

[Page 226]

on that it is from the making of people. God the Exalted said: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisa': 82]. And al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "Then none of these four [features], after being arranged in this secret arrangement, is free of a subtle point of eloquence: in the first there is the elision and the allusion to the purpose in the most delicate manner; in the second there is the grandeur contained in the definite article; in the third there is what is in placing the doubt before the adverbial complement; and in the fourth there is the elision, the placing of the verbal noun – which is guidance – in the position of the descriptive adjective, its being presented indefinite, and the brevity in mentioning the God-fearing." Ended.

So taqwa, in this sense, is the foundation of all good, and in its legal (shar'i) meaning, which is the ultimate goal of its linguistic meaning, it is the gathering of all good things. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "No word has been repeated in the Qur'an as often as the word taqwa, out of concern for its matter."

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 2, verse 3 (Part 1 of 2)**

﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾

It must be connected to His saying ﴿for the God-fearing﴾, as a description that follows their general description with a detail that clarifies the intended meaning. At the same time, it begins a digression that classifies people, according to their different states in receiving the Book that has been praised, into four categories. Before the Hijra they had been two categories. Before the Hijra there was a group of believers and a group of open disbelievers. After the Hijra two more categories were added: the hypocrites (munafiqun) and the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab). The open polytheists were the first enemies of Islam. The hypocrites appeared in Medina, and the earlier group was strengthened by them, those whom the Muslims had left in the abode of disbelief. The People of the Book had been occupied and did not take on the task of opposing Islam. When Islam became established in Medina next to them, they felt fear, so they allied themselves with the hypocrites and supported the polytheists.

It has been indicated that the believing God-fearing people are of two groups. One group is the God-fearing who embraced Islam from among those who had been polytheists, and for whom the Qur'an was guidance. This is shown by the contrast between this relative clause and the other relative clause introduced by His saying: ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾ [2:4] ... and so on. So those praised here are those who had been polytheists, who heard the Muhammadan call, reflected on salvation, feared the consequences of polytheism, and believed. The motive that moved them to Islam was God-consciousness (taqwa), not greed or experience. For example, Wa'il ibn Hujr, when he came from Yemen desiring Islam, was among the God-fearing. Musaylima, when he came with the Banu Hanifa harbouring enmity and seeking kingship, was not among the God-fearing.

Another group is mentioned by His saying ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾ [2:4] and what follows. These attributes have been applied to praise those who believed after having associated partners with God, since their guide to faith was God-consciousness and reflection on the outcome. For this reason He described them by His saying ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾, meaning: after they used to disbelieve in the resurrection and the return, as the Qur'an recounts about them in many verses. For this reason, in describing them by these three connected predicates, the present tense was used, which indicates renewal, signifying the continual renewal of their belief in the unseen, the continual renewal of their establishing prayer, and of their spending, since they were not characterised by these things except after the guidance of the Qur'an had come to them.

Sahib al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) permitted that it be an independent new sentence, with ﴿those are upon guidance﴾ as its predicate. In my view this is a permission that is not fitting, since beginning a new sentence requires a shift from one topic to another, which is called iqtida' (abrupt transition). In eloquence it is only good when the first topic has been spread out and fully developed until it is exhausted, or until the listener's weariness is feared. That is the place of expressions such as "amma ba'du" or "hadha" and similar phrases. Otherwise it would be a shortcoming on the part of the speaker or writer, especially since the style of a book is broader than that of oratory, because lengthy discussion of its topics is more possible.

The word "al-ghayb" is a verbal noun meaning absence (al-ghayba), as in His saying ﴿That is so that he (the Aziz) may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾ [12:52], and ﴿that God may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾ [5:94]. People sometimes say "bi-zahr al-ghayb" (in the back of the absence). Al-Hutay'a said:

"How (can) the satire (be)? She does not cease: a righteous (woman) of the family of Lam comes to me in her absence."

And in a hadith: "The supplication of a believer for his brother in his absence is answered." The meaning of "al-ghayb" is what is not perceived by the senses, of which the Messenger (ﷺ) clearly reported that it exists or will exist, such as the existence of God and His attributes, the existence of angels and devils, the signs of the Hour, and what God has kept exclusively to His knowledge.

If "al-ghayb" is explained as the verbal noun, i.e. absence, then the bā' is for accompaniment (mulabasa), and the phrase is a stationary adverbial complement. Then the attribute is an allusion to the hypocrites. If "al-ghayb" is explained as a noun, namely what has disappeared from the senses from the upper and otherworldly realms, then the bā' is connected to "yu'minun" (they believe). The meaning then is: those who believe in what the Messenger reported from the realm beyond the realm of witnessing, such as belief in the angels, the resurrection, the spirit, and similar things. In the hadith on faith (the Prophet said): "That you believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and that you believe in predestination, its good and its evil." All of these belong to the realms of the unseen. Then the attribute is an allusion to the polytheists who denied the resurrection and said ﴿Shall we show you a man who will tell you that when you are completely torn apart, you will be in a new creation?﴾ [34:7]. Thus this attribute combines explicit praise for the believers and, by allusion, censure of the polytheists for not being guided by the Book, and censure of the hypocrites who believe outwardly while concealing disbelief. He will follow this allusion with explicit description of them in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [2:6] and the following verses, and His saying ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God"﴾ [2:8].

"Yu'minun" means "yusaddiqun" (they affirm/believe). "Amana" is an augmented form of "amina" (to be safe), and the added hamza indicates transitivity. So the original meaning of "amana" is to cause someone to be safe, the opposite of "khafa" (to fear); "fa-amana" means he made another safe. Then they used "amana" to mean "saddaqa" (to affirm) and "wathiqa" (to trust). Abu Zayd related from the Arabs: "Ma amantu an ajida sahaba" (I did not feel secure that I would find a companion), said by a traveller when he delays his journey. So "amana" came to mean "saddaqa" either on the assumption that he made his informant safe from lying to him, or on the assumption that he made himself safe from fearing that the report was false, as an intensification of "amina", just as "aqdama 'ala al-shay'" means "to advance toward something and resolve upon it". Then it became an intransitive verb, either by considering the omission of the object because of frequent use, to the extent that the verb was treated as intransitive, or by considering the aforementioned intensification, meaning he attained safety, that is, from doubt and agitation of soul, and was reassured by this, since the meanings of safety and tranquillity are close. Then they also give "amana" the sense of "aqarra" (to acknowledge), so they say "amana bi-kadha" (he acknowledged it), as in this verse, and they give it the sense of "itmaanna" (to be at peace), so they say "amana lahu" (he trusted him), as in ﴿Do you then hope that they will believe you?﴾ [2:75]. The relative clause being a present-tense verb indicates that their faith is continuous and renewed, as you have just learned. That is, no doubt or suspicion befalls their faith.

The belief in the unseen was singled out for mention, rather than other objects of belief, because belief in the unseen, that is, what is hidden from the senses, is the foundation of accepting the possibility of what the messengers report about the existence of God and the upper world. When a person believes in it, he becomes ready to hear the call of the messenger and to reflect on what he conveys from God the Exalted, so that perceiving the proofs becomes easy for him. As for one who believes that behind the world of material things there is no other world, that is, what lies beyond nature, he has trained himself to turn away from the call to believe in the existence of God and the world of the Hereafter, as was the case of the materialists, called the Dahriyya, who said ﴿Nothing destroys us except time﴾ [45:24]. Close to their belief is that of the polytheists, which is why they worshipped embodied idols. Most of the Arabs affirmed from the unseen the existence of the Creator, and some of them affirmed the angels, but they did not believe in anything beyond that. The discussion of the reality of faith is not the place for this, and it will come at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and they are not believers﴾ [2:8].

* * *

﴿And establish prayer﴾

"Iqama" is the verbal noun of "aqama", which is the causative of "qama" (to stand). The causative prefix hamza indicates making something happen. "Iqama" means making something stand upright. It is derived from "qamat al-suq", when the market becomes brisk and people engage in buying and selling in it. This interpretation is supported by an expression of some language authorities who stated this implied meaning. Aymanu ibn Khurayn al-Asadi said:

"The gazelle established the market of striking (the camel) for the people of the two Iraqs for a whole year."

The original meaning of "qiyam" in language is standing upright, the opposite of sitting or lying down. A person stands up only with the intention of doing a difficult task that cannot be done from sitting. So the orator stands, the worker stands, the craftsman stands, the walker stands. Therefore standing has customary connotations drawn from its necessary accidents, and for this reason it has been used figuratively for activity, as in their saying "qama bi-al-amr" (he undertook the matter). Among the most famous uses of this figurative sense are their saying "qamat al-suq" (the market became active) and "qamat al-harb" (the war broke out). For its opposite they said "rakadat" (it stagnated) and "namat" (it slumped). It conveys, in everything connected with it, a meaning appropriate to its figurative activity. It belongs to the category of the metonymic figurative usage (majaz mursal), and this usage has spread until it became equal to the literal meaning, becoming like literal meanings. For this reason it is correct to build a second figurative usage and metaphor upon it. So "iqamat al-salat" (establishing prayer) is an implicit metaphor (isti'ara taba'iyya), in which perseverance in the prayers and attentiveness to them is compared to making something stand upright. I think that attaching this verb to "prayer" is one of the Qur'anic technical expressions.
