The Qur'an used it at the beginning of its revelation, as it occurs in Surat al-Muzzammil: ﴿and establish prayer﴾, and that surah is the third in order of revelation. Sahib al-Kashshaf mentioned other, distant interpretations far from the context of the verse.

Here He used the present tense, as in His saying "yu'minun", so that this would apply to those who established prayer in the past, namely those who believed before the revelation of this verse; to those who were about to establish prayer, namely those who believed at the time of the revelation of the verse; and to those who would later be guided to it, namely those who came after them. The present tense is suitable for all of this, because one who performed prayer in the past performs it now and will perform it tomorrow, and one who did not perform it either performs it now or will perform it tomorrow. All categories of this kind have been made into guidance for them by the Qur'an. The present tense conveys renewal, which reinforces what the root of "iqama" indicates of perseverance and repetition, so that the praise of them for perseverance in prayer would be clearer.

"Salat" is a fixed noun of the pattern fa'alat, with the middle letter vowelled (salawat). This word occurred in the speech of the Arabs with the meaning of supplication, as in the saying of al-A'sha:

"My daughter says, when I have set out on a journey, 'O Lord, keep my father from ailments and pain. May there be upon you the like of what you have prayed (for me), so close your eyes, for the side of a man must lie down.'"

It also occurred with the meaning of worship, as in the saying of al-A'sha:

"He alternates among the prayers of the Mali (?) between prostrating at times and crying out at other times."

As for the "salat" intended in the verse, it is the specific worship that includes standing, recitation, bowing, prostration, and salutation.

Ibn Faris said: The Arabs in their pre-Islamic time inherited their languages from their forefathers. Then when God, Exalted, brought Islam, circumstances changed and words were transferred from some meanings to other meanings with additions. Among what came in the Shari'a is "salat", although they already knew bowing and prostration, even if not in this form. Al-Nabigha said:

"Or a pearl from the oyster, whose diver, delighted, bows and prostrates when he sees it."

And although this is so, the Arabs did not define it in the same way the Shari'a did, with its numbers and times. End of quotation.

I say: there is no doubt that the Arabs knew prayer, prostration, and bowing. God, Exalted, has reported about Ibrahim, peace be upon him, that he said, ﴿Our Lord, that they may establish prayer﴾ [14:37]. The Jews lived among them, and they performed prayer, that is, they offered their worship in a specific form, and they called their synagogue a "salat". The Christians also lived among them and they prayed. Al-Nabigha, in mentioning the burial of al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith al-Ghassani, said:

"So those who prayed over him returned with a clear sign, and Hazm and Na'il were left behind at al-Jawlan."

According to the narration "musalluhu" with an unpointed sad (sa) meaning, he intended those who prayed over him at his burial from among the priests and monks, since he had been victorious, and the previous verse is from the same poem. They also knew prostration. Al-Nabigha said:

"Or a pearl from the oyster, whose diver, delighted, bows and prostrates when he sees it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 3 (part 2 of 2):

The leading philologists have disagreed about the derivation (ishtiqaq) of *al-salat* (prayer). One group said it is derived from *al-sala*, a thick vein in the middle of the back that divides at the coccyx and encircles it, so that the two are called *salawan*. Because the one who prays, when he bows in ruku' or in a similar posture, moves that vein, the word *salat* was derived from it. This is like the saying "anfa min kadha" (he disdained such-and-such), used when someone lifts his nose in disdain, because he raises it when he is repelled and feels great. This is derivation from a non-derived noun (*jamid*), like the expressions *istanwaqa al-jamal* (the camel became female-like) and *tanammara fulan* (so-and-so became a leopard-like fighter), and the saying of a woman: "My husband, when he enters, is a leopard, and when he leaves, is a lion." What points to this derivation here is that no other derivation is suitable. Therefore, the view is not weakened merely because derivation from non-derived nouns is rare, as al-Sayyid imagined.

The term was applied to supplication (*du'a'*) because it necessarily involves humility (*khushu'*), lowering oneself, and submission. Then they derived from *al-salat*, which is a non-derived noun, the verb *salla* (to perform the prayer), when one does the prayer. They also derived *sallā* from *al-salat* in the same way as they derived *sallā al-faras* (the horse "prayed") when it comes as a follower of the leader in a race of horses, because it comes competing with him in the race, placing its head on the *sala* (back) of the one who precedes it. From this they derived *al-musalli* as a name for the second horse in the race. This view of its derivation is drawn from their usage, and it is the one that must be relied upon, since no other derivation suits the original root of the word.

As for what al-Fakhr (al-Razi) raised in his *Tafsir*, namely that the claim that the word derives from the two *salawan* leads to a great discrediting of the Qur'an as proof, because the word *salat* is among the most widely known words, and its derivation from the movement of the two *salawan* is among the least known things among transmitters, so if we allow that it was obscure and effaced until only a few individuals knew it, then the same would be allowed for all other words, and we could not be certain that God's intended meaning of these words is what occurs to our minds in our time, since they may have been, at the time of the Messenger, assigned to other meanings that are hidden from us: this is answered by saying that there is no barrier to a widely known word being transferred (*manqul*) from a hidden meaning, because what matters for widespread use is usage, while derivation is a scholarly investigation. For this reason al-Baydawi said: "The fame of this word in the second meaning, along with its not being famous in the first, does not discredit its transfer from it."

[Page 234]

Among what supports that *salat* is derived from this root is its being written with a *waw* in the Qur'anic codices (*masahif*). If it were not intended to point to the root from which it is derived, there would be no reason for writing it with a *waw*. They also wrote *al-zakat*, *al-riba* and *al-hayat* with a *waw*, pointing to the original root.

As for the statement of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) that it is written with a *waw* according to the pronunciation of the *mufakhkham* (the "heavy" or emphatic pronunciation of the *lam*), that is, the dialect of emphasizing the *lam*, this is refuted by the fact that this was not done for other words containing emphatic *lams*.

The verbal noun (*masdar*) of *salla* by analogy is *al-tasliya*, which is rarely found in their speech. Al-Jawhari claimed that one does not say *salla tasliya*, and al-Fayruzabadi followed him. The truth is that it occurs rarely, as transmitted by Tha'lab in his *Amali*.

The word *al-salat* has been transferred in the language of the Shari'a (divine law) to submission through a specific bodily posture, a specific supplication, recitation, and a specific number [of units]. The view that its original meaning in the language is the posture in supplication and submission is closer to the legal meaning and more in harmony with the position of al-Qadi Abu Bakr (al-Baqillani) and those who followed him, who deny the existence of a legal technical meaning (*haqiqa shar'iyya*) and hold that the Shari'a has used no word except in its linguistic meaning, with additional conditions without which it is not accepted. The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said that the technical legal meanings were established by a new imposition, and are neither linguistic meanings nor figurative usages.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "The legal technical meanings are linguistic figurative usages that became famous for specific meanings." The truth is that these views return to categories that exist within the legal technical meanings.

* * *

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾

This is a third attribute (*sila*) in the description of the God-conscious (*muttaqun*), by which is realized the meaning of piety and the sincerity of faith, through giving up what is dear to the self, in seeking God's pleasure. Because faith has its seat in the heart and is expressed by the tongue, it needs evidence of the sincerity of its possessor, and that evidence is great deeds. Among these is adhering to its effects in the unseen, which indicate it: "﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾." Among them is persistence in performing the prayers, since they are evidence of the believer's remembrance of the One in whom he believes. Among them is generosity in giving wealth to the poor in obedience to God's command.

*Al-rizq* (provision) is what a person obtains from the existing things of this world by which he meets his necessities and needs and obtains what suits him. It is applied to everything by which the needs of life are met: food, livestock, animals, fruit-bearing trees, clothing, and what one acquires by means of it, such as the two precious metals (gold and silver). God the Exalted said: "﴿And when the division takes place, if the near of kin, the orphans and the needy are present, provide for them from it﴾" [al-Nisa': 8], meaning from what the deceased left behind. He said: "﴿God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾" [al-Ra'd: 26]; "﴿and they rejoiced in the life of this world﴾" [al-Ra'd: 26]. And regarding the story of Qarun, He said: "﴿And We gave him of the treasures﴾" [al-Qasas: 76], up to His saying: "﴿Do you not see that God extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it?﴾" [al-Qasas: 82], where *al-rizq* means the treasures of Qarun. And He said: "﴿If God had extended provision to His servants, they would have transgressed in the earth﴾" [al-Shura: 27]. The most common use of the word, according to what I have seen of Arab speech and the occurrences in the Qur'an, is what a person obtains of that. As for its application to what animals consume of pasture and water, it is figurative, as in God's saying: "﴿There is no creature on earth but its provision is upon God﴾" [Hud: 6]; His saying: "﴿He found with her provision﴾" [Al 'Imran: 37]; and His saying: "﴿No food will come to you that you are provided with﴾" [Yusuf: 37].

*Al-rizq* in the legal sense, according to the Ahl al-Sunna (the people of the Sunna), is like its linguistic sense, since the basic principle is that there is no transfer except by evidence. So the term *rizq* applies to both the lawful and the unlawful, since the attribute of lawfulness or unlawfulness is not considered here. The distinction between the lawful and the unlawful has other places [in the Shari'a], and God accepts only what is good (*tayyib*). That varies with the changing circumstances of legislation, such as wine and trade in it before its prohibition. Rather, the intended meaning is that they spend from what is in their hands.

The Mu'tazila disagreed on this point in a number of subsidiary issues concerning the question of the creation of evils and corruptions and their determination. The question of provision is among the matters on which debate took place between the Ash'ari school (Asha'ira) and the Mu'tazila, as was the question of the appointed terms of life and the question of prices. The Mu'tazila, regarding the question of provision, relied on proofs that do not yield the intended conclusion.

*Al-infaq* (spending) is giving provision in what benefits oneself, one's family and dependents, and whoever is desired to be maintained or drawn near to God by benefiting him, with food or clothing. Here it is intended to be distributed for the benefit of the poor and those in need, and to meet the calamities of the Muslims, by the indication of the praise and its being linked with faith and prayer. There is no doubt that here it is one of the characteristics of perfect faith. It is nothing other than spending in the way of good and general public interests, since no one is praised for spending on himself and his dependents, because that is something natural inclination already prompts, so religion does not especially encourage it. Among spending, some is obligatory, a right owed by the possessor of provision, to relatives, to needy members of the community, and to the calamities of the community, such as equipping armies and zakat. Some of it is fixed, and some of it is required by a necessary legal interest or need. This is detailed among the legal rulings in the books of jurisprudence (*fiqh*). Among spending is voluntary charity, which is what benefits those whom religion calls us to benefit. In attributing the verb *razaqna* (We provided) to God's pronoun, and in making its object "those who believe," there is an indication that what makes provision become provision for its owner is a particular right that God granted him by the rule of the Shari'a, according to the means and ways by which people's ownership of wealth and provisions is established. These are the means recognized in the Shari'a that require the entitlement of their owners and their exclusive right to them, through the effort made by a person with the strength of his body, which there is no doubt is his right. Examples are drawing water, gathering firewood, hunting, picking fruit, and collecting what no one owns and what is not in anyone's possession. Likewise is his service by his strength, such as carrying a load, walking to attend to the affairs of one who hires him, and confinement for guarding. Or it is what he makes of materials he owns and has the right to benefit from, such as baking bread, weaving, trade, forging iron, preparing foods, and shaping vessels from clay pottery. Or it is what he produces, such as planting, sowing and breeding. Or it is what he invents by his mind, such as teaching, invention, authorship, medicine, advocacy, judgeship, and similar functions and works that benefit the public or specific people. Or it is what someone who owns provision gives him by gifts, presents and bequests, or by permission to dispose of property, such as reviving dead land. Or it is what he obtained by exchange, such as sales, leases, rentals, partnerships and sharecropping (*mughārasa*). Or it is what passed to him from property whose owner has ceased to exist, by his being the most entitled person to it, such as inheritance.

Also included is taking ownership of a found object (*luqata*) after the required announcement, and the right to one-fifth (*khums*) of buried treasure (*rikaz*). All these and similar things are covered by God's saying "﴿and from what We have provided them﴾." No one, nor the whole of humanity, has a right to what God has made the provision of one individual among them, because no one has a right to property he did not strive to acquire by its means. Hind bint 'Utba, the wife of Abu Sufyan, came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "Abu Sufyan is a stingy man. Shall I spend from what he has for our dependents?" He said to her: "No, except in accordance with what is customary" (*illa bil-ma'ruf*), meaning except what is generally known to be something a wife may dispose of from what is in her house, which her husband placed in his house for that purpose, without stealth or secrecy.

The placement of the prepositional phrase (*majrur*), which is the object (*ma'mul*), before its governing verb *yunfiqun* (they spend) is for the mere emphasis on provision in people's common usage. In this fronting there is a notice that they spend while provision is dear to the self, as in God's saying: "﴿and they give food, in spite of their love for it﴾" [al-Insan: 8], while also observing the rhyme of the verses on the letter *nun*. In the use of *min* (from), which is for partitive meaning, there is a hint that the spending required by the Shari'a is spending part of one's wealth, because the Shari'a does not impose hardship on people. This part varies and is small or large according to the circumstances of those who spend. The obligatory portion is what the Shari'a has fixed as to its thresholds and measures, such as zakat and the spending on wives, children and slaves. What exceeds the obligatory has no fixed limit, and whatever exceeds it is good. Islam did not legislate the obligation for a Muslim to hand over to another what he has earned and acquired.

These attributes were specifically chosen for them over others because they were the first things legislated in Islam, so they became the emblem of the Muslims. They are complete faith, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat, for these two are the oldest of the legislated acts and are "siblings" in many verses of the Qur'an. And because these attributes are evidence of the sincerity of faith: faith in the state of being absent from the believers and in the state of the self's solitude is more indicative of certainty and sincerity, when fear and hope are absent, if what is meant by "the unseen" is what is absent. Or because faith in what the senses cannot reach is the strongest proof of the strength of certainty, to the point that one receives from the Lawgiver what reason has no ability to judge. The nature of souls is to recoil from believing in what they cannot perceive, since they incline toward the sensible. Believing in it despite its difficulties is evidence of the strength of trust in the one who informs, who is the Messenger, if what is meant by "the unseen" is that which is the opposite of "the witnessed." And because prayer is a bodily burden at times when the one who performs it does not remember it, that is, one who performs it well, except the one whose heart is filled with the remembrance of God the Exalted, along with its humility and manifestation of servanthood. And because zakat is the giving of wealth, and the stinginess of souls is well known. God the Exalted said: "﴿And when evil touches him, he is distressed﴾" [al-Ma'arij: 21]. And because the believers, after polytheism, were deprived of these [acts] during the time of polytheism, in contrast to the People of the Book. So mentioning them is a reminder of the blessing of Islam.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 4:

﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you, and what was revealed before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain.﴾

He conjoins to ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] a second group, distinct from the first group referred to by the words ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. Together they are two categories of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). After he informed that the Qur'an is guidance for the God-fearing who believed after polytheism, namely the Arabs of Makkah and others, and described them as ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ because they did not believe in it while they were polytheists, he mentioned another group of the God-fearing, namely those who believed in the divine books revealed before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) and then believed in Muhammad. These are the believers among the People of the Book (ahl al-Kitab), who at that time were the Jews, numerous in Madinah and its surroundings, in Qurayzah, al-Nadir and Khaybar, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, and some Christians, such as Suhayb al-Rumi and Dihyah al-Kalbi. Although they shared with the Muslims among the Arabs in being guided by the Qur'an, in believing in the unseen and in establishing the prayer, these qualities were among their characteristics before the coming of Islam. Therefore, he mentioned for them an additional quality beyond what was attributed to the earliest Muslims. The distinction between the two groups here is one of generality and specificity. Since the intention of singling them out by mention necessitates conjoining them, and conjoining without an indication that they are another group would give the impression that the Qur'an guides only those who believed in what was revealed before, because this is the last of the attributes and so it is what is intended, it would be supposed that those who believed after polytheism have no share of this praise. How could that be, when among them are the best of the believers from the Companions, who are the most fearful of God and the most guided, since they were not people who awaited a messenger before? Their guidance arose from divine grant. This assumption is removed by repeating the relative pronoun, to indicate that these are another group, different from the group upon whom the three earlier attributes were applied. Thereby it becomes clear that the intended referents of the first three attributes are those who believed after polytheism, due to the existence of the contrast. Both relative pronouns are for definiteness (al-'ahd). It is known that those who believe in what was revealed before are also among those who believe in the unseen, establish the prayer and spend, because that is among what was revealed to the Prophet. In the use of the present tense in his words ﴿they believe in what has been revealed to you﴾ there is an indication of renewal, as was mentioned previously in its parallels, because their belief in the Qur'an occurred anew. All of this is a specification of them with a distinction that must be taken into account, although precedence thereafter is by the strength of faith, its firmness, and the intensity of guidance. Thus Abu Bakr and 'Umar are better than Dihyah and 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.

Al-inzal (sending down) is making a thing descend, and al-nuzul (descent) is movement from a height to a low place. It is literal in the movement of bodies from a height. The verb inzal and its derivation are used by linguistic metaphor (majaz lughawi) for meanings that return to likening an action to descent, on account of a moral and immaterial elevation and nobility, as in His words ﴿We have sent down to you garments﴾ [al-A'raf: 26] and His words ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], because God's creation and His bestowal are treated as the arrival of a thing from a high source on account of its nobility. As for its application to the arrival of the revelation from God to the prophets, it is either an intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli), by attributing the descent to the revelation following the descent of the angel who conveys it, who connects to this world descending from the higher world, as He said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193], since the angel is associated with the speech commanded to be conveyed. Or it is a linguistic metaphor, by likening the meanings cast upon the Prophet to a thing that has reached from a high place, the point of resemblance being moral elevation, especially when the revelation is speech heard by the Messenger, like the Qur'an, and like what was sent down to Musa, and as the Prophet (ﷺ) described some states of revelation in the authentic hadith saying: "Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and it leaves me, and I have retained what it said." As for dream vision, like the dream of Ibrahim, it is not called inzal. The intended meaning of ﴿what has been sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ)﴾ is the portion of the Qur'an whose descent was established before the revelation of this verse, since praise of the guided is only for having attained faith in what descended, not for anticipating their faith in what will descend, because that does not need mention; it is known that one who believes in what has been sent down continues to believe in everything that descends upon the Messenger, since obstinacy and lack of tranquility occur only at the beginning, and when these are removed by faith they are secure from apostasy, and likewise faith when its cheerfulness mingles with hearts. Belief in what will descend in the future is attained by the implication of the discourse, which is the indication by analogy (dalalah ukhrawiyyah), so their belief in what will descend is intended by the speech and is not a signification of the word, which is in the past tense. Therefore there is no need to claim the predominance of the past over the future in His words ﴿by what was sent down﴾, and the intended meaning is what has been sent down and what will be sent down, as in al-Kashshaf.

He transitively used inzal with ila (to) because it is included in the sense of conveying (al-wasf), so the one to whom it is sent down is the endpoint of the descent. The more common and original usage is with the particle 'ala (upon), because it carries the sense of falling, as in His words ﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3]. When it is intended that the thing settled with the one upon whom it was sent down and was firmly established in him, He said ﴿And We sent down upon you manna and quails﴾ [al-Baqarah: 57]. The choice of one of the two transitive forms is variation in speech (tafannun).

Then, the benefit of using the relative pronoun here rather than saying "those who believe in you from among the People of the Book" is that the relative clause indicates that these had believed in what was established as sent down by God upon their messengers, without mixture with distortions that had turned their people away from entering Islam, such as the claim that the Torah does not accept abrogation, and that there would come at the end of time, from the descendants of Israel, one who would deliver the Children of Israel from captivity and servitude, and similar things not sent down in the previous books. Rather, these are among the fabrications or among corrupt interpretations. In it is therefore an allusion to the extremists among the Jews and Christians, whose extremism in their religion and their saying concerning God what is not true prevented them from following the Prophet (ﷺ).

His words ﴿and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ are a conjunction of a second attribute, namely the firm establishment of their faith in the Hereafter, i.e., their belief in a second life after this life. This attribute was singled out for mention in the praise of them among their other attributes, because it is the foundation of piety and fear, by which they were described, since all these attributes follow what the description "God-fearing" summarized. Certainty regarding the abode of reward and punishment is what necessitates caution and reflection on what saves the soul from punishment and grants it the reward; and that is what led them to faith in the Prophet (ﷺ). Also, this certainty about the Hereafter was among the distinctive features of the People of the Book among the Arabs in the age of ignorance, for the polytheists did not believe in a second life; they were materialists (dahriyyun). As for what is related about them, that they used to tie the mount of a dead man at his grave and leave it without eating or drinking until it died, claiming that when he was revived he would ride it and not be raised on foot, and calling it al-baliyyah, that is a confusion between the claims of polytheism and what they received without reflection from Christianized people among them.

In the terminology of the Qur'an, al-Akhirah is the Hereafter life. Al-akhirah is the feminine of al-akhir with a long vowel and a kasra on the kha', meaning what comes after something else in action or state. The feminine form of the attribute is considered as applying to a feminine-worded noun that was omitted due to its frequent use and its becoming known, and it is estimated as "the life of the Hereafter," in consideration of its opposite, the life of this world (al-hayat al-dunya), i.e., the near, meaning the present; for this reason it is called al-'ajilah. Then al-Akhirah became a proper name by predominance for the life after death, which is the life after resurrection, for the application of recompense to deeds. So the meaning of ﴿and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ is that they believe in the resurrection and life after death.

Yaqin (certainty) is knowledge of a thing through reflection and inference, or after a prior doubt, and doubt occurs only in a matter open to reflection. Thus it is more specific than iman and than 'ilm. Al-Raghib argued for this with His words ﴿If you knew with the knowledge of certainty﴾ [al-Takathur: 5] ﴿you would surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takathur: 6]. For this reason they do not apply yaqin to the knowledge of God nor to necessary knowledge. It has been said that it is the knowledge that does not admit possibility, and it may be applied to strong opinion in customary usage, where it does not come to mind that it is an opinion, and it is confused with firm knowledge, so it is synonymous with iman and 'ilm.

So the expression of their belief in the Hereafter with the root y-q-n (certainty) is because this root indicates that it is knowledge obtained through reflection and deep thought in the path of inference, since the Hereafter, being a life unseen and strange by ordinary standards, and since many doubts had led the polytheists and materialists to deny it and consider it impossible, belief in it was worthy of the root of certainty, on the basis that it is more specific than iman. Therefore, the choice of yuqinun here has a particularity fitting the eloquence of the Qur'an. Those who made iman and yaqin synonyms say that the mention of yuqinun is merely for variation in expression, to avoid repeating the word yu'minun after His words ﴿and those who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾. In His words ﴿and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ there is fronting of the prepositional phrase, which is the object of yuqinun, before its governing verb. This fronting is for mere emphasis, together with observing the rhyme (fasilah). I find that in this fronting there is praise of these people, that they were certain of the most important thing a believer is certain of. The fronting does not yield exclusivity, since the sense of restriction cannot stand here, that they are certain of the Hereafter only and not other things. The commentator al-Kashshaf and his commentators strained to derive restriction from this fronting, and the restriction moves from relating to the essence of what is restricted to relating to its states, and this is not usual in restriction.

His words ﴿they are certain﴾: the predicate-subject is placed before the verbal predicate to give strength to the statement, since it is a certainty established among them before the coming of Islam in general terms, even if the Torah was devoid of its detail, while the Gospel pointed to the life of the spirit, and the books of Ezekiel and Isaiah addressed its mention.

In both fronting constructions there is an allusion to the materialist polytheists and a rebuke of the lowness of their creed. As for those who followed the hanifiyyah in their assumption, such as Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt and Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, they were not considered, either because of their small number, or because they are classed with the People of the Book, having taken much of their laws from them on the ground that these were from the law of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord.﴾ The demonstrative (ism al-ishara) refers to the God-conscious (al-muttaqun) who were described by the attributes mentioned earlier, and so they were of two groups.

The basic function of the demonstrative is to refer to a specific, present, observable thing. However, the Arabs sometimes depart from this basic usage, so that it refers to a thing that is made present in the discourse after its attributes and conditions have been mentioned, which places it in the position of something present in the minds of the speaker and the listener. When the listener grasps those attributes, and they are significant or remarkable, whether for good or for ill, the one described by them becomes like something witnessed. The speaker then builds upon this and points to him as though he were present and visible. The demonstrative is used in this way because nothing makes a thing more distinctly identified, or more fully witnessed, than knowing its attributes, so the pointing suffices to identify it. This is the basic usage in presenting a demonstrative after the mention of attributes, when the thing pointed to is not physically present.

Then, they may follow the demonstrative that comes after these descriptions with judgments, and this indicates that the source of those judgments is the attributes that precede the demonstrative. Because these attributes were the means of making the referent present, the demonstrative pointing to the possessors of those attributes stands in place of the referents being pointed to. Just as judgments that come after the names of entities indicate that they are established for the named things, so judgments that come after what belongs to attributes indicate that they are established for the attributes. Thus His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ is equivalent to saying: those attributes are the cause of their being enabled to be guided by their Lord.

A parallel to this is the saying of Hatim al-Ta'i:

By God, there is a poor man who wrestles with his cares, and goes on forward, bold, against misfortunes and time.
A youth of aims, who does not see hunger a sorrow, nor satiety, if he attains it, a gain.

[p. 242]

Until he said:

So if he dies, his praise is good; and if he lives, he will not sit as a weak, blamed man.

His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance﴾ is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustanfa'a), a bayani resumption (isti'naf bayani), because the listener, on hearing the earlier attributes of praise for them, awaits the benefit of those attributes. The demonstrative here takes the place of mentioning their pronoun, and the demonstrative has a more striking effect, because it encompasses all of their earlier attributes. Al-Taftazani has verified in the chapter on separation and connection (al-fasl wa al-wasl) in the Sharh al-Mutawwal that resumption by means of the demonstrative is more eloquent than resumption by repeating the name of the entity being resumed.

This interpretation is clearer in meaning, more apt in eloquence, and better suited to the use of the demonstrative in such positions, because it shows more clearly that the pointing is for the purpose of highlighting those attributes that are pointed to, and the judgment that follows the demonstrative and arises from them. This can only be achieved by making the demonstrative the first subject at the beginning of a resumptive sentence. So His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ is a return to informing about them that the Qur'an is guidance for them. The use of the particle of elevation (harf al-isti'la', "upon") is a representation (tamthil) of their state, in that the form of their being established in guidance, their steadfastness in it, their striving for increase in it, and their journeying along the path of good deeds, is likened to the form of a rider who is raised above a mount, empowered to direct it, and able to tame it. Thus their state, abstracted from several elements, is likened to that other state, abstracted from several elements, by an implicit likeness (tashbih dimni) indicated by the particle of elevation, because elevation is the strongest kind of one thing's being established upon another. The reason we take it to imply a supposed mount, rather than a chair or a bench, for example, is that this is what their minds leap to when they hear what indicates elevation, since riding is the most common form of their elevation, so it is the one present in their minds. This is why, when they explicitly mention the thing likened to, or allude to it, they mention only the mount and its accessories. They say: "He made error a vehicle," "He mounted ignorance," and in the Maqamat: "when it sat upon the back of estrangement," and they say in proverbs: "He rode the back of a blind [mount]," and "He stumbled like a blind she-camel."

And al-Nabigha, satirizing 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl al-Ghanawi, said:

If 'Amir has spoken in ignorance,
then the mount of ignorance is youth.

So the word "upon" here is part of the compound expression that signifies the form being likened, by way of brevity,

[p. 243]

and its original form is: "Those are upon the mount of guidance." It is thus an explicit representational metaphor (tamthiliyya tasrihiyya), except that what is explicitly stated is a part of the signifying compound, not all of it.

This is how their commentators, al-Tibi, al-Tahtani, al-Taftazani and al-Baydawi, explained the words of al-Kashshaf on this point. Al-Qazwini in al-Kashf and al-Sayyid al-Jurjani held that the metaphor in the verse is a subsidiary restricted metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya muqayyada), in that the holding fast to guidance among the God-conscious is likened to a rider's being established upon a mount, and the likeness extended to the meaning of the particle, which is "upon." Al-Sayyid allowed a third possibility, namely that there is here an implicit singular metaphor (isti'ara makniyya mufrada), in which guidance is likened to a mount, and the particle of elevation is the indicator of this, following the method of al-Sakkaki in rejecting the subsidiary metaphor in favour of the implicit one.

Then al-Tibi and al-Taftazani added to these, holding that the verse contains a subsidiary metaphor alongside the representational one, saying that the occurrence of the word "upon" necessarily makes its meaning a metaphor for something similar to it, namely being established, so that there is necessarily a subsidiary metaphor there.

Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani championed the representational interpretation, and al-Sayyid al-Jurjani championed the subsidiary interpretation.

Al-Sayyid vigorously denied that it is representational, and considered it a combination of two contradictory things. This is because abstracting each of the two sides of the likeness from several matters requires that the composition be formed from several meanings. How can this be, when the meaning of a particle, which is one of the singular meanings, such as elevation here, is tied to something? If the likeness here is considered compound, it entails that the meaning of "upon" and what its meaning is tied to should be neither a likened thing nor a borrowed thing, neither as a subsidiary nor as a primary element. He elaborated on this in his marginal notes on al-Kashshaf and in his marginal notes on al-Mutawwal, just as Sa'd elaborated in his marginal notes on al-Kashshaf and in al-Mutawwal, and they exchanged the arrows of sharp debate.

We will intervene in the judgment between these two authorities by saying that there is no dispute among all of them that the verse contains a likening of things to things in general, arising from the establishment of guidance for the God-conscious and from the establishment of elevation upon a mount. The two groups differ only over identifying the method by which this likeness is achieved. Most of them consider it the method of the representational metaphor, in that the likeness of those things is achieved by abstraction and composition into a single form. Al-Sayyid considers it the method of the subsidiary metaphor, in that the likened and the likened-to are each a single one of those things, and knowledge of the remaining things is attained through the restriction of the two singular elements, the likened and the likened-to. The method of representation and the method of the implicit metaphor are also possible.

So the consideration here turns to which of the two methods is more weighty in consideration and more complete in eloquence, and to whether combining the representational and the subsidiary methods is considered contradictory according to the rules of rhetoric (ilm al-bayan), as al-Sayyid claimed.

It is established in the science of rhetoric that its scholars are most keen to consider the likeness of forms, so they do not turn away from it to the singular

[p. 244]

so long as its consideration is sound. For this reason al-Shaykh (Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani) said in Dala'il al-I'jaz, when mentioning the verse of Bashshar:

As if the dust-cloud above our heads
and our swords were a night whose stars have fallen.

He intended the likening of the dust-cloud and the swords in it to a night whose stars are falling, not the likening of the dust-cloud to the night on one side and the swords to the stars on the other side. For this reason it was necessary to judge that "our swords" is in the position of a complement to the verbal noun, meaning "raised" (muthar), so that the likeness would not be divided. The accusative case of "swords" is because the "wa" is in the sense of "with," not coordinating. When this is established, it becomes clear to you that the representational likeness has the greatest share among the people of eloquence. Its reason is that among the most important and first aims of eloquent speakers is the chapter on likeness, and it is the oldest of its arts. There is no doubt that representation is the most specific type of likeness, since it is the likening of a form to a form, so it is more striking to the souls and clearer for meanings.

We find the consideration of representation in the verse to be weightier, because it is clearer, more eloquent, more widely known, and better suited to the words of al-Kashshaf. As for its being clearer: the likeness of representation is an evident path with no effort involved, so it conveys the likening of the entire form of the God-conscious in their being characterized by guidance to the form of the rider, and so on, unlike the method of the subsidiary metaphor, which conveys only the likening of being established to elevation, and then the rest is derived through restriction.

As for its being more eloquent: since the context permitted both considerations by the agreement of both groups, the one more deserving of consideration is naturally the one containing stronger and more distinguished features. As for its being more widely known: representation is agreed upon, unlike the subsidiary metaphor.

As for its being better suited to the words of al-Kashshaf: the apparent meaning of his phrase "a likeness" (mathal) is that he intended representation, because in the speech of one like him from among the people of this discipline, the technical term does not depart from the common usage of its specialists toward its original linguistic meaning.

Since it is established that the representational is weightier, let us turn the discussion to the correction of combining it with the subsidiary, which is the second area of disagreement between the two authorities. Al-Sa'd and al-Tibi permit considering the subsidiary alongside the representational in the verse, while al-Sayyid prevents this, as you know, and says: if the likeness is abstracted from several things, then each part of the likened has been abstracted from the two parts of the likened-to, and this is the meaning of composition. How, then, can part of the likened-to be considered a borrowed term for part of the likened, so that the composition is broken?

This argument refers to the saying of the leading authorities of rhetoric that the original elements of a representational compound are to be used in their literal meanings, and that the metaphor lies in the whole of the compound, that is, in its application to the likened form. So al-Sayyid's statement stops at this point.

However, al-Taftazani saw no obstacle to considering a metaphor in some of the elements of the representational compound, provided there is no artificiality in it, and perhaps he regards this as an addition to the specific features of the inimitability (i'jaz) of this verse. It is incumbent upon the eloquent speaker not to forfeit any of the specific features required by the situation, and by this

[p. 245]

the eloquent differ, as has been established in the discussion on the definition of eloquence (balagha). The limit of inimitability is the highest level of eloquence, comprising the utmost of specific features, as we have explained in its proper place, and it is the preferred view. When it was found, in the likened form and the likened-to form, that there are two elements that can be likened one to the other by an independent likeness, not included in the likeness of the form, it was right in this context to liken the establishment to elevation. This is a striking likeness, and it is indicated by the word "upon." As for the other elements of the two forms, since it was not fitting to liken any of them to another, the singular likeness in them is set aside, for it is not fitting to liken the God-conscious specifically to the rider, nor guidance to the mount. Thus "upon" in this way is partly a compound metaphor, indicating it by one consideration, and a singular metaphor by another consideration.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 5 (part 2 of 2):

As for what I choose in this verse, it is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those are upon guidance﴾, is a metaphorical allegory (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) of the implicit (makniyyah) type, in which the state is likened to a state, and the word of the likened-to element has been omitted, namely the compound expression that indicates riding, as if one were to say "riding the mount of guidance." He retained what indicates the likened element, which is "those" and "guidance," and he alluded to the compound that indicates the likened-to element by one of its concomitants, which is the word "upon" (ʿalā), which indicates riding by convention, as you know. Thus the three divisions of the allegorical metaphor (tamthiliyyah) are complete for us: the metaphor (istiʿarah), as in the simple metaphor, so the allegory from it is a metonymy (majaz mursal), like the use of the report to express regret; and from it is an explicit metaphor (istiʿarah musarrahah), such as "I see you advancing one foot and delaying the other"; and from it is an implicit metaphor (makniyyah), as in this verse according to our view; and from it is a subordinate metaphor (tab'iyyah), as in the words of the Hamasi poet:

And a horseman plunged into the fray of death,
When he swears an oath upon something abhorrent, he is truthful.

For "plunged" (munghamis) is an allegory for the state of the causes of death encompassing him from every side, in the manner of one whom deadly waters have encompassed from every side. The word "plunged" is without doubt a subordinate metaphor. As for "guidance" being indefinite and not defined with the article (al-), this is because definition and indefiniteness are equal here; for had it been defined, the definition would have been the definition of the genus, so indefiniteness was preferred as a preparation for describing it as "from their Lord." It is distinct from the earlier guidance in His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], a distinction in consideration, since the aim here is to draw attention to the matter of guidance and, as a means to conveying the magnification of guidance, by the indication of the context of praise and by the mention of what denotes firm attainment; so the intent of magnification is determined. Thus His saying ﴿from their Lord﴾ is an acknowledgment of this guidance which requires its magnification, and all of this returns to the magnification of those characterized by firm attainment of it.

He described the guidance as "from their Lord" to draw attention to that guidance and to ennoble it, together with an indication that they are in a place of special care from God; likewise the attribution of the Lord to them is an attribution of magnification of the status of the one to whom it is attributed, by the context.

* * *

Page 246

﴿And those are the successful﴾. The referent of the second demonstrative is the same as the referent of the first. The purpose of repeating the demonstrative is to alert that each of the two attributes is worthy of attention and acknowledgment, so that neither is mentioned as a follower of the other; rather each is given a separate clause and a special demonstrative, so that their renown is renown for both sentences, and that they are among those of whom both statements are said.

The reason for conjoining with "wa" (and) without disjunction (fasl) is that between the two clauses there is an intermediate position between the two perfections of connection and disconnection. For if you consider the difference of their meanings and the time of their occurrence, the meaning of one of them, which is guidance, is attained in this world, and the meaning of the other, which is success, is attained in the Hereafter, and they would be disconnected. And if you consider the causation of the meaning of one from the meaning of the other, and that each of them is intended by the description, they are connected. Thus the conflict between the two perfections of connection and disconnection places them in the position of intermediates. So the commentators on the Kashshaf have established it, and it is known that the state of intermediacy requires conjunction, as has been established in the science of ma'ani (rhetoric). In my view its rationale is that when the two requirements conflict, conjunction is determined, because it is the basic principle in mentioning sentences one after another.

As for His saying ﴿they are the successful﴾, the pronoun is a separator (damir al-fasl), and the definite article in "the successful" (al-muflihun) is for the genus, which is the more apparent reading, since there is no known referent here according to the outward state; rather the purpose is to convey that these people are successful. The definition of the predicate with the article of genus, when it is taken as applied to a defined subject, conveys exclusivity (ikhtisas); so the separating pronoun serves merely to emphasize the attribution, that is, as emphasis for the exclusivity. But when the definition is for the genus, which is the apparent case, then the definition of the subject together with the predicate ordinarily conveys exclusivity; yet here it is devoid of conveying true exclusivity and conveys a certain degree of attention to the predicate, and therefore the definite was brought for it rather than the indefinite. ʿAbd al-Qahir illustrated this with the saying: "He is the brave defender," meaning: if you hear of the brave defender and have information about him, then he is so-and-so.

To this al-Zamakhshari alluded here in the Kashshaf with his words: "Or [it refers to] that they are those who, if the attribute of the successful is realized in them, and they are established in what they are, and they are conceived in their true form, then they are they." Al-Sakkaki did not follow the two shaykhs in this, so he departed from it in the Miftah, and God's excellence is with him.

Page 247

Al-falah: success and the good condition of affairs, so it applies to the affairs of this world and the affairs of the Hereafter. Its meaning in the terminology of the religion is success through deliverance from punishment in the Hereafter. The verb derived from it is aflaha, meaning he became one possessing success. The verb was derived from it through the intermediary of the hamzah that indicates becoming, because it is not an event subsisting in itself; rather it is a genus whose instances are attached to the one for whom it is decreed. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: "Consider how Allah, mighty and majestic, repeated the alerting to the exclusivity of the God-fearing in attaining what no one else attains, by various means: the mention of the demonstrative and its repetition, the definition of (the successful), and the placing of the separating pronoun between it and 'those,' so that He might show you their ranks, encourage you to seek what they sought, and stir you to advance what they advanced."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾

This is a transition from praise of the Book and of those who bear it, and from the description of its guidance and the effect of that guidance on those who were guided by it, along with the praise of them which returns to praise of the Book. Since praise only becomes apparent when the effects of the quality for which praise is deserved are realised, and since a thing is sometimes defined by its opposite, the discourse moved to speak of those for whom guidance through this Book does not occur. It records that their deprivation of guidance by its direction was only due to the corruption of their souls, since they turned away from it by them, so they were not among those who reflect upon the outcome of their affairs and fear the evil consequences, and so they were not among the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). For them, warning and its absence were equal, so they did not receive the warning with reflection; rather it was equal to them and its absence was the same to them. The verses have paired two groups: a group who concealed disbelief and openly declared it, and they are among the polytheists, as is the dominant usage of the Qur'an in the expression ﴿those who disbelieve﴾; and a group who showed belief while being deceivers, and they are the hypocrites referred to by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. This sentence was separated from the one before it because between them there is complete disconnection, since the preceding sentences were about guidance and those who are guided, while this one is about the misguided, so the separation between them is for the sake of opposition. It is known that these form a category opposed to the two categories mentioned before it, from the context of contrast.

The opening of the sentence with the particle of emphasis (inna) is either merely for drawing attention to the news and its strangeness, without rejecting denial or doubt, because the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and to the community and it is an address of novelty, such that no doubt had preceded its occurrence; and the coming of inna for emphasis is frequent in speech and in the Qur'an it is frequent. It may also be that inna here serves to reject doubt, taking the speech contrary to the apparent requirement, because the eagerness of the Prophet ﷺ for the guidance of the disbelievers makes him not cut off hope
صفحة ٢٤٨
in the benefit of warning to them, and his situation is like the situation of one who doubts the benefit of warning; or because the listeners, given the praise bestowed upon the Book in its reaching the highest degree of guidance, are led to hope that its guidance would affect the disbelievers who turn away, and would make them like those who doubt whether warning and its absence are the same; so the speech was taken contrary to the apparent requirement, and one who is not in doubt was placed in the position of one who doubts. It has been transmitted from al-Mubarrad that inna does not come to reject denial but only to reject doubt.

It has become clear that those who disbelieve mentioned here are a group of the polytheists who are despaired of regarding their faith. So the use of the relative pronoun for definition in mentioning them is either for definition by prior knowledge (al-'ahd), meaning by it a known people such as Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and their likes from the heads of polytheism and the leaders of obstinacy, excluding whoever was a polytheist at the time of the revelation of this verse and then believed afterward, such as Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and others from those who embraced Islam at the Conquest; or the relative pronoun is for definition of the genus, conveying totality, with the meaning of disbelief being its most intense kind, by the indication of His saying ﴿they will not believe﴾; so it is general, specified by sense-observation, since some of them did believe, or it is general but intended as particular by context. These two aspects are the ones restricted to by the verifying scholars among the exegetes, and both look to the fact that God informed concerning these that they would not believe, so it was necessary that they be among those who were later shown to have died in disbelief.

Among the exegetes is one who interpreted His saying, exalted is He, ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ to mean those for whom disbelief and wretchedness have been decreed, and compared it to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾ [Yunus: 96]. This is an interpretation far from the wording, and there is a great difference between it and the comparison. Among the exegetes is one who understood ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ to mean the chiefs of the Jews such as Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Abu Rafi', on the basis that the surah was revealed in Medina and that there were no disbelievers in it besides the Jews and the hypocrites. This is far from the custom of the Qur'an and a turning away from the intended context, which is the mention of those deprived of the guidance of the Qur'an in contrast to those for whom guidance through it occurred. In any case, the meaning according to all is that a specific group of disbelievers whose faith is not hoped for, namely those upon whose hearts and hearing God has set a seal; and this was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The intended purpose of this is that their non-guidance by the Qur'an was due to their lack of receptivity, not to a deficiency in the Qur'an's indication of good or its guidance toward it.

Kufr, with a dammah, is the concealment of a blessing; with a fatha, it is covering in general, and it is derived from kafara, meaning he covered. Since denying the Creator, or denying His perfection, or denying what His messengers brought, is a kind of ingratitude for His blessing by the one who denies it, the name kufr was applied to it, and its use became predominant in this meaning. In the Sharia it is the denial of what is indicated by decisive evidences, and all the valid previous religious laws transmitted it, until humanity knew it and their minds turned to investigating it and proofs were established for it, such as the unity of God, exalted is He, and His existence; and for this reason the people of polytheism in the interval between prophets (fatra) were counted as disbelievers. Denying what is known by necessity—the coming of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with it and his call to it, and counting it among the foundations of Islam—or obstinacy in acknowledging it, even while believing in his truthfulness, is also kufr; and for this reason the verse expressed it by denial rather than by false accusation.

Also joining kufr in applying the rulings of disbelief to it is every statement or act that a believing, affirming person would not dare to commit, such that it indicates the carelessness of its doer regarding faith, and his concealed intent to disparage the religion, and his use of that to undermine its foundations, or his humiliation of it in a way that does not admit of an apparent interpretation. In this last category there is room for the ijtihad of the jurists and the fatwas of the leading scholars, affirming and negating, according to the extent to which the statement or act indicates disparagement or doubt. Whoever considers the actions, or some specific part of them, to be part of faith considers their absence, or the absence of some specific part of them, to be part of disbelief.

Al-Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani said: "The view I hold is that disbelief in God is ignorance of His existence, and faith in God is knowledge of His existence. Thus disbelief occurs only through one of three matters: the first is ignorance of God, exalted is He. The second is that one performs an act or statement which God and His Messenger have declared, or which the believers have agreed, can only come from a disbeliever, such as prostrating to an idol. The third: that one has a statement or act with which knowledge of God, exalted is He, is not possible."

Ibn Rashid in al-Faiq transmitted from al-Ash'ari, may God have mercy on him, that kufr is a single trait. al-Qarafi said in al-Furuq (p. 241): "The root of kufr is a specific violation of the sanctity of lordship, and it occurs by ignorance of God and His attributes, or by audacity against Him; and this type is the difficult domain, because all sins are audacity against God."

His saying ﴿it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ is the predicate of ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, and "sawa'" (same) is a noun meaning equality. It is a verbal noun (ism masdar) indicated by the necessity of its being singular and masculine despite the difference of what it describes and reports; and when it is reported about or described, it is like a verbal noun in that what is meant by it is the meaning of the active participle for the purpose of emphasis. It has been said that sawa' is a noun meaning "like," so the obligation to keep it singular and masculine is because likeness does not multiply, even if what it qualifies is plural; you say "they are men who are sawa' to Zayd," meaning "like Zayd." Ibn 'Ashur notes that sawa' is here and elsewhere governed by 'ala rather than by 'inda and similar words, though the intended meaning of elevation in such a construction is what is meant; this indicates the firmness of equality in the speaker's view, that there is no turning away from it for him, and no hesitation in it for him. Thus the meaning is: the warning and its absence are equal to them.

Know that the Arabs use "sawa'" in two ways. One is to use sawa' in its original sense of indicating equality in a quality among a plurality, so that sawa' is preceded by something indicating plurality, such as the plural pronoun in His saying ﴿so they are equal therein﴾ [al-Nahl: 71], and such as the conjunction in the verse of Buthayna:

"Equal to us, O Jamil ibn Ma'mar, if you die, are the hardships of life and its ease."

Its i'rab follows what its position in the structure requires. The second is that it occurs with the hamza of equalization (hamzat al-taswiyah), which is nothing other than the interrogative hamza, and it frequently occurs after the word sawa' with am the connective (al-'atifah), which is called al-muttasilah, as in His saying ﴿It is the same for us whether we grow impatient or we endure﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]. This is the most common usage of the two, and the grammarians disagreed about its i'rab. The most apparent and safest of what they said is that (sawa'a) is a predicate preceding its subject, and that the verb following it, joined to the hamza, is in the interpretation of a subject (mubtada'), because it has become like a verbal noun, having been stripped of attribution and of time. So the estimate in the verse is: "It is the same for them your warning them and its absence."

What appears to me more correct than what they said is that the subject after sawa' is elided, indicated by the interrogation that occurs with it, and that the estimate is: "sawa' is the answer to 'did you warn them or did you not warn them.'" This proceeds like the speech of one who says "I knew: is Zayd standing?", since its estimate is "I knew the answer to this question." You may also make sawa' a subject raising a doer that takes the place of the predicate, because sawa' means "equal," and so it has the force of an active participle, raising a doer that takes the place of the predicate of the subject. The answer to such an interrogation, when it is one of two matters, is that reporting their equality in the speaker's view indicates two equal matters; and because the original of its predicate is singularity, the verb after sawa' is interpreted as a verbal noun. The eloquence in this is that these two matters are so obscure in their equality that people would ask: "Did so-and-so do such-and-such?" and it is said that the two are equal in not caring about them and not seeking an answer through the interrogation from either of them. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It is the same for them whether you warned them﴾ indicates that people, in their wonder at the continuance of the disbelievers in their disbelief despite the signs that came to them, to the extent that questioners would ask, "Did the Prophet warn them or did he not warn them?" being certain that if he had warned them they would not have hesitated in faith, it was said: "It is the same for them," as the answer to people's question about one of the two matters. By this, all the artificialities that the grammarians imposed here are dispelled, and we disclaim the objections raised against them, such as that the hamza would be outside the meaning of interrogation; how the action of what follows the interrogation could be valid upon what precedes it if sawa' is parsed as a predicate and the verb after the hamza as a subject stripped of time; and that the verb is intended to mean bare event; and the claim that the hamza in equalization is metaphorical by the relation of necessity; and that am means waw so that the speech concerns two things rather than one of two things; and similar matters. We also do not need to strain to answer the objection raised against taking the hamza to mean sawa', since it would revert to the meaning "the warning and its absence are equal to them," which would be a repetition devoid of benefit. It is answered by what is transmitted from the author of the Kashshaf, who said that its meaning is that the warning and its absence, which are equal in the knowledge of the addressee, are equal in not benefiting, so the aspect of equality differs, as al-Taftazani transmitted in his commentary on the Kashshaf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 6 (part 2 of 2):

It is necessary to parse "sawāʾ" in such a construction as a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted, indicated by the interrogative, its implied predicate being the answer to this interrogative. Thus "sawāʾ" in the verse is a second subject (mubtada' thānī), and the clause is its predicate: ﴿those who disbelieve﴾. Set aside all that the writers have disputed concerning al-Kashshaf. The particle "ʿalā" (on), which almost always accompanies the word sawāʾ, is for metaphorical elevation (al-istiʿlāʾ al-majāzī), intended to mean firm establishment (al-tamakkun); that is, this equality is firmly established in them and does not depart from their souls. For this reason, some adverbs may occur in the place of "ʿalā" with the word sawāʾ, such as ʿinda (with) and ladā (in the presence of). Abū al-Shaghb al-ʿAbsī said:

Do not blame me concerning Jundub, for Jundub
and the lion of the thickets are, in my sight, equal (sawāʾ).

The detailed treatment of this similar construction will come later, at His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Aʿraf: ﴿It is the same for you whether you call them or you remain silent﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 193].

Ibn Kathir recited ﴿أأنذرتهم﴾ with two hamzas, the first realized (muhaqqaqa) and the second eased (musahhala). Qalun, on the authority of Nafiʿ, and Warsh on his authority in the transmission of the Baghdadis, and Abu ʿAmr and Abu Jaʿfar likewise, with the insertion of an alif between the two hamzas. Both recitations are a Hijazi dialect. Hamza, ʿĀsim and al-Kisāʾī recited it with both hamzas realized, and this is the dialect of Tamim. The people of Egypt related from Warsh the replacement of the second hamza with an alif. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a lahn (error)." This weakens the transmission of the Egyptians from Warsh. This is a difference in the manner of performance, so it does not contradict tawatur (mass transmission).

* * *

﴿they do not believe﴾

The more evident view is that this clause is brought to affirm the meaning of the preceding clause, which is ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them﴾ etc. You may make it a second predicate of "inna," the emphasis being drawn from the context. You may also make it an emphatic (taʾkid). In both cases it is detached (fuṣṣilat): by necessity (jawāzan) according to the first, and obligatorily (wujūban) according to the second. They have proposed other possible parsings, which we do not dwell upon because of their weakness. Al-Kashshaf permitted making the clause ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) to the clause ﴿they do not believe﴾, but this is less preferred and was not accepted by al-Saʿd and al-Sayyid, since the locus of the information is not "they do not believe"; rather, what matters is informing about them the equality of warning and its absence in their sight, for in that is a rebuke of their obstinacy and dullness, an excuse for the Prophet ﷺ in his eagerness for their faith, and a recording that whoever does not open his hearing and heart to receive the truth and guidance, eagerness and seeking will not benefit him. Although this would be achieved on its (al-Kashshaf's) reckoning by making "they do not believe" a predicate, the intended meaning of the speech is more deserving of being the information. Also, the predicate would become unimportant, for it would be like saying: "Those who disbelieve do not believe." It is known that they disbelieved, so their non-belief is established. And if what is meant by "they do not believe" is the continuation of disbelief in the future, it is still a weak predicate, unlike when it is made an explanation of the predicate.

This verse has been used as evidence by those who hold that taklif (obligation) with what is impossible (taklif bi-ma la yuṭaq) occurs, arguing from it on the issue. The question of taklif with what cannot be borne remained for a time unsettled, and each one who saw in it an argument would use it as proof. They expressed it in various terms: some call it taklif bi-l-muḥāl (obligation with the impossible), some express it as taklif bi-ma laysa bi-maqdūr (obligation with what is not within capacity), and some as taklif bi-ma la yuṭaq. Then they look sometimes at rational essential impossibility (al-istiḥāla al-dhātiyya al-ʿaqliyya), sometimes at customary essential impossibility (al-dhātiyya al-ʿādiyya), sometimes at accidental impossibility (al-ʿaraḍiyya), and sometimes at strong hardship that causes the obligated one distress, and so they mix them with what cannot be borne. Abu Hamid al-Isfarayini, Abu Hamid al-Ghazali and their like clarified what lifts the veil from the face of the question, so that it no longer bewilders minds, and its thorns became thyme (i.e., its difficulty became easy). That is because the impossible includes what is impossible in itself by reason, such as the joining of two contradictories; and includes what is customarily impossible, such as ascending to the sky; and includes what involves hardship and distress, such as a man slaughtering his son, or one standing against ten of his peers; and includes what has become impossible by reference to something else, such as the faith of one whom God knows will not believe, and the pilgrimage of one whom God knows will not perform it. All of these are called "what cannot be borne," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], since what is meant is what causes great hardship. And impossibility is applied to them literally and by correspondence in some, by implication in some, and metaphorically in some. And the non-existence of what is within capacity is likewise applied to them, just as permissibility (jawāz) is applied to possibility, to possibility with respect to wisdom, and to occurrence.

From the difference of these divisions and the variance of these usages arose positions that filled the expanse, and they were for the opponents like a hard stone. When God raised up scholars who negated what resembled them and opened their locks, it became clear that the possibility of permissibility (al-jawāz al-imkānī) in all of them is established, because God, exalted is He, does what He wills if He wills; no Muslim disputes this. It is also established that permissibility fitting to wisdom (al-jawāz al-mulāʾim li-l-ḥikma) is negated in our view and in the view of the Mu'tazila, although we differ in the explanation of wisdom, since all agree that the benefit of taklif vanishes when what is obligated is impossible to occur.

It is also established that what is impossible due to the attachment of knowledge to its non-occurrence is nonetheless obligated, both in permissibility and in occurrence, and most obligations are not free of this. And what is more specific is established, namely the removal of external hardship beyond the customary limit, as a bounty from God, exalted is He, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and His saying: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to count it, so He turned to you [in mercy]﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], meaning: you cannot bear it, as Ibn al-ʿArabi indicated in al-Ahkam. This is the core of this question in a manner that gathers its scattered parts and makes its discordant parts agreeable.

It remains for us to clarify for you the way in which taklif is connected to one whom God knows will not comply, or to one whom God, exalted is He, has informed will not comply, as in this verse. This is more specific than the question of knowledge of non-occurrence, since informing has been added to knowledge, as is the basis of the argument of the one who cites it. The answer is that one whom God knows will not act is not addressed specifically by Him, nor is there a call directed to him in particular, since it is not established that the Prophet ﷺ singled out individuals with the call except that they believed, as he singled out ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab when he came to him, saying: "Has the time not come for you, O son of al-Khattab, to say: There is no god but Allah," and his saying to Abu Sufyan on the day of the Conquest something close to that statement, and he singled out his uncle Abu Talib with the like. And this verse had not yet been revealed at that time. So when the call was general and they were included in the generality, the argument from the verse and from the rational proof became void. Nothing remains but to ask: why was not the one whose non-compliance is known singled out from the generality of the call? The answer: singling out these would prolong the Sharia, embolden others, weaken the establishment of proof against them, and give the impression that the Message is not general. Moreover, God, exalted is He, has by His wisdom decreed the separation between what is in His decree and knowledge and what legislation and taklif require. The secret of wisdom in that we have explained in places that would take long to bring here and would go beyond the purpose of tafsir, and I think your awareness of its summary is not difficult.

[p. 254]

﴿God has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering.﴾ This sentence serves as an explanation of the ruling stated earlier in His words, ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6], and it clarifies its actual cause. Through it, it removes the wonder of those who marvel that warning has the same effect on them whether or not it is given, and that faith does not penetrate their souls despite the clarity of its proofs. Once it is known that there is a seal upon their hearts, and upon their hearing, and that there is a covering over their eyes, the cause of all of this becomes known and the wonder is dispelled. The sentence is therefore a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani), answering a questioner who asks about the reason they do not believe. The position of this sentence in the structure of the discourse corresponds to the position of the sentence ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. Thus this sentence has a standing in censuring its owners equal to the standing that the other has in praising its owners.

The khatm (sealing) is, in its literal reality, closing a vessel and locking a book with clay or the like, together with placing a mark engraved on a signet ring, so that this prevents the sealed object from being opened. If it is opened, its owner knows that it was opened for corruption that appears in the effect of the engraving. The Prophet ﷺ took a signet ring for this purpose. The Arabs used to seal the jars of wine so that the confinement of air would improve it and keep it free from impurities during the period of its ageing. As for calling the reaching of the end of a thing "khatm," it is because that place or that time is the vessel in which the seal is placed, so it is named after it by way of metonymy (majaz).

The khatim (signet, with a fatha on the ta') is the clay placed over the sealed place, and the term was extended to the engraved die in which a sign or inscription is carved, by which an impression is made on the clay used for sealing. The engraving of the Prophet's ﷺ signet was: "Muhammad, Messenger of God."

The clay of sealing is a special clay resembling gypsum (jibs). It is moistened with water or the like and fastened over the sealed place. When it dries, it becomes firmly fixed and is not easily removed. It comes in small pieces, each about the size of a morsel. They used to make it into seals on the necks of the dhimmis (protected non-Muslims). Bashshar said:

"Love for her has sealed upon my neck the place of the seal, [worn] by the people of protection."

The ghisha'ah (covering) is of the pattern fi'alah, derived from ghashahu and taghashsha-hu, meaning he covered it, when he veiled it. Among the forms used for what is attached to something is the pattern fi'alah with a kasra on the fa', meaning "being enveloped by something," such as 'imamah (turban), 'ilawah (covering) and lifafah (wrapping).

It has been said that the coining of this pattern for crafts, such as sewing (khiyatah), is because of the figurative meaning of enveloping in it. The meaning of ghisha'ah is a covering. The sealing upon the hearts and the hearing, and the covering over the eyes, are not literally meant here, as some exegetes imagined, as reported by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Rather, it is figurative. It is as if their hearts, that is, their intellects, were made unable to receive faith and truth and to be guided toward them; their hearing was made closed to hearing the verses and warnings; and their eyes were made unable to benefit from the miracles and cosmic proofs they see, as if they were sealed and covered over.

[p. 255]
