This may be either a metaphor (isti'ara) by likening the failure to attain the intended benefit from them to sealing and covering, then using the word khatama by way of the subordinate metaphor (tab'iyya) and the word ghisha'ah by way of the primary metaphor (asliyya), both of which are actual metaphors (isti'ara tahqiqiyya), except that the likened element is established by intellect, not by the senses.

You may also take the sealing and the covering as a figure of speech (tamthil), by likening an imagined, fancied state in their hearts, that is, in their perception, of persistence in disbelief and their refraining from reflecting on the proofs, as already mentioned, to the state of sealing; and likening a fancied state in their eyes, from their failure to reflect on divine oneness and the truthfulness of the Messenger, to the state of covering. Both are the likening of the intelligible to the perceptible.

You may also take the sealing and the covering as a metonymy (majaz mursal) through the relation of necessary consequence (luzum), meaning that they are described with the necessary consequence of that, which is that they neither understand nor perceive. In the technical usage of the Law, khatm means the continuance of misguidance in the misguided person himself, or the disposition of misguidance. Similar to it are tab' (stamping) and akinnah (coverings).

Apparently, His words ﴿and over their hearing﴾ are conjoined to His words "over their hearts," so the hearing is what is sealed. It is not an emphatic preposed predicate of the word "covering," in which case ﴿and over their eyes﴾ would be conjoined to it, because the covering suits the eyes and not the hearing, and because sealing suits the hearing as it suits the hearts, since both are likened to a container and the notion of locking and closing is imagined in them. The Arabs say: "His hearing was stopped up (istakka sam'uhu)" and "his hearing was heavy (waqara sam'uhu)," and they put their fingers in their ears.

By "hearts" here is meant the minds and intellects. The Arabs use the word "heart" for the conical organ, and they use it for perception and intellect, and they hardly use it for anything else with respect to man. Most of their speech about animals is of this kind, and this is what is meant here. Its seat is undoubtedly the brain, but the heart is what supplies it with the power by which the act of perception is performed.

The reason He used the singular for hearing, and did not pluralize it as He pluralized "their hearts" and "their eyes," is either that it is meant as a verbal noun (masdar) denoting the category, since "sam'" is not applied to the ears; do you not see that He pluralized when He mentioned the ears in His words ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19] and His words ﴿and in our ears is a heaviness﴾ [Fussilat: 5]? So when He expressed it with hearing (sam'), He used the singular because it is a verbal noun, unlike the hearts and eyes, for the hearts are plural, and "abşar" is the plural of basar, which is a noun and not a verbal noun. Or it is by supposing an omitted word, meaning "and over the sense organs of their hearing" or "the limbs of their hearing."

[p. 256]

There may be in the singularity of hearing a subtle point observed as part of the eloquence of the Qur'an: the hearts differ, and their occupation with reflecting on the matter of faith and religion varies with the difference in the clarity of the proofs and with abundance and scarcity, and they receive many kinds of verses, so each intellect has its share of perception. The eyes also differ in their attachment to visible things in which there are proofs of divine oneness, in the horizons and in the souls, in which there is indication. So each eye has its share of turning toward the verses, miracles, lessons and admonitions. Since the kinds of what they are attached to differ, they were pluralized.

As for hearing, it is attached only to hearing what is recited of the Qur'an. Groups who hear the Qur'an hear it in an equal way; they differ only in reflecting upon it, and reflection is the work of the intellects. Since their attachment to what is heard is unified, it was made a single hearing.

The use of the names of organs and limbs when the figurative sense of their actions and sources is intended permits applying them to other than the singular, both in singular and plural form, and both occur here. As for the literal application, it is not correct. Al-Jahiz said in al-Bayan: Someone said to his servant, "Buy me the head of two rams." It was said to him, "That is not possible." He said, "Then, the heads of a ram," and so his speech became even more absurd.

In al-Kashshaf it is said that they say that when there is no risk of ambiguity, as in the verse of the poet:

"Eat from some of your bellies, so you may be chaste,
for your time is a time of hunger."

This is similar to what Sibawayh said in the chapter on what is uttered in the dual though it is in the plural form, as in His words ﴿then your hearts have swerved﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], and they say "place their saddles (ḍa' riḥālahumā)," though they are two. This differs from al-Jahiz's view. It may be that what al-Jahiz counted as an error on the speaker is an error, because such a speaker does not intend the second meanings, so his speech is taken as an error because of his ignorance of Arabic and is not taken as the intention of a subtle rhetorical point. This differs from the verse of the poem, let alone the Qur'anic verse. Similar is the saying of 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, to one who asked him, when a funeral passed by, "Who is the one who has died (al-mutawaffi)?" in the form of the active participle. 'Ali said to him: "God." He knew that he had made a mistake and meant to say al-mutawaffa (the one who has died, in the passive form). Otherwise, it is correct to say "tawaffa fulan" in the active voice, so he is "mutawaffin," meaning he has completed his term. 'Ali himself recited His words ﴿those of you who die (yutawaffawna)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234] in the passive voice.

After the sealing has been established as a metaphor for the failure of the truth to take effect upon their intellects and hearing, and after that is necessarily caused by their turning away and obstinacy, this description has been attributed to God Most High, because He is the one who decrees it, following the manner of attributing similar descriptions in other verses of the Qur'an, such as His words ﴿Those are the ones whom God has sealed upon their hearts﴾ [al-Nahl: 108], and His words ﴿and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]. Similar instances are numerous in the Qur'an, in a number that makes interpreting them away unacceptable. Their meaning, in our view, according to verification, is that they are conveyed on the basis that everything that occurs is by the decree of God Most High, and that God guided and granted success to some, and misguided and forsook others, in decree and in creation. Therefore this does not contradict the occurrence of the verse and its like in the sense of censure of those so described and of condemning their state, because that is with regard to their inclination and acquisition. In verification, it is the power to act and to refrain, which is less than creation. God Most High decreed the evils and placed in people the power to commit them, but He forbade them from them, because He also placed in people the power to abstain from them. So there is no contradiction between divine decree and legal obligation, since each refers to a different aspect. This is contrary to what the Qadariyya imagined, so they denied decree, which is determination and knowledge; and contrary to what the Mu'tazila imagined, that God's power does not relate to the actions of the responsible persons, and that these actions are not created by Him, but rather that what is created by Him is their essences and the instruments of their actions. They did this in order to deny the validity of attributing such actions to God Most High, out of exalting Him above originating corruption, and to interpret what has come of that. Yet this does not avail them anything, because they themselves affirm His knowledge that they will act, and that He is able to take away power from them. So His leaving them with that power is a respite for them to commit the ugly act, and that is ugly. Therefore the verified position is that of the Ash'ariyya and others among the People of the Sunna: God is the one who decrees the actions of the servants, but the performance of those actions is from the servant, not from God. This is what Imam al-Haramayn and his like among the verifiers made clear.

It is not objected to us: how did He empower them to commit sins? Because this is also an objection against the Mu'tazila: how did He know, after empowering them, that they would begin sins, and yet did not remove power from them? So the Ash'ari position is more fitting to verification, and more in line with combining the proofs that the Book and the Sunna have overflowed with. We have a verification higher than this, which we expounded in the treatise on Power and Predestination (al-Qudra wa al-Taqaddur), which has not yet appeared.

The attribution of sealing, which is used figuratively, to God Most High is to indicate the firm establishment of the meaning of sealing in their hearts, and that it is not hoped that it will cease, as one says: "a natural disposition (khilqah) in so-and-so," and "the quality God placed in so-and-so, or granted to so-and-so." This attribution differs from attribution in the rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because here what is intended is the necessary meaning (luzum), whereas in the rational metaphor the verb is attributed to other than its agent because of a connection. It is generally correct to assume both considerations where either is suitable, and one resorts to what is more appropriate to the context.

[p. 258]

The clause ﴿and over their hearing﴾ is conjoined to His words "and over their hearts," with the repetition of the preposition to add emphasis, so that the conjoined element is intended, because "ʿalā" signals the thing to which it relates. It is as if "khatama" were repeated twice.

The commentary also notes that the hearing is singled out for sealing, since the conjunction does not function like an explicit repetition of the governing verb. The phrase ﴿and over their hearing﴾ is not a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam) for "a veil" (ghishawah), because a veil does not suit hearing; what suits hearing is sealing (sadd). Consider His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sealed upon his hearing and his heart, and placed over his sight a veil﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23]. Moreover, the fronting of ﴿and over their sights﴾ shows that it is the predicate, because fronting serves to validate beginning with an indefinite noun (ibtida' bi-al-nakirah). Had ﴿and over their hearing﴾ been the predicate, one of the two could have been fronted while the other remained in its original position of being delayed, so it would have been said: "and over their hearing is a veil, and over their sights."

In the placement of hearing before sight wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, there is evidence that hearing is more beneficial to its possessor than sight. Fronting indicates the importance of what is fronted. This is because hearing is the instrument for receiving the knowledge by which the perfection of the intellect is attained, and it is the means by which the call of the prophets reaches the understanding of nations in a more complete manner than it would reach them through sight, were hearing lost. Also, sounds reach the hearing from all six directions without any need to turn toward them, unlike sight, which requires turning to face directions that are not in front of it.

* * *

﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾. Al-'adhab (punishment) means pain. It has been said that its origin is al-i'dhab, the verbal noun of a'dhaba, meaning to remove sweetness (al-'udhubah), because punishment removes the sweetness of life; so a noun of the verbal noun (ism masdar) was derived from it by dropping the hamzah. Or it is a noun coined for pain without considering derivation from sweetness, since it does not necessarily follow that the word must become like its counterpart in letters. The description of the punishment as ﴿great﴾ shows that the indefiniteness of "punishment" (adhab) is for denoting a type (al-nau'iyyah), and this is an emphasis on explicitly stating its magnitude. Although indefiniteness can suffice to indicate magnification, it is not explicit in that. It is not permissible for "great" to be a ta'kid (emphatic repetition) of the magnification implied by indefiniteness, as the author of al-Miftah supposed, because the indication of magnification by indefiniteness is not a conventional (wad'i) one, and non-conventional indications are dispensed with when something conventionally indicating them occurs, so it is not counted as emphasis. As for the punishment in the verse, it is either the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter, or the punishment of killing and hunger in this world.

[p. 259]

﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers.﴾ This is another group, one that shows outward faith while harboring disbelief inwardly. It amounts to one of two things: either concealing polytheism (*shirk*), or concealing adherence to Judaism. What unites all of them is the display of faith as a lie. The particle *wa* (and) here conjoins one set of sentences to another, each set having its own purpose, and the connection between the two purposes is what brings them together in the discourse. In such cases, one does not require a connection between each sentence and the next within both purposes, but only a connection between the two purposes. This is what al-Taftazani established in his commentary on *al-Kashshaf*. Al-Sayyid said it is a great principle in the chapter on conjunction (*'atf*), one that many scholars have overlooked, and so matters became unclear to them in many places. Its origin is taken from the statement in *al-Kashshaf*: "The story of the hypocrites, from beginning to end, is conjoined to the story of those who disbelieved, just as one sentence is conjoined to another." By this comparison, he indicates that this is not the conjunction of one sentence to another. The verifier 'Abd al-Hakim said: "This is what al-Sakkaki neglected, namely in the section on *fasl* and *wasl* (disjunction and conjunction), and it was the sole contribution of the author of *al-Kashshaf*."

Know that when the preceding verses moved from praising the Qur'an, by mentioning those who are guided by it in both of their types, ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], and ﴿those who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4], up to what has already been mentioned, and moved from praising them to mentioning their opposites, who are the disbelievers, those who are explicitly meant by "the disbelievers," namely the polytheists, the listener may have supposed that those who displayed faith were included in the words ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. So the listener was not asking about another category, namely those who displayed faith while concealing polytheism or something else, and these are the hypocrites (*munafiqun*) who are meant here, as evidenced by His words ﴿and when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], and so on. Because this category is rare and its description so unusual that its existence does not readily come to mind, it was fitting to mention their matter to the listeners. For this reason, this sentence came conjoined with *wa*, since the preceding sentence neither necessitated it nor evoked its meaning in the listeners' minds. This contrasts with the sentence ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6], whose conjunction to the one before it was omitted, because the mention of its content after the believers was anticipated by the listener, who was thus like one asking about it. Therefore the disjunction came as an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), that is, a new sentence answering an implied question.

His words ﴿And among the people﴾ are an inevitably fronted predicate (*khabar muqaddam*). It may seem that informing about something of this sort has little benefit, since if the subject indicates a thing of its own kind, or a meaning that occurs only among people, then informing that it is "from the people" or "among the people" is unhelpful. This contrasts with your saying, "Khidr is from the people," meaning "not from the angels," where the benefit is evident. The rationale for the statement "from the people" in verses like this one, and in the words of one of my honored friends praising me on my appointment to the judgeship:

*Among the people is one who cast his necklace to a successor, so he forbade what he sought and permitted it.*

The intent is to conceal the meaning of the predicate from the listener, just as you say, "He said this, a person," when the speech attributes blame or deficiency. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "What is the matter with people who stipulate conditions that are not in the Book of God?" Fronting the predicate is common in this structure, because fronting it alerts the listener to something strange to be mentioned, and arouses in him the desire to learn what will complete the information. Were it delayed, its position would be superfluous, since the listener would already know that what the speaker mentions comes only from a human being, as in the words of Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi:

*And among men are sharpened spearheads, and those who are kindled, and a witness who is like an absent one.*

It has been said that the position of "from the people" indicates astonishment, and that the original purpose of the predicate is to inform that the doer of this act is from the people, lest the addressee think he is not from the people because of the act's abhorrence. This is far from the intent, because if it were as he said, fronting would have no benefit, and delaying it would be preferable, so that the matter which might lead one to suppose the subject is not human would first be settled. This is the justification for this usage: where the information that the subject is one of the people carries little benefit. If the aim is to inform of this where the addressee does not know it, as in your saying, "Among men is one who wears a veil," intending to inform about the people called "the veiled ones" from Lamtuna, or where the addressee is treated as ignorant, like the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr (with *fath* on the *zay* and *kasr* on the *ba'*):

*And among the people, if your ropes have decayed, is one who connects, and in the earth, away from the house of estrangement, is one who moves.*

When the addressees are in the state of one who supposes that the speaker finds no one to connect with if he himself severs ties, then mentioning "from the people" and similar phrases in such a context follows the original sense of the information. The fronting of the predicate here serves to create suspense about identifying the subject, and there is no implication of restriction. Since you have understood that the phrase "from the people" indicates that the group spoken of will be the subject of a blameworthy story and a shameful condition (since their mention is veiled only because their state is so shameful that the speaker is reluctant to state its characteristic openly), and since in this there is great belittling of hypocrisy and censure of it, thirteen verses were revealed about them, in which their depravity, their deceit, the bad end awaiting them, the feebleness of their minds, and their ignorance were condemned. This was followed by reproach, mockery, and depiction of their condition in the most hideous forms, and they deserve it. For the scheme they practiced combines many vices, since hypocrisy comprises lying, cowardice, cunning, weakness of judgment, foolishness, bad conduct, greed, wasting one's life, loss of trust, enmity with companions, and the decay of virtue.

Lying is evident. Cowardice is because, were it not for it, no one would be prompted to contradict what he conceals inwardly. Cunning is because it drives one to avoid being discovered by every possible means. Weakness of judgment is because that indicates feebleness of intellect, since there is no reason for it. Foolishness is because of ignorance that such deception cannot last long. Bad conduct is because the nature of hypocrisy is concealing blameworthy qualities, and blameworthy qualities, if they do not appear, cannot be changed by the one who educates, nor by a friend, nor by people in general, so they remain as they are and become more firmly rooted with the passage of time, until they become a habit that is difficult to remove. Greed is because hypocrisy mostly occurs out of desire for gain. Wasting one's life is because the mind becomes occupied with promoting the states of hypocrisy and what must be practiced with people, and with devising stratagems to conceal it, and this diverts the mind from occupation with what is beneficial. Loss of trust is because if people discover it, their suspicion grows, and they do not trust anything that comes from him, even if it is true. Enmity with companions is likewise, because if one knows that this is a trait of his companion, he fears his treachery and guards against him, and this leads to enmity. The decay of virtue is the result of all of this.

His words ﴿and they are not believers﴾ indicate lying; His words "they deceive" [al-Baqarah: 9] indicate cunning and cowardice; His words ﴿and they deceive none but themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9] indicate weakness of judgment; His words ﴿and they do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9] indicate foolishness; His words ﴿in their hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10] indicate bad conduct; His words ﴿so God increased their disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10] indicate the persistence and increase of this over time; His words ﴿they say, "We are only reformers"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11] indicate wasting one's life on what is not intended; His words, when they say ﴿"We are with you"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], emphasized with *inna*, indicate the scarcity of trust their companions place in them; His words ﴿so their commerce did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] indicate that their affair did not find acceptance among their companions; His words ﴿deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171] indicate the decay of virtue among them, and a detailed explanation of this will come.

Regarding His words ﴿in their hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10], the plural was used. "People" (*nas*) is a collective noun, from *insi* (with *kasra* on the *hamza* and the nisba *ya*), which is a substitute for *anasi*, the regular plural of *insan*. They substituted for *anasi* the form *unas* with *damma* on the *hamza* and omission of the nisba *ya*. This substitution is shown by its appearance in the words of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras al-Asadi, addressing Imru' al-Qays:

*Indeed, death looks upon the secure people.*

Then they dropped its *hamza* for lightness. Dropping the *hamza* for lightness is common, as they said *luqah* for *aluqah*, which is butter. The dropping of the *hamza* of *unas* has become the rule when the definite article *al* is attached to it, while the form without *al* commonly has both the *hamza* and its omission. It has also been said that *nas* is a plural in itself, and that it is one of the plurals that came on the pattern *fu'al* with *damma* on the first radical, like *zu'ar*, the plural of *zi'r* (a female camel's foster-mother), and *rukhal*, the plural of *rakhil*, which is a young female sheep. The pattern *fu'al* is rare among plurals in the speech of the Arabs. Lexicographers paid great attention to gathering what came of it, and Ibn Khalawayh in his book *Laysa*, and Ibn al-Sikkit, and Ibn Barri mentioned them. The earlier scholars counted eight of them, gathered in three verses attributed to al-Zamakhshari, though the correct attribution is to Sadr al-Afadil, his student. Then many lexicographers added other words to those eight, until they reached twenty-four plurals, which al-Shihab al-Khafaji listed in his commentary on *Durrat al-Ghawwas* and mentioned most of them in his gloss on al-Baydawi's commentary. This is a point of knowledge in the science of language, so refer to them if you wish.

It has been said that what came on this pattern are collective nouns, and the wording of *al-Kashshaf* indicates this. The singular of this plural is *insi*, *ins*, or *insan*, all derived from *anisa*, the opposite of *tawahhasha* (to be wild), because a human being is sociable and seeks company.

The definiteness in *al-nas* is generic (*li-l-jins*), because what I have known of its usage in their speech supports the intention of the genus. It is also permissible that the definiteness be specific (*li-l-'ahd*), where the referent is the people already mentioned in His words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6], or the people whom the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims know in this matter. The relative pronoun *man* is a relative, and what is meant by it is a group and a multitude, as indicated by His words ﴿and they are not believers﴾ and what follows it, which are plural forms. What is mentioned by His words ﴿And among the people are those who say﴾ and so on is a third category, contrasting with the two preceding categories, to distinguish all of them by their most prominent attributes. Even if some or all of them share attributes in general, there is no confusion about why the hypocrites are made a separate division from the disbelievers, though they are among them, because the purpose of the division is the distinguishing attributes.

The Qur'an mentioned only their statement ﴿"We believe in God and the Last Day"﴾, though they also displayed faith in the Prophet ﷺ, for brevity: the first is the starting point of all beliefs, since whoever does not believe in one Lord cannot arrive at faith in the Messenger, for belief in God is the foundation, through which belief is sound, and it is the root of action; the second is the restraint and motive in all actions, and in it lies the soundness of practical conduct.

Or it may be that they are the ones who restricted their statement to this, because, in their extreme disbelief, they could not bring themselves to affirm faith in the Prophet ﷺ, finding this acknowledgment burdensome. So they restricted themselves to mentioning God and the Last Day, giving the impression of sufficiency outwardly, while preserving their disbelief inwardly, because most of them and their leaders were Jews.

The use of the verb *yaqulu* ("says") in such a context hints that the statement does not correspond to reality, because when a report related from another is not intended to be quoted verbatim, and is reported using the word *yaqulu*, this indicates that it does not match his belief, or that the speaker is denying it. Thus it contains a preparation for His words ﴿but they are not believers﴾. The clause ﴿but they are not believers﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) with respect to the subject of *yaqulu*, meaning: he says this statement while they are not believers.

[End of part 1]

The verse refers to a group of disbelievers, namely the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). Some of them were from the people of Yathrib, some were Jews who outwardly professed Islam, and the rest were Bedouins living around them. A report in the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik states that the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk numbered about eighty-some. Among those known by name are 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the chief of the hypocrites; al-Jadd ibn Qays; Mu'attib ibn Qushayr; and al-Julas ibn Suwayd, concerning whom the verse was revealed: ﴿They swear by God that they did not say [it].﴾ [al-Tawba: 74]. Also among them are 'Abd Allah ibn Saba', the Jew, and Labid ibn al-A'sam of Banu Zuraiq, an ally of the Jews, as mentioned in the chapter on magic in the Book of Medicine in the Sahih of al-Bukhari; al-Akhnas Ubayy ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, who displayed affection and faith, and whose case will come up under the words of God, ﴿And among the people is one whose speech impresses you﴾ [al-Baqara: 204]; Zayd ibn al-Lusayt al-Qaynuqa'i; and Wadi'a ibn Thabit of Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf; and Mukhashshin ibn Himyar al-Ashja'i, the two of whom used to discourage the Muslims during the expedition to Tabuk. It has been said that Zayd ibn al-Lusayt repented and his condition improved, and it has been said otherwise. As for Mukhashshin, he repented, God pardoned him, and he was killed as a martyr on the day of Yamama.

In the Kitab al-Maratib al-Arba'a (The Book of the Four Ranks) by Ibn Hazm, he mentioned the people of Mu'attib ibn Qushayr al-Awsi of Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf among the hypocrites. This is false, because his presence at Badr undoubtedly refutes this assumption. Nevertheless, something appeared from him on the day of Uhud that indicated weakness of faith, so they accused him of hypocrisy. He is the one who said on the day of Uhud, ﴿If we had had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 154]. Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam narrated this from him. Ibn 'Atiyya said he was "suspected of hypocrisy" (maghmusan bi-l-nifaq).

Among the hypocrites was Abu 'Afak, one of Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, whose hypocrisy became evident when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had al-Harith ibn Suwayd ibn Samit killed. He composed a poem alluding disparagingly to the Prophet (ﷺ). The Messenger of God ordered the killing of Abu 'Afak, and Salim ibn 'Umayr killed him. Among the female hypocrites was 'Asma' bint Marwan of Banu Umayya ibn Zayd, who professed hypocrisy after Abu 'Afak was killed and composed a poem alluding disparagingly to the Prophet. 'Umayr ibn 'Adi al-Khatmi killed her, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him, "Two goats shall not butt heads over her" [i.e., no one shall take up her cause].

Among the hypocrites was Bashir ibn Ubayriq, who was a hypocrite who satirized the Companions of the Messenger of God. He witnessed Uhud. Among them was Tha'laba ibn Hatib, who had embraced Islam and was counted among the people of Badr. Among them was Bishr al-Munafiq, one of the Ansar, who is the one who quarreled with a Jew. The Jew invited Bishr to the judgment of the Prophet, but Bishr refused and demanded that the case be judged by Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. This is the one whom 'Umar killed. His story is connected to God's words, ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you?﴾ [al-Nisa': 60] in Surat al-Nisa'.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the hypocrites during the time of the Messenger of God numbered three hundred men and one hundred and seventy women. As for the hypocrites of Aws and Khazraj, the one who initiated hypocrisy for them and gathered them upon it was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, out of envy and rancor toward Islam. The people of Yathrib, after the wars of Bu'ath had ended between them and most of their chiefs had died in them, had agreed to make him their king and to crown him with a diadem.

Sa'd ibn 'Ubada said to the Prophet (ﷺ), in the hadith of al-Bukhari: "Pardon him, O Messenger of God, and overlook it. By God, God has given you what He has given you, and the people of this little valley (al-buhayra) had agreed to crown him with a diadem. When God turned that away through the truth that He gave you, he choked with rage over it." End of quote. As for the Jews, it is because they are people of deceit toward every religion that appears, and because they feared the loss of their present power in the regions of the Hijaz. As for the Bedouins, they follow these people, and for this reason came the words, ﴿The Bedouin are stronger in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾ [al-Tawba: 97], and so on, because they imitate without insight. Whoever comes after them with the same qualities falls under what God condemned them for. This is the meaning of the statement of Salman al-Farisi concerning the interpretation of this verse: "These have not yet come" (lam yaji' ha'ula' ba'du). Ibn 'Atiyya said: the meaning of his words is that they have not died out, but come forth in every age. End of quote. That is, Salman does not deny that this attribute applied to a group during the time of prophethood, but he does not see the purpose of the verse as restricting blame to them alone, but rather to those who come after them as well.

His words ﴿But they are not believers﴾ are phrased by negating their statement with a nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya), and it did not follow the pattern of their statement "We have believed" by saying "they did not believe" (wa ma amanu). This is because, when they affirmed faith for themselves, the use of the past tense was more comprehensive in meaning, since it implied the realization of faith in the past explicitly and its continuance implicitly, because the default is that belief does not change without a cause, especially since religion is itself unchanged. When the intention was to negate faith from them, its negation in the past does not necessarily imply its non-realization in the present, let alone the future. So his words ﴿But they are not believers﴾ indicate its negation from them in the present, because the active participle is literally in the time of the present, and that negation necessarily implies its negation in the past as well. Moreover, the verbal sentence indicates concern with the action rather than the agent, and therefore it was used to report their words, because when they saw the Muslims seeking to know whether their faith had been achieved, they said "We have believed." The nominal sentence, however, indicates concern with the agent, meaning that those who said "We have believed" did not actually possess any faith. Thus the concern with them within the negated action is a recording of their lie. This is one of the points of difference between the verbal and nominal sentences. It is consistent with the rule that fronting (taqdim) indicates emphasis in general, even though they neglected to point out the operation of that rule when they mentioned the differences between the verbal and nominal sentences in the books of rhetoric (ma'ani). The author of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari) alluded to this here with precise and subtle wording.

If you say: 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh had embraced Islam, then apostatized, and after his apostasy claimed that he used to write the Qur'an, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) would dictate to him "Mighty, Wise" for example, and he would write "Forgiving, Merciful" for example, and vice versa. This is a sign of lack of faith, so he would then be among the hypocrites who believed afterward. The answer is that this comes from the transmission of historians, and their words are not relied upon in matters of this kind, especially since 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh's governorship was among the things the rebels held against 'Uthman, and the historians' bias in this matter is well known, because they took it from the malcontents and their partisans. The legal proofs (al-adilla al-shar'iyya) refute this, because if it were true it would necessarily lead to doubt entering the religion. And if 'Abd Allah had attempted this, God would have informed His Messenger of it, because error and heedlessness are not permissible for the Messenger in matters relating to conveying the message. Moreover, it is rationally discredited, since if he had wanted to scheme against the religion, the more fitting thing would have been to distort something else. Furthermore, this is a statement he made at the time of his apostasy, and his statement at that time about religion is not credible, because he was accused of intending to promote his apostasy among the polytheists in Mecca. You have learned from the eighth introduction to this tafsir that the foundation of the Qur'an's verses rests upon the memorization of its memorizers and the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ). He ordered it to be written only for the purpose of consultation by the Muslims when they needed it. No one has narrated that there was a need to consult what had been written of the Qur'an except during the time of Abu Bakr, and it is not reported that the memorizers of the Qur'an found a discrepancy between what they had memorized and the written originals. Moreover, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh was not alone in writing the revelation, for others wrote with him.

Denying faith from them while they say "We have believed" is clear evidence that the designation of faith (musamma al-iman) is assent (tasdiq), and that uttering what indicates faith may be a lie, so that utterance is not faith. In the Sharia, faith is the firm conviction in the truth of what is known to be part of the religion by necessary knowledge ('ilm darurri), such that it is established by definitive proof according to all the imams of the religion, and whose being part of the constituents of Islamic belief, which is binding on every Muslim, is widely known among the elite scholars of religion and the common Muslims, so that there is no dispute about it. Thus faith in the Sharia has been transferred to a specific kind of assent. The authentic hadith from 'Umar has made this clear: "Jibril came and asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about faith. He said: Faith is that you believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and that you believe in predestination, its good and its evil."

The scholars of the Ummah have differed about the reality of faith, what it is, and they also went into the reality of Islam. We will gather the scattered reports from them together with the verified positions of the researchers in a brief summary. We have reduced their various statements on this matter to five positions.

The first position is that of the majority of the researching scholars of the Ummah, who said: faith is assent (tasdiq), with no designation other than that, and this is its linguistic meaning. It should not be transferred from its meaning, because the default is non-transference. However, it has been applied to a specific assent regarding matters among which is the religion. The use of a general term for some of its instances is not a transfer of it from its linguistic meaning, and it became prevalent in the speech of the legal scholars for that assent. They argued with several proofs, which are solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad), but they are so numerous that they are raised to the level of widely transmitted reports (al-mustafid).

Among them is the hadith of Jibril mentioned earlier, and the hadith of Sa'd, that he said: "O Messenger of God, what is wrong with you regarding so-and-so? I see him as a believer." He said: "Or a Muslim." They said: as for speech and actions, they belong to Islam, not to the concept of faith, because Islam is submission and compliance with the body rather than the heart. The evidence for the distinction between them is the language and the hadith of Jibril, and the words of God, ﴿The Bedouin say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14], and what Muslim narrated from Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah, that "a man came from Najd with disheveled hair, whose voice we could hear but could not understand what he was saying, and he was asking about Islam. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained to him that Islam is: testifying that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, establishing prayer, paying zakat, fasting Ramadan, and pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way to it."

This view is attributed to Malik ibn Anas, based on his statement in al-Mudawwana (a major Maliki legal compendium): "Whoever bathes while having submitted to Islam in his heart, it suffices him." Ibn Rushd said: because his Islam is in his heart, so if he dies he dies as a believer, and this is a distant inference. You will learn that Malik's position is contrary to this. It is also attributed to al-Ash'ari. Imam al-Haramayn said in al-Irshad, "and this is the one approved by us," and it was said by al-Zuhri from among the Successors (tabi'un).

The second position: faith is belief in the heart and verbal utterance of the two testimonies to affirm that belief. Thus faith is transferred in the Sharia to this meaning, and belief is not considered valid in the Sharia unless it is accompanied by utterance. This was reported from Abu Hanifa. Al-Nawawi attributed it to the majority of jurists, traditionists, and theologians. al-Fakhr (al-Razi) attributed it to al-Ash'ari and Bishr al-Marisi. al-Khafaji attributed it to the verifying Ash'aris, and Ibn al-'Arabi adopted it. Al-Nawawi said: by this, a person becomes among the people of the qibla.

قُلْتُ: ولا أحْسَبُ أنَّ بَيْنَ هَذا والقَوْلِ الأوَّلِ فَرْقًا، وإنَّما نَظَرُ كُلِّ قِيلٍ إلى جانِبٍ: فالأوَّلُ نَظَرَ إلى جانِبِ المَفْهُومِ، والثّانِي نَظَرَ إلى الِاعْتِدادِ، ولَمْ يَعْتَنُوا بِضَبْطِ عِباراتِهِمْ حَتّى يَرْتَفِعَ الخِلافُ بَيْنَهم. وإنْ كانَ قَدْ وقَعَ الخِلافُ بَيْنَهم في أنَّ الِاقْتِصارَ عَلى الِاعْتِقادِ هَلْ هو مُنْجٍ فِيما بَيْنَ المَرْءِ وبَيْنَ رَبِّهِ، أوْ لا بُدَّ مِنَ الإقْرارِ؟ حَكاهُ البَيْضاوِيُّ في التَّفْسِيرِ (التفسير: الشرح والتبيين للقرآن) ومالَ إلى الثّانِي. ويُؤْخَذُ مِن كَلامِهِمْ أنَّهُ لَوْ تَرَكَ الإقْرارَ لا عَنْ مُكابَرَةٍ كانَ ناجِيًا، مِثْلَ الأخْرَسِ والمُغَفَّلِ والمُشْتَغِلِ شُغْلًا اتَّصَلَ بِمَوْتِهِ.

واحْتَجُّوا بِإطْلاقِ الإيمانِ عَلى الإسْلامِ والعَكْسِ في مَواضِعَ مِنَ الكِتابِ والسُّنَّةِ، قالَ تَعالى: ﴿فَأخْرَجْنا مَن كانَ فِيها مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [الذاريات: ٣٥] ﴿فَما وجَدْنا فِيها غَيْرَ بَيْتٍ مِنَ المُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [الذاريات: ٣٦]. وفي حَدِيثِ وفْدِ عَبْدِ القَيْسِ أنَّ النَّبِيءَ (ﷺ) قالَ لَهم: «آمُرُكم بِأرْبَعٍ وأنْهاكم عَنْ أرْبَعٍ: الإيمانِ بِاللَّهِ، أتَدْرُونَ ما الإيمانُ بِاللَّهِ؟ شَهادَةُ أنْ لا إلَهَ إلّا اللَّهُ وأنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ، وإقامُ الصَّلاةِ» إلخ. وهَذِهِ أخْبارُ آحادٍ، فالِاسْتِدْلالُ بِها في أصْلٍ مِنَ الدِّينِ إنَّما هو مُجَرَّدُ تَقْرِيبٍ، عَلى أنَّ مُعْظَمَها لا يَدُلُّ عَلى إطْلاقِ الإيمانِ عَلى حالَةٍ لَيْسَ مَعَها حالَةُ إسْلامٍ.

القَوْلُ الثّالِثُ: قَوْلُ جُمْهُورِ السَّلَفِ (الأوائل من الصحابة والتابعين) مِنَ الصَّحابَةِ والتّابِعِينَ، أنَّ الإيمانَ اعْتِقادٌ وقَوْلٌ وعَمَلٌ، ذَلِكَ أنَّهم لِكَمالِ حالِهِمْ ومَجِيئِهِمْ في فاتِحَةِ انْبِثاقِ أنْوارِ الدِّينِ، لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَفْرِضُونَ في الإيمانِ أحْوالًا تُقَصِّرُ في الِامْتِثالِ. ونُسِبَ ذَلِكَ إلى مالِكٍ وسُفْيانَ الثَّوْرِيِّ وسُفْيانَ بْنِ عُيَيْنَةَ والأوْزاعِيِّ وابْنِ جُرَيْجٍ والنَّخَعِيِّ والحَسَنِ وعَطاءٍ وطاوُوسٍ ومُجاهِدٍ وابْنِ المُبارَكِ والبُخارِيِّ، ونُسِبَ لِابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ وحُذَيْفَةَ، وبِهِ قالَ ابْنُ حَزْمٍ مِنَ الظّاهِرِيَّةِ، وتَمَسَّكَ بِهِ أهْلُ الحَدِيثِ لِأخْذِهِمْ بِظاهِرِ ألْفاظِ الأحادِيثِ، وبِذَلِكَ أثْبَتُوا الزِّيادَةَ والنَّقْصَ في الإيمانِ بِزِيادَةِ الأعْمالِ ونَقْصِها، لِقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿لِيَزْدادُوا إيمانًا مَعَ إيمانِهِمْ﴾ [الفتح: ٤] إلخ. وجاءَ في الحَدِيثِ: «الإيمانُ بِضْعٌ وسَبْعُونَ شُعْبَةً»، فَدَلَّ ذَلِكَ عَلى قَبُولِهِ لِلتَّفاضُلِ.

[صفحة ٢٦٨]

وعَلى ذَلِكَ حُمِلَ قَوْلُهُ (ﷺ): «لا يَزْنِي الزّانِي حِينَ يَزْنِي وهو مُؤْمِنٌ»، أيْ لَيْسَ مُتَّصِفًا حِينَئِذٍ بِكَمالِ الإيمانِ.

ونُقِلَ عَنْ مالِكٍ أنَّهُ يَزِيدُ ولا يَنْقُصُ، فَقِيلَ: إنَّما أمْسَكَ مالِكٌ عَنِ القَوْلِ بِنُقْصانِهِ خَشْيَةَ أنْ يُظَنَّ بِهِ مُوافَقَةُ الخَوارِجِ الَّذِينَ يُكَفِّرُونَ بِالذُّنُوبِ.

قالَ ابْنُ بَطّالٍ: وهَذا لا يُخالِفُ قَوْلَ مالِكٍ بِأنَّ الإيمانَ هو التَّصْدِيقُ، وهو لا يَزِيدُ ولا يَنْقُصُ، لِأنَّ التَّصْدِيقَ أوَّلُ مَنازِلِ الإيمانِ ويُوجِبُ لِلْمُصَدِّقِ الدُّخُولَ فِيهِ، ولا يُوجِبُ لَهُ اسْتِكْمالَ مَنازِلِهِ، وإنَّما أرادَ هَؤُلاءِ الأئِمَّةُ الرَّدَّ عَلى المُرْجِئَةِ (الذين يرون أن الإيمان قول بلا عمل) في قَوْلِهِمْ إنَّ الإيمانَ قَوْلٌ بِلا عَمَلٍ. اهـ.

ولَمْ يُتابِعْهم عَلَيْهِ المُتَأخِّرُونَ، لِأنَّهم رَأوْهُ شَرْحًا لِلْإيمانِ الكامِلِ، ولَيْسَ فِيهِ النِّزاعُ، إنَّما النِّزاعُ في أصْلِ مُسَمّى الإيمانِ، وأوَّلِ دَرَجاتِ النَّجاةِ مِنَ الخُلُودِ. ولِذَلِكَ أنْكَرَ أكْثَرُ المُتَكَلِّمِينَ أنْ يُقالَ: الإيمانُ يَزِيدُ ويَنْقُصُ، وتَأوَّلُوا نَحْوَ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿لِيَزْدادُوا إيمانًا﴾ [الفتح: ٤] بِأنَّ المُرادَ تَعَدُّدُ الأدِلَّةِ حَتّى يَدُومُوا عَلى الإيمانِ، وهو التَّحْقِيقُ.

القَوْلُ الرّابِعُ: قَوْلُ الخَوارِجِ (الذين خرجوا على علي رضي الله عنه) والمُعْتَزِلَةِ (أصحاب الاعتزال)، إنَّ الإيمانَ اعْتِقادٌ ونُطْقٌ وعَمَلٌ، كَما جاءَ في القَوْلِ الثّالِثِ، إلّا أنَّهم أرادُوا مِن قَوْلِهِمْ حَقِيقَةَ ظاهِرِهِ، مِن تَرَكُّبِ الإيمانِ مِن مَجْمُوعِ الثَّلاثَةِ، بِحَيْثُ إذا اخْتَلَّ واحِدٌ مِنها بَطَلَ الإيمانُ. ولَهم في تَقْرِيرِ بُطْلانِهِ بِنَقْصِ الأعْمالِ الواجِبَةِ مَذاهِبُ غَيْرُ مُنْتَظِمَةٍ ولا مَعْضُودَةٍ بِأدِلَّةٍ، سِوى التَّعَلُّقِ بِظَواهِرِ بَعْضِ الآثارِ مَعَ الإهْمالِ لِما يُعارِضُها مِن مِثْلِها.

فَأمّا الخَوارِجُ فَقالُوا: إنَّ تارِكَ شَيْءٍ مِنَ الأعْمالِ كافِرٌ غَيْرُ مُؤْمِنٍ، وهو خالِدٌ في النّارِ، فالأعْمالُ جُزْءٌ مِنَ الإيمانِ. وأرادُوا مِنَ الأعْمالِ فِعْلَ الواجِباتِ وتَرْكَ المُحَرَّماتِ ولَوْ صَغائِرَ، إذْ جَمِيعُ الذُّنُوبِ عِنْدَهم كَبائِرُ.

وأمّا غَيْرُ ذَلِكَ مِنَ الأعْمالِ كالمَندُوباتِ والمُسْتَحَبّاتِ، فَلا يُوجِبُ تَرْكُها خُلُودًا، إذْ لا يَقُولُ مُسْلِمٌ إنَّ تَرْكَ السُّنَنِ والمَندُوباتِ يُوجِبُ الكُفْرَ والخُلُودَ في النّارِ، وكَذَلِكَ فِعْلَ المَكْرُوهاتِ.

وقالَتِ الإباضِيَّةُ مِنَ الخَوارِجِ: إنَّ تارِكَ بَعْضِ الواجِباتِ كافِرٌ، لَكِنَّ كُفْرَهُ كُفْرُ نِعْمَةٍ لا شِرْكٍ، نَقَلَهُ إمامُ الحَرَمَيْنِ عَنْهم، وهو الَّذِي سَمِعْناهُ مِن طَلَبَتِهِمْ.

وأمّا المُعْتَزِلَةُ فَقَدْ وافَقُوا الخَوارِجَ في أنَّ لِلْأعْمالِ حَظًّا مِنَ الإيمانِ، إلّا أنَّهم خالَفُوهم في مَقادِيرِها، ومَذاهِبُ المُعْتَزِلَةِ في هَذا المَوْضِعِ غَيْرُ مُنْضَبِطَةٍ، فَقالَ قُدَماؤُهم، وهو المَشْهُورُ عَنْهم: إنَّ العاصِيَ مُخَلَّدٌ في النّارِ، لَكِنَّهُ لا يُوصَفُ بِالكُفْرِ ولا بِالإيمانِ، ووَصَفُوهُ بِالفِسْقِ، وجَعَلُوا اسْتِحْقاقَ الخُلُودِ لِارْتِكابِ الكَبِيرَةِ

[صفحة ٢٦٩]

خاصَّةً. وكَذَلِكَ نَسَبَ إلَيْهِمُ ابْنُ حَزْمٍ في كِتابِ الفَصْلِ، وقالَ واصِلُ بْنُ عَطاءٍ الغَزّالُ: إنَّ مُرْتَكِبَ الكَبِيرَةِ في مَنزِلَةٍ بَيْنَ المَنزِلَتَيْنِ، أيْ لا يُوصَفُ بِإيمانٍ ولا كُفْرٍ، فَيُفارِقُ بِذَلِكَ قَوْلَ الخَوارِجِ وقَوْلَ المُرْجِئَةِ، ووافَقَهُ عَمْرُو بْنُ عُبَيْدٍ عَلى ذَلِكَ.

وهَذِهِ هي المَسْألَةُ الَّتِي بِسَبَبِها قالَ الحَسَنُ البَصْرِيُّ لِواصِلٍ وعَمْرِو بْنِ عُبَيْدٍ: اعْتَزَلَ مَجْلِسَنا.

ودَرَجَ عَلى هَذا جَمِيعُهم، لَكِنَّهُمُ اضْطَرَبُوا، أوِ اضْطَرَبَ النَّقْلُ عَنْهم، في مُسَمّى المَنزِلَةِ بَيْنَ المَنزِلَتَيْنِ، فَقالَ إمامُ الحَرَمَيْنِ في الإرْشادِ: إنَّ جُمْهُورَهم قالُوا: إنَّ الكَبِيرَةَ تُحْبِطُ ثَوابَ الطّاعاتِ وإنْ كَثُرَتْ، ومَعْناهُ لا مَحالَةَ أنَّها تُوجِبُ الخُلُودَ في النّارِ، وبِذَلِكَ جَزَمَ التَّفْتَزانِيُّ في شَرْحِ الكَشّافِ وفي المَقاصِدِ، وقالَ: إنَّ المَنزِلَةَ بَيْنَ المَنزِلَتَيْنِ هي مُوجِبَةٌ لِلْخُلُودِ، وإنَّما أثْبَتُوا المَنزِلَةَ لِعَدَمِ إطْلاقِ اسْمِ الكُفْرِ، ولِإجْراءِ أحْكامِ المُؤْمِنِينَ عَلى صاحِبِها في ظاهِرِ الحالِ في الدُّنْيا، بِحَيْثُ لا يُعْتَبَرُ مُرْتَكِبُ المَعْصِيَةِ كالمُرْتَدِّ فَيُقْتَلُ.

وقالَ في المَقاصِدِ، ومِثْلُهُ في الإرْشادِ: المُخْتارُ عِنْدَهم خِلافُ المُشْتَهِرِ، فَإنَّ أبا عَلِيٍّ (الجُبّائي) وابْنَهُ وكَثِيرًا مِن مُحَقِّقِيهِمْ ومُتَأخِّرِيهِمْ قالُوا: إنَّ الكَبائِرَ إنَّما تُوجِبُ دُخُولَ النّارِ إذا زادَ عِقابُها عَلى ثَوابِ الطّاعاتِ، فَإنْ أرْبَتِ الطّاعاتُ عَلى السَّيِّئاتِ دَرَأتِ السَّيِّئاتِ، ولَيْسَ النَّظَرُ إلى أعْدادِ الطّاعاتِ ولا الزَّلّاتِ، وإنَّما النَّظَرُ إلى مِقْدارِ الأُجُورِ والأوْزارِ، فَرُبَّ كَبِيرَةٍ واحِدَةٍ يَغْلِبُ وِزْرُها طاعاتٍ كَثِيرَةِ العَدَدِ، ولا سَبِيلَ إلى ضَبْطِ هَذِهِ المَقادِيرِ، بَلْ أمْرُها مَوْكُولٌ إلى عِلْمِ اللَّهِ تَعالى. فَإنِ اسْتَوَتِ الحَسَناتُ والسَّيِّئاتُ فَقَدِ اضْطَرَبُوا في ذَلِكَ، فَهَذا مَحَلُّ المَنزِلَةِ بَيْنَ المَنزِلَتَيْنِ.

ونَقَلَ ابْنُ حَزْمٍ في الفَصْلِ عَنْ جَماعَةٍ مِنهم، فِيهِمْ بِشْرُ المَرِيسِيُّ والأصَمُّ، أنَّ مَنِ اسْتَوَتْ حَسَناتُهُ وسَيِّئاتُهُ فَهو مِن أهْلِ الأعْرافِ، ولَهم وقْفَةٌ، لا يَدْخُلُونَ النّارَ مُدَّةً، ثُمَّ يَدْخُلُونَ الجَنَّةَ. ومَن رَجَحَتْ سَيِّئاتُهُ فَهو مُجازًى بِقَدْرِ ما رَجَحَ لَهُ مِنَ الذُّنُوبِ، فَمِن لَفْحَةٍ واحِدَةٍ إلى بَقاءِ خَمْسِينَ ألْفَ سَنَةٍ في النّارِ، ثُمَّ يَخْرُجُونَ مِنها بِالشَّفاعَةِ. وهَذا يَقْتَضِي أنَّ هَؤُلاءِ لا يَرَوْنَ الخُلُودَ. وقَدْ نَقَلَ البَعْضُ عَنِ المُعْتَزِلَةِ أنَّ المَنزِلَةَ بَيْنَ المَنزِلَتَيْنِ لا جَنَّةٌ ولا نارٌ، إلّا أنَّ التَّفْتَزانِيَّ في المَقاصِدِ غَلَّطَ هَذا البَعْضَ، وكَذَلِكَ قالَ في شَرْحِ الكَشّافِ.

وقَدْ قَرَّرَ صاحِبُ الكَشّافِ (الزمخشري) حَقِيقَةَ المَنزِلَةِ بَيْنَ المَنزِلَتَيْنِ بِكَلامٍ مُجْمَلٍ، فَقالَ في تَفْسِيرِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وما يُضِلُّ بِهِ إلّا الفاسِقِينَ﴾ [البقرة: ٢٦] مِن سُورَةِ البَقَرَةِ: والفاسِقُ في الشَّرِيعَةِ: الخارِجُ عَنْ أمْرِ اللَّهِ بِارْتِكابِ الكَبِيرَةِ، وهو النّازِلُ بَيْنَ المَنزِلَتَيْنِ، أيْ بَيْنَ مَنزِلَتَيِ المُؤْمِنِ والكافِرِ. وقالُوا: إنَّ أوَّلَ مَن حَدَّ لَهُ هَذا الحَدَّ أبُو حُذَيْفَةَ واصِلُ بْنُ عَطاءٍ، وكَوْنُهُ بَيْنَ بَيْنَ: أنَّ حُكْمَهُ حُكْمُ المُؤْمِنِ في أنَّهُ يُناكَحُ ويُوارَثُ ويُغَسَّلُ ويُصَلّى عَلَيْهِ ويُدْفَنُ في مَقابِرِ المُسْلِمِينَ،

[صفحة ٢٧٠]

وهُوَ كالكافِرِ في الذَّمِّ واللَّعْنِ والبَراءَةِ مِنهُ واعْتِقادُ عَداوَتِهِ، وأنْ لا تُقْبَلَ لَهُ شَهادَةٌ. اهـ. فَتَراهُ مَعَ إيضاحِهِ لَمْ يَذْكُرْ فِيهِ أنَّهُ خالِدٌ في النّارِ، وصَرَّحَ في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿ومَن يَقْتُلْ مُؤْمِنًا مُتَعَمِّدًا فَجَزاؤُهُ جَهَنَّمُ خالِدًا فِيها﴾ [النساء: ٩٣] في سُورَةِ النِّساءِ، بِما يُعَمِّمُ خُلُودَ أهْلِ الكَبائِرِ دُونَ تَوْبَةٍ في النّارِ.

قُلْتُ: وكانَ الشَّأْنُ أنَّ إجْراءَ الأحْكامِ الإسْلامِيَّةِ عَلَيْهِ في الدُّنْيا يَقْتَضِي أنَّهُ غَيْرُ خالِدٍ، إذْ لا يُعْقَلُ أنْ تَجْرِيَ عَلَيْهِ أحْكامُ المُسْلِمِينَ وتَنْتَفِيَ عَنْهُ الثَّمَرَةُ الَّتِي لِأجْلِها فارَقَ الكُفْرَ، إذِ المُسْلِمُ إنَّما أسْلَمَ فِرارًا مِنَ الخُلُودِ في النّارِ، فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ ارْتِكابُ بَعْضِ المَعاصِي مُوجِبًا لِانْتِقاضِ فائِدَةِ الإسْلامِ؟ وإذا كانَ أحَدٌ لا يَسْلَمُ مِن أنْ يُقارِفَ مَعْصِيَةً، وكانَتِ التَّوْبَةُ الصّادِقَةُ قَدْ تَتَأخَّرُ وقَدْ لا تَحْصُلُ، فَيَلْزَمُهم، ويَلْزَمُ الخَوارِجَ، أنْ يَعُدُّوا جُمْهُورَ المُسْلِمِينَ كُفّارًا، وبِئْسَ مُنْكَرًا مِنَ القَوْلِ.

عَلى أنَّ هَذا مِمّا يُجَرِّئُ العُصاةَ عَلى نَقْضِ عُرى الدِّينِ، إذْ يَنْسَلُّ عَنْهُ المُسْلِمُونَ لِانْعِدامِ الفائِدَةِ الَّتِي أسْلَمُوا لِأجْلِها، بِحُكْمِ ∗∗∗ «أنا الغَرِيقُ فَما خَوْفِي مِنَ البَلَلِ». ومِنَ العَجِيبِ أنْ يَصْدُرَ هَذا القَوْلُ مِن عاقِلٍ، فَضْلًا عَنْ عالِمٍ. ثُمَّ الأعْجَبُ مِنهُ عُكُوفُ أتْباعِهِمْ عَلَيْهِ، تَلُوكُهُ ألْسِنَتُهم، ولا تَفْقَهُهُ أفْئِدَتُهم، وكَيْفَ لَمْ يُقَيَّضْ فِيهِمْ عالِمٌ مُنْصِفٌ يَنْبَرِي لِهاتِهِ التُّرَّهاتِ فَيُهَذِّبُها أوْ يُؤَوِّلُها، كَما أرادَ جُمْهُورُ عُلَماءِ السُّنَّةِ مِن صَدْرِ الأُمَّةِ فَمَن يَلِيهِمْ.

القَوْلُ الخامِسُ: قالَتِ الكَرّامِيَّةُ: الإيمانُ هو الإقْرارُ بِاللِّسانِ إذا لَمْ يُخالِفِ الِاعْتِقادُ القَوْلَ، فَلا يُشْتَرَطُ في مُسَمّى الإيمانِ شَيْءٌ مِنَ المَعْرِفَةِ والتَّصْدِيقِ، فَأمّا إذا كانَ يُعْتَقَدُ خِلافَ مَقالِهِ بَطَلَ إيمانُهُ. وهَذا يَرْجِعُ إلى الِاعْتِدادِ بِإيمانِ مَن نَطَقَ بِالشَّهادَتَيْنِ وإنْ لَمْ يَشْغَلْ عَقْلَهُ بِاعْتِقادِ مَدْلُولِهِما، بَلْ يُكْتَفى مِنهُ بِأنَّهُ لا يُضْمِرُ خِلافَ مَدْلُولِهِما، وهَذِهِ أحْوالٌ نادِرَةٌ لا يَنْبَغِي الخَوْضُ فِيها. أوْ أرادُوا أنَّهُ تَجْرِي عَلَيْهِ في الظّاهِرِ أحْكامُ المُؤْمِنِينَ، مَعَ أنَّ الكَرّامِيَّةَ لا يُنْكِرُونَ أنَّ مَن يَعْتَقِدُ خِلافَ ما نَطَقَ بِهِ مِنَ الشَّهادَتَيْنِ أنَّهُ خالِدٌ في النّارِ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ. وفي تَفْسِيرِ الفَخْرِ (الرازي) أنَّ غَيْلانَ الدِّمَشْقِيَّ وافَقَ الكَرّامِيَّةَ.

هَذِهِ جَوامِعُ أقْوالِ الفِرَقِ الإسْلامِيَّةِ في مُسَمّى الإيمانِ.

وأنا أقُولُ كَلِمَةً أرْبَأُ بِها عَنِ الِانْحِيازِ إلى نُصْرَةٍ: وهي أنَّ اخْتِلافَ المُسْلِمِينَ في أوَّلِ خُطُواتِ مَسِيرِهِمْ، وأوَّلِ مَوْقِفٍ مِن مَواقِفِ أنْظارِهِمْ، وقَدْ مَضَتْ عَلَيْهِ الأيّامُ بَعْدَ الأيّامِ، وتَعاقَبَتِ الأقْوامُ بَعْدَ الأقْوامِ، يُعَدُّ نَقْصًا عِلْمِيًّا لا يَنْبَغِي البَقاءُ عَلَيْهِ.

ولا أعْرِفُنِي بَعْدَ هَذا اليَوْمِ مُلْتَفِتًا إلَيْهِ. لا جَرَمَ أنَّ الشَّرِيعَةَ أوَّلُ ما طَلَبَتْ مِنَ النّاسِ الإيمانَ والإسْلامَ، لِيَخْرُجُوا بِذَلِكَ مِن

[صفحة ٢٧١]

عَقائِدِ الشِّرْكِ ومُناوَأةِ هَذا الدِّينِ، فَإذا حَصَلَ ذَلِكَ تَهَيَّأتِ النُّفُوسُ لِقَبُولِ الخَيْراتِ، وأفاضَتِ الشَّرِيعَةُ عَلَيْها مِن تِلْكَ النَّيِّراتِ، فَكانَتْ في تَلَقِّي ذَلِكَ عَلى حَسَبِ اسْتِعْدادِها، زِينَةً لِمَعاشِها في هَذا العالَمِ ومَعادِها. فالإيمانُ والإسْلامُ هُما الأصْلانِ اللَّذانِ تَنْبَعِثُ عَنْهُما الخَيْراتُ، وهُما الحَدُّ الفاصِلُ بَيْنَ أهْلِ الشَّقاءِ وأهْلِ الخَيْرِ، حَدًّا لا يَقْبَلُ تَفاوُتًا ولا تَشَكُّكًا، لِأنَّ شَأْنَ الحُدُودِ أنْ تَكُونَ مُتَفاوِتَةً، كَما قالَ اللَّهُ تَعالى: ﴿فَماذا بَعْدَ الحَقِّ إلّا الضَّلالُ﴾ [يونس: ٣٢]. ولا يَدَّعِي أحَدٌ أنَّ مَفْهُومَ الإيمانِ هو مَفْهُومُ الإسْلامِ، فَيُكابِرُ لُغَةً تُتْلى عَلَيْهِ. كَيْفَ وقَدْ فَسَّرَهُ الرَّسُولُ (ﷺ) لِذَلِكَ الجالِسِ عِنْدَ رُكْبَتَيْهِ؟ فَما الَّذِينَ ادَّعَوْهُ إلّا قَوْمٌ قَدْ ضاقَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ العِبارَةُ، فَأرادُوا أنَّ الِاعْتِدادَ في هَذا الَّذِي لا يَكُونُ إلّا بِالأمْرَيْنِ. وبِذَلِكَ يَتَّضِحُ وجْهُ الِاكْتِفاءِ في كَثِيرٍ مِن مَوادِّ الكِتابِ والسُّنَّةِ بِأحَدِ اللَّفْظَيْنِ، في مَقامِ خِطابِ الَّذِينَ تَحَلَّوْا بِكِلْتا الخَصْلَتَيْنِ، فانْتَظَمَ القَوْلانِ الأوَّلُ والثّانِي.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 8 (part 4 of 4):

The cause of the divergence of opinions in distinguishing the reality of faith (*iman*, belief) from the reality of Islam (*islam*, submission) is two matters. The first is that the Muhammadan message called people to believe in the existence of God and His oneness, in the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), and in the unseen, and it called them to utter what indicates that this belief has taken root in the soul of the believer. This is because belief is not known except through speech. The Messenger did not accept from anyone what would produce a strong presumption that this belief had come to be in him, except that he acknowledge it with his speech, if he was able to.

The second is that the believers who responded to the Messenger's call did not have outward conduct that contradicted their beliefs, for there was none among them who was a Muslim while concealing disbelief. Thus the meaning of faith was attained for them together with the meaning of Islam, and it was true of them that they were believers and Muslims. Then, when hypocrisy emerged after the Hijrah, there arose the need to differentiate between the state of those who were characterized by faith and Islam and the state of those who displayed Islam while concealing disbelief. This differentiation was by way of warning and admonition, not by specifying and identifying the one described. Therefore, the words of the Qur'an and the speech of the Prophet generally proceeded in consideration of the prevailing condition of Muslims, who combined the two meanings. Sometimes they proceeded in consideration of rare conditions when there was a need to draw attention to them, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿Say: You have not believed; but say, "We have submitted," for faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14]. And as in the saying of the Prophet to one who said to him, "What is the matter with you concerning so-and-so? By God, I see him as a believer." He said: "Or a Muslim."

[p. 272]

The meaning of faith, therefore, is the attainment of belief in what must be believed. The meaning of Islam is a person's showing that he has submitted himself to following the religion and the call of the Messenger. God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women...﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35], to the end of the verse. Does any doubt occur to you that the Law (*shari'ah*) did not demand from people faith and Islam merely to populate the otherworldly realm with Paradise and Hell? God is capable of creating for these two places a creation that would inhabit them, should He will to create them. Rather, God willed to populate both the worldly and the otherworldly realms, and He made this world a polishing ground for human souls, preparing them to become qualified to populate the otherworldly realm, so that they might join the angels. God therefore made the laws to restrain people from the evil deeds that proceed from them by the motives of their desires, which corrupt their natural disposition. God also willed to preserve the order of this world, so that it would remain suitable for fulfilling God's purpose until the term He willed. He therefore legislated a law for people and called them to follow it and to enter its enclosure. That entry is called faith and Islam, since the two are required for the essential reality of joining under this law. Then this entails displaying the enabling of their souls to accept what is prescribed for them of conduct, willingly,

[p. 272 continued]

and with confidence in one of two ends: purity or defilement. This is what the deeds are, in obeying commands and refraining from prohibitions, and in doing and abstaining. This final aim is the one in which levels differ. However, the differing of its people in it does not diminish the foundation by which they entered. For the one who performs some of the good has done what is better than his state before faith, and the one who performs most of the good has surpassed the one below him, and the one who performs all of it to the extent of his capacity is the successful one. Thus the Law does not lack a benefit that arises from individuals of those who named themselves believers and Muslims. And among those levels is the protection of the domain and the defense of the core. Does anyone doubt that 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib, in the days when he did not see refraining from drinking wine as obligatory and said, "God said: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]," was told, "No"? His jihad on the day of al-Qadisiyyah indicated his faith and the realization of a great deal of the parts of his Islam. So is he to be regarded as equal to the disbelievers in that he will abide forever in the Fire?

Therefore, deeds have the second rank after faith and Islam, because they complete the purpose. No one disputes these two points, namely that deeds are in the second rank and that they are intended, except a stubborn person. Among what supports this most fully is what is related in the authentic collections (*al-sihah*) in the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, that the Prophet (ﷺ) had sent him to Yemen and said to him: "You are going to come to a people of the People of the Book. When you come to them, call them to bear witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God," meaning that they should utter this in speech matching their belief,

[p. 273]

"If they obey you in that, inform them that God has enjoined upon them five prayers in every day and night," and so on. Had it not been that faith and Islam have the first share, he would not have put it first. And had it not been that deeds have no place in the designation of Islam, he would not have distinguished between them. This is because calling to the truth must be in one step. Otherwise, approval of his remaining upon a part of disbelief, even for a moment, while expecting his acceptance of the religion, would be approval of disbelief, and that itself is a form of disbelief. How then would one command him to follow a path while being protected from approving anyone's remaining upon falsehood? Thus the third opinion is joined to the two opinions.

It is not doubtful that the deserving of reward and punishment is in proportion to the deeds, both of the heart and of the limbs. The matter without which none of what is sought is attained does not save from punishment unless all of it is present. It is therefore necessary that whoever does not believe and does not submit be eternal in the Fire, because nothing of the intended aim is attained from him without faith and Islam. As for matters whose doer comes closer to the goal in proportion to how far he advances along its paths, their reward is according to the extent of his performing them, and the punishment is according to the extent of his abandoning them. No one who is not stubborn should dispute this. For how could two men be equal before God, the All-Knowing, the All-Wise, one of whom did not believe and did not submit, and the other who believed, submitted, complied, and refrained, except that he followed the commanding soul to evil in one trait or one lapse? Would one then judge that both men are in punishment and abiding forever? Is there any benefit left for every perpetrator of disobedience in remaining upon Islam, if that for which he fled to Islam is attained in every case, namely eternal abiding in the Fire? Then, when he wishes to repent, he believes on that day. Does anyone deny that most of the Ummah are not free of being involved in disobedience, one or two acts of it, since infallibility is absent? If that was disbelief before repentance, does a reasonable person say that the Ummah in that state is characterized by disbelief? I do not think any reasonable person would commit to it after hearing it. Would anyone then conceal this and take from such a saying as God's words ﴿And God would not have wasted your faith﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], meaning the prayer, saying: "God named the prayer faith; and had deeds not been part of faith, it would not have been called so"? After we have shown that deeds are the ultimate aim of faith and Islam, the fourth and fifth opinions are joined to the three opinions for whoever follows the people of perfection in fairness.

Then the scholar saturated with knowledge of the objectives of the Law and its varied forms must distinguish between the situations of its address. Among them is the situation of admonition, encouragement, warning, glad tidings, and caution, and among them is the situation of instruction and verification. Each text from the texts of the Law is thus returned to its appropriate place, and it is not dragged between contradictory meanings in the manner of one who deceives. No one should argue from what is related concerning the most established attributes of a described person, where he affirms one of those attributes at one time in the context of praising him, since he is characterized by all of them. When he is described at one time with all of them, his being described at another time with one of them does not indicate that this one is equal to the rest. When we encounter legal reports that combine faith and deeds in the context of warning or exhortation, they are not evidence that the reality of one of them is composed of and constituted by the two together. Rather, a person argues only from a context of differentiation and negation, or from a context of instruction and clarification. One should not, then, presume to say of this view that it is foolish, arising from little reflection and a lack of comprehensive knowledge of the sources of the Law, and from overlooking its purpose, and that it leads to declaring most Muslims to be disbelievers and to the breaking of the Islamic community. Rather, one looks at the sources of the Law with a comprehensive view, so as not to be among those who have missed some things and grasped only a part. His ruling on the question should be like the ruling of the young woman of the quarter.

As for the question of God's pardon of the disobedient, it is a question related to our aim but is not part of it. The Ash'arites have expanded on it, while others have restricted it, and its matter is left to the knowledge of God. However, what has reached us from the Law is the consideration of promise and threat, for otherwise the deterrents would be like striking cold iron. When you know that the source of disagreement in it is the consideration of the proof of obligation or permissibility, you know that the disagreement in it has moved from the literal sense to the figurative sense. There is no wonder, and more wonderful still is the passage of times over a saying like that of the Kharijites, the Ibadis, and the Mu'tazilah, while none among the skilled scholars of those groups arises to refine the intended meaning or to interpret the statement of their predecessors in the customary way. It seems to me that the flash of insight of their intelligent ones has begun to shine through the gaps in the ashes.

[Page 275]

**Qur'an 2:9: "They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive none except themselves, and they are not aware."**

The clause "they seek to deceive" (yukhadi'una) is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause "they say" (yaqulu) in "We believe in Allah" (Qur'an 2:8), together with what follows it, because their saying that includes deception. Al-khida' is the verbal noun of khada'a, which indicates the sense of mufa'alah (the reciprocal form, denoting mutual action). Al-khad' is an act or statement accompanied by something that gives the impression that its doer intends by its literal meaning the benefit of another, while he in fact intends the opposite, and he strives to make it pass on to another in order to change that person from a state he is in, or to divert him from a matter he is about to do. The Arabs say: "The lizard deceived (khada'a al-dabb)," when it gives the impression to the one who hunts it that it is trying to leave by the side through which the hunter has inserted his hand, so that the hunter does not watch it, since he knows that he will certainly catch it; then the lizard exits from its nafiqa (a secret back exit in its burrow).

Deception is a blameworthy act, except in war. Being deceived (al-inkhida') is when the trick of the deceiver succeeds against the one deceived, and it is also blameworthy, because it stems from foolishness (al-balah). As for showing that one has been deceived while being aware of the trick, when the trick is not harmful, that is from generosity and forbearance. Al-Farazdaq said:

*They asked Quraysh for rain, every man who lets himself be deceived,*
*for indeed the generous man, when you deceive him, is deceived.*

In the hadith, "The believer is ghirr (naive) and generous (karim)." That is, among his attributes is forgiveness and overlooking, so that he is thought to be naive. For this reason it is followed by "generous," to dispel the naivety (al-ghirriyyah) that indicates foolishness. Faith increases shrewdness, because the foundations of its belief are built on rejecting everything that tends to mislead judgement and blind insight. Do you not see his saying: "The fortunate one is he who is admonished by others," together with his saying: "A believer is not stung from the same hole twice"? All of these proclaim that foolishness does not befit the believer. As for the meaning of "The believer is naive and generous," it is that when the believer's soul has been purified of evil thoughts and the notion of them occurring to his mind, and when he attributes to people a condition like his own, a state of trusting confidence comes upon him that resembles naivety. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*That girl whom I became attached to suddenly,*
*indeed the forbearing man and the man of Islam may be captivated.*

So he offers an excuse for the speed of his attachment to her and for her captivating his mind, by the nobility of his intellect and the soundness of his Islam, for all of this is among the causes of good judgement and tenderness of heart. So it is no wonder that he is quick to be affected by her.

The meaning of the deception issuing from their side towards the believers is clear. As for their deceiving Allah, which implies that the hypocrites intended to delude Allah, although no rational person intends that, since he knows that Allah is aware of hearts, and which implies that Allah deals with them by deception; likewise, the issuing of deception from the side of the believers towards the hypocrites, as the form mufa'alah requires, although that is among blameworthy acts that do not befit the believers to perform, so it cannot be attributed to Allah, nor can the hypocrites' intention be connected to their dealing with Allah. All of this necessitates an interpretation of the meaning of mufa'alah indicated by the form *yukhadi'una*, or of its implied agent on the other side, which is the explicitly mentioned object.

As for the interpretation of *yukhadi'una*, there are several aspects.

The first: the object of khada'a does not necessarily have to be the intended target of the deceiver (al-mukhadi'), since one may intend to deceive someone and it falls upon another, just as someone may deceive the agent of another in a matter of wealth, so it is said to him: "You are deceiving so-and-so and so-and-so," meaning the agent and his principal. So they intended to deceive the believers, because they denied that Islam was from Allah. Since their deception of the believers was for the sake of the religion, their deception returned to the Lawgiver of that religion. As for the interpretation of the meaning of Allah's deception of them and the believers' deception of them, it is the believers' overlooking their sudden outbursts, slips of the tongue, stumbles in actions, and errors, all of which indicate their hypocrisy, so that they continued to treat them as believers. For when this was from the believers by the permission of the Messenger (ﷺ), to the extent that he forbade the one who asked his permission to kill Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, that conduct was by the permission of Allah, so its ultimate source was Allah. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: "Indeed the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He is the one who deceives them" (Qur'an 4:142) in Surat al-Nisa', just as their deception of the believers returned to Him. This is an interpretation of deception from both of its sides, each according to what suits it.

The second is what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned: that "*yukhadi'una*" is a metaphor of analogy (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), comparing the state resulting from their dealings with the believers and with the religion of Allah, and from Allah's dealing with them in granting them respite and sparing them, and from the believers' dealing with them in applying the rulings of Muslims to them, to the state of those who deceive one another.

The third is that *khada'a* means *khada'a* (the same as the simple form), i.e., the act is not intended to occur from both sides, but rather the intent is exaggeration (al-mubalaghah). Ibn 'Atiyyah said, quoting al-Khalil: "It is said *khada'a* from one party, because in deception there is a delay (muhlah), just as one says 'I treated the patient' (*'alajtu al-mariḍ*) because of the delay." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is as if he is referring *fa'ala* to two parties, but there must be a delay, resistance and procrastination in it, so it is as if it contends with the meaning in which *fa'ala* is used." End of quotation.

This returns to making the form mufa'alah a metaphor for the meaning of exaggeration, by likening a strong act to an act that arises from two agents, by way of secondary implication. This interpretation is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Amir and those with him: *yakhda'una Allah* (they deceive Allah). This only removes the problem of attributing the issuing of deception to Allah and the believers, together with declaring Allah and the believers free of it; it does not remove the problem of the issuing of deception from the hypocrites towards Allah.

As for the interpretation of the implied agent of *yukhadi'una*, which is also the object, it is that the intended meaning is that they deceive the Messenger of Allah. The attribution to Allah, the Exalted, is then either by way of rational metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli), because of the connection between the Messenger and the one who sent him, or it is a metaphor by omission of the word meaning "the one who is in a relation with" (al-mudaf). Thus their intended meaning is not literally the deception of Allah. This leaves the possibility that the Messenger of Allah was deceived by them and also deceived them. As for permitting the deception of the hypocrites by the Messenger and the believers, on the grounds that it is a recompense to them for their deception, that is not appropriate.

His saying "*wa ma yukhadi'una*" (and they deceive not) is read by Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Khalaf as *yukhadi'una*, with an alif after the kha'. It is read by Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub as *yakhda'una* (with a fatha on the yaʾ and a sukun on the kha'). The clause "*wa ma yukhadi'una illa anfusahum*" (and they deceive none except themselves) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the first *yukhadi'una*; that is, they deceive while they deceive none except themselves, i.e., their deception is restricted to their own selves; none of it returns to Allah and the believers. Therefore it is necessary that the deception in His saying "*wa ma yukhadi'una*" is the same deception mentioned earlier in His saying "they seek to deceive Allah," and so there arises the problem of the validity of restricting deception to themselves while also affirming that they deceive Allah and the believers. The author of al-Kashshaf answered with what amounts to this: that the second deception is used in a necessary implication of the first meaning of deception, which is harm (al-darr). For it was first used for any dealing resembling deception, which is the dealing of the cunning one who treats others with contempt, and the word "deception" was applied to it by metaphor. Then it was applied a second time and what was meant was the necessary implication of the meaning of the metaphor, which is harm, because the one who is dealt with by cunning and contempt confronts his dealer in retaliation; he may find in himself capability, or find the other unguarded, and so he harms him. Thus the occurrence of harm to the one dealt with has become a customary matter necessarily associated with the one who deals. By this it is correct to use *yukhadi'u* in this sense, either by metaphor or by metonymy (kinayah). This is a case of building a metaphor upon a metaphor, because deception was first applied by metaphor, then treated as literal, and so was used by metaphor for the necessary implication of the meaning for which it was a metaphor. So the meaning is: "they harm none except themselves." The aspects concerning the application of the root *khida'* to their act apply here, and there arises the interpretation of the meaning of making their own selves a second side of the deception, even though the selves are themselves them. So deception is a metaphor for the dealing that resembles the act of the two deceiving parties, based on what is widespread in people's sense that the impulses which call to committing acts whose consequences are bad are an act of the self, which is distinct from the intellect, and which makes the human being see good at one time and evil at another. This is an imagined notion, based on moral exhortation, to create enmity between a person and his evil impulses, by making them come to him from a source other than his own essence, but rather from the self, so that he prepares himself to fight them and disobey their command. If they were attributed to him, he would see no way of resisting them. 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib said:

*My soul surged against me at the first time,*
*then it was turned back against what it disliked and settled.*

Ibn 'Atiyyah reports that Abu 'Ali al-Farisi recited to some Bedouin:

*You did not know what "no" is, and you will not say it,*
*your whole life, until the last of eternity.*

*And you did not consult your two souls, doubting*
*about it, nor about its sister, and you did not hesitate.*

He means by its sister the word "yes" (na'am), which is the sister of "no" (la). The meaning is that they are sisters in speech. I say: from this is also the saying of 'Urwah ibn Udhaynah:

*And when I find for her whisperings of consolation,*
*the heart intercedes with the conscience, so it wears it down.*

So when they disobeyed their souls, which call them to faith when they hear the verses and warnings, since the soul is never free of some return to the truth, their dealing with it in turning away from its advice, and its turning away from them in the scarcity of renewed counsel to them and their being left in their error, was like deception from these two sides.

Know that His saying "*yukhadi'una Allah wa alladhina*" (they seek to deceive Allah and those who believe) is read by all ten canonical readings with a dammah on the yaʾ and a fatha on the kha' followed by an alif. The word *nafs* (self) in the Arabic language means the essence and the inner power, which is expressed by the spirit and the thought of the intellect.

His saying "*wa ma yash'urun*" (and they are not aware) is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause "*wa ma yukhadi'una*." Shu'ur (awareness) is used for knowledge of hidden things. From it the poet is called *sha'ir* (poet), because of his knowledge of meanings which not everyone can reach, and his ability to measure and rhyme with ease, which not everyone does well. And the expression *layta sh'ri* (I wish I knew) is used for bewilderment in knowing a hidden matter; were it not for the hiddenness, one would not wish to know it, but would know it without wishing. So their saying "he is not aware" (*huwa la yush'ir*) is a description of lacking shrewdness, not of lacking sensation. This is more eloquent in blame, because blame with an attribute that is possible to attain is more painful than blame with something whose absence is certain. For their bodies are a matter known to them and to people, so it does not vex them to be described as lacking it; what vexes them is to be described as dull.

Moreover, the hiddenness of their deception of their own selves is something beyond dispute. The same expression was chosen for its counterpart in the hiddenness, which is "Unquestionably, they are the corrupters, but they are not aware" (Qur'an 2:12), because in both verses what is affirmed is the outcome and the end, and these are things that are hidden. And in His saying "Unquestionably, they are the foolish, but they do not know" (Qur'an 2:13), negation of knowledge was chosen rather than negation of awareness, because foolishness may become apparent to its possessor with the least glance at his conditions and conduct, since foolishness is closer to claiming manifestness than to deceiving one's own self when intending to deceive another, and than to the occurrence of corruption when intending reform. On this second meaning, the author of al-Kashshaf went: "They, because of the prolongation of their heedlessness, are like one who has no sense."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 10:

﴿In their hearts is a disease, so Allah increased their disease. And for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie.﴾

This is a pure resumptive clause (isti'naf) enumerating their evil qualities. It may also be explanatory (bayani), answering the question of one who is astonished upon hearing the states described before it in His saying: ﴿They deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive none except themselves, and they do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9].
