For whoever hears that a group deceives Allah the Exalted and deceives many people, and hopes that its deception will succeed over them, and then does not perceive that the harm of the deception is befalling it, is someone who deserves that the one who hears of their affair be astonished and ask how this occurred to their minds. So His saying ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾ is an explanation: that in their hearts there is a defect that has grown until it reached the limit of decay.

Page 279
For this reason the adverbial phrase ﴿in their hearts﴾ was placed first, for emphasis, because the hearts are the locus of thought in deception. Since what was asked about is its connection and its effect, it is what is emphasized in the answer. The tanwin of marad (a disease) is for magnification. The word "hearts" is used here for the locus of thinking, as was previously mentioned at His saying ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7]. "Disease" (marad) is literally an accident affecting the temperament that takes it out of the balance specific to the type of that body, a departure that is not complete; and in proportion to the departure, the pain intensifies. If the departure is complete, it is death. It is used metaphorically for the psychological conditions that afflict human characters, afflictions that take them out of their perfection. The application of "disease" to this is widespread and well known in Arabic speech. The management of the temperament to remove this accident and return it to its balance is true medicine, and there is a metaphorical sense of this as well. 'Alqamah ibn 'Abdah, known as al-Fahl, said:

"If you ask me about women, I am knowledgeable about the ailments of women, and a physician."

He mentioned the ailments and medicine in reference to the corruption of character and its reform.

The meaning of "disease" in this verse is undoubtedly its metaphorical meaning, because it is what the hypocrites are characterized by, and it is the intended object of their censure and of explaining the source of their evil deeds.

The meaning of ﴿so Allah increased their disease﴾ is that those blameworthy characters arising from hypocrisy and accompanying it kept increasing in them as the days passed, because it is the nature of characters, once they take root, to increase with the passing of days until they become fixed dispositions, as the poet al-Mu'allut al-Qurayi said:

"Encourage the youth toward good, as long as you see him in his youth, good, not ceasing to increase."

The same applies to evil. Hence it was said: "Whoever does not become forbearing in youth will not become forbearing in old age." And al-Nabighah said, satirizing 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl:

"You will surely become forbearing or cease, when you grow gray or the crow turns gray."

Hypocrisy necessarily causes the increase of the bad characters accompanying it, because hypocrisy conceals blameworthy characters, so they remain hidden from advisers, educators and guides, and thereby they take root and multiply without limit. Thus hypocrisy in concealing the bad characters is like a patient concealing his illness from the physician. Here is an explanation of what arises from hypocrisy of the moral diseases in the table mentioned here; and we have indicated what points to each of these traits in the verses occurring here or in other verses in this table.

Page 280

Page 281
Know that these are dispositions that arise from hypocrisy or accompany it as such, especially hypocrisy in religion. Allah the Exalted has alerted us to the blameworthiness of these, for instruction and education. Hypocrisy relies on three qualities: verbal lying, practical lying, which is deception, and accompanying these is fear, because lying and deception only proceed from one who guards against revealing the truth of his affair, and this happens only out of fear of harm or fear of failing in one's endeavor. Both indicate little courage, steadfastness, self-confidence and good conduct. Then each of these three blameworthy qualities gives rise to other ailments. Lying arises from some foolishness, because the liar believes his lie will pass among people, and this stems from little intelligence, since the discerning person knows that there are among people those like him and better than him. Then foolishness leads to ignorance of realities and of the levels of minds. And because lying accustoms the mind of its owner to distorted realities, and with prolonged persistence in that they become confused for him, to the point that he may believe what he has fabricated to be real. From both of these arises folly (sufah), which is a defect in judgment and a decay of intellect. The scholars of ethics and medicine have come to count lying among the diseases of the brain.

As for the arising of conceit, pride, disbelief and corruption of judgment from heedlessness, ignorance and folly, it is evident; likewise the arising of isolation, cowardice and concealment from fear. As for the arising of enmity among people from deception, it is because the enmity of opposites begins from their sense of being deceived by him, and it is followed by the enmity of companions, for when they see that companion's skill in hypocrisy and deception, doubt enters them that his sincerity which he shows them may be of the deception. When the enmity of both sides occurs, all people take precautions against him and retaliate against him, and he sets out to scheme against them and corrupt them in order to reach his aim. So people shoot at him from one bow, and what he gains from that is becoming a mockery to all people.

You have seen that what arises from the disease of hypocrisy and what increases in it is an increase of that arising, that is, its rootedness, its establishment, and the generation of other blameworthy traits from it. Perhaps the indefiniteness of "disease" in both places indicates this, for the indefiniteness of the first is to indicate variety or multiplicity, and the indefiniteness of the second is to indicate that the increase is another disease, according to the rule of repeating an indefinite as indefinite.

The increase of the disease of their hearts was attributed to Allah the Exalted, although the increase of these heart diseases is by its own nature, because when Allah the Exalted created this generation and its causes, and it was a hidden matter, He alerted people to the danger of indulging in evil intentions and reprehensible deeds, and that it is in its nature to increase those intentions in establishment in the heart, so that abandoning them becomes difficult or impossible after they are established. That increase was attributed to His name because Allah the Exalted became angry with them, so He left them to themselves and did not rescue them with His kindness that would awaken them from their heedlessness, in order to alert the Muslims to the danger of their affair, and that it is among what makes it difficult for its possessors to give it up, so that their caution in dealing with them is as strict as possible.

Thus the clause ﴿so Allah increased their disease﴾ is a declarative clause conjoined to His saying ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾, standing in the position of an explanatory resumption, included in dispelling astonishment: that is, the cause of their plunging into corruption and their attempting what cannot be attained is that there is a disease in their hearts, and because it is a disease that increases with the days by an increase decreed by Allah, so there is no hope of its removal.

Some exegetes said: it is an invocation against them, like the saying of Jubayr ibn al-Adbat:

"Fatlah moved far from me when I called upon him, 'Amin,' so Allah increased the distance between us."

This is an unsound interpretation, because it contradicts the original use of the conjunction fa', and because the Qur'an taking up insulting them in this way is not its custom, and because invoking against them with increase contradicts what is known of invoking for the misguided with guidance, as in "O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know."

His saying ﴿And for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿so Allah increased their disease﴾, completing the benefit. Thus with this conjunction the explanation is complete of what hypocrisy drew upon them of corruption of condition in this world and punishment in the Hereafter.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase ﴿for them﴾ is to draw attention to the fact that it is the predicate and not an attribute, so that upon merely hearing the subject, the knowledge that this is among their attributes is settled, and the soul does not neglect receiving it.

"Alim (painful) is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, because the more common usage of this form is that the quadriliteral verb has the meaning of mufil, and its origin is "'adhab mu'lim" (a painful punishment) in the form of the passive participle, meaning the one who is caused pain by it, by way of metonymy (majaz 'aqli), because the one in pain is the one punished, not the punishment, as they say "jadda jadduhu" (his fortune became great). Or it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il from alima, meaning became one who is in pain. Or it may be fa'il in the sense of mufil, i.e., mu'lim with kasra on the lam. It was said that this is not attested from the Arabs in this root, though it is attested in its counterpart, such as al-Hakim and al-Sami' in the sense of al-Musmi', as in the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"And horses I have advanced against with horses, a greeting among them is a blow that is painful."

That is, mu'lim (painful). There was disagreement regarding the permissibility of analogy upon it. The truth is that it is abundant in eloquent speech, and that the prohibition of analogy upon it by the later (muwallidun) was intended to keep away from violating analogy without a motive, lest the state of the ignorant be confused with that of the eloquent. So there is no obstacle to interpreting the eloquent speech upon it.

Page 283
His saying ﴿bima kanu yukadhdhibun﴾ — the ba' is causal. The majority (al-Jumhur) read (yukadhdhibun) with a damma on its first letter and shadda on the dhal. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a fatha on its first letter and without shadda on the dhal, i.e., because of their denial of the Messenger and their report that he is sent from Allah and that the Qur'an is the revelation of Allah to the Messenger. The root of the tafil form is for attributing to lying, like ta'dil (declaring someone upright) and tajrih (declaring someone unreliable). As for the reading with the lighter form, it refers to their specific lying in saying "We believe in Allah," and to their general lying in saying "We are only reformers." So the intended meaning is their lying in showing faith and in making themselves the reformers rather than the believers.

Lying is the opposite of truthfulness, and it will come at His saying ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103] in Surat al-Ma'idah. The ma after the ba' is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, and the verbal noun it forms with kana is the existence (al-kawn).

[Page 284 is marked here]

It appears to me that the clause "wa-idha qila lahum" ("and when it is said to them") is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause "fi qulubihim maradun" ("in their hearts is a disease"). The reason is that His words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth," they say, "We are only reformers."﴾ are an account of some of their strange conditions. Among those conditions is that they say "We are only reformers" while in fact they are corrupters. It is therefore coordinated with the nearest of the sentences that describe their conditions, although in meaning this amounts to its being coordinated with the relative clause (ṣila) in His words ﴿those who say, "We believe in God"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. Here "idha" serves merely as a temporal particle and does not carry the meaning of a conditional, just as it here refers to the past and not to the future. This is common with it, as in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿until, when you lost heart and disputed about the matter﴾ [Al ʿImran: 152], and so on.

Among the subtle points of the Qur'an that are overlooked is the restriction of this verb by the temporal clause. What comes first to mind is that the object of blame is that they say "We are only reformers" while being corrupters. But on reflection it becomes clear that the speakers of this statement are more deserving of blame when they utter it in reply to someone who says to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth." This reply, coming from corrupters, arises only from a sickness of the heart and a decay of judgement, for the nature of corruption is that it does not remain hidden. And if it is hidden, then insisting upon it and believing it to be righteousness, after being alerted to it and admonished, is excessive stupidity or obstinacy, and ignorance upon ignorance.

In my view, this is what necessitates placing the temporal clause before "qalu..." ("they said..."), because it is the more important, being the point of wonder at their condition. The subtleties of the Qur'an's inimitability are endless.

[Page 285 is marked here]

Those who said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth," were some of the believers who had knowledge of their condition through kinship or companionship. They sincerely offered them counsel and admonition, hoping for their faith, and they concealed their faults, out of fear for them of punishment, and knowing that the Prophet (ﷺ) overlooked their slips, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya indicated.

In their reply, "We are only reformers," there is an indication that those who said to them "Do not cause corruption on the earth" were certain that they were corrupters, because that is what the particle "innama" (only) requires, as will come. This is further indicated, in my view, by the construction of the verb "qila" in the passive, in accordance with what comes in His words, ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14]. It is not valid that the speaker to them was God or the Messenger, for if the revelation had descended and been conveyed to specific individuals among them, their disbelief would have been known. And if it had descended in general terms, as the admonitions of the Qur'an descend, their reply "We are only reformers" would not have been apt.

I have also come to think, in explaining their causing of corruption, that it has degrees. The first is their corrupting of themselves through persistence in those heart-diseases that we mentioned earlier, and what follows from them of blameworthy traits, and what issues from them of evils.

The second is their corrupting of people by spreading those qualities and calling to them, and their corrupting of their children and dependants by imitating them in their faults, as Noah, peace be upon him, said: ﴿If you leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will beget none but wicked, ungrateful disbelievers﴾ [Nuh: 27].

The third is their corrupting through actions from which the corruption of society arises, such as spreading slander and enmity, kindling strife, rallying factions against the Muslims, and placing obstacles in the path of the reformers.

Corruption (ifsad) is the doing of that by which corruption occurs, and the hamza in it indicates making (lil-jaʿl), that is, making things corrupt on the earth.

The root meaning of corruption (fasad) is the transformation of the benefit of a beneficial thing into harm, to it or to something else. It may also be used for the existence of a thing containing harm, even if it did not previously contain any benefit. One says: "fasada al-shayʾ" (the thing became corrupt) after it had been sound, and one says "fasid" (corrupt) if it was found corrupt from the very beginning. Likewise one says "afsada" (he caused corruption) if he deliberately targeted a sound thing and removed its soundness, and one says "afsada" also if he brought about corruption from the outset.

The more evident view is that "fasad" is placed for the common element of the two meanings, and is not a case of homonymy (al-wadʿ al-mushtarak). Therefore its application to both, as here, is not an instance of using a homonym in both its meanings.

Thus, corruption on the earth includes: making sound things harmful, as adulteration in foods; removing beneficial things, as by burning and killing the innocent; corrupting systems, as through strife and tyranny; and corrupting endeavours, as by increasing ignorance, teaching immorality, embellishing disbelief, and opposing the righteous reformers. Perhaps the hypocrites had taken of all these kinds of corruption, and therefore the object of "tufsidu" (you corrupt) is omitted, to emphasise the generality derived from the verb falling within the scope of negation.

Mentioning the locus in which they caused corruption, namely the earth, which contains it, is to make their corruption appear grave, since it is spread throughout this earth; for its occurrence in one part of it is a disfigurement of the whole. By "the earth" is meant this terrestrial globe with what it contains of things susceptible to corruption, of people, animals, plants, and all the systems and laws that God, Exalted is He, established for them. A parallel is His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the earth to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock, and God does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205].

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿They say, "We are only reformers"﴾ are a reply by reversal (naqd), for reform (iṣlah) is the opposite of corruption, that is, making a thing sound. Soundness (ṣalah) is the opposite of corruption; one says "ṣalaha" (it became sound) after it had been corrupt, and one says "ṣalaha" in the sense of being found sound from the very beginning. It is therefore placed for the common element, as we said.

They brought "innama", which conveys restriction (qasr), and the scholars of Arabic and of tafsir agree upon this; no account is taken of one who differs, as an anomaly in this matter. Here "innama" conveys the restriction of the described to the description, in reply to the one who said to them "Do not cause corruption," because that speaker had attributed to them the quality of corruption, either by believing that they had no part in righteousness at all, or by believing that they had mixed righteous and corrupt action. So they replied with restriction by reversal (qasr al-qalb), and this is not a real restriction, because the restriction of the described to the description is not real. Moreover, the particle "innama" is specific to restriction by reversal, as in Dalail al-Iʿjaz (of ʿAbd al-Qahir al-Jurjani). The particle "innama" was chosen in their speech because it is addressed to an addressee who persists in error, as in Dalail al-Iʿjaz. And the restrictive clause was made a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya) in order to convey that they regarded their being described as reformers as a fixed and permanent matter, since among the special features of the nominal sentence is the conveying of continuity.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 12:

﴿Surely, it is they who are the corrupters, but they do not perceive.﴾

It is a rebuttal of them in their delusion and in their confining themselves to righteousness. He rebutted them by means of one of the modes of restriction (qasr), which is more eloquent in this respect than the mode they had used, because the definiteness of the predicate (musnad) conveys the restriction of the predicate to the subject (musnad ilayh). Thus His saying ﴿Surely, it is they who are the corrupters﴾ conveys the restriction of corruption to them, such that it is not found in anyone other than them. This negates their confining themselves to reform and refutes it. It proceeds according to the rule of refutation (naqd) and according to the style of restriction achieved through definition by genus (ta'rif al-jins). Although the rebuttal could have been achieved simply by saying "they are corrupters" without a form of restriction, He used restriction to convey the claim of negating corruption from others.

This may also convey that the hypocrites are not among those who are counted as reformers, because the nature of the corrupter, by custom, is that he is not a reformer, since corruption is easy to bring about and only a restraining check (wazi') prevents it. When a person casts off that restraint and begins to corrupt, corruption becomes easy for him, and then it is repeated until it becomes a disposition and a habit that hardly leaves its possessor.

The particle "alā" (ألا) is for alerting (tanbih), announcing their description with corruption.

He also emphasised the restriction of corruption to them by the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl), as he emphasised the restriction with it in His saying ﴿And those are the successful﴾ (al-Baqarah: 5), as was mentioned shortly before. The entry of (inna) upon the sentence, and its being coupled with "alā," which conveys alerting, is part of the attention given to the report and its strengthening, indicating God's wrath upon them. The opening particles such as "alā" and "ammā," whose function is to alert the listeners, indicate attention to the report, its dissemination and its proclamation. Therefore they necessarily indicate the intensity of what the report contains of praise or blame or other things. This also indicates the complete manifestness of the content of the sentence to the eye, since the particles of alerting share with demonstrative nouns (asmā' al-ishārah) in alerting the addressee.

His saying ﴿but they do not perceive﴾ is to be understood in the same sense as His saying before it (﴿And they deceive none but themselves, and they perceive not﴾ (al-Baqarah: 9)). Their actions, in which they take delight and which they consider the peak of shrewdness and of service to pure benefit, inevitably lead to general corruption; yet they did not come to realise this, because of its obscurity and because of the veil cast over their hearts as a result of hypocrisy and of associating with its great men. The state of one's companion and the flimsiness of a doctrine obscure even clear minds, and lighten sound intellects, until one sees as good what is not good. The position of the particle of correction (istidrak) here is because the speech is a repudiation of what they had affirmed for themselves of sincere devotion to reform, so He removed that misconception by the particle of istidrak.

[Page 287]

﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed," they say, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?"﴾ This is part of the speech that precedes it, so its ruling is the same as that speech by coordination (ʿaṭf, grammatical conjunction), and so is its speaker. Here it is also possible that the speakers are a group of hypocrites who advise one another to abandon hypocrisy, because they have grown weary of it, tired of its burdens and its pitfalls, and their minds have become exhausted from devising stratagems and fabricating nonsense.

The object of āmanū ("they believed") is omitted, either because the comparison in the phrase ﴿as the people have believed﴾ makes it unnecessary, or because it is known to the listeners.

The phrase ﴿as the people have believed﴾: the kāf (ka, "as") here is for comparison (tashbīh) or for causation (taʿlīl), and the lām in al-nās ("the people") is for the genus (jins) or for customary totality (istighrāq ʿurfī). By "the people" is meant those other than the addressees. It is an expression the Arabs use to urge someone to act and to encourage him to it, because the nature of souls is to hasten to imitation and to follow the example of one who precedes them in a matter. For this reason they use this expression in contexts of urging, consolation, or emulation. ʿAmr ibn al-Barrāqa al-Nahmī said:

"We support our patron, knowing that he, like the people, is subject to what is imposed on him and to the one who imposes it."

The phrase ﴿Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?﴾ is an interrogation (istifhām) of denial (inkār). By it they intended to disavow faith in the most emphatic way, and they made the faith they disavowed resemble the faith of the foolish, as a way of reviling it and of implicitly insulting the Muslims, asserting that what moved them to faith was the foolishness of their minds. They also indicated that they understood the intention of the one who said to them, "as the people have believed," that by "the people" he meant the Muslims.

Safīh (plural sufahāʾ, "foolish") is one who is characterized by safāha (foolishness). Safāha is lightness of intellect and weakness in controlling affairs. Al-Samawʾal said:

"We fear that our wisdom will be made foolish, so that we will remain in obscurity forever along with the obscure."

The Arabs use safāha for weakness of opinion, and they also use it for poor management of property. God Most High said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 5], and He said: ﴿But if the one upon whom the obligation lies is foolish or weak﴾ [al-Baqara: 282], because such things arise only from weakness of judgment.

Their description of the believers as foolish is a slander (buhtān), since they assume that opposing them could come only from lightness in the believers' minds. It is not that they meant to belittle them, for how could they, when among the Muslims are the chiefs of the Arabs from among the Emigrants and the Helpers? This is the habit of the people of corruption and foolishness: they hurl at the reformers blameworthy descriptions, with slander and insolence, so as to distract them from pursuing their corruptions. For this reason Abū al-Ṭayyib said:

"When your blame comes to me from a deficient person, it is then a testimony to me that I am perfect."

This verse does not provide evidence for the ruling concerning the zindīq (heretic, one who conceals unbelief) when his zandaqa (heresy) becomes apparent and is established by proof, nor does it provide evidence against that ruling. This is because those who said to them, "Believe as the people have believed," were among their relatives or close associates from among the believers, who had not disclosed their affair. So the verse contains no evidence that their hypocrisy was made manifest to the Messenger in any usual manner. Rather, it was a matter that God made the Prophet aware of, and the interest lay in concealing it. Some of the believers became aware of it through their association with them, and they knew from the Prophet ﷺ his avoidance of spreading that matter. Therefore the verse does not indicate any legal ruling related to the rule of hypocrisy and heresy.

* * *

﴿Surely they are the foolish, but they do not know﴾

He came with what corresponds to the coarseness of their nature, in support of the believers. Had it not been for the coarseness of their words, ﴿Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?﴾, the Qur'an would not have taken up their reviling, although its custom is to turn away from the ignorant. But they had become a proverbial example: "You spoke, so you made it obligatory" (qulta fa-awjabta). Also, because this is a context of making clear the truth from falsehood, plainness and firmness are fitting in it, as established in the rules of rhetoric (ādāb al-khaṭāba). This was declared with the word alā ("surely"), which signals alerting the listener to a statement, and it came in the form of restriction (qaṣr) like what was established in ﴿Surely they are the corrupters﴾ [al-Baqara: 12], to indicate that foolishness is restricted to them and not to the believers. Thus it is necessarily relative (idāfī, restricted in relation to a specific contrast).

If foolishness is established for them, then forbearance (ḥilm) is necessarily negated for them, because the two are opposites in the qualities of intellect. Inna ("indeed") here is for emphasizing the statement, and what is emphasized is the content of the restriction. The separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl), huwa, is for emphasizing the restriction, as was mentioned previously. Alā here, like its counterpart mentioned earlier in ﴿Surely they are the corrupters﴾ [al-Baqara: 12], ...

His saying ﴿but they do not know﴾ negated knowledge of their being foolish, using the word yaʿlamūna ("they know") rather than yashʿurūna ("they perceive"), unlike the two preceding verses. This is because being characterized by foolishness is not something whose nature is to be hidden, such that knowledge of it would be perception and ignorance of it would be negation of perception. Rather, it is an obvious quality that is not concealed. Their meeting each group with a face, their vacillation in relying on one of the two conditions, and their lack of complete steadfastness in their religion, nor steadfastness in Islam in the same way, is sufficient for the call to their foolishness of judgment, for foolishness is a quality that is hardly hidden. The Arabs said: "Foolishness is like its name." Al-Nābigha said:

"I was informed that Zarʿa, and foolishness is like its name, brings me the strange poems."

Juzʾ ibn Kilāb al-Faqʿasī said:

"Ibn Kūz sought, and foolishness is like its name, to outdo us in the nights when we spent the winter."

So their assumption that what they were upon of disbelief is right guidance, and that what the Muslims adopted of faith is foolishness, indicates the absence of knowledge on their part. Thus the position of the particle of correction (ḥarf al-istidrāk, "but") is to dispel the astonishment of one who wonders at their contentment with being singled out by the attribute of foolishness.

**[Page 290]**

The phrase ﴿وإذا لَقُوا﴾ ("And when they meet") is conjoined to what it is conjoined to in ﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهم لا تُفْسِدُوا﴾ ("And when they are told, 'Do not cause corruption'") [al-Baqarah: 11] and ﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ آمِنُوا كَما آمَنَ النّاسُ﴾ ("And when it is said to them, 'Believe as the people have believed'") [al-Baqarah: 13]. The discussion of the adverbial (zarfiyya) and temporal force applies equally here.

The restriction by the phrase ﴿وإذا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ ("And when they meet those who believe") serves as a preparation (tamhid, a introductory setting) for ﴿وإذا خَلَوْا﴾ ("And when they are alone"). For this reason it carries an added benefit beyond what is in ﴿ومِنَ النّاسِ مَن يَقُولُ آمَنّا بِاللَّهِ﴾ ("Among the people are those who say, 'We believe in God'") [al-Baqarah: 8] and the verse that follows it. What is said here is therefore not a repetition of what was said there, because the purpose here is to describe what they did in the presence of the believers: giving the impression that they were among them, and meeting them with faces of sincerity. When they part from them and reach their own people and leaders, they cast off the cloak of concealment and openly declare what they conceal.

The reason for placing the adverbial phrase first has already been explained in the discussion of ﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهم لا تُفْسِدُوا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11]. The meaning of their saying "We believe" (āmannā) is "we were believers." Thus the faith meant in their saying "āmannā" is the legal faith (al-īmān al-sharʿī), which is the totality of the doctrinal and cognitive attributes by which believers are named and known, in the sense of God's words ﴿إنّا هُدْنا إلَيْكَ﴾ ("Indeed, we have turned to You") [al-Aʿrāf: 156]. That is, "we were upon the religion of Judaism." Therefore there is no object for "āmannā" that would require justifying its omission or supplying it. Alternatively, the sense may be "we believed in what you believed," but the first is more evident. Their meeting with those who believe is their presence in the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ) and in the gatherings of the believers. The meaning of ﴿قالُوا آمَنّا﴾ ("they say, 'We believe'") is that they showed that they were believers by mere utterance, not by conviction of the heart; that is, they pronounced the word of Islam and other expressions that convey faith.

His words ﴿وإذا خَلَوْا إلى شَياطِينِهِمْ قالُوا إنّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ ("But when they are alone with their devils, they say, 'Indeed, we are with you'") are conjoined to ﴿وإذا لَقُوا﴾, and the intended element is this conjoined clause. As for ﴿وإذا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾, it is a preparation for it, as you have learned. This is evident from the context, since everyone knows that the intended meaning is that they say "we believe" in a state of mockery, which they openly express when they are alone, as shown by the fact that it has already been mentioned that they refuse faith and say ﴿أنُؤْمِنُ كَما آمَنَ السُّفَهاءُ﴾ ("Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?") [al-Baqarah: 13], rejecting it. The conjunctive waw is suitable to indicate simultaneity (maʿiyya) or other relations according to context. The context is explaining their situation in two aspects: one aspect with the believers and one aspect with their leaders. The author did not present the content of the second clause in the form of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as in "saying to their devils when they were alone." Nor did he make the waw in ﴿وإذا خَلَوْا﴾ a circumstantial waw. As for the first point, the content of both clauses, being capable of being treated as an independent attribute indicating hypocrisy, was intended by the conjunction to establish the independence of each of them, since the purpose is to enumerate their faults. The content of ﴿وإذا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قالُوا آمَنّا﴾ stands alone as an exposure of their hypocrisy in that state. This is made clear by his words ﴿وإذا لَقُوا﴾, which indicate that this happens at a specific time. As for the second point, the original principle is that two similar clauses in wording share the same syntactic position, and this was explained earlier in the reason for avoiding the use of a circumstantial clause.

The word al-shayāṭīn ("the devils") is the plural of shayṭān, a broken plural (jamʿ taksīr). The reality of the shayṭān is that it is a kind of immaterial creature (mujarrad), whose nature is fiery heat, and they are of the species of the jinn. God said concerning Iblīs ﴿كانَ مِنَ الجِنِّ﴾ ("He was of the jinn") [al-Kahf: 50]. His mention has become well known in the speech of the prophets and the wise. The term shayṭān is also applied to one who corrupts and stirs up evil. The Arabs say: "So-and-so is one of the devils, and one of the devils of the Arabs," and this is a metaphor (istiʿāra). In the same way it is applied here to the leaders of the hypocrites in hypocrisy. God said ﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنا لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ عَدُوًّا شَياطِينَ﴾ ("And thus We made for every prophet an enemy: devils") [al-Anʿām: 112], and so on.

The morphological pattern (wazn) of shayṭān has been disputed by the grammarians of Basra and Kufa. The Basrans said it is fayʿāl from sh-ṭ-n in the sense of "to be far," because it was removed far from God's mercy and from Paradise, so its nūn is original (aṣliyya). The Kufans said it is faʿlān from shāṭa, meaning "to be agitated," "to burn," or "to perish," and the reason for the naming is evident. I do not think this disagreement is anything more than an inquiry into the derivation of the form, that is, an investigation into its root letters and whether its nūn is original or augmentative. Otherwise it is not to be supposed of the grammarians of Kufa that they would claim it is treated like an adjective with the augmentation of alif and nūn, like ghaḍbān, especially since it is agreed that it is not barred from diptotic inflection in God's words ﴿وحَفِظْناها مِن كُلِّ شَيْطانٍ رَجِيمٍ﴾ ("and We guarded it from every accursed devil") [al-Ḥijr: 17]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The Kufans' view is refuted by the fact that Sībawayh reported that the Arabs say tashayṭana, when someone acts like a devil. This shows that it derives from sh-ṭ-n; otherwise they would have said tashayyaṭa." End of quotation.

In al-Kashshāf: "Sībawayh treated the nūn of shayṭān as original in one place of his book and as augmentative in another." End of quotation.

The correct view is that since tashayṭana is a descriptive verb derived from the noun, like their saying tanammara ("to act like a tiger"), they kept the letters of the noun as they are, because they treated it as an uninflected noun and not as a derived form, since it is not derived from what the noun itself is derived from, but from the letters of the noun. Thus it is a derivation that occurred after the usage was established and after disregarding the original root of derivation. Therefore their saying this does not favor either of the two opinions. In my view, it is a rigid noun (ism jāmid) whose letters resemble a derived root, and it entered Arabic from an earlier language, because this name belongs to the names related to beliefs and religions, and the people of Iraq had precedence in them before their migration to the Hijaz and Yemen. This is supported by the closeness of the words that express this meaning in most ancient languages.

I had seen the view of one who said that its name in Persian is sīṭān. The verb khalaw means "to be alone" and is intransitive, and it is transitive by bi, li, min, and maʿa without any implicit transformation. It is transitive by ilā with the implicit meaning of "to return" (āba) or "to be sincere" (khalaṣa). It is transitive directly with the implicit meaning of "to pass beyond" (tajāwaza) or "to distance oneself" (bāʿada). From this comes the widespread saying "fʿal kadhā wa khalāka dhamm," meaning that the consequence or harm of the matter does not return upon you. Here it is transitive with ilā to indicate that their being alone took place in places that were their place of return and refuge, and that their meeting with the believers was merely by chance and fleeting glances. The words "laqū" and "khalaw" together convey all of this. This is among the wonderful eloquence and clarity of the words.

Know that their address to the believers is reported in a way that implies they did not add anything that confirms the report with emphasis. Their address to their devils is worded in a way that implies that they confirmed their continued adherence to their religion by emphasizing the report with the emphatic particle expressed in ﴿إنّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ ("Indeed, we are with you"), even though the apparent requirement would be that their speech be the reverse of this, because the believers doubt the faith of the hypocrites, while their own people do not doubt that they remain upon their religion. Thus the report of their speech came in agreement with its meaning, contrary to what the apparent requirement would suggest, in order to take into account what is more deserving of the eloquent speaker's attention than the apparent requirement. Thus they omitted from their address to the believers anything that would confirm the report, because they did not want to present themselves as one whose sincerity is open to doubt; for if they did so, they would awaken the believers to doubt, and that would be a sign of the flawlessness of their hypocrisy. Moreover, the believers may be free of doubt about the hypocrites because the hypocrites are not identified to them, so stripping the report of emphatic elements is the apparent requirement.

As for their saying to their own people "Indeed, we are with you" with emphasis, that is because when their hypocrisy showed in their meeting with the Muslims in a way that caused the suspicion of their great men regarding their remaining in disbelief, and suspicion reached the hearts of their leaders, they needed to emphasize what shows that they remain upon their religion. Likewise their saying ﴿إنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ ("we were only mocking") — by it they revealed the reason for what they displayed to the believers, and they used the restrictive form (qaṣr al-qalb, restriction by inversion) to repel their devils' belief about them that what they showed to the believers was real and sincere faith. The author of al-Kashshāf justified the omission of emphasis in their saying "āmannā" and the emphasis in their saying "Indeed, we are with you" by arguing that the address to the believers lacked what requires emphasizing the report, because the speakers' aim did not go beyond claiming the occurrence of their faith, since their souls would not help them to utter anything stronger than that, and because they knew that this would not be accepted by the Muslims. That is, they kept to the necessary meaning of the speech. The absence of emphasis in speech may be due to the speaker's lack of concern for establishing it, or his knowledge that emphasizing it would be futile because it would not be accepted by the listener. This is a curious point, its basis being the disregard of the listener's denial and the turning away from concern for the report. As for their address to their devils, they used emphasis in the report to indicate their concern with that report and the sincerity of their desire to utter it, and because they knew that it was accepted by those they addressed. Emphasis may indicate the speaker's concern with the report and its currency with the listener. That is, it is emphasis for the sake of concern, not for the sake of rejecting denial.

Their saying "﴿إنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾" ("we were only mocking") restricts themselves to mocking by a restriction of the relative type (qaṣr idāfī) directed at the heart, meaning: "we are not sincere believers." The clause ﴿إنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ explains ﴿إنّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ ("Indeed, we are with you"), because if they were with them, then what they showed of departing from their religion was mockery or something similar. The second clause may be a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) answering an implied question, as if a questioner were astonished at their claim that they remained upon their religion, given what they had perfected of the signs of hypocrisy in dealing with the Muslims, and he denies that they remain upon their religion, asking: "How was it possible to combine remaining upon the religion with showing affection to the believers?!" So they answered: "We were only mocking." This makes clear the reason for using the restrictive particle, because the denying questioner believes their claim "Indeed, we are with you" to be false, and claims the opposite. Or the clause may be a substitute (badal) for "Indeed, we are with you" as a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl), because whoever persists in disbelief and goes to extremes in it, which is what "with you" implies, that is, in your stubbornness, has belittled Islam and its people and treated them with contempt. The first aspect is the best of the aspects, because it combines what the substitution and the emphasis both convey, namely the confirmation of the content of the first clause, together with its indication of repelling the bewilderment that gives rise to the question. This is lost under the two interpretations of emphasis and substitution.

Mockery (istihzāʾ) means derision. One says hazaʾa bihi and istahzaʾa bihi, and the sīn and tāʾ are for emphasis, like istajāba ("to respond"). It means treating someone by deed or word in a way that produces contempt for him or belittlement of him, whether he is made aware of it or it is concealed from him. The bāʾ in it marks the cause. It was said that it is not transitive except with bāʾ, and it was said that it is transitive with min. It is synonymous with sakhira in meaning but not in root, as will come in Surat al-Anʿām. Abū Jaʿfar read "mustahzūn" without the hamza and with a ḍamma on the zāy, as a lightening (takhfīf), and this is an eloquent dialect form of the hamzated form.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 15:

﴿Allah mocks them.﴾

This sentence is not conjoined to what precedes it, because it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), an answer to an implied question. The listener, upon hearing their words to the believers, "We believe," and their words to their devils, "Indeed we are with you," etc., asks: "Their scheme has succeeded over the heedless Muslims who are unaware of their plotting. Is there anyone who perceives their condition among the Muslims so as to repay them for their mockery? Or is there anyone who will turn back what they have sought from the Muslims? Who will take up the task of countering their deeds?" So the resumption with His words ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ carries the utmost grandeur and eloquence. It also stands in the position of a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), and in parenthetical insertions the conjunction is usually omitted. The mention of "yastahzi'" (mocks) is an indication that the content of the sentence is a recompense for their mockery. Because the resumptive character is taken into account, the name of Allah the Exalted is placed before the verbal predicate. He did not say "yastahzi'u Allahu bihim" (Allah mocks them), because among the things that come to the mind of the questioner is to ask: "Who will take up the task of countering their evil conduct?" So it is made known that the one who takes up this is the Lord of Might, the Exalted. In this there is an exalting of the status of the one who gives victory to them, and they are the believers, as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed Allah defends those who believe﴾ [al-Hajj: 38]. Thus placing the subject before the verbal predicate here serves to express the strengthening of the judgment beyond doubt. Furthermore, it also conveys the restriction (qasr) of the predicate to the subject. For since placing the subject before a verbal predicate in an affirmative context comes to strengthen the judgment, and comes also for restriction according to the opinion of Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir and the author of al-Kashshaf, as he stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿And Allah measures the night and the day﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] in surah al-Muzzammil, the combining of the intention of strengthening and the intention of specification is permissible in the aims of eloquent speech. Al-Zamakhshari permitted this at His saying: ﴿so he fears neither loss nor oppression﴾ [al-Jinn: 13] in surah al-Jinn, because what the eloquent speaker attends to of particularities does not prevent bearing the eloquent speech upon it, so how much more so in the most eloquent of speech. For this reason it is said: "The subtleties do not crowd one another."

The hypocrites were deceived by what they saw of the Prophet's ﷺ forbearance toward them and the believers' turning away from making concessions to them, so they reckoned that their scheme and hypocrisy had succeeded. For this reason 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy said:

[p. 294]
﴿They will surely expel the more honorable from it the more humble﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. So the placing of the Name of Majesty (Allah) first is merely for the sake of emphasis, not for the purpose of strengthening, since there is no requirement for that.

The verb (yastahzi'u), predicated to Allah, is not used in its literal sense, because what is meant here is that He does to them in this world what is called "mockery," as indicated by His saying: ﴿and extends them in their rebellion﴾. No genuine mockery occurred in this world. It is therefore either a figurative representation (tamthil) of Allah's treatment of them in response to their mockery of the believers, by what resembles the act of one who mocks them, namely granting them respite until they think that they have escaped accountability for their mockery, so they suppose that Allah is pleased with them, or that their idols benefited them; then, when the punishment of this world descends upon them, in the form of killing and disgrace, they realize the opposite of what they had imagined, and so that was like the form of mockery directed at them. The imperfect verb in His saying (yastahzi'u) denotes the present time.

It is not to be understood as Allah's attribute of mockery in the literal sense according to the Ash'aris, because no meaning of mockery proceeded from Allah in this world. What makes this figurative representation fitting is the correspondence (mushakalah) it contains. It is also possible that ﴿He mocks them﴾ is literal on the Day of Resurrection, by commanding that they be mocked in the place of standing, which is a kind of punishment. In that case the imperfect (yastahzi'u) denotes the future. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan inclined to this meaning, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyyah. It is also possible that what is meant is the requital of their mockery in the form of punishment or the like of disgrace and humiliation, meaning: "He humiliates them," and it is expressed by mockery figuratively and by correspondence; or that what is meant is the consequence of mockery, namely the return of its evil upon them.

All of this, although permissible, has been specified here by the majority of scholars among the exegetes, as Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Qurtubi transmitted. Al-Fakhr al-Razi and al-Baydawi also specified it, and the Mu'tazila specified it too, because mockery is not fitting to be ascribed to Allah in the literal sense, for it is an ugly act from which Allah the Exalted is exempt, as in al-Kashshaf. This is based on what is customary among people.

In quoting their speech, the nominal predicate was used in their saying ﴿We are only mockers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], to convey the meaning of the continuity of mockery proceeding from them and its persistence, such that they cannot be turned away from it.

In His saying ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ the imperfect verb was used to convey renewal (tajaddud); that is, the renewal of Allah's granting them respite for a period until the punishment seizes them, so that the Muslims may know that what the people of hypocrisy enjoy of blessing is only respite, however long it lasts, as the Exalted said: ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196] ﴿a little enjoyment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197].

* * *

[p. 295]
﴿and extends them in their rebellion, wandering blindly﴾

It is necessarily conjoined to ﴿Allah mocks them﴾. (yamuddu) is a verb derived from madad, which means increase. It is said: "madda-hu" when he increased it. This is the original form in derivation, without need for the hamza, because it is transitive. The evidence for this is that they vowelled the 'ayn in the imperfect according to the pattern of the transitive geminate verb. They may also say "amadda-hu" with the hamza of transitivity, on the basis of the meaning "made him possessed of increase." Then the use of madda became predominant for increase in the thing itself, as in "madda lahu fi 'umurihi" (he extended his life for him), and "madda al-ard" (he stretched the land, i.e., made it extended and lengthened). And the use of hamzated amadda became predominant for increase for the object of things he needs, as in "amadda-hu bi-jaysh" (he supplied him with an army), and ﴿He has supplied you with cattle and sons﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 133]. This usage was applied in the place of the other form by the original usage; for this reason it has been said: "There is no difference between them in usage." It has also been said: hamzated amadda is specific to good, as in ﴿Do you supply me with wealth?﴾ [al-Naml: 36] and ﴿That with which We supply them of wealth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55]; and madda is specific to other than good. This is transmitted from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi in his book al-Hujjah, and Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted it from Yunus ibn Habib. Except for the form transitive by the preposition lam (la), which is specific to increase in lifespan and granting respite in it according to al-Zamakhshari and others, though some lexicographers disagree. They dispensed with distinguishing by the hamza, by the lam indicating that this is for benefit and for a term, with the consonant (jim) being quiescent, returning to the original form, lest they combine what requires transitivity, which is the hamza, with what requires intransitivity, which is the preposition lam. All of this is from the influence of patterns (amthilah) on those who examine them. This is their approach in many verbs whose lexical meaning branches into partial or restricted or figurative meanings: they specify some of its usages or some of its conditions with some of those meanings, following the explicit statement in speech and avoiding ambiguity as far as possible.

This is one of the subtleties of the usage of the Arabic language. So it is not said that the claim of the specialization of some usages to some meanings is a claim of homonymy (ishtirak) or a claim of metaphor, and both are contrary to the original (principle), as 'Abd al-Hakim raised. This is because that specialization, as you know, is a conventional usage in practice, not a multiplicity of coinage nor use in a meaning other than the one it was coined for. A parallel to this is their saying: faraqa and farraqa; wa'ada and awda'a; nashada and anshada; nazzala (the doubled form) and anzala. And their saying: "al-'ithar" is the verbal noun of 'athara when the verb is meant literally, and "al-'uthur" is the verbal noun of 'athara when the verb is meant figuratively, which is "discovering" (al-ittila'). The Arabs have differentiated among the verbal nouns of one verb and among the plurals of one noun according to the difference in conditions.

[p. 296]
The transitivity of the verb (yamuddu) to their pronoun, which indicates a condition or a disposition, although increase (madd) is transitive only to rebellion, has come in the manner of general statement (ijmal) followed by detail, so that the detail may settle in the mind of the listener, like the manner of the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). Al-Zajjaj and al-Wahidi held that its origin is: "yamuddu lahum fi tughyanihim" (He extends for them in their rebellion), so they omitted the lam of transitivity and the verb was joined to the object in the manner of the removal of the preposition (naza' al-khafid). But this is not the case.

Rebellion (tughyan) is a verbal noun on the pattern of ghufran and shukran, and it is an intensive form of taghy, which is excess in evil and arrogance. The attachment of the verb yamuddu-hum here to the pronoun of the persons is a general attachment, explained by His saying ﴿in their rebellion﴾. It may also be on the supposition of an omitted lam, meaning "He extends for them in their rebellion," that is, He grants them respite. In that case it is like some of what was explained by His saying ﴿Allah mocks them﴾. This is the view of al-Zajjaj and al-Wahidi, but it is far-fetched. Wandering blindly ('amah) is the obliteration of insight and the bewilderment of judgment. Its verb is 'amiha, so one is 'a'mih and 'amih.

The predication of extension in rebellion to Allah the Exalted, according to the first interpretation of His saying "yamuddu-hum," is the predication of creation and origination bound to the causes of origination, in accordance with Allah's sunnah concerning the coming about of effects at their causes. When hypocrisy enters hearts, one of its effects is that it does not cease from them. And since it is part of the nature of the attribute of hypocrisy that the vices we have already explained should spring from it, their formation in their souls results from various causes in their natures, linked in succession by the connection of effects to their causes, which are many and branching. This occurs through a disposition specific to them directly. But Allah withheld from them His success (tawfiq), which would have uprooted them from that innate constitution through combating their souls. So His withholding of success from them requires the continuation and growth of their rebellion through becoming firmly established. Thus the predication of its increase to Allah is because He is the creator of the systems which are the causes of its increase. This is counted among the common rational literal (haqiqah 'aqliyyah) statements, and it is not of the figurative kind, since the creation of causes is not considered according to what people customarily understand when they attribute to Allah the Exalted what its agent is hidden. For He is the creator of the original causes and the one who established their laws in a manner whose secret people do not know, and they have not witnessed anyone to whom it is attributed in the literal sense other than Him. This is unlike the statement "The Amir built the city," especially after the explicit predication to him in speech, such that there is no room left for "building" according to the usage of people. And this is unlike "His face increases him in beauty" and "Your sight delighted me," because that, although in reality it is from the act of Allah the Exalted, is not taken into account in common usage. Therefore Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir said: it is among the figurative statements that have no literal sense.

[p. 297]
He attributed the rebellion to the pronoun of the hypocrites and did not say "fi al-tughyan" (in the rebellion) with the definite article of kind, as He said in surah al-A'raf: ﴿and their brothers extend them in error﴾ [al-A'raf: 202]. This indicates the monstrousness of the status of this rebellion and its strangeness in its category, and that they are specifically characterized by it, to the extent that it becomes known by its attribution to them.

The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected to (yamuddu-hum). And (ya'mahun) is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hāliyyah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 16 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance.﴾
The demonstrative refers to ﴿those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8] and to the attributes coordinated with their relative clause. The plural demonstrative is used because the referent of (man, "those who") is a group of people. The sentence is separated from the one before it in order to affirm the meaning of ﴿And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]; its content is thus in the position of emphasis, and this calls for disjunction (fasl). It also serves to give the reason for the content of the sentence ﴿And He extends them in their transgression﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15], so it is an explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani) answering a questioner about the cause. It is also a summary (fadhlakah, a concluding recapitulation) of the preceding sentences that describe their conditions, and the nature of a summary is that it is not joined by a conjunction, as in His saying, ﴿That is ten complete﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. All these considerations require the absence of a conjunction, so there are three reasons for disjunction here. The position of this sentence within the structure of the discourse corresponds to the position of the sentence ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], and corresponds to the position of the sentence ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7], and so on. The demonstrative here does not point to individual persons, but to a category in which the attributes mentioned above are gathered, such that their conditions have become fully manifest, until they are as though present before the listener, so that they are pointed at. This usage occurs frequently in eloquent speech.
There is no indication in this demonstrative of distance or nearness that would convey contempt arising from distance, because this is among the demonstratives most commonly used in Arabic speech, so there is no deviation in it that would indicate a purpose. Moreover, the thing referred to here is not perceptible such that it would have a specific rank, so that deviation from its wording would be for the sake of a second meaning. Compare His saying ﴿That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], where the Book is near to the one reciting its verses, yet the expression is a deviation from pointing to the near with a demonstrative for the distant, and it conveys exaltation. The reverse of this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:
"Whenever this death comes, it will not find a need of mine unfulfilled except that I have fulfilled it."
Here death is distant from him, so it should have been pointed to with the distant demonstrative, but he deviated to the demonstrative of the near in order to show his contempt for it.
Page 298
The verb ishtara (to buy) is a form of the reflexive derivation (iftial) from shara, and its base verb sharā, which means "to sell," just as ishtara means "to buy" (ibtā'a). Both ishtara and ibtā'a are reflexive (muṭāwi') forms of their base verb. The lexicographers noted that the doer of this reflexive form is the one who accepts the action and undertakes it, and by this they indicated that he takes something out of desire for it. Since the meaning of sale requires a taker and a giver, each of the two is seller and buyer depending on the perspective. The verb "sold" (bā'a) is considered primarily with regard to giving, while the verb "bought" (ibtā'a) is considered primarily with regard to taking. If the speaker regards the party as taking what has come into his hand, he expresses it with "buyer" (mubtā') and "purchaser" (mushtarī); if he regards him as giving up what has left his hand as the price, he expresses it with "seller" (bā'i') and "vendor" (shārī). By this the two verbs proceed along a single pattern.
Many lexicographers have stated that sharā is used with the meaning of ishtarā, and what emboldened them to this was a careless reading of His saying ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams﴾ [Yusuf: 20], where they took the pronoun to refer to the Egyptians, although its referent is clear and near, namely the caravan (sayyārah) in His saying ﴿And a caravan came﴾ [Yusuf: 19], meaning they sold him. Sufficient as evidence for this is His saying ﴿And they were among those who had no interest in him﴾ [Yusuf: 20]; as for the one who bought him, he was among those who desired him. Do you not see His saying to his wife, ﴿Make his residence honorable﴾ [Yusuf: 21]? On these two perspectives regarding the verbs of buying and selling, their transitivity to the object was as follows: they both transitively govern the primary intended object directly, and govern the other by the preposition bi-, so one says "he sold his horse for a thousand" and "he bought the horse of so-and-so for a thousand," because the horse is the thing for which the contract was made, since the one who brought it out to sell knew that people desire it, and the one who came to buy it is likewise.
The use of "buying" here is a metonymic figurative usage (majaz mursal) through the relation of necessary consequence ('alaqat al-luzum): it applies "buying" to its second necessary consequence, which is eagerness for something and disinterest in its opposite, that is, they were eager for error and disinterested in guidance, since there was no exchange of one thing for another in what the hypocrites did, for they had not previously been guided.
It is also possible that "buying" is used with the meaning of exchange (istibdal), which is its first necessary consequence, and its use with this consequence is well known. Bashama ibn Hazn said:
"We are the sons of Nahshal; we do not claim a father other than him, and he does not exchange us (yashrīnā) for the sons."
That is, he does not sell us, i.e., replace us. And 'Antarah ibn al-Akhras, one of the poets of the Hamasa, said:
"And one who, if you sell a dwelling for another, you have alighted by his command and move by it."
Page 299
That is, if you exchange one house for another. This differs from the saying of Abu al-Najm:
"I took by the thick-haired one a bald head, and by the long-lived one a fine-looking old man, as the Muslim bought when he became a Christian."
Here the sense would be that their mingling with the Muslims and their display of faith is a state resembling the condition of the guided, in which they clothed themselves; when they went privately to their devils, they cast it off and exchanged it for the state of error. On this second interpretation it is also valid for "buying" to be a metaphor (isti'arah), by likening those two states to the condition of one who buys something that was not lawful for him, which he accepted; this is the view he approved in al-Kashshaf.
The relative pronoun in His saying ﴿those who bought﴾ carries the customary (al-'urf) sense with the definite article of genus, so the construction conveys restriction (qasr) of the predicate to the subject. This is a claimed (ida'i) restriction, on the basis that they reached the utmost limit in buying error and in eagerness for it, since they combined disbelief, folly, deception, corruption, and mockery of the guided.

﴿So their commerce did not profit, nor were they guided.﴾
The particle fa' (so) makes the absence of profit, conjoined by it, and the absence of guidance, conjoined to it, follow from the buying of error in exchange for guidance, because both are the result of the aforementioned buying in existence and manifestation; for when they bought error in exchange for guidance, they bought what does not benefit and gave up what benefits, so it is inevitable that they be losers and that it be established that they were not guided. Although the absence of guidance preceded the buying of error in exchange for guidance, or is identical with it, or is its cause, nevertheless, since it is an absence, its manifestation to people in existence occurs only when its effect appears, and that effect is this buying; when its effect appears, the cause becomes clear to people. Therefore it is correct that it is ordered by the particle of sequence (fa'), and it resembles the final cause (al-'illah al-ghā'iyyah). For this reason He expressed it with ﴿they were not guided﴾ rather than ﴿they did not become guided﴾, because "mā kānū" is more emphatic in negation, as it indicates that the negation of guidance from them is a rooted, prior, ancient matter, since kāna indicates the attribution of its predicate to its subject from the past; so negating being in the past tense was more fitting for this consequence.
Profit (ribh) is the success of trade and the coincidence of desire for goods at a higher amount than the prices with which the merchant bought them; and "profit" is also applied to the wealth obtained by the merchant over and above his capital.
Tijarah (commerce), with a kasra on its first letter, is on the pattern fi'alah, which is the pattern of crafts; the meaning of tijarah is the undertaking of buying goods for the purpose of selling them at a price
Page 300
higher than what was paid, so that one may gain from that surplus what he spends or accumulates as wealth. Since this does not succeed without persistence and renewal, it was given the pattern of crafts. The negation of profit in the verse is a comparison of the condition of the hypocrites, who, having aimed at an end through hypocrisy, saw their efforts fail and their purposes lost, to the condition of merchants who gained no profit from their commerce. Therefore there is no regard for capital in commerce, such that it might be said that if they did not profit, the benefit of the capital remained for them. It is answered that the negation of profit implies the loss of capital, because it is consumed in expenditure on food and clothing, since all this is not considered; for metaphor relies on what is intended from the aspect of resemblance, and it does not require resemblance in all matters, as is established in the science of rhetoric (bayan).
The attribution of profit to commerce occurred so that it could be negated of it, because profit, being caused by commerce, and the one who profits being the merchant, it is correct to attribute it to commerce, since commerce is its cause; this is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli). For, were it not for this metaphorical attribution, it would not be correct to negate of a thing what everyone knows is not among its attributes, since that would become informing of the known by necessity. So do not suppose that the negation in such a case is literal and abandon it; rather, the negation of profit from commerce is a fixed and established fact, because commerce is not described as profitable. Likewise you say in such expressions as Jarir's verse:
"And I slept, though the night of the riding camels is not a sleeper."
In contrast to your saying "its night is not long," here the negation is a rational metaphor, because it is a branch of considering the attribute of commerce as leading to loss, and describing it as profitable is a metaphor. The rule for this is that in negation you look at what is negated, were it affirmed: if you find its affirmation to be a rational metaphor, then make its negation likewise; otherwise make its negation literal, because only what can be affirmed can be negated.
This is the approach by which the verifier al-Taftazani resolved the matter in al-Mutawwal, and he departed from it in the marginal notes to al-Kashshaf, though the former is more sound than what he turned to.
The saying ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾ has provided a supporting elaboration (tarshih) for the metaphor in "they bought," for the essence of tarshih is that the metaphor is followed by what suits it, whether that supporting element is literal, such that nothing is gained from it except strengthening the metaphor, as when you say "he has a long hand" or "he is a lion with bloodied claws," or whether the supporting element is distinct, or borrowed for another meaning that is among the suitable features of the first metaphor, whether or not it is also fitting to stand alone as a metaphor, as in this verse, where the negation of profit is a supporting elaboration of "they bought."
Similar is the verse of a poet, related by Ibn al-A'rabi, as in Asas al-Balaghah of al-Zamakhshari, without attribution:
Page 301
"When I saw the eagle had overcome Ibn Dayah, and had built its nest in his two cheeks, my chest was stirred for him."
Here, having likened gray hair to an eagle and black hair to a crow, the poet made the coming of gray hair into the two temples of blackness like a bird nesting in the place of another bird, which is valid. Or the supporting element may not be fitting except together with the first metaphor, as in the verse of one of the valiant Arabs about his mother, which he recited in al-Kashshaf, without identifying its speaker:
"And the mother of al-Rudayn, though she boasts, is not one who knows the ways of the noble.
When Satan has crept into her back, we have dug her out with the twin rope."
Here, having borrowed "qassa'a" (crept in, like a lizard into its burrow) for the entry of Satan, that is, his whispering, which is a good metaphor, since he likened Satan to a lizard (dabb) that enters to whisper, and its entry through its customary entrance, the qasa'a (the hole of the burrow). He made their remedy and the removal of his whisperings like tanaffuq, that is, seeking the lizard's exit from its emergency hole (naafiqa') after the qasa'a has been blocked against it; and this second image is not good except as a consequence of the first. The verse under discussion is not of this type. His saying ﴿and they were not guided﴾ is already known from His saying ﴿they bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ up to ﴿and they were not guided﴾, so it is determined that the guidance negated is guidance in its original linguistic sense, which is knowing the path that leads to the goal, and it is not in the legal sense mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿they bought error in exchange for guidance﴾. So there is no repetition in meaning, and it is not objected that when He reported of them that they bought error in exchange for guidance, it was already known that no guidance remained among them.

The negation of guidance is a metonymy for the loss of purpose, meaning that they wasted what they strove for, and did not know what would lead to the good of the other (world) nor what would harm the Muslims. This is a rebuke against them for foolishness of opinion and recklessness, and it is, as you have known from what preceded, functioning in the manner of the reason (ʿillah) for the non-profit of the trade. Thus the poor course of their conduct, even in their disbelief, was likened to the poor conduct of one who wants profit and so falls into loss. Therefore His saying ﴿and they were not guided﴾ is an allegorical depiction (tamthīliyyah), and it is valid to take from it also a metonymy for loss and the wasting of everything, because whoever is not guided has wasted the profit and has wasted the capital by his bad conduct.

[Page 302]

﴿Their parable is like the parable of one who kindled a fire﴾

Having followed the detailed description of their attributes, he (Allah) depicted all of them together in a single image, likening their condition to a tangible form. This is the method of *tashbih al-tamthil* (representational simile, in which a composite state is likened to a composite image), attaching those intelligible conditions to concrete things, since the soul is more inclined toward the tangible.

It also completes the exposition by gathering scattered elements into one hearing, with the lengthening of the wording, in one image, because summarising after detailing has an effect on the hearers' souls. Restating what has preceded in the mind in an image different from the one previously depicted is also valued, because the renewal of the image in the soul is more beloved than its repetition.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: The Arabs' coining of parables and the scholars' citing of examples and analogies is a matter that is not hidden in bringing out the hidden meanings and lifting the veils from realities, until it shows you the imagined in the form of the verified, the supposed in the guise of the certain, and the absent as if it were witnessed.

And, as evidence for what the totality of those attributes contains of evil condition, failure of effort, and corrupt outcome, one of the benefits of simile is the intent to make the likened thing appear abominable. Also, to bring close what is in their situation in religion of contrast and opposition, between a beautiful outward appearance and an ugly inward reality, by means of a strange state among the states of the world; for one of the benefits of simile is showing the possibility of the likened thing and making its strange features analogous to their counterparts in the thing used for comparison.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: For some purpose, Allah the Exalted has multiplied His parables in His Clear Book, and they have spread in the speech of His Messenger (ﷺ) and in the speech of the prophets and the wise. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And these parables We strike for people, but none understands them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43]. End of quotation.

*Tamthil* (parabolic illustration) is a noble and wondrous method among the methods of the eloquent, which none reaches the excellences of except its elite. Here it falls under the category of simile, not metaphor, because it contains the mention of the likened thing, the thing used for comparison, and the particle of comparison, which is the word *mathal* ("parable").

The clause ﴿Their parable is like the parable of one who kindled a fire﴾ is a sentence that occupies the position of explanation, confirmation, and summation relative to the preceding sentences. Thus there is complete connection between it and what precedes it, and for this reason it is detached and not joined by a conjunction. The situation whose depiction is intended will be explained at the end of the exegesis of the verse.

The root meaning of *mathal* (pronounced with two fathas) is "counterpart" and "resemblance." It is also said *mithl* (with a kasra on the mim and a sukun on the tha'), and *mathil*, just as it is said *shibh*, *shabah*, and *shabih*; and *badal*, *bidl*, and *badil*. There is no fourth word among these in the pattern *fa'al*, *fi'l*, and *fa'il* with one meaning.

[Page 303]

The word *mathal* (with two fathas) has been specifically used for a strange and remarkable state, because it is such that it illustrates things for people, clarifies them, and likens them, whether or not it is itself likened, as in His saying ﴿the description of Paradise﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35]. It is also used for a saying uttered in a strange situation, which is remembered and spreads among people because of its eloquence and originality. So people continue to recall the situation in which that saying was uttered, following its mention. How many a strange situation has occurred and been forgotten, because no eloquent saying was uttered in it that would make it remembered by its mention, and so it is called a *mathal*. The Arabs' proverbs are a branch of their eloquence and have been specially compiled, and they define it as a saying whose application is likened to its origin; I shall mention this shortly.

So it is apparent that the application of *mathal* to a striking saying that circulates among people, uttered by its speaker in a strange situation, is an application derived from the use of the name *mathal* for the strange situation. They hardly ever coin a *mathal* or consider it fit for circulation and worthy of currency unless it is a saying containing eloquence and distinction in the excellence of its wording, its conciseness, and the abundance of its meaning. The *mathal* is thus a rare saying, not among the common sayings of ordinary speech, but one of the outstanding utterances of eloquence. For this reason it is described as *gharib* (strange), i.e., rare, like their saying: "The summer, you have wasted the milk," and their saying: "An order is not obeyed for a short man." You will learn the reason for this.

Since the use of the word *mathal* with a fatha and sukun has become widespread for a strange-circumstanced situation, the eloquent, when they wish to liken a composite state to another composite state (that is, two attributes abstracted from a multiplicity), use the word *mathal* on the side of the likened thing and the thing used for comparison together, or on the side of one of them, and they attach the *kaf* (like) and similar particles of comparison to the thing used for comparison from among them. They do not apply this to simple simile, so they do not say "the likeness of so-and-so is like the lion." Rarely do they liken a composite state to a composite state while relying only on the *kaf*, as in His saying ﴿like one who stretches out his hands toward water so that it reaches his mouth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 14]. Rather, they usually mention the word *mathal* on both sides, as in this verse, and sometimes they mention the word

[Page 304]

*mathal* on only one side, as in His saying ﴿The likeness of the life of this world is only like water We sent down from the sky﴾ [Yunus: 24], etc. This is so that it will immediately occur to the hearer that the intent is the likening of a state to a state, not of an essence to an essence, nor of a state to an essence. Thus the word *mathal* in likening a configuration has come to be detached from its original imposition and used in the sense of "state." For this reason they do not dispense with the particle of comparison even when the word *mathal* is present. So the *kaf* in His saying (kamathali) indicates comparison and is not superfluous, as al-Radi asserted in his commentary on *al-Hajibiyya*.
