'Abd al-Hakim followed him in his remark on the Qur'anic phrase ﴿or like a rainstorm﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], adhering to the original imposition and disregarding the usage. Do you not see how the word *mathal* was dispensed with when conjoined in His saying ﴿or like a rainstorm﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], but the *kaf* was not dispensed with?

From the widespread use of the word *mathal*, the scholars of rhetoric (*'ulama' al-bayan*) borrowed their technical term for naming the composite simile *tashbih al-tamthil*, and for naming the use of a composite expression that indicates a configuration abstracted from a multiplicity, in other than what it was imposed for, as a unit by the relation of resemblance, *isti'ara tamthiliyya* (representational metaphor). The explanation of some of this has already preceded at His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. I have traced their discourse and found that representational simile is subject to what befalls simple simile, so it comes in four types.

The first is what is explicitly stated with the particle of comparison, or in which it is omitted, in the manner of eloquent simile, as in this verse, and in His saying ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16], if we estimate "those" as "like those who have bought," as we previously stated.

The second is what follows the manner of the explicit representational metaphor: they mention the expression that indicates by correspondence the configuration used for comparison, and omit what indicates the configuration being likened. An example is the well-known proverb: "I see you advancing one foot and delaying the other."

The third: a representational *makniyya* (implicit), which is that a configuration is likened to a configuration, but the expression indicating the configuration likened to is not mentioned; instead it is alluded to by something necessarily and famously associated with it. I used to consider as an example of this type specifically the proverbs known by this title, such as "The summer, you have wasted the milk" and "By my hand, not by the hand of 'Amr," and others like them, for they are expressions uttered on occasions and became famous and spread until their mention indicates the situations in which they were uttered, even if the expression indicating the state is not mentioned. The reason for their fame will come later. Then no example of the implicit representational simile outside the category of proverbs occurred to me, until one day I attended a funeral. When they had buried the deceased and finished covering him with dust, some people cried out with the words: "O God, there is no life but the life of the Hereafter, so forgive the Ansar and the Muhajirat." I said: Those who established this saying in such a situation intended nothing but to liken the condition of their digging for the deceased to the condition of those who used to dig the trench with the Prophet (ﷺ), since they used to repeat this saying, as recorded in the books of Sunna. By this comparison the intent was that their digging should be like the digging of the trench in the Battle of the Confederates, by the common factor of hoping for acceptance with Allah the Exalted. So they did not mention what indicates the thing used for comparison, but they concealed it and alluded to it by something necessarily associated with it by which it is known, namely the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying of that statement. Then I came upon the words of Ahmad ibn 'Abd Rabbih al-Andalusi:

*Say to him who blames me for my youthful folly: "Step aside a little from the road."*

I saw this as implicit representational simile, for he omitted the thing used for comparison, which is the state of one who obstructs a traveller on his path, blocking him and preventing him from passing; and he brought something from the necessary features of this state, which is the traveller's saying to the obstructer: "Step aside from the road."

The fourth is the subordinate representational simile (*tamthiliyya taba'iyya*), as in the words of Abu 'Ata al-Sindi:

*I remembered you while the Khatti spear passes between us, and the dark lances have already drunk from me.*

He affirmed "drinking" for the spears, likening them to the state of one who drinks: what they strike of the blood of the wounded time after time, as if they were never quenched by what they first struck; then he used *nahilat* (drank) in a subordinate manner.

Among this category, according to al-Taftazani, is the metaphor in *'ala* (upon) in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], and the discussion of it has already preceded there.

As for the *mathal* which is a saying whose application is likened to its origin, which I promised to mention just now: the meaning of likening its application to its origin is that a situation arises that has a resemblance to the situation in which that saying was uttered. The speaker recalls the situation in which the saying was uttered, likens the situation that has arisen to it, and utters the saying that was spoken during the situation of the thing used for comparison, to remind the hearer of that situation and that the situation of today is similar to it. The utterance of that saying, which was spoken in that situation, is made the sign of mentioning it.

On careful reflection you will find that this act belongs to the category of implicit representational metaphor, because those expressions called proverbs have circulated and been transmitted among the eloquent in those events, so they are necessarily among the necessary features of the situations used for comparison, due to their being joined with them in people's minds. So they are customary associations of these situations among the people of literature, and they have become among the attendants of those situations. Mentioning those proverbs was a symbol referring to consideration of the situations in which they were spoken. For this reason it is impossible to change them from their wording as transmitted, because if they are changed they no longer remain in their preserved and familiar wording, and their association in minds with the images of the events in which they were said disappears, so their mention no longer serves as a symbol for the thing used for comparison, of which they are necessarily attendants. In this there is what suffices without seeking the reason for the Arabs' caution against changing proverbs, so that they are spared the confusion in judging between the author of *al-Kashshaf* and the author of *al-Miftah*. For the author of *al-Kashshaf* made the cause of preventing proverbs from being changed to be the strangeness they contain, and he said: "They did not coin a *mathal*, nor did they consider it fit for circulation or worthy of currency, unless it was a saying containing strangeness from some aspect. For this reason it was preserved and protected from change." So its commentators differed about his intended meaning of strangeness. Al-Tibi said: Strangeness is the obscurity and rarity of speech, and this is either with respect to meaning or with respect to wording. As for the first, it is like a saying in which the trace of contradiction appears, though it is not a contradiction, such as the saying of al-Hakam ibn 'Abd Yaghuth: "Many a shot from one who is not a shooter." That is, many a shot that hits its mark from one who is not a skilled archer. And His saying ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179], since it made killing into life. As for the second, that there are strange words in it that the common people do not use, such as the saying of Hubab ibn al-Mundhir:

*I am its little stump that is rubbed smooth, and its palm-tree trunk propped up.*

Or there is ellipsis and implied omission, as in "a throw from one who is not a thrower" (ramyatun min ghayri rāmin). Or there is mushākala (correspondence of terms), as in "as you judge, so you will be judged" (kamā tadīnu tudānu), where he intended "as you do, so you will be repaid."

Some of them explained gharāba (strangeness, uniqueness) as balāgha (eloquence) and faṣāḥa (clarity), until it became wondrous. In my view, he did not mean by gharāba anything other than that it is a unique, singular saying, since the gharīb is the opposite of the ma'lūf (the familiar), and gharāba is the absence of familiarity — he means the absence of familiarity with it in terms of its elevated rank.

As for the author of al-Miftāh, he made the prohibition of altering it (the proverb) due to its occurrence by way of metaphor (istiʿāra). He said: "When the figurative comparison (al-tashbīh al-tamthīlī) becomes widespread and its use by way of metaphor is well known, it is called only a proverb (mathal), and nothing else." End of quote.

Al-Taftazani and al-Sayyid inclined to his method. You have known its secret and its explanation from what we have clarified.

Because proverbs occur by way of metaphor, they are not altered from the wording in which they appeared originally, in terms of masculine and feminine forms and other such features.

So the meaning of their definition of the proverb with this usage — "a saying whose place of striking (maḍrib) is likened to its source (mawrid)" — is as follows: its maḍrib is the comparand situation (al-ḥāla al-mushabbaha). It is called maḍrib because it stands in the position of the place where that saying is struck, i.e., placed, i.e., uttered. One says: "the proverb was struck" (ḍuriba al-mathal), meaning it was likened and represented. God the Exalted said: ﴿that He should strike a parable, whatever﴾ [al-Baqara: 26]. As for its mawrid, it is the comparison situation (al-ḥāla al-mushabbaha bihā), which is the situation in which that saying appeared, i.e., was issued at the time of its occurrence. It is called mawrid because it stands in the position of the water-place which those who draw water come to. And one says: "the travelling proverbs" (al-amthāl al-sā'ira), i.e., the widespread ones which people pass on and circulate among the various tribes and lands, so that it is as if they travel from one country to another.

﴿Those who kindled a fire﴾ is singular, meaning a single comparand, because the kindler of a fire is one person, and there is no sense in a group gathering to kindle one fire. Do not be troubled by the fact that the situation of the comparand is the situation of a group of hypocrites: the likening of one configuration to another relates only to depicting the comparand configuration by the comparison configuration, not to its being in the same form as the comparand configuration. For the intent is to liken the state of the hypocrites in the appearance of the trace of faith and its light — together with its being followed by misguidance and its persistence — to the state of one who kindled a fire. Istawqada means awqada (kindled), so the sīn and tāʾ in it are for emphasis, as they are in God's words ﴿so their Lord responded to them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 195], and in the saying "the matter became clear" (istabāna al-amr). This is like the saying of one of the Banū Bawlān of Ṭayy in the Ḥamāsa:

"We kindle arrows with the lowland, and we hunt souls built on generosity"

He meant: fuel that falls with intensity at the time of shooting. Likewise, in the verse, the purpose is to present the representation of the state of the hypocrites in displaying faith through the state of one seeking fuel — indeed, it is the state of the one who kindles.

* * *

God's words: ﴿So when it illuminated what was around him, God took away their light﴾ are a consequence (mufarra') of istawqada. And lammā (when) is a particle indicating that one thing occurs at the occurrence of another, so the occurrence of its answer is concurrent with the occurrence of its condition. This is the meaning of the scholars' saying: "a particle of existence for existence" — i.e., a particle indicating the existence of the answer for the existence of its condition, meaning that its answer is like an effect (ma'lūl) for the existence of its condition, whether it is from the ordering of the effect upon the cause, or from the ordering of the conventional result upon the cause, or from the ordering of the concurrent upon the concurrence of the prepared (al-muhayya'), or the concurrent occurring by chance. All of these are usages occurring in the speech of the Arabs and in the Qur'an.

An example of the ordering of the effect upon the cause: "When its humours decayed, he had fever" (lammā ta'affanat akhlāṭuhu ḥumma). An example of the ordering of the result upon the cause:

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them﴾ [Hūd: 77], and the saying of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdī Karib:

"When I saw our women scrambling over the goat-hair (of the tent) in haste, / I attacked their ram, and I found no escape from fighting the ram."

An example of the concurrent prepared: the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"So when we passed the courtyard of the tribe, and he (the mount) turned us toward the belly of a valley with a winding sand-dune, / I bent her head by its two sides, and she swayed toward me, the slender-waisted, soft-ankled one."

An example of the concurrent occurring by chance: ﴿When Our messengers came to Abraham with good tidings﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 31], ﴿they said, "Peace"﴾ [Hūd: 69]; and His saying ﴿When they entered upon Joseph, he took his brother to himself﴾ [Yūsuf: 69]. So whoever thinks that lammā indicates causality, deceived by their saying "existence for existence" — taking the lām in their expression to mean causation — has committed an error and has not found in the speech of the leading scholars any lapse. And aḍāʾa (to illuminate) comes transitively, and that is the original usage, since its bare form is ḍāʾa; then its hamza is for transitivity, as in Abū al-Ṭamaḥān al-Qaynī's saying:

"Their noble lineages and faces illuminated the darkness of the night, until the piercer pierced the trunk."

It also comes intransitively with the meaning of ḍāʾa, so its hamza is for becoming (ṣayrūra), i.e., it became possessing light, and thus equals ḍāʾa. Like Imru' al-Qays describing lightning:

"Its gleam lights up, or the lamps of a monk, which olive oil with twisted wicks has tilted."

The verse admits both: so when the fire illuminated the regions around it — which is the meaning of the rising of its rays and the radiance of its flame — then mā ḥawlahu is an object (mafʿūl) of aḍāʾat, which is the more immediate reading.

It may also be from the intransitive aḍāʾa, i.e., the fire illuminated, i.e., it blazed and its light increased in itself; and in this case mā ḥawlahu is a locative adverb (ẓarf) for the fire, i.e., the light of the fire occurred around it, not far from it. Ḥawlahu is an adverb of nearby place, and it need not be understood as encompassing. So ḥawlahu here means ladayhi (beside him). Whoever imagines that mā ḥawlahu requires encompassment falls into difficulties from which he finds no escape except with great hardship.

The plural pronoun in His words ﴿with their light﴾, despite being adjacent to the singular pronoun in ﴿mā ḥawlahu﴾, observes the comparand situation (al-ḥāla al-mushabbaha), which is the situation of the hypocrites, and not the comparison situation (al-ḥāla al-mushabbah bihā), which is the situation of the single kindler, in a wonderful manner of returning to the primary purpose, namely the extinguishing of the light of faith from them. So it returns to the hypocrites and not to "the one who" (alladhī), somewhat like the return of the last part upon the first part (radd al-ʿajuz ʿalā al-ṣadr), so it resembles the stripping of the single metaphor (tajrīd al-istiʿāra al-mufrada), and it is of the kind of tafnīn (variation of style), like Ṭarafa's saying:

"And in the tribe is a dark-eyed gazelle, shaking the hair of the sand-coloured, displaying a double strand of pearls and emerald."

This is a wonderful return. Close to it is the return that occurs by way of parenthetical insertion in His later words ﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqara: 19]. Its beauty is that the representation combined mention of the comparand and mention of the comparison, so the speaker has the choice in observing both of them, because the description applies to both. Thus that part is one type in both the comparand and the comparison, so what is established for the comparison is treated as established for the comparand.

This requires that the clause ﴿God took away their light﴾ be the answer of (lammā), so that the plural pronouns in ﴿with their light and left them﴾ are a departure from the expected form, since the expected form would be "God took away its light and left it." That is why the word "light" was chosen here instead of "fire" mentioned at the start, to alert to the transition from the representation to the reality, to indicate that God removed the light of faith from the hearts of the hypocrites. This is a wonderful conciseness, as if it were said: "When it illuminated, God took away its fire," so likewise God took away their light. This is a style for which the Arabs have no precedent, so it is among the styles of inimitability (i'jāz). Close to it is His saying: ﴿Nay, they said, "We found our fathers upon a community, and we are guided by their footsteps"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]; ﴿And likewise, We did not send before you any warner into a town except that its affluent ones said, "We found our fathers upon a community, and we are following in their footsteps"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23]; ﴿He said, "Even if I brought you something better guidance than that upon which you found your fathers?" They said, "Indeed, we are, in what you have been sent with, disbelievers"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 24]. So His saying "you have been sent" is a quotation of the address of the peoples of the messengers in answer to Muhammad's ﷺ question to his people with His saying "even if I brought you" [al-Zukhruf: 24]. By this, what is in this verse agrees with what is in the verse after it, His saying ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾ [al-Baqara: 19], since its return is determined to some of the comparison and not to the comparand.

The author of al-Kashshaf permitted that His saying ﴿God took away their light﴾ be a new sentence (isti'nāf), and that the representation ended at His saying ﴿So when it illuminated what was around him﴾, and that the answer of lammā is omitted, indicated by the resumed sentence. This is close to what I have mentioned, except that the consideration differs.

The meaning of ﴿God took away their light﴾: He extinguished their fire. He expressed it with "light" because it is the intended goal of kindling. He attributed the removal to God the Exalted because it happened without a cause of wind, rain, or extinguishing by an extinguisher. The Arabs and people attribute to God's name a matter whose cause is not clear, as already mentioned at His saying ﴿and He extends them in their transgression﴾ [al-Baqara: 15].

صفحة ٣١٠

The transitive form with bāʾ (dhahaba bihi) is more emphatic than the transitive form with hamza (adhhaba). This emphasis in transitivity with bāʾ arises from the original usage: the original sense of dhahaba bihi is that the two went away together, so it is stronger in establishing the going of the companion, as in His saying ﴿when they took him away﴾ [Yūsuf: 15]. And adhhabahu means he made him go by his command or sending. Since one who wishes to remove a person's going, removing it without doubt, takes charge of that himself until he is certain of the execution of his command, dhahaba bihi came to carry the meaning of adhhabahu. Then this was forgotten through frequent use, so they say dhahaba bihi and the like, even when he did not accompany him in going, as in His saying ﴿He brings the sun from the east﴾ [al-Baqara: 258], and His saying ﴿and brought you from the desert﴾ [Yūsuf: 100]. Then the hamza was made merely for transitivity in usage, so they say "gambling took away the money of so-and-so," and they do not mean that it went with him. But they were careful not to use that except in a context emphasizing the removal, so the emphasis remained in it. The singular pronoun in His saying "what was around him" observes the comparison situation.

The choice of the word "light" in ﴿God took away their light﴾ rather than "illumination" or "fire" is because the word "light" is most suitable: what resembles fire from the comparand situation is the outward manifestations of Islam that they display. The expression of Islam as "light" has become widespread in the Qur'an, so choosing the word "light" here is like stripping the metaphor, since it is more suitable to the comparand situation; and he expressed what corresponds to it in the comparison situation with a word that suits both, or is more suitable to the comparand in the speaker's terminology, as we have indicated in the aspect of the plural pronoun in His saying "with their light."

* * *

﴿And He left them in darkness, not seeing﴾

This clause includes a confirmation of the content of "God took away their light," because whoever loses his light remains in darkness and does not see. Its purpose is to add clarity to the state into which they came, for the explicit indication has an impression in the hearer's mind that the implicit indication does not have. His saying "God took away their light" indicates that when they kindled a fire and it went out, the benefit was lost and their efforts failed. But the hearer may be distracted from what they came to in that state, so His saying after that "and He left them in darkness, not seeing" serves as a reminder of that and an alert to it.

For they do not intend from eloquence anything but intensity in depicting meanings, and for this reason they elaborate, liken, represent, describe the known, bring the state, enumerate reports and attributes. So this is wonderful elaboration, as in Ṭarafa's saying:

"My companions are white like stars, and a singing-girl who comes to us between a striped cloak and a silken garment."

صفحة ٣١١

For His saying "comes to us" etc. indicates no more than depicting the state of the singing-girl and beautifying her companionship. This clause also indicates that they did not return to illumination from afar, on what is in His saying "and He left them" of the indication of their humiliation, and what is in the plural "darkness" of the indication of the intensity of darkness. This is an additional benefit beyond what is implicitly derived from "God took away their light," and beyond what the plural "darknesses" requires of the estimation of three comparisons for three misguidances among their misguidances, as will come.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 17 (part 3 of 3):

In view of this additional consideration beyond restating the content of the preceding clause, it is conjoined to the clause (*'uṭifat 'alā al-jumla*) and not separated from it.

The reality of *tark* (leaving, abandoning) is that a person separates from something that was previously with him in a place, and leaves it in that condition. Often they mention the state (*ḥāl*) in which the agent left the object. In this usage it frequently becomes a *majāz* (figurative usage) for the meaning of *ṣayyara* (to make, render) or *ja'ala* (to make). Al-Nabigha said:

*"So do not leave me to threats, as if I were, among the people, a mangy camel smeared with tar."*

That is, do not make me (*lā tuṣayyirannī*) into this likeness. And 'Antara's saying:

*"Every abundant spring has poured upon it, and so they left every hollow like a dirham."*

He means "made them." Most often, in this usage, it is used as a metonym for devaluing its object, as in the verse of al-Nabigha, or for belittling it, as in this verse.

The difference between what is considered as containing the meaning of *ṣayyara* such that its second accusative is an object (*mafʿūl*), and what is considered such that the second accusative is a state (*ḥāl*), is this: if the intent is to inform of abandonment and withdrawal from it, then the second accusative is a state; but if the intent is first to that second accusative, which is the locus of the benefit, then the second accusative is an object and carries the sense of a statement. Neither of them, then, admits any meaning other than that, even if the wording admits it.

The plural *ẓulumāt* (darknesses) is used to express the intensity of the darkness, like His saying: ﴿Say: Who rescues you from the darknesses of land and sea?﴾ [al-An'am: 63], and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Injustice is darknesses on the Day of Resurrection." For plurality was, in common usage, the cause of strength, so they applied it to absolute strength even where there is no multiplicity or abundance, like the word *kathīr* (many), as will come at His saying: ﴿Call not today for one destruction but call for many destructions﴾ [al-Furqan: 14] in surah al-Furqan. From this is the mention of the plural pronoun for glorification referring to one, and the first-person pronoun accompanied by others for glorification, and the plural form is of that kind. It has been said that the word *al-ẓalama* (the wrongdoers, in the singular form) is not mentioned in the Qur'an. Perhaps the word *ẓulumāt* is more commonly used in eloquent speech. Its explanation will come at His saying: ﴿And made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1] in surah al-An'am. This is unlike His saying:

[p. 312]

﴿In three darknesses﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], for multiplicity is intended there by the indicator of its qualification with *thalāth* (three). But the eloquence of the Qur'an and of the speech of the Messenger, peace be upon him, does not permit the use of a plural not intended to convey an added meaning beyond its singular form. In this verse it is determined that the plural *ẓulumāt* refers to states of the hypocrites, each state of which is suitable to be likened to darkness. These are: the state of disbelief, the state of lying, the state of mocking the believers, and what follows these states of the effects of hypocrisy. This simile is a figurative depiction (*tamthīl*) of the condition of the hypocrites in their vacillation between the manifestations of faith and the inner reality of disbelief. So the basis of comparison (*wajh al-shabah*) is the appearance of a beneficial matter followed by its disappearance before benefit is gained from it. For in their outward display of Islam with the believers there is a semblance of the goodness and radiance of faith, because Islam has light and blessing. Then they soon return, when they are alone with their devils, and that departs from them, and they return to the darkness of disbelief more severely than they were before, because they were in disbelief and then they became in disbelief, lying, and what branches off from hypocrisy of blameworthy qualities. For one who kindles a fire in the dark seeks to see things, and when the fire is extinguished he becomes more bewildered than at the start, because the light of the fire had accustomed his sight. So the effect of darkness appears more strongly the second time, and disbelief becomes firmly rooted in them. By this the subtle point of the expression is made clear in the clause *lā yubṣirūn* (they do not see), to depict the state of one whose light has gone out after having been illuminated by it.

The object of *lā yubṣirūn* is omitted for the purpose of generalizing the negation of visible things. So the verb is treated as intransitive and no object is posited for it, as if it were said: "There is no perception of sight for them," like the saying of al-Buhturi:

*"The grief of his envious ones and the rage of his enemies is that a seer sees and a hearing listener hears."*

The basis of comparison has been left implicit in the likening of the state of the hypocrites, relying on the listener's discernment, for he extracts it from the totality of what has preceded of the explanation of their state, beginning from His saying: ﴿And among the people is one who says: "We believe in God"﴾ [al-Baqara: 8], etc. And among what the two parables include is an indication of the aspects of resemblance between the parts of their states and the parts of the state being likened. For their outward display of faith by their saying ﴿We believe in God﴾ [al-Baqara: 8], their saying ﴿We are only reformers﴾ [al-Baqara: 11], and their saying when meeting the believers, "We believe," are good states and manifestations that appear on the hypocrites when they attend the Prophet's (ﷺ) assembly and when they feign Islam, prayer, and charity with the Muslims. Good speech and upright conduct issue from them, and the prophetic lights shine upon them, so that the light of faith nearly penetrates into their souls. But soon that good state is followed by a state contrary to it when they disperse from those pure assemblies and withdraw to their inner circles of great men or followers, and so the blameworthy states return to them: [p. 313] practicing disbelief, deceiving the believers, harboring rancor against them, mocking them, and describing them as foolish. That feigning and that reversal are depicted by the state of one who kindled a fire and then its light went away from him.

Among the marvels of this parable is that, along with its composition of the image likened and its contrast with the composed image of their state, it is capable of being analyzed into single similitudes: each part of the image of their states corresponds to a single part of the image likened. Thus their listening to the Qur'an is likened to the kindling of fire, and this includes the likening of the Qur'an in guiding people to good and truth to fire in illuminating paths for travelers. Their return to their disbelief is likened to the going away of the fire's light, and their disbelief is likened to darknesses, and they are likened to people whose sight has been cut off.

Predicate (akhbar) of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), a pronoun referring back to what the pronoun in ﴿mathaluhum﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] refers to. It cannot refer to "alladhi istawqada" (the one who kindled), because the beginning and end of the simile would not fit together: His saying ﴿like the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] requires that the one kindling be someone who sees, since otherwise kindling would not be possible from him. Omitting the subject in this context is a common usage among the Arabs: when they mention a person described by attributes or predicates, they treat him as though he were already known to the listener, saying "Fulan" (so-and-so), "fata" (a youth), "rajul" (a man), or similar, with the implied sense "he is Fulan." From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿a reward from your Lord, a gift in sufficient measure﴾ [al-Naba': 36], ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ [al-Naba': 37], the implied sense being "He is the Lord of the heavens." (Rabb) was not made an appositive substitute of (Rabbika).

And the verse of the Hamasi poet:

I will thank 'Amr if my death is delayed, for favours he did not reproach me for, however great they were.

A youth who does not withhold his wealth from his friend, nor shows complaint when the sandal slips.

Al-Sakkaki named this omission "the omission in which the usage that is reported to be left is followed."

The predication about them with these predicates came in the manner of the eloquent simile (al-tashbih al-baligh): they were likened, in the absence of any traces of perception in them, to the deaf, the mute and the blind; that is, each one of them has all three attributes combined. This is the case with predicates in plural form following a subject that is a noun denoting a plurality. So the meaning is that each one of them is like the deaf, mute, blind person. The meaning is not distributive, so it is not understood that some of them are deaf, some mute and some blind. This is not metaphor (isti'arah) according to the verifying scholars of rhetoric (muhaqqiqu ahl al-bayan).

The author of al-Kashshaf said: If you say, "Is what is in the verse called metaphor?" I say: this is disputed, and the verifiers insist on calling it an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), not a metaphor, because the thing being compared (al-musta'ar lahu) is mentioned, and they are the hypocrites. End quote. That is, metaphor depends on the mention of either the borrowed term (al-musta'ar minhu) or the thing to which it is borrowed (al-musta'ar lahu) within the metaphorical expression; when both are mentioned together, it is a simile. Mentioning the term of the thing borrowed-to outside the metaphorical expression does not harm, since it is evident that, were it not for knowledge of the thing borrowed-to in the speech, the metaphor would not appear. For this reason they agreed that the saying of Ibn al-'Amid:

A soul dearer to me than my own soul has stood shading me from the sun,
and, by wonder, a sun has stood shading me from the sun.

in which his saying "sun" (shams) is a metaphor, and the mention of the thing borrowed-to earlier, in his saying "a soul dearer," and its pronoun in his saying "has stood shading me," did not prevent them from calling it metaphor. Likewise, when the term of the borrowed item is not intended as the basis of the comparison, it does not prevent metaphor, as in the saying of Abu al-Hasan Ibn Tabataba:

Do not marvel at the wearing out of his undershirt, for he has buttoned its buttons over the moon.

For the pronoun was not mentioned in order that the comparison be built upon it; rather, the comparison came after it.

"Summ" (deaf), "bukm" (mute) and "'umy" (blind) are plurals of "asamm," "a'mα" and "abkam," and they are those who are characterised by deafness (samam), muteness (bakam) and blindness ('ama). Deafness is the absence of the perception of hearing in one who by nature should hear; muteness is the absence of speech in one who by nature should speak; blindness is the absence of sight in one who by nature should see.

His saying ﴿so they do not return﴾ is a consequence (tafri') of the sentence ﴿deaf, mute, blind﴾, because whoever is afflicted with these attributes lacks understanding and the ability to make others understand, and hope of his returning to guidance or rightness becomes remote.

"Ruju'" (return) is departing from a second place of residence to a first place of residence, and it is here used figuratively (majaz) for desisting from disbelief (kufr).

[Page 315]

﴿Or like a downpour from the sky, in which are darkness, thunder and lightning﴾

This is coordinated with the preceding simile, which is His saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. The description of their state is restated through another allegory, taking into account other attributes. It is an allegory for the state of the hypocrites (munafiqun), whose condition is mixed between opposing pulls and impulses: when the pull of goodness draws their souls upon hearing the admonitions and guidance of the Qur'an, and the pull of evil, arising from the roots of their dispositions and from mockery of the Muslims, draws them the other way, their state is like that of a downpour from the sky in which rains of benefit and lights are mingled with frightening things and troubles. It follows the manner of the eloquent Arabs in varying their similes, a practice they competed in, especially with allegorical (tamthili) similes. This manner indicates the speaker's mastery of description and his range within it.

I have observed from their usage that they sometimes follow the method of coordinating one simile with another, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays in his Mu'allaqa:

*Friend, do you see a lightning flash whose glimmer I show you, like the flashing of two hands in a striped cloak?*
*Its brightness shines like the lamps of a monk, when the oil pours out onto the twisted wick.*

And the words of Labid in his Mu'allaqa, describing his mount:

*Upon her, at the reins, is a swaying, as if she were a camel of pale hue, whose rain-clouds have moved swiftly with the south wind,*
*or a shining one, watered for a two-year-old stallion, whom the driving off of stallions and their beating and their running-about have worn down.*

It is common for such coordination to use *aw* (or) rather than *wa* (and). *Aw* is placed for one of two things or among several things, so from it arises the sense of equivalence (taswiyah). Sometimes they follow the method of restating the simile in the form of a question with the interrogative hamzah, meaning: "so choose the simile with this or with that." An example is Labid's words after the two verses mentioned above:

*Is she that, or a wild cow hunted by beasts, who has been forsaken, and whose herd's leader has lost her?*

Dhu al-Rummah said, describing the swift pace of his she-camel:

*She leapt, the swift one from the tail-ends of a bound she-camel, as if he were [a dark/dim] one uncertain of the mark, or a flank.*

Then he said:

*Is that it, or a freckled one, its forelegs bearing the saffron, its cheek a dark mark, a runner with a bright patch...*

Then he said:

*Is that it, or one dyed with ochre in its pasture, a father of thirty, who at evening returns...*

Sometimes they coordinate with *wa* (and), as in His saying ﴿Allah sets forth a parable: a man with partners quarrelling [with one another]﴾ [al-Zumar: 29], to the end of the verse, and then His saying ﴿and Allah sets forth a parable: two men﴾ [al-Nahl: 76], to the end of the verse. Also His saying ﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ [Fatir: 19], ﴿nor are the darknesses and the light﴾ [Fatir: 20], ﴿nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾ [Fatir: 21], to the end of the verse. Indeed, they sometimes juxtapose without any coordinating particle, as in His saying ﴿until We made them a harvest, extinguished﴾ [al-Anbiya': 15]. These are beautiful variations in eloquent speech. How much more so, then, when they occur in an allegorical simile, since such a simile is rare in isolation, and it is therefore difficult to repeat it.

The *aw* here coordinates the word *sayyib* (downpour) with the one who kindled (alladhi istawqada), with the understanding of the word "mithl" (likeness) between the *kaf* (like) and *sayyib*. The repetition of the particle of comparison together with the coordinating particle, which dispenses with repeating the governing element, is used in their speech. Its beauty here is that it indicates the difference between the two compared states, as we shall explain. They generally do not repeat it in coordination.

The allegory here is for the state of the hypocrites when they attend the gathering of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and hear the Qur'an and its verses of threat for those like them and verses of glad tidings. So the purpose of this allegory is to depict a state different from the one depicted in His saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled [a fire]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], with a different kind of restriction and generalization.

His saying ﴿or like a downpour﴾ is to be understood as "or like a people possessing a downpour," that is, like a people in a manner similar to what preceded in His saying ﴿like one who kindled﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. The mention of a people is indicated by His saying ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾ and His saying ﴿the lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾, to the end of the verse. This is because these attributes cannot be attributed to the hypocrites themselves in the same way as what was permissible in His saying ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], and so forth. Thus the state of the hypocrites is likened to the state of a people traveling at night in the land of a people upon whom rain has fallen, and whose inhabitants were sheltering in their dwellings, as is known from His saying ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾. That rain benefited the people of the land, and the thunder and thunderbolts connected with it did them no harm. But for those passing through it, it brought no benefit and harmed them, through the darkness, thunder and lightning connected with it.

So the *sayyib* (downpour) is a metaphor for the Qur'an and the guidance of Islam, and its comparison to rain is well-established. In the authentic hadith: "The likeness of what Allah has sent me with of guidance is like the rain that fell upon a land, and some of it was pure..." etc. In the Qur'an: ﴿like the rain whose vegetation pleased the disbelievers﴾ [al-Hadid: 20]. You will not find a state more suitable for depicting a condition in which benefit and harm are mixed than the state of rain and clouds, and this is one of the wonders of Qur'anic allegory. From it Abu al-Tayyib took his words:

*A youth like a dark, heavy cloud, hoped for and feared: one hopes for its rain, while its thunderbolts are feared.*

"Darkness" (zulumat) is a metaphor for the loneliness that afflicts the disbelievers upon hearing it, just as the loneliness of clouds afflicts the one traveling at night, because it hides from him the light of the stars and the moon.

"Thunder" is for the rebukes and warnings of the Qur'an. "Lightning" is for the manifestation of the lights of its guidance through its admonitions. It is thus clear that this compound allegory is suitable for the considerations of dividing the simile into its parts, which is the highest form of allegory.

*Sayyib* is of the pattern *fay'al*, from *sabba yasubbu sawban*, meaning to descend with force. Al-Marzuqi said its *ya'* is for transferring the word from the verbal noun to a noun, so it is a description of rain in terms of the intensity of darkness resulting from the density of the clouds and the darkness of night. The apparent view is that His saying ﴿from the sky﴾ is not a restriction on *sayyib*; rather it is a clarifying attribute, brought to increase the vividness of the image of the downpour in this allegory, since the context is one of elaboration (itnab), as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*Like a boulder of rock which the torrent has hurled down from a height.*

The listener already knows that a torrent does not hurl down a boulder except from above, but the poet intended to create a picture. Similarly, His saying ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38], and His saying ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed in the land﴾ [al-An'am: 71]. And He said ﴿Rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. "Sky" (sama') is applied to the high atmosphere above us, which we imagine as a blue dome, and to the lofty air, as He said ﴿like a good tree whose root is firm and whose branches are in the sky﴾ [Ibrahim: 24]. It is also applied to the clouds, and it is applied to the rain itself. In the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us after a sky..." etc. Since the formation of rain occurs in the high, frigid layer of the atmosphere, its beginning is attributed to the sky, and this usage recurs in the Qur'an.

It is also possible that His saying ﴿from the sky﴾ is a restriction on *sayyib*, either in the sense of "from all regions of the atmosphere," if we say that the definite article in "al-sama'" is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), as al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) held, though this is somewhat distant, since the particle of comprehensiveness is not known to enter except upon a universal noun with individuals, not upon a noun denoting a whole with parts, which would require treating the parts as if they were the individuals of a class, and there is no known parallel for this in usage. What appears to me, if we make His saying ﴿from the sky﴾ a restriction on *sayyib*, is that the intended meaning of "sky" is the highest elevation, and rain coming from a point directly opposite and at a great height is more lasting, unlike rain that comes from the sides of the atmosphere and is near the earth, not elevated.

The pronoun in "fihi" (in it) refers to *sayyib*, and the locative sense is metaphorical, meaning "with it." The "darknesses" have already been discussed just above, and what is meant by them is the darkness of night, that is, like a cloud whose color is the darkness of night. A cloud of the night is more intense in rain and lightning, and is called *sariyah*. "Thunder" is sounds that arise in the clouds.

"Lightning" is a fiery, luminous flash that appears in the clouds. Thunder and lightning arise in the clouds from an electrical effect present in the clouds. When two clouds gather in the atmosphere, one of which has a stronger electrical charge than the other, and they rub against each other, the stronger one draws the weaker, and by this a rupture occurs in the air with force and speed, producing a loud sound, which is called thunder. It is an atmospheric crackling caused by electricity. At that moment the two electrical charges meet, and this causes lightning to flash.

You know now that the *sayyib* is an allegory for the Qur'an, and that the darknesses, thunder and lightning are an allegory for the impulses of the threat, in that they delight some people, namely those who benefit from the rain, and distress travelers other than the people of that land. Likewise, the verses delight the believers, for they find themselves saved from being condemned, and they distress the hypocrites, for they find the verses applying exactly to their own circumstances.

* * *

[Page 319]

﴿They put their fingers in their ears because of the thunderbolts, fearing death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers.﴾
﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight. Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it; and when darkness falls upon them, they stand still. And if Allah willed, He would surely take away their hearing and their sight. Indeed Allah is powerful over all things.﴾

The apparent view is that the clause *yaj'alun* (they put) is a circumstantial clause (hal), by which the intended meaning of the form being compared is made clear, since that form was stated in a general way. As for the clause ﴿the lightning nearly snatches﴾, it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause relating to the subject of *yaj'alun*, since it fully clarifies the form being compared. It is also permissible for it to be a resumptive clause (isti'naf), explaining the state of the group at the lightning, following the explanation of their state at the thunder. The clause ﴿whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ is a circumstantial clause either of the lightning or of the pronoun of "their sight," and only these two. In this there is an allegory for the alarm of the hypocrites at the verses of threat, by the condition of one standing under the sky at the time of thunder, lightning and darkness: he fears the deafening of his hearing, fears the thunderbolts for fear of death, the lightning dazzles him with its intense brightness, and after its glow has ceased it confuses his path for him. His saying ﴿whenever it lights up for them﴾ is an allegory for the bewilderment of the hypocrites by the bewilderment of travelers in the dark, thundering and flashing night.

His saying ﴿and Allah encompasses the disbelievers﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) serving as a reminder that the intended purpose is the allegory of the state of the hypocrites in their disbelief, and not merely the display of variety in allegory. His saying ﴿and if Allah willed, He would surely take away their hearing and their sight﴾ is a return to the threat against the hypocrites, who are the actual object of the allegory. Thus the pronouns in the clause ﴿and if Allah willed﴾ refer to the original subject of discourse, and the distribution of the pronouns is indicated by the context.

Thus He expressed the admonitions of the Qur'an by the thunderbolts, and the decline of the hearts of the hypocrites, which are their insights, from the settled light of faith within them, by the lightning snatching away their sight. A similar meaning is indicated by the words of Ibn 'Atiyah, quoting the majority of the commentators. This is a widespread metaphor: one says "so-and-so thunders and lightens" (yar'ad wa yabruq). Moreover, its construction here upon the previous metaphor increases its acceptability. He expressed what happens to the hypocrites of doubt about the soundness of their belief by the walking of one traveling in darkness when the lightning illumines him, and their abandonment of that doubt when they return to their disbelief by the standing of the walker when the lightning ceases, in the manner of allegory. He interspersed all of this with a threat that suits none but the two parties compared, namely what is conveyed by the parenthetical clause ﴿and Allah encompasses the disbelievers﴾ and His saying ﴿and if Allah willed, He would surely take away their hearing and their sight﴾. He brought these circumstantial and resumptive clauses to draw attention to the aspect of resemblance, and to establish the strength of the likeness between the admonitions and the signs of guidance and faith on the one hand and thunder and lightning on the other, in producing the two effects of benefit and harm, together with a variety in eloquence and in the methods of literal and figurative speech.

Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, made the three clauses resumptive, each following from the other: the first is a resumption from ﴿or like a downpour﴾, the second, ﴿the lightning nearly snatches﴾, is a resumption from *yaj'alun* (they put), since thunderbolts imply lightning, and the third, ﴿whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾, is a resumption from His saying ﴿the lightning nearly snatches﴾. The meaning upon this reading is weak, and in some of these it is weaker than in others, as we have pointed out just above.

[Page 320]

The verb *al-ja'l* (placing, making) and *al-aṣābiʿ* (the fingers) are used in their literal senses according to the view of some exegetes, because *al-ja'l* here means *al-nawṭ* (suspending, inserting), and the sense of location (*al-ẓarfiyyah*) does not require full enclosure. Placing part of a finger in the ear is therefore a placing of the finger. Some scholars of rhetoric (*ʿulamāʾ al-bayān*) cited this verse as an example of a metaphor (*majāz*) whose relation (*ʿalāqah*) is partiality (*al-juzʾiyyah*), but that is a loose usage (*tasāmuḥ*). For this reason the author of the *Kashshāf* (al-Zamakhsharī) expressed it by saying: "This is among the broad usages of the language that the enumerator can hardly count, such as ﴿So wash your faces﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 6] and ﴿So cut off their hands﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 38], and from it your saying: *I wiped with the handkerchief* and *I entered the town*." It has also been said that this is a metaphor in the fingers, and it has been said that it is a metaphor in the placing. Whoever wishes may take it as a metaphor in the sense of location, in which case it follows the particle *fī* ("in").

The *min* in His saying ﴿from the thunderbolts﴾ is causal, meaning "for the sake of the thunderbolts," since the thunderbolts are the reason for placing the fingers in the ears. There is no harm in the placing being for the purpose of guarding against them, so as to say that it requires a supplied noun such as "leaving" or "avoiding," since there is no need for it. A parallel to this is the saying: *saqāhu min al-ʿaymah* ("he gave him to drink because of the ʿaymah"), with a fatḥah on the ʿayn and a sukūn on the yāʾ, meaning the desire for milk, because the ʿaymah is the cause of the giving to drink, and what is intended is its removal. The object of purpose (*al-mafʿūl li-ajlihi*) is the motive whose existence prompts the action, whether or not it is also the end of the action, which is the usual case, or not, as here.

*Al-ṣawāʿiq* is the plural of *ṣāʿiqah*, a fire that bursts forth from the electricity of the clouds, as was mentioned earlier. His saying ﴿fear of death﴾ is an object of purpose, and here it is both a cause and an end.

Among the excellent qualities of this image is that, together with what it contains of the composite form that is the likeness, it represents the state of the hypocrites when the attractions to guidance in their souls contend with the attractions to persistence in disbelief: they await what may be bestowed upon their souls of acceptance of the Prophet's call and his guidance, while they protect themselves from that guidance taking hold of them when they are alone with their devils. It is also capable of being divided, in its individual elements, into separate likenesses, so that each part of the composite form of the likeness corresponds to a part of the composite form of a people struck by a rain-cloud with darkness, thunder, and thunderbolts, whom they cannot bear to hear crashing, and whom they fear death from; and a fierce lightning that nearly takes away their sight, while they are in bewilderment between walking and stopping.

His saying ﴿God encompasses the disbelievers﴾ is a parenthetical statement that returns to the hypocrites, since the image has been fully applied to them and their state has become clear, so it is time to warn them and threaten them. In this there is a return to the main purpose, like the return in His exalted saying ﴿God took away their light and left them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], as was mentioned earlier, except that here it occurs by way of parenthesis.

The word *iḥāṭah* (encompassment) is a metaphor for complete power. The power that does not lose what it wills is likened to the encompassing of the encompasser over the encompassed, in the manner of an inherited (*tabaʿiyyah*) or a representational (*tamthīliyyah*) metaphor, even though not every element that indicates the whole composite that signifies the likened form has been mentioned. This statement has been used for its implication, which is that they will not escape Him, and that He will requite them for the evil of their deeds.

*Al-khaṭf* is seizing with speed. *Kullamā* is a word that conveys the generality of what follows it. The *mā* is a particle that serves to replace the genitive construction (*kāffah li-kull ʿan al-iḍāfah*), or it is a temporal verbal noun (*maṣdariyyah ẓarfiyyah*), or an indefinite relative noun (*nakirah mawṣūfah*); the generality in it is derived from the word *kull*.

The mention of *kullamā* on the side of the illumination and of *idhā* on the side of the darkness indicates their eagerness to walk, and that they watch for the illumination, so they do not miss any moment of its occurrence, in order to see the path in their walking because of the intensity of the darkness. The verb *aḍāʾa* is used intransitively and transitively according to the meaning, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿When it illuminated what was around him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. *Aẓlama* is used intransitively very often and transitively rarely. Apparently *aḍāʾa* here is transitive, so the object of *aḍāʾa* is omitted, the indication being the verb *mashaw* ("they walked") that follows it. Its supplied object is "the walkway" or "the path"; that is, the lightning illuminated the path for them. Likewise *aẓlama*, meaning: and when it darkens the path for them, the lightning ceases its flashing. So the attribution of darkening to the lightning is metaphorical, because it was the cause of the darkening. The meaning of *qiyām* ("standing") is not walking, that is, standing still in the place.

His exalted saying ﴿And if God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾: the object of *shāʾa* is omitted, the indication being the answer clause. That is the rule of the verb of will and desire and the like when it is connected to something that can indicate its object, like its occurrence as a relative clause for a relative pronoun that requires a predicate, as in: *mā shāʾa Allāh kāna* ("what God willed came to be"), meaning: what He willed its existence came to be. Likewise when it occurs as the condition of *law* (if), because it is evident that the answer is the indicator of the object. Likewise when there is in the preceding speech, before the verb of will, something that indicates the object of the verb, such as His exalted saying ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 6] ﴿except what God wills﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 7].

[Page 321]

Al-Shaykh (ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī) said in *Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz* (*Proofs of Inimitability*): The eloquence lies in its being brought in this way, with the object omitted. In some cases it may happen that stating the object is better, as in the verse of the poet, who is Isḥāq al-Khuraymī, a client of the Banū Khuraym, one of the poets of the era of al-Rashīd, lamenting Abū al-Haydhām al-Khuraymī, his grandson, the son of ʿImārah's son:

*If I wished to weep blood, I would have wept it for him,*
*but the courtyard of patience is wider.*

The reason for its beauty is that it is as if it were a strange novelty for a person to wish to weep blood. Since this is so, it is better to state it explicitly, to establish it in the mind of the listener, etc. Al-Zamakhsharī followed him and added to it that they do not omit the object when speaking of something strange. He said: "They rarely make the object explicit except in the case of something strange, etc." This is to be interpreted as meaning that in such a case non-omission is frequent.

In my view, omission is the basic form, for the sake of brevity. The eloquent speaker sometimes dispenses with the answer clause and intends the explanation after the ambiguity; this is the most common in the speech of the Arabs. Ṭarafah said:

*And if you wish, you do not make her trot; and if you wish, she trots.*

Sometimes the speaker clarifies, by mentioning the condition, the basis of the omission in the answer clause, as in the verse above and in His exalted saying ﴿If We had wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 17]. This is good when the object is strange, so mentioning it serves to begin establishing it, as in the verse of al-Khuraymī. Brevity is achieved in every case, because there is an omission either from the first clause or from the second. The discourse of the masters of rhetorical meanings may give the impression that a strange object must be mentioned, but that is not so. God, exalted is He, said ﴿They said: If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 14], although the sending down of angels is a strange matter. Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī said:

*If you wish, claim that whoever is upon its back*
*are your slaves, and call upon your God, and He will testify.*

Such a claim is a strange claim.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿with their hearing and their sight﴾ apparently refers to the people of the rain-cloud, who are the likeness for the state of the hypocrites, because the report of the possibility of destroying their hearing and sight fits the people of the rain-cloud who are likened to them, according to His saying ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ and His saying ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾. The intended meaning is that the thunder and lightning that occur in the likened image are thunder and lightning that have reached the extreme of their kinds' power, such that the crash of the thunder does not prevent the destruction of the hearing of its hearers, and the flash of the lightning does not prevent the destruction of the sight of its beholders, except that God wills for that not to happen, for a wisdom. The benefit of mentioning this in the likened state is that its counterpart should extend to the state being likened, which is the state of the hypocrites. They are on the verge of having no benefit from their hearing and sight, a complete loss, because of the intensity of their obstinacy and their turning away from the truth. But God did not will that, as a respite for them and a granting of time, so that they might increase in sin, or as a delay for them and an excuse, perhaps some of them will turn back to guidance. This meaning has been formulated in this style because of what it contains of directing a threat at them: that God may take away their hearing and sight because of their hypocrisy, if they do not hasten to abandon hypocrisy. That has the effect of terror in their hearts, as it happened to ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah when the Prophet ﷺ recited to him ﴿Say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 13].

So the purpose of introducing *law* into this conditional is not to convey what *law* normally implies, namely the negation of the condition, because the intention is not to inform about God's power over that. Rather the intention is to convey the implication of the negation, which is that the causes of the lightning and thunder taking away their sight, in the likeness, are fully present, namely their ingratitude for the blessing that comes from them. For they were provided with them for the sake of contemplating the cosmic signs and hearing the legal signs. When they turned away from both matters, they deserved to have the blessing taken away. But God did not will that, as a respite for them and to establish proof against them. So *law* is used figuratively, as a loose metonymy, for mere conditionality, to show that the causes are abundant if not for the presence of an obstacle, in the manner of the saying of Ubayy ibn Sulmā ibn Rabīʿah, one of the poets of the *Ḥamāsah*, describing his horse:

*Even if a one-hoofed creature had flown before her,*
*she would have flown; but she did not fly.*

That is, the cause of flying was fully present in her. The meaning is: If God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and sight by increasing the strength of the lightning and thunder, so that the thunder and lightning reach near the extreme of their strength.

His saying ﴿Indeed God is over all things Competent﴾ has a wonderful placement. His saying ﴿Indeed God is over all things Competent﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*), and in it there is a reinforcement (*tarshīḥ*) of the intended directive for the threat, increasing their admonition, conveying it to them, and cutting off their excuses in this world and the Hereafter.

[Page 315]

﴿Or like a downpour from the sky, in which are darkness, thunder and lightning﴾

This is coordinated with the preceding simile, which is His saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. The description of their state is restated through another allegory, taking into account other attributes. It is an allegory for the state of the hypocrites (munafiqun), whose condition is mixed between opposing pulls and impulses: when the pull of goodness draws their souls upon hearing the admonitions and guidance of the Qur'an, and the pull of evil, arising from the roots of their dispositions and from mockery of the Muslims, draws them the other way, their state is like that of a downpour from the sky in which rains of benefit and lights are mingled with frightening things and troubles. It follows the manner of the eloquent Arabs in varying their similes, a practice they competed in, especially with allegorical (tamthili) similes. This manner indicates the speaker's mastery of description and his range within it.

I have observed from their usage that they sometimes follow the method of coordinating one simile with another, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays in his Mu'allaqa:

*Friend, do you see a lightning flash whose glimmer I show you, like the flashing of two hands in a striped cloak?*
*Its brightness shines like the lamps of a monk, when the oil pours out onto the twisted wick.*

And the words of Labid in his Mu'allaqa, describing his mount:

*Upon her, at the reins, is a swaying, as if she were a camel of pale hue, whose rain-clouds have moved swiftly with the south wind,*
*or a shining one, watered for a two-year-old stallion, whom the driving off of stallions and their beating and their running-about have worn down.*

It is common for such coordination to use *aw* (or) rather than *wa* (and). *Aw* is placed for one of two things or among several things, so from it arises the sense of equivalence (taswiyah). Sometimes they follow the method of restating the simile in the form of a question with the interrogative hamzah, meaning: "so choose the simile with this or with that." An example is Labid's words after the two verses mentioned above:

*Is she that, or a wild cow hunted by beasts, who has been forsaken, and whose herd's leader has lost her?*

Dhu al-Rummah said, describing the swift pace of his she-camel:

*She leapt, the swift one from the tail-ends of a bound she-camel, as if he were [a dark/dim] one uncertain of the mark, or a flank.*

Then he said:

*Is that it, or a freckled one, its forelegs bearing the saffron, its cheek a dark mark, a runner with a bright patch...*

Then he said:

*Is that it, or one dyed with ochre in its pasture, a father of thirty, who at evening returns...*

Sometimes they coordinate with *wa* (and), as in His saying ﴿Allah sets forth a parable: a man with partners quarrelling [with one another]﴾ [al-Zumar: 29], to the end of the verse, and then His saying ﴿and Allah sets forth a parable: two men﴾ [al-Nahl: 76], to the end of the verse. Also His saying ﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ [Fatir: 19], ﴿nor are the darknesses and the light﴾ [Fatir: 20], ﴿nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾ [Fatir: 21], to the end of the verse. Indeed, they sometimes juxtapose without any coordinating particle, as in His saying ﴿until We made them a harvest, extinguished﴾ [al-Anbiya': 15]. These are beautiful variations in eloquent speech. How much more so, then, when they occur in an allegorical simile, since such a simile is rare in isolation, and it is therefore difficult to repeat it.

The *aw* here coordinates the word *sayyib* (downpour) with the one who kindled (alladhi istawqada), with the understanding of the word "mithl" (likeness) between the *kaf* (like) and *sayyib*. The repetition of the particle of comparison together with the coordinating particle, which dispenses with repeating the governing element, is used in their speech. Its beauty here is that it indicates the difference between the two compared states, as we shall explain. They generally do not repeat it in coordination.

The allegory here is for the state of the hypocrites when they attend the gathering of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and hear the Qur'an and its verses of threat for those like them and verses of glad tidings. So the purpose of this allegory is to depict a state different from the one depicted in His saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled [a fire]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], with a different kind of restriction and generalization.

His saying ﴿or like a downpour﴾ is to be understood as "or like a people possessing a downpour," that is, like a people in a manner similar to what preceded in His saying ﴿like one who kindled﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. The mention of a people is indicated by His saying ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾ and His saying ﴿the lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾, to the end of the verse. This is because these attributes cannot be attributed to the hypocrites themselves in the same way as what was permissible in His saying ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], and so forth. Thus the state of the hypocrites is likened to the state of a people traveling at night in the land of a people upon whom rain has fallen, and whose inhabitants were sheltering in their dwellings, as is known from His saying ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾. That rain benefited the people of the land, and the thunder and thunderbolts connected with it did them no harm. But for those passing through it, it brought no benefit and harmed them, through the darkness, thunder and lightning connected with it.

So the *sayyib* (downpour) is a metaphor for the Qur'an and the guidance of Islam, and its comparison to rain is well-established. In the authentic hadith: "The likeness of what Allah has sent me with of guidance is like the rain that fell upon a land, and some of it was pure..." etc. In the Qur'an: ﴿like the rain whose vegetation pleased the disbelievers﴾ [al-Hadid: 20]. You will not find a state more suitable for depicting a condition in which benefit and harm are mixed than the state of rain and clouds, and this is one of the wonders of Qur'anic allegory. From it Abu al-Tayyib took his words:

*A youth like a dark, heavy cloud, hoped for and feared: one hopes for its rain, while its thunderbolts are feared.*

"Darkness" (zulumat) is a metaphor for the loneliness that afflicts the disbelievers upon hearing it, just as the loneliness of clouds afflicts the one traveling at night, because it hides from him the light of the stars and the moon.

"Thunder" is for the rebukes and warnings of the Qur'an. "Lightning" is for the manifestation of the lights of its guidance through its admonitions. It is thus clear that this compound allegory is suitable for the considerations of dividing the simile into its parts, which is the highest form of allegory.

*Sayyib* is of the pattern *fay'al*, from *sabba yasubbu sawban*, meaning to descend with force. Al-Marzuqi said its *ya'* is for transferring the word from the verbal noun to a noun, so it is a description of rain in terms of the intensity of darkness resulting from the density of the clouds and the darkness of night. The apparent view is that His saying ﴿from the sky﴾ is not a restriction on *sayyib*; rather it is a clarifying attribute, brought to increase the vividness of the image of the downpour in this allegory, since the context is one of elaboration (itnab), as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*Like a boulder of rock which the torrent has hurled down from a height.*

The listener already knows that a torrent does not hurl down a boulder except from above, but the poet intended to create a picture. Similarly, His saying ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38], and His saying ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed in the land﴾ [al-An'am: 71]. And He said ﴿Rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. "Sky" (sama') is applied to the high atmosphere above us, which we imagine as a blue dome, and to the lofty air, as He said ﴿like a good tree whose root is firm and whose branches are in the sky﴾ [Ibrahim: 24]. It is also applied to the clouds, and it is applied to the rain itself. In the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us after a sky..." etc. Since the formation of rain occurs in the high, frigid layer of the atmosphere, its beginning is attributed to the sky, and this usage recurs in the Qur'an.

It is also possible that His saying ﴿from the sky﴾ is a restriction on *sayyib*, either in the sense of "from all regions of the atmosphere," if we say that the definite article in "al-sama'" is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), as al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) held, though this is somewhat distant, since the particle of comprehensiveness is not known to enter except upon a universal noun with individuals, not upon a noun denoting a whole with parts, which would require treating the parts as if they were the individuals of a class, and there is no known parallel for this in usage. What appears to me, if we make His saying ﴿from the sky﴾ a restriction on *sayyib*, is that the intended meaning of "sky" is the highest elevation, and rain coming from a point directly opposite and at a great height is more lasting, unlike rain that comes from the sides of the atmosphere and is near the earth, not elevated.

The pronoun in "fihi" (in it) refers to *sayyib*, and the locative sense is metaphorical, meaning "with it." The "darknesses" have already been discussed just above, and what is meant by them is the darkness of night, that is, like a cloud whose color is the darkness of night. A cloud of the night is more intense in rain and lightning, and is called *sariyah*. "Thunder" is sounds that arise in the clouds.

"Lightning" is a fiery, luminous flash that appears in the clouds. Thunder and lightning arise in the clouds from an electrical effect present in the clouds. When two clouds gather in the atmosphere, one of which has a stronger electrical charge than the other, and they rub against each other, the stronger one draws the weaker, and by this a rupture occurs in the air with force and speed, producing a loud sound, which is called thunder. It is an atmospheric crackling caused by electricity. At that moment the two electrical charges meet, and this causes lightning to flash.

You know now that the *sayyib* is an allegory for the Qur'an, and that the darknesses, thunder and lightning are an allegory for the impulses of the threat, in that they delight some people, namely those who benefit from the rain, and distress travelers other than the people of that land. Likewise, the verses delight the believers, for they find themselves saved from being condemned, and they distress the hypocrites, for they find the verses applying exactly to their own circumstances.

* * *

[Page 319]

﴿They put their fingers in their ears because of the thunderbolts, fearing death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers.﴾
﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight. Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it; and when darkness falls upon them, they stand still. And if Allah willed, He would surely take away their hearing and their sight. Indeed Allah is powerful over all things.﴾

The apparent view is that the clause *yaj'alun* (they put) is a circumstantial clause (hal), by which the intended meaning of the form being compared is made clear, since that form was stated in a general way. As for the clause ﴿the lightning nearly snatches﴾, it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause relating to the subject of *yaj'alun*, since it fully clarifies the form being compared. It is also permissible for it to be a resumptive clause (isti'naf), explaining the state of the group at the lightning, following the explanation of their state at the thunder. The clause ﴿whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ is a circumstantial clause either of the lightning or of the pronoun of "their sight," and only these two. In this there is an allegory for the alarm of the hypocrites at the verses of threat, by the condition of one standing under the sky at the time of thunder, lightning and darkness: he fears the deafening of his hearing, fears the thunderbolts for fear of death, the lightning dazzles him with its intense brightness, and after its glow has ceased it confuses his path for him. His saying ﴿whenever it lights up for them﴾ is an allegory for the bewilderment of the hypocrites by the bewilderment of travelers in the dark, thundering and flashing night.

His saying ﴿and Allah encompasses the disbelievers﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) serving as a reminder that the intended purpose is the allegory of the state of the hypocrites in their disbelief, and not merely the display of variety in allegory. His saying ﴿and if Allah willed, He would surely take away their hearing and their sight﴾ is a return to the threat against the hypocrites, who are the actual object of the allegory. Thus the pronouns in the clause ﴿and if Allah willed﴾ refer to the original subject of discourse, and the distribution of the pronouns is indicated by the context.

Thus He expressed the admonitions of the Qur'an by the thunderbolts, and the decline of the hearts of the hypocrites, which are their insights, from the settled light of faith within them, by the lightning snatching away their sight. A similar meaning is indicated by the words of Ibn 'Atiyah, quoting the majority of the commentators. This is a widespread metaphor: one says "so-and-so thunders and lightens" (yar'ad wa yabruq). Moreover, its construction here upon the previous metaphor increases its acceptability. He expressed what happens to the hypocrites of doubt about the soundness of their belief by the walking of one traveling in darkness when the lightning illumines him, and their abandonment of that doubt when they return to their disbelief by the standing of the walker when the lightning ceases, in the manner of allegory. He interspersed all of this with a threat that suits none but the two parties compared, namely what is conveyed by the parenthetical clause ﴿and Allah encompasses the disbelievers﴾ and His saying ﴿and if Allah willed, He would surely take away their hearing and their sight﴾. He brought these circumstantial and resumptive clauses to draw attention to the aspect of resemblance, and to establish the strength of the likeness between the admonitions and the signs of guidance and faith on the one hand and thunder and lightning on the other, in producing the two effects of benefit and harm, together with a variety in eloquence and in the methods of literal and figurative speech.

Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, made the three clauses resumptive, each following from the other: the first is a resumption from ﴿or like a downpour﴾, the second, ﴿the lightning nearly snatches﴾, is a resumption from *yaj'alun* (they put), since thunderbolts imply lightning, and the third, ﴿whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾, is a resumption from His saying ﴿the lightning nearly snatches﴾. The meaning upon this reading is weak, and in some of these it is weaker than in others, as we have pointed out just above.

[Page 320]

The verb *al-ja'l* (placing, making) and *al-aṣābiʿ* (the fingers) are used in their literal senses according to the view of some exegetes, because *al-ja'l* here means *al-nawṭ* (suspending, inserting), and the sense of location (*al-ẓarfiyyah*) does not require full enclosure. Placing part of a finger in the ear is therefore a placing of the finger. Some scholars of rhetoric (*ʿulamāʾ al-bayān*) cited this verse as an example of a metaphor (*majāz*) whose relation (*ʿalāqah*) is partiality (*al-juzʾiyyah*), but that is a loose usage (*tasāmuḥ*). For this reason the author of the *Kashshāf* (al-Zamakhsharī) expressed it by saying: "This is among the broad usages of the language that the enumerator can hardly count, such as ﴿So wash your faces﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 6] and ﴿So cut off their hands﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 38], and from it your saying: *I wiped with the handkerchief* and *I entered the town*." It has also been said that this is a metaphor in the fingers, and it has been said that it is a metaphor in the placing. Whoever wishes may take it as a metaphor in the sense of location, in which case it follows the particle *fī* ("in").

The *min* in His saying ﴿from the thunderbolts﴾ is causal, meaning "for the sake of the thunderbolts," since the thunderbolts are the reason for placing the fingers in the ears. There is no harm in the placing being for the purpose of guarding against them, so as to say that it requires a supplied noun such as "leaving" or "avoiding," since there is no need for it. A parallel to this is the saying: *saqāhu min al-ʿaymah* ("he gave him to drink because of the ʿaymah"), with a fatḥah on the ʿayn and a sukūn on the yāʾ, meaning the desire for milk, because the ʿaymah is the cause of the giving to drink, and what is intended is its removal. The object of purpose (*al-mafʿūl li-ajlihi*) is the motive whose existence prompts the action, whether or not it is also the end of the action, which is the usual case, or not, as here.

*Al-ṣawāʿiq* is the plural of *ṣāʿiqah*, a fire that bursts forth from the electricity of the clouds, as was mentioned earlier. His saying ﴿fear of death﴾ is an object of purpose, and here it is both a cause and an end.
