Among the excellent qualities of this image is that, together with what it contains of the composite form that is the likeness, it represents the state of the hypocrites when the attractions to guidance in their souls contend with the attractions to persistence in disbelief: they await what may be bestowed upon their souls of acceptance of the Prophet's call and his guidance, while they protect themselves from that guidance taking hold of them when they are alone with their devils. It is also capable of being divided, in its individual elements, into separate likenesses, so that each part of the composite form of the likeness corresponds to a part of the composite form of a people struck by a rain-cloud with darkness, thunder, and thunderbolts, whom they cannot bear to hear crashing, and whom they fear death from; and a fierce lightning that nearly takes away their sight, while they are in bewilderment between walking and stopping.

His saying ﴿God encompasses the disbelievers﴾ is a parenthetical statement that returns to the hypocrites, since the image has been fully applied to them and their state has become clear, so it is time to warn them and threaten them. In this there is a return to the main purpose, like the return in His exalted saying ﴿God took away their light and left them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], as was mentioned earlier, except that here it occurs by way of parenthesis.

The word *iḥāṭah* (encompassment) is a metaphor for complete power. The power that does not lose what it wills is likened to the encompassing of the encompasser over the encompassed, in the manner of an inherited (*tabaʿiyyah*) or a representational (*tamthīliyyah*) metaphor, even though not every element that indicates the whole composite that signifies the likened form has been mentioned. This statement has been used for its implication, which is that they will not escape Him, and that He will requite them for the evil of their deeds.

*Al-khaṭf* is seizing with speed. *Kullamā* is a word that conveys the generality of what follows it. The *mā* is a particle that serves to replace the genitive construction (*kāffah li-kull ʿan al-iḍāfah*), or it is a temporal verbal noun (*maṣdariyyah ẓarfiyyah*), or an indefinite relative noun (*nakirah mawṣūfah*); the generality in it is derived from the word *kull*.

The mention of *kullamā* on the side of the illumination and of *idhā* on the side of the darkness indicates their eagerness to walk, and that they watch for the illumination, so they do not miss any moment of its occurrence, in order to see the path in their walking because of the intensity of the darkness. The verb *aḍāʾa* is used intransitively and transitively according to the meaning, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿When it illuminated what was around him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. *Aẓlama* is used intransitively very often and transitively rarely. Apparently *aḍāʾa* here is transitive, so the object of *aḍāʾa* is omitted, the indication being the verb *mashaw* ("they walked") that follows it. Its supplied object is "the walkway" or "the path"; that is, the lightning illuminated the path for them. Likewise *aẓlama*, meaning: and when it darkens the path for them, the lightning ceases its flashing. So the attribution of darkening to the lightning is metaphorical, because it was the cause of the darkening. The meaning of *qiyām* ("standing") is not walking, that is, standing still in the place.

His exalted saying ﴿And if God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾: the object of *shāʾa* is omitted, the indication being the answer clause. That is the rule of the verb of will and desire and the like when it is connected to something that can indicate its object, like its occurrence as a relative clause for a relative pronoun that requires a predicate, as in: *mā shāʾa Allāh kāna* ("what God willed came to be"), meaning: what He willed its existence came to be. Likewise when it occurs as the condition of *law* (if), because it is evident that the answer is the indicator of the object. Likewise when there is in the preceding speech, before the verb of will, something that indicates the object of the verb, such as His exalted saying ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 6] ﴿except what God wills﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 7].

[Page 321]

Al-Shaykh (ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī) said in *Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz* (*Proofs of Inimitability*): The eloquence lies in its being brought in this way, with the object omitted. In some cases it may happen that stating the object is better, as in the verse of the poet, who is Isḥāq al-Khuraymī, a client of the Banū Khuraym, one of the poets of the era of al-Rashīd, lamenting Abū al-Haydhām al-Khuraymī, his grandson, the son of ʿImārah's son:

*If I wished to weep blood, I would have wept it for him,*
*but the courtyard of patience is wider.*

The reason for its beauty is that it is as if it were a strange novelty for a person to wish to weep blood. Since this is so, it is better to state it explicitly, to establish it in the mind of the listener, etc. Al-Zamakhsharī followed him and added to it that they do not omit the object when speaking of something strange. He said: "They rarely make the object explicit except in the case of something strange, etc." This is to be interpreted as meaning that in such a case non-omission is frequent.

In my view, omission is the basic form, for the sake of brevity. The eloquent speaker sometimes dispenses with the answer clause and intends the explanation after the ambiguity; this is the most common in the speech of the Arabs. Ṭarafah said:

*And if you wish, you do not make her trot; and if you wish, she trots.*

Sometimes the speaker clarifies, by mentioning the condition, the basis of the omission in the answer clause, as in the verse above and in His exalted saying ﴿If We had wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 17]. This is good when the object is strange, so mentioning it serves to begin establishing it, as in the verse of al-Khuraymī. Brevity is achieved in every case, because there is an omission either from the first clause or from the second. The discourse of the masters of rhetorical meanings may give the impression that a strange object must be mentioned, but that is not so. God, exalted is He, said ﴿They said: If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 14], although the sending down of angels is a strange matter. Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī said:

*If you wish, claim that whoever is upon its back*
*are your slaves, and call upon your God, and He will testify.*

Such a claim is a strange claim.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿with their hearing and their sight﴾ apparently refers to the people of the rain-cloud, who are the likeness for the state of the hypocrites, because the report of the possibility of destroying their hearing and sight fits the people of the rain-cloud who are likened to them, according to His saying ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ and His saying ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾. The intended meaning is that the thunder and lightning that occur in the likened image are thunder and lightning that have reached the extreme of their kinds' power, such that the crash of the thunder does not prevent the destruction of the hearing of its hearers, and the flash of the lightning does not prevent the destruction of the sight of its beholders, except that God wills for that not to happen, for a wisdom. The benefit of mentioning this in the likened state is that its counterpart should extend to the state being likened, which is the state of the hypocrites. They are on the verge of having no benefit from their hearing and sight, a complete loss, because of the intensity of their obstinacy and their turning away from the truth. But God did not will that, as a respite for them and a granting of time, so that they might increase in sin, or as a delay for them and an excuse, perhaps some of them will turn back to guidance. This meaning has been formulated in this style because of what it contains of directing a threat at them: that God may take away their hearing and sight because of their hypocrisy, if they do not hasten to abandon hypocrisy. That has the effect of terror in their hearts, as it happened to ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah when the Prophet ﷺ recited to him ﴿Say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 13].

So the purpose of introducing *law* into this conditional is not to convey what *law* normally implies, namely the negation of the condition, because the intention is not to inform about God's power over that. Rather the intention is to convey the implication of the negation, which is that the causes of the lightning and thunder taking away their sight, in the likeness, are fully present, namely their ingratitude for the blessing that comes from them. For they were provided with them for the sake of contemplating the cosmic signs and hearing the legal signs. When they turned away from both matters, they deserved to have the blessing taken away. But God did not will that, as a respite for them and to establish proof against them. So *law* is used figuratively, as a loose metonymy, for mere conditionality, to show that the causes are abundant if not for the presence of an obstacle, in the manner of the saying of Ubayy ibn Sulmā ibn Rabīʿah, one of the poets of the *Ḥamāsah*, describing his horse:

*Even if a one-hoofed creature had flown before her,*
*she would have flown; but she did not fly.*

That is, the cause of flying was fully present in her. The meaning is: If God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and sight by increasing the strength of the lightning and thunder, so that the thunder and lightning reach near the extreme of their strength.

His saying ﴿Indeed God is over all things Competent﴾ has a wonderful placement. His saying ﴿Indeed God is over all things Competent﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*), and in it there is a reinforcement (*tarshīḥ*) of the intended directive for the threat, increasing their admonition, conveying it to them, and cutting off their excuses in this world and the Hereafter.

[Page 324]

This is a new, independent sentence (*istiʾnaf ibtidaʾi*, a resumptive sentence). With it, God turns the discourse to admonishing each of the four groups mentioned above, with an admonition suited to its condition. This comes after He has fully described each group by its traits, and after their conditions have been illustrated and their parables struck. Once He had completed the descriptions of the believers and their opposites, the idolaters and the hypocrites, the situation was ripe for addressing all of them together with what benefits them, as guidance for them and as mercy toward them. He does not desire misguidance for them. And the evil conduct mentioned just before did not stand as a barrier to renewing His guidance of them and turning to them in address. In this there is a comforting of their souls after He had threatened them, reproached them, and condemned their conduct, so that they would know that the harshness toward them was nothing but zeal for their welfare, and that He is independent of them. This is like the nurturing, sincerely advising educator who, when he rebukes or censures, sees the spirit of the one he is raising broken, and so he mends his heart with a gentle word, to show him that he only wronged him for the sake of correction and out of love for his good. Thus He does not withhold His mercy toward His creation even in their state of rebellion and misguidance, and in their state of being carried toward their own welfare.

Furthermore, this comforting and mending of hearts increases the doers of good in their goodness, and restrains the wrongdoers from their evil conduct. Thus each of the groups mentioned earlier takes its share of it.

The intended meaning of the address in His words ﴿O people﴾ is to turn attention to the admonition to abandon polytheism. This is the predominant usage of the Qur'an in addressing with "O people." The indication of this here is His words ﴿So do not set up rivals to God while you know﴾ (2:22). He opened the address with the vocative to give it prominence. *Yā* (O) is a particle of address, and it is the most frequently used of the vocative particles. Hence it is the origin of the vocative particles, and for this reason no other particle is presumed when the vocative particle is omitted. And because it is the origin, it was used in common for addressing the near and the far, as in the *al-Qamus*. Al-Radi said in his commentary on *al-Kafiyah*: The use of *yā* for the near and the far alike is established, and claiming a metaphorical use for one of them, or an interpretation, is contrary to the original usage.

He intends by this to refute al-Zamakhshari, when he said in *al-Kashshaf*: *Yā* is a particle originally laid down for addressing the distant, then it was used for calling one who is heedless or inattentive even if near, treating him as if he were distant. He did the same in his book *al-Mufassal*.

*Ayyu* (which) in origin is an indefinite noun that denotes an individual of a genus, followed by a noun connected to it by way of apposition (*idafah*), as in "*ayyu rajulin*" (what man), or by way of substitution (*ibdal*), as in "*yā ayyuhā al-rajul*" (O you man). Among its uses is that of specification (*ikhtisas*), like your saying to your companion: "I have taken care of your concern, O you who are sitting beside you." They sometimes address the one being addressed by his generic name or by his attribute, because that is the way of knowing him, or because it is more comprehensive for bringing him to attention, as here. Thus the addressed may then be put in indefinite form, intended or unintended. Sometimes they use the generic name or attribute defined by the generic *al-* (*al-lam al-jinsiyyah*), indicating that definiteness extends to it as a whole, as a variation in style. So their usage became that in such a case they bring, with the *al-*, a demonstrative noun, to emphasize its definiteness, and they separate between the vocative particle and the addressed noun in such a case by the word "*ay*." This is a construction not in line with the analogy of the language, and perhaps it is a remnant of an archaic usage.

They have contracted the demonstrative noun, retaining the reminder particle "*hā*" and dropping the demonstrative noun. So the origin of "*yā ayyuhā al-nās*" is "*yā ayyuhāʾulāʾi*." They have stated this explicitly in some of their speech, as in the saying of an unknown poet:

*Ayyuhadhāni kullā zādaykumā*
(O you two, each of your provisions!)

Sometimes they intended to address an unknown person present in essence as well, by means of something indicating the manner of his presence, from a state he is in, considering him as an individual of a genus. So they arrived at this by means of the relative noun, which indicates the state through its clause and indicates the genus, because the relative noun comes to what the *al-* comes to. Thus they insert *ayyu* in this way, as in His words ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾ (15:6). The word "people" (*al-nās*) has already been discussed in its derivation at His words, exalted is He, ﴿And among the people﴾ (2:8). It is a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*), addressed here, and defined by *al-*. It encompasses all the individuals of what it names, because collective nouns defined by *al-* are general, so long as no specific reference is established, as is settled in the principles of jurisprudence. Their possibly meaning a specific reference is weak, since the norm is a specific reference to individuals. For this reason, in generality it is more explicit than the generality of the singular noun defined by *al-*.

If you look at the form of the address, then it was addressed to people who were hearing it, so its generality extends to whoever was not present at the time this verse was heard, and to whoever will come into existence later. This is by the indication of the generality of obligation and the non-intention of restricting it to those present. That is a matter established both by transmission and by meaning. So it is no wonder that it encompasses all, without any need for analogy. And if you look at the fact that this is one of the types of address that is not directed at a specific person, so the specification is left out in order to include everyone who is fit to be addressed with it, and this is the practice of the address issued by preachers, rulers, and authors in their books, such as their saying: "O people," "O young man," "you see," "you know by this," and the like. So what do you think of the address of the messengers, and of an address that descends from God, exalted is He, which is general to everyone whom the wording includes, without seeking help from any other proof?

This is the verification of the question which the jurists of principles pose and express with the address of direct speech (*khitab al-mushafahah*) and face-to-face address (*khitab al-muwajahah*): does it encompass all, or not? The majority, although they said that it addresses those present and not those after them, based on the view that this is what direct address requires, to the point that al-ʿAḍud said that denying this is obstinacy. Al-Taftazani discussed it, and they said: the extension of the ruling to those who come after them is among what is established by the generality of the mission, and that its rulings encompass creation in all ages, as al-Baydawi indicated.

I say: The apparent view is that the addresses of legislation and the like do not follow the familiar pattern of the direction of address in the origins of languages, because the lawgiver does not intend a specific group. Likewise the address of caliphs and governors in decrees and appointment documents. So the indication that those present are not intended is firm and clear. The most that can be said is that its connection to those present is an original, obligatory connection, and its connection to those who come after is a notional, informative connection, in the manner established regarding the connection of the command in the science of the principles of jurisprudence. So we posit something like it in the direction of the address.

Worship (*ʿibadah*) in origin is humbling oneself and submission. Its meaning was discussed at His words ﴿You alone we worship﴾ (1:5). Since humbling oneself and submission arise only from true certainty, faith in God and affirming His unity in divinity is the starting point of worship, because whoever associates with the one who deserves worship that which does not deserve it has moved far from humbling himself and submitting to Him. So those addressed by the command to worship are the idolaters among the Arabs, the materialists (*dahriyyun*) among them, the People of the Book, and the believers, each according to the worship obligatory upon him: affirming the Creator and His unity, faith in the Messenger, submission to the religion, and compliance with what He has legislated, and beyond all that, up to the furthest point of worship, even by constancy and perseverance with respect to the Messenger ﷺ and the believers with him. For they are included in the address, as is established in the principles. So the commandedness is the common element, so that the shared term is not forced to be used in all its meanings according to whoever uses it in that way. Yet we do not reject this if the context allows it, as evidenced by His saying after that, ﴿So do not set up rivals to God﴾ (2:22), as a consequence of His words ﴿Worship your Lord﴾ and the verse. Therefore there is no proof in this verse for the view that the unbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Sharia, because the command to worship, with respect to them, refers only to faith, affirming the unity of God, and confirming the Messenger. Their being addressed with that is agreed upon. And this is a repugnant question.

The discussion of the meaning of *Rabb* (Lord) has already passed at His words ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ (1:2) in Surat al-Fatihah. The reason for turning away from other means of definiteness, such as the proper name, by not saying "worship God," is that the use of the word *Rabb* indicates that the command to worship Him is most appropriate. For the one who manages the affairs of creation is worthy of worship, because worship carries the meaning of gratitude and the manifestation of need.

The singular form of the name *Rabb* indicates that what is meant is the Lord of all creation, who is God, exalted is He, since there is no lord who deserves this name in its singularity and its attribution to all people except God. For even though the idolaters associated with God other gods, some tribes had a special attachment to some idols, just as Thaqif had a special attachment to al-Lat, as was mentioned in Surat al-Fatihah. The Aws and the Khazraj followed them, as will come in the explanation of His words ﴿Whoever makes the pilgrimage to the House or performs the minor pilgrimage﴾ (2:158) in this surah. So the turning to the attribution here is because it is the shortest way to indicate this purpose. It is shorter than the relative clause. For if other than God had been intended, it would have said: "worship your lords." Therefore His words ﴿worship your Lord﴾ are clearly an invitation to the unity of God. For this reason, His words ﴿who created you﴾ are an additional explanation of the basis for worship, or an additional explanation of what the attribution implies, namely the inclusion of the meaning of exclusivity in the worthiness of worship.

His words ﴿and those before you﴾ serve to remind the materialists among those addressed, who claim that their fathers were the ones who created them, and so they said ﴿We die and we live, and nothing destroys us but time﴾ (45:24). So His words ﴿and those before you﴾ were a reminder to them that their first fathers must lead back to a first father, and he is a creature of God, exalted is He. This is perhaps the reason for the emphasis by the added particle *min* in His words ﴿min qablikum﴾ (from before you), which could be dispensed with by merely saying "qablikum" (before you). For *min* originally indicates the starting point, so it points to the first of those characterized by priority. Thus its mention here is a retention of its original meaning together with the emphasis that predominates when it occurs with *qabl* and *baʿd*.

The creation (*khalq*) is originally bringing into existence according to a measure and arrangement. From it comes the saying: "He created the leather when he prepared it to cut and sew it." Jubayr said about Hiram ibn Sinan:

*Wa-innaka tafrī mā khalaqta wa-baʿḍu l-qawmi yakhluqu thumma lā yafrī*
(You indeed cut what you have created, while some people create and then do not cut.)

The term *khalq* in the Qur'an and in the language of the Sharia is applied to bringing into existence things that did not exist. It is bringing things out from non-existence into existence, a bringing forth in which there is no human craftsmanship. For the bringing into existence of things by human craftsmanship is only giving them a form by assembling their scattered parts and fixing the required measures of them, like the potter's craft. So creation and the bringing into existence of worlds and kinds and species of existents, and the generation of some of them from others through the order of existence that the divine nature has placed in them, such as the formation of embryos in animals within their wombs and eggs, the formation of plants in the seeds of grain, and the formation of water in clouds, all of this is creation, and it is from God's formation, exalted is He. There is no consideration for what may accompany some of this bringing into existence of human treatment, such as marriage, or throwing seed and pits into the earth for growth. So the bringing into existence, which is bringing forth from non-existence into existence without human action,

[Page 328]

Ibn 'Ashur, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir, commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 21 (part 2 of 2)

It is specified by the name "creation" (khalq) in the terminology of the Shari'ah, because the word khalq is, in the Arabic language, the closest of words in indicating the meaning of bringing into existence from non-existence, which is an attribute of God Most High. That meaning became the signified sense of the root kh-l-q in the terminology of the people of Islam. Therefore its application in the language of Islam is specific to God Most High: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then remember?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], and He said ﴿Is there any creator other than God?﴾ [Fatir: 3]. The name al-Khaliq (the Creator) is specific to Him, Most High, and is not applied to anyone else. If someone were to apply it to other than God Most High on the basis of the linguistic literal meaning, its application would be presumptuous (ajrafah), and it must therefore be warned against being abandoned.

Al-Ghazali said in al-Maqsad al-Asna: "The servant has no share in His name the Creator, Most High, except by a far-fetched kind of metaphor. When he attains, in governing himself and governing creation, a level at which he alone devises matters that no one has preceded him in, and is able also to do them, he is like one who invents what had no existence before, and so it is permissible to apply the name—that is, the Creator—to him metaphorically." End of quote.

He made the permissibility of applying the verb of creation to the invention of some servants conditional upon this rare state, and yet he considered it a distant metaphor. What God related in the Qur'an of the words of 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, I create for you from clay like the form of a bird; then I breathe into it, and it becomes a bird by permission of God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 49], and God Most High's words ﴿And when you create from clay like the form of a bird by My permission﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]—this is governed by the original linguistic application before the usage of the root kh-l-q became dominant for the creation that none can do except God Most High. Then the restriction of that root to God Most High's bringing existence into being of the existents. For this reason He Most High said ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14].

The clause ﴿la'allakum tattaqun (that you may be God-fearing)﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the command "worship" (u'budu), and therefore it is detached (fusilat), meaning: I commanded you to worship Him in hope that you would become God-fearing.

La'alla (لَعَلَّ) is a particle indicating hope (raja'). Hope is the report of the readiness of an event to occur in the future, occurring with certainty. Thus it becomes clear that la'alla is a particle whose signification is declarative (khabari), because it is a report of the certainty of the occurrence of a thing, while its meaning is composed of the speaker's hope regarding the addressee, which is a particular, particle-type meaning. Among the exegetes and the scholars of the sciences, the perplexity regarding the intended sense of la'alla occurring in the speech of God Most High has become widespread, because the meaning of expectation (tarajji) requires that the speaker not be certain of the occurrence of the hoped-for matter; so there is an aspect of doubt in its meaning, to the extent that al-Jawhari said: "La'alla is a word of doubt." This is not consistent with God's knowledge of the states of things before they occur. Also, it has occurred in reports even when the hoped-for outcome did not happen, as in His words ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits, that they might remember﴾ [al-A'raf: 130], although they did not remember, as the subsequent verses clarify.

Regarding the interpretation of la'alla occurring in the speech of God Most High, there are several views:

First: Sibawayh said: "La'alla is on its original usage, and the expectation or anticipation is only within the sphere of the addressees." That is, it is a report that the addressee is the one who is hoped for. Al-Radi adopted this, saying: "Because the principle is that it should not wholly depart from its meaning."

I say: Sibawayh does not mean that this meaning was the original basis of the word; rather he means that it is a metaphor close to the real meaning, because there is a restriction in one of the two components of the real meaning. For hope requires a one who hopes and one who is hoped from. So the particle of hope signifies the sense of the verb of hope, though only as a particular meaning, and each of the agent and the object is signified by the meaning of the verb by implication. When a context indicates the suspension of the particle of hope's signification regarding the agent of hope, there is no metaphor in the particle or the verb, since metaphor only applies to linguistic signifieds, not rational ones; and likewise when the hoped-for act does not occur.

Second: that la'alla is for enticement (ith'am). You say to one who intends: "La'allaka tanal bughyataka (perhaps you will attain your aim)." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It has come in the manner of enticement in several places in the Qur'an." Enticement is also a metaphorical meaning of hope, because hope entails proximity, and proximity entails enticement; so enticement is a necessary consequence at two levels.

Third: that it is for causation in the sense of kay (in order that). This was said by Qutrub, Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and Ibn al-Anbari. I suppose that their intention with this meaning is in the contexts where the sense of hope does not appear, so it is not objected to them that it does not apply in such a verse as ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17], since the meaning of hope is valid with respect to the addressee. Nor is it objected to them that this is asserting a meaning in la'alla for which there is no witness in the speech of the Arabs. Al-Zamakhshari made it a view branching from the view that made it for enticement, saying: "Because it is an enticement from a generous one: when he is enticed, he acts." Whoever says that la'alla means kay has a metaphorical meaning arising from another metaphor, so this is a composition of metaphor upon necessity with three levels.

Fourth: what the author of al-Kashshaf held, that it is a metaphor (isti'arah). He said: "La'alla occurs in the verse in the position of metaphor, because God Most High created His servants so that He might have them worship Him, and placed in their hands the reins of choice, and desired good and piety from them. So they are in the form of one from whom hope is held that they will be God-fearing, so that their affair may tilt, while they are free to choose between obedience and disobedience, just as the state of one who hopes is weighed between doing and not doing." Its evidence is His words ﴿That He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7]. Testing and examining are only for one whose outcomes are hidden from him; but the testing was likened to the structuring of their affair upon choice. Thus al-Kashshaf makes la'alla in God's speech a figurative (tamthili) metaphor, since he made it the likeness of a composite state of the one who desires and what is desired from him and the desire, with a composite state of the one who hopes, the one hoped from, and the hope. So the composite expression that is set for hope is borrowed for the meaning of the composite that signifies desire.

I have another independent view: that la'alla occurring in the context of giving the reason for a command or prohibition has a usage that differs from the usage of la'alla that begins a sentence, whether it occurs in the speech of God or in other speech. When you say: "Check on so-and-so, perhaps you will advise him," it is a report of the nearness of the occurrence of the thing, and that it is within the realm of possibility if what is conditioned upon it is accomplished. As for its requiring that the speaker not be certain of the occurrence, that is a generally prevalent implied meaning, which may be known to be absent through context; and that absence is more evident in the speech of God. So our belief that everything that has not occurred or will not occur in the future is the context that suspends this implied meaning, without need for interpretation in the sense of hope that la'alla conveys, so that it would be metaphor or figure. Because la'alla is only used because the context requires the sense of hope. Therefore, binding the interpretation of this implication in every place in the Qur'an is a suspension of the sense of hope that the context requires. The scholars resorted to interpretation because they looked at la'alla with a single gaze across all its positions of usage, unlike the initiating la'alla, which is closer to the performance of hope than to the report of it.

In any case, the meaning of la'alla is different from the meaning of the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah). Taqwa is guarding against what is disliked; it is common among the Arabs and the religious in its causes, and it is the attainment of the qualities of perfection that religiosity gathers. Its discussion has already preceded at the words of God Most High ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. Since taqwa is the result of worship, the hope of it was made an effect of the command to worship. The meaning is: worship your Lord in hope that you will be God-fearing, so that you become perfect and God-fearing; for taqwa is the purpose of worship. So the hope of its attainment at the command to worship and at the worshipper's worship, or at the will of creation and origination, has clear benefit.

[331]

It is necessary that His saying, ﴿Who made the earth for you a resting-place (firash)﴾, be a second attribute of the Lord, because its context is the context of His saying ﴿Who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. The purpose is to point to another reason why He alone deserves to be worshipped and singled out for worship. When He made it obligatory to worship Him, on the ground that He is the Creator of all people, He followed this with another attribute that requires them to worship Him alone: His continuous blessings upon them, together with the signs of His great power within them. He enabled them to have the means of livelihood, and the first of these is a place suitable for settling on without fatigue. He made it like a bed (firash) for them. Among the blessings is that this settled place is surrounded by air that is beneficial to their life, which is the nourishment of the animal spirit (al-ruh al-hayawani). This is what is indicated by His saying ﴿and the sky as a structure (binā')﴾. Also, through that atmospheric sphere, people are protected from the harm of layers above it, which extend very high, such as extreme cold (zamharir) or strange, deadly, suffocating elements. The atmospheric sphere is placed above this world, so it is like a building (binā') for it, and its benefit is like the benefit of a building. Therefore it is likened to a building by way of the eloquent simile (al-tashbih al-baligh). And [He blessed them] by bringing forth for people what sustains the straightness (awad) of their life, through the combination of rainwater with the strength of the earth, which is fruit.

The word "sky" (al-sama') here is used in its customary sense among the Arabs, namely what appears to the observer as a blue dome. It is the sphere of air surrounding the earth, as is intended in His saying ﴿or like a downpour from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]. This is the predominant meaning when "sky" is used in the singular, without the plural.

The meaning of "He made the earth a bed" is that it is like a bed in allowing one to settle and lie down upon it, and that is the most specific form of settling. The meaning is that He made it intermediate between the harshness of rocks, which would hurt a person's skin, and the softness of mud, in which a creature would slip and sink. This is a great favour.

As for the aspect of resemblance between the sky and a building, it is that God made the atmospheric sphere a barrier between the terrestrial sphere and the ethereal sphere (al-kurah al-athiriyyah). It is thus like a building in what a building is for, namely protection from descending harms. The atmospheric sphere repels several harms, the most evident of which is repelling the flooding of the seas over the earth, and repelling the harms of the arrival of airs that are emitted from some of the stars toward us, and softening them until they mix with the air, or the air holding them back from us. There is also the resemblance of the atmospheric sphere to the shape of a dome, and a dome is a tent of leather (adam) that is arched, and it is called a building (binā').

[332]

In the speech of the Arabs, a building is whatever is raised high above the ground for protection, whether made of stone, leather or hair. From this comes their saying "he built upon his wife" (bana 'ala imra'atihi) when he married, because the one who marries makes a house in which he lives with his wife. The use of "building" for a leather tent is well known, and for this reason they called the leather from which domes are made mabnāh, with the mim either open or with a kasra. This is like His saying in surat al-Anbiya': ﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾ [al-Anbiya': 32].

If you say: your speech implies that the favour of making the sky like a building for the protection of people belongs to the scientific miracles that you indicated in the tenth introduction, and that is understood only by the generations that came after the time of revelation. Then what is the share of the Muslims and others among whom the verse was revealed, in relation to His saying ﴿and those who came after them﴾ [al-Hashr: 10], across many generations? For the people of the Jahiliyyah did not perceive that the sky has the property of a building in protection. What they imagined at most was that the sky resembles the ceiling of a dome, as the Bedouin woman said when she was asked about knowing the stars: "Can anyone be ignorant of beads hanging from his ceiling?" Thus the verse serves to convey lessons from that wondrous creation. However, it contains no share of the favour that is conveyed by His saying "for you" (lakum). So should we restrict the connection of "for you" to the expressed verb "made" (ja'ala), rather than its connection to the implied verb under the conjunction wāw, or make it connected to "bed" (firash), so that His saying ﴿and the sky as a building﴾ becomes coordinated with the object of the verb "made" when it is unrestricted by any connected complement?

I say: this leads to an arbitrary restriction of the connection of "for you," an arbitrariness for which the hearer has no evidence. Rather, the correct view is that "for you" is connected to the verb "made." For the favour of the creation of the sky, it suffices that the hearers of this verse are made aware that in the creation of the sky in that form there is what there is in the building of a structure in terms of general benefits, so that the hearers may conceive it according to the measure of their intuitions and understanding. Then its full interpretation comes in later generations.

"For you" (lakum) is omitted when the sky is mentioned, for brevity, because its mention in His saying ﴿made the earth for you a bed﴾ is evidence for it.

If "made" (ja'ala) means "brought into existence" (awjada), then the favour is borne by that meaning if both are in this state. If it means "transformed" (sayyara), then it indicates that the earth and the sky have moved from one state to another until they became as they are. "Became" (sara) is more apparent in the meaning of transition from one attribute to another, and the rules of the science of geological strata (al-jiyulujya, geology) indicate this second aspect. Thus there are two favours and two lessons in the verse, in making them as we have seen, and in the stages through which they passed by the power and permission of God Most High. This is like His saying: ﴿Have not those who disbelieved seen that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, and We separated them?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 30], up to His saying ﴿and We made the sky a protected ceiling, yet they turn away from its signs﴾ [al-Anbiya': 32].

[333]

God has bestowed favour and set forth the lesson through the nearest and most evident things to all people, both the settled and the nomadic, and through the first of the things that are conditions of this life. In them are the most beneficial things: air, and water that springs from the earth. In them the first benefits of humankind were realised. The specific mention of the earth and the sky has another subtle point, which is the preparation for His saying that follows: ﴿and sent down water from the sky﴾, and so on. He began with the earth because it is the first thing that comes to the mind of the reflecting person; then with the sky, because after the reflecting person looks at what is before him, he looks at what surrounds him.

His saying ﴿and sent down water from the sky, and by it brought forth﴾, and so on, is a favour concerning what follows creation: what preserves it from disruption. It is a replacement for what the innate heat (al-hararah al-gharizziyyah), nervous activity and cerebral activity consume of bodily strength, so that the constitution of the body may endure through nourishment. The origin of nourishment is what comes out of the earth. The earth brings forth vegetation only by water descending upon it from the sky, that is, from the clouds and the upper layers.

Know that the water's descending from the sky is due to its formation in the layers of the atmosphere, from the effects of vapour that is in the atmosphere. The atmosphere is always filled with vapours rising into it by the heat of the sun from the waters of seas and rivers, from the moisture of the earth, and from vegetation. This is why we find a vessel filled with water empty after days if left uncovered to the air. When the vapour reaches the high regions of the atmosphere, it cools by their coldness, especially in the winter season. When it cools, it tends to condense, and becomes a cloud. Then it remains for a little or a long time according to the proportion between the coldness of the atmospheric layers and the heat of the vapour. When the coldness increases upon it, the cloud contracts and grows heavy and condenses, so the watery bubbles gather in it and weigh upon it, and it sends down rain. This is what His saying indicates: ﴿and He produces the heavy clouds﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12]. Likewise, when the cloud is struck by a wind coming from the direction of the sea, which is a moist wind, the air rises to the upper atmosphere, cools, and becomes liquid. Perhaps the cloud was small, so the wind drives another cloud to it, and one joins the other and they send down rain. This is why rain frequently follows the blowing of a sea wind. In the hadith: "When a sea wind arises and then turns to the north, that is a heavy, copious rain (ghudayqah)."

It is a principle that heat and lower pressure increase the rising and expansion of vapour, while cold and greater pressure turn vapour into liquid. It has been observed that the rising of vapour increases in proportion to the nearness of a region to the equator, and decreases in proportion to its distance from it. Some of this is indicated by what is related in the hadith: "Rain descends from a rock beneath the Throne." The Throne ('arsh) is the name of one of the heavens, and the rock is an approximation of a place of coldness. You have known that rain is produced by coldness, which condenses the cloud into water. Thus coldness is the begetter of the rain.

[334]

The "min" (from) in His saying ﴿from the fruits﴾ is not partitive (lil-tab'id), since partition is not suitable to the context of favour. Rather, it is either explanatory, indicating what the provision is that was brought forth, and placing the explanation before what is explained is common in Arabic speech; or it is additional (za'idah), for the emphasis of the connection of the bringing forth to the fruits.

* * *

﴿So do not set up rivals to God while you know﴾

The fa' (so) comes to order this sentence upon the preceding speech, which is ordered upon the command to worship. "Do not" (la) is prohibitive, and the verb is jussive (majzum). It is not negative, so that the verb would be in the subjunctive as an answer to the command in His saying ﴿worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. What is meant here is its specific causation, namely that it results from a proof that requires it, which is that the One Whom He commanded you to worship is the One deserving of exclusive worship. Thus it is more specific than the general opposite of worship, because the opposite of worship is the absence of worship. But since associating partners with the worshipped in worship resembles abandoning worship, abandoning association is made equivalent to the contrary of worship, because association is nothing but abandonment of the worship of God at the times of honouring their associates.

The word nidd (rival), with a kasra on the nun, means one equal and similar in some matter, such as glory or war. Some lexicographers added that it is one who opposes, that is, who is hostile. They seem to have considered its derivation from nadda, meaning to flee or to oppose. But this is not necessary, since it may be a fixed noun. I think that the reason the word nidd signifies opposition and contrariety is that these are among the necessary consequences of similarity in custom among the Arabs. It is the nature of an equal among them to compete with his equal and contend with him for what he desires, so opposition results.

A parallel to this in the reverse is their calling the equal qari' (a contender), since the qari' is one who wrestles and strikes. Since no one would take on the challenge of one who is above him out of fear, nor one who is beneath him out of contempt, contending entails equality. Likewise, their saying qirn is for a warrior equal to him in courage. It is said "he made for him a nidd" when he equated another with him.

The meaning is: do not establish for God rivals that you make by your making, though they are not rivals. He called them rivals as a mockery of their claim, because the condition of the Arabs in their worship of them is like the condition of one who equates God with them, even though the people of the Jahiliyyah said that the gods are intercessors, and said: "We worship them only so that they may bring us near to God." They made God the Creator of the gods, and they said in the talbiyah (the call of pilgrimage, "Here I am"): "Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You; You possess him and what he possesses." But when they worshipped them, and forgot, through worshipping them, and through striving toward them, making vows at them and holding festivals around them, that the worship was of God, their deeds became the deeds of one who believes in equating them with God Most High, because it is the deed that counts, not the speech. In this there is an element of allusive reproach against them, and a charge of the disorder of their condition and the contradiction of their words by their deeds.

[335]

Ibn 'Ashur's words on the verse "Do not set up rivals to Allah while you know" (2:22):

His saying ﴿and you know﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah). The object of "you know" (ta'lamun) is omitted, because the verb was not intended to be linked to an object; rather, it was intended only to affirm the attribute of knowledge to its doer, so the verb is treated as intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lazim). The meaning is: "while you are people of knowledge." By "knowledge" (ilm) here is meant complete intellect ('aql tamm), which is the soundness of judgment that is contrasted, in their view, with ignorance (jahl), as in His saying ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]. This circumstantial clause has been made the focus of both the prohibition and the negation, as a subtle rhetorical device that combines rebuke with the stirring of resolve. He affirmed for them knowledge and soundness of judgment in order to stir their resolve and draw their insight to the proofs of God's oneness. He forbade them from taking rivals (or negated that), while they were characterized by it, and he made it incompatible with knowledge, as a rebuke for what they neglected of the gifts of their minds and squandered of the soundness of their perception. This is a great method of moral education (manza tahdhibi 'azim): that the educator deliberately combines, for the one he educates, what points to a remaining perfection in him, so that he does not kill his resolve through despair of his own perfection. For if his opinion of himself becomes bad, his determination weakens and his gifts disappear. And he also brings what points to his deficiencies, so that he seeks perfection and does not rest from the toil of striving for lofty aims and perfection.

His saying ﴿and you know﴾ has also indicated that they know that Allah has no equal, but they feigned ignorance and forgot, and so they said:
"Except a partner who is yours."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 23 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it, and call upon your witnesses other than God, if you are truthful.﴾

This is a transition to establishing the second of the two parts of faith (īmān), after the first part has been established through what preceded it, namely His saying, ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:21), and so on. This is the connection (munāsabah) that required this sentence to be conjoined to the sentence ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:21). Also, the prohibition against making rivals (andād) for God came from God, so they were likely to deny that God had forbidden the worship of their intercessors and those close to Him, since in their error they claimed that God had commanded them to do so. He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And they say, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:20). Thus they offered as a justification for worshipping idols that God had established them as intermediaries between Himself and them. With this, the connection of conjoining His saying ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾ to His saying ﴿So do not set up rivals to God﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:22) was strengthened. The particle ʾin ("if") was used in the conditional clause of this condition, which is their being in doubt. It is known in the science of rhetoric (ʿilm al-maʿānī) that ʾin is specific to a situation in which the occurrence of the condition is not certain. This is because the meaning of this condition is surrounded by evidences which should uproot the condition from its root, such that its occurrence is hypothetical. Therefore, the use of ʾin, while the listener is known to be in doubt, indicates the speaker's knowledge that the condition is fulfilled, as a rebuke for the fulfilment of that condition, as if their doubt about the Qur'an were a weakly-occurring thing. The reason for this is that the wording and meanings of the Qur'an are so refined that, if sound reason contemplated them, it would be certain that it is from God, exalted is He. It came with an eloquence and rhetorical excellence the like of which they had not known from their most accomplished masters of eloquence, and these were numerous and abundant among them. To the point that some of them prostrated because of its eloquence, and some of them acknowledged that it was not the speech of a human being. It included meanings which their poets, orators and sages had never touched upon, and even meanings which some of the scholars of the nations had not attained. Throughout the length of time, knowledge has continued to reveal the hidden secrets of the Qur'an and to prove the truth of its being from God. These attributes are therefore sufficient for them to perceive this, and they are people of sound intellect and clear perception, as shown by their poetry, their reports, their spontaneity and their debates, and which the nations have testified to them in every age. How, after all of that, could there remain any path to doubt about it open to them, let alone their being immersed in it?

The use of fī (in), which denotes enclosure, indicates that doubt has taken possession of them and surrounded them as a container surrounds what is contained. The use of fī in the sense of attachment (mulābasah) is common in the speech of the Arabs, as in their saying: "He is in blessing" (huwa fī niʿmah). The verb nazzala is used rather than anzala because the Qur'an was sent down in installments (nujūman). It has already been mentioned at the beginning of the tafsir that the form faʿʿala indicates a gradual passing away, bit by bit. Moreover, the author of al-Kashshāf mentioned that its choice here, in the context of the challenge (taḥaddī), is to take into account what they used to say: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" So when this was one of the sources of their doubts, it was appropriate to mention it in their challenge: that they should produce a surah like it, arranged in installments (munajjamah).

A surah is a specific portion of the Qur'an, distinguished from other similar portions by a beginning and an end, comprising three or more verses, in one complete purpose or several purposes.

Using the word surah as a generic noun for portions of the Qur'an is a technical usage (iṣṭilāḥ) brought by the Qur'an itself. It is derived from al-sūr, which is the wall that surrounds a town or an enclosure. Thus the name surah is specific to the defined portions of the Qur'an, and not to other books. Its detailed explanation has been given in the eighth introduction of this tafsir. The challenge was made with a surah and not with the measure of a surah from the verses of the Qur'an, because among the aspects of its inimitability (iʿjāz) are matters whose distinctive qualities only become apparent when considering a complete discourse on one of the purposes. The surahs of the Qur'an were revealed for specific purposes, so there is no escape from considering the particularities appropriate to the openings and closings of speech according to its purpose, completing the purpose which the speech is driving towards, the correctness of the division, the subtleties of summary and detail, the rules of transition from one art to another among the arts of the purpose, the connections of digression, interjection, departure and return, the separation and joining of sentences, brevity and elaboration, and similar matters which pertain to the subtleties of the whole composition of the speech. These are not clearly apparent in their correspondence unless the speech is complete and the purpose has fully attained its due. Therefore, the arrangement of the Qur'an and the excellence of its fusion have an inimitability which exceeds human capacity, which is other than the inimitability found in its sentences, its structures and the eloquence of its words.

Thus a surah of the Qur'an is in the position of a preacher's sermon or a poet's ode: it is not judged to be superior except by considering the whole of it after considering its parts.

Al-Ṭībī, in his marginal commentary on al-Kashshāf, said, at His saying ﴿So you did not kill them﴾ (al-Anfāl 8:17) in the surah of al-Anfāl: "And because of the secret of the Qur'anic composition, the challenge was made with a surah, even if it is short, and not with verses, even if they are numerous."

The indefinite form (tankīr) is for singularity or for kind: that is, with one surah of the category of surahs. This is fulfilled by the shortest surah which is designated by a name specific to it. The shortest surahs in number of verses are the surah of al-Kawthar. The polytheists in Medina were following the polytheists in Mecca, and the revelation of this surah was at the beginning of the period after the emigration to Medina. All the polytheists were a confederacy against the Prophet (ﷺ), contriving to incite and to turn people away from following him. So the challenge of the inimitability of the Qur'an was renewed for them, the challenge that had already been made in the surahs of Yunus, Hud and al-Isra.

The challenge was first made with bringing a book like that which had been sent down. In the surah of al-Isra, He said: ﴿Say: "If mankind and the jinn were to gather to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if some of them were to others assistants."﴾ (al-Isrāʾ 17:88). When they were unable to do so, they were brought down to producing ten surahs like it, in the surah of Hud. Then they were brought down further to producing a single surah like it, in the surah of Yunus.

The word mithl (like) originally means the similar, and the one that is completely alike. It is therefore originally an adjective that follows a described noun. Then its use spread to refer to the similar and equivalent thing.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿like it﴾ (min mithlihi) may refer to what We have sent down, meaning "of the like of the Qur'an". It may also refer to "Our servant". If it refers to what We have sent down, meaning "of the like of the Qur'an", then the most apparent reading is that min is for origin (ibtidāʾiyyah), meaning "a surah derived from the like of the Qur'an", that is, "a book like the Qur'an". The prepositional phrase is then an adjective of surah. It may also be partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah), explanatory (bayāniyyah), or superfluous (zāʾidah).

All of this has been said, though these are weaker opinions. In all cases, the prepositional phrase is an adjective of surah, meaning: it is a part of the like of what We have sent down, with mithl being a noun in this case in the sense of "one that is alike". Or: "a surah like what We have sent down", with mithl being an adjective according to the two possibilities that min is explanatory or superfluous. All of these possibilities require that the like, whether it is an adjective or a noun, is a hypothetical like based on their belief and their supposition. It does not require that this like actually exists, because the speech is driven towards demonstrating their incapacity. If the pronoun refers to "Our servant", then min is for the transitive complement of the verb ʾtū ("produce"), and it is for origin. In that case the prepositional phrase is a complement of a non-fixed (ghayr mustaqirr) adverbial type. It is permissible for the prepositional phrase to be an adjective of surah on the basis that it is a fixed adverbial. The meaning in both cases is: "Produce a surah derived from a man like Muhammad in his unlettered state." The word mithl in that case is a noun.

It has become clear to you that the word mithl in the verse cannot mean that it is a metonymy (kināyah) for the thing that is added to, on the model of His saying: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ (al-Shūrā 42:11), on the basis that the word mithl is a metonymy for the thing it is added to. This is because the meaning would not be correct if the sense were: "So produce a surah from the Qur'an", or "from Muhammad". This is contrary to someone who imagined this from the words of al-Kashshāf. Rather, the word mithl is used in its clear meaning, except that it resembles a metonymy for the very thing it is added to, in the sense that the like here, on the assumption that it is a noun, is not actually existing. However, the reason for the non-existence of its actuality is that it is supposed, since commanding in the sense of incapacitation requires the impossibility of what is commanded. None of these aspects requires the existence of a like of the Qur'an, so that some of these aspects would be intended, as al-Taftazānī imagined. In my view, all the possibilities that His saying ﴿like it﴾ can bear are intended, in order to refute the claims of the deniers, since their claims differ. Among them is one who said: "The Qur'an is the speech of a human being." Among them is one who said: "It is copied from the fables of the ancients." Among them is one who said: "A human being teaches it."

These aspects of the verse's meaning refute all these claims. If it is the speech of a human being, then produce something like it or its equal. If it is from the fables of the ancients, then you produce a part of these fables. If a human being teaches it, then you produce from your own side a surah, for he is not stingy with you if you ask him.

All of this is a loosening of the reins of opposition and a recording of the inimitability for when opposition is absent.

So the challenge concerning the truthfulness of the Qur'an is the totality of the resemblance of the Qur'an in its words and structures, and the resemblance of the Messenger to whom it was sent down in that he is unlettered, has not previously received any instruction, and does not know the earlier books. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book?﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt 29:51). This is the meaning of resemblance. So if they were to produce something from the sermons or poetry of their eloquent men which did not contain the particularities that the Qur'an contains, that would not be producing what He challenged them with. And if they were to produce a discourse containing legislative meanings, or wisdom, from the composition of a learned and wise man, that would not be producing what He challenged them with. Therefore, making min for origin does not imply that it would suffice for them to produce something from the speech of their eloquent men, because that resemblance is not complete.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and call upon your witnesses other than God﴾ is conjoined to ﴿then produce a surah﴾, meaning: "produce it, and call upon your witnesses." The verb "to call" (duʿāʾ) is used in the sense of requesting the presence of the one called, and in the sense of soliciting and asking him for some act. Abū Firās addressed Sayf al-Dawlah, asking him to ransom him from the captivity of the king of the Romans:

I called you for a tearful eye, sleepless with me,
and for a sleep that is driven away and dispersed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 23 (part 2 of 2):

Al-shuhada' (the witnesses) is the plural of shahid, on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active participle), from shahida, meaning "to be present" (hadara). Its original meaning is "the present one." Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the witnesses do not refuse when they are called﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. Then this word was used for that which necessarily involves presence, figuratively or metonymically, not by its original lexical application. It was also applied to the helper, by way of metonymy, since the witness supports the statement of the one witnessed for and aids him against his opponent. The term shahid is not applied to the imam and the exemplar, and al-Baydawi affirmed it, but it is not recognized in the books of lexicography nor in the speech of the exegetes. Perhaps he was led to it from the Kashshaf's explanation of the resultant meaning of the verse, so he mistakenly took it for a lexical meaning. Here, then, the intended sense is: call your gods, by the indication of His saying ﴿besides Allah﴾, that is, call them besides Allah, just as you habitually resort to them in your grave matters, turning away from calling upon Allah and seeking refuge in Him to calling upon them and seeking their aid. Thus in the verse there is an incorporation (idmaj) of rebuking them for polytheism within the context of the challenge to produce a counterpart. This incorporation is among the refinements of eloquence: that the eloquent speaker has two purposes, and he joins the purpose for which the speech is primarily directed with the second purpose. In it the eloquent speaker's capability is manifested, since he brings about that combination without departing from his primary purpose and without affectation. Al-Harith ibn Hillizah said:

Asma' has announced to us her separation, / and many a sojourner is wearied by his stay.

His saying "many a sojourner" when mentioning the beloved's distance and lamenting it is a metonymy that she is not of the kind whose sojourn becomes wearisome. He has thus settled the right of pleasing her by indicating that he does not care for the residence of anyone else. The incorporation has been counted among the decorative embellishments (muhassinat badi'iyyah), and it is worthy of being classed among the rhetorical chapters under the topic of prolixity (itnab) or the diversion of speech from what the apparent context requires. Indeed, their gods are helpers to them in their own assumption.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning is: call your helpers from among the people of eloquence, so that it becomes a challenge to both the common folk and the elite.

And call whoever testifies to the likeness of what you have produced to what We have sent down, in the manner of His saying the Exalted: ﴿Say: Bring your witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this﴾ [al-An'am: 150]. And His saying ﴿besides Allah﴾, in these aspects, is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the pronoun in (ud'u, "call") or from (shuhadaa'akum, "your witnesses"), meaning: while you are not calling upon Allah in that, or while the witnesses are other than Allah, in the sense: make the side of Allah who sent down the Book like the side witnessed against. We have informed you of this, making it easy for you, because the severity of exposing incapacity is in proportion to the facilitation of the causes of action. It is also permissible that (dun, "besides") means "in front of" and "in the presence of," that is, call your witnesses in the presence of Allah. As evidence for this, they cite the saying of al-A'sha:

She shows you the speck before her, while she is beneath it; / when one tastes it, one smacks his lips.

Also permissible is that ("besides Allah") means "besides the party of Allah," who are the believers, that is: bring witnesses from among those who share your religion, for we have accepted them as witnesses. The skilled practitioner of a craft does not consent to testify to the correction of its corruption or the reverse, out of aversion to being attributed with poor knowledge or injustice, and both are things a person of honor does not accept. Long ago the Arabs used to seek arbitration and go to judgment before their wise men and their arbiters, and they did not hold against them an error or an injustice. Al-Samaw'al said:

When the inclinations of desire lean toward us, / and the listener is silent to the speaker,
we do not make falsehood truth, nor / do we press against the truth with falsehood.
We fear that our forbearance be made foolish, / so that we become forgotten through ages along with the obscure.

According to this interpretation, the statement of the jurists comes into place: the testimony of people of expertise in establishing defects or in soundness is not conditioned on uprightness (adala). I used to explain this in lessons of jurisprudence by saying that the purpose of uprightness is the realization of a restraint against false testimony, and the scholarly restraint in the testimony of experts has taken the place of religious restraint, because the expert is eager, as far as he can, that no error or mistake be attributed to him, and that is sufficient as a restraint against deliberately committing it, and his knowledge is sufficient as a presumption of hitting the correct answer. Thus the purpose of testimony is achieved.

His saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾ is an interjection at the end of the speech and a concluding appendage (tadhyil). He used "in" (the conditional particle), whose original condition is that its occurrence is not certain, because their truthfulness is not something that can be certainly realized. The clause ﴿if you are truthful﴾ (concerns) whether the Qur'an is the speech of a human being and whether you produced its like.

Sidq (truthfulness) is the opposite of kadhib (falsehood), and they are two attributes of a report, neither of which is free of one of them. Truthfulness is that the meaning of an informative statement corresponds and is similar to reality in the external world, that is, in external existence, as distinct from mental existence. Falsehood is the opposite of truthfulness, and it is that the meaning of an informative statement does not correspond, that is, is not similar to reality in the external world.

Speech is established for truthfulness, whereas falsehood is a rational possibility. A performative (insha') utterance is not described as truthful or false, since there is no sense in its correspondence to what is in the reality of the matter, because it is the bringing into being of a meaning, not of external affairs.

This is the meaning of truthfulness and falsehood in the well-known usage. Falsehood may also be used as a term of blame, and in that case its meaning is understood as: its deviation from reality was deliberate. Al-Jahiz imagined that the quiddity of falsehood is constituted by the non-correspondence of a report to reality and to belief together, and this constitutive condition extended to the quiddity of truthfulness, so he made its essence correspondence to the external and belief together. From here he affirmed an intermediate position between truthfulness and falsehood. Close to this is the statement of al-Raghib, and it is likely that the dispute is verbal; the full discussion belongs to the sciences of usul and rhetoric.

The meaning: if you are truthful in your claim that the Qur'an is the speech of a human being. The object of (sadiqin, "truthful") is omitted due to the indication of what preceded it. The apodosis of the conditional is omitted, indicated by a clause implied after the clause ﴿and call your witnesses besides Allah﴾, since the implied sense is: then you will bring a surah like it. The implied clause is indicated by his saying before it ﴿so bring a surah like it﴾, and the implied clause serves as evidence for the apodosis of the condition, so the clause ﴿if you are truthful﴾ becomes a repetition of the challenge. In this verse there is an arousing of their zeal, as it implicitly questions their truthfulness, so that their motives toward producing a counterpart are stirred.

[Page 342]

﴿فَإنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا ولَنْ تَفْعَلُوا فاتَّقُوا النّارَ الَّتِي وقُودُها النّاسُ والحِجارَةُ أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾

﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it, then guard yourselves against the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, prepared for the disbelievers.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the conditional clause and its response. That is: if you do not produce a sūrah, or if you produce what you claim is a sūrah (and your witnesses have been unable to do so, under either interpretation), then know that you have dared against God by denying His Messenger, who was supported by the miracle (mu'jizah) of the Qur'an. So guard yourselves against His punishment, which is prepared for the likes of you.

The object of "taf'alū" (you do) is omitted, but the context indicates it: "If you do not do that," namely, produce a sūrah like it. The discussion of omitting the object in a similar construction will come at the words of the Exalted, ﴿وإنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلْ فَما بَلَّغْتَ رِسالاتَهُ﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 67], in the sūrah of al-Mā'idah.

The conditional particle "in" is used, which in principle does not imply certainty. Yet the non-performance is the more likely outcome, given the context of challenge and incapacitation (taḥaddī wa-ta'jīz). The purpose is to present this condition as an unlikely one, in order to heighten their motivation to counter-argue, by means of gentleness and encouragement, and to exhaust their capacity to do so. This is like drawing in the opponent's bird (istinzāl ṭā'ir al-khaṣm), restraining the wild stubbornness of his obstinacy, and disputing with him "in the manner that is best" (Qur'an 16:125). When he comes to the truth and is fair to himself, he rises with the argument to higher degrees of disputation. That is why "and you will never do it" follows. It is as if the challenger is contemplating their situation and weighing their affair: he first says, "Produce a sūrah," then says, "Suppose you are unable to produce anything like it, and prepare an escape for that situation," and then says, "Now I have become certain, and you have become certain, that you are unable to produce anything like it." This also has the effect of heightening their motivation to counter-argue, by means of harshness and warning.

For this reason the particle "lan" (never), which indicates negation of the future, is well placed. Negation with it is stronger than negation with "lā." Hence Sībawayh said: "lā" negates "yaf'al" (he does), and "lan" negates "sa-yaf'al" (he will do). Al-Khalīl said that "lan" is a contracted particle from "lā" (not) and "an" (the particle of the future subjunctive). This is a good opinion. Since it negates the future, it generally indicates a perpetual negation, because the future has not been limited by any of its limits, and so it indicates the encompassing of all its times, since none of them is more deserving than another. For this reason al-Zamakhsharī said that it conveys perpetuity (ta'bīd), literally or figuratively, which is emphasis (ta'kīd). I have surveyed its uses in the Qur'an and the speech of the Arabs, and I found that it is only used in a context where a strongly emphasized or perpetual negation is intended.

The words of al-Khalīl on its original usage support this. Whoever among the grammarians says that it conveys neither emphasis nor perpetuity has indeed been obstinate.

The words "and you will never do it" are among the greatest miracles of the Qur'an, for it is a miracle from two aspects. The first: it establishes that they did not counter-argue, because the desire to counter-argue would have been stronger in them had they been able to. All of this is confirmed by the earlier words, ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23] (if you are truthful), and this is evidence of their inability to produce anything like it, which indicates that it is speech whose power is beyond the capacity of humans.

[Page 343]

The second: it informs that they will not produce anything like it in the future. No one among them, nor among those who came after them, produced anything that counter-argues the Qur'an. Thus this verse is a miracle of the type of the inimitability (i'jāz) through reporting the unseen, which continues through the succession of years. The many verses of challenge in the Qur'an were recited to the ears of the stubborn Arabs who refused to believe the Messenger. The reports of this spread among them and travelled with the caravans, so that it cannot be claimed that they were unaware of it, while their motivations to counter-argue were present. Among their elite, there was what they felt at ease with, since they were qualified for speaking eloquently, and they were their poets and orators.

They had gatherings for debate and assemblies for consultation and cooperation. Among their common people and their poor, there was eagerness to urge their elite to ward off the disgrace of defeat from their tribes and religion, to support their gods, and to halt the flood of their men entering the religion of Islam. In addition, the Arab was known for his refusal to accept defeat and his dislike of humiliation. Thus the whole community refrained from producing anything like the Qur'an only because they were unable to do so. This is proof that it was sent down from God, the Exalted. If one or a group had counter-argued it, they would have rushed to it with joy, spread it, and passed it around, for they were accustomed to transmitting the sayings of their eloquent people even before the challenge spurred them on. So what do you think they would have done had they found something of it with which to ward off this humiliation? The failure to find anything claimed of this kind necessitates certainty that they refrained from countering it. We will explain this in detail at the end of the commentary on this verse.

The first "taf'alū" is necessarily jussive by "lam," because the conditional "in" entered upon the verb after it was considered negated. Thus the meaning of the condition governs "lam" and its verb. It is clear that this is not a case of dispute (tanāza') between "in" and "lam" in governing "taf'alū," because the two meanings differ. Thus the disagreement among the grammarians about the validity of two particles governing one operand does not apply here, as Ibn al-'Ilj, one of the grammarians of al-Andalus, imagined; Ibn al-'Ilj was cited for it in al-Taṣrīḥ 'alā al-Tawḍīḥ. Moreover, the truth is that there is no barrier to it when the requirement is the same in meaning. Its permissibility has been derived from the words of Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī in al-Masā'il al-Dimashqiyyāt and from his book al-Tadhkira, where he considered the verse of the rajaz poet:

"Until you see them, as if 'ka-anna' and 'ka-an' (their necks) are raised ornaments in a necklace."

to be a case of dispute between the heavy "ka-anna" and the light "ka-an."

The words ﴿فاتَّقُوا النّارَ﴾ (so guard yourselves against the Fire) are a result (athar) of the response of the conditional in the words ﴿فَإنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا﴾ (but if you do not), and they indicate omitted sentences

[Page 344]

for the sake of brevity. The response of the condition in meaning is that for which the condition was brought, which is what is implied by the words ﴿وإنْ كُنْتُمْ في رَيْبٍ مِمّا نَزَّلْنا عَلى عَبْدِنا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23] (and if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant). So the estimated response to the words "But if you do not" (﴿فَإنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا﴾) is: "then be certain that what Muḥammad has brought is sent down from Us, and that he is truthful in what he has commanded you regarding the obligation to worship God alone; and beware, if you do not comply with his command, of the punishment of the Fire." So the words ﴿فاتَّقُوا النّارَ﴾ (so guard yourselves against the Fire) take the place of the response, as they indicate it and point to it. This is a wonderful brevity, because guarding against the Fire was not something they believed in before, since they denied the Resurrection. When the truthfulness of the Messenger became clear, belief in the Resurrection and the recompense became obligatory for them.

The phrase used was ﴿لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا ولَنْ تَفْعَلُوا﴾ (you do not, and you will never do it) rather than "if you do not produce that, and you will never produce it," as in the words of the Exalted, ﴿قالَ ائْتُونِي بِأخٍ لَكم مِن أبِيكُمْ﴾ [Yūsuf: 59] (He said, "Bring me a brother of yours from your father") up to His words ﴿فَإنْ لَمْ تَأْتُونِي بِهِ﴾ [Yūsuf: 60] (but if you do not bring him to me), and so on. This is because the word "taf'alū" here contains a brevity that is not present in the other verse, since the "coming" that is challenged in this verse is a coming qualified by a specific manner, namely that the thing brought be like this Qur'an, and be witnessed against them, and be supported by their witnesses.
