Thus the word "taf'alū" includes, in its encompassing of those attributes and restrictions, a brevity that the "coming" in the sūrah of Yūsuf does not require.

"Al-waqūd" (the fuel), with a fatḥah on the waw, is a noun for what is kindled with, and with a ḍammah it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is said the reverse. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: "The ḍammah and the fatḥah have been transmitted for both the firewood and the verbal noun." The analogy for "fa'ūl" with a fatḥah on the fā' is that it is a noun for what is done with it, like "wuḍū'" (ablution), "ḥanūṭ" (embalming spices), "sa'ūṭ" (nasal medicine), and "wujūr" (medicine poured into the mouth), except for seven words that came with the fatḥah for the verbal noun, and they are: al-walūl, al-qabūl, al-wuḍū', al-ṭahūr, al-wazūʿ, al-lughūb, and al-wuqūd. The fatḥah here is the required one, because what is meant is the noun. It was also read with a ḍammah in the anomalous reading, and that is on the basis of taking the ḍammah as a verbal noun, or on the basis of an omitted possessive, meaning "the possessors of its fuel are men."

The word "men" (al-nās) is intended to denote a category of them, namely the disbelievers. Its definiteness is the definiteness of conventional comprehensiveness (ta'rīf al-istighrāq al-'urfī). It is also possible that it is the definiteness of reference (ta'rīf al-'ahd), because their being polytheists is known from many other verses.

"Al-ḥijārah" (the stones) is the plural of "ḥajar" (stone), in an irregular pattern, and this is a rare form in their speech. They formed the plural of ḥajar as aḥjār, and attached the feminine ending (tā' marbūṭah) to it. Sībawayh said that they attached it as they attached it to "bu'ūlah" and "fuḥūlah." It is related from Abū al-Haytham that the Arabs add the ha' (the feminine ending) to every plural of the pattern fi'āl or fu'ūl, because when it is pause-stopped, two consonants come together at the pause: the quiescent alif and the letter on which one pauses. That is, they found it pleasant that it be light when they pause on it. This is not the forbidden coming together of two quiescent letters. Examples include "'iẓāmah," "nifārah," "fiḥālah," "ḥibālah," "dhikārah," "fuḥūlah," and "ḥumūlah" as plurals, and "bikārah," the plural of "bakr" with a fatḥah on the bā', and "mihārah," the plural of "muhr."

[Page 345]

The meaning of "its fuel is stones" is that the stone is placed for it in place of the firewood, because when it is kindled it becomes more intensely burning and slower to be extinguished. Among the stones are their idols, for they are stones. This is explicitly stated in the words of the Exalted: ﴿إنَّكم وما تَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 98] (Indeed you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell). In this verse there is an allusion (ta'ārīḍ) that threatens the addressees. The meaning alluded to is: "Beware lest you yourselves and what you worshipped become the fuel of the Fire." The indicator of the allusion is His words "guard yourselves" and His words "and the stones," because when they were commanded to guard against it with a command of warning, they knew that they were the men, and when the stones were mentioned, they knew that they were their idols. Thus it followed that the men are the worshippers of those idols. The allusion here is of varying degrees: the first is through one intermediary, and the second through two.

The wisdom of casting the stones of the idols into the Fire, even though no wisdom of recompense appears in them, is that this is a degradation of them, and an increase in the manifestation of the error of their worshippers in what they worshipped. It also repeats their regret over the humiliation of the idols, and their regret too that what they had prepared as a cause of their honour and pride became a cause of their punishment, and what they had prepared for their salvation became a cause of their punishment. The Exalted said: ﴿إنَّكم وما تَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 98], and so on.

The definiteness of "the Fire" (al-nār) is definiteness of reference (ta'rīf al-'ahd). Its description by a relative clause implies that the addressees know the relative clause, as is generally the case with relative clauses, in order to treat the ignorant as if he were knowing, with the aim of affirming the existence of Hell. Or, the description of Hell with this has already been established in the Qur'an revealed earlier, such as the words of the Exalted in the sūrah of al-Taḥrīm: ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قُوا أنْفُسَكم وأهْلِيكم نارًا وقُودُها النّاسُ والحِجارَةُ﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 66:6] (O you who have believed, guard yourselves and your families against a Fire whose fuel is men and stones). Although the sūrah of al-Taḥrīm is counted among the sūrahs revealed after al-Baqarah, there is room to question the accuracy of that count. Or, it was known to them from the reports of the People of the Book.

In making men and stones a fuel there is evidence that the Fire of Hell is kindled before men are cast into it, and that men and stones are only kindled by it, because the Fire of Hell is the source of all heat, as the ḥadīth in the Muwaṭṭa' indicates: "The intensity of heat is from the breath (fayḥ) of Hell. When a human being comes into contact with it, he is set alight and his skin is roasted, and when stones come into contact with it, they are melted." In burning by electric current there is a model that brings this closer to people today.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbās that Hell is kindled with stones of sulphur, so its model is the burning volcanoes.

The words ﴿أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ (prepared for the disbelievers) are a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) that was not conjoined (lam yu'taf), for the purpose of alerting that it is intended as a statement of fact. Had it been conjoined, the conjunction would have given the impression that it is a second attribute or another relative clause. Making it a separate statement is more awe-inspiring, more majestic, and more effective in striking terror into the hearts of the addressees. It is also an allusion that it was prepared for them from the outset, because the discourse is with them.

This verse has established the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an by mass-transmitted evidence (tawatur), which distinguishes the Qur'an from the rest of the miracles. For the miracles of the prophets, and of our Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon them, were established only by single-narrator reports (akhbar ahad), and what is common to all of them is a shared core: the occurrence of the basic miracle is established by meaning-based mass transmission (tawatur ma'nawi), like the generosity of Hatim or the bravery of 'Amr. As for the Qur'an, its inimitability is established by transmitted mass transmission (tawatur naqli). The Arabs perceived its miracle through direct sense-perception (hiss), and the general population of others perceived it through transmission (naql). Some of the elite among others may also perceive it through direct sense-perception, as we will explain.

As for the Arabs' perception of the Qur'an's miracle, it is evident from this verse and its like. They denied the Prophet (ﷺ), opposed him, and turned away from following him. So He argued with them to establish his truthfulness by a speech that Allah revealed to him, and He made the proof that it is from Allah their inability to produce its like. It is composed of the letters and words of their language and according to the styles of its structures, and it contains such rhetorical qualities as they knew to be found in the speech of their eloquent orators and poets. Then He made them the judges in deciding whether to affirm or deny it, by an easy and just standard, which is their producing its equivalent, or their inability to do so. The Qur'an declared this in more than one place like this verse, and they were unable to oppose it. So their inability to oppose it could only be one of two things:

Either their inability is because the Qur'an reached, in what it contains of rhetorical qualities required by the situation, a limit beyond the capacity of the minds of the eloquent of mankind to encompass. So that even if their minds were gathered, their intuitions were kindled, and they conspired and consulted in their assemblies, their valleys, and the markets of their seasons, and every eloquent man put forward what occurred to him of subtleties and qualities, they would find that all of that is already fulfilled by the verses of the Qur'an in its like, and that they bring something greater than it. Then if a later one joined them, and a successor came after them and put forward subtleties they had not put forward, he would find that verse in which the understandings of the predecessors were kindled, and which included what they had counted of its qualities, already containing what occurred to this latter and more than it. This is the extent that the eloquent Arabs perceived by their natural disposition, so they turned away from opposing it, knowing that they had no power to produce its like. They were, in their lofty resolve and soundness of judgment, such that they would not expose themselves to disgrace nor accept diminishment for themselves. Therefore they saw that refraining from opposition was more beneficial to them, and they bore the taunt of being unable to oppose it in a verse like this. Perhaps they saw that silence receives interpretations with dignity that a deficient opposition, falling short of the eloquence of the Qur'an, does not receive. Thus it is established that it is inimitable, for it reached a limit that mankind cannot attain. This speech was therefore extraordinary beyond the custom, and a proof that Allah brought it into being in this way so that it would be a proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger. So the inability to oppose it, in this respect, was due to lack of capacity to produce its like.

This is the view of the majority of the People of the Sunna, the Mu'tazila, and the leading Ash'aris, such as Abu Bakr al-Baqillani and 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani, and it is the well-known position of al-Ash'ari.

It is also possible that they were capable of producing its like, and that opposition was made possible for them, but Allah diverted them from undertaking it despite the strong motives for it. Their being prevented from doing so, despite the difference in their circumstances, would then be an extraordinary matter beyond custom as well, and that is the proof of the miracle. This is an opinion held by a group, and al-Baqillani mentioned it in his book on the inimitability of the Qur'an without naming any proponent. Al-Taftazani in the book al-Maqasid attributed it to those who say that the inimitability is by diversion (sarfa), which is the view of al-Nazzam among the Mu'tazila and many of the Mu'tazila. Al-Khafaji attributed it to Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini, 'Iyad attributed it to Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, but it is not well known from him. Al-Sharif al-Murtada of the Shi'a held it, as in al-Maqasid. Although it is sufficient to explain that their inability to oppose by Allah's rendering them incapable is a path, it is a weak one. The discussion of the aspects of the Qur'an's inimitability has been detailed earlier in the tenth introduction of this commentary.

If you say: why could it not be that the Arabs' abstention from opposition was a demonstration of unwillingness rather than inability? Moreover, how do we know that the Arabs did oppose the Qur'an and that what they opposed it with was not transmitted to us? I say: it is impossible that their act was a feigned inability, for Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent to a people who were hostile to him and opposed him, not as Moses was sent to the Children of Israel, who were supportive, helpful, and loyal to him. The Arabs as a whole were opposed to the Prophet (ﷺ), for they denied him and slandered him with madness, sorcery, and other things. Only a small band followed him, weak among their people with no support at the beginning of the call. Then their people boycotted him, then ordered him to leave, between a plan to kill him and a limitation to expelling him. All of this is established from them in their reports and sayings, transmitted by a transmission in which it is impossible for us to have colluded upon falsehood. They continued their opposition to him after his departure in the same way, blocking him from the Hajj and persecuting his followers, until the end of what is known in history and biographies. That opposition was not within a short period in which events could be concealed and the spreading of an opposition suppressed, for it lasted nineteen years until the day of the conquest of Makkah.

Without doubt, their greatest desire during that period was to make his denial manifest, defending themselves and their gods and displaying victory among the tribes of the Arabs. All of this is established by mass transmission among all the neighboring nations: Persians, Byzantines, Copts, and Abyssinians.

Without doubt, the Qur'an shortened for them the distance of argument and prepared for them the path of holding them to the truth of what they attributed to him. It came to them as a book revealed in installments, and it called them to oppose it by producing a short piece like it, and to gather their witnesses and helpers for that. This book declared that, and all of this is established by mass transmission. For this book is mass-transmitted among the Arabs, and the people of religion among the nations are not without knowledge of its existence. And that it contains a challenge to opposition is established by a transmission known to us, for it is this very book that the Muslims believed in and memorized before the conquest of Makkah, and that all the Arabs believed in after the conquest of Makkah, so they learned it as it is today. The generations have testified to this, generation after generation.

Those who were challenged and called to opposition were known for their standing: soundness of judgment, uprightness of minds, weight of intellect, and the fact that counterfeit was not current among them, and for their capacity and power to vary in meanings and expressions. All of that is transmitted from them through what has been reported of their speech in verse and prose, and through what is famously and mass-transmitted of their rare sayings and reports among the common transmitted material. It would not have been difficult for them to oppose him had they found it in the familiar manner of their speech, for the soundness of their minds perceived that it exceeded the limit known to them. Therefore they turned away from opposition, despite the strength of their natural motive and their eagerness, had they found a way to it. Their turning away from opposition is established by mass transmission, for had such a thing occurred they would have publicized it and spread it, and people would have passed it on, since it is a momentous event. Instead they shifted from opposition by tongue to war and confrontation. This is established by mass transmission without doubt among historians and others.

Whatever you consider the cause of their turning away from opposition, whether the speech's exceeding human capacity or Allah diverting their minds from it, it is a proof of a matter beyond custom, which occurred by the decree of the Creator of destiny and the Incapacitator of mankind.

Behind all this is another proof, which informs us that the Arabs, by the goodness of their natural disposition, perceived the truthfulness of the Messenger and grasped the inimitability of the Qur'an, and that it is not speech habitually produced by humans, and that they denied him only out of stubbornness, arrogance, eagerness for leadership, and aversion to admitting error. That proof is the conversion to Islam of all the Arab tribes and their successive delegations after the conquest of Makkah. For they had been following Quraysh in opposition, while magnifying following this religion for fear of reproach from some of them, especially Quraysh and those who supported them. When Quraysh was overcome, nothing remained to prevent the rest of the Arabs from coming obediently and acknowledging it without compulsion by force. For those tribes were able to stand firm in combat more than Quraysh had stood, since among those tribes were people of valor and strength from the Arabs of Najd, Tayy, and others, by whom Islam was later strengthened. It is not known in the customs and habits of nations that great and numerous tribes abandon the religions they hold to be true and all come submissively, rejecting their religion within a few months of the year of delegations, with no assembly gathering them, no envoys circulating among them, and no congregation mustering them, unless they were already prepared for this acknowledgment, held back by nothing except a weak obstacle, namely arrogance and obstinacy.

Furthermore, in this verse there is a lasting miracle, which is His saying ﴿but you will never do it﴾. Centuries and generations have passed over it, and its truthfulness is clear, for no opposition has come from any of those addressed nor from any who followed them until today. If you say: this establishes that the Qur'an is a miracle for the Arabs, and thereby it was established for them that it is a miracle and that the truthfulness of the Messenger was established for them by it, but this was not established for one who is not like them; so what is the miracle for others? I say: the establishment of inimitability does not require that people be equal in the way it is established. For when it renders the Arabs incapable, it is established that it is beyond custom, by the two aspects previously mentioned. Thus the inimitability is known to the Arabs by immediate perception, and to those who came after them by reasoning and proof, and these are two paths to attaining knowledge.

Furthermore, whoever wishes to grasp the inimitability as the Arabs grasped it must busy himself with learning the language, its literature, and its characteristics until he equals or nearly equals the Arabs in their taste for their language, and then consider the Qur'an's relation to the speech of their eloquent ones. No age has been without a group that undertook to understand Arabic eloquence and grasped the inimitability of the Qur'an, namely the scholars of rhetoric and of correct Arabic literature.

Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir said in the introduction to Dala'il al-I'jaz: If someone says: we have a way to the inimitability of the Qur'an other than what you have mentioned, namely that it depends on the science of eloquence (bayan), which is our knowledge of the Arabs' incapacity to produce its like and their abstention from opposing it despite the repeated challenge against them and the long reproach to them for their incapacity to do so. And if the matter were as such, the proof would not have stood for non-Arabs as it stood for the Arabs, and people would not be equal in it in general, and the ignorant one in the Arabic tongue would not be silenced by the Qur'an. It is said to him: tell us about what the Muslims agree upon concerning the particularity of our Prophet, peace be upon him, that his miracle remains across the ages. Do you know any meaning for that other than that the proof from it remains manifest, open to everyone who wishes to know it, and that knowledge of it is possible for whoever seeks it; and that there is no meaning to the miracle remaining in the Qur'an except that the quality by which it was a miracle remains in it forever. End quote.

Al-Sakkakī said, in the course of drawing attention to some issues of taqdīm (fronting or prioritizing in word order), his statement: "Thereby seeking to refine the aspect of inimitability (i'jāz) in the Revelation, moving from what the challengers' inability (ʿajz) to match it had summarized for you to its details."

I have already set out, in the Tenth Introduction, details of its aspects of inimitability. This verse comprises several categories of inimitability: it conveyed the inimitability through mass transmission (tawātur), it was itself inimitable by its eloquence (balāgha), and it was inimitable in respect of its reporting of the entire future, all of which has been confirmed as true. Glory be to the One who sent it down and who bestows it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 25 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾

In al-Kashshaf: It is the custom of Him, Mighty and Majestic, in His Book to mention encouragement together with warning, and to follow good tidings with admonition, desiring to stir people to acquire what brings them near (to Him), and to restrain them from committing what destroys them. So when He mentioned the disbelievers and their deeds and threatened them with punishment, He followed this with the good tidings to His servants who combined belief with righteous deeds. [End of quotation.]

He treated the clause (﴿and give good tidings﴾) as coordinated with the whole group of clauses presented to explain the punishment of the disbelievers, meaning all that was detailed from His words, ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23] to His words, ﴿prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24]. Thus He coordinated a whole set of reports about the reward of the believers with a whole set of reports about the punishment of the disbelievers. The connection is clear and justifies coordinating a group with a group. This is not the coordination of one specific clause with another specific clause, which requires agreement between the two clauses in being informative (khabariyya) or directive (insha'iyya). Compare it with your saying: "Zayd is punished with shackles and hardship, and give 'Amr good tidings of pardon and release." Al-Sayyid al-Jurjani gave this type of coordination the designation "coordination of story to story" ( 'atf al-qissa 'ala al-qissa), because the coordinated element is not a clause over a clause but a group of clauses over another group. A parallel in single words is what has been said about the first and third waw in His words, ﴿He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward﴾ [al-Hadid: 3]: they are not like the second waw, because each of the first and third waws serves to combine the two opposing attributes, whereas the second serves to coordinate the group of the two opposing attributes that follow it over the group of the two opposing attributes that precede it. Had one considered the coordination of "the Outward" alone over one of the two preceding attributes, there would be no harmony. This is its substance.

[Page 351]

He means that the waw coordinates a clause with an omitted subject and two predicates over a clause with an expressed subject and two predicates. Thus the implied sense is: "He is the Outward and the Inward." It is not meant that the subject in it is implied in order to dispense with the conjunctive particle; rather, it is omitted because of the indication (qarina) or the connection in coordinating the clause of "the Outward and the Inward" over the clause of "the First and the Last."

They are two opposing attributes that are established for one referent, the one for whom two other opposing attributes are established.

Al-Sayyid said: The author of al-Miftah did not mention the coordination of story over story, so the rigid followers were perplexed by his words in this context and imagined that the intent of the author of al-Kashshaf here is coordination of clause over clause, and that the preceding statement is implicitly a command, or vice versa, so that the two clauses would harmonize. But the wording of al-Kashshaf is explicit in something other than that. Al-Sayyid intended by this to refute an understanding that Sa'd al-Din had derived from the words of al-Kashshaf and included in his extended commentary on al-Talkhis.

The author of al-Kashshaf also permitted that His words, (﴿and give good tidings﴾), be coordinated over His words, (﴿so guard yourselves﴾), which is the answer to the conditional, so it would have the same ruling as the answer. This is because the condition, (﴿but if you do not do it﴾) [al-Baqarah: 24], is the cause of both: when they are unable to produce an equal, the truthfulness of the Prophet becomes evident, so guarding against the Fire, which is the warning for whoever persists in disbelief, becomes obligatory, and the good tidings become due to those who believe. The reason that the element coordinated over the answer differs from it is that the verse is directed as an address to the disbelievers through the tongue of the Prophet. When it was intended to establish the warning for them and the good tidings for the believers, the answer was made a direct address to them, because they were the ones first addressed, and an address to the Prophet so that he would address the believers, since the believers are not mentioned in this address. So there was no way to address them except by sending the message to them.

[Page 352]

This view has been deemed weak on the grounds that the grammarians established the impermissibility of coordinating an imperative addressed to one party over an imperative addressed to another party unless it is accompanied by a vocative (nida'), as in: "O Zayd, write! O 'Amr," and there is no vocative here.

The author of al-Miftah permitted that (﴿give good tidings﴾) be coordinated over an implied "say" (qul) before (﴿O mankind, worship﴾) [al-Baqarah: 21]. Al-Qazwini said in al-Idah that it is coordinated over an implied element after His words, (﴿prepared for the disbelievers﴾) [al-Baqarah: 24], meaning: "So warn those who disbelieved." All of this is a forced interpretation for which there is no need, except for adhering to the apparent meaning of the grammarians' statements. Yet the author of al-Kashshaf did not regard it. 'Abd al-Hakim said: The grammarians' prohibition applies when there is no indication showing that the addressees are different, and the vocative is a kind of indication, as in His words, ﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and you (woman), ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Yusuf: 29]. [End of quotation.]

He means that anything that indicates the intended addressee in the address is sufficient. The grammarians specified the vocative only because it is the clearest indication. The difference between the two imperatives here, marked by the plural and singular forms, itself indicates the intended addressee. Whatever the case, the coordinated clauses were made to correspond to what is in the clauses they are coordinated over. Thus the warning in His words, ﴿so guard against the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24], is matched by the good tidings; (﴿mankind﴾), meaning the polytheists, is matched by (﴿those who believe﴾); and (﴿the Fire﴾) is matched by (﴿the Garden﴾). Thus three antitheses arise.

Tabshir (good tidings) is the report of a matter that is loved, so it is more specific than khabar (report). Some scholars restricted the meaning of tabshir to the condition that the one informed (al-mukhbar, in the passive) does not already know that report. The truth is that it suffices that the informer (al-mukhbir, in the active) not be certain that the one informed (al-mukhbar) knows it, for the informer is not obliged to investigate the addressee's knowledge. So if the informer is certain that the addressee knows it, it is not correct to report it, unless the report is used for a necessary consequence of its meaning or for rebuke or the like.

Al-salihat is the plural of saliha, which means a good deed. Its origin is an adjective that has come to function like nouns, because they say saliha and hasana without supposing an omitted modified noun. al-Hutay'a said:

"How is the satire, while the houses of Lam still come to us in absence with the attentions of their daughters?"

Perhaps this is the reason for its feminine form, as it moved from being a descriptive word to a noun. The definite article here is for totality (istighraq), and it is a conventional totality whose extent is determined by the legal obligation, capability, and the legal evidences, such as the fact that avoiding the major sins expiates the minor ones, so that it renders them as if nonexistent. If you ask: why did He not say "wa 'amilu al-salihah" in the singular, since they have said that the totality of the singular is more comprehensive than the totality of the plural? I say: that is an expression that spread to them from the words of the author of al-Kashshaf in this passage of his commentary,

[Page 353]

where he said: When the definite article of the genus (lam al-jins) enters a singular noun, it is suitable that the noun be intended as the genus until it is exhausted, and that it be intended as some of it down to a single member of it. When it enters a plural, it is suitable that the noun be intended as the whole genus, and that it be intended as some of it, but not down to a single member of it. [End of quotation.] The author of al-Miftah adopted it, and the scholars transmitted it without clarifying its explanation.

Perhaps someone will ask about the reason the Arabs used plurals after the totalizing "al" when the singular would perform its function. I say: the definite "al" comes for specific reference ('ahd), and comes for the genus intended as the quiddity (mahiyya), and for the genus intended as all its individuals, beyond which it has no other location. When they intend totality from it, they look: if the indication of totality is evident, either from a word or from context, as in His words, ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 2], ﴿except those who believe﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 227], ﴿and you believe in the Book entirely﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119], and ﴿and the angels will be on its edges﴾ [al-Haqqa: 17], they are satisfied with the singular form, because it is the original and lighter form. If they see the indication of totality as hidden or absent, they shift to the plural form, because the form of the plural indicates a number of individuals and not a single individual. Since specific reference does not usually apply to a number of individuals, it is determined that its use here is for totality, as in His words, ﴿and God loves the good-doers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134], lest one suppose the discourse is about a particular good-doer; and as in the words of (the wife of al-'Aziz), ﴿and that God does not guide the scheme of the treacherous﴾ [Yusuf: 52], lest one suppose the discourse is about a specific treacherous person, meaning herself. Thus in these contexts the plural becomes an indication of the intent of totality.

(al-salihat) is in the accusative as the object of (wa 'amilu), according to the well-known position of the leading Arabic grammarians. But Ibn Hisham in the sixth section of Mughni al-Labib claimed that if the object of a verb can exist only with the existence of its verb, it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) and not a direct object (maf'ul bihi). So in His words, ﴿they did righteous deeds﴾, it is an absolute object, and likewise in ﴿God created the heavens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 44]. He supported this with the claim by Ibn al-Hajib in his commentary on al-Mufassal that the absolute object can be a clause, as in: "qala Zayd: 'Amr munTaliq" (Zayd said: 'Amr is departing). Ibn Hisham's words are an error, and Ibn al-Hajib's are similar, and Ibn Hisham himself refuted it. The correct view is that the absolute object is the verbal noun of its verb or what functions in its place.

Al-jannat is the plural of jannah. Jannah in origin is a form from janna-hu, meaning he covered it. They applied the term to the place whose trees have multiplied and whose branches have intertwined so that its shade has become dense. This is among the means of luxury and comfort for all humans, especially in a land dominated by heat, such as the lands of the Arabs. God says: ﴿and gardens of dense foliage﴾ [al-Naba': 16].

[Page 354]

The literal meaning of jarayan (flowing) is very rapid movement in walking, and it is used figuratively for the flow of water in a continuous and successive stream. The best water is that which flows and does not stand still, for it is thereby fresh each time a drinker takes from it or a bather bathes in it.

Al-anhar is the plural of nahr, pronounced with a fatha or sukun on the ha, the fatha being more eloquent. al-Nahr is the trench in which water flows over the ground. It is derived from the root n-h-r, which indicates splitting and widening, and it may be large or small. The most beautiful feature of gardens is the flowing of water within them, and all people agree that this is among the finest sights, because water holds the nature of life, and because the viewer sees a wondrous sight and something delightful.

This love of such things is placed in souls. Either because God, exalted, has prepared the bliss of the righteous in the Garden in the manner of what their souls became accustomed to in this world, for familiarity has a firm hold on souls and spirits through their passage through this world, the world of matter; they acquired knowledge and familiar things that they continue to yearn for and regard as the ultimate desire. For this reason God has prepared for them lasting bliss in those forms. Or because God, exalted, made these things beloved to souls in this world, since they are in the manner of what they were accustomed to in the higher worlds before descending into bodies, through their familiarity with that in the world of archetypes (alam al-mithal). The cause of their aversion to crooked shapes and repulsive forms is that they are not familiar with their likes in their own worlds.

The first explanation that appeared to me seems stronger to me in explaining why the pleasures of Paradise come in the forms of the familiar pleasures of this world. This will be useful to us at His words, ﴿and they will be brought to them in similitude﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25].

The meaning of (﴿beneath them﴾) is from below them. The pronoun refers to the gardens, taking into account their whole, which includes the trees and the land growing in them. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the gardens with respect to the trees, because they are the most important part of the gardens. This qualifier is merely for disclosure, since rivers are only like that. This qualifier conveys the description of the state of the rivers to increase the beautifying of the description of the gardens, like the words of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"Its waters were poured from a bent spring with dark, clear water, in a valley that has become mixed."

[The text continues with the second verse.] The author of al-Kashshaf gave a justification for the definiteness of (al-anhar) and its difference from the indefiniteness of (jannat): either that the definite article is meant to define the genus, so it functions like an indefinite noun; or that the definite article is meant for specific reference, but it is a presumed reference, because when the gardens were mentioned, their accompaniments and associated features were brought to the hearer's mind, so it became appropriate for the speaker to point to them.

[Page 355]

**[Page 356]**

Its meaning refers to that known thing, so the definite article *al-* was used. This is what he meant by his statement, "or it is intended that its rivers (*anhāruhā*)," so the definiteness of the genitive construction was replaced by the definite article. He means that the speaker in such a context is torn between using the rivers defined by an annexation to the gardens and defining them by *al-* of prior reference (*al-ʿahdiyya*), taking it as a notional prior reference. The second was chosen to avoid the burden of the annexation and to draw attention to the fact that the rivers are an independent blessing, worthy of not making the enjoyment of them subordinate to the enjoyment of the gardens. He does not mean that *al-* is a substitute for the genitive complement, in the manner of the Kufan grammarians (*nuḥāt al-Kūfa*), because he has rejected that in his explanation of the verse ﴿Indeed, Hellfire is the refuge﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 39]. Rather, he meant that the annexation and the *al-* are interchangeable here, and that this is not suitable in every context. Moreover, I consider the Kufans' position acceptable, and they only intended to explain the resulting meaning of that definiteness, since the supposition of the genitive complement is what made the mentioned noun seem like a known thing, so the definite article of prior reference was attached to it.

In my view, the motive for the definiteness is variety (*tafannun*), so that the indefinite is not repeated a second time. Thus the two were differed in wording, for the sake of the strength of the definite form.

His statement ﴿from beneath them﴾ appears to be a descriptive qualifier intended to bring vividly before the hearer the scene of the rivers flowing, since rivers do not in some circumstances flow from above. This description was brought to depict the scene for the listener, with the aim of encouragement. This is one of the purposes of eloquent speakers, for the eloquent speaker does not limit himself to mere conveying of meaning. Close to this is the statement of al-Nābigha describing the horse of the hunter and his dogs:

*From a swift, sleek-coated (steed), beneath whom run greyhounds,*
*as if their lower jaws were fishing hooks.*

The *taḥt* (beneath) is a noun for the lower direction of place, and it is the opposite of *aʿlā* (above). Every place has a top and a bottom, and this does not imply that what *taḥt* is annexed to is elevated above the *taḥt*. Rather, its full signification is only that it is in the direction of its lower part. God, the Exalted, said, relating from Pharaoh: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 51]. Therefore there is no need here to interpret the Garden as meaning the trees in order to correct the *taḥt*, nor any other of the forced interpretations.

* * *

**[Page 357]**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Whenever they are provided with fruit therefrom as provision, they say, "This is what we were provided with before," and it is brought to them in resemblance; and for them therein are purified spouses; and they therein abide forever.﴾

The clause ﴿Whenever they are provided﴾ may be a second qualifier of "gardens," and it may be a predicate of an omitted subject, which is the pronoun of "those who believed." Then it is an independent nominal clause whose purpose is to explain another aspect of the affairs of those who believed. And because of the complete connection between it and the clause ﴿that for them are gardens﴾, it was separated from it as predicates are separated when multiple.

*Kullamā* is an adverb of time, because *kull* was annexed to *mā* as a temporal verbal conjunction (*mā al-ẓarfiyya al-maṣdariyya*), so it became for the comprehensiveness of the times restricted by the clause of the verbal *mā*. It has absorbed the meaning of the conditional, for the conditional is nothing but a dependence upon times restricted by the signification of the conditional verb. For this reason many words of generality have shifted to the meaning of the conditional when combined with the temporal *mā*, such as *kayfamā*, *ḥaythumā*, *annamā*, *aynamā*, *matā*, *mā*, and *mahmā*. The governing element of *kullamā* is the apodosis, because the conditional character is an incidental attribute that is not consistent with it, unlike *mahmā* and its counterparts.

Since *kullamā* is explicit in the generality of times, it is determined that the statement *min qablu* (before), which is built on a *ḍamma*, is by an implied annexed noun whose implication is evident, that is, *min qabli hādhihi al-marra* (before this occasion). This implies that this is the regular practice of the attributes of their fruits: that they come to them in the forms of what was presented to them the previous time. This either is a report about the attribute of the fruits of the Garden, and there is no specific intention of favour in it, so the meaning is that the fruits of the Garden are uniform in appearance but differ in flavours. The reason for this, and God knows best, is that the differences of shapes in this world arise from the differences of temperaments and compositions, while the existents of the Hereafter are the elements of things, so shape does not afflict them, and they come in one shape, which is the elemental shape. It is also possible that in this there is an element of wonder for them, and a marvellous thing is pleasing to souls, which is why people desire to see wonders and rarities. This possibility is the more apparent from the context. It is also possible that *kullamā* is for a generality other than the first time, so it is a general term intended to refer to a specific sense by means of a contextual indicator, and the meaning of *min qabl* ("before") is the first time upon entering the Garden.

Some exegetes understood his statement *min qabl* ("before") as implying *min qabli dukhūli al-janna*, i.e., "before entering the Garden," meaning "this which we were provided with in the world." Its justification in the *Kashshāf* is that a person is more at ease with the familiar. But this is weak, because it entails that the generality of *kullamā* is intended as a specific reference to the bringing of it the first time in the Garden, and because it implies a difference of taste and a difference of shapes, and this is weaker in producing wonder. Also, among the people of the Garden there are some who do not know all the kinds of fruits, so this entails restricting the kinds with respect to him.

His statement ﴿and it is brought to them in resemblance﴾ clearly indicates that the resemblance is among what is brought, not between it and the fruits of this world.

Then God bestowed upon them the blessing of companionship with spouses, and He exempted the women from the defects of the women of this world, from those things at which the soul recoils, were it not for forgetfulness. Thus He, glory be to Him, gathered for them the pleasures in the manner to which they were accustomed, so it was a blessing upon a blessing.

*Azwāj* is the plural of *zawj*, which is said of both the male and the female, because he made the other, after it had been single, a *zawj* (pair). It may be said of the female *zawja* with the *tāʾ*, and this occurs in the ḥadīth of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir in al-Bukhārī: "Indeed, I know that she is his wife in this world and the Hereafter," meaning ʿĀʾisha. And al-Farazdaq said:

*Indeed, he who strives to corrupt my wife*
*is like one who runs to the lions of the thicket to seduce her.*

His statement ﴿and for them therein are purified spouses﴾ is in the form of the singular, and the apparent expectation would be that it be said *muṭahharāt*, as it was read thus. But the Arabs often avoid the plural together with the feminine, because both are burdensome: the feminine is contrary to what is familiar, and the plural is likewise. So when the two are combined, they avoid the plural by using the singular, and this is frequent and widespread in their speech, and needs no citation of evidence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 26–27 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is above it.﴾

It may appear at first glance that there is no connection between the flow of the preceding verses and the flow of this verse. While the previous verse was a praise of this Clear Book, a description of the state of those who are guided by its guidance and those who deviate from its path, and an explanation of its inimitability and its challenge, along with the admonitions, warnings, clear proofs, and marvelous similitudes that were interspersed and followed this, suddenly the speech comes with a report that Allah, the Exalted, is not concerned to present an example with something base or not base.

The discerning reader, upon reflection, should see the connection to this transition. The preceding verses contained a challenge to the eloquent to produce a surah like the Qur'an. When they were unable to contend with its composition (naẓm), they followed the method of attacking its meanings, so they confused the people by claiming that the Qur'an contains foolish meanings from which the speech of Allah should be free, in order to reach by this the invalidation of the Qur'an being from Allah, by casting doubt into the souls of the believers and sowing discord to repel the polytheists and hypocrites.

Al-Wahidi narrated in Asbab al-Nuzul from Ibn 'Abbas that when Allah revealed His saying ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it. And if the fly should steal from them a thing, they could not recover it from it﴾ [al-Hajj: 73], and His saying ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider that takes a home﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 41], the polytheists said: "Look at what is made with this!" So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is above it.﴾ It is also reported from al-Hasan and Qatadah that when Allah mentioned the fly and the spider in His Book and struck examples with them, the Jews laughed and said: "This does not seem to be the speech of Allah," so Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed﴾, the verse. The correct approach is to combine the two narrations and explain what they both contain: that the polytheists used to turn to the Jews of Yathrib in consultation regarding the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, especially after the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Medina, and they would receive from them forms of deceit and agitation. Thus both parties came together in attacking the eloquence of striking examples with the spider and the fly. When Allah revealed the similitude of the hypocrites as "the one who kindled a fire," and most of them were Jews, their resentments were stirred and their throats constricted, so they varied these criticisms, and each group said what was attributed to it in one of the two narrations. The verse came to refute both groups, and the dawn became clear to one who has two eyes.

It is possible that this was said by the Jewish scholars who had no share in eloquence, or they said it knowingly of the arts of striking examples out of obstinacy and feigned ignorance. That the speakers were the Jews agrees with the fact that the surah was revealed in Medina, and the most stubborn opponents there were the Jews; and it also agrees with His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And He does not lead astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient﴾, ﴿those who break the covenant of Allah﴾, and this is the attribute of the Jews. Also, the Jews were widespread in pessimism and excessive caution regarding the implications of words, to the extent that they became known for using speech directed with insult and blame, such as their saying "Ra'ina," and Allah said ﴿But those who did wrong among them changed the word from that which had been said to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 162], as its interpretation is recorded in the Sahih. Such was not the custom of the Arabs. Or the speaker may have been the polytheists of Mecca, knowing that similar expressions occurred in the speech of their eloquent ones, such as their saying: "More daring than a fly," "More hearing than a tick," "More flighty than a butterfly," and "Weaker than a mosquito." This second possibility is more evident that they only said "What is this example?" out of obstinacy and contention, for when they were overcome by the challenge and were unable to bring a surah like it, they clung in their excuses to these trivialities. The obstinate one speaks what he does not believe, and the one overcome and confounded distorts the straight and conceals the clear. To this second view the words of the author of al-Kashshaf incline, and it is more in accord with the context.

Although the surah is Medinan, the polytheists never ceased to cast doubts on the validity of the message and spread them after the Hijra through the hypocrites. This meaning is indicated by His saying after it: ﴿As for those who believed, they know that it is the truth from their Lord; but as for those who disbelieved﴾ up to His saying ﴿and by it He leads many astray﴾. If it is said: the refutation did not come immediately after the revelation of the verses containing the example they denied, for hastening to refute one whose speech carries a faint doubt would cut off his doubt more decisively than delaying it for a time. We say: the reason for delaying its revelation is that the refutation should come after bringing marvelous examples demanded by the situation of comparing states. This is like a generous man withholding a gift from his enemy, so the one withheld blames him with the blame of stinginess; or like a warrior holding back from the battlefield as a stratagem, so some people think him a coward, while the first conceals it in his soul until the seeker comes to him and gives him a generous gift, and the second until he charges a charge that will be decisive against his foe. Likewise, when the Qur'an brought the greatest and most striking examples, namely His saying ﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], ﴿or like a rain-cloud﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], and the verses, and His saying ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18], it followed that with the refutation of them. This explains to you the connection of the revelation of this verse immediately after the one before it, and the commentators neglected to explain it.

The word "mathal" here means likeness in general, not specifically a compound image, unlike His saying earlier ﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], because what is intended here is what they criticized in the Qur'an's similitudes, such as His saying ﴿will never create a fly﴾ [al-Hajj: 73] and His saying ﴿like the spider that takes a home﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 41]. The placement of "inna" here is clear.

As for the use of the subject as a proper name (ʿalam), "Allah," rather than other attributes, this is because this name comprises all the attributes of perfection; so mentioning it is more effective in persuading that His speech is the highest speech in observing what is truly deserving of observance. In this there is also a refutation of their deception that the Qur'an's including such an example is evidence that it is not from Allah. Therefore it is not the meaning of the verse that someone other than Allah ought to be ashamed to present an example of this kind.

For this reason also, the predicate was chosen to be specifically the verb "to be ashamed" (yastahyi), as an added rebuttal of them, because they denied the striking of examples with these things out of regard for people's disgust, and such a thing is a form of shame, as we will explain. So they were alerted that the Creator is not ashamed of that, since it is not something one should be ashamed of. Also, created things are equal in weakness in relation to their Creator and the One who disposes of them. And the mention of shame here may be an echo of their saying: "Is the Lord of Muhammad not ashamed to strike examples with the fly and the spider?"

If you say: if the use of these words denoting base meanings does not detract from eloquence, why do we see many critics criticizing the speech of eloquent authors that contains such an example, such as the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Out of their pride, Kulayb walled up her house with a fence, as if the lice were near it."

And the verse of Abu al-Tayyib:

"Ignorance has killed you before your death, and the ant has dragged you out of lightness."

And the verse of al-Tirimmah:

"Even if a flea upon the back of a louse should charge against the flanks of Tamim, they would turn away."

I say: the principles of literary criticism return to explaining what it is not good for the speech of a writer to include, from the aspect of the craft of speech, and from the aspect of forms of meanings, and from the aspect of what is praiseworthy and what is disliked among them. This third kind varies with the variation of customs, the faculties of minds, and the soundness of understandings according to the prevailing condition of the people of the literary craft. Do you not see that a word may be accepted by one people and not accepted by others, and accepted in one age and rejected in another? Do you not see the words of al-Nabigha addressing the king al-Nu'man:

"Indeed you are like the night which will overtake me, even if I think that the one who is far from you is spacious."

For the comparison of a king to the night, if it occurred in the age of the Muwallads, would be counted as rudeness or boorishness. Likewise their comparison to a snake in boldness and destroying the enemy, in the words of Dhu al-Isba':

"Help, O clan, from the enemies, who were like a snake of the earth."

And the words of al-Nabigha in lamenting al-Harith al-Ghassani:

"What calamity have we suffered from him, a male snake, pouring out misfortunes, a coiling viper."

It is claimed by some people of letters that Ali ibn al-Jahm praised the caliph al-Mutawakkil with the words:

"You are like the dog in your loyalty to the covenant, and like the he-goat in clashing with calamities."

And that when he settled in Baghdad and the people's freshness clung to his imagination, he said at the beginning of what he said:

"The eyes of gazelles between al-Rusafa and the bridge have brought desire from where I know not and do not know."

Bashshar criticized Kuthayyir's saying:

"Verily Layla is a rod of bamboo, which becomes soft when they touch it with their palms."

He said: if he had made her a rod of marrow or a rod of butter, it would not have gone beyond being a rod. Yet Bashshar himself is the one who said:

"When she rises for her neighbor she sways, as if her bones were of bamboo."

And Bashshar likened 'Abda to a snake in his saying:

"And as if she, when she walked, was a female snake swaying in the sand dune."

"Istihya" (shame) and "haya'" (shyness) are one and the same; the sin and ta' in it are for intensification, like istaqdama and ista'khara and istajaba. It is the contraction of the soul from the occurrence of an act or from receiving it, from sensing that it is not fitting or not good according to the customary norms of its like. It is a state that affects the soul, of the type of emotion, whose effect appears on the face, and in refraining from what it would naturally do.

Here "istihya'" is negated as a description of Allah, the Exalted, so there is no need for interpretation in the correctness of its attribution to Allah. The justification for this, that the negation of an attribute implies the validity of the attribution, is an unsound justification.

The verb "daraba" in His saying ﴿an yadriba mathalan﴾ ("to present an example") is used metaphorically in the sense of placing and making, from their saying: "daraba khaymatan" (he pitched a tent) and "daraba baytan" (he built a house). 'Abda ibn al-Tabib said:

"Indeed she who pitched a house, emigrating, in the garrison town of Kufa, the ghoul has destroyed her love."

And al-Farazdaq's saying:

"The spider has spun its web over you, and the revealed Book has decreed against you by it."

That is: he made something a mathal, i.e., a likeness. Allah said ﴿So do not set forth examples for Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 74], i.e., do not make for Him any equal from His creation. So "mathalan" is in the accusative as the direct object. Some linguists permitted that the verb "daraba" be derived from "darb" in the sense of resembling, so "mathalan" is in the accusative of the absolute object for emphasis, because "mathal" is synonymous with the verbal noun of its verb on this assumption, and the meaning is: he is not ashamed to liken [something] to any thing. "Mathal" means likeness and similarity, and it has become predominantly used for the likeness of one state to another state. This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], and the meaning of striking an example in the other sense was discussed there too. The indefiniteness of "mathalan" is for classification, as shown by its explanation with "ba'ūḍatan fa-mā fawqahā" (a mosquito or what is above it).

"Ma" here is indefinite (ibhamiyya), attached to the indefinite noun to confirm its meaning, whether for classification, magnification, or belittling, as in: "li-amrin ma" (for some matter) and "a'taahu shay'an ma" (he gave him something). The more apparent view is that it is extra (zā'ida), so that its indication of emphasis is stronger. It was also said to be a noun meaning the undetermined indefinite.

"Ba'ūḍatan" is a substitute or explanatory apposition of "mathalan". "Ba'ūḍa" is a single mosquito, and it is a small flying insect with a fine proboscis that hovers around a human to suck blood from him with its proboscis as food for itself. It is known in the dialect of Hudhayl as "al-khumūsh," and the people of Tunisia call it "al-nāmūs," its singular being "al-nāmūsa." It is made an example here for extreme weakness and baseness.

Ibn ʿĀshūr's commentary (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrah al-Baqarah, verses 26–27 (part 2 of 4):

His words ﴿fa-mā fawqahā﴾ are conjoined to "baʿūḍatan" (a gnat). The root meaning of fawqa (above) is a noun for a place elevated above another thing, so it is an indeterminate noun (ism mubham), and for this reason it is always attached to a genitive (iḍāfa), since its direction is only specified by the noun to which it is added. It is therefore one of the directional nouns that always require an iḍāfa, either explicitly or implicitly. It is used figuratively for exceeding something else in a quality, an excess that is evident, by analogy with the visible elevation of a thing above another upon which it stands. Thus fawqa in such usage means domination and excess in a quality, whether the quality is praiseworthy or blameworthy. One says: "So-and-so is base, and beyond the base (fawqa al-khasīs)," and "So-and-so is brave, and beyond the brave (fawqa al-shujāʿ)," and you say: "So-and-so was given beyond his right (fawqa ḥaqqihi)," meaning more than his right. In this verse it is suitable for both meanings: what is lower than the gnat in insignificance, and what is greater in size.

A parallel to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No Muslim is pricked by a thorn or anything above it (fa-mā fawqahā) except that a degree is recorded for him by it and a sin is erased from him by it." Related by Muslim. It may refer to something less than a thorn in harm, such as the sting of an ant, as occurs in another hadith, or to something greater than a thorn, such as being stabbed with a knife. This is one of the varied uses of the word fawqa in speech, and for this reason its choice in this verse, rather than the word aqall (less) or, for example, aqwā (stronger), is a point of concise eloquence (ījāz).

The fāʾ is conjunctive (ʿāṭifa), conjoining mā fawqahā to baʿūḍatan, and it indicates that both are included in the striking of the parable. Its proper function is to indicate sequence and immediate succession (tartīb wa taʿqīb), but here it does not indicate immediate succession. It is used to mean graded progression in rank among the objects of (﴿an yaḍriba﴾). It does not indicate that the striking of the parable occurs with the gnat and is immediately followed by striking it with what is above it. Rather, the intent is to state the parable as being the gnat and what rises in degrees of strength above it, one rank after another. The fāʾ in such a case is a figurative metonymic usage (majāz mursal) whose relation is absoluteness from the condition, because the fāʾ is established for taʿqīb, which is a specific connection, so it is used for connection in general. Or it is metaphorically borrowed for gradual progression, because it resembles taʿqīb in lateness of comprehension, just as taʿqīb is lateness in occurrence. From this is the saying: "May God have mercy on those who shave their heads, then those who trim them."

The meaning is: that He strikes a gnat as a parable, then strikes what is above it, that is, another degree, namely something more insignificant than the gnat, such as the ant, and greater than it, such as the spider and the donkey.

* * *

﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. But as for those who disbelieve, they say: "What did God intend by this as a parable?"﴾

The fāʾ is for mention-based sequence (taʿqīb dhikrī), not for sequence in occurrence. That is, it sequences the detailed statement after the summarized statement. It conjoins the implied element in His words ﴿lā yastaḥyī﴾ (He is not ashamed), because its implied form is: "He is not ashamed before people," as was mentioned earlier. Since among people there are believers and disbelievers, and both groups received that parable and their conditions differed in benefiting from it, an implied summary arose in the speech which required a detailed explanation of their conditions. He conjoined with the fāʾ because the detail follows directly after the summary.

And ʾammā (as for) is a particle established to detail a summary, whether spoken or implied. Since a summary demands that the listener anticipate its detail, undertaking to detail it is like a hypothetical question, as if the speaker says: "If you wish its detail, its detail is such and such." For this reason ʾammā carries the sense of a condition, and for this reason the fāʾ is required in the clause after it, since it is like the response to a condition. It may be void of the sense of detail, specifically in the Arabic saying: "ʾammā baʿdu" (as for what follows), which becomes purely conditional. In reality this is because the sense of detail is obscure, since it is based on the listener's anticipation of speech after his first speech.

Sībawayh interpreted it in the sense of mahmā yakun min shayʾin (whatever may be the case), and the grammarians after him adopted this. In my view it is a supposed meaning to justify the entry of the fāʾ into its response, but there is something in the soul about it, because the claim that the intent is the generality of the condition is not clear. When the particle of detail, which carries the sense of a condition, is used, this indicates the speaker's greater concern with that detail, and so it gives strengthening to the speech, which al-Zamakhsharī called emphasis (taʾkīd). It is nothing but an indication of concern with the speech, that its content is established, and were it not so he would not have been concerned with it. By this the excellence of His words ﴿ʾammā alladhīna āmanū fa-yaʿlamūna﴾ and so on becomes evident, compared with saying: "Those who believe know" without ʾammā and the fāʾ. He made the division of people in this verse into two categories, because people, in relation to legislation and revelation, are initially of two kinds: believer and disbeliever. The purpose of mentioning the believers here is to praise them for the steadfastness of their faith and to dishearten those who wanted to cast doubt upon them, so that they know that their hearts have no entry for that doubt. By "those who disbelieved" here is meant either specifically the polytheists, as is the usage of the Qur'an in most cases, or what includes them and also the Jews, based on what preceded regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse.

He expressed concerning the believers with "yaʿlamūna" (they know) as an allusion that the disbelievers only said what they said out of obstinacy and arrogance, and that they know that this is a parable that hit the mark. How could they not, when they are the people of language and the knights of eloquence? But the way of the obstinate and arrogant is to say what he does not believe, out of envy and stubbornness. The pronoun in ʾannahu refers to the parable. Al-ḥaqq (the truth) has meanings that return to the conformity of a thing with what ought to occur, and here it is that which conforms to the rightness and eloquence of the speech. The phrase ﴿min rabbihim﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "al-ḥaqq," and min is for origin (ibtidāʾiyya), meaning that it came from God, not as those who disbelieved claimed, that it contradicts what is correct. It thereby indicates that it is the speech of One from whom error does not occur.

The original form of mādhā is a compound of the interrogative mā and the demonstrative dhā. For this reason its original use is to ask about a thing being pointed to, as in the saying of one who says "mādhā," pointing to a present thing, equivalent to saying "mā hādhā" (what is this). However, the Arabs extended its use, employing it as a compound interrogative of two words, in cases where the thing asked about is expressed by another word other than the demonstrative, so that the demonstrative with the other expression is merely for emphasis, as in "mādhā al-tawānī" (what is this delay). Or where there is no place for pointing, as in ﴿wa-mādhā ʿalayhim law āmanū billāh﴾ (An-Nisāʾ 39). For this reason the grammarians say that dhā is inoperative (mulghāh) in such a construction.

They have extended it further, making dhā a relative pronoun (ism mawṣūl), when the one asked about is known to the addressee in some respect of his circumstances. They then follow it with a clause or something similar as its relative clause (ṣila), as in ﴿mādhā anzala rabbukum﴾ (An-Naḥl 24). On both of these other possibilities its parsing as a subject (mubtadaʾ) is valid, and its parsing as a fronted object (mafʿūl muqaddam) is valid when a verb follows it.

The interrogative here is denunciatory (inkārī), meaning the speech is put in the form of a question as a metonymy (kināya) for denial, since the thing denied is asked about regarding its occurrence. The use of the interrogative for denial is thus a kind of metonymy, and such a question is generally not answered, since it is not intended to seek information. Its original meaning may sometimes be taken into account, so it is answered, because metonymic usage does not prevent the intended original meaning, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ʿamma yatasāʾalūn﴾ (An-Nabaʾ 1) ﴿ʿan al-naba al-ʿaẓīm﴾ (An-Nabaʾ 2). The indication in His words "bihādhā" (by this) conveys belittlement, by the context, as in His saying: ﴿ʾahādhā alladhī yadhkuru ālihatakum﴾ (Al-Anbiyāʾ 36). The word mathalan is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyīz) of "hādhā," because it is indeterminate and so is entitled to a specifier. It is parallel to the specifier of the pronoun in the saying "rubbahu rajulan" (how many a man).

* * *

﴿He leads many astray by it and He guides many by it, and He leads astray by it none but the defiantly disobedient (al-fāsiqīn), who break the covenant of God after its ratification, and sever what God has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption in the land. Those are the losers.﴾

This is an explanation and elaboration of the two clauses introduced by ʾammā, in the manner of inverted correspondence (al-nashr al-maʿkūs), since the meaning of these two clauses is comprised in summary within the meaning of the two preceding clauses. The believers' knowledge that it is the truth from their Lord is guidance, and the disbelievers' saying "What did God intend" and so on is misguidance. It is most apparent that His words ﴿He leads many astray by it and He guides many by it﴾ are not a response to the interrogative in the disbelievers' words "What did God intend by this as a parable?", because that is not a genuine question, as has been mentioned.

It may be taken as a response to their question, as a redirection of the speech into the wise style (al-uslūb al-ḥakīm), by taking their question at face value, to alert them that what befits them is to ask about the wisdom behind what God intended by those parables. Then His words ﴿He leads many astray by it and He guides many by it﴾ are an answer to them, a rebuttal to them, and an explanation of the condition of the believers. This does not contradict the question before it being a metonymy for denial, as you have just understood, since there is no obstacle to combining the metonymic and the original meanings.

That each of the two groups includes many who are led astray and many who are guided, in itself, does not contradict His words ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ (Saba' 13), because the strength of gratitude implied by the intensive form is more specific to being guided.

Al-fāsiq is a word from the transferred terms of the Sharīʿa. Its root is the active participle of fisq with a kasra on the fāʾ. The literal meaning of fisq is the fruit's coming out of its skin, and this is a defect or inferiority in the fruit. It is thus a blameworthy emergence, counted among blemishes, as al-Nābigha said:

Small pits, tightly packed, whose skin, when the skin of the date flies off from them, does not fly away like a bird.

They said: it was not heard in their speech in any sense other than this, until the Qur'an transferred it to the departure from God's binding command by committing major sins. After that it occurred in the speech of Muslims. Ruʾba said describing camels:

Defiant (fawāsiq), deviating from their course, going astray, / Going in Najd and in deep valleys.

Fisq has many degrees, some of which reach unbelief. Fisq has been applied in the Book and the Sunna to all of them. But what is extracted from combining the evidences is what the Ahl al-Sunna among the theologians (mutakallimūn) and jurists (fuqahāʾ) have settled upon: that fisq is other than kufr, and that sins, however many, do not remove faith, and this is the truth. God has given the title "defiantly disobedient" to the Jews in many places in the Qur'an, and I think this is what is meant here. Ibn Kathīr attributed this view to a majority of the exegetes.

The attribution of misguidance to God, exalted is He, is considered in that He is the One who enabled the misguided to acquire and choose, through the intellects He created for them and the means of good and its opposite that He distinguished for them.

In choosing to attribute it to God, exalted is He, despite the validity of attributing it to the one who is misguided's own act, there is an indication that this misguidance has become firmly rooted in their souls until it became like innate nature in them, so they are hopeless of being guided, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿God has sealed their hearts﴾ (Al-Baqarah 7). Thus the attribution of misguidance to God, exalted is He, is viewed in relation to His creating its near and distant causes. Otherwise, God commanded all people to be guided, and this is a question that is settled in the science of theology (ʿilm al-kalām).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 26–27 (part 3 of 4):

And His saying ﴿And He does not lead astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)﴾ is either delivered to show that defiant disobedience (al-fisq) has an effect in increasing misguidance, because disobedience stains the hearts and brings darkness upon the souls, so they fall into misguidance time after time in succession, until it becomes a habit for them. This is what the attaching of the description by a derived noun (al-mushtaqq) indicates, if what is meant here is its derivational meaning (al-ma'na al-ishtiqaqi). It is as if it were said: "These are defiantly disobedient, and there is no defiantly disobedient person who is not astray; so misguidance is established only by the establishment of defiant disobedience," in the manner of the conjunctive syllogism (al-qiyas al-iqtirani). Or it is delivered to show that misguidance and defiant disobedience are brothers, so wherever one of them is realised, it announces the realisation of the other, in the manner of the syllogism of equality (qiyas al-musawat). If what is meant by "the defiantly disobedient" is the well-known title-meaning (al-ma'na al-laqabi), then it does not indicate a causal explanation. Or it is for showing that the misguidance [p. 367] that is manifest in denying the parables is misguidance together with stupidity, so it proceeds only from the Jews, and they are known by this description.

As for the discussion of the views of the scholars of Islam on defiant disobedience and its effect on faith, this is not the place to explain it, since it is not the intended purpose of the verse. If the sense of "the defiantly disobedient" is taken to include the polytheists and the Jews who criticised the parable, then the restriction in His saying ﴿And He does not lead astray thereby﴾ and so on is relative to the believers, so that the intended meaning of the one led astray and the one guided is distinguished. If the sense of "the defiantly disobedient" is taken to be the Jews, then the restriction is real but claimed (haqiqi idda'i), meaning: He leads many astray thereby, and they are the ones who criticise it, and the most misguided of them are the defiantly disobedient. The reason for this is that the polytheists are further from being guided by the Book, because they are in their polytheism, whereas the Jews are People of the Book, and it is their nature to know the varieties of the heavenly Books and the striking of parables; so their denial of it is the utmost misguidance, as if there were no misguidance other than it.

The clause ﴿who break﴾ to the end of the verse is a description of "the defiantly disobedient," to confirm their being characterised by defiant disobedience, because these traits are among the greatest kinds of disobedience, in the sense of going out of the command of God the Exalted. It is permitted that it be a separate, resumptive clause (maqta'ah mustaani'ah), with "those who" as the subject (mubtada') and His saying ﴿those are the losers﴾ as the predicate (khabar). Even so, it does not depart from the meaning of describing the defiantly disobedient by those traits, since the resumption, when it comes right after the narration of a state of the defiantly disobedient, requires in the rules of eloquence that this relative clause be among their attributes and conditions, because of the necessity of unity in the imaginative comprehensive (al-jami' al-khayali). Otherwise the speech would become fragmented and scattered. So there is no difference between the two considerations except in the grammatical analysis (al-i'rab), while the meaning is one. For this reason its grammatical analysis as a description is preferred or required, since there is no call to consider it separated.

The coming of the relative pronoun here is for defining the intended sense of "the defiantly disobedient," that is, the defiantly disobedient who are known by these three traits. The clearest view is that the intended sense of "the defiantly disobedient" is the Jews, and this description has been applied to them in several places in the Qur'an, and they are known by what the relative clause indicates, as we shall explain here. Indeed, the books of their prophets testify against them that they broke God's covenant more than once, and they themselves acknowledged this, so it is fitting that breaking be made the relative clause, because they are famous for it. The reason for singling them out with this is that criticising this parable led them to increase criticism of Islam, and so they increased in misguidance upon their previous misguidance in altering their religion and in disbelieving in Jesus. As for the polytheists, their misguidance does not admit of increase. Moreover, the Surah of al-Baqarah was revealed at Madinah, and most of the refutation in the Madinan verses is directed at the People of the Book.

[p. 368] The word naqd (breaking) in the language is literally the undoing and untying of what was assembled and joined, by an action opposite to the action by which it was assembled. I have added to my words "by an action" etc. only so that cutting and burning are excluded, so one says naqada al-habl (he unpicked the rope) when he unties what he had tightly twisted, and naqada al-ghazl (he unravelled the spun thread), and naqada al-bina' (he demolished the building).

The word naqd has been used here metaphorically for the annulment of the covenant, by the indication of its being attached to "God's covenant." This is a metaphor (isti'arah) of the Qur'an's own innovation, built on what was common in the speech of the Arabs in likening a covenant and everything in it that is a connection to a rope. This is a common likeness in their speech. Among it is the saying of Malik ibn al-Tayyihan al-Ansari to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of the Pledge of 'Aqabah: "O Messenger of God, between us and the people there are ropes, and we are going to cut them; we fear that if God grants you victory and supremacy, you will return to your people," meaning the covenants that existed in the Jahiliyyah between the Quraysh and the Aws and the Khazraj. It was common in speech to use the words for cutting and severing, and what is in their meaning, for annulling a covenant as well. Imru' al-Qays said:

"And if you have resolved to sever me, then do it graciously."

And Labid said:

"Did not Nawar know that I am
one who joins a bond whose strands are severed?"

And he said:

"Rather, Nawar is remembered, though she has gone far,
and her cords and reins are cut."

And he said:

"Cut the tie of one who, having been attached, has turned away from union,
for the worst of those who join in friendship is the one who severs."

The reason for choosing the metaphor of naqd, which is the undoing of the strands of a rope, for the annulment of a covenant is that it represents the annulment of a covenant gradually, over repeated times and with working at it. Naqd is more eloquent in indicating annulment than cutting, severing and the like, because in naqd there is corruption of the form of the rope and the disappearance of hope of its return, whereas cutting is dividing into parts.

In naqd there is an allusion to a metonymic metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), because naqd is among the attributes (rawadif) of the rope. Thus two metaphors are combined here, a metonymic one and an explicit one (tasrihiyyah), and this latter is a figurative one (tamthiliyyah). It has been established in the science of rhetoric (ilm al-bayan) that what is signalled by means of the omitted comparandum (al-mushabbah bihi al-matruh) in a metonymic metaphor may be used with a literal meaning, in the manner of imaginative representation (al-takhyil). This occurs when the stated comparandum in the form of the metonymic metaphor has no attribute that can be likened to an attribute of the omitted comparandum. Examples are the attributing of claws to death, as in their saying "the claws of death" (azfar al-maniyyah), and the attributing of talons and fangs to warriors in the saying of Abu Firas al-Hamdani:

"When the battle grew fierce, we were
sharper in claws and keener in fangs."

And the attributing of a hand to the north wind in the saying of Labid:

"And on a day of wind, when I uncovered it, and of cold,
when the north wind had put its reins in its hand."

It may also be used with a figurative meaning when the comparandum in the metonymic metaphor has an attribute that can be likened to an attribute of the omitted comparandum. Such is His saying: ﴿they break the covenant of God﴾.
