When the work of the temperament stops and its effects are suspended, the living being becomes like the dead, as in the state of one who has fainted and the state of a paralyzed limb. When the work of the temperament ceases, that is death. Death is a privation (adam) and life is a faculty (malakah), and both are existent created things. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ (Al-Mulk 67:2), in the surah of al-Mulk.

The purpose of His words, ﴿when you were dead and He gave you life﴾, is not to express favor (imtinan). Rather, it is pure argumentation, mentioning one thing that people consider a blessing and another thing that they do not consider a blessing, namely the two deaths. Therefore there is no difficulty in the occurrence of the word "dead" and His words, ﴿then He will cause you to die﴾, within the context of the verse.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 2, verse 28 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying ﴿Then He will bring you back to life; then to Him you will be returned﴾, this is a derivative continuation of the argument, and it is not itself a proof, since the polytheists deny the Hereafter. It is therefore an incidental addition (idmaj) and an instruction, not an argument. Alternatively, the proofs already established that there is a second life have taken the place of knowledge of it, even if knowledge has not actually been attained. For whoever knows the existence of the Creator, who is just and wise, and sees people not conducting themselves according to the requirements of His commands and prohibitions, so that he sees the corrupter on earth in bounty and the righteous in hardship, knows that the justice and wisdom of God would not allow the work of any worker to be lost, and that there is a life more judicious and more just than this life, in which the states of people will be according to the measure of their deserving and the loftiness of their realities.

His saying ﴿then to Him you will be returned﴾ means that your return will be to Him. It is likened to the presence for reckoning, by way of the return of a traveler to his abode, on the basis that God created the creation, so they proceeded, as it were, from His presence; when He brings them back to life after death, it is as if He has returned them to Him. This is an affirmation of the Gathering (hashr) and of recompense.

The fronting of the complement before its governing verb (taqdim al-muta'allaq 'ala 'amilihi) conveys restriction (qasr), and it is a true restriction (qasr haqiqi), directed at the addressees to inform them of it, since they were deniers of it. It also carries a discouragement for them from hoping for benefit from their idols, since the polytheists used to argue against the Muslims that if there is a resurrection and gathering, they would find their gods supporting them.

The verb (turja'un) is read with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the jim in the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur); Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the jim. The first reading is according to the consideration that God returned them, even if they were unwilling, since they denied the resurrection; the second reading is according to the consideration of the return occurring from them, regardless of choice or compulsion.

[Page 378]

﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾

This is either a second argument against the monstrousness of their disbelief in God, the Exalted, and an indication that it is among the things that are astonishing. The signs of God's lordship and oneness are manifest in the creation of human beings and in the creation of everything on the earth, so this is an advance in argument by means of the multiplicity of created things. The separation (fasl) of this sentence from the preceding one may be for the sake of perfect connection between the two sentences, because this is like a conclusion drawn from the first argument. The creation of the earth and of everything in it, and the fact that all of this is for the benefit of humankind, complete their existence, which was referred to in His words ﴿And you were dead, and He gave you life﴾ [2:28], because the purpose of existence is not complete except by supplying the existent with what secures it from the pains of need for the things that sustain its existence.

It is also possible that the omission of the conjunction (ʿatf) is to prevent the conjunction from giving the impression that the argument is the combination of the two matters. By omitting the conjunction, it is known that the first argument is independent in itself. In the first there is a remoteness, and in the second there is a departure from the original rule, because the original rule of separation is not to be cut off, on the basis that this is an unfounded assumption that does no harm.

Or His words ﴿It is He who created﴾ may be a reminder of blessings bestowed upon them, to record that their associating others with God is ingratitude for the blessing. Into this is incorporated an argument that He is the creator of what is in the earth, of animals, plants, and minerals, an argument from what is a visible blessing, as indicated by His words ﴿for you﴾. In that case the separation between the two sentences is as established just above. The difference in this sentence from the first, in respect of being a reminder of blessings, has not been taken into account, because the argument incorporated into it favoured considering the separation.

Creation (al-khalq) has already been explained at His words, exalted is He, ﴿O humankind, worship your Lord who created you﴾ [2:21]. The earth (al-ard) is a name for the spherical world comprising land and sea, which is inhabited by humans, animals, plants and minerals, these being the three kinds of generated beings (al-mawalid al-thalatha). This earth is an existent entity that is a container (zarf) for the kinds of created beings within it. Since the lesson is to be found in observing existent things among the three kinds of generated beings, creation here is attached to what is in the earth, that which its container holds, outwardly and inwardly, and it was not attached to the essence of the earth, because most people are heedless of drawing lessons from the wondrous creation of the earth itself. Yet the creator of the contained is worthy of creating the container, since a container is only intended for the sake of what it contains. If the container were not by the workmanship of the creator of the contained, then it would necessarily follow either that the container came after its contents, which entails the destruction of the contents (and observation negates this), or that the container came before them, which is futile.

So the understanding that He created the earth is derived by way of implication (fahwa). It is remote for the author of al-Kashshaf to allow that by "the earth" is meant the lower direction, just as by "the heaven" is meant the upper direction. This is remote for two reasons.

[Page 379]

The first is that "the earth" has never been applied except to the terrestrial globe, save metaphorically, as in the verse of a poet which the author of al-Miftah cited in the discussion of definition by the article (al-ta‘rif bi-l-lam), without ascribing it to anyone, and neither did his commentators:

(People are earth in every land, and you are a heaven above them.)

This is unlike "heaven", which has been applied to everything that is high and overshadows. The difference between them is that the earth is a visible thing, while the heaven is not conceived except as a thing that is elevated. The second reason, granting the analogy, is that "heaven" has not been applied to the upper direction such that applying "earth" to the lower direction would be valid. Rather, "heaven" is applied to a high thing, not to the direction itself.

The sentence ﴿It is He who created for you﴾ is a form of restriction (qasr), and it is a true restriction (qasr haqiqi). It is addressed to the polytheists who, without doubt, hold that God is the creator of what is in the earth. But they are treated as one ignorant of that, so the restricted statement is addressed to them, because in their disbelief, their turning away from thanking Him, and their failure to consider His call and worship, they are like one who is ignorant that God is the creator of all existent things. A parallel to this is His words ﴿Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not take heed?﴾ [16:17], and ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides God will never create a fly, even if they gather together for it﴾ [22:73]. For the polytheists did not ascribe to their idols any power to create, but made them intercessors and intermediaries, worshipped them, and turned away from worshipping God as He should be worshipped, forgetting the creation that is attached to them and to what surrounds them of living things. In my view, the purpose of the speech, which agrees with eloquence, is to remind them that God is the creator of the earth, of what is upon it, and of what is within it, and that He created all of that in proportion to our benefit from it and from what is in it across different times and circumstances. So the speech is brief with a wondrous concision, through the insertion of the words ﴿for you﴾, which dispenses with a whole sentence. The discourse is thus directed to display the greatness of power, to display the greatness of favour upon humankind, and to display the greatness of the status of the human being with God, the Exalted. All of these require the uprooting of disbelief from their souls.

There are two benefits in this verse. The first is that the particle of causation (lam al-ta‘lil) indicates that the creation of what is in the earth was for the sake of humankind. Here there is an explanation (ta‘lil) of the creation and a statement of its fruit and benefit, and from this arises the question of God's acts being explained by purposes (ta‘lil af‘al Allah bi-l-aghrad). This question is disputed among the theologians (mutakallimun) in a dispute that resembles being merely verbal. For all Muslims agree that God's acts arise from will and choice and in accordance with His knowledge, and that all of them include wisdoms and benefits, and that these wisdoms are the fruits of God's acts, arising from the occurrence of the act, so that they are for the sake of their occurrence at the act, yielding ends. All of this is undisputed. The dispute is only over whether they may be described as purposes and final causes (ʿilal ghaʾiba) or not.

[Page 380]

A group affirmed this, citing reports such as His words, exalted is He, ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [51:56]. The followers of al-Ash‘ari, as Fakhr al-Din attributed to them in his commentary, denied it, arguing that whatever is done for a purpose must necessarily be benefiting from that purpose, since the existence of that purpose is preferable, by comparison, to its non-existence, so the agent benefits from that preference. And it follows from that purpose being a cause of the act that the agent is deficient in his agency, requiring the occurrence of the cause. It has been answered that the necessity of benefiting and of perfecting oneself applies when the benefit returns to the agent, but when the benefit returns to another, as in beneficence, it does not apply. Fakhr al-Din rejected this, saying that if beneficence is more preferable and more fitting than other things, then benefiting follows. This rejection is invalid, because preferability never entails benefiting; it only entails the attachment of will. Benefiting would follow only if we claimed that the choice is determinate and obligatory.

The conclusion is that the argument they used contains two sophistical premises. The first is their saying: if the act is for a purpose, then the agent necessarily becomes perfected by it. This is a sophistry in which the beneficial purpose to the agent was confused with the purpose in the sense of the motive for the act; what returns to something suitable to its perfection does not make its perfection depend upon it. The second is their saying: if the act is for a purpose, then the purpose is a cause that entails the agent's incapacity. This is a sophistry in which the cause in the sense of the motivator was confused with the cause whose existence necessarily entails existence and whose non-existence entails non-existence, though both are called "cause".

It is a marvel that they concede that God's acts are not free of fruit and wisdom, yet they deny that those wisdoms are causes and purposes, even though the fruit of the act of an agent who knows everything cannot but be a purpose, because it is what motivates the act, given the certainty of the agent's knowledge and will. I do not know what difficulty they saw when they prohibited the explanation of God's acts and their purposes.

It seems to me that this question was required by the consistent application of principles in disputation. For when the Ash‘aris denied that God's acts are obligatory on the basis of the good and the best (al-salah wa-l-aslah), the Mu‘tazila objected to them, or they themselves imagined that the objection would be raised against them: that God does nothing except for a purpose and wisdom, and purposes are nothing but benefits. So they committed themselves to the view that God's acts are not tied to purposes and are not expressed as causes. This is indicated by the fact that, when they raised this question, they mentioned in their proofs beneficence to others and the preservation of benefit. There is another reason for raising the question, namely avoiding describing God's acts with what suggests benefit to Him or to another, and both are invalid, because He does not benefit from His acts, and because for another, God's act may not be a benefit in relation to that other.

Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi in al-Muwafaqat reported from the majority of jurists and theologians that God's rulings (ahkam) are explained by benefits and the averting of harms. Ibn ‘Arafa gathered the opinions in his commentary and said: this is the explanation of God's acts, and there is disagreement about it, but as for His rulings, they are explained by reasons.

The second benefit: the scholars derived from His words, exalted is He, ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾ that the basic principle regarding the use of things for any of the kinds of use is permissibility (ibahah), unless a proof indicates their prohibition, because He made what is in the earth created for our sake and bestowed favour upon us by it. Al-Imam al-Razi, al-Baydawi, and the author of al-Kashshaf said this. It is also attributed to the Mu‘tazila and to a group of Shafi‘is and Hanafis, among them al-Karkhi, and it is attributed to al-Shafi‘i. But the Malikis, the majority of the Hanafis, and the Mu‘tazila, according to Ibn ‘Arafa's report, held that the basic principle regarding things is suspension (waqf), and they did not regard the verse as a proof. Ibn al-‘Arabi said in his Ahkam: God, exalted is He, mentioned this verse only in the context of demonstrating and drawing attention to the way of knowledge, power, and the direction of created beings according to the requirement of measure and mastery, with knowledge, and so on.

The truth is that the verse is general (mujmala), intended to draw attention to the power of the Creator by creating what is in the earth, and that it was created for our sake. Yet creating it for our sake does not entail the permissibility of using it in every way one might intend. Rather, it was created for us in general. Moreover, the favour holds if each person has some portion of what is in the world, in the sense that the verse indicates that the whole is for the whole, not each one for each one, as al-Baydawi pointed out. Especially since God addressed it to a people who were disbelievers, rebuking them for their disbelief, so how could they know permissibility or prohibition from it? The place of admonition is only what God created of things that people have never ceased to benefit from in many ways.

Another group held that the basic principle regarding things is prohibition (hazr). This was reported from some people of hadith and some Mu‘tazila. So the Mu‘tazila have the three opinions, as al-Qurtubi said. Al-Hamawi said in his commentary on Ibn Nujaym's al-Ashbah, reporting from al-Imam al-Razi: the fruit of the question appears in

[Page 382]

the ruling on things during the interval (fatrah) before prophethood, that is, concerning what people committed of indulgence in appetites and the like. For this reason the more correct view is that the matter is suspended, and that things have no attribute by which reward or punishment is consequent upon them.

In my view, scholars need not posit this, because the people of the fatrah have no sacred law, and their acts have no rulings except regarding the obligation of monotheism according to some. As for after the revelation of the sacred law, the law has already dispensed with that. If an act is found for which no proof exists from text, analogy, or sound inference, then the sound view is that the basic principle regarding harms is prohibition and regarding benefits is permissibility. This is what al-Imam chose in al-Mahsul, so the question bears fruit in this category of new matters in Islam.

* * *

﴿Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens, and He is Knower of all things﴾

This is a transition from the argument drawn from the creation of the earth and what is in it, which is something whose knowledge is necessary for people, to the argument drawn from the creation of what is greater than the earth, namely the heavens. People also often overlook reflecting on this as evidence for the existence of God. This transition may be a digression (istitrad) meant to complete the alerting of people to the magnitude of God's power.

And *thumma* (then) conjoins the clause *istawa* (He turned to) to the clause *khalaqa lakum* (He created for you). The indication of *thumma* for sequence and interval in conjoining a single word to a single word is, in conjoining a clause to a clause, an interval of rank (*muhlah rutbiyyah*). This interval is originally an imagined one (*takhyiliyyah*), indicating that what is conjoined by *thumma* is more deeply rooted in the meaning contained in the clause it follows, so that the mind seems to pause before reaching it after the first statement, and the listener takes note of it lest he overlook it in light of what he heard earlier. This usage became common until it came to be treated as literal. It is called the rank-based ordering (*al-tartib al-rutbi*) and the ordering of information (*tartib al-ikhbar*, with a kasra on the hamza), as in the Almighty's saying: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep ascent﴾ [al-Balad: 11], ﴿And what can make you know what the steep ascent is?﴾ [al-Balad: 12], ﴿It is freeing a slave﴾ [al-Balad: 13], up to His saying ﴿Then he was of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17]. Here His saying ﴿It is freeing a slave﴾ [al-Balad: 13] is the predicate of an omitted subject. Since mentioning these matters, whose due fulfilment is difficult, distracts the listener from another great matter, attention is drawn to it by conjoining it with *thumma*, to indicate that it is more emphatic and more important. From this is the saying of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd describing his riding camel:

*A swift, strong-necked she-camel, then her two shoulders were made into a high, raised ridge*

For when he had mentioned a number of her good qualities, he drew attention to another, more important attribute among the attributes of her neck, namely the length of its height. Al-Marzuqi said in his commentary on the Hamasa, in explaining the verse of Ja'far ibn 'Ulba al-Harithi:

*None removes the calamity except the son of a noble mother, who sees the surges of death and then visits them.*

He said: Indeed *thumma*, although in conjoining a single word to a single word it indicates a lapse of time, in conjoining a clause to a clause it does not mean this. He mentioned the saying of the Almighty ﴿Then he was of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17]. End of quotation.

The indication of rank-based lapse is what is taken into account when *thumma* conjoins clauses, whether or not it agrees with the existential order, or whether its conjunct is prior in existence. Eloquent speech has also come with what indicates the sense of "afterness" intended as afterness in rank, even if it is the reverse of the existential order. In that case the afterness is figurative, based on likening a non-physical separation to a spatial or temporal distance. From this is the Almighty's saying ﴿A slanderer, going about with malicious talk﴾ [al-Qalam: 11], ﴿Hinderer of good, transgressor, sinful﴾ [al-Qalam: 12], ﴿Brutal, and after that, of doubtful lineage﴾ [al-Qalam: 13]. For his being brutal and of doubtful lineage is prior in existence to his being a slanderer and going about with malicious talk, since these are innate attributes, unlike ﴿a slanderer, going about with malicious talk﴾ [al-Qalam: 11]. Likewise the Almighty's saying ﴿Indeed God is his protector, and Gabriel and the righteous of the believers, and the angels after that are supporters﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. When *thumma* is purely for rank-based lapse, it is interpreted accordingly. If it admits both rank-based and temporal lapse, then the apparent meaning of al-Marzuqi's statement, that in conjoining a clause it does not mean this, is that it does not then admit temporal lapse. However, it appears that both possibilities are permissible, in cases where the conjunct comes later in occurrence than what precedes it while still being as in the verse of Ja'far ibn 'Ulba.

I say: this is either a loose metonymy (*majaz mursal*) or an implicature (*kinayah*). If *thumma* is used and what is meant is the necessary implication of lapse, namely the distance of magnification, just as magnification is meant by the demonstrative noun that is set for what is distant, then the relation, though distant, is not rejected because of its fame in their speech and usage and with the accompanying indicators.

Know that I have traced this usage through its occurrences and found that it occurs most often when the clauses are predications about a single subject. By contrast, when the subject differs, *thumma* is definitively for temporal sequence, as in the Almighty's saying ﴿And when We took your covenant: You shall not shed your blood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 84], up to His saying ﴿Then you, these are they who kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85]. That is: after We had taken the covenant by a period of time, you became those who kill yourselves. Like your saying: "The company of the Ansar passed by, then the company of the Muhajirun passed by."

As for this verse, if the creation of the heavens is later than the creation of the earth, then *thumma* is necessarily for rank-based lapse together with temporal lapse. If the creation of the heavens is prior, then *thumma* is for rank-based ordering only. The apparent meaning is the second. Among the early scholars there was disagreement about what the reports on the creation of the heavens and the earth imply. Mujahid and al-Hasan, the majority of them, and it is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, said that the creation of the earth precedes the creation of the sky, because of the Almighty's saying here ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, and His saying in Surah Ha Mim al-Sajdah ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days?﴾ [Fussilat: 9], up to His saying ﴿Then He turned to the heaven, and it was smoke﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. Qatadah, al-Suddi and Muqatil said that the creation of the heaven precedes, and they argued by the Almighty's saying ﴿He built it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27], ﴿He raised its height and made it level﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 28], up to His saying ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30]. It has been answered that the earth was created first, then the heaven was created, then the earth was spread out. Thus what comes after the creation of the heaven is the spreading out of the earth, in accordance with the view of the scholars of the layers of the earth (*tabaqat al-ard*), that the earth was at extreme heat and then began to cool until it hardened, and a solid crust formed from it, then it cracked and burst, and parts of it sank and other parts rose through pressure. However, the scholars of the layers of the earth estimate the time for this to occur as extremely long periods, while God's power is capable of bringing about what causes that transformation in a short span, by coinciding with events that hasten the transformation of created things from their present state.

The more probable of the two views is that the heaven was created before the earth, because the phrase *ba'da dhalika* (after that) is more evident in indicating lateness than His saying ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾. Also, the views of the astronomers hold that the earth is a sphere that separated from the sun like the rest of the planets of the solar system. The apparent meaning of the Book of Genesis (*Sifr al-Takwin*) also requires that the creation of the heavens precedes the earth. I think that the Qur'an's approach in these verses is the method of generality on this matter, to settle the dispute between the proponents of the two theories.

As for "the heaven," if what is meant is the atmosphere surrounding the terrestrial sphere, then it is subordinate to it and later than its creation. If what is meant is the upper celestial bodies, and that is the more fitting reading in light of His saying ﴿And He completed them as seven heavens﴾, then the celestial bodies are greater than the earth and so are prior in creation. It may be that each of the two possibilities is intended in some Qur'anic passages while the other is not intended in those same passages.

Al-istiwa' (turning, rising to) originally means straightness and the absence of crookedness. It is said *sirat mustawin* (a straight path), *istawa fulan wa fulan* (so-and-so and so-and-so became equal), and *istawa al-shay'* (the thing became level), as the reflexive of *sawahu* (he made it level). It is used figuratively for resolving upon a thing with determination and haste, as if one goes toward it straight without turning aside for anything, and it is then construed with *ila* (to). Here *ila* is the indicator of the figurative usage, and it is a figure of speech. Therefore the meaning of God's *istiwa'* toward the heaven is the attachment of His decisive will to bringing it into being, an attachment resembling *istiwa'* in readiness for a great and perfectly executed work. The form of *istawa* is *if'al* (*istaf'ala*), because the *sin* in it is an original radical letter, and this is a figurative *if'tial*. In it there is an indication that when He began creating the creatures, He created the heavens and those in them, to be a preparation for the creation of the earth, then He created humankind, and it is for them that the account has been brought.

And *sawwahunna* (He made them level) means He created them in straightness, and the straightness of creation is its being ordered in a way with no defect or fracture. Between *istawa* and *sawwahunna* there is a *jinas muharraf* (a paronomastic pun with a slightly different vowel or letter). The word *sama'* (heaven) is derived from *sumuww* (height), meaning elevation. The name *sama'* is applied to a single entity and to a genus of the upper worlds that are above the terrestrial world. What is meant here is the genus, by the indicator of His saying ﴿and made them seven heavens﴾, since He made them seven. The pronoun in ﴿He made them level﴾ refers to *al-sama'* in view of the intended genus, because it has the sense of plurality. The author of al-Kashshaf permitted that what is meant by *al-sama'* here is the direction of height, and although this is correct, there is no reason for it, as al-Taftazani stated.

God the Exalted counted the heavens as seven in this verse and elsewhere, and He knows them and what is meant by them best. Nevertheless, the apparent meaning indicated by the rules of the sciences is that what is meant by the heavens is the great upper bodies, namely the wandering planets (*al-kawakib al-sayyarah*) that are organized together with the earth in the solar system. Several things indicate this:

First: The heavens are mentioned in most places of the Qur'an together with the mention of the earth, and their creation is mentioned here together with the creation of the earth. This indicates that they are worlds like the terrestrial world, and this holds for the planets.

Second: They are mentioned together with the earth in that they are signs of God the Exalted's wondrous craftsmanship. Therefore it fits that their interpretation be those observable bodies known to people and to nations, whose orderly motion and dazzling light indicate the greatness of their Creator.

Third: They are described as seven, and the astronomers have known the seven planets since the age of the Chaldeans, and astronomers succeeded one another from that age to the age in which the Qur'an was revealed, and they did not differ that they are seven.

Fourth: These planets are the stars whose motion is regulated by an order linked with the order of the motion of the sun and the earth, and for this reason the later astronomers call them the solar system. So it fits that they are the ones whose creation is coupled with the creation of the earth.

Some interpret the heavens as the spheres (*aflak*), but this interpretation is not sound, because the spheres are the paths traversed by the wandering planets in space, and they are hypothetical lines having no real existence outside the mind.

Furthermore, God the Exalted has mentioned the heavens as seven here and in other verses, and has mentioned the Throne and the Chair in a way that indicates that they encompass the heavens, and He has placed all the heavens opposite the earth. This supports what the astronomers hold, that the wandering planets are nine. Their names in order of their distance from the earth are: Neptune, Uranus, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and Pluto.

The earth, in their terminology, is a wandering planet, but in the terminology of the Qur'an it is not counted with them, because it is that from which the planets are observed. In its place the moon is counted, though it is one of the earth's satellites, so counting it among them is a substitute for counting the earth, bringing things closer to the understanding of the listeners. As for the fixed stars, they are, according to the astronomers, suns floating in vast distances from the earth, and concerning that there are doubts. Perhaps God did not make them heavens with an order like the order of the seven planets, so He did not count them among the heavens; or God only counted for us the heavens that are linked to the order of our earth.

His saying ﴿And He is Knower of everything﴾ is a conclusion drawn from what He mentioned of the signs of power, which can proceed only from one who knows. For this reason the theologians said: the power's objects of attachment proceed in accordance with the will, and the will follows knowledge.

In it there is an allusion censuring their disbelief and expressing wonder at it, for one who knows everything condemns disbelief in Him.

This verse is evidence for the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge. All the Muslim communities (*al-milliyyun*) have held this, as the researcher al-Salkuti transmitted in al-Risalah al-Khaqaniyyah. The philosophers denied His knowledge of particulars (*al-juz'iyyat*) and claimed that the attachment of knowledge to particulars is not fitting for divine knowledge, and this is an illusion for which there is no reason.

The majority of readers pronounced the *ha'* of (هو) with a *damma* (*huwa*), in accordance with the original form. Qalun, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read it with a *sukun* (*huwa*), for lightness, when a conjunction (*harf al-'atf*) is attached to it. The *sukun* is more common than the *damma* in their speech, and this happens with *wa* (و), *fa* (ف) and the *lam* of initiation (*lam al-ibtida'*). Its rationale is that particles consisting of a single letter, when they are attached to a word, take the position of a part of it. The word thus becomes heavy with the addition of that letter, so it is lightened with a *sukun*, just as they did with the vowel of the *lam* of command (*lam al-amr*) after *wa* and *fa*.

What shows that the most eloquent of the Arabic dialects is the *sukun* on the *ha'* of (هو) when a particle is attached to it is that you find it in poetry, where the line does not scan (*yattazin*) except by reading the *ha'* as silent. You rarely find otherwise, to the extent that the claim that it is a poetic necessity (*darurah*) cannot be sustained.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 30 (part 1 of 3)

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I am going to place a successive authority (khalifah) on the earth."﴾

The conjunction (al-waw) joins the story of the creation of the first human beings to the story of the creation of the heavens and the earth. This moves the argument forward, to establish that God is One and to refute their polytheism. It also transitions from mentioning the creation of the heavens and the earth to the creation of the species that holds authority over the earth and manages its affairs. This combines the multiplicity of proofs with the variety of the creation of the worlds and their origin, so that the Muslims may know what the People of the Book knew of the knowledge with which they used to boast over the Arabs, namely what is in the Book of Genesis (Sifr al-Takwin) of the Torah.

Know that the point at which the creation of Adam serves as proof of God's oneness is that the creation of the origin of the species is something perceived necessarily, because every person, when he turns his mind to his own existence, knows that his existence was preceded by the existence of an origin for him, by what he observes of children arising from parents. Thus he is certain that this species has a first origin, to which its emergence ends. Since the lesson concerned the creation of everything on the earth in its entirety, a favour was incorporated into it, namely His saying "for you" (lakum), which requires that the creation of what is on the earth was for their sake. Their souls were thereby prepared to hear the story of bringing into being the origin of mankind, for whose sake the earth was created, so that the signs of power in it are comprehended along with the great favour. That favour is the favour of creation, from which many virtues arise, and the favour of preference, and the favour of God's succession (khilafah) on the earth. Thus the creation of our origin was the most wondrous manifestation of our existence, which is the foundation of the creation of what is on the earth for us. Therefore the appropriateness of transitioning to a reminder of it is clear, along with the excellence of the transition to mention of its wondrous report. The use of the conjunction waw here is to show the independence of this story in its own right, in the greatness of its matter.

(Idh) is among the indefinite nouns of time. It indicates a time of a past relation in which another past relation occurred concurrently with it. Thus (idh) requires two sentences: a principal sentence, which indicates the time-frame (al-mazruf), and this is the one that accompanies all the time-adverbs; and a sentence that specifies what the time-frame is, because (idh), being indefinite, needs something to specify its time from the rest of the times. For this reason it is always obligatory for it to be followed by sentences. In general usage, (idh) is in the position of an adverb of the time of the verb, and thus it is in the accusative position as an adverbial object (maf'ul fihi). Sometimes (idh) departs from the accusative as an adverb to the objective case (maf'ulliyyah), like the inflected time-nouns, according to what Sahib al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) held, and this is the preferred view of Ibn Hisham, in contrast to the apparent meaning of the words of the majority (al-Jumhur). Thus it becomes an indefinite, inflected adverb of time. A time-noun may be annexed to it, such as yawma'idhin ("on that day") and sa'ata'idhin ("at that hour"), and it is then put in the genitive by a formal annexation, so that mentioning it serves as a means to omitting the sentence that is annexed to it. This is because (idh) is always bound to annexation. When its sentence is omitted, the listener knows that there is an omission. When they wished to omit a sentence with a time-noun other than (idh), they feared that the listener would not be guided to something omitted until he sought its evidence. So they made (idh) an indicator of annexation and omitted the sentence, to alert the listener so that he seeks the evidence of what is omitted.

In this verse, it may be an adverb, and the majority so parsed it, and they made it dependent on the verb "they said" (qalu). This leads to the conclusion that the intended point of the story is the speech of the angels. That is far-fetched, because the intended point of the lesson is God's address to them, which is the origin of the lesson, and what it includes of the honouring of Adam and his instruction, after the reminder of the bestowal of the origin of the human species, which is the locus of the lesson. This is from His saying "How can you disbelieve" (Q 2:28), and the verses thereafter. Also, in its parallel, which is His later saying "And when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,' so they prostrated" (Q 2:34), the presence of the particle of sequence (fa') prevents making the adverb dependent on what follows it. Also, the more evident view is that His saying "they said" is a narration of the exchange and dialogue, in the manner of similar passages, as we shall verify. What the composition of the discourse suggests here is that the conjunction is to be read as connected to His saying "He created for you all that is on the earth" (Q 2:29). That is, He created for you what is on the earth, and He said to the angels, "I am creating the origin of man," because we have already stated that mention of the creation of what is on the earth, and that it is for our sake, prepares the listener to await mention of our own affair after the mention of what was created for our sake, namely the heaven and the earth. On this reading, (idh) is superfluous, for emphasis. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna, who cited the verse of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

"Then when that (was), its remembrance is no beauty,
and time follows the good with corruption."

He related it as "fa-idh" (with the vowel of idh), so that the line has the prosodic licence of al-tayy (zihaf al-tayy). In another transmission it is "fa-idha," and then there is no licence. The word "mahah" (with two h's) means beauty. It is not an objection to this that the rule for additions is that they occur in particles, because idh, idha, and similar words are treated as particles. Or it may be that the conjunction is of one story to another story, and this is supported by the fact that wondrous stories that indicate God's power, the Exalted, begin with it. Do you not see that it is mentioned also in His saying, "And when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam'" (Q 2:34), and it is not mentioned in between them? In this reading, (idh) is a noun of time, an object (maf'ul bihi), with the implied verb "remember" (udhkur). Its parallel is abundant in the Qur'an. The intended point of linking the remembrance and the story to a time is what occurred in that time of circumstances. The specification of the noun of time rather than the noun of place is because people have customarily attributed historical events and stories to the times of their occurrence.

God's speech to the angels is applied to what they understand of His will, which is what is expressed as the inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsi). It is possible that it is a speech they heard, so the application of "saying" to it is literal, and its attribution to God is because He created that saying without a customary means. It is also possible that it is another indicator of the will, so the application of "saying" to it is metaphorical, because it is an indication for rational beings. The metaphor here is stronger than the metaphor in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "The Fire complained to its Lord," and in His saying, "Then He said to it and to the earth, 'Come willingly or unwillingly.' They said, 'We come willingly'" (Q 41:11), and in the words of Abu al-Najm:

"When the branches said to the belly, 'Be pressed!'"

There is no benefit in investigating the determination of one of the two possibilities.

The word "angels" (al-mala'ikah) is the plural of "malak". The original form of the plural is "mala'ik", and the ta' is for emphasizing plurality, because the ta' carries an indication of the meaning of a group. The apparent view is that the feminine form of "malaikah" spread into the language of the Arabs from the speech of the Christianized among them, since they believed that the angels are the daughters of God, and the Arabs also believed this. God, the Exalted, said, "And they attribute to God daughters, glory be to Him" (Q 16:57). So "malaʾik" is the plural of "mal'ak", like "shama'il" and "shamal". What also indicates this is the saying of one of the poets of 'Abd al-Qays or another:

"You are not of humankind, but of an angel
descended from the air of the sky, pouring down."

Then they said "malak" as a lightened form. They differed on its derivation. Abu 'Ubayda said it is a noun of place (maf'al) from la'aka, meaning "sent," and from it comes their saying in the command to convey a message, "alikni ilayh," meaning "be my messenger to him." The original of "alikni" is "al'akni," although no verb for it is known. The name of the angel is derived from sending, because the angels are God's messengers, either by conveyance or by creation, as in the hadith, "Then He sends to it, that is, to the foetus in its mother's womb, an angel, and he breathes the spirit into it." On this view, it is a mimetic verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle. Al-Kisa'i said it is metathesized (maqlub), and its present form is ma'fal, and its original is ma'lak, from al-Alūk. Al-Alūkah is the message. It is said ma'lak and ma'lakah, with the lam vowelled or unvowelled. They performed a local metathesis in it, so they said mal'ak, and so it is an adjectival form (sifah mushabbahah). Ibn Kaysan said it is derived from al-malk (with a fatha on the mim and sukun on the lam), and al-malk in the sense of power, as God, the Exalted, said, "Over it are angels, harsh and strong" (Q 66:6). The hamza is added, so its pattern is fa'al with a sukun on the ayn and a fatha on the hamza, like shamal. It was refuted by saying that the claim of adding a letter without a purpose is a far-fetched claim. The view of al-Kisa'i was refuted by saying that metathesis contradicts the original form, so the view of Abu 'Ubayda was preferred. Al-Qurtubi transmitted from al-Nadr ibn Shumayl that he said: there is no derivation of "malak" among the Arabs. He means that they arabized it from the Hebrew language. This is supported by the fact that the Torah calls the angel "mal'ak," with lightening. The existence of a word of close form and meaning in two languages does not indicate that it was transferred from one to the other, except with other evidence.

The angels are luminous, heavenly creatures, created upon goodness, able to take on forms beyond the customary order, because light is capable of taking on forms in various modes, and because its parts do not crowd one another. Their light has no ray, and therefore it does not illuminate when it contacts the earthly world. They take shape when God wishes one of them to appear to one of His messengers and prophets in a manner that breaks the customary order.

God, the Exalted, has given them the power of directing themselves toward the things that God wishes to bring into being, so they take charge of arranging them. These angelic directings have many aspects and ranks which cannot be fully encompassed. They are opposed to the directings of the devils. Thus good inspirations are from the directings of the angels and their connection to human souls, and the inspirations of evil are the opposite.

The khalifah (successor), in its original sense, is one who succeeds another or who is a substitute for him in a task he performs. It is a fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active), and the ta' in it is for intensifying the description, as in 'allamah. The meaning of khalifah here may be either the figurative sense, namely one who undertakes a task that the one who appoints him wishes, like the agent (wakil) and the executor (wasi), that is, "I am placing in the earth a manager who will do what We wish in the earth." This is a metaphor or a figurative use of a general relation (majaz mursal), and not a literal meaning, because God, the Exalted, was not indwelling in the earth nor performing in it the work that He placed in man, which is dominion over the beings of the earth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 2 of 3):

And because God, exalted is He, has not abandoned a task that He used to perform and then entrusted it to man. Rather, the supreme governance has always belonged to God, exalted is He. Man is the only existent that, by what God deposited in his creation, has been able to act upon the creatures of the earth in great and endless ways, unlike other animals. Or the word "khalifa" (vicegerent) may be taken in its literal sense, if it is established that the earth was previously inhabited by a group of creatures called the Hinn and the Binn, with an unpointed ḥāʾ and a kasra and a nūn at the beginning, and with a single kasra-marked bāʾ and a nūn at the second. It has been said that their names are al-Ṭamm and al-Ramm, with a fatḥa on the first letter of each. I consider this to be among the baseless claims, and that the coining of these two names is in the manner of people saying "Hayyān ibn Bayyān," as a reference to something non-existent or unknown. Perhaps this is more suitable for the storytellers than the fables of the Persians or the Greeks. The Persians claimed that before man there existed on the earth a kind called al-Ṭamm and al-Ramm. The Greeks believed that the earth had been inhabited by creatures called "the Titans," and that "Zeus," who is Jupiter, the greatest of the gods in their belief, expelled them from the earth because of their corruption. All of this is contradicted by the context of the verse, for the mention of the creation of the earth followed by the heavens, and then the mention of His, exalted is He, will to appoint a vicegerent, is evidence that the appointment of the vicegerent was the first state on the earth after its creation. The khalifa here is one who succeeds the owner of a thing in disposing of his possessions, and it does not follow that the one created had previously been settled in the place. The khalifa is Adam, and his vicegerency consists in his carrying out God's purpose of populating the earth, through inspiration or revelation, and instructing his offspring in God's purpose from this earthly world. Among what this disposal includes is Adam's disposal by establishing order for his people and their households, according to the abundance of their number and the extent of their dealings. Thus the verse, in this respect, is an allusion to mankind's need to establish a vicegerent to implement judgment among people in their disputes, since no order that unites humanity can stand without that. God has sent the messengers and explained the laws, so that sometimes prophethood and vicegerency were united and sometimes they were separated, according to what God willed in His laws, until Islam came and united prophethood and vicegerency, because the religion of Islam is the ultimate aim of God's purpose in the laws, and it is the final law. And because the fusion of religion and kingship is the most perfect manifestation of the two functions. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by God's leave﴾ [al-Nisa': 64]. For this reason, the Companions of the Messenger of God, after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), agreed on the appointment of a khalifa to preserve the order of the community and implement the law, and no one among the elite or the common people disputed this, except those who turned back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them, from the rough Bedouins and the callers to strife. Debating with such people is futile.

[Page 400]

The khalifa has conditions, the explanation of which is found in the books of jurisprudence and theology, and their relevance will come in upcoming verses. The apparent view is that God's address to the angels here was at the completion of Adam's creation, at the breathing of the spirit into him, or before the breathing, and the first is more apparent. Then the one informed about his appointment as vicegerent is that very creature, just as one who is writing a letter in the presence of a companion says: "I am sending a letter to so-and-so," and the listener understands that what is meant is that the one he is in the process of writing is a letter for so-and-so. It is also possible that this address to them was before Adam's creation. In all these interpretations, the active participle in His saying "jāʿil" (one who will appoint) refers to the future, because the description of vicegerent did not yet apply to Adam at that time.

This statement of God is directed to the angels in the form of information, in order to lead them to know the excellence of the human species, in a way that removes what God knew to be in their souls of ill opinion of this species. It also serves as a consultation with them, honoring them, so that it becomes instruction in the form of honor, like a teacher delivering a benefit to the student in the form of a question and answer, and in order to establish the practice of consultation in affairs, and to alert the angels to what is subtle and hidden of the wisdom in Adam's creation. Thus did the exegetes mention.

In my view, this consultation was made to be a reality concurrent with the existence of the first human, so that it becomes a law impressed upon the souls of his descendants. For the concurrence of some states and meanings with the formation of a thing creates an affinity between that being and what accompanies it. Perhaps this concurrence exists in the meanings that do not exist except as subordinate to the essences in the station of the command of creation in essences. Just as His command, when He wills a thing, that is, the bringing into being of an essence, is to say to it "Be!" and it is, so His command, when He wills the concurrence of a meaning with an essence or a species, is that the origin of that meaning be determined to occur at the formation of the root of that species or at the formation of the essence. Do you not see that when He, exalted is He, willed that the acceptance of knowledge should be among the distinguishing features of man, He taught Adam the names at the moment He created him?

This is the reason for the legitimacy of mentioning God's name at the beginning of actions, so that the concurrence of the beginning of an act with the utterance of His name may pour blessing upon all parts of that act. For this reason also, the Law has required us to choose the most perfect states and the best times for beginning virtuous deeds and important undertakings. This has been discussed in the commentary on the basmala. We will mention what relates to consultation (shūrā) at His saying, exalted is He, "and consult them in the affair," in surah Āl ʿImrān.

[Page 401]

The narration of this statement has been attributed to God, glorified is He, under the title "the Lord," because it is a statement that announces a great governance in the appointment of a vicegerent on the earth. In that appointment there is a blessing of governance mixed with kindness and righteousness, and that is among the meanings of lordship (rubūbiyya), as was previously mentioned in His saying: "﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha: 2]." Since this blessing encompasses the entire species, the title of Lord is attributed to the pronoun of the noblest individual of the species, who is the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), along with honoring him with the distinction of being present in the address.

* * *

﴿They said: "Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?"﴾

This is the answer of the angels to God's statement to them, "﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a vicegerent﴾." The implied sense is: "They said," in the same pattern as His saying, "And when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,' and they prostrated." The answer is separated without being joined by "fa" or "wa," following an established method in the Qur'an in narrating dialogues, which is an Arabic method. Zuhayr said:

It was said to them, "Ride up!" so they said, all of them, "A thousand!"

That is, "so ride up," and he did not say "so they said." Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj said:

The paternal cousins said, "O Salma! Even if he is a poor, destitute man," she said, "Even if..."

They omitted the conjunction in such cases out of dislike of repeating the conjunction with the repetition of the verbs of saying, since dialogue generally requires repetition. So they applied the rule and omitted the conjunction in all of them, and this is frequent in the revelation. Sometimes they joined that with "fa" for a reason that calls for departing from the usual usage, although joining with "fa" is the apparent and original form. This is among what I have not been the first to uncover of the styles of Arabic usage. Among the instances joined with "fa" is His saying: ﴿So he said, "O my people, worship God; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 23] ﴿So the eminent chiefs said﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24] in surah al-Mu'minun. It may also be joined with "wa," as in His saying: ﴿So We sent among them a messenger from themselves, [saying], "Worship God; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 32] ﴿And the eminent chiefs of his people said﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 33] etc., in surah al-Mu'minun. This happens when the intent is not to narrate the dialogue, but rather to report sayings that occurred, or when the sayings reported occurred at different times or different places. This will be evident to you in His saying: ﴿They said, "Kill the sons of those who believed with him"﴾ [Ghafir: 25], up to His saying, "And Pharaoh said, 'Leave me, let me kill Moses'" [Ghafir: 26]. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Moses said, "I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [Ghafir: 27], then He said: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh said﴾ [Ghafir: 28], etc., in surah Ghafir. And in His saying "qalū ataj'alu" there is no answer to "idh" functioning as its governing element, for the reason we have just mentioned: that would lead to the statement "Will You place in it" being the purpose of the story, and the clause introduced by "idh" would become subordinate to it, since the adverbial phrase is subordinate to what it modifies.

[Page 402]

The interrogative reported from the speech of the angels is taken in its literal sense, with the implication of wonder and disbelief at the idea that wisdom would be connected with this. The indication of the interrogative for this meaning here is by way of implicature, together with a demand for what would remove their denial and disbelief. Therefore it was necessary to keep the interrogative in its literal sense, contrary to those who imagined the interrogative here was merely for wonder. What led the angels to this question was that they knew that God, when He informed them, wished them to show their knowledge in response to this news, because they were created upon truthfulness and integrity free from any ambiguity. When this arose in their souls, it was expressed by a sign that God, exalted is He, knows from their conditions, especially since part of the completeness of consultation is that the one consulted should state what he sees as sincere advice. In a hadith: "The one consulted is trusted, and he has the choice as long as he has not spoken," meaning that if he speaks, it is incumbent upon him to fulfill the trust of sincere counsel.

He expressed it with the relative pronoun and its clause to allude to the reason for the construction of the statement, which is the interrogative and wonder, because one who is characterized by corruption and bloodshed is not fit for building, for if he builds he will undo what he has built. The conjunction of bloodshed to corruption is for emphasis on it. The repetition of the pronoun of the earth is for emphasis on it and to remind of the matter of its population and the preservation of its order, so that this is more effective in the wonder at the vicegerency of Adam, and in turning the will of God, exalted is He, away from that, if there is any suggestion in the consultation.

Corruption (ifsād) has been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Surely they are the corrupters﴾ [al-Baqara: 12]. Shedding (safk) is pouring out, and in their speech it has become predominant to link it with blood (dimāʾ). As for the pouring out of anything other than blood, it is safḥ with a ḥāʾ. The use of the clause as a verbal sentence in the relative clause indicates the expectation that this corruption and bloodshed would recur from this creature. They conjectured this conjecture about this creature because of what they perceived of the attributes of this creature being made a vicegerent, through their luminous perception of the bodily, intellectual, and speech configuration of its creation, either from God's description of this vicegerent to them, or from their seeing the form of its composition before the breathing of the spirit into it and after it. The more apparent view is that they saw it after the breathing of the spirit into it, so they knew that it is a composition whose possessor can depart from natural disposition toward acquisition, and from obedience toward disobedience. For the intellect comprises appetite, anger, and reason, and from the combination of these, or the combination of some of them, arise compositions of thought, beneficial and harmful. Then the power in the limbs can carry out whatever the intellect conceives and its faculties wish to do. Then speech can display the opposite of what is real and promote falsehood. Thus there arises great corruption from these states, and from them also arises great good. The nature of the use by a possessor of power of his faculties requires that he will bring about everything these faculties are capable of, both its good and its evil, so there results a mixed act from

[Page 403]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 3 of 3):

...good and evil. The mere sight of the angels of this wondrous creature, whom He intends to make a khalifa (vicegerent) on earth, is sufficient for them to grasp the wondrous attributes it contains, in the manner that will become apparent from them in external reality. This is because their faculties are supremely elevated, being free from the turbidity of matter. If individual human beings vary in their awareness of hidden things, in the orientation of the luminous souls toward known things, and in the discernment and insight into essences, in proportion to their variation in the attributes of the soul, whether innate, acquired, or bestowed (ladunniyya), the highest of which is prophethood, then what do you think of purely angelic souls?

In this there is enough to dispense with what some exegetes have strained to explain regarding how the angels knew the attributes of man before they manifested in him: through revelation (tawqif) and knowledge of what is in the Preserved Tablet, that is, the knowledge of God; or by analogy with a previous nation that had passed away and become extinct; or by analogy with the predatory beasts, since they existed on earth before Adam was created, as in the Book of Genesis of the Torah. Through this you also know that the angels' judgment, that this creature would act in such and such a way, was not directed at one individual rather than another, because it was a judgment upon them before the actions had proceeded from them, and it is only a judgment about what they are capable of by potential. Therefore this does not indicate that their judgment was upon the children of Adam rather than upon Adam himself, since he did not cause corruption. For this view is heedless of the clarification we have mentioned.

The present tense was chosen in His saying ﴿who will cause corruption﴾ and ﴿shed blood﴾ because the present tense indicates renewal and occurrence, not permanence. That is, one from whom corruption occurs at times and bloodshed at times, since corruption and bloodshed are not constant characteristics of human beings.

Their saying ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein?﴾ is evidence that they knew that God's purpose in creating the earth is its righteousness and the orderliness of its affairs. Otherwise, the interrogation mixed with astonishment would have had no place. They knew this purpose of God either from their receiving it from Him, glory be to Him, or from the requirement of the reality of vicegerency, or from the indications of the circumstances of God's care for the creation of the earth and what is upon it, in systems that require its survival for a period. Many verses indicate that the reform of the world is an aim of the Lawgiver. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Would you, if you were given authority, cause corruption on earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ [Muhammad: 22]; ﴿Those are the ones whom God has cursed﴾ [al-Nisa: 52]; and He said: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock, and God does not like corruption﴾ [al-Baqara: 205].

It should not be objected here that this statement is backbiting (ghiba), and they are free of it, because that world is not a world of obligation (taklif), and because there is no backbiting in consultation (mashwara) and the like, such as betrothal and the impugning of character, since the benefit depends on mentioning what is in the one consulted regarding faults, and the benefit outweighs the harm of mentioning someone in a way he dislikes. Also, the one described by this is not specified, since the judgment is upon the species. Thus all the harms that result from backbiting in the actual situation are absent, and for this reason the angels did not refrain from it.

* * *

﴿while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾

The waw is definitely the waw of the circumstantial clause (ḥāliyya), since there is no place for conjunction here. Although what follows the waw is part of their speech and reported from them, the waw belongs to the reported speech and not to the reporting. Their saying ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise﴾ admits of two meanings. One is that the purpose of it is to delegate the matter to God, the Exalted, and to disclaim their knowledge of what they indicated, as the consultant does with one he knows to have a sounder opinion and more perfect intellect: he indicates, then delegates, as the counselors of Bilqis said when she said ﴿Advise me in my affair; I would not decide a matter until you witness﴾ [al-Naml: 32]. They said ﴿We are possessors of strength and possessors of great might﴾ [al-Naml: 33], meaning the opinion is that we should fight him and turn him back from what he desires, as she said ﴿and come to me in submission﴾ [al-Naml: 31], ﴿and the matter is yours, so look at what you will command﴾ [al-Naml: 33]. It is also like the student with the teacher in his discussion with him, then he declares that this is the extent of his knowledge and that the final word belongs to the teacher. Or it is a declaration of the transcendence of the Creator, that nothing that appeared to them as an obstacle to the appointment of Adam could be hidden from Him, and a disavowal of any trace of objection. God, although He knows their innocence of that, their speech followed the manner of expressing what is in the heart without intending to inform others. Or because in this very declaration there is blessing and worship, or it is a proclamation to the people of the exalted assembly (al-mala' al-a'la) of this.

If this is so, then conjunction is not permissible, because when a clause reported by a verb of saying is conjoined with another clause of speech, the rule is that conjunction is not intended on the assumption of the governing verb of saying, unless the two sayings are at two different times, as in His saying ﴿and they said, "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], according to one of the interpretations regarding the conjunction of the clause "the best Guardian" according to those who do not hold that conjoining an imperative to a declarative is valid. Although the correct view is that conjoining an imperative to a declarative and vice versa is valid, and that this does not contradict the eloquence of speech. Therefore the conjunction had no part here. Do you not see that when they relate an incident that has befallen them or a great calamity, they follow it with something like "God is sufficient for us and He is the best Guardian," or "Indeed we belong to God and to Him we shall return," or the like, and they do not conjoin such things? So the waw was the waw of circumstance, indicating that this is a matter present to them in the state of their saying ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption?﴾, and not something that occurred to them after they had gone deep into wonder and astonishment.

The second possibility is that the purpose of their saying ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise﴾ is an allusion that they are more deserving of the vicegerency, because the nominal clause indicates permanence, while the clause ﴿who will cause corruption therein﴾ indicates the expectation of corruption and bloodshed. So the meaning is that his vicegerency will involve both righteousness and corruption, and those from whom disobedience to God's will does not proceed are more deserving of vicegerency than one from whom corruption is expected. Thus it is a circumstantial clause that establishes what the clause ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption?﴾ implies, completing the astonishment. Its governing element is "You place" (taj'al), and this is what the Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari) indicated in its example.

The governing element of the circumstantial clause is the interrogative, because it contains the meaning of a verb, especially when its intent is also astonishment, since the estimate of "Will You place therein" etc. is "we marvel at Your making him a vicegerent."

Glorification (al-tasbih) is a saying, or a complex of saying with action, that indicates the magnification and transcendence of God, the Exalted. For this reason the remembrance of God is called tasbih, and prayer is called subha (a rosary-like devotion). Tasbih is also applied to the saying "Glory be to God" (subhan Allah), because that saying is part of transcendence. Some have mentioned that tasbih is derived from sabh, which is swift movement in water, since its meaning has been broadened, as it is used metaphorically for the passage of stars in the sky, as God said: ﴿and each in an orbit floats along﴾ [Ya Sin: 40], and for the running of a horse. They said: perhaps the notion of swift passage in the worship of God was taken into account in tasbih. More apparent than this is that sabbaha means "to attribute to the sabah," that is, distance, and the intended distance is the figurative distance, which is elevation, that is, transcendence from states of deficiency. It has also been said that sabaha is heard unduplicated and unemphasized, meaning "to transcend," as mentioned in the Qamus (al-Qamus al-Muhit).

In my view, the derivation of tasbih from sabh by way of metaphor is remote. The correct view is that it is derived from the expression subhana (Glory be to Him), and for this reason they insisted that it be on the pattern fa''ala (the intensive form) with doubling, so it has not been heard in an unduplicated form.

Since, as we have said, tasbih is a saying, or a saying and action, that indicates magnification, then the attachment of His saying "with Your praise" to it here, and in most places in the Qur'an, is clear, because the saying includes praising God, the Exalted, glorifying Him, and extolling Him. So the bā' is the bā' of accompaniment, meaning: we glorify You with a glorification accompanied by praise to You. By this, all the artificial explanations given here are removed.

Taqdis is transcendence and purification. It is either by act, as the word muqaddas is applied to the monk in the verse of Imru' al-Qays describing dogs clinging to a wild bull:
They seized him by the leg and the sinew, as the boys tear the garment of the consecrated one.
Or it is by belief, as in the hadith: "A nation is not sanctified (lā quddisat ummatun) in which the weak is not taken from the strong," meaning God has not transcended it nor purified it from Satanic impurities.

The verb qaddasa is transitive by itself, so the bringing of the lām with its object in the verse serves to emphasize the realization of the action, as in "I thanked you (shakartu laka)" and "I advised you (nasahtu laka)." In the hadith, when the man who found a dog panting from thirst took his leather sock, lowered it into the well, and gave the dog water, and God thanked him (fa-shakara Allahu lahu), that is, He thanked him with emphasis, so that it would not be supposed that his thanks were weak, as though it were only for a good deed toward an animal. So the emphasis with the lām removes this misunderstanding. This is among the most eloquent of speech. So do not follow those who made His saying "for You" (laka) attached to a deleted element, the estimate being "praising" (ḥāmidīn), or that it is attached to "we glorify" (nusabbiḥu) with the lām meaning "for Your sake," in the sense that the object of "we glorify" is deleted, so the meaning is "we glorify ourselves," that is, we transcend them from deficiencies for Your sake, that is, for Your obedience. That is a departure from eloquent speech. You may make the lām the lām of specification (lām al-tabyīn), which we will discuss when we come to His saying ﴿and give thanks to Me and do not be ungrateful﴾ [al-Baqara: 152]. Thus the meaning of ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾ is: we magnify You and transcend You. The first is by saying and action, and the second by belief in attributes of perfection fitting to the exalted Essence. So no repetition is to be supposed between "we glorify" and "we sanctify."

The nominal clause was chosen in His saying ﴿and we glorify﴾ to indicate permanence and steadiness, that is, this is their constant description, inseparable from their nature. The fronting of the subject (ism) before the verbal predicate, without a negation particle, may mean specification by the permanence the nominal clause indicates: that is, we are the constantly persevering in glorification and sanctification, not this creature. The more apparent view is that the fronting is for mere emphasis, as in "He gives abundantly."

* * *

﴿He said, "Indeed I know that which you do not know."﴾

This is a reply to their speech, so it follows the style of dialogue in discourse, as previously mentioned. That is: I know what is in mankind of attributes of goodness and attributes of corruption, and I know that their goodness brings about the purpose of populating the earth, and that their corruption does not reach the purpose so as to nullify it, and that in all of this there are great benefits and manifestations of the differences among human beings in ranks, and an illustration of a model of the ultimate ends of God's knowledge, will, and power, through what human beings manifest of the furthest results of intellects, sciences, crafts, virtues, and laws, and other things. How much more so, since among the most wondrous of these is that the combination of two blameworthy attributes produces attributes of virtue, such as the emergence of courage from between the two extremes of recklessness and cowardice. This is a general indication, in reminding them, that God's knowledge is broader than what they knew, so they are certain in general that there is wisdom in this. It is known that there is no need here to estimate "and what you know" after "what you do not know," because it is well known to every listener, and because the point does not depend on mentioning it, but on mentioning His knowledge of what escaped them. This statement of God, the Exalted, was a conclusion of the dialogue and a general argument against the angels, that the breadth of God's knowledge encompasses what their knowledge did not encompass, and that when He willed to make Adam a vicegerent, His will was based on knowledge that he was fit for vicegerency. The emphasis of the clause with inna is to treat the angels, in their objection and their heedlessness of wisdom, as those in doubt.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 31 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them.﴾

This is conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to His saying ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ (Q. 2:30). It conjoins the narrative of the detailed proof (*al-dalil al-tafsili*) to the narrative of the summary argument (*al-istidlal al-ijmali*) that is implied by His saying ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ (Q. 2:30). The teaching of Adam the names, and the manifestation of his excellence by his acceptance of this teaching, to the exclusion of the angels, made it a proof against His statement to them ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ (Q. 2:30). That is, what you do not know of the fitness of this creature for the vicegerency on earth. The mention of Adam after the mention of God's statement to the angels and the mention of their dialogue indicates that this vicegerent is Adam, and that "Adam" is the name of that vicegerent. This style is among the excellent forms of summary, detail and brevity, as al-Nabigha said:

*I said to them: "I will not know the choice she-camels, the young ones from the two sides of Arik and 'Aqil..."*

The verses continue, and then he said after them:

*I have been so frightened that my fear does not exceed
the fear of a goat, in Dhi al-Matara, of 'Aqil.*

*Fearing 'Amr, lest his horses
be led to us, between barefoot and shod.*

This indicates that what he mentioned earlier of the choice she-camels between Arik and 'Aqil, and of the booty of livestock, is what was expected from the raid of 'Amr ibn al-Harith al-Ghassani upon the abodes of Banu 'Awf, of his own people.

*Page 408*

"Adam" is the name of the first human, the father of mankind, in the language of the Arabs. It is said that it is a loanword from Hebrew, because *adama* in Hebrew means "the earth." This is plausible, since the Torah speaks of the creation of Adam and elaborates on his circumstances. So it is not far-fetched that the name of the father of mankind became known to the Arabs through the Jews and their accounts. It is also possible that this name was known to both the Arabs and the Hebrews together from the original Semitic languages, so that its cognates agreed upon it. In the Book of Genesis of the Torah he is named by this name, Adam. It is recorded in the Arabic *Dā'irat al-Ma'ārif* (encyclopaedia) that Adam named himself *Īsh*, meaning "the one possessing substance," and its translation is "human" or "one who is read." I say: perhaps this is a distortion of *Īth*, as you will learn at His saying ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾ (Q. 2:35). The first human has other names in the languages of the nations. The ancient Persians named him Kayumarth, with a fatha on the *k* at the beginning and a *t* with two dots above at the end. He is also called Kayamarthan, with an alif in place of the waw, a kasra on the *r*, and an *n* after the *t* with two dots above. They said that he remained in the Garden for three thousand years, then descended to earth and lived on earth for another three thousand years. His name in Hebrew is Adam, as he is named in the Torah. This name passed into the European languages from the books of the Christian religion, and they called him "Adam," with the *d* lengthened. So it is a noun on the pattern *fā'il*, formed that way arbitrarily. It has been pluralised as *Awadim*, on the pattern *fawā'il*, just as *khatam* is pluralised. This is what the author of the *Kashshaf* points to. He made the attempt to derive it [from a root] like the attempt to derive Ya'qub from *'aqib*, or Iblis from *iblas*, and similar things, meaning that it is a slight attempt. And this is the truth.

Al-Jawhari said: its origin is *ā'dam* with two hamzas, on the pattern *af'al*, from *udmah*, which is the colour of brownness. The second of the two hamzas was changed into a long vowel. The plural rules this out, although it is possible to interpret it as follows: its origin is *ā'adam*, then the second hamza was changed into a waw in the plural because it has no root, as al-Jawhari answered. Perhaps the derivation of the name of the colour *udmah* from the name Adam is more likely than the reverse.

"Names" (*al-asma'*) is the plural of *ism*. In language it is a word that indicates a meaning that the mind of the hearer understands. It applies specifically to words, whether what they signify is an entity, which is the primary first category, or an attribute, or an action, in respect of what humans came to need in their help of one another. From that arose single or compound words, and this is what "name" means by convention, since no transfer of meaning has occurred. So what is said, that "name" applies to whatever indicates a thing, whether its word, its attribute or its action, is a supposition in the language. Perhaps they were led to it by deriving it from *simah*, meaning "mark." Even if this is granted, it does not require that it remain equal to the original basis of its derivation.

It has been said: it is derived from *sumuww* (height), because when it indicates the essence it brings it out. It has also been said: it is derived from *wasm* (branding), because it is a mark upon the thing signified. The more evident view is that it is derived from *sumuww*, and that its pattern is *simw*, with a kasra on the *s* and a sukun on the *m*, because they pluralised it as *asma'*. If its origin were not *simw*, there would be no reason for the hamza added at its end, since it is a substitution for a waw in final position after an extra alif. They would have pluralised it as *awsam*.

It is evident that the names that Adam was taught are words indicating the essences of things, which the human species needs to express, because of its need to call them, to summon them, or to convey the occurrence of some of them with others.
