The latter, meaning the conveying, is what we today call "statements" or "description." So it is evident that the names intended in the first instance are the names of the essences of existent things, such as proper names, and the names of genera among animals, plants, stones and stars, which the human eye falls upon first, such as the name of Garden, angel, Adam, Eve, Iblis, tree and fruit. We find this according to the first human language. For this reason we prefer that there was nothing among what Adam was first taught of the names of meanings and events. Later these came to be, so that when he wanted to report the occurrence of an event or a meaningful matter for a thing, he would join the name of the thing with the name of the event, such as "water of coolness," meaning "cool water." Then after that the positing of verbs and attributes came about, and he said "the water is cool" or "the water became cool." This favours the view that the basis of derivation is the verbal noun (*masdar*) and not the verbs, because verbal nouns are a fine category of the species of names. The Qur'an's saying ﴿Then He presented them﴾ indicates this, as will come.

The definite article in "the names" is the definite article of the genus, intended to express comprehensiveness (*istighraq*), to indicate that He taught him all the names of the things known at that time in that world. It is a conventional comprehensiveness, like "the amir gathered the goldsmiths," meaning the goldsmiths of his land. This is the evident view, because it is the measure by which excellence is manifested, and whatever exceeds it is not fitting for teaching by wisdom, although God's power is capable of that.

The definiteness of "the names" indicates that God taught Adam every name together with what it names and signifies. The use of the plural here is required, since it would not be correct to say "and He taught Adam the name." What has spread, that comprehensiveness by a singular noun is more inclusive than comprehensiveness by a plural noun in the definite with *al*, is an unrefined statement. Its origin is taken from the words of al-Sakkaki, and we shall verify it at His saying ﴿But righteousness is in one who believes in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book﴾ (Q. 2:177) in this surah. "All of them" (*kullaha*) is an emphasis on the meaning of comprehensiveness, lest it be supposed that it refers to a specific known set. The word *kull* did not add generality by itself, but it removed the possibility of the other meaning. *Kull* is a noun indicating totality and encompassing of what it is added to. It most often comes added to a pronoun referring back to what precedes it, and it is then parsed as a corroborative (*tawkid*) following what precedes it. It may also be independent in its grammatical function when emphasis is not intended but encompassment is intended. It is always tied to an addition, either explicitly or by implication. When the thing it is added to is not mentioned, it is compensated for by tanween. Because it is always tied to an addition, it is considered definite by addition, so the definite article does not enter upon it.

God's teaching Adam the names was either by way of instruction, by presenting the named thing to him, so that when He showed it to him its name was made known to him by a created sound that he heard, and he knew by a necessary knowledge that that utterance indicates that essence. Or the teaching was by casting a necessary knowledge into the soul of Adam, such that the name of a thing comes to his mind when it is presented to him, and he then assigns it a name, by His inspiring him with the positing of names for things, so that he could convey them to others. This is done by creating in him the faculty of speech and making him capable of establishing a language, as He said ﴿He created man﴾ (Q. 55:3) ﴿taught him the explanation﴾ (Q. 55:4). All of this is teaching, since teaching (*ta'lim*) is the verbal noun of *'allamahu*, meaning "he made him a possessor of knowledge," like *addabahu* ("he made him well-mannered"). So it is not restricted to instruction, although instruction is what comes to mind first by convention. Whatever the manner of teaching, it was the cause of man's preference over the rest of his kind through the faculty of speech and the creation of linguistic conventions for expressing what is in the mind. It was also the cause of the differences among individual humans, some over others, through what arises from speech, namely the acquisition of the unknown from the known, which is the origin of the sciences. Since man was created speaking and expressing what is in his mind, he was created perceiving, that is, knowing, and he was created as a teacher. This is the origin of the arising of sciences and laws and their branches. For if you look at all knowledge, you will find that it consists of positing names for named things, defining the meanings of those names, and specifying them, to facilitate conveying what occurs in the mind to the mind of another. Both of these matters were denied to the rest of the species of animals. For this reason their individuals did not differ except by a weak difference, in beauty of form, usefulness, or lack of incomprehensibility, let alone the rest of the kinds, such as plants and minerals.

From this you learn that the lesson in God's teaching Adam the names is achieved whether what He taught him were the names of the existent things of that day or the names of everything that would exist. And whether this was in one language, the one with which human speech began from the time of that teaching, or in all the languages that his descendants among the nations would speak. And whether the names were names of essences only, or names of meanings and attributes. And whether what is intended by names is words indicating meanings, or everything that indicates a thing, whether verbal or otherwise, such as the properties, attributes and actions of things, as has been mentioned. For attempting to verify this has no value for the interpretation of the Qur'an.

Perhaps many of the exegetes found it easy to suppose that the preference of Adam by God's teaching was tied to knowing a number of words indicating existing meanings. So they tried to magnify this teaching by expanding it, and they neglected the place of the lesson and the criterion of excellence, which is the bringing into being of this great faculty, whose first manifestation was the teaching of those names. For this reason, the demonstration of the angels' incapacity to attain this level was by their not being taught any of the names. Had the superiority and preference of Adam consisted in his being taught all the names that would come to be in the languages, it would have sufficed to demonstrate the angels' incapacity that they were not taught the mass of names. God taught Adam only the names of all the things existing that day, so that his informing the angels of them would be more striking to them regarding his excellence.

This verse does not contain proof that languages are *tawqifiyya* (revealed or divinely taught), meaning that God taught them to mankind through the tongue of Adam, nor proof of the opposite, because the manner of teaching in His saying ﴿And He taught Adam the names﴾ is general and admits of several modes, as we have already stated. People agree that the capacity for these is an inspiration from God, and that is a teaching from Him, whether He taught Adam one language or all the languages of mankind. Or He inspired him with that, or created for him the speaking faculty. The question is assumed in the knowledge of God and in the principles of jurisprudence, and there are opinions about it. This difference has no consequence, neither in jurisprudence nor elsewhere. Al-Mazari said that its only effect is on the permissibility of altering language. The truth is that altering the legal terms is forbidden, and other alterations are permitted. Al-Mazari was right, and whoever has tried to make a consequence of this disagreement other than what has been mentioned has erred. The investigation of that and its refutation is lengthy, and its matter is not hidden from those of sound intellect.

* * *

﴿Then He presented them to the angels and said, "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful."﴾

Some have said that its conjunction with "thumma" (then) is because there is an interval between the beginning of the teaching and the presentation, namely the period in which the names were taught to Adam, or the period of his being inspired to assign the names to the named things. The more apparent view is that "thumma" here denotes sequence of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), as is its usage when it conjoins sentences, because the rank of this presentation, the manifestation of the angels' lack of knowledge, the manifestation of Adam's knowledge, and the manifestation of the effect of God's knowledge and wisdom, all of this is higher in rank in showing Adam's distinction and his worthiness for the caliphate, than the mere rank of his having been taught the names. Had it remained unconnected to him, none of the whole event that occurred would have happened.

Since the concept of the word "ism" (name) is one of the relational concepts whose conceptualization depends on conceptualizing something else, for "ism" cannot be except as the named thing (musamma), the mention of the names necessarily evokes the named things, so it is permissible for the eloquent speaker to rely on this and omit the word "the named things" for brevity. The pronoun in "ʿaradahum" (He presented them) refers to the named things, because they are what is presented, by the indication of His saying ﴿Tell Me the names of these﴾, and by the indication of His saying ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾, for "ism" implies a named thing. This is an instance of brevity by omission. As for the names themselves, they are not presented, because presentation (ʿarḍ) is the manifestation of an essence after its concealment, and from it comes "ʿarḍ al-shay'" (presenting a thing for sale) and "yawm al-ʿarḍ" (the day of presentation). Words do not become manifest in this way, so it is determined that what is presented is the referents of the names, either by presenting only images of the essences, and they are asked about knowing their names, that is, knowing the words that signify them, or about explaining their qualities and properties; or by presenting the essences and the meanings by creating forms that indicate the meanings, such as presenting courage in the form of its possessor's act, and knowledge in the form of a scholar's instruction in his lesson or his writing, as we see in the sculpted or painted images of intelligible meanings among the Greeks, Romans and Persians, and the mental images among the Europeans, such that the angels, on witnessing that form, find that what is presented is the meaning of courage or the meaning of knowledge. This is close to what happens in dream visions. The summary is that the situation mentioned in the verse is the situation of a world wider than the world of the sensible and of matter.

The return of the pronoun for rational masculine beings to the named things in His saying ﴿ʿaradahum﴾ is by way of prevalence (taghlib), because the most noble of things presented are the essences of rational beings and their attributes. Moreover, the use of such a form with words originally for rational beings is an Arabic usage, such as His, the Exalted, saying ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about it﴾ [al-Isra': 36]. The purpose of this is that it be known from the outset that the presented items are other than the names, so that the listener's understanding does not go astray before hearing the indication ﴿Tell Me the names of these﴾. His saying ﴿He said: Tell Me﴾ is a consequence of the presentation, and it is joined with "fa" (so) for this reason. The imperative in His saying ﴿Tell Me﴾ is an imperative of incapacitation (amr taʿjiz), by the indication that the one commanded knows that the commander is aware of this, so this is not a case of commanding the impossible, as some exegetes have thought. The use of the imperative form in the sense of incapacitation is figurative. Then, that figurative meaning entails the commander's knowledge of the commanded one's incapacity, and that entails the commander's knowledge of the thing commanded.

"Inba'" (telling) is informing with a "naba'", which is a report of great benefit and importance, such that listeners are eager to acquire it. For this reason, "inba'" includes the meaning of informing, because the thing reported is counted among what is known and believed in a more specific way than the belief in a report in general, so it is more specific than "khabar" (report).

His saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾ either means: if you are truthful in your claim that you are more excellent than this creature, if their saying ﴿while we glorify You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] etc. is an allusion that they are deserving of that. Or it means: if you are truthful regarding Adam's unworthiness for the caliphate, as indicated by their saying ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]; their saying ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] was merely a delegation of the matter, or a declaration to the listeners of the exalted assembly of their freedom from any taint of objection to what We have chosen.

The connection between telling of the names and their truthfulness in what they claimed, which the linkage of the consequent to the condition requires, is that knowledge of the names is an expression for the speaking faculty fit to acquire and transmit knowledge, or an expression for knowing the realities and properties of things, or an expression for knowing the names of essences and meanings. All of this entails the actual or potential attainment of worldly knowledge, and the bearer of this attribute is the one worthy of vicegerency on earth, because the function of this vicegerency is management, guidance, direction, and placing things in their proper places without needing instruction in most of its activities. All of this requires the speaking faculty or its branches, while the instinctive faculties, however noble, are only fit for specific tasks for which they have been subjected, which they do not exceed and in which they do not act through analysis and synthesis. What is mentioned about the variety of their actions and the correctness of their works is only from God's direction of them and His inspiration, expressed as subjugation. By this the connection of the command to the telling under this condition becomes clear, though many have been puzzled by it.

When telling is negated, their truthfulness in denying Adam's caliphate is negated. If the object of truthfulness is their claim that they are more deserving, then its absence is established. If the object of confirmation is their claim that man is unfit for vicegerency, then the negation of telling does not indicate the negation of their claim, but it is a preparation for it, because after it comes Adam's telling of the names, since the context indicates that when they were commanded with a command of incapacitation, and the commanded matter was made a proof of truthfulness, there was behind that another telling awaited from the one whose worthiness they had impugned. This is also indicated by His, the Exalted, saying to them ﴿Indeed I know what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

[p. 414]

"Qālū" (they said) is stripped of the conjunctive *fa'* because it is a dialogue, as was explained earlier at His words, ﴿They said: Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. Opening their speech with glorification (*tasbīḥ*) is a stance of courtesy and exaltation toward the One of absolute majesty. *Subḥānaka* is a verbal noun (*ism al-maṣdar*, a noun functioning as a verbal noun) of the verb *sabbaḥa* (doubled form), and it is not a true verbal noun (*maṣdar*), because it does not follow the patterns of the verbal nouns of the quadriliteral form. It has been said that it is the *maṣdar* of *sabaḥa* (undoubled, lightened form) in the sense of *nazzaha* (to declare free from imperfection). In that case it is like *ghufrān*, *shukrān* and *kufrān* from *ghafara*, *shakara* and *kafara*. Its use in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ūl muṭlaq*) with its verb suppressed is very common, as in *ma'ādh Allāh* (God forbid). Rarely it departs from this, as in the saying: "*Subḥānaka Allāhumma dhā s-subḥān*" (Glory be to You, O God, Lord of glorification).

When they restricted its usage to declaring God free from imperfection by making it like a proper name (*'alam*), they departed from the analogy of its derivation, so *subḥāna* became like a generic proper name (*'alam jinsī*), such as *barra* and *fajār* with a kasra on the *rā'*, in the verse of al-Nābigha:

"So Barra bore, and Fajār bore [the burden]."

They prohibited its declension (*ṣarf*) because of its status as a proper name and the addition of the *alif* and *nūn*. Sībawayh said: As for omitting the tanwīn of *subḥāna*, it is because it has become definite in their usage.

The statement of the angels, ﴿We have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾, is an informative sentence intended to express acknowledgment of incapacity, not to report their state, because they are certain that God knows what their speech contains, nor did they intend its necessary implication, which is that the speaker has knowledge of what he reports. It is therefore determined that the informative form is used to express acknowledgment. Moreover, their speech indicates that their knowledge is limited and not open to increase; it is restricted to what God has inspired in them and what He commands them. So for the angels there is the knowledge of receiving meanings (*'ilm qabūl al-ma'ānī*), not the knowledge of deriving them (*'ilm istinbāṭihā*).

In opening their speech with *subḥānaka* there is an allusion to an apology for their rejoinder, ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. It is an opening of the type of the skill of the opening (*barā'at al-istihlāl*), the apology being at its start. Although the apology is achieved by their words ﴿We have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾, its achievement from that is by way of implicature (*kināya*) and not explicit statement, and it occurs at the end of the beginning. So opening their speech with declaring God free from imperfection is a hastening toward what indicates adherence to the great aspect of courtesy.

﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾: they placed it in the manner of a causal explanation for their words "We have no knowledge except what You have taught us," because the One whose knowledge encompasses everything and who perfectly orders every creation, when He does not give any of His creatures a way to knowledge of a thing, they have no means to knowing it. Attainment is according to capacity for receiving and readiness; that is, there is no hope for us to go beyond knowledge to what You have not prepared for us to know according to our nature.

What shows that this statement is given as a causal explanation and is not merely praise is its introduction with *inna* in a context that is neither a rejection of denial nor of doubt.

The Shaykh [ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī] said in *Dalā'il al-I'jāz*: It is among the characteristics of *inna* when it comes in this manner, i.e., that it follows a statement and is merely for emphasis, that it can serve in place of the connecting *fā'* (then), for example, and that it conveys from the linking of the sentence with what precedes it a wondrous matter; so you see the speech with it as both disconnected and connected. He recited the verse of Bashshār:

"Hasten, my two companions, before the midday heat,
Indeed that success lies in early rising."

And the saying of one of the Arabs:

"So sing to her, and she is your ransom,
Indeed the singing of camels is the driving chant."

For both of these have dispensed, by mentioning *inna*, with the *fā'*. When Khalaf al-Aḥmar asked Bashshār why he did not say "Hasten, so success lies in early rising," Bashshār answered him that he had brought it in its Arab, Bedouin form, and that if he had said "fa-al-najāḥ" it would have become the speech of the muwallads (later non-Bedouin poets); that is, he answered him with an answer that referred him to taste. The Shaykh 'Abd al-Qāhir explained its reason. The Shaykh also said in another place: Do you not see that the purpose of his saying "Indeed that success lies in early rising" is to clarify the meaning in his saying to his two companions "Hasten," and to argue for himself in the command to hasten early, and to show the benefit of it? End of quote.

*Al-ʿAlīm* means one of great knowledge, and according to the correct view it is among the forms of intensification (*mubālagha*). It is permissible for it to be an attributive adjective (*ṣifa mushabbaha*) on the supposition of transforming *ʿalima* with a kasra on the *lām* into *ʿalula* with a ḍamma on the *lām*, so that it becomes one of the verbs of innate characteristics, as we established in the case of *al-Raḥīm*. But we are content without this strained reasoning, since there should be no disagreement that the pattern *faʿīl* comes for the meaning of intensification. Those who claimed that *faʿīl* does not come for intensification are the ones who created these far-fetched explanations.

*Al-Ḥakīm* is *faʿīl* from *aḥkama*, when someone perfects the workmanship by protecting it from defect. The root *ḥ-k-m* in the language of the Arabs originally means preventing corruption and defect. From it comes *ḥakama al-dābba* (the bridle of the animal, with a fatḥa on the *ḥā'* and kasra on the *kāf*, pronounced with vowel movement), the iron placed in the horse's mouth to prevent it from disturbing its course. *Aḥkama fulānun fulānan* means he prevented him. Jarīr said:

"Sons of Ḥanīfa, restrain your foolish ones,
Indeed I fear for you that I may become angry."

*Al-ḥikma* with a kasra on the *ḥā'* is the mastery of knowledge and its completeness. So *al-Ḥakīm* is either in the sense of one who perfects all affairs, or in the sense of one who possesses wisdom. Whichever it is, it has come in the pattern *faʿīl* from a non-triliteral verb, and that is attested. ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib said:

"From the fragrance of the caller, the one who hears, does it keep me awake,
While my companions are asleep?"

Among the grammatical evidences is what Abū ʿAlī recited without attributing it:

"So whoever has not had noble parents, his mother and father,
Indeed for us there is the noble mother and the noble father."

He meant the *mother* who bears noble children (*al-umm al-munjiba*), as is shown by his saying "his father did not bear noble offspring." And in the Qur'an, ﴿the Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 117], and the description of "the Wise," and the Arabs apply the patterns of some derived forms to others. So there is no need for strained interpretation of ﴿Badīʿ al-samāwāt wa al-arḍ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 117] as "the wondrous of His heavens and earth," meaning that *al* is a substitute for the genitive complement, so that the thing described as wise would be the heavens and the earth, which are firmly created. For the context of the verse is glorification of the Creator, not the wonders of created things, so that it would have an intelligible meaning. Nor is there need to interpret *al-Ḥakīm* as "the one possessing wisdom," because that does not help in removing the question of its coming from a non-triliteral root.

The following of *al-ʿAlīm* by *al-Ḥakīm* is the following of a description by one more specific than it, for the concept of wisdom exceeds the concept of knowledge, since wisdom is perfection in knowledge. So it is like their saying "an eloquent orator" (*khaṭīb miṣqaʿ*) and "a superb poet" (*shā'ir mufliq*).

In *Maʿārij al-Nūr* by the Shaykh Luṭf Allāh al-Arḍarūmī: *Al-Ḥakīm* is the possessor of wisdom, which is knowledge of a thing and perfection of its work, and it is bringing it into existence in relation to Him, and governing it with the utmost of what the governed (with a fatḥa on the *bā'*) is prepared for, and comprehension of the realities of affairs. End of quote.

Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī said in *al-Maqṣad al-Asnā*: *Al-Ḥakīm* is one who possesses wisdom, and wisdom is an expression for knowledge of the best of things. The best of knowledge is knowledge of God, and the most exalted of things is God, and it has already been said that none other knows Him in the full reality of His knowledge. The grandeur of knowledge is according to the grandeur of the object known. So He is the true *Ḥakīm*, because He knows the most exalted things with the most exalted knowledge, since the most exalted knowledge is the eternal, pre-eternal knowledge whose cessation cannot be conceived, which corresponds to the object known with a correspondence into which no obscurity or doubt can enter, and such is not conceivable except in the knowledge of God. End of quote.

The discussion of wisdom will come at His words, ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269].

The *anta* in ﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾ is a separating pronoun (*ḍamīr faṣl*), and its placement in the middle is one of the forms of restriction (*qaṣr*). So the meaning is the restriction of knowledge and wisdom to God, a restriction of reversal (*qaṣr qalb*) to refute their belief that they themselves had some share of knowledge and wisdom when they responded with their words, ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], or treating them as those who believe that, according to the two possibilities mentioned earlier. Or it is a real restriction (*qaṣr ḥaqīqī*) of a claimed kind (*āddhā'ī*), intended to restrict perfect knowledge and wisdom to Him, exalted is He.

[Page 417]

When this statement became part of the dialogue, the sentence was also left without a *fa'* (conjunction), as was mentioned earlier with its counterparts. Although it turns toward those addressed by the speech in a different manner from those who were addressed by the preceding statements, it has the force of an address to them. The purpose of addressing Adam with this command is that his subsequent superiority over them in knowledge, from this direction, should become manifest. Thus the address stands as though it were directed to them, given His saying after that: ﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth?"﴾. The beginning of the address to Adam with his name, even though he was not far from hearing the divine command, serves to honor Adam and to make his name prominent among the exalted assembly, so that he may gain a good reputation, along with the honor he receives in the sight of the one who commands. This is because it is the practice of one who commands or addresses (with *kasr*, i.e., the speaker) when he is gentle toward the one addressed (with *fath*, i.e., the listener) to mention his name and not to limit himself to the pronoun of address, so that he does not equate his address to him with every address. From this is what came in the hadith of intercession, after mentioning the prostration of the Prophet and his praise of God with praises that God inspires him with, when it is said: "O Muhammad, raise your head; ask and you shall be given; intercede and your intercession shall be accepted." This is the subtle point of mentioning the name even in the midst of direct address, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*Fatima, gently, enough of this coquetry*

Sometimes they have used the vocative as a means to bring the explicit name into presence, since there is no way to bring it into presence during direct address except through the vocative. Thus the vocative in every case is used in its figurative meaning.

* * *

﴿So when he informed them of their names﴾

*Al-inba'* (informing) means telling them the names, and in it there is an indication that what is told is something important. The pronoun in the genitive construction is the pronoun for the named things, like the pronoun in (*'aradahum*, "He presented them"). Using for them the form of the pronouns for rational beings is explained in His saying ﴿Then He presented them﴾ [2:31]. As for His saying ﴿So when he informed them of their names﴾, the pronoun in *anba'* refers to Adam, and the pronoun in *qala* refers to the Name of Majesty (God). The subject was not stated as an explicit noun, even though it follows the pattern applied to one other than its owner, meaning that it came after the pronouns of Adam in His saying ﴿Inform them﴾ and ﴿he informed them﴾, because the context is evidence that this statement could not have come from someone like Adam.

* * *

﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth?"﴾

This is the answer to *lamma* (when). The speaker is God Most High, who is mentioned in His saying ﴿And when your Lord said﴾ [2:30]. The pronouns of *qala innī a'lamu* ("He said, 'I know'"), *'allama* ("He taught"), and *'aradahum* ("He presented them"), and the pronouns before them, refer back to Him. This is a reminder to them of His statement to them at the beginning of the dialogue: ﴿I know what you do not know﴾ [2:30]. Although that statement does not explicitly contain ﴿I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, it implies it, because the generality of what you do not know includes all of that. Therefore His statement here, ﴿I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, is an explanation of what was stated in general in the first statement, since it is equal to it in extension, for "what you do not know" is the unseen of the heavens and the earth. The explanation here, however, goes beyond what was explained by His saying:

* * *

﴿And I know what you disclose and what you were concealing﴾

The general statement was given before the proof appeared, and the detailed statement was given after it appeared, according to the method of argumentation: the claim is stated in general, and the conclusion is stated in detail. This is because a claim before proof may be met with doubt from the listener, who may take it as exaggeration or something similar, but after proof it is proper for the one making the claim to make the defeated party recognize his error or something similar, and to triumph over him with the authority of his proof, for truth has its own force. A parallel to this is the statement of the companion of Moses: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾ [18:78], ﴿As for the boat﴾ [18:79], through His saying ﴿and I did not do it of my own accord﴾ [18:82], then he said ﴿That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾ [18:82], where he used the demonstrative for the distant to exalt the interpretation after its manifestation. This is a method followed by writers and orators, and it goes back to the principle of deriving conclusions from premises in the art of composition, as I explained in my book *Usul al-Insha' wa al-Khitabah* (The Principles of Composition and Oratory). Most orators reach the purpose of their sermon only after premises and preliminaries. The verse follows the method of orators and eloquent speakers in what we have mentioned, as a teaching for creation and in accordance with the customary requirement of the situation, without regard for the side of divinity, for the angels do not doubt that His statement is the truth and His promise is the truth, so they have no need for the setting out of proofs.

In His statement ﴿and what you were concealing﴾, the *kuntum* ("you were") is most likely superfluous, serving to emphasize the certainty of the concealment. Whoever knows what has been intensely concealed knows what has not been eagerly concealed, and knows the outward states by a fortiori reasoning. The present tense in *tubdūna* ("you disclose") and *taktumūna* ("you conceal") indicates the renewal of that from them, and so it implies the renewal of God's knowledge of it whenever it occurs from them.

Some have made far-fetched interpretations here, by taking *kuntum* as indicating past time and *tubdūna* as indicating the future, and by assuming an ellipsis on both sides, namely "and what you used to disclose and what you conceal," and an ellipsis regarding the unseen of the heavens and the earth, meaning "and their witnessed part." None of this has any justification.

God Most High made Adam's knowledge of the names and the angels' inability regarding that a sign of the capacity of the human species for the vicegerency on earth, rather than the angels. This is because vicegerency on earth is God Most High's vicegerency in carrying out what He willed of cultivation (*'umran*) in all its states and branches. That is to say, God Most High entrusted to the human species the completion of His purpose for the world. Thus the disposal of this species over the earth stood in place of the direct exercise of God Most High's power in all the works that humans perform. There is no doubt that this vicegerency cannot be realized except through knowledge, namely the acquisition of the unknown from the known, and the realization of the proportion between things and their places, their correlations, and their connections. This is acquired knowledge, by which a human perceives good and evil and is able to do good and evil, each in its proper place. Only the rational faculty is suited for this knowledge, namely the faculty of thought, whose most evident manifestation is knowing the names of things and the names of their properties, and which is able to produce opposite actions. This is because it is the faculty whose objects are not confined and whose known things do not come to an end, as has been observed of the states of the human species from its origin until now and until what God Most High wills. The angels, since they were not created prepared for this, were overcome by the task of assigning names to named things. They were created with a single disposition, the disposition of good, which does not vary or deviate. Therefore they were not qualified to derive the unknown from the known, so that their knowledge would not stop. Nor were they sources of the evils whose occurrence is necessary for the reform of the world. Thus their goodness, although it is suitable for the rectitude of their pure world, was not suitable for the order of a mixed world. The wisdom of this mixing is the manifestation of the ultimate of divine knowledge, as Abu al-Tayyib said:

*Placing generosity in the place of the sword, in matters of honor, is as harmful as placing the sword in the place of generosity.*

The verse implies a great distinction for this species in this respect and in the excellence of knowledge. But it does not indicate the superiority of the human species over the angels, for distinction does not necessarily entail superiority, as Shihab al-Qarafi explained in the ninety-first Distinction (*al-Farq al-Hadi wa al-Tis'un*). This is an excellence from one aspect only. Absolute preference depends on the totality of excellences, as indicated by the hadith of Moses and al-Khidr.

The interrogative in His statement (*"Did I not tell you"*) etc. is affirmative (*taqriri*), because that statement certainly took place, and the angels know its occurrence and do not deny it. The interrogative was placed on the negation of the statement because most affirmative interrogatives include what conveys negation, with the aim of widening the scope of what is being affirmed, so that it seems to the addressee that he is being asked about the negation of the occurrence of the thing. If he wishes to claim its negation, the one who affirms has granted him that latitude, but he realizes that he cannot deny it. Therefore the affirmer makes him confirm its negation, and when he confirms it, his confirmation becomes binding on him and he has no way out of it.

This is the rule of the affirmative interrogative, which is generally predominant, and it is what recurs in the Qur'an, and the author of *al-Kashshaf* built upon it the meanings of its verses, among them His statement ﴿Do you not know that God is powerful over all things?﴾ [2:106]. Ibn Hisham in *Mughni al-Labib* hesitated about this, and its commentator responded to him. Affirmation may also occur through a positive form in its basic sense, as in ﴿Did you say to the people﴾ [5:116], which is an affirmation intended to nullify the claim of the Christians, and His statement ﴿They said, "Did you do this to our gods, O Abraham?"﴾ [21:62].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 34 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers.﴾ This is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority (khalifa)"﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. It is the coordination of one account with another account. The repetition of "idh" (when) after the coordinating particle, which dispenses with repeating its adverbial phrase, is an indication that this clause is intended in its own right, because it is distinguished by this remarkable account. It has come in a style that signals independence and importance. Because of this consideration, this account was not introduced with the consequential particle "fa" (so), which would have said "So We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam'", even though its content in reality is a consequence of the content of the preceding one. The command to them to prostrate to Adam was only for the sake of the manifestation of his superiority over them, since he knew what they did not know. This is what the ordering of these accounts one after another has required, beginning with the creation of the heavens and the earth, and what came after it of the stages of the origins of those who would inhabit the earth and what is between it and the heaven. For the default in speech is that the order of its composition should follow the order in which its meanings occur in external reality, unless an indicator points to a departure from that.

Do not be troubled by His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat al-Hijr: ﴿Indeed, I am going to create a human from clay from black, altered mud﴾ [al-Hijr: 28], ﴿and when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down to him in prostration﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. This is because that surah related the account in summary, so it passed over its details, and its explanation has come in what is repeated of it in other verses. The clearest of them is the verse of al-Baqara, because the preceding verse requires that Adam's excellence was not made manifest to the angels except after his being taught the names, and presenting them to them, and their inability to inform about them. Before that, they were awaiting the clarification that would uncover their suspicion about Adam, that he would be a corrupter on the earth, after they had kept to the position of withholding judgment because of what Allah had said to them: (﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]). So Adam's informing them of the names, at their inability to inform of them, was a clarification to remove their doubt, and so they deserved to bring forth what contains an excuse for their lack of knowledge of his right.

[p. 421]

The purpose of this account is to show the distinction of the human species, that Allah specializes the kinds of His creatures and their types with the characteristics and distinctions that His wisdom has required, so that no one of them is free from benefit in its existence in this world. It also serves to show the excellence of knowledge, and to clarify that the one who possesses knowledge is deserving of being honored by those around him. It shows what the wicked, satanic souls have of corruption and depravity. It clarifies that acknowledging the truth is among the qualities of angelic virtues, and that corruption, envy, and arrogance are among the blameworthy traits of those possessing intellects.

The discussion of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "idh" is like the discussion that preceded it in the explanation of His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. The mention of the word "al-malaʾika" (the angels) and the word "Adam" here, rather than using pronouns for them, as in His saying (they said, "Exalted are You") and His saying (﴿When he informed them﴾ [al-Baqara: 33]), is so that the coordinated account is titled with a title like the title of the account it is coordinated with. This indicates that the coordinated account deserves to be an intended account, not merged into the account before it.

The style of attributing the speech to Allah was varied. It is presented here attributed to the pronoun of greatness ("And when We said"), while in the preceding verse it was attributed to the Lord of the Prophet ("And when your Lord said"), for variety, and because the speech here includes a command to an act which involves humiliation for those commanded, so the manifestation of the greatness of the one commanding is fitting for it. As for the preceding speech, it is merely an informing from Allah of His purpose, in order to make manifest their opinion. Also, because of the intent to connect consultation with the beginning of the creation of the first individual of the human species, who needed consultation, the attribution to the one described with lordship (rububiyya), which indicates the management of the affairs of those who are nurtured, is fitting. It is added to the pronoun of the most noble of those nurtured, who is the Prophet ﷺ, as has preceded at His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ [al-Baqara: 30].

The reality of prostration (sujud) is the lowering of the body, or placing it upon the earth, with the intention of venerating something visible before the eyes, such as prostrating to a king or a lord, or prostrating to the stars. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾ [Yusuf: 100], and He said: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon﴾ [Fussilat: 37]. Al-A'sha said:

"When he came to us after the sleep, we prostrated to him and removed the turbans."

He also said:

"He alternates from the prayers of the one who is ... (al-Malik), at times prostration and at times supplication."

Or [the intention is] toward something imagined and visualized in the mind, which is prostration to Allah. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾ [al-Najm: 62]. Prostration is a pillar of the prayer in Islam. As for the prostration of the angels, it is a representation of a state in them that indicates veneration. Allah's saying has gathered its meanings: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant﴾ [al-Nahl: 49]. So prostration was the first greeting that humans received at the creation of the world. Prostration has been known since the most ancient eras of history. On the Chaldean monuments, since the nineteenth century BCE, there is an image of Hammurabi, king of Chaldea, bowing before the sun. On Egyptian monuments were found images of war captives prostrating to Pharaoh. The forms of prostration differ according to differing customs.

The form of prostration in prayer differs according to the differing religions. Prostration in the prayer of Islam is falling to the ground with the forehead, the two hands, and the two feet.

The transitive use of "usjudu" (prostrate) with the name "Adam" by the preposition "li-" (to/for) indicates that they were charged with prostration to his very person. This is the primary meaning of the preposition "li-" of purpose when attached to the root of prostration, like His saying: ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾ [al-Najm: 62] and His saying: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon﴾ [Fussilat: 37]. It is not an objection to this that prostration to other than Allah is forbidden in Islam, because this is a new law that abrogated what was in the earlier laws (naskh). Also, the prostration of the angels is one of the deeds of the higher world, and that is not included among the obligations of the people of the earth. So there is no benefit in extending the discussion about whether Adam was prostrated to, or whether he was a direction of prayer for those who prostrate, like the Kaʿba for Muslims. There is no need to strain by making the "li-" carry the meaning of "ila" (to), as in the verse of Hassan:

"Was he not the first to pray toward your qibla? Indeed, necessity has its rulings."

This does not befit comparing with it the most excellent of speech in arrangement. In this verse there is a wonderful indication of the grandeur of knowledge and the worthiness of scholars for veneration and honor. Because Allah, when He taught Adam a knowledge that He had not qualified the angels for, made Adam a model for the innovations, inventions, and sciences that would appear among humans afterward, and those that will appear until the end of this world.

[p. 423]

Abu Ja'far, according to the most famous narration from him, read (lil-malaʾikatu usjudu) with a damma on the "ta'" in the state of continuity, following the vowel of the "ta'" to the damma of the "jim" in "usjudu", because the intervening quiescent letter is not counted, as it is a weak barrier. His reading is a narration, and it follows a weak dialect in such a case. Therefore al-Zajjaj and al-Farisi said: "This is an error from Abu Ja'far." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is not permissible to eliminate the grammatical vowel by the vowel of assimilation except in a weak dialect, like the reading of al-Hasan (al-hamdi lillahi) with a kasra on the dal." Ibn Jinni said: "What Abu Ja'far went to is only permissible when what precedes the hamza is a sound quiescent letter, such as His saying: ﴿And she said, 'Come out to them'﴾ [Yusuf: 31] in Surat Yusuf." End of quote. They only gave this judgment because his reading is counted among the mutawatir (widely transmitted) readings, so such an anomaly would not be fitting in them, even if it is an anomaly in modes of recitation that does not contradict the script of the Mushaf.

The coordination of "fa-sajadu" (so they prostrated) with the particle "fa" of immediate sequence indicates the angels' swiftness in compliance, and what was in their souls of apprehension, lest this creature become a locus of corruption and bloodshed, did not hinder them, because they are free from disobedience.

The exception of Iblis from the pronoun of the angels in "fa-sajadu" is a disjunctive exception (istithna munqati', an exception not of the same genus). This is because Iblis was not of the genus of the angels. Allah said in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]. But Allah made his states like the states of angelic souls, with a grace that overcame his nature, so that his association with them and his conduct according to their manner could be realized. Thus the exception of his state from their states was permissible, in the expectation that he would be like those among them.

The verse indicates that Iblis was intended in the report that was given to the angels, when He said to them: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority﴾ [al-Baqara: 30], and in the command that He gave to the angels, when He said to them: "Prostrate to Adam." That is because the genus of the immaterial beings was, in that world, submerged in the type of the angel, since Allah created from their type many individuals, as indicated by the plural form in His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. Allah did not create from the type of the jinn except their origin, who is Iblis. And He created from the type of humankind their origin, who is Adam. Allah established Iblis among the angels in a station of training and cultivation, and subjected him to follow their practice. So he continued upon those ways for a long period, which no one knows except Allah. Then what was in his type of wickedness became manifest, as His saying indicates: (﴿So he defied the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]) in Surat al-Kahf. So he disobeyed his Lord when He commanded him to prostrate to Adam.

[p. 424]

Iblis is the name of the first devil, who is the progenitor of the devils. So Iblis stood to the kind of devils and jinn in the position that Adam stood to the kind of humankind. "Iblis" is a name arabicized (muʿarrab) from a non-Arabic language, which the lexicographers did not specify. But what indicates that it is arabicized is that the Arabs did not give it diptote treatment (triptotic inflection, i.e., they prevented it from taking nunation), and there is no cause for that except being a proper name and being non-Arabic. For this reason al-Zajjaj made its hamza original, and said: "Its pattern is fiʿlil." Abu 'Ubayda said: "It is an Arabic name derived from al-ibласʾ (despair), which is distance from good and hopelessness of mercy." This is a fine derivation, were it not that it conflicts with its being prevented from nunation. They made its pattern ifʿil, because its hamza is augmentative. The justification for its being prevented from nunation has been offered: that since it has no counterpart among Arabic names, it is counted in the position of a non-Arabic word. This justification is weak.

Most of those who enumerated the arabicized words in the Qur'an did not count the name Iblis among them, because they did not ascertain that, and because the name is suitable for an Arabic root and fits it.

The clauses ﴿He refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers﴾ are an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), indicating that the divergence of his state from the state of the angels in prostrating to Adam is something that would naturally raise a question in the mind of the listener: how did Iblis not do what he was commanded, and how did he oppose the state of his group, and what was the cause of that? Because his opposition to the state of his kind is a strange opposition, since the norm is agreement among groups, as Durayd ibn al-Simma said:

"Am I anything but of Ghaziyya? If Ghaziyya goes astray, I go astray, and if Ghaziyya is rightly guided, I am rightly guided."

So [the Qur'an] clarified the cause by saying that he refused, and was arrogant, and disbelieved in Allah.

Abu'l-Ibā' (refusal) is abstaining from an act or refusing to accept it. Al-istikbār (arrogance) is an intensified form of kibr (pride). The sīn and tā' in it may indicate counting, meaning that he counted himself great, as in istaʿẓama (he deemed something great) and istaʿdhaba al-sharāb (he found the drink sweet). Alternatively, the sīn and tā' may indicate intensification, as in istajāba (he responded) and istaqarra (he settled), so that istakbara means he became characterised by pride. The meaning is that he was arrogant towards God by denying that Adam deserved for him to prostrate to him. This was a denial born of determination, not of consultation or seeking counsel, as other verses indicate, such as His saying: ﴿He said, "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay."﴾ [al-A'rāf 7:12]. On this basis, Iblīs's act contradicted the statement of the angels when ﴿they said, "Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:30], because theirs was a pause regarding wisdom, which is why they said: ﴿"While we exalt You with praise and sanctify You"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:30]. Through his refusal, Iblīs disrupted the innate nature in which he had been created at first, so it was transformed into another nature, in the manner of the change that befalls the rational person when his mind becomes disordered, or the capable person when some of his limbs are paralysed. Among ailments are physical ailments and among them are spiritual ailments, as the poet said:

*So I was like one with two legs: one healthy, and the other which Time afflicted and paralysed.*

Istikbār is therefore an increase in pride, since the sīn and tā' in it indicate intensification and not request, as you have understood. Among the subtleties of the Arabic language is that the root denoting being characterised by pride occurs only in the form *istifʿāl* or *tafaʿʿul*, indicating that one who possesses the attribute of pride is only ever one who seeks pride or affects it, and is not truly great. Here it is fitting to mention the words of Abu'l-ʿAlāʾ:

*You rose high, then you showed humility, with confidence; when peoples showed humility in heedlessness.*

On the reality of pride, Ḥujjat al-Islām (the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazālī) said in *Iḥyāʾ* (The Revival of the Religious Sciences): Pride is a trait in the soul, and it is the sense of ease and reliance upon a person's belief that he is above those he is proud over. Pride requires one who is proud and one over whom he is proud, and by this pride is distinguished from self-admiration (ʿujb), for self-admiration requires no one other than the self-admirer. It is not enough for a person to deem himself great in order to be proud, for he may deem himself great yet see another as greater than himself or equal to him, and so he is not proud towards him. Nor is it enough for him to belittle another, for even so, if he sees himself as lowlier, he does not become proud; and if he sees another as equal to himself, he does not become proud either. Rather, he must see for himself a rank and for another a rank, and then see his own rank as above the other's. When these three beliefs are present, the trait of pride arises. This belief blows into it, so that in the soul arises self-regard, might, joy, and reliance upon what he believes. He becomes mighty in his own soul because of this. That might, that exhilaration, and that reliance upon that belief is the trait of pride.

This verse and its like have been a source of disagreement among the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (*uṣūl al-fiqh*) concerning what the implication of an exception (*istithnāʾ*) is regarding a ruling that applies to the excepted item (*mustathnā*). The majority said: the exception requires that the excepted item be characterised by the opposite of what was ruled concerning the item from which it is excepted (*mustathnā minhu*). For this reason, the exception is frequently used without being followed by a specific ruling for the excepted item, whether the statement is affirmative or negative.

This becomes clear in the statement of witness, *lā ilāha illā Allāh* (there is no god but God). Were it not that the exception indicates that the excepted item is characterised by the opposite of what was ruled concerning the item from which it is excepted, the statement of witness would convey nothing beyond denying divinity to all besides God. Its conveying the oneness of God would then be by implication. Abū Ḥanīfa said: an exception from a negative statement establishes for the excepted item the opposite of what was ruled concerning the item from which it is excepted. An exception from an affirmative statement, however, indicates only that the excepted item is characterised by the opposite of the ruling, not the opposite of the attribute ruled. Thus the excepted item is like one whose attribute is left unstated, so according to the majority the excepted item is removed from the attribute ruled for the item from which it is excepted, while according to Abū Ḥanīfa the excepted item is removed from the ruling upon it, so it is like one left unmentioned.

The later Ḥanafīs equated exception from a negative statement with exception from an affirmative statement, in that neither indicates that the excepted item is characterised by the opposite of what was ruled for the item from which it is excepted. This is a weak opinion, which neither the language nor the usages of the Sharīʿa support.

According to the majority's view, the clause *abā wa-istakbara* (he refused and was arrogant) is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'nāf bayānī*). According to the Ḥanafī view, it is an explanation of the generality implied by the exception. Neither view yields a proof that settles the dispute between the two sides.

The clause *wa-kāna min al-kāfirīn* (and he was among the disbelievers) is coordinated with the resumptive clauses. *Kāna* indicates only that he was characterised by disbelief in a past time before the time of the revelation of the verse. It does not mean that he was characterised by it before his refusal to prostrate to Adam. Most exegetes were perplexed in explaining the meaning of the verse, because they took the verb *kāna* as indicating characterisation by disbelief in the past relative to the time of the refusal to prostrate. It is self-evident that there was no group at that time described as disbelievers, so they had to contrive that Iblīs was among the disbelievers in God's knowledge. Some contrived that Iblīs was outwardly displaying obedience while inwardly concealing disbelief, out of hypocrisy, and God was aware of his inner state, but did not inform the angels of it. They took this divine awareness to be what His saying indicates: ﴿"Indeed, I know what you do not know."﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:30]. All of this is contrivance for which there is no need, given what you know, that the past tense indicates the occurrence of the act before the time of speaking. The most reasonable of them in method were those who took *kāna* to mean *ṣāra* (became), as this is a usage among the usages of *kāna*. God the Exalted said: ﴿"And the waves came between them, so he became one of the drowned."﴾ [Hūd 11:43], and He said: ﴿"And the mountains will be crumbled to dust"﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa 56:5], ﴿"and they will become scattered dust."﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa 56:6], and the words of Ibn Aḥmar:

*In a waterless desert, with the mounts appearing like the sandgrouse of the sandy plain, whose eggs had become chicks.*

That is: he became a disbeliever by not prostrating, because his refusal arose from his arrogance towards God and his belief that what he was commanded was not in accordance with the truth of wisdom. You have understood that the change that befell Iblīs in his nature was a change of contempt for the wisdom of God the Exalted, and therefore by it he became an explicit disbeliever.

What I consider the best interpretation of *wa-kāna min al-kāfirīn* is this: the apparent requirement would be to say *wa-kafara* (and he disbelieved), just as he said *abā wa-istakbara* (he refused and was arrogant). Instead, he deviated from the apparent requirement to *wa-kāna min al-kāfirīn* (and he was among the disbelievers), because in this usage *kāna* indicates that the meaning of the predicate is firmly established in its subject. The meaning is: he refused, was arrogant, and disbelieved, a deep disbelief within himself. This is like His saying: ﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife; she was among those who remained behind.﴾ [al-A'rāf 7:83], and like His saying: ﴿"We will look to see whether you will be guided or whether you will be among those who are not guided."﴾ [al-Naml 27:41], rather than saying *an lā tahtadī* (that you will not be guided). For when she saw the sign of the alteration of her throne and was not guided, she was firmly established in the attribute of not being guided.

As for the use of the predicate of *kāna* as *min al-kāfirīn* (among the disbelievers), rather than saying *wa-kāna kāfiran* (and he was a disbeliever), this is because ascribing an attribute to a subject under the designation that he is one of a group who are all characterised by that attribute establishes the attribute more firmly in him than ascribing the attribute to him alone. This is based on the principle that the individual becomes more attached to his action when a group shares it with him, for the more he sees of those who are engaged in the same act as his, the further his soul is from hesitating over the soundness of his deed. On this basis came His saying: ﴿"Have you spoken the truth, or have you been among the liars?"﴾ [al-Naml 27:27], and His saying which we have mentioned just now: ﴿"or will you be among those who are not guided?"﴾ [al-Naml 27:41]. This is an implicative indication (*dalīl kināʾī*) and a rhetorical usage upon which the structure of the verse is built, even though there was no group of disbelievers at that time, and Iblīs was alone in disbelief.

This is a line of reasoning I have derived from tracing the occurrences of this construction with respect to these two particularities: the particularity of the addition of *kāna*, and the particularity of ascribing an attribute to a subject under the description that he is one of a group characterised by it. This will come shortly, at His saying: ﴿"And bow with those who bow"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:43]. Since there was no group of disbelievers at the time of Iblīs's refusal to prostrate, His saying *wa-kāna min al-kāfirīn* follows the customary usage of such implicit statements.

In this deviation from the apparent requirement there is also observance of what the rhyme endings (*fawāṣil*) require. The three predicates have been arranged in mention according to the order of their concepts in existence, and this is the basic principle in composition, that the arrangement of speech should correspond to the arrangement of the meanings of its clauses, as in His saying: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed for them and felt powerless to protect them, and he said, "This is a trying day."﴾ [Hūd 11:77]. I have pointed this out in my book *Uṣūl al-Inshāʾ wa'l-Khaṭābah* (The Principles of Composition and Oratory).

[p. 428]

﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden, and eat from it freely wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers."﴾ This is a conjunction with ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:34]. That is, after that had ended, We said: "O Adam, dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden." This is an honour with which God honoured Adam, after He had honoured him with the honour of reverence from the angels.

The calling of Adam before his being granted residence in the Garden is a call to draw attention to his name among the Exalted Assembly (al-mala' al-a'la), because his being called draws the attention of the inhabitants of the Exalted Assembly, so that they look forward to what he is about to be addressed with. It is also derived from this verse that the person of knowledge is deserving of honour through a pleasant life, just as it was derived from the preceding verse that he is deserving of veneration. The command in His words "dwell" (uskun) is used in the sense of bestowing favour through granting settlement and empowerment, and it is not a command to him to strive by himself to reach residence in the Garden, since he has no capacity for that striving, and so he is not charged with it.

The pronoun "you" (anta) is placed for the purpose of conjoining "and your spouse" (wa-zawjuka) to the hidden pronoun in "dwell" (uskun). This is the usage of Arabic when conjoining a noun to an attached pronoun in the nominative position, which they almost never omit. By this they intend to increase the clarity of the conjoined element, so that the benefit of affirming the meaning of the conjoined element is obtained, lest the follower (the conjoined) be more prominent than the thing it follows in the utterance. Therefore, the separation by such a pronoun is not a restricted emphasis of the predication, because the use of the pronoun is obligatory and the speaker has no choice in it, so it is not a requirement of the situation, and the listener does not know that the speaker intends it as emphasis. Yet it does not lack the effect of affirming the meaning of the implied pronoun, which is what al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) indicated by his collective statement: "and 'you' is an emphasis of the hidden pronoun so that the conjunction upon it may be correct."

The zawj (spouse, pair) is every thing that is second with another thing, between which there is a pairing in some state. It appears to be a non-derived noun (jamid), because all its inflections in speech carry the sense of being the second of two or of being like another. So each of two paired together in some state is called a zawj for the other. God the Exalted said (﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾ [al-Shura 42:50]), meaning He makes for one of the two children a zawj for him, that is, other than him of a different kind. Close to this usage is the usage of the word shaf' (one of a pair). The female who is a man's partner by marriage is called zawj because she is joined to him and makes him second, and the man is likewise called zawj for her for that reason without distinction. Therefore one does not say zawjah (with the feminine ending) for a woman, because it is a noun and not an adjective. The grammarians faulted al-Farazdaq in his saying:

[p. 429]
"Indeed he who strives to corrupt my spouse
is like one who runs to the lions of the thicket, seeking to take her."

The jurists were lenient in attaching the feminine marker to zawj when they intended by it a man's wife, for the purpose of removing ambiguity in establishing rulings in their books, as in their saying: "the statement is the statement of the zawj (husband)" or "the statement is the statement of the zawjah (wife)." This is a good practice. In Sahih Muslim, from Anas ibn Malik: "The Prophet ﷺ was speaking with one of his wives, when a man passed by him, and he called him: 'O so-and-so!' and he came, and he said to him, 'This is my zawjati (wife), so-and-so,'" the hadith to its end. So his saying zawjati with the feminine ending (ta') is decisive that it is part of the wording of the narrator of the hadith in the chain of transmission to Anas, and not the wording of the Prophet ﷺ.

In this verse, He omitted the creation of Adam's spouse, though it is mentioned in other verses, such as His saying: ﴿He who created you from a single soul and created from it its spouse﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:1]. This will come in Surat al-Nisa' and Surat al-A'raf.

The name of Adam's spouse is not mentioned in the Qur'an. Among the Arabs her name is Hawwa' (Eve). Her name is mentioned in a hadith narrated by Ibn Sa'd in his Tabaqat from Khalid ibn Khidash, from Ibn Wahb, reaching back to the Messenger of God ﷺ that he said: "The people are to Adam and Hawwa' like a measure (tuff) to a ṣā' that they will never fill," the hadith to its end. The "ṭaff" of a measure, with the ṭa' vowelled with fatḥa or kasra, is what is near its being full, meaning they do not seek perfection, for every perfection among human beings is open to increase. Khalid ibn Khidash is a Basran; Ibn Ma'in, Abu Hatim and Sulayman ibn Harb declared him trustworthy, while Ibn al-Madini declared him weak.

So the name of Adam's spouse among the Arabs is Hawwa', and her name in Hebrew is disputed. In the Book of Genesis (Sifr al-Takwin), chapter 2, her name is "woman" (imra'ah), which Adam named her as such, saying: "because she was taken out of man." In chapter 3, Adam called his wife's name Hawwa' "because she is the mother of every living thing." Ibn Sa'd said: Adam slept, and Hawwa' was created from his rib; he awoke and found her beside him, and said "atha," meaning "woman" in Nabataean; that is, her name in Nabataean is "the woman," as Adam named her. Earlier, at His saying ﴿And He taught Adam the names﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:31], it was mentioned that Adam called himself "īsh." So perhaps "atha" is a corruption of "ishā."

Her name in Hebrew is Khamwā', with a Khā' (kh) and a heh after the alif, and it is also said Ḥayvā with a ḥā' and an alif at the end; in Arabic it became Hawwa', and in Italian it became Eva; and in French, Ève. In the Torah, Hawwa' was created in the Garden after Adam had been settled in the Garden, and God created her to comfort him. God the Exalted said ﴿and made from it its spouse that he might find rest in her﴾ [al-A'raf 7:189], meaning that he might be at ease. The imperative in "dwell" (uskun) is an imperative of granting: God made Adam, together with his spouse, reside in the Garden.

[p. 430]
Settlement (suknā) is taking a place as a dwelling for the greater part of a human's conditions. The Garden is a piece of land in which there are fruit trees and water, and it is the best dwelling for a human when the heat of the sun scorches him, he eats of its fruit when he is hungry, drinks from the waters from which the trees drink, and its sight pleases him in all of that. The Garden therefore gathers what human nature aspires to of pleasures. The definiteness of "the Garden" (al-jannah) is definiteness of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), and it is a Garden known to Adam, which he sees, if the definiteness in "the Garden" is a report of what is equivalent to it in what Adam was addressed with, or what is meant by it is what is known to us, if it is a report of God's speech to us in meaning, and that is permissible in reporting speech.

The scholars of Islam have differed in identifying this Garden. What the majority of the early generations (al-salaf) held is that it is the Garden of Eternity (jannat al-khuld) which God promised to the believers and to those who affirmed His messengers, and they were certain that it exists in the upper world, the world of the unseen, that is, in the heaven, and that God prepared it for the people of goodness after the Resurrection. This is what the people of the Sunnah among the theologians adopted, as did Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i, and it is what the apparent sense of the verses and the reports transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ attest. These apparent indications are numerous, though they yield only a probable conviction (ghalabat al-zann), and this question has no effect on creed.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, Muhammad ibn Bahr, Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi, and the Mu'tazila other than al-Jubba'i held that it is a garden on earth that God created to settle Adam and his spouse. al-Bayḍawi transmitted from them that it is an orchard in Palestine, or that it is between Fars and Kerman. I suppose this arises from their seeking to specify the place that is named in the Torah by the name 'Eden (Adan).

In the Torah, in chapter 2 of the Book of Genesis: "And the Lord God took Adam and put him in the Garden of Eden to work it and keep it, then..." She said: "So the Lord God brought him out of the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken." This implies that the Garden of Eden is not on earth, but what the commentators of the Torah hold is that the Garden of Eden is on earth, and this is the apparent sense of the description of the river of this Garden which waters it, that it is a river that flows out of Eden, and waters the Garden, and from there it divides and becomes four heads. The name of the first is Pishon, which encompasses all the land of Havilah, and they are of the sons of Cush, as in the chapter of Genesis. The name of the second river is Gihon, which encompasses all the land of Cush. The name of the third river is Hiddekel, which flows east of Asshur, the Tigris. The fourth river is the Euphrates.

I have not found the vocalization of this Eden. In the book of 'Abd al-Haqq al-Islami al-Sabti, who was a Jew and became a Muslim, and who composed a book refuting the Jews named "al-Husam al-Mahdud fi al-Radd 'ala al-Yahud," which he wrote in Ghidin and vocalised with the marks, with a kasra on the ghayn with a dot and a kasra on the dal without a dot, I saw it; perhaps the dot on the letter 'ayn is an error of the copyist. That is the source of the saying of those who say it is in 'Adan, or in Palestine, or between Fars and Kerman. What compelled them to that is that the Garden of reward is an abode of perfection, in which disobedience is not fitting, and that it is an abode of eternity whose inhabitant does not leave it, and that is a state of the Garden's people, not an effect of the place; all of it is God the Exalted's doing, when He wills it. The people of the Sunnah argued that the "al-" in "al-jannah" is for the definiteness of external reference ('ahd khariji), and there is no known referent other than it. The definiteness is determined to be external reference because the generic reading is not valid in its three kinds: there is no sense in reading it as the lam of reality (lam al-haqiqah), because settling (the act of residence) is attributed to it, and there is no sense in its relating to the reality itself, unlike the example "the man is better than the woman." Nor is there sense in reading it as mental reference ('ahd dhihni), since the individual of the reality here is a specific intended one, because the command to settle is a reward and an honour, so it must relate to a known Garden. Nor is there sense in reading it as comprehensive (istighraq), since that is evident. Since the intended matter is the reward, it is determined that it must relate to a specific known referent, and there is no known referent except the well-known Garden, especially since it is the technical term of the Law (shar').

It may be said that the "lam" is for prior reference, and perhaps the referent known to Adam is a Garden on earth, specific, pointed to by definiteness of prior reference. For this reason I myself choose that His saying ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾, since its purpose is to narrate to us, is related with words familiar to us, as a translation of the words of the language in which Adam was addressed, or from the inspiration that was cast upon Adam. Then the definiteness of "the Garden" is viewed in relation to what is customary for us, and Adam had known the intended meaning of his dwelling by another way than definiteness, and it has been related to us in the manner of definiteness, because the word "the Garden," when it is accompanied by the definite article in our speech, indicates the very thing indicated by the other way by which Adam knew God's intended meaning. That is: "We said to him, 'Dwell in the plot which you today call the Garden.'" The conclusion is that the more apparent view is that the Garden in which Adam was settled is the Garden counted as an abode for the reward of the doers of good.

The meaning of eating from the Garden is eating from its fruit, because the Garden entails fruits, and they are among the things sought for eating. For this reason "min" (from) is made partitive, by treating part of what the place contains as part of that place. It is permissible that "min" be a "min" of origin, indicating that the permitted eating is eating of what that Garden bears, like your saying "this fruit is from Khaybar."

[p. 432]
"Raghadan" is an adjective of a noun understood from the context, that is, "eating raghadan," and raghad is pleasant ease in which there is no hardship and no stinginess. His saying ﴿wherever you wish﴾ is an adverb of place, that is, from whatever places you desire to eat from. Since their will is not restricted to particular places, the generality of the permission is understood by implication. In making the eating of fruit one of the conditions of Adam and his spouse at the time of their creation, there is an indication that God made nourishment a natural disposition for the human being, such that his life does not last except by it.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary, part 2 of 2:

God's words ﴿And do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers﴾ mean: do not eat from the tree, because approaching it is only for the purpose of eating from it. The prohibition on approaching is more emphatic than the prohibition on eating, because nearness to a thing creates an inclination and a desire for it. In a hadith: "Whoever grazes around the protected pasture is close to falling into it." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "I heard al-Shashi in a session of disputation say: When it is said *lā taqrab* (with a fatha on the *rā*), its meaning is 'do not engage in the act.' When it is said with a damma on the *rā*, its meaning is 'do not draw near to it.'" End of quotation.

This is strange, for *qaruba* and *qariba* are like *karuma* and *sami'a* in meaning: both mean "drew near." So whether one places a damma or a fatha on the *rā* in the imperfect, the intended meaning is a prohibition on drawing near. However, drawing near is partly figurative, namely engaging in an act, and partly literal. A figurative sense does not have a distinct morphological form in verbs; otherwise it would belong to homonyms rather than to literal and figurative usage. The exception would be if usage restricted the figurative sense to certain conjugations, in which case that pattern would serve as a verbal clue to the figurative meaning. That is good, and it is one of the fine distinctions in the use of synonymous words in the Arabic language, such as the distinction between *ba'ida* (with a kasra on the 'ayn), which is specific to complete separation, and *ba'uda* (with a damma on the 'ayn), which is specific to moving away from a place. For this reason the supplication with the kasra form is specific in the saying addressed to a traveller: *lā tab'ad* ("do not be far away"). Fatima bint al-Ahjam al-Khuza'iyya said:

"My brothers, do not ever be far away,
but by God, they have gone far."

In the linking of the prohibition to approaching the tree there is an indication of the principle of *sadd al-dharā'i'* (blocking the means to what is forbidden), which is one of the foundations of the school of Malik, may God have mercy on him. This principle has detailed treatment established in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (*uṣūl al-fiqh*).

The demonstrative *hādhihi* ("this") refers to a tree that was visible to Adam and his wife, and the intended meaning is either a tree of its kind or a single tree in the Garden. The narrators of stories (*ahl al-qaṣaṣ*) differed in specifying the type of this tree. From 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi it is reported that it was the vine. From Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and the majority of exegetes it is reported that it was wheat. From Qatada and Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Jurayj attributed it to a group of Companions, it is reported that it was the fig tree. The Book of Genesis in the Torah leaves it unspecified and calls it the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

[Page 433]

God's words ﴿so that you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ mean: among the transgressors. The most well-known meaning of *ẓulm* (wrongdoing) in Arabic usage is transgression (*i'tidā'*). Transgression is either a violation of the prohibition of the one who forbids, if the purpose of the prohibition is a definite command to abstain, or a transgression against the self and its excellence, if the purpose of the prohibition on eating from the tree is to preserve Adam's excellence of comfort in the Garden. On the first view, the wrongdoing is to their own selves by incurring God's anger and punishment. On the second view, the wrongdoing is to their own selves by depriving them of the continuation of honour.

[Page 434]
