The *fa* (ف) here is a conjunction linking to His words "﴿and do not approach this tree﴾". Its basic function is to indicate sequence (*al-ta'qib*, immediate succession). The sequence is customary, because the slip occurred after a period of time that, compared with the duration intended for residence in the Garden, is like a short span. The better view is to take the *fa* as signalling a consequence (*al-tafri'*) without any sense of immediate sequence.

*Al-izlal* (causing to slip) means making someone a slipper, i.e., one in whom slipping (*al-zalal*) occurs. It is like *al-zalaq*, where the two feet move across the ground involuntarily because the ground has become slippery with mud or the like. That is, his feet go without his intending it. This is a well-known metaphor for committing a sin or a harmful error, and from it disobedience and similar acts are called *al-zalal*.

The pronoun in His words "(*'anha*) [from it]" may refer to the tree, because it is the nearer antecedent, and so that the cause of the slip and the cause of the expulsion from the Garden are both made clear. If the pronoun is not taken as referring to the tree, the story would be devoid of mention of the cause of the expulsion. The preposition *'an* ("from") is in its original meaning here: He caused them to slip, a slip arising *from* the tree, that is, from eating of it. The omitted noun is indicated by His words "﴿and do not approach this tree﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]". *'An* does not indicate causation. Those who claim it does mean the resulting sense of the phrase. Abu 'Ubaydah said of His words "﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3]" that its meaning is "nor does he speak *with* desire." Al-Radi said: the better view is that *'an* keeps its own meaning, and the prepositional phrase is an adjunct to an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a speech issuing *from* desire."

It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the Garden, with *'an* kept in its literal sense, and *al-izlal* used metaphorically for expulsion by force. The intended meaning is descent from the Garden as unwilling parties, like one who is dislodged from his position and falls, as in the line: "And how many a dwelling, had I not been there, would you have been overturned."

His words "﴿so He caused them to leave what they were in﴾" contain a consequence (*tafri'*) drawn from the slip, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the tree.

[Page 435]

The relative pronoun and its clause are meant to convey magnification, as in the expression "What was, was." If you take the pronoun in "from it" as referring to the Garden, this consequence becomes a consequence of detail from the general (*tafri' al-mufassal 'an al-mujmal*), and the *fa* then indicates mention-order consequence without sequence, as in His words "﴿And how many a town We destroyed, and Our might came upon it at night or while they were resting at noon﴾ [al-A'raf: 4]" and His words "﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and they denied Our servant and said, 'Mad!' and he was rebuked﴾ [al-Qamar: 9]." As for the magnifying sense of the relative clause, it is the same in either case.

Hamzah read "﴿fa-azalla-huma﴾" with an *alif* after the *zay*, from *al-izalah* (removal), in the sense of distancing. On this reading it is definitely required that the pronoun in "from it" refers to the Garden and not to the tree. The reading is specified with a clear indication, even though it is known that whoever leaves the Garden has left what he was in. This is to bring this great loss vividly to the minds of the hearers, so that it is not understood only by implication, which can be obscure. Thus the restatement in this relative clause, using a synonym, is like the restatement with the same wording in His words "﴿Then the sea covered them with what covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78]."

The verse stirs regret in the souls of the children of Adam over what befell Adam as a result of his failure to comply with God's command. It is also an admonition that alerts them to the obligation of stopping at commands and prohibitions, and an encouragement to strive toward what returns them to this Garden which was their father's. It also nurtures enmity between them and Satan and his soldiers, since Satan was the cause of this calamity for their father. Thus they will always be avengers for their father, opposed to Satan, mistrustful of his whispering and of his incitement, as His words indicate: "﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]." His words here, "﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾," also point to this. This is a great principle in educating the common people, and for this reason leaders of nations used to recount to their people the past enmities of their rivals and of those who defeated them in wars, so that this would arouse them to take revenge.

The conjunction of "﴿And We said: descend﴾" is by *wa* and not *fa*, because it is not a consequence of the expulsion; rather it precedes it. The mention of the expulsion before it is for the sake of the context of what Satan did and his deception of Adam. Therefore "﴿so He caused them to leave﴾" is placed right after "﴿so Satan caused them to slip﴾."

As for the plural form of the pronoun in "descend" (*ihbitu*), it is said that because the descent of Adam and Eve required that their offspring not exist in the Garden, their descent was a descent for their offspring. It is also said that the address is to them and to Iblis. Although Iblis was made to descend when he refused to prostrate, as indicated by His words in Surah al-A'raf: "﴿He said: I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]; ﴿He said: Descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein, so go out; you are among the debased﴾ [al-A'raf: 13]," down to His words: "﴿He said: Go out from it, reproached and expelled﴾ [al-A'raf: 18]," and on to "﴿O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 19]." This is a second descent, in which entry into the Garden was forbidden to him. The first descent was a descent of deprivation of honour, while he was still enabled to enter in order to whisper. Both views are remote. What I see is that the plural pronoun is meant to indicate the dual, because of the aversion to successive dual forms, both explicit and implicit, in His words "﴿and eat from it freely﴾." The Arabs find this heavy to pronounce. Imru' al-Qays said:

*They halted, my companions, their mounts over me, saying: "Do not perish from grief; be patient."*

He had only two companions, because of his words "*Halt, let us weep*," and so on. He also said, "﴿Your two hearts have certainly inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]," which will come in Surah al-Tahrim.

His words "﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾" may mean by "some" some of the kinds, namely the enmity of humans and jinn, if the pronoun in "descend" refers to Adam, his wife, and Iblis. It may also mean the enmity of some individuals of the human species, if the pronoun in "descend" refers to Adam and Eve. In that case it is an announcement to them of an effect of their action that will be inherited by their offspring. This is also the beginning of the appearance of disorder in the formation of their nature, in that their disobedience produced in themselves and in their descendants the impulse toward deception and cunning, in accordance with His words "﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children there are enemies to you﴾ [al-Taghabun: 14]," for character traits are inherited. How could they not be, since they are acquired by long association and companionship? Abu Tammam said:

*You infected me with forbearance, for nobility is contagious.*

The relationship between this effect and its origin, which is eating from the tree, is that eating from the tree was a violation of God's command and a rejection of it. Bad opinion about the benefit of the command led to violating it: greed and desire for gaining a benefit for themselves, namely eternal life in the Garden and sole possession of its good things, together with bad opinion of the One who had forbidden them to eat from it. He informed them that if they ate from it they would wrong themselves, as Iblis said to them: "﴿Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become among the immortals﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]." Likewise, the enmity among individuals of mankind, despite their natural inclination to intimacy, companionship, and unity, has its origin in rejecting that intimacy and unity for the sake of obtaining benefit for the self and neglecting the benefit of others. Thus there is no doubt that between that thought which moved them to eat from the tree and its trace that remained in their souls, which they will pass on to their offspring, the offspring are created with minds composed to be disposed to that same disposition which arose in the minds of their two parents. There is no doubt that this disposition, which returns to preferring the self in goodness and to thinking ill of others, is the source of all enmities, because one does not oppose another except from belief in competition over a benefit, or from bad opinion of him as a source of harm.

[Page 436]

In this there is an indication of an ethical question: the origin of morals, good and bad, is the good and evil thoughts. Then a thought becomes a trait when it is followed by an action. If its bearer resists it and does not act, that resistance becomes a cause for the dissolving of that thought. For this reason the Sharia warned against resolving upon sins, and abstaining from doing what one has resolved upon is rewarded as a good deed. It commanded good thoughts, so the reward of merely resolving upon a good deed is a good deed even if one does not do it. And doing it is rewarded tenfold, as in the authentic hadith: "Whoever resolves upon a good deed and does not do it, God records it with Him as a complete good deed. Then he said: Whoever resolves upon an evil deed and does it, one evil deed is recorded for him." And He made pardon for the inner discourse of the soul a favour and forgiveness from God Most High, in the hadith: "God has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper to them."

God Most High created man good, that is, free from evil and from evil thoughts, upon a angelic nature. This is the meaning of "﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4]." Then He made him into stages. The first of these is the stage of teaching him speech and assigning names to things, because that is the beginning of knowledge, and through it instruction occurs: some of his kind teach others what they know and the other does not know. Thus His inspiring him with language became the beginning of the movement of human thought. This beginning is suitable for good and helps toward it, because through it people taught one another. For this reason you see a child who sees a thing hurrying to his companions, calling them so that they may see it with him, eager to inform them. Thus man is a teacher by nature, and this helps his goodness. Yet it is also suitable for using speech for deception and lying.

Then, when God Most High forbade him from a matter, He imposed on him a duty which was within his capacity to comply with or to violate. That capacity was the beginning of the movement of his soul in greed and self-preference. God's creating him with that capacity became the beginning of a new stage, indicated by His words "﴿then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 5]." Then He guided him through the Sharia, so that by following it he reaches the ranks of the angels and returns to his first formation. This is the meaning of His words "﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 227]." This final stage is indicated by His words later: "﴿And if guidance comes to you from Me, then whoever follows My guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38]," and so on.

The clause "﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾" is either a fresh, independent resumption (*istί'nāf ibtida'i*) or a circumstantial clause (*jumlat hal*) from the pronoun in "descend." It is a nominal sentence lacking the *waw*. There is a difference among Arabic grammarians about treating a nominal clause without *waw* as a circumstantial clause. Al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari forbade it, while Ibn Malik and a group permitted it. In my view the truth is that the circumstantial clause dispenses with *waw* when there is a pronoun, and with a pronoun when there is *waw*. When it has the force of an attribute of its subject, it contains a pronoun referring to him or to his related pronoun, and so it dispenses with *waw*, as in this verse and as in "Zayd came, his hand upon his head," or "his father accompanying him." Otherwise *waw* is required, since no other link is then available, as in "Zayd came while the sun was rising," and the line of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran:

*He mingled with the level ground; the rock did not wound him with any wound, while death was disgraced, looking on.*

His words "﴿and for you on earth is a settlement﴾" have a pronoun that refers, on all the readings, to what the pronoun in "descend" refers to. *Al-hin* means a time, and what is meant by it is the time of the extinction of the human and satanic species with the ending of the world. It is possible that the pronoun in "for you" (*lakum*) is meant distributively, that is: "and for each one of you on earth is a settlement and enjoyment until a time." This is called enjoyment because life is something desired by all humans, and life is never free of pleasures and enjoyment of what God has bestowed upon us of agreeable things. This holds if the predicate is taken collectively, i.e., for all of you together. If it is taken distributively, then *al-hin* is the time of each individual's death, in the way that you say to an army, "These horses are yours," meaning each one of you has a horse.

فَتَلَقّى آدَمُ مِن رَبِّهِ كَلِماتٍ فَتابَ عَلَيْهِ إنَّهُ هو التَّوّابُ الرَّحِيمُ

Ruled by "فَ" (fa'), which signals that Adam was quick to seek pardon.

Talaqqi (receiving) means receiving with honour and joy. God says: ﴿And the angels will receive them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103]. Its indication of this meaning lies in the form tafa''ala (تَفَعَّلَ) from laqiya (لَقِيَ). This form indicates effort in obtaining something and seeking it, and effort and seeking are applied only to the meeting of something desired. By contrast, laqiya (لاقى) does not indicate that what is met is desired; one says laqiya al-'aduw (لاقى العَدْوَ, he met the enemy). Liqa' (meeting) is presence before someone, intentionally or unintentionally, and for good or evil. God says: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing (for battle)﴾ [al-Anfal: 15]. Thus the expression talaqqa here indicates that the words Adam received were beneficial to him. It is therefore known that they were not words of rebuke and reproach, but words of pardon, forgiveness and acceptance. They were either words which God taught Adam so that he might say them, seeking forgiveness, or words of information from God to him that He had pardoned him after lowering him from the Garden, being satisfied with that as the punishment.

What shows that they were words of pardon is the coordination of "فَتابَ عَلَيْهِ" (so He accepted his repentance) with fa' (فَ), since if they were words of rebuke the causation would not be valid. Adam's receiving of the words was either by way of revelation (wahy) or inspiration (ilham).

Scholars differ on identifying these words, and they have various reports, which we set aside because of the little benefit in occupying oneself with that. Adam said the words, and so he was forgiven. Let us concern ourselves with what benefits us of good speech and good action.

Eve's repentance is not mentioned here, although it is mentioned in other places, such as God's saying: ﴿They said: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. This is because it is apparent that she followed him in all his conditions and that he guided her to what he was guided to. It is not mentioned in this verse because the discourse began with the honouring of Adam and his being placed on earth as a khalifa (vicegerent), so the focus was on mentioning his changing circumstances.

The original meaning of taba is "raja'a" (returned). Its counterpart is tha'aba with the letter thа' (ث). Since repentance is the return of the penitent to obedience and the casting off of disobedience, and since its acceptance is the return of the One who accepts it to contentment and good treatment, the return of the disobedient from disobedience and the return of the one disobeyed from punishment were both described with this word. They say: "Fulan taba li-fulan, fa-taba 'alayhi" (so-and-so repented to so-and-so, and he accepted his repentance), because they included in the second word the meaning of compassion and contentment. Thus the different meanings of this verb depend on the different prepositions with which it is construed, and its original usage was based on parallelism (al-mushakala).

Repentance is composed of knowledge, a state, and action. Knowledge is recognition of the sin; the state is the soul's pain at that harm, which is called nadam (regret); and action is abandoning sin and making up what can be made up. This last is the real aim of repentance, whereas regret is the motive for action. That is why the hadith says: "Regret is repentance" (al-nadam tawba), as al-Ghazali stated. I say: that is, because it is its necessary cause, since one who truly regrets has not fallen short, for one of the two parts is not knowledge.

Then, the expression "تابَ عَلَيْهِ" (He accepted his repentance) here implies that Adam's eating from the tree was a sin and a transgression. However, the sin at that time did not entail any otherworldly punishment or any deficiency in religion. Rather, it necessitated immediate discipline, because man at that stage was like a stage of childhood. For this reason, committing it does not discredit Adam's prophethood. Moreover, it does not appear that it should be counted among the major sins; at most it is among the minor ones, since there is no meaning in it indicating a lack of concern for the matter, nor does it result in corruption. The question of the infallibility of prophets from minor sins is disputed between the followers of al-Ash'ari and al-Maturidi, and it is in the books of theology (kalam). Moreover, Adam's prophethood apparently came after his descent to earth, so he had no infallibility before that, since infallibility accompanies prophethood.

In my view, and part of this is taken from their words, that world was not a world of obligation (taklif) in the sense known among the people of the sacred laws, but a world of training (tarbiya) only. So Adam's sin and disobedience were a disciplinary violation (mukhalafa ta'dibiyya). For this reason, the consequence of it followed the manner of disciplinary punishments, namely deprivation of what had led him to disobedience. Therefore, the application of the terms disobedience (ma'siya), repentance (tawba), and wronging oneself (zulm al-nafs) to all of this is not in the legally known sense, rather it is a great disobedience, and a repentance in the sense of regret and returning to the commitment to good conduct. God's acceptance of his repentance means contentment, not forgiveness of sins. Wronging oneself means causing oneself to be deprived of many pleasures for the sake of a small pleasure. Thus he went against what he should not have gone against. This is indicated by God's saying after that: ﴿Then whenever guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance﴾ [al-Baqara: 38], down to His saying: ﴿abiding therein﴾ [al-Baqara: 39]. For it is He who explained to them that disobedience after that day is punished by Hell.

Then one of the sharp students of the lesson objected to me: if that world was not a world of obligation, how did Iblis (Satan) disbelieve by his objection and refusal to prostrate? I answered him that the indication of God's divinity in that world is achieved by direct observation, a stronger attainment than every indication, in addition to the indication of reason. This is because Iblis witnessed through the senses the signs of God's sole divinity, creation, and absolute disposal, and of His knowledge and wisdom and His attributes of perfection, just as knowledge of the like was attained by the angels. Therefore his objection to His action and his criticism were a denial of what those attributes require, and thus it was a violation of the indications of faith, so he disbelieved by it. As for command and prohibition, obedience and disobedience, and their consequences, these are received only through legal reports, and these had not yet taken place that day. They took place only through His saying to them: ﴿Whoever follows My guidance﴾ and so on. Thus the difference became clear.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read "آدَمُ" (Adam) in the nominative and "كَلِماتٍ" (words) in the accusative. Ibn Kathir read it with "آدَمَ" in the accusative and "كَلِماتٌ" in the nominative, interpreting talaqqa as "balaghat-hu kalimat" (words reached him). In that case talaqqa is a metaphor for reaching, through the relation of causation.

His saying: ﴿Indeed He is the Oft-Returning, the Most Merciful﴾ is a concluding remark (tadhyil) and a reason (ta'lil) for the preceding clause, "فَتابَ عَلَيْهِ" (so He accepted his repentance). It conveys its meaning with additional generality and emphasis, and this is amplification (itnab), as established in the science of rhetoric (ilm al-ma'ani). The intensive sense of al-tawwab means that He is the one who accepts repentance abundantly, that is, because of the great number of penitents. It is an intensive form of "taba" transitive with "ʿalā", meaning accepting repentance, indicating that this is not restricted to one penitent over another. It is a concluding remark to His saying "فَتَلَقّى آدَمُ مِن رَبِّهِ" (Adam received words from his Lord), implying that Adam repented and God accepted his repentance; here al-tawwab means the one who inspires His many servants to repent, since intensive forms may come without multiplicity. Thus al-tawwab here means the one who inspires repentance, and it is a metonymy for accepting the penitent's repentance.

Its following with al-Rahim (the Most Merciful) is because al-Rahim functions as a reason for al-Tawwab, since accepting the repentance of His servants is a kind of mercy towards them. Otherwise, repentance would only benefit the penitent himself by not returning to sin, and sins would then be consequences upon him. As for the sin that results, it would be just for its punishment to be realised, but mercy preceded justice here by a promise from God.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 38–39 (part 1 of 2):

[Page 440]
﴿We said, "Go down from it, all of you. And when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance – there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve."﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs – those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

The phrase ﴿We said, "Go down"﴾ is repeated. Its repetition may be for the sake of linking the structure of the Qur'anic verse, without indicating that its meaning is repeated in the speech addressed to Adam. Thus this repetition serves only to connect what is related to the content of "And We said, 'Go down'" – namely His words ﴿some of you will be an enemy to others﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36] – and His words ﴿And when guidance comes to you from Me﴾. For these two related parts were separated by what intervened between them: His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance; indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37]. Had He followed that directly with ﴿And when guidance comes to you from Me﴾, the connection would not have been fully coherent, and the listener might have imagined that it was an address to the believers, according to the Qur'an's habit of variation (tafannun). To avert this, the words ﴿We said, "Go down"﴾ were repeated. It is therefore one statement repeated twice for the sake of connecting the discourse. For this reason the word "qulna" is not joined by a conjunction (waw), because between them there is near-complete connection, since the statement ﴿We said, "Go down, all of you"﴾ descends from the statement ﴿And We said, "Go down, some of you an enemy to others"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36] in the position of a verbal emphasis. Then His words ﴿And when guidance comes to you from Me﴾ and so on were built upon it. It differs from what was built upon His words ﴿And We said, "Go down, some of you an enemy to others"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36], so that some new benefit may arise in the speech, lest the repetition of "Go down" be mere emphasis. In the science of rhetoric (badi') this style is called tardid (repetition), like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought and love to be praised for what they have not done – do not think them safe from punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 188]. Its benefit of emphasis is achieved by the mere repetition of the wording.

It has also been said that it is a second command to descend: that Adam was made to descend from the Garden to the lowest heaven by the first command, then was made to descend from the lowest heaven to the earth. Thus the repetition of "We said, 'Go down'" serves to draw attention to the difference in time of the two statements and the descents. This interpretation implies that stages and distances are of no consequence to the traveler. Also, the pronoun in "from it" (minha), which is definitively referring back to the Garden, is consistent with the arrangement of pronouns in His words ﴿and eat from it freely﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]
[Page 441]
and His words ﴿so Satan caused them to slip from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36]. This prevents the meaning of "go down" from being from the heaven all together, since no return to the heaven has preceded. Therefore, in my view, if the second "go down" is not for linking the structure of the discourse, the preferable reading is that it relates an additional command to Adam to descend, lest one think that God's acceptance of his repentance and His pleasure with him, upon his prompt repentance following the command to descend, had necessitated pardon from the descent from the Garden. So He repeated to him the command to descend after accepting his repentance, so that he would know that this is inevitable, because it is the will of God, exalted is He, and one of the stages of what God willed in making him a khalifah (successor) on earth, which He had informed the angels of. There is also another indication in this: that pardon comes from the one who repents regarding reproaches and punishments. As for the realization of the effects of disobedience, which is the corrective punishment, pardoning it is corruption in the world; for the doer of disobedience, if he does not see the effect of his act, he will not be disciplined in the future. Thus leniency with him in this matter defeats the requirement of wisdom. For example, if a child soils a place and his educator becomes angry with him, then he repents and he is pardoned, the pardon concerns the punishment; but imposing on him that he remove with his own hand the soiling he caused is not something in which leniency is appropriate. Accordingly, when God accepted Adam's repentance, He was pleased with him and did not seize him with punishment or deterrent in this world, yet He did not pardon him regarding the realization of the effect of his disobedience, which is the descent from the Garden, so that he would see the effect of his greed and his bad opinion. This is how the interpretation should be if the intended meaning of the second "go down" is the relating of a second command to descend addressed to Adam.

"Jami'an" is a circumstantial accusative (hal). "Jami'an" is a noun for those gathered, like the word jam', and therefore they kept it in one fixed state. It is not originally an adjective; otherwise they would have said "ja'u jami'in" (they came gathered), because fa'il in the sense of fa'il agrees with the thing it describes. The grammarians have interpreted the verse of Imru' al-Qays,
"If indeed a soul were to die gathered (jami'atan)"
by saying that the ta' in it is for intensification, and the meaning is: "Go down, gathered together in the descent, joined in it," because they both shared in committing the cause of the descent.

His words ﴿So if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance﴾ are a conditional upon a conditional, because "imma" is a compound conditional particle made of "in" (the conditional) and the added "ma," which indicates emphasis of the conditional linkage. Since "in" alone indicates the condition, the addition of "ma" to it is not like its addition to "mata," "ayy," "ayna," "ayyana," "ma," "min," or "mahma" (according to the view that their origin is "mama"); because those additions were to make them convey the meaning of condition, whereas these words were not originally set for that, unlike "in" and "qad." The Arabs consistently used the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid) with the verb of the condition after "imma," to add emphasis to the conditional linkage by the presence of its marker on its particle and on its verb. This is an emphasis that does not establish the actual occurrence of the answer, because that would contradict the conditional. For this reason the answer of the condition is not emphasized with nun; rather, it establishes the binding, i.e., that the answer's occurrence being dependent on the occurrence of the condition is a matter that is certainly established, since the conditional is nothing but a statement of information, its substance being the report that the occurrence of the recompense depends on the occurrence of the condition. Therefore it is, like other statements, capable of emphasis. The verb of the condition with "imma" has rarely been without the energetic nun, as in the words of al-A'sha:
"If you see us barefoot, without sandals for us – indeed we are thus: we go barefoot and we wear sandals."
This is not good according to Sibawayh and al-Farisi, while al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said it is prohibited, making the absence of it a necessity (darurah).

His words ﴿whoever follows My guidance﴾: "man" is conditional, as shown by the entry of the fa' into its answer ﴿then there is no fear for them﴾. Although the fa' often enters the predicate of a relative pronoun, that is by treating it as a conditional; so it is to be understood here as conditional, for brevity.

The word "guidance" is made explicit in His words "hudaya," though it is the very same guidance in His words ﴿guidance from Me﴾. The context called for a resumptive pronoun for the second conditional, but it was made explicit to give emphasis to guidance, so that it would become more firmly fixed in the minds of the addressees, in the manner of ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15] ﴿but Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16]. And so that this sentence would be self-standing, not containing a pronoun requiring a referent, so that it could function like a proverb or advice, to be noticed, remembered, and retained by souls for refinement and discipline. Similarly, the noun was made explicit in His words ﴿Say, "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood is ever bound to vanish"﴾ [al-Isra': 81], so that this last sentence would travel like a proverb. From this is the saying of Bashshar:
"When opinion reaches the point of consultation, seek help from the opinion of a sincere advisor or the advice of a discerning man."
"And do not make consultation a burden upon you; its place is strength for the primary feathers, as the secondary feathers are for the flight."
"Draw near to consultation the one whose opinion is upright, and do not let consultation be heard by a man who is not a keeper of secrets."
He repeated "consultation" three times in the second and third verses, so that each half would travel as a proverb. By this the reason becomes clear for defining the second "guidance" by annexation to the divine pronoun rather than with "al," although "al" is the original form for placing an explicit noun in the position of a resumptive pronoun; this is so that nothing included in the first sentence is lost from this self-standing sentence. The first sentence included describing guidance as coming from God, and the annexation in the second sentence conveys this same meaning.

[Page 442]
The coming in His words ﴿if there come to you﴾ with the conditional particle, which indicates non-certainty of the occurrence of the condition, is a sign of a remaining reproach for not complying with the first guidance, and an implicit suggestion that attempting to guide you in the future is of no use. It is like a master saying to his servant, when he did not act on what he instructed him and he became angry with him, then the servant apologized and he became pleased: "If I instruct you another day about something, do not return to a deed like your deed," implicitly suggesting that the attachment of the purpose to his instruction in the future is a doubtful matter, since perhaps it will be of little benefit. This is an eloquent point which escaped the author of al-Kashshaf, whose attention was diverted from it by his strained effort to force the verse to be evidence for the Mu'tazilite view that sending messengers is not obligatory, since guidance is attained by reason in belief in God, while God's guidance of mankind is obligatory in their view. That kind of strain occurs often in his book, and it is not befitting the firmness of his foot in knowledge. So his statement here is like an apology for the view that sending messengers is not obligatory, since guidance is not restricted to belief, in which reason dispenses with revelation according to them; rather, most of it is guidance regarding obligations, many of which reason cannot perceive. And it is, according to their own principles too, obligatory upon God to convey it to mankind. The difficulty then remains regarding the use of the particle of doubt here, so it stands. Therefore the verse is more favorable to our school, O Ash'aris, against the obligation of all guidance upon God, exalted is He, if we wished to use it as evidence for that, as al-Baydawi did; but we do not see it as coming for that purpose.

His words ﴿if there comes to you from Me guidance﴾ and so on have the sense of a covenant which God took from Adam, so that his descendants are bound to follow every guidance that comes to them from God, and that whoever turns away from guidance coming from God has incurred punishment.

[Page 444]
It thus includes all divine laws addressed to the groups of mankind, because "guidance" occurs indefinite in the context of a condition, and that is one of the forms of generality. The most fitting and most deserving of being obeyed is the guidance which came from God to all of mankind, which is the religion of Islam, addressed to all the children of Adam. By this the place is prepared for His words "those who disbelieve" and so on. Thus God took a covenant from Adam onward to follow the general guidance, like His words ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81] and so on. This verse indicates that God does not hold mankind accountable for the error they commit until after He sends to them one who guides them. As for the details of the laws, there is no doubt about that and no disagreement. As for the Oneness of God, exalted is He, and what it entails of attributes of perfection, there is a difference among our scholars regarding holding the people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah) accountable for shirk. Perhaps the verse indicates that the guidance coming from God in this matter had been present from the time of Adam and Noah, and all of mankind knew it; thus it is a binding address which mankind cannot claim ignorance of. This is one of two opinions from al-Ash'ari; it is also said otherwise. According to the Mu'tazilah and the Maturidiyyah, it is a rational proof.

His words ﴿then there is no fear for them﴾ are a negation of the genus of fear. "Khawf" is in the nominative in the recitation of the majority; Ya'qub read it as built on fatha. These are two readings concerning the noun of "la" of negation for the genus. The narration of the fourth woman in the hadith of Umm Zar' has been transmitted with both readings: "My husband is like the night of Tihamah: neither hot nor cold, no fear and no weariness." Building the noun on fatha is explicit in negating the genus; its being nominative is open to negating the genus and negating a single instance. Therefore, when ambiguity is removed, both readings are equal, as here, since the context is clearly indicating negation of the genus.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on the verse: "And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs..." (Qur'an 2:39)

His saying, ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾, may be part of what was said to Adam, so completing the mention of it here is a comprehensive reference to the categories of Adam's descendants, and in it is an allusion to the polytheists among Adam's descendants. It includes everyone who denied all the miracles, and among them the Qur'an. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the conditional (man) in His saying ﴿Whoever follows My guidance﴾, etc., so it is the coordination of a nominal clause with a nominal clause. He used a non-conditional clause for the coordinated part, despite the conditional's greater strength of linkage and explicitness regarding the consequence following the condition and its inseparability from it. The meanings of consequence (tartīb), causation (tasabbub) and inseparability have been achieved by other means, so the sense of the condition is derived from the implication of His saying ﴿Whoever follows My guidance, there is no fear for them﴾, for it is good news whose implication signals a warning to whoever does not follow it, so he is fearful and grieved. The listener thus anticipates what will clarify this fear and grief, and this is achieved by His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny﴾, to the end of the verse. As for the meaning of causation, it is achieved from attaching the predicate to the relative pronoun and its clause, which alludes to the basis and cause of the predicate according to one of the two interpretations concerning the allusion to the basis of the predicate. As for inseparability, it is required by the report about them as "companions of the Fire", which implies constant attachment, then the explicit statement in His saying ﴿They therein abide forever﴾.

Page 445

It may also be a concluding statement (tadhyīl) with which the story of Adam is concluded, because of the mention of the guided ones, and it is not part of what was said to him. The purpose of this concluding statement is to threaten the polytheists and to return to the presentation of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [2:21] and His saying ﴿How can you disbelieve in God﴾ [2:28]. Thus the waw in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾ is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya). By "those who disbelieve" is meant those who denied the Creator, denied His prophets and rejected His covenant, as is the Qur'anic usage. The meaning is: "And those who disbelieve in Me and in My guidance," as the contrast indicates.

"Āyāt" is the plural of āya, which is a thing that indicates a matter that is by nature hidden. For this reason, the markers of paths are called āyāt, because they set them up to guide to the hidden routes in the sands. Proof is also called āya, because it reveals a hidden truth, as al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza said:

"Who has for us with him of good signs (āyāt), three, in all of which is the judgment?"

He means three proofs of their sincere counsel, their good service in war, and their connection to the king ʿAmr ibn Hind. God called the proofs of His existence, of His oneness, and of the invalidity of the doctrine of polytheism "āyāt," saying: ﴿And no sign comes to them from the signs of their Lord but they turn away from it﴾ [6:4], and He said ﴿And it is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea. We have detailed the signs for a people who know﴾ [6:97], up to His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ [6:99]. He said ﴿And they swore by God their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it﴾ [6:109]. The Qur'an also called itself a sign, saying: ﴿And they say, "Why is not a sign sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Signs are only with God"﴾ [29:50], up to His saying ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book being recited to them?﴾ [29:51] in Surat al-ʿAnkabut. He called its parts āyāt, saying: ﴿And when Our signs are recited to them as clear evidence, you recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve the denial; they nearly assault those who recite to them Our signs﴾ [22:72], and He said ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra. These are the signs of the Book, and that which is revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [13:1], because every surah of the Qur'an is such that mankind is unable to produce its like, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Then bring a surah like it﴾ [2:23]. Thus it was evidence of the Messenger's truthfulness in what he brought, and its sentences were āyāt, because in them is part of the miraculous measure. The parts of the other heavenly books were not called āyāt. As for what occurs in the hadith of stoning, that Ibn Ṣūriyā, when he unfolded the Torah, placed his hand on the verse of stoning, this is by likening a part of the Torah to a part of the Qur'an, and it is an expression of the narrator of the hadith.

The original form of āya, according to Sibawayh, is

Page 446

"faʿala" with a fatḥa, "ayiyah" or "awiyah," depending on the disagreement over whether it is waw-based or yāʾ-based, derived from ayy (the interrogative) or from awā. When the two weak letters in it became vowelled, one of them was changed, and the first was changed for lightness, contrary to analogy; for the analogy for two weak letters suitable for alteration is that the second be altered, except for what is rare, such as āya, wiqāya, ṭāya, thāya and rāya.

So what is meant by "Our signs" here is the signs of the Qur'an, i.e., "and they denied with the Qur'an, i.e., revelation from God."

The bāʾ in His saying ﴿and denied Our signs﴾ is a bāʾ that frequently enters upon the object of the root of denial, although denial is transitive by itself. I have not found in the statements of the leading lexicographers the particular features of its attachment to this root and form. It may be that it serves to emphasize the attachment, for intensity in denial, as in the bāʾ in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [5:6], and the verse of al-Nābigha:

"To you is the good, since the earth has concealed you, one [man]."

It may also be that its original sense is causal, and that the original usage was "kadhdhaba fulānan bi-khabarihi" (he denied someone by his report), then it became common so that "kadhdhaba bihi" and "kadhaba bihi" came to have the same meaning, though the more common usage is "kadhdhaba fulānan" and "kadhaba bi-l-khabar al-fulānī." So His saying "bi-āyātinā" is governed by the two verbs "kafarū" and "kadhdhabū." His saying ﴿They therein abide forever﴾ explains the content of His saying ﴿companions of the Fire﴾, for "companion" here means one who is constantly attached; therefore the clause "therein they abide forever" is separated from the first, as it stands in the place of explanation, so there is perfect connection between them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 38–39 (part 1 of 2):

[Page 440]
﴿We said, "Go down from it, all of you. And when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance – there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve."﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs – those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

The phrase ﴿We said, "Go down"﴾ is repeated. Its repetition may be for the sake of linking the structure of the Qur'anic verse, without indicating that its meaning is repeated in the speech addressed to Adam. Thus this repetition serves only to connect what is related to the content of "And We said, 'Go down'" – namely His words ﴿some of you will be an enemy to others﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36] – and His words ﴿And when guidance comes to you from Me﴾. For these two related parts were separated by what intervened between them: His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance; indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37]. Had He followed that directly with ﴿And when guidance comes to you from Me﴾, the connection would not have been fully coherent, and the listener might have imagined that it was an address to the believers, according to the Qur'an's habit of variation (tafannun). To avert this, the words ﴿We said, "Go down"﴾ were repeated. It is therefore one statement repeated twice for the sake of connecting the discourse. For this reason the word "qulna" is not joined by a conjunction (waw), because between them there is near-complete connection, since the statement ﴿We said, "Go down, all of you"﴾ descends from the statement ﴿And We said, "Go down, some of you an enemy to others"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36] in the position of a verbal emphasis. Then His words ﴿And when guidance comes to you from Me﴾ and so on were built upon it. It differs from what was built upon His words ﴿And We said, "Go down, some of you an enemy to others"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36], so that some new benefit may arise in the speech, lest the repetition of "Go down" be mere emphasis. In the science of rhetoric (badi') this style is called tardid (repetition), like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought and love to be praised for what they have not done – do not think them safe from punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 188]. Its benefit of emphasis is achieved by the mere repetition of the wording.

It has also been said that it is a second command to descend: that Adam was made to descend from the Garden to the lowest heaven by the first command, then was made to descend from the lowest heaven to the earth. Thus the repetition of "We said, 'Go down'" serves to draw attention to the difference in time of the two statements and the descents. This interpretation implies that stages and distances are of no consequence to the traveler. Also, the pronoun in "from it" (minha), which is definitively referring back to the Garden, is consistent with the arrangement of pronouns in His words ﴿and eat from it freely﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]
[Page 441]
and His words ﴿so Satan caused them to slip from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36]. This prevents the meaning of "go down" from being from the heaven all together, since no return to the heaven has preceded. Therefore, in my view, if the second "go down" is not for linking the structure of the discourse, the preferable reading is that it relates an additional command to Adam to descend, lest one think that God's acceptance of his repentance and His pleasure with him, upon his prompt repentance following the command to descend, had necessitated pardon from the descent from the Garden. So He repeated to him the command to descend after accepting his repentance, so that he would know that this is inevitable, because it is the will of God, exalted is He, and one of the stages of what God willed in making him a khalifah (successor) on earth, which He had informed the angels of. There is also another indication in this: that pardon comes from the one who repents regarding reproaches and punishments. As for the realization of the effects of disobedience, which is the corrective punishment, pardoning it is corruption in the world; for the doer of disobedience, if he does not see the effect of his act, he will not be disciplined in the future. Thus leniency with him in this matter defeats the requirement of wisdom. For example, if a child soils a place and his educator becomes angry with him, then he repents and he is pardoned, the pardon concerns the punishment; but imposing on him that he remove with his own hand the soiling he caused is not something in which leniency is appropriate. Accordingly, when God accepted Adam's repentance, He was pleased with him and did not seize him with punishment or deterrent in this world, yet He did not pardon him regarding the realization of the effect of his disobedience, which is the descent from the Garden, so that he would see the effect of his greed and his bad opinion. This is how the interpretation should be if the intended meaning of the second "go down" is the relating of a second command to descend addressed to Adam.

"Jami'an" is a circumstantial accusative (hal). "Jami'an" is a noun for those gathered, like the word jam', and therefore they kept it in one fixed state. It is not originally an adjective; otherwise they would have said "ja'u jami'in" (they came gathered), because fa'il in the sense of fa'il agrees with the thing it describes. The grammarians have interpreted the verse of Imru' al-Qays,
"If indeed a soul were to die gathered (jami'atan)"
by saying that the ta' in it is for intensification, and the meaning is: "Go down, gathered together in the descent, joined in it," because they both shared in committing the cause of the descent.

His words ﴿So if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance﴾ are a conditional upon a conditional, because "imma" is a compound conditional particle made of "in" (the conditional) and the added "ma," which indicates emphasis of the conditional linkage. Since "in" alone indicates the condition, the addition of "ma" to it is not like its addition to "mata," "ayy," "ayna," "ayyana," "ma," "min," or "mahma" (according to the view that their origin is "mama"); because those additions were to make them convey the meaning of condition, whereas these words were not originally set for that, unlike "in" and "qad." The Arabs consistently used the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid) with the verb of the condition after "imma," to add emphasis to the conditional linkage by the presence of its marker on its particle and on its verb. This is an emphasis that does not establish the actual occurrence of the answer, because that would contradict the conditional. For this reason the answer of the condition is not emphasized with nun; rather, it establishes the binding, i.e., that the answer's occurrence being dependent on the occurrence of the condition is a matter that is certainly established, since the conditional is nothing but a statement of information, its substance being the report that the occurrence of the recompense depends on the occurrence of the condition. Therefore it is, like other statements, capable of emphasis. The verb of the condition with "imma" has rarely been without the energetic nun, as in the words of al-A'sha:
"If you see us barefoot, without sandals for us – indeed we are thus: we go barefoot and we wear sandals."
This is not good according to Sibawayh and al-Farisi, while al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said it is prohibited, making the absence of it a necessity (darurah).

His words ﴿whoever follows My guidance﴾: "man" is conditional, as shown by the entry of the fa' into its answer ﴿then there is no fear for them﴾. Although the fa' often enters the predicate of a relative pronoun, that is by treating it as a conditional; so it is to be understood here as conditional, for brevity.

The word "guidance" is made explicit in His words "hudaya," though it is the very same guidance in His words ﴿guidance from Me﴾. The context called for a resumptive pronoun for the second conditional, but it was made explicit to give emphasis to guidance, so that it would become more firmly fixed in the minds of the addressees, in the manner of ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15] ﴿but Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16]. And so that this sentence would be self-standing, not containing a pronoun requiring a referent, so that it could function like a proverb or advice, to be noticed, remembered, and retained by souls for refinement and discipline. Similarly, the noun was made explicit in His words ﴿Say, "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood is ever bound to vanish"﴾ [al-Isra': 81], so that this last sentence would travel like a proverb. From this is the saying of Bashshar:
"When opinion reaches the point of consultation, seek help from the opinion of a sincere advisor or the advice of a discerning man."
"And do not make consultation a burden upon you; its place is strength for the primary feathers, as the secondary feathers are for the flight."
"Draw near to consultation the one whose opinion is upright, and do not let consultation be heard by a man who is not a keeper of secrets."
He repeated "consultation" three times in the second and third verses, so that each half would travel as a proverb. By this the reason becomes clear for defining the second "guidance" by annexation to the divine pronoun rather than with "al," although "al" is the original form for placing an explicit noun in the position of a resumptive pronoun; this is so that nothing included in the first sentence is lost from this self-standing sentence. The first sentence included describing guidance as coming from God, and the annexation in the second sentence conveys this same meaning.

[Page 442]
The coming in His words ﴿if there come to you﴾ with the conditional particle, which indicates non-certainty of the occurrence of the condition, is a sign of a remaining reproach for not complying with the first guidance, and an implicit suggestion that attempting to guide you in the future is of no use. It is like a master saying to his servant, when he did not act on what he instructed him and he became angry with him, then the servant apologized and he became pleased: "If I instruct you another day about something, do not return to a deed like your deed," implicitly suggesting that the attachment of the purpose to his instruction in the future is a doubtful matter, since perhaps it will be of little benefit. This is an eloquent point which escaped the author of al-Kashshaf, whose attention was diverted from it by his strained effort to force the verse to be evidence for the Mu'tazilite view that sending messengers is not obligatory, since guidance is attained by reason in belief in God, while God's guidance of mankind is obligatory in their view. That kind of strain occurs often in his book, and it is not befitting the firmness of his foot in knowledge. So his statement here is like an apology for the view that sending messengers is not obligatory, since guidance is not restricted to belief, in which reason dispenses with revelation according to them; rather, most of it is guidance regarding obligations, many of which reason cannot perceive. And it is, according to their own principles too, obligatory upon God to convey it to mankind. The difficulty then remains regarding the use of the particle of doubt here, so it stands. Therefore the verse is more favorable to our school, O Ash'aris, against the obligation of all guidance upon God, exalted is He, if we wished to use it as evidence for that, as al-Baydawi did; but we do not see it as coming for that purpose.

His words ﴿if there comes to you from Me guidance﴾ and so on have the sense of a covenant which God took from Adam, so that his descendants are bound to follow every guidance that comes to them from God, and that whoever turns away from guidance coming from God has incurred punishment.

[Page 444]
It thus includes all divine laws addressed to the groups of mankind, because "guidance" occurs indefinite in the context of a condition, and that is one of the forms of generality. The most fitting and most deserving of being obeyed is the guidance which came from God to all of mankind, which is the religion of Islam, addressed to all the children of Adam. By this the place is prepared for His words "those who disbelieve" and so on. Thus God took a covenant from Adam onward to follow the general guidance, like His words ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81] and so on. This verse indicates that God does not hold mankind accountable for the error they commit until after He sends to them one who guides them. As for the details of the laws, there is no doubt about that and no disagreement. As for the Oneness of God, exalted is He, and what it entails of attributes of perfection, there is a difference among our scholars regarding holding the people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah) accountable for shirk. Perhaps the verse indicates that the guidance coming from God in this matter had been present from the time of Adam and Noah, and all of mankind knew it; thus it is a binding address which mankind cannot claim ignorance of. This is one of two opinions from al-Ash'ari; it is also said otherwise. According to the Mu'tazilah and the Maturidiyyah, it is a rational proof.

His words ﴿then there is no fear for them﴾ are a negation of the genus of fear. "Khawf" is in the nominative in the recitation of the majority; Ya'qub read it as built on fatha. These are two readings concerning the noun of "la" of negation for the genus. The narration of the fourth woman in the hadith of Umm Zar' has been transmitted with both readings: "My husband is like the night of Tihamah: neither hot nor cold, no fear and no weariness." Building the noun on fatha is explicit in negating the genus; its being nominative is open to negating the genus and negating a single instance. Therefore, when ambiguity is removed, both readings are equal, as here, since the context is clearly indicating negation of the genus.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on the verse: "And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs..." (Qur'an 2:39)

His saying, ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾, may be part of what was said to Adam, so completing the mention of it here is a comprehensive reference to the categories of Adam's descendants, and in it is an allusion to the polytheists among Adam's descendants. It includes everyone who denied all the miracles, and among them the Qur'an. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the conditional (man) in His saying ﴿Whoever follows My guidance﴾, etc., so it is the coordination of a nominal clause with a nominal clause. He used a non-conditional clause for the coordinated part, despite the conditional's greater strength of linkage and explicitness regarding the consequence following the condition and its inseparability from it. The meanings of consequence (tartīb), causation (tasabbub) and inseparability have been achieved by other means, so the sense of the condition is derived from the implication of His saying ﴿Whoever follows My guidance, there is no fear for them﴾, for it is good news whose implication signals a warning to whoever does not follow it, so he is fearful and grieved. The listener thus anticipates what will clarify this fear and grief, and this is achieved by His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny﴾, to the end of the verse. As for the meaning of causation, it is achieved from attaching the predicate to the relative pronoun and its clause, which alludes to the basis and cause of the predicate according to one of the two interpretations concerning the allusion to the basis of the predicate. As for inseparability, it is required by the report about them as "companions of the Fire", which implies constant attachment, then the explicit statement in His saying ﴿They therein abide forever﴾.

Page 445

It may also be a concluding statement (tadhyīl) with which the story of Adam is concluded, because of the mention of the guided ones, and it is not part of what was said to him. The purpose of this concluding statement is to threaten the polytheists and to return to the presentation of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [2:21] and His saying ﴿How can you disbelieve in God﴾ [2:28]. Thus the waw in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾ is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya). By "those who disbelieve" is meant those who denied the Creator, denied His prophets and rejected His covenant, as is the Qur'anic usage. The meaning is: "And those who disbelieve in Me and in My guidance," as the contrast indicates.

"Āyāt" is the plural of āya, which is a thing that indicates a matter that is by nature hidden. For this reason, the markers of paths are called āyāt, because they set them up to guide to the hidden routes in the sands. Proof is also called āya, because it reveals a hidden truth, as al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza said:

"Who has for us with him of good signs (āyāt), three, in all of which is the judgment?"

He means three proofs of their sincere counsel, their good service in war, and their connection to the king ʿAmr ibn Hind. God called the proofs of His existence, of His oneness, and of the invalidity of the doctrine of polytheism "āyāt," saying: ﴿And no sign comes to them from the signs of their Lord but they turn away from it﴾ [6:4], and He said ﴿And it is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea. We have detailed the signs for a people who know﴾ [6:97], up to His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ [6:99]. He said ﴿And they swore by God their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it﴾ [6:109]. The Qur'an also called itself a sign, saying: ﴿And they say, "Why is not a sign sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Signs are only with God"﴾ [29:50], up to His saying ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book being recited to them?﴾ [29:51] in Surat al-ʿAnkabut. He called its parts āyāt, saying: ﴿And when Our signs are recited to them as clear evidence, you recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve the denial; they nearly assault those who recite to them Our signs﴾ [22:72], and He said ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra. These are the signs of the Book, and that which is revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [13:1], because every surah of the Qur'an is such that mankind is unable to produce its like, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Then bring a surah like it﴾ [2:23]. Thus it was evidence of the Messenger's truthfulness in what he brought, and its sentences were āyāt, because in them is part of the miraculous measure. The parts of the other heavenly books were not called āyāt. As for what occurs in the hadith of stoning, that Ibn Ṣūriyā, when he unfolded the Torah, placed his hand on the verse of stoning, this is by likening a part of the Torah to a part of the Qur'an, and it is an expression of the narrator of the hadith.

The original form of āya, according to Sibawayh, is

Page 446

"faʿala" with a fatḥa, "ayiyah" or "awiyah," depending on the disagreement over whether it is waw-based or yāʾ-based, derived from ayy (the interrogative) or from awā. When the two weak letters in it became vowelled, one of them was changed, and the first was changed for lightness, contrary to analogy; for the analogy for two weak letters suitable for alteration is that the second be altered, except for what is rare, such as āya, wiqāya, ṭāya, thāya and rāya.

So what is meant by "Our signs" here is the signs of the Qur'an, i.e., "and they denied with the Qur'an, i.e., revelation from God."

The bāʾ in His saying ﴿and denied Our signs﴾ is a bāʾ that frequently enters upon the object of the root of denial, although denial is transitive by itself. I have not found in the statements of the leading lexicographers the particular features of its attachment to this root and form. It may be that it serves to emphasize the attachment, for intensity in denial, as in the bāʾ in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [5:6], and the verse of al-Nābigha:

"To you is the good, since the earth has concealed you, one [man]."

It may also be that its original sense is causal, and that the original usage was "kadhdhaba fulānan bi-khabarihi" (he denied someone by his report), then it became common so that "kadhdhaba bihi" and "kadhaba bihi" came to have the same meaning, though the more common usage is "kadhdhaba fulānan" and "kadhaba bi-l-khabar al-fulānī." So His saying "bi-āyātinā" is governed by the two verbs "kafarū" and "kadhdhabū." His saying ﴿They therein abide forever﴾ explains the content of His saying ﴿companions of the Fire﴾, for "companion" here means one who is constantly attached; therefore the clause "therein they abide forever" is separated from the first, as it stands in the place of explanation, so there is perfect connection between them.

[Page 447]

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and fulfill My covenant; I will fulfill your covenant. And fear none but Me.﴾

This is a transition from the admonition of the polytheists (mushrikun) to the admonition of the disbelievers among the People of the Book, and with it the admonition of the groups mentioned earlier is completed, because the group of hypocrites (munafiqun) can only be either polytheists or Jews from among the People of the Book. The address here is directed to the Children of Israel, who are the most renowned of the peoples who possessed a famous Book and an extensive law (shari'ah). This is because this Qur'an came to guide to that which is most upright (al-lati hiya aqwam), so this sura, which is its tent-pole (fusatatuhu), contained the purpose for which it came. The fulfillment of this purpose came in the most marvelous styles and the most complete aspects of eloquence. Its opening therefore draws attention to the status of this Book, the effects of its guidance, and the success (falah) that its followers gain in this world and the Hereafter, and it warns against the evil outcome of whoever turns away from its guidance and deviates from its path. In the course of this, it described the states of people in their reception of this Book: believer, disbeliever and hypocrite. After that, it turned to these categories with the call to the intended goal. The three categories of people who receive this Book, with respect to their attitude toward the Islamic call, are confined to two kinds, because they are either a polytheist or a religious adherent, that is, a People of the Book. The hypocrite category is included within the religious category, because they are from among the Jews, as we have previously stated.

So He called the polytheists to worship Him, exalted is He, by His saying ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. If "mankind" here refers to the polytheists, as is the usual terminology of the Qur'an, as was previously mentioned, then it is evident.

If it refers to all mankind, then His saying ﴿worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21] is necessarily addressed to them, since the believers are not included in it. He reminded them of the signs of the Creator's craftsmanship, which are the creation of their origins and the origins of the blessings of life, namely the creation of the earth and the heavens and the sending down of water from the sky to bring forth fruits. He also marveled at their disbelief despite the clear evidences for affirming the Creator in life and death. He reminded them of a great blessing, namely the honoring of their father (Adam) and His accepting his repentance. All of this was a limitation to what is established in their innate nature (fitrah), since they did not have among their religious foundations anything that could be made a reference point in dialogue and debate by which they would be convinced. In addressing them about establishing the truthfulness of the Messenger, He also addressed them through this with the proof that their rhetorical sensibilities perceive, saying ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a sura like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], and so on in the verses.

When He had given all of this its due, He turned the address here toward the second category, namely the people of the laws and the Book, and He singled out from among them the Children of Israel, because they are the best nation possessing a Book renowned throughout the entire world. They are unique in this description among the speakers of the Arabic language who dwelt in Medina and its surroundings. They are also the ones from whom obstinacy and opposition to this religion appeared. For this reason, He did not call the Jews to monotheism or to acknowledging the Creator, because they were already monotheists. Rather, He called them to remember God's blessings upon them and to what their prophets encountered from their deniers, so that they would recall that this was the custom of God, and so that they would turn back upon themselves with the same reproach they used to direct at whoever denied their prophets. He also reminded them of the good tidings brought by their messengers and prophets concerning a prophet who would come after them.

There is another way of directing the address to them: He argued with them through religious and scholarly proofs and by establishing the truthfulness of the message through what they were familiar with regarding the conditions of the messengers. He did not turn to establishing truthfulness through the evidence of the Qur'an's inimitability (i'jaz), because they were not knights of this field, as we previously mentioned in the commentary on His saying ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to present any example﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. So their address here was through religious proofs and the arguments of the Mosaic law, so that the evidence of the Messenger's truthfulness would be in considering his circumstances and that he came in accordance with the states of his brother messengers who preceded him.

The Qur'an has elaborated on this and progressed in it from one level to its counterpart, with a marvelous method of debating the addressees, and it has conveyed through it the teaching of the Muslims, so that the scholars of the Children of Israel would not escape them. God, exalted is He, said ﴿Was it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 197]. Knowledge at that time was the knowledge of legislation, the knowledge of the reports of the prophets and of past nations, the states of the two worlds (the higher and the lower), together with moral counsels and ethical admonitions. By this, the Jews surpassed the Arabs, and because of it the Arabs would seek their guidance in affairs. The Jews were distinguished over the Arabs in their lands by the civic way of thinking. The knowledge of the general Jewish populace in this matter was weak; this knowledge was monopolized by their scholars and rabbis. So the Qur'an, in these debates, was also teaching the Muslims and joining them with the scholars of the Children of Israel, so that the highest rank would belong to them, because they combine this knowledge with their linguistic sciences and their intellectual acumen. Thus the general body of Muslims would become equal in knowledge to the elite of the Israelites. This is a great meaning among the meanings of universalizing education and of joining in the race for civilization (tamaddun).

By this, there is revealed to you one of the wisdoms behind the Qur'an's recounting of the stories of nations and their conditions, for in that, along with the lesson, there is a formal teaching (ta'lim istilahi). We might even count this among the miracles of the Qur'an: that it described aspects of the conditions of the Children of Israel that none knows except their rabbis and their elite, despite their eagerness to conceal them and to keep them to themselves out of fear of competition for status and benefits. Yet the Qur'an came through the tongue of one most distant from them and from their knowledge, openly stating what none but their elite knew. Thus this miracle was, for the People of the Book, in the place of the rhetorical miracle for the unlettered (ummiyyun). This matter was previously touched upon in the seventh introduction.

In this transition, the order of the books of the Torah was also observed, for it followed the Book of Genesis (Sifr al-Takwin) with the Book of Exodus (Sifr al-Khuruj), that is, a description of the conditions of the Children of Israel during the time of Pharaoh and then the mission of Moses. From the Book of Genesis it mentioned only the creation of Adam and his settling on earth, because that is the locus of the lesson, and then it moved on from that to the conditions of the Children of Israel, because in them there are many lessons for them and for the community.

As for His saying ﴿O Children of Israel﴾, it is an address to the descendants of Ya'qub (Jacob), and within his descendants all of the Jewish community is confined. He addressed them with this description rather than saying "O Jews," because "Israel" is the name of the lineage, whereas "Jews" is the name of the religious community and creed. Also, whoever followed the Jewish faith from outside the Children of Israel, such as the Himyar, was not counted, because they were followers of the Children of Israel. So if the Children of Israel had believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), their followers would have believed, because the one who follows another's taqlid is a follower of the one he imitates.

Also, because this address is for reminding them of the blessings God bestowed upon their forebears and the honors He conferred upon them, it was more fitting for their being called by the title of being the sons of Ya'qub and his descendants. Do you not see that when they were reminded by the title of adherence to the religion of Moses, they were reminded with the description of "those who are Jews" in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62], the verse, as will come shortly. The address directed to all the Children of Israel includes both their scholars and their common people, because what they are addressed with is the reminder of God's blessing upon their forebears and of God's covenant with them. Likewise, we find that His address to them in matters intended to put a charge upon all of them comes in such terms as "O People of the Book," or with the description "those who are Jews," or with the description "Christians." But when the purpose is to put a charge upon their scholars, the Qur'an titles them with the description ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101] or ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 121]. It may also dispense with that by the report being of a kind that pertains specifically to their scholars, such as His saying ﴿And there was a group among them who used to hear the words of God, then they distorted it after they had understood it, while they knew﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75]; and like ﴿and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41]; and like ﴿and do not mix the truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 42]; ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79], the verse; ﴿And when there came to them a Book from God confirming what was with them, and they had previously been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, but when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]; ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance, after We have made it clear for the people in the Book, those are the ones God curses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 159]; ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145], the verse.

So when the address comes in a style that encompasses both their scholars and their common people, it is directed to each of the two groups with what is fitting for it.

As for "banun" (sons), it is among the words that are attached to the sound masculine plural but are not truly part of it, because it underwent broken plural formation (taksir) by the deletion of its third radical and the addition of a hamzat al-wasl at its beginning. So its proper plural is "abna'." There has been disagreement about the root of "ibn." It has been said that it is derived (mushtaqq) from "bana" (to build), so it is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, like "khalq" (creation), so its original form is "bany," meaning "mabni" (built), because his father built him and formed him. Its final radical was deleted for lightness and a hamzat al-wasl was substituted in its place. So there is a correspondence in the sense of derivation (ishtiqaq), except that the deletion in this case is not according to regular analogy, since there is no requirement for deleting the ya' except by a contrived argument that the ya' moved while the preceding letter was quiescent, so its vowel was transferred to the quiescent letter, treating it as if it were the medial radical of the word. Then, when it became an alif according to that rule, it was feared it would be confused with the verb "bana," so its lam was deleted and a hamzat al-wasl was substituted for it. It has also been said that its root is a waw, on the pattern of "banw" or "banaw," with the nun either quiescent or vocalized, and the waw was deleted as it was deleted from its counterparts such as "akh" (brother) and "ab" (father). But this view is far from derivation and far from its counterparts, because when the final radicals of its counterparts were deleted, no hamzat al-wasl was substituted in their place.

"Israel" is the epithet (laqab) of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them. Ibn 'Abbas said its meaning is "servant of God," because "Isra" means "servant" and "Il" is a name of God; that is, it is compounded of two words, "Isra" and "Il," the name of God, exalted is He, just as they say "Bayt Il" (Beth-El), the name of a village called Luz in the land of Canaan, where Ya'qub, peace be upon him, stayed during his migration fleeing from his brother Esau ('Isu), and he built an altar there and called its name Beth-El. What is found in the books of the Jews is that the reason for Ya'qub's being named Israel is that, when he was fearful during his migration lest his brother Esau overtake him to take revenge on him, a figure appeared to him one night. Ya'qub knew that he was his Lord, that is, an angel from among the angels of God. So he seized him and wrestled with him all night until the break of dawn. He said to him, "Let me go, for the dawn has broken." Ya'qub said to him, "I will not let you go until you bless me." He said to him, "What is your name?" He said, "Ya'qub." He said, "Your name shall no longer be called Ya'qub after today, but you are Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men and have prevailed," and he blessed him there. This indicates that "Isra" in this name refers to the meaning of "capture" in war, as it does in Arabic. So if this is from the original Torah, then it is by interpretation of a vision Ya'qub saw, through which God granted him honor, or an angel similarly encountered him.
