Then, Ya'qub had twelve sons, who are known as the "Asbat" (tribes), because they are the tribes (asbat) of Ishaq son of Ibrahim. To these tribes the lineage of all the Children of Israel traces back. The mention of the tribes will come in this sura.

[Page 452]

*Wa-dhkurū* is an imperative from *al-dhikr*. *Al-dhikr*, whether pronounced with a kasra or a damma on the *dhāl*, is used for a thing occurring to the mind of someone who has forgotten it. For this reason it was said: "How can one remember what one does not forget?" It is also used for uttering the name of a thing that occurs to people's minds. Then it was applied, without restriction, to explicit mention with the tongue, because the usual case is that no one utters the name of a thing unless it has come to his mind. Some lexicographers distinguished between the *dhāl* with kasra and the *dhāl* with damma: they assigned the kasra to the verbal (*lisānī*) and the damma to the mental (*'aqlī*). This is perhaps a usage-based distinction that arose later (*muwalladah*), since the user of a language cannot be restricted to assigning one of the two verbal nouns of a single verb to one of the verb's meanings in speech. Thus it becomes a conventional usage (*istilāḥī*, *isti'mālī*) and not a lexical coinage (*waḍ'*), so that it would not count as a pair of synonyms. The uniformity of the verb prevents the claim that the two verbal nouns are synonymous. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The remembrance of Allah that is better than remembrance with the tongue is remembrance of Allah at the moment of His command and His prohibition." So he called both kinds *dhikr*. What is intended here is mental remembrance, since the meaning is not remembrance of the blessing with the tongue.

The "blessing" (*al-ni'mah*) here refers to everything Allah has bestowed upon the addressees, either directly or through the bestowal upon their forefathers. The blessing upon the forefathers is also a blessing upon their descendants, since it is a source of good repute for them, a model they follow, and a baraka that reaches them from it. The present good condition of their affairs was due to it. Some blessings lie in the natural endowments Allah gave to man: intelligence and soundness of disposition. Such qualities may be inherited by descendants.

Had it not been for those blessings, their predecessors would have perished or their condition would have been bad, and their descendants would have come into a worse state. This therefore includes all the blessings Allah bestowed upon them. It is as if He said: "Remember My blessings upon you." This generality is derived from the attribution of *ni'mah* to the pronoun of Allah, the Exalted, since attribution (*idāfah*) conveys what the *lām* conveys. The *lām* of *al-'ahd* (the specific reference) cannot apply here, because there is no particular blessing previously known in the discourse. The *lām* of *al-jins* (the generic sense) also cannot apply. Therefore the attribution must be on the meaning of the *lām* of *al-istighrāq* (comprehensiveness, all-inclusiveness). The generality is thus obtained from the attribution of *ni'mah* to a definite noun. Few scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (*uṣūl al-fiqh*) mention a singular noun defined by attribution as one of the forms of generality. Imam al-Razi mentioned it in *al-Maḥṣūl* in the course of his argumentation. Walī al-Dīn said: "According to the Imam, attribution is more indicative of generality than the *lām*." Ibn al-Subki said in his commentary on Ibn al-Ḥājib's *Mukhtaṣar*: "The indication of generality by a singular noun in attributive form, when no specific previous reference has been established, is the correct view." An example is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So let those who oppose His command beware﴾ [al-Nur: 63], meaning every command of His. The intention of generality for the blessing is further supported by the fact that the context is one of reminding of favour and of inviting to Islam, so the multiplicity of blessings fits this context.

What is meant is the blessings Allah bestowed upon their forefathers and upon those of them present at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an, since the blessing upon their forefathers is a blessing upon them. Blessings followed one another upon them when He settled them in villages in the lands of the Arabs after their own lands, Palestine, had been taken from them. He placed them in comfort and ease of life, with security, wealth, and peace with the Arabs.

The command to remember the blessing here intends its necessary consequence, which is thanking for it. The first level of thanks is abandoning obstinacy in receiving what is attributed to Allah of the message, by examining its proofs and following what the messengers bring. Thus His saying ﴿which I bestowed upon you﴾ is a descriptive clause that points to the obligation of thanking for blessings, by what the relative pronoun and its clause imply of causation. It is of the type of His saying: ﴿and that He may complete His blessing upon you, that you may be grateful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. In addition, it conveys the command to them to reflect upon the blessings He bestowed upon them, so that they turn away from envy of others. Reminding the envious person of the blessings he has is an admonition to him and a turning of him away from the envy that arises from preoccupation with the blessings of others. This is an allusive reproach to them: they envy the Arabs for what they were given of the Book and wisdom through the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ), and for the transfer of prophethood from the Children of Israel to the Arabs. They were reminded of this because the self is heedless of what is within it and busies itself with the conditions of others, since sense perception is the origin of knowledge. When the envious person sees the blessings of others, he forgets that he too is in a blessing. When it is desired to turn him away from envy, he is reminded of his own blessings, so that his envy may lessen, since their envy was what prevented them from believing in him. This is comparable in its structure to His saying: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ [al-Nisa': 54]. Its placement before His saying ﴿and fulfil My covenant﴾ is of the type of placing *al-takhliyah* (clearing away what is undesirable) before *al-taḥliyah* (adorning with what is desirable). The opening of their address with this reminder prepares their souls to receive the address with sound disposition and fairness.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and fulfil My covenant﴾ is a hamzated verb from *wafā* in its basic form. The original meaning of *wafā* is completing a matter. One says *wafaytuhu ḥaqqahu* ("I gave him his due in full"). Since the basic form is transitive to the object, and the hamzated form does not add transitivity, since "wafaytuhu ḥaqqahu" and "awfaytuhu ḥaqqahu" are equivalent, the augmentation must be for mere intensification of fulfilment, like *bāna* and *abāna*, *shaghala* and *ashghala*. As for the doubled form *waffā*, it is more emphatic than *awfā*, because *fa''ala*, although it shares meanings with *af'ala*, indicates the gradual passing of one thing after another, and so it is more indicative of intensification, since a matter performed step by step is usually more perfected. The word *wafā'* has been applied to the fulfilment of a promise and a covenant in a widespread usage that has made it a true (conventional) meaning. The meaning of *'ahd* was explained at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27] in this surah.

*Al-'ahd* here is the commitment to another party regarding a transaction, a commitment that the contracting party does not neglect until they both dissolve it between them. The covenant attributed to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is used metaphorically for accepting what He imposes upon them of religion. It is used figuratively for accepting the obligations and entering the religion. The noun attributed to the pronoun of the addressees is used for the promise of reward for that in the Hereafter and victory in this world. So you may take each *'ahd* as a single metaphor: the first *'ahd* is used for the obligations, the second *'ahd* is used for the promise of reward and victory, and *al-īfā'* (fulfilment) with both is used for fulfilling what both parties committed to, borrowed from the suitable element of the figurative source to the suitable element of the target, as a *tarshīḥ* (a supporting element) for its metaphor. You may also take the whole as a metaphor of image (*isti'ārah tamthīliyyah*), in that the state arising from their saying, regarding what Allah commanded them and that they should not fall short in acting upon it, and from Allah's promise to them of reward for that, is likened to the state of parties who mutually bind themselves to a commitment in which each one does work for the other, and the other fulfils his covenant by not violating it. For this state, the speech containing His saying ﴿fulfil My covenant, I shall fulfil your covenant﴾ is borrowed. This second option is better, and by it the reason for using the word *'ahd* a second time in His saying ﴿I shall fulfil your covenant﴾ becomes clear, and it is brought closer by *al-mushākalah* (harmonization of the wording).

In both interpretations, *al-'ahd* in both places is an object-attributive (*muḍāf li-l-maf'ūl*), which is what the author of *al-Kashshāf* held. This is because its attribution to the object is necessary when the fulfilling is connected to it, since no one fulfils except a covenant of his own. When the covenant, which is the object of *awfū* (fulfil), is attributed to something other than the agent of fulfilment, its attribution must be to the object. With this, the *tarshīḥ* of the metaphor is completed if it is a single word, as al-Muḥaqqiq al-Taftazani indicated. If it is a compound, then it is even more fitting, because the expression that is originally applied to the compared image (*al-hay'ah al-mushabbah bihā*) is necessarily attributed, with the restriction of fulfilment, to its object.

Among the subtleties of the Qur'an in its choice of the word *'ahd* for the metaphor here, regarding Allah's imposition upon them, is that this is an address to them in a term familiar to them from their books. The Torah revealed to Moses, peace be upon him, is called among them *al-'ahd*, because it is the commandments of Allah, the Exalted, to them. For this reason it is expressed in several places in the Qur'an as *al-mīthāq* (the covenant). This is one of the ways of scientific inimitability (*i'jāz 'ilmī*), which none knows except their scholars, who are more stingy with it than with anything else, so that only the particular people of the religion know it. Its coming through the tongue of the unlettered Arab Prophet is evidence that it is a revelation from the Knower of the Unseen.

The covenant was taken from their forefathers through their messengers and prophets. Allah, the Exalted, said: [Page 454] ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom, then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must support him"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81], and so on. Since the addressees of the verse had received the law from their forefathers with what it contains of covenant, the covenant was binding upon them, and fulfilment was obligatory upon them, because they are the ones among whom the promised Messenger came.

His saying ﴿and fear Me, and only Me﴾: the conjunction *wāw* coordinated the clause ﴿and of Me﴾ with the preceding clauses from His saying ﴿and fulfil My covenant﴾ to its end, by way of moving from one meaning to the meaning that arises from it. This is the original method of those who compose speech: they observe the external order between report and command, since that is the basic arrangement unless a factor arises requiring a change from the natural order. Among its examples in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed by them and felt powerless to protect them, and said, "This is a difficult day."﴾ [Hud: 77], ﴿and his people came rushing towards him﴾ [Hud: 78], etc. For when He opened their address with reminding them of the blessing, which arouses gratitude to the Benefactor and attentiveness to His right, and which purifies them from envy (since envy prevents recognition of the blessing, as we mentioned), then He joined to it His saying ﴿and fulfil My covenant﴾, which is the beginning of the purpose of the command to believe the promised Messenger, through the tongues of their prophets. Then He followed this with His saying ﴿and fear Me, and only Me﴾. This is a completion of the earlier command, through a prohibition against whatever stands between them and fulfilling the covenant properly. That is the obstruction by their elders and rabbis, who prevented them from moving away from what they were upon, adherence to the Torah. These are the people who said to the king of their lands, Pharaoh of Egypt, on the day of the sending of Moses: "We will never prefer you over what has come to us of clear proofs and Him who created us." They were thus fit to address their leaders and rabbis with the same address at the Muhammadan mission.

So the placement of the object here is necessarily for restriction (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), so that the clause conveys both affirmation and negation: the command to fear Allah, the Exalted, is conveyed explicitly, and the prohibition against fearing others is conveyed implicitly. The restriction by the placement of the object was chosen among the ways of restriction, rather than by *innamā* (only), so that what is conveyed by the explicit statement is the command to fear Allah, the Exalted, and the prohibition against fearing other than Him is conveyed by implication. For when they fear Allah, the Exalted, they are eager to fulfil the covenant. Since their fear of their rabbis would prevent them from fulfilling the covenant, the prohibition against fearing other than Allah was incorporated (*udmija*) with the command to fear Allah in a single form.

Placing the object while its verb is attached to its pronoun (*īyāya ārhabūnī*) is more emphatic in conveying restriction than placing the object before a verb that is not attached to its pronoun (*īyāya ārhabū*). Thus *īyāya ārhabūnī* is more emphatic than something like *īyāya ārhabū*, as indicated by the author of *al-Kashshāf* when he said: "It is from your saying *zaydan rahibtuhu* ("Zayd, I feared him"), and it is more emphatic in conveying restriction than *iyyāka na'budu* ('You alone we worship')." End of quote.

My view on this is that the placement of the object admits of restriction, but its original function is to indicate

[Page 455]

عَلى الِاخْتِصاصِ إلّا إذا أقامَتِ القَرِينَةُ عَلى التَّقْوى، فَإذا كانَ مَعَ التَّقْدِيمِ اشْتِغالُ الفِعْلِ بِضَمِيرِ المُقَدَّمِ نَحْوَ: زَيْدًا ضَرَبْتُهُ، كانَ الِاخْتِصاصُ أوْكَدَ، أيْ كانَ احْتِمالُ التَّقْوى أضْعَفَ. وذَلِكَ لِأنَّ إسْنادَ الفِعْلِ إلى الضَّمِيرِ بَعْدَ إسْنادِهِ إلى الظّاهِرِ المُتَقَدِّمِ يُفِيدُ التَّقْوى، فَتَعَيَّنَ أنَّ تَقْدِيمَ المَفْعُولِ لِلِاخْتِصاصِ دُونَ التَّقْوى، إذِ التَّقْوى قَدْ حَصَلَ بِإسْنادِ الفِعْلِ أوَّلًا إلى الِاسْمِ أوِ الظّاهِرِ المُتَقَدِّمِ، وثانِيًا إلى ضَمِيرِ المُتَقَدِّمِ. ولِهَذا لَمْ يَقُلْ صاحِبُ الكَشّافِ: "وهو أكْثَرُ اخْتِصاصًا" ولا "أقْوى اخْتِصاصًا"، إذِ الِاخْتِصاصُ لا يَقْبَلُ التَّقْوِيَةَ. بَلْ قالَ: "وهو أوْكَدُ في إفادَةِ الِاخْتِصاصِ"، أيْ أنَّ إفادَتَهُ الِاخْتِصاصَ أقْوى، لِأنَّ احْتِمالَ كَوْنِ التَّقْدِيمِ لِلتَّقْوى قَدْ صارَ مَعَ الِاشْتِغالِ ضَعِيفًا جِدًّا.

ولَسْنا نَدَّعِي أنَّ الِاشْتِغالَ مُتَعَيِّنٌ لِلتَّخْصِيصِ، فَإنَّهُ قَدْ يَأْتِي بِلا تَخْصِيصٍ في نَحْوِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿إنّا كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْناهُ بِقَدَرٍ﴾ [القمر: ٤٩]، وقَوْلِهِ: ﴿أبَشَرًا مِنّا واحِدًا نَتَّبِعُهُ﴾ [القمر: ٢٤]، وقَوْلِ زُهَيْرٍ:

فَكُلًّا أراهم أصْبَحُوا يَعْقِلُونَهُ          صَحِيحاتِ مالٍ طالِعاتٍ بِمَخْرَمِ

لِظُهُورِ أنْ لا مَعْنى لِلتَّخْصِيصِ في شَيْءٍ مِمّا ذَكَرْنا. غَيْرَ أنَّ الغالِبَ أنْ يَكُونَ التَّقْدِيمُ مَعَ صِيغَةِ الِاشْتِغالِ لِلتَّخْصِيصِ، إذِ العَرَبُ لا تُقَدِّمُ المَفْعُولَ غالِبًا إلّا لِذَلِكَ. ولا التِفاتَ إلى ما وجَّهَ بِهِ صاحِبُ المِفْتاحِ مِن أنَّ احْتِمالَ المَفْعُولِ في الِاشْتِغالِ التَّخْصِيصُ، والتَّقْوى باقٍ عَلى حالِهِ، ولَكِنَّكَ إنْ قَدَّرْتَ الفِعْلَ المَحْذُوفَ مُتَقَدِّمًا عَلى المَفْعُولِ كانَ التَّقْدِيمُ لِلتَّقْوى، وإنْ قَدَّرْتَهُ بَعْدَ المَفْعُولِ كانَ التَّقْدِيمُ لِلتَّخْصِيصِ، فَإنَّهُ بَناهُ عَلى حالَةِ مَوْقِعِ الفِعْلِ المُقَدَّرِ، مَعَ أنَّ تَقْدِيرَ الفِعْلِ اعْتِبارٌ لا يُلاحِظُهُ البُلَغاءُ، ولِأنَّهم يَنْصِبُونَ عَلى مَوْقِعِهِ قَرِينَةً، فَتَعَيَّنَ أنَّ السّامِعَ إنَّما يَعْتَدُّ بِالتَّقْدِيمِ المَحْسُوسِ وبِتَكْرِيرِ التَّعَلُّقِ. وأمّا الِاعْتِدادُ بِمَوْقِعِ الفِعْلِ المُقَدَّرِ فَحَوالَةٌ عَلى غَيْرِ مُشاهَدٍ، لِأنَّ التَّقْدِيرَ إنْ كانَ بِنِيَّةِ المُتَكَلِّمِ فَلا قِبَلَ لِلسّامِعِ بِمَعْرِفَةِ نِيَّتِهِ، ولا يَصِحُّ أنْ يَكُونَ الخِيارُ في التَّقْدِيرِ لِلسّامِعِ.

هَذا، والتَّقْدِيمُ إذا اقْتَرَنَ بِالفاءِ كانَ فِيهِ مُبالَغَةٌ، لِأنَّ الفاءَ كَما في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ مُؤْذِنَةٌ بِشَرْطٍ مُقَدَّرٍ، ولَمّا كانَ هَذا الشَّرْطُ لا دَلِيلَ عَلَيْهِ إلّا الفاءَ تَعَيَّنَ تَقْدِيرُهُ عامًّا نَحْوَ: إنْ يَكُنْ شَيْءٌ، أوْ مَهْما يَكُنْ شَيْءٌ، كَما أشارَ لَهُ صاحِبُ الكَشّافِ في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿ورَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ﴾ [المدثر: ٣] حَيْثُ قالَ: "ودَخَلَتِ الفاءُ لِمَعْنى الشَّرْطِ، كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: مَهْما كانَ فَلا تَدَعْ تَكْبِيرَهُ."

فالمَعْنى هُنا: ﴿وأوْفُوا بِعَهْدِي أُوفِ بِعَهْدِكُمْ﴾ [البقرة: ٤٠]، ومَهْما يَكُنْ شَيْءٌ فَإيّايَ ارْهَبُونِ. فَلَمّا حُذِفَتْ جُمْلَةُ الشَّرْطِ بَعْدَ واوِ العَطْفِ بَقِيَتْ فاءُ الجَوابِ مُوالِيَةً لِواوِ العَطْفِ، فَزُحْلِقَتْ إلى أثْناءِ الجَوابِ كَراهِيَةَ تَوالِي

[صفحة ٤٥٦]

حَرْفَيْنِ، فَقِيلَ: ﴿وإيّايَ فارْهَبُونِ﴾ بَدَلًا عَنْ أنْ يُقالَ: ﴿فارْهَبُونِ﴾. والتَّعْلِيقُ عَلى الشَّرْطِ العامِّ يَسْتَلْزِمُ تَحَقُّقَ وُقُوعِ الجَوابِ، لِأنَّ التَّعْلِيقَ الشَّرْطِيَّ بِمَنزِلَةِ رَبْطِ المُسَبَّبِ بِالسَّبَبِ، فَإذا كانَ المُعَلَّقُ عَلَيْهِ أمْرًا مُحَقَّقَ الوُقُوعِ لِعَدَمِ خُلُوِّ الحَدَثانِ عَنْهُ، تَعَيَّنَ تَحَقُّقُ وُقُوعِ المُعَلَّقِ. وهَذا مَبْنِيٌّ عَلى مَذْهَبِ سِيبَوَيْهِ في بابِ الأمْرِ والنَّهْيِ، إذ يُخْتارُ فِيهِما النَّصْبُ في الِاسْمِ الَّذِي يُبْنى عَلَيْهِ الفِعْلُ، وذَلِكَ مِثْلَ قَوْلِكَ: زَيْدًا اضْرِبْهُ، ومِثْلَ ذَلِكَ: أمّا زَيْدًا فاقْتُلْهُ. فَإذا قُلْتَ: "زَيْدٌ فاضْرِبْهُ" لَمْ يَسْتَقِمْ أنْ تَحْمِلَهُ عَلى الِابْتِداءِ. ألا تَرى أنَّكَ لَوْ قُلْتَ: "زَيْدٌ فَمُنْطَلِقٌ" لَمْ يَسْتَقِمْ؟ ثُمَّ أشارَ إلى أنَّ الفاءَ هُنا في مَعْنى فاءِ الجَزاءِ، فَمِن ثَمَّ جَزَمَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ بِأنَّ هاتِهِ الفاءَ مَهْما وُجِدَتْ في الِاشْتِغالِ دَلَّتْ عَلى شَرْطٍ عامٍّ مَحْذُوفٍ، وإنَّ الفاءَ كانَتْ داخِلَةً عَلى الِاسْمِ فَزُحْلِقَتْ عَلى حُكْمِ فاءِ جَوابِ أمّا الشَّرْطِيَّةِ. وأحْسَبُ أنَّ مِثْلَ هَذا التَّرْكِيبِ مِن مُبْتَكَرِ أسالِيبِ القُرْآنِ، ولَمْ أذْكُرْ أنِّي عَثَرْتُ عَلى مِثْلِهِ في كَلامِ العَرَبِ.

ومِمّا يُؤَيِّدُ ما ذَهَبَ إلَيْهِ صاحِبُ الكَشّافِ المَبْنِيَّ عَلى كَلامِ سِيبَوَيْهِ مِنِ اعْتِبارِ الفاءِ مُشْعِرَةً بِشَرْطٍ مُقَدَّرٍ: أنَّ غالِبَ مَواقِعِ هاتِهِ الفاءِ المُتَقَدِّمِ مَعَها المَفْعُولُ عَلى مَدْخَلِها أنْ تَقَعَ بَعْدَ نَهْيٍ أوْ أمْرٍ يُناقِضُ الأمْرَ والنَّهْيَ الَّذِي دَخَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ تِلْكَ الفاءُ، نَحْوَ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿ولَقَدْ أُوحِيَ إلَيْكَ وإلى الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكَ لَئِنْ أشْرَكْتَ﴾ [الزمر: ٦٥] إلى قَوْلِهِ: ﴿بَلِ اللَّهَ فاعْبُدْ﴾ [الزمر: ٦٦]، وقَوْلِ الأعْشى:

ولا تَعْبُدِ الشَّيْطانَ واللَّهَ فاعْبُدا

فَكانَ ما يَتَقَدَّمُ هاتِهِ الفاءَ يَتَوَلَّدُ مِنهُ شَرْطٌ في المَعْنى، وكانَتِ الفاءُ مُؤْذِنَةً بِذَلِكَ الشَّرْطِ وعَلامَةً عَلَيْهِ، فَلِأجْلِ كَوْنِهِ مَدْلُولًا عَلَيْهِ بِدَلِيلَيْنِ: أصْلِهِ وفَرْعِهِ، كانَ كالمَذْكُورِ، كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: ﴿لَئِنْ أشْرَكْتَ لَيَحْبَطَنَّ عَمَلُكَ﴾ [الزمر: ٦٥]، وفَإنْ كُنْتَ عابِدًا شَيْئًا فاللَّهَ فاعْبُدْ، وكَذا في البَيْتِ. وهَذِهِ فائِدَةٌ لَمْ يُفْصِحْ عَنْها السَّلَفُ فَخُذْها ولا تَخَفْ.

[صفحة ٤٥٧]

قالَ التَّفْتَزانِيُّ: ونُقِلَ عَنْ صاحِبِ الكَشّافِ أنَّهُ قالَ: إنَّ في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى ﴿وإيّايَ فارْهَبُونِ﴾ وُجُوهًا مِنَ التَّأْكِيدِ: تَقْدِيمُ الضَّمِيرِ المُنْفَصِلِ وتَأْخِيرُ المُتَّصِلِ، والفاءُ المُوجِبَةُ، مَعْطُوفًا عَلَيْهِ ومَعْطُوفًا: تَقْدِيرُهُ: إيّايَ ارْهَبُوا فارْهَبُونِ؛ أحَدُهُما مُقَدَّرٌ والثّانِي مُظْهَرٌ، وما في ذَلِكَ مِن تَكْرارِ الرَّهْبَةِ، وما فِيهِ مِن مَعْنى الشَّرْطِ بِدِلالَةِ الفاءِ، كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: إنْ كُنْتُمْ راهِبِينَ شَيْئًا فارْهَبُونِ. اهـ. يُرِيدُ أنَّ في تَقْدِيمِ الضَّمِيرِ إفادَةَ الِاخْتِصاصِ، والِاخْتِصاصُ تَأْكِيدٌ. قالَ صاحِبُ المِفْتاحِ: لَيْسَ الحَصْرُ والتَّخْصِيصُ إلّا تَأْكِيدًا عَلى تَأْكِيدٍ. وأمّا تَأْخِيرُ الضَّمِيرِ المُتَّصِلِ فَلَما في إعادَةِ الإسْنادِ مِنَ التَّقْوى. ومُرادُ الزَّمَخْشَرِيِّ بِقَوْلِهِ "مَعْطُوفًا عَلَيْهِ ومَعْطُوفًا" العَطْفُ اللُّغَوِيُّ، أيْ مُعَقَّبًا ومُعَقَّبًا بِهِ، لا العَطْفُ النَّحْوِيُّ، إذْ لا يَسْتَقِيمُ هُنا.

فَتَحَصَّلَ أنَّ في التَّعْبِيرِ عَنْ مِثْلِ هَذا الِاخْتِصاصِ في كَلامِ البُلَغاءِ مَراتِبَ أرْبَعًا:
- مُجَرَّدُ التَّقْدِيمِ لِلْمَفْعُولِ، نَحْوَ ﴿إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ﴾ [الفاتحة: ٥]؛
- وتَقْدِيمُهُ عَلى فِعْلِهِ العامِلِ في ضَمِيرِهِ، نَحْوَ: زَيْدًا رَهِبْتُهُ؛
- وتَقْدِيمُهُ عَلى فِعْلِهِ مَعَ اقْتِرانِ الفِعْلِ بِالفاءِ، نَحْوَ ﴿ورَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ﴾؛
- وتَقْدِيمُهُ عَلى فِعْلِهِ العامِلِ في ضَمِيرِهِ مَعَ اقْتِرانِ الفِعْلِ بِالفاءِ، نَحْوَ ﴿وإيّايَ فارْهَبُونِ﴾.
فالثّانِيَةُ والثّالِثَةُ والرّابِعَةُ أوْكَدُ مِنهُما.

وحُذِفَتْ ياءُ المُتَكَلِّمِ بَعْدَ نُونِ الوِقايَةِ في قَوْلِهِ ﴿فارْهَبُونِ﴾ لِلْجُمْهُورِ مِنَ العَشَرَةِ في الوَصْلِ والوَقْفِ، وأثْبَتَها يَعْقُوبُ في الوَصْلِ والوَقْفِ. وجُمْهُورُ العَرَبِ يَحْذِفُونَها في الوَقْفِ دُونَ الوَصْلِ، وهُذَيْلٌ يَحْذِفُونَها في الوَقْفِ والوَصْلِ، وأهْلُ الحِجازِ يُثْبِتُونَها في الحالَيْنِ. وإنَّما اتَّفَقَ الجُمْهُورُ هُنا عَلى حَذْفِها في الوَصْلِ مِثْلَ الوَقْفِ، لِأنَّ كَلِمَةَ ﴿فارْهَبُونِ﴾ كُتِبَتْ في المُصْحَفِ الإمامِ بِدُونِ ياءٍ وقُرِئَتْ كَذَلِكَ في سُنَّةِ القِراءَةِ.

ووَجْهُ ذَلِكَ أنَّها وقَعَتْ فاصِلَةً فاعْتَبَرُوها كالمَوْقُوفِ عَلَيْها. قالَ سِيبَوَيْهِ في بابِ ما يُحْذَفُ مِن أواخِرِ الأسْماءِ في الوَقْفِ وجَمِيعِ ما لا يُحْذَفُ في الكَلامِ: "وما يُخْتارُ فِيهِ أنْ لا يُحْذَفَ يُحْذَفُ في الفَواصِلِ والقَوافِي." ولِأنَّ لُغَةَ هُذَيْلٍ تَحْذِفُها مُطْلَقًا، وقِراءَةُ يَعْقُوبَ بِإثْباتِ الياءِ في الوَصْلِ والوَقْفِ جَرى عَلى لُغَةِ أهْلِ الحِجازِ، ولِأنَّهُ رَواها بِالإثْباتِ وهو وجْهٌ في العَرَبِيَّةِ، ويَكُونُ قَدْ تَأوَّلَ كِتابَتَها بِدُونِ ياءٍ في المُصْحَفِ أنَّهُ اعْتِمادٌ عَلى أنَّ القارِئَ يُجْرِيها عَلى رِوايَتِهِ. ولِذَلِكَ لَوْ لَمْ تَكُنْ ياءُ المُتَكَلِّمِ في كَلِمَةٍ هي فاصِلَةً مِنَ الآيِ لَما اتَّفَقَ الجُمْهُورُ عَلى حَذْفِها، كَما في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدّاعِي إذا دَعانِ﴾ [البقرة: ١٨٦] كَما سَيَأْتِي.

[Page 458]

﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾

This begins the call of the Children of Israel to Islam and to the guidance of the Qur'an. This is the real purpose of addressing them, but before it He introduced what prepares their souls to accept it, just as a preface (muqaddimah) precedes the main subject, and clearing away (takhliyah) comes before adorning (tahliyah).

Belief in the Book sent down from God, or in the Books of God, though it is among the things covered by the covenant referred to in His words ﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40], is not considered here from that angle. This is because they had made covenants with God concerning many things, as has already been mentioned, and among them was belief in the messengers and books that would come after Moses, peace be upon him. However, that is stated in general terms in the covenant. So it is not necessarily the case that what Muhammad ﷺ brought is among the things they covenanted with God to believe in. Rather, they are called here to affirm that it is from God and that the one who brought it is a messenger of God.

So the conjunction of "and believe" with "and fear Me" [al-Baqarah: 40] is like the conjunction of the purpose with the preface. Its conjunction with "And fulfil My covenant" [al-Baqarah: 40] is of the type of conjoining the specific with the general in meaning. But this is conjunction of sentences, so it is not called conjoining the specific with the general, because that applies only to conjoining a part with a whole among single words, not to conjoining sentences. We only intended to bring out the position of the sentence and the reason for presenting it connected rather than separated.

In attaching the command to the relative phrase "what" (mā unzilat), rather than to other names such as "the Book," "the Qur'an," or "this Book," there is a hint at the reason for the command to believe in it: that it is sent down from God. They had already agreed to believe in every book that is established as being sent down from God.

For this reason He brought the circumstantial clause (ḥāl), which is the reason for the relative clause, since He made its confirming what is in the Torah a sign that it is from God. This is the religious sign suitable for the scholars among the People of the Book. Just as He made the verbal inimitability (i'jāz lafẓī) a sign that the Qur'an is from God for the people of eloquence and rhetoric among the Arabs, as indicated by His words ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1], ﴿That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], up to His words ﴿then bring a sūrah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], so too He made the inimitability of meaning (i'jāz ma'nawī), which is its containing guidance, the characteristic of divine books, a sign that it is from Him for the people of religion and the knowledge of the laws. Then, believing in the Qur'an necessarily entails believing in the one who brought it and the One who sent it down.

What is meant by "what is with them" are the four books of the Torah and what has been added to them from the books of the prophets of the Children of Israel,
[Page 459]
such as the Psalms (Zabūr), the Book of Isaiah (Ashya'), Jeremiah (Armiyā'), Ezekiel (Ḥizqiyāl), Daniel (Dāniyāl), and others. For this reason the expression "what is with you" was chosen rather than "the Torah," even though "the Torah" is used in other places, because in the books of the prophets after Moses, peace be upon him, there are clearer glad tidings of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ than in the Torah. So drawing attention to them was more effective.

What is meant by the Qur'an being confirming of what is with them is that it contains the guidance to which their prophets called: monotheism, commanding virtues, avoiding vices, establishing justice, and promises, threats, admonitions, and stories. Whatever in it agrees with them is clearly so, and whatever differs from them does so only because of differences in interests and eras, while all remain under one principle. For this reason that difference was called abrogation (naskh), because naskh is the removal of an established ruling, and it was not called nullification or denial. Thus it is clear that it confirms what is with them, even in what comes differing from what is with them. This is because it proclaims that the difference is a change of rulings in accordance with the change of circumstances of interests and harms due to the variation of ages, such that the one who changes and the thing changed are each true according to its time. That is not nullification or denial. He, exalted is He, said ﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things﴾ [al-Nisā': 160], and so on.

Therefore, believing in the Qur'an does not contradict their clinging to their old religion, nor the earlier covenant their messengers took from them to follow it.

Among what the confirmation of the Qur'an of what is with them includes is that the attributes the Qur'an contains, and the religion of Islam and the one who brought it, agree with what their books gave good news of. So its arrival is a miracle for their prophets and another confirmation of their religion. This is one of the two aspects mentioned by al-Fakhr (al-Rāzī) and al-Bayḍāwī. Thus the meaning of confirmation (taṣdīq) must be interpreted as verification (taḥqīq). This is because taṣdīq, in informing the one who is told (with the vowel on the bā'), means that the report of the informant corresponds to reality, either by his saying "you have spoken truly" or "so-and-so has spoken truly," as occurs in the hadith of Gabriel in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, when he asked about faith, Islam, and excellence (iḥsān), and when he had informed him, the questioner said, "You have spoken truly." He said, "We marvelled at him: he asks him and then confirms him." Or it means that a man reports a report similar to what another has reported, so that his second report is a confirmation of the first report.

As for applying the word taṣdīq to something's indicating the truth of a certain report, that is a metaphorical use. The intended meaning is describing the Qur'an as confirming what is with them through its reports and its rulings, not describing the religion or prophethood, as is not hidden.

* * *

[Page 460]

﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾

The pronoun in "do not be" is plural while "disbeliever" (kāfir) is singular. This indicates that what is meant by the disbeliever is a group to which disbelief is attributed, not a single individual. So the construct "first of" (awwal) with "disbeliever" (kāfir) is an explanatory construct (iḍāfah bayāniyyah), conveying the meaning of a group which is the first of the groups of disbelievers.

The pronoun in "in it" (bihi) apparently refers to "what I have sent down," because that is what is intended. It is conjoined to the clause "And believe in what I have sent down," and this is an escalation in the call and in winning hearts. When He commanded them to believe in the Qur'an, and the form of the command allowed for obeying it immediately or later, and since they were known for intense hostility to the religion of Islam, He conjoined to their command to believe in the Qur'an a prohibition against being the first to disbelieve in the Qur'an. That is understood in several senses: some drawn from the proper structure of the expression, some from its necessary implications, and some from what follows from it. The verse can bear all of them.

The first meaning is that the phrase "first disbeliever" is taken in its literal sense of "first," meaning one who precedes others. So from the conjoined sentence there results an emphasis of the sentence it is conjoined to, by the indication of direct correspondence. Thus the prohibition from disbelief in the Qur'an emphasizes "And believe in what I have sent down." Then the description "first" implies restriction of the prohibition by the description. But the context indicates that restricting the prohibition of disbelief to the state of their being first in disbelief is not intended. The aim is not merely to forbid them from hastening to disbelief or from preceding others in it, since that would be of little benefit. Rather, the more important aim is that they should be the first of the believers. This is conveyed by way of an allusive metonymy (kināyah talwīḥiyyah). The word "first" basically means one who precedes others in some action or matter, so precedence and hastening are necessary implications of the meaning of "first," since they are part of what the word signifies. And since belief and disbelief are contradictories, if one is negated the other is established. So the prohibition against being the first of the disbelievers necessarily implies being the first of the believers.

The purpose of the prohibition is to rebuke them for lagging in following the call of Islam. So this expression is used as a metonymy for two meanings among its necessary implications: the meaning of hastening to Islam, and the meaning of rebuke implied by the prohibition. Thus the meaning of the prohibition is intended, and its implication, which is the command to hasten to faith, is also intended, and it is the main aim. So the statement is a metonymy in which the implicating and the implicated are combined together. From the viewpoint of the implication, the prohibition has the sense of a command, so the command preceding it is reinforced, as if it were said: "And believe in what I have sent down, and be the first of the believers." From the viewpoint of the implicating, it is a prohibition against disbelief after the command to believe. Thus two aims are achieved.
[Page 461]

This metonymy is an allusive indirect expression (taʿrīḍ), because the aim of the implied meaning is other than the aim of the explicit meaning. This is what I have derived in clarifying the meaning of taʿrīḍ: that the aim of the ruling indicated by it is other than the aim of the ruling expressed explicitly, or that the one to whom the ruling is attributed is other than the one to whom the explicit ruling is attributed. This view rests on what is apparent, and it brings together the scattered statements of the scholars about the well-known taʿrīḍ within kināyah. By this, two separate objections are dispelled. One of them arises from what precedes it. The first: how is the prohibition against being the first of the disbelievers valid, when its implication requires that if they were to disbelieve in it a second time, their disbelief would not be forbidden? The second: the people of Mecca had already preceded them in disbelief, because the verse of al-Baqarah addressed to the Jews was revealed in Medina. So it is established that the Jews were not the first of the disbelievers, and the prohibition against being the first of the disbelievers would be achieving the already achieved.

The answer to the objection is that the more important aim is the allusive meaning (taʿrīḍ), and it serves as an indication that the purpose of the prohibition is that they should not be among those who hasten to disbelief, that is, they should not be late in believing. This is the first of the interpretations of the verse according to the author of al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī), and al-Bayḍāwī chose it and limited himself to it.

Know that the allusive indirect expression concerns specifically the description "first" (awwal). As for the basic prohibition against their being disbelievers in it, that is the direct and explicit meaning of the words. The allusion is of the type of allusive metonymy because of the hidden transition from the meaning to its implications. Some allusion arises from the context of the circumstances at the time of speech, and perhaps this is not described as literal, figurative, or metonymic. It is one of the implications of expressions and their rational indications. Further clarification of this will come at the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you allude to of the proposal to women﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235] in this sūrah.

The second meaning is that the aim is an allusion to the polytheists, and that they are worse than the Jews in disbelief, that is, "do not be among them." Perhaps this is the meaning intended by the author of al-Kashshāf when he said: "It is also permissible that it means: do not be like the first disbeliever in it, that is, those among the people of Mecca who associated partners with God." He did not intend that this is a powerful simile, although his statement may suggest it, and its commentators remained silent about it.
[Page 462]

The third meaning: "first" is taken to mean the one who hastens and rushes, because this is a necessary implication of being first, as God, exalted is He, said ﴿So I am the first of the worshippers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81]. And Sa'īd ibn Miqrūm al-Ḍabbī said:

So they called me to a duel, and I was the first to dismount,
and how could I ride it if I did not dismount?

His saying "first to dismount" does not mean to establish that no one had dismounted before him. He meant that he hastened together with the people, for the custom is that when a people calls to a duel, all the listeners dismount. But he meant that he was among those who did not wait. The meaning then is: "Do not hasten to declare disbelief before reflection." So the intended sense of disbelief here is insisting upon it, not remaining in what they were upon. So the metonymy is with a single word, namely "first."

The fourth meaning: "first" is a metonymy for leadership in the matter, because chiefs, standard-bearers, and the like go before the people. God, exalted is He, said ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Hūd: 98]. And Khālid ibn Zuhayr, who was the nephew of Abū Dhu'ayb al-Hudhalī, said:

Do not be distressed over a custom you have followed,
for the first to be content with a custom is the one who walks in it.

That is, the most worthy and the supporter of a custom. The meaning is: "Do not be those who approve of the disbelievers in your disbelief, for if they witness your disbelief, they will disbelieve following your example." This too is a metonymy with a single word.

The fifth meaning: "first" is intended in relation to the second call, which is the call in Medina, because what came after the migration (hijrah) was a second state of Islam, in which Islam appeared distinct and independent.

This whole discussion is based on taking the pronoun in the phrase ﴿kafirin bihi﴾ ("a disbeliever in it"), attached to the preposition bi-, as referring to ﴿what I have sent down﴾, meaning the Qur'an. This is the apparent meaning, because the phrase is mentioned in contrast to belief in it. It has been said that the pronoun refers to what is with you, namely the Torah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "According to this view, the phrase ﴿awwala kafirin﴾ ("the first disbeliever") remains straightforward in its literal sense of priority." It is not hidden, however, that this view is strained, because it requires interpretation: their disbelief in the Qur'an, which came in the manner described by the Torah and the books of their prophets in their predictions of a prophet and a scripture that would come after Musa, means that when they denied that, they disbelieved in the truth of what is in the Torah, and this leads to disbelief in what is with them.

Al-Taftazani said: "All of this holds only if their disbelief in it means their claim that it is entirely false. But if they disbelieved that it is the word of God while believing that it contains truth and falsehood, then it does not hold. For this reason this view is weaker." 'Abd al-Hakim refuted it with what does not befit it.

[Page 463]

With all of this it becomes clear that the statement ﴿and do not be the first disbeliever in it﴾ should not be understood as implying that the negation applies to the qualifier, such that it would mean there is no prohibition against being the second or third disbeliever, owing to the apparent context. Nor is "first disbeliever" a qualifier inseparable from its subject, so that it would be the same whether the qualifier is mentioned or not, as in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Upon a well-trodden road whose landmarks are no guide"*

and the verse of Ibn Ahmar:

*"You do not see the lizard hiding in it"*

as will come in the statement of God, exalted is He, ﴿and do not trade My signs for a small price﴾, after this.

* * *

﴿And do not trade My signs for a small price﴾

This is coordinated with the prohibition before it, and this prohibition is directed at the scholars of the Children of Israel, who were the examples for their people. The connection is that what prevented them from accepting the call of Islam was their fear that their leadership among their people would disappear. So they pretended to deny the Qur'an so that the common people of their community would rally around them, and their leadership would remain over them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If ten Jews had believed in me, all the Jews would have believed in me."

*Ishtira'* (purchase, trade) was discussed earlier at the statement of God, ﴿those who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqara: 16]. It is the exchange of specific things for other things of equal value, or for their price in gold and silver and the like, such as paper money and bills of exchange. The word *ishtira'* is used here metaphorically for exchanging one thing for another without an actual sale.

*Ayat* is the plural of *ayah*, and its original linguistic meaning is a sign marking a dwelling or a road. al-Nabigha said:

*"I recognised the marks of it, and I knew them after six years, and this year is the seventh."*

Then the word *ayah* was applied to proof, because proof is a sign of the truth. al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

*"Who has for us from the good things three signs, in all of which is the decision?"*

For this reason the miracle of the Messenger was called an *ayah*, as in the statement of God, ﴿among the nine signs to Pharaoh and his people﴾ [al-Naml: 12], and ﴿and when you do not bring them a sign﴾ [al-A'raf: 203]. It was also applied to a complete sentence of the Qur'an. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is He who sent down to you the Book, in it are clear verses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. In the authentic hadith the Messenger of God said: "Does not the verse of summer suffice you?" ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning the kalala﴾ [al-Nisa': 176]. This is because the sentences of the Qur'an are proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger, since their eloquence is miraculous.

As for applying *ayah* to a sentence of the Torah in the hadith of stoning, in the narrator's words, "the Midras placed his hand on the verse of stoning," that is a metaphor upon a metaphor, through the relation of resemblance.

The point of resemblance between their turning away and the act of buying is that their turning away from the verses of the Qur'an was for the sake of preserving leadership, and the benefit in this world resembles the exchange of the buyer in that he gives what he has no need for and takes what he needs, and in it he has his benefit. So in *tashtaruu* ("trade") there is a realised metaphor (*isti'ara tahqiqiyya*) in the verb. It is also permissible that *tashtaruu* be a sent metaphor (*majaz mursal*) through the relation of necessity (*'alaqat al-luzum*) or through the relation of using the restricted in place of the general, as was discussed before at the statement, ﴿those who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqara: 16]. But here the metaphor is more apparent, because the relation of resemblance is clearer, and the relation of resemblance needs no search for a reason for departing from the literal to the figurative, since the intention of comparison alone is sufficient for turning to metaphor, for comparison is among the aims of eloquent speakers.

Since the verb *ishtira'* requires two things, one of which is exchanged for the other, the desired counter-value, which is what is bought, is what is taken, and it is directly connected to the verb. The other counter-value, which is what is given and is called the price (*thaman*), is connected to the verb by the preposition *bi-*, which indicates the sense of exchange.

Here the verb *ishtira'* is connected to the verses by *bi-*, so the verses are the element occupying the place of the price, because the price is what the *bi-* enters. The entry of *bi-* indicates that the verses have been likened to the price in being the less valuable of the two counter-values in the eyes of the one who exchanges. Mentioning *bi-* is a sign (*qarina*) of the implicit metaphor (*makniyya*), because it enters on the price, and it cannot be a subsidiary metaphor (*tab'iyya*), since there is no meaning whose proper expression is by a particle which has been likened to the meaning of *bi-*. Therefore it is necessary here to follow the approach of al-Sakkaki in reducing the subsidiary metaphor to the implicit metaphor. Nor is it correct to make *bi-* an imaginative indicator (*takhyiliyya*), since it does not indicate an independent meaning that can be imagined.

Then the object of the buying was expressed by the word *thaman* ("price"), whereas the apparent expectation would have been to give the word *thaman* to what the *bi-* enters, or to express each by a different word, as one would say, "do not trade My signs for a small goods (*mata'an*)." So the speech departed from what the apparent context requires. He expressed the goods and the like by the word *thaman* by way of realised metaphor, to liken this counter-value from leadership or wealth to the price, or because it resembles the price in being objects and perishable matter, which are given in exchange for a beneficial thing. In this there is an allusion (*ta'ridh*) against them, that they are defrauded in the transaction, since they gave up the most precious thing and took a small and paltry share. Thus both counter-values in the verse are likened to the price, except that the verses are likened to it in being the less valuable for the one who exchanges, while the goods they take are likened to the price in being a material thing that everyone can obtain. Or it is to indicate that each of the verses and the price is something cheap for one group: the verses were cheap for the rabbis, and wealth was cheap for the common people. The genuinely cheap is specified by giving it the real word indicating that it is cheap, while what is cheap in appearance is given the figurative *bi-*. Each of the two metaphors is a sign of the other. Also, since the expression "the price" had become common for gold and silver, the use of that word for what they take was chosen as an allusion that they take wealth in return for changing the legal rulings of the Sharia, as in God's statement, ﴿they take the goods of this lowly life﴾.

It has been said that the statement *thaman* ("price") is the sign of the metaphor in the statement *la tashtaruu* ("do not trade"). The reasoning is that once *bi-* was attached to the verses, it became fixed that the verses are the price of the buying. So when the speech afterward expressed the object of *tashtaruu* by the word *thaman*, the hearer knew that the first was not a real price, and so he knew that the buying was a metaphor. Then he also knows that what is expressed by "price" afterward is not a real price either, following his knowledge of the metaphor in the verb that governs it.

It has also been said that the statement *thaman* is an abstraction (*tajrid*), and its explanation is like the explanation of it being a sign, if we take the sign to be the statement *bi-ayati* ("for My signs").

It has been said that it is an intensification (*tarshih*), since the word *thaman* belongs to the vocabulary suited to buying. This is close to what we have already presented about it being a metaphor, since intensification itself may be a metaphor drawn from what suits the figurative term (*mushabbah bihi*) to what suits the thing compared (*mushabbah*). In all the possibilities, they all indicate their ignorance and their rebuke.

The verses themselves are not exchanged in their essences, so an implied noun must be supposed, meaning: do not trade the acceptance of My verses for a price.

The attribution of the verses to the pronoun of majesty (*damir al-jalala*) is for honour. Shaykh Muhammad ibn 'Arafa said: "The greatness of the verses is by two things: plurality and their attribution to the pronoun of majesty, and he belittled the counter-value by two ways of belittling it: indefiniteness and describing it as small." End of quote. That is, in this there is an allusion to the defrauding of their transaction, since they exchanged the precious for the base. I say: the description *qalilan* ("small") is a clarifying qualifier, because the price for which the loss of the verses is sold is small, even if it is the greatest wealth compared to what the one who takes that price has lost. On this meaning, the words of Ibn 'Arafa should be understood.

The counter-value for which they exchanged the verses has been left general, and it is not specified whether it is leadership or the bribes they take, so that this includes the difference of their circumstances, for they differ in the aims that prevent them from following Islam according to the differences of their ambitions.

[Page 466]

The description of *thaman* ("price") by the words *qalilan* ("small") does not mean a restriction implying a prohibition against taking a small counter-value while permitting taking a counter-value that has value. Rather, it is a qualifier inseparable from the price taken as a counter-value for exchanging the verses, for every price in that transaction is small. So mentioning this restriction is intended to belittle every price in that matter. Therefore this negation resembles the negation of restrictions inseparable from the restricted thing, so as to imply the negation of both the restriction and the restricted together, as in the famous verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Upon a well-trodden road whose landmarks are no guide, when the Dayafi camel pushes and bellows along it."*

That is, there is no landmark for it that could be followed, because being guided is inseparable from the landmark. Likewise is the statement of Ibn Ahmar:

*"Its terrors do not frighten the hare, and you do not see the lizard hiding in it."*

That is, there is no hare in it that would be frightened by its terrors, and no lizard in it that would hide. Likewise is al-Nabigha's statement:

*"Like a glass bottle which has not been applied with kohl for ophthalmia."*

That is, an eye that has not had ophthalmia, so that it would be treated with kohl, because applying kohl is inseparable from an inflamed eye. Similar things are numerous in eloquent speech.

*Thaman* ("price") occurs indefinite in the context of prohibition, which is like negation, so it includes every counter-value. Likewise the verses occur as a plural attributed to a pronoun, so they include every verse. Likewise the verb occurs in the context of negation, so it includes every act of buying, since the verb is like an indefinite noun.

Although the address is to the Children of Israel, the Qur'an's addresses and its narratives concerning other nations are intended for taking lessons and warning. So we are warned, with even greater reason, against the like of what they fell into, because we are more deserving of spiritual perfections. As Bashshar said:

*"The free man is blamed, and the stick is for the slave."*

And like the well-known verse:

*"The slave is struck with the stick, and a gesture suffices the free man."*

So our scholars are forbidden to do what the Children of Israel were forbidden from, namely turning away from the truth for the sake of worldly aims. Such too was the way of the early generations, may God be pleased with them.

From here a question arose which the commentators made connected to this verse, though its connection to it is weak. It is the question of taking a wage for teaching the Qur'an and religion, and from it branches the question of taking a wage for teaching knowledge and on

[Page 467]

part of the commentary arrives mid-argument, so I translate exactly from "بَعْضِ ما فِيهِ عِبادَةٌ".

...some of which is an act of worship, such as the call to prayer (adhan) and leading the prayer (imamah). The summary of the discussion on this is that the majority of scholars permitted taking a wage for teaching the Qur'an, let alone for jurisprudence and knowledge. Permission for this was given by al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Sha'bi, Ibn Sirin, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Thawr and the majority. Their proof is the sound hadith from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The most deserving of what you take a wage for is the Book of Allah." Accordingly, this verse has no place, in their view, in this meaning at all, because the "purchase" (ishtira') in it is meant figuratively, and there is no exchange, no deviation, and no squandering in teaching.

Ibn Rushd reported a consensus of the people of Madina on permissibility, and perhaps he means the consensus of the majority of their jurists. In al-Mudawwanah: "There is no harm in taking a fee for teaching the Qur'an." Ibn Shihab (al-Zuhri) among the Successors, from the jurists of Madina, prohibited it, as did Abu Hanifa and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh. They relied on the verse, on the argument that teaching for this purpose is obedience and worship like prayer and fasting, so one does not take payment for it, and on what is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The dirhams of teachers are unlawful." And from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "I taught some people of the People of the Suffah the Qur'an and writing, and one of them gave me a bow as a gift. I asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'If you would like to be given a collar of fire with it, then accept it.'" Al-Qurtubi answered this by saying that the verse is to be understood as applying to one for whom teaching has become obligatory, who refuses except for a wage. But there is no evidence for what al-Qurtubi answered with.

The correct view is that this was at the beginning of Islam and during the spreading of the call; if payment had been allowed for it then, much teaching would have been neglected, because few would be able to spend on it, since most of them could not afford it. The hadith of Ibn 'Abbas is to be understood as applying to the period after that, when Islam had spread and the memorisers of the Qur'an had increased. I say: there is no need for all of this, because the verse is far from this purpose, as you have come to know. Al-Qurtubi answered the analogy (qiyas) by saying that prayer and fasting are purely personal acts of worship, whereas teaching is an act of worship whose benefit extends to others, so taking a wage for that act is permissible; and this is a significant distinction.

As for the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and the hadith of 'Ubadah, both are weak in terms of their chains of transmission, as al-Qurtubi explained. I say: I do not think al-Zuhri relied on such things, nor on the verse, nor on that analogy; rather, he regarded it as obligatory, so no wage may be taken for it. Later Hanafi jurists have issued fatwas permitting taking a wage for teaching the Qur'an and jurisprudence. In al-Durar and its commentary it is said: "Today the validity of it is ruled, i.e., the hiring for teaching the Qur'an and jurisprudence. The principle is that hiring is not permitted in our school for acts of obedience or sins, but when weakness set in with religious affairs, the later scholars permitted it." End of quote.

Among the branches of this issue is the permissibility of taking a wage for the call to prayer and leading the prayer. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "It is derived from the question of wages for teaching the Qur'an, and their ruling is one." In al-Mudawwanah: hiring for the adhan is permitted, and for the adhan and prayer together; but for prayer alone Malik disliked it. Ibn Shas said: it is permitted for the adhan, because the muezzin is not obliged to perform it; but if it is combined with prayer, the wage is for the adhan alone. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam permitted hiring for leading the prayer, and its basis is that he undertakes to perform the prayer at that place and that time. Ashhab reported from Malik: "There is no harm in a wage for the Ramadan taraweeh," and he disliked it for the obligatory prayer. Al-Qurtubi said: Abu Hanifa and his companions disliked it. In al-Durar: "Today the validity of it is ruled, for teaching the Qur'an and jurisprudence, leading the prayer and the adhan, and the employer is compelled to pay the wage and may be imprisoned."

Al-Qarafi said in the Fifteenth and Hundredth Difference (al-Furuq): "Hiring for leading the prayer is not permitted according to the well-known view of Malik's school, because it is a contract of bargaining among exchanges, so it is not permissible that two considerations come to one person, since the reward for the prayer is his; if he takes a return for it, he gathers two considerations." End of quote.

This is a reasoning built on a feeble principle which he stated in the Fourteenth and Hundredth Difference; and whether it is a branch of that principle is open to doubt, which we will not elaborate on here, so consult it, for I have alerted you to it. The truth is that the dislike reported from Malik is a dislike of discouragement (karahat tanzih).

This question once arose between Ibn 'Arafa and al-Dakkali. In about the year 770 AH (around 770 AH), a pious man from the Maghrib named Muhammad al-Dakkali arrived in Tunis. He would not pray with the congregation nor attend Friday prayer, arguing that the imams of Tunis take wages for leading the prayer, and that this is a blemish on the one who does it. Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa objected to him, his affair became known among the common people, a dispute arose among the people, and he left for the East, fleeing with himself. It was reported that he had gone to Egypt, so Ibn 'Arafa wrote to the people of Egypt verses:

O people of Egypt, and whoever shares with them in religion,
be alert to a perplexing question that has come down.

The necessity of your being sinners, or of the sinner whose sayings claim
that he has acted in accordance with the truth,

in his abandoning the Friday prayers and the congregations behind you,
while the condition for the obligation of the whole ruling has been met.

If your concern is piety, then others
have fallen into sin, to the point that even the one who is upright has been called unjust.

And if it is the reverse, then the matter is reversed:
speak the truth, for the truth is what has been withdrawn from.

It is said that the people of Egypt answered him with verses, among them:

It is not among the traits of the righteous to brand
a shaykh who is naturally inclined to good deeds as a sinner.

No, but when they see a flaw,
they clothe it in the fine garments of their good interpretations.

Did not its author say in al-Minhaj
that this is permissible for one who fears a slip?

Among them: It has been reported from Ibn al-Qasim al-'Utaqi,
in what I have abridged, a statement that clarifies the paths:

A testimony is not rejected from one who abandons it,
if he is adorned with knowledge and piety.

Yes, and there was in the highest rank,
apart from the congregations and Friday prayers, and he withdrew from them,

like Malik, who did not offer any excuse for it
until his death, and was not asked, and was not blamed. Now, what he has put forward as sound is
that taking a wage by the imams is prohibited, as transmitted.

Even if you suppose that you see its permissibility through reasoning,
your own ijtihad is not more deserving of correctness, nor is it like this.

These verses are attributed in some biographical books to the people of the Maghrib, and it is said that they were sent from the people of Egypt; but it has also been said that some people of Tunis composed them in support of al-Dakkali. Al-Khafaji mentioned this in Taraz al-Majalis, and said that the one who answered was Abu al-Hasan 'Ali al-Sulami al-Tunisi, and he mentioned that al-Siraj al-Bulqini mentioned this incident in his fatawa, and that his father answered the question with a rhyming poem (lamiyyah) which you may consult there.

* * *

"And fear Me, so be mindful of Me" (﴿وإيّايَ فاتَّقُونِ﴾). The discussion of it is like the discussion of "And fear Me, so dread Me" (﴿وإيّايَ فارْهَبُونِ﴾) [al-Baqarah: 40], except that the expression in the first is "fear Me" (irhabun) and in the second "be mindful of Me" (ittaqun), because dread (rahbah) precedes taqwa, since taqwa is a dread in which action is required: carrying out what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden. This differs from mere dread, which is belief and emotion without action. Also, the preceding verse commands them to fulfil the covenant, so it was fitting that they be warned against breaking it; and this verse commands them to believe in the Qur'an, which the remnant of their common folk prevented them from, so it was fitting that they be commanded to fear none but Allah. Taqwa has a legal meaning that was mentioned in His saying, "a guidance for the mindful" (﴿هُدًى لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾) [al-Baqarah: 2], and in that meaning it is necessarily more specific than dread. I do not think that this is what is intended here.

The discussion of the deletion of the first-person ya' in "fa-ittaquni" is similar to the discussion of it in "fa-rhabuni" [al-Baqarah: 40].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 42:

[p. 470]
﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while you know [it].﴾
It is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the whole of what preceded from His saying ﴿Remember My favour which I have bestowed upon you﴾ [2:40] up to here, because these sentences were not all intended such that each one is coordinated only with the one before it, but rather with everything preceding them. This is especially so for His saying ﴿and do not mix﴾, for it is the starting point of a transition from the purpose of warning against misguidance (dalal) to the purpose of warning against leading others astray (idlal), after He had placed between them His saying ﴿and do not trade My signs for a small price﴾ [2:41], as has been mentioned.

If you wish, you may make each [sentence] coordinated with the one before it, in which case it is coordinated with the one before it, given that what precedes it is itself coordinated with what precedes it in the same way. This is the case with coordinated sentences, except when it is intended to coordinate a sentence with a specific sentence because the second is more closely connected to the one it follows than the rest. This is like the coordination of ﴿and conceal the truth﴾ upon ﴿and do not mix﴾. It is necessarily determined to be coordinated with ﴿do not mix﴾ if it is coordinated, which is the apparent meaning, since both matters are forbidden, and the emphasis in the prohibition against combining them is clear by a fortiori reasoning.

They permitted that ﴿and conceal the truth﴾ be in the accusative governed by an implied ʾan after the waw of accompaniment (wa al-ma'iyya), so that the basis of the prohibition is the combining of the two matters. This is far-fetched, because each of them is forbidden, and separating the forbidden items implies the prohibition of combining them a fortiori, but not the reverse. Unless it is said that they were forbidden from the two matters together, in the manner of combination, as an allusion to them that nothing more than leaving off this mixing can be expected from them, namely leaving off mixing that is accompanied by concealing the truth, since its being a transgression in religion is a plain matter. As for leaving off mixing in the sense of distorting interpretation, it cannot be expected of them, since there is no hope for their immediate reform. Truth (haqq) is a matter that is established; when it is established and binding, and it is what all souls acknowledge regardless of their desires.

Falsehood (batil) in their speech is the opposite of truth, for it is that which is transient and lost. It is said: "batala batlan, buţūlan, and buṭlānan" when it goes to waste, is lost, and "his blood went to waste (buṭlan)," meaning in vain (hadran).

What is meant by it here is that which souls reject and remove as long as they are free of purpose or desire. It was called batil because it is an act that goes to waste and loss for its doer. Mixing (labs) is the blending of things that resemble one another in their attributes, such that distinguishing them becomes difficult or impossible. It is transitive to the one confused by it with several particles, such as ʿala, al-lam, and al-ba', according to the context which determines the meaning of some of these particles.

It may be governed by the adverbial phrase ʿinda, and it may be unrestricted by a particle. It is applied to the confusion of meanings, which is the most common usage; and the apparent meaning of al-Raghib's words in Mufradat al-Qur'an is that

[p. 471]
this is the literal meaning. It is said of a matter, "lubsa" with a damma on the lam, meaning ambiguity (ishtibah). In the hadith of the splitting of the chest, "I feared that it had become mixed up with me (iltabasa bi)," meaning confusion arose in my mind such that it could not distinguish between vision and imagination. Its verb is of the pattern "daraba." As for the verb "labisa" meaning to wear clothes, it is of the pattern "samia."

Thus, mixing the truth with falsehood is presenting falsehood in the form of truth. This mixing is the starting point of misguidance and heresy in well-known matters, for those who engage in it are not deceived into thinking they intend to nullify them. The way of one who wants to nullify them is to resort to mixing truth with falsehood until he gives the impression that he wants the truth. God the Exalted said: ﴿And thus their partners made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children, to destroy them and to confuse them regarding their religion﴾ [6:137], because they made them believe that this was an act of worship drawing them closer to the idols. Most kinds of misguidance that have entered Islam are of this type of mixing truth with falsehood. The apostates among the Arabs who withheld zakat said: "We used to give zakat to the Messenger and obey him, so we owe no obedience to anyone after him." This is a breaking of the unity of the religion under the guise of refusing to obey other than God. Their poet, al-Khuteyl ibn Aws, said:

"We obeyed the Messenger of God while he was among us. So, servants of God, what [claim] does Abu Bakr have?"

The rebels against ʿUthman, may God be pleased with him, did the same, dressing up matters that they made attractive to the common people. Such as their saying: "He climbed the pulpit into the seat of the Prophet ﷺ," which is belittling, since each of the two caliphs before him descended from the step on which his predecessor used to sit. And the Seal of the Prophet ﷺ fell from his hand, which is a symbol of the fall of his caliphate. The Kharijites said: "There is no judgement except God's," and ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, said: "A word of truth by which falsehood is meant."

Some people distorted verses by remote interpretation, then called that "the esoteric" and claimed that the Qur'an has an outward and an inner meaning, and much confusion arose from that. Then from that arose the sect of the Batiniyya. Then the interpretations of the philosophers regarding the Sharia, such as the authors of the Epistles known as the Brethren of Purity (Ikhwan al-Safa').

Then arose the confusion of the preachers, those who encourage and those who warn, and the Murji'a. They took some verses and publicised them, and concealed what restricts and qualifies them, such as God's saying: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of God's mercy﴾ [39:53]. Thus they gave people the impression that forgiveness is general for every sin and every sinner, even if he does not repent, and they ignored the verses of threat and the verses of repentance. To avoid this description which God condemned, the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) said: interpretation is not valid unless a strong proof indicates it. If an interpretation occurs for what is thought to be a proof, it is a

[p. 472]
false interpretation; and if it occurs without any proof at all, it is play, not interpretation. For this reason the jurists forbade quoting the Qur'an in a sense other than that for which it came, as Ibn al-Rumi said:

"Even if you erred in your praise of me, you were not wrong in your refusal of me.
I have lodged my needs in a valley with no crops."

His saying ﴿while you know﴾ [2:42] is a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is more emphatic in the prohibition, because such conduct from one who knows is more grave. The object of "you know" is omitted, indicated by what preceded, that is: "while you know that," meaning your mixing the truth with falsehood.

Al-Tayyibi said, regarding God's saying later, ﴿Do you not then reason?﴾ [2:44]: God's saying ﴿while you know﴾ [2:42] is not placed in the position of an intransitive verb, because if it were placed in the position of an intransitive verb, it would indicate that they are described with knowledge, which is an attribute of perfection, and that would contradict His later saying ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people and forget yourselves?﴾ [2:44] up to His saying ﴿Do you not then reason?﴾ [2:44], since He denied them the attribute of reason. How then does He affirm for them here the attribute of knowledge without qualification?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 43:

﴿And establish prayer and give zakah and bow with those who bow.﴾

He commanded adherence to the emblem of Islam immediately after the command to hold the creed of Islam, so His saying ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming that which is with you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41] and so on, refers back to faith in the Prophet ﷺ, and to what is the means to that and what is its end. The means is ﴿Remember My favor﴾ [al-Baqarah: 47] up to ﴿and fear Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]; the aim is ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming that which is with you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41]; and the end is ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾. Interspersed among these are prohibitions against corruptions that would prevent them from the commanded acts, placed appropriately among the commands.

So His saying ﴿And establish prayer﴾ and so on is a command to the greatest of the Islamic foundations after faith and the utterance of the word of Islam. It also contains an allusion to a good opinion of their responding and complying with the earlier commands, and that the required matters have been completed for them.

In this command there is also an allusion to the hypocrites. Faith is an inward conviction of the heart, which is indicated only by utterance, and verbal utterance is an easy matter that one who does not hold the belief may readily engage in, when he is not extreme in his religion; so he does not scruple to utter a statement that contradicts the religion, if he does not believe its meaning, as the Exalted said: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14] and so on. Therefore they were commanded to perform prayer and zakah, because the first is an act that indicates the glorification of the Creator, prostration to Him, and renunciation of the deities. A polytheist does not perform such an act, because it enrages his gods through the act and through the saying "Allahu Akbar," and a People of the Book does not perform it, because it opposes their worship. And because zakah is the spending of wealth, which is dear to the soul, a person does not give it in ways that do not benefit him except out of belief in an otherworldly benefit, especially when that wealth is spent on an enemy of the religion. Therefore He followed the command to believe with the command to establish prayer and give zakah, because only a sincere believer undertakes them.

Hence it was said concerning the hypocrites: ﴿And when they stand up to prayer, they stand lazily﴾ [al-Nisa': 142], and His saying: ﴿So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 4-5]. And in the Sahih it is reported that "the prayer of 'Isha' is the heaviest prayer upon the hypocrites."

In this verse there is evidence for Malik regarding the killing of one who refuses to perform prayer, when it is established that he has not performed it from the beginning of the time of any prayer until its time has passed, if that time is agreed upon among the scholars of Islam, because He made that refusal, in the absence of an excuse, a proof of the absence of his faith. But since he explicitly professes faith, Malik said he is to be killed as a hadd punishment, combining the evidences and preventing the pretext of breaching the religion. It is likely that this is evidence for those who say that one who abandons prayer is a disbeliever, were it not for the opposing evidences.

It also contains evidence for what Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, did in fighting those who withheld zakah and applying the name apostates to them; because Allah made prayer and zakah the sign of the truthfulness of faith when He said to the Children of Israel: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾. For this reason Abu Bakr said, when 'Umar debated with him about his resolve to fight the people of apostasy when they refused to give zakah, and said to him: "How will you fight them, when they have said, 'There is no god but Allah,' and the Messenger of Allah said, 'I have been commanded to fight people until they say, "There is no god but Allah." When they say it, they have protected their blood and their property from me, except by its right'?" Abu Bakr said: "By Allah, I will fight whoever separates prayer from zakah, for zakah is the right of wealth." Thus from his expression, concise as it is, there is an answer to 'Umar's evidence.

His saying ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾ is an emphasis on the meaning of prayer, because the Jews have a prayer in which there is no bowing; so that they would not say "we establish our prayer," He removed this misconception with His saying ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾. Ruku' is lowering the head and bending the back for the purpose of glorification or veneration. The Arabs used to do it to some of their nobles. Al-A'sha said:

When Abu Malik comes to us, we bow to him and remove the turban.
It is also narrated: "we prostrated to him and removed the 'amara," and the 'amara is the turban.

His saying ﴿with those who bow﴾ is an indication of the obligation of the Muslims resembling one another in performing the obligatory rites of Islam. So by "those who bow" is meant the Muslims, and in it is an indication of performing the prayer with its pillars and conditions.

[p. 474]

﴿Do you command the people to righteousness while you forget yourselves, though you recite the Book? Will you not then use your reason?﴾

This is an interjection (i'tiraḍ, a parenthetical clause) placed between His saying ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43] and His saying ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45]. The reason for its placement here is that when He commanded them to perform the rites of Islam, namely establishing the prayer and giving zakat, and concluded that with His saying ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43], He was pointing to their prayer, which they perform but which no longer benefits them. It was therefore fitting to add that they do not uphold the righteousness their religion commands as they should. Hence this interjection was introduced. The fact that it is not joined by the conjunction "wa" (and) signals that it is an interjection, lest one suppose that the primary purpose is to urge commanding righteousness and adhering to it. The aim here is to proclaim the depth of their loss and the extent of the evil state they have reached, to the point that they take up preaching and teaching as a craftsman takes up his craft or a merchant his trade, intending only to discharge their religious duties in full so that they may thereby earn the ranks and stipends they are paid. They do not look to the condition of their own souls in relation to those commands which they enjoin upon people.

The addressees of His saying ﴿Do you command﴾ are all the Children of Israel who were addressed earlier. This implies that this condition applies to all of them, meaning that each one of them is found to proclaim the commands of his religion and spread them among people, yet does not comply with them himself. It is also possible that the intended address is a group among them, since an address directed to communities and tribes is taken by each group according to its share of that address. In that case the intended group would be their rabbis and scholars, who are most particularly concerned with commanding righteousness.

On the first interpretation, the word "the people" (al-nās) may refer either to the polytheistic Arabs, since the Jews used to tell them what their religion had brought and the Arabs used to swear by hearing their statements, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And previously they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]. Or "the people" may refer to whoever is considered in the matter, as when you say "I do as people do," and as in His saying: ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 173]. That is, does one person command another and forget himself? On the second interpretation, "the people" refers to the common folk of the Jewish community, meaning: how do you command your followers and your common people to righteousness while you forget yourselves? In this there is a censure of the state of their rabbis, or an implication that they know that what the Messenger of Islam brought is the truth, yet they command their followers with admonitions and do not seek the salvation of their own souls.

The interrogative here is for rebuke, because it is not sound to take it as a genuine question. It is therefore used for rebuke by way of metaphor (majāz), indicated by the context. It is a metonymy (majāz mursal, a figurative usage based on a relation other than resemblance), because rebuke necessarily accompanies the interrogative. The reason is that one who commits what deserves rebuke is naturally questioned by people about whether the act is indeed his, and they direct the question to him; thus it passes from questioning to rebuke, and from it there arises the sense of wonder at the state of the one being rebuked. This is because the condition for which they are rebuked is a strange one, since it involves desiring good for others while neglecting oneself. Therefore it is fitting that every hearer should marvel at it. Wonder is not necessarily entailed by the meaning of rebuke in every context, but only in cases like this, where the thing for which one is rebuked is unusual and not familiar among sensible people. When the interrogative is used for a single necessary concomitant (lāzim), its being a metonymy is evident. When it is used for two necessary concomitants, one of which arises from the other or which are close to each other, it is still one metonymy, because the multiplicity of concomitants does not require multiplicity of the relation, nor repeated usage, since figurative meanings are derived from the relation and not from the lexical coinage. Thus the multiplicity of figurative senses for one word is broader than the use of a homonym. In any case, it is a metonymy according to what al-Sayyid chose in his gloss on al-Muṭawwal, in the chapter on inshā' (non-declarative speech), and its relation is necessary connection (luzūm). Al-Taftazānī hesitated in specifying its relation and said that it is among the matters on which no one has ventured an opinion.

[p. 475]

Al-birr, with a kasra on the bāʾ, means goodness in deeds, whether in matters of this world or the Hereafter, and in dealings. Its verb is usually of the pattern ʿalima, except for al-barr in an oath, which occurs in both the pattern ʿalima and the pattern ḍaraba. Among the transmitted sayings is that righteousness is threefold: righteousness in the worship of God, righteousness in regard to relatives, and righteousness in dealing with strangers. This follows from fulfilling goodness abundantly in the rights of these three domains.

Al-nisyān (forgetting) is the departure of a known matter from a person's memory due to weakness of mind or heedlessness. It is synonymous with al-sahw (inadvertence).
