It has been said that al-sahw is a slight heedlessness such that one wakes at the least reminder, whereas al-nisyān is its complete removal. Some lexicographers explained al-nisyān as mere abandonment in general, and the author of al-Asās considered this a metaphorical usage. This is the correct view, and it occurs frequently in the Qur'an. Here al-nisyān is used metaphorically for abandoning, deliberately or through negligence, what one should bear in mind regarding righteousness in some way.

It has been said concerning His saying ﴿Those who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Māʿūn: 5] that the meaning is: and you abandon yourselves in this respect, that is, in commanding them to righteousness; or: and you forget to command yourselves to righteousness. On this estimation, forgetting remains in its literal sense, because when a long time passed for them in neglecting to adorn themselves with the matters of religion and in daring to interpret revelation according to what their desires dictated without guidance, they came to forget that they were themselves engaged in the very things they forbade. So when they set themselves to admonish their people, or to preach to them, or to command them to good and forbid them from evil, they would forbid them from vices in which they themselves were already involved. But habituation to them caused them to forget these, and so it made them forget the command of their own souls to righteousness, because they had forgotten its cause. A person may see the fault of another because he observes it, but not see his own fault because he does not observe it, and because habit makes him forget his own condition. The remedy for this forgetting is self-examination. Thus righteousness refers to everything contained in the preceding commands in their details. They commanded others to these details and forgot themselves when hearing them. This includes believing in the religion of Islam, since it is among what the Torah contains, the Torah which they used to command the people to follow.

The clause ﴿And you forget yourselves﴾ may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the pronoun in "you command", in which case the object of rebuke and wonder is the commanding of people to righteousness qualified by being in a state of forgetting. It may also be a clause coordinated with "you command", in which case it is itself the object of rebuke and wonder, and His saying ﴿Do you command the people﴾ serves as a preface to it, meaning that the locus of the enormity that calls for censure is the combination of the two matters together.

From this you know that it is not to be supposed that the intent is a prohibition concerning the content of either clause. The intent is rebuke for the attribution of a horrendous state, which is not among the characteristics of sincere advisers, and not a prohibition. So do not fall into the perplexity of one who wonders about the sense of a prohibition in this, nor into the delusion of one who says that the verse indicates that a sinner may not command good or forbid evil, as al-Fakhr reported from them in his tafsir. For the intent is not a prohibition or a ruling of unlawfulness, but rather to express the enormity of the condition. This is shown by the fact that He concluded it with ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ and did not say ﴿Will you not then be mindful of God?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 65] or something similar.

Al-anfus is the plural of nafs, with the fāʾ pronounced with a sukūn. It denotes the whole of a person's self, consisting of the body and the spirit, as here. On the basis of this composite structure within the self, the word nafs has been used broadly in Arabic speech: sometimes for the whole self, as in the emphatic usage "So-and-so came himself" and in His saying ﴿A life for a life﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 45] and His saying ﴿You kill your own selves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85]; sometimes for a part, as in the speaker's saying "I disowned my self," and in His saying ﴿And you forget yourselves﴾; and sometimes for the inner perception, as in His saying ﴿You know what is in my self﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 116], meaning my inner mind. It is also applied to the spirit by which perception occurs: ﴿Indeed the self is greatly commanding to evil﴾ [Yūsuf: 53]. A fuller clarification of this will come at His saying ﴿On the Day when every self comes pleading for itself﴾ [al-Naḥl: 111] in Surat al-Naḥl.

His saying ﴿while you recite the Book﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya) by which the rebuke and wonder are further qualified. For their forgetting of themselves is more strange and more heinous when two things are with them that should remove it, namely commanding people to righteousness, since the nature of commanding righteousness is to remind the one who commands of his own soul's need for it when he is heedless of himself; and the recitation of the Book, that is, the Torah, through which they pass over commands and prohibitions, which should remind them of the contradiction between their condition and what they recite.

His saying ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ is an interrogative inquiring about the absence of their reasoning, used for denunciation and rebuke. They were treated as if their reason were absent, and so it was denied to them. The point of resemblance between their condition and that of those who do not reason is that one who continually neglects himself and neglects to reflect on his own well-being, while keeping company with two things that should remind him, has come close to being described as lacking reason.

The verb ta'qilūn (you reason) is treated as intransitive, or it is intransitive, and in this there is a proclamation of the completeness of their heedlessness and the disorder of their state. That this is a shameful and dreadful matter among human conditions is not doubted by any sensible person.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 2, verses 45–46:**

﴿Seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is burdensome except for the humble (khāshiʿīn),﴾ ﴿those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that they will return to Him.﴾

This is an address to the Children of Israel, guiding them to what will help them acquire all the commands and prohibitions He has enumerated for them, which lead to adorning oneself with praiseworthy qualities and divesting oneself of blameworthy ones. It has a most excellent effect in eloquence. When they were addressed with encouragement and warning, and with exaltation and disparagement, it was presumed of them that no path remained in their souls for Satan and no room for abandonment (khidhlān). It was presumed that they had been created eager to comply and to follow. Yet that old habituation weighs down their feet in stepping toward this straight path. So He described for them the remedy by which their righteousness is achieved, and He made patience and prayer into the two primary feathers of the wing.

The command to seek help through patience is because patience is the foundation of guidance. Among what turns nations away from following a sound religion is attachment to their ancient circumstances and the weakness of souls in bearing separation from them. When they arm themselves with patience, following the truth becomes easy for them.

As for seeking help through prayer, the intended meaning is to emphasize the command to it, which is found in His saying ﴿And establish prayer and give zakāt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43]. This is a demonstration of a good opinion of them, and it is a wondrous method among the methods of encouragement.

Among the exegetes is one who claimed that the address in His saying "seek help" etc. is to the Muslims, by way of a shift from one address to another. This is an error, because the presence of the conjunctive particle indicates otherwise. Moreover, His saying ﴿except for the humble﴾ means, by it, except for the believers, as is clarified by His saying ﴿those who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾ and so on. The only exception would be an instance of explicit noun in place of the pronoun, which is contrary to the apparent sense, in the absence of any reason for it. What deceived them into this interpretation is the assumption that one is not commanded to seek help through prayer if he has not yet believed. But what is strange about this? Close to it, just before, is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And establish prayer and give zakāt and bow with those who bow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43], addressed certainly to the Children of Israel.

Patience was defined by al-Ghazālī in *Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn* as the steadfastness of the motive of religion against the motive of desire. This is a definition specific to the legal (sharʿī) patience, and it is suitable to serve as an explanation of the verse, because the verse concerns legal patience. As for patience considered in itself, which is a quality of perfection, it is the endurance of the soul toward a matter that does not suit it, either because its outcome is agreeable, or because there is a great reward for it, so it resembles what has an agreeable outcome, or because of the inability to shift from it to something else, together with avoiding anxiety and impatience. Thus patience is endurance and steadfastness upon what is unsuitable. The least of its types is that which arises from inability. For this reason it is reported in the authentic collection: "Patience is only at the first shock." That is, complete patience is that which occurs before knowing that escape from that matter is impossible. Otherwise, patience at the belief that escape is impossible, when no anxiety or impatience issues from one, is patience in truth. Thus the form of restriction in His words "patience is only" is a restriction by claim to completeness, as in the saying "You are the man."

The word "prayer" here is intended in its legal meaning in Islam, and it is a totality of acts of praise of God, exalted is He, in speech, action, and belief. Therefore the seeking of help commanded here is necessarily related to two things: patience and gratitude. It has been said that faith is half patience and half gratitude, as in *al-Iḥyāʾ*, and this is a fine statement. Most virtues have patience as their foundation, since virtues flow from noble qualities, and noble qualities return to the strength of will and restraining the reins of the soul from following its desires, by turning back the two forces, the appetitive and the irascible, from what does not yield perfection or from what produces deficiency. So patience is the foundation of the virtues. Forbearance, generosity, learning, piety, courage, justice, and work on earth and the like are nothing but kinds of patience.

Among what is transmitted from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: "Courage is an hour's patience." Zufar ibn al-Ḥārith al-Kilābī said, excusing his people's defeat:

*We gave them a cup, and they gave us its like, but they were more patient in the face of death.*

Sufficient to show the excellence of patience is that God made it the completer of the cause of success in His saying ﴿By time﴾ [al-ʿAṣr: 1], ﴿indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-ʿAṣr: 2], ﴿except those who believed and did righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [al-ʿAṣr: 3]. And here He said ﴿seek help through patience and prayer﴾. Al-Ghazālī said: God mentioned patience in the Qur'an in over seventy places, and He attributed most good and ranks to patience and made them its fruit. So the Mighty and Majestic said ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient﴾ [al-Sajdah: 24], and He said ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled upon the Children of Israel because of what they patiently endured﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 137], and He said ﴿Indeed, God is with the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153]. End of quotation.

If you reflect, you will find that the root of religiosity and faith is among kinds of patience. For in it is the opposition of the soul to its desire and its habitual attachments, in affirming what is unseen by the sense to which it is accustomed, and in obeying one of its own kind whom it does not see as superior in creation, and in opposing the custom of its fathers and peoples from earlier religions.

When patience becomes a character trait of its possessor, it makes easy for him the opposition to all of that for the sake of truth and proof. Thus the aspect of the command to seek help toward faith and what branches from it through patience becomes clear, for it is a trait that opens the doors of souls to accepting what they have been commanded in this regard.

As for seeking help through prayer, this is because prayer is gratitude, and gratitude reminds one of the blessing, which moves one to obey the Benefactor. Moreover, in prayer there is patience in several respects: in opposing a person's habitual state, and in adhering to a state at a specified time from which he is not permitted to lag behind or depart. Furthermore, in prayer there is a divine secret, perhaps arising from the manifestation of the Lord's good pleasure upon the one praying. For this reason we find in prayer a great secret in dispelling sorrows and removing the distress of the soul. It has been reported in a ḥadīth that "when the Prophet ﷺ was distressed (ḥazabahu, with the letters zāy and bāʾ), that is, when a matter befell him, he turned to prayer." This is something that whoever observes those who pray will find. And God, exalted is He, said ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 45], because it combines various kinds of worship.

As for gratitude, considered in itself, as an aid to good, it is among the requirements of His saying ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 7].

His saying ﴿and indeed, it is burdensome﴾: the exegetes differed about the referent of the pronoun in "indeed, it" (innahā). It has been said that it refers to prayer, and the meaning is: prayer is difficult upon souls because it is a prison for the soul. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the seeking of help through patience and prayer, understood from "seek help," in the manner of His saying ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 8]. And it has been said that it refers to the preceding commands from His saying ﴿Remember My favor﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40] up to His saying ﴿and seek help through patience and prayer﴾. This last view is one that al-Kashshāf's author permitted, and perhaps it is one of his original ideas. It is the clearest of the sayings and the most comprehensive, and the interpretations are all admissible.

What is meant by "burdensome" (kabīrah) here is difficult, something that is hard upon souls. The application of greatness to a difficult and arduous matter is a well-known metaphor in the speech of the Arabs, because hardship is a necessary consequence of a great matter in bearing or achieving it. God, exalted is He, said ﴿And indeed, it would have been burdensome except upon those whom God has guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], and He said ﴿And if their turning away has been difficult for you﴾ [al-Anʿām: 35], the verse. And He said ﴿Difficult for the polytheists is that to which you call them﴾ [al-Shūrā: 13].

His saying ﴿except upon the humble﴾: that is, those who are characterized by humility (khushūʿ). Khushūʿ linguistically is withdrawing and lowering. Al-Nābighah said:

*And a boundary-stone like the stump of a pool, its edge worn away, humbled.*

That is, the height of its sides has disappeared. Submission (tadhallul) is khushūʿ. Jaʿfar ibn ʿAbla al-Ḥārithī said:

*So do not think that I have become humble after you for anything, nor that I fear death.*

It is a metaphor for the humbling of the soul, which is stillness and contraction from turning toward refusal or disobedience. What is meant by the humble here is one who subdues his soul, breaks its ferocity, and accustoms it to be at rest in God's command, seeking good outcomes, and not to be deceived by what present desire adorns. This one, whose soul has this description, has readied itself to accept good.

It seems that what is meant by the humble here are the fearful, those who look to outcomes, so that seeking help through patience and prayer is light for them, together with the restraint of the soul in patience, and the commitment to specified times and purity in periods in which the servant may be occupied with what he desires or with what gains him wealth or pleasure. Close to this is the saying of Kuthayyir:

*I said to her: "O ʿAzz, every calamity, when the soul has made itself ready for it one day, becomes humbled."*

I suppose that the legislation of many rulings, of which the most important is fasting, was intended by the Lawgiver to achieve this meaning. It is not correct to restrict khushūʿ here to khushūʿ specifically in prayer, on account of the state arising in the soul from the servant's sense of standing before God, exalted is He, as Ibn Rushd explained at the beginning of the first question in the book of prayer in *al-Bayān wa al-Taḥṣīl*. For that, which is the meaning indicated by His saying ﴿The believers have certainly succeeded﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 1], ﴿who are humble in their prayer﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 2], is all among the attributes of prayer and the perfection of the one praying. So it is not correct that it be what lightens the burden of prayer upon one who seeks help through prayer, as is not hidden.

God, exalted is He, described the humble as ﴿those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that they will return to Him.﴾ This is a relative clause that has a close connection with the meaning of khushūʿ. So it carries the sense of explanation of "the humble" and the sense of stating the source of their humility. This indicates that what is meant by ẓann here is the firm conviction. The use of ẓann in the speech of the Arabs in the sense of certainty is very common. Aws ibn Ḥajar, describing a hunter who shot a wild ass with an arrow, said:

*He released it, certain of the assumption that it [the arrow] pierces between the lower ribs, penetrating.*

Durayd ibn al-Ṣimmah said:

*I said to them: "Assume you face two thousand armored men, their chieftains upon saddled Persian horses."*

So it is shared between firm conviction and dominant conviction. Meeting (mulāqāh) and returning (rujūʿ) here are two metaphors for reckoning and resurrection, or for seeing and reward, because the literal sense of meeting, which is the nearness of two bodies, and the literal sense of returning, which is arriving at a place from which one departed, are impossible here.

What is intended by His saying ﴿and indeed, it is burdensome﴾ and so on is an indirect allusion to praise of the Muslims, and an exhortation to the Children of Israel to be resolute in imitating the believers. And if the address in "seek help" is taken to be to the Muslims, then His saying ﴿and indeed, it is burdensome﴾ becomes an indirect allusion to others, namely the Jews and the hypocrites.

Mulāqāh is a form of the verb laqiya, and liqāʾ is presence, as already mentioned in His saying ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37]. What is meant here is presence before God for reckoning, that is, those who believe in the resurrection. A detailed explanation of it will come at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And fear God, and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223], in this sūrah, and in Sūrat al-Anʿām at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They have certainly lost who denied the meeting with God﴾ [al-Anʿām: 31].
