Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 47:

[Page 482]
﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾

The address to the Children of Israel is repeated in the form of a vocative (nida'), resembling what occurred in their first address, for the purpose of repetition, to give emphasis to this address and to what follows from it. The first address was intended to remind them of the favours of Allah Most High, so that this reminder would be a motivation to comply with what comes to them from Allah in the form of commands and prohibitions, through His Prophet (ﷺ). However, since the aim intended from that was compliance, the rule of eloquence (balaghah) is that the eloquent speaker should reach the intended goal and not lengthen the introduction. Rather, he touches upon it briefly and alludes to it in summary, drawing attention to the goal, given the great importance of that goal. Orators and eloquent speakers have always regarded such conduct as a mark of the orator's acuity, and they mention it in praise of the vizier of al-Andalus, Muhammad ibn al-Khatib al-Salmani, when he said, while on his embassy from the king of Granada to the king of the Maghrib, Ibn 'Anan, his famous verses which he improvised upon entering to him, whose opening is:

O Caliph of Allah, fortune has aided your loftiness, as the moon has not shone in the darkness.
Then he said:

All the people in the land of al-Andalus, ∗∗∗ had they not been for you, would not have settled nor flourished.

Their souls have distressed them, ∗∗∗ so they directed me to you and waited.
Then Abu 'Anan said to him: "You will not return to them except with all of your demands." He permitted him to sit, and he greeted him. The judge Abu al-Qasim al-Sharif, who was among the delegation, said: "We have never heard of an envoy who concluded his embassy before greeting the sultan, except this one."

Thus, brevity in the introduction fulfilled the right of its precedence by being placed first; reaching the intended goal fulfilled its right of attention; and returning to the detailed enumeration of the favours fulfilled their right of being counted. For the mention of favours is an exaltation of the Bestower, an honouring of the one bestowed upon, and an admonition to him and to whomever the news of that reaches, which stirs one to gratitude.

[Page 483]
Thus, the repetition here carries the subtlety of combining the two statements after they had been separated, and the subtlety of enumeration, since it contains a summary of the meaning of favour.

The word "favour" (ni'mah) here is intended to mean all favours, because it is a noun in the genitive construction (jins mudaf), and so it has the ruling of the plural, as in His Most High saying: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, I shall fulfil your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]. And His Most High saying: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ is conjoined to "My favour," meaning: and remember My preferring you over the worlds. This preference is a specific favour, so its conjunction to "My favour" is a specific conjunction to a general one. It is the starting point for the detailing and enumeration of the favours. Perhaps the enumeration of favours is sufficient in lieu of a command to obedience and compliance, because it is part of the nature of noble souls to comply with the command of the Benefactor, since favour generates love. Mansur al-Warraq said:

You disobey God while you show His love; by my life, this is a wondrous thing in analogy.

Had your love been sincere, you would have obeyed Him; indeed, the lover is obedient to the one he loves.

This reminder is intended to urge one to adopt what befits that favour and to preserve that bounty.

The meaning of "the worlds" was explained at His saying: ﴿Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2]. The intended meaning here is a category of created beings. There is no doubt that created beings are classified into diverse kinds according to the classification of the speaker or the listener. Thus, "the worlds" in the context of mentioning creation are the kinds of created beings, such as humankind, animals, birds, and fish. "The worlds" in the context of mentioning the virtues of creation, or of nations, or of tribes, refers to the kinds of that which is being spoken of. Therefore, it is inevitable that the intended meaning of "the worlds" here is the human nations, encompassing all nations, since it is a plural definite with the article (al-); however, its generality here is customary (
'urfi), restricted to the nations of their time, just as the plural "the goldsmiths" in the phrase of the amir is restricted to the goldsmiths of his place, i.e., his city. It is also restricted to the well-known nations, just as the plural "the goldsmiths" is restricted to those who take goldsmithing as a profession, rather than everyone who knows goldsmithing. This is like your saying, "He is the most famous of scholars and the most distinguished of students." Thus the verse points to the preference of the Children of Israel, the addressees or their predecessors, over the nations of their era, not over some groups that followed a complete religion, such as the Christians of Najran. It has no connection to the question of preferring the prophets over the angels in any way. Nor does one heed what deviates within every nation or tribe in the form of individuals. Therefore, it does not entail the preference of every individual of the Children of Israel over individuals of other nations who attained a righteous rank or prophethood, because preference in such matters is intended as the preference of the whole group, just as you say, "Quraysh is more excellent than Tayy," even though among Tayy there was Hatim the generous.

[Page 484]
Likewise, the preference of the Children of Israel is over all the nations of their era, and among those nations are great nations such as the Arabs, the Persians, the Romans, the Indians, and the Chinese, among whom were scholars, sages, reformers, and prophets, because it is the preference of a whole over a whole in all eras. The meaning of this preference is that Allah had gathered for them the praiseworthy qualities which nations and tribes are characterised by, which He did not gather for others. These are: nobility of lineage; perfection of character; soundness of creed; breadth of law; freedom; courage; and the care of Allah Most High for them in all their conditions. This is alluded to in the verse: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you when He appointed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone of the worlds"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 20]. These attributes were established for their predecessors at the time when they were combined. It is well known that virtues accrue to later generations through a good reputation, even if the addressees on that day were not in a state of preference over the worlds; rather, they were reminded of what their forebears had been. The virtues of nations are not assessed by individuals or by particular eras. As for the qualification of the favour with the phrase ﴿which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40], its explanation has passed in its sister verse earlier.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 48:**

﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any ransom be taken from it, nor will they be helped.﴾

He connects the warning (al-tahdhir) to the reminder (al-tadhkir). When He reminded them of the blessing, especially their being preferred over the worlds of their time, and this was the source of their delusion, since they took it as an inherent preference, they supposed that falling short in righteous deeds would not harm them. So He followed it with a warning against this.

Here taqwa (piety, guarding oneself) is used in its linguistic sense, not its technical legal sense. Yawman (a Day) is in the accusative as a direct object (maf'ul bihi), not as an adverb of time (zarf). For this reason it was not read without tanwin (nunation).

Fearing the Day means guarding oneself against what happens in it of terrors and punishment. It is thus a case of using the name of a time for what occurs in it, as when you say "makan makhuf" (a dreadful place).

*Tujza* is the imperfect of *jaza*, which in the sense of "to fulfil on someone's behalf" (qada haqqan 'an ghayrih) is transitive with *'an* to one of its two objects. So *shay'an* is its first object. It is also permissible for it to be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) if some kind of recompense is meant, with the object then omitted.

[Page 485]

The clause *la tajzi nafs* is a qualifier (sifa) of *yawman*. The rule is that a clause functioning as a predicate, qualifier, circumstantial (hal) or relative complement (silah) should contain a pronoun referring back to what it modifies. This pronoun is often omitted when it is in the accusative or is a pronoun governed by a preposition, and it is then omitted together with its preposition, especially when the preposition is known because the verb in the clause only takes one specific preposition, as is the case here. Its omission is allowed because the omitted element is determined by the sentence. It may also be omitted when there is an indicator (qarina), as in the omission of the relative pronoun when it is governed by the same preposition that governs the relative noun. A parallel to this omission is the verse of al-'Uryan al-Jarmi of the Jarm of Tayy:

*Fa-qultu laha: la wal-ladhi hajja Hatimun*
*Akhununki 'ahdan innani ghayru khawwan*

(I said to her: "No, by Him to whom Hatim made pilgrimage,
I will be faithful to you in covenant; I am not a betrayer.")

The estimate is: *hajja Hatimun ilayhi* (Hatim made pilgrimage to Him).

The indefiniteness of *nafs* in both places, while it falls within the scope of negation, indicates the generality of souls: that is, it does not avail anyone, whoever he may be. Thus the idols and intercessors of the unbelievers will not avail them, whatever their creeds about those beings' help. The meaning is the negation of their help to them by standing between them and the punishment of God the Exalted, that is, the negation that they would offer a recompense that would prevent God from requiting them with evil, out of regard for their allies. Here what is meant is help through the respect due to a person and the fear of his anger. This is the help of a match for the enemy, whom the enemy fears, as was known among the nations of that day: their guarding themselves against the might of their enemies' master, and their refraining from what would incur his anger out of fear of his deceit, his harm, or the denial of his benefit. Al-Samaw'al said:

*Wa ma darranaa anna qalilun wa jaruna*
*'Azizun wa jaru al-akthareena dhalilu*

(It does us no harm that we are few, while our protector is mighty,
and the protector of the many is humbled.)

And al-'Anbari said:

*Law kuntu min Mazinin lam tastabih ibili*
*Banu al-Shaqiqati min Dhuhlin ibn Shaybana*

(Had I been of Mazin, the sons of al-Shaqiqa of Dhuhl ibn Shayban would not have seized my camels.)

By this it becomes clear that the import of His words *la tajzi nafs 'an nafsin shay'an* differs from what is mentioned after it in His words *wa la yuqbalu minha shafa'a* and so on. His words *la tajzi nafs 'an nafsin shay'an* have the same meaning as God's words: *yawma la tamliku nafsun linafsin shay'an wal-amru yawma'idhin lillah* ("The Day when no soul will have power for another soul at all, and the command that Day is God's" [82:19]). As for His words *wa la yuqbalu minha shafa'a wa la yu'khadhu minha 'adl*, the two pronouns refer to the second *nafs*, governed by *'an*. That is: no intercession that it brings will be accepted from a soul, and no ransom by which it might be compensated will be accepted, because the primary aim is to invalidate a belief that excuses the criminal from God's punishment unless God wills it. Thus the pronoun in His words *wa la hum yunsarun* [Page 486] refers back to the referent of the two pronouns before it. This despair entails the belittling of those whom the unbelievers supposed to be intercessors, and the refutation of what they claimed would shield them from God's wrath through the offerings they made and the disputations they prepared, saying: "These are our intercessors with God." (Cf. the verse: *yawma ta'ti kullu nafsin tujadilu 'an nafsiha*, "The Day when every soul will come pleading for itself" [16:111].)

Some exegetes interpreted His words *la tajzi nafs 'an nafsin shay'an* in a way that encompasses recompense in general. Thus they made what is mentioned after it a case of specific after general. For this reason Shaykh Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This verse encompasses the meanings by which the children of Adam were accustomed to be rescued in this world, for one who is in distress is not freed except by being interceded for, or ransomed, or helped." End of quote. He omitted gathering them under the condition that people avoid bringing him into distress out of fear of his allies. What we have explained is more elegant.

The speech of the elders of the Banu Asad was gathered together when they spoke with Imru' al-Qays concerning the blood of his father. They said: "The best of the conditions in this matter is that you recognise your obligation in one of three things: either that you choose from the Banu Asad the most noble of their houses and we deliver him to you with a rope that goes with the edges of your sword, along with the rest of its sheath; or a ransom from what the Banu Asad's herds bring each evening, and they are thousands. Or you make a truce with us until the pregnant women give birth, the waistcloths are let down and the veils are tied over the banners." End of quote.

The majority read *wa la yuqbalu* with a yā' (the masculine form), the yā' of the imperfect with a masculine subject, to match His words after it: *wa la yu'khadhu minha 'adl*. It is permissible for every feminine noun that is not truly feminine to be treated as masculine, because the masculine form is the basic form in speech and so requires no reason. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a tā' (feminine form), in regard for the feminine form of the word *shafa'a*.

*Al-shafa'a* (intercession) is the striving and mediation for obtaining a benefit or warding off harm, whether the mediation is at the request of the one who benefits, or is merely the striving of the mediator. The one who asks for intercession is called *mustashfi'*.

It is derived from *al-shaf'* (pair), because the seeker or the penitent comes alone; when he finds no acceptance he goes and brings someone whom he uses as a means, and that second person becomes an intercessor (*shafi'*) for the first, that is, his state becomes a pair (*shaf'*).

*Al-'adl* (with a fatha on the 'ayn) means compensation and ransom. It was named with the verbal noun because the redeemer equates the redeemed with its like in value or substance and makes them equal. It is said *'adala kadha bikadha*, meaning he made the one equal to the other.

*Al-nasr* (help) is aiding the opponent in war or otherwise by the strength and dominance of the helper.

The subject was placed first for the sake of added emphasis, which indicates that the negation of their help is certain, beyond what is conveyed by the negation of the verb with its ascription to the passive voice, as we have indicated just above.

The Jews used to suppose, or believe, that their connection to the prophets and the honour of their forefathers before God would place them in safety from His punishment for disobedience and rebellion, as is the way of nations in the dawn of their ignorance and decline.

[Page 487]

His words, exalted is He, have indicated this: *wa qalati al-yahudu wal-nasara nahnu abna'u Allahi wa ahibbau'uhu qul fa-lima yu'adhdhibukum bidhunubikum* ("The Jews and the Christians said: 'We are the sons of God and His beloved.' Say: 'Then why does He punish you for your sins?'" [5:18]). The Mu'tazila have held fast to this verse as evidence for their doctrine of denying intercession for the people of major sins on the Day of Resurrection, on account of the generality of *nafs* in a negated context, which requires that every soul be such that intercession is not accepted from it. They hold that this generality was not restricted by anything else. The matter is disputed between the Mu'tazila and the followers of al-Ash'ari.

The Muslims agreed on the existence of intercession on the Day of Resurrection for the obedient and the penitent, to raise their ranks. The Ash'aris and the Mu'tazila did not differ on this. Thus this is a consensus on the initial restriction of the generality. The disagreement concerns intercession for the people of major sins. According to us, intercession for them occurs with respect to the reduction of their evil deeds at the time of reckoning, or after entering Hell, because of the sound hadiths that are well known on this, such as his words (ﷺ): "Every prophet has a granted supplication, and I have saved my supplication as an intercession for my community." And other such reports. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani said: "The reports on this have reached the level of being mutawatir in meaning" (widely transmitted in sense, *mutawatir ma'nawi*, meaning that the content is established by many reports even if each report differs in wording), as al-Qurtubi indicated when quoting his words.

According to the Mu'tazila, there is no intercession for the people of major sins, for several reasons. Among them are the verses that indicate that intercession does not benefit, such as this verse, and His words: *fa-ma tanfa'uhum shafa'atu al-shafi'in* ("So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them" [74:48]); *min qabli an ya'tiya yawmun la bay'a fihi wa la khullatun wa la shafa'a* ("before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession" [2:254]); *ma lilzalimina min hamimin wa la shafi'" ("The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor intercessor" [40:18]). They said: "Disobedience is wrongdoing." Among them is His words: *wa la yashfa'una illa limani artada* ("And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves" [21:28]), and the person of a major sin is not one who is approved. Among them is His words: *faghfir lilladhina tabu* ("So forgive those who repent" [40:7]). The answer to all of these is that the location of all of that is the unbelievers, reconciling the evidences, and that His words *li-man artada* [21:28] indicate that there is permission for intercession, as He said: *illa li-man adhina lahu* ("except for one whom He has permitted" [34:23]). Otherwise Islam together with the commission of some sins would be equal to unbelief, and the wisdom of God does not accept this. As for His words *faghfir lilladhina tabu* [40:7], it is a supplication, not an intercession.

It appears that what prompted the Mu'tazila to deny intercession is that it contradicts the eternal punishment of the person of major sin, which is the doctrine of the majority of them, who interpreted the saying of Wasil ibn 'Ata' about "the intermediate position between the two positions" to mean that the disobedient is given the ruling of the Muslim in this world and the ruling of the unbeliever in the Hereafter. There is no doubt that intercession contradicts this principle. So what they held fast to of the verses is only for the purpose of asserting eternity, and to oppose the evidences of the People of the Sunna with their like.

[Page 488]

We have not seen their answer concerning the hadith of intercession, and I suppose that they answer it by saying that single-transmitted reports (akhbar al-ahad) do not overturn the foundations of religion. That is why al-Qadi Abu Bakr had to argue from mutawatir in meaning. The truth is that the matter is more closely related to the subsidiary rulings (furu') than to the foundations (usul), because it does not concern the essence of God or His attributes. Even if we went along with them in saying that it is obligatory to reward the obedient and punish the disobedient, the wisdom would still appear without eternity, and with the occurrence of intercession after remaining in punishment. So since we do not find in establishing intercession anything that overturns their foundations, we say to them: "This is nonetheless a legal ruling concerning the one who has committed a major sin and has not repented, and it is received from the Lawgiver. On this basis, the punishment is limited to a specific period, or until God's pardon occurs, or together with intercession. Perhaps intercession occurs when God wills to end the period of punishment."

Furthermore, it is required by wisdom that unbelievers and sinners not be equal in the duration of punishment or in its measure. This is a weak opinion among their views, even by the standard of their own principles. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani relates the consensus of the community before the emergence of innovations on the existence of intercession in the Hereafter, and this is the truth. Sawad ibn Qarib said, addressing the Messenger of God (ﷺ):

*Fa-kun li shafi'an yawma la dhu shafa'atin*
*Bi-mughnin fatilan 'an Sawadi ibn Qaribi*

(So be for me an intercessor on a Day when no one with intercession
will avail a fatil (a trifle) on behalf of Sawad ibn Qarib.)

As for the Great Intercession (al-shafa'a al-kubra), which is general for all the people of the standing place of reckoning, concerning which there is the sound and well-known hadith, the principles of the Mu'tazila do not reject it.

His words, *wa la yu'khadhu minha 'adl*: *al-'adl* (with a fatha on the 'ayn) is applied to a thing that is equal to another thing and like it. For this reason, what is given as a ransom for something is called *'adl*, and this is what is meant here, as in His words: *aw 'adlu dhalika siyaman* ("or its equivalent in fasting" [5:95]). So the meaning is: "nor will there be accepted from it" what it might ransom itself with as a substitute for its crime.

Help (*nasr*) is aiding an enemy against his enemy and opponent, either by standing with him in defence or by attacking with him. In common usage it is meant as defence by one's own strength. As for its application to defence by argument, as in *man ansari ila Allah* ("Who are my helpers toward God?" [3:52]), and to partisanship and following, as in *in tansuru Allaha yansurkum* ("If you help God, He will help you" [47:7]), it is a metaphor.

[Page 489]

**"And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted on you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord"** (2:49). This is coordinated ('atf) with His words "My favour," so that *idh* (when) is treated as an object (mafʿul bihi), as in His words: **"And remember when you were few and He multiplied you"** (7:86). Here it is a noun of time that is not an adverb (zarf) of a verb, and the implied meaning is: "Remember the time when We delivered you." Since nouns of time are commonly followed by clauses, and the clause after them has the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar), the implied meaning is: "Remember the time of Our delivering you."

The purpose of using this construction rather than the explicit verbal noun is that by using *idh*, which introduces a clause, the wondrous scene produced by the form of the verb is brought to mind. When the mind conceives of a verbal noun, it conceives only the meaning of an event; but when it hears a clause that indicates it, it conceives the occurrence of the act together with its agent, object and related elements all at once, and thus a wondrous image arises. So the effect of using the verbal noun is like that of a single-word metaphor (isti'ara mufrada), and the effect of using the verb is like that of an allegorical metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya).

It is not coordinated with the clause "Remember" (udhkurū), as some exegetes have stated, because that would make *idh* an adverb of time, which requires an element it depends on, and there is none. Nor does the conjunctive particle serve this purpose, because the conjunction in the coordination of clauses only conveys sharing in the ruling of the clause coordinated with; it does not stand in for a governing word. Do not be disturbed by the separation between the coordinated and that to which it is coordinated, namely "And when We delivered you" and the clause "And fear a Day," for you may think it is a sign of coordination with the clause. As you have learned earlier, His words "And fear" arise from the reminder, so it is connected to the discourse and is not foreign to it. Moreover, there is nothing in the grammarians' statements that requires the prohibition of separating the coordinated from that to which it is coordinated by a foreign element, since the two coordinated elements are not in the closeness of the governor and the governed.

He has transitively linked the verb *anjayna* (We delivered) to the pronoun of the addressees, although the deliverance was in fact of their ancestors. This is because the deliverance of their ancestors is a deliverance for their descendants, for if their ancestors had remained in Pharaoh's torment, that would have extended to their descendants. Therefore the favour of deliverance was two favours: a favour upon the earlier generation and a favour upon the later generation, and so its thanks was obligatory upon each generation among them. For this reason their law obliged them to celebrate, on each year, the days corresponding to the days of this blessing upon them; these are their festivals. And Allah said to Moses: **"And remind them of the days of Allah"** (14:5).

*Āl* (family/people) of a man means his household. The origin of *āl* is *ahl*; its *h* was changed to a hamza for lightness, so that by this the hamza could be eased into a long vowel. The evidence that its origin is *ahl* is that the *h* returns in diminutive form, for they say *uhayl*, and *uwayl* has not been heard, contrary to al-Kisa'i.

**[Page 490]**

*Ahl* and *āl* are used to mean relatives, kinsfolk, clients, and especially a person and his followers. What is meant by "the people of Pharaoh" is his guards (wuzʿa) and his agents. *Āl* is specifically attached to someone of worldly rank and honour among rational beings; so one does not say "the *āl* of the criminal" or "the *āl* of Mecca." Since Pharaoh was great in this world, and the address concerned a worldly deliverance from a worldly great power, the term *āl* was applied to his followers. So there is no hesitation about this, such that it would need to be interpreted as sarcasm, as was the case with His words **"Enter, O people of Pharaoh, the severest torment"** (40:46), because that is a quotation of words to be said on the Day of Resurrection, when Pharaoh will be humiliated and his dominion gone.

If you say: The word *ahl* is also used for the relatives of a person of rank, since it is the general term, so why was it not used here, so that the phrase would not apply to the people of Pharaoh in a way that praises them? I answer: The particular feature of the word *āl* here is that the context is the magnification of the favour and the full giving of its due thanks, and a favour is magnified by what surrounds it. Deliverance from torment, although it is a favour in absolute terms, is greater when the torment is from a powerful and eminent person, because hardly anyone escapes from him, as the poet said:

*"There is no stability at the roar of a lion."*

The deliverance is attributed to the people of Pharaoh rather than to Pharaoh himself, although he was the one who commanded the torment of the Children of Israel, as a linking of the act with one of its related persons, according to the rational figurative attribution (ḥaqīqa ʿaqliyya), and as an alert that these guards and those charged with the Children of Israel were exceeding the limit commanded in oppression, in the manner of executors, for they are less merciful and narrower in spirit than rulers. As the poet al-Ra'i said, addressing ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan:

*"Indeed those whom you ordered to act justly
did not do, of what you ordered, even a fatil."*

History records that the beginning of the settlement of the Children of Israel in Egypt was due to Joseph, peace be upon him, entering into the care of al-Aziz Tifar, the chief of police of Pharaoh.

**[Page 491]**

Egypt was divided into two parts: Upper Egypt, the southern part, known today as the Sa'id, ruled by Coptic pharaohs, whose capital was Thebes (Tiwa); and Lower Egypt, the northern part, whose capital was Memphis (Manfis), which was the great capital and the seat of the pharaohs. The latter had been overcome by the Amalekites, of the Semites, cousins of Thamud, who are called in Egyptian history the "Wandering Shepherds" and the "Hyksos," around the year 3300 or 1900 BCE, with disagreement arising from disagreement over the length of their stay in Egypt, which ended around 1700 BCE, at the rise of the Eighteenth Dynasty.

So Joseph was with the chief of police of Pharaoh, who was an Amalekite. The name of the Pharaoh at that time was Apophis or Abibi. The people of the stories and those who took their words from the exegetes called him Rayyan ibn al-Walid; this is one of their illusions. This was around the year 1739 BCE. Then the Children of Israel dwelt in Egypt because Jacob and his sons moved to Egypt when the matter of Joseph became manifest and the rule of the Lower Egyptian kingdom came into his hand.

The relations of the Israelites with the Egyptians were good for a long time, but the Israelites preserved their religion, their language and their customs; they did not worship the gods of the Egyptians, and they all settled in a region called the land of Goshen. The Israelites remained in this state for about four hundred years, during which the Egyptian kings overcame the Amalekite kings and expelled them from Egypt, until the Nineteenth Dynasty arose in Egypt, whose kings ruled all the Egyptian lands. Among them emerged Ramesses II, called "the Great," around the year 1311 BCE. He was a brave warrior, and the kingdoms which his father had subjugated rose against him, including the peoples on the borders of the Arabian Peninsula. So circumstances, or bad suspicions, led to the Copts turning against the Israelites; they imposed the hardest labours on them and enslaved them in service of the fields, the buildings, and the making of bricks.

The Torah says that they built for Pharaoh the storage city of Pithom (Pithom) and the city of Raamses. Then Pharaoh feared that the Israelites would be helpers to his enemies against him, and he ordered their extermination. It seems that he had learned of some assistance from them to their kinsmen, the Amalekites and the Arabs, so he ordered the slaughter of their sons, the capture of their women, and the enslavement of their elders. This must have been because of what he saw of their turning against him, or because the Copts, when they overused the Hebrews in service, Pharaoh knew that if his armies became entangled in a war, he would not be safe from an uprising of the Israelites, so he ordered their extermination.

As for what the storytellers relate, that a priest told Pharaoh that the loss of his kingdom would come at the hand of a youth from the Israelites, I do not think it is sound, for it is unlikely that such a thing would be circulated

**[Page 492]**

among the ruler of a kingdom so that he would destroy a group of his subjects because of it. Unless the priests had incited Pharaoh against the Jews intentionally, in order to free the kingdom from foreigners; or they had perceived ill intentions among the Children of Israel and fabricated that priestly prophecy in order to persuade Pharaoh of the necessity of caution toward the Israelites. It is also possible that the slaughter of the sons was an act of the Egyptians, done out of contempt for the Jews, so that they would kill a Jew over a minor quarrel, as the verse indicates: **"So the one from his faction sought his help against the one from his enemy"** (28:15). The conclusion is that history indicates in general that a great enmity arose between the Copts and the Jews, which ended with the Copts uprooting the Israelites.

The Qur'an was marvellous in summarizing it, since its detailed accounts were numerous, and the purpose of the reminder does not depend on explaining them.

The clause **"who inflicted on you the worst torment"** is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "the people of Pharaoh," by which is made clear what the deliverance was from, namely the severe torment which the Israelites suffered from the treatment of the Copts toward them.

The meaning of *yasumūnakum* is "they treat you in the manner of one who is humiliated by what he has been subjected to." It is said *sāmahu khasfan* when one humiliates and despises him; so *sāma* is used in the sense of "to inflict" and "to give," and for this reason it takes two objects, which are not originally the subject and predicate. The literal sense of *sāma* is to put forward a price (*sawm*), that is, a price.

*Sū' al-ʿadhāb* means its worst and most appalling form; it is the torment of forced labour and exhaustion, and the imposition of severe punishment through the slaughter of sons and the capture of women. The meaning is: "They slaughter the sons of your fathers and spare the women of your earlier people."

As for "the sons," it has been said that it means the children of the Jews; and it has been said that men are meant, by the evidence of its being contrasted with "women." This second view is more apparent and more fitting to the conditions of peoples, since it is presumed that extermination and uprooting are aimed at adults; and because on the first view the verse would be silent about men, unless it is said that they used to slaughter the young to cut off descent, and take the mothers as slaves, and keep the men for service until they died out gradually.

To keep men in such a condition is harder than killing them. Or perhaps there was a failing from the women of the Children of Israel, the nursing mothers and the raising mothers of the young, and its cause was their preoccupation with the affairs of their sons; so whenever their oppressors became angry at that, they killed the infant.

*Istiḥyāʾ* is a form X (istif'āl) which indicates a seeking of life, that is, they keep them alive or they seek their lives. The reason it is mentioned here, in the context of reminding them of the calamities that befell them, is that this sparing of the women had an evil purpose, namely that they would violate their honour, and they would have no choice but to comply, by the rule of captivity and enslavement. So His words "and spare your women" are a metonymy (kināya) for a particular sparing; and for this reason it was included in the reference in His words **"and in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord"** (2:49). Had the intended meaning of sparing been its apparent sense, there would have been no reason for its being coordinated with that calamity.

**[Page 493]**

It has also been said that *istiḥyāʾ* is from *ḥayāʾ* (modesty/shame), which means the private parts, that is, they examine the women in their wombs to know whether there is a pregnancy in them. This is very far-fetched. Better than this would be to say that it is a metonymy, as we mentioned just above.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary, part 2 of 2, on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 49.

The Torah has related that Pharaoh instructed the midwives to kill every male newborn. The clause ﴿They slaughter your sons﴾ and what follows is an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿they inflicted upon you the worst torment﴾. Accordingly, the intended meaning of "the worst torment" here is specifically the slaughtering of the sons and what is conjoined to it, namely ﴿and let your women live﴾, since, as you have understood, both of them are an explanation of "the worst torment." Therefore any other form of torment is not considered significant in comparison with this.

You may also make the clause a substitute (badal) of part (badal al-ba'd), specifying the greatest states of the worst torment by mention. This is what agrees with the verse in Surah Ibrahim in which it is mentioned ﴿and they slaughter your sons﴾ [Ibrahim: 6] by conjunction (ʿatf) upon "the worst torment." The phrase "and they let your women live" is not a new independent sentence completing the detail of Pharaoh's conduct; rather it is part of the explanation (bayan) or substitution (badal) for the torment. What supports this is the verse elsewhere: ﴿He slaughters their sons and lets their women live; indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾ [al-Qasas: 4], where He followed the two verbs with His saying, "indeed, he was among the corrupters."

Al-balaʾ (بلاء): testing (al-ikhtibar) through good and evil. God the Exalted said: ﴿And We tested them with good things and bad things﴾ [al-A'raf: 168]. It is a well-known metaphor (majaz mashhur), whose original meaning is the wearing and decay of a garment (balaʾ al-thawb), with the ba' pronounced with a fatha and a long vowel, or with a kasra and a short vowel, meaning its becoming worn and threadbare. Since testing entails distress and weariness, it was called balaʾ, as if it wears down the self. Then it spread to testing through evil, because it is more distressing to the self. Its most familiar usage, when used without qualification, is for evil, and when they intend good by it they need a qarina (indicator) or an explicit statement, as in the saying of Zuhayr:

May God reward with goodness what the two of them did with you,
And what the two of them tested you with, the best of testing that tests.

It is therefore generally applied to the calamity that befalls the servant, because through it the measure of patience and forbearance is tested. The intended meaning here is calamity, as shown by His saying "a great" (ʿaẓīm). It has been said that He meant by it deliverance, and that balaʾ means testing of gratitude, but this is distant here.

The deliverance (al-injaʾ) is connected to the addressees, because the deliverance of their predecessors is a deliverance for them; for had He left their predecessors there, the addressees would have suffered the worst torment and the slaughter of the sons. Or it is by omission of a noun (ḥadhf muḍaf), meaning "We delivered your fathers." Or it is an expression about the absent through the pronoun of address, either for the sake of making present his condition, or because the addressees are his example and likeness, for what is established of virtues for the fathers of a tribe is established for their descendants. So the use of the second-person pronoun contrary to what the apparent sense requires is on the pattern of what is said in His saying ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11]. The address is therefore not an iltifat (shift of person), because the consideration of the states of tribes is applied to later generations for what was established of their predecessors.

**[Page 495]**

This is an addition to the detail, mentioning another great blessing that breaks the normal course of things. With it, the rescue of the family of Pharaoh was complete. It shows the extent of God Most High's honouring of them, and it is a miracle (mu'jizah) for Musa (Moses), peace be upon him. The verb ﴿فَرَقْنا﴾ ("We divided") takes the pronoun of the addressees through the particle *bi* (with), in the same way that the verb ﴿نَجَّيْناكُمْ﴾ ("We saved you") [al-Baqarah: 49] takes their pronoun, as was mentioned earlier.

*Faraqa* and *farraqa* (both meaning "to separate") are used with and without the doubling of the middle letter with one meaning, since the doubling makes the verb transitive. Its meaning is separating the parts of a thing whose parts are joined together. However, *farraqa* indicates intensity of separation, which is the case when the separated parts were more closely joined. It has been said that *farraqa* is used for physical bodies and *faraqa* for abstract meanings. This was transmitted by al-Qarafi from some of his teachers, but it is not complete, as was explained in the first introduction of this commentary, by the evidence of this very verse. The correct view is that *farraqa* (with doubling) is used when there is treatment and effort involved, and that both the undoubled and doubled forms are literal (ḥaqīqah) in the separation of physical bodies, while in the separation of ambiguous meanings they are figurative (majāz). The ten widely transmitted (mutawātir) recitations agree on reading ﴿فَرَقْنا﴾ without doubling. The unDoubled reading is considered in light of the great power of God Most High, so that this intense separation became easy.

Great things become small in the eye of the Great. The definite article in *al-baḥr* ("the sea") refers to the sea they knew, namely the Gulf of Suez (al-Qulzum), which is today called the Red Sea, and which the Torah (al-Tawrah) called the Sea of Suph.

The *bā'* in *bikum* ("by you") is either for accompaniment (mulābasah), as in *ṭārat bihi al-'anqā'* ("the phoenix flew with him") and *'adā bihi al-faras* ("the horse ran with him"). That is, the division of the sea took place in connection with you, and the meaning of accompaniment is that it was divided while you were entering it, so the division occurred on your side. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) allowed that the *bā'* is causal (sababiyyah), meaning "because of you," that is, for your sake.

The address here is like the address in His saying ﴿وإذْ نَجَّيْناكم مِن آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ ("And when We saved you from the family of Pharaoh") [al-Baqarah: 49], and His saying ﴿فَأنْجَيْناكم وأغْرَقْنا آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ ("So We saved you, and We drowned the family of Pharaoh"). It is the place of favour and mention of the blessing, which is their deliverance from destruction and the destruction of their enemy. Al-Farazdaq said:

*How do you see me, [bowing my head as a] slave who has no shield? God has killed Ziyad for me.*

So His saying ﴿وإذْ فَرَقْنا بِكُمُ البَحْرَ﴾ serves as a preparation for the favour, because it is the cause of both matters: the salvation and the destruction. Along with that, it is a miracle for Musa, peace be upon him.

The verse alludes to what happened to the Children of Israel after their departure from Egypt, namely the pursuit of Pharaoh's army after them to prevent them from leaving the Egyptian lands. When they went out at night, either with Pharaoh's permission, as the Torah says in some passages, or secretly, as the Torah expresses it by "flight," Pharaoh came to regret releasing them, or some of his helpers incited him to stop them from leaving, because their departure meant the loss of the work for which they had been forced labourers. Or, when he saw them taking a route other than the familiar one for crossing Egypt towards Syria, he assumed they intended to spread into some parts of his Egyptian kingdom, so he feared their harm if they went far from the centre of his rule and the gathering place of his strength and army.

When the Children of Israel left the outskirts of Egypt, which at that time was the city of Memphis (Manfis), they did not take the familiar road to the lands of Syria, since they were not allowed to take the road along the shore of the Mediterranean Sea (Bahr al-Rum), entering the Sinai desert without crossing the sea and without covering more than twelve stages, that is, two hundred and fifty miles. Instead they took a route to the south-east around the upper part of the Red Sea, so that they would not take the familiar road used by Egyptian caravans and Pharaonic armies, which would have blocked them from continuing their journey or caused Pharaoh to send someone to turn them back. This is because Musa knew by revelation, as God Most High said: ﴿وأوْحَيْنا إلى مُوسى أنْ أسْرِ بِعِبادِي إنَّكم مُتَّبَعُونَ﴾ ("And We revealed to Musa: Travel by night with My servants; you will certainly be pursued") [al-Shu'ara': 52]. Pharaoh would not hesitate to stop them from continuing their march. Therefore, by divine command, he led them on an untrodden path. They were compelled to stand before the sea at a place called Fam al-Hayrut. There the miracle appeared, when God split the sea for them with His overwhelming power. Musa was commanded to strike it with his staff, and it split, and a dry path appeared in it. The Children of Israel crossed over it, while Pharaoh's army, which had caught up with them and tried to force its way into the sea after them, was enveloped by the sea and drowned.

**[Page 496]**

His saying ﴿وأغْرَقْنا آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ ("and We drowned the family of Pharaoh") means his army and his helpers. Pharaoh's own drowning is not mentioned in this verse, because the place of favour is the destruction of those who were directly responsible for enslaving the Children of Israel and torturing them, and who constituted Pharaoh's strength. The drowning of Pharaoh is mentioned in other verses, which we will discuss in their place, God willing. This took place in the time of the king Mentuhotep (Manfatah), who is also called Mentuhotep or Mineptah, one of the Pharaohs of the nineteenth dynasty in the order of the Pharaohs of Egypt according to historians.

His saying ﴿وأنْتُمْ تَنْظُرُونَ﴾ ("while you were looking on") is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah ḥāliyyah*) from the subject, which is the pronoun of Majesty (*ḍamīr al-jalālah*, referring to God) in *faraqna*, *anjayna* and *aghraqna*. It restricts the three verbs by way of grammatical dispute (*tanāzu'*) concerning them. In such a dispute over a circumstantial phrase, one cannot conceive of pronoun-deletion (*iḍmār*) in the second verb if the first verb is taken as the governing one, because a clause is not deleted, just as a adverbial of place or time is not deleted in disputes, as in *sakana wa qara'a 'indaka* ("he dwelt and read at your place"). This perhaps requires that the first verb governs. This circumstantial clause adds emphasis and magnification to the blessing, since the beneficiary's witnessing of the blessing is a great pleasure, especially since witnessing the drowning of the enemy is also an additional blessing, just as witnessing the division of the sea is a great blessing, because it involves witnessing a miracle that increases their faith and an event that cannot be witnessed by anyone else. It is also possible that the clause is a circumstantial clause from the object, which is "the family of Pharaoh," meaning "while you were looking at them." The object of *tanzurūn* ("you look") is then omitted, and it is not acceptable to treat it as an intransitive verb.

The attribution of looking to them is based on the consideration that their ancestors were the ones looking at that, because a blessing upon the forebears is necessarily a blessing upon their descendants. Therefore the pronoun of address is figurative (majāz).

[Page 497]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 51–52 (Part 1 of 2)

﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights; then you took the calf [for worship] after him, while you were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, so that you might give thanks.﴾

This is a reminder to them of the blessing of God's pardon for their great crime of worshipping other than Him. The earlier generation had committed this act, so the attribution of these actions to the addressees is based on what is coordinated with it, namely His saying ﴿Then We pardoned you﴾. For pardon granted to the fathers is a favour to them and to their sons, and the sons must give thanks for it, as was explained earlier at His saying ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ [2:47].

In al-Kashshaf, the tafsir of al-Baghawi, and the tafsir of al-Baydawi, it occurs that God promised Moses to give him the Law after the Children of Israel had returned to Egypt following the destruction of Pharaoh. This is a mistake, for the Children of Israel never returned to Egypt at all after their departure. How could they, when the verses are explicit that the revelation of the Law took place at Mount Sinai, and that their departure was so that God would give them the Holy Land which God had prescribed for them? Al-Kashshaf, in its commentary on Surah al-Dukhan, pointed to hesitation regarding this, but there should be no hesitation about it.

His saying ﴿then you took the calf after him﴾ is the main point. As for what was mentioned before it, it serves as a preface and foundation for it, and as an amplification of the magnitude of that crime, to show the vastness of God's pardon and His forbearance towards them. The placing of the reminder of pardon for this evil between the mention of the blessings is in observance of the order in which they came into existence, so that two purposes are achieved: the purpose of reminding, and the purpose of presenting the history of the Law.

What is meant by the appointment (al-muwa'adah) here is God's command to Moses to set apart forty nights for intimate conversation (munajah) with God. The use of the term "promise" (wa'd) for this matter is because it is an honour for Moses and a promise to him of God's speech and of the giving of the Law. The reading of the majority is ﴿wa-wa'adna﴾ with an alif after the waw, in the form of mufa'alah, which implies that the promise came from two sides: the one promising and the one promised. The mufa'alah here is not in its original function but serves merely to emphasise, like "safara" and "'afahu Allah" and "'alaja al-mariḍa" and "qatalahu Allah." Thus it is figuratively used for affirmation (tahqiq), because mufa'alah implies the repetition of the action from two agents. When it is removed from its original function, only repetition remains, without regard to the agent. Then what is intended by repetition is its necessary implication, which is intensification and certainty, so it functions like a verbal emphasis (ta'kid lafzi).

The more well-known view is that since the usual state of muwa'adah is that the promise comes from both sides, its form became widely used for promise in general. Its form has also become widely used specifically for mutual arrangement of a meeting, as occurred in the hadith of the Hijrah: "they both arranged with him the cave of Thawr" (wa-wa'adahu ghar Thawr). And the words of the poet:

"So arrange a meeting with her at the two trees of Malik, or at the hill between them, and make it easy."

It is used here because intimate conversation and speaking require closeness, so it is by way of metaphor like a meeting. For this reason the object of the promise is omitted, since it is clear from the form of muwa'adah.

It has also been said that the mufa'alah is in its original function, on the understanding that God promised Moses to give him the Law and commanded him to attend for intimate conversation, so Moses promised his Lord to comply with that. Thus the promise came from both parties, and this is sufficient to validate the mufa'alah, regardless of the difference in what is promised. This does not contradict the mufa'alah, because the basis of the mufa'alah form is the occurrence of a similar act from two sides, especially when the object is not mentioned in the wording, as here, for the sake of concise eloquence and to magnify the object from both sides. You may also say that the omission of the object was permitted because the addressees know it, since this statement is intended as a reminder and not as information, and a reminder requires only the slightest indication. Thus omission and mention are equal, and concision is preferred, even though the usual practice is to mention it.

Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿wa-'adna﴾ without an alif after the waw, in its literal sense.

Moses is the messenger of God to the Children of Israel and the bearer of the Law of the Torah. He is Moses son of 'Imran. The name of his grandfather is not mentioned, but what has come in the Torah is that he and his brother Aaron were from the tribe of Levi son of Jacob. He was born in Egypt around the year 1500 BCE. When his mother gave birth to him, she feared that the Copts would take him and kill him, because at the time of his birth the Copts had subjected the Children of Israel to terrible torment for unlawful reasons, as was explained earlier at His saying ﴿they slaughter your sons﴾ [2:49]. The king of Egypt had therefore commanded the killing of every male child born among the Children of Israel. His mother was called Yuhanadh, and she was also from the tribe of Levi. Her husband had died when she gave birth to Moses, so she devised a way to hide him from the Copts for a period of three months. Then God inspired her to nurse him once, and she placed him in a basket woven from papyrus reeds, smeared it with bitumen and pitch so that water would not penetrate it, placed the child in it, and set it adrift on the Nile near the dwellings of Pharaoh, on the bank of the Nile. She assigned a sister of his, named Maryam, to watch the place where the Nile would carry it and what would be done with him. The king of Egypt at that time was approximately Pharaoh Ramesses II. When the river carried him, Pharaoh's daughter, named Thermutis, was with her maidservants walking along the bank of the river, intending to bathe and cool herself in its water. It is said that they were in the city of 'Ain Shams. When she saw the basket, she sent one of her maidservants to look at it. When they opened it they found the infant, and Pharaoh's daughter took him to her mother. Maryam, the sister of Moses, revealed herself to Pharaoh's daughter. When she saw the tenderness of Pharaoh's daughter towards the infant, she said: "Shall I go and call for you a nurse among us who may suckle him?" She said, "Yes." So she went and brought Moses' mother. Pharaoh's wife took the child, adopted him, and named him Musha. It is said that it is composed of the word (mu), meaning water, and the word (sha), meaning rescuer, and it became Musa in Arabic. But the more apparent view is that this name is composed from the Hebrew language, not from Coptic, so perhaps he had another name in Pharaoh's palace, and he changed his name after that.

Moses grew up in Pharaoh's house as a child of his. When he grew older, he learned that he was not the son of Pharaoh and that he was an Israelite. Perhaps his mother informed him of this and gave him signs by which he would be certain. God raised him with a love of justice and a support of the weak. Moses was strong and sturdy of build. When he reached his maturity, around forty and some years of age, an incident occurred in which he killed a Copt in support of an Israelite. Perhaps this was after he had left Pharaoh's palace, that is, after the death of his foster-father. Moses feared that he would be retaliated against, so he migrated from Egypt, passed during his migration through Midian, married the daughter of Shu'ayb, then left Midian after ten years, when he was about forty-odd years old.

God revealed to him on his way that he should bring the Children of Israel out of Egypt and rescue them from the oppression of Pharaoh. So he entered Egypt, met his brother Aaron among his people in Egypt, and strove to bring the Children of Israel out of Egypt in the manner that God recounted in His Book. His departure with the Children of Israel from Egypt was around the year 1460 BCE in the time of Merneptah II. Moses, peace be upon him, died near Jericho on Mount Nebo in the year 1380 BCE, and was buried there, and his grave is not known to anyone, as is the text of the Torah.

His saying "forty nights" is put in the accusative as a time adverb (zarf) for the object of ﴿wa-wa'adna﴾, which is the meeting promised. This adverb takes the place of the object, meaning intimate conversation and other things during forty nights, if we take wa-wa'adna as stripped of the mufa'alah sense. If we keep it in its apparent sense, we posit two objects. In both estimations, the accusative of "forty" is in the adverbial sense for that omitted element, on the basis that using the name of a time for what occurs in it is a common figurative usage in the speech of eloquent speakers. Among it is ﴿and fear a Day when no soul will avail another﴾ [2:48], as was explained earlier. The matters that the forty nights comprised are known to the addressees, who recall them merely by allusion to them.

By what we have explained in His saying ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾, you are spared the lengthy discussions and possibilities that have circulated in the speech of writers here, from various aspects which al-Taftazani and 'Abd al-Hakim mentioned. The aspect we have presented includes their good points. He made the appointed time into nights because their reckoning was by lunar months.

The clause ﴿then you took the calf after him﴾ is joined by the particle thumma, which in the coordination of clauses indicates gradual sequence, to point to an order in the degrees of greatness of these situations. Thumma also coordinates ﴿then We pardoned you after that﴾, because the rank of the great pardon is distant from the greatness of their offence. Therefore, in this sequence, it was observed that what these clauses contain are great matters, both of good and of its opposite, to draw attention to the vastness of God's mercy towards them before their disobedience and after it. The omission of the second object of ﴿you took﴾ is because it is evident and known to them, and because of the ugliness of mentioning it, and the estimated object is "a god" (ma'budan aw ilahan). Through this, the benefit of mentioning "after him" (min ba'dihi) becomes apparent, for added condemnation: they were worthy of awaiting the Law, which would increase them in perfection, not of reverting to what they had been upon of monotheism and immersion in God's blessings. They were also worthy of fidelity to Moses, so they should not have introduced what they introduced in his absence, after they had seen his miracle and after he had forbidden them this worship when they said to him ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾, and he said, ﴿Indeed you are a people who are ignorant﴾ [7:138], and so on. The benefit of mentioning "min" (from) is to indicate that the taking began from the very first times after the absence of Moses, peace be upon him.

This too is a strange state, for the nature of deviation from a covenant is that it occurs after a long absence, though that itself is a weakness in the covenant, as al-Harith ibn Kaldah said:

"I do not know whether distance changed them, or the long passage of the covenant, or wealth which they acquired."

So in His saying "after him" there is an allusion to the scarcity of their fidelity in keeping the covenant of Moses. His saying "after him" means after his absence. The omission of the noun governed by "after" (ba'd) when it is attached to the name of the one spoken about is common in Arabic speech, because it is apparent from the context. When there is no context indicating what is meant, the most common usage is that it refers to after death, as in His saying ﴿You said: "God will never send a messenger after him."﴾ [40:34], and His saying ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses?﴾ [2:246].

They took the calf only in imitation of the Canaanites, who entered their land, and they are the Phoenicians, inhabitants of the coasts of the land of the Levant. They were worshippers of idols, and the calf was sacred to them. They represented their greatest god in the form of a man of copper with the head of a seated calf, on a throne, extending his arms as one who reaches for something to embrace. They heated it with fire from a pit beneath its throne which people did not notice. They offered sacrifices to it, and sometimes they offered their young children to it. When the child was placed on its arms, it was roasted, and they took that to be a sign of the acceptance of the offering. Woe to their ignorance and to what they did.

It was called among them Ba'l, and sometimes they named it Molech. They were a Semitic people whose language and customs in most respects resemble the language and customs of the Arabs. When the Children of Israel passed by them, they said to Moses, "Make for us a god as they have gods." Moses rebuked them, and they feared him. When he went for intimate conversation and appointed Aaron as his successor over them, they regarded him as weak and thought that Moses had perished. So they took the calf, which they made from gold and silver of their ornaments, and worshipped it.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 51–52 (part 2 of 2):

His saying "and you were wrongdoers" (wa-antum zalimun) is a qualifying circumstantial clause (hal) attached to "you took" (ittakhadhtum), so that the taking (al-ittikhadh) is linked with wrongdoing from its beginning to its end. The benefit of the circumstantial clause is to indicate that their excuse for what they did is cut off, and that there is no interpretation (ta'wil) available to them regarding the worship of the calf. Or, because during their stay in Egypt they were constantly adhering to monotheism (al-tawhid), guarding the injunction of Abraham and Jacob to their offspring to hold fast to monotheism, their shift to association (al-ishrak) after a messenger had come to them was a remarkable shift. Therefore they were wrongdoers in this deed with a doubled wrong (zulman mudaa'afan).

Apparently, the meaning of "wrongdoing" in this verse is not shirk and disbelief (kufr), although it is among the meanings of "wrongdoing" in the technical usage of the Qur'an, because it is evident that taking the calf is a wrong (zulm), so there is no expectation of the clause with it. After this I came across the commentary of Shaykh Muhammad ibn 'Arafa al-Tunisi, and I found that he said: "and you were wrongdoers" means: you have no doubt (shubha) in taking it.

His saying, ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾, is the place of favour (mahall al-minna), and its being conjoined with "then" (thumma) is because of the great remove in rank of this pardon, in that it is greater than all those blessings previously enumerated; so there is in it an increase of favour. The intended point of the speech is what is conjoined with "then". As for what preceded, His saying, ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾ and so on, it is a preparation for it and a description of what surrounds this pardon of the great sin.

His saying "after that" (min ba'di dhalika) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "We pardoned" (,'afawna), qualifying the pardon for emphasis on it, i.e., it is a pardon that occurs after that great sin. It is not an adverbial phrase (zarf laghw) attached to "We pardoned", such that it could be said that "then" indicates its meaning, making it an emphasis on the implication of "then". The delay of the pardon is in it, and the showing of its gravity by delaying the pardon regarding it.

His saying "that" (dhalika) came with the second-person singular kaf in plural address because it is the most frequently used demonstrative with singular reference; the singular address is the more common usage, so it was used for plural address, alerting that the kaf has departed from the intention of address to the meaning of distance. Similar usage is abundant in Arabic speech, because the dual and plural are two things contrary to the original and are not resorted to except when their meaning is specified; so when specifying their meaning is not intended, resorting to them is purely a matter of choice.

His saying, ﴿so that you might be thankful﴾ (la'allakum tashkurun), expresses hope for the occurrence of your gratitude. He departed from the lam of causation, indicating that their gratitude, despite this, is a matter that admits the possibility of failing. So mentioning the particle of hope rather than the particle of causation is an excellent eloquence (min badi' al-balagha). Thus interpreting la'alla as meaning li-kay (in order that) conveys this particularity. The manner in which la'alla indicates hope in the speech of God Most High has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 21] up to His saying "so that you may be mindful" (la'allakum tattaqun). The meaning of gratitude (shukr) was discussed at His saying, ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha: 2]. Al-Ghazali has an extensive chapter on it, which we have refrained from mentioning due to its length; refer to it in the Ihya' (Revival of the Religious Sciences).
