It is said that they were in the city of 'Ain Shams. When she saw the basket, she sent one of her maidservants to look at it. When they opened it they found the infant, and Pharaoh's daughter took him to her mother. Maryam, the sister of Moses, revealed herself to Pharaoh's daughter. When she saw the tenderness of Pharaoh's daughter towards the infant, she said: "Shall I go and call for you a nurse among us who may suckle him?" She said, "Yes." So she went and brought Moses' mother. Pharaoh's wife took the child, adopted him, and named him Musha. It is said that it is composed of the word (mu), meaning water, and the word (sha), meaning rescuer, and it became Musa in Arabic. But the more apparent view is that this name is composed from the Hebrew language, not from Coptic, so perhaps he had another name in Pharaoh's palace, and he changed his name after that.

Moses grew up in Pharaoh's house as a child of his. When he grew older, he learned that he was not the son of Pharaoh and that he was an Israelite. Perhaps his mother informed him of this and gave him signs by which he would be certain. God raised him with a love of justice and a support of the weak. Moses was strong and sturdy of build. When he reached his maturity, around forty and some years of age, an incident occurred in which he killed a Copt in support of an Israelite. Perhaps this was after he had left Pharaoh's palace, that is, after the death of his foster-father. Moses feared that he would be retaliated against, so he migrated from Egypt, passed during his migration through Midian, married the daughter of Shu'ayb, then left Midian after ten years, when he was about forty-odd years old.

God revealed to him on his way that he should bring the Children of Israel out of Egypt and rescue them from the oppression of Pharaoh. So he entered Egypt, met his brother Aaron among his people in Egypt, and strove to bring the Children of Israel out of Egypt in the manner that God recounted in His Book. His departure with the Children of Israel from Egypt was around the year 1460 BCE in the time of Merneptah II. Moses, peace be upon him, died near Jericho on Mount Nebo in the year 1380 BCE, and was buried there, and his grave is not known to anyone, as is the text of the Torah.

His saying "forty nights" is put in the accusative as a time adverb (zarf) for the object of ﴿wa-wa'adna﴾, which is the meeting promised. This adverb takes the place of the object, meaning intimate conversation and other things during forty nights, if we take wa-wa'adna as stripped of the mufa'alah sense. If we keep it in its apparent sense, we posit two objects. In both estimations, the accusative of "forty" is in the adverbial sense for that omitted element, on the basis that using the name of a time for what occurs in it is a common figurative usage in the speech of eloquent speakers. Among it is ﴿and fear a Day when no soul will avail another﴾ [2:48], as was explained earlier. The matters that the forty nights comprised are known to the addressees, who recall them merely by allusion to them.

By what we have explained in His saying ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾, you are spared the lengthy discussions and possibilities that have circulated in the speech of writers here, from various aspects which al-Taftazani and 'Abd al-Hakim mentioned. The aspect we have presented includes their good points. He made the appointed time into nights because their reckoning was by lunar months.

The clause ﴿then you took the calf after him﴾ is joined by the particle thumma, which in the coordination of clauses indicates gradual sequence, to point to an order in the degrees of greatness of these situations. Thumma also coordinates ﴿then We pardoned you after that﴾, because the rank of the great pardon is distant from the greatness of their offence. Therefore, in this sequence, it was observed that what these clauses contain are great matters, both of good and of its opposite, to draw attention to the vastness of God's mercy towards them before their disobedience and after it. The omission of the second object of ﴿you took﴾ is because it is evident and known to them, and because of the ugliness of mentioning it, and the estimated object is "a god" (ma'budan aw ilahan). Through this, the benefit of mentioning "after him" (min ba'dihi) becomes apparent, for added condemnation: they were worthy of awaiting the Law, which would increase them in perfection, not of reverting to what they had been upon of monotheism and immersion in God's blessings. They were also worthy of fidelity to Moses, so they should not have introduced what they introduced in his absence, after they had seen his miracle and after he had forbidden them this worship when they said to him ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾, and he said, ﴿Indeed you are a people who are ignorant﴾ [7:138], and so on. The benefit of mentioning "min" (from) is to indicate that the taking began from the very first times after the absence of Moses, peace be upon him.

This too is a strange state, for the nature of deviation from a covenant is that it occurs after a long absence, though that itself is a weakness in the covenant, as al-Harith ibn Kaldah said:

"I do not know whether distance changed them, or the long passage of the covenant, or wealth which they acquired."

So in His saying "after him" there is an allusion to the scarcity of their fidelity in keeping the covenant of Moses. His saying "after him" means after his absence. The omission of the noun governed by "after" (ba'd) when it is attached to the name of the one spoken about is common in Arabic speech, because it is apparent from the context. When there is no context indicating what is meant, the most common usage is that it refers to after death, as in His saying ﴿You said: "God will never send a messenger after him."﴾ [40:34], and His saying ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses?﴾ [2:246].

They took the calf only in imitation of the Canaanites, who entered their land, and they are the Phoenicians, inhabitants of the coasts of the land of the Levant. They were worshippers of idols, and the calf was sacred to them. They represented their greatest god in the form of a man of copper with the head of a seated calf, on a throne, extending his arms as one who reaches for something to embrace. They heated it with fire from a pit beneath its throne which people did not notice. They offered sacrifices to it, and sometimes they offered their young children to it. When the child was placed on its arms, it was roasted, and they took that to be a sign of the acceptance of the offering. Woe to their ignorance and to what they did.

It was called among them Ba'l, and sometimes they named it Molech. They were a Semitic people whose language and customs in most respects resemble the language and customs of the Arabs. When the Children of Israel passed by them, they said to Moses, "Make for us a god as they have gods." Moses rebuked them, and they feared him. When he went for intimate conversation and appointed Aaron as his successor over them, they regarded him as weak and thought that Moses had perished. So they took the calf, which they made from gold and silver of their ornaments, and worshipped it.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 51–52 (part 2 of 2):

His saying "and you were wrongdoers" (wa-antum zalimun) is a qualifying circumstantial clause (hal) attached to "you took" (ittakhadhtum), so that the taking (al-ittikhadh) is linked with wrongdoing from its beginning to its end. The benefit of the circumstantial clause is to indicate that their excuse for what they did is cut off, and that there is no interpretation (ta'wil) available to them regarding the worship of the calf. Or, because during their stay in Egypt they were constantly adhering to monotheism (al-tawhid), guarding the injunction of Abraham and Jacob to their offspring to hold fast to monotheism, their shift to association (al-ishrak) after a messenger had come to them was a remarkable shift. Therefore they were wrongdoers in this deed with a doubled wrong (zulman mudaa'afan).

Apparently, the meaning of "wrongdoing" in this verse is not shirk and disbelief (kufr), although it is among the meanings of "wrongdoing" in the technical usage of the Qur'an, because it is evident that taking the calf is a wrong (zulm), so there is no expectation of the clause with it. After this I came across the commentary of Shaykh Muhammad ibn 'Arafa al-Tunisi, and I found that he said: "and you were wrongdoers" means: you have no doubt (shubha) in taking it.

His saying, ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾, is the place of favour (mahall al-minna), and its being conjoined with "then" (thumma) is because of the great remove in rank of this pardon, in that it is greater than all those blessings previously enumerated; so there is in it an increase of favour. The intended point of the speech is what is conjoined with "then". As for what preceded, His saying, ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾ and so on, it is a preparation for it and a description of what surrounds this pardon of the great sin.

His saying "after that" (min ba'di dhalika) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "We pardoned" (,'afawna), qualifying the pardon for emphasis on it, i.e., it is a pardon that occurs after that great sin. It is not an adverbial phrase (zarf laghw) attached to "We pardoned", such that it could be said that "then" indicates its meaning, making it an emphasis on the implication of "then". The delay of the pardon is in it, and the showing of its gravity by delaying the pardon regarding it.

His saying "that" (dhalika) came with the second-person singular kaf in plural address because it is the most frequently used demonstrative with singular reference; the singular address is the more common usage, so it was used for plural address, alerting that the kaf has departed from the intention of address to the meaning of distance. Similar usage is abundant in Arabic speech, because the dual and plural are two things contrary to the original and are not resorted to except when their meaning is specified; so when specifying their meaning is not intended, resorting to them is purely a matter of choice.

His saying, ﴿so that you might be thankful﴾ (la'allakum tashkurun), expresses hope for the occurrence of your gratitude. He departed from the lam of causation, indicating that their gratitude, despite this, is a matter that admits the possibility of failing. So mentioning the particle of hope rather than the particle of causation is an excellent eloquence (min badi' al-balagha). Thus interpreting la'alla as meaning li-kay (in order that) conveys this particularity. The manner in which la'alla indicates hope in the speech of God Most High has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 21] up to His saying "so that you may be mindful" (la'allakum tattaqun). The meaning of gratitude (shukr) was discussed at His saying, ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha: 2]. Al-Ghazali has an extensive chapter on it, which we have refrained from mentioning due to its length; refer to it in the Ihya' (Revival of the Religious Sciences).

This is a reminder of the blessing of the revelation of the Law (al-shari'ah), through which their affairs are set right, their lives are ordered, and their community is united. It also points to the completeness of the blessing. They regard it as the emblem (shi'ar) of their glory and nobility, because of the breadth of the Law revealed to them, so that it became a Book, and by it they became ahl kitab (people of a scripture), that is, people of legislative knowledge. The Book intended here is the Torah given to Musa, so the definite article is for previous reference (al-'ahd). What was appended to it is also included, in the manner we mentioned in the commentary on His words, ﴿That is the Book﴾.

[Page 502]

Al-furqan is a verbal noun of the pattern fu'lan, derived from al-farq, which is separation. It was borrowed for distinguishing truth from falsehood, so it is a linguistic description of differentiation. It may be applied to the Book of the Law, to the miracle, to the victory of truth over falsehood, and to the proof established for the truth. Verses came in this sense: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the furqan upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan: 1], ﴿And We had certainly given Musa and Harun the furqan﴾ [al-Anbiya': 48], and ﴿On the day of the furqan, the day the two hosts met﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], meaning the day of victory, the day of Badr. He also said, ﴿And He sent down the furqan﴾ [Al 'Imran: 4], coordinated with ﴿He has sent down upon you the Book in truth﴾, and ﴿and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3], and the verse continues. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to the miracle or the proof, so that it does not entail the coordination of an attribute with the thing it qualifies, if al-furqan is taken to mean the Book that separates truth from falsehood, since an attribute cannot follow its qualified noun by conjunction. The one who deduced this from the verse of the poet:

To the lordly king, son of the bold hero, and the lion of the battalion in the thick of the press, fa-qaddasaha [so he sanctified it].

This is because it is the coordination of some attributes with others, not the coordination of an attribute with the thing it qualifies, as Abu Hayyan pointed out.

His words, ﴿so that you may be guided﴾, are the locus of the favour (minnah, divine bounty), because if the bringing of the Law were not for their guidance, and it were restricted to Musa's acting upon it, it would not have been a blessing upon them. The discussion of ﴿la'allakum tahtadun (so that you may be guided)﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿la'allakum tashkurun (so that you may be grateful)﴾ earlier.

﴿And [recall] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf [for worship], so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator." Then He turned to you in forgiveness. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

This is another blessing, namely the blessing of abrogating a severe obligation that had been imposed on them as an atonement (jabir) for the sin of worshipping the idol they had committed. Pardon was granted to them without that obligation, and so the favour was complete. On this basis, it is valid to count this as a separate favour, following the favour contained in the words of Allah, Exalted is He, "Then We pardoned you after that" (2:52). This is because pardon from being held accountable for a sin in the Hereafter may occur together with a worldly punishment, such as a legal penalty (hadd) or the like, and in that case it is still a favour. For had Allah willed, He could have made for the sin two punishments, one worldly and one otherworldly, just as the sinner had committed a sin against both soul and body. But Allah, by His mercy, made the legal penalties (hudud) expiations (jawabir) in Islam, as in the authentic hadith. So when Allah pardoned the Children of Israel on condition that they kill themselves, He graciously removed the otherworldly punishment, which is the consequence of the sin. And when He abrogated their obligation to kill themselves, He again showed favour in that respect. Thus there are two favours.

[Page 503]

So Moses' words to his people, "Indeed you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves," constitute the legislation of a ruling that could only come through revelation, not through personal reasoning (ijtihad). Even if ijtihad is permissible for prophets, this ruling contradicts the principle of preserving lives, which it is said all of Allah's laws agree upon. It therefore indicates that He obligated them to kill themselves literally. This could be either by each person who worshipped the calf killing himself, so that "the souls" means the spirits within the bodies, in which case the agent and the object are the same, differing only in aspect, as in His saying "you have wronged yourselves," and in the verse of Ibn Udhayna:

"When you find for them [the whispers of the heart] a consolation, the heart, having interceded, will bring the conscience to forget them."

Or it could be that those who did not worship the calf kill those who worshipped it. The Torah's account of this matter is extremely ambiguous. Its apparent meaning is that God commanded Moses to instruct the Levites, who are of the tribe of Levi from which Moses and Aaron came, to kill with the sword those who worshipped the calf; they did so and killed three thousand souls. Then Moses interceded for them, and God forgave them. Accordingly, the ruling to kill themselves would have been abrogated after it had been acted upon. The meaning would then be "let some of you kill others." Thus "souls" refers to persons, as in His saying, "When you enter houses, greet one another" (24:61), meaning that some of you should greet others; and His saying, "And when We took your covenant, that you would not shed your blood" (2:84), meaning that some of you would not shed the blood of others; and His following words, "Then you, these people, kill yourselves" (2:85). In this case the agent and the object are distinct.

Some people have interpreted the command to kill the self here as a metaphorical killing, meaning subduing and taming, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"In the depths of a heart subdued (muqattal)."

And in the phrase "a wine that is muqattala or maqtula," meaning one whose strength has been tempered with water. Bujayr ibn Zuhayr said:

"The one you handed me, I refused it. It was killed, killed; so bring it, it was not killed."

But this is far removed from the wording, and it contradicts the purpose of expressing favour, because taming and subduing the self is a law that has not been abrogated.

[Page 504]

Here, "wrong" (zulm) means transgression and disobedience, in the sense of His saying, "Indeed, associating others with Allah is a great wrong" (31:13). The fa' in His saying, "so turn in repentance" (fa-tubu), is the fa' of causation, because wrongdoing is the cause for the command to repent. So the fa' serves to link the command to the statement. It is not, according to al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Hajib, a conjunctive fa' ('atf), since there is no sequential relationship in existence between a declarative statement (khabar) and an imperative (insha'). Some grammarians do not consider the fa' to be out of the conjunctive function, and this is the common view in the formulations of the majority, such as the author of Mughni al-Labib (Mughni al-Labib 'an Kutub al-A'arib, Ibn Hisham's grammar). He therefore takes it as the conjunction of an imperative with a declarative. There is no harm in this. The mention of repentance has already occurred in His saying, "Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He turned to him in forgiveness" (2:37). The fa' in His saying, "so kill yourselves," clearly indicates that their killing themselves is an explanation of the repentance prescribed for them. Thus the fa' is for mentioned sequence (al-tartib al-dhikri), which is the conjunction of a detailed statement to a general one, as in His saying, "They asked Moses for even greater than that, saying, 'Show us Allah openly'" (4:153). This is as stated in Mughni al-Labib. It implies that the fa' indicates sequence in mention, not immediate succession.

As for the author of al-Kashshaf, he permitted two interpretations of it. One is to take the preceding verb as meaning the resolve to act, so that what follows is ordered upon it and immediately follows it. This interpretation is not mentioned by the author of Mughni, and it does not apply to His saying, "They asked Moses for even greater than that, so they said..." (4:153). The second is to make the required repentance encompass statements and actions, the last of which is their killing themselves, so that the fa' indicates both order and immediate succession.

In my view, when the second sentence functions as an explanation of the first, and the first is conjoined by fa', the second should originally be detached from the conjunction. When it is attached with fa', as in this verse, the second fa' emphasizes the first. This may be appropriate in any two sentences where the first is a non-perceptible action and the second is a perceptible action that clarifies the first. The second then takes the place of the result of the first, and is joined by fa' because the first action is not completed until it has been firmly established in the soul. That is why the author of al-Kashshaf brought it closer by interpreting the first action, in some places, as a resolve.

The baari' (Creator) is the one who creates creation with proportion and balance. He is therefore more specific than the khaliq (creator). That is why He follows khaliq with it in His saying, "He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner" (59:24). Moses' expression, peace be upon him, in his speech, using a term that conveys the meaning of the word bari' in Arabic, is an incitement to repentance, since repentance is a return from disobedience, and so it contains the sense of gratitude. The fact that creation is in a balanced pattern further incites gratitude to the Creator.

[Page 505]

His saying, "Then He turned to you in forgiveness" (fa-taba 'alaykum), clearly indicates that it is part of the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, when He reminds them of the favour. This is the place of reminder in His saying, "And [recall] when Moses said to his people," and so on. The past tense is used in its normal sense of narration. It is in the manner of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), because the context required speech in the first person, so it shifts to the third person. Its preference here is due to the earlier mention of the referent of the third-person pronoun in the report of Moses' speech. The fa' is conjoined to an omitted element for brevity, meaning "so you did, then He turned to you in forgiveness," or "so you resolved, then He turned to you in forgiveness," in the same manner as His saying, "Strike the sea with your staff," and it split (26:63), meaning "so he struck, and it split." The fa' is used to indicate that the repentance of Allah toward them followed immediately upon their sin, and that it was not delayed until after the destruction of all who worshipped the calf. Rather, the abrogation occurred shortly after its legislation, either after acting upon it briefly or without acting upon it. In this there is great mercy toward them, since pardon was granted for a great sin without imposing on them a severe repentance, but merely with the sufficiency of their remorse and their resolve not to return to it.

It is far-fetched that "so He turned to you in forgiveness" is part of Moses' speech, because this would require an omission in the speech whose indicator is unclear. It would entail supposing a condition such as "If you do it, He will turn to you in forgiveness," which would mean the future tense, with the fa' being an eloquent fa' (fa' fasiha). Moreover, it would empty this verse of the locus of the favour being reminded of, except implicitly.

The sentence "Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful" is a statement and a praise of Allah. Its emphasis with an emphatic particle (inna) is to treat them as one who doubts that repentance will be accepted from them, since their state, given the magnitude of their offence, is that of someone who doubts the acceptance of repentance. The reason He combined "the Accepting of repentance" with "the Merciful" is that His repentance toward them consisted in pardoning the lapse of taking the calf, which is a great lapse that none but the Most Forgiving (al-Ghaffar) could forgive, and in abrogating the ruling to kill themselves, which is an act of mercy. Therefore the Merciful has a great place here, and it is not merely a formula of praise.

[p. 506]

**Ibn ʿAshur's commentary (al-Taḥrīr wa'l-Tanwīr) on Sūrat al-Baqarah, verses 55–56:**

﴿And when you said, "O Mūsā, we will never believe you until we see God openly," the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾ ﴿Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might give thanks.﴾ This is a reminder of another blessing, one that came after a punishment for the coarseness of your nature. The locus of the favour and the blessing is His saying, ﴿Then We raised you up﴾, and what precedes it is a preparation for it and a foundation for its structure, as was explained earlier in His saying, ﴿And when We appointed for Mūsā forty nights﴾ [al-Baqarah: 51], and so on. The speakers were the forebears of those addressed, for they said to Mūsā, ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly.﴾

[p. 506 continued]

The apparent meaning is that this statement was made by them after the pardon for their worship of the calf, as is evident from the order of the verses. Al-Baghawī related this from al-Suddī. It has also been said that they asked this during his private conversation with God, and that the askers were the seventy whom Mūsā chose for the appointed time, who are referred to in the Torah as the priests and the elders of the Children of Israel. It has also been said that a group of the common people of the Children of Israel, numbering about ten thousand, asked this. Al-Zamakhsharī (in al-Kashshāf) related these two opinions. The Torah contains nothing explicit to favour one of the two opinions, nor anything explicit about this request actually occurring. However, the apparent meaning of what is in the Book of Deuteronomy indicates that this proposal was indeed made, and that it happened after God's first speech to Mūsā. When it recounts Mūsā's reminder to the Children of Israel, it mentions something that differs from the manner of the first private conversation: "When you heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, while the mountain was burning with fire, all the heads of your tribes and your elders came near to me, and you said, 'Behold, the Lord our God has shown us His glory and His greatness, and we have heard His voice out of the midst of the fire.' … For if we hear the voice of the Lord our God any more, we shall die. … Go near, and hear all that the Lord our God shall say, and speak to us all that the Lord our God shall speak to you," and so on. This indicates that there was among them an eager expectation of seeing God, Exalted, and that what befell them brought them to the point of death. Furthermore, the Qur'an is a proof over other scriptures, confirming what is before it and watching over it. The apparent meaning is that this occurred in the third month after their departure from Egypt.

The meaning of "we will not believe you" may include that they anticipated disbelief if they did not see God, Exalted; that is, that they would apostatise in the future from the faith they had previously held. It may also include that they intended the complete faith whose proof is direct witnessing; that is, that one of these two kinds of faith would be lost if they did not see God openly. This is because *lan* negates the future. Sībawayh said: "*Lā* negates *yafʿalu* (he does), and *lan* negates *sa-yafʿalu* (he will do)." Just as your saying *sa-yaqūmu* (he will stand) does not imply that he is not standing now, there is nothing in the verse that shows they disbelieved at the moment of their saying this. Rather, it indicates their rudeness and their little regard for the blessings they had been given and the miracles they had witnessed, to the extent that they desired to see God openly. If they did not see Him, doubt would enter them regarding the truthfulness of Mūsā. This is like the saying of one who says, "If it is so, then I am an unbeliever." Neither the Qur'an nor anything else indicates that they said this out of disbelief.

The verb *nu'min* is followed by *lām* because it is implicitly given the meaning of acknowledging God, and so the sense is "we will not acknowledge to you the truth." What indicates this omitted verb is the *lām*, and this is the method of *tadmīn* (the implicit conveying of one verb's meaning through another).

[p. 507]

*Jahrah* is a verbal noun of the form *fa'lah*, from *al-jahr*, which is clear and manifest appearance. It is used for the manifestation of essences and of voices in the literal sense, according to al-Rāghib's words: "*al-jahr* is the appearance of a thing in an excessive manner, either through the sense of sight, as in *ra'aytuhu jihāran* (I saw him openly), and from this *jahara al-bi'r* (he made the well's water manifest) when he brought its water to light; or through the sense of hearing, as in *wa-in tajhar bi'l-qawl* (and if you speak aloud)." The words of al-Zamakhsharī indicate that *al-jahr* is a metaphor for seeing, by likening the one who sees with the eye to one who speaks aloud, and the one who sees with the heart to one who speaks quietly. What led him to this was the widespread use of *al-jahr* for the voice. But all of this is far-fetched, since there is no evidence that the loud voice is the literal meaning, and there is no way to claim that it is the common usage for the loud voice, so that one could say the commonness is a sign of the literal meaning. Moreover, commonness is known to be a sign of a rarely used metaphor, and being more common is not a sign of the literal meaning. Furthermore, there is no point in this metaphor, nor any purpose that would return to the thing likened by this comparison, since the manifestation of essences is clearer than the manifestation of voices.

*Jahratan* is in the accusative as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*), to explain the kind of the verb *tara* (you see). This is because among seeing there is that which is a glance, or which occurs with a transparent intervening thing, and such seeing is not clear.

The reason for deviating from saying *ʿiyānan* (in plain sight) to saying *jahratan* is that *jahratan* is more eloquent in wording, because of its lightness. It does not begin with a throat letter, and beginning with a throat letter is more tiring to the throat than its occurring in the middle of speech. It is also free of a weak letter. Likewise, eloquent speakers choose some words over others for the goodness of their effect in speech and for their lightness to the ear. The Qur'an has the highest share in this, and it is at the utmost level of eloquence.

His saying, ﴿the thunderbolt seized you﴾, means as a punishment for them for the coarseness and little regard for the miracles that had appeared from them. This is a worldly punishment, and it does not indicate that the thing punished was forbidden or disbelief, especially since it has been determined that their death by the thunderbolt did not last long, so it was not like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd. By this you know that there is in the striking of the thunderbolt upon them no indication that seeing God, Exalted, is impossible, nor that asking for it and insisting upon it is disbelief, as the Muʿtazilah claimed. Nor is there any need to answer this by saying that the thunderbolt struck them because they believed that He, Exalted, resembles bodies, so they were unbelievers thereby. This is because there is no evidence in the verse, nor elsewhere, that they disbelieved. How could that be, when Mūsā, upon him be peace, himself asked to see Him?

The *ṣāʿiqah* (thunderbolt) is an electrical fire from the clouds that burns whoever it strikes. Sometimes the fire does not appear, but its air reaches the living beings, and they suffocate because of what mixes with the air they breathe, of acids arising from the intensity of electricity. It has been said that what struck them was fire, and it has been said that they heard a blast and died.

[p. 508]

His saying, ﴿while you were looking on﴾ [al-Baqarah: 50]: the restriction by this condition, according to the author of al-Kashshāf, serves to indicate that the thunderbolt which struck them was the fire of the thunderbolt, not its intense sound, because the condition shows that what struck them was something that could be seen. Al-Qurṭubī said: that is, "while some of you were looking at others," that is, gathered together.

In my view, the object of *tanẓurūna* (you were looking) is omitted, and *tanẓurūna* has the meaning of *tuḥaddiqūna al-anẓār* (you were gazing intently), at the sight of the cloud over Mount Ṭūr, hoping that God would appear to them through it. This is because they had become accustomed to God speaking to Mūsā in words he heard through the cloud, as the Torah says in many places. So the benefit of the condition is to show that the punishment struck them at the very moment of their misdeed and their rudeness, when they were eager for what could not be attained for them.

His saying, ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾, is a wonderful concision. That is, "you died from the thunderbolt, then We raised you up after your death." This was an extraordinary event that God made a miracle for Mūsā, in answer to his supplication and intercession, or as an honour for them after their chastisement, if the askers were the seventy, for they were among the righteous of the Children of Israel.

If you say: if the askers were the righteous, then how were they punished? I say: you have already learned that this is a worldly punishment, and it may befall the righteous. The Ṣūfīs call it *ʿitāb* (gentle reproach), and it does not contradict honour. A parallel to this is that Mūsā asked to see his Lord, and God manifested Himself to the mountain, so He made it crumble to dust, and Mūsā fell down unconscious. When he recovered, he said, "Glory be to You, I repent to You." If you say: death requires the dissolution of the bodily composition, so how can there be resurrection after it outside the Day of the Resurrection of creation? I say: death is the cessation of the movement of the heart and the suspension of the functions of the blood circulation. When it occurs from corruption in these, no life follows it except on the Day of the Resurrection of creation. This is the meaning of His, Exalted, saying, ﴿They will not taste death therein except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhān: 56]. But when it occurs from a sudden, overpowering obstacle that prevents the functions of the heart from working, the body has the judgment of death in that state, yet it accepts return if the causes of life come back to it after the obstacles that arose are removed. Physicians today regard some conditions that stop the work of the heart as death, and they treat the heart with surgical procedures that restore its movement.

Death by the thunderbolt, when it is from suffocation or from the force of the pressure of the sound upon the heart, may be followed by life when pure, fresh air reaches the person. Customarily, this kind of death may last a few hours. But since this event was an extraordinary event, it is possible that their death lasted a day and a night, as has been related in some reports, and it is possible that it was less than that.

[p. 506]

**Ibn ʿAshur's commentary (al-Taḥrīr wa'l-Tanwīr) on Sūrat al-Baqarah, verses 55–56:**

﴿And when you said, "O Mūsā, we will never believe you until we see God openly," the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾ ﴿Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might give thanks.﴾ This is a reminder of another blessing, one that came after a punishment for the coarseness of your nature. The locus of the favour and the blessing is His saying, ﴿Then We raised you up﴾, and what precedes it is a preparation for it and a foundation for its structure, as was explained earlier in His saying, ﴿And when We appointed for Mūsā forty nights﴾ [al-Baqarah: 51], and so on. The speakers were the forebears of those addressed, for they said to Mūsā, ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly.﴾

[p. 506 continued]

The apparent meaning is that this statement was made by them after the pardon for their worship of the calf, as is evident from the order of the verses. Al-Baghawī related this from al-Suddī. It has also been said that they asked this during his private conversation with God, and that the askers were the seventy whom Mūsā chose for the appointed time, who are referred to in the Torah as the priests and the elders of the Children of Israel. It has also been said that a group of the common people of the Children of Israel, numbering about ten thousand, asked this. Al-Zamakhsharī (in al-Kashshāf) related these two opinions. The Torah contains nothing explicit to favour one of the two opinions, nor anything explicit about this request actually occurring. However, the apparent meaning of what is in the Book of Deuteronomy indicates that this proposal was indeed made, and that it happened after God's first speech to Mūsā. When it recounts Mūsā's reminder to the Children of Israel, it mentions something that differs from the manner of the first private conversation: "When you heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, while the mountain was burning with fire, all the heads of your tribes and your elders came near to me, and you said, 'Behold, the Lord our God has shown us His glory and His greatness, and we have heard His voice out of the midst of the fire.' … For if we hear the voice of the Lord our God any more, we shall die. … Go near, and hear all that the Lord our God shall say, and speak to us all that the Lord our God shall speak to you," and so on. This indicates that there was among them an eager expectation of seeing God, Exalted, and that what befell them brought them to the point of death. Furthermore, the Qur'an is a proof over other scriptures, confirming what is before it and watching over it. The apparent meaning is that this occurred in the third month after their departure from Egypt.

The meaning of "we will not believe you" may include that they anticipated disbelief if they did not see God, Exalted; that is, that they would apostatise in the future from the faith they had previously held. It may also include that they intended the complete faith whose proof is direct witnessing; that is, that one of these two kinds of faith would be lost if they did not see God openly. This is because *lan* negates the future. Sībawayh said: "*Lā* negates *yafʿalu* (he does), and *lan* negates *sa-yafʿalu* (he will do)." Just as your saying *sa-yaqūmu* (he will stand) does not imply that he is not standing now, there is nothing in the verse that shows they disbelieved at the moment of their saying this. Rather, it indicates their rudeness and their little regard for the blessings they had been given and the miracles they had witnessed, to the extent that they desired to see God openly. If they did not see Him, doubt would enter them regarding the truthfulness of Mūsā. This is like the saying of one who says, "If it is so, then I am an unbeliever." Neither the Qur'an nor anything else indicates that they said this out of disbelief.

The verb *nu'min* is followed by *lām* because it is implicitly given the meaning of acknowledging God, and so the sense is "we will not acknowledge to you the truth." What indicates this omitted verb is the *lām*, and this is the method of *tadmīn* (the implicit conveying of one verb's meaning through another).

[p. 507]

*Jahrah* is a verbal noun of the form *fa'lah*, from *al-jahr*, which is clear and manifest appearance. It is used for the manifestation of essences and of voices in the literal sense, according to al-Rāghib's words: "*al-jahr* is the appearance of a thing in an excessive manner, either through the sense of sight, as in *ra'aytuhu jihāran* (I saw him openly), and from this *jahara al-bi'r* (he made the well's water manifest) when he brought its water to light; or through the sense of hearing, as in *wa-in tajhar bi'l-qawl* (and if you speak aloud)." The words of al-Zamakhsharī indicate that *al-jahr* is a metaphor for seeing, by likening the one who sees with the eye to one who speaks aloud, and the one who sees with the heart to one who speaks quietly. What led him to this was the widespread use of *al-jahr* for the voice. But all of this is far-fetched, since there is no evidence that the loud voice is the literal meaning, and there is no way to claim that it is the common usage for the loud voice, so that one could say the commonness is a sign of the literal meaning. Moreover, commonness is known to be a sign of a rarely used metaphor, and being more common is not a sign of the literal meaning. Furthermore, there is no point in this metaphor, nor any purpose that would return to the thing likened by this comparison, since the manifestation of essences is clearer than the manifestation of voices.

*Jahratan* is in the accusative as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*), to explain the kind of the verb *tara* (you see). This is because among seeing there is that which is a glance, or which occurs with a transparent intervening thing, and such seeing is not clear.

The reason for deviating from saying *ʿiyānan* (in plain sight) to saying *jahratan* is that *jahratan* is more eloquent in wording, because of its lightness. It does not begin with a throat letter, and beginning with a throat letter is more tiring to the throat than its occurring in the middle of speech. It is also free of a weak letter. Likewise, eloquent speakers choose some words over others for the goodness of their effect in speech and for their lightness to the ear. The Qur'an has the highest share in this, and it is at the utmost level of eloquence.

His saying, ﴿the thunderbolt seized you﴾, means as a punishment for them for the coarseness and little regard for the miracles that had appeared from them. This is a worldly punishment, and it does not indicate that the thing punished was forbidden or disbelief, especially since it has been determined that their death by the thunderbolt did not last long, so it was not like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd. By this you know that there is in the striking of the thunderbolt upon them no indication that seeing God, Exalted, is impossible, nor that asking for it and insisting upon it is disbelief, as the Muʿtazilah claimed. Nor is there any need to answer this by saying that the thunderbolt struck them because they believed that He, Exalted, resembles bodies, so they were unbelievers thereby. This is because there is no evidence in the verse, nor elsewhere, that they disbelieved. How could that be, when Mūsā, upon him be peace, himself asked to see Him?

The *ṣāʿiqah* (thunderbolt) is an electrical fire from the clouds that burns whoever it strikes. Sometimes the fire does not appear, but its air reaches the living beings, and they suffocate because of what mixes with the air they breathe, of acids arising from the intensity of electricity. It has been said that what struck them was fire, and it has been said that they heard a blast and died.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 57:

[p. 509]
﴿And We shaded you with the clouds, and sent down upon you the manna and the quail. "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you." And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ The clause "﴿And We shaded you﴾" is coordinated (ʿatf) upon "﴿We raised you up﴾" [al-Baqarah: 56], and following the mention of the distress with the mention of a gift is the way of the Merciful in the upbringing of His servant. The apparent meaning is that the shading by the clouds and the sending down of the manna and quail took place before their request to see God openly (jahratan), because the Torah mentions the descent of the manna and quail when they entered the wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai, on the twelfth day of the second month after their departure from Egypt, when they longed for the eating of bread and meat. For in their journey they did not cook; rather, the apparent meaning is that they subsisted on the milk of their livestock, which they had brought with them, and on what the earth produced. As for their being shaded by the cloud, the apparent meaning is that it occurred after they asked to see God, because the shading by the cloud took place after Moses had set up for them the Tent of Meeting, the place of offerings, the place of Moses' secret conversation (munajat), and the qiblah of the Children of Israel who prayed in the wilderness of Sinai. When the Tent was completed in the second year after their departure from Egypt, a cloud covered the Tent of Testimony, and whenever the cloud lifted from the Tent, that was a permission for the Children of Israel to move on; and when the cloud settled, they settled, etc. Thus their books say.

When the Children of Israel asked for bread and meat, the manna would descend upon them in the morning, and the quail would fall upon them in the evening, in the amount sufficient for all of them for their day or their night, except on Friday, when a double quantity of both would descend upon them, because on the Sabbath the descent ceased.

Manna is a gummy, airborne substance that falls upon the trees of the desert, resembling moistened flour; it has a sweetness tending toward sourness, and its color tends toward yellow. It is abundant in the valleys of Turkistan, and it may descend in small quantities elsewhere, and it was not known before in the wilderness of Sinai. The Torah has described it as fine like flakes, falling as dew like frost upon the earth, and it is like coriander seed, white, and its taste is like wafers with honey. The Children of Israel named it manna. They were commanded not to keep any of it until morning, because worms would breed in it, and to gather it before the sun grew hot, because the sun would melt it. So when they gathered it, they ground it with a millstone or pounded it in a mortar, cooked it in pots, and made it into cakes; its taste was like the taste of qata'if in oil. They ate it for forty years until they came to the edge of the land of Canaan, meaning Hebron.

[p. 510]
As for the quail (salwa), it is a collective noun of a kind, its singular being salwah. It is said that it has no singular, and it is said that its singular and plural are the same (sawa'). It is a wild bird with delicious flesh, easy to hunt; the south wind would drive it to them every evening, and they would catch it by hand. This bird is also called al-sumani, with a dammah on the sin, a fathah on the mim, lightened, followed by an alif and a nun, maqsur, like hubara. It is also a term that applies to both the singular and the plural; it is said that it is the plural, and its singular is sumanah.

His saying ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾ is a statement of a suppressed verb of saying, because those addressed at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an were not commanded with this; thus it indicates that it is part of the continuing report about their forebears.

His saying ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾ — the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) estimated it as coordinated upon a suppressed element, i.e., "so they wronged," and his commentators established it on the basis that "they did not wrong Us" is a negation of wronging related to a specific object, namely the divine name (the pronoun of majesty), and this negation implies, in the rhetorical context, that there is wronging related to something other than this object; for if wronging had not occurred, it would have been negated absolutely by saying "they did not wrong." That is not the meaning. It is only that al-Kashshaf estimated the omitted verb as connected with the fa', because the fa' in coordinating clauses conveys, along with sequence and immediacy, the meaning of causality in most cases, so that the coordinated clause is caused by the clause coordinated upon. Thus the occurrence of their wronging when they were ungrateful for the blessing immediately after the kindness is likened to the sequence of the effect after the cause in occurrence, without delay and without reflection upon that kindness, so that it is as if they bring wronging as a recompense for the blessing. The likened term is alluded to by its companion, which is the fa' of causality, and the indication of this is what the listener knows, that wronging cannot be caused by bounty, as in your saying, "I did good to so-and-so, and he harmed me." His exalted saying ﴿And they make your provision that you deny﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82] means: you make the thanks for your provision that you deny; so the fa' is metaphorical for non-sequence, in the style of your saying, "I bestowed a favor upon him, and he disbelieved." You may say that the original meaning of the coordinating fa' is sequence and immediacy only, and this is the meaning inseparable from it in all the places where it is used, for regularity is a sign of the literal sense. As for sequence, that is, causality, it is an accidental matter attached to it; it is either metaphor or one of the consequences of constructions. Do you not see that it is found at times and is absent at others? It is absent in the coordination of single words, as in "Zayd came then 'Amr," and in many coordinations of clauses, such as His exalted saying ﴿You were in heedlessness of this, so We removed from you your covering﴾ [Qaf: 22]. Therefore the meaning of causality, wherever it is understood, needs indications; if you do not seek a connection for it, you say: it is one of the consequences of constructions, by the indication of context; and if you seek a connection for it — and it will not be lacking — you say: it is metaphor, because most matters occurring after others have the cause of sequence in them, even if by custom or by supposition. So the departure of the fa' from sequence is not the metaphor; rather the matter is the reverse.

Among what shows that the literal sense of the coordinating fa' is sequence and immediacy only is that some rhetoricians made His exalted saying ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy﴾ [al-Qasas: 8] the lam in it metaphorically used for the meaning of the fa' of immediacy, i.e., "so he became for them an enemy." They made the fa' literal in immediacy; and if it were for sequence, it would be equal to the lam and the metaphor would not stand. Thus the reason that moved al-Zamakhshari to estimate the omitted verb connected with the fa' is that he saw the coordination of wronging upon "﴿We shaded you with the clouds﴾" and what follows with the waw, and it is not fitting because there is no common aspect between the favor and the blame. Connection by the waw is conditioned by suitability, unlike coordination by the fa'; so it is fixed either to estimate "they wronged" as an independent sentence without coordination — and it is evident that there is no meaning in the independent reading — or to link "they wronged" by a coordinator other than the waw; and there is nothing suitable here except the fa', because the coordinated element occurred immediately after the coordinated-upon element, so that this succession in external reality substitutes for the common aspect. For this reason the fa' does not demand the strength of suitability that the waw demands, but only suitability in imagination; and it is found here, because the coordinated element occurring in reality immediately after the coordinated-upon element is what makes it present in the imagination of one speaking about the coordinated-upon element. As for the ugliness of such a phrase as "Zayd came then the rooster crowed," it is because of the slight benefit of this report; you see that it becomes good if by your saying "the rooster crowed" you mean the timing by dawn. By this it becomes clear that there was no way to link the supposed wronging with the two verbs before it except the fa'.

In that report, the linkage, and the attention to explaining it along with the strangeness of this sequence, there is an allusion to their blame, since they met kindness with ingratitude; and in it there is an allusion to their folly, since they turned away from thanks as if they were harming the Benefactor, whereas they were only inflicting harm upon themselves. This is the elaboration of what is said on the estimate of the author of al-Kashshaf.

What appears to me is that there is no need for the estimate, and that the sentence ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾ is coordinated upon what precedes it, because it is like it in being among the states of the Children of Israel; and the occasion for mentioning this sentence is what some of the preceding sentences included, that wronging had occurred from them: from His saying ﴿Then you took the calf after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 51], and His saying ﴿Indeed you have wronged yourselves by your taking the calf﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54], and what your saying included ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55], which indicates that this was a punishment they drew upon themselves. So He brought this sentence as a summation of what the preceding sentences included, like His saying "And they deceive none but themselves" after His saying ﴿They deceive God and those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9], and like His saying ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾ [Saba': 19] after the preceding discourse, which is His saying ﴿And We placed between them and the cities which We had blessed visible cities﴾ [Saba': 18], up to the verse.

[p. 512]
He changed the style in this sentence, shifting from addressing the Children of Israel to speaking about them with the third-person pronoun, in order to prompt admonition from their condition and as an allusion that they persist in their error and are not returning from their straying; they are such that they do not acknowledge that they wronged themselves.

This wronging that was supposed in the composition of the verse is their complaint about persistence in eating the manna and quail, which will be mentioned later by His exalted saying ﴿And when you said: O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], up to the verse. So His saying ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾ served as a preparation for it and as a hastening to record the scarcity of their thanks for God's blessings and His care for them, since their disposition was not softened by admonitions or by generosity.

As for His saying ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾, He placed the object first for restriction (qasr). The restriction had already occurred initially by the mere combination of negation and affirmation, then it was emphasized by the fronting, because their condition is like that of one who harms another, as it is said: the ignorant person does to himself what the enemy does to his enemy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 58–59 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We said, "Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in ease, and enter the gate prostrating, and say, 'Hittah (relief from sin),' and We will forgive you your sins and increase the doers of good."﴾ ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them, so We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they used to defiantly disobey.﴾ This is a reminder of another blessing which they were granted, but they neither accepted it well nor observed it with its due observance, so they were deprived of it for a time, and those who were the cause of its not being accepted were punished.

In the reminder of this blessing there is a favour upon them by bestowing the blessing upon them, because a blessing is a blessing even if the one who is blessed does not accept it; and it stirs up their regret over what their forefathers missed and what they suffered as a result of their self-admiration in their opinions; and it is an admonition to them not to fall into what the earlier ones fell into, for they knew that whenever they turned away from the due measure of blessings, calamities befell them.

Shaykh Ibn 'Ata' Allah said: "Whoever does not give thanks for blessings has exposed them to their loss, and whoever gives thanks for them has tied them down with their cord." Because the addressees knew what this verse meant, its wording was abridged to a degree that left many of the exegetes in this verse bewildered. They adopted various methods of drawing out the detailed meaning from its summary, but they did not arrive at anything convincing, and you would find their statements here: when some of them are reconciled with the arrangement of the verse, others are not reconciled, and perhaps all of them contradict what occurs in other verses.

What I hold as the account regarding the interpretation of this verse is that it refers to a known story contained in their books, namely that when the journey had driven the Children of Israel to the wilderness of Paran, they camped at the city of Kadesh, and so they found themselves on the borders of the land of Canaan, which is the Holy Land that God promised to the Children of Israel. That was during the second year after their departure from Egypt. Moses sent twelve men to spy out the land of Canaan, one man from each tribe, and among them were Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh. They went up and came to the city of Hebron, and they found the land abounding in good things, and they cut from its grapes, its pomegranates and its figs, and they returned to their people after forty days, and they informed Moses, Aaron and all the Children of Israel, and showed them the fruit of the land, and told them that it truly flows with milk and honey, but that its people are people of might and its cities are very fortified. Moses then commanded Caleb, and Israel listened to Moses, and he said, "We shall go up and possess it," and so did Joshua. As for the other ten, they spread among the Children of Israel a disparagement of the land, that it devours its inhabitants and that its inhabitants are giants, so the Children of Israel feared the inhabitants of the land and shrank from fighting. Joshua and Caleb then stood among them saying, "Do not fear the enemy, for they are a morsel for us, and God is with us." But the people did not heed them, and God revealed to Moses that the Children of Israel had thought ill of their Lord and that He would destroy them. Moses interceded for them, and God pardoned them, but He forbade them from entering the Holy Land for forty years, wandering, so that none of those present that day would enter it except Joshua and Caleb. And God sent a plague upon the ten discouraging spies, which destroyed them.

This verse thus corresponds perfectly to this story, especially when one joins to it the verse of Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has prescribed for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21] up to His saying ﴿the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 25]. His saying ﴿enter this town﴾ apparently means by it Hebron, which was close to them, and to which their spies went and from which they brought its fruits. It has been said that by "the town" is meant the whole region, as al-Qurtubi related from 'Amr ibn Shabbah, for the word qaryah is applied to a farm; but this is far-fetched by His saying ﴿and enter the gate﴾, since "gate" is applied to the passage between two mountains. However it is, it fits with His saying ﴿and eat from it wherever you wish, in ease﴾, which points to the abundant fruits there.

His saying ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them﴾ is necessarily an allusion to what the ten spies spread of disparagement of the land and its difficulty, and that they did not say the like of what Moses said, when the people were made to listen by the tongue of Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He, in Surah al-A'raf: ﴿So those who did wrong among them substituted a statement﴾ [al-A'raf: 162], i.e., from among those to whom it was said, "Enter the town." And the punishment that befell those who did wrong was the plague that struck the ten spies. This also fits with His saying in the verse of al-Ma'idah: ﴿And do not turn back upon your heels, lest you become losers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21], ﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed in it are a people of giants"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22], etc., and His saying ﴿Two men from among those who feared, upon whom God had bestowed favour, said, "Enter upon them through the gate"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23], for the gate suits the town. And His saying ﴿He said, "Then it is forbidden to them"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 26]. This is the correct interpretation, which conforms to the clear history. So His saying ﴿And when We said﴾ means, through the tongue of Moses, who conveyed it to the people by means of the silencing of the audience by Caleb son of Jephunneh. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 58–59 (part 2 of 2):

*I have been exchanged, from the cloak of youth's finery, for a worn-out garment, and wretched is the recompense of the one who exacts (a debt).*

The purpose of stating the word "qawl" (saying) explicitly, rather than saying "so they substituted it," is to rule out the supposition that they changed only the word *ḥiṭṭah* (remission, a word of repentance) and obeyed the rest of the command. Or it is like eating a grain together with a hair, which chokes the one who eats it, or a grain of wheat together with a barley-corn.

﴿And when We said, "Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in ease, and enter the gate prostrating, and say, 'Hittah (relief from sin),' and We will forgive you your sins and increase the doers of good."﴾ ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them, so We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they used to defiantly disobey.﴾ This is a reminder of another blessing which they were granted, but they neither accepted it well nor observed it with its due observance, so they were deprived of it for a time, and those who were the cause of its not being accepted were punished.

In the reminder of this blessing there is a favour upon them by bestowing the blessing upon them, because a blessing is a blessing even if the one who is blessed does not accept it; and it stirs up their regret over what their forefathers missed and what they suffered as a result of their self-admiration in their opinions; and it is an admonition to them not to fall into what the earlier ones fell into, for they knew that whenever they turned away from the due measure of blessings, calamities befell them.

Shaykh Ibn 'Ata' Allah said: "Whoever does not give thanks for blessings has exposed them to their loss, and whoever gives thanks for them has tied them down with their cord." Because the addressees knew what this verse meant, its wording was abridged to a degree that left many of the exegetes in this verse bewildered. They adopted various methods of drawing out the detailed meaning from its summary, but they did not arrive at anything convincing, and you would find their statements here: when some of them are reconciled with the arrangement of the verse, others are not reconciled, and perhaps all of them contradict what occurs in other verses.

What I hold as the account regarding the interpretation of this verse is that it refers to a known story contained in their books, namely that when the journey had driven the Children of Israel to the wilderness of Paran, they camped at the city of Kadesh, and so they found themselves on the borders of the land of Canaan, which is the Holy Land that God promised to the Children of Israel. That was during the second year after their departure from Egypt. Moses sent twelve men to spy out the land of Canaan, one man from each tribe, and among them were Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh. They went up and came to the city of Hebron, and they found the land abounding in good things, and they cut from its grapes, its pomegranates and its figs, and they returned to their people after forty days, and they informed Moses, Aaron and all the Children of Israel, and showed them the fruit of the land, and told them that it truly flows with milk and honey, but that its people are people of might and its cities are very fortified. Moses then commanded Caleb, and Israel listened to Moses, and he said, "We shall go up and possess it," and so did Joshua. As for the other ten, they spread among the Children of Israel a disparagement of the land, that it devours its inhabitants and that its inhabitants are giants, so the Children of Israel feared the inhabitants of the land and shrank from fighting. Joshua and Caleb then stood among them saying, "Do not fear the enemy, for they are a morsel for us, and God is with us." But the people did not heed them, and God revealed to Moses that the Children of Israel had thought ill of their Lord and that He would destroy them. Moses interceded for them, and God pardoned them, but He forbade them from entering the Holy Land for forty years, wandering, so that none of those present that day would enter it except Joshua and Caleb. And God sent a plague upon the ten discouraging spies, which destroyed them.
