[p. 518]

This is a reminder of another blessing, one that combined three blessings: quenching thirst after thirst. That is a greater blessing than the provision of food, which is why the image of quenching the thirsty person's need has become common. Providing drink where it is not expected to be found is a miracle for Musa and an honour for his community, because it is a favour to them.

That the springs were twelve meant that each tribe would have its own watering-place, so they would not crowd one another. His words "wa-idh" (and when) are connected to "udhkuru" (remember). The verse alludes to a well-known incident among the Jews. When they camped at Rafidim, before reaching the wilderness of Sinai, and after leaving the wilderness of Sin, around the third month after the Exodus, they became thirsty, and there was no water at that place. They complained against Musa and said: "Have you brought us up out of Egypt to die of thirst, we and our children and our livestock?" Musa called upon his Lord, and God commanded him to strike with his staff a rock there at Horeb. He struck it, and water gushed from it. The Torah does not mention that the springs were twelve. That division was a kindness to them, lest they crowd one another and perish because of their great numbers. This is among the things God clarified in the Qur'an.

His words "Musa asked for water" (istasqa Musa) clearly indicate that the one who asked for water was Musa alone. He asked it of God, and his people did not share in the supplication, so that his dignity would appear alone. Likewise, the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeking rain on Friday from the pulpit, when a Bedouin said to him: "The crops and the livestock have perished, so pray to God to send us rain." The hadith is in the Two Sahihs.

His words "to his people" indicate that thirst did not afflict Musa, because he set out on that journey certain that God was guarding them and bringing them to the Holy Land. For this reason God protected him from hunger, thirst and fatigue. This is the condition of the prophets. The Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith on continuous fasting: "I am not like your condition. I spend the night with my Lord, who feeds me and gives me drink." Ibn 'Arafa said in his tafsir: "Al-Mazari took from this verse the permissibility of asking for rain on behalf of the barren from the fertile, because Musa, peace be upon him, did not suffer the thirst that they suffered. Ibn 'Arafa refuted this by saying that he was their messenger and was with them." End of quote.

This is a firm refutation, since what is meant by seeking rain for the barren from the fertile is not individuals. Rather, it means that the people of a land not struck by drought seek rain for the people of a land that is struck by drought. The matter to which al-Mazari pointed is disputed among our (Maliki) scholars. Al-Lakhmi chose the permissibility of seeking rain for the barren from the fertile, because it is cooperation in righteousness, and because a Muslim's supplication for his brother in his absence is answered. Al-Mazari said: "There is scrutiny in it, because the predecessors did not do it."

The staff of Musa is the one he threw before Pharaoh's court, and it swallowed the serpents of the sorcerers. It was also the staff in his hand when God spoke to him in the wilderness of Sinai before he entered Egypt. Reports have been transmitted about it, none of which is authentic. It is said that it was from the tree of Paradise which Adam brought down with him, and that Musa inherited it. Had this been authentic, Musa would have counted it among its attributes when he said: ﴿It is my staff﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:18] and so on, for this is its greatest attribute. The word "'asa" (staff) is always written without the final ha'. Whoever says "'asahu" (his staff) with a ha' has committed a grammatical error (laḥn). It is narrated from al-Farra' that the first grammatical error to appear in Iraq was their saying "'asati" (my staff).

The "al-" in "al-hajar" (the rock) is for generic definition, meaning: strike any rock you wish. Or it is for specific reference, pointing to a rock that Musa knew by revelation from God. It is a rock on Mount Horeb, the mountain from which God spoke to Musa, as occurs in the Book of Exodus. Weak reports have been transmitted about it.

The fa' in His words ﴿fanfajarat﴾ (so it gushed forth) is called fa' al-fasiha (the "eloquent" fa'). They said that the meaning of the eloquent fa' is that it is the coordinating fa', since what follows it cannot be coordinated with what precedes it. Therefore, one must assume another coordinated element between them, which is then coordinated with what follows the fa'. This is the approach of al-Sakkaki, and it is the best approach. It has also been said that it indicates an omitted element before it. If that element is a condition, the fa' is the fa' of the response; if it is a single noun, the fa' is coordinating. The term fa' al-fasiha includes both. This is the approach of the majority in both cases, and it is called "eloquent" because it reveals an omitted element. The estimate in such a case is: "fa-daraba fa-nfajarat" (so he struck, and it gushed forth). In the verse of 'Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf:

They said: "Khurasan is the farthest that is aimed at us, then the return,"
So we have come to Khurasan.

That is, if the return comes after arriving at Khurasan, then we have come to Khurasan; that is, let us return, for we have come.

In my view, the fa' is not considered eloquent unless coordinating what follows with what precedes is not appropriate. When that coordination is appropriate, it is the coordinating fa'. The omission is for brevity, and estimating the omitted element is for clarifying the meaning. This is because the gushing of water follows God's words to Musa: "Strike the rock with your staff." It is evident that Musa is not one whose compliance is doubted. Moreover, every person who asks about a matter and is told "do such-and-such" should understand that what he was commanded is the thing that contains its answer. For example, a student says, "What is the ruling on such-and-such?" and you say, "Open the book of al-Risala at the chapter on such-and-such." Of the same kind is God's later words: ﴿Go down to a city﴾ [2:61]. As for estimating a condition here, meaning "if you struck, then it gushed forth," that is not clear, and it is strange that it was mentioned in al-Kashshaf.

His words ﴿each people knew its drinking-place﴾ were considered a resumptive sentence (istinaf) by al-'Ukbari and Abu Hayyan. They meant the explanatory resumption (al-istinaf al-bayani). That is why it is separated, as if a questioner asked about the reason the gushing of water was divided into twelve springs, and it was answered: "Each tribe knew its drinking-place." In my view, the more apparent reading is that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) stripped of the waw, because it addresses those who know the story, so there is no sense in assuming a question. What is meant by "people" (unas) is every tribe of the tribes.

His words ﴿Eat and drink of God's provision﴾ are the content of an omitted saying. It combined eating and drinking, although the topic is watering, because the sending down of manna and quails had preceded it. It was said there: ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾ [2:57]. So when that was followed by water, the two favours were united.

His words ﴿and do not spread corruption on the earth, causing corruption﴾ are part of what was said to them. The reason for this prohibition is that blessing may cause the servant to forget his need of the Creator, so he abandons the law and falls into corruption. God said: ﴿Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [96:6-7]. The word ﴿la ta'thaw﴾ (do not spread corruption) is the present tense of "'athiya," on the pattern of "radiya." This is the dialect of the Hijaz and is the eloquent form. Its verbal noun, according to the lexicographers, should be on the pattern of "ridan," though I have not seen anyone state this explicitly. The Lisan al-'Arab lists verbal nouns: al-'uthiyy and al-'ithiyy, with the 'ayn vowelled with a ḍamma or a kasra, with the thā' kasred in both and the yā' doubled in both; and al-'athayan with two fatḥas. In the dialect of non-Hijazis, "'athā ya'thū," like "samā yasmū." None of the reciters read ﴿wa-la ta'thū﴾ with a ḍamma on the thā'. It is the most severe corruption. It has been said that it means corruption in general. On both views, ﴿mufsidin﴾ (causing corruption) is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida) for its operator.

In al-Kashshaf, the meaning of ﴿la ta'thaw﴾ was given as: do not persist in your corruption. Thus the prohibited thing was made the continuation of the act. Apparently, al-Zamakhshari rejects the validity of an emphatic circumstantial clause for a verbal sentence, so he tried to differentiate between ﴿la ta'thaw﴾ and ﴿mufsidin﴾ to avoid emphasis. That is the view of the majority, but many verifiers disagreed with it. Ibn Malik chose a detailed position: if the meaning of the circumstantial clause is the same as the meaning of its operator, he treated it as similar to an emphatic clause for its subject, as here. He restricted the emphatic clause for the content of a clause to what follows a nominal sentence, as in: "Zayd is your father, kind," and in the verse of Salim ibn Dara al-Yarbu'i:

I am the son of Dara, known by it is my lineage,
And is there, O people, any shame in Dara? [206]

[Page 521]

These [clauses] are joined (ma'tufa) to the clauses before them in the same style. Attributing the saying to the second-person plural pronoun follows what has preceded in its parallels. What the clauses before it contain is part of enumerating the blessings bestowed upon them, either purely or mixed with their poor gratitude, and with the blessing being connected to that act through pardon and the like, as has preceded. So the apparent meaning is that the content of this clause is also a blessing.

The exegetes are perplexed about what this refers to. From the words of al-Fakhr (al-Razi) it is taken that the statement of God Most High, ﴿Go down to a city, for you will have what you asked﴾, is like an answer to what they requested, meaning that the answer is a bounty. But if it were conditional upon entering a town among the towns, it is very far-fetched, because their being given what they asked for is not established as having occurred.

And from the words of the exegetes that al-Fakhr began by quoting, and that 'Abd al-Hakim directed, it is taken that their request for the substitution of the manna and the quails with herbs and the like was a disobedience, because in it there is a dislike of the blessing that God bestowed upon them, since they expressed their consuming of it as ﴿endurance﴾ [al-sabr]. Endurance (al-sabr) is the soul's compelling itself to a disliked matter. What indicates this is that He disapproved of them with His saying ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower﴾. So the locus of the blessing would be the pardoning of this sin and the dealing gently with them until the answer with His saying "Go down." But it is far-fetched, since there is no blessing in His saying "Go down," nor in their request is there anything indicating that they disobeyed, because seeking a transfer from one blessing to another for a known purpose is not counted as disobedience, as al-Fakhr explained.

So what I hold regarding the interpretation of the verse is that it is a transition from enumerating blessings, which are followed by further blessings, to explaining the poor choice they made regarding their desires. Choosing is the proof of the intellect of the discerning, even if one chooses what is permissible. Along with this is the rudeness in the form of their request and the lack of courtesy toward the Messenger and toward the Bestower, since they said "we will not endure," expressing the consumption of the manna and quails with "endurance," which entails aversion. They also brought in what the "lan" (never) indicates in the reporting of their words, that they would not consume the manna and quails from now on. For (lan) indicates the total negation extending over all the times of the verb "nasbiru" (we will endure) from its beginning to its end, which is the meaning of perpetuity (ta'bid). In this there is a compulsion for Musa to hasten with the request, as they supposed that they had despaired him of accepting the manna and quails after that time. So God's answer to them in this request was that He cut off His care for them, neglected them, and left them to their own selves, and did not show them what He had accustomed them to: the sending down of food, the gushing of springs after the splitting of the sea, and the shading of the clouds. Rather He said to them, ﴿Go down to a city﴾, commanding them to strive for themselves, and that is enough as discipline and rebuke.

The Shaykh Ibn 'Ata' Allah, may God have mercy on him, said: "Among the ignorance of the disciple is that he behaves discourteously and the punishment is delayed for him, so he says: 'If there were in this an offence, I would have been punished.' Perhaps the supply is cut off from him from where he does not perceive it, and even if it were only the withholding of increase. And he may be placed in the position of distance from where he does not know. And if it were only that He leaves you to what you desire..." The purpose of this is that the discourse moves from enumerating blessings to explaining their receiving them with contempt, so that it moves from that to mentioning the reversal of their conditions and the causes of their abandonment. None of that is required by the request being a disobedience, for worldly punishments and the deprivation of virtues are not among the effects of the address of obligation (khitab al-taklif, the divine address that imposes duties), but they are of the kind of the address of legal causation (khitab al-wad', the address that establishes causes, conditions and obstacles), returning to the ordering of effects upon their causes, and that is among the laws of the order of the world. What indicates that the thing requited is a disobedience is only the otherworldly punishment. With this, the perplexity disappears, every difficulty is resolved, and the thread of the discourse is put in order.

The verse alludes to a story that the Torah mentions in a brief and scattered way: that when they departed from the wilderness of Sinai from Horeb and descended in the wilderness of Paran in the last part of the second month of the second year of the Exodus, travelling toward the regions of Hebron, they said, "We remember the fish that we used to eat in Egypt for nothing," meaning they would catch it with their own hands, and the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic, "and our souls have dried up, and we see nothing but this manna." So they wept. God became angry with them, and Musa asked Him for pardon, so He pardoned them and sent down on them the quails, and they stored up food for a full month from them.

The expression with "lan," which indicates the perpetuity of negation, in the Arabic language serves to convey the meaning of their reported words here: extreme vexation and aversion reaching the limit beyond which they had no capacity.

For perpetuity indicates the totality of negation across all parts of eternity, its beginning and its end. Thus "lan," in negating verbs, is like "la" of general negation (la al-tabri'a) in negating indefinite nouns.

They described the food as "one" (wahid), though it was two, the manna and the quails, because what is meant is that it recurs every day.

The clause "that He bring forth for us..." to its end is the content of what they asked Him to request. So it has the meaning of the object of an implied verb of saying, as if it were said, "Say to your Lord: 'Let Him bring forth for us...'". The apparent requirement would be to say "an yukhrija" (that He bring forth) for us, but He turned away from that to using a jussive verb in the form of an answer to their request, as a hint that they were confident that if he called upon his Lord, He would answer him, so that bringing forth what the earth produces seems to happen merely by Musa's supplication to his Lord. This is a style repeated in the Qur'an, such as His saying ﴿Say to My servants who have believed that they should establish the prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31], and ﴿Say to My servants that they should say that which is best﴾ [al-Isra': 53], and it is frequent. So it is equivalent to a conditional and a response, as if it were said: "If you call upon your Lord that He bring forth for us, He will bring forth for us." This is by treating the cause of the cause as the cause itself. So the verb sought was put in the jussive as an answer to the command with the request for it to God, to indicate the certainty of its occurrence because of their confidence in God Most High's answering Musa's supplication. In it there is an incitement to bring about what the answer is conditioned upon, as though it were a matter within his power. If he does not do it, he has been stingy toward them in what benefits them.

"Ikhraj" (bringing forth) is making something appear from the earth. The first "min" (from) is partitive (tab'idiyya) and the second is explanatory (bayaniyya), or the second is also partitive, because they do not request all the herbs but only some of them. In this there is ease for the one asked. The phrase ﴿from its herbs﴾ may be a circumstantial clause (hal) of "ma" (what), or it may be a substitute (badal) for "ma tunbitu al-ard" by repeating the preposition.

It is related from al-Hasan: "They were a people of farming, so they reverted to their original dispositions." It has been disputed regarding "al-fum." It is said it is garlic (al-thum) with the letter thaʼ, and the replacement of the thaʼ with the fa' is common in the speech of the Arabs, as they said "jadath" and "jadaf," and "thalagh" and "falagh." This is the most apparent and the most consistent with what was enumerated with it and with what is in the Torah. It is said that al-fum is wheat. Al-Zajjaj recited for Uhayha ibn al-Julah:

"I was indeed the richest of people, a single person,
when he came to Medina from the farms of fum."

He means the wheat farms. It is said that al-fum is chickpeas, in the dialect of the people of al-Sham.

His saying ﴿He said: Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ is from the speech of Musa, and it is said to be from the speech of God. It is a severe rebuke, because He stripped it of persuasive devices and of reproach, and confined Himself to the interrogation whose purpose is wonder, so it is a rebuke. In the exchange of the better for the lower there is the proclamation of the extremity of their foolishness and the badness of their choice.

His saying ﴿Would you exchange (atastabdiluna)﴾: the "sin" and "ta'" in it are for emphasizing the event and are not for requesting, so it is like His saying ﴿and God is self-sufficient (istaghna)﴾, and their saying "istajaba" in the sense of "ajaba" (he answered), and "istakbara" in the sense of "takabbara" (he became arrogant). From this is His Most High saying ﴿its evil was spreading (mustatiran)﴾ [al-Insan: 7] in Surat al-Insan. The verb "istabdala" is derived from "al-badal" (substitution) with a fatha on the ba' and a sukun on the dal, like "shabah" (resemblance), and it is said with a kasra on the ba' and a sukun on the dal, like "shibh," and it is said "badil," like "shabih." Among its derivatives there has been heard "istabdala," "abdala," "baddala," and "tabaddala," and all of these are augmented verbs. There has not been heard from it an unaugmented (mujarrad) verb, and it seems they dispensed with the unaugmented form by these augmented forms. The apparent meaning of the words of the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari), in Surat al-Nisa', at His saying ﴿and do not substitute the bad with the good﴾ [al-Nisa': 2], is that "istabdala" is its root and most of it, and that "tabaddala" is modeled upon it, because the form "tafa''ala" in the sense of "istaf'ala" is abundant, and from it "ta'ajjala" in the sense of "isti'jal" (hastening) and "ta'akhkhara" in the sense of "isti'khar" (delaying).

All the verbs of the root b-d-l indicate placing one thing in the place of another, whether of essences or of attributes, or substituting one thing for another, whether of essences or of attributes.

Since the meaning of the event from which the verb is formed requires that these verbs be transitive to two complements, they are either transitive to both objects together, as with the verb "ja'l" (making), or transitive to one object while the other is governed by a preposition, as with the complements of verbs of exchange such as "ishtara" (to buy). This latter is the common usage. When the verb is transitive to two objects, like His saying ﴿on the day the earth will be changed into another earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48], the first object is what is removed and the second is what replaces it, like His saying ﴿those, God will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾ [al-Furqan: 70], and ﴿on the day the earth will be changed into another earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48], and their saying "abdaltu al-halqata khatiman" (I replaced the ring with a seal). When it is transitive to one object and transitive to the other with "bi" (with), which is the more common usage, the accusative object is what is taken and the object with the preposition is what is given. Such as His saying here ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾, and His saying ﴿And whoever substitutes disbelief for faith has strayed from the right way﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108], and His saying in Surat al-Nisa' ﴿and do not substitute the bad with the good﴾ [al-Nisa': 2]. And the second complement may be governed by a preposition that means "bi" of substitution (bi al-badaliyya), as in the verse of Abu al-Shish:

"I was exchanged for the robe of youth's bloom
a worn-out garment, and evil is the reward of the one who seeks it."

And the transitivity of the verb may be turned away from the object being replaced and be made transitive to the one receiving the exchange, so that it becomes of the pattern of "a'ta" (gave), taking two accusative objects, and the omitted one is indicated by something like "min kadha" (from such-and-such) or "ba'da kadha" (after such-and-such), such as His Most High saying ﴿and He will certainly change for them, after their fear, security﴾ [al-Nur: 55]. The estimate is: "He will certainly change their fear into security." This is the exposition of the method of using these verbs.

In al-Kashshaf, at His Most High saying ﴿and do not substitute the bad with the good﴾ [al-Nisa': 2], there occurs something that implies that the verb "baddala" has a usage different from the usage of "istabdala" and "tabaddala," in that when it is transitive to the second object by "bi," what is governed by "bi" is what is taken, and what is accusative is what is abandoned and given. Al-Qutb (al-Razi) explained it in his commentary in a way whose apparent meaning is that "baddala" cannot, in the sense of its transitivity, be other than contrary to "tabaddala" and "istabdala." Al-Taftazani explained it by saying that it has two usages when it is transitive to the second object by "bi": one of them agrees with the usage of "tabaddala," and the other is the opposite. But in my view the more apparent is that there is no difference between "baddala," "tabaddala," and "istabdala," and that the words of al-Kashshaf are problematic. It suffices you that this is not found in the speech of the imams of the language, nor in its own speech in the book al-Asas.

So the command in His saying "Go down" (ihbitu) is for permission mixed with rebuke, meaning: if this is your aim, then go down, by the indication of His saying ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾. So the meaning is ﴿Go down to a city﴾, one of the cities, meaning. In it there is a turning away from their request, since there was no town near them at that time which they could reach.

It is also said that He meant "ihbitu Misr," that is, the land of Egypt, the land of the Copts, meaning: return to Egypt from which you came out. The command in this case is merely for rebuke, since it was not possible for them to return to Egypt.

[Page 525]

Know that Misr, on this meaning, may be treated as non-diptote (mamnu' min al-sarf) if it is interpreted as a specific territory, so it has both proper-name status (al-'alamiyyah, the status of being a proper name) and feminine gender (al-ta'nith). It may also be treated as diptote (munsarif) if it is interpreted as a general place, or because it is a feminine triliteral with a quiescent middle letter (sakin al-wasat), like Hind. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it appears without tanwin (nunation), and in the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it appears without an alif, and it appears without an alif in some of the Mushafs of 'Uthman. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyyah, who also mentioned that Ashhab said: Malik said to me, "It is, in my view, Misr, your village, the dwelling of Pharaoh." (End of quotation.)

Musa's saying to them ﴿Go down to a city﴾ may be a command intended as a threat, reminding them of the days of their humiliation and hardship, and of their longing to return to that way of life, as if he were saying to them: Return to what you were in, since you were unable to appreciate the excellence of the self (al-fada'il al-nafsiyyah) and the blessing of freedom and independence. Perhaps his saying "Go down" without "let us go down" (linahbit) indicates this, because he does not intend to include himself in this matter. This recalls the verse of Abu al-Tayyib:

"If your year pleased you,
then return to Homs in the coming year."

As for His saying ﴿Then indeed for you is what you asked for﴾, the apparent reading is that the fa' indicates sequence (al-ta'qib), joining the clause "indeed for you is what you asked for" to the clause "Go down," to show that the attainment of their request follows immediately upon their descent to Misr. Alternatively, it does not express causation (al-ta'lil), since the command to descend does not require a causal explanation of the kind this clause provides, because the intended meaning is clear from His saying ﴿Go down to a city﴾, and because this is not a context of encouragement toward this descent, such that the one addressed would be encouraged by a reason for the command. The apparent reason for using the fa' of sequence is that causation is not intended, for if causation were intended, then inna would serve in place of the fa', as Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir has explicitly stated in Dala'il al-I'jaz, in the fifth and eleventh chapters of his "Various Discourses on Composition" (Fusul shatta fi al-nazm), where he says: "Know that it is among the characteristics of inna, when it comes in this manner" — i.e., in the verse of Bashshar:

"Hurry, my two companions, before the midday heat,
indeed success lies in hastening."

— that it can take the place of the coordinating fa', and that it conveys a remarkable matter in linking the clause to what precedes it. You see the speech with it as both newly begun and not newly begun, both severed and connected at once. He also said: You see that when a clause enters with inna, it becomes linked to what precedes it and blends with it, so that the two statements seem poured in a single mould. But if inna is removed, you find the second of them has turned away from the first and its meaning has diverged from the meaning of the first, until you bring in the fa' and say, for example:

"Hurry, my two companions, before the midday heat,
hurry, then success lies in hastening."

Then you do not find the fa' restoring the two clauses to the harmony they had. This pattern is very frequent in the revelation, for example His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord; indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ [al-Hajj: 1], and His saying ﴿O my son, establish prayer﴾ [Luqman: 17], up to His saying ﴿Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Luqman: 17], and He said ﴿And pray for them; indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103], and so on.

The apparent meaning of the Shaykh's words is that when inna is present in a clause whose purpose is causation and linkage, it dispenses with the use of the fa', and that using the fa' in such a case is not appropriate to eloquent speech, since it is like combining the substitute and what it substitutes for. So when we find the fa' with inna, we know that the fa' is merely for coordination, while inna is intended to express causation and the linking of the two coordinated clauses beyond the mere meaning of sequence.

From this it is derived that the places of causation are those in which its meaning lies between the contents of the two clauses, as in the examples he cited.

Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr al-Muhit, considered the clause ﴿Then indeed for you is what you asked for﴾ to be the response (jawab) to the command, and claimed that just as a command is answered by a verb, it may also be answered by a nominal sentence. But it is not hidden that both of these views are weak here, because there is no intention to encourage this descent so that it should be given a reason or made conditional. Rather, this is an utterance of anger, as has been explained earlier. The linking of the clause with inna, the emphatic particle, serves to treat them as if they were in doubt because of the long time since they made their request, to the point that they doubt whether they will find it, out of their intense longing; and the lover is spurred on by bad expectation.

* * *

﴿And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with anger from Allah﴾ is coordinated with the preceding clauses by the particle wa (and), without repeating idh (when). As for its coordination, this is because this clause has a particular closeness to the clauses before it, being in the sense of a result and effect of what the clauses before it signify, from His saying ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49]. The content of those clauses is the mention of what Allah, Exalted is He, bestowed upon them of the blessing of liberating them from the enslavement of the Copts and from being driven to the land He had promised them. This included the two blessings of liberation and of establishment in the land, which is making courage subservient to them, if they had acted. But they did not appreciate its worth, and they longed to return to the way of life in Egypt, saying ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾, as We explained to you there, from what the Torah related; and they shrank back from entering the town and were cowardly in facing the enemy, as the preceding verse indicates and as the verse of al-Ma'idah details. Therefore, since they did not give thanks for the blessing nor appreciated it, it was inevitable that it be taken away from them and stripped from them, and that they be given in its place its opposite, namely humiliation (al-dhillah), which is the opposite of courage, since they did not trust in Allah's help for them; and poverty (al-maskanah), which is servitude. Thus the verse is presented as a recompense for the preceding speech. This is the reason for the coordination.

As for its being joined by wa rather than fa', this is so that it be a statement intended in itself, and not a consequence following from Musa's words to them ﴿Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾, because they did not give thanks for the blessing. For giving thanks for a blessing is the manifestation of its intended effects, like manifesting victory for the truth through the blessing of courage, relieving the distressed through the blessing of generosity, and sharpening minds through the blessing of knowledge. Thus whoever does not give thanks for a blessing deserves to have it taken from him and to be given its opposite in exchange. Allah, the Exalted, said ﴿So they turned away, and We sent upon them the flood of al-Arim and replaced their two gardens with two gardens bearing bitter fruit, tamarisk and some lote-trees﴾ [Saba': 16], and so on. Had it been coordinated without wa, its mention would have followed the mention of its cause, and it would not have had enough independence to command attention.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿And they were stamped upon﴾ and ﴿they returned﴾ and so on refers to all of the Children of Israel, not only to those who refused to enter the town and those who said ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾. This is shown by His saying ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right﴾, for those who killed the prophets were the sons of those who refused to enter the town and said ﴿We will not endure﴾. Thus the use of the third-person pronoun here follows the expected norm, since they are not the ones addressed. It is therefore not an iltifat (shift of pronoun), since the statement ﴿And humiliation was stamped upon them﴾ and so on is not a continuation of Musa's reply to them, as you know, because it includes both those who are described as refusing to enter the town and others who came after them. So the third-person pronoun has come in its original form. As for its including the addressees, this is only by way of ta'rid (indirect allusion), namely that the children inherit the character and dispositions of their fathers, as we established in explaining the earlier addresses in His saying ﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 50] and the verses that follow. This is supported by the causal explanation that comes afterward with His saying ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve﴾, which indicates that whoever is characterized by this is deserving of the same ruling that applied to the others.

In the usage of the Arabs, al-darb (striking) returns to the meaning of a forceful contact of the outer surface of one body with the outer surface of another body. One says "he struck with a staff," "with his hand," "with the sword," and "he struck the earth with his hand" when he pressed it to the ground. From this there branch out figurative meanings that return to the idea of intense adhesion. Among them: "he struck in the earth," meaning he travelled far; and "he struck a dome or a tent in such-and-such a place," meaning he fixed it firmly and secured it into the earth. 'Abdah ibn al-Tabib said:

"Indeed she who pitched a tent as an emigrant..."

Ziyad al-A'jam said:

"In a dome struck upon the son of al-Hashraj..."

And he struck the mud upon the wall, meaning he plastered it.

All of these senses were discussed earlier under His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example — a mosquito or what is above it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. So His saying ﴿And humiliation was stamped upon them﴾ is a metaphor by implicit comparison (isti'arah makniyyah), in which humiliation and poverty are likened, in their encompassing of them and their clinging to them, to a tent or dome that the occupant pitches so as to remain in it. The mention of "stamping" is a takhyil (imaginative metaphor), since it has no counterpart among the features of the thing compared. It is also possible that "stamped" is an indirect metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah), without an implicit comparison, by likening the clinging of humiliation to them and its adherence to them to the adherence of mud to a wall. The meaning of "indirect" is that what is considered in the comparison is the event and the attribute, not the essence; that is, the metaphor applies to the verb in the sense of its being an event, not in the sense of its being attached to a subject, as in the imaginative metaphor. Rather, it is in the sense of its being an event, and this is what is meant by their saying that it was applied to the verb following the application of the metaphor to the verbal noun. From this the difference becomes clear between taking "stamped" as imaginative and taking it as an indirect metaphor. This is a view in the verse that al-Tibi adopted in his commentary on al-Kashshaf, and al-Taftazani disagreed with him and took "stamped" to be an indirect metaphor in the sense of encompassing and covering, whether the comparison is to a dome or to mud. These are two intended possibilities in this context, which eloquent speakers perceive.

Furthermore, His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And humiliation was stamped upon them﴾ is not of the kind of Ziyad al-A'jam's line:

"Indeed generosity, manliness, and bounty
are in a dome struck upon the son of al-Hashraj."

Because the dome in the verse is the thing compared to something that does not actually exist, whereas the dome in the line can be literal. So the verse is a metaphor and an explicit expression, while the line is literal and a metonymy (kinayah), as al-Tibi pointed out. Al-Taftazani took the verse, on both possibilities of the metaphor, to be a metonymy for the Jews being humbled and abased. These are subtle points that do not clash with one another.

Al-dhillah means humiliation or abasement, and it is always with a kasrah on the dhal, nothing else. It is the opposite of 'izzah (honour). For this reason, al-Samaw'al or al-Harithi placed them in antithesis in his verse:

"Our being few did us no harm, while our neighbour
is honoured, and the neighbour of the majority is humiliated."

Al-maskanah means poverty, derived from sukun (stillness), because poverty reduces the movement of its possessor. It is also used for weakness, and from it comes miskin (the needy one) for the poor.

The meaning of the stamping of humiliation and poverty upon the Jews is that they lost fortitude and courage, and the marks of poverty and need appeared upon them despite the abundance Allah had bestowed upon them. When they became weary of it, it became for them as if it did not exist. For this reason, greed became for them an enduring disposition that persisted in their descendants.

Al-bawu' means to return, and here it is used figuratively for the transformation of their condition from what pleases Allah to His anger.

* * *

[Page 529]

﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right, and that is because they disobeyed and were transgressing﴾

This is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), prompted by the matter of their condition, which was so reprehensible in its consequences, namely the stamping of humiliation and poverty upon them and the mention of His saying ﴿And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with anger﴾. The demonstrative noun is singular to treat the thing pointed to as the one mentioned, and this is more appropriate to permit singularity than the singular pronoun in the verse of Ru'bah:

"In it are lines of blackness and whiteness,
as if on its skin is the splash of white patches."

Abu 'Ubayda said to Ru'ba: "If you mean the lines (of writing), say ka-annahā; if you mean the blackness and the whiteness, say ka-annahumā." Ru'ba replied: "I meant ka-anna dhālika, woe to you." The reason the form in the verse is more fitting with the singular is that humiliation (dhilla), poverty (maskana) and anger (ghaḍab) are things that cannot be seen, so one does not point to their essence; rather one points to the content of the speech, which is one thing, namely what has been mentioned and said. From this is the words of the Most High: ﴿That We recite to you of the signs and the wise reminder﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 58], meaning: that narrative which preceded. And from it is the words of the Most High: ﴿Neither old nor young, but between that﴾ [al-Baqara: 68], which will come. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "What made this good is that the demonstratives (asmāʾ al-ishāra), their dual, their plural and their feminine forms are not so in the true sense, and likewise the relative pronouns; for this reason alladhī came to mean the plural." End of quote.

It has been said that he meant by this that the plural and dual forms of the demonstratives were not formed by adding markers, but by special words for those situations; therefore using some of them in the sense of others is easier when there is a interpretation (taʾwīl). This is of little benefit, because the matter rests on interpretation and metaphor (majāz), whether in using a word in another sense or using a form in another meaning; there is therefore no particular merit attached to these words, as far as is apparent. Perhaps he meant that (dhā) is placed for the category of what is pointed to.

As for alladhī, it is placed for the category of what is known through a relative clause (ṣila), so it is suitable for application to the singular, dual, plural, masculine and feminine. What occurs of demonstratives and relative pronouns for the dual, such as dhāni, and for the plural, such as ulāʾika, is only a noun with the meaning of the dual and the plural, not that it is an inflection of a singular form or a plural of a singular form. Thus dhā is used to point to the dual and plural, but not the reverse; for this reason it is good to use the singular of them to indicate the multiple.

The bāʾ in His words ﴿because they used to disbelieve﴾ is causal (sababiyya), meaning that their disbelief and what accompanied it was a cause of their punishment: in this world by humiliation and poverty, and in the Hereafter by the anger of God. It contains a warning against falling into the like of what they fell into.

Page 530

His words ﴿and they killed the prophets without right﴾ refer specifically to the generations of the Jews who committed this great crime, whether those who carried out the killing and ordered it, or those who remained silent about it and did not support the prophets.

The Jews had killed among the prophets Isaiah (Ashiyāʾ) son of Amoz, who lived in the middle of the eighth century BCE; he was killed by King Manasseh, king of the Jews, in the year 700 BCE, being sawn in two on a tree trunk.

And Jeremiah (Armiyāʾ) the prophet, who lived in the middle of the seventh century BCE, because he gave the Jews many rebukes and admonitions, so they stoned him until he died; there is disagreement about this. And Zechariah (Zakariyyāʾ), the last, father of Yahya, was killed by Herod the Hebrew, king of the Jews on behalf of the Romans, because Zechariah tried to save his son Yahya from being killed; this was during the time of the mission of ʿĪsā. Yahya son of Zechariah was killed by Herod because the daughter of Herod's sister was angry with Yahya.

His words ﴿without right﴾ mean without a ground recognized in their own law, for in it is: ﴿whoever kills a soul, other than for a soul or for corruption on the earth, it is as if he had killed all mankind﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 32]. This restriction is therefore an argument against the Jews from the foundations of their own religion, to make their blame perpetual. Otherwise, the killing of prophets is never by right in any circumstance. He said "the prophets" because messengers are not given power over by their enemies, since that contradicts the wisdom of the mission, which is conveying the message. The Most High said: ﴿Indeed We help Our messengers﴾ [Ghāfir: 51], and He said: ﴿And God protects you from the people﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 67]. Hence the claim of the Christians that the Jews killed ʿĪsā is a claim contradicting the wisdom of sending; but God ended the period of his mission by the attainment of the purpose for which he was sent.

His words ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾ may be understood such that the demonstrative refers to the same thing indicated by the first "that", so it is a repetition of the reference for the sake of greater distinction of what is pointed to, eager to know it; and disobedience and transgression are then two other causes for the imposition of humiliation and poverty and for the anger of God upon them. The verse in this case is of the type of repetition, which dispenses with conjunction, like His words: ﴿Those are like cattle; nay, they are more astray; those are the heedless﴾ [al-A'rāf: 179]. It may also be that what is pointed to by the second "that" is disbelief in the signs of God and their killing of the prophets, so that this is an indication of the cause of imposing humiliation, etc.; what follows the word "that" is then the cause of the cause, to alert that persistence in disobedience leads to becoming immersed in it and moving from its smaller forms to its greater ones.

The bāʾ in both cases is causal in its basic meaning. There is no need to make one of the two bāʾs mean "with" (maʿa), when the second demonstrative is taken as a repetition of the first, following the Kashshaf, which al-Ṭībī dwelt upon, lengthening its explanation and exhausting its interpretation; for there is in it such artificiality that the composition of the Qur'an rejects.

What prompted the adoption of this view is that the speech is devoid of a conjunction linking "because they disobeyed" to "because they used to disbelieve," if the demonstrative is merely for repetition. We have already pointed out earlier how to answer this: that repetition serves the function of conjunction.

[Page 532]

Surah 2, verse 62 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians (al-Ṣābi'ūn), whoever believed in God and the Last Day and did righteous deeds, will have their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾

This verse falls between verses about the Children of Israel, concerning the blessings God bestowed upon them and their response to those blessings with ingratitude and indifference. It comes as a parenthetical insertion between these passages, for a reason that every eloquent reader will grasp. The earlier account of their poor treatment of God's blessings had brought upon them the stroke of humiliation and destitution, and their return with wrath from God. Since this affliction was bound to drive them to seek deliverance from God's anger, God, who never abandons His practice of mercy toward His creation and His desire for their welfare, made clear in this verse that the door of God is open to them and that turning to Him is an easy matter for them. This is achieved by believing and doing righteous deeds. It is a wonderful feature of eloquence that God joined with them in this matter a remnant of other nations. This serves to comfort the Jews in their loneliness after the harsh admonitions of the preceding verses, to do justice to the righteous among them, to acknowledge their virtue, and to give good news to the righteous of the nations, including the Jews and others, who passed away, such as those who lived before Jesus and obeyed their prophets, and such as the disciples (al-Ḥawāriyyūn), and those who existed at the time of the revelation of this verse, such as 'Abd Allāh ibn Salām and Ṣuhayb. Thus the verse has fulfilled the right of both groups with encouragement and good news, and it has observed the two correspondences with the preceding verses: the correspondence of pairing encouragement with warning, and the correspondence of mentioning the opposite after speaking of its opposite.

The particle (inna) here serves merely to emphasize the statement and to confirm it, in order to dispel the misconception that the preceding reproaches cover all Jews. Many people imagine that the earlier nations who went astray were like them in their misguidance. Some of my companions were astonished when I told them that when I stayed in Rome I sought blessing by visiting the tomb of Saint Peter, supposing that his tomb is in the church of Rome. I explained to them that he was one of the disciples (al-Ḥawāriyyūn), the companions of the Messiah Jesus, peace be upon him.

Mention of the believers came first in order to give attention to their status, so that they stand at the forefront of those who are cited with praise. The mention of people of goodness is never made without mentioning them alongside it. Among the consideration of this purpose is God's saying in Surat al-Nisā' ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them﴾ [al-Nisā' 4:162], meaning those who were Jews, ﴿and the believers believe in what has been revealed to you﴾ [al-Nisā' 4:162], and so on, and because they are the model for others, as God said: ﴿So if they believe in the same as you have believed, then they are guided﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:137]. Therefore, what is meant by "those who believed" in this verse is the Muslims who affirmed the Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ), and this is a title for the Islamic community in the usage of the Qur'an.

﴿Those who were Jews﴾ are the Children of Israel, and their discussion has already passed. What we mention here is the reason for describing them as "those who were Jews." The meaning of "were Jews" (hādū) is that they became Jews or adhered to the religion of the Jews.

The origin of the name Yahūd is a word transferred into Arabic from Hebrew. In Hebrew it ends with a dhāl with a dot, and it is the name of one of the tribes of Israel. This name was applied to the Children of Israel after the death of Solomon, in the year 975 BCE. After his death the kingdom of Israel split into two kingdoms: the kingdom of Rehoboam son of Solomon, which was followed only by the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, and it was called the kingdom of Judah, because most of its followers were from the tribe of Judah, and it made its seat the same seat as that of his father, Jerusalem. And there was a kingdom whose king was Jeroboam son of Nebat, the servant of Solomon, who was brave and noble. The remaining ten tribes made him king over them, and he made the seat of his kingdom Samaria, and he was called king of Israel. However, he and his people corrupted the Mosaic religion and worshipped idols, and because of this they separated from the Israelite community. Their rule in Samaria lasted only two hundred and some fifty years, and then it was ended at the hands of the kings of the Assyrians, who uprooted the Israelites in Samaria, destroyed it, and carried the Children of Israel to the land of Assyria as slaves. They settled a group of Assyrians in the land of Samaria. From that day on, the Children of Israel had no kingdom except the kingdom of Judah in Jerusalem, ruled by the descendants of Solomon, peace be upon him. From that time the name Jews, that is, Judah, prevailed over the Children of Israel, and their kingdom continued until around the year 120 BCE, when it became Christian during the time of the Roman emperor Hadrian, who expelled the Jews with the final expulsion. They scattered across the regions under the name of Jews, they and those who joined them from the remnants of the rest of the tribes.

Perhaps this is the reason for choosing the expression "those who were Jews" in the verse instead of "the Jews," to indicate that they are those who attributed themselves to the Jews, even if they were not from the tribe of Judah.

Then the name "Jews" became applied generally to those who adhere to the religion of the Torah. God said: ﴿The Jews said, "The Christians are not on anything"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:113], and so on. It is said "tahawwada" when one follows the law of the Torah. In a hadith: "Every child is born upon the fiṭrah (natural disposition), then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian." It is also said "hāda" when one adopts Judaism. God said: ﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾ [al-An'ām 6:146]. As for the saying of Moses in Surat al-A'rāf, ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [al-A'rāf 7:156], that has the meaning of repentance.

As for "al-Naṣārā" (the Christians), it is a collective noun of naṣrī, with a fatḥa then a sukūn, or nāṣirī, a relative adjective referring to al-Nāṣira (Nazareth), a village from which Mary, mother of the Messiah, peace be upon them both, originated. Mary left Nazareth heading for Jerusalem, and she gave birth to the Messiah in Bethlehem. For this reason the Children of Israel called him Yashū' al-Nāṣirī or al-Naṣrī. This is the reason for naming his followers "the Christians."

As for His saying "al-Ṣābi'īn" (the Sabians), the majority read it with a hamzah after the bāʾ, in the form of the plural of ṣābi' with a hamzah at its end. Nāfi' alone read it with a sākin yā' after the kasra-vowelled bāʾ, as the plural of ṣāb, a defective noun. According to the reading of the majority, al-Ṣābi'ūn is probably the plural of ṣābi', and ṣābi' is probably the active participle of ṣaba'a with hamzah, meaning appeared and rose. It is said ṣaba'a al-najm, meaning the star rose. It is not from ṣabā yaṣbū, meaning to incline, because the reading with the hamzah indicates that leaving the hamzah unsoftened in other readings is a softening, since the original principle is the agreement of the readings in meaning.

Some scholars among the Europeans claimed that they were called Ṣābi'a because their religion was brought by a people from Sheba (Saba'). As for the reading of Nāfi', they made it the plural of ṣāb, like rām (one who throws), as an active participle of ṣabā yaṣbū, meaning to incline. They said: because the people of this religion inclined away from every religion toward the religion of worshipping the stars. It would have been better to say that they inclined away from many religions, since they took their religion from them, as you will know.

It has also been said that Nāfi' softened the hamzah of al-Ṣābi'īn and made it a yā', like his reading sāla sā'il (a questioner asked), and this kind of softening is transmitted by report, because there is no reason to soften a moving hamzah after a moving letter.

In my view, the more apparent conclusion is that the origin of the word al-Ṣābī, or al-Ṣābi'a, or what branches from them, is an ancient word from an ancient Arabic or Semitic language, the language of the Arabs of Mesopotamia in Iraq. In the Encyclopaedia of Islam it is stated that the name al-Ṣābi'a is derived from a Hebrew root (ṣ-b-' ), meaning to immerse, by which a sect known as the Mandaeans was identified. They are a Jewish-Christian sect in Iraq who practice baptism like the Christians. They are called al-Ṣābi'ūn in the form of the plural of ṣābi', and al-Ṣābi'a as a description of an implied noun, meaning the Sabian nation, namely those who adhere to the religion of the Sabians. This religion is known only by the name al-Ṣābi'a, under the assumption of a genitive construction, meaning "the religion of the Sabians," with the description of its followers. It is also said "the religion of the Sabians."

This religion is an ancient one that appeared in the land of the Chaldeans in Iraq, and most of its followers spread between the Khābūr and the Tigris, and between the Khābūr and the Euphrates. They were in the marshes (baṭā'iḥ) and Kaskar in the fertile lands of Wāsiṭ, and in Ḥarrān in the lands of al-Jazīra.

The people of this religion were Nabateans in the land of Iraq. When the Persians gained control over the region of Iraq, they removed the kingdom of the Sabians and prevented them from worshipping idols, so they no longer dared to worship their idols. Likewise, the Romans prevented the people of Syria and al-Jazīra from the Sabians. When Constantine became Christian, he compelled them by the sword to become Christian, and from that time the worship of idols among them ceased, and they outwardly professed Christianity. When Islam prevailed over their lands, they were counted among the Christians. The Sabians of the lands of Kaskar and the marshes were considered a sect of the Christians who trace their lineage to the prophet Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā (John son of Zechariah). Nevertheless, they have books which they claim God revealed to Seth son of Adam, and they call him Aghathā Dīmūn. The Christians call them the Yūḥannāsiyya, attributed to Yūḥannā, who is Yaḥyā.

The essence of this religion is the worship of the wandering planets, the Moon, and some stars, such as the North Star. They believe in the Creator of the world, that He is one, wise, and holy, exalted above the attributes of created things. However, they said that humans are unable to reach the majesty of the Creator, so it is necessary to draw near to Him through intermediary beings close to Him, which are pure, holy, incorporeal spirits. They claimed that these spirits dwell in the stars and descend to human souls and connect with them to the extent that human souls approach the nature of spiritual beings. Thus they worshipped the stars with the intention of turning toward their spiritual natures. Because those spiritual beings descend upon human souls, it becomes necessary to purify the soul by cleansing it from the effects of the appetitive and irascible powers as much as possible, and to devote oneself to worship through humble supplication to the spirits, and by purifying the body, fasting, almsgiving, and perfuming. They obligated themselves to the four fundamental virtues of the soul, which are chastity, justice, wisdom, and courage, and to the particular virtues branching from the four, which are righteous deeds, and to avoiding the particular vices, which are the opposites of the virtues, namely evil deeds.

Among the scholars there are those who say that they hold that there is no need for the sending of messengers, and they give as their reason that a claimant to prophethood is a human, so he cannot be an intermediary between people and the Creator. Among the scholars there are some who transmit from them that they claim to be upon the religion of Noah. They also say that the first teachers of the religion of the Sabians were Aghathā Dīmūn and Hermes, and they are Seth son of Adam, and Idrīs. They take from the words of the sages whatever helps toward perfection, so their speech frequently resembles the sayings of Greek sages, especially Solon, Plato, and Aristotle. In my view it is not improbable that those sages borrowed some opinions from the ancient Sabians of Iraq, for there is a resemblance between them in the worship of the stars, considering them gods, and in affirming a God of gods.

They built temples for the stars so that they would be descent-places for the spirits of the stars, and they took care to purify and perfume them so that spiritual beings would be drawn to them. They sometimes made images of the stars in forms, intending by them to imitate the forms of spiritual beings according to their belief.

Among their religion are three prayers each day, and their qibla is toward the direction of the north wind. They perform ablutions before prayer, and their recitations and supplications are called al-zamzama (muttering) with two zāy's, as occurs in the translation of Abū Isḥāq al-Ṣābi'.

They have a fast of thirty days in the year, distributed over three seasons of the year.

[Page 536]

It is obligatory to perform the ghusl of major impurity (*ghusl al-janabah*) and the ghusl of a menstruating woman. Celibacy is forbidden. A man may marry as many women as he wishes, but he may marry only a Sabian woman who follows his religion. If he marries a woman who is not Sabian, or a Sabian woman marries a man who is not Sabian, both leave the religion, and repentance from them is not accepted. They wash their dead, shroud them, and bury them in the ground. They have a religious leader whom they call the *Kimr*, spelled with a kaf, a mim, and a ra. This religion became well known in Harran, a town in the region of al-Jazirah. For this reason, in the books of Islamic doctrine (*kutub al-'aqa'id*) the Sabians are known as *al-Harnaniyyah*, with two nuns, after Harran, contrary to the usual rule of derivation, as stated in the *al-Qamus* (dictionary). Ibn Hazm said in *Kitab al-Fisal*: "The religion held by the Sabians was the oldest of religions on the face of the earth and the most dominant in the world, until they introduced innovations into it. Then God sent Ibrahim, peace be upon him, with the *hanifiyyah* (the upright monotheistic faith)." End of quotation.

[Page 536, continued]

The religion of the Sabians was known to the Arabs in the pre-Islamic era, because the lands of the Sabians in Iraq and Syria bordered the dwellings of some Arab tribes, such as Diyar Bakr and the lands of the Anbat, which were adjacent to the lands of Taghlib and Quda'ah.

Do you not see that when Muhammad ﷺ was sent, the polytheists described him as a Sabian? Sometimes they called him "Ibn Abi Kabshah," and Abu Kabshah was one of the forefathers of Aminah al-Zuhriyyah, the mother of the Prophet ﷺ. He had openly practiced the worship of the stars among his people. They claimed that the Prophet had inherited this from him, but they lied. In the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, they were on a journey with the Prophet ﷺ when their water ran out. They sought water and met a woman between two water-skins on a camel. They said to her, "Go to the Messenger of God." She said, "The one who is called the Sabian?" They said, "He is the one you mean." He then related the hadith about the multiplication of water.

They used to call the Muslims *al-Sabah* (those who have turned away), as reported in the account of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, who was a friend of Umayyah ibn Khalaf. Whenever Sa'd passed through Makkah, he would stay with Umayyah. When the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Madinah, Sa'd set out one day to perform 'umrah and stayed with Umayyah in Makkah. He said to Umayyah, "Watch for me a moment when it is quiet, so that I may circumambulate the House." So Umayyah took him out, and Abu Jahl met them. He said to Umayyah, "O Abu Safwan, who is this with you?" Sa'd answered, and Abu Jahl said to him, "Do I see you circumambulating in Makkah in safety, when you have given shelter to the Sabah?"

In the account of Khalid ibn al-Walid's expedition against Jadhimah, he offered them Islam or the sword, but they did not know how to say "We have submitted" (*aslamna*), so they said "We have turned away" (*saba'na*). [The hadith continues.]

It has been said that a people of Tamim worshipped the star *Najm al-Dabaran*; that a people of Lakhm and Khuza'ah worshipped *al-Shi'ra al-'Abur*, which is one of the stars of the constellation Gemini (*burj al-Jawza'*) in the circle of Cancer; and that a people of Kinanah worshipped the moon. Some have assumed that these people were Sabians. I suspect they adopted the worship of these stars through poor investigation of the true nature of the Sabian religion. Al-Zamakhshari did not assert with certainty that there were Sabians among the Arabs. He said in *al-Kashshaf*, in his commentary on Surah Fussilat, on God's words ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon﴾ [Fussilat: 37], "Perhaps some of them used to prostrate to the sun and the moon, like the Sabians, and so they were forbidden from that."

The Muslim scholars differed about how to apply the rulings to the Sabians. According to Mujahid and al-Hasan, they are a group between the Jews and the Magians (*al-Majus*). Al-Baydawi said: they are a people between the Christians and the Magians. Some scholars classed them with the People of the Book, and some classed them with the Magians. The cause of this disagreement is the obscurity of their conditions, their concealment of their religion, and the confusion that entered it because of the subjugation of the nations that dominated their lands. The section that was overcome by the Persians had its religion mixed with Magianism, and those overcome by the Romans had their religion mixed with Christianity. Ibn Shas said in *al-Jawahir al-Thaminah*: Shaykh Abu al-Tahir, meaning Ibn Bashir al-Tanukhi al-Qayrawani, said: "They prohibited the slaughter of the Sabians because they are between Christianity and Magianism." Without doubt, he meant the Sabians of Iraq, who before Islam conquered their lands followed Magianism.

In *al-Tawdih* on the abridgment of Ibn al-Hajib, in the chapter on slaughter, al-Tartushi said: "The slaughter of a Sabian is not eaten, but it is not forbidden in the way the slaughter of a Magian is forbidden." In the same work, in the chapter on hunting, Malik said: "The game of a Sabian is not eaten, nor is his slaughtered animal."

In the commentary of 'Abd al-Baqi on Khalil: "The claim that the Sabian is of Christianity is not strong, as Abu Ishaq al-Tunisi mentioned. And from Malik: a Muslim may not marry a Sabian woman."

Al-Jassas said in his commentary on Surat al-Ma'idah and Surat Bara'ah: It is related from Abu Hanifah that the Sabians are People of the Book, while Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said they are not People of the Book. Abu al-Hasan al-Karkhi used to say: "The Sabians who are in the region of Harran worship the stars, so they are not People of the Book according to all of them." Al-Jassas said: "The Sabians who are known by this name at this time do not include any People of the Book. Their creed is originally one, I mean those in the region of Harran and those in the region of al-Bata'ih and Kaskar in the countryside of Wasit. The disagreement between those in the region of Harran and those in the region of al-Bata'ih concerns some of their laws, and among them there are no People of the Book. What is most likely in my view, regarding Abu Hanifah's opinion, is that he witnessed some of them declaring that they were Christians out of dissimulation (*taqiyyah*). These are the ones who were in the region of al-Bata'ih and Kaskar, and the Christians call them *Yuhanna Siyyah*. They claim descent from Yahya ibn Zakariyya, and they hold books which they claim were revealed by God to Shith and Yahya.

As for those whose belief among the Sabians is as we have described, namely the Harranians in the region of Harran, who are idol-worshippers and do not claim descent from any of the prophets, nor hold any of the books of God, there is no disagreement among the jurists that they are not People of the Book, that their slaughter is not eaten, and that their women may not be married. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said that the Sabians are not People of the Book, and they did not distinguish between the two groups. Likewise is the view of al-Awza'i and Malik ibn Anas." End of his words.

[Page 537]

As for the reason that the verse mentions these three religions together with Islam, and not others such as Magianism, the dahriyyun (materialists), and the zanadiqah (heretics): this is the context of calling them to enter Islam and turn away from their religions, which had been invalidated. They are more receptive to accepting Islam than the Magians and the dahriyyun, because they affirm one God who alone created the world and who follow virtues, though they differ among themselves in this. Therefore the verse specified them, drawing them near to entering Islam. Do you not see that He mentioned the Magians with them in His words ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated partners [with God] — indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Hajj: 17], because that was a context of affirming the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims.

God's words ﴿whoever believes﴾ may be read as "man" being a conditional (*shart*) in the position of the subject, and "then for them is their reward" as the response of the condition. The condition together with its response is the predicate of *inna*, and so the meaning is: "Indeed, those who believed — whoever among them believes in God, then for him is his reward." The connecting pronoun between the sentence and the subject of *inna* is omitted, because the conditional *man* is general, so the generality served as the connector that encompasses the subject, namely the noun of *inna*. The meaning of the speech is then in the future, because the past verb falls within the scope of the condition: i.e., whoever among them believes in God and does righteous deeds, for him is his reward. The intended purpose is to open the door of return for them after they were struck by the earlier calamities, and to mention among these nations those for whom no disbelief is recorded, to fit what the reason implied in this statement: that they used to disbelieve. It also reminds the Jews that they have no special status over other nations, so that they do not rely on the illusion that they are beloved of God and that their sins are forgiven. In this there is also an indication that sincere believers among the Jews and others from earlier times, such as the leaders who were present at the secret conversation with Musa, and such as Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yafunah, share this ruling: that they have a reward with their Lord. This is because attaching the reward to a derived condition indicates causation. Indeed, those who did these things before the condition was specified are more deserving of the ruling. Thus the verse fulfils the right of both groups.

It is also possible that *man* is a relative pronoun (*maw-sulah*), a substitute (*badal*) for the noun of *inna*. The past verb in that case remains in the past, because there is nothing that turns it to the future. The *fa'* (then) enters "then for them is their reward" either because it enters the predicate, as in the line of the poet, which is among the examples in the book of Sibawayh, and as in the saying of a woman of Khawlan: "So marry their young women"; and as in God's words ﴿Indeed, those who tormented the believing men and believing women and then did not repent — for them is the punishment of Hell﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], according to other than Sibawayh. Or it is because the relative clause is treated like a condition, to signal causation, and so the *fa'* was introduced as an indicator of this. In that case, the meaning drawn from the verse is the exception of the righteous of the Children of Israel from the ruling of humiliation, poverty, and the wrath of God. The mention of the rest of the righteous of the nations alongside them, on this reading, indicates that this is the way of God in His dealings with His creation and in recompensing each for his deeds.

The mention of those who believed among these groups, and the application of the words *man amana billah* to them, has been regarded as problematic, since they are already believers, so mentioning them is "obtaining what is already obtained." It has been said that by this is meant only those who believed with their tongues, namely the hypocrites. It has also been said that it refers to all of them, and that "whoever believed" refers to whoever persisted in belief with respect to the sincere, and to whoever was sincere with respect to the hypocrites. These two answers are very far-fetched. It has also been said that the words ﴿whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾ refer specifically to the groups who were Jews, Christians, and Sabians, and not to the believers, by the context of the situation, since they were described as "those who believed." This is good. In my view, there is no need for any of this. The condition and the relative clause are composed of two things: faith and righteous deeds. Even if the sincere ones have faith, righteous deeds still remain incumbent upon them. Since the condition or the relative clause is composed of two matters, each people knows its own path, and each attribute returns to the one who needs it, wholly or partly.

The meaning of "whoever believes in God" is complete faith, which is belief in the message of Muhammad ﷺ, by the context of the situation and by the context of His words "and does righteous deeds," since the condition for the acceptance of deeds is legal faith, according to God's words ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17]. He counted not believing in the message of Muhammad ﷺ as equivalent to not believing in God, because obstinate denial of the miracles, which stand in place of God's confirmation of the Messenger who was challenged by them, amounts to denying God's confirmation of that message. Therefore one who obstinately denies is not a believer in God with true belief.

From this it is known that there is no basis for the claim that this verse is abrogated by God's words ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 85], since there is no soundness in claiming abrogation of a report, unless it is said that God informed of it concerning believers among the People of the Book and the Sabians who believed in what the messengers of God brought, without alteration, distortion, or disobedience, and who died upon that before the mission of Muhammad ﷺ. Then the meaning of the verse would be like the meaning of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, in what he related about the one who will be given his reward twice: "A man of the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and then believed in me — for him are two rewards."

As for those who say it is abrogated, I suppose their interpretation is that God gave them respite at the beginning, when they first received the call of the Messenger of God ﷺ, so that they might reflect. When they persisted in opposition, He abrogated it by His words ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾, so that their claim would not lead to the claim of abrogating a report.
