Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 62 (part 3 of 3):

His saying, ﴿So they will have their reward with their Lord⦈, uses "reward" (ajr) for the recompense figuratively, because it stands in exchange for righteous deeds, and what is meant by it is the bliss of the Hereafter, not a worldly reward, by the indication of the context. His saying ﴿with their Lord⦈ is a figurative "with" (indiyya), used to establish the certainty of the promise, just as it is used to establish the certainty of an acknowledgment in their saying, "I have such-and-such with me" (laka 'indi kadha).

The way that 'inda in this kind of usage indicates certainty is that 'inda denotes place. When it is applied to something that does not, by its nature, reside in a place, it is used to mean the necessary consequence of place, namely the existence of something that is of the kind that could be in a place. Moreover, attaching 'inda to the name of the Lord, exalted is He, is among the things that increase the reward in certainty, because the one it is attached to is the most generous of the generous, so the reward that is with Him is not lost.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿their reward with their Lord⦈ is in the plural only in observance of what the relative pronoun "man" refers to, while its predicate or relative clause is in the singular in observance of its wording. What made this fitting here and placed it at the highest level of eloquence is that these two permissible Arabic usages, in the return (ma'ad) of relative pronouns and conditional particles, have been combined in a manner that signals the intention of generality in the relative or conditional. Therefore, He brought the pronoun in its relative clause or verb in agreement with its wording, for the purpose of generality. Then, when the pronoun is brought with the predicate or the response, it is made plural so that it returns to the beginning, and thus it connects with the subject of "inna," which was introduced by the relative or conditional as a substitute for it or as a predicate about it, so that one knows that this general ruling is intended to include that specific group first. It is as if it were said: "Indeed, those who believed, etc.; everyone who believed in God and did, etc.; then for those who believed, their reward is theirs." Thus it is known that they are among those covered by the generality, in the manner that logicians mention when a premise is implicitly included in some premises for knowledge of it. This is from the general statement that came in connection with a specific cause.

His saying ﴿and no fear shall be upon them⦈: the reading of the majority is with the nominative (raf'), because the negated thing is a specific fear, namely the fear of the Hereafter.

The expression of negating fear with a nominal sentence, which is ﴿no fear shall be upon them⦈ [Yunus: 62], serves to convey the negation of the genus of fear as a steady negation, because the nominal sentence indicates permanence and stability. The expression of negating fear with a verbal sentence, which is
صفحة ٥٤١
﴿nor shall they grieve⦈, serves to restrict them to the negation of grief in the Hereafter, that is, unlike those who do not believe.

Since fear and grief are mutually connected, the specificity of each of them extends to the other. Know that His saying ﴿so they will have their reward⦈ corresponds to His saying ﴿and they incurred wrath from God⦈ [al-Baqarah: 61], and for this reason it is joined with "'inda," which indicates care and approval. His saying ﴿and no fear shall be upon them⦈ corresponds to ﴿and humiliation was struck upon them⦈ [al-Baqarah: 61], because humiliation is the opposite of honor, and the humiliated person fears, since he dreads hostility, killing, and raids, whereas the honorable person is brave, since he does not fear harm and knows that what has been decreed for him will happen. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And honor belongs to God, His Messenger, and the believers⦈ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. His saying ﴿nor shall they grieve⦈ corresponds to His saying ﴿and destitution⦈ [al-Baqarah: 61], because destitution imposes grief on its bearer and the wish for a good life. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life⦈ [al-Nahl: 97]. Thus the fear that is negated is the fear arising from humiliation, and the grief that is negated is that arising from destitution.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 2, verses 63–64:**

﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God."﴾ ﴿Then you turned away after that, and but for the grace of God upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers.﴾

This is a reminder of another story in which God showed their forefathers both His might and His mercy, yet they neither took heed nor gave thanks. It is that the covenant was taken from them through Moses, peace be upon him, that they would act by the Sharīʿah (sacred law). This happened when God manifested Himself to Moses, peace be upon him, on the Mount (al-Ṭūr) in a special manifestation directed at the mountain. The mountain shook, quaked and trembled, and smoke, cloud, thunder and lightning enveloped it, as described in the nineteenth chapter of the Book of Exodus (Sifr al-Khurūj) and in the fifth chapter of the Book of Deuteronomy (Sifr al-Thaniyah). So perhaps, from the intensity of the tremors, the mountain, because of the clouds, smoke and thunder that appeared around it, began to appear as if it were a cloud. For this reason it is described in the verse of al-Aʿrāf with His words, "﴿And when We lifted the mountain over them as though it were a canopy﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 171]." _Nataqa_ means he shook it violently and tore it loose, until it seemed to them that it was swaying. This is similar to their saying _istaṭārahu_, meaning he startled it and it became agitated. So they gave the pledge and complied with everything God commanded them, and they said: "Whatever God speaks, we will do." Then God said to Moses, "Let them believe in you forever." There is nothing in the books of the Children of Israel, nor in the sound hadiths, indicating that God uprooted the Mount from its place and lifted it above them. Rather, that is reported only in weak narrations, and therefore we have not relied on it in this exegesis.

The pronouns of address serve to burden the later generation with the consequences of the earlier generation, so that they would not fall into the like of it, and so that they would seek forgiveness for their forefathers for it. The word _mīthāq_ (covenant) in this verse is like _ʿahd_ (pledge) in the preceding verses: it refers to the Sharīʿah, and He promised them to act by it. Their books have named it a pledge, as we mentioned earlier, and it is still so called in their books to this day. This is a scientific miracle for our Messenger (ﷺ).

Al-Ṭūr is the proper name of a mountain in the Sinai desert. It is said that al-Ṭūr is a generic noun for mountains in the language of the Canaanites, which was transferred into Arabic, and they recited the verse of al-ʿAjjāj:

*He brought close his two wings from the mountain, so that the falcon's flight was cut short when the falcon swooped.*

If that is correct, then its application to this mountain is a proper name by dominance in Hebrew, because they found the Canaanites mentioning it, saying _al-Ṭūr_ meaning the mountain. It was a word they had not previously known, so they supposed it to be its proper name and called it al-Ṭūr.

His words, "﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you﴾," are the object of an omitted verb of saying, its estimated form being: saying to them, "Hold firmly." That is what the covenant was taken upon. Taking (_akhdh_) is a metaphor for receiving and understanding. Strength (_quwwah_) is a metaphor for keeping it safe, mastering its reception, and resolving to act upon it, as in His saying, "﴿O John, take the Book with strength﴾" [Maryam: 12]. It is also permissible that _dhikr_ (remembrance) is a metaphor for compliance, meaning: remember it when you resolve to do the deeds, so that your deeds accord with what is in it. Or the intended meaning of _dhikr_ is understanding, as evidenced by the particle _fī_ (in), which indicates a figurative sense of place, meaning deriving the branches from the roots. What is meant by "what He gave them" is what was revealed to Moses, namely the Ten Words, which are the foundations of the Torah's Sharīʿah.

The clause "﴿that you may be mindful of God﴾" is the cause (ʿillah) of the command in His words "﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you with strength﴾" and "remember what is in it." That is why it is separated without a conjunction.

The hope which the particle _laʿalla_ (perhaps, that) implies is used to mean bringing close the cause of piety by urging them to hold firmly, and to keep remembering what is in it. Thus this bringing close and clarifying resembles the hope of one who hopes. It is also permissible that _laʿalla_ is an indicator of a metaphor depicting God's situation, when He prepared for them the means of guidance, in the state of one who hopes for their piety. On this basis is the interpretation of the occurrences of the word _laʿalla_ in speech attributed to God, the Exalted. It was discussed earlier at His words, "﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾" [al-Baqarah: 21], and so on.

His words, "﴿Then you turned away after that﴾," refer to their worshipping the calf during the period of Moses' private conference (with God), and that God forgave them by His grace. Had it not been for that, they would have been among the losers, those destroyed in this world, or in this world and the Hereafter.

There is no need for us to delve into the question of compulsory obligation (_al-taklīf al-iljāʾī_, obligation under compulsion) and the incompatibility of compulsion with obligation, which is the question of the obligation of one who is forced (_taklīf al-malja'_) mentioned in the works of legal theory (_al-Uṣūl_), because it has been built here upon the remnants of the reports narrated about the uprooting of the Mount and lifting it above them, and Moses' saying to them: "Either you believe, or the Mount will fall upon you." Moreover, even if those reports were sound, there would be no compulsion in them at all, since setting forth signs and miracles and warning are not compulsion. They are rather an indication and proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger and the correctness of what he brought. What is impossible in obligation is obligation in a state of compulsion, not warning in order to complete the obligation. So do not be heedless.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 2, verses 65–66:**

﴿Indeed you knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them: "Be apes, despised and cast out."﴾ ﴿So We made it a deterrent punishment for what was before it and what came after it, and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾

This is among the reports that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned as a reminder to the Jews of what their predecessors had done in treating the commands of Allah, exalted is He, lightly, and of the warnings, mercy and repentance that were presented in the course of that account. The reason the narrative of this story departs from the style used for the stories before and after it, which introduce the account with the word *idh* ("when"), indicating the time of the story and implying that its occurrence is certain, up to His saying here, ﴿Indeed you knew﴾, is a subtle meaning that is among the aspects of the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the Qur'an. This story referred to in this verse is not among the narratives contained in the books of the Torah, unlike the other stories that are introduced with *idh*, because those are widely transmitted among them. Rather, this story occurred in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him), so it was not recorded in the ancient books, but it was known to their scholars and rabbis. Allah, exalted is He, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) about it, and that is an unseen miracle. He also revealed in its wording what indicates that knowledge of it is more obscure than knowledge of the other stories. So He attributed the matter in it to their knowledge when He said, "﴿Indeed you knew﴾".

*I'tida'* (transgression) is on the pattern *ifti'al* from *'adw*, which means going beyond the limit of a course, a boundary or an end. The term *i'tida'* became predominantly used for opposing the truth and wronging people. Here what is meant is transgressing the legal command (*amr shar'i*), because a legal command is likened to a boundary in that what is covered by it is taken, and what lies beyond it is not taken. The transgression committed by them was their transgressing the command of Allah, exalted is He, which He had imposed on them since the time of Musa, to observe the ruling of the Sabbath and to refrain from earning in it, so that they might devote themselves to worship with a heart free from preoccupation with worldly affairs. A group of the inhabitants of Ayla on the sea saw the abundance of fish on the shore on the Sabbath day, because when they did not see the boats and nets of the fishermen, they felt secure and so they approached the shore, opening their mouths in the water to swallow what was on the shores of food remnants, small fish and other things. They said, "If we dig pools for them and channel streams to them on Friday, the pools will hold the fish until Sunday, and we will catch them." They did this, so Allah, exalted is He, became angry with them for this greed for provision, or because they would occupy their minds on the Sabbath with thinking about what they had gained, or because they devised tricks to get around working on the Sabbath. What I consider to be the case is that this was accompanied by treating the command lightly and by their belief that they had understood what their law had not guided them to, so Allah, exalted is He, punished them with what He mentioned here.

So His saying *fi al-sabt* ("in the Sabbath") may have *fi* as a particle of time (*zarfiyya*). *Al-sabt* is a verbal noun from *sabata al-yahudi*, on the pattern *darab* and *nasar*, meaning he honoured and magnified the Sabbath. The meaning is: they transgressed while honouring the Sabbath, or at the time of honouring the Sabbath. It is also possible that *fi* indicates cause (*'illa*), meaning they transgressed for the sake of what the honouring of the Sabbath required, namely the cessation of work. Perhaps the prohibition of hunting in it was so that it would be a safety for animals.

It is also possible that *fi* is a particle of time (*zarfiyya*) and that *al-sabt* means the day. The transgression is attributed to it even though the digging took place on Friday, because its effect, upon which the disobedience was based, namely the entry of the fish into the pools, occurs on the Sabbath day.

As for His saying ﴿So We said to them: "Be apes"﴾, *kunu* is a command of creation (*amr takwin*, a command by which a thing comes into being). *Al-qiradah* with a kasra on the *qaf* and a fatha on the *ra'* is the plural of *qird* (ape). Their being made apes may be by transforming their bodies into the bodies of apes while the human faculty of perception remains. This is the view of the majority of scholars and exegetes. It may also be by transforming their minds into the minds of apes while the human form remains, and this is the view of Mujahid. The lesson is established under both considerations. The first is more apparent in the lesson, because in it they and people consider themselves in light of them, unlike the second. The second is closer to history, since no transformation (*maskh*) is reported in the books of the history of the Hebrews. Power is capable of both, and the whole is a miracle for the Shari'ah or for Dawud. For this reason al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "Mujahid's view is not very far-fetched, but it contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse, and the verse is not explicit about transformation." The meaning of their being apes is that, since they did not receive the Shari'ah by understanding its purposes and meanings, but took the outward form of the words, they resembled the dumb animals in halting at sensible things. Thus they were not distinguished from the dumb animals except by human form, and apes share with them this resemblance. This is the meaning of Mujahid's statement: it is a transformation of hearts, not a transformation of essences.

Furthermore, those who hold that transformation of bodies occurred agreed, or nearly agreed, that the transformed does not live more than three days and that it does not reproduce. Ibn Mas'ud reported this from the Prophet (ﷺ) in Sahih Muslim, that he said: "Allah has never destroyed a people, or punished a people, and then given them offspring." This is explicit on the matter. Among the scholars there are those who permitted the reproduction of the transformed and claimed that the elephant, the ape, the lizard (*dabb*) and the pig are among the transformed nations. The Arabs used to believe this about the lizard. A man from the Banu Sulaym, when he brought a lizard to his wife and she refused to eat it, said:

She said, and you were a shrewd man: "By the life of Allah, this is Israina."

Some jurists even held that eating the elephant and the like is forbidden, on the basis of the possibility that its origin is human offspring. Ibn al-Hajib said: "As for what is mentioned as transformed, such as the elephant, the ape and the lizard, the school's position is that it is permissible, due to the generality of the verse. The prohibition applies to what is mentioned, that is, to the generality of the verse on edible things." The author of *al-Tawdih* attributed to Malik the correctness of permissibility. Muslim also narrated in various hadiths from the end of his Sahih from Abu Hurayra that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said: A nation of the Children of Israel has disappeared, and it is not known what became of it, and I think it is only the mouse. Do you not see that when milk of camels is placed before it, it does not drink it, and when milk of sheep is placed before it, it drinks it?" End.

Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Rushd in *al-Bayan*, and many other scholars, interpreted this as meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) said it by his own reasoning (*ijtihad*), before Allah informed him that the transformed does not live more than three days and does not reproduce, as is explicit in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. I say: what supports this is that he said it by his own reasoning, as shown by his saying "and I do not think". There is no doubt that these kinds of animals existed before the transformation, and that the transformation to them is evidence of their existence and of people's knowledge of them.

This creative command was for the sake of punishment for their audacity in treating the divine command lightly, to the point that they devised tricks against it. In this there is evidence that Allah, exalted is He, does not approve of devising tricks to get past His commands and prohibitions, for the laws of Allah, exalted is He, are instituted for benefits and wisdoms. So devising tricks to breach those wisdoms by carrying out acts in forms that are legally valid, while the purpose behind them is actually nullified, is audacity against Allah, exalted is He. There is no proof for those who claim the permissibility of tricks (*hiyal*) from His saying, exalted is He, in the story of Ayyub: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾, because that was a ruling from Allah, exalted is He, to a Prophet, to avoid breaking an oath, which could be dealt with by expiation. But Allah did not approve for His Prophet the breaking of the oath in itself, because it is contrary to what is better, so He gave him a ruling by what he said. This helps explain the wisdom of avoiding breaking an oath, because in it there is preservation of the honour of the name of Allah, exalted is He, so there is no loss of wisdom in that. The question of legal tricks (*al-hiyal al-shar'iyya*) we may address in the commentary on Surah Sad, where there is thorough examination.

As for His saying ﴿So We made it a deterrent punishment﴾, the pronoun refers to the punishment understood from His saying ﴿So We said to them: "Be apes"﴾. *Al-nakal* with a fatha on the *nun* is severe punishment that deters the one punished from returning to the crime and deters others from committing the like of it. It is derived from *nakala*, meaning he refrained. It is said *nakkala bihi tankilan wa nakalan*, meaning he punished him with what prevents him from returning.

What is meant by ﴿what was before it and what came after it﴾ is what accompanied it of their disobediences and what preceded it. That is, that deed was the last of what they did, so the punishment came upon it. And "what was before it" means the nations nearby, and "what came after it" means the distant nations. The *maw'iza* (admonition) is that by which admonition is given, and it is warning against evil.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 2, verses 65–66:**

﴿Indeed you knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them: "Be apes, despised and cast out."﴾ ﴿So We made it a deterrent punishment for what was before it and what came after it, and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾

This is among the reports that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned as a reminder to the Jews of what their predecessors had done in treating the commands of Allah, exalted is He, lightly, and of the warnings, mercy and repentance that were presented in the course of that account. The reason the narrative of this story departs from the style used for the stories before and after it, which introduce the account with the word *idh* ("when"), indicating the time of the story and implying that its occurrence is certain, up to His saying here, ﴿Indeed you knew﴾, is a subtle meaning that is among the aspects of the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the Qur'an. This story referred to in this verse is not among the narratives contained in the books of the Torah, unlike the other stories that are introduced with *idh*, because those are widely transmitted among them. Rather, this story occurred in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him), so it was not recorded in the ancient books, but it was known to their scholars and rabbis. Allah, exalted is He, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) about it, and that is an unseen miracle. He also revealed in its wording what indicates that knowledge of it is more obscure than knowledge of the other stories. So He attributed the matter in it to their knowledge when He said, "﴿Indeed you knew﴾".

*I'tida'* (transgression) is on the pattern *ifti'al* from *'adw*, which means going beyond the limit of a course, a boundary or an end. The term *i'tida'* became predominantly used for opposing the truth and wronging people. Here what is meant is transgressing the legal command (*amr shar'i*), because a legal command is likened to a boundary in that what is covered by it is taken, and what lies beyond it is not taken. The transgression committed by them was their transgressing the command of Allah, exalted is He, which He had imposed on them since the time of Musa, to observe the ruling of the Sabbath and to refrain from earning in it, so that they might devote themselves to worship with a heart free from preoccupation with worldly affairs. A group of the inhabitants of Ayla on the sea saw the abundance of fish on the shore on the Sabbath day, because when they did not see the boats and nets of the fishermen, they felt secure and so they approached the shore, opening their mouths in the water to swallow what was on the shores of food remnants, small fish and other things. They said, "If we dig pools for them and channel streams to them on Friday, the pools will hold the fish until Sunday, and we will catch them." They did this, so Allah, exalted is He, became angry with them for this greed for provision, or because they would occupy their minds on the Sabbath with thinking about what they had gained, or because they devised tricks to get around working on the Sabbath. What I consider to be the case is that this was accompanied by treating the command lightly and by their belief that they had understood what their law had not guided them to, so Allah, exalted is He, punished them with what He mentioned here.

So His saying *fi al-sabt* ("in the Sabbath") may have *fi* as a particle of time (*zarfiyya*). *Al-sabt* is a verbal noun from *sabata al-yahudi*, on the pattern *darab* and *nasar*, meaning he honoured and magnified the Sabbath. The meaning is: they transgressed while honouring the Sabbath, or at the time of honouring the Sabbath. It is also possible that *fi* indicates cause (*'illa*), meaning they transgressed for the sake of what the honouring of the Sabbath required, namely the cessation of work. Perhaps the prohibition of hunting in it was so that it would be a safety for animals.

It is also possible that *fi* is a particle of time (*zarfiyya*) and that *al-sabt* means the day. The transgression is attributed to it even though the digging took place on Friday, because its effect, upon which the disobedience was based, namely the entry of the fish into the pools, occurs on the Sabbath day.

As for His saying ﴿So We said to them: "Be apes"﴾, *kunu* is a command of creation (*amr takwin*, a command by which a thing comes into being). *Al-qiradah* with a kasra on the *qaf* and a fatha on the *ra'* is the plural of *qird* (ape). Their being made apes may be by transforming their bodies into the bodies of apes while the human faculty of perception remains. This is the view of the majority of scholars and exegetes. It may also be by transforming their minds into the minds of apes while the human form remains, and this is the view of Mujahid. The lesson is established under both considerations. The first is more apparent in the lesson, because in it they and people consider themselves in light of them, unlike the second. The second is closer to history, since no transformation (*maskh*) is reported in the books of the history of the Hebrews. Power is capable of both, and the whole is a miracle for the Shari'ah or for Dawud. For this reason al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "Mujahid's view is not very far-fetched, but it contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse, and the verse is not explicit about transformation." The meaning of their being apes is that, since they did not receive the Shari'ah by understanding its purposes and meanings, but took the outward form of the words, they resembled the dumb animals in halting at sensible things. Thus they were not distinguished from the dumb animals except by human form, and apes share with them this resemblance. This is the meaning of Mujahid's statement: it is a transformation of hearts, not a transformation of essences.

Furthermore, those who hold that transformation of bodies occurred agreed, or nearly agreed, that the transformed does not live more than three days and that it does not reproduce. Ibn Mas'ud reported this from the Prophet (ﷺ) in Sahih Muslim, that he said: "Allah has never destroyed a people, or punished a people, and then given them offspring." This is explicit on the matter. Among the scholars there are those who permitted the reproduction of the transformed and claimed that the elephant, the ape, the lizard (*dabb*) and the pig are among the transformed nations. The Arabs used to believe this about the lizard. A man from the Banu Sulaym, when he brought a lizard to his wife and she refused to eat it, said:

She said, and you were a shrewd man: "By the life of Allah, this is Israina."

Some jurists even held that eating the elephant and the like is forbidden, on the basis of the possibility that its origin is human offspring. Ibn al-Hajib said: "As for what is mentioned as transformed, such as the elephant, the ape and the lizard, the school's position is that it is permissible, due to the generality of the verse. The prohibition applies to what is mentioned, that is, to the generality of the verse on edible things." The author of *al-Tawdih* attributed to Malik the correctness of permissibility. Muslim also narrated in various hadiths from the end of his Sahih from Abu Hurayra that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said: A nation of the Children of Israel has disappeared, and it is not known what became of it, and I think it is only the mouse. Do you not see that when milk of camels is placed before it, it does not drink it, and when milk of sheep is placed before it, it drinks it?" End.

Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Rushd in *al-Bayan*, and many other scholars, interpreted this as meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) said it by his own reasoning (*ijtihad*), before Allah informed him that the transformed does not live more than three days and does not reproduce, as is explicit in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. I say: what supports this is that he said it by his own reasoning, as shown by his saying "and I do not think". There is no doubt that these kinds of animals existed before the transformation, and that the transformation to them is evidence of their existence and of people's knowledge of them.
