So devising tricks to breach those wisdoms by carrying out acts in forms that are legally valid, while the purpose behind them is actually nullified, is audacity against Allah, exalted is He. There is no proof for those who claim the permissibility of tricks (*hiyal*) from His saying, exalted is He, in the story of Ayyub: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾, because that was a ruling from Allah, exalted is He, to a Prophet, to avoid breaking an oath, which could be dealt with by expiation. But Allah did not approve for His Prophet the breaking of the oath in itself, because it is contrary to what is better, so He gave him a ruling by what he said. This helps explain the wisdom of avoiding breaking an oath, because in it there is preservation of the honour of the name of Allah, exalted is He, so there is no loss of wisdom in that. The question of legal tricks (*al-hiyal al-shar'iyya*) we may address in the commentary on Surah Sad, where there is thorough examination.

As for His saying ﴿So We made it a deterrent punishment﴾, the pronoun refers to the punishment understood from His saying ﴿So We said to them: "Be apes"﴾. *Al-nakal* with a fatha on the *nun* is severe punishment that deters the one punished from returning to the crime and deters others from committing the like of it. It is derived from *nakala*, meaning he refrained. It is said *nakkala bihi tankilan wa nakalan*, meaning he punished him with what prevents him from returning.

What is meant by ﴿what was before it and what came after it﴾ is what accompanied it of their disobediences and what preceded it. That is, that deed was the last of what they did, so the punishment came upon it. And "what was before it" means the nations nearby, and "what came after it" means the distant nations. The *maw'iza* (admonition) is that by which admonition is given, and it is warning against evil.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 2, verse 67:**

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in mockery?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾

This verse addresses a narrative from the stories of the Children of Israel, in which there appears a lack of reverence toward their Prophet, excessive questioning, and insistence in inquiry. This was either to evade compliance, or due to the distance of their understanding from the intent of the Lawgiver, and their desire to have restrictions placed on something that had no intended purpose.

It has been said that the beginning of this story is what is mentioned in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 72] and so on, and that Moses' words, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow," arise from the killing of the soul mentioned there. It has also been said that Moses' words are mentioned here first because Moses' address to them, peace be upon him, gave rise to a kind of their blameworthy conduct in receiving the legislation, which is treating the command lightly, when they thought it was mockery, and insisting on questioning. Thus, by placing this part of the story first, the intent was to multiply their rebuke. This is what the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) and those who defended his words have stated. But it should not be overlooked that what they offered as justification for placing this part of the story first only requires dividing the story into two stories, each titled with the phrase "And when," while the order remains the same. Moreover, the blameworthy conduct may be known by narrating it and drawing attention to it through expressions such as His words, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant," and His words, "and they nearly did not do it." What appears to me is that these are two stories. The first, which is narrated here, refers to Moses' command to them to slaughter a cow. This is the story that the Torah (the Tawrah) refers to in the Fourth Book, which is the Second Book of Legislation, Deuteronomy (Tathniyah), in Chapter 21, that when a slain person is found and his killer is not known, then the elders of the city nearest to the place where the slain person was found shall go out and bring a heifer that has never been worked and has not pulled in a yoke, and they shall bring it down to a valley with flowing water that has not been plowed or sown, and there they shall break the heifer's neck. The priests from the sons of Levi shall approach, and the elders of that city shall wash their hands over the heifer in the valley, and say, "Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it being shed. Forgive, O Lord, Your people Israel..." and the blood shall be forgiven them. End quote. This story has been mentioned in summary, which obscured its purpose and left vague the aim of this slaughter: was it to dispose of that blood without purpose, or was it when the accused killer could not be identified? Whatever the case, this is a cow that is prescribed whenever a soul is killed and its killer is unknown, and this is what is referred to here. Then there occurred the killing of the slain man, whom his cousins had killed, and they came demanding retribution for his blood. That incident occurred on the day the cow was slaughtered, so Allah commanded them to strike the slain man with a part of that cow, which by its nature is to be slaughtered when a killer of a soul is unknown.

By this, the reason for mentioning them as two stories becomes clear. The Qur'an has summarized the mention of the two stories, because the place of reminder and lesson in them is what occurred within them, not the detailed description of events. The first story was a legislation that had already been mentioned, together with their excessive questioning at the time they received the command, which indicates weakness in understanding the Sharia and seeking things that should not be thought to be the concern of the legislation. The second story was a favor upon them, a sign of Allah's signs and a miracle of their Messenger, which Allah made clear to them so that they might increase in faith. For this reason it was concluded with His words, ﴿And He shows you His signs that you may understand﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 73], and followed by His words, ﴿Then your hearts became hard after that﴾.

The emphasis in His words, "Indeed, Allah commands you," is a quotation of what Moses expressed of his concern with this report, which, had it been stated in Arabic, would have come emphasized with *inna*.

Their words, "Do you take us in mockery?" is a genuine interrogative, because they thought that the command to slaughter a cow to clear oneself of the blood of a slain man was like a game. The verb *tattakhidhuna* here means "make us" (taj'aluna). The origin of the verb *ittakhadha* will be explained later at His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ in Surah Al-An'am. The noun *huzu'* (هُزُؤًا), with a *damma* on the *ha'* and the *zay*, and with a sukun on the *zay*, is the verbal noun of *ihza' bihi* (اهْزَأْ بِهِ), meaning "to mock him." Here it is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, like *al-sayd* (the game caught) and *al-khalq* (the created). The majority of readers recite (هُزُؤًا) with two *dammas* and a hamza after the *zay*, both in continuous recitation and at pause. Hamzah recites it with a sukun on the *zay* and with the hamza in continuous recitation, and at pause he softens the hamza into a waw. It is written in the Mushaf with a waw. Hafs recites it with a *damma* on the *zay* and softens the hamza into a waw both in continuous recitation and at pause.

Moses' words, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant," are a disavowal and a declaration of his freedom from mockery, because it does not befit noble and virtuous people. For mockery is more specific than jesting, since in mockery there is jesting together with belittling and contempt toward the one jested with. Moreover, jesting is not befitting in public gatherings and sermons. Furthermore, it does not befit the station of a Messenger. For this reason Moses disavowed it by denying that he was among the ignorant, which is a *kinayah* (a figurative expression, i.e. metonymy) for denying jesting by denying what necessarily accompanies it. He intensified the declaration of his freedom with the words, "I seek refuge in Allah," meaning "from it," because seeking refuge in Allah is the most emphatic of expressions of negation. For a person does not seek refuge in Allah unless he wishes to be protected against a great matter that none can overcome but Allah, Exalted is He.

The form "that I be among the ignorant" is more emphatic in negating ignorance than if he had said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being ignorant," as will be explained in Surah Al-An'am at His words, "And I am not among the guided" (Al-An'am: 56). *Al-jahl* (ignorance) is the opposite of knowledge and the opposite of forbearance (*hilm*), and both meanings occur in the language of the Arabs. Of the first, there is the saying of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

Ah, let none among us act ignorantly, lest we act more ignorantly than the ignorant among them.

Of the second is the saying of al-Hamasi: "The knower and the ignorant are not equal." And the saying of al-Nabigha:

"The one ignorant of a thing is not like one who knows it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 68:

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is." He said: "Indeed He says it is a cow neither old nor virgin, but between that; so do what you are commanded."﴾

The manner in which their challenge to their Prophet is related follows the familiar style of narrating dialogues, namely the omission of the conjunction between the verbs of saying. We have already explained this to you in the story of the creation of Adam.

The phrase "ud'u lana" (call upon for us) may be understood as du'a' (supplication) in its true sense, which is a request made with humility and eagerness to obtain what is sought. In that case the statement expresses their desire for clarification in order to obtain the benefit hoped for from slaughtering a cow that meets the qualities required in the various kinds of sacrifices (qara'in, sacrificial offerings) with differing purposes. They built this on what they had inherited from the idol-worshipping nations, who stipulate qualities and conditions for the offerings that are brought near (to God), which vary according to the purpose intended from the sacrifice. It may also be understood that they meant simply asking, and expressed this by "du'a'" because it is a request from a lower to a higher party.

It may also be understood that by du'a' they meant a loud calling, on the basis of their supposition that God is far away, so that one who asks Him must raise his voice. Muslims were forbidden to supplicate aloud in the early period of Islam. The lam in His saying "lana" is the lam of purpose, meaning: "call upon (your Lord) on our behalf."

The jussive form of "yubayyin" (He will make clear) is in answer to "ud'u" (call upon), by treating the effect as though it were the cause, meaning: if you call upon Him, He will hear and make clear; and this has already been mentioned.

His saying "ma hiya" (what is it) relates their question by means of what indicates it through the interrogative "ma" in the speech of the Arabs, which is a question about the attribute. For "ma" is used to ask about the attribute, as when one who hears people mention Hatim or al-Ahnaf, and knows that they are two men but does not know their qualities, says: "What is Hatim? Or what is al-Ahnaf?" and it is answered: "Generous," or "forbearing." "Ma" is not established for asking about the genus, as some who read the Kashshaf have supposed, who then strained to justify it, since the genus of the cow is known; they treated this particular cow ordered to be slaughtered as an individual of an unknown genus because of the strangeness of the wisdom of ordering its slaughter, and they thought that the purpose here is a question with "ayy" or "kayf." This is a misconception that al-Taftazani pointed out in his commentary on the Kashshaf, and he supported this with the words of the Miftah, which made genus and attribute two categories of questions with "ma."

The truth is that the context here is for a question with "ma," because "ayy" is used to ask about the distinguishing of a thing from individuals of its kind with which it is confused, and the sign of this is the mention of the genitive after "ayy," as in: "Which of the two groups is better?" and "Which of the two cows pleased you?" Here there are no particular cows whose one is to be distinguished.

His saying "Qala innahu yaqulu innaha baqaratun" (He said: "Indeed He says it is a cow") has emphasized both the saying of Musa and the saying of God the Exalted with "inna," in imitation of the concern contained in the speech of Musa with relating the saying of God the Exalted, and so he emphasized it with "inna"; and what is contained in the implication of God's speech to Musa of confirming His will in that, treating them as those who deny what had appeared of their obstinacy and evasion. It is also possible that the emphasis in the speech of Musa is to treat them as though God had said that to Musa, following their earlier accusation in their saying: "Do you make us a mockery?" (Al-Baqarah: 67), in answer to His saying "Indeed Allah commands you" (Al-Baqarah: 67).

His saying "la fariduni wa la bikrun" (neither old nor virgin) takes the place of an attribute of "baqarah" (cow), and the particle "la" is inserted into it because the attribute is by the negation of one quality and then by the negation of another, meaning the affirmation of a quality intermediate between the two negated qualities. When the particle "la" is brought in, the case-ending is applied to what follows it, because "la" does not govern anything, so what comes before "la" is considered as governing what follows it, whether it is an attribute as here, or His saying the Exalted "a olive tree neither eastern nor western" (al-Nur: 35), or the verse of Juwayriyya or Huwayrithah ibn Badr al-Rami:

"And the calamities have overtaken me while they are many: spears of a people, neither weak nor unarmed."

Or as a circumstantial clause, like the saying of the poet, which is among the witnesses of grammar: "You have conquered the enemies, not seeking help from a band, but by kinds of deception and cunning." Or as a qualifier of an annexed noun, like the saying of al-Nabigha: "And his disposition is neither feeble nor weak in strength, and a striving one who, when the seekers fail, rises." Or as the predicate of a subject, as occurred in the hadith of Umm Zar': the first one's saying: "Neither is he easy so that one climbs, nor is he fat so that one is moved," according to the narration with the nominative, meaning: he, that is the husband, is neither easy nor fat.

The majority of grammarians hold that this "la" must be repeated in the predicate, the attribute and the circumstantial clause, meaning that the predicate and the like are two or more things; if it is not so, it is not permissible to introduce "la" into the predicate or the like. They regarded the verse of Juwayriyya or Huwayrithah as a poetic necessity, and al-Mubarrad disagreed with this. The "la" in such usage does not function like "laysa" nor like "inna." The grammarians' mention of this usage in one of these two sections is merely for the sake of connection.

Know that the negation of two attributes with the particle "la" may be used to express the affirmation of a third attribute that is intermediate between the states of those two attributes, as in this verse, by the evidence of His saying "between that," and like His saying the Exalted: "wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those" (al-Nisa': 143). It may also be used to intend merely the negation of those two attributes, because they are among what is sought in the purpose to which they relate, and no other intermediate attribute between them is intended; and this is the more common usage, as in His saying the Exalted concerning scorching wind, boiling water and a shade of black smoke: "neither cool nor generous" (al-Waqi'ah: 43-44).

The fariduh is the aged cow, because she has broken her teeth, i.e. cut them; "al-fard" means cutting, and the old one is also called fārid. The bikr is the young one in her prime, derived from "al-bukrah" with a damma, which is the beginning of the day, because the bikr is at the beginning of her years of life. The 'awan is the one of middle age.

The 'awan was chosen for them because she is the most precious and the strongest, and for this reason the 'awan became a metaphor for severity in the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Whoever awaits the calamities, they will descend upon him: a great misfortune, 'awan, not a virgin," meaning a grave calamity, i.e. great. And they described a severe war by saying: "a war 'awan."

His saying "bayna dhalika" (between that) means between these two ages, so the demonstrative refers to what has been mentioned in plural.

For this reason the annexation of "bayna" to the demonstrative is valid, just as it is annexed to a pronoun indicating a plurality, even though it is one word, as in "baynahā." The singular form of the demonstrative is by interpretation as referring to what has been mentioned, as has been mentioned shortly before in His saying the Exalted: "That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah" (al-Baqarah: 61). In his answer they came with this lengthy elaboration rather than saying at the start of the answer: "It is 'awan," as an allusion to their dullness and their need for an increase in description, so that it leaves them no room to repeat the question.

If you say: They asked about an unspecified attribute, so how did Musa know that they were asking about the age, and how did he know from their later question with "ma hiya" also that they were asking about her being trained for service?

I say: It is possible that "ma hiya" is an abbreviation of their question that includes clarification, and this abbreviation is among the marvels of the Qur'an, being sufficient with what the answer indicates. It is also possible that what is related in the Qur'an is a synonym of their question, so that Musa's peace be upon him answer with that, knowing that the first thing on which the purposes of people depend in knowing the conditions of animals is the age, for it is the most important attribute of the beast. And when they asked him about the colour, then asked the second, vague question, it was known that nothing remained of the attributes in which people's purposes regarding animals differ except the state of being unburdened, i.e. not being used in service, because that is a weak matter, for a precious animal may be used in service and then be honoured by whoever acquires it afterwards, so the traces of service and its dishevelment disappear.

His saying "fa-if'alu ma tu'marun" (so do what you are commanded) — the fa is the fa of expressiveness (fa al-fasihah), and its position here is the position of cutting off excuses together with urging compliance, as it is in the saying of 'Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf:

"They said: 'Khurasan is the furthest of what is aimed at,' so I said: 'Then the return; for we have come to Khurasan.'" meaning: what you pretended as a reason, the length of the journey, has already been achieved. The meaning is: hasten to what you have been commanded, which is the slaughter of the cow. "Ma" is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is omitted after omitting its preposition, by way of extension, since they say "amartuka al-khayr" (I commanded you the good), so they reached by omitting the preposition the omission of the pronoun.

In Musa's urging them to hasten to slaughter the cow after they had been charged with choosing her as an 'awan, there is evidence that they were commanded to slaughter a cow in general, without any intended restrictive attribute, because when he commanded them to hasten to the slaughter at that time, we and they knew that what they were charged with afterwards, of seeking that she be yellow, bright in colour, and free from the traces of service, was not what God the Exalted intended when He charged them at the first. And this is the truth, for how could those attributes be intended, when they are attributes of an incidental nature having no effect on the wisdom of the command to slaughter? For whether it was a command to slaughter her for charity, or for sacrifice, or for sprinkling on the impure, or for the oath of the qasamah, none of these attributes has any relevance to the ruling. By this it is known that their being commanded with all these attributes is an incidental legislation, intended as a discipline for them because of their questioning. If their question was for delay and evasion, then the demand for those burdensome attributes is a discipline for bad conduct and for using pretexts to disobey. And if the question arose from their supposition that concern with this cow requires that unusual attributes be intended from her, as is apparent from their later saying: "And indeed we, if Allah wills, are guided" (al-Baqarah: 70), then charging them with these attributes, which are difficult to find together, is a scholarly discipline for their misunderstanding of the legislation, just as a student of knowledge is disciplined when he asks a question that is not fitting for his rank in knowledge.

'Umar said to Abu 'Ubaydah concerning the incident of fleeing from the plague: "If someone other than you had said it, O Abu 'Ubaydah." Among the forms of discipline is imposing a difficult task. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ disciplined his uncle 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the estimation (of dates), when he took from the fifth of the spoils more than his need, and he could not lift it, so he said to him: "Order someone to lift it for me." He said: "I will not order anyone." He said: "Then lift it yourself for me." He said: "No." So 'Abbas began to scoop from the wealth and return it to its heap until he was able to carry what remained, and he went off while the Prophet ﷺ followed him with his gaze, marvelling at his greed, as in Sahih al-Bukhari.

What indicates that it is a charge for the purpose of discipline is that the verse is cast in the manner of censure of them, and the story is counted among the accounts of their faults and their bad reception of the Law, in various kinds of shortcoming in action, gratitude and understanding, as shown by His saying the Exalted at the end of the verses: "and they nearly did not do it" (al-Baqarah: 71), together with what is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Had they slaughtered any cow, it would have sufficed them, but they were strict upon themselves, so Allah was strict upon them."

By this you know that there is no evidence in the verse for delaying the clarification beyond the time of address, nor for the occurrence of abrogation before the possibility of acting upon it, because what arose was a specific charge for the purpose of hardship. Moreover, addition to the text is not abrogation according to the verifiers; the naming of it as abrogation is the terminology of the earlier scholars.

[p. 553]

﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a yellow cow, intensely yellow in color, pleasing to the beholders."﴾

They asked with "what" (*bima*) about the quiddity (*mahiyyah*, the essential nature) of the color and its genus, because it is the second thing on which the aims of those who desire animals depend. The discussion of the jazm (apocopation) in *yubayyin* and of the emphatic particle in *innahu yaqulu innaha baqarah* is the same as the discussion of what came before. As for His saying *safra'u faqi'un lawnuha*, the yellow is emphasized with *al-fuqu'* (intense brightness), which means the intensity of yellowness, because the yellow of cows often approaches red. So He emphasized it with *faqi'*. *Al-fuqu'* is specific to yellow, just as *al-ahmar* is specific to *qani* (deep red), *al-aswad* to *halik* (deep black), *al-abyad* to *bayqaq* (pure white), *al-akhdar* to *mudhhamm* (dark green), *al-awraq* to *khutbani* (a grayish-blue, rendered as *khutbaniyy*, derived from *al-khutban*, with a *damma* on the *kha*, a plant like the *hilyun*), *al-armak*, which is the color of ashes, to *raddaniyy* (saffron-colored, with a *ra* at its beginning). *Al-raddan* is saffron. This is what is in al-Tibi. In al-Kashshaf and al-Tibi it is written with an *alif* after the *dal*. In the Qamus it is stated that it is of the pattern *sahib*, and in one copy of al-Kashshaf, one copy of the margins of al-Qutb on it, and one copy of the margins of al-Hamdani on it, the *ra* is vocalized with a *damma*, which contradicts what is in the Qamus.

And *al-nusu'* (pure clarity) applies to all colors, and it is the purity of the color from being mixed with another color.

As for *lawnuha*, it is either the subject of *faqi'* or a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). Its being an idafa to the pronoun of the cow indicates that it is the yellow color. So its description as *faqi'* is a true (haqiqi) description. However, He turned away from saying *safra' faqi'ah* to *safra' faqi' lawnuha*, so that its description with *al-fuqu'* occurs twice, since He described the color with *al-fuqu'*. Then, since the color is an idafa to the pronoun of the yellow (*al-safra'*), what is predicated of it of attributes proceeds according to its two causes, in the manner stated by the author of al-Miftah concerning the predicate being a verb: that the verb is ascribed to the pronoun first, and then, through that pronoun's returning to the subject, it is ascribed to the subject at the second level.

Al-Tibi, in his commentary on al-Kashshaf, thought that the words of the author of al-Kashshaf indicate that the ascription of *faqi'* to *lawnuha* is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), and this is an error, since it has nothing to do with rational metaphor. As for the example given by the author of al-Kashshaf with his saying *jaddu jaddihi*, it is an analogy only regarding the mere conveying of emphasis.

As for His saying *tasurru al-nazirin*, that is, its sight brings joy into their souls. *Al-masarrah* is a psychological pleasure that arises from perceiving what is agreeable, or from believing that it has come about. Among the things that produce it is wonder at a thing and admiration of it. This color is among the finest colors of cows, and therefore the verb *tasurru* was ascribed to the pronoun of the cow, not to the pronoun of the color. So it does not imply that the yellow color in general pleases the beholders. The expression *al-nazirin* was used instead of *al-nas* and the like

[p. 554]

to indicate that the joy enters them upon looking at it, by way of deriving the causation from the attachment to a derived noun (*ism mushtaqq*).

[Page 555]

The discussion of *ma hiya* is the same as the discussion of its counterpart. If God, exalted is He, related the equivalent of their words in the language of the Arabs, then the answer to them is: "She is a cow that is not tractable" (*dhalul*), because it is known that none of the attributes on which purposes depend remain except nobility and high value. If what is related in the Qur'an is an abridgment of their speech, the matter is evident.

Moreover, God knew what they meant and informed them of it.

The clause ﴿إنَّ البَقَرَ تَشابَهَ عَلَيْنا﴾ ("Indeed, the cows have become similar to us") is a resumptive clause (*istinaf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question). They knew that their repeating the question would produce in Musa's mind a wondering about the reason for this repetition. Their statement "the cows have become similar to us" is an excuse for repeating the question. They did not offer an excuse in the first two instances but did so now, because the third repetition has a particular effect on the soul, in terms of emphasis, weariness, and other things. This is why the setting of times by threes is common in human affairs and in their laws.

The emphatic particle (*inna*) has been used in a report that Musa does not doubt is true. It is therefore fixed that the use of the emphatic particle is merely for expressing concern. Then, through this concern, one arrives at conveying the meaning of consequence and causation (*tafri'* and *ta'lil*), so that *inna* conveys the import of the conjunctive *fa'* of consequence and causation. This is what Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir was keen to point out in *Dala'il al-I'jaz*, and he illustrated it with the verse of Bashshar:

"Go early, my two companions, before the midday heat,
Indeed, that success lies in going early."

Its mention has already occurred at God's saying ﴿إنَّكَ أنْتَ العَلِيمُ الحَكِيمُ﴾ ("Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise") [2:32] in this surah, where he mentioned a story.

As for their saying ﴿وإنّا إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَمُهْتَدُونَ﴾ ("And indeed, if God wills, we will surely be guided"), it is an encouragement to Musa and a promise to him of compliance, so that he will be energized to pray to his Lord for clarification. It also dispels from him the weariness of their repeated questioning, whose signs had appeared in their saying "so do what you are commanded" [2:68]. It also shows the goodness of their intention in asking so much, and that their aim was not to cause difficulty, to avoid Musa's anger at them. The conditioning with "if God wills" is for courtesy toward God in referring the matter to Him in seeking the attainment of good. The discussion of the purpose of the emphasis in "indeed, he says, it is a cow" is the same as the discussion of its first counterpart.

[Page 556]

*Al-dhalul* (tractable, broken to work), with a *fatha* on the *dhal*, is a *fa'ul* form from *dhalla dhullan* (with a *kasra* on the *dhal* in the verbal noun), meaning "became soft and easy." As for *al-dhull* with a *damma* on the *dhal*, it is the opposite of *al-'izz* (honor). The two are verbal nouns of a single verb, and usage has restricted one of the two verbal nouns to one of the two meanings. The meaning is that she has not reached the age at which she may be plowed and irrigated, that is, she is a young heifer who has nearly reached this age, and this is consistent with what her age was specified as in the Torah (*al-Tawrah*).

*La dhalul* is an attribute of *baqarah* (cow). The clause ﴿تُثِيرُ الأرْضَ﴾ ("that plows the earth") is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to *dhalul*.

*Ithārat al-ard* (stirring the earth) means plowing it and turning over the inner part of its soil so that the outer part becomes inner. The verb "stirring" is applied to plowing as a figurative comparison, since the earth's parts are turned over like a thing being moved from its place to another place, as God said ﴿فَتُثِيرُ سَحابًا﴾ ("then it stirs up clouds") [30:48], meaning it raises and carries them. A parallel usage is His saying in Surat al-Rum: ﴿وأثارُوا الأرْضَ﴾ ("and they plowed the earth") [30:9]. ﴿وَلا تَسْقِي الحَرْثَ﴾ ("nor irrigates the tilth") is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause.

The insertion of *la* after the conjunction in ﴿ولا تَسْقِي الحَرْثَ﴾, although the conjunction after a negated item already makes repeating the negation unnecessary, is only to observe the eloquent usage in every attribute, or what has the same sense, into which the particle *la* is inserted. This is as already mentioned in God's saying ﴿لا فارِضٌ ولا بِكْرٌ﴾ ("neither old nor a virgin") [2:68]. When the attribute *dhalul* was restricted by the clause "irrigates the tilth," the sense of the speech became: "she is a cow that does not plow the earth nor irrigate the tilth." So the verse followed the eloquent usage of repeating *la*. For this reason, this verse provides no evidence for al-Mubarrad, as becomes apparent upon reflection.

The imperfect verb was chosen in *tuthiru* and *tasqi* because it is more suitable to *dhalul*, since the description resembles the imperfect, and because the imperfect indicates the present. *Musallamah* means "free from defects of her kind." It is a passive participle from *sullimat* (passive form), and the attributes that arise in the original creation are frequently mentioned with the passive form, both in the verb and in the adjective, since it does not occur to the speaker to specify who the agent of that is. Most of the verbs that are obligatorily in the passive form are of this kind.

His saying *la shiyata fiha* (no mark on her) is another attribute distinguishing this cow from others. *Al-shiyah* means the mark, and it is of the pattern *fi'lah* from *washa al-thawb* when one weaves a garment with colors. The original of *shiyah* is *wishyah*. The Arabs say *thawb muwashsha* (a garment woven with patterns) and *thawb washi* (patterned cloth), and they say *thawr muwashsha al-akarui* (a bull with patterned legs), because in the legs of a wild bull there is blackness mixed with its yellowness, so it is a *thawr ashyah*. Similar to this are their expressions *faras ablaq* (a horse with mixed coloring), *kabsh adra'* (a ram with mixed coloring), *taysun azraq* (a he-goat with blue-gray coloring), and *ghurab abqa'* (a crow with white patches), meaning "mixed in two colors."

His saying ﴿قالُوا الآنَ جِئْتَ بِالحَقِّ﴾ ("They said: Now you have brought the truth") means that by "the truth" they intended a firm matter that admits of no doubt, as one says "he came with the matter as it should be." They did not mean by "truth" the opposite of falsehood, because they did not deny their prophet.

[Page 557]

If you ask: Why was it stated here with the word *al-haqq* (the truth)? Why was it not said "Now you have brought the explanation" or "the certainty"?

I answer: Perhaps the verse relates the meaning of what the Jews expressed to Musa with a word that in their language allows both interpretations, so it related it with its Arabic equivalent, to draw attention to their lack of care in choosing decent words when addressing their prophets and their elders, just as they used to say to the Prophet ﷺ "Ra'ina" (a word with a double meaning), so we were forbidden from saying it, by God's saying ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تَقُولُوا راعِنا وقُولُوا انْظُرْنا﴾ ("O you who believe, do not say 'Ra'ina' but say 'Unzurna' and listen") [2:104]. Because they had little aptitude for understanding the laws, they imagined that in the command to slaughter a cow without specifying its attributes there was a deficiency, as though they thought the command to slaughter was like the command to buy. So they began asking about all its attributes, and they kept pressing Musa until, when he explained to them the attributes by which people's purposes in acquiring cattle differ, they supposed that knowledge of these worldly purposes was a perfection in the prophet. Therefore, after the explanation they praised him, saying "now you have brought the truth," just as an examiner says to a student after going through the forms of a question, "Now you have hit the answer." Perhaps they did not distinguish, in legislation, between a descriptive attribute that is merely incidental and other attributes. So let the Muslims beware of falling into an understanding of the religion in any way similar to what those people fell into, for which they were blamed.

[p. 557]

The fa' (فَ) conjoins the clause "fa-dhabahuha" (﴿فَذَبَحُوها﴾) to an understood, known antecedent, namely "fa-wajaduhā" (they found it), or "fa-zafiru bihā" (they obtained it), or something similar. This is an instance of concise ellipsis (ijaz al-hadhf al-iqtisari). Since the conjoined clause takes the place of the clause it is conjoined to, it is correct to say that the fa' here is the fa' al-fasiha (the "explanatory fa'," which reveals an omitted antecedent), because it occupies the position of an omitted clause that contains an explanatory fa'. You may also say that the explanatory fa' is simply that which reveals an understood antecedent in general, as has been mentioned.

His saying ﴿وما كادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("and they were not about to do it") is a rebuke aimed at them, by mentioning a state of their poor reception of the Shari'a: at times by turning away and neglecting it, and at times by excessive hesitation and overdoing it. It also contains a teaching for the Muslims in the foundations of jurisprudence (tafaqquh) in the Shari'a, and in adopting the influential attributes (al-awsaf al-mu'aththira) that bear on the meaning of the legislation, rather than the incidental attributes (al-awsaf al-tardiyya). For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "Had they slaughtered any cow whatsoever, it would have sufficed them, but they made it strict, so God made it strict upon them."

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bazzar and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, with their chains of transmission, to al-Hasan al-Basri, from Rafi', from Abu Hurayra, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Had they picked out the least of the cows and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them, but they made it strict, so God made it strict upon them." In its chain is 'Ubada ibn Mansur, who is weak.

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to forbid his companions from excessive questioning, and said: "Those before you were destroyed only by the abundance of their questions and their disputing with their prophets." He also explained to the one who asked him about a found object (luqata) what he should do concerning it. The questioner said: "What about the lost sheep?" He said: "It is yours, or your brother's, or the wolf's." The questioner said: "What about the lost camel?" The Messenger of God became angry and said: "What is it to you? It has its hooves and its water-skin; it drinks water and grazes the trees until its owner finds it."

[p. 558]

The clause ﴿وما كادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ may be understood as a circumstantial clause (hal) or as a new independent clause (isti'nafiyya). The first is more apparent, because it binds the clause more tightly, and that is the original form of clauses; the meaning being: "they slaughtered it in a state that approaches the state of one who does not do it." The meaning is that they slaughtered it under compulsion, or as if under compulsion, because of the delay they had shown. On this reading, the time of the slaughter and the time of the attribute of approaching its negation are one and the same time, a unity in common usage according to the rhetorical contexts, indicating that their procrastination coincided with the very first times of the slaughter. On the independent reading, the difference of the two times is permissible: i.e., "they slaughtered it at that point," that is, at the completion of the attributes, and their condition before that had been the condition of one who was not about to do it.

Then, by its lexical structure, ﴿ما كادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ requires the negation of the meaning of kada, since its meaning is approximation (al-muqarabah). Negating the approximation of an act requires that the act not occur, a fortiori. So the question arises: how does this agree with the occurrence of the slaughter expressed by ﴿فَذَبَحُوها﴾? On the independent reading, one can answer that the negation of approximation was prior to the slaughter, when they repeated the questions and displayed their delay, and then the slaughter occurred afterwards. Some have answered in this manner, meaning that the act happened suddenly after they had been far from it. However, this answer is based on making the waw an independent clause, and you know how far that is.

The solution that removes the difficulty is this: the grammarians (a'immat al-'arabiyya) have differed about the implication of negated kada in such constructions as ﴿ما كادَ يَفْعَلُ﴾ ("he was not about to do it"). A group, among them al-Zajjaji, held that its negation indicates the negation of the approximation of the act, and that this is evidence for the non-occurrence of the act a fortiori. Thus the affirmation of kada is the negation of the predicate, as in your saying kada yaqum (he was about to stand), i.e., he approached (qarib), for it is not said except when he approached and did not do it. And the negation of kada is a negation of the act by way of the implication of the discourse (fahwa al-khitab), so it is like the explicit statement. And whatever occurs that seems to contradict this is interpreted as referring to two different times, so that it is like two statements. Among such is God's saying ﴿وما كادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ in this verse, meaning: "so they slaughtered it now, and they were not about to do it before that." Perhaps they take the combination of two apparently contradictory statements as an indication that two times are intended. To this view Ibn Malik went in the Kafiya, when he said:

"By the affirmation of kada, the predicate is negated, and when kada is negated, that is more fitting.
Other than this, it comes in two statements: 'Hind gave birth, and she was not about to give birth.'"

[p. 559]

This position stands by the analogy of the lexical form (qiyas al-wad'). Another group held that the affirmation of kada necessitates the negation of the predicate in the manner we have established in presenting the first position, and that its negation becomes an affirmation contrary to analogy. This became well known among the grammarians, to the point that Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri made it into a riddle in his saying:

"O grammarian of this age, what is this word
that came in the tongues of Jurhum and Thamud?
When used in the form of denial, it affirms;
and when affirmed, it takes the place of denial."

They argued for this position with God's saying ﴿فَذَبَحُوها وما كادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾. This is among the strange usages that run contrary to the lexical convention. A literary anecdote occurred on this matter, which Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir mentioned in Dala'il al-I'jaz: 'Anbasa al-'Ansi the poet said: Dhu al-Rumma came to Kufa and stopped upon his she-camel at al-Kunasa, reciting his rhyming ode (al-ha'iyya) whose beginning is:

"Are these the two abodes of Mayy? Peace be upon you both,
despite the distance, the distant one loves and advises."

Until he reached his saying in it:

"When distance changes the lovers, the trace of passion does not
cease (lam yakad) to depart from love for Mayya."

Among those present was Ibn Shubruma, who called out to him: "O Ghaylan, I see that it has ceased (bara)!" He said: So Dhu al-Rumma pulled his she-camel's rein, began to hold back with it, and reflected; then he said: "I did not find a replacement for 'lam yakad.'" 'Anbasa said: When I left, I told my father, and he said to me: "Ibn Shubruma was wrong when he objected to Dhu al-Rumma, and Dhu al-Rumma was wrong when he changed his poetry in response to Ibn Shubruma's objection. It is only like the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿ظُلُماتٌ بَعْضُها فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ إذا أخْرَجَ يَدَهُ لَمْ يَكَدْ يَراها﴾ ("darknesses, one above another; when he stretches out his hand, he can hardly see it"); it actually means 'he did not see it,' and 'he was not about to.'"

Some, among them Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni, 'Abd al-Qahir, and Ibn Malik in al-Tashil, held that the original meaning of kada is that its negation negates the act a fortiori, as the majority said, except that its negation may be used to indicate that the act occurred after slowness and exertion, and after it had been unlikely to occur. 'Abd al-Qahir pointed out that this is a usage that became customary; he meant by this that it is a figurative, illustrative metaphor (majaz tamthili), in which the state of one who performs an action after hardship is likened to the state of one far from doing it, so that the compound expression which denotes the state of the thing compared (al-mushabbah bihi) is used for the state of the thing compared to it (al-mushabbah). Perhaps they take something like His saying ﴿فَذَبَحُوها﴾ as an indication of this intention. In al-Tashil he said: "Kada is negated to inform of the occurrence of the act with difficulty, or of its non-occurrence and the absence of its approximation." In his commentary on al-Tashil, he excused Dhu al-Rumma for changing his verse by saying that he changed it to remove the possibility of this usage.

[p. 560 continues below]

Some held that if kada is negated in the imperfect form (al-mudari'), it indicates the negation of approximation; and if it is negated in the perfect form (al-madi), it indicates affirmation. Their basis is that it came that way in the two verses ﴿لَمْ يَكَدْ يَراها﴾ and ﴿وما كادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾, and that negation of a perfect verb does not necessitate continuation up to the present time, unlike negation of the imperfect.

Some claimed that the saying ma kada yaf'alu, when they mean "kada ma yaf'alu" (he was about to do what he does not do), is among the common inversions (al-qalb al-shai'). But in my view the correct position is the second, namely that its negation has the sense of affirmation. This is because, when they found it in the affirmative form conveying the sense of negation, they made its negation the reverse, as they did with law and lawla. This is supported by the places where it is used in negation, for you will find all of them meaning the approximation of negation (muqarabat al-nafy), not the negation of approximation. Perhaps this is among the constant inversions (al-qalb al-muttarid), so that the saying ma kada yaf'alu and lam yakad yaf'alu means "kada ma yaf'alu." It is not improbable that this usage is a remnant of an ancient dialect of Arabic which placed the negative particle, whose proper place is after, at the front. Perhaps this is what al-Ma'arri alluded to in his saying "it came in the tongues of Jurhum and Thamud." What confirms this as the intended meaning is that Dhu al-Rumma changed his verse, and he was one of the people of the language and men of taste; although he was of the Muwallad era, because of his withdrawal to live in the desert he was in the rank of the poets of the Arabs, to the point that he was counted among those whose poetry is cited as evidence. Someone like him would not have changed his poetry after reflection if it had a valid basis. Therefore the excuse Ibn Malik offered for him in his commentary on al-Tashil is weak.

As for the claim of figurative usage in it, the consistency of this usage, even in the verse ﴿لَمْ يَكَدْ يَراها﴾, weakens that claim: for one standing in darkness who stretches out his hand sees it only with effort. Ta'abbata Sharran said:

"So I returned to Fahm, and I was not about to return."

And God the Exalted said: ﴿ولا يَكادُ يُبِينُ﴾ ("and he can hardly express himself clearly"). He said ﴿وما كادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ and did not say "yadhbahuna" (they slaughter), out of dislike of repeating the word, for the sake of variety in expression.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 72–73:**

﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed over it, while Allah was to bring forth what you were concealing.﴾ ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it." Thus Allah brings the dead to life and shows you His signs that you may understand.﴾

Its introduction with "when" (idh), in the manner of relating what preceded of the enumeration of blessings and kindnesses and their response to them with ingratitude and contempt, indicates that this is a story other than the story of the slaughter, but it occurred following the command to slaughter

[p. 560]

to show some of the wisdom of that command, which they had shown their disapproval of when they heard it, when they said, "Do you take us for a laughingstock?" In this there is also the manifestation of a miracle for Musa. It has been said that what is related in this verse is the beginning of the story and what came earlier is its end, and they mentioned a point for the advancement (of the one before the other), the discussion of which, and its refutation, has already preceded.

As far as I have seen in the books of the Jews, there is nothing that refers to this story. Perhaps it was incorporated into the story of the cow mentioned earlier. The surah did not mention it because it was a miracle for Musa, peace be upon him, and was not a legislation after him.

His saying "you killed" points to the occurrence of a killing among them, and this is the Qur'anic manner of attributing the acts of some to all, following the Arab manner of saying "the clan of so-and-so killed so-and-so." al-Nabigha said, describing the Banu Hunn:

"They killed the Ta'i man in the open by force, Abu Jabir, and took Umm Jabir as a wife."

The reason was that a group of Jews killed their only cousin in order to inherit from his uncle, and they threw him in the quarter of a people, and came to Musa demanding the blood of their cousin, falsely. The accused denied it. So Allah commanded him to strike the slain with part of that cow, so that he would speak and inform about his killer. The word "nafs" (soul) for a single person of humankind is because he is a possessor of a nafs, that is, a spirit and breath, and it is derived from breathing. In a hadith: "There is no breathing soul (nafs manfusa)..." Because of its implication of the meaning of breathing, there has been disagreement over whether it is permissible to apply "nafs" to Allah and to attribute it to Allah. It has been said that it is permissible, because of His saying, related from the speech of Jesus, "You know what is in my self (nafs), and I do not know what is in Your self," and because of His saying in the Hadith Qudsi, "And if he mentions Me in his self (nafs), I mention him in My self." It has also been said that it is not permissible except by way of mushakala (matching of expressions), as in the verse and the Hadith Qudsi. The apparent view is that it is permissible, and the original derivation of the word from breathing carries no weight. So "nafs" means the essence. He, the Exalted, said: "On the Day when every soul (nafs) comes pleading for itself." And "nafs" is applied to the spirit of a human being and his perception. From this is His saying, "You know what is in my self." And the saying of the Arabs: "I said in myself," meaning in my reflection without verbal speech. From this is the usage of the scholars of the term "inner speech" (al-kalam al-nafsi) for the meanings that are in the mind of the speaker, which are expressed by the utterance.

"Idda'artum" is an ifti'al form. Its original is "tada'artum," a tafa'ul form, from al-dar' which is repelling, because each party repels the crime from itself. When the assimilation of the "ta" into the "dal" was intended, according to the rule of the "ta" of the iftial with "dal" and "dhal," a hamzat al-wasl was brought in to facilitate the sukun for the assimilation.

His saying "while Allah was to bring forth" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "idda'artum," meaning: you disputed while Allah was going to bring forth what you concealed. So the active participle in it refers to the future with respect to its governing verb, which is "idda'artum."

[p. 561]

The address here is similar to the address in the preceding verses, which is based on treating the addressees as their ancestors, so as to bear their consequences upon them, on the basis of what has been established: that the character of the predecessors passes on to the successors, as we explained earlier and will explain, if Allah wills, at His saying "Do you hope that they will believe for you?" [2:75]. The will of Allah, the Exalted, was connected to exposing the state of the killers of this slain man, although his blood was not the first blood shed among the nations, as an honour to Musa, peace be upon him, that blood should not be lost among his people while he was among them and within his sight and hearing. Especially since the killers intended to deceive Musa and devised the scheme by showing the demand for his blood. If Allah, the Exalted, had not made this blood manifest among a nation, its certainty in its messenger would have weakened, and that would have increased their doubt in his truthfulness, so they would have turned into disbelievers. So the manifestation of this blood was an honour for Musa and a mercy to the nation, lest it go astray. Therefore, it should not be problematic for you that blood was lost in the time of our Prophet (ﷺ), as in the hadith of Huwayyisa and Muhayyisa that follows, because the difference between the two situations is clear: the scheme was not devised, and the nation had no doubt about its messenger, and it is the best nation brought forth for mankind.

His saying "Thus Allah brings the dead to life" refers to an omitted element for brevity, meaning: so they struck him, and he came to life and informed about who had killed him. That is, thus is the revival: Allah brings the dead to life. So the comparison is in the certainty (of the event), even though the manner of the compared thing is stronger and greater, because it is a life from non-existence, unlike this. So the purpose of the comparison is to demonstrate the possibility of the compared thing, like the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

"Though you surpass mankind, and you are one of them, Musk is but a part of the blood of the gazelle."

His saying "Thus Allah brings the dead to life" is part of what was said to the Children of Israel, so it is necessary to assume: "And We said to them, 'Thus Allah brings the dead to life.'" Because the reference is to a thing witnessed by them, and it is not an interjection intended to address the Islamic nation, because they did not witness that revival so that Allah's revival of the dead could be likened to it.

His saying "that you may understand" is an expression of hope that they would understand. The assumption regarding them did not reach the level of certainty, despite all these proofs.

It has been the custom of our jurists to argue from this verse for the legitimacy of considering the statement of the slain person, "My blood is with so-and-so," as grounds for the qasama (the oath procedure in cases of homicide), and they make the argument from it for that dependent upon the argument from the law of those before us. In this there is an indication that the locus of the inference from this verse for the legitimacy of that is that the revival of the dead was not intended except to hear his statement. This shows that the statement of the slain person was taken into account in matters of blood.

The Torah has summarised the matter of blood in an extremely brief manner in the story of the slaughter of the cow that we have already presented. Yes, the verse does not indicate

[p. 562]

the occurrence of the qasama with the statement of the slain person. But it does indicate that the statement of the slain person is considered a cause among the causes of retaliation (qisas). And since the presumption regarding that law is that no one is killed merely on the basis of a claim against the accused, it is necessary that there be something that strengthens the claim, which is the qasama. The Malikis' argument from it has been objected to on the grounds that this is one of the breaches of customary norms (kharq al-'adat), and these do not establish rulings. Ibn al-'Arabi answered that the miracle lies in the revival of the dead, and once he came to life his speech became like the speech of all other living persons. This is a subtle answer, but it is not conclusive. The disagreement over judgment by qasama, both affirmation and negation, and over the extent of judgment by it, is expounded in the books of jurisprudence, and al-Qurtubi has investigated it thoroughly, but it is not among the purposes of the verse.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 72–73:**

﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed over it, while Allah was to bring forth what you were concealing.﴾ ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it." Thus Allah brings the dead to life and shows you His signs that you may understand.﴾

Its introduction with "when" (idh), in the manner of relating what preceded of the enumeration of blessings and kindnesses and their response to them with ingratitude and contempt, indicates that this is a story other than the story of the slaughter, but it occurred following the command to slaughter

[p. 560]

to show some of the wisdom of that command, which they had shown their disapproval of when they heard it, when they said, "Do you take us for a laughingstock?" In this there is also the manifestation of a miracle for Musa. It has been said that what is related in this verse is the beginning of the story and what came earlier is its end, and they mentioned a point for the advancement (of the one before the other), the discussion of which, and its refutation, has already preceded.

As far as I have seen in the books of the Jews, there is nothing that refers to this story. Perhaps it was incorporated into the story of the cow mentioned earlier. The surah did not mention it because it was a miracle for Musa, peace be upon him, and was not a legislation after him.
