Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 74:

﴿Then your hearts became hardened after that, so they were like stones, or even harder. For indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed, among them are those that split open and water comes out of them, and indeed, among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾

Thumma (then) here denotes the sequence of rank (al-tartib al-rutbi), which is what arises when you conjoin sentences; meaning: despite all of that, your hearts did not soften and the signs did not benefit you, so your hearts became hard, and their hardness was of a remarkable degree. His words ﴿after that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 52] express amazement at the ways in which the heart becomes hard after all the preceding signs were repeated, which are referred to collectively by "that," in the manner of the saying of al-Qatami:

"Ungrateful after the death was turned back from me, and after your gift of the camels in their herds?"

That is: how could I be ungrateful for your favour, meaning I would not be ungrateful for it, given that you saved me from death, and so on. The reason that "ba'da" (after) is used in this sense is that it is a metaphor for "ma'a" (with), because the caused thing normally comes after its cause. Since the purpose was not to draw attention to its being later, as this is known, but to draw attention to the fact that it accompanies it, whether in affirmation or negation, he used "ba'da" to express the meaning of "ma'a," while indicating the sequence of rank.

Qaswah (hardness) and qasawah are attributed both to physical bodies and to souls, which are expressed as hearts. So the meaning that unites the two descriptions is the non-acceptance of change from the existing state to a state that opposes it.

Whether hardness was originally assigned to the common notion shared by these two meanings, the sensory and the heart-related (a weak possibility), or was originally assigned to physical bodies in actual usage and applied to hearts metaphorically (which is the correct view), this usage has spread until it equals the literal and no longer needs a context. The word has thus come to indicate the shared notion through usage rather than through original assignment. This is shown by the conjunction in His words ﴿or even harder﴾, as will come. His words ﴿so they were like stones﴾ are a comparison of a branch with the particle fa', intended to make the comparison evident after the state expressed by "qasat" (became hard) has been related, because hardness is the point of resemblance, and because the best-known example of this quality is the stone. So when hardness is mentioned, the comparison with the stone is already prepared; hence the use of fa'. That is: when you know they are hard, then liken them to stones, like the saying of al-Nabighah describing the pilgrims:

"Upon them are dishevelled ones devoted to their Lord, so they are like the tips of the bent branches, humbled."

The hardness of stone was more widely known and familiar to people, because it is perceptible, and so it was used for comparison. In my view this technique is called preparing the comparison (tahayyu' al-tashbih), and it is one of its excellences. If you examine the methods of comparison in their speech, you will find them of two kinds: one in which the comparison is not prepared, which is the more common, and one in which it is prepared, as here. The conjunction with fa' in such a case is very good. As for a speaker bringing something that does not suit the comparison, in my view this is considered blameworthy. I have seen a line that combined both the preparation of the comparison and the deviation from it, the saying of Ibn Nubatah:

"In the saliva there is intoxication, and in the sideburns there are curls; this is the wine, and those are the clusters of grapes."

When he mentioned intoxication, the comparison with wine was prepared, but his words "curls" do not suit "clusters." If you say: why do you count it as blameworthy, when it is nothing but a case of the abstraction (tajrid) of a metaphor?

I say: no, because abstraction comes after the metaphor has been repeated and is known, so it is a subtle variation, unlike what comes before the comparison is known.

His words ﴿or even harder﴾ are in the nominative, being the predicate of a subject indicated by His words ﴿so they were like stones﴾. The "or" (aw) here means "rather" (bal) of transition (al-intiqali), because its condition is met, which is that the item it conjoins is a sentence.

This meaning derives from the meaning of choice for which "aw" is originally placed, or because the transition arises from choice: after the hearts were likened to stones, and it is normal that the thing compared is weaker in the quality than the thing to which it is compared, the comparison is built upon starting with what is better known, and then the comparison is followed by an ascent to surpassing in the point of resemblance, in the manner of the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"She appeared like the sun's horn in the brightness of the forenoon, and her form, or you in the eye are more beautiful."

So "aw" is not for choice in the comparison; that is, it is not conjoining the word "stones" which is governed by the kaf (like), because that has a place only when the thing compared to is repeated, as we have already explained at His words, exalted is He, ﴿or like a downpour from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]. It may be for choice in the report, conjoining the predicate "like stones"; that is: "so they are like stones, or they are stronger than stones." The purpose of the choice is that the speaker indicates that he does not hurl his words recklessly, nor does he blame them out of bias, but he is careful and diligent regarding their condition, so he attributes to them only what has become clear to him through investigation and scrutiny. He equated them with stones in one quality, then examined and saw that they were stronger in it. It is as if he says to the addressee: if you wish, equate them with stones in hardness, and you may also say they are harder than them. This conveys the same sense as the transition indicated by "bal" (rather). It is only good in the context of blame, because it contains gentleness; in the context of praise, the better expression is "bal," as in the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"She said to us: welcome and ease, and she provided us with the honey of the bees, but what she provided from it is sweeter."

The reason the hearts are preferred over stones in hardness is that the hardness attributed to the hearts, although it is a different kind from the hardness of stones, shares with it the genus of hardness, which returns to the meaning of non-acceptance of change, as already explained. Thus the hardness of these hearts, upon close examination, is greater than the hardness of stones, because stones may undergo change from their firmness and strength through scattering and splitting, whereas these hearts have not been benefited by any attempt.

His words ﴿And indeed, among stones are those...﴾ and so on are an explanation of the reason for the preference, since it is the kind of thing that is to be regarded as strange. The position of this first "wa" in His words ﴿And indeed, among stones﴾ is difficult. It has been said that it is for the state (hal) of "stones," implied after "ashadd" (harder); that is, harder than stones in hardness, meaning the preference of the hearts over stones in hardness appears in these conditions described of stones. The qualification means that the preference is more evident in these conditions. It has also been said that the "wa" is for conjunction to His words ﴿so they are like stones, or harder in hardness﴾, as said by al-Taftazani. It seems that he takes the content of these conjoined items as not returning to the meaning of comparing the hearts to stones in hardness, but makes them a report of excellences by which stones are superior to these people's hearts, through the benefits that come from these stones, while the hearts of these people are idle and produce no benefit. It has also been said that the "wa" is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), and that it is a concluding statement for the preceding sentence, but this is remote, as Ibn 'Arafah explicitly stated. The apparent view is that it is the parenthetical "wa" (al-wawu al-i'tiradiyyah), and that the sentence ﴿And indeed, among stones﴾ and what is conjoined to it are parenthetical clauses between His words ﴿then your hearts became hard﴾ and the clause of the circumstance that follows it, which is His words ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ The emphasis with "inna" is for the importance of the predicate, and this importance indicates the causal explanation; the presence of the conjunction particle before it does not conflict with this, as already explained at His words, exalted is He, ﴿so for you is what you asked for﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. Among the remarkable transitions is the late placement of His words, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed, among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah﴾. The expression of the subjection of stones to the command of creation by "fear" is so that the preference of stones over their hearts appears fully in their states, whose end is compliance with the creational command, while their hearts disobey the legal command, so as to make possible the transition to His words ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do,﴾ and to His words ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75]. The verse has indicated that the gushing of water from the earth through rocks is confined to these two states. This is what has been established in the science of physical geography: water descending upon the earth bores through the earth gradually, because the nature of water is to descend, following the rule of gravity. When it is pressed by its own weight from its abundance, or by another force from the air-pockets of the earth, it seeks to emerge, until it reaches a rocky or clayey stratum and floats there. Sandstone absorbs water, while rocks and clay are not pierced by water unless the rocks are composed of calcareous materials and the water has carried in its flow particles of carbonic acid, for it has power to dissolve lime. It then creates a hole in the calcareous rocks until it pierces them, and it emerges from them as springs. When the springs gather in one place, rivers arise from them, like the Nile emerging from the Mountains of the Moon. As for non-calcareous rocks, water does not crumble them, but they may be cracked by earthquakes or by the splitting of tools, and water emerges from them either onto the surface of the earth, as we see in wells, or it may emerge into a stratum beneath them, where it is stored until it comes out in one of the previous conditions. Water may also, in its course before entering under the rock or after it, find an outlet into earthy land and emerge floating from the surface of the rocks over which it passed. Water may also, in its course, find depressions within the earth, where it settles, and when other quantities join it, it seeks to come out by one of the previously mentioned routes. This is why rivers often burst forth after earthquakes.

Khashyah (fear) in its true sense is fear that prompts the fearful to piety. It is a legal technical term in the context of compliance with the legal command, since it is what prompts compliance. Here it is used figuratively for acceptance of the creational command, either as an absolute metonymy (mursal) with regard to its generality and restriction, or as an image (tamthil) depicting the state of the creational command by the state of the one addressed by the legal command, since stones have no fear, as they have no intellect. It has been said that the attribution of "yahbitu" (falls down) to the stone is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), and that the intended meaning is the falling down of hearts, that is, the hearts of those who look upon the rocks and mountains, meaning their submission. The falling down is attributed to the stones because they are its cause, as they say "a trading she-camel," meaning she prompts whoever sees her to bargain over her.

His words ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ are a concluding statement in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: you did what you did, while Allah is not unaware of all your doings. The majority read it with the second-person ta' (taʿmalūna), completing the address to the Children of Israel. Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub and Khalaf read "ya'malūna" with the third-person ya', which is a shift from addressing them to addressing the Muslims; therefore the style was changed to the third person. This is not an iltifat (shift of pronoun), because the reference of the two pronouns differs, since the branching of His words ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75] upon it shows that the speech was transferred from addressing the Children of Israel to addressing the Muslims. It is a report meant as a threat and warning to them, either directly or by allusion.

[Page 567]

This is a digression (istitrad) placed between the earlier narrative and the narrative that begins with ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: Do not worship except Allah﴾ (2:83). Every sentence from His words ﴿Do you hope that they will believe in you?﴾ up to ﴿And when We took﴾ (2:83) falls within this digression. The fa' (فاء) here introduces a rhetorical question of denial or wonder, and it is connected either to the phrase ﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾ (2:74), or to the whole group of preceding sentences, since all of them point to despair of their believing in what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought. It is as if it were said: "Do not hope that they will believe in you," or "Be amazed at your hoping." The precise role of the interrogative particle together with the conjunction in similar contexts will be clarified later, at His words ﴿Is it that whenever a messenger comes to you with what your souls do not desire, you become arrogant?﴾ (2:87). Ṭama' (طمع) means to anticipate the attainment of something loved; it is synonymous with raja' (رجاء, hope) and is the opposite of despair (yaʾs). Ṭama' normally takes fi (في, "in") after it, and here that fi has been omitted before anna (أنْ, "that").

If it is asked: how can one be forbidden to hope for their belief, or be marvelled at for it, when the Prophet and the Muslims are always commanded to call those people to faith? And is there any connection between the meaning of this verse and the question of taklif bil-muhal (تكليف بالمحال, imposing an impossible obligation), which is deemed impossible because Allah's knowledge is attached to its non-occurrence?

I say: We are forbidden to hope for their belief, not from calling them to belief. We call them to belief even though we despair of it, in order to establish the proof against them in this world when the rulings of disbelief are applied to them, and in the Hereafter as well. Also, the call to the truth may reach a pure soul and benefit it. The judgment that their belief is unlikely is a judgment on most of them and their majority, whereas the call falls upon each individual among them. The matter here is narrower than that other question, because the question of taklif bil-muhal, on the basis that Allah's knowledge is attached to its non-occurrence, concerns what Allah knows will not occur. On that we have already given you a clear answer: although Allah knows the non-belief of someone like Abu Jahl, He has not informed us of what He knows about him. The legal commands do not single out anyone for a call such that one could ask how he is commanded when Allah knows he will not believe. As for this verse, it has shown the denial of expectation regarding the belief of those whose habit is these states. So the answer to it returns to the more general answer, which is that the call is made in order to establish the proof. This is the more general answer of our companions (scholars) regarding the question of imposing an obligation with what Allah knows will not occur. Moreover, some of their conditions may change, so that expectation may have a share after that.

The lam (ل) in His words ﴿for you﴾ is used to imply the meaning of yuqirru (يُقِرُّوا, "acknowledge"), as if there is a hint that their belief in the truthfulness of the Messenger is already present, but they are stubborn and deny it, in the manner of His words ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it as they recognise their sons﴾ (2:146) and so on. How wonderful is the weaving of the Qur'an! It is also permissible to take the lam as indicating cause, and to treat yu'minu (يُؤْمِنُوا, "believe") as if it were intransitive, as a rebuke to them, meaning that they have not believed in the truth that came to them through their prophets, and they are the people most closely bound to those prophets. So: do you hope that they will acknowledge it for your sake?

His words ﴿And there was a group among them who used to hear the speech of Allah﴾ form a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), which is a qualification of the denial of hope for their belief. Thus the denial is supported by two causes: the first is the consequence (tafrī') based on what we have known, and the second is the restriction by what we have known. His words ﴿a group among them﴾ may mean a group from their earlier forefathers, or from those present at the time the verse was revealed. Their hearing the speech of Allah, under either interpretation, is the hearing of revelation through the Messenger if the group is among those of the time of Moses, or through transmission if the group came after him. As for hearing the speech of Allah directly, that happened only to Moses (peace be upon him). In any case, the intended group is a number of their scholars, not their common people. Tahrif (تحريف, distortion) originally is the verbal noun of harrafa al-shay' (حرف الشيء), meaning to incline a thing toward its edge (ḥarf), and it implies departing from the main path.

Since the comparison of truth, rectitude, guidance, and noble qualities to the main road and to the straight path became widespread, the opposite comparison also became widespread: describing what opposes these as deviation and as the twisting paths of the road. Al-Ashtar said:

"I kept my wealth and turned away from lofty deeds, and I met my guests with a frowning face."

Among the branches of this figure are the expressions zāgha (زاغ, went astray), ḥāda (حاد, deviated), maraqa (مرق, passed out), and alḥada (ألحد, inclined). His words ﴿And among mankind is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾ (22:11) also fit this usage. So the meaning of tahrif is taking revelation and the law away from what they were revealed to convey, either by altering it, which is rare, or by concealing part of it and forgetting it, or by far-fetched interpretation, which is the most common type of distortion.

His words ﴿and they know﴾ are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "a group," and it is a qualification of a qualification, meaning: they hear it, then they understand it, then they distort it, while they know that they are distorting. And a people who inherited this characteristic from one another are not to be hoped for in their belief, because those who did this are either their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their paternal cousins. Generally, their dispositions are one and their natures are close, as Noah (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And they will not beget any but a wicked disbeliever﴾ (71:27). The Arabs and the wise have many sayings on this meaning, all returning to the principle that natural dispositions are inherited. That is why they described a tribe by the characteristics of its majority.

Alternatively, by "the group" is meant their scholars and rabbis. Then the meaning is: you have no hope in the belief of a people whose elite (scholars) has these characteristics. So how do you expect their common people to be? For the elite in every nation is the showcase of its praiseworthy qualities and perfections. When the elite reaches a shameful degree of decline, know that the common people are even more heinous and more disgraceful. By "the common people" is meant those among them who existed at the time of the Qur'an, because although there were scholars among them, they were like the common people in bad judgment and weakness of restraint.

[p. 569]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 76–77:

﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone with one another, they say, "Do you tell them what Allah has disclosed to you, so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord? Do you not then use your reason?"﴾ ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾

The more apparent view is that the pronoun in لَقُوا (laqu, "they met") refers to the Children of Israel, in keeping with the pronouns in the preceding verses, in His words ﴿Do you hope that they will believe?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75] and what follows it. The pronoun subject of قالوا (qalu, "they said") refers to them as a group, namely those among them who displayed belief out of hypocrisy or, out of fear of the harsh confrontation and argument. This is indicated by the context of their words "We believe." Such usage is common in the pronouns of nations, tribes and the like, as in His words, ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 232]. The pronoun in طلقتم (talaqtum, "you divorced") refers to the men who divorce, and the pronoun in تعضلوا (ta'dulu, "prevent") refers to the guardians, because the whole is directed to one side, namely the addressees among the Muslims, since it includes both categories. Of this kind is your saying: "If you visit the clan of so-and-so, they will honour you," when in fact only their chiefs and noblemen will honour you. The pronoun in His words بعضهم (ba'duhum, "some of them") refers to the whole, meaning: some of the whole went off to some other part, and it is well known that the speaker is one who did not practise hypocrisy addressing one who did. Then the pronouns harmonise after that in يعلمون (ya'lamun, "they know"), يسرون (yusirrun, "they conceal") and يعلنون (yu'linun, "they reveal") without strain. This is the approach taken by the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari), and I prefer it because it restricts the interpretation to what is needed, and interpretation is required only when its evidence is absent, whereas here the evidence, namely آمنّا ("we believe"), is right beside it.

The clause إذا لقوا (idha laqu, "when they meet") is coordinated with the clause ﴿Some of them had indeed heard the word of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75], as a circumstantial clause of similar kind describing the Jews. The purpose of it is to restrict the prohibition, or to express wonder at the hope of their belief. So it is coordinated with the circumstantial clause, under the interpretation: "and there was another group among them who, when they met..." The words ﴿when they are alone with one another﴾ are coordinated with إذا لقوا and this is the intended sense of the circumstantial relation; that is, while the situation is that there comes from them the totality of this. Mere saying "we believe" would not be a cause for wonder at the hope of their believing; so the pronoun in بعضهم refers to what لقوا refers to, namely the Jews in general. The point in using the expression قالوا آمنّا is similar to its counterpart earlier at the beginning of the surah.

His words أتحدثونهم (a-tuhaddithunahum, "Do you tell them?") form an interrogative for denial, or for affirmation, or for rebuke. The context indicates this, since the situation shows that there had been talk among them about what was being revealed of the Qur'an, exposing the conditions of their ancestors and the disgraceful aspects of their conduct with their prophets and their law.

In my view the apparent meaning is that when they heard from the Qur'an what exposed their conditions, and the mention of matters that only their elite knew, they supposed that this had leaked to the Prophet through some of their followers who had displayed belief, and that their hypocrisy had reached the point where they informed the Muslims of some of their people's stories, in order to conceal their inner disbelief. So they rebuked them with a rebuke of denial, meaning: how far does your hypocrisy go that you would do this? Also, in some display of affection towards the Muslims there is sufficiency, in accordance with the saying of the proverb which Bashshar related in his verse:

"Be content with what the son of Dhi Yazan said in a dream; the noble ones amuse themselves and do not forget their lineage."

So Allah related this about them as a report of their bewilderment and the disorder of their affairs. For they used to send some men from their people as spies upon the Prophet and the Muslims, who displayed Islam while concealing Judaism. Then they accused them of folly in opinion and poor management, and that they had gone off spying and thereby disclosed the conditions of their own people. What supports this in my view is His words that follow: ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾

There are also reports transmitted from some of the Successors (tabi'un), with chains of transmission, which clarify who was speaking about it. From al-Suddi: some of the Jews used to tell the Muslims about what their ancestors had been punished with. From Abu al-Aliyah, who said: some of the hypocrites said, "The Prophet is mentioned in the Torah." From Ibn Zayd: they used to inform about some of the stories of the Torah.

The meaning of ﴿what Allah has disclosed﴾ (bima fataha Allah) is either: what Allah has decreed of conditions and calamities, for the word fath (opening, disclosure) in this sense means decree, as in His words, ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 89]; and al-Fattah (the judge) is the term for a judge in the dialect of Yemen. Or it means clarification and instruction, and from this comes the phrase "opening (the recitation) for the imam in prayer," meaning showing him the verse. This is a well-known metonymy (kinayah), because judging entails clarifying the truth. From this also is His word, ﴿Previously they used to seek victory against those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89], that is, they asked them for knowledge of legislative matters. According to one of the two interpretations, the meaning is: "what Allah has taught you of the religion."

His words ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾ (li-yuhajjukum bihi 'inda rabbikum) use the form of mufa'alah (reciprocal form), but the intention is not that the action occurs from two sides. Rather the form serves to emphasise the argument, meaning: "so that they may argue against you with it," that is, with what Allah has disclosed to you. The lam in His words li-yuhajjukum is the lam of purpose, but it is used here in the sense of consequence, figuratively, or as a supporting device (tarshih) for the figurative use of the interrogative in denial or affirmation. For since the interrogative, which is originally for seeking knowledge, is used here for denial or affirmation figuratively, because seeking knowledge entails acknowledgement, and what is affirmed is by necessity something that is denied, and the argument before Allah was a consequence of talking about what Allah had disclosed to them, he made the consequence of the occurrence of the denounced talk as if it were a cause that is being questioned about. That is: your act would have been caused by their arguing against you. This is an extreme form of denial, for how could anyone strive to bring about something by which evidence will be established against himself? So the indicator is that the context is one of denial, not interrogation, and for this reason the lam is also a distinct supporting device.

The more apparent view is that His words 'inda rabbikum (before your Lord) is a adverbial phrase in its proper sense, meaning the presence of judgement, which fits His words yuhajjukum. That is the Day of Resurrection without doubt; that is, they would make it a proof against you before Allah, regarding the truthfulness of their Messenger and your following of them in not believing in him. This follows the description of the belief of the Jews, in which they likened the Lord, glory be to Him, to human judges, in that stratagems succeed against Him, and that He takes effects only from their apparent causes. For this reason they used to resort to tricks in their law. You find their books full of what indicates that Allah came to know such-and-such, and learned that such-and-such a matter was contrary to what had been supposed. Like their saying in the Book of Genesis: "And the Lord said, Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil." And in it: "The Lord saw that the wickedness of man had multiplied, and the Lord regretted that he had made man on the earth, and grieved in his heart, and said, I will blot out from the face of the earth the man whom I have created." And in Genesis also: when Isaac grew old and his eyes dimmed from seeing, he called his eldest son Esau and said to him, "I am old, and I do not know the day of my death. Now take your equipment, go out to the wilderness, hunt game for me, and prepare savoury food for me, so that I may bless you before I die." Rebekah heard this, so she spoke to her son Jacob and said, "Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats, so that I may prepare them as savoury food for your father, that he may bless you before his death." Jacob said to his mother, "Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man. Perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall be in his eyes as a deceiver, and I shall bring upon myself a curse." She said, "Listen to my word." So she went and prepared the food for him, and she took the garments of her eldest son Esau and put them on Jacob, and she put the skins of the young goats on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck. Then Jacob went in to his father and said, "My father, I am your eldest son; I have done as you told me." Isaac felt him and said, "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau." So he blessed him, that is, made him a prophet. Then Esau came and spoke to his father with a stratagem, and said to his father, "Bless me too." He said, "Your brother has come in the morning and taken your blessing," and so on. So what do you think of a people whose beliefs reach such extremes, that they would not say, "Do not inform them, lest they argue against you before Allah on the Day of Resurrection"? By this the objection of al-Baydawi and others is dispelled, to the effect that the meaning of "before your Lord" could not be the Day of Resurrection, on the grounds that concealing the truths on the Day of Resurrection benefits no one who attempts it. They went to such lengths in interpreting the meaning of His words "before your Lord" that they took extremely contrived paths, analogising from the situation of the Jews to the situation of the beliefs of Islam. So they interpreted "before" (inda) to mean "the Book," or with an elided genitive (mudaf) or an elided relative pronoun. Then their critics went to extreme lengths of strangeness in its grammatical analysis.

His words ﴿Do you not then use your reason?﴾ (afala ta'qilun) are part of what they said to their own people. It is not valid to take it as an address from Allah to the Muslims, as a closing remark to His words ﴿Do you hope that they will believe for you?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75], because the Muslims, including the Messenger ﷺ, are not deserving of such a rebuke. What they contain of the interrogative, of wonder or of prohibition, is enough for them.

If you say: the verse does not mention the reply of the addressees disavowing that they had told the believers what Allah had disclosed to them, as was mentioned in His earlier words, ﴿When they are alone with their devils, they say, "We are truly with you; we were only mocking"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14]. I say: the Qur'an is not concerned with relating their disputes and conditions, for these are less than that. Rather it relates from them what contains the shamefulness of their condition, the badness of their conduct, the persistence of their obstinacy, and the baseness of their morals. Their disavowal of the accusation that their elders had been charged with is therefore known, because it is certain that they did not tell the Muslims anything, and because of what is indicated by His later words, ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows...﴾ and so on. As for what appears in the earlier verse of their disowning by their words "We are truly with you," this is because in it there is a recording against them in His words in it, ﴿we were only mocking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14].

As for His words ﴿Do they not know?﴾ and the verse that follows, the interrogative here is not in its literal sense. It is either a figurative use for affirmation, meaning: they do not know that; and the intended affirmation is by its necessary implication, which is that if Allah knows it, then His Messenger knows it too. This is a conventional, assumed necessary implication in a rhetorical context. Or it is a figurative use for rebuke, and the meaning is the same. Or it is a figurative use for exhortation, meaning: was the existence of the secrets of their religion in the Qur'an something that caused them to know that Allah knows what they conceal? The intended meaning is the necessary consequence of that, namely: they know that it was sent down from Allah. That is: would it not have been a proof of the Messenger's truthfulness, instead of being a cause for the accusation against them by their people, who had verified their sincerity in Judaism? This latter view is the more apparent to me, and it is supported by the use of the present tense ya'lamun (they know) rather than 'alimu (they knew). The placement of the interrogative together with the conjunction in His words ﴿Do you not then use your reason?﴾ and His words ﴿Do they not know?﴾ will be discussed when we reach their counterparts, and the disagreement of the grammarians of Arabic about it will be addressed at His words, ﴿Whenever a messenger comes to you with what your souls do not desire, do you become arrogant?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87].

﴿And among them are unlettered people who know not the Book, except wishful fancies, and they do not do anything but guess.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf, grammatical coordination) with His saying ﴿And a group of them used to hear the Word of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75], as the coordination of one state with another state. "Among them" is a predicate placed before its subject (khabar muqaddam), and placing it first serves to create suspense (tashwīq) about the subject, as already explained in His saying ﴿And among mankind is he who says﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. The meaning is: How can you hope that they will believe in you, when a group of them were distorters, and a group were ignorant? And if the faith of the people of knowledge among them, who were expected to seek the saving truth and to distinguish it from falsehood, is negated, then they used to distort the religion and to be stubborn about what they heard of the inimitability of the Qur'an in its reports about the secrets of their religion. So how can you hope also for the faith of the unlettered group, who are further from knowing the truth, more heedless of seeking it, more misguided in distinguishing truth from falsehood, and more deserving of following their leaders and scholars? Thus the first group are the predecessors.

On this basis, the clause ﴿And among them are unlettered people﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿And a group of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75] etc., in view of its being a counterpart (muʿādil) to it in respect of what it includes, namely that it describes the state of a group of them, and this is the state of another group. As for his saying ﴿And when they meet﴾ and his saying ﴿And when they are alone﴾, these are coordinated with the clause ﴿And a group [used to hear]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75], likewise as coordination of state upon state, but in view of what the first clause includes, namely the word "they hear", which is a state of the Jews. For this reason, in the clause ﴿And among them are unlettered people﴾ there does not arise the option (takhyīr) based on the disagreement over coordinating several items one upon another: whether the last is made coordinated with what precedes it among the coordinated items, or coordinated with the first object, because that applies when the basis of coordination is one aspect, whereas here the aspect differs.

The ummī (unlettered) is one who does not know reading and writing. The more apparent view is that it is derived from ummah (the nation), in the sense of common people, so it is synonymous with ʿāmmī (common). It has also been said that it is derived from umm (mother), meaning that he has remained in the state in which he was during the period of his mother's nurturing of him, so he has acquired no new knowledge. It is not an objection to this that, if it were so, the correct relative form would be ummahī, on the basis that the relative form restores words to their roots. They have indeed said, for the plural of umm, ummahāt, thereby restoring the singular to its root, which indicates that the root of umm is ummah, because when names are transferred from the state of derivation to being proper nouns, a change may occur in their root.

The Jews were well known among the Arabs by the description "People of the Book", and therefore it is said here ﴿And among them are unlettered people﴾, meaning that not all of them are People of the Book.

Being unlettered was not a term of blame among the Arabs, but among the Jews it was a term of blame, as indicated by His saying ﴿That is because they said: "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 75]. Ibn Ṣayyād said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I testify that you are the messenger of the unlettered." This is because of what being unlettered entails of little knowledge. For this reason, being unlettered was a miracle (muʿjiza) for the Prophet (ﷺ), since he was the most knowledgeable of people while having grown up unlettered before prophethood. Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī said: Allah taught His Prophet reading and writing after the miracle of being unlettered had been established, by making him aware of what would enable him to know that when needed, relying on al-Bukhārī's hadith concerning the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyya. A group of scholars supported him in this, while most of them rejected it, as is explained at length in his biography in the book al-Madārik by ʿIyāḍ. He intended only to show his opinion.

The word "the Book" (al-Kitāb) is either in the sense of the Torah, as a name for what is written, or it is a verbal noun of kataba (to write), meaning "they do not know writing". The latter is made unlikely by His saying after it ﴿except wishful fancies﴾. On the first interpretation, His saying ﴿who know not the Book﴾ is a consequence of being unlettered, meaning they do not know the Torah except with a mixed knowledge obtained from what they hear, which they do not master. On the second interpretation, the clause is a descriptive clarification explaining the meaning of "the unlettered", like the saying of Aws ibn Ḥajar:

"The wise one who suspects you of suspicion, as if he had seen and heard."

The word amānī, with a shadda, is the plural of umniyya, on the pattern afāʿīl, and it has also come with the lightening (without shadda), in which case it is a plural on the pattern afāʿil according to al-Akhfash, just as miftāḥ is pluralized as maftāḥ and mafātīḥ. Umniyya is like uthfiyya and uḍḥiyya, on the pattern ufʿūla, like ujūba (a wonder), uḍḥūka (a joke), ukdhūba (a lie), and ughlūṭa (an error); and amānī is like aʿājīb, aḍāḥīk, akādhīb, and aghālīṭ. It is derived from manā, like ramā, in the sense of decreeing a matter. For this reason it is said tamannā, meaning to undertake to estimate the occurrence of something unattainable or difficult. And mannāhu means he made him one who decrees, i.e. determined, as a metaphor for a false promise, because it moves the one promised from estimating the occurrence of a thing today to estimating its occurrence tomorrow. So too, as Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr said:

"Do not let them deceive you by what they desire and promise; indeed, wishes and dreams are delusion."

And because the liar lies only because he wishes that what is in reality would agree with his report, the connection between lying and wishing arose, so umniyya was used for a lie. Thus amānī are psychological estimations, i.e. beliefs which their holder considers to be true but which are not true; or they are the practices which the common people consider part of the religion but which are not part of it, rather they forget the religion and preserve these; this is the habit of misguided nations concerning their law, that they consider the customs, traditions and festivals they have as law; or they are the estimations which the rabbis put in place of divine revelation, either adding to it until they make them forget the original, or to mislead. This is the most apparent of the views.

It has been said that amānī here means falsehoods, i.e. what those who distorted the religion put forward for them. It has also been said that amānī means recitation, i.e. they know the Book only as words they memorize and study, without understanding any meaning from them, as is the habit of misguided nations who limit their books to recitation without understanding. They cited as evidence on this the saying of Ḥassān in lamenting ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him:

"He wished for the Book of Allah at the first of his night, and at its end he met the death decreed by destiny."

That is, he recited the Qur'an at the beginning of the night in which he was killed at its end. In my view, amānī here means wishes, and this is the extreme in describing them with compound ignorance, i.e. they claim that they know the Book while they are unlettered and do not know it, but they claim that because they wished to be scholars, and when they did not attain knowledge they claimed it falsely, for one who is not a scholar but is branded with the mark of scholars shows that he wishes he were a scholar. Whatever the intended meaning, the exception (istithnāʾ) is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), because none of these meanings is part of the knowledge of the Book.

﴿Then woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah," that they may purchase with it a small price. Woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.﴾

The *fa'* (then/therefore) indicates sequence and causation, so what follows it is consequent upon what precedes it. The apparent reading is that what follows is consequent upon His words, ﴿And there was a party of them who heard the words of Allah, then they distorted it after they had understood it, while they knew﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75], which indicates that they deliberately committed distortion. Thus the report that they deserve an evil state is made consequent upon it. Or it is made consequent upon the creation of a statement of the horror of their condition, and within this the content of the preceding clause, which was stated in summary, is repeated in detail.

The meaning of ﴿they write the Scripture with their own hands﴾ is that they write something that did not come to them from their messengers, but rather they invent and originate it, as indicated by His words ﴿then say, "This is from Allah"﴾, which suggests that this saying is merely what they utter with their mouths and does not correspond to the reality of the matter.

*Thumma* (then) here denotes the sequence of rank (*al-tartib al-rutbi*), because this statement was included among the things that made them deserve woe for writing the Scripture with their own hands, since it is the intended purpose. This statement is not delayed after their writing of what they wrote in time; rather, the two are concurrent.

*Wayl* (woe) is a word denoting evil or destruction, and no verb has been heard from its root; therefore it is said to be an *ism al-masdar* (a noun standing in place of a verbal noun). Ibn Jinni said it is a *masdar* (verbal noun) whose verb the Arabs refrained from using, because if it were conjugated, its first and middle radicals would have to be weakened, so that two weakenings would converge in it, making it heavy. *Wayl* means calamity, and its feminine form is *way(i)la*. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿They said, "O woe to us!"﴾, and Imru' al-Qays said:

*Fa-qalat laka al-waylatu innaka murjili*
(She said, "Woe to you! Indeed, you are making me walk on foot.")

*Wayl* is used without the vocative particle, as in this verse, and it is used with the vocative particle, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿They said, "O woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 14], just as one says *ya hasrata* (O my regret).

As for its grammatical position (*i'rab*), when it is not annexed to a following noun, it takes the case of nouns that begin a sentence and its predicate is introduced by the preposition *li-* (for), as in this verse and His saying, ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1]. Al-Jawhari said it may be put in the accusative, as in *wayla-n li-Zayd* (woe to Zayd). Sibawayh considered that ugly, and he required that when it begins a sentence it be in the nominative. When it is annexed, it is generally annexed to a pronoun, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for those who believe﴾ [al-Qasas: 80], and His saying, ﴿Woe to you! Believe﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17], in which case it is in the accusative. It may also be annexed to an explicit noun, and then it is inflected as an unannexed word, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Abu Basir, "Woe to his mother, a kindler of war!" (*waylu ummihi mis'ara harb*).

Since in its grammatical inflection it resembles the following verbal nouns that replace their verbs, in the accusative and nominative, such as *hamdan li-Llah* (praise be to Allah) and *sabrun jamil* (beautiful patience), as was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2], most of the imams of Arabic said it is a verbal noun whose verb has been dropped (*umita fi'luhu*). Some of them claimed it is a noun, and they took its accusative case in the annexed state to be an accusative of address, with the vocative particle omitted due to frequent usage. Thus the original of *waylahu* is *ya waylahu*, as evidenced by the appearance of the vocative particle with it in their speech. They sometimes treated it like the *mandub* (lamented), saying *waylah* (alas for him). Al-Zajjaj parsed it in this way in Surah Ta-Ha.

Some claimed that when it is in the accusative, it is governed by an implied verb. Al-Zajjaj said, regarding His saying, ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61], in Ta-Ha, it is permissible that the implied meaning is "Allah has imposed upon you a woe."

Al-Farra' said that *wayl* is a compound word made of *way*, meaning grief, and *la-* (the preposition) with a kasra, which is governed. When the use of *la-* with *way* became frequent, they made the two into a single particle and chose to open the *lam* with a fatha, as they said *ya la-Dabba* (O for Dabba), opening the *lam*, though originally it is with a kasra. It is used as supplication, as an expression of wonder, and as a rebuke, like the expressions *la aba laka* (may you have no father) and *thakilatka ummuka* (may your mother be bereaved of you).

The meaning of ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture﴾ is a supplication used to express anger and rebuke. Sibawayh said: "It should not be said that *wayl* in *woe to the defrauders* is a supplication, because it is ugly in wording; rather, the servants were addressed in their own speech, and the Qur'an came in their language according to the measure of their understanding." That is, these are among those to whom this statement applies. Words like *wayh*, *way's*, *wayb*, *wayh* and *wayk* have also come in the pattern of *wayl*.

The mention of ﴿with their own hands﴾ is an emphasis, like *I saw it with my own eyes*, and like ﴿they say with their mouths﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167], and His saying, ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. Its purpose is to affirm that the writing actually occurred, to remove any metaphorical sense from it, and to affirm that they were deliberate and intentional in it.

His saying, ﴿that they may purchase with it a small price﴾ is like His saying, ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41]. The price intended here is either the pleasing of the common people, by changing for them the rulings of the religion to accord with their desires, or claiming knowledge for themselves while they are ignorant. They composed worthless books of stories and simple known information in order to show off with them in gatherings. Since their minds did not reach true knowledge, and they were eager for leadership and false prominence, they fabricated superficial fragments and gathered topics and voids that do not stand up to the touchstone of true knowledge. Then they spread them and attributed them to Allah and His religion. This is the way of ignorant people who aspire to leadership without qualification, so that they may appear in the guise of scholars before the eyes of the common people, and of those who cannot distinguish between fat and tumor.

His saying, ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn﴾, is a detailing of the genus of woe into two woes: the evil that befalls them because of what they have fabricated, and the evil that befalls them because of what they have acquired as a result of that. So it is a requital of evil for the means and for the end. There are not three woes in the verse, as some have imagined.

It seems that this verse alludes to what happened among the Children of Israel of the disappearance of the Torah after the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis in the time of Bukhtnassar, and then in the time of Titus, the Roman commander. The Torah which Musa (peace be upon him) wrote, he was commanded to place in the Ark of the Covenant, as is mentioned in the Book of Deuteronomy. Musa had placed this Ark in the Tent of Meeting, then Sulayman placed it in the Temple. When Bukhtnassar invaded them in the year 588 BC, he burned the Temple and the entire city with fire, and took most of the Jews and sold them as slaves in his land. He left a small group in Jerusalem, confining them to planting and cultivation. Then they rebelled against Bukhtnassar, killed his deputy, and fled to Egypt with Irmiya (Jeremiah), so the kingdom of the Jews was ruined. It is known that on that day they were not able to save the Torah, and they were not among its keepers, because their law made the Torah a trust in the hands of the Levites, as the Book of Deuteronomy contains. Musa commanded the people to recite the Torah to them after every seven years had passed, and Musa said, "Place this Book beside the Ark of the Covenant, so that it may be a witness against you there, for I know your rebelliousness, and you have already resisted your Lord while I am alive, so how much more will you do so after my death."

It is not hidden that the Jews repudiated their religion more than once and worshipped idols in the days of Rehoboam son of Sulayman, king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam, the servant of Sulayman, king of Israel, before the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis. This indicates the forgetting of the religion. Then the well-known destruction came upon it. This was followed by the Roman destruction in the time of Titus in the year 40 AD, and then in the time of Hadrian, by whose hand the city of Jerusalem was destroyed, so that he turned it into a farm, and those whom the sword spared of the Jews were scattered throughout the regions of the world.

For this reason, the research scholars who investigate the history of religion agree that the Torah was subject to distortion, addition and disappearance, and that when they gathered their affairs after some of their great calamities, they found the Torah missing, so they wanted to collect it from the scattered pages and remnants of their writings. Lingerk, one of the Christian theologians among the scholars of the Europeans, said that the Book of Deuteronomy was written by a Jew who was residing in Egypt in the time of King Josiah, king of the Jews. Others said that the five books which together form the Torah had much distortion introduced into them from the knowledge of Samuel or Ezra (Uzayr, 'Izra).

Our scholars mention that the Jews only said "Uzayr is the son of Allah" because he claimed that he had found the Torah. All of this indicates that the Torah had disappeared and been torn apart. What is found in the Second Book of Kings in their books, in chapter twenty-one, is that while they were engaged in restoring Bayt al-Maqdis in the time of Josiah, king of Judah, the priest Hilkiah claimed that he had found the Book of the Law in the House of the Lord, and the priest handed it to the king's scribe. When the scribe read it to the king, the king tore his garments and repented of his apostasy from the Law, and commanded the priests to establish the words of the Law written in the book that Hilkiah the priest had found in the House of the Lord. End of quotation. This is strong evidence that the Torah had been unknown to them for a long time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 80–82:

[p. 579]
﴿And they say, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." Say, "Have you taken a covenant from Allah – so Allah will not break His covenant? Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?"﴾ ﴿Yes! Whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him – those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds – those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

It has been said that the waw (wa) is for conjoining the sentence to the sentence "and a group of them had already [heard the word of Allah, then distorted it]" (2:75), so that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) similar to it, meaning: How do you hope that they will believe for you while they hear the speech of Allah, then distort it, and say, "The Fire will not touch us"?

What appears more evident to me is that the waw is a conjunction to his saying "they write," etc. (2:79), meaning: they did that, and [they] said, "The Fire will not touch us." The point of connection is that their saying "The Fire will not touch us" indicates a firmly established belief in their souls, which they spread among people with their tongues. It gives news of a great delusion, from the nature of which it is that they would proceed to that crime and others, since they considered themselves safe from accountability except for a few numbered days, equal to the days of the worship of the calf, or days, one day for every thousand years of the world. That [punishment] is a punishment written upon all of them, so they do not refrain from advancing into sins because of it. Thus, by conjoining it to their reports, the benefit of informing about a creed from their misguidances is achieved.

Due to the position of this conjunction, the benefit of the explanatory resumption (al-isti'naf al-bayani) is achieved, since the listener marvels at their audacity toward this crime.

His saying "and they said" means that they said it out of conviction, because the original state of speech is truthfulness, until evidence indicates that it is a statement contrary to belief, as in His saying "They said, 'We believe'" (2:14). And because the original state of speech is that it should accord with belief, the use of "said" in the sense of supposing and believing became permissible, as in the expressions of their saying "Mālik said," and in the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib: "Why do you say the spear weighs upon my shoulder?"

The root meaning of "massa" (touch) is the contact of a hand with a physical body, and likewise "lamasa." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who disbelieved in Our signs – the punishment will touch them﴾ (6:49). He expressed their negation with the particle "lan," which indicates the perpetuity of negation, as an emphasis on the removal of punishment from them after emphasis. And because "lan" indicates the comprehensiveness of times, the exception from the generality of times was made possible by His saying ﴿except for a few numbered days﴾, in the manner of a branching-off; so it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf).

The description "numbered" (ma'dūdah) indicates fewness, because what is meant by "the counted" is that which people count when they see it or speak of it. It has become common in custom and habit that people do not intentionally count many things, to avoid tedium or due to occupation, whether they know arithmetic or not, because what is meant is counting by the eye and tongue, not counting by summing calculations, since that is not intended here.

[p. 580]
The feminine form of "ma'dūdah," which is an adjective of "ayyāman" (days), is used with consideration of the interpretation of the plural as a group. This is a well-known Arabic usage, and for this reason it is common, when describing a plural with a feminine form, to use the singular form, unless they intend to interpret the plural as groups. This will come in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿ayyāman ma'dūdāt﴾ (2:184).

His saying ﴿Say, "Have you taken a covenant from Allah?"﴾ is a response to their speech; for this reason it is separated in the manner of dialogues, as we have previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ (2:30). The interrogation is not real, as evidenced by His saying after it, "Yes." It is an interrogation of affirmation (taqrir) to compel acknowledgment of the more truthful of the two matters. It is not a denial, because of the presence of the counterpart, which is "or do you say," since a denying interrogation has no counterpart.

By "covenant" is meant a promise confirmed, so it is a metaphor, because the original meaning of covenant is a promise confirmed by oath and commitment, and the promise of one who does not break promises is like a covenant. It is also permissible that "covenant" here be used literally, since it is in the context of affirmation, indicating the negation of that.

He mentioned "taking" rather than "have you made a covenant with" or "has He made a covenant with you," because "taking" carries the confirmation of the covenant, and with "ʿinda" (with/at) for added emphasis they say: "He took a hand with so-and-so." His saying ﴿so Allah will not break His covenant﴾: the fa' is an eloquent fa' indicating an implied condition and its consequent, and what follows the fa' is the reason for the consequent. The estimate is: "If that is so, then you have an excuse in your saying, because Allah does not break His covenant." This was preceded at His saying ﴿So there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾ (2:60). Because what follows the eloquent fa' is an indication of a condition and its consequent, it is not necessary that what follows it be caused by what precedes it, or consequent upon it, so that there would be a difficulty over the non-validity of the consequent's following from the implied condition in the verse, since "lan" is for the future. As for His saying ﴿or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾, the equalization is with the interrogative hamza, so it is a connected (muttasilah) "am," after which a clause occurs, as Ibn al-Hajib explicitly stated in al-Idah, and this is the verified position, as 'Abd al-Hakim said. What the author of al-Miftah said, that the sign of a disconnected "am" is that what follows it is an imperative clause in most cases, and there is no sense of disconnection here, because that would spoil what the interrogation conveyed of compulsion and affirmation.

His saying "Yes" is a refutation of their saying ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾. Responsive particles enter upon the preceding speech, not upon what follows them; so the meaning of "yes" is "rather, you will be touched by the Fire for a long period." His saying ﴿Whoever earns an evil deed﴾ is a support for what "yes" contains of the refutation of their saying, meaning: you are none other than among those who earned an evil deed, etc.

﴿Whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him – then those are the companions of the Fire, so you are among them without doubt,﴾ on the pattern of the saying of Labid:

"My two daughters wished that their father would live, and am I anything but of Rabi'ah or Mudar?"

That is: I will not be made eternal just as the sons of Rabi'ah and Mudar were not made eternal. The "man" in His saying ﴿Whoever earns an evil deed﴾ is conditional, as evidenced by the entry of the fa' into its consequent, and in the condition it is among the forms of generality; for this reason it indicated an omitted clause, which is indicated by the sequence of "yes" with this generality, because if the generality were not meant to include the addressees among its members, then mentioning the generality after it would be disjointed speech. So there is an elision of brevity in the speech, so that what is mentioned is like the major premise of the proof of His saying "yes." What is meant by "evil deed" here is a great evil deed, which is disbelief, as evidenced by the conjunction to it in His saying: "and his sins encompassed him." His saying "and his sins encompassed him": "khati'ah" is a noun for what a person commits of crimes, and it is of the form fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ulah, from "khata'a" when he did evil. Encompassing is metaphorical for not being free of a thing, because what encompasses a person leaves him no outlet to turn to anything else. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they supposed that they were encompassed﴾ (10:22). The encompassing of sins is the state of disbelief, because it emboldens one toward all transgressions, and no righteous deed is counted alongside disbelief, as His saying indicates: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ (90:17). For this reason this verse contains no proof for those who claim that the companions of major sins among the Muslims abide eternally in the Fire, since a Muslim is not encompassed by sins; rather he is not free of a righteous deed, and it is enough of that that his belief is sound from disbelief and his tongue is safe from uttering the wicked word of disbelief.

The restriction derived from the definition in His saying ﴿then those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ is a restriction relative to reversing their belief. His saying ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds – those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally﴾ is a concluding supplement (tadhyil) following the warning with good tidings, according to the custom of the Qur'an. The meaning of "eternity" here is its literal meaning.

His saying "and they said" means that they said it out of conviction, because the original state of speech is truthfulness, until evidence indicates that it is a statement contrary to belief, as in His saying "They said, 'We believe'" (2:14). And because the original state of speech is that it should accord with belief, the use of "said" in the sense of supposing and believing became permissible, as in the expressions of their saying "Mālik said," and in the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib: "Why do you say the spear weighs upon my shoulder?"

The root meaning of "massa" (touch) is the contact of a hand with a physical body, and likewise "lamasa." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who disbelieved in Our signs – the punishment will touch them﴾ (6:49). He expressed their negation with the particle "lan," which indicates the perpetuity of negation, as an emphasis on the removal of punishment from them after emphasis. And because "lan" indicates the comprehensiveness of times, the exception from the generality of times was made possible by His saying ﴿except for a few numbered days﴾, in the manner of a branching-off; so it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf).

The description "numbered" (ma'dūdah) indicates fewness, because what is meant by "the counted" is that which people count when they see it or speak of it. It has become common in custom and habit that people do not intentionally count many things, to avoid tedium or due to occupation, whether they know arithmetic or not, because what is meant is counting by the eye and tongue, not counting by summing calculations, since that is not intended here.

[p. 580]
The feminine form of "ma'dūdah," which is an adjective of "ayyāman" (days), is used with consideration of the interpretation of the plural as a group. This is a well-known Arabic usage, and for this reason it is common, when describing a plural with a feminine form, to use the singular form, unless they intend to interpret the plural as groups. This will come in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿ayyāman ma'dūdāt﴾ (2:184).

His saying ﴿Say, "Have you taken a covenant from Allah?"﴾ is a response to their speech; for this reason it is separated in the manner of dialogues, as we have previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ (2:30). The interrogation is not real, as evidenced by His saying after it, "Yes." It is an interrogation of affirmation (taqrir) to compel acknowledgment of the more truthful of the two matters. It is not a denial, because of the presence of the counterpart, which is "or do you say," since a denying interrogation has no counterpart.

By "covenant" is meant a promise confirmed, so it is a metaphor, because the original meaning of covenant is a promise confirmed by oath and commitment, and the promise of one who does not break promises is like a covenant. It is also permissible that "covenant" here be used literally, since it is in the context of affirmation, indicating the negation of that.

He mentioned "taking" rather than "have you made a covenant with" or "has He made a covenant with you," because "taking" carries the confirmation of the covenant, and with "ʿinda" (with/at) for added emphasis they say: "He took a hand with so-and-so." His saying ﴿so Allah will not break His covenant﴾: the fa' is an eloquent fa' indicating an implied condition and its consequent, and what follows the fa' is the reason for the consequent. The estimate is: "If that is so, then you have an excuse in your saying, because Allah does not break His covenant." This was preceded at His saying ﴿So there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾ (2:60). Because what follows the eloquent fa' is an indication of a condition and its consequent, it is not necessary that what follows it be caused by what precedes it, or consequent upon it, so that there would be a difficulty over the non-validity of the consequent's following from the implied condition in the verse, since "lan" is for the future. As for His saying ﴿or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾, the equalization is with the interrogative hamza, so it is a connected (muttasilah) "am," after which a clause occurs, as Ibn al-Hajib explicitly stated in al-Idah, and this is the verified position, as 'Abd al-Hakim said. What the author of al-Miftah said, that the sign of a disconnected "am" is that what follows it is an imperative clause in most cases, and there is no sense of disconnection here, because that would spoil what the interrogation conveyed of compulsion and affirmation.

His saying "Yes" is a refutation of their saying ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾. Responsive particles enter upon the preceding speech, not upon what follows them; so the meaning of "yes" is "rather, you will be touched by the Fire for a long period." His saying ﴿Whoever earns an evil deed﴾ is a support for what "yes" contains of the refutation of their saying, meaning: you are none other than among those who earned an evil deed, etc.

﴿Whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him – then those are the companions of the Fire, so you are among them without doubt,﴾ on the pattern of the saying of Labid:

"My two daughters wished that their father would live, and am I anything but of Rabi'ah or Mudar?"

That is: I will not be made eternal just as the sons of Rabi'ah and Mudar were not made eternal. The "man" in His saying ﴿Whoever earns an evil deed﴾ is conditional, as evidenced by the entry of the fa' into its consequent, and in the condition it is among the forms of generality; for this reason it indicated an omitted clause, which is indicated by the sequence of "yes" with this generality, because if the generality were not meant to include the addressees among its members, then mentioning the generality after it would be disjointed speech. So there is an elision of brevity in the speech, so that what is mentioned is like the major premise of the proof of His saying "yes." What is meant by "evil deed" here is a great evil deed, which is disbelief, as evidenced by the conjunction to it in His saying: "and his sins encompassed him." His saying "and his sins encompassed him": "khati'ah" is a noun for what a person commits of crimes, and it is of the form fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ulah, from "khata'a" when he did evil. Encompassing is metaphorical for not being free of a thing, because what encompasses a person leaves him no outlet to turn to anything else. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they supposed that they were encompassed﴾ (10:22). The encompassing of sins is the state of disbelief, because it emboldens one toward all transgressions, and no righteous deed is counted alongside disbelief, as His saying indicates: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ (90:17). For this reason this verse contains no proof for those who claim that the companions of major sins among the Muslims abide eternally in the Fire, since a Muslim is not encompassed by sins; rather he is not free of a righteous deed, and it is enough of that that his belief is sound from disbelief and his tongue is safe from uttering the wicked word of disbelief.

The restriction derived from the definition in His saying ﴿then those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ is a restriction relative to reversing their belief. His saying ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds – those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally﴾ is a concluding supplement (tadhyil) following the warning with good tidings, according to the custom of the Qur'an. The meaning of "eternity" here is its literal meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 80–82:

[p. 579]
﴿And they say, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." Say, "Have you taken a covenant from Allah – so Allah will not break His covenant? Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?"﴾ ﴿Yes! Whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him – those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds – those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

It has been said that the waw (wa) is for conjoining the sentence to the sentence "and a group of them had already [heard the word of Allah, then distorted it]" (2:75), so that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) similar to it, meaning: How do you hope that they will believe for you while they hear the speech of Allah, then distort it, and say, "The Fire will not touch us"?

What appears more evident to me is that the waw is a conjunction to his saying "they write," etc. (2:79), meaning: they did that, and [they] said, "The Fire will not touch us." The point of connection is that their saying "The Fire will not touch us" indicates a firmly established belief in their souls, which they spread among people with their tongues. It gives news of a great delusion, from the nature of which it is that they would proceed to that crime and others, since they considered themselves safe from accountability except for a few numbered days, equal to the days of the worship of the calf, or days, one day for every thousand years of the world. That [punishment] is a punishment written upon all of them, so they do not refrain from advancing into sins because of it. Thus, by conjoining it to their reports, the benefit of informing about a creed from their misguidances is achieved.
