[p. 582]

﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but God; be good to parents, to kindred, to orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer and give zakat." Then you turned away, except for a few of you, and you were averse.﴾

Ibn 'Ashur: The mention of the conditions of the Children of Israel is resumed after that varied digression (istitrad), and so the earlier style is resumed: the conjunction by repeating the word "when" (idh), as at the beginning of the narratives. Here the phrase "Children of Israel" is made explicit, and the earlier style, in which the address was in the second person, meaning the predecessors and successors of those addressed, is abandoned, for two reasons.

The first is that this is a return to the argument with the Children of Israel and to making them face their faults. It is thus a second opening, following the style of the opening in the words of God Most High: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, I shall fulfil your covenant﴾ [al-Baqara: 40], and so on.

The second is that what will be mentioned here is among the conditions that characterized both predecessors and successors. Since the primary purpose of it is to establish the evil conduct of those present in the time of the Qur'an, it was necessary to express their predecessors by an explicit term, so that it would be possible to direct the address afterwards to those addressed, so that it would not be supposed that it is of the kind of address in which the predecessors are meant, as in the case of ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqara: 49], or as in ﴿Then you took the calf after Him﴾ [al-Baqara: 92]. The words ﴿covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ mean their predecessors, because they were the ones who gave the covenant to Moses to obey what God had sent down in the Torah, as we have previously mentioned. Or the phrase "Children of Israel" may mean both earlier and later generations. The address in ﴿you turned away﴾ refers specifically to "those after them", because they are the ones who turned away. So there is no iltifat (shift of grammatical person) in the speech. This is preferable to making what "confirms the Children of Israel" refer to what "confirms the pronoun of you turned away", and to holding that the speech contains an iltifat.

The words ﴿Worship none but God﴾ are a report with the meaning of a command. The use of a report for a command is more emphatic than the imperative form, because the report is used in a sense other than its literal one, by the relation of resemblance between a command whose compliance is certain and a thing already achieved, to the extent that one reports it. The clause ﴿Worship none but God﴾ is the beginning of an explanation of the covenant, and so it is detached, and what follows it is conjoined to it so that it shares with it the explanatory sense, whether you estimate an (an, "that") or do not estimate it, or estimate an omitted saying.

The words ﴿and to parents, goodness﴾ are among what the covenant was taken upon them to observe. This is an emphatic command confirming what is indicated by the fronting of the complement before its governed element, which are ﴿to parents, goodness﴾; the original order is "and goodness to parents", and the verbal noun (masdar) is a substitute for its verb, the estimate being "and do good to parents". Let it not disturb you that it is a complement of a verbal noun, which cannot precede its governing element according to the Basrians, because that is a feeble claim, prompted by the view that the verbal noun has the meaning of "that" plus the verb, so it is in the status of a relative clause, and the complement of a relative clause cannot precede it. Moreover, it is "that" and the verb which have the meaning of the verbal noun, not the reverse. It is strange that Ibn Jinni followed them in his commentary on the Hamasa on this point, at the verse of the poet of the Hamasa:

"And some forbearance in the face of ignorance is submission to humiliation."

According to their method, the words "to parents" are linked to a deleted verb whose estimate is "and do good". The words "goodness" is a verbal noun. It is refuted by saying that deleting the governing verb of an emphatic verbal noun is impermissible, because the benefit of emphasis obtained by repetition is thereby nullified, so there is no need for all that. We are certain that the prepositional phrase is fronted before the verbal noun; moreover, the expansion in prepositional phrases is a common matter and a settled principle.

The plural "orphans" (yatama) is the plural of "yatim", like "nadama" for "nadim", and this is rare in the plural pattern fa'il.

He made goodness toward the rest of people to be by speech, because it is the measure by which it is possible to deal with all people. The origin of speech is that it should come from belief, so when they speak kindly to people, they have hidden good for them within themselves, and this is the basis of good dealing with creation. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself." God Most High has taught us this in His words: ﴿and do not place in our hearts any rancour toward those who believe﴾ [al-Hashr: 10]. Further, if something arises that requires the disturbing of the mind, then good speech removes the turbidity in the speaker's soul, and he sees clarity in the one addressed, so he deals with him only with clarity. Al-Ma'arri said:

"The vinegar, like water, shows me its inner thoughts with clarity, and hides them with turbidity."

Moreover, God commanded good in action where it is determined and falls within the capacity of the one commanded: that good is to parents, kindred, orphans, the needy, and the giving of zakat. And He commanded good in speech when action is impossible, in the manner of the words of Abu al-Tayyib:

"Let speech then be helpful, if the state does not help."

As for His words ﴿Establish prayer and give zakat﴾, zakat is applied to charity in general, or to obligatory charity on wealth. The meaning is not an allusion to the Islamic law, because, as you know, these conjunctions follow the explanation of the covenant, which is the covenant of Moses, peace be upon him.

His words ﴿Then you turned away, except for a few of you﴾ are an address to those present, and it is not an iltifat, as you have known just now. The meaning is: We took the covenant of the Israelite community to monotheism and the basics of goodness, so you were among those who turned away from that and disobeyed a law which you had followed. Tawalli means aversion and nullifying what they had committed themselves to. Its complement is deleted because of what preceded it, meaning: you turned away from all that the covenant was taken from you to observe, that is, you associated others with God, worshipped idols, disobeyed parents, mistreated kin, orphans and the needy, spoke the most vile speech to people, abandoned prayer and withheld zakat. It is permissible that the address in "you turned away" refers to those addressed at the time of the revelation of the verse, and some of those before them from the middle periods of the Israelite generations; so the pronoun of address is used by way of predominance (taghlib). Its wisdom is to show the innocence of those upon whom the covenant was first taken from breaking it; this is from the report using the plural. The intention is distribution: "you turned away", so among you are those who did not do good to parents and kindred, and so on; this is one of the attributes of the Jews at the time of the revelation of the verse, as will come in the commentary on the next verse. Among you are those who associated others with God; this was not transmitted of the Jews at the time of revelation, but it is one of the attributes of those who preceded them after Solomon, for among the kings of Israel there were idol-worshippers, and this recurred among them many times, as is recorded in the books of Kings, First and Second, of the Torah. The particle thumma (then) here is for two orders: the sequential order and the external order.

His words ﴿except for a few of you﴾ are a fairness to them in their rebuke and censure, and a declaration of the virtue of those who kept the covenant.

His words ﴿and you were averse﴾ form a circumstantial clause. Because it is a nominal sentence, it indicates that aversion is a fixed attribute of them and a well-known habit of theirs, as al-Kashshaf indicated. This is based on considering the active participle as derived from a verb used in the sense of an intransitive verb, with no complement to be estimated for it. It is also permissible to estimate it as derived from a verb whose complement is deleted, relying on the context, meaning: "and you are averse" from the commandments which contained that covenant, that is, you turned away deliberately, boldly, with little regard for the commandments, and neglecting to reflect upon them and act by them.

[p. 585]

The address here varies in style, following the pattern of the verse before it. Here it refers to all the Children of Israel with the second-person pronoun, through *taghlib* (the figure of speech in which the dominant group stands for the whole). This is because the people addressed at the time the Qur'an was revealed are the ones intended by this admonition. Alternatively, it is by treating later generations as if they were the earlier ones, as was mentioned before, because the motive for the shift to the explicit address when moving from the digression (*istitrad*) back to the main subject of the previous verse has already fulfilled its purpose, so the mode of address returns to what it was.

The discussion of ﴿لا تَسْفِكُونَ﴾ ("you shall not shed") is like the discussion of ﴿لا تَعْبُدُونَ إلّا اللَّهَ﴾ ("you shall worship none but God") [2:83]. *Safk* means pouring out. The attribution of "blood" to the pronoun of the subject of *tasfikūna* requires that the object of *tasfikūna* be the blood of those who shed it. The intended meaning is not a prohibition against a person shedding his own blood or expelling himself from his own home, because the natural inclination restrains a person from such things, and it is not the concern of the Sharia to prohibit them. Rather, what is meant is that no one should shed the blood of another or expel another from his home, in the manner of His saying ﴿فَإذا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتًا فَسَلِّمُوا عَلى أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ ("When you enter houses, greet one another") [24:61], meaning: let some of you greet others. The reason for attributing the blood to the pronoun of those who shed it is that in rulings related to a community or tribe, the pronouns in them refer to the people collectively. When rulings are connected to those pronouns, whether as predicates, objects or as possessives, each is returned to what suits it, by way of distribution. This is frequent in the Qur'anic usage. Its subtle point is to indicate that the difference in the rights of individuals within the community is a formal difference, which returns to one thing, namely the comprehensive benefit or the comprehensive harm. Similar to this is His saying ﴿لا تَأْكُلُوا أمْوالَكم بَيْنَكم بِالباطِلِ﴾ ("Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood") [4:29]. Of this kind is the saying of the poet al-Hamasi, al-Harith ibn 'Ilzah al-Dhuhli:

*My people are the ones who killed my brother Umaym; so when I shoot, my arrow strikes me.*
*So if I pardon, I shall pardon a great offence; and if I strike, I shall break my own bone.*

He means that when his arrow hits his people, it harms himself. Ibn 'Atiyya pointed to this interpretation and called it *al-laff fi al-qawl* (wrapping in speech), that is, a generalized statement whose intended meaning is distribution. The author of the *Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) held that it is a case of treating the other as oneself, because of the strong connection of the other to oneself in lineage or religion. So if one kills someone closely connected to him by lineage or religion,

[p. 586]

then it is as if he had killed himself. This is close to the first view, and its basis is a metaphor in the possessive pronoun attached in His saying *dimā'akum* ("your blood") and *anfusakum* ("yourselves"). It has also been said that the meaning is: you shall not shed your own blood by causing the killing of another, so that retaliation is taken against you; and you shall not expel yourselves from your homes by committing an offence against another, so that you are banished from your homes. This is based on a metonymic metaphor in *tasfikūna* and *tukhrijūna* by the relation of causation.

This verse also refers to two of the divine commandments in the covenant known as the Ten Words, revealed to Moses, peace be upon him: "Do not kill; do not covet your neighbour's house." The prohibition against coveting a neighbour's house is, by implication of the address, a means of blocking the pathway to seizing it from him.

Accordingly, the attribution of *mīthāq* ("covenant") to the pronoun of the addressees takes into account that, since they adhered to the religion of the Torah, they bound themselves to all that it contains.

His saying ﴿ثُمَّ أقْرَرْتُمْ وأنْتُمْ تَشْهَدُونَ﴾ ("Then you affirmed it while you were witnesses") is arranged in a sequence of rank (*tartib ruteb*). That is: He took your covenant and you affirmed it, meaning you acted upon it and bore witness to it. The two pronouns in ﴿أقْرَرْتُمْ وأنْتُمْ تَشْهَدُونَ﴾ refer to what the pronoun of "your covenant" referred to and what followed it, so that the pronouns are in one pattern within the composition. The clause ﴿وأنْتُمْ تَشْهَدُونَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause, meaning: you do not deny your affirmation of that, since you took it upon yourselves and bound yourselves to adhere to it.

The conjunction *thumma* ("then") in His saying ﴿ثُمَّ أنْتُمْ هَؤُلاءِ تَقْتُلُونَ أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ ("Then you are these who kill yourselves") [2:85] indicates sequence in rank: all of that occurred, and then you are these who kill. The address is to the Jews present at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an, as indicated by the word *hā'ulā'* ("these"), since the demonstrative is not used to refer to someone absent. This is like their saying *ha anā dhā* ("here I am") and *ha antum ulā'* ("here you are"). So the addition of the demonstrative serves only to specify the meaning of the pronoun. This is an Arabic usage which is generally restricted to contexts of wonder at the condition of the one addressed. This is because the basic principle of a predication is that there should be a difference between the speaker and the one spoken of in concept, while being identical in reality. This is known among the logicians as "predication by derivation", as in *anta sādiq* ("you are truthful").

For this reason, the predicate and the subject are usually required to differ in being fixed or derived, or else to share the same derivation. You will not find both of them fixed except by interpretation.

Furthermore, the Arabs sometimes intend by the predication the meaning of the speaker's coming upon a thing that is exactly what he was searching for in his mind, such as (*anta Abā Jahl*, "you are Abu Jahl"), said to him by Ibn Mas'ud on the day of Badr, when he found him badly wounded and prostrate. And the addressee's coming upon this in the speaker's belief is like His saying ﴿قالَ أنا يُوسُفُ وهَذا أخِي﴾ ("He said: I am Joseph and this is my brother") [12:90]. When they intend this, they expand the manner of predication, so that it is valid to say (*anā dhālik*, "I am that") when the reference is to something established in the hearer's mind while he does not know that it is the very subject. Such as the saying of Khufaf ibn Nudba:

*Consider Khufaf, for I am that one.*

And the saying of Tarif al-'Anbari:

*So recognise me, for I am that one of yours.*

And broader than this among them is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

*I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry.*

Then, when they want to emphasise the identity, they bring the particle of alerting *ha* and say *ha anā dhā* ("here I am"), which the speaker says to someone who might doubt that he is the person. Such as the saying of the poet:

*Indeed the young man is the one who says "here I am".*

When the cause that justifies the predication is known, the speaker confines himself to that. Otherwise he follows that construction with a clause indicating the situation that required the predication. They have several levels of this. The first is ﴿ثُمَّ أنْتُمْ هَؤُلاءِ تَقْتُلُونَ﴾ ("Then you are these who kill") [2:85]. The second is ﴿ها أنْتُمْ أُولاءِ تُحِبُّونَهُمْ﴾ ("Here you are, you love them") [3:119], and from it is *ha anā dhā ladaykumā* ("here I am with you both"), said by Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt. The third is ﴿ها أنْتُمْ هَؤُلاءِ جادَلْتُمْ عَنْهُمْ فِي الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ ("Here you are, you argued on their behalf in the life of this world") [4:109]. The sense of wonder is mostly derived from context, as when you say to someone whom you find present, though you were not expecting his presence, "Here you are!" Or else it is derived from the clause following it, if its implication is strange, as you have seen in the examples. The more apparent view is that the pronoun and the demonstrative are subject and predicate, and the clause following them is a circumstantial clause. It has also been said that the clause is a new sentence explaining the origin of the wonder. It has also been said that the clause is the predicate and the demonstrative is an interjected vocative. Sibawayh prohibited this. It has also been said that the demonstrative is in the accusative by way of specification, but this view is weak.

Concerning the difference over the position of the clause, there is also disagreement about what happens if *anta dhā* and similar expressions are followed by a single noun. It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial, and it has been said that it is in the nominative as a predicate. No example from the Arabs has been heard except one which the grammarians cited, namely the saying:

*O Abu Hakam, here you are, the star of Mujalid.*

For this reason Ibn Malik wrote in the preface of *al-Tashil*: "*wa-ha anā sā'in fīmā intudibtu ilayhi*" ("and here I am, striving in what I have been appointed to"). And Ibn Hisham wrote in the preface of *al-Mughni*: "*wa-ha anā mubīḥun bimā asrartuhu*" ("and here I am, revealing what I have concealed").

The grammarians also differed over whether the pronoun after the alerting particle *ha* must necessarily be followed by the demonstrative. Ibn Malik said in *al-Tashil*: it is frequent but not obligatory. Ibn Hisham said: it is obligatory. He stated this in the margins of *al-Tashil* by quoting al-Damamini in the Egyptian marginal notes, in the preface and on the separate *ha*. Al-Radi said: the particle *ha* in reality attaches to the demonstrative, as is well known in their saying *hadha* ("this"), and it is separated from the demonstrative by a separator. Among the separators is the separate pronoun in the nominative, as you have seen, and among them is an oath, as in the saying of a poet cited by al-Radi:

*Know, by the life of God, here is an oath; so estimate with your measuring cubit, and see where it will run.*

Other than this, there are rare cases, such as the saying of al-Nabigha:

*Here, indeed, Ta'idha, if it has not benefited, then its owner has indeed wandered in the land.*

His saying ﴿تَقْتُلُونَ﴾ ("kill") is either a circumstantial clause or a predicate. He used the present tense to indicate renewal and that this is part of your nature. The same applies to His saying ﴿تُخْرِجُونَ فَرِيقًا مِنْكُمْ﴾ ("you expel a group of you") [2:85]. In the *Kashshaf*, the address in all of these expressions in this verse is taken to mean the ancestors of those present. And he took the saying ﴿ثُمَّ أنْتُمْ هَؤُلاءِ تَقْتُلُونَ﴾ ("Then you are these who kill") [2:85], despite its implying a difference between those pointed to and those to whom the address was directed, to refer to a difference of description, namely a difference in the attributes of one addressee, due to his changing attributes. This is a forced interpretation, driven by the desire to make the addresses in this verse agree with the addresses in the verses before it. You know that this is not necessary, and that the difference is intended here and the sense is sound, so there is no need for this forced reading.

This verse has also referred to the strife and neglect among the Jews, in failing to carry out what their law commanded them. The more apparent view is that what is meant is the Jews of Qurayza, al-Nadir and Qaynuqa'. And what is meant in particular is what happened among them in the wars of Bu'ath, which took place between the Aws and the Khazraj. When the Aws and the Khazraj fought, the Jews stood aloof from both groups for a long time, while the Aws were defeated in most of the days of fighting. So the Aws resolved to go out seeking alliance with Qurayza and al-Nadir. When the Khazraj learned of this, they threatened the Jews that if they did so they would act against them. They said to them: "We do not ally with the Aws, nor do we ally with you." Then the Khazraj demanded from the Jews forty boys from the youths of Qurayza and al-Nadir as hostages, and they handed them over. Then 'Amr ibn al-Nu'man al-Bayadi of the Khazraj enticed his people to move into the homes of Qurayza and al-Nadir, because of the goodness of their land and their palm groves. He sent to Qurayza and al-Nadir, saying: "Either you vacate your homes for us, or we shall kill the hostages." The people feared for their hostages and consulted Ka'b ibn Usayd al-Qurazi. He said to them: "O people, defend your homes and let him kill the boys. It will not be more than a night before one of you has intercourse with his wife and she gives birth to a child like one of you." When Qurayza and al-Nadir answered 'Amr that they would defend their homes, 'Amr attacked the boys and killed them. For this reason Qurayza and al-Nadir allied with the Aws. Then the Khazraj sought alliance with Banu Qaynuqa' of the Jews, and from this a fight arose among the factions of the Jews. This took place at the day of Bu'ath five years before the Hijra. The Jews fought one another, expelled the defeated from their homes and took them captive. Then, when the war ended, they gathered wealth and ransomed the Jewish captives who had fallen into the custody of the allies of one of the two groups, the Aws or the Khazraj. The Arabs reproached the Jews for this, saying: "How do you fight them, then ransom them with your wealth?" They said: "Their fighting has been forbidden to us, but we are ashamed to abandon our allies. We have been commanded to ransom captives." That is His saying: ﴿وإنْ يَأْتُوكُمْ أُسارى تُفادُوهُمْ وهو مُحَرَّمٌ عَلَيْكُمْ إخْراجُهُمْ﴾ ("And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while their expulsion was forbidden to you") [2:85].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 85–86:

﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while their expulsion was forbidden to you. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part? So what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the life of this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the severest punishment. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones who bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter; so their punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped.﴾

The waw([wa]) in His saying ﴿And if they come to you as captives﴾ may be a conjunction (li-l-'atf), so it is coordinated with His saying ﴿you kill yourselves and expel a group of you﴾. It is then part of what was rebuked, namely the breaking of the covenant. [p. 590] Although there was no earlier mention of what covenant was taken from them that indicates this, when it returns to the expulsion of people from their homes, it falls within the category of prohibited acts. You may also make the wawa a circumstantial (li-l-hal) particle relating to His saying ﴿and you expel a group﴾, meaning: you expel them, while the situation is that if you take them captive, you ransom them. Whichever way you assess it, His saying ﴿while their expulsion was forbidden to you﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating to His saying ﴿they come to you﴾, either as a circumstance of the coordinated element or as a circumstance of a circumstance, since ransoming a captive is not blameworthy in itself; rather, its blame is due to what accompanies it of the cause of the ransom. So the locus of the rebuke is the combination of ransoming together with the expulsion being forbidden, and after they had killed them and expelled them. Therefore the clause ﴿while their expulsion was forbidden to you﴾ is circumstantial relating to the pronoun in ﴿you ransom them﴾, and it is introduced by the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n) for the sake of emphasis and to show that this prohibition is an established, well-known matter among them. It is not coordinated with His saying ﴿and you expel a group of you﴾, and what lies between them is an interjection (i'tiraad), because its benefit is slight, since that has already been established by His saying ﴿and you do not expel yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 84]. In His saying ﴿while their expulsion was forbidden to you﴾ there is a reproach and a rebuke for them, since they imagined nearness to God in what is one of the effects of disobedience. That is: how do you commit the crime while claiming that you draw near to God through ransoming? The ransoming that is legislated is the ransoming of captives from the hands of enemies, not from your own hands. So why did you not abandon what necessitates ransoming? In my view, the verse indicates a preference for the opinion of Imam al-Haramayn, that one who exits from usurped property is neither performing an obligatory act nor a prohibited one, but the prohibition's obligation has ceased for him, and that nearness to God is not nearness unless it does not arise from disobedience.

Al-usara (الأُسارى), with a damma on the hamza, is the plural of asir (أسِيرٌ), formed by analogy with kaslan (كَسْلانَ), just as they formed kaslan on the analogy of asir, so they said kasla (كَسْلى). This is the view of Sibawayh, because the analogical plural of asir is asra (أسْرى), like qatla (قَتْلى). It has been said that it is a rare plural and not built on analogy, as they said qudama (قُدامى) as the plural of qadim. It has also been said that it is a plural of a plural: asir is pluralized as asra, and then asra is pluralized as usara, and this is the most apparent view.

Asir is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (passive), from asarahu, meaning he tied him up. It is a verb derived from a fixed noun, since al-isar is the strip of leather with which a prisoner or a bound person is tied. They used to bind the vanquished in war with strips of leather. Al-Nabigha said:

"None remained except one who is driven off, not escaping, or one bound in the thongs of rawhide, plundered."

The majority read usara, and Hamza read (asra) (أسْرى). Nafi', al-Kisa'i, 'Asim and Ya'qub read tufadu-hum (تُفادُوهم) in the form of mufa'ala, which is used for intensification in ransoming, that is: you ransom them with an eager ransom. So the use of fada here carries the sense of comparison (maslub al-mufadalah), like 'afahu Allah (عافاهُ اللَّهُ), and the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"He ran with a run between a bull and a she-goat, a dirak, and did not sprinkle himself with water, so he was not washed."

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read (تَفْدُوهم) with a fatha on the taa' and sukun on the fa', without an alif after the fa'. Al-muharram is the forbidden, and the root h-r-m in the speech of the Arabs means prevention. Al-haram is what is prohibited with strong prohibition, or what is prohibited by religion. For this reason they said al-ashhur al-hurum (الأشْهُرُ الحُرُمُ) and Shahr al-Muharram.

His saying ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ is a rhetorical question of denunciation and rebuke, meaning: how did you deliberately oppose the Torah in fighting your brethren, while following it in ransoming their captives? Following and turning away have been called belief and disbelief by way of metaphor (isti'arah), in order to disfigure the one compared and as a warning that deliberately opposing the Book may lead its possessor to disbelieve in it. The verb ﴿you believe﴾ fell within the scope of the denial to indicate that combining the two matters is strange, and this implies that they nearly denied the prohibition of their expulsion, or perhaps they did deny it. Denying what is definitive in religion is apostasy from religion.

The fa' is coordinated with ﴿you kill yourselves﴾ and what is coordinated to it. It has coordinated the question, or it has coordinated an implied element indicated by the question. The verification of this will come shortly at His saying ﴿Whenever a messenger comes to you﴾. The fa' in His saying ﴿So what is the recompense of those among you who do that﴾ is an eloquent fa' (fa' fasihah), coordinating with an omitted element indicated by the denunciatory question, or coordinating with the question itself because of the rebuke it contains.

'Abd al-Hakim said that the clause is an interjection, and that an interjection with a fa' is distant both in meaning and in wording. As for the first, an interjection at the end of speech, called al-tadhyil (التذييل), is only beneficial if it confirms what came before without introducing a new judgment. As for the second, the attachment of an interjected clause to a particle other than the wawa is not known in their speech.

Al-khizy (الخِزْيُ), with a kasra, is a humiliation of the self that suddenly befalls it because of a disgrace that reached it, or a shame that came from it, or a trick and domination that prevailed over it. It is a noun for what results from that, and its verb is from the pattern sami'a with a fatha on the kha'. What is meant by disgrace here is what befell the Jews after those wars of abasement: the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir from their homes, the killing of the Banu Qurayza, the conquest of Khaybar, and the humiliation that was decreed for them among the nations.

Al-Jumhur read (yuraddun) and (ya'malun) with the ya' of the third person. 'Asim, in one narration from him, read (turaddun) with the ta' of address, considering the meaning of man and His saying ﴿among you﴾. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read (ya'malun) with the ya' of the third person, while the majority read it with the ta' of address.

This verse indicates that God punishes those who deviate from the path with punishments in this world and punishments in the Hereafter. What is said about ﴿bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter﴾ is like what is said about ﴿bought error at the price of guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]. What is said about ﴿so their punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped﴾ is close to what is said about ﴿no intercession from it will be accepted, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48].
