﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, and We followed him up with messengers. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you became arrogant? Some of them you denied, and some of them you killed.﴾

This is a transition from the rebuke of the Children of Israel for their conduct toward the Prophet Moses, peace be upon him, in the form of disobedience, aversion, and evasion in accepting the Law, and for what they violated of the rulings of the Torah after his death, down to the time close to the coming of Islam. It is a rebuke for their evil treatment of the messengers who came after Moses, such as Joshua, Elijah, Jeremiah, and David, who confirmed his Law, explained it, and roused the community to renew its practice of the Law. These messengers differed in their methods of calling to that purpose, some gentle and some harsh, some encouraging and some warning. Then came Jesus, confirming, abrogating in part, and giving good news. Yet their response to all of them was aversion, arrogance, and wicked conduct. This is a sign that they turned away from the truth only because the truth opposed their desires. Otherwise, how is it that in the course of these eras, among all these different methods, they did not find anything that agreed with the truth and sincerely offered counsel?

Indeed, a people whose habit this is, and which their later generations inherit from their earlier ones, deserve to be rebuked further. This serves as a proof against them: that their denial of the Muhammadan call is obstinacy and envy, so that their argument may be cut off. For if their opposition to Islam had been their first action, they would have made people think that they turned away only because falsehood had become clear to them. Thus this is connected to His saying ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41], and it is a preface to the rebuke of them for their response to the Muhammadan call, which will be mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are uncovered"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88]. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾ is a preparation for the conjoined clause, which is His saying ﴿and We followed him up with messengers﴾, on which the expression of wonder in His saying ﴿Is it that whenever a messenger came to you﴾ is built. Thus His saying ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾ is a preparation for a preparation, since it is already known from the preceding verses, and there is no need to inform of it independently here. Rather, it is mentioned so that what follows may be built upon it. It is thus like a summary of what came before, meaning: "And indeed there was what had occurred of what preceded, namely the giving of the Book to Moses, and We also followed him up with messengers." It is like the addition of a further matter, or like a speaker's saying, "This happened, and that had also happened."

*Qaffā* is the doubled form of *qafā*. One says *qafawtu fulānan* ("I followed someone") when you come behind him, because at that time you are, as it were, heading toward the back of his neck (*qafā*). It is thus among the verbs derived from solid nouns, like *jabahahu* ("he struck him on the forehead," from *jabhah*). The doubled form becomes *qaffāhu bi-fulān*, *taqfiyatan*, because you made him commanded to follow, by an act from you and not of his own accord. That is, you made another follow him. Since the object is single, when the form is doubled they put the second object after the verb with the transitive particle *bi* ("with"), so that the follower is not confused with the one followed. Thus they say *qaffā Zaydan bi-ʿAmr* instead of saying *qaffā Zaydan ʿAmran*.

The meaning of ﴿We followed him up with messengers﴾ is "We sent messengers." The object of *qaffaynā* has been omitted because it is known, and it is the pronoun referring to Moses. His saying *min baʿdihi* ("after him") means after his departure, that is, after his death. In this there is an implication of reproach to the Jews, that the coming of messengers after Moses is no novelty.

The plural in *al-rusul* ("the messengers") is for multiplicity, and the definite article is for the genus. It is intended to express abundance. This was said by the author of al-Kashshaf: since the nature of a definite generic noun, when there is no specific reference, is to indicate comprehensiveness (*istighraq*), and since comprehensiveness is impossible here, it indicates abundance by way of metaphor, due to the resemblance of a great number to all the individuals of the genus. Compare your saying, "No one in the town failed to see the new moon," when many groups saw it. This is close to the customary sense of comprehensiveness (*al-istighraq al-ʿurfī*).

The prophets of the Children of Israel who came after Moses were called messengers, although they did not bring a new law, taking into account that God commanded them to uphold the Torah, explain it, and derive from it. Thus He gave them a legal function, and by this they exceeded mere prophethood, which has no connection with legislation, neither in establishing principles nor in deriving rules. Al-Baqillani said, as al-Fakhr reported from him: "These messengers must have brought a new law, even if they kept the first law, or renewed what had been effaced of it." This is close to what we have said. God, exalted is He, said ﴿And indeed Elias was among the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat: 123], and ﴿And indeed Jonah was among the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat: 139]. Jesus, peace be upon him, was no different from them in that he brought no new rulings except a few.

Jesus was singled out from among the other prophets who came after Moses for mention, as an added chastisement for the Jews, because they disbelieved in him and denied him. For this reason too He singled him out with His saying ﴿and We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾. Also, none of the messengers who came after Moses reported that Gabriel had brought them revelation, whereas Jesus had a wider mission than they did.

*ʿIsā* is an arabicised name derived from *Yashūʿ* or *Yasūʿ*. This is the name of Jesus son of Mary. In arabicising it, they transposed it by a metathesis, so that it would follow a light pattern, out of dislike for combining the heaviness of foreignness with the heaviness of the arrangement of its letters. For the two weak letters in the word, a *shīn*, and a final guttural letter would not match the natural arrangement of letters with the breath in pronunciation. So they put the *ʿayn* first, because it is a guttural and thus the origin of speech. Then they moved its letters with suitable vowels, and changed its heavy pointed *shīn* into an unpointed *sīn*. How eloquent Arabic is, by God!

The meaning of *Yashūʿ* in Hebrew is "lord" or "blessed." Maryam is the mother of Jesus, and this is her name in Hebrew, transferred to Arabic in its original form because of its lightness. In Arabic, *Maryam* has no meaning other than being a proper name. However, Arabs who had become Christians treated it as an adjective, meaning a woman who keeps away from seeing women, because this attribute became famous for Mary, since she was the first Hebrew woman to serve the Temple of Jerusalem. That is why they say *imraʾatun Maryam* ("a woman Maryam"), meaning one who turns away from the attributes of women, just as they say *rajulun Ḥātim* ("a man Ḥātim") meaning generous. This is known among them in famous names characterized by attributes. For this reason Ru'bah said:

"I said to Zīr, whom Maryamah did not visit."

So it is not derived from *rāma yarīmu* ("to seek, to move away"), as might be supposed. The pattern of the word should be *faʿīl* with a fatḥah on the *fāʾ*, even though this is rare.

[Page 595]

Jesus, peace be upon him, is the son of Mary. God created him in her womb without any man touching her. His mother Mary was the daughter of ʿImrān, from the tribe of Judah.

Jesus was born during the reign of Augustus, king of Rome, and during the rule of Herod over Jerusalem on behalf of the Roman authority, in the year 430 [or 620] before the Muhammadan Hijrah. His birth took place in a village known as Bethlehem in Judea. When he reached thirty years of age he was sent as a messenger to the Children of Israel, and he remained in the world until he was thirty-three years old.

As for his mother Mary, she was Mary daughter of ʿImrān son of Māthān, from the tribe of Judah. She bore Jesus when she was thirteen years old. Her birth was thirteen years before the birth of Jesus. She died after she had grown old, and the year of her death is not known. Her father had died before her birth, so she was cared for by Zechariah of the sons of Abijah, who was the husband of Elizabeth, Mary's maternal aunt. He was a priest among the rabbis of the Jews, as will come in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān.

*Al-bayyināt* is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "the clear signs and miracles." *Ayyadnāhu* means "We strengthened him, reinforced his arm, and aided him." It is derived from a solid noun, *yad* ("hand"). So *ayyada* means "made him possessor of a hand," and "hand" is metaphorically used for power and ability. Thus the pattern of *ayyada* is *afʿala*. You may also make it derived from *al-ayd*, which means strength. In that case its pattern is *faʿʿala*.

*Ta'yīd* means strengthening and enabling for inward action. It is derived from *al-ayd*, meaning strength. God, exalted is He, said ﴿Remember Our servant David, the one of strength﴾ [Ṣād: 17]. *Al-ayd* is derived from *al-yad*, since it is the instrument of power. The better view is that it is derived from *al-yad*, meaning "he made him possessor of a hand," that is, of strength. The meaning here is spiritual strength: the strength of the message and the strength of patience in bearing the harm of his people. Later, in Sūrat al-Anfāl, His saying will come: ﴿He is the One who strengthened you with His help﴾.

*Al-rūḥ* is a subtle luminous substance, that is, not perceived by the senses. It is applied to the human soul by which humans live. It is applied to what gives life to animals only by the word *nafs* ("soul"). God, exalted is He, said ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: "The spirit is of the command of my Lord"﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 85]. It is also applied to a power from God, exalted is He, by which a wondrous act is performed, and from this is His saying ﴿So We breathed into it of Our spirit﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 91]. It is applied to Gabriel, as in His saying ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has descended with it upon your heart, that you may be among the warners﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 193]. This is what is meant in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr: 4], and in His saying ﴿On the day when the Spirit and the angels stand﴾ [al-Naba': 38].

*Al-quds*, with two *ḍammas* or with one *ḍammah* and a sukūn, is a verbal noun or a noun of action, meaning purity and cleanness. *Al-muqaddas* means purified. This was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

[Page 596]

*Rūḥ al-quds* ("the Holy Spirit") is a spirit attributed to holiness. It is possible that what is meant is the Spirit that God breathed into the womb of Mary, so that Jesus came from it. This was for his strengthening, because his formation through that holy, divinely given spirit is what prepared him to perform the great miracles. It is also possible that what is meant is Gabriel, and the strengthening through him is clear, since he is the one who brings him revelation and speaks through his tongue in the cradle and at the time of calling people to the religion. This application is more apparent here. In the authentic hadith: "The Holy Spirit breathed into my heart that no soul will die until it has fully received its provision and its term."

On both views, the construction *rūḥ* + *al-quds* is either an annexation of what should be described to what it should be derived from, but the annexation to the source of the adjective is considered because the annexation is more indicative of particularity with the genus annexed to. For annexation implies association between the annexed and the annexed-to, and this association here amounts to description. At-Taftazānī, in his commentary on al-Kashshaf, held this view, and he denied that the annexed-to in such a construction is a true adjective, so as to make it a description by a verbal noun.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So whenever a messenger came to you﴾ is the purpose of the preceding speech, and what precedes it, namely His saying ﴿And indeed We gave﴾, is a preparation for it, as already stated. The *fāʾ* indicates causation, and the interrogative expresses wonder at their transgression and at their confronting all the messengers in all times with one and the same response, in which the later generations equaled the earlier ones. This indicates that such a disposition is common to them all.

[p. 597]

The placing of the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham, the interrogative particle "a") before the conjunctive particle (harf al-'atf) that signifies sharing the same ruling is a common usage in Arabic speech. Its outward form, however, seems strange, because it implies that the interrogation governs both the conjunction and what is conjoined, and that the interrogation governs the conjunctive particle is strange. For this reason the grammarians turned it away from its outward meaning, and they have two approaches to this.

The first is the approach of the majority, who said: the interrogative hamza is placed earlier than its original position. Its original position was after the conjunctive particle, but it was moved in front of it because interrogation deserves to begin its sentence. They singled out the hamza for this fronting, rather than other interrogative words, because the hamza is rooted in interrogation: it is the particle set for interrogation and the most frequently used for it. As for the other words, they are terms that have absorbed the meaning of interrogation. Some of them are nouns, such as "أيْنَ" (where). Others are the particle of confirmation, "هَلْ" (hal), which carries the sense of "قَدْ" (qad). When the interrogative hamza came to be frequently prefixed to it, they dropped the hamza because of its frequent use. Thus the original form of "هَلْ فَعَلْتَ" (did you do?) is "أهَلْ فَعَلْتَ". The estimated form here is "أفَكُلَّما جاءَكم رَسُولٌ" (so whenever a messenger came to you...), and it was then inverted. It has also been said that the estimated form is "أفَكُلَّما جاءَكم رَسُولٌ". On this approach the interrogation is conjoined, and the sentence is conjoined to the one before it, or conjoined to an omitted element, according to what the context allows.

The second approach is that of the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari). In Mughni al-Labib it is stated that al-Zamakhshari was the first to hold this view. Al-Damamini claimed that al-Zamakhshari was preceded in it, but he did not specify who preceded him. Al-Zamakhshari had permitted the approach of the majority, and he also permitted that the interrogative hamza be the beginning of the sentence, with the thing interrogated about being omitted and indicated by what is conjoined to it by the conjunctive particle. The estimate in such a case is: "أتُكَذِّبُونَهم فَكُلَّما جاءَكم رَسُولٌ" (Do you deny them? So whenever a messenger came to you...), and so on.

On this approach the sentence is an interrogative, newly begun, with its remainder omitted, and then what is conjoined is conjoined to it. There is no effect of this except in the difference of consideration and estimate, for the meaning of the speech does not change under either consideration, because both the conjunction and the interrogation are directed at the sentence that follows them. The apparent view of the author of al-Kashshaf in this verse, and in his statement of the Most High in Surat Al 'Imran, "﴿أوَلَمّا أصابَتْكم مُصِيبَةٌ قَدْ أصَبْتُمْ مِثْلَيْها﴾" (Or when a calamity strikes you, although you had struck twice as much [of it]...) [Al 'Imran: 165], is that both approaches are permissible in all positions where the interrogation occurs with a conjunctive particle. This is the truth. As for his not addressing this at the verses "﴿أفَتَطْمَعُونَ أنْ يُؤْمِنُوا لَكُمْ﴾" (Do you hope that they will believe you?) [al-Baqarah: 75], "﴿أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾" (Will you not then use your reason?) [al-Baqarah: 76], and "﴿أفَتُؤْمِنُونَ بِبَعْضِ الكِتابِ﴾" (Do you believe in part of the Book?) [al-Baqarah: 85] earlier in this surah, that is an oversight on his part, and he has made up for it here. In my view there is a third approach that is permissible: that the interrogation is about the conjunction, and the meaning is: "أتَزِيدُونَ عَلى مُخالَفاتِكُمُ اسْتِكْبارَكم كُلَّما جاءَكم رَسُولٌ إلَخْ" (Do you add to your acts of disobedience your arrogance, whenever a messenger came to you...?). This applies to the three conjunctive particles, as has been shown in the examples of waw and fa' above, and to the statement of the Most High "﴿أثُمَّ إذا ما وقَعَ آمَنتُمْ بِهِ﴾" (Is it then, when it has occurred, that you believe in it?) [Yunus: 51] in Surat Yunus, and to the verse of al-Nabigha:

Athamma ta'adharani ilayya minha
fa-inni qad sami'tu wa-qad ra'aitu

(Is it then that the two of you make excuses to me for it?
Indeed I have heard, and I have seen.)

I have surveyed this usage, and I found its occurrences to be specific to the non-literal interrogation, as you have seen from the examples.

The meaning of the "فَ" (fa') here is that it expresses the causation of the astonished, reproachful interrogation, based on what was established among them regarding Musa being followed by the messengers. That is: We followed up Musa with messengers. So it is one of the strange aspects of your affair that every messenger who came to you, you were arrogant toward. The author of al-Kashshaf also permitted that the conjunction is to an estimated element, i.e., "آتَيْنا مُوسى الكِتابَ إلَخْ" (We gave Musa the Book...), then you did [such and such], then He rebuked them with His saying "أفَكُلَّما" (So whenever...). In that case the hamza is for rebuke, and the fa' is then conjoining an estimated element to the estimated element that is qualified for rebuke. This is a distant view. The aim of both views is that the clause "آتَيْنا مُوسى الكِتابَ إلَخْ" is not intended to convey its meaning as information.

"كُلَّما" (kullama, whenever) is in the accusative as a substitute for the adverb of time, because it is annexed to "ما" (ma) of the temporal verbal type, and its governing element is the statement "اسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ" (you were arrogant). The adverb is placed first so that it follows the interrogation intended for astonishment, to make clear that the locus of the wonder is the continuity of this behavior from them, which indicates that it is their disposition, and that it is not due to an incidental cause that occurred in some of the messengers or at some times. The estimate is: "أفاسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ كُلَّما جاءَكم رَسُولٌ" (So were you arrogant whenever a messenger came to you?). The adverb was placed first for emphasis, because it is the locus of wonder. The generality contained in "كُلَّما" indicates that the denial or killing includes all the messengers sent to them, because the generality of times entails the generality of the individuals contained within them.

"تَهْوى" (tahwa) is the present tense of "هَوِيَ" (hawiya) with a kasra on the waw, when one loves. What is meant by it is what their souls incline toward: casting off the legal restraints, immersing in various pleasures, and insisting upon misguided beliefs.

"الِاسْتِكْبارُ" (al-istikbar, arrogance) is the state of being characterized by pride. Here it means lofty disdain for following the messengers, and the self-admiration of the arrogant, and the belief that they are too high to obey the messengers and to be followers of them. Thus the "سين" (sin) and the "تاء" (ta') in "اسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ" are for intensification, as has been mentioned previously in the statement of the Most High "﴿إلّا إبْلِيسَ أبى واسْتَكْبَرَ﴾" (except Iblis, who refused and was arrogant) [al-Baqarah: 34]. His statement "﴿فَفَرِيقًا كَذَّبْتُمْ وفَرِيقًا تَقْتُلُونَ﴾" (so a group you denied and a group you kill) is caused by the arrogance, so the fa' is for causation. When they were arrogant, their disobedience reached the point that they denied a group, i.e., they openly denied them, or treated them as liars, and they killed a group.

This is like the statement of the Most High about the people of Madyan: "﴿قالُوا يا شُعَيْبُ ما نَفْقَهُ كَثِيرًا مِمّا تَقُولُ وإنّا لَنَراكَ فِينا ضَعِيفًا ولَوْلا رَهْطُكَ لَرَجَمْناكَ﴾" (They said, "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed we see you among us as weak; and were it not for your tribe, we would have stoned you.") [Hud: 91].

The object is placed first here, because it contains the indication of detail, so it was fitting to place it first to show that. This is like the statement of the Most High "﴿فَرِيقًا هَدى وفَرِيقًا حَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ الضَّلالَةُ﴾" (a group He guided, and a group upon whom misguidance was justified) [al-A'raf: 30]. This is a common Arabic usage with the word "فَرِيقٌ" (fariq, group) and what has its meaning, such as "طائِفَةٌ" (ta'ifah, a party), when it occurs as the object of a verb in a context of division, as in the statement "﴿يَغْشى طائِفَةً مِنكم وطائِفَةٌ قَدْ أهَمَّتْهم أنْفُسُهُمْ﴾" (a party of you [being] overcome with drowsiness, and another party concerned only for themselves) [Al 'Imran: 154].

The detail refers back to the generality in the word "رَسُولٌ" (rasul, messenger), because "كُلَّما جاءَكم رَسُولٌ" (whenever a messenger came to you) expresses the generality of messengers, and this includes Musa, peace be upon him. Although they did not deny him in explicit words, they treated him as one who is denied, since they doubted what he told them about Allah, the Exalted, more than once, and thought ill of Him regarding His legislative commands repeatedly, and they attributed to him the intention of deceiving them and striving to destroy them. This is as they said when they reached the Red Sea, and when he commanded them to attend to hear the speech of Allah, the Exalted, and when he commanded them to enter Ariha (Jericho), and other instances. As for the rest of the messengers, they denied them in explicit speech, like 'Isa (Jesus), and they killed some of the messengers, like Ishaya (Isaiah), Zakariyya (Zechariah), his son Yahya (John), and Irmiya (Jeremiah).

The present tense "تَقْتُلُونَ" (taqtulun, you kill) is used in place of the past tense to bring the terrible situation vividly before the mind, namely the situation of their killing their messengers, as in the statement of the Most High "﴿واللَّهُ الَّذِي أرْسَلَ الرِّياحَ فَتُثِيرُ سَحابًا فَسُقْناهُ﴾" (And it is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir clouds, and We drive them...) [Fatir: 9]. In addition, the form "تَقْتُلُونَ" observes the rhyme of the verses. Thus the eloquence of the meaning and the beauty of the composition are complete.

[Page 599]

﴿And they say, "Our hearts are wrapped," but Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so little is it that they believe.﴾

Either it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His saying "اسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ" (you were arrogant), or with "كَذَّبْتُمْ" (you denied). On the second reading, it is an explanation (tafsīr) of the arrogance, meaning that if it is coordinated with "كَذَّبْتُمْ," it falls within the detailing of the arrogance, indicating that their arrogance takes several forms: denial, killing, and turning away.

On both readings there is an iltifāt (shift from address to third person) and a distancing of them from the station of presence. This is the kind of iltifāt whose purpose is that the qualities of deficiency and monstrosity attributed to the addressee have made him so repugnant that the mind turns away from him. This distancing is indicated by addressing him with the form of distance, so it is a kināya (metonymy).

The iltifāt is also made pleasing by the fact that it signals a shift of the discourse to the evil of their opposition to the Muhammadan call, which is a new theme. When the speech spoke about them in matters concerning their dealings with their prophets, it directed the address to them. When the intention was to speak about them in their turning away from the Prophet (ﷺ), the address continued with the believers, and the pronoun of the third person was applied to the Jews.

It is also possible that their saying "قُلُوبُنا غُلْفٌ" (our hearts are wrapped) was not declared openly. What supports this is that the style of address continued in the third person from the beginning of this verse until His saying, ﴿And certainly Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf﴾ [al-Baqara: 92]. The word "القُلُوب" (hearts) is used with the meaning of minds, following the manner of Arabic speech in applying "القلب" (heart) to the intellect.

"الغُلْف" (ghulf), with a ḍamma and then a sukūn, is the plural of "أغْلَفَ" (aghlaf), which means hard or closed. The noun "الغِلاف" (ghilāf, covering) is derived from "غَلَّفَهُ" (he covered it), when one makes a covering for it. It is the container that protects a thing and screens it from the arrival of what is disliked. This was a saying that they used to say to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he called them to Islam. They intended by it mockery and cutting off his hope of their conversion. It is like the saying of the polytheists, ﴿Our hearts are under coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a screen﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 5].

In the expression there is a tawjīh (a directing or interpretive angle), because the basic meaning of the aghlaf is that he is screened from what does not suit him, for that is the meaning of the ghilāf. They imagine that their hearts are veiled from understanding, and they mean that they are protected from grasping misguidance. For this reason the exegetes said that it indicates the meaning that they do not comprehend what they say, even if they did comprehend it.

[Page 600]

These two meanings, which the expression includes, are met by the rejection in His saying, ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾. That is, their not believing is not due to a deficiency in their understanding, nor to the swelling of their minds from accepting the like of what they were called to. Rather, it is because they disbelieved, so Allah cursed them for their disbelief and removed them far from good and its causes.

By this, the two intended meanings are achieved without the need to posit the possibility that "غُلْفٌ" is the plural of "غِلاف," which involves an elaborate omission of the genitive complement (muḍāf ilayhi), so that one would have to assume they are containers for knowledge and truth, so that falsehood does not seep into them. His saying, ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾, is a recording against them and an exposure of them, that they were resolute in disbelief and in clinging to their religion, without turning to the proof of the Prophet (ﷺ). When they were resolute in that, Allah punished them with the curse and removal far from mercy and good. He deprived them of success and of insight into the signs of the Messenger's truthfulness. So the curse came upon them as a punishment for their resolve in disbelief and their turning away from the truth. In this is a refutation of what they had given the impression of, that their hearts were created far from understanding, because Allah created them like all other rational beings, able to grasp the truth had they turned to it with reflection and abandoned obstinacy. This is the belief of the People of Truth among the believers, unlike the Jabriyya (determinists).

His saying, ﴿So little is it that they believe﴾, is a consequence (tafrīʿ) of "لَعَنَهم" (He cursed them). "قَلِيلًا" (little) is an adjective of an omitted noun indicated by the verb, and the estimate is: "فَإيمانًا قَلِيلًا" (so their belief is little). "ما" is an extra particle (zāʾida) for the sake of emphasis in minimizing. The pronoun refers to the collective of the Children of Israel. It is also permissible that "قَلِيلًا" is an adjective of the time implied by the verb, meaning: "فَحِينًا قَلِيلًا يُؤْمِنُونَ" (so they believe for a little while).

"قَلِيلٌ" (little) may be permissible to keep in its literal sense, referring to their belief in some of the Book, or to their belief in some of what the Prophet (ﷺ) calls to that agrees with their ancient religion, such as monotheism and the prophethood of Moses. Or it refers to the belief of certain individuals among them at some times, for the belief of a few of them entails the occurrence of belief from the collective of the Children of Israel in short periods, or the occurrence of a few acts of belief.

It is also permissible that "قَلِيلًا" here is used in the sense of non-existence, for "القِلَّة" (fewness) is used for non-existence in Arabic speech. Abū Kabīr al-Hudhalī said:

"Little complaining at the affliction that befalls him,
Much desire, scattered in its distances and paths."

He meant that he does not complain. And ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba ibn Masʿūd said about the land of Nusaybin: "Many scorpions, few relatives." He meant "without relatives." And they say, "So-and-so has little shame," and all of that is either a majāz (metaphor), because "little" is likened to non-existence, or a kināya (metonymy). The latter is more apparent, because when a thing becomes little it approaches dissolution, so non-existence is a customary (ʿurfī) necessary consequence of fewness, claimed (iddiʿāʾī). In that case "ما" is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya).

Both possibilities were indicated by al-Zamakhsharī in the Kashshāf in brief. In his commentary on His saying in Sūrat al-Naml, ﴿Is there a god with Allah? Little is it that you remember﴾ [al-Naml: 62], he adopted only the second of them, saying: "The meaning is the negation of remembrance." Fewness is used to express negation. The likely reason for this is that remembering, by its nature, brings about knowledge. So had the polytheists addressed in the verse remembered, knowledge would have arisen in them that Allah is one with no partner. How could they, when the address "أإلَهٌ مَعَ اللَّهِ" (is there a god with Allah?) [al-Naml: 60] is meant as a denial, on the basis that they do not believe that?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 89:

﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah, confirming what was with them, though before that they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved. Yet when there came to them that which they recognised, they disbelieved in it. So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers.﴾

This is conjoined to His saying ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are uncovered"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88], for the purpose of increasing the reproach against them by rebuke. For had they turned away from the Muhammadan call with a turning-away stripped of any proofs, there would have been some excuse in their turning away. But they turned away and disbelieved in the Book that came confirming what was with them, and which they had formerly been using to seek victory over the polytheists. So His saying ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to "came to them" and is not an attribute, because it is not a matter witnessed and known such that it could be described by it. His saying ﴿confirming what was with them﴾ is a description of state, for the purpose of increasing the branding of them with blame in this disbelief. The discussion of its interpretation has already passed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41]. And istiftah (seeking opening) apparently means seeking a victory (fath), i.e. help. He, exalted is He, said ﴿If you seek a victory, then there has certainly come to you the victory﴾ [al-Anfal: 19]. They (the scholars) have explained it as: when the Jews fought the polytheists, i.e. the people of Madinah, they sought help against them by asking Allah to send to them the Messenger promised in the Torah.

And it is permissible that yastaftihun means yaftahun, i.e. they inform and make known, as one says fataha ʿala al-qari (he opened to the reciter), i.e. he taught him the verse he had forgotten. So the sin and the ta' are merely for emphasis, like their addition in istaʿsama, istasrakha and istaʿjaba. The meaning is that they used to inform the polytheists that a messenger would be sent who would support the believers and punish the polytheists. His saying ﴿when there came to them what they recognised﴾ means: that which they had been seeking victory by, i.e. when the Book they recognised came, they disbelieved in it. The expression "a Book" was avoided in favour of "that which" so that the wording would be more comprehensive, encompassing both the Book and the Messenger who brought it, for a Book does not come except with a Messenger.

Page 602

The relative pronoun ma was used rather than man for the sake of this comprehensiveness, and because indefiniteness suits the relative which is more general; for the truth is that ma is used for what is more general than the rational.

By "what they recognised" is meant the Qur'an, i.e. they recognised it through the attribute established in external reality, even though they were ignorant of its applying to the Qur'an, owing to their misguidance. For the apparent meaning is that most of the Children of Israel did not believe in the truthfulness of the Qur'an and the truthfulness of the Messenger, while some of them did believe this but forgot and ignored it out of envy. He, exalted is He, said ﴿out of envy from themselves, after the truth had become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109]. The meaning of the verse thus becomes: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah, confirming what was with them﴾, and they recognised that it was the one by which they had been seeking victory over the polytheists.

The clause ﴿though before that they had been seeking﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and its benefit here is to call to mind their astonishing condition: that they denied the Book and the Messenger while they were awaiting his coming and expecting victory through him, and this is the utmost of forsaking and slander.

His saying ﴿Yet when there came to them what they recognised﴾, with the fa' (then), is conjoined to the clause "they used to seek", and the second (lamma) contends with the first (lamma) for the response, which is His saying "they disbelieved in it". So the position of the clause "and they used to... etc." with respect to the Book being confirmatory is the position of a circumstantial clause, since seeking victory by it or giving good tidings of it suits the belief that it is ﴿confirming what is with them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91]. Its position with respect to the Book and the Messenger being known to them through signs and proofs is the position of the initiating clause from that which is derived from it. Yet the import of the clause ﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah﴾ etc. and the clause ﴿Yet when there came to them what they recognised﴾ etc. is one. The repetition of (lamma) in the second clause, rather than saying ﴿And they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved before, then when there came to them what they recognised﴾ etc., was intended to show the unity of meaning of the two clauses introduced by lamma and to increase the linkage between the two meanings, since it is separated by the circumstantial clause, and by this there results a wondrous arrangement and a marvellous conciseness. The method of repeating the governing element while the object is one is a eloquent Arabic method. He, exalted is He, said ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought, and love to be praised for what they have not done, do not think them safe from the punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 188], and He said ﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 35], repeating "that you" before the predicate of the first. We have, in this explanation, departed from the method of al-Zajjaj, the method of al-Mubarrad and the method of al-Farra' mentioned in the margin of al-Khafaji and ʿAbd al-Hakim, and we have drawn from the good points of all those methods, because of the opposition to the apparent meaning found in each of them.

His saying ﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾ is a clause of supplication against them and against those like them. Supplication from Allah, exalted is He,

Page 603

is a decree and a determination, because nothing can overpower Him, and none other than Him is sought by supplications. This is like His saying ﴿And the Jews said, "The hand of Allah is chained up"; their hands were chained up﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and His saying ﴿May Allah fight them; how are they turned away?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30]. Its explanation will come at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Upon them is the circle of evil﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98] in Surat Bara'ah. The fa' (so) is for causation, and what is meant is a mentioned causation, meaning that what precedes it, namely the conjoined element, causes the speaker to utter what follows it, like the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"I was a man who would not hear, through the ages, a reproach I was reviled by without uncovering its veil,
So I am, in the fierce war, one charged with a boldness of soul whose survival I do not desire."

Here he conjoined "so I am" to "I uncovered its veil", because this statement requires the explanation that he is bold in war. The lam in "the disbelievers" is for totality (istighraq), by the indication of the context of supplication; it includes those spoken of, for they are among the individuals of this generality, indeed they are the first of its individuals to come to the mind, because the cause of the general term's revelation is definitely included in the generality from the outset. This is an eloquent Arabic method of attributing a ruling to a generality while the intended meaning is the initial portion of its individuals, for the entry of the intended into it is then by a demonstrative method, as the conclusion enters into a syllogism. Bashshama ibn Hazn al-Nahshali said:

"We greet you, O Salma, so greet us back, and even if you give drink to the noble of people, give us drink."

He meant by it a metonymy for their generosity, that they are given drink when the noble of people are given drink.

**[Page 604]**

This is a resumptive statement (*istinaf*, a new sentence that continues the argument) condemning them and mocking their judgment, since they were content for themselves to disbelieve in the Qur'an and in Muhammad (ﷺ). They turned away from considering what their scriptures contained of the promise of the coming of a messenger after Moses, in satisfaction of the urge of envy. Yet they imagined that by disbelieving in the Qur'an they had nevertheless preserved their souls upon the truth. This is therefore a warning to them, directing them toward recognizing the one who calls them to disbelief, and a public exposure, before the Muslims, of what he conceals.

"*Bi'sama*" (بِئْسَما) is composed of *bi'sa* (بِئْسَ, "how wretched") and the *ma* (ما) that is superfluous. Concerning *bi'sa* and its opposite *ni'ma* (نِعْمَ, "how excellent"), there is a difference of opinion as to whether they are verbs or nouns, and the more correct view is that they are verbs. Concerning the *ma* attached to them there are several positions. The first is that it is a complete definite *ma* (*ma ma'rifa tamma*), meaning it is explained by a definite noun with the definite article, and does not require a relative clause (*sila*), in order to distinguish it from the relative *ma* (*ma al-mawsula*). Accordingly, his saying "*bi'sama*" is explained as "*bi'sa al-shay'*" (how wretched is the thing). This is the view of Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i. The other position is that it is a relative pronoun, the view of al-Farra' and al-Farisi. These two are the clearest interpretations. When *ma* alone follows them, it is a complete definite *ma*, as in His saying ﴿إنْ تُبْدُوا الصَّدَقاتِ فَنِعِمّا هِيَ﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 271), meaning "*ni'ma al-shay'u hiya*" (how excellent is the thing it is). If after *ma* there comes a clause that could serve as a relative clause, then *ma* is a defective definite *ma*, that is, a relative pronoun, as in His saying here ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾. Here *ma* is the subject (*fa'il*) of *bi'sa*.

After *bi'sa* and *ni'ma* there is often mentioned a noun which specifies the intended object of dispraise or praise, and which in the terminology of Arabic grammar is called the *makhsus* (the specified object). It may also be omitted when it is evident from the context, or because something preceding it indicates it. Thus His saying "*an yakfuru*" (أنْ يَكْفُرُوا) is the *makhsus* of dispraise. The implied meaning is "their disbelief in the signs of God." You may also take it as a subject with an omitted predicate, or as a predicate with an omitted subject, or as an apposition (*badal*) or an explanatory elaboration (*bayan*) of *ma*. In that case His saying "*ishtaraw*" (اشْتَرَوْا) is either a qualifier of the definite *ma*, or a relative clause of the relative *ma*, and "*an yakfuru*" is the *makhsus* of dispraise, the predicate of an omitted subject. This is in the pattern of your saying "*ni'ma al-rajulu fulan*" (how excellent a man is so-and-so).

*Al-ishtira'* means purchase (*ibtiya'*), and it has already been discussed in His saying ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ بِالهُدى﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 16). Therefore His saying here ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ is a metaphor, in which "*ishtira'*" is used for preserving a thing that is desired, by way of comparing the preserving of it to the purchase of a desired thing. They preferred their own selves in this world, and preserved them by disbelieving in the Qur'an out of envy. If they believed that they were right in turning away from the call of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they held fast to the Torah, and that His saying earlier ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَهم ما عَرَفُوا﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 89) means "when there came to them what they recognized," meaning they recognized its description, though they neglected to apply it to the one described, then the meaning of "purchasing their souls" is in accordance with their belief, because they thought they had saved them from punishment. Thus His saying ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ means "how wretched is what it actually is." As for it being a purchase, that is according to their belief. His saying ﴿أنْ يَكْفُرُوا بِما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ is also according to reality, and in it is a warning to them about the true nature of their situation: that they disbelieved in a messenger sent to them, in order to persist in a law that had been abrogated (*nusikha*).

If they believed in the truthfulness of the Messenger, and their turning away was merely out of obstinacy, as His saying before it ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَهم ما عَرَفُوا﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 89) indicates according to one of the two previously mentioned possibilities, then "*ishtira'*" means preserving worldly status: that is, how wretched is the exchange, their giving up of disbelief and their contentment with it, for the sake of preserving leadership and reputation, and not acknowledging the message of the truthful one. The verse is then like His saying ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الحَياةَ الدُّنْيا بِالآخِرَةِ﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 86).

It has also been said that "*ishtaraw*" means "*baa'u*" (sold), that is, they offered up their souls, and what is meant is offering them to punishment in exchange for satisfying their obstinacy and envy. This interpretation looks back to His saying before it ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَهم ما عَرَفُوا كَفَرُوا بِهِ﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 89). However, it is distant from the wording, because using *ishtira'* in the sense of *bay'* (selling) is a remote metaphor, since it leads to introducing confusion for the hearer and corrupting the distinction that the language has established. What prompted its proponent to it was his intention to clarify the overall meaning. Furthermore, you already know that it is possible to combine what His saying "*ma 'arafu*" implies with His saying here ﴿اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾, so you have no need of artificial construction.

On both interpretations, "*ishtaraw*" together with what derives from it, His saying ﴿فَباءُوا بِغَضَبٍ عَلى غَضَبٍ﴾, forms an allegory (*tamthil*) for their situation in the case of one who attempts a trade in order to profit, but suffers loss. This allegory admits that some of its parts may be a metaphor (*isti'ara*), and that is among the excellences of allegorical expression (*tamthiliyya*).

The imperfect form was used in His saying "*an yakfuru*" (أنْ يَكْفُرُوا), and it was not given in a form that suits what is clarified, which is "*ma ishtaraw*" (ما اشْتَرَوْا), which implies that the purchase has already taken place. This is to indicate that they had openly declared disbelief in the Qur'an before the revelation of the verse. Thus it has become clear that their purchase of their souls with disbelief was an act that was established and had already passed. Then, when it was intended to clarify what they had purchased their souls with, attention was drawn to the fact that they were continuously disbelieving, and it is known that they had disbelieved in the past as well, since what is clarified by "*an yakfuru*" is expressed in the past tense by His saying "*ma ishtaraw*."

His saying "*baghyan*" (بَغْيًا) is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*, a noun giving the reason for an action), the cause of His saying "*an yakfuru*," because it is the nearer to it. It is also permissible that it is the cause of "*ishtaraw*," because the purchase here applies to disbelief, which is the *makhsus* of the ruling of dispraise, and which is the very thing being condemned. *Al-baghy* here is the verbal noun of *baghā yabghī*, meaning to wrong, and by it is meant here a specific kind of wrongdoing, namely envy (*hasad*). Envy was called wrongdoing because wrongdoing is treating someone without right. Envy is wishing the removal of a blessing from the one envied, and the envier has no right in that, since he gains no benefit from its removal, nor harm from its continuance. Abu al-Tayyib has excelled when he took up this meaning in his saying:

"The most wrongful of God's creatures is he who spends the night envious of one who spends the night turning in his blessings."

His saying "*an yunazzila Allah*" (أنْ يُنَزِّلَ اللَّهُ) is connected to "*baghyan*" by the omission of the preposition, which is the preposition of elevation (*isti'la'*), since "*baghyan*" is interpreted to mean "*hasadan*" (out of envy).

Thus the Jews disbelieved out of envy at the prophethood coming forth from among themselves to the Arabs. This is what is indicated by His saying ﴿عَلى مَن يَشاءُ مِن عِبادِهِ﴾ (upon whomever He wills of His servants). His saying ﴿فَباءُوا بِغَضَبٍ عَلى غَضَبٍ﴾ means they returned from that transaction, which was the purchase of their souls, with manifest loss. It is an allegory for their situation, like the situation of one who goes out with his merchandise for trade, but is struck by loss, and returns to his home a loser. It likens their outcome of loss to the return of the losing merchant, after adding His saying ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾.

The apparent meaning of "*bi-ghadabin 'ala ghadab*" (with wrath upon wrath) is intense wrath, in the manner of His saying ﴿نُورٌ عَلى نُورٍ﴾ (Al-Nur: 35), meaning a great light, and His saying ﴿ظُلُماتٌ بَعْضُها فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ﴾ (Al-Nur: 40), and the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

"Sleeplessness upon sleeplessness, and one like me stays awake."

This is an instance of repetition with variation of form to express the meaning of strength and intensity, like the saying of al-Hutay'a:

"The family of Shammas ibn La'y have come, and indeed there came to them with them the forbearance and the abundant *'add* (lineage)."

That is, the numerous, i.e., the great. And al-Ma'arri said:

"Sons of the bright lineage and abundant glory."

That is, the great. Al-Qurtubi said: some of them said that what is meant by it is the intensity of the state, and not that He intended two wraths, namely the wrath of God upon them for disbelief and for envy, or for disbelief in Muhammad and Jesus, peace be upon them both.

His saying ﴿ولِلْكافِرِينَ عَذابٌ مُهِينٌ﴾ (and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment) is like His saying ﴿فَلَعْنَةُ اللَّهِ عَلى الكافِرِينَ﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 89), meaning: and for them is a humiliating punishment, because they are among the disbelievers. *Al-muhin* means the one who humiliates, that is, it contains the manner of their being despised.

[Page 607]

This is conjoined (ma'tuf, grammatically linked) to His saying ﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:89], which is itself conjoined to His saying ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are uncovered"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:88]. On this basis it is also valid to treat it as conjoined to ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are uncovered"﴾ [2:88], according to the familiar view on conjoining something to what is already conjoined. All of this belongs to the conjoining of accounts of their states in their excuses for turning away from the Islamic call. When they are called, they say, "Our hearts are uncovered." When they hear the Book, they turn away from it after having been awaiting it, out of envy that it was sent down upon a man from other than them. When they are admonished, warned, and called to believe in the Qur'an, and that Allah sent it down, and to consider the proofs that it was sent down from Allah, they turn away and say ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us﴾, meaning, in what Allah sent down to our Messenger Moses. This is the sum of their misguidance and the source of their obstinacy. Therefore the Qur'an undertook to prolong the argument against them concerning this, with what is here and what follows it, as a preparation for His later saying ﴿Whatever a sign We abrogate﴾ [2:106] and the verses after it.

[Page 608]

Their saying ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us﴾ was intended as an excuse and a way of consoling themselves. For when it was said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down," they knew that if they simply refused, the ugliness of refusing to believe in what is claimed to have been sent down by Allah would be counted against them. So in their excuse, and to satisfy themselves, they said, "We believe in what was sent down to us," meaning that the merit of being affiliated with belief in what Allah has sent down has already been attained by them, so they are content with what was sent down to them. They added to this by holding firmly to it and not abandoning it. This is the reason for the expression in their account with the present tense, *nu'minu* (we believe), meaning that we persist in believing in what was sent down to us. They were also implying that they do not believe in anything other than it. This is because the expression "we believe in what was sent down to us," given in reply to those who said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down," while it is known that the speaker means belief in the Qur'an, suggests that they believe only in what was sent down to them, since they consider believing in anything else to require disbelief in it. So what is derived here from the combination of the two clauses, "Believe in what Allah has sent down" and its reply, "We believe in what was sent down to us," is this.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they disbelieve in what is beyond it﴾, the present tense was used as an imitation of their saying *nu'minu bima unzila 'alayna* (we believe in what was sent down to us), and as an explicit statement of what they had hinted at, and as a rebuttal to them. That is, they persist in believing in what was sent down to them, and they likewise disbelieve in what is beyond it. For they consider that believing in it necessitates disbelief in anything else. Furthermore, the present tense has an effect on the meaning of astonishment and strangeness.

Joining it with the circumstantial *waw* (*wāw al-hāl*, the conjunction introducing a circumstantial clause) carries an indication of rejecting them, and His saying ﴿while it is the truth, confirming what is with them﴾ adds to this. *Al-warā'* (beyond, behind) originally is the name of a place for the direction that is behind a thing, and it is strongly used as an adverb of place; its origin is not a verbal noun. *Al-warā'* was made a figurative usage or a metonymy for the absent, because a person does not see it. It is also used figuratively for what exceeds, because when a thing is in front of the traveler, he is heading toward it; when it becomes behind him, he has passed it and moved away from it. The poet al-Nabigha said:

*And for a man there is no seeking beyond God.*

It is also used in the sense of pursuit and following up. You say, *warā'iy fulān*, meaning he follows me up and seeks me. From this is God's saying, exalted is He, ﴿And there was behind them a king who seizes every boat by force﴾ [al-Kahf 18:79], and the saying of Labid:

*Is there not behind me, since my death has been delayed, a state like the staff's binding, around which the fingers are bent?*

From this, some scholars claimed that *al-warā'* is applied to both what is behind and what is in front, in the manner of applying a name to two opposites, and they cited Labid's verse and the Qur'anic verse *and there was before them a king* [al-Kahf 18:79]. But you know that there is no proof in this. For this reason al-Amidi, in *al-Muwazana*, denied that it is an antonym.

So what is meant by ﴿what is beyond it﴾ in the verse is what is other than it and exceeds it, that is, other than it. The intended object of this "other" here is specifically the Qur'an, by the indication of the context: the earlier words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down"﴾, and by its being followed by ﴿while it is the truth, confirming﴾.

[Page 609]

The clause "while it is the truth" is circumstantial (*hāliyya*). The *lām* in *al-haqq* (the truth) is for the category, and the intended meaning is to make the subject well known by this category, that is, while it is the one famous for truthfulness, which is acknowledged for it, in the manner of Hassan's saying:

*Indeed, the summit of glory belongs to the family of Hashim; the sons of the daughter of Makhzum, and your father is the slave.*

Hassan did not intend to restrict servitude to the father, but he meant that he is the one known for that and famous for it. So the *lām* here does not indicate restriction, because defining the predicate with *al-* does not consistently indicate restriction, according to what is in *Dala'il al-I'jaz* (Proofs of Inimitability) by al-Jurjani.

It has been said that it indicates restriction by the consideration of the qualifier, namely His saying *muṣaddiqan* (confirming). That is, He is the one restricted to being truth while also confirming, for other heavenly books are truth, but they do not confirm what is with them. Perhaps the author of this tafsir (*ṣāḥib hādhā al-tafsīr*) regards the Gospel as not addressing the confirmation of the Torah, but rather as limited to permitting some of the prohibited things, and that resembles not confirming.

So in the verse there is a rebuke to the Children of Israel for not responding to the Qur'an with the same treatment they gave to the Gospel, and an increase in their reproach.

His saying *muṣaddiqan* (confirming) is a confirming circumstantial clause (*ḥāl mu'akkida*) for His saying *wa huwa al-ḥaqq* (and it is the truth). This verse is a famous example for illustrating the confirming circumstantial clause. But in my view it is an establishing circumstantial clause (*ḥāl mu'assisa*), because His saying *muṣaddiqan limā ma'ahum* (confirming what is with them) indicates a description added to the content "it is the truth," since a book may be true without confirming another book or denying it. And in having a circumstantial clause follow a circumstantial clause there is an increase in bringing their conditions and states to mind.

His saying ﴿Say, "Why then do you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you are believers?"﴾ is separated from what precedes it, because it is an interjection (*i'tirāḍ*) in the course of mentioning their states. It is intended as a rebuttal to them in this excuse of theirs, to show that opposing the prophets is a habit of theirs, and that their saying ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us﴾ is a lie. For if it were true, their forefathers would not have killed the prophets who were of their own people and who called them to support the Torah and to act according to it. But they turn away from everything that does not agree with their desires. This is a censure of those present for what their forefathers did, because they regard them as being right in what they did of killing the prophets.

The use of the present tense in His saying *taqtulūna* (you kill) even though the killing has already passed is for the purpose of bringing to mind the terrible situation. The indication of this is His saying *min qablu* (before). This is like the poet al-Hutay'a using the past tense with a future meaning in his saying:

*Al-Hutay'a witnessed on the day he meets his Lord that al-Walid is more deserving of excuse.*

The indication is his saying *yawma yalqā rabbahu* (on the day he meets his Lord).

The prophets of Allah intended here are those we mentioned at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:61].

[Page 609]

﴿And certainly Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf [for worship] after him while you were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And [recall] when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you, [saying], "Take what We have given you with determination and listen." They said, "We hear and we disobey," and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, "Wretched is what your faith enjoins upon you, if you are [truly] believers."﴾

This is a continuation of His saying, ﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91]. Its purpose is to teach the shift in argument with them to what further refutes their claim: believing only in what was revealed to them. After He refuted them in that by His saying, ﴿Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], as we have explained, the discourse moves on to mention their conduct in facing the call of Moses, whom they claim they believe in exclusively, since they believed only in what came to them through him. Yet they opposed his call with disobedience, both in word and in deed. If they turned away from the Muhammadan call with the excuse that they believe only in what was revealed to them, then why did they confront the call of their prophets after Moses with killing? And why did they confront the call of Moses with what they did? This is the reason for mentioning these verses here. Although similar verses have preceded in earlier places, their mention here serves a different argument and a new aim. I have already explained that the Qur'an is not like a book of knowledge in which one refers back to what came before. Rather, it is a collection of admonitions, reminders, calamities, and disputations, revealed at many times and in various circumstances. Therefore its themes recur, as the context requires their mention at that moment, in connection with the occasion of revelation of those verses.

In al-Kashshaf [of al-Zamakhshari], it is said that the repetition of the account of raising the mount here serves the additional meaning attached to it beyond what is in the previous verse, in His saying, ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾, and this is a subtle point at the second level.

Al-Baydawi said that the repetition of the story is to alert that their way with Muhammad ﷺ is the way of their predecessors with Moses. This is a subtle point at the first level. This constitutes a charge against them for the deeds of their predecessors, on the basis that the branch follows its root, and the son is a copy of his father. It is a rhetorical argument.

The discussion of these verses is like the discussion of the preceding ones, and likewise the discussion of "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat). However, His saying "and listen" (wasma'u) is intended to mean compliance (imtithal). It is a kinaya (metonymy), as you say: "So-and-so does not hear my words," meaning he does not comply with my command. The command here is not about hearing in the sense of attentive listening to the Torah, because His saying, ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾, includes that as a beginning. The intended meaning of taking with determination is giving it full attention, and the first step of giving attention to speech is hearing it.

[Page 610]

Apparently His saying, ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾, does not include compliance. Therefore His saying "and listen" signifies a new meaning and is not an emphasis. You may, however, make it an emphasis of the implication of ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾, such that taking with determination includes the intention to comply. In that case, the point of emphasis is to signal that they are prone to neglect and failure, so that this was emphasized upon them before their non-compliance becomes evident in what follows. Thus in this verse there is further clarification of His saying in the first verse, "Then you turned away after that."

Know that among the signs of prophethood and the scientific miracles is the Qur'an's allusion to the expressions that Moses uttered to the Children of Israel, which were written in the Torah. The command to listen was repeated in the occasions when Moses addressed the chiefs of the Children of Israel with the words, "Hear, O Israel." This is one of the subtle reasons for choosing this word to indicate compliance over others that are clearer than it. This is like what we mentioned concerning the expression "covenant" (al-'ahd).

His saying, ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾, may mean that they said it at one time, answering His saying, "and listen." They answered him with two matters, because His saying "listen" contained two meanings: an explicit meaning and an implicit meaning (kinaya). They answered by complying with the explicit command, but as for the implicit command, they rejected it. This also includes the answer to His saying, ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾, because it contains what "and listen" contains. This interpretation is clearly remote, since it is not known of them that they confronted their prophet directly with the intention to disobey.

It has also been said that His saying "We hear" is an answer to His saying "Take what We have given you," meaning: we heard this speech. His saying "and we disobey" is an answer to His saying "and listen," because it means "comply," so that every statement has been answered. This is made remote by the fact that their use of the word "We hear" in their answer indicates that it is an answer to His saying "Listen," since the nature of an answer is that it includes the wording of the statement being answered. And His saying (so that every statement has been answered): you know that making "We hear and we disobey" an answer to "and listen" obviates the need to seek an answer to "Take," so there is brevity in it. Therefore the proper interpretation of the meaning of this verse is what al-Fakhr [al-Razi] transmitted from Abu Muslim, that their saying "we disobey" was by the tongue of the state (lisan al-hal), that is, "qalu" is used in its literal and figurative senses together, meaning: they said, "We hear and we disobey." It is as if their tongues were saying, "We disobey."

It is also possible that their saying "we disobey" occurred at a time later than the time of the revelation of the Torah, by their saying "we disobey" in response to some of the commands, like their saying to Moses when he said to them, "Enter the town," "We will never enter it" [al-Ma'idah: 24]. These two interpretations are closer than the first. In this is a clarification of His saying in the first verse, "Then you turned away after that."

[Page 611]

Al-ishrab (causing to drink) is making a thing drink, and it is used metaphorically for making a thing connected to and penetrating another thing. The point of resemblance is intense connection and permeation, because water is the most pervasive of substances in other things. Hence the physicians say: water is the vehicle of foods and medicines, the conveyance by which they travel to the regions of the body. Therefore they used "ishrab" for intense penetration, as a subordinate metaphor (isti'ara taba'iyya). Some poets said:

Love of 'Athma penetrated my heart, so its manifest and hidden parts flow together.
It penetrated where no drink had reached, nor grief, nor joy had reached.

From this is the saying: "The cloth was made to drink the dye." Al-Raghib said: It is their custom, when they want to mix love or hatred into something, to borrow for that the name of a drink. End of quotation.

The figurative meaning has become well known, so the use of "ishrab" in the sense of watering has fallen out of use. The mention of hearts is an indication that the causing of the calf to be drunk is, by estimation, an omitted genitive construction (mudaf mahdhuf), such as "the worship of the calf" or "the deification of the calf."

The reason their love for the calf was described as making them drink it is to indicate that their love for the calf reached the level of a matter over which they had no choice, as if someone else had made them drink it, like the saying "he was made enamoured with such-and-such" or "he was infatuated."

"The calf" is the object of "were made to drink," with an omitted genitive construction, which is well known in such expressions, where rulings are attributed to entities, as in His saying, ﴿Prohibited to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], meaning the eating of its flesh.

They were infatuated with it out of approval and belief that it was their god and that it benefited them, because when they saw it made of gold, they sanctified it out of excessive love for gold.

This admiration for it grew stronger through their excessive belief in its divinity. For this reason, He, Exalted, said "because of their disbelief," since belief increases the believer's immersion in love of what he believes.

Attributing the causing to drink to the pronoun of their selves, then clarifying it with His saying "into their hearts," is an intensification (mubalagha). It is like what occurs in badal al-ba'd (partial substitution) and al-ishtimal (inclusion), and what occurs in tamyiz al-nisba (specification of a relation). Close to this is His saying, ﴿They only eat fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa': 10]. It is not like what is here, because eating is purely limited to being confined to the belly, unlike causing to drink, which has no restriction to the hearts.

His saying, ﴿Say, "Wretched is what your faith enjoins upon you, if you are [truly] believers."﴾ is a tadhyil (concluding appendix) and an i'tiradh (parenthetical interjection) arising from their saying "We hear and we disobey." It is a summary of the refutation of their saying, ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], after that was refuted

[Page 612]

by the evidence of history, which is His saying, ﴿Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], and His saying, ﴿And certainly Moses came to you with clear proofs﴾, and His saying, ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey."﴾ For this reason He separated it from His saying, ﴿Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], because it functions, relative to the former, as an affirmation and clarification of its substance. The meaning is: Say to them, "If you are believers in what was revealed to you, as you claim, that is the Torah, then wretched is what this faith enjoined upon you, since you did what you did of atrocities, such as killing the prophets and associating others with Allah, while the Torah was among you. How then [can you claim this] when today you know of the Law only a little, especially if this faith, according to their claim, prevents them from believing in Muhammad ﷺ?" The entire conditional sentence is the content of the saying "Say," and the imperative here is used figuratively to mean causation (tasabbub).

He made this one of the things their faith enjoined upon them, although they did not claim it, because when they did it while claiming that they are firmly bound to holding to what was revealed to them, to the point that they do not deviate from it even slightly, and do not listen to any book that came after it, then there is no doubt that the tongue of their state proclaims that they do nothing except what is permitted to them by their book. This is the aspect of the implication (mula zama). As for the fact that these actions are blameworthy and abominable, that is known by necessity. Thus it follows that their faith in the Torah enjoins them to commit atrocities. This is the apparent meaning of the speech, and its intent is to disparage their claim to believe in the Torah and to refute it by a method that brings down their bird (of pride) and casts them into the abyss of submitting to the argument. Thus He presented their faith, whose absence is certain, in the guise of a possible supposition, in order to arrive from that at rebuking them and silencing them, like His saying, ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81]. For this reason, faith was attributed to their pronoun to show that the blameworthy faith is their faith, that is, the one that has been corrupted and disordered by distortion. This is because it is known that belief in the books and the messengers is only for the welfare of people and to bring them out of darkness into light. Therefore, those who commit these abominations are certainly not part of believing in the Book that contains guidance and light, in any respect. Thus their being believers is refuted, and that is the aim.

As for His saying, "﴿Wretched is what your faith enjoins upon you﴾", it is the answer to the condition, placed before it, or, say, it is the evidence of the answer. For this reason, in this condition, "in" (in) is used, whose nature is that its condition is doubtful in its occurrence, and it moves from doubt about its occurrence to its being supposed, as a hypothetical state is supposed. This is what is meant here, because the speaker knows that the condition does not hold, and because the addressees believe that the condition holds. So the apparent state of the speaker requires that the conditional clause containing their being believers should not be introduced except as negated, and the apparent state of the addressee requires that it should not be introduced except with "idha" (when). But the speaker, while knowing that the condition does not hold, supposes it, as an impossibility is supposed, in order to bring them down from their pride.

The use of "in" indicates this

[Page 613]

supposition, so that they fall into doubt about their own state and move from doubt to certainty that they are not believers at the time the answer arrives, which is "﴿Wretched is what your faith enjoins upon you﴾". To this the author of al-Kashshaf pointed, as al-Taftazani reported, and this does not contradict that the purpose is rebuke, because these are successive meanings, some of which lead to others. From supposition arises doubt, and from doubt rebuke becomes evident.

There is no sense in making "﴿if you are believers﴾" the beginning of a speech with an omitted answer, whose estimate would be (so your faith does not enjoin you to kill the prophets and worship the calf…), etc., because that severs the bonds of the discourse and is an unnecessary estimation, while His saying, ﴿Say, "Wretched is what your faith enjoins upon you"﴾, etc., requires further consideration, and its parallels in the verses of the Qur'an are numerous.

Moreover, the meaning of that estimation does not fit the preceding statement that affirmed that their faith enjoined them to these blameworthy acts. How, then, could it deny after this that their faith enjoins them?

"Bi'sama" (an evil thing is that) here is similar to the "bi'sama" mentioned earlier in His words ﴿Evil is that for which they have sold themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90], except that this one is not introduced with a specific noun for the blame, because of the indication in His words ﴿And the calf was made to sink into their hearts because of their disbelief﴾. The meaning is: "Evil is what your faith commands you to do: the worship of the calf."
