Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 94–95:

﴿Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is specifically for you, to the exclusion of other people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.﴾ ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forth. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾

This is a refutation of a deep-rooted claim in their souls, which was implied by their saying, ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], by which they meant to excuse their turning away from the call of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the ground that they are steadfast in holding to the Torah and do not transgress it, and that by this they deserve Allah's love, and the Last Abode is theirs. When their claim of believing in what was revealed to them was refuted, by holding them to the lie in their claim on the evidence of what their forebears, namely their ancestors, did of abominations against their prophets and of departing from the commands of the Torah by associating others with Allah through the worship of the calf, he followed that by refuting what they held in their beliefs, namely that they are the sole people who are the recipients of Allah's mercy so long as they hold to the Torah, and that whoever opposes it has no share in the Hereafter. In refuting this belief, he employed the method of referring to what they had based their belief upon, namely their confidence in a good outcome, or to their doubt about that. When their doubt about this is established for them, they know that their belief in the Torah is not firmly grounded in its truth, and that is the most damaging thing to their resolve and the most disheartening to them, because anticipating a share in the Hereafter is the most important thing that a religiously devout believer is concerned with, for that is the everlasting life and the enduring bliss.

It has been said that this verse is a response to another claim issued by the Jews, which indicates that they make Paradise exclusively theirs, like their saying ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and their saying ﴿None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. To this view al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi inclined. In that case, the mention of the response to them is clear merely for the sake of relevance, in refuting another false belief of theirs, not specifically in the purpose for which the preceding verses were directed, on the basis that verses do not necessarily have to be fully relevant to one another. We do not support that. Accordingly, on this view, this verse was revealed here together with its predecessors to respond to their scattered statements reported in other verses. It has been joined with the verses returning to the refutation of their claim of believing in what was revealed to them only for the sake of relevance, by gathering the refutation of all their claims. But in what we have mentioned there is sufficiency. In any case, this verse challenges the Jews just as the Qur'an challenged the idolaters of the Arabs by His saying ﴿So bring a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23].

This sentence has been separated from what precedes it because the context differs: this verse is a laying down of a proof against them, whereas the preceding verses are a denunciation of their conditions. Although there is argumentation in each of these, the shift from one style to another made separation (fasl) the better choice rather than conjunction (atf), especially with the opening of the argument with "Say" (qul).

The speech with "la-kum" (for you) indicates that what is meant by "the Last Abode" is its bliss. "La-kum" is the predicate of "kanat" and has been placed first to indicate restriction (hasr), in accordance with their belief, as in its placement in the verse of al-Kumayt praising Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik when he pardoned him, from a qasidah:

To you are the two mosques of Allah that are visited, and the pebbles; to you is its share, between the rich and the poor.

"Indda Allah" (with Allah) is an adverbial complement attached to "kanat", and the sense of "'indiyyah" is one of honour and storing up: that is, it is stored up for you with Allah. In this there is an indication that by "the Last Abode" is meant Paradise. "Khalisah" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the subject of "kanat", and there is no basis for the hesitation of some grammarians regarding the coming of a hal from the subject of kana. The meaning of "khalisah" is pure, free from sharing with others, so it reverts in meaning to: exclusively for you.

As for His saying ﴿min duni al-nas﴾ (to the exclusion of other people): "dun" originally is an adverb of place denoting the nearer place in relation to another place, not inflected, and it is used metaphorically for separation, so it indicates differing attributes or conditions. You say, "This is yours, to the exclusion of Zayd," meaning Zayd has no right to it. Thus His saying "min duni al-nas" is an emphasis of the meaning of exclusivity derived from the fronting of the predicate, and from His saying "khalisah," to rule out the possibility that the intended meaning of purity is being free from one who shares in their ranks while still having a share of bliss. What is meant by "al-nas" (the people) is all people, so the lam in it is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), because they said ﴿None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. His saying ﴿fa-tamannaw al-mawt﴾ (then wish for death) is the answer to the condition. The connection between the condition, which is that the Last Abode is theirs, and its consequence, which is wishing for death, is that no one reaches the Last Abode except through the spirit when it departs the body, and the departure of the spirit from the body is death. So when death is the cause of their arrival at the good things, it would be fitting for them to wish for its arrival, as was the case with the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), as 'Umayr ibn al-Humam (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

Rushing towards Allah without provision, except piety and the deed for the return.

Ja'far ibn Abi Talib recited a rajaz verse on the day of the battle of Mu'tah when he stormed the idolaters, saying:

How wonderful is Paradise and its nearness, pure and cool is its drink.

'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah said when he set out for the battle of Mu'tah, and the Muslims supplicated for him and for those with him that Allah return them safe:

But I ask the Most Merciful for forgiveness, and a blow that spills forth the foam,
or a thrust from the hand of one who is a Harranite, a deadly one, with a spear that pierces the entrails and the liver,
so that when they pass by my grave they will say: "May Allah guide you, O one who fought and was rightly guided."

The sentence ﴿wa-lan yatamannawhu abadan﴾ (But they will never wish for it, ever) up to its end is parenthetical between the sentence ﴿Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is specifically for you﴾ and the sentence ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97]. The speech is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, as information for them so that they might increase in certainty, and so that a challenge to the Jews arises from it, since they hear it and would wish to contradict it, lest it stand as a proof for the truthfulness of the one who reports it, and then it would be necessary for them that the Last Abode is not theirs.

His saying ﴿bi-ma qaddamat aydihim﴾ (because of what their hands have sent forth) points to the fact that they have come to hold a mixed and contradictory belief, like the beliefs of the deluded ignorant. They believe that the Last Abode is theirs, as indicated by their saying, "We believe in what was revealed to us" [al-Baqarah: 91], and their saying, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved" [al-Ma'idah: 18]. Then they acknowledge that they have dared against Allah and acquired evil deeds, as inscribed against them in the Torah and in the books of their prophets. So they make excuses that the Fire will touch them for a number of days, and for this reason they fear death, fleeing from punishment.

What is meant by ﴿bi-ma qaddamat aydihim﴾ is the sins they committed, whether done by the hand or by other means, by the context. It has been said that "hands" is used here metaphorically for the self, as in His saying ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195], and as "eye" is used for the self in the context of emphasis, because the hand is the most important instrument of action. It has also been said that "hands" is meant literally, because most of people's crimes are committed by them, and it is a metonymy for all deeds. This was stated by al-Wahidi. Perhaps the choice of expressing it by hands rather than anything else is because the most comprehensive and most grievous of their sins were committed by the hand: the most comprehensive is the distortion of the Torah, and the most grievous is the killing of the prophets, for by that they deprived people of a great guidance.

The attribution of the "sending forth" to the hands is literal according to the first interpretation, and is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli) according to the second. His saying ﴿wa-llahu 'alimun bi-l-zalimin﴾ (And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers) is a statement used in the sense of threat, because when the All-Powerful knows of the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer, He does not delay in punishing him. This is like the saying of Zuhayr:

Whatever Allah conceals, He will know.

This verse has been counted among the proofs of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), because it negated the occurrence of wishing for death while they were most eager to show the falsity of this verse. It cannot be said that perhaps they wished for death in their hearts, because if such wishing had occurred in their hearts, they would have spoken it with their tongues, intending to announce the refutation of this stigma. Their silence therefore indicates that it did not occur, even though wishing (tamanni) has its place in the heart, since it is an inward seeking, being the love of the attainment of a thing. It was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿except wishes (amani)﴾ that "umniyyah" is what is imagined in the heart. This is clearly the case with regard to the Jews addressed at the time of revelation, for it is not transmitted from any of them that he wished for death, as the verse reports. It is also among the greatest proofs, in the view of those Jews, of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), for each of them was certain that he would not wish for death, and was certain that the rest of his people would not wish for it either, because if any of them had wished for it, he would have announced it, knowing the eagerness of each of them to refute the ruling of this verse.

By this there is derived a general miracle across the succession of generations, just as it indicated the inability of the Arabs to produce its equal, and all researchers know that the Qur'an is miraculous and that it is from Allah.

Moreover, the apparent meaning is that the verse includes the Jews who come after the time of revelation, since it is not known that any Jew has wished for death up to today. This is an elevation in the proofs of prophethood. The sentence ﴿wa-llahu 'alimun bi-l-zalimin﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of nominative case in "yatamannawhu," meaning: Allah knows what is in their souls, so He informed His Messenger that he should challenge them. This is an addition to recording their abstention from wishing for death. What is meant by "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers) is the Jews, so this is the placement of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, to describe them with wrongdoing.

[Page 617]

﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life, even more than those who associate others with God. One of them wishes he could live a thousand years, yet being granted long life would not remove him from the punishment. And God is Seeing of what they do.﴾ It is conjoined (ʿaṭf, conjunction) to His saying, ﴿and they will never wish for it [death], ever﴾. This indicates that their not wishing for death is not in the usual manner found among humans, who dislike death as long as a person is in good health. Rather, they have gone beyond that to being more eager for life than all other humans, including the polytheists, who do not hope for resurrection, rising again, or bliss. For them, bliss is the bliss of this world. [The verse also indicates] that they wish to be granted the utmost extent of lengthy life, despite the wretched condition that accompanies the possessor of such a lifespan and the baseness of such living.

Because the emphasis (taʾkīd) found in these conjoined sentences reinforces the content of the sentence to which they are conjoined, they were placed after it. And because of the added intensity in describing them as excessively eager, it was conjoined to it and not separated from it. Had it been merely for emphasis, it would have been separated, as emphasis is normally separated from what it emphasizes.

His saying, ﴿and you will surely find them﴾, is from the mental finding (wijdān qalbī), which takes two objects. The word "people" (al-nās), in its apparent sense, refers to all people, that is, all of humankind. Thus they are the most eager of them for life, since eagerness for life is an innate disposition in people. However, people differ in it in strength, manner and causes. Abu al-Tayyib said:

*I see that all of us love life through our striving,
eager for it, enamored by it,*

*the coward's love of self brings him to it,
and the love of the brave for self brings him to war.*

He used "life" (ḥayāh) in indefinite form intentionally, to indicate variety, meaning whatever that life may be. The Jews of Tunis say something whose meaning is: "Life, and that is enough."

His saying, ﴿and of those who associated [others with God]﴾, is conjoined to "people," because the noun in a genitive construction with the elative form (afʿal al-tafḍīl, comparative/superlative form) must necessarily be understood with the partitive sense (min al-tafḍīliyyah, the "of" of comparison). When it is conjoined, it is permissible to make it explicit, and it becomes obligatory to make it explicit if the preferred item is not of the same kind as the item it is preferred over, because the genitive construction is then impossible, as here. The Jews are among the people, but they are not among those who associated [others with God].

According to Sibawayh, the genitive construction is on the presumption of the preposition lām (meaning "for"). Thus his saying, ﴿and of those who associated [others with God]﴾, according to him, is conjoined by considering the meaning, or by presuming an omitted conjoined term whose presumed form is "most eager." It is governed by "those who associated [others with God]." Al-Zamakhsharī in al-Kashshāf inclined to this view.

[Page 618]

His saying, ﴿one of them wishes﴾, is an explanation of their eagerness for life and a confirmation of the generality of the species in the indefinite "life," to remove the suspicion that their eagerness does not reach the degree of longing for life lasting a thousand years. For even if that were impossible, were it to be granted to them, it would be a life of humiliation and the most abject living. One might think that their love of life does not extend to wishing for it. Al-Harīrī said:

*Death is better for the youth
than a life of living like a beast.*

So this sentence was brought to affirm that this eagerness includes even this despicable life. Because this sentence explains the content of the sentence before it, it was separated from it. The word "wadd" means love, even if for the sake of wishing. It is a quotation of the wording with which they wished, and the use of the third-person masculine singular form is in consideration of the meaning. It is also permissible for "law" (lau) to be a verbal particle (maṣdariyyah, which turns the following verb into a verbal noun), and the implied meaning would be: "one of them loves the granting of a thousand years."

His saying, ﴿would be given a life of a thousand years﴾, is an explanation of "wadd" (love). That is, the love whose explanation is "if he were given a life of a thousand years." The original function of "law" is that it is a conditional particle for the past or the future. The original position with the verb "wadd" and similar verbs is that it introduces a clause explaining the clause of "wadd," by way of concision. The implied meaning in such a case is: "one of them loves that he would be given a thousand years, [and this] would not make him weary or averse." Since the meaning of the conditional clause introduced by "law" and the meaning of the object of "wadd" are the same, they dispensed with the object of the verb by using the conditional verb, and they omitted the object. The conditional particle together with its verb took the place of the object. Therefore the particle with the conditional clause became equivalent to the object and acquired the nominal force in meaning. The conditional verb was then interpreted as a verbal noun derived from it. For this reason the particle "law" came to function like the verbal particle "an," because the verb after it is interpreted as a verbal noun. The conditional clause became used in the sense of a verbal noun, a usage that became dominant with "law" when it follows the verb "wadd." Things similar to it in meaning, such as verbs indicating love and desire, may also be included.

This is the detailed account of the usage of "law" in such constructions according to the view of the verifying grammarians. Because this usage is common and this omission is widespread, some grammarians held that "law" is used as a verbal particle, and they assigned it, among its positions, the position after "wadd" and similar verbs. This is the view of al-Farrāʾ, Abu ʿAlī al-Fārisī, al-Tibrīzī, al-ʿUkbarī and Ibn Mālik. They say there is no omission, and they treat "law" as a particle merely for forming a verbal noun, like "an," with the verb becoming a verbal noun. The implied meaning is: "one of them loves the granting [of long life]." This view is weaker in verification and easier in assumption.

His saying, ﴿and it would not remove him from the punishment﴾, may have the pronoun referring to "one of them," or it may be an ambiguous pronoun explained by the verbal noun after it, in the manner of Zuhayr's saying:

[Page 619]

*War is only what you know and have tasted,
and it is not a story told in confused speech.*

He did not take the pronoun as a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), because negation enters upon it, as in the verse cited. Nevertheless it is close to the pronoun of the matter, because its purpose is to emphasize the predicate, and because what follows it has the form of a sentence. It was also said that it refers to the granting of long life implied by ﴿would be given a life of a thousand years﴾, and that his saying, ﴿that he be granted long life﴾, is an apposition to it. This is far-fetched. "Muzaḥzih" means one who removes far away.

His saying, ﴿and God is Seeing of what they do﴾: "Seeing" (baṣīr) here means "Knowing," as in the saying of ʿAlqama al-Faḥl:

*So if you ask me about women, I am
knowing of women's ailments, a physician.*

This is a statement used for threat and reproach, because the Powerful, when He knows what the one who disobeys Him commits, and informs him that He knows it, knows that punishment will certainly descend upon him. Zuhayr's saying is of this kind:

*Do not conceal from God what is in your souls,
so that it may not be hidden; whatever you conceal, God knows it.*

*It is delayed, placed in a book and stored
for the Day of Reckoning, or hastened and avenged.*

He made his saying "knows" mean knowledge returning to threat, as evidenced by his replacing it with "is delayed," the verse. Close to this is al-Nābigha's saying about al-Nuʿmān:

*I know that you watch over me with a discerning eye,
and send guards and watchers over me.*

[Page 617]

﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life, even more than those who associate others with God. One of them wishes he could live a thousand years, yet being granted long life would not remove him from the punishment. And God is Seeing of what they do.﴾ It is conjoined (ʿaṭf, conjunction) to His saying, ﴿and they will never wish for it [death], ever﴾. This indicates that their not wishing for death is not in the usual manner found among humans, who dislike death as long as a person is in good health. Rather, they have gone beyond that to being more eager for life than all other humans, including the polytheists, who do not hope for resurrection, rising again, or bliss. For them, bliss is the bliss of this world. [The verse also indicates] that they wish to be granted the utmost extent of lengthy life, despite the wretched condition that accompanies the possessor of such a lifespan and the baseness of such living.

Because the emphasis (taʾkīd) found in these conjoined sentences reinforces the content of the sentence to which they are conjoined, they were placed after it. And because of the added intensity in describing them as excessively eager, it was conjoined to it and not separated from it. Had it been merely for emphasis, it would have been separated, as emphasis is normally separated from what it emphasizes.

His saying, ﴿and you will surely find them﴾, is from the mental finding (wijdān qalbī), which takes two objects. The word "people" (al-nās), in its apparent sense, refers to all people, that is, all of humankind. Thus they are the most eager of them for life, since eagerness for life is an innate disposition in people. However, people differ in it in strength, manner and causes. Abu al-Tayyib said:

*I see that all of us love life through our striving,
eager for it, enamored by it,*

*the coward's love of self brings him to it,
and the love of the brave for self brings him to war.*

He used "life" (ḥayāh) in indefinite form intentionally, to indicate variety, meaning whatever that life may be. The Jews of Tunis say something whose meaning is: "Life, and that is enough."

His saying, ﴿and of those who associated [others with God]﴾, is conjoined to "people," because the noun in a genitive construction with the elative form (afʿal al-tafḍīl, comparative/superlative form) must necessarily be understood with the partitive sense (min al-tafḍīliyyah, the "of" of comparison). When it is conjoined, it is permissible to make it explicit, and it becomes obligatory to make it explicit if the preferred item is not of the same kind as the item it is preferred over, because the genitive construction is then impossible, as here. The Jews are among the people, but they are not among those who associated [others with God].

According to Sibawayh, the genitive construction is on the presumption of the preposition lām (meaning "for"). Thus his saying, ﴿and of those who associated [others with God]﴾, according to him, is conjoined by considering the meaning, or by presuming an omitted conjoined term whose presumed form is "most eager." It is governed by "those who associated [others with God]." Al-Zamakhsharī in al-Kashshāf inclined to this view.

[Page 618]

His saying, ﴿one of them wishes﴾, is an explanation of their eagerness for life and a confirmation of the generality of the species in the indefinite "life," to remove the suspicion that their eagerness does not reach the degree of longing for life lasting a thousand years. For even if that were impossible, were it to be granted to them, it would be a life of humiliation and the most abject living. One might think that their love of life does not extend to wishing for it. Al-Harīrī said:

*Death is better for the youth
than a life of living like a beast.*

So this sentence was brought to affirm that this eagerness includes even this despicable life. Because this sentence explains the content of the sentence before it, it was separated from it. The word "wadd" means love, even if for the sake of wishing. It is a quotation of the wording with which they wished, and the use of the third-person masculine singular form is in consideration of the meaning. It is also permissible for "law" (lau) to be a verbal particle (maṣdariyyah, which turns the following verb into a verbal noun), and the implied meaning would be: "one of them loves the granting of a thousand years."

His saying, ﴿would be given a life of a thousand years﴾, is an explanation of "wadd" (love). That is, the love whose explanation is "if he were given a life of a thousand years." The original function of "law" is that it is a conditional particle for the past or the future. The original position with the verb "wadd" and similar verbs is that it introduces a clause explaining the clause of "wadd," by way of concision. The implied meaning in such a case is: "one of them loves that he would be given a thousand years, [and this] would not make him weary or averse." Since the meaning of the conditional clause introduced by "law" and the meaning of the object of "wadd" are the same, they dispensed with the object of the verb by using the conditional verb, and they omitted the object. The conditional particle together with its verb took the place of the object. Therefore the particle with the conditional clause became equivalent to the object and acquired the nominal force in meaning. The conditional verb was then interpreted as a verbal noun derived from it. For this reason the particle "law" came to function like the verbal particle "an," because the verb after it is interpreted as a verbal noun. The conditional clause became used in the sense of a verbal noun, a usage that became dominant with "law" when it follows the verb "wadd." Things similar to it in meaning, such as verbs indicating love and desire, may also be included.

This is the detailed account of the usage of "law" in such constructions according to the view of the verifying grammarians. Because this usage is common and this omission is widespread, some grammarians held that "law" is used as a verbal particle, and they assigned it, among its positions, the position after "wadd" and similar verbs. This is the view of al-Farrāʾ, Abu ʿAlī al-Fārisī, al-Tibrīzī, al-ʿUkbarī and Ibn Mālik. They say there is no omission, and they treat "law" as a particle merely for forming a verbal noun, like "an," with the verb becoming a verbal noun. The implied meaning is: "one of them loves the granting [of long life]." This view is weaker in verification and easier in assumption.

His saying, ﴿and it would not remove him from the punishment﴾, may have the pronoun referring to "one of them," or it may be an ambiguous pronoun explained by the verbal noun after it, in the manner of Zuhayr's saying:

[Page 619]

*War is only what you know and have tasted,
and it is not a story told in confused speech.*

He did not take the pronoun as a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), because negation enters upon it, as in the verse cited. Nevertheless it is close to the pronoun of the matter, because its purpose is to emphasize the predicate, and because what follows it has the form of a sentence. It was also said that it refers to the granting of long life implied by ﴿would be given a life of a thousand years﴾, and that his saying, ﴿that he be granted long life﴾, is an apposition to it. This is far-fetched. "Muzaḥzih" means one who removes far away.

His saying, ﴿and God is Seeing of what they do﴾: "Seeing" (baṣīr) here means "Knowing," as in the saying of ʿAlqama al-Faḥl:

*So if you ask me about women, I am
knowing of women's ailments, a physician.*

This is a statement used for threat and reproach, because the Powerful, when He knows what the one who disobeys Him commits, and informs him that He knows it, knows that punishment will certainly descend upon him. Zuhayr's saying is of this kind:

*Do not conceal from God what is in your souls,
so that it may not be hidden; whatever you conceal, God knows it.*

*It is delayed, placed in a book and stored
for the Day of Reckoning, or hastened and avenged.*

He made his saying "knows" mean knowledge returning to threat, as evidenced by his replacing it with "is delayed," the verse. Close to this is al-Nābigha's saying about al-Nuʿmān:

*I know that you watch over me with a discerning eye,
and send guards and watchers over me.*

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 98–99 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel – for he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of God, confirming what came before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97] ﴿Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels and His messengers, and Gabriel and Michael – then indeed God is an enemy to the disbelievers.﴾ The position of this sentence is the position of the sentences before it, from His saying ﴿Say: Why then do you kill the prophets of God?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], and His saying "Say: Wretched is what your faith enjoins upon you," and His saying "﴿Say: If the Last Abode with God is yours alone...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 94]". All of them are a response to what their saying "We believe in what was revealed to us" included, because they used it to show an excuse for turning away from the Muhammadan call, and it is a false excuse, by which they concealed the real cause, which is envy at the Qur'an being sent down to a man from among other than themselves. So these disputations, introduced by "Say", came to nullify their excuse and expose their intention.

He first nullified what their saying "﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾" [al-Baqarah: 91] included, namely that they accept only what was revealed to their own messengers, by showing that they had also met their messengers with denial, harm and disobedience. This is in His saying "﴿Say: Why then do you kill...﴾" and His saying "Say: Wretched is what..." etc.
Page 620
He secondly nullified what it included, that they are fiercely attached to what was revealed to them, eager to act upon it, and keen to keep far from anything that distances them from it, for the sake of salvation in the Hereafter, by His saying "﴿Say: If the Last Abode with God is yours alone...﴾" [al-Baqarah: 94]. Thirdly, he nullified that this excuse be what diverts them from faith, while establishing that what diverts them is envy, by His saying here "﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel...﴾" [al-Baqarah: 97], etc. This connection is confirmed by the pronoun in His saying "nazzalahu" referring to what God sent down in the verse answered by these nullifications. For this reason this sentence is disconnected (fasl), as its sisters were, and because it has no relation to the sentences near it, so it is not conjoined to them; therefore it came as a new sentence (mustan'afah).

"Al-'aduww" means the one who hates, and it is derived from "ʿadā ʿalayhi yaʿdū", meaning "to leap upon", because the one who hates leaps upon the one he hates to take vengeance on him; its pattern is faʿūl. "Jibril" is a Hebrew name for the angel sent by God with revelation to His messengers, and it is a compound of two words. It has several dialects, the most famous of which is "Jibrīl" on the pattern of "qiṭmīr", which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and the majority (al-Jumhur) read with it. ("Jabrīl" with a fatha on the jīm and a kasra on the rāʾ occurs in the reading of Ibn Kathīr; this is the pattern faʿlīl, for which no example is found in the speech of the Arabs, as said by al-Farrāʾ and al-Naḥḥās.) "Jabraʾīl" with a fatha on the jīm also, and a fatha on the rāʾ, with a kasrated hamza between the rāʾ and the yāʾ, is the dialect of Tamim, Qays and some people of Najd, and Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read with it. "Jabraʾil" with a fatha on the jīm and the rāʾ, with a kasrated hamza between it and the lām, is what Abū Bakr recited from ʿĀṣim, and there are other dialects recited in the irregular readings (al-shawādhdh).

It is a compound name of two words: the word "Jabr" and the word "Īl". As for "Jabr", its meaning according to the majority, transmitted from Hebrew, is "servant" (ʿabd); but the verified view is that in Hebrew it means "strength" (al-quwwa). As for "Īl", according to the majority it is one of the names of God the Exalted.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī went against the majority view, claiming that "Jabr" is the name of God the Exalted and "Īl" is the servant; this contradicts what is in the Hebrew language according to those who know it. Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī followed the opinion of Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī at the beginning of his epistle addressed to ʿAlī ibn Manṣūr al-Ḥalabī, known as Ibn al-Qāriḥ, which is known as "Risālat al-Ghufrān", where he said: "The Jabr to whom Gabriel is ascribed is known, and in all goodness there is a path, that in my dwelling there is a..." etc. That is, God, to whom Gabriel is ascribed by his name, that is by his name Jabr, is known; he intends by this an oath. This is an obscure claim from him and an alert to his lack of familiarity with the language.

The enmity of the Jews toward Gabriel arose from the time of his bringing the Qur'an down upon Muhammad (ﷺ)
Page 621
It was also said that it is because he descends upon the nations that denied their messengers with punishment and threat; al-Qurtubi transmitted this from a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi. His saying "﴿Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾" [al-Baqarah: 97] is a general condition intended as particular, namely the Jews. He intended the inclusiveness so that they would know that God does not care about them, nor about others who oppose Gabriel, if he has any other enemy.

The Jews were known in Medina as enemies of Gabriel. In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, he said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam heard of the arrival of the Messenger of God while he was in his land gathering dates. He came to the Prophet and said: 'I will ask you about three things which none knows except a prophet: What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food of the people of Paradise? And why does the child resemble its father or its mother?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Gabriel has just informed me of them.' He said: 'That is the enemy of the Jews among the angels; for they hate him, because he brings what contains severity and the command to fight'," and the hadith continues. In the Book of Daniel among their books, in chapters eight and nine, they mention that Gabriel interpreted for Daniel a vision he saw and warned him of the destruction of Jerusalem. The commentators mention other reasons for their hatred of Gabriel. Among the wonders of the incoherence of their belief is that they affirm that he is an angel sent by God and yet hate him; this is among the lowest depths of degradation in intellect and creed. Without doubt, confusion of belief is among the greatest signs of a people's decline, because it indicates that their opinions converge upon error and illusions.

His saying "﴿So indeed he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of God﴾" [al-Baqarah: 97]: the pronoun in the accusative governed by "nazzalahu" refers to the Qur'an, either because it was mentioned in His saying "﴿And when it is said to them: believe in what God has sent down﴾" [al-Baqarah: 91], or because the verb suits nothing but it here, in the manner of "﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾" [Sad: 32] and "﴿Why, when it reaches the throat﴾" [al-Waqiʿah: 83]. This sentence stands in place of the answer of the condition.

It is evident that the intended meaning is that there is no cause for their enmity toward him, because he is an intermediary whom God permitted to descend with the Qur'an; so in hating him they are in fact hating God the Exalted. The estimate is: "Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, let him not be his enemy, and let him be an enemy to God the Exalted." This view is better than what they mentioned, more fitting to His saying "by the permission of God," and clearer in connection with His saying after it: "﴿Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels﴾," as you will know. It is also possible that the estimate is: "for indeed He has sent it down to you, whether they love it or oppose it," so it is in the sense of provoking rage, like "﴿Say: Die in your rage﴾" [Al ʿImran: 119], as in the words of al-Rabiʿ ibn Ziyad:

Whoever is delighted by the killing of Malik, let him come to our courtyard at the time of daybreak;
he will find the women unveiled, wailing for him at night before the dawn breaks.

That is: he should not rejoice at his killing, for we have killed his slayer before the morning came, since his slayer is one of the allies of him who was delighted by his killing. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: "for indeed it descended with him from God, confirming their book, and in it is guidance and good tidings," and this condition calls for love of the one who brought it; so from their folly and obstinacy is their enmity toward the one who brought it. The estimate is then: "he has cast off the noose of reason or the ornament of fairness." The use of the emphatic particle in "fa-innahu nazzalahu" is because they deny that.

"Al-qalb" here means the self (nafs) and that by which memory and understanding occur; the Arabs apply "qalb" to this immaterial matter, as in "﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾" [Qaf: 37], just as they also apply it to the inner conical organ, as said:

As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry...

"Muṣaddiqan" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in the accusative of "anzalahu", i.e., the Qur'an, which is the cause of the Jews' enmity toward Gabriel; that is, He sent it down accompanied by a state that does not necessitate their enmity toward it, for He sent it down confirming what is before it of the books, namely the Torah and the Gospel. "Muṣaddiq" is one who reports the truthfulness of someone. The particle of emphasis (lam al-taqwiyah) was introduced to the object of "muṣaddiqan" to indicate the strengthening of that confirmation; that is, it is a firm, established confirmation that is not tainted by anything of denial or correction, for the Qur'an praised the Torah and the Gospel and described each as guidance and light, as in Surah al-Ma'idah.

The confirmation of earlier messengers is among the first proofs of the truthfulness of the one who confirms, because impostors who claim prophethood come with denial of those before them, since what they bring of guidance opposes the misguidance of the deceivers, so they cannot afford to confirm them. For this reason the earlier prophets warned against the lying pretenders, as is found in several places of the Torah and the Gospels.

The intended meaning of "what is before it" (mā bayna yadayhi) is what preceded it, and it is a metaphor (kināyah) for precedence, because the precedent comes before the preceded. Since it is a metaphor for precedence, it does not contradict the long duration between the earlier books and the Qur'an, and because the practice of them continued among their nations until the coming of the Qur'an; so their precedence was made continuous up to the time of the coming of the Qur'an, and thus their precedence was connected.

"Hudan" is a description of the Qur'an by the verbal noun, for the purpose of emphasizing the attainment of guidance through it. "Bushra" is the report of the occurrence of a joyful matter, or of the expectation of its occurrence. So the Qur'an gave good tidings to the believers that they are upon guidance, perfection and the pleasure of God the Exalted, and gave them good tidings that God will grant them the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter.

Thus there have been obtained five attributes of the Qur'an: that it was sent down from God by the permission of God; that it was sent down upon the heart of the Messenger; that it confirms the books that preceded it; that it is a guide to the most eloquent guidance; and that it is good tidings for the believers. Praise of the Qur'an for the nobility of its origin, the nobility of its abode, the nobility of its people, the overflowing of good upon its virtuous followers: immediate good, and a promise to them of the good outcome. These are the qualities of the noble man: his lineage, his house, and his people; generous in giving, and promising what he gives. These are qualities that the verse of Ziyad al-A'jam considered:

Indeed generosity, manliness and liberality are in a dome raised over the son of al-Ḥashraj.

His saying "﴿Whoever is an enemy to God﴾" etc. Its excellent position has become clear from what you have known of the sense of "So indeed He has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of God": that is, since their enmity toward Gabriel was on account of their enmity toward the Messenger, and it ultimately returned to obliging them to be enemies to God who sent him, because the cause of the enmity is his bringing the message, it became possible to record against them that they are enemies of God, since He is the sender; enemies of His messengers, since they opposed the Messenger; and enemies of the angels, on that account. Thus their enmity toward Gabriel became like the middle term in a syllogism, which is not itself looked at; rather one looks to the two premises, the minor and the major. Their enmity toward God is like the major premise, since it is the cause in meaning upon reflection; and their enmity toward the Messenger is like the minor premise, since it is the particular cause establishing it. So it is not objected that there is no reason to mention enmity toward God here, to be answered by saying that enmity toward the angels and messengers is enmity toward God, in the manner of "﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾" [al-Nisa: 80], for that is far-fetched.

He has attributed to them enmity toward the angels and messengers, although they only opposed Gabriel and Muhammad; because when they opposed the two of them, they were opposing Gabriel on account of his performance of what is特 of his angelic kind, namely conveying God's commanding order, for that is their distinguishing feature. He said: "﴿And they act by His command﴾" [al-Anbiya: 27]. Their enmity toward him for this reason led back to enmity toward the whole kind of angels, since this path is one in which Gabriel is not unique. Likewise, when they opposed Muhammad on account of his coming with the message by a particular cause related to his own person, their enmity toward him led back to enmity toward the attribute that constitutes the kind of messenger. So whoever opposes one of them is bound to oppose all of them; otherwise his action is arbitrary, and he has no excuse in it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 98–99 (part 2 of 2):

Gabriel (Jibril) is singled out for mention here to heighten attention to the punishment of his enemies, and so that Michael (Mika'il) may be mentioned along with him. Perhaps they opposed both of them together. Or it may be because they claimed that Gabriel is the messenger of punishment and destruction, and that Michael is the messenger of fertility and peace, and they said: "We love Michael." When the aim is to warn them that their enmity toward the angels draws God's enmity upon them, Gabriel's name is repeated to give him prominence, and Michael is joined to him by conjunction, lest they imagine that their love for Michael earns the believers his enmity.

For Michael there are several forms (lughat). The first is Mikha'il (مِيكائِيلُ), with a hamza after the alif and a yā' after the hamza, and the majority of readers (al-Jumhur) recited it this way.

The second is (مِيكائِلُ), with a hamza after the alif and without a yā' after the hamza, and Nafi' recited it this way.

The third is (مِيكالُ), without hamza and without yā', and Abu 'Amr and Hafs recited it this way. It is the dialect (lughat) of the people of the Hijaz.

His saying, ﴿indeed God is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾, is the answer to the conditional clause. "Enemy" (al-'Aduww) is used in its figurative sense, namely what this entails of retribution and destruction, and that He will not let such a person escape, as al-Nabigha said:

"For you are like the night that overtakes me,"

and the rest of the verse. And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and found God with him, so He paid him his account in full﴾ [al-Nur: 39]. How then would one think of the one whom God has made an enemy? For this reason the name of God (Ism al-Jalalah) is mentioned in its apparent form, and He did not say "indeed I am an enemy" or "indeed He is an enemy," because the apparent form here conveys great power, in the manner of the caliph, the Commander of the Faithful, saying: "The Commander of the Faithful orders such-and-such," urging obedience.

The intended meaning of "the disbelievers" is all the disbelievers. The general term is used so that their inclusion within it is like establishing a ruling through evidence. It also shows that God is their enemy because of their disbelief, and that this enmity is itself disbelief. And so the sentence serves as a concluding clause (tadhyil) for what precedes it.

Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī followed the opinion of Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī at the beginning of his epistle addressed to ʿAlī ibn Manṣūr al-Ḥalabī, known as Ibn al-Qāriḥ, which is known as "Risālat al-Ghufrān", where he said: "The Jabr to whom Gabriel is ascribed is known, and in all goodness there is a path, that in my dwelling there is a..." etc. That is, God, to whom Gabriel is ascribed by his name, that is by his name Jabr, is known; he intends by this an oath. This is an obscure claim from him and an alert to his lack of familiarity with the language.

The enmity of the Jews toward Gabriel arose from the time of his bringing the Qur'an down upon Muhammad (ﷺ)
Page 621
It was also said that it is because he descends upon the nations that denied their messengers with punishment and threat; al-Qurtubi transmitted this from a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi. His saying "﴿Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾" [al-Baqarah: 97] is a general condition intended as particular, namely the Jews. He intended the inclusiveness so that they would know that God does not care about them, nor about others who oppose Gabriel, if he has any other enemy.

The Jews were known in Medina as enemies of Gabriel. In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, he said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam heard of the arrival of the Messenger of God while he was in his land gathering dates. He came to the Prophet and said: 'I will ask you about three things which none knows except a prophet: What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food of the people of Paradise? And why does the child resemble its father or its mother?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Gabriel has just informed me of them.' He said: 'That is the enemy of the Jews among the angels; for they hate him, because he brings what contains severity and the command to fight'," and the hadith continues. In the Book of Daniel among their books, in chapters eight and nine, they mention that Gabriel interpreted for Daniel a vision he saw and warned him of the destruction of Jerusalem. The commentators mention other reasons for their hatred of Gabriel. Among the wonders of the incoherence of their belief is that they affirm that he is an angel sent by God and yet hate him; this is among the lowest depths of degradation in intellect and creed. Without doubt, confusion of belief is among the greatest signs of a people's decline, because it indicates that their opinions converge upon error and illusions.

His saying "﴿So indeed he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of God﴾" [al-Baqarah: 97]: the pronoun in the accusative governed by "nazzalahu" refers to the Qur'an, either because it was mentioned in His saying "﴿And when it is said to them: believe in what God has sent down﴾" [al-Baqarah: 91], or because the verb suits nothing but it here, in the manner of "﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾" [Sad: 32] and "﴿Why, when it reaches the throat﴾" [al-Waqiʿah: 83]. This sentence stands in place of the answer of the condition.

It is evident that the intended meaning is that there is no cause for their enmity toward him, because he is an intermediary whom God permitted to descend with the Qur'an; so in hating him they are in fact hating God the Exalted. The estimate is: "Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, let him not be his enemy, and let him be an enemy to God the Exalted." This view is better than what they mentioned, more fitting to His saying "by the permission of God," and clearer in connection with His saying after it: "﴿Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels﴾," as you will know. It is also possible that the estimate is: "for indeed He has sent it down to you, whether they love it or oppose it," so it is in the sense of provoking rage, like "﴿Say: Die in your rage﴾" [Al ʿImran: 119], as in the words of al-Rabiʿ ibn Ziyad:

Whoever is delighted by the killing of Malik, let him come to our courtyard at the time of daybreak;
he will find the women unveiled, wailing for him at night before the dawn breaks.

That is: he should not rejoice at his killing, for we have killed his slayer before the morning came, since his slayer is one of the allies of him who was delighted by his killing. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: "for indeed it descended with him from God, confirming their book, and in it is guidance and good tidings," and this condition calls for love of the one who brought it; so from their folly and obstinacy is their enmity toward the one who brought it. The estimate is then: "he has cast off the noose of reason or the ornament of fairness." The use of the emphatic particle in "fa-innahu nazzalahu" is because they deny that.

"Al-qalb" here means the self (nafs) and that by which memory and understanding occur; the Arabs apply "qalb" to this immaterial matter, as in "﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾" [Qaf: 37], just as they also apply it to the inner conical organ, as said:

As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry...

"Muṣaddiqan" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in the accusative of "anzalahu", i.e., the Qur'an, which is the cause of the Jews' enmity toward Gabriel; that is, He sent it down accompanied by a state that does not necessitate their enmity toward it, for He sent it down confirming what is before it of the books, namely the Torah and the Gospel. "Muṣaddiq" is one who reports the truthfulness of someone. The particle of emphasis (lam al-taqwiyah) was introduced to the object of "muṣaddiqan" to indicate the strengthening of that confirmation; that is, it is a firm, established confirmation that is not tainted by anything of denial or correction, for the Qur'an praised the Torah and the Gospel and described each as guidance and light, as in Surah al-Ma'idah.

The confirmation of earlier messengers is among the first proofs of the truthfulness of the one who confirms, because impostors who claim prophethood come with denial of those before them, since what they bring of guidance opposes the misguidance of the deceivers, so they cannot afford to confirm them. For this reason the earlier prophets warned against the lying pretenders, as is found in several places of the Torah and the Gospels.

The intended meaning of "what is before it" (mā bayna yadayhi) is what preceded it, and it is a metaphor (kināyah) for precedence, because the precedent comes before the preceded. Since it is a metaphor for precedence, it does not contradict the long duration between the earlier books and the Qur'an, and because the practice of them continued among their nations until the coming of the Qur'an; so their precedence was made continuous up to the time of the coming of the Qur'an, and thus their precedence was connected.

"Hudan" is a description of the Qur'an by the verbal noun, for the purpose of emphasizing the attainment of guidance through it. "Bushra" is the report of the occurrence of a joyful matter, or of the expectation of its occurrence. So the Qur'an gave good tidings to the believers that they are upon guidance, perfection and the pleasure of God the Exalted, and gave them good tidings that God will grant them the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter.

Thus there have been obtained five attributes of the Qur'an: that it was sent down from God by the permission of God; that it was sent down upon the heart of the Messenger; that it confirms the books that preceded it; that it is a guide to the most eloquent guidance; and that it is good tidings for the believers. Praise of the Qur'an for the nobility of its origin, the nobility of its abode, the nobility of its people, the overflowing of good upon its virtuous followers: immediate good, and a promise to them of the good outcome. These are the qualities of the noble man: his lineage, his house, and his people; generous in giving, and promising what he gives. These are qualities that the verse of Ziyad al-A'jam considered:

Indeed generosity, manliness and liberality are in a dome raised over the son of al-Ḥashraj.

His saying "﴿Whoever is an enemy to God﴾" etc. Its excellent position has become clear from what you have known of the sense of "So indeed He has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of God": that is, since their enmity toward Gabriel was on account of their enmity toward the Messenger, and it ultimately returned to obliging them to be enemies to God who sent him, because the cause of the enmity is his bringing the message, it became possible to record against them that they are enemies of God, since He is the sender; enemies of His messengers, since they opposed the Messenger; and enemies of the angels, on that account. Thus their enmity toward Gabriel became like the middle term in a syllogism, which is not itself looked at; rather one looks to the two premises, the minor and the major. Their enmity toward God is like the major premise, since it is the cause in meaning upon reflection; and their enmity toward the Messenger is like the minor premise, since it is the particular cause establishing it. So it is not objected that there is no reason to mention enmity toward God here, to be answered by saying that enmity toward the angels and messengers is enmity toward God, in the manner of "﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾" [al-Nisa: 80], for that is far-fetched.

He has attributed to them enmity toward the angels and messengers, although they only opposed Gabriel and Muhammad; because when they opposed the two of them, they were opposing Gabriel on account of his performance of what is特 of his angelic kind, namely conveying God's commanding order, for that is their distinguishing feature. He said: "﴿And they act by His command﴾" [al-Anbiya: 27]. Their enmity toward him for this reason led back to enmity toward the whole kind of angels, since this path is one in which Gabriel is not unique. Likewise, when they opposed Muhammad on account of his coming with the message by a particular cause related to his own person, their enmity toward him led back to enmity toward the attribute that constitutes the kind of messenger. So whoever opposes one of them is bound to oppose all of them; otherwise his action is arbitrary, and he has no excuse in it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 98–99 (part 2 of 2):

Gabriel (Jibril) is singled out for mention here to heighten attention to the punishment of his enemies, and so that Michael (Mika'il) may be mentioned along with him. Perhaps they opposed both of them together. Or it may be because they claimed that Gabriel is the messenger of punishment and destruction, and that Michael is the messenger of fertility and peace, and they said: "We love Michael." When the aim is to warn them that their enmity toward the angels draws God's enmity upon them, Gabriel's name is repeated to give him prominence, and Michael is joined to him by conjunction, lest they imagine that their love for Michael earns the believers his enmity.

For Michael there are several forms (lughat). The first is Mikha'il (مِيكائِيلُ), with a hamza after the alif and a yā' after the hamza, and the majority of readers (al-Jumhur) recited it this way.

The second is (مِيكائِلُ), with a hamza after the alif and without a yā' after the hamza, and Nafi' recited it this way.

The third is (مِيكالُ), without hamza and without yā', and Abu 'Amr and Hafs recited it this way. It is the dialect (lughat) of the people of the Hijaz.

His saying, ﴿indeed God is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾, is the answer to the conditional clause. "Enemy" (al-'Aduww) is used in its figurative sense, namely what this entails of retribution and destruction, and that He will not let such a person escape, as al-Nabigha said:

"For you are like the night that overtakes me,"

and the rest of the verse. And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and found God with him, so He paid him his account in full﴾ [al-Nur: 39]. How then would one think of the one whom God has made an enemy? For this reason the name of God (Ism al-Jalalah) is mentioned in its apparent form, and He did not say "indeed I am an enemy" or "indeed He is an enemy," because the apparent form here conveys great power, in the manner of the caliph, the Commander of the Faithful, saying: "The Commander of the Faithful orders such-and-such," urging obedience.

The intended meaning of "the disbelievers" is all the disbelievers. The general term is used so that their inclusion within it is like establishing a ruling through evidence. It also shows that God is their enemy because of their disbelief, and that this enmity is itself disbelief. And so the sentence serves as a concluding clause (tadhyil) for what precedes it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 100–101:

﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieves in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 99] ﴿Is it [not] that every time they make a covenant, a party of them throws it aside? Rather, most of them do not believe﴾. ﴿And when there came to them a messenger from Allah, confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Scripture threw the Book of Allah behind their backs, as if they did not know﴾

This is a conjunction with His saying ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97]. It is the conjoining of one narrative with another, to mention their disbelief in the Qur'an, so it is among their conditions. This sentence is the answer to an omitted oath, so He conjoined it to ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97]; it is a conjunction of an imperative with an imperative. It contains an added refutation of their saying, "We believe in what was sent down to us." Moving to address the Prophet ﷺ shows attentiveness to him and consolation for him regarding what he encountered from them, and that what was sent down to him is denied only by one whose denial carries no weight, because this sent-down revelation contains clear proofs that are not deficient in convincing them of its truth; but they display to themselves that they have not been certain of its truth.

The lam is a preparatory particle for an omitted oath, so here is an oath-clause whose answer is the omitted oath, indicated by the lam.

His saying ﴿And none disbelieves in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 99] is a conjunction with "We have certainly sent down," so it is also an answer to the oath.

Page 625
Al-fasiq (the defiantly disobedient) is one who goes out of something, from "fasaqat al-tamrah" (the date came out of its skin), as was previously explained in His saying ﴿And He leads astray thereby none except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. Its application has become widespread to one who goes out of the path of goodness, because that attribute in the date is a blameworthy description, and the description of the Jews with it has become widespread in the Qur'an. The meaning is: none disbelieves in these signs except one for whom defiant disobedience is his character and habit, because that makes him prepared for disbelief in such signs. So the intended meaning of "the defiantly disobedient" is those who exceed the limit in disbelief and are rebellious in it. The report is expressed with the present tense, which indicates renewal, and the description is expressed with the active participle defined by the lam.

His saying ﴿Is it [not] that every time they make a covenant, a party of them throws it aside?﴾ is an interrogative used for rebuke, conjoined to the clause of the oath, not to the specific answer. The hamzah was placed first, in keeping with its position of precedence, as is its rule with conjunctive particles.

The view that the hamzah is for a question about an omitted supposition, and that the waw is conjunctive for what follows the omitted element, you have come to know its refutation at His saying: "Is it that whenever a messenger comes to you," and the placement of "kullama" follows the placement of the interrogative particle, and its explanation was previously given at His saying ﴿Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you waxed arrogant?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87].

Al-nabdh is throwing a thing from the hand, and here it is a metaphor for breaking the covenant. He likened the nullifying of the covenant and failing to fulfill it to casting aside a thing that was held in the hand, just as they called keeping to a covenant and fulfilling it "tamassuk" (holding fast). Ka'b said:

"And you do not hold fast to the promise which you made."

The covenant intended is the covenant of the Torah, namely what it contained of taking a covenant from the Children of Israel to act upon what they were commanded, a repeated taking, until the Torah itself was called "the covenant." Their breaking of covenants with their prophets was repeated, and among the covenant that was taken from them is that they should believe in the messenger who confirms the Torah.

The throwing aside is ascribed to "a party" either in consideration of the eras in which they broke the covenants, as "kullama" indicates, or as a safeguard against the blame extending to those among them who believed. It is not intended that this party was few among them, so that He points out that most of them are such by His saying ﴿Rather, most of them do not believe﴾. This is one of the refinements of eloquence: that the speaker shows he gives his opponent in the dispute his due, so he does not attribute blame to him except gradually and with reflection before refutation. You may also take it as a transition from one matter to what is stronger than it for that purpose, since throwing aside may mean non-practice without disbelief, and the first is more apparent.

His saying "﴿And when there came to them a messenger﴾" etc. is conjoined to His saying "Is it that whenever," conjoining one narrative to another because of the strangeness of these matters. The messenger is Muhammad ﷺ, as shown by "﴿confirming what was with them﴾." Throwing (nabdh) is casting a thing from the hand, so it requires prior taking. "The Book of Allah" is evidently intended to be the Qur'an, because it is most complete in its attribution to Allah. So throwing, on this view, means abandoning it after hearing it; hearing is treated as taking, and disbelief in it after hearing is treated as throwing.

It has been said that "the Book of Allah" means the Torah. Al-Zamakhshari indicated preferring this by its being placed first, because throwing requires prior taking of what is thrown, and they did not hold fast to the Qur'an. The basic principle regarding the unqualified use of a word is that it is literal in both wording and meaning. It has been said that a definite term repeated as a definite term is the same as the first; but this is questionable, since that applies to repeating a noun defined by the lam. Or you may make throwing a figure for the state of one who turns away from a thing and pays it little regard, so it is not meant in its literal sense.

His saying "behind their backs" is a metaphor for turning away, because whoever turns away from something passes beyond it and leaves it behind his back. The addition of "behind" (waraa') to "backs" (zuhur) is to emphasize the remoteness of what is abandoned, such that he will not encounter it afterward; thus the back is made to have a "behind," though here "back" itself has the sense of "behind." The genitive is like an explanatory one. By this one answers what Ibn 'Arafa transmitted from the jurist Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn 'Ablun, that he used to say: the implication of this is that they cast the Book of Allah in front of them, since what is behind the back is the face, and just as the back is behind the face, so the face is behind the back. Ibn 'Arafa said: it is answered that the intended meaning in mentioning the back is to emphasize the sense of "behind," as in the expression "from behind behind."

His saying ﴿as if they did not know﴾ is a recording against them that they know that the Qur'an is the Book of Allah; or it means "as if they did not know the Torah and what it contains of the good news of the sending of the Messenger from the descendants of Isma'il."

﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieves in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 99] ﴿Is it [not] that every time they make a covenant, a party of them throws it aside? Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 102 (part 1 of 5):

﴿And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic﴾ His saying "and they followed" is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the conditional clause whose response is in his saying ﴿And when there came to them a messenger from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101], the verse, by mentioning a strange characteristic of theirs, which is their clinging to falsehoods, after mentioning another characteristic, which is their rejecting the true Book. This is the reason for the conjunction of this report upon the one before it. If the intended meaning of "the Book of Allah" in his saying "﴿the Book of Allah behind their backs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101]" is the Qur'an, then the meaning is that when the Messenger of Allah came to them confirming what was with them, they rejected his Book on the pretext that they adhere to the Torah, so they do not follow what contradicts its rulings. Yet they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon, which contradicts the Torah, since it forbids magic and polytheism. So, just as it was said to them in the past, "Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?" it is said to them: "Do you believe in the Book at one time and disbelieve in it at another?"
Page 627
And if the intended meaning of "the Book of Allah" is the Torah, then the meaning is that when the Messenger of Allah came to them, they cast aside what was in the Torah of the proofs of the truthfulness of this Messenger; and they had already cast it aside before, when they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon, although that contradicts the rulings of the Torah. Al-Qurtubi said: Ibn Ishaq said: When the Prophet ﷺ mentioned Solomon among the prophets, the Jews said: "Muhammad claims that Solomon was a prophet, but he was not a prophet; he was only a sorcerer." So this verse was revealed.
And "the devils" (al-shayatin) may refer to devils from the jinn, which is the well-known usage. It may also mean people who rebelled, disbelieved, and committed hidden abominations, so they were called devils by way of comparison, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. The indication of this is His saying "teaching people magic," for it clearly means they were teaching it to people. Likewise His saying after it: "but the devils disbelieved," since this use of "but" (istidrak) in the report indicates that they are from mankind, because the disbelief of the devils of the jinn is an established matter that does not need to be reported.
Also from Ibn Ishaq: when Solomon, peace be upon him, died, the devils set about writing kinds of magic and said: "Whoever wishes to attain such-and-such should do such-and-such," listing kinds of magic; they sealed it with a seal resembling the seal of Solomon, attributed it to him, buried it, and claimed that Solomon had buried it and that they knew its burial place; they guided people to that place, and they dug it up. The Jews then said: "Solomon was only a sorcerer, and his kingdom was established only by this." It was also said that Asaf ibn Barakhya, Solomon's scribe, used to write wisdom by Solomon's command and bury his books beneath Solomon's throne so that later generations would find them. When Solomon died, the devils incited people to bring out those books, and they added into the lines of their pages magic and disbelief, and attributed all of it to Solomon. So the Jews said: "Solomon disbelieved."
The meaning of the verse, together with its occasion of revelation if it was revealed concerning a specific occasion, is that when Solomon, peace be upon him, died, the kingdom of Israel was divided shortly after him into two kingdoms: one is the kingdom of Judah, whose king was Rehoboam ibn Solomon, whom they made king after his father. The children of Israel had grown weary of Solomon's rule, because he burdened them with what contradicted their desires. Their notables came, led by Jeroboam ibn Nabat, a client of Solomon, to speak with Rehoboam, saying: "Your father was harsh with us; so lighten for us the servitude of your father, that we may obey you." He answered them: "Go, then return to me after three days." Rehoboam consulted the elders of his father and his ministers, who advised him to be gentle with the nation so that it would obey him.
He then consulted his companions among the young men, who advised him to say to the nation: "My little finger is thicker than my father's loins. If my father disciplined you with whips, I will discipline you with scorpions." When the elders of the children of Israel returned to him on the third day, and he answered them with what the young men had advised, the children of Israel renounced his obedience and made Jeroboam king over them. Only the tribes of Judah and Benjamin remained loyal to Rehoboam, and he took refuge in Jerusalem. His entire nation did not exceed one hundred and eighty thousand fighting men, meaning men capable of bearing arms. From that day the kingdom was divided into two kingdoms: the kingdom of Judah, whose capital was Jerusalem, and the kingdom of Israel, whose seat was Samaria. This was in the year 975 BC, as we mentioned earlier when discussing His saying, Exalted is He, (﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews and the Christians and the Sabians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62]) the verse. The condition of a nation in such a transition is not hidden. When Rehoboam's adversaries stripped him of material strength, they did not neglect to undermine what sustained him of moral strength, namely that he was the son of Solomon ibn Dawud, from the house of kingship and prophethood, and of good reputation. So his enemies spared no effort in dismantling this moral strength, by gathering the managers of the affair to fabricate lies about Solomon and spread them among the common people, to achieve two aims. The first: attributing to Solomon sorcery and disbelief, to diminish the reputation of his son Rehoboam, just as the propagandists of the Abbasid state did with the reports they fabricated about the Umayyads. The second: encouraging the common people, who held Solomon's and his son's kingdom in great esteem, to rebel against his son, by claiming that Solomon's kingdom was established only through those charms and talismans, and that once they had obtained them they could establish a kingdom like Solomon's, just as the promoters of regime change in Islamic history did by fabricating hadiths about awaiting the Mahdi, and as they do by spreading reports about the righteous that announce the imminent fall of the state.
It is not hidden what such illusions stir in the souls of the common people: certainty of the success of the endeavor, and a sense of security from the failure of their deeds and from being punished. When the purpose is achieved through that report, its impact clings to people, so the harm of its misguidance remains after its fruits have been gathered.
Following (ittiba') in origin is walking behind another, and it is used figuratively for acting upon another's saying and opinion, and for believing in another's belief. You say: he followed the school of Malik, and he followed the creed of al-Ash'ari. Following here is necessarily figurative, because its object cannot be literally followed. Recitation (tilawah) is reading what is written and the Book, and presenting what is memorized from the heart; its verb is transitive by itself, as in "they recite to you My verses." Its being transitive here by the preposition of elevation ('ala) indicates that it implies the meaning of "lying" (takdhib), i.e., they recite a recitation of lies over the kingdom of Solomon, as one says "he lied upon so-and-so," meaning he said about him what he had not said. This meaning was understood only from the particle ('ala).
The kingdom here means either the period of the kingdom or the cause of the kingdom, by the indication that recitation does not relate to the kingdom itself. Omitting the genitive-modified noun when what remains indicates the time is common in Arabic speech, as when they say: this occurred in the life of the Messenger of Allah, or in the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, and the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr:
"It was nothing but in a waist-wrap and a cord, the raid of Ibn Hammam upon the clan of Khath'am."
He means the times of the raid of Ibn Hammam. Likewise the omitted noun is elided when the intended meaning is events or causes, as you say: so-and-so spoke about the caliphate of ʿUmar, or: this is a book on the kingdom of the Abbasids. This is because when a name is known for an attribute or a story, it is valid to use it while intending that attribute or story, such that if it appeared it would be attached to the name. Al-Nabigha said:
"And a night I endure, slow of stars."
He meant the hardships of a night, because the night is well known among lovers as the time of longing and sleeplessness.
As for "the devils" (al-shayatin): it has been said that it means the devils of mankind, i.e., the misleaders, and this is the apparent meaning. It has also been said that it means the devils of the jinn, and the definite article (al) is for the genus under both views. In my opinion, the intended meaning of "the devils" is the people of tricks and the sorcerers, as they say: so-and-so is one of the devils of the Arabs, and Nashib al-A'war, one of the men of the Day of al-Waqit, was counted among them.
As for His saying "tatlu" (recites), it came in the present form to narrate a past situation, according to the majority. Or it is a present tense in its proper use, according to what we have chosen, that the devils are their rabbis, for they never ceased reciting that; so the meaning is that they "followed," i.e., believed in, what the devils recited, and that they never stopped reciting it.
Solomon is the Prophet Solomon ibn Dawud ibn Yasai, of the tribe of Judah. He was born in the year 1032, two and thirty and a thousand years before Christ, and died in Jerusalem in the year 975, five and seventy and nine hundred years before Christ. He ruled over Israel in the year 1014, fourteen and a thousand years before Christ, after the death of his father Dawud the Prophet, king of Israel. The kingdom of the children of Israel flourished during his time. He is the one who ordered the building of the Masjid of Bayt al-Maqdis. He was a prophet, wise, and a poet, and he made for his kingdom a great navy whose ships sailed the seas to distant regions, such as the east of Africa.
His saying: (﴿And Solomon did not disbelieve﴾) is a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah), whose interjection was prompted by what His saying ﴿what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon﴾ implies, namely that they lied about Solomon and attributed disbelief to him. It is therefore interposed between the clause "and they followed" and His saying "and what was sent down to the two angels," if "and what was sent down" is conjoined to "what they recited"; and between "they followed" and "and they certainly knew that whoever purchased it," etc., if "and what was sent down" is conjoined to "magic." You may also take it as conjoined to "they followed" if the intended meaning of the devils is the rabbis of the Jews, because this ruling then falls within the states of the Jews, since its outcome is (they followed and disbelieved). And "Solomon did not disbelieve" was placed first because it is the more important, hastening the affirmation of his purity and infallibility; and because the belief in his disbelief was a cause of misguidance for those who followed what the devils wrote. There is no doubt that the ruling on the followers and the ruling on the followed is one, so this was a report about the Jews as well.
The Jews had believed in Solomon's disbelief in their books. In the First Book of Kings it came that in his old age his foreign wives, the Egyptian, Sidonian, and Ammonite women, inclined his heart toward their gods, like Ashtoreth, god of the Sidonians, and Molech, god of the Ammonites (the Phoenicians), and he built temples for these gods. So Allah was angry with him, because his heart had turned away from the God of Israel, who had charged him not to follow other gods.
His saying ﴿teaching people magic﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "disbelieved," and its purpose is to denounce the state of their disbelief, since it was accompanied by teaching magic, like the saying "a disbelief short of disbelief." So it is a specifying circumstantial clause (hal mu'assisah).
Magic (sihr) is trickery (sha'wadhah), which is the deception of tricks by concealing them under movements and states, such that the observer thinks these are what produce the effect, while the actual cause remains hidden. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate from the heaven, and they continued to ascend through it, they would say: "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched"﴾ [al-Hijr: 14]. For this reason the word magic was applied to deception; you say: "I sahhartu the child" when you amused him with something. Labid said:
"So if you ask us what we are, we are sparrows of this bewitched people."
Then it was applied to what has an apparent form while its cause is hidden, namely deception, confusion, imagining what is not real as real, and promoting the impossible. The Arabs say: a she-goat is "masurah" when her udder becomes large and her milk little; and land is "masurah" when nothing grows in it. Abu ʿAta said:
"By Allah, I do not know, and I am truthful: is it an ailment that has befallen me from your love, or is it magic?"
