Meaning: a thing whose cause is not known. The Arabs held that the ghouls (ghiylan) are sorceresses of the jinn, because of the forms they take on and the shapes they present to humans. Sorcery (sihr) is among the ancient sciences that appeared at the source of the first civilization, that is, in the lands of the East, for it appeared in the lands of the Chaldeans and the Babylonians and in Egypt in one era, namely in the fortieth century before Christ. This indicates that it was among the teachings of a people who arose before those two nations. Indeed, Egyptian magical remains have been found from the era of the Fifth Dynasty and the Sixth Dynasty of the Pharaohs, 3951–3703 BCE.

The Arabs had a wide imagination concerning sorcery. They believed that sorcery alters physical things, alters hearts, and makes the bewitched person submissive to the sorcerer. For this reason they used to say that the ghoul is a sorceress of the jinn, and therefore she takes on various forms to the one who sees her. When the Quraysh saw the miracles of the Messenger of Allah, they said: "He is a sorcerer." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic."﴾ [al-Qamar: 2]. Allah the Exalted also said: ﴿And even if We opened for them a gate from the heaven, and they continued to ascend through it, [they] would surely say, "Our eyes have only been intoxicated; rather, we are a people affected by sorcery."﴾ [al-Hijr: 14–15].

In the Hadith of al-Bukhari, on the authority of ʿImran ibn Husayn: "The people became thirsty during a journey with the Messenger of Allah, so they sought water and found a woman on her camel, who had two water-skins. They brought her to the Messenger of Allah, and the Messenger of Allah gave drink to the whole army, then returned to her both her water-skins, full. She said to her people: 'By Allah, he is the greatest sorcerer between this and this,' meaning the heaven and the earth." And in a hadith: "Indeed, among eloquence there is sorcery."

I have not seen anything indicating that the Arabs practised sorcery, for sorcery is derived from the special properties of natural things and their composition. The Arabs had no skill in manual crafts; their skill was purely intellectual. The Arabs used to claim that the most knowledgeable people in sorcery were the Jews and the Sabians, who are the people of Babylon, and the context of the verse indicates the fame of these people for sorcery among the Arabs.

The Muslims believed that the Jews of Yathrib had bewitched them, so that they could not have children; therefore they rejoiced when ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr was born, and he was the first child born to the Emigrants in Medina, as in Sahih al-Bukhari. For this reason mention of sorcery did not become frequent among the Arab Muslims except after they migrated to Medina, where the Jews were, and who used to give the impression that they bewitched people. The one who treats sorcery is the ʿarraf (diviner), and the remedy for sorcery is the salwah (sulwa), which are known beads rubbed in water, and its water is drunk.

The prohibition of sorcery appears in the Torah, and it is counted among the characteristics of polytheism. The Torah has described the people of idols with it. It has come in the Book of Deuteronomy, chapter 18: "When you enter the land which the LORD your God gives you, you shall not learn to act according to the abominations of those nations. There shall not be found among you anyone who makes his son or his daughter pass through the fire, or who practises divination, or an augur, or a soothsayer, or a sorcerer, or one who casts a spell, or a medium, or a spiritist, or one who inquires of the dead, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD."

In the Book of Leviticus, chapter 20: "(6) As for the person who turns to mediums and spiritists, to play the harlot after them, I will set My face against that person and will cut him off from among his people. (27) If there is a man or a woman who is a medium or a spiritist, they shall surely be put to death; they shall stone them with stones; their blood shall be upon them."

They made it a religious principle for addressing the spirits of the dead, subjugating the devils, and healing diseases. Its affair flourished in the land of the Chaldeans, and they mixed it with the sciences of the stars and the science of medicine. The Egyptians traced the magical knowledge to the body of mathematical sciences that "Tut," whom they claim to be Idris, bestowed upon them, and who is Hermes according to the Greeks.

The Chaldeans and the Egyptians employed in it secrets of the natural, philosophical and spiritual sciences, intending to bring things out in their most dazzling appearances, so that they would be captivating or deceptive and apparent, like extraordinary feats. However, it spread among their common people, and after they strayed from its scientific purpose, it became an expression for deception, delusion, and bringing falsehood out in the form of truth, or ugliness in a beautiful form, or harm in the form of benefit.

Among the Chaldeans and the Egyptians it became a special matter in the hands of the priests, who at that time were the people of knowledge, those who combined in themselves religious and scientific leadership. They adopted the principles of the mathematical, philosophical and moral sciences to subjugate the common people to themselves and to submit them through what they displayed of the ability to treat diseases, to perceive hearts through physiognomy, and through the influence of the evil eye and through plots.

The nations took it from these two peoples, and most of what they transmitted they took from the Chaldeans. The Syriacs (the Assyrians), the Jews, the Arabs, and all the other religious nations, the Persians, the Greeks and the Romans acquired it from them.

The roots of sorcery are three. The first is the subjugation of souls through preliminaries of delusion and intimidation, through the psychological influence that the sorcerer habitually exerts on himself, through the weakness in the soul of the bewitched, and through precedents the bewitched has witnessed and believed; when the sorcerer turns toward him, he is subjugated to him. To this root refers His saying, exalted is He, concerning the sorcerers of Pharaoh: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people and terrified them﴾ [al-A'raf: 116].

The second is the use of influences from the properties of bodies, from animals and minerals. This returns to natural properties, like the property of mercury. Among it are drugs that affect minds for good or for ill, that weaken resolve, and narcotics and sedatives, with varying degrees of effect. To this refers His saying, exalted is He, concerning the sorcerers of Pharaoh: ﴿What they have produced is only the trick of a sorcerer﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69].

The third is sleight of hand (shaʿwadhah) and the use of hidden matters of motion, speed and oscillation, until an inanimate object is imagined to be moving. To this refers His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It appeared to him, because of their magic, that their ropes and staffs were moving﴾ [Ta-Ha: 66].

These are the roots of sorcery by induction. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) in his tafsir divided it into eight categories, none of which exceeds these three roots, and some of which overlap. The scholars of the Franks have another division, which has little benefit.

These three roots are all direct actions upon the bewitched and connected to him, and they have an effect upon him in proportion to the receptiveness of his weak soul, while he is unaware of them. Their totality is what the verse indicates, and it is what there is no disagreement about affirming in general, without detail. Whatever else there is of illusions and claims is something without effect. That is every act that has no direct contact with the person who is to be bewitched, and where the practitioner is absent from him, yet claims that he affects him. Such as drawing figures called talismans (talasim), or tying knots of threads and blowing upon them with specific incantations that include invoking the stars, or the names of devils, jinn, and the gods of the ancients; and likewise writing the name of the bewitched in figures, or placing his image or some of his clothing and belongings and directing words toward them, under the claim that this affects the very essence of the bewitched; or they use special gestures toward his direction or toward his land, which they call astrological observations (arsad). Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi mentioned in al-Qabas that when the Prophet ﷺ pointed with his finger during the tashahhud, the Quraysh said: "This Muhammad bewitches the people." Or joining specific parts and combining some of them with others, with the intention that that figure or combination affects a specific person with harm, benefit, love, hatred, sickness or health, especially if it is coupled with the name of the bewitched and his image or with his birth horoscope. All of that is among the illusions, and there is no proof of its effect from reason, nor from nature, nor from what the Law establishes. The proofs for establishing realities are confined to these proofs. It is among the wonders that al-Fakhr in his tafsir attempted to establish it with what is not convincing.

Some have held fast, to establish the effect of this type of sorcery, to what is narrated in the two Sahihs from the saying of ʿAyshah that Labid ibn al-Aʿsam bewitched the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet's ﷺ vision that two angels informed him of that sorcery. In al-Nasa'i, on the authority of Zayd ibn Arqam, is something similar but abridged. One should be careful about its wording and then about its interpretation. There is no doubt that Labid tried to bewitch the Prophet ﷺ, for the Jews were sorcerers in Medina, and Allah informed His Messenger ﷺ of what Labid had done, so that it would be a miracle for the Prophet ﷺ in nullifying Labid's sorcery, and so that the Jews would know that he is a prophet whom their harm does not reach. And just as the sorcery of the sorcerers did not affect Moses, likewise the sorcery of Labid did not affect the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Rather, a physical ailment befell the Prophet ﷺ, from which Allah healed him, and it coincided with what Labid ibn al-Aʿsam had done in attempting his sorcery. The Prophet's ﷺ vision was information from Allah to him about what Labid had done. The description of the form of that vision was in general terms, for visions are symbols, and no explanation of what it contained is reported in the report; therefore it cannot be a basis for detailing the story.

Furthermore, for the effect of these causes or the three roots there are conditions and circumstances, some of which are in the sorcerer himself and some in the bewitched. It is required of the sorcerer that he be exceptionally intelligent, devoted to repeatedly renewing sorcerous attempts, bold, of strong will, discreet with secrets, little disturbed by events, sound of constitution, disciplined in thought, and subtle in plotting and stratagem. For this reason most sorcerers were men; but the Abyssinians used to make sorcerers women, and likewise was the prevalent practice among the Persians and the Arabs. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ [al-Falaq: 4], so He used the plural feminine. The pre-Islamic Arabs used to say that the ghouls are old women among the jinn who are sorceresses, and therefore they are able to take on various forms. The teachers of sorcery used to test the fitness of their students for this knowledge by exposing them to frightening things and ordering them to undertake hardships, as a test of the measure of their resolve and obedience.

As for what is required in the bewitched: vanity of intellect, weakness of resolve, delicacy of constitution, and foolishness of mind. For this reason the people most susceptible to it are women, children, the common folk, and those who are amazed at everything. Accordingly, among the roots of sorcery is the delivery of false statements to the bewitched in order to test the measure of his intellect in believing worthless things and in trusting the sorcerer. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but clear magic."﴾ [Hud: 7], so they made that strange statement a sorcery.

Then there surround sorcery acts whose purpose is deception, and these acts are of several kinds.

[Page 636]

The second type is one whose purpose is to conceal the real causes of their deceptions, so that people do not learn their true nature. They therefore attribute their acts to false causes, such as calling on names they have invented that have no referents, drawing figures on paper or on walls which they claim have special powers of influence, and relying on the rising of certain stars at specific times, especially the Moon. Part of this is their display to people of an appearance of asceticism and lofty aspiration.

The third type is one used to enable the magic to take effect: spying and prying into hidden matters and the secrets of people through tale-bearing (*namimah*) and sowing enmity among relatives, friends and spouses, until each of them reveals the other's secret. The sorcerer then uses these secrets as a means of striking terror into the hearts of their owners by showing that he knows the unseen and people's inner thoughts. He then commands those whom he has terrified and whom he employs, and they obey him. He orders a wife to rebel against her husband and seek separation from him, and orders a husband to divorce his wife, and so on. In this category the sorcerer's intellectual capacity becomes apparent, and through it his harms and dangers to people multiply, along with his boldness in committing frightful and abominable acts. It includes the destruction of wealth by theft, carried out by someone whom the victim does not suspect, and this includes his doing so against his own close associates, his children and his wife, whom the sorcerers beguile and enslave to devote themselves to them. The sorcerers' conduct in this matter may reach the point of taking lives, those who they feel have seen through their deception, or who have defied their commands. They incite against those who are most secure from them. Then there is the probing of people's consciences through covert inquiries and gradual questions, with which he creates the illusion that he is asking them in order to inform them about their future.

The fourth type is one employed as a test of the level of people's minds regarding his susceptibility to magic. This is done by placing objects in food, out of fear of discovery, to see whether the one who placed them will notice them. It also includes producing phantoms or apparitions, which he makes the onlooker believe are jinn, devils or spirits, when they are nothing but disguised forms or some of his disguised helpers. The purpose is to see whether the beholder is convinced by what the sorcerer tells him about them, or whether he seeks to uncover their reality or to trace their traces.

Thus magic has been the companion of a corrupt soul, a corrupted religion, evil conduct, and the frightening and terrorising of people. For this reason the true religions have never ceased to warn people against it and to regard occupation with it as apostasy from the obedience of God, Exalted is He. This is because it is founded on the belief in the influence of the gods and of the jinn attributed to the gods in the beliefs of the ancients. Moses warned his people against magic and its practitioners. In the Book of Deuteronomy, chapter 18, it is stated that among what Moses, peace be upon him, addressed to his people was: "When you enter the land which the LORD your God gives you, you shall not learn to do according to the abominations of those nations. There shall not be found among you anyone who makes his son or his daughter pass through the fire, or one who practises witchcraft, or a soothsayer, or an interpreter of omens, or a sorcerer, or one who casts spells, or a consulter with familiar spirits or a wizard, or one who calls up the dead." The Torah also made the penalty for sorcerers death. In the Book of Leviticus, chapters 20 to 27: "If there is a man or a woman who is a medium or a wizard, they shall surely be put to death."

It is reported from Malik that he said: "The names which sorcerers write in amulets are the names of idols."

Islam has warned against practising magic and has censured it in several passages. This does not necessarily imply the affirmation of an existential reality of magic in every respect, but it is a warning against corruption of beliefs, the removal of the restraints of religion, and vile morals. The scholars of Islam have differed over affirming and denying the reality of magic, and in my view this disagreement concerns states of affairs, for each group looked at a category of what is called magic.

ʿIyad, in *Ikmal al-ʿIlm*, reports that the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) affirmed its reality. I say: their words contain no description of the manner of the magic whose reality they affirmed, for they affirmed it only in general terms. The majority of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) held that magic has no reality and is merely deception, imagination and a kind of sleight of hand and charlatanry, and some of Ahl al-Sunnah agreed with them, as ʿIyad's report in *Ikmal* implies. I say: among those named from them is Abu Ishaq al-Isti'rabadhi of the Shafi'is.

The question, in all its details, is one of the derivative juristic (*furuʿ fiqhiyyah*) matters. It falls under the penalties for apostates, murderers and those who cheat people of their wealth, and it does not fall under the foundations of religion (*usul al-din*). Although the atheists deny it, denying it does not amount to disbelief. This verse is not explicit on the matter. As for the hadith, you have just learned it. The jurists made the penalty for practising it severe. Malik said: "The sorcerer is killed and is not given the chance to repent if he is a Muslim. If he is a dhimmi, he is not killed but is disciplined, unless his magic causes harm to a Muslim, in which case he is killed, because he has then broken the covenant, since among the terms of the covenant is that they do not harm the Muslims." Al-Baji said in *al-Muntaqa*: "Malik regarded magic as disbelief, polytheism and evidence of it, and since its practitioner conceals his act, it is like heresy (*zandaqah*), the outward display of Islam with inward unbelief. For this reason Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam, Ibn al-Mawwaz and Asbagh said: 'He is like the zindiq. If he conceals his magic he is not given the chance to repent, and if he displays it he is asked to repent.' This is an explanation of Malik's statement, and there is no disagreement about it." Al-Baji said: "He is not killed until it is established that what he does is the magic that God described as disbelief." Asbagh said: "Those who know its reality will reveal that, and it will be established before the imam."

In *al-Kafi* by Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr: if he practises magic in order to kill, and kills by it, he is killed, even if it is not disbelief. Malik included magic in the chapter on assassination (*al-ghilah*) in the *Muwatta'*. Ibn al-ʿArabi said in *al-Qabas*: "The reason for this is that the one bewitched does not know about the magic until it befalls him." I say: there is no doubt that the magic whose penalty is death is that which is explicit disbelief, accompanied by concealment, or that which results in the destruction of lives. This is because the sorcerer would promise the one who came to him for magic that so-and-so would die tonight or tomorrow, or that he would be struck with madness. Then he would scheme to deliver hidden poisons from drugs to the bewitched person, placed in his food through people of the bewitched person's household, so that the bewitched person would wake up dead or mentally deranged. This is what Malik meant by saying that its penalty is death, that is, if it kills. For this reason he said: "His repentance is not accepted." Without this interpretation the jurisprudence of this question cannot be sound. Malik's statement on magic is not based on a specific proof concerning magic in particular, but is a matter of verifying the applicable ruling (*tahqiq al-manat*), by applying the rules of discretionary punishment (*taʿzir*) and harm. Some of the jurists of the school, in reporting this question, have made astonishing generalisations which are surprising coming from such people. Moreover, magic is most often sought to subjugate the beloved to the lovers, so it is mostly a means to fornication or to revenge against the beloved or the spouse.

Malik was asked about one who ties men to women (by magic), and about a slave-girl who gives a man something to eat so that his mind departs. He said: "Neither of them is killed. As for the one who ties, he is disciplined. As for the slave-girl, she has committed a grave matter." It was asked: "Is she then to be killed?" He said: "No." Ibn Rushd said in *al-Bayan*: "He considered that her act is not of the magic (category)," end quote.

Abu Hanifa said: "A male sorcerer is killed and is not given the chance to repent. As for a female, she is imprisoned until she abandons it." Thus he gave the sorcerer the ruling of the apostate. Abu Yusuf justified this on the basis that he combined his disbelief with striving on earth for corruption. It is reported from Shaykh Abu Mansur that the statement that magic is disbelief in every respect is an error. Rather, its reality must be investigated. If it involves rejecting what is necessarily part of the conditions of faith, it is disbelief; otherwise it is not. What is not disbelief but involves the destruction of a soul receives the ruling of highway robbers (*qutaʿ al-tariq*), and in this men and women are equal, and his repentance is accepted if he repents. Whoever says that it is not accepted has erred, for the repentance of Pharaoh's sorcerers was accepted, end quote. This is an argument from the law of those before us.

Al-Shafiʿi said: "The sorcerer is asked about his magic. If something that is disbelief appears from him, he is like the apostate and is asked to repent. If he persists, he is killed. If it appears from him that he permits altering forms by reciting those myths or by fumigating with medicines, and it is known that he does a forbidden thing, then his ruling is that of an offence (*jinayah*). If he confesses to bewitching a person, and that his magic usually kills, he is killed by retaliation (*qawad*), meaning if it is established that the person died because of it. If he says that my magic may kill and may not kill, it is quasi-intentional homicide (*shibh ʿamd*). If his magic was for something other than killing and the person died from it, it is accidental homicide (*qatl khata'*), for which blood money is due, lightened, from his property."

It is necessary to extract from their disagreement and from their scattered opinions what provides insight into applying to the practices called magic, and to its practitioner called the sorcerer, the treatment given to the crimes of their like, and to the measure of the transgression that it has caused, without exaggeration or illusions. Today the name sorcerer is sometimes applied to the performer of sleight-of-hand tricks at entertainments. That is one of the kinds of amusement, so it should not be counted as a crime.

* * *

﴿And [they followed] what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. And they taught no one until they had said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve."﴾

It is clear that *ma* (what) is a relative pronoun, and it is coordinated with the phrase "the kingdom of Solomon", meaning: "and what the devils recited over what was sent down to the two angels." What is meant by "what was sent down" is a kind of magic, but one that involves great disbelief, teaching submission to other than God together with contempt for religion and harm to people, as we have explained above. So it is a coordination with "what they recited", which refers to magic in general. "What was sent down" is coordinated with it because it is a type of magic more severe than what the devils recited, who taught it to people along with the magic that they had themselves invented. The coordination is either for the difference of consideration, or to draw attention to the fact that the origin of magic is derived from what appeared at Babylon in the time of these two teachers. The coordination of a thing with itself by reason of a difference in concept and consideration occurs in speech, as in the verse of the poet (and it is among the examples cited in grammar):

[Page 639]

*To the mighty king, son of the bold hero, and the lion of the battalion in the crush of battle.*

It has also been said that what is meant is a lighter kind of magic than what the devils set down in the time of Sulayman, because the most that is attributed to this (the magic that appeared in Babylon in the time of these two teachers) is that it separates a man from his wife, and that is not disbelief. But this view is weak.

The widely transmitted (mutawatir) reading is *al-malakayni* ("the two angels"), with a fatha on the lam. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Ibn Abza read it with a kasra on the lam (*al-malikayni*, "the two kings").

All of these readings require that something was sent down upon the two in Babylon. That is what the context of the verse means when you work out how these two teachers taught the science of magic.

The sounder view is that the phrase *wa ma unzila* ("and what was sent down") is conjoined to *mulk Sulayman* ("the kingdom of Sulayman"), and so it is governed by *tatlu*, which here means *takdhibu* ("to falsify"). The meaning is then the invalidity of this report: what the devils falsely claim (*takdhibuhu*) about what was sent down upon the two angels in Babylon, that is, they attribute some magic to what was sent down at Babylon. Al-Fakhr said: this is the view chosen by Abu Muslim [55]. Abu Muslim denied that magic was sent down upon the two angels, since God would not command it, and how could the angels take on teaching it when it is disbelief or wickedness?

[Page 640]

It has also been said that *ma* is a negation, conjoined to *(ma kafara Sulayman)* ("Sulayman did not disbelieve"). That is: "Sulayman did not disbelieve by composing magic, as those who composed it claim, nor was magic sent down upon the two angels at Babylon."

The definiteness of "the two angels" is either generic (*ta'rif al-jins*) or definite by prior reference (*ta'rif al-'ahd*), meaning the two angels were already known to those acquainted with the story of the emergence of magic. It has also been said that Harut and Marut are a substitute (*badal*) for "the devils," and that by "devils" are meant two devils who originated magic for people, Harut and Marut, on the grounds that the plural is used for the dual, as in His words ﴿your hearts﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:4]. But this interpretation (*ta'wil*) is mistaken, because then the phrase "upon the two angels" would become a superfluous filler statement.

On the apparent sense of this verse there are four difficulties. First: the magic being sent down, if "sending down" is taken in its familiar sense, namely sending down from God. Second: the one who carries this out being two angels, according to the widely transmitted reading. Third: how the two angels can combine between their saying (*nahnu fitnatun*, "we are only a trial") and their saying (*fa-la takfur*, "so do not disbelieve"); how can the intention of causing a trial combine with a warning against falling into it? Fourth: how do they restrict their own state to being a trial, and what is the wisdom in their undertaking this? For if they are angels, the difficulty is obvious; and if they are kings (with a kasra), then they know the harm of disbelief, since they forbid it, and they know the meaning of trial, by their saying (﴿we are only a trial﴾). So why did they get themselves into this situation?

The resolution of this entire difficulty is that "sending down" (*al-inzal*) means "conveying" (*al-iisal*). When it is followed by *'ala* ("upon"), it indicates conveying from a height, and this is well known in the conveying of knowledge through revelation, inspiration or the like. So "sending down" here means inspiration and placing into the intellect, or into the natural disposition, such that the two angels had excelled in this magic and devised methods which they had not received from any teacher. This is the state of the scholar who has mastered his field and who originates the aspects of questions, their causes, their variations and their branches.

It is my clear view that the meaning of "sending down" is not the sending down of magic, since magic was already in existence before. Rather it is the sending down of a matter to the two angels, or the sending down of revelation or inspiration to the two angels, so that they undertook to spread the hidden secrets of magic among learners, in order that the monopoly of a small group over its knowledge would be ended. Thus the first and second difficulties are removed.

Then, the wisdom behind the general teaching of it is that the magicians in Babylon had taken magic as a means to subjugate the common people, in their bodies, their minds and their wealth. Then they aspired from it to establishing the worship of idols and the stars, and they claimed that they (that is, the magicians) were interpreters for them and spoke by the will of the gods. So great corruption occurred and error became widespread. God, according to His customary wisdom, wished to rescue creation from this, so He sent, or revealed, or inspired, Harut and Marut to disclose the subtleties of this craft to people, so that all people would share in it, and they would know that the magicians were not upon anything, and people would return to a state of soundness. Thus the third difficulty is removed.

[Page 641]

As for the fourth difficulty, you will learn its resolution when explaining His words ﴿and they do not teach anyone﴾ [al-Baqara 2:102], the verse. In the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, *al-malikayni* (with a kasra on the lam) is a sound reading in meaning. Its meaning is that two kings who ruled in Babylon had mastered the science of magic. On the reading with a fatha on the lam, the more evident interpretation is that it is a metaphor, and that they were two righteous men who were judges of the city of Babylon and had come to know the secrets of magic which the magicians of Babylon practised. Or they were the ones who originated its basis, and there was no disbelief in it, but people later introduced disbelief into it.

It has also been said that they were two angels whom God sent down, appearing to people in human form, teaching them magic in order to expose the secrets of the magicians. This is because the magicians used to claim that they were gods or messengers, and they subjugated the common people to themselves. So God wished to refute them, defending the station of prophethood, and He sent down two angels for this purpose.

It has been answered that learning magic in the time of Harut and Marut was permissible, as a trial from God for His creation: the obedient would not learn it, and the disobedient would hasten to it. But this is invalid, because it contradicts the generality of His words ﴿they teach people﴾. They said: just as God tested the people of Talut with the river, etc. But the flaw in this analogy is not hidden.

Babylon is an ancient city among the cities of the world. The origin of the name in the Chaldean language is *Bab-Ilu*, that is, "Gate of God." Its equivalent in Hebrew is *Bab-El*. It is a city situated on both banks of the Euphrates, such that the Euphrates cuts through it. Its site is close to the location of the present-day city of Hilla, at a distance of miles from the confluence of the Euphrates and the Tigris.

It was among the greatest cities of the ancient world. It is said that the sons of Noah first built it after the Flood. Then the attention of the people of civilisation to the regions of Iraq continued, in the time of King Nimrod, in the third generation of the sons of Noah. But the beginning of Babylon's greatness was around the year 3755, that is three thousand seven hundred and fifty-five years before Christ. It was one of the four capitals of the Chaldean kingdom, and the greatest and most famous of them. The aspirations of the kings of the two Chaldean and Assyrian dynasties remained directed to building up this city and adorning it. So it was a city of wonders in its buildings and gardens, and a source of Asian knowledge and magical marvels. In ancient times they attributed to it aged wine and magic. Abu al-Tayyib said:

*May God water the days of youth with what delights them, and do the deed of aged Babylonian wine.*

Because Babylon was famous among the ancient nations for the knowledge of magic, as we mentioned earlier in defining magic, it is correct to take the relative clause *"sent down upon the two angels at Babylon"* as an allusion to a story they know.

Harut and Marut are a substitute for "the two angels." They are two Chaldean names, into which a change of definiteness has entered in order to make them conform to the lighter Arabic patterns. The apparent view is that Harut is an arabicised form of *Haruka*, the name of the Moon among the Chaldeans, and that Marut is an arabicised form of *Ma-Rudakh*, the name of Jupiter among them. They used to count the wandering planets among the sacred objects of worship, which are below the gods, especially the Moon, since it is the planet of greatest influence among them in this world, and it is the symbol of the female. Likewise Jupiter, which is the noblest of the seven planets among them, and perhaps it was the symbol of the male among them, just as Baal was among the Canaanites, the Phoenicians.

It is well known that ascribing this sanctity to the stars arose from their belief that these two had been among the righteous and holy, and that after their deaths they were raised to the heavens in the form of stars. So *Haruka* and *Marudakh* had been among their ancient scholars and righteous men, and rulers of the lands, and they were the two who originated magic. Perhaps this is the reason why in the story they are referred to as the two angels with a fatha on the lam.

Among the storytellers there is a fabricated tale, one of the inventions of the Jews in their recent myths, which some exegetes customarily mention, including Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi. The verifying scholars such as al-Baydawi, al-Fakhr, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Arafa have pointed out that it is false and that it is among the narrations of Ka'b al-Ahbar. Some lax narrators of hadith have erred regarding it, attributing its transmission to the Prophet (ﷺ) or to some of the Companions through weak chains. It is surprising that Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may God have mercy on him, narrated it with a chain traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ). Perhaps it was inserted into Imam Ahmad's work, or perhaps the outward appearance of its narrators deceived him, although among them is Musa ibn Jubayr, who is criticised. 'Abd al-Hakim made an excuse, saying that the report is authentic, but what is narrated relates to the reports of the Jews, so it is false in itself while its narrators are truthful in what they relate. This is an ugly excuse, because the report was attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn 'Arafa said in his tafsir: the shaykhs used to criticise Ibn 'Atiyya at this point because of his mention of this story. Some have reported from al-Qarafi that Malik, may God have mercy on him, denied this regarding Harut and Marut.

[Page 643]

His words ﴿and they do not teach anyone﴾ form a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*) relating to Harut and Marut, and *ma* is a negation. The use of the present tense expresses the narrated state (*hikayat al-hal*), indicating that their saying to those learning magic, ﴿we are only a trial﴾, is a statement made simultaneously with the time of teaching, not one that follows it. From this it is known that they were teachers, and this was omitted because it is dispensed with by the implication of this clause. So this is concision by ellipsis (*ijaz al-hadhf*), or it is an implicit meaning understood from the context (*lahn al-khitab*), understood from the clear purpose.

His words ﴿we are only a trial﴾: the word *fitna* (trial) combines the meaning of confusion and disorder in a person's affairs, the scattering of his mind through fear and danger to his life and property, without justice or order. It may be restricted or generalised according to what it is attached to or according to the context. One says "the trial of wealth" and "the trial of religion."

Since this situation causes people's steadfastness to differ according to the soundness of their minds, their patience and their ability to find good ways out of it, testing and examination are among its necessary consequences. So this is among the meanings that the word *fitna* frequently refers to. For this reason some scholars of the language were lax and explained *fitna* as "testing," and what emboldened them to do so is the common saying "I smelted the gold or the silver" when one melts them with fire to distinguish the bad from the good. This usage, if it is not a later (muwallad) usage, is such that the meaning of examination is not regarded in the word *fitna*; rather what is regarded is the turmoil and confusion that occur in melting. The Qur'an called Harut and Marut a *fitna* and said ﴿Indeed, those who put the believing men and believing women to trial﴾ [al-Buruj 85:10], and said ﴿Let not Satan tempt you﴾ [al-A'raf 7:27]. Their reporting about themselves that they are a *fitna* is a report using the verbal noun for emphasis. The emphasis is reinforced by a restrictive construction (*al-hasr al-idafi*). The intention behind this is that they used to declare that there was nothing of divine good in their knowledge, and that it was pure trial, a test from God for His servants regarding the extent of their adherence to their religion. They were a trial only because everyone who learned from them acted upon it. So do not disbelieve, as the magicians disbelieved when they attributed the effects to the gods, and you have come to know its secret. In this there is something that weakens the view that their purpose in teaching people magic was to show the falsity of the magicians who claimed divinity or prophethood.

What appears in the interpretation of this sentence is that their saying ﴿we are only a trial﴾ is a claimed restriction (*qasr idda'i*) for emphasis. They made the great extent to which people were drawn into trial by the magic they undertook to teach equivalent to their attributes being confined to trial. The aspect of

[Page 644]

**[Page 644]**

...their beginning. With this sentence, they (the two angels) should make clear to whoever they teach that this knowledge, in its early stages, appears as a trial and an evil, so that the student is likely to disbelieve when these teachings suddenly confront him, if his soul had already become settled in the belief that the appearance of extraordinary events (*khariq al-'adat*) is a sign of the divinity of the one who displays them. Their saying "﴿So do not disbelieve﴾" means: do not hasten to adopt that belief about us. For if you go deeply into the knowledge of magic, you will know that these phenomena are caused by causes arising from the properties of souls or the properties of things. The trial occurs for the one who learns magic when he sees its outward manifestations and wonders at the hands of magicians, and for the one who is at the beginning of instruction. But when it is verified in his knowledge, the trial is dispelled. This is the meaning of their saying "﴿So do not disbelieve﴾," which is equivalent to "so do not be tempted." Thus the fourth objection mentioned earlier is resolved.

* * *

﴿And they learn from the two what causes separation between a man and his wife. Yet they cannot harm anyone thereby except by God's permission. And they learn what harms them and does not benefit them.﴾

This is a consequence of what is implied by His saying "﴿And they teach no one until they say﴾," which entails that teaching took place, so "they learn" follows. The pronoun in "they learn" refers back to "anyone" (*ahad*) occurring within the scope of negation, governed by the *min* of universal quantification (*min al-istighraqiyya*) in His saying "﴿And they teach no one﴾," for it carries the meaning of "every one," so its signification becomes plural.

His saying "﴿what causes separation between a man and his wife﴾" points to a particular instance of the kinds of magic, and it is its greatest effect, for in it there is the separation between the two parties of a firm bond, which is a bond of affection and mercy. God, exalted is He, said: "﴿And among His signs is that He created for you mates from among yourselves that you may find tranquillity in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy﴾" [al-Rum: 21]. Affection alone is a great bond, namely the bond of friendship and brotherhood and their branches; mercy alone is a bond which includes fatherhood and sonship. So what do you think of a bond that combined both matters and was by God's appointment, and what is not by God's appointment is at the utmost degree of perfection? Our noble shaykh Salim Abu Hajib used to allude to this meaning in His saying "﴿and He placed between you affection and mercy﴾" [al-Rum: 21]. This separation occurs either by using substances that corrupt the intellect of one of the spouses until he hates his spouse, or by casting deceptions, illusions, and slander until they are separated.

His saying "﴿Yet they cannot harm anyone thereby except by God's permission﴾" is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'tarida*). The pronoun in "they" refers back to "anyone" in His saying "﴿And they teach no one﴾," because it occurs in a context of negation and so generalizes to every one of the learners; that is, the learners do not harm anyone by magic. This is a warning that magic has no effect in itself, but that the effect of its tricks varies according to the susceptibility of the one bewitched, and this susceptibility differs and has many states, which the verse summarizes through the exception in His saying "﴿except by God's permission﴾." That is, God makes the causes of susceptibility to the effect of magic present in some souls. This is a good and fitting summary for the condition of the Muslims to whom the address is directed, because they have adopted the character of glorifying God, exalted is He, and His power. The context is not one of detailing the causes and influences, but the intent is to refute the idea that magic has an inherent state and unvarnished rules. Thus the *ba'* in "by God's permission" is for accompaniment (*lil-mula-basa*).

The basic meaning of *idhn* (permission) in the language is the allowance of an act, and *istadhana* means to request permission for an act or to enter a house. The Qur'an has used it metaphorically to mean enablement, either by creating the causes of the act beyond the customary order, as in His saying "﴿and you heal the blind and the leper by My permission﴾" [al-Ma'idah: 110], or by the continuance of the causes deposited in things and powers, as in His saying, exalted is He, "﴿And whatever befell you on the day the two hosts met, it was by God's permission﴾" [Al 'Imran: 166]. So His saying "﴿Yet they cannot harm anyone thereby except by God's permission﴾" means: except by what God has prepared in the receptivity to magic of readiness to be harmed by it, for this readiness and the possibility of being affected is created in its subject, and so it is by God's permission and will. Thus al-Raghib established it, and it returns to a usage in which the word *idhn* is employed. From this category and its like is the word *amr* in His saying "﴿For him are successive angels before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of God﴾" [al-Ra'd: 11], that is, by what God created of things which bring harm upon people. This usage has become well known in the language of the Law until it became a conventional meaning for will and volition. Therefore it should be associated with those terms whose meanings the theologians distinguished: satisfaction, love, command, will, and volition. So the meaning is not that magic may harm and may not harm; rather the meaning is that it causes no harm except what is the delivery of things that are harmful by their nature.

His saying "﴿And they learn what harms them and does not benefit them﴾" means: what harms people with a harm other than separation between a man and his wife. So the pronoun in "harms them" refers to something other than what the pronoun in "they learn" refers to. The meaning is that nothing comes from the matters of magic except harm, that is, in this world. Thus the magician cannot use magic on anyone to make him clever after being dull, or rich after poverty. This is an additional warning about the feebleness of the minds of those occupied with it, and this is the aim of the verse. With this interpretation, the conjunction of His saying "and does not benefit them" is founding, not emphatic. What is considered in this harm and benefit is what occurs in this world. As for their state in the Hereafter, His saying will convey it: "﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾." The verse, by combining the affirmation of harm with the negation of benefit, which is its opposite, conveys the sense of restriction, as if it were said: "they learn what is nothing but harm," like the saying of al-Samaw'al and 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Harithi:

*"Our souls flow over the edges of swords, and over other than the edges of swords they do not flow."*

He turned away from the form of restriction (*qasr*) for the aforementioned subtlety, which is the warning that it is harm. The repetition of the verb "they learn" with the conjunction particle is due to the intervening parenthetical clause.

* * *

﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. And wretched is that for which they sold their souls, if only they had known.﴾

This is coordinated with His saying "﴿and they followed what the devils recited﴾," meaning: they followed all of that, and they certainly knew, etc. The pronoun refers to the Jews, following the pronoun in "they followed." Or the *wa* is for the circumstantial clause, meaning: while their knowledge was verified. The *lam* in "they certainly knew" may be the *lam* of oath (*lam al-qasam*), which is the *lam* that by nature enters the answer of an oath to link it to the oath, and then they often omit the oath, relying on the answer to indicate it by implicit indication, since an answer cannot be arranged without something answered.

It may also be the *lam* of inception (*lam al-ibtida'*), a *lam* that serves to emphasize the oath and frequently enters the beginning of a sentence; for this reason it is called the *lam* of inception. Both possibilities exist in any utterance suitable for an oath in which there is no oath, for omitting the word of oath indicates, in a discursive context, that the speaker is not eager for additional emphasis, just as mentioning *inna* alone for emphasizing a nominal sentence is weaker in emphasis than combining it with the *lam* of inception, since both are instruments of emphasis. Al-Radi said that the positions of the *lam* of oath, in the view of the majority, are all *lams* of inception. The Kufans do not affirm the *lam* of inception and interpret its positions as meaning the omitted oath, and the disagreement on this is close.

The *lam* in His saying "﴿for whoever purchased it﴾" may also be a *lam* of oath, for emphasis of what is known, that is, they knew with certainty that the purchaser of magic has no share. It may also be a *lam* of inception. *Ishtira'* (purchasing) is acquiring a thing by giving something else in exchange, so the meaning is that they acquired it by giving up their faith, which is expressed later in His saying "their souls." *Khalaq* means a portion of good specifically.

In a hadith: "Only the one who has no share (*khalaq*) wears this." And al-Bu'ayth ibn Huraith said:

*"Even if I come close one day, I am not one who sells my share (khalaqi) or my religion to seek the pleasure of love."*

The negation of *khalaq*, which is an indefinite noun, together with the emphasis of the negation by the universal *min*, is evidence that practicing this magic is a crime of disbelief or something less, and therefore its practitioner has no portion of good in the Hereafter. And when every portion of good is negated, all evil is established, because freedom from evil is good, and this is the state of sufficiency, which the virtuous have desired, or something less, out of fear of God, exalted is He.

His saying "﴿And wretched is that for which they sold their souls﴾" is coordinated with "and they certainly knew," a coordination of an expressive (*insha'i*) statement upon a declarative (*khabari*) one. "Sold" (*shara*) here means "gave up," meaning "spent," and it is the counterpart of His saying "whoever purchased it." The meaning of giving up the soul is causing it to be ruined and destroyed.

His saying "﴿if only they had known﴾" implies negation of knowledge by way of the counterfactual *law* (*law al-imtina'iyya*). The knowledge negated of them here is other than the knowledge affirmed for them in His saying "and they certainly knew." What they knew is that the acquirer of magic has no share in the Hereafter, while what they were ignorant of here is that magic is a blameworthy thing. This involves a rebuke to them, since they knew that its practitioner has no share, but they did not realize that the negation of share entails loss, for what follows the truth is only error. This is the correct interpretation, because "﴿if only they had known﴾" is appended to His saying "﴿and wretched is that for which they sold their souls﴾," which indicates that it is the indicator of its object. By this the objection is removed concerning the affirmation and negation of knowledge about one and the same known matter, on the basis that knowing that the practitioner of magic has no share is the very meaning of magic being blameworthy. So how could they be considered as not knowing its blameworthiness? You have known its aspect, and this is what the verse is to be understood as meaning.

There are other answers to resolve the objection, among them: what the author of al-Kashshaf held, and the author of al-Miftah followed, that the intended negation of knowledge is that, since they were in their knowledge like one who does not know by not acting upon it, knowledge is negated from them for not regarding it as valid, that is, this is said as mockery of them. Second: the intended negated knowledge is knowledge that what they practiced is among the forbidden kinds of magic, as though they knew the blame of magic in a universal sense, but did not perceive that their conduct was of it, as they said: the jurist knows the major premise of the syllogism, while the judge and the mufti know the minor premise, and the jurist is like the pharmacist, while the judge and the mufti are like the physician. This is the view we have chosen. Third: the intended "﴿if only they had known﴾" is what follows from it of punishment in the Hereafter; that is, they thought that absence of opposition does not entail punishment, and this is close to what we have mentioned. Fourth: the intended negated knowledge is reflection, and the affirmed knowledge is innate knowledge. This is a very distant view, since it is not possible that their knowledge that whoever acquired magic has no share should be innate knowledge. Had it been said: conceptual knowledge and assentive knowledge, it would have been acceptable. In combining "they certainly knew" with "if only they had known" there is a remarkable antithesis (*tibaq*).

There is another answer, based on the difference in the referent of the pronoun in "they knew" and the two pronouns in "if only they had known." The pronoun in "they certainly knew" refers to the jinn who know magic, and the two pronouns in "﴿if only they had known﴾" refer to the humans who learned magic and sold their souls by it. This was said by Qutrub and al-Akhfash, and by this, those to whom knowledge is affirmed are other than those from whom it is negated.

**[Page 645 marker reference as in source]**

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 103:

﴿And if they had believed and been mindful of God, a reward from God would have been better, if only they knew.﴾

That is: if they had believed in Muhammad and been mindful of God, and so had not proceeded to deny what their scriptures gave good tidings of, there would have been a reward for them from God, and God's reward is better than every benefit that drove them to obstinacy.

"Law" (lau) is a conditional particle indicating the impossibility of the consequent due to the impossibility of the condition, and its condition is joined with anna (that) while the verb in its clause is in the past tense, in accordance with the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Had what I strive for sufficed me for a meager livelihood, and I had not sought a little of wealth..."

Anna, together with its complement, occupies the position of a subject (mubtada') according to the Basran grammarians of the majority, and what is in the complement clause of predicate and subject completes the meaning and so dispenses with a predicate (khabar). It was said that its predicate is omitted, its estimated form being "established" (thabit), that is: "and had their belief been established".

As for his saying "lamathubatun" (a reward), it is more probable that it is the answer (jawab) of lau, for it is joined with the lam that commonly accompanies the answer of an affirmative lau. The answer here is a nominal clause, and it does not usually occur as the answer of lau. This answer was not clearly ordered and dependent upon the conditional clause, because God's reward is better whether the Jews believed and were mindful or did not do so.

Some grammarians said: the answer is omitted, that is: "they would have been rewarded, and a reward from God is better." Sahib al-Kashshaf deviated from this and said: "The nominal clause was preferred in the answer of lau over the verbal one, because of what this implies about the reward's firmness and stability, just as he deviated from the accusative to the nominative in 'salamun 'alaykum' (peace be upon you) for this reason."

His meaning is that the estimated answer is: "they would have been rewarded by God, a better reward for them than what they sold their souls for," or "lamathubatan" in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) substituting for its verb. In either case, the verb or its substitute indicates occurrence (huduth), so it has no indication of permanence and stability.

Since the context requires the reward's occurrence, its stability, and the stability of its being better, so that the combined meanings are achieved, he deviated from the accusative, which signals the verb, to the nominative, because the nominal clause does not indicate occurrence but establishment (thubut). It moves from indicating establishment to indicating continuity and stability. So the indication of the verse on the stability of the reward lies in the change from the accusative of the verbal noun to its nominative, as in "salamun 'alaykum" and "al-hamdu lillah." Its indication of the stability of the attribution of goodness to the reward lies in the attribution being derived from a nominal clause, so the clause becomes like two clauses. The original status of a verbal noun that substitutes for its verb is to indicate an attribution to its agent. If it were said "lamathubatan" in the accusative, its estimated form would be "they would have been rewarded a reward." When it is changed to the nominative verbal noun, what was in it of attribution before the nominative must be taken into account, and since the nominative verbal noun has no attribution in it, the hearer knows that the estimate is "lamathubatun" for them, just as when you say "salaman and hamdan," the hearer knows you mean "I greeted with a greeting and praised with praise," whereas if you say "salamun and hamdun," the estimate is "a greeting from me and praise from me." This is the aspect of the Kashshaf's analogy. The evidence that this verbal noun was originally accusative is its occurrence as the answer of lau, which is rooted in the verbal form. Then, when he hears his saying "khayrun," the hearer knows it is a predicate concerning the reward after its change, and so he acquires the stability of goodness. For this reason the author of the Kashshaf did not address explaining that the clause indicates the stability of goodness for the reward, because by its clarity it needs no explanation, for every nominal clause indicates the stability of its predicate for its subject.

By this the order becomes clear, because the intent of informing about the reward as being better is that it would be established for them if they believed. I have another view, which is to say: his saying "lamathubatun min 'indi Allahi khayrun" is an indication of the answer by way of allusion (ta'rid), for when it was made dependent on his saying "and if they had believed and been mindful," it was understood that in this statement there is something that concerns them. Since lau is an impossibility particle and a complete declarative clause occupies the place of its answer, the hearer knows that this statement's establishment is impossible for whoever has failed the condition of lau, so it is a rebuke against them and a reproach upon them.

It has been said that lau is for wishing (tamanni), in the manner of "lau anna lana karratan" (Q. 2:167). The verification is that the lau used for wishing is the conditional lau, imbued with the meaning of wishing, because the one who is prevented wishes for what is beloved, "and the dearest thing to man is what is withheld." This is supported by the fact that when it comes for wishing it takes two kinds of answer: an accusative answer like the answer of laita (would that), and an answer joined with lam like the answer of the impossibility lau, as in the saying of al-Muhalhil:

"Had he dug up the graves for Kulayb, he would inform about the Dhanaib, what kind of Zir..."

"And on the day of al-Sha'thamayn, my eye would have been cooled, and how is meeting with those under the graves?"

The answer was given by his saying "fa-yukhbiru" and his saying "laqarra 'ayna." The wishing, according to this estimate, is a metaphor from God, exalted be He, for calling to faith and obedience, or an illustration of the state of one who calls to that by the state of one who wishes, so it uses for it the composition established for wishing. Or it is what, if an Arab spoke it in this context, he would have spoken with wishing, in the manner of what was said about His saying "la'allakum tattaqun" (Q. 2:21) and the like. On this view, his saying "lamathubatun" is a fresh resumption, and the lam is for an oath.

Al-mathubah is the verbal noun of "athaba" when he gives reward, and ath-thawab is the recompense given to the one who does good. It is said "thawaba" and "athwaba" in the sense of "athaba," so al-mathubah is on the pattern of al-maf'ulah, like al-masdaqah, al-mashurah, and al-makruhah.

His saying "law kanu ya'lamun" (if only they knew) is a second conditional whose answer is omitted, because of what precedes it, and the object of "ya'lamun" is omitted, because of "lamathubatun min Allahi khayrun." That is: if they knew God's reward, they would not have bought magic.

The repetition of a word or clause in the endings of the Qur'an is not a fault of monotony (iytha'), because monotony is only faulted in poetry and not in prose, since in prose one only takes into account conformity to the situation's demand. The benefit of this repetition is to record against them that they do not know what the true benefit is.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 104:

﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Raina" (Ra'ina), but say, "Unzurna" (Unzurna), and listen. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾

In a verse such as this, it is necessary to seek its occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) so that its place and the aspect of its meaning become clear. The prohibition against the believers saying a word in which there is neither blame nor levity must have a cause. They have mentioned, regarding its occasion of revelation, that when the Prophet (ﷺ) delivered the Law and the Qur'an to the Muslims, they would ask him to repeat it and to speak slowly in his delivery until they understood it and retained it. So they would say to him, "Raina, O Messenger of Allah," meaning: do not be burdened by us, and be gentle with us. The hypocrites among the Jews would revile the Prophet (ﷺ) secretly in their private gatherings. They had a word in Hebrew that resembled the word "raina" in Arabic, and its meaning in Hebrew was abuse. It was also said that its meaning was, "May you not hear," as a supplication. So some of them said to others, "We used to revile Muhammad in secret, so let us now do it openly," or they said this and meant by it the active participle of "ra'ana," meaning one who is characterized by foolishness, as will come. Thus they would say this word to the Muslims while intending by it abuse. Allah exposed them and nullified their scheme by forbidding the Muslims from saying this word, so that the hypocrites would desist from it and would know that Allah had informed His Prophet of their secret.

The occasion of the revelation of this verse, following the preceding verses about sorcery and what arose from condemning it, is this: as we have mentioned, sorcery returns to deception (tamwih). Among the kinds of sorcery is deception by words, and it is founded on the belief that words have an effect on the one who is bewitched according to the intention of the sorcerer and his psychological orientation toward the one bewitched. This had become deeply rooted among the Jews, who were convinced of it in opposing their enemies. Since harming a person by a word or an act whose meaning is not known, such as addressing him with a word that conveys a meaning while the speaker intends harm by it, or an insult that depicts him, or trampling on his shadow, all of this returns to relying on intention and orientation in bringing about harm, this resembled some kinds of sorcery. For this reason, it was a mark of those whom sorcery had enticed and who had bought it. So the mention of this condition among their states was appropriate, following the discussion of their being seduced by sorcery and their love for it, rather than the rest of their states mentioned earlier. This appropriateness is the reason for the sequencing in mention. This verse is separated from what precedes it because the two aims differ: this verse is for the discipline of the believers, and then there arises from it an allusion to the Jews in their hypocrisy and their harm, and an indication to them that Allah has informed His Prophet of their scheme. They used to consider the bewitched person's awareness of sorcery as nullifying its effect, so awareness of evil intentions resembles it. Also, the explicit verses before it concern their religious conditions, which contradict the foundations of their religion. Moreover, a speech that opens with a vocative and an admonition, such as "O people" (ya ayyuha al-nas), "O Zayd" (ya Zayd), and "Alla" (alla) and similar, does not suit being joined by conjunction to what precedes it. It should be considered that a speech which opens in such a way that it can only be conjoined by "fa" (fa) when it is sequential to what precedes it, because conjunction by "fa" is more distant from conjunction by "wa" (wa) and broader in terms of appropriateness.

"Raina" is an imperative from "raa-ahu, yurawiihi," and it is an intensive form of "ra-ahu, yar'aahu," meaning he guarded it with his gaze from destruction and loss. "Ra'i" is like "ra'a," as Tarafa said: "A gentle one who tends to a gazelle in a thicket." It was used metaphorically for preserving a person's interest, being gentle with him, and watching over his benefit. This metaphor became so common that it became a conventional literal meaning. From it comes "ra'aaka Allah" (may Allah watch over you) and "ra'a dhimamahu" (he honored his covenant). So the Muslims' saying to the Prophet (ﷺ), "Raina," is an imperative verb from pasturing in the figurative sense, that is, gentleness and watchfulness, meaning: do not be burdened by our request, and be gentle with us. His saying, "﴿And say, 'Unzurna'﴾," replaced their saying "raina" with a word that equals it in literal and figurative meaning, in number of letters, and in intended sense, without the disbelievers being able to use it as a pretext to harm the Prophet (ﷺ). This is among the most eloquent of rhetorical features. If "unzur" is taken literally in the sense of watching over, and it becomes figurative for managing interests, and from it comes the jurists' saying, "This is of consideration (min al-nazar)," meaning gentleness and watchfulness in facilitation, then it is established that his saying "unzurna" is with a pronounced hamzat al-wasl and a pronounced "zay," and that it is from "al-nazar" (looking/considering) and not from "al-intizar" (waiting).

This verse indicates the legitimacy of a principle of the foundations of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), which is among the foundations of the Maliki school, and is called blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i'), namely the means by which one reaches a forbidden matter.

His saying, "﴿and listen﴾," is intended as a particular kind of hearing, which is comprehension and greater attentiveness, so that they would not need to ask for consideration or attention. It was also said that by "listen" he meant "obey the commands of the Messenger." This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya, and it is more apparent.

His saying, "﴿And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾," the definite article is for prior reference (al-ahd), and by "the disbelievers" is meant the Jews specifically, meaning: behave courteously yourselves toward the Messenger, and do not imitate the Jews in their statements, for they will have a painful punishment. The expression "the disbelievers" instead of "the Jews" is an increase in their condemnation. It is not a concluding generalization (tadhyil) here, because the preceding speech is addressed to the believers, so what follows cannot suitably be a general rule about the disbelievers as a conclusion to what precedes it.
