**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 105:**

﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, and the polytheists, do not wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord. But God singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and God is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ It is separated from what precedes it because the two purposes differ. The verse before it concerns the discipline of the believers, with an allusion to the Jews. This verse explains the envy of the Jews and others toward the Muslims. The connection between the two verses is clear, since their outcome is the same, and because the motive for abuse and harm is envy.

This verse returns to uncovering the cause that prevented the Jews from believing in the Qur'an when they were told: (Believe in what God has sent down. They said: "We believe in what was sent down to us.") That is, what turned them away was not their adherence to what was revealed to them, but envy of what God revealed to the Prophet and the Muslims of good. He then demonstrated the evidence that their obstacle was not their rigidity and adherence to their religion, through His saying ﴿Say: Why then did you kill the prophets of God?﴾ (2:91), and what came between that and what resulted from it of disputes, the exposure of their turning away from the commands of their religion, and their following of magic. Now he clarifies the true nature of the obstacle and the cause of insult and false speech, in order to move from that to explaining abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one).

Al-widd (with a damma on the waw) means love. Whoever loves something wishes for it, so widd is not specifically wishing, nor is it excessive love, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) verified.

He mentioned "those who disbelieve" here rather than "the Jews" in order to make this ruling include both the Jews and the Christians together, as a preparation for what comes later about the wisdom of abrogation and His saying ﴿They say: None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ (2:111), and so on. By His saying ﴿those who disbelieve among the People of the Book﴾, rather than "what the People of the Book wish," he draws attention to the fact that they did not follow their Book, because their Books command them to follow the truth wherever they find it, and to believe in the Prophet who comes after them. In the Torah and the Gospel there are many passages containing the taking of a covenant on this. So when they envied the Prophet ﷺ for prophethood, and envied the Muslims, they disbelieved in what their books had commanded. With this, the discourse reached a combination of admonishing the Christians together with admonishing the Jews.

Since the context's expression "those who disbelieve among the People of the Book" might suggest that "among the People of the Book" is a restricting condition, and that disbelievers other than the People of the Book do not envy the Muslims, he joined to it His saying "nor the polytheists," as a safeguard, and so that the ruling would encompass all of them. Thus it has a share in the preparation for His saying later ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God from having His name mentioned in them?﴾ (2:114).

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read *an yunazzala* with the *zay* doubled and fatha. The use of *tanzil* rather than *inzal* reflects the actual event, since the Qur'an was revealed in installments (munajjaman), to make it easier to memorize, understand and write down, and for ease upon those under obligation in establishing the rulings gradually. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the *zay* lightened and also fatha, on the basis that the negation of their wishing is connected to the general sending down of the Qur'an, whether it was all at once or in installments.

Al-khayr means blessing and bounty. Al-Nabigha said:

*"I am not upon a good that came to you with an envier."*

Here he intends by it prophethood and what supported it of revelation, the Qur'an and victory, which is what is expressed by mercy in His saying ﴿God singles out for His mercy﴾ and His saying ﴿God singles out for His mercy whom He wills﴾. It is coordinated with *yawaddu* (what they wish), because it implies that God wanted that, even if they did not want it. Mercy here is like the good sent down to them, and that is an inclusion (idmaj) of a favour upon them, that what was sent down to them is mercy for them. The meaning of *ikhtisas* (singling out) is making it for one person rather than another, because the root of *ikhtisas* and *takhsis* goes back to this meaning, namely making a ruling specific rather than general, whether it singles out one or more. The object of the will (mashi'a) is omitted, as is usual when a phrase precedes it or follows it, meaning: whoever He wills to single out for mercy. Mashi'a is irada (will). Since God's will is connected to what He wills in accordance with His knowledge, exalted is He,

[Page 654]

His will, that is His determination, proceeds in accordance with His wisdom, which is one of the modes of God's knowledge. So it is among the connections of divine knowledge to the bringing forth of events as they should be. This matter has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You are indeed the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾.

So God singles out for His mercy whomever He knows to be worthy of it, especially the mercy whose intended meaning is prophethood, for God singles out for it among His creatures whoever is receptive to it. He creates him with a pure inner nature and a sound disposition suitable for receiving revelation little by little. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when he reached his maturity and was firm, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾ (28:14). And God said: ﴿He knows best where to place His messages﴾ (6:124). For this reason prophethood is not attained by acquisition, because God creates for prophethood whoever He wills for it, due to the great importance of its matter, unlike other virtues. These are attainable by acquisition, like righteousness, knowledge and others. Thus many a sinner has had his condition set right, and many a utterly ignorant person has become learned through striving and acquisition. Yet even so, the recipient of prophethood must have some readiness in general. Beyond that is success (tawfiq) and God's care for His servant.

Since the readiness for the degrees of mercy, from prophethood downward, is not apparent to people, he folded up the carpet of its detailed explanation, because it is impossible, and left it to God's will, which is connected only to what He knows and what His wisdom, glorified is He, requires, out of kindness to the understandings of the addressees.

His saying ﴿and God is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil), because bounty (fadl) includes the giving of good and treating with mercy. It is also an alert that the duty of one who desires good is to seek out God's bounty and to desire Him, that He may manifest Himself to him in the attribute of bounty and mercy, so that he withdraws from sins and vices and adorns himself with virtues and acts of obedience, perhaps his Lord will love him. In the authentic hadith: "Get to know God in ease, and He will know you in hardship."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 106–107 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Whatever abrogation We abrogate, or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it.﴾ The connection (munasabah) of this verse with the verses before it is that the Jews made an excuse for their turning away from believing in the Prophet (ﷺ) by saying: ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], by which they meant that they disbelieve in anything other than it. In this excuse of theirs, they claimed that their law (shari'ah) cannot be abrogated, and they said that Muhammad (ﷺ) described the Torah as true and that he came confirming it, so how could his law nullify the Torah? They deceived people with what they named al-bada' (the notion of a change of divine intention), which is the necessity that God, exalted is He, would not know what legislation is good, and that the matter would appear to Him, then He would turn away from it and replace one law with another.

We have already mentioned that God, exalted is He, refuted their excuse and exposed them by showing that they do not truly adhere to their law such that they would be steadfast in it, and this is from His saying: ﴿Say: Why then did you kill the prophets of God before?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], and His saying
Page 655
﴿Say: If the Last Abode with God is yours alone﴾ [al-Baqarah: 94], etc., and that they have no motive except envy, by His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book do not wish that any good be sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105], up to His saying "the Possessor of great bounty," indicating that the cause is envy. When He had clarified the refutation of them in all of that, He intended to dismantle that sophistry or doubt which they sought to promote among people by denying abrogation. The primary purpose of this is to teach the Muslims a foundational principle of the laws, namely the principle of abrogation, which occurs when one law is replaced by a law after it, and occurs when some rulings of one law are replaced by rulings from that law that nullify them. Because this is the primary purpose, He turned away from addressing the Jews with a refutation and directed the address to the Muslims, as indicated by His saying "Do you not know" and His connecting it to it with His saying: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108], and His saying: ﴿Whatever abrogation We abrogate﴾, and He did not say "of a law." In this there is a turning away from addressing the Jews, because teaching the Muslims is more important, and this entails a refutation of the Jews by way of parity, for when the wisdom of changing some rulings for a benefit becomes apparent, the wisdom of changing some laws becomes apparent.

Some exegetes have mentioned a occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) for this verse. In al-Kashshaf and al-Ma'alim it is said: it was revealed when the Jews said: "Do you not see Muhammad commanding his companions with a matter and then forbidding them from it?" In the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi, the Jews criticized the change of the qiblah and said: "Muhammad commands his companions with something and forbids them from it, so this Qur'an is only from himself, and for that reason some of it contradicts other parts."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (nansakh) with a fatha on the first nun and a fatha on the sin, and this is the basic form of the imperfect of (nasakha). Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the first nun and a kasra on the sin, as the imperfect of (ansakha) with the hamzah of transitivity, meaning: We command the abrogation of a verse. (ma) is conditional, and its original is the relative pronoun, which has absorbed the meaning of the condition; therefore it is a noun of condition that takes the i'rab of objects, and it is clarified by what explains its vagueness. It also imposes vagueness regarding the times of the connection, because the connection, which is the conditional linkage, when attached to something vague becomes vague, so it does not indicate a specific time among the times of linking the response to the condition and its connection to it.

And "min ayah" is an explanation (bayan) of (ma). The word (ayah) originally means a proof and a sign of a matter. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:
Who among us has, from the good in his presence, three signs, in all of which is judgment?
Page 656
Its pattern is fi'alah, with the middle letter vowelled, according to al-Khalil, and its middle letter is a ya' or a waw, which became alif because it was vowelled and the letter before it was open. The relative form is ayiyy or awiyy. Then the word ayah was applied to the miracle, because it is the proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger; God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We send not the signs except as a warning﴾ [al-Isra': 59]. The word ayah is also applied to a portion of the Qur'an containing a legal ruling, an admonition, or the like, and this is a Qur'anic usage; God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another—and God knows best what He sends down—they say: "You are only a fabricator." Rather, most of them do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 101]. This is supported by the fact that among the meanings of ayah in Arabic speech is the sign that the sender gives to the messenger so that the recipient will confirm him. When they sent a message or news with a messenger, they attached a sign which they called an ayah, especially when a captive was sent to his people with a message, as Nashib al-A'war did when he was a captive among the Banu Sa'd ibn Malik and sent a message to his people in La'nabar, intending to warn them of what their enemies who captured him were plotting against them, and he said to the messenger: "Tell them such and such, with the sign that I ate with you hays." And Suhaym al-Abd said:
By your life, O youth, convey to her from me, with the sign of what came to us swaying gently.
For this reason they also called a message an ayah, naming a thing by the name of what is customarily associated with it. The meaning of ayah here is the ruling of the verse, whether its wording is removed or its wording is kept, because the aim is to explain the wisdom of nullifying rulings, not the removal of Qur'anic words.

Naskh (abrogation) is the removal of one thing by another, as al-Raghib said. It is thus an expression for removing a form or substance and establishing something else in its place. One says: the sun abrogated the shade, because its ray removed the shade and replaced it in its place; and the shade abrogated the sun in the same way, because the image of the body which came between the illuminated body and the ray of the sun that lit it has replaced the ray in its place. It is also said: I transferred (nasakhtu) what was in the hive of bees and honey to another hive. It may be used for removal alone without replacement, as when they say: the wind abrogated the trace. It may also be used for establishment, but for a specific establishment, namely the establishment of what removes. As for its use for mere establishment, I do not think this is correct in the language, even though the apparent sense of al-Raghib's words may suggest it. It has also been derived from it that they say: "I abrogated the book" when you copy the letters of its like into your page, since they found it to be pure establishment; but this is a misconception, because the use of naskh for copying the letters of a book is a figurative usage by way of the image, or a representation of the state by the state of one who removes the letters from the original book to the copied book, after which the copy came about from that. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We were having your deeds copied﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29], and He said: ﴿And in its copy is guidance and mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 154]. As for the saying of people, "the child is a copy of his father," it is a metaphor upon a metaphor. Naskh is not used for cessation without removal; one does not say "the night abrogated the day," because the night is not an existing matter but rather the original darkness resulting from the absence of the luminous body.

The meaning of naskh here is removal and the establishment of a replacement, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿We bring one better than it or similar to it﴾. This is what the scholars of usul (usuliyyun) know as the lifting of a legislative ruling by a textual address (khitab). Thus, new legislation (al-tashri' al-musta'naf) is excluded, since it is not a lifting. And by our saying "legislative ruling," the lifting of the original exemption (al-bara'ah al-asliyyah) by new legislation is excluded.

For the original exemption is not a legislative ruling; rather it is the remaining in the absence of obligation (taklif) that people were in before the coming of the law, such that the law does not address the stipulation of the permissibility of permissible things except in a place where there is a suspicion of their prohibition, or in a place restricting the prohibited things or the obligatory things. The first is like His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198], regarding trade during the Hajj, since the Muslims thought trade was forbidden during the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah as the Jahiliyyah had practiced after departing from Dhu al-Majaz, as will come. An example of the second is His saying: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], after mentioning the forbidden women, and His saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to approach your wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], to restrict the obligation of abstention to the specific time of the day. From their saying in the definition "lifting of a ruling" it is understood that this ruling was established were it not for its lifting, and some have stated this explicitly. Therefore we chose to add a qualifier to the definition, namely "the lifting of a legislative ruling whose continuity is known, by a textual address that lifts it," so as to exclude from the definition of naskh the lifting of a legislative ruling limited by an end-point when that end-point is reached, and the lifting of a ruling derived from a command that has no evidence of repetition.

Since the wisdom of abrogating verses has become clear, the wisdom of abrogating laws by one another is known from it, and this is what they denied. They denied that Islam had abrogated the Torah, and they claimed that the continuity of the Torah prevents belief in Islam, just as they said: "We believe in what was revealed to us." And abrogation of laws has several states. The first: the coming of a law for a people in a temporary manner for the duration of the life of the Messenger who was sent with it.
Page 658
When he dies, the law is lifted, as with the laws of Noah, Abraham, Joseph, and Shu'ayb. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Joseph had already come to you﴾ [Ghafir: 34] up to His saying ﴿until when he perished, you said: "God will never send after him a messenger"﴾ [Ghafir: 34]. The people remained in an interval (fatrah), and everyone who wanted guidance could follow that law or part of it, just as they followed the law of Abraham. When a law came after it, the second is not truly abrogating the first, but it is an abrogation by which people are given the choice in following it, which was their right during the interval, just as the tribe of 'Abs, for example, was permitted to follow the law of Abraham; when Khalid ibn Sinan came to them with his law, following it became obligatory upon them. The second: a law comes for a people who are commanded to remain upon it, as the law of Moses, and then a law comes after it which does not lift that law in its entirety, but lifts some of its rulings and confirms others, as the law of Jesus. This is an abrogating law in general, since it abrogates some and clarifies some. The Messiah was a messenger who abrogated part of the Torah, namely what he explicitly stated to be abrogated; as for the rest, it remains upon the rulings of the Torah, so he is mostly an explainer, reminder, and interpreter, like those who preceded him among the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah the elder, Daniel, and their like. This type does not contradict the abrogation of the rulings of a single law except by means of a second messenger. The third: the coming of one law after another in such a way that the second nullifies the first in a general nullification, such that that law is regarded as invalid, whether in those rulings where the second law states something that contradicts what is in the first, or in what the second law is silent about. This is Islam in relation to the laws that preceded it, for it lifted all the laws such that it is not permitted for any Muslim to adopt anything from the earlier laws in matters the Islamic law has not addressed at all; rather he derives the rulings of such matters by inference (istinbat), analogy (qiyas), and other methods of the principles of Islam. It has been disputed whether the law of those before us is a law for us where no abrogating text has come; but that disagreement concerns another piece of evidence, namely His saying: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. His saying "or cause it to be forgotten": Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read (nunsihā) with a damma on the first nun and a kasra on the sin, then a ha'. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (nansa'hā) with a fatha on the first nun and a fatha on the sin, followed by a silent hamzah, then a ha'. On the reading without hamzah, it is from forgetting (nisyan), and the hamzah is for transitivity, its object is omitted for generality, meaning: We cause people to forget it, by the command of the Prophet (ﷺ) to stop reciting it until the Muslims forget it. On the reading with hamzah, the meaning is "or We postpone it," that is, We postpone its recitation or We postpone acting upon it, and the aim is the nullification of acting by its recitation or by its ruling.
Page 659

[Page 660]

Thus it was described metaphorically as *al-nasi'* (postponement), which is another category, opposed to *naskh* (abrogation). It is that the Messenger does not remind people to act upon a legislated ruling, and does not order those who neglect it to make up for it, until people forget to act upon it. That would amount to nullifying the ruling, because if it were still in force, the Messenger would not have stayed silent about reiterating the command to it, nor would one who neglects its obligation have been left unrebuked when its requirement applied. I have not found an example of this in the Qur'an. Its parallel in the Sunnah is the saying of the Messenger of God: "None of you should prevent his neighbour from placing a piece of wood in his wall," according to those who hold that the prohibition in it is for forbiddance (*tahrim*). This was the view of Abu Hurayra, and for this reason he used to mention this hadith and say: "Why do I see you turning away from it? By God, I will strike it among you."

The meaning of *al-nasa'* (postponement) implies a delay that is followed by confirmation. Accordingly, the meaning is either that the ruling remains for a period without being abrogated, or that the verse remains in the Qur'an for a period without being abrogated. Or the intended meaning may be causing the verse to be forgotten, in the sense of delaying its coming, with God's will that this occur after a time. The hypothetical possibilities regarding the abrogation of a ruling of the Shari'a apply to the abrogation of one Shari'a by another, and to its causing to be forgotten or its postponement.

His saying ﴿We bring something better than it or its like﴾ is the answer to the conditional clause. Making it an answer implies that these two states, namely abrogation and causing to be forgotten or postponement, do not separate from two states: the bringing, at the time of abrogation and at the time of causing to be forgotten, of something better than the abrogated or its like, or better than the forgotten or postponed or its like. So what is brought with abrogation is the abrogating (*nasikh*) Shari'a or ruling, and what is brought with causing to be forgotten, from forgetting, is also the abrogating Shari'a or ruling, or it is a ruling that comes from the rulings which is not abrogating but is a contrary ruling descending after the other. What is brought with postponement, that is, delay, is what accompanies the remaining ruling from the rulings revealed during the period in which there is no abrogation.

I have left the aspects of being better and being similar in general terms, so that the mind of the listener may go in every possible direction, and you will find it intended. For being better may be in terms of including what suits the interest of the people, or what averts harm from them, or what brings about praiseworthy outcomes, or what contains great reward, or what contains gentleness toward those under obligation and mercy toward them in times of hardship, even if imposing hardship upon them may sometimes be more beneficial.

It is not meant that every form of the hypothetical cases of abrogation, causing to be forgotten, or postponement includes both the better and the similar together. Rather, what is meant is that each form of them does not lack including either the better than it or the similar to it. For this reason ﴿or⟩ was used in His saying ﴿something better than it or its like﴾, so it conveys one of the two things, while the combination is still permissible.

[Page 660 continues]

The realisation of these forms is in your hands. Let us give examples that point to the intended meaning and suffice in place of the rest, without adhering to the order of presentation, according to the most correct view. We say:

(1) Abrogation of a Shari'a together with bringing something better than it, like the abrogation of the Torah and the Gospel by Islam.

(2) Abrogation of a Shari'a together with bringing one similar to it, like the abrogation of the Shari'a of Hud by the Shari'a of Salih. Each has a benefit similar to the other in determining the conditions of two nations with closely related customs and morals. Hud forbade them from building a monument on every high place as a diversion, whereas Salih did not forbid this, but forbade harming the she-camel.

(3) Abrogation of a ruling within a Shari'a by something better than it, like the abrogation of the disapproval of wine established by His saying ﴿In them is great sin and benefits﴾ [al-Baqara: 219] by its prohibition absolutely. This abrogating ruling is better in terms of benefit, but not in terms of gentleness. The abrogating ruling may also be better in gentleness, like the abrogation of the prohibition of eating, drinking, and approaching women during the nights of Ramadan after the time of breaking the fast at sunset, when the fasting person had slept before having the evening meal, by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to approach your wives﴾ [al-Baqara: 187], up to His saying: "from the dawn." In the hadith in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, it is said: "So the Muslims rejoiced at its descent."

(4) Abrogation of a ruling in the Shari'a by a ruling similar to it, like the abrogation of the bequest to parents and relatives by the determination of the shares of inheritance. Each is beneficial to all in giving them wealth. And like the abrogation of the obligation of fifty prayers by five prayers, with the reward of the fifty being granted for the five, so both are equal in terms of reward. And like the abrogation of the verse ﴿And for those who are able to fast, there is a ransom of feeding a poor person﴾ [al-Baqara: 184] by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], up to His saying ﴿and that you fast is better for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 184]. So the affirmation that fasting is better than the ransom.

(5) Causing to be forgotten in the sense of postponement of a Shari'a together with the coming of something better than it: the delay of the appearance of the religion of Islam at the time of the coming of Shari'as which preceded it, each of which was better in relation to the nation for which it was legislated and the age in which it was legislated. Shari'as come to people with what suits their conditions, until all of mankind becomes prepared to accept the final Shari'a, which is the religion with God. So the betterness here is in some of its meanings, and it is relative.

(6) Causing a Shari'a to be forgotten in the sense of postponing its coming, with God's will that it occur after a time, and together with bringing one similar to it, like the postponement of the Shari'a of Jesus at the time of bringing the Shari'a of Moses, while it is better than it in that it includes most of the interests and what the nation needs.

(7) Causing to be forgotten in the sense of postponing the intended ruling together with bringing something better than it, like the postponement of the prohibition of wine, which was intended, together with bringing its disapproval or its prohibition only during the times of the prayers. For what was brought is better than the prohibition in terms of gentleness toward people in bringing them to abandon something they had become attached to by their love for it.

(8) Causing a Shari'a to be forgotten in the sense of its remaining unabrogated until a known term, together with bringing something better than it, that is, more extensive and more general in benefit, and greater

[Page 661]

in reward, but in another nation, or one similar to it likewise.

(9) Causing a verse of the Qur'an to be forgotten in the sense of its remaining unabrogated until a known term, together with bringing something better than it in another chapter, that is, more general in benefit, or one similar to it in another chapter, that is, similar in benefit or reward, like the prohibition of wine at the time of the prayers. During that period there descends the prohibition of trading at the time of the Friday prayer.

(10) Forgetting a Shari'a in the sense of its dissolution, like the Shari'a of Adam and Noah with the coming of the Shari'a of Moses, which is more excellent and more extensive, and like the Shari'a of Idris, for example, which is similar to the Shari'a of Noah.

(11) Forgetting the ruling of a Shari'a together with the coming of something better than it or similar to it. In what was revealed were ten known sucklings that establish prohibition, which were abrogated by five known sucklings. Then both were forgotten together, and the verse ﴿and your sisters through nursing﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] came in absolute terms. All are equal in establishing the foster relationship, and there is no hardship upon those under obligation in one suckling or ten, because the quantity is close.

It has been said that what is meant by forgetting (*nisyan*) is abandonment (*tark*). In that case its meaning and forms return to the meaning and forms of causing to be forgotten in the sense of postponement.

The purpose of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We bring something better than it or its like﴾ is to show the ultimate of wisdom and to refute them, by [showing] that it does not matter to them whether a Shari'a is abrogated by a Shari'a, or a ruling in a Shari'a by another ruling. This does not detract from God's knowledge, nor from His wisdom, nor from His lordship. For He did not abrogate a law or a ruling, nor abandon it, except that He had already compensated people with what is more beneficial to them than it at that time, or with what is similar to it in terms of time and circumstance. And whenever He postponed a ruling for a period and then manifested it afterward, He had already compensated people, during the time of its postponement, with what fills its place according to their conditions. This is the manifestation of lordship (*rububiyya*), for He nurtures creation and guides them to their interests together with gentleness toward them and mercy. God's intention in all those times and circumstances is one: the preservation of the order of the world and the regulation of people's conduct within it in a manner that protects their conditions from disorder according to the eras, the nations, and the circumstances, until He brought the final Shari'a. This is God's intention from people, and for this reason He said, ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 19], and He also said, ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura: 13], and the verse.

The apparent meaning is that bringing something better or something similar applies to each of abrogation and causing to be forgotten. So bringing something better than the abrogated or the forgotten, or something similar to it, is the case, and the statement is not of the figure of speech called *laff wa nashr* (wrapping and unfolding). Thus His saying, exalted is He, (﴿We bring something better than it or its like﴾) is either the bringing of compensation or the bringing of reinforcement. The distribution of this rule over the previously mentioned forms is not difficult.

[Page 662]

And the meaning is: We have not left creation in a time without guidance (*suda*). And that there is nothing in abrogation from which *bada'* (a change of mind in God's knowledge) might be supposed.

In the verse there is a wonderful brevity in division, which has gathered these forms that you have heard, and forms that branch out from them, which I do not ask you to supply, because no form is assumed after this except that you have already recognised it.

Among what makes the hair stand on end, and what should not be turned to, is what some of the exegetes said regarding His saying, "*nunsiha*" (We cause it to be forgotten): that it means God's causing the Muslims to forget the verse or the chapter, that is, removing it from their hearts, or His causing the Prophet ﷺ to forget it. Then the forgetting of all people of it at one time would be evidence of abrogation. They cited for this a hadith which al-Tabarani narrated with its chain to Ibn 'Umar: "He said: Two men recited a chapter which the Messenger of God ﷺ had taught them. They stood one night praying, but could not recall a single letter of it. So they went in the morning to the Messenger of God ﷺ and mentioned that to him. He said to them: 'It is of what was abrogated and caused to be forgotten, so leave it aside.'" Ibn Kathir said: "In the chain of this hadith is Sulayman ibn Arqam, and he is weak." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is a munkar hadith, which al-Tabarani alone narrated as a gharib. How could the like of it remain hidden from the imams of hadith?"

The correct view is that the forgetting by the Prophet of what God intended to abrogate, and did not intend to establish as Qur'an, is permissible, that is, though it did not occur. As for forgetting that is a flaw among humans, the Prophet is protected from it before conveyance. After conveyance and the Muslims' preservation of it, it is permissible. It has been related that he dropped a verse from a chapter during prayer, and when he finished he said to Ubayy: "Why did you not remind me?" He said: "I thought it had been lifted." He said: "No, but I forgot it." End of quotation. My view is that the incidental forgetting which is afterward remembered is permissible, and the verse is not to be understood as referring to it, because it contradicts the apparent meaning of His saying: (﴿We bring something better than it or its like﴾). As for the continuous forgetting of the Qur'an, I think it is not permissible. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6] is evidence for this, and His saying: (﴿except what God wills﴾ [al-A'la: 7]) is an expansion of the promise. The explanation of that will come in the chapter of al-A'la.

As for what is related in the Sahih of Muslim from Anas, who said: "We used to recite a chapter which we likened in length to *Bara'a*, and then it was forgotten, except that I retained from it: 'If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would seek a third; and nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust; and God turns in forgiveness to whoever repents.'" End of quotation. This is *gharib*, and its interpretation is that there was a chapter whose recitation and rulings were abrogated. The forgetting by the Muslims of what its wording was abrogated from the Qur'an is not strange. Moreover, it is a *gharib* hadith.

This verse has indicated that abrogation occurs. The scholars of Islam have agreed on the permissibility of abrogation and its occurrence. None has disagreed about this except Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, Muhammad ibn Bahr. It has been said that his disagreement is verbal, and the detail

[Page 663]

...in the books of the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*). They divided the abrogation (*naskh*) of the textual evidences for rulings and their implications into categories. The first is the abrogation of both the recitation and the ruling together, which is the basic form, and they illustrated it with what was narrated from Abu Bakr: "It was among what was revealed: *Do not turn away from your fathers, for it is disbelief in you to turn away from your fathers.*" The second is the abrogation of the ruling while the recitation remains. This does occur, because preserving the recitation serves the purpose of keeping the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the verse through its eloquence. An example is the verse ﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast ones﴾ [al-Anfal: 65] and the verses that follow it. The third is the abrogation of the recitation while the ruling remains. They illustrated it with what was narrated from Umar: "It was among what was recited: *The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, then stone them both.*" In my view, however, there is no benefit in abrogating the recitation while the ruling remains. They have interpreted Umar's words, "It was among what was recited," to mean that it was recited among the people in order to publicize its ruling.

Many of the Companions held that when the ruling of a verse is abrogated, its writing is not kept in the codex (*mushaf*). In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, in the chapter on tafsir, Ibn al-Zubayr said: I said to Uthman, "Concerning ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 240], it has been abrogated by the other verse, so why do you write it?" He said: "O son of my brother, I will not change anything of it from its place."

* * *

﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things capable?﴾ ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper?﴾ These are brought to explain the wisdom of abrogation and the bringing of something better or similar, in a non-detailed explanation following the method of the wise style (*al-uslub al-hakim*). This is because, after finishing his warning that the abrogation which they considered improbable and used as a pretext to deny the Messenger is never separate from replacing the abrogated ruling with something better than it or similar to it, or from strengthening what remains with something similar, he wished to move from that to uncovering the doubt that remained. That doubt is that the denier would say: "What is the benefit of abrogation, such that it requires a replacement?" The apparent course would have been to take up the explanation of the differences in interests (*masalih*), their suitability to circumstances and eras, and the detailed explanation of what is better or similar in each abrogating and abrogated ruling. But since undertaking that is something the minds of the listeners cannot grasp, because of the difficulty of understanding the ranks of interests and their variation, which requires establishing rules from foundational principles of the Shari'ah and of governance, he turned them away from explaining that, and the interest was summarized for them by referring them to the power of Allah, which nothing possible and willed escapes, and to the vastness of His dominion, which indicates the greatness of His knowledge, and to the creatures' need of Him, since they have no lord other than Him and no guardian besides Him. That is sufficient as proof that He will guide them to their interests in all circumstances. What makes this turn even more fitting is that undertaking the explanation would open the door to dispute over establishing the interest and over the variation of that according to the differences in minds and understandings.

Also, because the causes of legislation and abrogation are of different kinds: some of them have their wisdom manifest through the text, so it is possible to make them understand it, as in His saying ﴿Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91] and the verse that follows it, after His saying ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] and the verse that follows it, and as in ﴿And He knew that there is weakness among you﴾ [al-Anfal: 66] and the verse that follows it. And some of them are difficult for them to grasp, because they require knowledge and detailed analysis that belongs to the legislators and the scholars of the principles, such as the matters known through analogy (*qiyas*) and the principles of legislation.

And some of them concern a wisdom that has not been disclosed in that time or in the times following it. Since most of these details are difficult to make them understand, or it is not appropriate to make them understand, the aforementioned turn occurred. And because this general statement serves in the position of an explanation of the first, it has been separated from it.

The address in "*ta'lam*" (do you not know) is not intended to be directed to a single specific person, namely the Prophet (ﷺ) himself. Rather it is either an address to an unspecified audience, in the manner of metaphor (*majaz*), by treating the one who is not present for the address as if he were the addressee, because of the fame of this matter, with the purpose that it include every suitable addressee, namely everyone who is presumed or imagined not to know that Allah is over all things capable, even if by not acting in accordance with what that knowledge requires. It was to this method that al-Qutb and al-Taybi, among the commentators of the *Kashshaf*, inclined. According to this, the address includes the Jews and the polytheists from the outset, and whoever the matter might be unclear to or the doubt might be circulated among weak Muslims. As for others, they are apparently in no need of this affirmation, and they were included only so that others might hear it.

Or it is intended in its apparent sense, namely a single addressee, so the one addressed is the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant by it is the Muslims. Thus it moves from addressing the Prophet to addressing his community through an implicit transition (*kinayah*), because the knowledge of the community is a necessary consequence of the knowledge of the Messenger insofar as he is a Messenger, by customary necessity. Hence every ruling attached to him under the title of messengerhood is meant for his community, because what is established for him of the known matters in the domains of belief and legislation is also established for them. Sometimes what is intended by the address is that the content of the address is directed to him and to his community, and sometimes what is intended is that the content is directed to his community alone, according to the principle of writing that permits intending both the literal meaning and the implicit meaning together. Here, however, the content cannot be directed to the Messenger, because he would not be asked to affirm that Allah is over all things capable, let alone be rebuked for denying it. The affirmation is directed only to the community, and the purpose of that implicit expression is an indirect allusion to the Jews. The reason for choosing this route rather than using the pronoun for the addressed plural is the eloquence and emphasis contained in following the path of implicit expression, together with the brevity of the pronoun's wording.

The interrogative is affirmative (*taqriri*) in both readings, and this is the nature of an interrogative that enters upon a negation, as was previously mentioned at His saying ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33]. That is, you know that Allah is capable, and you know that He is the owner of the heavens and the earth with what occurs in them of states, and so that dominion is also His, and He directs creation as He wills. Al-Zamakhshari in the *Kashshaf* indicated that it is affirmative, and al-Qutb stated this explicitly in his commentary. No interrogative entering upon a negation has been heard in the speech of the Arabs except that it is intended to affirm.

As for His saying ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, al-Baydawi said: It is placed in the position of a proof relative to the sentence before it, because the one to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth is certainly capable of everything. For this reason this sentence has been separated from the one before it. In my view, the reason for the separation is that this sentence is in the position of a repetition of the first, because both the situation of affirmation and the situation of rebuke are situations of repetition of that by which affirmation and denial are made, as an enumeration to the addressee.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 106–107 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Whatever abrogation We abrogate, or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it.﴾ The connection (munasabah) of this verse with the verses before it is that the Jews made an excuse for their turning away from believing in the Prophet (ﷺ) by saying: ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], by which they meant that they disbelieve in anything other than it. In this excuse of theirs, they claimed that their law (shari'ah) cannot be abrogated, and they said that Muhammad (ﷺ) described the Torah as true and that he came confirming it, so how could his law nullify the Torah? They deceived people with what they named al-bada' (the notion of a change of divine intention), which is the necessity that God, exalted is He, would not know what legislation is good, and that the matter would appear to Him, then He would turn away from it and replace one law with another.

We have already mentioned that God, exalted is He, refuted their excuse and exposed them by showing that they do not truly adhere to their law such that they would be steadfast in it, and this is from His saying: ﴿Say: Why then did you kill the prophets of God before?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], and His saying
Page 655
﴿Say: If the Last Abode with God is yours alone﴾ [al-Baqarah: 94], etc., and that they have no motive except envy, by His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book do not wish that any good be sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105], up to His saying "the Possessor of great bounty," indicating that the cause is envy. When He had clarified the refutation of them in all of that, He intended to dismantle that sophistry or doubt which they sought to promote among people by denying abrogation. The primary purpose of this is to teach the Muslims a foundational principle of the laws, namely the principle of abrogation, which occurs when one law is replaced by a law after it, and occurs when some rulings of one law are replaced by rulings from that law that nullify them. Because this is the primary purpose, He turned away from addressing the Jews with a refutation and directed the address to the Muslims, as indicated by His saying "Do you not know" and His connecting it to it with His saying: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108], and His saying: ﴿Whatever abrogation We abrogate﴾, and He did not say "of a law." In this there is a turning away from addressing the Jews, because teaching the Muslims is more important, and this entails a refutation of the Jews by way of parity, for when the wisdom of changing some rulings for a benefit becomes apparent, the wisdom of changing some laws becomes apparent.

Some exegetes have mentioned a occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) for this verse. In al-Kashshaf and al-Ma'alim it is said: it was revealed when the Jews said: "Do you not see Muhammad commanding his companions with a matter and then forbidding them from it?" In the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi, the Jews criticized the change of the qiblah and said: "Muhammad commands his companions with something and forbids them from it, so this Qur'an is only from himself, and for that reason some of it contradicts other parts."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (nansakh) with a fatha on the first nun and a fatha on the sin, and this is the basic form of the imperfect of (nasakha). Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the first nun and a kasra on the sin, as the imperfect of (ansakha) with the hamzah of transitivity, meaning: We command the abrogation of a verse. (ma) is conditional, and its original is the relative pronoun, which has absorbed the meaning of the condition; therefore it is a noun of condition that takes the i'rab of objects, and it is clarified by what explains its vagueness. It also imposes vagueness regarding the times of the connection, because the connection, which is the conditional linkage, when attached to something vague becomes vague, so it does not indicate a specific time among the times of linking the response to the condition and its connection to it.

And "min ayah" is an explanation (bayan) of (ma). The word (ayah) originally means a proof and a sign of a matter. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:
Who among us has, from the good in his presence, three signs, in all of which is judgment?
Page 656
Its pattern is fi'alah, with the middle letter vowelled, according to al-Khalil, and its middle letter is a ya' or a waw, which became alif because it was vowelled and the letter before it was open. The relative form is ayiyy or awiyy. Then the word ayah was applied to the miracle, because it is the proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger; God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We send not the signs except as a warning﴾ [al-Isra': 59]. The word ayah is also applied to a portion of the Qur'an containing a legal ruling, an admonition, or the like, and this is a Qur'anic usage; God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another—and God knows best what He sends down—they say: "You are only a fabricator." Rather, most of them do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 101]. This is supported by the fact that among the meanings of ayah in Arabic speech is the sign that the sender gives to the messenger so that the recipient will confirm him. When they sent a message or news with a messenger, they attached a sign which they called an ayah, especially when a captive was sent to his people with a message, as Nashib al-A'war did when he was a captive among the Banu Sa'd ibn Malik and sent a message to his people in La'nabar, intending to warn them of what their enemies who captured him were plotting against them, and he said to the messenger: "Tell them such and such, with the sign that I ate with you hays." And Suhaym al-Abd said:
By your life, O youth, convey to her from me, with the sign of what came to us swaying gently.
For this reason they also called a message an ayah, naming a thing by the name of what is customarily associated with it. The meaning of ayah here is the ruling of the verse, whether its wording is removed or its wording is kept, because the aim is to explain the wisdom of nullifying rulings, not the removal of Qur'anic words.

Naskh (abrogation) is the removal of one thing by another, as al-Raghib said. It is thus an expression for removing a form or substance and establishing something else in its place. One says: the sun abrogated the shade, because its ray removed the shade and replaced it in its place; and the shade abrogated the sun in the same way, because the image of the body which came between the illuminated body and the ray of the sun that lit it has replaced the ray in its place. It is also said: I transferred (nasakhtu) what was in the hive of bees and honey to another hive. It may be used for removal alone without replacement, as when they say: the wind abrogated the trace. It may also be used for establishment, but for a specific establishment, namely the establishment of what removes. As for its use for mere establishment, I do not think this is correct in the language, even though the apparent sense of al-Raghib's words may suggest it. It has also been derived from it that they say: "I abrogated the book" when you copy the letters of its like into your page, since they found it to be pure establishment; but this is a misconception, because the use of naskh for copying the letters of a book is a figurative usage by way of the image, or a representation of the state by the state of one who removes the letters from the original book to the copied book, after which the copy came about from that. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We were having your deeds copied﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29], and He said: ﴿And in its copy is guidance and mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 154]. As for the saying of people, "the child is a copy of his father," it is a metaphor upon a metaphor. Naskh is not used for cessation without removal; one does not say "the night abrogated the day," because the night is not an existing matter but rather the original darkness resulting from the absence of the luminous body.

The meaning of naskh here is removal and the establishment of a replacement, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿We bring one better than it or similar to it﴾. This is what the scholars of usul (usuliyyun) know as the lifting of a legislative ruling by a textual address (khitab). Thus, new legislation (al-tashri' al-musta'naf) is excluded, since it is not a lifting. And by our saying "legislative ruling," the lifting of the original exemption (al-bara'ah al-asliyyah) by new legislation is excluded.

For the original exemption is not a legislative ruling; rather it is the remaining in the absence of obligation (taklif) that people were in before the coming of the law, such that the law does not address the stipulation of the permissibility of permissible things except in a place where there is a suspicion of their prohibition, or in a place restricting the prohibited things or the obligatory things. The first is like His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198], regarding trade during the Hajj, since the Muslims thought trade was forbidden during the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah as the Jahiliyyah had practiced after departing from Dhu al-Majaz, as will come. An example of the second is His saying: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], after mentioning the forbidden women, and His saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to approach your wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], to restrict the obligation of abstention to the specific time of the day. From their saying in the definition "lifting of a ruling" it is understood that this ruling was established were it not for its lifting, and some have stated this explicitly. Therefore we chose to add a qualifier to the definition, namely "the lifting of a legislative ruling whose continuity is known, by a textual address that lifts it," so as to exclude from the definition of naskh the lifting of a legislative ruling limited by an end-point when that end-point is reached, and the lifting of a ruling derived from a command that has no evidence of repetition.

Since the wisdom of abrogating verses has become clear, the wisdom of abrogating laws by one another is known from it, and this is what they denied. They denied that Islam had abrogated the Torah, and they claimed that the continuity of the Torah prevents belief in Islam, just as they said: "We believe in what was revealed to us." And abrogation of laws has several states. The first: the coming of a law for a people in a temporary manner for the duration of the life of the Messenger who was sent with it.
Page 658
When he dies, the law is lifted, as with the laws of Noah, Abraham, Joseph, and Shu'ayb. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Joseph had already come to you﴾ [Ghafir: 34] up to His saying ﴿until when he perished, you said: "God will never send after him a messenger"﴾ [Ghafir: 34]. The people remained in an interval (fatrah), and everyone who wanted guidance could follow that law or part of it, just as they followed the law of Abraham. When a law came after it, the second is not truly abrogating the first, but it is an abrogation by which people are given the choice in following it, which was their right during the interval, just as the tribe of 'Abs, for example, was permitted to follow the law of Abraham; when Khalid ibn Sinan came to them with his law, following it became obligatory upon them. The second: a law comes for a people who are commanded to remain upon it, as the law of Moses, and then a law comes after it which does not lift that law in its entirety, but lifts some of its rulings and confirms others, as the law of Jesus. This is an abrogating law in general, since it abrogates some and clarifies some. The Messiah was a messenger who abrogated part of the Torah, namely what he explicitly stated to be abrogated; as for the rest, it remains upon the rulings of the Torah, so he is mostly an explainer, reminder, and interpreter, like those who preceded him among the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah the elder, Daniel, and their like. This type does not contradict the abrogation of the rulings of a single law except by means of a second messenger. The third: the coming of one law after another in such a way that the second nullifies the first in a general nullification, such that that law is regarded as invalid, whether in those rulings where the second law states something that contradicts what is in the first, or in what the second law is silent about. This is Islam in relation to the laws that preceded it, for it lifted all the laws such that it is not permitted for any Muslim to adopt anything from the earlier laws in matters the Islamic law has not addressed at all; rather he derives the rulings of such matters by inference (istinbat), analogy (qiyas), and other methods of the principles of Islam. It has been disputed whether the law of those before us is a law for us where no abrogating text has come; but that disagreement concerns another piece of evidence, namely His saying: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. His saying "or cause it to be forgotten": Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read (nunsihā) with a damma on the first nun and a kasra on the sin, then a ha'. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (nansa'hā) with a fatha on the first nun and a fatha on the sin, followed by a silent hamzah, then a ha'. On the reading without hamzah, it is from forgetting (nisyan), and the hamzah is for transitivity, its object is omitted for generality, meaning: We cause people to forget it, by the command of the Prophet (ﷺ) to stop reciting it until the Muslims forget it. On the reading with hamzah, the meaning is "or We postpone it," that is, We postpone its recitation or We postpone acting upon it, and the aim is the nullification of acting by its recitation or by its ruling.
Page 659

[Page 660]

Thus it was described metaphorically as *al-nasi'* (postponement), which is another category, opposed to *naskh* (abrogation). It is that the Messenger does not remind people to act upon a legislated ruling, and does not order those who neglect it to make up for it, until people forget to act upon it. That would amount to nullifying the ruling, because if it were still in force, the Messenger would not have stayed silent about reiterating the command to it, nor would one who neglects its obligation have been left unrebuked when its requirement applied. I have not found an example of this in the Qur'an. Its parallel in the Sunnah is the saying of the Messenger of God: "None of you should prevent his neighbour from placing a piece of wood in his wall," according to those who hold that the prohibition in it is for forbiddance (*tahrim*). This was the view of Abu Hurayra, and for this reason he used to mention this hadith and say: "Why do I see you turning away from it? By God, I will strike it among you."

The meaning of *al-nasa'* (postponement) implies a delay that is followed by confirmation. Accordingly, the meaning is either that the ruling remains for a period without being abrogated, or that the verse remains in the Qur'an for a period without being abrogated. Or the intended meaning may be causing the verse to be forgotten, in the sense of delaying its coming, with God's will that this occur after a time. The hypothetical possibilities regarding the abrogation of a ruling of the Shari'a apply to the abrogation of one Shari'a by another, and to its causing to be forgotten or its postponement.

His saying ﴿We bring something better than it or its like﴾ is the answer to the conditional clause. Making it an answer implies that these two states, namely abrogation and causing to be forgotten or postponement, do not separate from two states: the bringing, at the time of abrogation and at the time of causing to be forgotten, of something better than the abrogated or its like, or better than the forgotten or postponed or its like. So what is brought with abrogation is the abrogating (*nasikh*) Shari'a or ruling, and what is brought with causing to be forgotten, from forgetting, is also the abrogating Shari'a or ruling, or it is a ruling that comes from the rulings which is not abrogating but is a contrary ruling descending after the other. What is brought with postponement, that is, delay, is what accompanies the remaining ruling from the rulings revealed during the period in which there is no abrogation.

I have left the aspects of being better and being similar in general terms, so that the mind of the listener may go in every possible direction, and you will find it intended. For being better may be in terms of including what suits the interest of the people, or what averts harm from them, or what brings about praiseworthy outcomes, or what contains great reward, or what contains gentleness toward those under obligation and mercy toward them in times of hardship, even if imposing hardship upon them may sometimes be more beneficial.

It is not meant that every form of the hypothetical cases of abrogation, causing to be forgotten, or postponement includes both the better and the similar together. Rather, what is meant is that each form of them does not lack including either the better than it or the similar to it. For this reason ﴿or⟩ was used in His saying ﴿something better than it or its like﴾, so it conveys one of the two things, while the combination is still permissible.

[Page 660 continues]

The realisation of these forms is in your hands. Let us give examples that point to the intended meaning and suffice in place of the rest, without adhering to the order of presentation, according to the most correct view. We say:

(1) Abrogation of a Shari'a together with bringing something better than it, like the abrogation of the Torah and the Gospel by Islam.

(2) Abrogation of a Shari'a together with bringing one similar to it, like the abrogation of the Shari'a of Hud by the Shari'a of Salih. Each has a benefit similar to the other in determining the conditions of two nations with closely related customs and morals. Hud forbade them from building a monument on every high place as a diversion, whereas Salih did not forbid this, but forbade harming the she-camel.

(3) Abrogation of a ruling within a Shari'a by something better than it, like the abrogation of the disapproval of wine established by His saying ﴿In them is great sin and benefits﴾ [al-Baqara: 219] by its prohibition absolutely. This abrogating ruling is better in terms of benefit, but not in terms of gentleness. The abrogating ruling may also be better in gentleness, like the abrogation of the prohibition of eating, drinking, and approaching women during the nights of Ramadan after the time of breaking the fast at sunset, when the fasting person had slept before having the evening meal, by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to approach your wives﴾ [al-Baqara: 187], up to His saying: "from the dawn." In the hadith in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, it is said: "So the Muslims rejoiced at its descent."

(4) Abrogation of a ruling in the Shari'a by a ruling similar to it, like the abrogation of the bequest to parents and relatives by the determination of the shares of inheritance. Each is beneficial to all in giving them wealth. And like the abrogation of the obligation of fifty prayers by five prayers, with the reward of the fifty being granted for the five, so both are equal in terms of reward. And like the abrogation of the verse ﴿And for those who are able to fast, there is a ransom of feeding a poor person﴾ [al-Baqara: 184] by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], up to His saying ﴿and that you fast is better for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 184]. So the affirmation that fasting is better than the ransom.

(5) Causing to be forgotten in the sense of postponement of a Shari'a together with the coming of something better than it: the delay of the appearance of the religion of Islam at the time of the coming of Shari'as which preceded it, each of which was better in relation to the nation for which it was legislated and the age in which it was legislated. Shari'as come to people with what suits their conditions, until all of mankind becomes prepared to accept the final Shari'a, which is the religion with God. So the betterness here is in some of its meanings, and it is relative.

(6) Causing a Shari'a to be forgotten in the sense of postponing its coming, with God's will that it occur after a time, and together with bringing one similar to it, like the postponement of the Shari'a of Jesus at the time of bringing the Shari'a of Moses, while it is better than it in that it includes most of the interests and what the nation needs.

(7) Causing to be forgotten in the sense of postponing the intended ruling together with bringing something better than it, like the postponement of the prohibition of wine, which was intended, together with bringing its disapproval or its prohibition only during the times of the prayers. For what was brought is better than the prohibition in terms of gentleness toward people in bringing them to abandon something they had become attached to by their love for it.

(8) Causing a Shari'a to be forgotten in the sense of its remaining unabrogated until a known term, together with bringing something better than it, that is, more extensive and more general in benefit, and greater

[Page 661]

in reward, but in another nation, or one similar to it likewise.

(9) Causing a verse of the Qur'an to be forgotten in the sense of its remaining unabrogated until a known term, together with bringing something better than it in another chapter, that is, more general in benefit, or one similar to it in another chapter, that is, similar in benefit or reward, like the prohibition of wine at the time of the prayers. During that period there descends the prohibition of trading at the time of the Friday prayer.

(10) Forgetting a Shari'a in the sense of its dissolution, like the Shari'a of Adam and Noah with the coming of the Shari'a of Moses, which is more excellent and more extensive, and like the Shari'a of Idris, for example, which is similar to the Shari'a of Noah.

(11) Forgetting the ruling of a Shari'a together with the coming of something better than it or similar to it. In what was revealed were ten known sucklings that establish prohibition, which were abrogated by five known sucklings. Then both were forgotten together, and the verse ﴿and your sisters through nursing﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] came in absolute terms. All are equal in establishing the foster relationship, and there is no hardship upon those under obligation in one suckling or ten, because the quantity is close.

It has been said that what is meant by forgetting (*nisyan*) is abandonment (*tark*). In that case its meaning and forms return to the meaning and forms of causing to be forgotten in the sense of postponement.

The purpose of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We bring something better than it or its like﴾ is to show the ultimate of wisdom and to refute them, by [showing] that it does not matter to them whether a Shari'a is abrogated by a Shari'a, or a ruling in a Shari'a by another ruling. This does not detract from God's knowledge, nor from His wisdom, nor from His lordship. For He did not abrogate a law or a ruling, nor abandon it, except that He had already compensated people with what is more beneficial to them than it at that time, or with what is similar to it in terms of time and circumstance. And whenever He postponed a ruling for a period and then manifested it afterward, He had already compensated people, during the time of its postponement, with what fills its place according to their conditions. This is the manifestation of lordship (*rububiyya*), for He nurtures creation and guides them to their interests together with gentleness toward them and mercy. God's intention in all those times and circumstances is one: the preservation of the order of the world and the regulation of people's conduct within it in a manner that protects their conditions from disorder according to the eras, the nations, and the circumstances, until He brought the final Shari'a. This is God's intention from people, and for this reason He said, ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 19], and He also said, ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura: 13], and the verse.

The apparent meaning is that bringing something better or something similar applies to each of abrogation and causing to be forgotten. So bringing something better than the abrogated or the forgotten, or something similar to it, is the case, and the statement is not of the figure of speech called *laff wa nashr* (wrapping and unfolding). Thus His saying, exalted is He, (﴿We bring something better than it or its like﴾) is either the bringing of compensation or the bringing of reinforcement. The distribution of this rule over the previously mentioned forms is not difficult.

[Page 662]

And the meaning is: We have not left creation in a time without guidance (*suda*). And that there is nothing in abrogation from which *bada'* (a change of mind in God's knowledge) might be supposed.

In the verse there is a wonderful brevity in division, which has gathered these forms that you have heard, and forms that branch out from them, which I do not ask you to supply, because no form is assumed after this except that you have already recognised it.

Among what makes the hair stand on end, and what should not be turned to, is what some of the exegetes said regarding His saying, "*nunsiha*" (We cause it to be forgotten): that it means God's causing the Muslims to forget the verse or the chapter, that is, removing it from their hearts, or His causing the Prophet ﷺ to forget it. Then the forgetting of all people of it at one time would be evidence of abrogation. They cited for this a hadith which al-Tabarani narrated with its chain to Ibn 'Umar: "He said: Two men recited a chapter which the Messenger of God ﷺ had taught them. They stood one night praying, but could not recall a single letter of it. So they went in the morning to the Messenger of God ﷺ and mentioned that to him. He said to them: 'It is of what was abrogated and caused to be forgotten, so leave it aside.'" Ibn Kathir said: "In the chain of this hadith is Sulayman ibn Arqam, and he is weak." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is a munkar hadith, which al-Tabarani alone narrated as a gharib. How could the like of it remain hidden from the imams of hadith?"

The correct view is that the forgetting by the Prophet of what God intended to abrogate, and did not intend to establish as Qur'an, is permissible, that is, though it did not occur. As for forgetting that is a flaw among humans, the Prophet is protected from it before conveyance. After conveyance and the Muslims' preservation of it, it is permissible. It has been related that he dropped a verse from a chapter during prayer, and when he finished he said to Ubayy: "Why did you not remind me?" He said: "I thought it had been lifted." He said: "No, but I forgot it." End of quotation. My view is that the incidental forgetting which is afterward remembered is permissible, and the verse is not to be understood as referring to it, because it contradicts the apparent meaning of His saying: (﴿We bring something better than it or its like﴾). As for the continuous forgetting of the Qur'an, I think it is not permissible. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6] is evidence for this, and His saying: (﴿except what God wills﴾ [al-A'la: 7]) is an expansion of the promise. The explanation of that will come in the chapter of al-A'la.

As for what is related in the Sahih of Muslim from Anas, who said: "We used to recite a chapter which we likened in length to *Bara'a*, and then it was forgotten, except that I retained from it: 'If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would seek a third; and nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust; and God turns in forgiveness to whoever repents.'" End of quotation. This is *gharib*, and its interpretation is that there was a chapter whose recitation and rulings were abrogated. The forgetting by the Muslims of what its wording was abrogated from the Qur'an is not strange. Moreover, it is a *gharib* hadith.

This verse has indicated that abrogation occurs. The scholars of Islam have agreed on the permissibility of abrogation and its occurrence. None has disagreed about this except Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, Muhammad ibn Bahr. It has been said that his disagreement is verbal, and the detail

[Page 663]

...in the books of the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*). They divided the abrogation (*naskh*) of the textual evidences for rulings and their implications into categories. The first is the abrogation of both the recitation and the ruling together, which is the basic form, and they illustrated it with what was narrated from Abu Bakr: "It was among what was revealed: *Do not turn away from your fathers, for it is disbelief in you to turn away from your fathers.*" The second is the abrogation of the ruling while the recitation remains. This does occur, because preserving the recitation serves the purpose of keeping the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the verse through its eloquence. An example is the verse ﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast ones﴾ [al-Anfal: 65] and the verses that follow it. The third is the abrogation of the recitation while the ruling remains. They illustrated it with what was narrated from Umar: "It was among what was recited: *The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, then stone them both.*" In my view, however, there is no benefit in abrogating the recitation while the ruling remains. They have interpreted Umar's words, "It was among what was recited," to mean that it was recited among the people in order to publicize its ruling.

Many of the Companions held that when the ruling of a verse is abrogated, its writing is not kept in the codex (*mushaf*). In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, in the chapter on tafsir, Ibn al-Zubayr said: I said to Uthman, "Concerning ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 240], it has been abrogated by the other verse, so why do you write it?" He said: "O son of my brother, I will not change anything of it from its place."
