﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things capable?﴾ ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper?﴾ These are brought to explain the wisdom of abrogation and the bringing of something better or similar, in a non-detailed explanation following the method of the wise style (*al-uslub al-hakim*). This is because, after finishing his warning that the abrogation which they considered improbable and used as a pretext to deny the Messenger is never separate from replacing the abrogated ruling with something better than it or similar to it, or from strengthening what remains with something similar, he wished to move from that to uncovering the doubt that remained. That doubt is that the denier would say: "What is the benefit of abrogation, such that it requires a replacement?" The apparent course would have been to take up the explanation of the differences in interests (*masalih*), their suitability to circumstances and eras, and the detailed explanation of what is better or similar in each abrogating and abrogated ruling. But since undertaking that is something the minds of the listeners cannot grasp, because of the difficulty of understanding the ranks of interests and their variation, which requires establishing rules from foundational principles of the Shari'ah and of governance, he turned them away from explaining that, and the interest was summarized for them by referring them to the power of Allah, which nothing possible and willed escapes, and to the vastness of His dominion, which indicates the greatness of His knowledge, and to the creatures' need of Him, since they have no lord other than Him and no guardian besides Him. That is sufficient as proof that He will guide them to their interests in all circumstances. What makes this turn even more fitting is that undertaking the explanation would open the door to dispute over establishing the interest and over the variation of that according to the differences in minds and understandings.

Also, because the causes of legislation and abrogation are of different kinds: some of them have their wisdom manifest through the text, so it is possible to make them understand it, as in His saying ﴿Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91] and the verse that follows it, after His saying ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] and the verse that follows it, and as in ﴿And He knew that there is weakness among you﴾ [al-Anfal: 66] and the verse that follows it. And some of them are difficult for them to grasp, because they require knowledge and detailed analysis that belongs to the legislators and the scholars of the principles, such as the matters known through analogy (*qiyas*) and the principles of legislation.

And some of them concern a wisdom that has not been disclosed in that time or in the times following it. Since most of these details are difficult to make them understand, or it is not appropriate to make them understand, the aforementioned turn occurred. And because this general statement serves in the position of an explanation of the first, it has been separated from it.

The address in "*ta'lam*" (do you not know) is not intended to be directed to a single specific person, namely the Prophet (ﷺ) himself. Rather it is either an address to an unspecified audience, in the manner of metaphor (*majaz*), by treating the one who is not present for the address as if he were the addressee, because of the fame of this matter, with the purpose that it include every suitable addressee, namely everyone who is presumed or imagined not to know that Allah is over all things capable, even if by not acting in accordance with what that knowledge requires. It was to this method that al-Qutb and al-Taybi, among the commentators of the *Kashshaf*, inclined. According to this, the address includes the Jews and the polytheists from the outset, and whoever the matter might be unclear to or the doubt might be circulated among weak Muslims. As for others, they are apparently in no need of this affirmation, and they were included only so that others might hear it.

Or it is intended in its apparent sense, namely a single addressee, so the one addressed is the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant by it is the Muslims. Thus it moves from addressing the Prophet to addressing his community through an implicit transition (*kinayah*), because the knowledge of the community is a necessary consequence of the knowledge of the Messenger insofar as he is a Messenger, by customary necessity. Hence every ruling attached to him under the title of messengerhood is meant for his community, because what is established for him of the known matters in the domains of belief and legislation is also established for them. Sometimes what is intended by the address is that the content of the address is directed to him and to his community, and sometimes what is intended is that the content is directed to his community alone, according to the principle of writing that permits intending both the literal meaning and the implicit meaning together. Here, however, the content cannot be directed to the Messenger, because he would not be asked to affirm that Allah is over all things capable, let alone be rebuked for denying it. The affirmation is directed only to the community, and the purpose of that implicit expression is an indirect allusion to the Jews. The reason for choosing this route rather than using the pronoun for the addressed plural is the eloquence and emphasis contained in following the path of implicit expression, together with the brevity of the pronoun's wording.

The interrogative is affirmative (*taqriri*) in both readings, and this is the nature of an interrogative that enters upon a negation, as was previously mentioned at His saying ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33]. That is, you know that Allah is capable, and you know that He is the owner of the heavens and the earth with what occurs in them of states, and so that dominion is also His, and He directs creation as He wills. Al-Zamakhshari in the *Kashshaf* indicated that it is affirmative, and al-Qutb stated this explicitly in his commentary. No interrogative entering upon a negation has been heard in the speech of the Arabs except that it is intended to affirm.

As for His saying ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, al-Baydawi said: It is placed in the position of a proof relative to the sentence before it, because the one to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth is certainly capable of everything. For this reason this sentence has been separated from the one before it. In my view, the reason for the separation is that this sentence is in the position of a repetition of the first, because both the situation of affirmation and the situation of rebuke are situations of repetition of that by which affirmation and denial are made, as an enumeration to the addressee.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 108:

﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before? And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the sound way.﴾

"Am" (أمْ) is a conjunctive particle (harf 'atf) specific to interrogation and what has the meaning of interrogation, namely equalization (al-taswiyah). When it conjoins one of two singular terms while inquiring about the determination of one of them, whether as a genuine question or as one that equates the two in the possibility of occurrence, it carries the meaning of the disjunctive "aw" (or), and the grammarians call it "muttasilah" (connected). When it conjoins a full sentence, it indicates a shift from the preceding speech to a question, so it carries the meaning of the transitional "bal" (rather), and the grammarians call it "munqati'ah" (disconnected). In both cases the interrogative remains attached to what follows it. Here it is necessarily "munqati'ah", because the two interrogatives preceding it carry the meaning of a statement, since they are for affirmation (taqrir), as has already been explained. Nevertheless, their occurrence in the form of interrogation, even if for affirmation, makes it appropriate for "am" to come after them, as is most common. The interrogative that follows them here is one of denial (inkar) and warning (tahdhir). The connection in this transition is complete, for the affirmation preceding it is intended to warn against error and against being like one who does not know, and the interrogative following it is likewise intended as a warning. What is warned against in all of them is shared in being among the blameworthy conditions of the Jews. It is not correct for "am" here to be "muttasilah", because the two interrogatives preceding it are necessarily not genuine questions, as has already been explained.

Al-Qazwini, in al-Kashf upon the Kashshaf, permitted that "am" here be "muttasilah" in a less preferred respect, and al-Baydawi followed him, and both labored for this in a way that the usage of Arabic speech does not support. 'Abd al-Hakim, in his gloss upon al-Baydawi, went to excess and claimed that reading it as "muttasilah" is preferable, because it is the original usage, especially with the agent of the two verbs joined by "am" being one and the same, and because it indicates that when they asked as the people of Moses asked, they knew that God is powerful over all things, and they only intended obstinacy; and all of them were heedless of the inability of the two preceding interrogatives to be taken in their genuine sense of questioning.

Her saying "turidun" (do you wish) is addressed to the Muslims without doubt, by the indication of her saying "rasulakum" (your Messenger). That this is so is not made preferable by the two addresses before it being directed to the Muslims, because the shift of speech after the disconnected "am" permits a shift of address. Her saying "turidun" indicates that the questioning has not occurred, but perhaps it stirred in the hearts of some of them, or perhaps the doubts of the Jews, in their denial of abrogation and their casting of the doubt of al-bada' (change of divine decision), and the like, aroused it in their hearts, which may impel some Muslims to question the Prophet ﷺ.

Her saying ﴿as Moses was questioned﴾ is a comparison, whose aspect is that among the questions of the Children of Israel to Moses were many questions that led them to disbelief, such as their saying ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138], or of arrogance, such as their saying ﴿We will not believe you until we see God openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55]. Thus the warning is against the chain of questions that leads to the like of that. It is also permissible that it refers to the questions of the Children of Israel about what does not concern them and what brings them hardship, such as their saying "What is its color?" and "What is it?" Al-Fakhr said: The Muslims used to ask the Prophet ﷺ about matters in which there was no good for them in seeking to know them, just as the Jews asked Moses. End.

Others have mentioned other occasions of revelation, among them that the Muslims asked the Prophet ﷺ during the expedition of Khaybar, when they passed by Dhat Anwat, which belonged to the polytheists, that he make for them a similar one; and similar to this, which is based on weak reports. All of that is a burdening of oneself with what is not needed, for the verse is brought in the manner of warning denial, as shown by her saying "turidun", aiming at counseling trust in God and His Messenger; and counsel and warning do not require the act to occur, but rather require its absence. The intended aim is the warning against the entry of doubt concerning the suitability of the rulings that were abrogated before their abrogation, not concerning the suitability of the abrogating rulings when they occur.

Her saying ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾ is a concluding generalization (tadhyil) to the preceding warning, indicating that what is warned against is disbelief or leads to disbelief, because it contradicts the sanctity of the Messenger, trust in him, and trust in the judgment of God the Exalted. It is possible that by "disbelief" is meant the conditions of the people of disbelief, that is: do not exchange your manners for adopting the customs of the people of disbelief in their questioning, as he ﷺ said in the hadith of the two Sahihs: "The ones before you were destroyed only by the abundance of their questions and their disputing with their prophets." The application of "disbelief" to the conditions of its people, even when they are not disbelief, is common in the terminology of the Sharia and the terminology of the early generations, as Jamilah bint 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, wife of Thabit ibn Qays, said: "I dislike disbelief," meaning adultery. For the mention of one sentence after another indicates a connection between the two sentences; so when the meaning of the two sentences is not clearly related, the listener knows there is a connection which the eloquent speaker alludes to. Here you know that apostasy from faith to disbelief is a universal general meaning under which their questioning the Messenger falls, as the Children of Israel questioned Moses; so that matter is disbelief. This is the purpose of the tadhyil defined in the chapter on prolixity (itnab) as: following a sentence with a sentence containing its meaning, which stands in the position of proof for the content of the first sentence, and by which the emphasis of the first sentence's meaning and an increase is obtained. Thus tadhyil is a kind of prolixity, in that it establishes the meaning of the first sentence and adds to it a new benefit related to the benefit of the first sentence. The most excellent of it is what is expressed in the manner of proverbs, because of its generality of ruling and concise wording, like this verse and the saying of al-Nabigha:

"You will not keep a brother whom you do not blame for his faults; who among men is refined?"

What is emphasized by the sentence ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾ is the implied meaning of the sentence ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger﴾, not its explicit wording, so it is like the tadhyil in the verse of al-Nabigha. Concerning the transitivity of the verb "yatabaddal" (exchanges), the discussion has passed at His saying ﴿He said: Do you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. The saying "faqad dalla" (has certainly strayed) has been made the answer of "man" (whoever) in the conditional, because the intended straying is its greatest form, which results immediately upon the exchange of disbelief for faith. There is no doubt that the answer is consequent upon the condition. Do not be troubled by the answer of the conditional coming as a past verb, although the condition is a stipulation about the future, nor by the past verb being joined with "qad" which indicates the certainty of past occurrence; for this is good Arabic usage, in which they bring the response in the past tense intending to indicate the intensity of the consequence following the condition and the certainty of its occurrence with it, so that when the content of the condition occurs, the response has already occurred, as though it had occurred before the condition, as in ﴿And whoever His anger befalls has certainly fallen﴾ [Ta-Ha: 81]. Upon this every response that comes in the past is to be understood, for the indication of it is that the content of the answer does not come about except after the condition occurs; and they use "qad" as a sign of this intention. For this reason, a past response to a present-tense condition is rarely without "qad" accompanying the response, to the point that it has been said that its absence is a necessity of verse and was not found in the Qur'an, as al-Radi stated, contrary to this, since with "qad" there are many instances in the Qur'an.

They may also make the response a past verb intending that the occurrence of the content of the condition reveals that the content of the response has already occurred, or that people have recalled it, as in ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has already stolen before﴾ [Yusuf: 77]. In that case, the realization of the response in such a case is what the answer contains of the meaning of revelation, precedence, or other things according to the contexts, before it is estimated. So do not be surprised that a brother of his had already stolen. It is possible to derive this verse upon that, by estimating ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾ as: the cause of it is that he had already strayed from the sound way until he fell into apostasy, as you say: "Whoever has fallen into the pit has certainly stumbled blindly," if by the past is meant that it occurred, and by straying is meant what surrounds the apostate of doubts and abandonment which led him to apostasy; but this is far from the purpose of the verse. "Al-sawa'" is the middle of everything. Balʿa' ibn Qays said:

"I overcame him while he was in a dark, brave host, with a sharp sword that struck the middle of the head and split it."

The middle of the road is the clear, well-trodden road, because it lies between the minor paths which do not reach the goal.

[Page 669]

﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after your belief, out of envy from their own selves, after the truth has become clear to them. So pardon and overlook, until Allah brings His command. Indeed, Allah has power over all things.﴾ ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah. And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

Its connection to what precedes it: what came before was a report about the envy of the People of the Book, especially the Jews among them, and the end of that passage was the objection concerning abrogation (naskh). So in this verse there is an explicit statement of the implied meaning of His words ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book do not wish that any good be sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105], because when they do not wish for the coming of this religion which the Muslims follow, they wish for those who have embraced Islam to remain in their disbelief, and they wish that after their Islam they would return to disbelief. He digressed between it and the previous verse with His words ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate﴾ for the reasons mentioned earlier.

For this reason, this sentence was separated (from what precedes it, in the grammatical sense of fasl), because, being part of the sentence before it, it serves as an explanation (bayan), since it explains both its explicit meaning (manṭūq) and its implied meaning (mafhūm). In the tafsirs of Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Kashshaf, and in Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, it is reported that Huzayfah ibn al-Yaman and 'Ammar ibn Yasir came to the House of Study (bayt al-midras), in which were Finhas ibn 'Azura, Zayd ibn Qays, and others of the Jews. They said to Huzayfah and 'Ammar: "Did you not see what befell you on the day of Uhud? If you were upon the truth you would not have been defeated. Return to our religion, for it is better, and we are more guided than you." The two of them rejected this and remained steadfast in Islam. Al-wadd (wishing, affection) has already been discussed in the previous verse.

He attributed this judgment to "many of them," whereas He had attributed His words ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book do not wish...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105] to all of them. This is because their wish that no religion be sent down to the Muslims entails their wish that the polytheists follow the religion of the Jews or the Christians, so that this religion would spread throughout the lands of the Arabs. When Islam came, their hearts were all constricted by this. As for their scholars and rabbis, they were disappointed, and they knew that what the Muslims had come to was better than what they had been upon of polytheism, because they had come to the Oneness of Allah and to belief in His prophets, messengers, and books. In that is belief in Moses and Jesus, even if they did not follow our religion. So they do not wish for the Muslims to return to the old polytheism, because in wishing that there is a wish for disbelief, and he is content with it. As for the common Jews and their ignorant ones, envy and rage have driven them

[Page 670]

to wish that the Muslims would return to polytheism and would not remain in this good state which accords with the religion of Moses in most of its aspects, out of spite toward the Muslims and toward the Prophet (ﷺ). The Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, who believe in jibt and taghut and say to those who disbelieved, "These are better guided than those who believed, as to the way"?﴾ [al-Nisa: 51]. In this rich meaning there is what shows you the reason for the expression "yaruddunakum" (they would turn you back) rather than "law kafartum" (if you disbelieved). This is to indicate that their wish is that the Muslims return to polytheism, because returning (radd) is only to a prior state. If it had been said "law kafartum" (if you disbelieved), there would have been some excuse for the People of the Book, because it could be understood that they wished for the Muslims' destination to be Judaism. From this appears the reason for the word "kuffaran" (disbelievers) being in the accusative as a complement of the complement of "wadda kathirun" (many wished), to indicate that they wished that the Muslims would return as disbelievers in Allah, that is, disbelievers in a form of disbelief agreed upon even among the People of the Book, namely polytheism. So it is not an expression of the actual referent of what they wished, but rather an expression of the concept (mafhum) of what they wished. From this also appears the reason for His words ﴿after the truth has become clear to them﴾, for it became clear that what the Muslims follow is true in respect of the Oneness of Allah and belief in the messengers, unlike polytheism. Or it means: after the truth of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had become clear to them, according to them, if by "many of them" is meant specifically their scholars. And Allah is fully aware of them.

"Law" (لو) here has the meaning of "an" (أن) of the verbal-noun type (al-maṣdariyyah), and for this reason what follows it is interpreted as a verbal noun (maṣdar).

"Hasadan" (حسدًا, out of envy) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in "wadda" (wished), meaning that this wish has no cause except envy, not a desire for disbelief.

As for His words ﴿from their own selves﴾ (مِن عِنْدِ أنْفُسِهِمْ), the initial "min" (مِن, from) is used to indicate the rootedness of this envy in them and its emanating from their souls. He emphasized this with the word "'inda" (عِنْدِ, with/from), which indicates permanence, so that the explanation of its firm establishment might increase. It is connected to "hasadan" (envy), not to His word "wadda" (wished). The Muslims were commanded to pardon and overlook them specifically in this context because what was related about the People of the Book here is something that stirs the anger of the Muslims, because of their intense aversion to disbelief. The Exalted said: ﴿And He made disbelief hateful to you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 49:7]. So inevitably, whoever wishes that for them, they regard as their greatest enemy. Since this report stirred anger, it was feared that they would lash out at the Jews, and that is not what Allah wants from them, because Allah wanted them to be a repository of pardon and forbearance, so that they would be exemplars in virtues.

[Page 671]

Al-'Afw (العفو) is leaving off punishing the wrongdoer. Al-saft (الصفح), with the ṣād vowelled with a fatḥah, is the verbal noun of "ṣafḥan," meaning he turned away. This is because when a person turns away from something, he turns the side of his face (ṣafḥat wajhihi) away from it. "Ṣafaḥa wajhahu" means he turned his side and width away from it. It is a metaphor for not confronting him with the mention of that wrong, that is, not blaming him or reproaching him for it. This is more eloquent than pardon, as is reported from al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani). For this reason, He connected the command to overlook it to the command to pardon, because the command to pardon does not necessarily imply it. He did not suffice with "aṣfaḥū" (overlook) alone, for the purpose of gradualness in commanding them with what may conflict with what their souls incline toward, namely retaliation, as a gentle kindness from Allah toward the Muslims in bringing them to the noble moral qualities.

His words ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾ mean: until what contains the healing of your rage comes. It was said that it is the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir and the killing of Qurayzah. It was also said that it is the command to fight the People of the Scripture, or the imposition of the jizyah (poll-tax).

The apparent meaning is that it is an indefinite end-point for the pardon and overlooking, to reassure the hearts of those commanded, so that they would not despair of the removal of the harm of the wrongdoers from them in the end. This is a method used in urging a person toward something that does not suit him, like the saying of people, "so that Allah may decree a matter that was to be done." So when the command of Allah comes to abandon pardon, the end-point has ended. Among this is the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir.

Perhaps in His words ﴿Indeed, Allah has power over all things﴾ there is a teaching to the Muslims of the virtue of pardon, that is: indeed Allah is powerful over all things, and He pardons and overlooks. In the authentic hadith: "No one is more patient toward harm he hears from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when they ascribe a rival to Him, while He provides for them." Or it means that He has power over all things, so if He willed He would destroy them now, but in His wisdom He commanded you to pardon them. All of this comes back to imitating the action of Allah, the Exalted. It has been said that all wisdom is in assimilating oneself to the Creator to the extent of human capacity. So the sentence "Indeed, Allah has power over all things" is an appended conclusion (tadhyil) brought in the manner of a justification (ta'lil). The sentence ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾ up to His words "﴿And they say, none will enter﴾" [al-Baqarah: 111] is a consequential sentence with an interjection (tafri' ma'a i'tiraḍ). The interjected sentence (i'tiraḍ) is one placed between two sentences that are very closely connected in terms of the purpose the speech is directed toward, and the interjection is the coming of something whose purpose the speech was not directed toward, but which has a relation to the speech and its purpose and completes it. The consequence here is introduced by the particle "fa" (ف) in the sense of deriving one statement from another, not deriving the meaning of one concept from another concept, because the meaning of pardon does not follow from the wishing of the People of the Book. Rather, the command to it follows from the mention of this wish, which is itself a harm. An interjected sentence may come with "wa" (و) and with "fa" (ف), where the conjoined element is an interjection. The author of al-Kashshaf permitted this in his commentary on the Exalted's words ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 16:43] in Surat al-Nahl. Ibn Hisham permitted it in Mughni al-Labib and argued for it with the Exalted's words ﴿Then Allah is more worthy of both﴾ [al-Nisa: 4:135]

[Page 672]

according to a view and a report from some students of al-Zamakhshari, that he was asked about the Exalted's words in Surat 'Abasa: ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder﴾ [80:11], ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾ [80:12], ﴿in honored sheets﴾ [80:13], that he said: it is not correct for the sentence ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾ [80:12] to be an interjection, because an interjection does not occur with "fa." He was refuted by the author of al-Kashshaf, who said it is not correct to attribute that to him, because it contradicts what he said in the verse of Surat al-Nahl.

His words ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾ are meant as a command to remain steadfast in Islam, for prayer and zakah are its two pillars. So the command to them implies the command to persist in what you are upon, by way of metonymy (kinayah).

His words ﴿And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ are appropriate to the command to remain steadfast in Islam and to the command to pardon and overlook. In it is an allusion (ta'rid) to the Jews, that they do not appreciate the measure of your pardon and forbearance, but it is not lost with Allah. For this reason He restricted Himself to the words "with Allah." Al-Hutay'ah said:

Whoever does good will not lose its rewards; kindness does not vanish between Allah and people.

His words, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, are an appended conclusion to what precedes it. Al-basir here means the All-Knowing, as already mentioned. It is a metonymy for not neglecting to recompense the good-doer and the evil-doer, because the All-Knowing, All-Powerful, when He knows something, arranges upon it what is appropriate to it, since ignorance does not distract Him and incapacity does not hinder Him. In this there is a promise to them which contains a warning for others, because if He is Seeing of what the Muslims do, He is Seeing of what others do.

Indeed, it is a reminder﴾ [80:11], ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾ [80:12], ﴿in honored sheets﴾ [80:13], that he said: it is not correct for the sentence ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾ [80:12] to be an interjection, because an interjection does not occur with "fa." His words ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾ are meant as a command to remain steadfast in Islam, for prayer and zakah are its two pillars. So the command to them implies the command to persist in what you are upon, by way of metonymy (kinayah).

His words ﴿And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ are appropriate to the command to remain steadfast in Islam and to the command to pardon and overlook. In it is an allusion (ta'rid) to the Jews, that they do not appreciate the measure of your pardon and forbearance, but it is not lost with Allah. For this reason He restricted Himself to the words "with Allah." Al-Hutay'ah said:

Whoever does good will not lose its rewards; kindness does not vanish between Allah and people.

His words, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, are an appended conclusion to what precedes it. Al-basir here means the All-Knowing, as already mentioned. It is a metonymy for not neglecting to recompense the good-doer and the evil-doer, because the All-Knowing, All-Powerful, when He knows something, arranges upon it what is appropriate to it, since ignorance does not distract Him and incapacity does not hinder Him. In this there is a promise to them which contains a warning for others, because if He is Seeing of what the Muslims do, He is Seeing of what others do.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 111–112:

﴿And they say: None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians. Those are their wishful thoughts. Say: Bring your proof, if you are truthful.﴾ ﴿Yes! Whoever submits his face to God while doing good, his reward is with his Lord, and there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "Ṣaḍḍa kathīrun" (Many of the People of the Book wish...), and what lies between them, from His saying ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109] to the end of the verse, is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ), as explained earlier. The pronoun refers to all the People of the Book, both Jews and Christians, as indicated by His saying after it, "except those who are Jews or Christians." The object of the saying differs according to the speaker: the Jews said, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews," and the Christians said, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Christians." The Qur'an combined their two statements in a concise manner, by gathering what they share, namely the denial of entry into Paradise for the omitted exception-subject, in order to make the exception (istithnāʾ) follow from it. Then came the separation of what is specific to each group, which is His saying "Jews" or "Christians."

So the word "aw" (or) is part of the narrator's speech in his reporting, and is not part of the reported speech. Here "aw" is for dividing the two statements, so that the listener assigns each statement to its speaker. The evidence that "aw" is not part of their reported speech is that, if it were, it would imply that neither group has confidence in salvation, and that each believes the other's salvation is possible. What is known of the condition of the adherents of each religion is the opposite: each of the Jews and Christians does not doubt its own salvation and does not doubt the misguidance of its opponent. This is also evidence for determining each of the two predicates of kāna for the rest of the shared sentence that each group said, by referring "Hūdan" to the Jews' statement and "Naṣārā" to the Christians' statement.

Thus "aw" here is for distribution (tawzīʿ), which is a kind of division (taqsīm) that derives from its being used for one of two things. This is a concise expression combining concision by omission (ījāz al-ḥadhf), since the exception-subject is omitted, and gathering the two statements in one verb, which is "qālū." It also includes concision by restriction (ījāz al-qaṣr), because this omission was not based merely on a context requiring an estimate, but rather pointed to the omitted part of the two statements through the introduction of the particle "aw" or "kānat"/"aw", or through expressing the omitted part with the shortest phrase. Therefore it should be counted as a third type of concision, namely concision of both omission and restriction together.

Al-Qazwini, in Talkhīṣ al-Miftāḥ, made this verse an example of al-laff wa al-nashr al-ijmālī (the general "wrapping and unfolding"), taking this from the words of al-Kashshaf, namely the statement of the author of al-Kashshaf: "So he wrapped the two statements together, trusting that the listener would return each statement to its group, and we were safe from confusion because the enmity between the two groups was known." His saying "he wrapped the two statements together" means by it the "laff" that is the title of the rhetorical embellishment called al-laff wa al-nashr. For this reason they sought a "nashr" (unfolding) for this "laff," and the "laff" in the verse is illustrated by His saying "qālū," together with what it contains. It is a general "laff," which its "nashr" that follows it clarifies, and for this reason they named it the general "laff." Then the "nashr" of this "laff" came with His saying "except those who are Jews or Christians," so from the particle "aw" it is known that the "nashr" distributes to what suits each of the two groups.

Al-Taftazani said in his commentary on al-Miftāḥ: "It is the usage in general negation that its unfolding is mentioned with the word 'aw' (or)."

"Hūd" is the plural of hāʾid, meaning one who follows Judaism. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62]. The plural of fāʿil on the pattern fuʿl is not common, and it is an irregular (samāʿī) form, from it the saying "ʿawwadh," the plural of ʿāʾidh, which refers to young female animals of gazelles, horses and camels that have recently given birth. From it also "ʿāʾiṭ" and "ʿawṭ" for a woman who remained years without giving birth; and "ḥāʾil" and "ḥawl" (barren camel/cow), "bāzil" and "bazl" (camel in its full maturity), and "fārih" and "furh" (skilful/strong, of horses).

"Hūdan" came in plural form, although the predicate of "kāna," referring to its pronoun, is singular, because "man" is singular in its wording while its meaning is plural. So its pronoun followed its wording, and its predicate and pronoun followed its meaning.

The demonstrative "tilka" refers to the statement uttered by them, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians," as is apparent. Describing it in the plural form is either because, since it was the wish of each one of them, it became many wishes; or because it intends that all their wishes are like this, and as is their habit in them, so this is an eloquent metaphor (tashbīh balīgh).

"Amānī" (wishes) was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿They know not the Book except as wishful thinking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78]. The clause "Tilka amānīyuhum" is a parenthetical insertion. His saying "Say: Bring your proof" is a command that they be answered with this, and for this reason He separated it, because it is in the context of dialogue, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, "They said: Will You place in it...?" [al-Baqarah: 30]. He used "inna," which indicates doubt about their truthfulness, while in fact there is certainty of their untruthfulness, in order to lead them on, until they know that they are not truthful when they cannot produce proof, because every belief whose holder cannot establish evidence for it is a false belief, since if it had evidence, he would be able to express it. Even more so, it cannot be true in the sight of one who wants to promote his belief to others.

"Balā" (Yes/Indeed) is a refutation of their claim. "Balā" is a word used to answer a negative statement in order to affirm the opposite of the negation, which is affirmation, whether it occurs after an interrogative about a negation, which is the most common case, or after a negated statement, as in His saying, ﴿Does man think that We shall not assemble his bones? Yes (balā)...﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3], and the saying of Abu Ḥayya al-Numayri:

"The slanderers inform you that I will never love you. Yes (balā), and the veils of God are those with forbidden things."

His saying "man aslama" (whoever submits) is a new independent sentence after "balā," as an answer to a question from one who seeks to know how the denial of entry into Paradise for other than these two groups was overturned. It is intended to show that Paradise is not restricted to anyone, but rather it is deserved only by whoever submits, and so on, because His saying "then for him is his reward" means "for him is entry into Paradise," and this is the answer of the conditional, since "man" is certainly a conditional particle. Whoever estimates here a verb after "balā," meaning "whoever submits will enter it," intends an estimate of meaning, not an estimate of grammatical parsing, since there is no need for an estimate here.

"Islām al-wajh li-llāh" (submitting one's face to God) is the surrender of the self to the commands of God, the Exalted, meaning the utmost compliance, because "aslama" means to lay down arms and abandon resistance. God, the Exalted, said, ﴿So if they dispute with you, say: I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 20]. "Wajh" here means the self. He expressed the self by the face, because it is the most noble part of the self, as al-Shanfara said:

"When they cut off my head, and in the head is what is most (of me)."

Among the uses of "wajh" for the self is His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And there remains the face of your Lord, Full of Majesty and Honour﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 27]. "Wajh" is also used for the reality of a thing. You say: "He came with the matter according to its face," meaning according to its reality. Al-Aʿshā said:

"And the first of judgment is according to its face, not a judgment by unjust desire."

And "wujūh al-nās" means the nobles among them.

It is also possible that "aslama" means "akhlaṣa" (sincerely devoted), derived from "salāma" (soundness), meaning making it sound. From it: ﴿A man belonging to one master﴾ [al-Zumar: 29].

His saying "wa huwa muḥsin" (while he is a doer of good) is brought as a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya), to show that the submission of the heart alone is not sufficient, nor is action without sincerity; rather, there is no salvation except by both of them. And God's mercy is beyond that, since no person is free from shortcoming.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿And there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾ is plural, in consideration of the generality of "man," just as the pronoun in His saying ﴿His face to God, while he is a doer of good﴾ is singular, in consideration of the singular wording. This is one of the varieties of Arabic usage, to avoid the tedium of repetition.
