It is conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to His saying: ﴿They say, "None will enter Paradise unless he be a Jew or a Christian."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], in order to further explain that baseless assertion is their habit, and that dismissing those who oppose them as misguided is an old trait among them. They label opponents as astray merely because they oppose them. Long ago the Jews labelled the Christians as astray, and the Christians labelled the Jews with the same. So do not be surprised at the judgement each group passes on the Muslims, that they will not enter Paradise. This verse also rebukes the People of the Book, reassures the hearts of the Muslims, and removes from the polytheists the doubt that they might use the criticism of the People of the Book against Islam as a justification for their hostility towards it and for their persistence in their polytheism.

By "saying" is meant the explicit statement of the words. They did say this openly when the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and among them were the chief religious figures of the Christians. When they reached the Jews, the Jews met them while they were with the Prophet (ﷺ). They debated with them about the religion and disputed with them until they insulted one another. The Jews then disbelieved in Jesus and in the Gospel, and said to the Christians, "You are not upon anything." The delegation of Najran disbelieved in Moses and in the Torah, and said to the Jews, "You are not upon anything."

Their words "upon anything" (*'ala shay'*) are an indefinite noun in a negative context. The word "thing" here is used for emphasis, meaning: they are not upon any matter that is of worth. Thus the thing negated is a conventional thing, or else it is understood with a deleted qualifier, as in the verse of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"I have been in war one who bears the blows, yet I was not given anything, nor was I withheld."

That is, I was not given anything beneficial or sufficient, as indicated by his words "nor was I withheld." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about soothsayers (*kuhhan*) and he said, "They are not anything." The form is a general form, but in the course of speech it is meant to negate anything of worth in the matter under discussion, according to the context. It is therefore used figuratively, like a general expression intended in a particular sense. That is, they are not in possession of any share of the truth. Here, then, the meaning is "they are not upon any part of the truth." This is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the invalidity of what is in their hands of the revealed Book. Each of the two groups said to the other that what it has of the Book has no share of good in it, as indicated by His saying after it, ﴿while they recite the Book﴾. His saying ﴿while they recite the Book﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*), brought to add to the astonishment at their state, that they should say such things while each group of them recites the Book. Every Book they recite contains the truth, if its people followed it as it should be followed. No people of a true Book fail to follow either some of what is in their Book or most of it. Therefore the claim of the other that they are not upon anything is not to be accepted. The circumstantial clause is used because its indication of the state is stronger than that of a single circumstantial word, since a circumstantial clause, by containing a declarative relation, conveys that what should have been a predicate has been turned from predication to claim that the subject is known to be characterised by it. So it is placed in the position of a single circumstantial word, to draw attention to and direct the mind towards it, and so it becomes a circumstance for it. The pronoun in His saying "they" refers to the two groups, though it has also been said that it refers to the Christians alone, since they are the nearest antecedent.

The definite article in "the Book" was taken by the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) as the definite article of the genus, and he intends by this that what is meant is that they are people of knowledge, just as they are called "People of the Book" in contrast to the "Unlettered" (*ummiyyin*). What led him to this is His saying after it, "Thus said those who have no knowledge." So the meaning is that they have reached the extreme of misguidance, while they are among the people of knowledge, to whom baseless assertion is unbecoming, and who ought to be fair by pointing out the errors of their opponents.

Ibn 'Atiyya took the definite article as referring to a known thing, and took the known thing to be the Torah, that is, because it is the book both groups read. The aspect of astonishment on this reading is that the Torah is the root of Christianity, and the Gospel bears witness to its truth. So how can the Christians permissibly claim it is not anything, as the Christians of Najran did? And the Torah bears witness to the coming of messengers after Moses, so how could the Jews permissibly deny the messenger of the Christians?

If the pronoun is taken to refer to the Christians alone, the known book may be the Torah, as we have mentioned, or the Gospel which bears witness to the truth of the Torah. In His saying "they recite" there is an indication of this, because then the astonishment becomes mixed with a kind of excuse, namely that they read without reflection. This is a form of sarcasm (*tahakkum*). Otherwise it would have said "while they know the Book." By this it becomes clear that this verse is not revealed to defend either of the two groups or both of them.

His saying ﴿Thus said those who have no knowledge the like of their saying﴾ means: this statement resembles the saying of another group other than the two groups. These are the ones who have no knowledge, and they are the counterpart of "those who recite the Book." By them are meant the polytheists of the Arabs, who have no knowledge because they are unlettered. The application of "those who have no knowledge" to the polytheists occurs in the Qur'an. Among such examples is His later saying, ﴿Those who have no knowledge say, "Why does God not speak to us, or a sign come to us?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 118], indicated by His saying ﴿Thus said those before them, the like of their saying﴾ [al-Baqarah: 118], meaning: thus said the Jews and the Christians. The meaning here is that the polytheists denied all the religions, the Jewish, the Christian and Islam. The purpose of the comparison is to disfigure the thing compared, by showing it resembles the saying of the people of pure misguidance.

This is a digression (*istitrad*) to rebuke the polytheists for what they responded with to the Islamic call. That is, they said to the Muslims the like of the saying of the two groups of the People of the Book towards one another. The Qur'an has recounted their saying in His words, when they said, ﴿God did not send down anything upon any human being﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. The comparison derived from the particle "thus" (*kazialika*) is a comparison in the claim that they are not upon anything. The implied meaning is: like that saying which the Jews and the Christians uttered, "those who have no knowledge said." For this reason the phrase "the like of their saying" serves as an emphasis (*ta'kid*) of what the particle of comparison has conveyed. This emphasis indicates that the resemblance between the saying of those who have no knowledge and the saying of the Jews and the Christians is complete, since when they said "God did not send down anything upon any human being," they denied the Jews, the Christians and the Muslims.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing verb "said" is either merely to give importance to showing the similarity, or to dispense with a conjunction in moving from one statement to another, as a wonderful brevity. This is because the function of the conjunction is to join, and the function of the particle of comparison is also to join, since comparison is a joining in a quality. And for the sake of emphasis, or to increase it, he emphasised "thus" with "the like of their saying." So it is also a qualifier of the deleted object of "they said," meaning: they said a statement like their saying. You may also take "thus" as an emphasis of "the like of their saying," and consider its being placed first as a fronting from a later position. But the first is more evident.

The author of al-Kashshaf and a group of others permitted that neither "the like of their saying" nor "thus" should be an emphasis of the other. They held that the basis of the comparison is the manner of the saying and its method of issuing from caprice, while the basis of the similarity is similarity in wording. In their view this makes for a repetition of the comparison from two aspects, to indicate the strength of the resemblance.

His saying ﴿God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ﴾ comes with the particle "then" (*fa*) because the threat of judgement among them on the Day of Resurrection, and the disclosure of what their hearts concealed of caprice and envy, is a consequence of these statements and is caused by them. It is a declarative statement intended as rebuke and threat. The pronoun in the genitive after "between" (*bayna*) refers to the three groups. And "that about which they used to differ" includes what has been mentioned and other things. The sentence is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 114:

﴿And who does greater wrong than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them and strives for their ruin? Those would not have entered them except in fear. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with ﴿The Jews say, "The Christians are not upon anything"﴾ [al-Baqara: 113], in consideration of the preceding verses that show the various ways of the People of the Book in boldness and evil speech. That is, their statement and what precedes it is wrongdoing, and none is like the wrongdoing of one who prevents the mosques of Allah. This is a digression (istitrad) that falls as an interjection between the mention of the states of the Jews and the Christians, to mention the evils of the polytheists in their bad reception of the call to Islam, which came to guide them and save them.

The verse was revealed concerning the polytheists of the Arabs, as in the narration of ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās, and this is what is required by His saying ﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear﴾ and what follows, as will come. It points to the prevention by the people of Makkah of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims from entering Makkah, as came in the hadith of Saʿd ibn Muʿādh when he entered Makkah secretly, and Abū Jahl said to him: "Do I not see you circumambulating the House safely, while you have sheltered the Ṣubāʾ?" And this recurred in the year of Ḥudaybiyya.

It was also said that it was revealed concerning Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Ashur, and his raid on Bayt al-Maqdis in three raids. The first was in the year 606 BCE, in the time of the king of the Jews, Yehoiakim, in which he took captive a group of the people of Israel. The second was eight years later, in which he took captive the leaders of the kingdom and the king Yehoiachin ibn Yehoiakim, and he plundered the Holy Mosque of all its precious things and treasures. The third was ten years after that, in the time of the king Zedekiah. He captured the king, blinded his eyes, burned the Al-Aqsa Mosque and the whole city, took captive all the Children of Israel, and by that the kingdom of Judah came to an end. That was in the year 578 BCE, and this event is called the Third Captivity. So he, in all of that, prevented the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis from having the name of Allah mentioned in it, and caused its ruin.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning the attack of Titus the Roman upon Urshalim (Jerusalem) in the year 79 CE, when he ruined Bayt al-Maqdis, burned the Torah, and left Bayt al-Maqdis in ruins until the Muslims rebuilt it after the conquest of the Levantine lands. According to these last two narrations, there is no apparent connection for mentioning it right after what preceded, so it is not appropriate to base the tafsir upon them.

The correct view is to rely upon the first narration, which is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās. The connection is that, after the People of the Book were given their due by exposing their intentions regarding the religion of Islam and its people, and explaining that this is a deeply rooted habit in them towards everyone who brings them what opposes their desires, and after he had indicated at His saying ﴿Neither those who disbelieve among the People of the Book nor the polytheists wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 105] that the polytheists resembled them in that, the discourse turned to explain what branches from the polytheists' unwillingness for the Qur'an to be revealed. So He made clear that their wrongdoing in this had not been reached by anyone before them, for they prevented the mosques of Allah, blocked the path of guidance, and stood between the people and visiting the Sacred Mosque, which is their pride and the source of their status. This is not the attitude of one who seeks the good of creation, but the attitude of the envious, enraged one.

The interrogative with "man" (who) is for denial (inkari). Since the original of "man" is that it is an indefinite modified noun (nakira mawsufa), it has taken on the meaning of interrogation, and since the denying interrogative has the meaning of negation, the sentence became an indefinite noun in a context of negation. Therefore they interpreted it as meaning "there is no one more unjust."

Wrongdoing (ẓulm) is transgression upon the right of another by disposing of it in a way that he does not approve. It is also applied to placing a thing in a place other than that which it deserves to be placed in, and both meanings are suitable here.

They were the most unjust of people only because they committed a strange wrong, for they wronged the Muslims by barring them from the Sacred Mosque, though they were the most entitled people to it, and they wronged themselves by the bad reputation among the nations.

He used the plural "mosques," although the polytheists prevented only the Kaʿba. This is either for glorification, since the plural comes for glorification, as in His saying ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37]; or because of what it contains of places of worship, namely the House, the Sacred Mosque, the Station of Ibrahim, and the Ḥaṭīm; or because of what is connected to it also, such as al-Khayf, Mina, and al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām, and all of these are mosques. The idafa (construct) in these aspects is in the sense of the definite article of prior reference (lam al-ʿahd). Or it is for the purpose of including all the mosques of Allah, since it is a plural made definite by the idafa and it occurs in the context of "prevention," which has the meaning of negation, so that the threat encompasses every one who ruins a mosque or prevents worship by closing it off from the performance of acts of worship. In this case the polytheists enter initially into it, according to the ruling that a general wording comes upon a specific cause, and the idafa in this aspect is in the sense of the definite article of comprehensiveness (lam al-istighraq). Perhaps the plural pronoun in the accusative in His saying "that they enter them" supports that the intended mosques are specific known mosques, because this threat does not extend to everyone who prevents a mosque, since it is a worldly punishment whose consistency is not required in similar cases of the punished.

The intended meaning of prevention is preventing worship at its specific times, such as circumambulation and congregational prayer, when prevention is intended to deprive a group of those qualified for them from them. It does not include closing the mosques outside the times of congregational prayer, because the individual prayer is not preferred in the mosque over elsewhere, and likewise closing them to prevent children and travelers from sleeping in them. Ibn ʿArafa was asked about this in a tafsir lesson, and he said: "Closing the door of the mosque outside the times of prayer is protection and preservation." End of quotation. Likewise is preventing one who is not qualified from entering it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prevented the polytheists from circumambulation and the Hajj, and Mālik prevented the disbeliever from entering the mosque, and the prohibition of the one in a state of major impurity (junub) and the menstruating woman is well known.

Al-saʿy (striving) originally means walking, then it became a well-known metaphor for purposeful causing, like a conventional literal meaning, as in His saying ﴿Then he turned away, striving﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 22]. It is governed by fi, which indicates causation, as in: "I strove in your need." So the prevention here is literal according to the first narration mentioned in the occasion of revelation, and the striving is a metaphor for causing that was not purposeful, so it is a metaphor upon a metaphor. As for the other two narrations, the prevention is a metaphor and the striving is literal, because Bukhtansar and Titus did not prevent anyone from mentioning Allah, but they caused the ruin by ordering destruction, and this led to prevention and resulted in it.

His saying ﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear﴾ is a new resumptive sentence (isti'nāf), which removes the need for a question arising from His saying "who does greater wrong" or from His saying "strives." This is because the hearer, when he learns that the doer of this is the most unjust of people, or hears this boldness, which is striving for ruin, seeks an explanation of the recompense of one who has these qualities or who did this. It is also possible that it is an interjection between "who does greater wrong" and His saying ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾. The demonstrative "those" (ulāʾika), after mentioning the three attributes concerning them, is to draw attention to the fact that they have been brought to mind by these attributes, so that after this demonstrative they may be informed of a predicate that they deserve. This is like what preceded in ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5]. This indicates that the purpose of these clauses is not to explain the recompense for their deed or to warn against it, but rather to explain this strange state of the polytheists after explaining the marvels of the People of the Book, and then to arrange the punishment upon it, so that you may know their deserving of it. He mentioned two punishments for them: a worldly one, which is fear and disgrace, and an otherworldly one, which is the great punishment.

The meaning of ﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear﴾ is that after this deed, it will not be possible for them to enter those mosques that they prevented except while they are fearful. Indeed, "mā kāna" when followed by "an" and the present tense in its predicate indicates negation of the future, even though the word "kāna" is in the past form. This "an" is the one that is concealed when the lām (of purpose or emphasis) comes, as in "mā kāna Allāh li-yuʿadhdhibahum" (it was not for Allah to punish them), so there is no indication in this clause of the past. The lām in His saying "la-hum" is for entitlement, meaning it is not fitting for them to enter in any state except the state of fear, so they are deserving of it and fitting for it in the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. This is a threat that Allah has decreed that their hands be removed from managing the Sacred Mosque and the rites of Allah there, and that they become subject to the Muslims, so that after that they will not enter the Sacred Mosque except in fear. It is also a promise to the believers. Allah fulfilled His promise, for on the day of the conquest of Makkah they were fearful and anxious, until the herald of the Prophet (ﷺ) proclaimed: "Whoever enters the Sacred Mosque is safe." Many of them entered it in terror, fearing they would be seized by the sword before they entered.

According to the interpretation of "mosques of Allah" in its generality, His saying ﴿They would not have entered them﴾ means: they prevented the mosques of Allah while it was fitting for them to enter them humbly before Allah. Fear is then interpreted as awe before Allah, and for this reason they were wrongdoers, by placing arrogance in the place of submission. The lām in His saying "la-hum" on this reading is for specification (ikhtisas). However, although many exegetes adopted this view, the position of the demonstrative noun, which indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes, contradicts it, because this aspiration is established and prior to the prevention and striving for ruin.

His saying ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾ is a second resumptive sentence, and it was not conjoined to what precedes so that it would be intended by the resumption, for emphasis on it, because the conjoined element, being a follower, is not given the full attention of the hearers. Also, it functions in relation to the resumption before it as explanation relates to what it explains. Disgrace is fear, and disgrace is humiliation and abasement, and that is what befell the leaders of the polytheists on the day of Badr of the horrible killing and capture, and what befell them on the day of the conquest of Makkah of the disgrace of defeat. His saying ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ is conjoined to what precedes because it completes it, since the intended meaning of the two together is that they have two punishments: a punishment in this world and a punishment in the Hereafter.

In my view, the revelation of this verse indicates an argument against the polytheists concerning the cause of the Prophet's turning away from facing the Kaʿba after his migration, for their preventing the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque is more severe than facing other than the Kaʿba in prayer, in the manner of His saying: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is great, but averting from the way of Allah, disbelief in Him, and [preventing access to] the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is greater with Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 217].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 115:

﴿To Allah belongs the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

When He mentioned their threat and promised the believers, He followed that with consolation for the believers over their departure from Makkah, and with a rebuke to the polytheists by undoing their gloating over the believers' departure from it and their exclusive claim to the privilege of dwelling near the Ka'bah. So He made clear that the whole earth belongs to Allah the Exalted, and that its directions are not distinguished except by their being a means of drawing near to Him, the Exalted, and of remembering His blessings and His great signs. Thus, when a person's orientation is toward the good pleasure of Allah the Exalted, then wherever he turns, he has attained the pleasure of Allah the Exalted. And when his orientation is disbelief, delusion and wrongdoing, then seeking refuge in sacred places does not benefit him; rather, he is an intruder there who will soon be uprooted from them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they were not its protectors. Its protectors are only the God-fearing﴾ [al-Anfal: 34]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the Children of Israel: "We have more right to Moses than they do."

So what is meant by "the east and the west" in the verse is the generalization of the directions of the earth, because with respect to the course of the sun it divides into two parts: a part that begins from where the sun rises, and a part that ends where it sets. This is a conventional division, which was well known among the earlier scholars, because it is based on observation and suits all people. The natural division of the earth, however, is its division into northern and southern parts, because it is a division founded on the differing effects of the earth's movement.

It has been said that this verse is a permission for the Messenger (ﷺ) to face any direction he wished in prayer. Perhaps the intent of this speaker is that the verse alludes to that legislation, because the apparent reading is that the verse was revealed shortly before the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis, since the usual pattern is that verses were revealed in succession, and the verse on the abrogation of the qiblah is close in position to this one. The more apt view is that the purpose of the verse is general, as is usual, so it includes the emigration from Makkah and the turning away from facing the Ka'bah.

The fronting of the adverbial phrase ("li-Llah al-mashriq wa al-maghrib") serves exclusivity, meaning that the earth belongs to Allah the Exalted alone and not to them. Therefore they have no right to prevent any part of it from the servants of Allah who are sincere.

"The Face of Allah" means the essence, and this is a linguistic reality: one says "li-wajh Zayd," meaning his essence, as was mentioned earlier at His saying "whoever submits his face to Allah." Here it is a metaphor for his deed: since He commanded them to face Bayt al-Maqdis, His pleasure is tied to compliance with that. It is also a symbolic metaphor for His pleasure at the emigration of the believers in the path of the religion to the land of Abyssinia and then to Madinah. What supports the face being in this sense is His saying in the concluding phrase, "Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing." So His saying "All-Encompassing" is a closing supplement to the meaning of "To Allah belongs the east and the west." What is meant is the vastness of His dominion or the vastness of His facilitation. The purpose is the greatness of Allah, and that He has no direction; rather, the directions from which His pleasure is sought are preferred over others. And He is All-Knowing of whoever turns in intention to seek His good pleasure. This verse has been interpreted as meaning the qiblah in prayer.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 116:

﴿And they say: "Allah has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are obedient to Him.﴾

The pronoun subject of "qālū" refers to all three groups: the Jews, the Christians, and "those who do not know," indicating another error in which the three groups agreed. It has also been read with a conjunctive waw, "wa-qālū," as being coordinated with his statement "and the Jews said" (qālat al-Yahūd), and this is the reading of the majority (al-Jumhūr). Ibn 'Amir read it without the conjunctive waw, and the verse is likewise recorded thus in the Imam Codex (al-Muṣḥaf al-Imām) sent to Syria. In that case it is a resumptive new sentence (isti'nāf), as though the listener, after hearing what had passed concerning the wonders of these three groups, both collectively and separately, were able to say: "You have made us hear strange things of their evils. Have their evils ended, or do they have further evils? For what we have heard indicates that these are evils that can only issue from corrupt natures."

These three groups have united upon this error just as they agreed upon what preceded it. The Jews said: "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and the idolaters said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." This verse therefore returns to their collective grouping in one saying, completing the collective description of their conditions that occurred in His words ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would not love...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105], and in His words ﴿Thus say those who do not know, the like of their words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113]. This verse has been concluded with a verse that gathers the third group in another saying, namely His exalted words ﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 118], up to His words ﴿Thus said those before them, the like of their words. Their hearts are alike﴾ [al-Baqarah: 118]. The word "qawl" (saying) here is in its literal sense, namely spoken speech, and for this reason the sentence is in the accusative (naṣb) form; it is also intended that they believed this, because in general speech conforms to belief.

His words "Allah has taken a son" came with the expression "ittakhadha" (has taken) as a veiled mockery of them, in that their speech is not coherent: they affirm a son for Allah while saying that Allah "took" him. Ittikhadh means acquisition, and it contradicts sonship, since sonship is born without any making; when making enters, servitude inevitably comes. This kind of contradiction is what is termed in the science of dialectic (ʿilm al-jadal) "fasād al-waḍʿ" (invalidity of the premise), which is to infer the existence of a thing from the existence of its opposite, as when someone says: "Killing is a great crime, so it is not expiated, like apostasy."

The origin of this saying, with regard to the idolaters, arises from ignorance, and with regard to the People of the Two Books, arises from their excessive immersion in the misunderstanding of the religion, to the point that they imagined figurative expressions and metaphors to be literal realities. The description of the righteous as "sons of Allah" was given in the manner of a figure of speech, and the Christians' book contains the description of Allah, exalted is He, as "the Father of Jesus" and "the Father of the nation," so minds that do not know interpretation seized upon it and did not support their belief with clear evidence, so they took it in its literal sense.

In the Torah, in Chapter 14 of the Book of Deuteronomy: "You are children to the LORD your God; you shall not cut yourselves." In the Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 5: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God." And in it: "Pray for those who persecute you and revile you, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven." And in Chapter 6: "Look at the birds of the air; they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them." This is repeated in the Gospels more than once. They understood these by a bad understanding according to the surface of their wording, and did not observe the principles of the religion which require interpreting them. Do you not see that when Muslims encountered similar expressions, they interpreted them well and made clear their evidence, as in the hadith: "The creation is the dependents of Allah" (al-khalq ʿiyāl Allāh).

His words "Glory be to Him" are an declaration of Allah's transcendence above this abominable saying. It also contains an indication that sonship is a deficiency with respect to Allah, exalted is He, even though it is a perfection among created beings; for it is a perfection among created beings only insofar as it fills some of their deficiencies in weakness and poverty, and takes their place at their decline, while Allah is exempt from all of that. Thus, if He had a son, that would indicate temporality (ḥudūth) and need for him.

His words ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ are a rejection (iḍrāb) of their saying, in order to nullify it, and he established the proof of the nullification by his words "to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth." So the sentence is a fresh inceptive resumption (istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī), the lam is for ownership (lil-mulk), and "what is in the heavens and the earth" means what exists, for the heavens and the earth are the totality of the upper and lower worlds. Among the forms of generality, there is none that applies to rational beings and non-rational beings alike and to the collective; this is the most correct view, which al-Zamakhshari adopted in al-Mufaṣṣal and which al-Radi chose.

It has been said that "mā" predominantly or exclusively applies to non-rational beings, and that "man" applies exclusively to rational beings, and that each is sometimes used for the other. This is the well-known view among the grammarians, although it is weak. On this basis they answer regarding verses like this one that it is of the kind of taghlīb (predominance of one category), treating rational beings, in their being the work of Allah, as being on the same level as the rest of existing things, to diminish the status of every existent.

Al-qunūt means submission and compliance together with fear. "Qānitūn" came in the masculine sound plural form, which is specific to rational beings, by way of taghlīb, because they are the people of qunūt by will and insight.

The omitted genitive complement after "kull" is indicated by His words "what is in the heavens and the earth," meaning: all that is in the heavens and the earth, i.e., the rational beings, "are obedient to Him." The tanwīn on "kull" is the tanwīn of compensation (ʿiwaḍ) for the omitted genitive complement, and its explanation will come at His words ﴿For each there is a direction toward which he turns﴾ [al-Baqarah: 148] in this surah. In His words "all are obedient to Him" there is a third argument against the existence of a son, because submission is the emblem of servants, whereas a son has a claim of privilege over his father; he is dutiful to him but does not submit. Therefore the affirmation of qunūt is a kināya (implicit indication) of the negation of sonship, through the negation of its necessary consequence, since the equivalent of a contradictory is a contradictory, and affirming the contradictory entails negating what it contradicts.

The separation of the sentence "all are obedient to Him" is intended to make it independent as an argument, so that the listener does not think it completes the proof introduced by "to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth." Some jurists have used it as evidence that whoever owns his child is freed upon him, because Allah, exalted is He, made the negation of sonship by the affirmation of servitude, which indicates the incompatibility of the two realities; and this is a fine inference.

[Page 686]

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth; and when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾

Here it is in the nominative (*bi-l-raf'*) as the predicate of an omitted subject, following the practice of omitting the subject (*hadhf al-musnad ilayhi*) in accordance with usage, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿deaf, dumb﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18]. This is of the same kind as what the grammarians call the *na't maqta'* (the detached epithet).

*Badi'* (the Originator) is derived from *ibda'*, which means creating something without a prior model. It refers to bringing things into existence without any previous pattern, and this means creating the origins of the species and what is generated from them. Thus the creation of the heavens is *ibda'*, the creation of the earth is *ibda'*, the creation of Adam is *ibda'*, and the creation of the system of reproduction is *ibda'*. It is on the pattern *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* (active participle). It is said that it is derived from the unaugmented *bada'a*, like *qadara* when it is sound, and *bada'a* is attested in the sense of *qadara* (to be able) but rarely. Or it is derived from *abda'a*, and the occurrence of *fa'il* from *af'ala* is rare. From this is the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"Is it from Rayhanah that the summoner who hears keeps me awake, while my companions sleep?"

He means "the one who makes (others) hear" (*al-masma'*). From it also is the verse of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"The trusted one gave you to drink from it a full cup, so the trusted one gave you full draughts of it and then a second."

That is, a cup that is *marwiyyah* (quenched/satisfying). So this is among what has come rarely, and we have already discussed it in His saying, ﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾, and it will come in His saying, "as a bearer of good tidings and a warner" (*bashiran wa nadhiran*). Various contrived interpretations have been given for the verse, but the truth is that it is a rare usage, preserved in a number of eloquent words, such as *nadhir* and *bashir*. Yet its rarity does not remove it from eloquence, because its being well known prevents it from being regarded as obscure. As for its being contrary to analogy, this does not prevent its use, except in the case of a later (*muwallad*) speaker who wishes to make analogy from it in another root.

[Page 687]

The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) held that *badi'* here is a *sifah mushabbahah* (attributive adjective of quality), derived from *bada'a* with the *dal* vowelled with a *damma*, meaning that originating was an essential attribute of Him, by way of interpreting it as "the originating of the heavens and the earth," which are among His creatures. It was then attributed to its true agent, treating Him as analogous to the object (*mushabbahan bi-l-maf'ul bihi*), and the attribute was applied to the Name of Majesty (Allah) so that His pronoun would be the grammatical subject in form, as in: "Zayd has a handsome face" (*zayd hasan al-wajh*). Just as one says, "So-and-so is original in poetry," meaning "his poetry is original."

As for the verse of 'Amr, they only specified it for comparison, and they did not allow the possibility that *al-sami'* means *al-masmu'* (the one heard), for several reasons. The first: *sami'* in the sense of *masmu'* is not attested, and *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* is not regularly used. The second: *sami'* was used as a description of the agent, namely the summoner, and the rule of *sami'a* when it is applied to what does not hear is that it becomes one of the sisters of *zanna* (verbs taking two objects), which requires a second object after the implicit agent, and this is absent. The third: the meaning is not that the summoner is described as *masmu'* (heard), but rather as *musmi'* (making heard), that is, the summoner who intends to make others hear and who raises his voice, and this indicates that he is calling to an important matter. The description of Allah the Exalted as "Originator of the heavens and the earth" is intended to mean that He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth from among the created things. In this description there is an argument against the sonship of those who claimed He had a son, because since He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and what is in them, none of those existing things is fit to be His child. Rather, everything between them is a servant of Allah the Exalted, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾. For this reason the denial of offspring is connected to His being the Originator of the heavens and the earth in Surat al-An'am, by His saying: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth; how could He have a son when He has no consort and He created all things?﴾ [al-An'am: 101]. His saying, ﴿and when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾, etc., is an explanation of the doubt of the Christians and an argument that He does not take a son, but rather brings all beings into existence by a single act of bringing into being, and all of them are subject to His bringing into being. This is because the Christians imagined that the coming of the Messiah without a father was proof that he was the son of Allah. So Allah the Exalted made clear that the bringing into being of the states of existing things from nothing is more remarkable than that, and that all of it returns to creation and decree, whether what came into being through a complete intermediary, or an incomplete one, or without any intermediary. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. So the creation of Jesus from a mother without a father is not a necessary consequence of his being a son of Allah the Exalted.

In the verse, *kun* is a complete verb that does not require a predicate; that is, He says to it: "Exist" (*ijad*), so it comes into existence. The apparent view is that there is a speaking and a spoken word. The effect here is an image illustrating the swiftness with which beings come into existence when the will and power are directed toward them. He likened the act of Allah the Exalted to the bringing about of a thing, the thing's coming into being immediately afterward without any delay, to the commander's address to the one commanded with the word of command, and his compliance immediately after that. This is because that is the nearest of the familiar situations by which one can approximate matters for which language does not have room to express. The author of *al-Kashshaf* inclined to this and supported it with the verse of Abu al-Najm:

"When the reins said to the lean-bellied one: 'Forward!' it turned like a rutting stallion camel."

What indicates that this is an image is that it is not conceivable to address one who is not existent in such a way that he would be existent. Therefore this statement by al-Zamakhshari is not based on the Mu'tazilah's denial that the attribute of speech subsists in the Essence of Allah the Exalted, for there is nothing in the verse that compels them to affirm the subsistence of the attribute of speech, since they could interpret it by the same interpretation they gave to many verses. For this reason Ibn al-Munir remained silent about it, contrary to what the words of Ibn 'Atiyyah seem to imply.

﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign not come to us?" Likewise said those before them, the same as their words. Their hearts are alike. We have indeed made the signs clear for a people who are certain.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon his saying ﴿And they said: Allah has taken a son﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116], which is itself conjoined upon his saying ﴿And the Jews say: The Christians have nothing [to stand on]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113], due to the affinity of the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians in false statements and misguided beliefs. However, in the previous verse he placed the statement of the People of the Book first, which is ﴿And the Jews say﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113], because they were the ones who initiated this when they disputed about the superiority of their religions. At that time the polytheists had no reason requiring them to occupy themselves with this, until Islam came and they said the same as the People of the Book. He gathered them all together in ﴿And they said: Allah has taken a son﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116]. Yet none of the three groups borrowed it from the other. Rather, all of it arises from exaggeration in sanctifying exalted beings, and its source is poor understanding of the creed, whether it was taken from a book, as was previously mentioned regarding the origin of the saying of the two groups of the People of the Book, "Allah has taken a son," or taken from the statements of their leaders, as the Arabs said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah."

[Page 689]

He placed the statement of the polytheists here because this statement is more closely tied to the polytheists, since it is new among them and widespread among them. Since they were the originators of this statement, it was attributed to them. Then the people before them were considered in relation to them, namely the Jews and Christians, since they said the like of it to their messengers.

Here "lawla" is a particle of urging (taḥḍīḍ), intended to express challenge (taʿjīz) and to offer an excuse for not paying attention to the Messenger, out of arrogance, by considering themselves worthy of prophethood and of hearing the speech of Allah the Exalted. This is an exaggeration in ignorance that the People of the Book, who affirmed prophethood and the need for messengers, do not say.

As for his saying ﴿or a sign come to us﴾, they meant any sign at all, so the indefiniteness is for the category. In that case it is obstinacy and denial of the signs that had come to them, and it is enough to mention the greatest of them, which is the Qur'an. This is the apparent meaning of the indefiniteness. They had asked for proposed signs and said, ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 90], and so on. They thought the signs were wondrous events or created things, but they did not realize that the rational, knowledge-based sign is the clearest of miracles because of its universality and permanence. The Messenger challenged them with the Qur'an, and they were unable to oppose it. That should have sufficed them as a sign, had they been people of fairness.

As for his saying ﴿Likewise said those before them, the same as their words﴾, meaning: in the manner of this their statement, those before them among the nations said the same as their words. What is meant by "those before them" is the Jews and Christians. The Jews said to Moses, ﴿We will not believe you until we see Allah openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55], and the Christians asked Jesus, ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 112]. In this statement there is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), that what he encountered from his people is like what the messengers before him encountered. For this reason this verse was followed by his saying ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 119], and so on.

Then it is permissible that the clause ﴿Likewise said those before them, the same as their words﴾ is positioned as a reply to the statement of those who do not know. It is a general reply, in which he restricted himself to comparing their condition with the condition of those before them. That comparison is then a metaphor (kināya) for turning away from answering their statement, and that they do not deserve to be answered, because they are not of the rank of those whom Allah speaks to, and their understandings are not fit to grasp what is in the descent of the Qur'an, which is the greatest of signs. The clause ﴿Their hearts are alike﴾ would then be an affirmation, meaning: their intellects were alike in weakness of judgment and poor reasoning. The clause ﴿We have indeed made the signs clear for a people who are certain﴾ would be a justification for turning away from answering them, on the grounds that they are not fit for an answer, because those fit for an answer are the people who are certain, and the verses of the Qur'an have made clear to them by what it contains of proofs. As for these people, they are not fit for an answer because they are not a people who are certain; rather their habit is obstinacy.

It is also permissible that the clause ﴿Likewise said﴾ through to its end is a parenthetical insertion between the clause ﴿And those who do not know said﴾ and the clause ﴿We have indeed made the signs clear﴾. Then the clause ﴿We have indeed made the signs clear﴾ becomes the answer to their statement, and the meaning is: the sign has indeed come to you, namely the verses of the Qur'an, but only those who are certain will understand it, that is, not you. This would be on the pattern of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51]. The turning away from answering their saying ﴿Why does Allah not speak to us?﴾ occurred because it is self-evidently false, as the Exalted said: ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?" They have indeed become arrogant within themselves and have overstepped in great overstepping﴾ [al-Furqan: 21].

As for the referent of the comparison and likeness in his saying "likewise" (kadhālika), ﴿said those before them, the same as their words﴾, it is in the same manner as the discussion of the previous verse, ﴿Likewise said those who do not know, the same as their words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113]. His saying ﴿Their hearts are alike﴾ is an affirmation of the meaning of ﴿said those before them, the same as their words﴾, meaning: their intellects were similar in weakness of judgment and poor reasoning, so for this reason they agreed in their statement. Here "hearts" means intellects, as is customary in the Arabic language. His saying "tashābahat" (are alike) is one of the forms of expressing likeness, and it is stronger in this than its particles, and closer to eloquent metaphor (al-tashbīh al-balīgh). Among the finest examples of this is the saying of the poet al-Sabi':

My tears resembled my wine when they flowed, so my eye pours out what is in the cup.

In this verse, the Jews and Christians are made equal to the polytheists in this statement, because the polytheists are more deeply rooted in it, since they associated with Allah others besides Him. Their claim that Allah has a son is no more than their claim that idols share divinity with Allah. So the Jews and Christians were attached to them, because the claim of a son for Allah came upon them and was not part of the original foundation of their religion. By this method, a return to explaining the particular conditions of the two groups of the People of the Book was achieved, which is the return of the last to the first.

The present tense verb was used in "yūqinūn" (who are certain) to indicate renewal and continuity, as a metaphor that faith is a disposition for them. As for those whose habit is turning away from reflection and obstinacy after the truth has become manifest, turning away prevents the attainment of certainty, and obstinacy prevents benefiting from it, so it is as though it has not been attained. Thus the possessors of these two dispositions are not among those who are certain.

[Page 690]

The clarification of the signs is what has come of the Qur'an, which is miraculous for humankind, with which He challenged all of them, and they were unable to produce anything like it, as was mentioned earlier. In a hadith: "There is not a prophet among the prophets except that he was given signs such that people believed because of them, but what I was given is a revelation that Allah revealed to me, so I hope to be the most numerous of them in followers on the Day of Resurrection." So the meaning is: We have indeed made the signs clear for a people whose nature it is to be certain and not to make themselves doubtful, or to turn away until that prevents them from attaining certainty. Or the meaning is: We have indeed made the signs clear for a people who manifest certainty and acknowledge the truth, not for people like you among the obstinate.

This is an interposed clause between accounts of the condition of the polytheists and the People of the Book. Its purpose is to console the Messenger (ﷺ) for his grief over what he encountered from the People of the Book, which resembles what he encountered from the polytheists. He had been eager that the People of the Book would believe in him, so that Islam would be strengthened by them against the polytheists. Instead, he met from them what he had met from the polytheists, or worse. He had said: "If ten Jews had believed in me, all the Jews would have believed in me." God's reminder to him that He sent him therefore serves to soothe his noble heart, to excuse him for having delivered the message, and to reassure him that he is not answerable for a people who chose the Blaze for themselves. It also paves the way for despair of the faith of the Jews and the Christians. The emphatic particle (ta'kid) is used, although the Prophet did not doubt this, because of the great concern with this report and to show that it is announced for what it contains of elevating the Messenger's status.

The subject (al-musnad ilayh, the grammatical subject of the predication) is the pronoun of majesty (ḍamīr al-jalāla), used to honour the Prophet (ﷺ) with the high honour of being in the presence of the act of speaking with the Creator, exalted and sanctified be He. It is as if God were addressing him directly with this speech without an intermediary; for this reason He did not say, "God has sent you." His words "with the truth" (bi-l-ḥaqq) are connected to "We have sent you." The truth (al-ḥaqq) is guidance, Islam, the Qur'an, and other aspects of the Qur'an and the miracles, all of which attach to the Prophet (ﷺ) in his mission: some by way of conveying it and some by way of its being supported. The meaning is that you are the Messenger of God, and that the Qur'an is a truth sent down from God.

His words "a bringer of good news and a warner" (bashīran wa-nadhīran) are two circumstantial states (ḥāl), and both are in the pattern fa'īl in the sense of fā'il (active participle). They are derived from bashshara (the doubled form) and andhara (the augmented form). Their coming from the quadriliteral (rubā'ī) is therefore contrary to analogy (qiyās), like the discussion of "Originator of the heavens and the earth" mentioned earlier. It has been said that bashīr is derived from bashara with a lightened shin, from the pattern naṣara, but there is no need for this.

His words "and you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire" (wa-lā tus'alu 'an aṣḥābi al-jaḥīm): the wāw is for coordination, and it is either coordinated with the clause "We have sent you," or with the state in "bashīran wa-nadhīran." The wāw may also be a wāw of circumstance (li-l-ḥāl).

Nāfi' and Ya'qūb read the verb with a fatḥa on the second-person prefix and a sukūn on the lām, taking lā as a prohibitive particle that jazms (apocopates) the imperfect. This is then the coordination of a directive (inshā') with an informative statement (khabar). Here the question (su'āl) is used in the sense of concern and eagerness to know the state of affairs, as a metonymy (majāz mursal) through the relation of necessity, because one who is eager to know the circumstances of a thing asks about it often. Alternatively, it is an allusion (kināya) to the monstrousness of the conditions of the polytheists and the disbelievers, such that one who reflects on their final state is forbidden from occupying himself with it, because these are conditions that description cannot encompass and the intellect cannot reach the essence of, in their horror and abomination. The prohibition against asking is used to magnify the matter asked about, as in 'Ā'isha's words: "He prayed four [rak'ahs], so do not ask about their beauty and length." For this reason it became common among the scholars to present difficult questions in the form of a question, such as "If you say..." (fa-in qult), for emphasis.

The majority of the ten readers read it with a ḍamma on the second-person prefix and a rafʿ on the lām, taking lā as a negative particle, meaning: God will not question you about the companions of the Blazing Fire. This is an affirmation of the content of "Indeed, We have sent you with the truth." The question here is an allusion to being held to account and blamed, like his (ﷺ) saying: "Each of you is responsible for his flock" (wa-kullukum mas'ūlun 'an ra'iyyatihi), meaning you are not held to account for the disbelievers remaining in their disbelief after you have conveyed the call to them.

As for what has been said, that the verse was revealed concerning the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition from asking about the state of his parents in the Hereafter, this relies on a weak report. Even if it were authentic, interpreting the verse in that way would be incompatible with eloquence, since you already know that "Indeed, We have sent you" is consolation and reassurance. Bringing in with it something that recalls distressing matters departs from the purpose, and this is what is called a defect in the arrangement (fasād al-waḍ').

[Page 693]

It is an extension (ʿaṭf) of His saying ﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 119], or of His saying ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾. This statement that discourages them from believing comes after the earlier reassurance and consolation, in the same manner as the reproach that comes after the pardon in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿May Allah pardon you. Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. This is one of the honours Allah bestowed upon His Prophet (ﷺ).

The negation with lan is an intensification in reassurance, because it negates the future and makes that negation perpetual. The millah (religion), with a kasra on the mim, is the dīn and the sharīʿah (sacred law). It is a collection of beliefs and practices that a group of people adhere to and agree upon, and it unites them as a path that they follow. It may also be derived from amalla al-kitāb (dictated the book), so the sharīʿah was called millah because the Messenger, or the founder of the religion, dictates it to the people and makes them recite it. It was called dīn (religion, judgment, submission) in view of the community's acceptance of it, their obedience and their submission.

The meaning of the limit in ﴿until you follow their religion﴾ is a metaphor (kināyah) for despair of the Jews and Christians following the sharīʿah of Islam at that time. Since they will not be pleased unless he follows their religion, they will not follow his religion. Since the Prophet's following their religion was impossible, their being pleased with him was likewise impossible, in the manner of the saying ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 40], and His saying ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ [al-Kāfirūn: 2], ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kāfirūn: 3]. The explicit repetition of the negative particle lā after the conjunction particle in His saying ﴿nor the Christians﴾ serves to specify that each of them is independently included in the negation. The conjunction particle was used to generalise the disbelief in following, because it was thought that they might do otherwise, since they showed some affection towards the Muslims, as in His saying: ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe are those who say, "We are Christians"﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 82]. This verse also contains that they do not believe in the Prophet, because he does not follow their religion, and that they do not confirm the Qur'an, because it came with the abrogation (naskh) of their two scriptures.

His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ is a command to answer what was implied by His saying ﴿nor will the Jews be pleased with you﴾, from the essence of statements they made, whose meaning requires that nothing of what the Prophet calls them to will please them, except that he follow their religion. They say: their religion is guidance, so there is no harm for him if he follows it, like their saying "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians" [al-Baqarah: 111], and other vacillations in turning away from the call. For this reason their answer was phrased in the usual style of response, using the verb of saying without a conjunction.

It is also possible that they said what the verse contains in His saying ﴿until you follow their religion﴾. The guidance of Allah is what He decrees for the person of success (tawfīq). That is, say to them: "I do not possess guidance for you, except that Allah guides you." So the restriction is real (ḥaqīqī). It is also possible that what is meant by the guidance of Allah, which He sent down to me, is "the guidance", meaning: the Qur'an is the guidance, refuting their delusion that what they follow of religion is the guidance, and that what opposes it is misguidance. The meaning is that the Qur'an is the guidance, and what you follow is not from the guidance, because most of it is falsehood. So the attribution of guidance to Allah is an honouring, and the restriction is relative (idāfī). In it there is an implicit criticism that what they followed at that time was something they had altered and fabricated. The restriction may then be either a real restriction of ascription (qaṣr ḥaqīqī āddhāʿī), meaning that it is "the guidance" in its full completeness, so the guidance of other scriptures is, relative to the guidance of the Qur'an, not entirely guidance, because the guidance of the Qur'an is more comprehensive and more perfect. This does not negate the affirmation of guidance in their scripture, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 44], and His saying ﴿And We gave him the Gospel, in which is guidance and light, confirming what was before it of the Torah﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 46]. Or it may be a relative restriction, meaning: it is the guidance, rather than what you follow of a religion that has been changed and mixed with misguided beliefs. By this also, guidance is not negated from many of the sound teachings and advice that come from wise people and people of sound intellect and experience, but it is incomplete guidance.

His saying ﴿it is the guidance﴾: the pronoun "huwa" is a separate pronoun (ḍamīr munfaṣil, the pronoun of separation). The definite article in "al-hudā" is the definite article of the genus (taʿrīf al-jins), which indicates comprehensiveness (istighrāq). Thus there are two of the methods of restriction (ḥaṣr) in it: the separating pronoun and the definition of the two parts (of the predication). Combining them conveys the confirmation of the meaning of restriction and its emphasis, because of the importance given to it. So whichever of them you consider to be the means of restriction, the other is an emphasis of the restriction and also of the predication.

The emphasis with inna is to confirm the predication, confirm its attribution, and nullify the hesitation of the one who hesitates. Because the purpose of the relative restriction is to reject the belief of the addressee, the addressee may not perceive what it requires of emphasis. So another emphasis is added here, namely the particle "inna", out of concern for emphasising this ruling. Thus several emphases are gathered in this sentence: the particle inna, and the restriction, since restriction is emphasis upon emphasis, as in al-Miftāḥ (of al-Sakkākī), so it is in the force of two emphases, together with the emphasis of the restriction by the separating pronoun. This resolves into four emphases, because the restriction is equivalent to two emphases, to which is added the emphasis of the restriction by the separating pronoun and the emphasis of the sentence by the particle inna.

Perhaps the verse indicates that the Prophet's (ﷺ) facing the qiblah in prayer, the same direction the Jews face, was to cut off the excuse of the Jews, as will come in His saying ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you were on except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. So He informed His Messenger, by His saying ﴿nor will the Jews be pleased with you﴾ and the Christians, that this does not soften the Jews' obstinacy in their opposition. Thus it is an allusion to paving the way for the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis.

His saying ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after what has come to you of knowledge﴾: the lām is a preparatory lām (lām al-muwaṭṭiʾah), that is, it prepares for the oath, and this is an emphasis on the predication and its confirmation. He expressed their way there by the term "millah", in view of their belief and the fame of that among the Arabs. He expressed it here by "desires" (ahwāʾ), after preparing for it with His saying ﴿Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾, because desire (hawā) is an opinion arising from appetite, not from evidence. For this reason the pronoun referring back to the millah was not used, and it was expressed by the apparent noun. So their desires included denial of the Prophet and of the Qur'an, and their belief that their religion would not be abrogated by another law.

His saying ﴿you would have no protector or helper against Allah﴾ is a warning to everyone who has received Islam, that after Islam they should not follow the desires of other nations. It came in the manner of warning the Prophet (ﷺ), like His saying ﴿If you associate others with Him, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], which is the answer to the oath and the evidence for the answer to the condition, because the lām is preparatory for the oath, so the answer belongs to it. The conditional particle in ("in"), which is used in situations where the occurrence of its condition is not certain, was used, because this is a weak supposition regarding the Prophet and the Muslims. The walī (protector) is the near relative and the ally.

The naṣīr (helper) is everyone who assists someone against one who intends harm to him. Both of them are of the form faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil (active). The "min" in His saying "min Allāh" (from Allah) is connected with walī, because it implies the meaning of "one who prevents from His punishment". Something similar is to be understood after "nor a helper", meaning: "a helper from Allah." The "min" in His saying "min walī" (any protector) is emphasising the negation. The coordination of the helper with the protector is a precaution, because the negation of a protector does not require the negation of every helper, since a person may have no protector by being a stranger in a tribe, while his helpers are from among his neighbours. The purpose of negating the protection was an implicit allusion to them, in their belief that they are the sons of Allah and His beloved, so He negated that from them, since they did not follow the call of Islam. Then He negated the more general thing than it. This is the reason for not limiting the negation to the more general thing.

The sentence "And if you were to follow their desires" to its end includes a warning against hoping that Jews or Christians would be brought closer through some appeasement of them, in hope of their conversion by winning their hearts. So He emphasised that warning with ten emphases: the oath implied by the preparatory lām for the oath; the emphasis of the answer clause by inna; the lām of commencement in its predicate; the nominal form of the answer clause, which is "you would have no protector or helper against Allah"; the emphasis of the negation by min in His saying "min walī"; the generalisation followed by specification by mentioning the relative pronoun and clarifying it by His saying "of knowledge"; making "what has come" (i.e., "what was sent down to him") to be the whole of knowledge, because nothing else is considered, since it is deficient; and the emphasis of "min walī" by the conjunction of "nor a helper", which returns to its meaning though its concept differs, so it is like emphasis by a synonym.

[Page 696]

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it as it should be recited. It is they who believe in it. And whoever disbelieves in it, it is they who are the losers.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that follows on from what precedes it), arising from His saying: ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 120), together with His saying: ﴿Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [only] guidance﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 120). This is because it implies that the Jews and Christians, on that day, possess nothing of guidance. It is as if a questioner asked: how can they be [said to be without guidance] when they adhere to a law? And who is upon guidance, out of those who follow these two laws?

So the answer is: those who were given the Book and recited it as it should be recited are the ones who believe in it. It is also permissible that this be a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*, a sentence placed within or at the end of a discourse) to explain the state of the sincere believers among the People of the Book, with the aim of nullifying their belief that they are upholding faith in the Book. This verse looks back to His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down," they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and they disbelieve in what is beyond it﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 91), and so on. That verse is the opening of these discussions, and of the examples, lessons, and clarifications that were interspersed among them. Thus His saying ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ is a summation (*fadhlaka*, a concluding recapitulation) of what came before, and a decisive answer to their earlier excuse. This is of the type of *radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-ṣadr* (returning the end of a passage to its beginning).

For one of these two possibilities, the sentence is disconnected (not joined by a conjunction), because it has the sense of an answer, and because what is reported by it contrasts with what it opposes. That opposition is contained in His saying ﴿They say, "We believe in what was sent down to us"﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 91). It has moved from that to His saying ﴿And they say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 116), and His saying ﴿And those who do not know say﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 118). His saying ﴿reciting it as it should be recited﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to ﴿those to whom We have given the Book﴾, since they are now reciting it as it should be recited. The phrase *ḥaqqa tilāwatihi* is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ūl muṭlaq*, a cognate accusative), and its annexation to the verbal noun is of the type of an adjective annexed to its noun, meaning: a recitation that is true (*ḥaqqan*).

Here *al-ḥaqq* is the opposite of *al-bāṭil* (falsehood). That is, a recitation that fully preserves the essentials of its kind, lacking nothing of what is considered in recitation. This is the recitation that comes with understanding the purposes of the speech being recited, for speech is intended to convey meaning to the hearer. So if the reciter recites it without understanding everything its speaker intended, his recitation is deficient. Therefore *ḥaqq al-tilāwah* is knowledge of what is contained in the text recited.

His saying ﴿It is they who believe in it﴾ is a sentence that is the predicate of the subject, and the subject is the relative pronoun. The demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishārah*, "those" or "it is they") is used in describing them, rather than a pronoun or anything else, to draw attention to the fact that the qualities mentioned earlier, by which they were presented and then pointed to through their being characterised by them, are what make them deserving of the judgment attributed to the demonstrative, in the manner of His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 5). There is no doubt that their reciting the Book as it should be recited establishes that they alone (*awḥadiyyah*) believe in that Book, because the belief of others in it is as nothing. Thus the restriction (*qaṣr*) is claimed (*idda'ā'ī*, a restriction asserted by way of claim rather than strict logic).

The pronoun in "in it" refers to the Book in His saying ﴿those to whom We have given the Book﴾. And if they are the ones who believe in it, then they are believers in Muhammad (ﷺ), because the attributes that are in their scriptures apply to him, and because a covenant was taken from them to believe in the Messenger who follows (the earlier prophets), and to strive to distinguish between the truthful of the prophets and the liars, until they are certain that the attributes apply to the promised Prophet. For this reason some commentators have said that the pronoun in "in it" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), although no antecedent was previously mentioned for it.

It is also permissible that the pronoun in His saying "they believe in it" refers to the guidance in His saying ﴿Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [only] guidance"﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 120). That is, they believe in the Qur'an that it is sent down from Allah. In that case the pronoun governed by the preposition *bi-* refers to the Book in His saying ﴿We have given them the Book﴾. What is meant by it is the Torah and the Gospel. The definite article in "the Book" is either generic (*lil-jins*, referring to the category of revealed books) or refers only to the Torah, because it is the principal of the two religions, while the Gospel is a supplement. In that case the article is one of specific reference (*lil-'ahd*). Among these believers were 'Abd Allah ibn Salam from the Jews, and 'Adi ibn Hatim and Tamim al-Dari from the Christians.

The discussion of His saying ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, it is they who are the losers﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿It is they who believe in it﴾. It is an explicit statement of the judgment implied by the sense of ﴿It is they who believe in it﴾ (*mafhūm*, the implied meaning), and it dispenses with stating explicitly the judgment of the stated meaning (*manṭūq*), which is that those who believe in it are the winners. Thus the verse contains an excellent conciseness (*ījāz*), since it indicates that those who were given the Book and recite it as it should be recited are the believers and no others. So those who disbelieve are the losers, while those who believe in it are the successful.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 122–123:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another at all, nor will compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.﴾

The address "O Children of Israel" is repeated in the manner of warning, admonition and reminder, following the same method of repetition in the purpose for which the preceding discourse was brought. For he (may Allah be pleased with him) first began their address with a similar exhortation at the start of the reminder, concerning their many conditions, good and bad, right after His words ﴿and that they are to return to Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46]. The mention of this sentence there is like the mention of the objective (matlub) in the science of logic (sina'at al-mantiq) before establishing the proof (burhan), and its mention here is like the mention of the conclusion (natijah) in logic after the proof, as confirmation of what preceded and as a summary (fadhlakah) of it, and this is one of the forms of "returning the last to the first" (radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr).

This verse has been repeated in the same wording in which it was mentioned there, to draw attention to the subtle point of repetition for the sake of reminding. The two verses differ only in the order between "compensation" (al-'adl) and "intercession" (al-shafa'ah). There he placed ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48] first and then ﴿nor will compensation be taken from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48] after it. Here he placed "nor will compensation be accepted from it" first and delayed the word "intercession," attributing to it "will benefit it," and this is variation (tafannun). Variation in speech removes the tedium of repetition while the purpose of repetition is still achieved. Along with the variation, a subtle point has been achieved: in the preceding verse, intercession was attributed acceptability, so it was placed before compensation because its acceptability was negated; and negating the acceptance of intercession does not entail negating the taking of ransom, so he conjoined the negation of taking ransom as a precaution (li al-ihtiras). In this verse, he placed ransom first because acceptability was attributed to it, and negating the acceptance of ransom does not entail negating the benefit of intercession, so he conjoined the negation of intercession's benefit to the negation of ransom's acceptance, also as a precaution. The summary is that what is negated of being accepted was placed first in both verses and the other mentioned after it. As for negating acceptance once of intercession and once of compensation, this is because the conditions of peoples in seeking release from their offenders differ: sometimes they offer ransom, and if it is not accepted they offer intercessors; and sometimes they offer intercessors, and if their intercession is not accepted they present ransom.

His words ﴿nor will compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it﴾ mean that there is no compensation that is accepted, nor any intercession of an intercessor they might find whose intercession would be accepted, because the payment of ransom is impossible and the mediation of an intercessor for people like them is forbidden, since no intercessor intercedes except for one whom Allah has permitted. Ibn 'Arafah said: "So the negation of the benefit of intercession here is of the type of his saying:

*On a path whose signpost does not guide one*

He means that it is a kinaya (metonymy) for negating the thing described by negating its inseparable attribute," like their saying:

*"And you do not see the lizard entering its burrow there."*

This is what the logicians express by saying that a negative proposition is true when the subject is negated; this happens by way of kinaya, but as for it being usage in the original Arabic language, that is not so, and the logicians followed in this the methods of the Greeks.

The discussion of the remaining verses is unnecessary given what has preceded regarding their counterparts.

Here he concluded the argument with the People of the Book in this surah, and this is from the excellence (bara'ah) of the section's ending.

[Page 700]

When the proofs had been fully established against the People of the Book and the idolaters of the Arabs, who were deep in their misguidance through their turning away from Islam, and when their evil intentions, which prevented them from being guided by its guidance and benefiting from its bounty, had become clear, the Qur'an recorded this against the leaders of the obstinate, namely the Jews, beginning with His words "O Children of Israel" twice. It also incorporated the Christians along with them by way of an intended digression. Then, after those among them who were fair-minded, "who recite the Book as it ought to be recited," received their due, the discourse turned to directing rebuke and reminder to the Arabs, who claim that they are the best of the descendants of Ibrahim (Abraham), that they cling to his creed (millah), that they are the offspring of Isma'il (Ishmael), and that they are the custodians (sadana) of the House that he built. They had been stung by an aspect of allusion (ta'rid) in the course of the debates that had taken place with the People of the Book, concerning the quality that united them with those people in envying the Prophet and the Muslims for the good that had been sent down upon them, and for their saying, "The Muslims are upon nothing," and their saying, "Allah has taken a son," and their saying, "Why does Allah not speak to us?"

When the Jews and the Christians had received their full share of warning and admonition regarding what was specific to them, and the idolaters had received their share of that regarding what they shared, the occasion was prepared for turning toward the idolaters of the Arabs to give them their full share of admonition regarding what was specific to them.
