[Page 700 continues]

Thus, the connection between mentioning the virtues of Ibrahim, his station with his Lord, and his supplication for his progeny, placed after the mention of the conditions of the Children of Israel, is the unity of purpose. The aim of reminding the Children of Israel of the blessings and warning them is to urge them to be fair in receiving the Islamic call, to strip themselves of obstinacy and envy, and to abandon worldly interests in order to attain the happiness of the Hereafter.

The purpose of mentioning the story of Ibrahim is to admonish the idolaters primarily and the Children of Israel secondarily, because the Arabs have a stronger connection to Ibrahim in that they trace their lineage to him and, in addition, they are the guardians of his sanctuary (haram), and they have long been affiliated with the hanifiyya (the primordial monotheistic faith), and no religion has come upon them that contradicts the hanifiyya, unlike the People of the Two Books. It is therefore fitting that we take his saying "﴿And when﴾ [Ibrahim] was tested" as coordinated (ʿatf) with the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority (khalifa)"﴾ (2:30), as is indicated by its opening with "idh" (when), in the manner of the opening of the mention of the creation of Adam with the words ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ (2:30). The first is a reminder of the blessing of the first creation, and it came after the expression of wonder at the disbelief of the idolaters in the Creator in His words ﴿How do you disbelieve in Allah while you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ (2:28). Then this reminder was followed by a warning to whoever among the progeny of Adam disbelieves in the signs of Allah, in His words ﴿And if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ (2:38) and what follows. Then, among the progeny of Adam, the Children of Israel were singled out, to whom the covenant of faith and of confirming the Messenger who would come confirming what was with them was entrusted through the tongue of Musa (Moses), because they became like witnesses over the progeny of Adam.

Thus the occasion was prepared for reminding both groups of their closer forefather, who is Ibrahim, in whatever manner the address is primarily directed to the Arabs, while including the other group together with them in one conjunction. For this reason, most of the praise of Ibrahim concerns the building of the Sacred House and what followed from it, until the qibla (direction of prayer) was mentioned in the midst of that. Then he passed over, by transition, to mention the predecessors of the Children of Israel with His words ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub (Jacob)?﴾ (2:133), so that it would lead to His words ﴿And they say, "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided."﴾ (2:135). It then returns to the exaltation of the hanifiyya and the information that it is the origin of Islam, and that the idolaters have no share in it, and likewise the Jews and the Christians.

The opening of mention of these two phases (tawran) was with the excellence of mentioning the virtue of the two fathers, Adam and Ibrahim. So the two reports came in one style, in the most wondrous manner and the most precise arrangement. It is therefore determined that the implied sense of the speech is: "Remember when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord with words."

Some people have claimed that his saying "﴿And when﴾ [Ibrahim] was tested" is coordinated with his saying "My blessing," meaning: remember My blessing and My testing of Ibrahim. This entails restricting this admonition to the Children of Israel, and the words ﴿and fear a Day﴾ (2:123) intervene between the two coordinated items, and that narrows the comprehensiveness of the verse. The words ﴿and of my descendants﴾ and His words ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ have been incorporated into this. In this verse there is another purpose, which is to prepare the transition to the virtues of the Sacred Land (al-Balad al-Haram) and the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram), in order to establish the proof against those who were astonished by the abrogation of the direction toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and who used that as a pretext to attack Islam on account of the occurrence of abrogation in it, and to repel the common People of the Book from following it, because it changed their qibla. This was so that it might show them that the Ka'ba is more worthy of being faced, and that Allah preserved it for this Ummah, as an alert to the excellence of this religion.

Al-ibtila' (testing) is an iftiʿal form derived from al-bala' (trial), and the iftiʿal form here is for intensification. Al-bala' means examination, and it was mentioned previously in His words ﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord﴾ (2:49). It is a well-known metaphor, because the one who imposes a task upon another involves in that imposition the expectation of his doing or abstaining from something, and so he entails testing. Thus it is a metaphor upon a metaphor. What is meant here is imposition (taklif), because Allah imposed upon him commands and prohibitions, either of virtues and good manners, or of specific legal obligations pertaining to him. There is no difficulty in attributing testing to Allah the Exalted once you know that it is a metaphor for imposition. You may also take it as a metaphorical allegory (istiʿara tamthiliyya). In any case, the path of imposition is necessarily revelation. This indicates that Ibrahim was given revelation of a prophecy so that his soul would be prepared to receive the Law, and when he carried out what he was commanded, he was revealed the mission (risala), which is in His saying ﴿Indeed, I will make you an imam (leader) for the people﴾. So the clause ﴿Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people﴾ is a partial substitution (badal baʿd) for the clause "when he was tested." It is also permissible that the testing is the revelation of the mission, and that His saying "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people" is an explanation of "was tested."

The imam is the messenger and the exemplar (qudwa). Ibrahim is the name of the great messenger known by the title al-Khalil (the Friend), and he is Ibrahim son of Tarah. The Arabs call Tarah "Aazar, son of Nahur, son of Suruj, son of Ra'w, son of Falih, son of Abir, son of Shalih, son of Arfakshad, son of Sam, son of Nuh (Noah)," thus says the Torah. The meaning of Ibrahim in the language of the Chaldeans is "a compassionate father" or "a merciful father," as stated by al-Suhayli and Ibn 'Atiyya. In the Torah, the name of Ibrahim is Abram, and when Allah revealed to him and spoke to him, He commanded him to be named Ibrahim, because He would make him a father to a multitude of nations. So the meaning of Ibrahim according to this is "father of many nations." He was born in Ur of the Chaldeans in the year 1996, one thousand nine hundred and ninety-six (i.e. 1996 from the Creation, in the reckoning cited), before the birth of the Messiah. Then his father moved him to the land of Kan'an (Canaan), which is the land of the Phoenicians, and they settled in Harran (it is Hawran),

[Page 702]

then he left it because of a famine that struck Harran. He entered Egypt with his wife Sarah. There the king of Egypt desired to take Sarah, but he saw a sign that turned him away from his purpose. He honored her and gifted her an Egyptian slave-girl named Hajar (Hagar), who became the mother of his son Isma'il. Allah later named him Ibrahim, and he settled his son Isma'il and his mother Hajar in the valley of Makka. Then, when Isma'il grew up, Ibrahim built the Sacred House there.

Ibrahim died in the year 1773, one thousand seven hundred and seventy-three (i.e. 1773 from the Creation, in the reckoning cited), before the birth of the Messiah. As for his name, the Arabs have dialects: the first is Ibrahim, which is the well-known form, and most readers recited with it. The second is Ibrahaam, which occurs in the recitation of Hisham from Ibn 'Amir wherever the name Ibrahim occurs. The third is Ibrahim (with the vowel of the ha dropped), which occurs in a rajaz (verse) of Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl:

"I have sought refuge in what Ibrahim sought refuge in, facing the Ka'ba while standing."

Abu Shama mentioned in his commentary on Hirz al-Amani, from al-Farra', that Ibrahim has six forms: Ibrahim, Ibrahaam, Ibrahuum, Ibrahim with the ha kasra, Ibraham with the ha fatha, and Ibrahum with the ha damma. The majority of the ten readers recited only with the first, and some recited with the second in thirty-three places, which will be pointed out in their places. Despite the difference of these recitations, it is not written in most of the original codices (masahif) except Ibrahim with the ya' included. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: "I have not found in the codices of Iraq and Sham the word Ibraham written with a mim after the ha, nor was Ibrahaam written with an alif after the ha in any of the codices, in accordance with the recitation of Hisham." Abu Zur'a said: "I heard 'Abd Allah ibn Dhakwan say: I heard Abu Khulayd the reciter say that in the Qur'an there are thirty-six places of Ibrahaam." Abu Khulayd said: "I mentioned that to Malik ibn Anas, and he said: 'We have an ancient codex,' and he looked into it, then informed me that he found it so." Abu Bakr ibn Mihran said: It is related from Malik ibn Anas that he was told: "The people of Damascus recite Ibrahaam and claim that it is the recitation of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him)." Malik said: "Here is the codex of 'Uthman with me," then he called for it, and in it was as the people of Damascus recited.

The placement of the object, which is the word Ibrahim, first is because the intended purpose is to ennoble Ibrahim by joining the name of the Lord to his name, while observing brevity. Therefore He did not say "when Allah tested Ibrahim."

The "words" (kalimat) are the speech that Allah revealed to Ibrahim, since a kalima is an utterance that signifies a meaning. What is meant here is sentences (jumal), as in His words ﴿No! It is but a word he says﴾ (23:100). He summarized them here, since the purpose is not to detail the law of Ibrahim, nor to expand the story and narration. Rather, the purpose is to explain the excellence of Ibrahim by showing the manifestation of his resolve and his compliance with obligations, which he carried out completely, so he was rewarded with a great reward. This is the custom of the Qur'an in summarizing what is not the place of need. Perhaps the plural form of kalimat, the sound masculine plural, indicates that what is meant by them is the foundations of the hanifiyya, which are few in number but heavy in burden. Perhaps among them is the command to sacrifice his son, and his command to undergo circumcision, and the emigration with Hajar to a far region. The greatest of that is his command to sacrifice his son Isma'il, by revelation from Allah to him in a dream. This has been called a trial in His words ﴿Indeed, this is a manifest trial﴾ (37:106).

His saying "﴿and fulfilled them﴾" (fa-atammahunna) comes with the fa' to indicate immediacy in compliance, and that is from the intensity of resolve. Itmam (completion) originally means bringing the act to its end, or completing the last parts of a thing that has been made.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 124 (part 2 of 2):

The transitive use of the verb atamma (to complete) with the pronoun referring to "words" (kalimat) is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), in which the verb is attached to that which contains the object, since the words are like the place for it. Among the meanings of completion is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And Abraham, who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾ [al-Najm: 37], and His saying: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Saffat: 105]. Thus the form af'ala here means carrying out the act in the most complete manner. The intended sense of the hamza is not that of making (taṣyir), i.e., that He made them complete after they had been incomplete, because the intended meaning is not that he performed some of them and then came to the rest. Thus His saying "fa-atammahunna" ("and he fulfilled them"), despite its brevity, indicates compliance, perfecting it, and promptness in it. This clause is the goal of this part of the story, so its coordination (by fa-) serves to indicate that he was tested and complied, like your saying: "I called so-and-so, and he answered."

The clause "Qāla innī jā'iluka lil-nāsi imāman" ("He said: Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people") is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) of explanatory type (istī'nāf bayānī), arising from what the saying of His, "And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with words," required, namely the magnification of the report and drawing attention to it, since the adverbial phrase idh indicates a story from great historical reports. So the hearer anticipates what follows from its narration. It is also possible that the disconnection is in the manner of a dialogue (muqāwala), because this saying is a response to what is implied by His saying "ibtalā" (tested).

The word imam is derived from amm, with a fatha on the hamza, which means intention (qasd). It is of the form fa'āl, one of the forms of instrument by transmission (samā'an), like 'imād (pillar), niqāb (veil), izār (waistwrap), and ridā' (mantle). Its root is therefore "that by which one intends," i.e., the aim. Since the one who points to the way is followed by the traveller, imam came to signify the model to be followed and the guide.

The intended meaning of imam here is the Messenger, for prophethood is the most complete kind of imamate, and the Messenger is the most complete individual of this category. He turned away from the specification "rasulan" (messenger) to "imaman" (imam) so that this would indicate that his message benefits the nation to which he was sent by way of conveying, and benefits other nations by way of emulation. Abraham, peace be upon him, travelled to many horizons, moving from the lands of the Chaldeans to Iraq, to the Levant, the Hijaz and Egypt, and in all his dwellings he was a place of veneration. Without doubt, veneration arouses emulation. It has been said that the religion of Brahma followed in India has its origin attributed to the name Ibrahim, peace be upon him, with a distortion introduced into that religion, just as distortion was introduced into the hanifiyya. And so that brevity may be achieved in the report of Abraham's later words, "And of my offspring" (wa min dhurriyyati), he would have asked that the imamate in its various kinds—prophethood, kingship and exemplary leadership—be among his descendants according to their readiness for it. The least kind of imamate is that a perfect man be a model for his sons, his family members and his students.

His saying "﴿Qāla wa min dhurriyyatī﴾" ("He said: And of my offspring") is a reply that came from Abraham, and therefore it is related with qāla without a conjunction, in the manner of relating dialogues, as was previously mentioned at His saying: ﴿They said: Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. The spoken statement is coordinated with God's address to him, which they call the coordination of suggestion (ʿaṭf al-talqīn), which is the coordination by the addressee of a statement onto what occurred in the speech of the speaker, placing himself in the position of the speaker, completing for him something the speaker left out either through heedlessness or through brevity, so that the hearer suggests its completion, such that from the two statements a complete utterance results in the belief of the addressee.

In the authentic hadith, Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah said: "I pledged allegiance to the Prophet upon the testimony that there is no god but Allah, etc., and he stipulated for me ... and sincere advice to every Muslim." From this is the saying of Ibn al-Zubayr to one who asked him and he did not give, so he said: "May Allah curse the she-camel that carried me to you." Ibn al-Zubayr said: "And its rider." They have given it the title ʿaṭf al-talqīn, as in the commentary of al-Taftazani on the Kashshaf. That is because most occurrences of its like are in the position of coordination. It is better to delete the word ʿaṭf and call this type of speech by the name talqīn, which is the hearer suggesting to the speaker what he sees as fit to join to his speech. It may be by the way of coordination, which is the most common, as here, and it may be by way of the denying interrogative and the state, like His saying: ﴿They said: Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon. Even though their fathers did not reason anything, nor were they guided?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170]. The "wa" together with "law" (even if) is the wa of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), not the wa of coordination, so it is a denial of their attaching to the questioned matter their saying and claim. It may also be by way of exception, like the saying of al-ʿAbbas: "When the Prophet ﷺ said in the sanctuary of Makkah: 'Its trees must not be cut,' al-ʿAbbas said: 'Except idhkhir for our houses and our smiths.'"

The coordinated statement of suggestion takes the same ruling as the statement coordinated to, whether informative or directive. When it is in the manner of presentation, as here, it is known that the speaker endorses it, either by his affirmation as in the verse, or by explicit statement as occurred in the hadith, "except idhkhir." Then, in an imperative statement, if the coordinated element is an object of the imperative, it entails that the coordinated element has the ruling of what it is coordinated to. Since the one who coordinates in the imperative is the addressee of the imperative, the coordination of suggestion in it must be interpreted as intending coordination on a necessary object of the imperative. So in a command, if the one commanded coordinates an object onto the object of the commander, the meaning is "increase me from the command, for I am ready to comply." Likewise in a prohibition. The coordinated element is omitted, indicated by the context, i.e., "and some of my offspring," or "and the one who makes some of my offspring [imams]."

Dhurriyya is the progeny of a man and what proceeds from him and from his sons and daughters. It is derived either from dharr as a noun, meaning small ants; or from dharr as a verbal noun, meaning scattering; or from dhurrā and dharw (with yā' and wāw), the verbal noun of dharat al-rīḥ when it swept away; or from dhar' with a hamza, meaning creation. Its pattern is therefore either fu'liyya, in the form of a relative adjective to dharr, with the dhāl vowelled with a ḍamma in the relative adjective contrary to analogy, as they said in the relative adjective to dahr, dahrī, with the dāl vowelled with a ḍamma; or fu'ayyila or fu'ūla from dhurrā, dharw or dhar', with the two yā's merged, or the yā' with the wāw, or the yā' with the hamza after changing it to yā'. All of this is morphological derivation by the coiner's etymology, so it is not the analogy of morphology.

Abraham said "wa min dhurriyyatī" and did not say "wa dhurriyyatī" because he knew that God's wisdom in this world did not operate in such a way that the entire offspring of any person would be fit to be followed. So he did not ask for what is customarily impossible, since asking for that is not among the etiquettes of supplication.

He asked on behalf of his progeny, and did not restrict the request to his immediate descendants, as is customary in the partisanship of one who speaks to the people of his religion according to the natural disposition, which does not require distinction. He regards the sons of a son and the sons of a daughter as equal in closeness to the grandfather; rather, they are equal in the ruling of kinship. As for the foundation of tribal affiliation, it rests on customary considerations that return to support and pride. As for the verse of the poet:

"Our sons are the sons of our sons, and our daughters' sons / Are the sons of distant men."

this is a pre-Islamic delusion; otherwise the sons of sons are also, in turn, the sons of distant women, and no offspring comes into being except from a father and a mother. Likewise the saying of ...

And as for the verse:

"Our mothers are but vessels / In which we were created, and the children are the children [of the fathers]."

that is sophistry. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the one who asked him who has the greatest right to his good companionship among his parents: "Your mother, then your mother, then your mother, then your father." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents: his mother carried him in weakness upon weakness﴾ [Luqman: 14]. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ is an implied answer, concisely and clearly indicating the group in whom Abraham's supplication is fulfilled and the group in whom it is not, by restricting to one of them, because the ruling of one of two opposites establishes its contradiction for the other, by way of brevity. The category in whom the supplication is fulfilled was not mentioned because the purpose is to mention the other category, as an allusion that those who claim on that day that they are the most entitled to Abraham, namely the People of the Book and the idolaters of the Arabs, are the ones who are deprived of his supplication. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a hanif, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67]. ﴿Indeed, the people most entitled to Abraham are those who followed him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 68]. And because the educator intends to warn against corruptions before exhorting to benefits, the explanation of those in whom the supplication is not fulfilled takes precedence over the explanation of the others.

"Yanal" is the present tense of nāla, nayl, with the yā', when one attains something and reaches it, i.e., "does not reach My covenant the wrongdoers," meaning it does not encompass them. So "ʿahd" here means the emphatic promise.

God's promise is called a covenant ('ahd) because God does not break His promise, as He informed of that, so His promise became a covenant. For this reason the Prophet called it a covenant in his saying: "I beseech You by Your covenant and Your promise." That is, My promise of answering your supplication does not reach the wrongdoers among them. It is not fitting to interpret "ʿahd" here otherwise, although in some places in the Qur'an it is intended in another sense; the mention of ʿahd will come in Surat al-A'raf.

Among the precision of the Qur'an is the choice of this term here, because the Jews claimed that God made a covenant with Abraham that He was with his offspring. So mention of the word ʿahd contains an allusion to them, although the plain wording is for rebuking the idolaters. The wrongdoers here primarily means the polytheists, i.e., those who wronged themselves by associating partners with God. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. Wrongdoing also includes committing major sins, as occurred in His saying: ﴿And among their offspring is one who does good and one who clearly wrongs himself﴾ [al-Saffat: 113]. The Qur'an has described the Jews with the description of wrongdoers in His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. So the wrongdoing intended is major sins, the highest of which is associating partners with Allah, the Exalted.

In the verse there is an indication that the People of the Book and the idolaters at that time were not worthy of the imamate, because they were characterized by kinds of wrongdoing, such as polytheism, distorting the Book and interpreting it according to their desires, and persistence in sins. When they presented themselves to this description, they knew it applied to them. The attaching of the ruling to the description of wrongdoers is an indication of the reason for negating that God's covenant reaches them, so it is understood from the reason that when the attribute of wrongdoing is removed, the covenant reaches them.

In the verse there is also that one who is characterized by a major sin is not deserving of being entrusted with the imamate, meaning all the public offices of the Muslims: the caliphate, the emirate, judgeship, giving legal opinions, transmitting knowledge, leading prayer, and the like. Fakhr al-Din said: "The majority of jurists and theologians said: the sinner, during his sinfulness, may not be appointed to the imamate." In the tafsir of Ibn 'Arafa there is an acceptance of this, and Ibn 'Arafa transmitted from al-Mazari and al-Qurtubi from the majority: if the imam was validly appointed and then became corrupt and tyrannical, then if his corruption was through disbelief, it is obligatory to depose him; but if it was through other sins, the Kharijites, the Mu'tazila and some of the People of the Sunna said he should be deposed. The majority of the People of the Sunna said he is not deposed by corruption, tyranny, and suspension of the hudud; rather, it is obligatory to admonish him and to refrain from obeying him in what is not obligatory to obey, and this is with the ability to depose him. If he cannot be deposed except through strife and war, they agreed on forbidding rising against him, and that patience under his injustice is better than exchanging security for fear, shedding blood, and letting loose the hands of fools and sinners in the land. This is the ruling of every office according to the scholars of the Sunna. What is transmitted from Abu Hanifa about the permissibility of a sinner being a caliph but not a judge, Abu Bakr al-Razi al-Jassas said, is an error in transmission.

The majority of the ten readers read "ʿahdī" with a fatha on the yā' of the first person, which is one of the modes of the yā' of the first person; and Hamza and Hafs read it with the yā' sukun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 125 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And [mention] when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, and [said], "Take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer." And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il: "Purify My House for those who circumambulate it, those who stay in devotion there, and those who bow and prostrate."﴾ This is a progression in mentioning the virtue of Ibrahim, in that God made his House to have this excellence, and in that He attributed it to His majesty, saying "My House," and it is an introduction to the excellence of the Islamic qibla. The waw is a conjunction upon "ibtala" (tested), and "idh" is repeated to draw attention to the independence of the narrative, and that it is worthy of being counted with a separate intention. There is no concern with whether the content of this occurred after the other or before it, since there is no purpose in that in the context of mentioning virtues, and because the waw does not indicate sequence.

"Al-Bayt" (the House) is a generic noun for a place taken as a dwelling by one person or a number of people for some purpose. It is a place of the earth surrounded by what distinguishes it from the rest of its plot of land, so that the dweller is independent with it for himself and for whoever follows him, so that it is a settled place for him, and it shelters him from cold and heat, and a covering in which he hides from people, and a place for his furnishings and affairs. It may be for a particular person, which is the most common, and it may be for a group, like the Dar al-Nadwa among the Arabs and the Tent of Meeting among the Children of Israel. It may be a house whose enclosure is of stone and clay, like the Ka'ba and Dar al-Nadwa; it may be of leather, like tents; and it may be of woven wool or hair. God the Exalted says: ﴿And He made for you from the hides of livestock houses which you find light to carry﴾ [al-Nahl: 80]. A structure is not called a house unless its top is covered against heat and cold, and that is by a roof for houses of stone, houses of leather, and tents.

"Al-Bayt" is a proper name by predominance for the Ka'ba, just as "al-najm" (the star) became predominant for al-Thurayya. The origin of the "al" found in proper names by predominance is the "al" of definiteness by previous reference (al-'ahdiyya): when the mention of one individual of a class becomes frequent among a group or people, the name of its class together with the "al" of previous reference becomes like a proper noun for it. Then they may retain alongside this the original meaning, as in "al-najm" for al-Thurayya, "al-kitab" for the Qur'an, and "al-bayt" for the Ka'ba; and the original meaning may be forgotten, either through little need for it, as "al-Sa'iq" is a name for Khuwaylid ibn Nufayl, or through the class being confined to it, as "al-shams" (the sun).

The Ka'ba is a house which Ibrahim, peace be upon him, built for the worship of God alone, without partner, so that whoever holds to monotheism may take refuge in it, and whoever intends to magnify God the Exalted circumambulates it. For this reason He attributed it to God the Exalted in this sense, as He said: "Purify My House for those who circumambulate it," and in His saying: ﴿Near Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]. The Ka'ba has been known by the name "the House" since the time of Jahiliyya. Zuhayr said:

So I swore by the House which those around it circumambulated, men whom Quraysh and Jurhum built.

"Al-mathaba" is a noun of place from thaba yathubu, meaning to return; it is said mathaba and muthab, like maqama and maqam. What is meant by "mathaba" is that people come to it with veneration and seek refuge in it. What is meant by "the people" is the inhabitants of Makka from the descendants of Isma'il, and everyone who neighbours them and enters into their alliance. The definiteness of "al-nas" is of the class known, and the attachment of "lil-nas" to "mathaba" is distributive, meaning that people visit it and depart, and other people replace them.

Since the purpose of this is to mention the virtue of the House and the favour upon its inhabitants, the aim is to remind of God's blessing in making it such that no group departs from it except that other groups replace them. Those who replace the visitors thus stand in their place with respect to the House and its inhabitants. It is also permissible to take the definiteness of "al-nas" as previous reference, meaning that the people who are accustomed to it return to it, namely the perfect visitors, who return to it repeatedly; and so it was the custom among the Arabs.

"Al-amn" (security) is a verbal noun which is predicated of the House on the basis that it is a cause of security, so it is treated as if it were security itself, for emphasis. Security is the protection of people from harms: the dispersal of brigands, guarding the land, paving roads, and lighting paths are security; and the exacting of retribution from criminals, striking the hands of oppressors, and restoring rights to their owners are security. Thus security is interpreted in every case according to what suits it. Since the prevailing condition of the Jahiliyya was that the strong seized the wealth of the weak, and there was no mutual judgement or law among them, security on that day was the barrier between the strong and the weak. So God made the House a security for the people on that day, meaning that it prevents the strong from seizing the weak within it. God the Exalted says: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary while people are snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67]. This is therefore a favour upon the people of the Jahiliyya. As for in Islam, God the Exalted has sufficed through what He legislated of His rulings and what He established of His rulers, and that was sufficient security. Al-Suhayli said: His saying, the Exalted, "the station of Ibrahim, and whoever enters it shall be secure," is merely information about the magnification of its sanctity in the Jahiliyya, a favour from Him, the Exalted, upon the people of Makka; and in that was a benefit for the descendants of Isma'il, peace be upon him.

The jurists have differed concerning the use of this verse and its like as evidence for the ruling on carrying out the hudud and punishments within the Haram; its detail will come at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqara: 191], and it is not the purpose of this verse.

The meaning of "ja'l" (making) in the verse is either the creational making, since God decreed that and brought about its causes, so that it became settled among the people of the Jahiliyya and facilitated their veneration of it; or the making by God's command to Ibrahim, so that Ibrahim conveyed it to his son Isma'il, and he spread it among his descendants, who received it as a matter taken for granted. Thus that security persisted through the ages and generations from the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, until God made it unnecessary through what He legislated of rulings on security in Islam everywhere, and the will of God the Exalted was fulfilled. So let not what happened at the Sacred Mosque of fear during the siege of al-Hajjaj in the strife of Ibn al-Zubayr disturb you, nor what happened there of terror, killing and plunder in the time of the Qaramita, when al-Hasan ibn Bahram al-Junnabi, a nisba to a town called Junnaba with a doubled nun, the leader of the Qaramita, attacked it, for he killed thousands of people in Makka, and he would say to them: "O dogs, did not Muhammad of Makka say to you: ''And whoever enters it shall be secure'' [Al 'Imran: 97]? What security is here?!" He was ignorant and foolish, because God intended the matter, that He would make the Sacred Mosque a refuge during the period of the Jahiliyya, when people had no restraint against injustice. Or it is a report meant as a command, like ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqara: 228].

His saying, ﴿and take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer﴾, was read by Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir with the past tense form (ittakhadhu), coordinated upon ja'alna, so that this taking is one of the effects of that making. The meaning is: We inspired the people to take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer, or We commanded them to do so through the tongue of Ibrahim, and they complied and took it. It thus indicates that the making occurred by way of the implication of necessity (dalalat al-iqtida'), as if it were said: "We made that, so they took it." The remaining ten readers read it with the kasra on the kha' in the imperative form, on the assumption of a verb of saying, meaning "We said: take," by the indication of the address; so the governing verb coordinated is omitted by indication, and its object remains, like the saying of Labid:

So the branches of al-Ayhaqan grew tall, and its gazelles and ostriches gave birth to young in the two sides.

He meant "and its ostriches laid eggs", for young of birds are not called "atfal". Thus the outcome of the two readings returns to one meaning.

"Maqam Ibrahim" is applied to the Ka'ba, because Ibrahim used to stand beside it worshipping God the Exalted and calling to His monotheism. Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said: "I take refuge in what Ibrahim took refuge in, facing the Ka'ba while standing." And with this application it came in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The station of Ibrahim, and whoever enters it shall be secure﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], since entering is among the connections of the House. "Maqam Ibrahim" is also applied to the stone on which Ibrahim, peace be upon him, stood when building the Ka'ba, in order to rise to place the stones on the top of the wall, as al-Bukhari reported; and the traces of his two feet have been established in the stone. Anas ibn Malik said: "I saw in the Maqam the trace of his fingers and the sole of his two feet, except that the rubbing of people's hands has removed it." This stone is known to this day as the Maqam. The Prophet ﷺ prayed two rak'as at its place after the tawaf of arrival, so bowing there became a sunna upon completing the tawaf.

"Al-musalla" is the place of prayer, and their prayer on that day was supplication and humility to God the Exalted. Ibrahim had placed the Sacred Mosque around the Ka'ba and placed the stone on which he rose for the building around it, so the musalla was on the stone called the Maqam; thus the musalla is "taken from the station of Ibrahim" under both applications.

The two readings imply that taking the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer was from the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and the stone on which Ibrahim stood in the building was not specifically designated for prayer there, but it was included in prayer in the Sacred Mosque. When Islam came, the matter remained so until the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage or the year of the Conquest, when the Messenger of God ﷺ entered the Sacred Mosque with 'Umar ibn al-Khattab; then prayer at the Maqam was established as a sunna upon the tawaf of arrival.

Al-Bukhari reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters: I said, 'O Messenger of God, if only we took the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer,' and then it was revealed: ﴿And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer﴾." This report raises another meaning of the verse, namely that the address is directed to the Muslims, so that the phrase ﴿and take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer﴾ is an interjected clause between the phrase "We made the House a place of return for the people" and the phrase "And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il", as a digressive interjection. To bring together the three possibilities in the verse, the interpretation of 'Umar's words "then it was revealed" is that the ruling of prayer at the stone of the Maqam was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ after it had not been prescribed for them, so that the combination of the meanings of the two readings is consistent: "wa-ttakhadhu" in the past tense and in the imperative form. For the past tense admits only the narration of what was in the time of Ibrahim, while the imperative admits that, and also admits that what is meant is the sense of legislation for the Muslims, applying the Qur'an with everything its words can bear, as we have explained in the ninth introduction.

His saying, ﴿And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾: "'ahd" originally means a promise made firm in its occurrence, and it has been mentioned above at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqara: 124]. When it is followed by "ila", it means a command emphasised upon the one commanded to act upon it. So "'ahida" here means "arsala 'ahdan ilayhi", i.e., sent to him a covenant, taking from them a covenant. The meaning is: "We commanded Ibrahim and Isma'il." His saying "an tahhara" is an explanatory "an", because the command contains the sense of speech without its letters; so the explanation is of an implicit saying, and what follows "an" is the explanation. There is no elision in the sentence; and had the intention not been to relate the speech, it would not have come after "an" with the imperative form, but would have said "bi-tathhir bayti" etc.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 125 (part 2 of 2):

The intended meaning of "purifying the House" is what the word "purification" indicates in the sensory sense, by protecting it from filth and dirt so that the worshipper in it may devote himself to worship without disturbance, and in the non-sensory sense, by keeping away from it whatever is unfitting to the purpose of its construction, such as idols and acts that contradict truth, like transgression (al-'udwan) and grave sin (al-fusuq), and acts that contradict chivalry (al-muru'ah), like circumambulating naked without the garments of men and women. In this there is an allusion that the polytheists are not fit to maintain the Sacred Mosque, because they did not purify it of what must be purified. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they were not its guardians; its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾ [al-Anfal: 34], and He said: ﴿O you who believe, the polytheists are only impure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. "Those who circumambulate, those who stay in devotion (al-'akifun), those who bow and those who prostrate" are categories of worshippers in the House, through circumambulation, seclusion, and prayer. They are the categories of those characterised by these attributes, whether some groups are distinguished by some of these attributes alone or the attributes are combined in one group or several groups. All of this applies to the Ka'bah before the Sacred Mosque was established, and these are Isma'il, his sons, his in-laws from Jurhum, and everyone among their neighbours who believed in the religion of hanifiyyah.

The plural sound form (jam' salamah) was used for "al-ta'ifin" and "al-'akifin," and the broken plural (jam' taksir) for "al-raki'" and "al-sajid," as a variation in speech and a departure from repeating the same pattern more than once, unlike His saying: ﴿Muslim women, believing women, obedient women, penitent women﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35]. Ibn 'Arafah said: "He used the sound plural for al-ta'ifin and al-'akifin because it is closer to the wording of the verb, as in yatufun, meaning they renew the circumambulation, to indicate the reason for purifying the House, which is the nearness of these two to the House. By contrast, bowing and prostration do not necessarily occur in the House or near it, so the sound plural was not used for them." This statement indicates a distinction between the sound plural and the broken plural in terms of indicating occurrence and renewal. Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinni's commentary on al-Hamasah supports this, regarding the verse of al-Ahwas al-Ansari: "Fa-idha tazulu tazulu 'an mutakhammitin ∗∗∗ tukhsha bawadiruhu 'ala al-aqran." Abu al-Fath said: "It is permissible for 'ala to be connected to bawadir, even though it is a broken plural, and the verbal noun, when it takes a broken form, becomes more distant from resembling the verb because of its breaking. And since it is permissible for the object to be connected to a verbal noun in broken form, as in mawa'id 'Urqub akhahu, the connection of the prepositional particle to it is even more permissible." The clear sense of his statement is that breaking (taksir) distances what has the meaning of the verb from resembling the verb.

The bowing and prostration were differentiated as an added variation in style; otherwise the one who prostrates is pluralised as sujjad. However, the more common practice with these two when they occur together is to vary their forms. Kuthayyir said:

"Law yasma'una kama sami'tu kalamaha ∗∗∗ kharru li-'Izzata rukka'an wa sujudan"

You know from grammar and morphology that the plural of fa'il on fu'ul is transmitted (sama'i), and from it come shuhud, huju', hujud, and sujud.

He did not conjoin "al-sujud" to "al-ruka'" because the two descriptions are mutually inseparable; had he conjoined them, it would have been assumed that they were two separate descriptions.

[Page 714 begins]

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary" (2:125). It introduces a third virtue of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), concerning the granting of his supplication regarding the excellence of Makkah and the blessing upon its inhabitants if they are thankful. It is also a third admonition to the polytheists of Makkah at that time, so that they may remember the supplication of their father Ibrahim, which indicates his eagerness for their faith in God and the Last Day, to the point that he singled out the believers among his descendants with his supplication. The polytheists thus present themselves to the state their father requested, and it becomes clear to them that they are in a different state. This prompts them to adopt that state, because people have a desire to follow their forefathers and a longing for their conditions. All of this contains an implicit reproach to them: what they boast of, namely their lineage to Ibrahim, the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque, and the rites of the Hajj, does not avail them against associating partners with God. Likewise, the earlier verses alluded to the Jews and Christians, and this is found in His words here: "Then I shall compel him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination." Through this, the connection of mentioning this virtue immediately after the words of the Exalted, "And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary," becomes evident. The demonstrative in His words "this a land" (hādhā baladan) refers to the place where Ibrahim stood at the time of his supplication, which is the place where he left his wife and son and resolved to build the Kaʿbah, if the supplication was before the building, or the place in which the Kaʿbah was built, if the supplication was after the building. The direct presence of the referent makes the sensory pointing unnecessary, because its being distinguished for the addressee is sufficient in place of pointing to it. Therefore, the use of the demonstrative is clear in that context.

The original function of demonstratives is to dispense with additional verbal specification of the referent, since pointing is itself a form of clarification. Sometimes, however, they add further clarification by mentioning after the demonstrative a noun that is in apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) or a substitute (badal) for it, to indicate that the referent is intended to be brought to mind through some of its attributes, as in your saying: "This man says such-and-such." This is strengthened if one omits the pointing with the hand, relying on the presence of what is meant by the demonstrative. Here, however, he (the Qur'an) has departed from specifying the referent, being content with what is present at the time of the supplication, for Ibrahim made his supplication while standing in the place where he built the Kaʿbah. The purpose is not to detail the circumstances of the supplication, but to state the granting of his supplication, the excellence of the place of the supplication, the making of Makkah a secure land, and the provision of its people with fruits. This is the Qur'an's practice of omitting what has no bearing on the intended meaning. Do you not see that when He made "land" the second object, He dispensed with specifying the demonstrative? In Sūrat Ibrahim, when He made "secure" the second object, He specified the demonstrative with the word "land." Thus, from the two verses it results that Ibrahim prayed for a land that it be secure.

"Land" (balad) is a spacious place of the earth that is distinct, whether inhabited or uninhabited, and it is also the earth in general. Ṣannān al-Yashkurī said:

"But it is the pool of one who destroyed his brothers,
the vicissitude of fate, and it became the egg of the land."

He means the egg of the ostrich in its nest, that is, the place of its eggs. "Land" is also applied to a village composed of several houses for the dwelling of its people, and this is a literal usage which is more well-known than its application to a spacious tract of earth. Apparently, the supplication of Ibrahim related in this verse was before Makkah was settled, since there was then only the house of Ismaʿil, or one or two other houses, because Ibrahim began its construction by building the House of stone. Also, God's inspiration to him for this was due to His will that it become a place of great civilization in that region, as a preparation (irhāṣ) for the prophethood of our master Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also possible that the place was inhabited by people at the time of the arrival of Ibrahim, his wife, and his son. The Arabs mention that in that region there were clans of Jurhum, Quṭūrā, the Amalekites, and the Karkar, in the areas of Ajyad and ʿArafat.

"Secure" (āmin) is an active participle from amina, the opposite of khāfa (to fear). In its unrestricted sense it means the absence of fear of an enemy or of fighting, and this is what God distinguished Makkah by, among all the other lands of the Arabs. The term "security" may also be applied to the absence of fear in general, in which case it is necessary to mention what it relates to. Security is only predicated of what can be characterized by fear, which is that which possesses perception. Therefore, the description of the land as "secure" is either by making the form fāʿil here in the sense of relation, meaning "possessing security," as in the saying of al-Nābigha:

"Leave me alone for a worry, O Umayma, one who is fatigued,"

meaning one possessing fatigue; or by the intention of "its people are secure," by way of metaphor of attribution (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī) through the association of the place. Then, if the referent at the time of Ibrahim's supplication was a land in which there was one or two houses, the meaning of the speech is: "Make this place a secure city," that is, a secure village. Thus it is a supplication that it become a village and that it be secure.

If the referent at the time of his supplication was a village that people had built around it and settled beside it, which is the more apparent view and what the speech of al-Kashshāf here and in Sūrat Ibrahim implies, then it was a supplication for the land that security be granted to it. As for the narration of his supplication in Sūrat Ibrahim with His words, "Make this land secure" (14:35), that was a supplication for it after it had become a land.

This supplication of Ibrahim is among the comprehensive expressions of prophetic speech, for the security of lands and roads entails all the qualities of a good life. It requires justice, honor, and prosperity, since there is no security without them. It also entails prosperity and attention to what benefits, and wealth. Security is not disturbed unless these three are disturbed: the first (security), and when it is disturbed, the last three are disturbed. He intended by this to facilitate residence in it for its inhabitants, so as to consolidate the means for what he desired for that land, namely that it be the source of Islam.

"Fruits" (thamarāt) is the plural of thamara, which is what the tree bears and produces, from what contains nourishment for humans or fruit for them. It seems that its name is derived from the name of the dates with the letter tāʾ (thamar, with the single dot), for the people of the Ḥijāz mean by thamar with the three-dot thāʾ the fresh dates, and with the two-dot tāʾ the dried dates.

The word thamara has several plurals: thamar (with vowel modification), thimār, thumur (with two ḍammas), athmār, and athāmīr. They said there is no parallel to this except for akama, whose plurals are akam, ikām, ukum, āḵām, and akāmīm.

The definite article in "the fruits" (al-thamarāt) is the article of comprehensiveness (taʿrīf al-istighrāq), and it is a customary comprehensiveness, that is, of all the fruits known to people. The evidence that it is the article of comprehensiveness is the coming of "min" (from), which indicates partiality. In this there is a supplication for them for prosperity, so that their souls do not aspire to depart from it.

His words, "whoever among them believes in God," is a partial substitute (badal baʿḍ) for his words "its people." It indicates its specification, because "its people" is general, being a collective noun with a pronoun attached, and the partial substitute is specifying.

Ibrahim specified the believers for the request of provision for them, out of eagerness for the spread of faith among its inhabitants. For when they know that the supplication of Ibrahim was specific to the believers, they avoid whatever turns them away from faith. Thus he made the facilitation of provision for them conditional upon their faith, as an incentive for them to believe. Or he intended to show good manners with God, and so he asked Him in a way closer to being answered. Perhaps he sensed from God's response to him the general scope of his earlier supplication, when he said, "And of my offspring," and He said, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers" (2:124), that those who do not believe are not worthy of having God's provision bestowed upon them. God followed up his supplication with His words, "And whoever disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little while." The purpose of Ibrahim in this supplication was that the means of residing in Makkah be abundantly available to its people, so that need would not compel them to settle in another land. For he hoped that they would be callers to what the Kaʿbah was built for: the establishment of monotheism and the qualities of ḥanīfiyya, which are qualities of perfection. This is the first manifestation of the formation of the virtuous city (al-madīna al-fāḍila) which Plato called for, some ten or more centuries later.

The clause "He said, 'And whoever disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment'" came in the manner of relating statements in dialogues and replies, separated (from the preceding clause). The pronoun in "He said" refers back to God. Whoever allows that the pronoun in "He said" refers to Ibrahim, and that the repetition of the statement is due to the length of the first statement, has neglected the meaning, the usage, and the pronoun in His words "I will grant him enjoyment."

As for His words, "whoever disbelieves" (wa-man kafara), the most apparent view is that it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause "and provide for its people," in respect of the condition, which is His words "whoever among them believes." Thus His words "whoever disbelieves" would be a subject (mubtadaʾ), and the relative pronoun has the sense of a conditional, which is why the predicate is joined with the particle fa- (then), in a common manner for such constructions, as we have mentioned under His words, "And of my offspring" (2:124): that the coordination of an instruction in a directive, when it proceeds from the one addressed by the directive, is evidence of the attainment of the purpose of the directive and its extension beyond it. Therefore, the meaning here amounts to God Most High showing His favor to Ibrahim by providing for his descendants, both believer and disbeliever, or showing the breadth of His mercy by providing for all the inhabitants of Makkah, believers and disbelievers alike.

The meaning of "I will grant him enjoyment" (umatti'uhu) is: I will make the provision for him an enjoyment. "A little" (qalīlan) is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (maṣdar) after his words "I will grant him enjoyment," and the little enjoyment is the enjoyment of this world, as the contrast with His words "then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire" indicates.

In this verse there is evidence for the view of al-Bāqillānī, the Māturīdiyya, and the Muʿtazila that the disbelievers are granted blessings of this world. Al-Ashʿarī said: the disbeliever is not granted blessings, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter; rather, God gives them respite (istidrāj) in this world as a form of ease. The question is counted among the matters of disagreement between the Ashʿarī and the Māturīdī, and it seems that the disagreement between them is verbal, although al-Subkī counted it among the disagreements of meaning.

His words, "then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire," are a precaution against the disbeliever being deceived into thinking that the bestowal of blessings upon him in this world indicates God's pleasure. Therefore He mentioned punishment here.

[The particle] "then" (thumma) indicates a delay in rank (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), as is its usage in coordinating sentences, without regard to the fact that his destination to punishment is delayed relative to his being granted the little enjoyment.

The word "iḍṭirār" originally means being driven to seek refuge. It is of the pattern iftaʿala and is the reflexive (muṭāwiʿ) of aḍarrahu, meaning he made him possessed of necessity (ḍarūra), that is, need. Thus the original form was that iḍṭurra would be intransitive, because the basic meaning of the reflexive is non-transitivity. However, its usage came to be transitive with an object, and this is an eloquent usage, though not following the regular pattern. One says iḍṭarrahu ilā kadhā, meaning he compelled him to it. A parallel to this verse is His words in Sūrat Luqmān: "We grant them enjoyment for a little while, then We compel them to a harsh punishment" (31:24).

His words, "and wretched is the destination," are a concluding summary (tadhyīl). The waw is for parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) or for circumstance (ḥāl), and the predicate is deleted, being the object of the dispraise (al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-dhamm), and its estimate is "it" (hiya).

This is a third virtue of Abraham, peace be upon him, and a reminder of the nobility of the Ka'bah. It is also a third means of alluding to the polytheists after His saying, ﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You, and of our descendants a Muslim nation﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:128], and so on. It also paves the way for a refutation of the Jews, who deny the direction of prayer toward the Ka'bah, a matter that comes at His saying, ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:142]. Because this verse is independent by virtue of these three purposes, which the preceding verses contain, it is conjoined to what precedes it with the particle ﴿when﴾ (idh), as an alert to its independence.

The style that the apparent meaning would require in narrating the past is the past tense, so that it would say, "and when Abraham raised..." Instead it is in the present tense, ﴿raises﴿ (yarfa'u), to evoke the situation.

The narration is presented as though it were being witnessed, because the present tense indicates the time of the present. Its use here is a secondary metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya): the past is likened to the present because of its fame and because of the repeated mention of it among them. For out of their love for Abraham and their veneration of him, they never cease to mention his virtues, and the greatest of them is the building of the Ka'bah. Thus the past is likened to the present for this reason. Also, what has preceded in the verses about Abraham, from His saying, ﴿And when his Lord tested Abraham﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:124] up to here, is of the kind that fills the minds of the listeners with Abraham and his affairs, until it is as though he were present among them and his circumstances were present and witnessed. The word ﴿when﴾ (idh) is an indicator of this presentation, because its common usage is for past time. This is the meaning of the statement of the grammarians (nuhat) that idh transforms the present tense into the past.

The qawa'id (foundations) is the plural of qa'idah, which is the base of a building, rising from the ground, on which the building's stability rests. This term was applied to them because they resemble one who sits (qa'id) in their adherence to the earth. Thus the original designation of qa'idah is a metaphor for adherence to the earth, and then for the intended sense of firmness in the earth. The feminine ending in it is for emphasis, like the ending in 'allamah.

Raising the foundations means bringing them out of the ground and building upon them, so that they become walls, because the structure joins part to part and becomes like one thing. Thus when the wall is joined to the foundation, the foundation is raised. It is also permissible to take qawa'id to mean the walls of the House, just as they were called arkan (pillars). Raising them means extending them. The height of the walls of the House has been given as nine cubits.

It may also be understood from the choice of the root r-f-' (raising) rather than the root of extension or similar, that there is a meaning of honoring. Attributing this to the foundations is a metonymy (kinayah) for its being established for the House. Attributing the raising, in this sense, to Abraham is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because Abraham was the cause of the said raising, that is, by his supplication accompanying it.

The conjunction of Isma'il with Abraham is an honoring of him, since he was his helper and the one who handed him the stones.

To indicate the difference between the action of Abraham and the action of Isma'il, the conjunction was placed on the agent after mentioning the object and the complements. This is, as it appears to me, one of the peculiarities of Arabic in the style of conjunction, and I cannot recall at present a similar usage in the speech of the Arabs. The principle is this: if you wish to show a difference between two agents in the performance of the verb, you place the conjunction of one of them after the completion of what relates to the first agent. If you wish to make the conjoined and the conjoined-to equal in the performance of the verb, you make the conjoined follow directly after the conjoined-to.

Isma'il is the name of the firstborn son of Abraham, peace be upon him, and he is his son by his concubine Hajar the Egyptian.

He was born in the land of the Canaanites, between Qadesh and Barad, in the year 1910 BC (written as "nineteen hundred and ten" in the text). In Hebrew, the meaning of Isma'il is "God has heard," that is, God's answering, because God answered the supplication of his mother Hajar when she left, pregnant with Isma'il, leaving the place where Sarah, her mistress, was, when Sarah became jealous of Hajar after Hajar conceived, and Sarah had no children at that time. It is also said that it is an Arabicized form of Yishma'el in Hebrew, and its meaning is "the one whom God hears." When Isma'il grew up, Abraham saw a vision of revelation in which he was to sacrifice him, and he resolved to slaughter him, but God ransomed him. At that time Isma'il was Abraham's only son, before the birth of Isaac. Isma'il lived in Makkah around the Ka'bah. He died in Makkah in the year 1773 BC, approximately, and was buried in the Hijr that is around the Ka'bah.

The clause ﴿Our Lord, accept from us; indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is the object of a suppressed statement, which is to be understood as a circumstantial clause (hal) for ﴿raises﴿ (yarfa'u), with Abraham as the subject. This statement is from the speech of Abraham, because supplication for his descendants is what suits him, since Isma'il was then young.

The shift from mentioning the saying to the speech of the speaker himself, with what the one narrated about had said, is a kind of evoking the situation. The present-tense report in His saying ﴿and when [Abraham] raises﴾ has prepared the way for it, until it is as though the speaker himself were the one who said it. This is a kind of elaboration (iyghal).

The clause ﴿indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for the request that they be accepted from them both. The definiteness of the two parts of this clause and the bringing of the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) indicate two restrictions (qasr), for the sake of emphasis on the perfection of the two attributes for Him, the Exalted, by making the hearing and knowledge of others as though they did not exist.

It is also permissible that it be a true restriction (qasr haqiqi) with regard to a specific object: that is, "He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing of our supplication, which none other than You knows." This is a restricted true restriction, a type different from the relative restriction (qasr idafi), which the scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-ma'ani) have not drawn attention to.

﴿Our Lord, make us both submissive to You, and from our descendants a submissive community to You, and show us our rites, and turn to us. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

The purpose of repeating the address "Our Lord" is to show humble supplication to God Most High, and to show that each of these requests is sought in its own right. For this reason, the address is repeated only when moving from one supplication to another.

[p. 720]

The first supplication seeks the acceptance of the deed, and the second seeks guidance. Thus the address clause is an interjection (jumla i'tiradiyya) between the conjoined phrase here and the phrase it is conjoined to in His saying, later: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a Messenger﴾ [al-Baqara: 129]. By "submissive to You" (muslimayn laka) is meant those who yield to God Most High, since islam is submission (al-inqiyad). Since submission to the Creator in truth includes belief in His existence, not associating anyone with Him in worship, and knowing His attributes as indicated by His acts, the reality of islam is inseparable from the reality of faith (iman) and monotheism (tawhid). The reason this is called islam will come at His saying ﴿so do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqara: 132]. As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Say: You have not believed, but say: We have submitted﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14], it separates the two, because their submission was out of fear and not out of conviction. Thus faith and islam are different in concept, and between them there is a partial overlap in extension (umum wa khusus wajhi fi al-masdaq). Monotheism during the period of fatra (the interval between prophets) is faith, from which submission is not expected, since submission arises only through deeds. And the submission of one who is overcome and coerced is islam that did not arise from conviction of faith. Nevertheless, the two cases of separation, of faith without islam and of islam without faith, are rare.

God inspired Abraham with the name islam, then reserved it after him for the Muhammadan religion. So this name was forgotten after Abraham, and no other religion was given it as a title, because God willed that the Muhammadan religion be the completion of the hanifiyya, the religion of Abraham. An explanation of this will come at His saying, ''﴿Abraham was neither a Jew﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 67]'' in the Surah of Ali 'Imran.

The meaning of the request that He make them both submissive is a request for increase in the islam they already have, and a request for its continuance, because God had already made them submissive before, as indicated by His saying ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit"﴾ [al-Baqara: 131] and what follows.

As for His saying ﴿and from our descendants a submissive community to You﴾, it is necessary that both (min dhurriyyatina) and (muslima) be objects (ma'mulan) of the verb "make us" (aj'alna) by way of conjunction. This is a supplication that their religion remain among their descendants. The "min" in His saying "min dhurriyyatina" is partitive (lil-tab'id). They asked this only for some of the descendants, combining eagerness for the descendants to attain this excellence with courtesy in supplication, because Abraham's prophethood implied his knowledge that his descendants would be many nations, and that God's wisdom in this world has been that it does not lack the inclusion of both the righteous and the wicked. So he asked God for what is ordinarily possible, and this is part of the etiquette of supplication. A parallel to this was mentioned before in His saying, ﴿He said, "And of my descendants"﴾ [al-Baqara: 124].

From here began the allusion to the polytheists who turned away from monotheism and followed polytheism, and the preparation for the honour of the Muhammadan religion.

[p. 721]

The word "umma" is a homonym (ism mushtarak) applied to many meanings. What is meant here is a great group gathered by a unifying bond of considerable importance, whether of lineage, religion or time. For example, the "Umma of Muhammad" is said of Muslims, because they have come together in belief in the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. It is of the form fi'la, and this form indicates the passive (maf'ul), like laqta (what is picked up), dihka (a laugh at someone), and qudwa (exemplar). So "umma" means "ma'mūma" (that which is followed), derived from "umm" with an initial fatha, which means intention (al-qasd), because the umma is intended by the many factions gathered under a unifying bond encompassing the whole umma, like the Arab umma, because the tribes of the Arabs trace back to it, and the Islamic umma, because the Islamic schools trace back to it. As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you﴾ [al-An'am: 38], it is in the sense of eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), meaning "like communities." If you reflect on the wisdom in the perfection of their creation and the order of their conditions, you will find them like communities similar to you, because people were heedless of this consideration.

The supplication of Abraham was answered regarding the Muslims from among the Arabs, who followed one another into islam before the Hijra and after it, until all the Arabs had embraced islam, except a few tribes whose presence does not break the unifying bond of the umma. This meaning was indicated by His saying ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a Messenger from among them﴾ [al-Baqara: 129]. As for those from the Children of Israel who embraced islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, the number of them did not gather to form a community (umma).

His saying ﴿and show us our rites﴾ is a request for guidance on the manner of the Hajj, which they had been commanded to perform earlier in a general way. So the verb "arina" is from the cognitive sense of "ra'a" (to see/know), and this is an established usage of the verb of seeing, as al-Raghib affirmed in al-Mufradat and al-Zamakhshari in al-Mufassal, and it transitively takes two objects through the causative hamza.

The original usage of "ra'a" is that it takes one object, because its origin is visual sight. Then it was used figuratively for knowledge, by likening certain knowledge to visual sight. When the causative hamza enters it, it takes two objects. As for the transitivity of "arā" to three objects, it is contrary to the original usage and is a special usage. This occurs when the speaker wants to report knowledge of an attribute of an essence. He mentions the name of the essence first, and knows that this does not convey his intended meaning, so he completes it by mentioning a necessary state, to complete the meaning. He says, "I saw the crescent rising," for example, and then says, "So-and-so showed me the crescent rising." The same applies to the verb "'alima" (to know) and its sisters from the category of "zanna" (to think) entirely, and similarly the category of "kana" (to be) and its sisters. Do you not see that if you turned away from the second object in the category of "zanna," or from the predicate in the category of "kana," to bringing a verbal noun in the place of the noun in the verbs of these two categories, you would dispense with the predicate and the second object? So you say "kana hudur fulan" (the presence of so-and-so occurred), meaning "hasala" (it happened), "'alimtu majī' sahibika" (I knew the coming of your companion), and "zanantu tuluu al-shams" (I thought the sun's rising). It has been transmitted, the saying of al-Fand al-Zimmani:

"Perhaps the days will return a people to what they once were."

And the saying of Hatit ibn Ya'fur:

"Show me a horse that died of emaciation, so that perhaps I may see what you see, or a miserly one kept forever."

For the clause "mata huznan" (died of emaciation) is not a predicate of "jawadan" (a horse), since the subject cannot be indefinite. By this it becomes clear that the correct view is that the predicate in the category of "kana" and the second object in the category of "zanna" are necessary states for the completion of the meaning, and that calling that accusative element by the name of predicate or object is a loose usage and an old expression.

Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read (wa-arna) with a sukun on the ra' for lightness. Abu 'Amr read it with the kasra on the ra' weakened (ikhtilas) for lightness as well. The clause ﴿indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the clauses of supplication.

"Manasik" is the plural of "mansak," which is a noun of place from "nasaka nusukan" (to worship, of the pattern nasara), meaning "ta'abbada" (to devote oneself in worship), or from "nasuka" (with a damma on the sin) "nasakha" (to slaughter as an act of drawing near to God). The more apparent is the first, because it is what rightly calls for a request for success. It will come in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾ [al-Baqara: 200].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 129:

﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, and teach them the Book and the wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾

The invocation (nida') was repeated because it introduces a different purpose within this supplication, namely the request for the coming of the message among their descendants, to honour them and out of eagerness for the completeness of their guidance.

He said "among them" (fihim) and not "to them" (lahum) so that the call would be for the coming of a messenger with a universal message, and that messenger would not be a messenger only to them. For this reason he omitted the object of "messenger" (rasulan) so that it would be general. Thus the invocation in His words "Our Lord, and send" is a parenthetical insertion between the coordinated clauses of the supplication. The manifestation of this supplication is Muhammad ﷺ, for he is the messenger who is a descendant of both Ibrahim and Isma'il. As for other messengers from non-Arab peoples, they are not descendants of Isma'il. Shu'ayb was a descendant of Ibrahim but not of Isma'il, and Hud and Salih were from the Arab 'Arabah (the original Arabs), so they were neither descendants of Ibrahim nor of Isma'il.

Page 723

The Torah, in Chapter 17 of Genesis, states: "The LORD appeared to Abram, that is Ibrahim, and said to him: I am God Almighty; walk before Me and be perfect. And I will make My covenant between Me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly." And in verse 20: "As for Ishmael, I have heard you. Behold, I will bless him and make him fruitful and multiply him exceedingly."

'Abd al-Haqq al-Islami al-Sabti, who had been a Jew and then embraced Islam together with his children and family in Ceuta, and who was present there in the year 736 (seven hundred and thirty-six), mentioned in a book he named al-Husam al-Mahdud fi al-Radd 'ala al-Yahud (The Sharpened Sword in Refutation of the Jews) that the phrase "exceedingly" (kathiran jiddan) originally corresponds in the Hebrew text to "mada mada," and that it is a symbol in the Torah for the name of Muhammad by the reckoning of the jummal (abjad numerals), because the number of letters of "mada mada" by the jummal reckoning among the Jews adds up to ninety-two, which is the number of letters of Muhammad. End of quote. Al-Biqa'i in Nazm al-Durar followed him in this.

The meaning of "He recites to them Your verses" (yatlu 'alayhim ayatika) is that he reads them to them in the manner of reminder, and in this there is an indication that he will come to them with a Book containing law (shar').

"Ayat" is the plural of "ayah," which is a sentence among the sentences of the Qur'an. It was called an ayah because of its indication of the truthfulness of the Messenger through the totality of what it contains of the evidence that the like of it could issue from an unlettered man who neither reads nor writes, and through the arrangement of its composition, which rendered people unable to produce the like of it, and because of what it contains of the decisive proof of the Oneness of God and the perfection of His attributes, a proof that left no path to error in the beliefs of the community, such that this community was safe from associating partners with God. The Prophet ﷺ said in the Farewell Pilgrimage sermon: "Indeed, Satan has despaired of being worshipped in this land of yours." The present tense "yatlu" is used to indicate that this Book's recitation is repeated.

"Wisdom" (al-hikmah) means knowledge of God and the subtleties of His laws; it is the meanings of the Book and the detailed explanation of its purposes. From Malik: wisdom is knowledge of jurisprudence (fiqh) and religion and following them. From al-Shafi'i: wisdom is the Sunnah of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Both of these views consider that the conjunction of "wisdom" with "the Book" requires some difference, by adding a further meaning. The detailed explanation of the meaning of wisdom will come at His words, exalted is He, ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269] in this surah. "Tazkiyah" is purification from deficiencies, and the greatest of deficiencies is associating partners with God. In this there is an allusion to those who turned away from following the Qur'an and refused except to remain in polytheism.

The arrangement of these clauses in mention follows the order of their occurrence, because the first conveyance of the message is the recitation of the Qur'an, then there is teaching its meanings, as He said: ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾. Then indeed, its explanation is upon Us. Then knowledge, through which purification is attained, and it is in acting upon the guidance of the Qur'an.

Page 724

His words ﴿Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ are a concluding phrase (tadhyil) bringing the answer near, meaning: because no great matter overcomes You, and nothing escapes Your knowledge and wisdom. "Al-Hakim" in the sense of "al-muhkim" (the one who perfects and makes firm) is a form of fa'il in the sense of maf'il, and its like has preceded in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10], and His words ﴿They said: Glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32].

[Page 724]

The placement of these verses in relation to what precedes them is that of a conclusion after a proof. When he had explained Abraham's virtues in the words "And when his Lord tested Abraham..." up to this point, the reader understands that whoever possesses these virtues would not turn away from his religion and from following him except one who is foolish in mind and weak in judgment. Accordingly, the apparent requirement is that this sentence be joined to what precedes it with the particle *fa'* (so, then). Instead, the speech shifts from *fa'* to *wa-* (and), so that the meaning of this sentence stands independently in completing the praise of Abraham's status, and so that this ruling applies to the religion of Abraham in every respect, not only to the particular matters he was described as doing in the earlier verses. It also contains an allusion (*ta'rid*, indirect reference) to those who deviated from the religion that came embodying the religion of Abraham.
