The implication of consequence is not lost, because the sentence's placement after its predecessors, containing this meaning, is evidence that it is a result of what preceded it, just as you say, "So-and-so managed the important affair well, and he is a wise man," and you do not need to say, "So he is a wise man."

The interrogative form here is for denial (*inkar*) and deeming unlikely (*istib'ad*). Its use for denial may occur while the intended meaning could still be a question, in which case it is a metonymy (*kinaya*). It may also occur where the question meaning cannot be intended, in which case it is a figure of speech (*majaz*) for denial, and its meaning is that of negation. The more apparent view is that it is a metonymy here, since turning away from the religion of Abraham, while knowing its excellence and clarity, is a matter that is denounced and considered unlikely.

Since it is the nature of a denounced and unlikely matter that one asks about its doer, the interrogative is used for its necessary concomitant, which is denial and deeming unlikely, by way of metonymy. Yet if one were asked about this turning away, the question would be fitting. The exception (*istithna'*) is an indicator of the intended negation and of using the expression in two metonymic meanings, or it is an ornamentation (*tarshih*) of the metonymic meaning, which is denial.

The interrogative does not involve what the scholars said about using a homonymous term in both of its meanings, or using a term in its literal and figurative senses, or in its two figurative senses. This is because the indication of the metonymic meaning is by way of reason ('aql), unlike the indication of the two meanings for which it was literally coined, or of the literal and figurative meanings. Those who considered that prohibited argued that intending the indication by the word of one of the two meanings requires that it not indicate the other, since it is a single word. So when it indicates one meaning, its indication is complete. Also, the indication of two figurative meanings is an indication by the word of one of the two meanings, which implies that it was transferred from its literal meaning to a figurative meaning, and this requires that it not indicate anything else, since it is a single word. We have refuted this in the ninth introduction. As for the metonymic meaning, the indication of it is rational, whether the word still indicates its literal meaning or its indication of it has been suspended. You may also make the use of the interrogative in the sense of denial a figure of speech by the relation of necessary concomitance, as has been repeated in every metonymy in which the original meaning does not appear. This is more apparent, because it is a well-known figure that has become a customary literal usage. Thus the grammarians said: "The denying interrogative is a negation, and therefore *istithna'* (exception) comes after it." The verified view is that it does not invariably mean negation, but that this usage is frequent in it, because the nature of a denounced thing is that it should be nonexistent. For this reason, the exception here may be an exception from a statement implied by the interrogative, as if a respondent had answered the questioner with the words: "None turns away from it except one who has made himself foolish."

*Al-raghba* (desire) is the seeking of a beloved thing. Its verb should govern *bi-* (in), but it may govern *'an* (from) when it implies the meaning of deviating from a matter. This implication became so frequent in speech that it became forgotten. *Al-milla* is religion, and its explanation was given earlier at the saying of the Exalted: "The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion" (2:120). *Safiha* means "he belittled," because *al-safaha* is lightness of mind and its disturbance. It is said: *tasaffahahu* (he made him light), i.e., belittled him. Dhu al-Rumma said:

*"They swayed as spears sway, their tips made light by the passing of the scattering winds."*

From this comes *al-safaha* in action, which is committing acts that people of honor do not approve of. And *al-safah* in wealth is squandering it, being careless about it, and mismanaging its growth. *Safahahu* means "he belittled him and humiliated him," because belittling leads to humiliation. *Safiha* means he became foolish, and the *fa'* may be vowelled with a *damma* in this.

The accusative of *nafsahu* (himself) is either an object: i.e., he neglected it and belittled it, and was not concerned with its loss in this world and the next. Or it may be an accusative of specification (*tamyiz*) transferred from the subject; its original form was "his self became foolish," i.e., it became light and disturbed. The predication was transferred to the possessor of the self by way of the rational figure (*al-majaz al-'aqli*) because of the close connection, intending exaggeration, namely that the foolishness flowed from the self to its owner, from the intensity of its firm hold on him, until it became an attribute of his body. Then the subject was put in the accusative as a specification explaining that ambiguity in the figurative predication. The occurrence of a definite specification by annexation does not contradict this, because indefiniteness is the usual form of specification.

The intended meaning of "And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who has made himself foolish" is to call the polytheists foolish for their turning away from the call to Islam, after the Messenger (ﷺ) explained to them that Islam is established on the foundation of *al-hanifiyya* (pure monotheism), which they know to be the religion of Abraham. The Exalted said: "Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a *hanif*" (16:123). He also said in the previous verse: "Our Lord, make us submitting to You, and from our descendants a Muslim community submitting to You" (2:128), and He said: "And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and Jacob..." up to His saying: "Do not die except as Muslims" (2:132).

The sentence "And We had certainly chosen him" is conjoined to the preceding sentences, which indicate the elevated rank of Abraham with God, the Exalted, since He made him an *imam* (leader) for the people, guaranteed prophethood among his descendants, commanded him to build a mosque for His monotheism, and answered his supplications.

These sentences indicated God's choosing of him, so this sentence was necessarily joined after them, because it gathers their summation and adds by mentioning that he will be among the righteous in the Hereafter. The *lam* is the response to an omitted oath, and in this there is emphasis on establishing his choosing and his righteousness in the Hereafter.

Because of the concern with this final report, it was emphasized with the words: "And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous." So the phrase "And indeed he is in the Hereafter..." to its end is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) between the clause "We had chosen him" and the adverbial clause "When his Lord said to him: Submit," since "when" is an adverb modifying *isṭafaynāhu* and what is conjoined to it. The purpose of this adverbial placement was to move on to another virtue, because that time is the proof of his choosing, when God addressed him by revelation and commanded him with what the word "submit" includes of meanings, whose sum is monotheism, disavowal of power and strength other than God's, and sincere obedience. It was also the time when it became evident that God intended to set right his condition in the Hereafter, since each person is facilitated for what he was created for.

It has been understood that the object of "submit" and its complement are omitted, known from the context, i.e., "Submit yourself to Me," as indicated by the answer: "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds." Omitting the object of "submit" became common, so the verb was treated as intransitive. One says *aslama* (he submitted), meaning he embraced Islam, as indicated by the Exalted's saying: "But he was a *hanif*, a Muslim" (3:67), as will come shortly.

[Page 725]

His saying "He said: I have submitted" is joined in the manner of narrating dialogues, as we previously mentioned at "And when your Lord said to the angels: I am placing a successor on the earth" (2:30). His saying "He said: I have submitted" indicates that he responded immediately without hesitation, as the fact that it came as an answer requires. Ibn 'Arafa said: "He only said 'to the Lord of the worlds' and did not say 'I have submitted to You,' so that he would have brought Islam along with its proof." That is, Abraham had already known that this world has a knowing Creator, which he had attained by inspiration from God. So when God revealed to him the call to faith, it met a mind that was already rightly guided.

[Page 724]

The placement of these verses in relation to what precedes them is that of a conclusion after a proof. When he had explained Abraham's virtues in the words "And when his Lord tested Abraham..." up to this point, the reader understands that whoever possesses these virtues would not turn away from his religion and from following him except one who is foolish in mind and weak in judgment. Accordingly, the apparent requirement is that this sentence be joined to what precedes it with the particle *fa'* (so, then). Instead, the speech shifts from *fa'* to *wa-* (and), so that the meaning of this sentence stands independently in completing the praise of Abraham's status, and so that this ruling applies to the religion of Abraham in every respect, not only to the particular matters he was described as doing in the earlier verses. It also contains an allusion (*ta'rid*, indirect reference) to those who deviated from the religion that came embodying the religion of Abraham. The implication of consequence is not lost, because the sentence's placement after its predecessors, containing this meaning, is evidence that it is a result of what preceded it, just as you say, "So-and-so managed the important affair well, and he is a wise man," and you do not need to say, "So he is a wise man."

The interrogative form here is for denial (*inkar*) and deeming unlikely (*istib'ad*). Its use for denial may occur while the intended meaning could still be a question, in which case it is a metonymy (*kinaya*). It may also occur where the question meaning cannot be intended, in which case it is a figure of speech (*majaz*) for denial, and its meaning is that of negation. The more apparent view is that it is a metonymy here, since turning away from the religion of Abraham, while knowing its excellence and clarity, is a matter that is denounced and considered unlikely.

Since it is the nature of a denounced and unlikely matter that one asks about its doer, the interrogative is used for its necessary concomitant, which is denial and deeming unlikely, by way of metonymy. Yet if one were asked about this turning away, the question would be fitting. The exception (*istithna'*) is an indicator of the intended negation and of using the expression in two metonymic meanings, or it is an ornamentation (*tarshih*) of the metonymic meaning, which is denial.

The interrogative does not involve what the scholars said about using a homonymous term in both of its meanings, or using a term in its literal and figurative senses, or in its two figurative senses. This is because the indication of the metonymic meaning is by way of reason ('aql), unlike the indication of the two meanings for which it was literally coined, or of the literal and figurative meanings. Those who considered that prohibited argued that intending the indication by the word of one of the two meanings requires that it not indicate the other, since it is a single word. So when it indicates one meaning, its indication is complete. Also, the indication of two figurative meanings is an indication by the word of one of the two meanings, which implies that it was transferred from its literal meaning to a figurative meaning, and this requires that it not indicate anything else, since it is a single word. We have refuted this in the ninth introduction. As for the metonymic meaning, the indication of it is rational, whether the word still indicates its literal meaning or its indication of it has been suspended. You may also make the use of the interrogative in the sense of denial a figure of speech by the relation of necessary concomitance, as has been repeated in every metonymy in which the original meaning does not appear. This is more apparent, because it is a well-known figure that has become a customary literal usage. Thus the grammarians said: "The denying interrogative is a negation, and therefore *istithna'* (exception) comes after it." The verified view is that it does not invariably mean negation, but that this usage is frequent in it, because the nature of a denounced thing is that it should be nonexistent. For this reason, the exception here may be an exception from a statement implied by the interrogative, as if a respondent had answered the questioner with the words: "None turns away from it except one who has made himself foolish."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 132:

﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and [so did] Jacob: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims."﴾

Since it is part of the nature of the people of truth and wisdom to be keen on the reform of their own souls and the reform of their community, it is among the things that complete this that they be keen to preserve the truth among people as something followed and well known. Thus it was among their practices to enjoin those whom they regarded as successors to them among the people, that they should not deviate from the path of truth and should not neglect what they had attained of it. For its attainment came through the striving of souls and the passing of ages, so it was a precious matter, fitting to be safeguarded.

Al-iysa' (enjoining, bequest) is a command or prohibition related to the welfare of the one addressed, whether specifically or generally, and losing it entails harm. Thus the wasiyya (testamentary charge) is more emphatic than a bare command or prohibition, and it is used only where there is fear of its being missed, either with respect to the one who enjoins, which is why enjoining became frequent when death was anticipated, as will come in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Jacob, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?"﴾ [al-Baqara: 133]. In the hadith of al-'Irbad: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ admonished us with an admonition that made hearts tremble and eyes overflow with tears, so we said, 'O Messenger of Allah, it is as if it were the admonition of one bidding farewell, so enjoin us,'" and the hadith continues. Or it is with respect to the one enjoined, as with the charge during travel in the hadith of Mu'adh when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him to Yemen: "The last thing the Messenger of Allah instructed me, when I had put my foot in the stirrup, was: 'Make your character good toward people.'" And a man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said to him, "Enjoin me," and he said, "Do not become angry."

So the enjoining of Abraham and Jacob was either at the time of death, as the following verse indicates, when death approached Jacob, or in situations where there is fear of it being missed.

The pronoun in the genitive with bi- refers either to the religion (millah) or to the word (kalima), namely His saying, ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqara: 131]. If it refers to the religion, the meaning is that he enjoined them to hold fast to what they had been upon with him during his lifetime; if it refers to the second, the meaning is that he enjoined them with this statement, which is a motto comprising the meanings of what is in the religion.

The sons of Abraham were eight: Isma'il, who was his eldest son, and his mother was Hajar; Ishaq, and his mother was Sarah, and he was his second son; Madyan, Madan, Zimran, Yiqshan, Bishbaq, and Shuh. These latter had as their mother Qatura, whom Abraham married after the death of Sarah. Beyond Isma'il and Ishaq there is no detailed account in the Torah, except that the apparent sense of the Torah is that Madyan is the forefather of the people of Madyan, the companions of al-Aykah, and that when Moses, peace be upon him, left Egypt in fear, he settled in the land of Madyan, and that Yithro or Ra'uel is Shu'ayb, who was the priest of the people of Madyan. As for Jacob, he is the son of Ishaq by his wife Rifqa the Aramean, whom he married in the year 1836 BC, during the lifetime of his grandfather Abraham, so he was a man in the time of Abraham. He was given the title Isra'il, and he is the forefather of all the Children of Israel. Jacob died in the land of Egypt in the year 1989 BC and was buried in the cave of Machpelah in the land of Canaan, the city of Hebron, where his grandfather and father were buried, peace be upon them.

The conjunction of Jacob with Abraham here is an intended embedding (idmaj) aimed at reminding the Children of Israel, whose forefather is Jacob, of the bequest of their grandfather. Just as it alluded to the polytheists in their turning away from a religion their father enjoined, it likewise alludes to the Jews, because, although they trace their lineage to Isra'il, who is Jacob, the one who unites their lineage after Abraham, the proof is established against them concerning the obligation of following Islam.

His saying "O my sons" etc. is a quotation of the form of Abraham's bequest, and the mention of Jacob's bequest will come. Since the verb awsa (enjoined) contains the sense of speech, it is correct for a clause to follow it that is suitable for quoting the bequest, so that it explains the clause "enjoined." The explanatory an (that) was not used, though it often comes after a clause that carries the sense of saying without its letters, because the explanatory an may mean that what follows is reported in its wording or in its meaning, and the more common practice is to report by meaning. Since here it is intended to make explicit that this clause is a quotation of Abraham's statement in its exact wording, apart from the difference in Arabic vocabulary, it is treated as the verb of saying itself, for after it the explanatory an never comes in any case. For this reason

ال​بصريون (the Basrans) say about this verse that it is an implied, omitted verb of saying, in contrast to the Kufans, who hold that awsa and similar verbs govern the quoted clause directly; and the disagreement between them seems to be merely verbal.

"﴿اصطفى لكم﴾" means: chose for you the religion, namely the complete religion. This contains an indication that He chose it for them from among the religions and that He favored them with it, because "chose for you" indicates that He reserved it for their sake. By it he meant the religion of ḥanifiyya, called Islam, and therefore he said: "so do not die except while you are Muslims." The meaning of "so do not die except while you are Muslims" is a prohibition against departing from Islam, meaning the religion of Abraham, throughout all the times of their lives. This is a metonymy for remaining in it for the duration of life, because a living person does not know when death will come to him. So forbidding anyone from dying other than as a Muslim is a command to be characterized by Islam at all times of life. The intended purpose of such a prohibition is intense eagerness to avoid what is forbidden.

The Arabs have three methods for a prohibition whose intended meaning is a prohibition of its necessary concomitant. First: they make the thing forbidden something the addressee has no ability to avoid, and by this they indicate that the intended meaning is the negation of its concomitant, like their saying "Do not forget such-and-such," meaning "Do not engage in the causes of forgetting," and like their saying "I do not want to see you doing such-and-such," meaning "Do not do it, so I will recognize you," since the speaker's knowledge is not something the addressee can be forbidden from; and in the hadith: "Let no people be driven away from my pool." Second: the thing forbidden is within the addressee's ability, but the speaker does not intend prohibiting it directly; rather he prohibits what is connected to it or accompanies it, so he states the prohibition about one thing and restricts it by its accompaniment, knowing that the forbidden thing is bound to occur, so that when it occurs, its accompaniment is necessarily realized, as in your saying "I do not want to see you in disfigured clothes." Among this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so do not die except while you are Muslims﴾. Third: the thing forbidden is possible to occur, and he makes the prohibition useful while allowing the context to admit that the prohibition is against both matters if they are combined, even if one of them is not done, as in your saying "Do not come to me as a beggar," while you mean that he should not ask you; then either he comes and does not ask, or he does not come at all. In the second case there is an affirmation that the sons of Abraham and Jacob were upon the religion of Islam, and that Islam brought what Abraham and his sons were upon when no one had authority over them. There is also in it an allusion that what befell his sons after that of the laws was only prompted by circumstances that arose, which fell short of the perfection Abraham possessed. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 19], and He said: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship; it is the religion of your father Abraham. He named you Muslims before this﴾ [al-Hajj: 78].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 133 (part 1 of 2):

Page 730
﴿Or were you witnesses when death came to Ya'qub, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God; and to Him we are submitting."﴾
This is a detailing of the bequest of Ya'qub, that he commanded his sons to be upon the millah (religious creed) of Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq. It is similar to what Ibrahim enjoined upon his sons, but here it is stated in summary, relying on what was made explicit in His saying earlier, ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132]. This is an emphasis on the hanifiyyah (pure monotheism), which is the foundation of Islam, and a preparation for refuting their saying ﴿Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], and a refutation of their claim that Ya'qub was upon Judaism and bequeathed it to his sons, so that his descendants were bound to it and would not be turned away from it.
It has been mentioned that the Jews said this; al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi related it without a chain of transmission. What points to it is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Or do they say that Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq and Ya'qub and the tribes were Jews or Christians?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 140], and so the detailing of Ya'qub's bequest has been brought here, refuting the claims of the Jews and undermining their belief, which has no evidence, as the denunciation in His saying ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ etc. indicates.
The "am" (or) here is coordinating the clause "kuntum shuhada'" (were you witnesses) upon the clause "wa-wassa bihā Ibrahīm banīhi" (and Ibrahim enjoined it upon his sons), for am is one of the particles of coordination wherever it occurs. Here it is disjunctive (munqati'ah), for the transition from the report about Ibrahim and Ya'qub to disputing those who believed contrary to that report. Since am is always accompanied by interrogation, as already passed at His saying, ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108] etc., the interrogation here is not genuine, since it is evident that their not having witnessed Ya'qub's death is certain; so it is determined that the interrogation is figurative. Its interpretation is denial (inkar), because it is the most well-known of the figurative meanings of interrogation, and because such an object of interrogation is common in denying interrogation. Furthermore, the fact that the interrogation is denunciatory prevents the address in it from being to the Muslims, since they are not in the condition of one who claims the opposite of reality such that they would be denounced. This contradicts those commentators who permitted the address to be to the Muslims, who imagined that denial equates completely to negation and overlooked the difference between denunciatory interrogation and bare negation. Denunciatory interrogation is used for denial figuratively by direct signification, and it implies negation by implicative signification. It is strange that al-Zamakhshari fell into this oversight. So it is determined that the addressees are the Jews, and that the denial is directed at a belief they held, known from the context of the speech
Page 731
and its antecedents, namely their claim that Ya'qub died upon Judaism and bequeathed it, so that his descendants were bound to it. Thus the target of denial upon the Jews is clear: they claimed what they had no means of knowing, since they did not witness it, as will come. The meaning is: "You were not witnesses to Ya'qub's death." Then the story is completed for instruction, detailing and thoroughness in argument, by mentioning what Ya'qub said at his death and what his sons answered; this is not within the scope of the denial. The denial ends at the word "death," and the remainder is a completion of the story. The indication of both matters is clear, relying on the customary usage in such cases, for the object of interrogation is not extended in denial. Do you not see His saying, ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]? So when He said here, "Or were you witnesses when death came to Ya'qub," the hearer knows the target of denial. Then he knows that the saying of Ya'qub's sons, "We will worship your God," was not among the claims of the Jews, such that it would fall within the scope of denial; for had they claimed it, it would not have been denounced, since it is precisely the intended content of the report. With this, both statements settle in their place. There was no reason to make the "am" connective with an omitted element before it that it would correspond to, as if one were to suppose "Were you absent when death came to Ya'qub, or witnesses?" with the address to the Jews or the Muslims and the interrogation being for confirmation; nor to make the address in "kuntum" to the Muslims in the sense of making the interrogation pure negation, i.e., "You did not witness Ya'qub's death," as al-Zamakhshari and his followers attempted, as in "and you were not on the western side" and "you were not with them when they cast their pens." What led him to this was his analogizing it to the most common uses of this kind of construction, although its position here is an unusual position. It is from the concision and completeness, for it combines denunciation of them for slandering one they did not witness, and instruction of them in what they did not know. For the sake of drawing attention to this wondrous combination, "idh" is repeated in His saying "idh qala li-banīhi," so that it serves as an apposition to "idh ḥaḍara Ya'qūba al-mawt," and thus is intended with the judgment too.

"Shuhada'" is the plural of "shahid" in the sense of "shahid" (present), i.e., present for the matter and the affair. The way the negation of witnessing indicates the negation of what they attributed to Ya'qub is that alerting them to the fact that they did not witness that stirs doubt in their souls regarding their belief.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They said, "We will worship your God"﴾ is part of the remainder of the story, whose witnessing by the addressees is negated. This is from the occurrence of "they said" in dialogues, as we have mentioned, like His saying ﴿They said, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. So the statement is a negation of their witnessing together with conveying that bequest, i.e., even if you had witnessed, you would have believed the contrary.
Page 732
So when they held a belief like a necessity, he rebuked them and denounced them, until they would return to consider the means upon which they relied and know that they are means that do not lead to the goal. By this you know the reason for restricting it to negating presence, even though negating presence does not indicate the falsity of the claimant, because failing to find does not indicate non-existence. So the aim here is a gradual drawing-out (istidraj) in refuting the claim by introducing doubt about its proponent.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿idh qala li-banīhi﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿idh ḥaḍara Ya'qūba al-mawt﴾. The benefit of bringing the report in this manner, rather than saying "Or were you witnesses when Ya'qub said to his sons at death," is the intent of making the report independent, the importance of the story, the intent of narrating it in the order of its occurrence, and the intent of summary then detail, because the state of the presence of death is not free of a significant event that will be related after it, so the hearer awaits it.

This bequest came at death, which is the time of intensified eagerness to convey counsel, at the last of what remains of the speech of the testator, so that it has firm roots in the souls of those charged. Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related from al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) admonished us with an admonition from which hearts trembled and eyes shed tears. We said, 'O Messenger of Allah, it is as if it were the admonition of one bidding farewell, so advise us.'" The hadith continues.

Ya'qub, in his bequest, used the form of interrogation in order to observe the degree of their steadfastness upon the religion, until he would be informed of the sincerity of their inner intentions, so that he could then impart to them what he would advise them with of reminder. In the question, "ma" (what) is used rather than "man" (who), because "ma" is the original form when generality is intended, since he asked them about what could be worshipped by worshippers.

The adverbial phrase "ba'di" (after me) is joined with the particle "min" for emphasis, for this "min" is originally inceptive (ibtida'iyyah). Your saying "I came from after noon" indicates that you came at the very beginning of the times after noon; then it was treated as a particle of emphasis.

"Banu Ya'qub" are the Asbat, that is, the Asbat of Ishaq, and from them branched the tribes of the Children of Israel. They were twelve sons: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun; their mother was Leah. Joseph and Benjamin, whose mother was Rachel; Dan and Naphtali, whose mother was Bilhah; Gad and Asher, whose mother was Zilpah. The Qur'an has reported that all of them became prophets, and that Joseph was a messenger.

The singular of "Asbat" is "sibt," with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the ba', and it means a grandson, i.e., a grandchild. The derivation of "sibt" has been disputed. Ibn 'Atiyyah, in his commentary on His saying, ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations﴾ [al-A'raf: 160] in Surat al-A'raf, related from al-Zajjaj: "The more apparent view is that 'sibt' is Hebrew, arabicized." End of quote. I say: In Hebrew it is "sibat," with a yod after the sin, and the sin is vowelless.

The clause ﴿They said, "We will worship your God"﴾ is an answer to his saying "what you worship," and came in the manner of dialogues without a waw. It is not a resumption (istinaf), because resumption occurs only after the completion of speech, and there is no completion before the answer is obtained. As for their saying "your God" in the form of an idafa rather than the proper name, saying "we will worship Allah," the reason is that the idafa of "ilah" to the pronoun of Ya'qub and to his fathers conveys all the attributes by which Ya'qub and his fathers described God, in what was taught to them from their upbringing; and because they had dwelt in the land of Canaan and Palestine, mixing and intermarrying with peoples who worshipped idols, from the Canaanites, Philistines, Hittites and Aramaeans. Then Ya'qub died in the land of the Pharaohs, who worshipped other gods.

Also, among the benefits of defining what they worship by way of idafa to the pronoun of their father and to the word "fathers" is that it contains an allusion that they follow their predecessors.

In the use of the appositive (ʿatf al-bayān) in their saying "Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq" there is a kind of embellishment of consistency (muhassin al-intiraad), honoring the names of these forefathers, like the saying of Rabi'ah ibn Nasr ibn Qa'in:

"If they kill you, you have destroyed their foundations
by 'Utaybah ibn al-Harith ibn Shihab."

The noun repeated in His saying ﴿wa-ilaha aba'ika﴾ is because repeating the governing noun along with the conjoined noun over the genitive is more eloquent in speech, though not obligatory. The application of "fathers" to what includes Isma'il, who is paternal uncle of Ya'qub, is an application by way of predominance (taghlib), and because an uncle is in the position of a father.

The introduction to Ibrahim and Isma'il has already passed.

As for Ishaq, he is the son of Ibrahim, and he was fourteen years younger than Isma'il; his mother was Sarah. He was born in the year 1896 (of the Hebrew calendar?) [sic: the text reads] six and ninety and eight hundred and a thousand before the birth of the Messiah, and he is the grandfather of the Children of Israel and others of nations near to them.

The Jews say that the son whom Allah commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice and whom Allah ransomed was Ishaq. The truth is that the one commanded to be sacrificed was Isma'il, in his youth, when Ibrahim had no child other than him, so that the perfection of submission would appear.
Page 733
Strangely, when the Torah mentioned the story of the sacrifice, it described him as the only son of Ibrahim, though Ishaq was never the only one. Ishaq died in the year 1708 before the birth (of Christ), and was buried with his father and mother in the Cave of Machpelah in Hebron, the city of al-Khalil.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿one God﴾ is a clarification of the attribute of the God whom they worship. So His saying "ilahan" (a god) is a state (hal) of "ilahika," and the use of "ilahan" as a state of "ilahika," even though it is synonymous with it in its wording and meaning, is only by way of applying the attribute to it, "wahidan" (one). So the state in reality is that attribute, and "ilahan" was repeated but not restricted to describing "wahidan" for the sake of greater clarity, because the context calls for expansion (ita'nab). So in the repetition there is an emphasis on the Return and a confirmation of what precedes it, and this is a style of eloquence, in which the word is repeated in order to build upon it a description or a complement, and along with that there is incidental confirmation of the preceding word, and the aim of that is not mere confirmation. Among its instances is His saying, ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72], and His saying, ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾ [al-Isra': 7], and His saying, ﴿Fear the One who has aided you with what you know﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 132], ﴿He aided you with cattle and sons﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 133], where He repeated the verb "amadda-kum." And the saying of al-Ahwas al-Ansari:

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 133 (part 2 of 2):

*"Then when he [the lion] moves, he moves away from one who is furious, whose sudden attacks his equals fear."*

Ibn Jinni said in his commentary on the Hamasa (Sharh al-Hamasa): "It is impossible to say, 'If I stand, I stand,' because the second clause contains nothing beyond what is in the first. The line may say, 'Then when he moves, he moves,' only because the second verb is joined to a prepositional particle (harf al-jarr), from which the meaning is derived." A similar case is the words of God Most High: ﴿These are the ones whom we misled; we misled them as we ourselves were misled﴾ (28:63). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) had refrained from applying this principle to this verse, but in my view the matter here is as I have explained to you.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) allowed that his saying "one God" (ilahan wahidan) may be a substitution (badal) for "your God" (ilahika), on the basis of permitting the substitution of an indefinite qualified noun (nakira mawsufa) for a definite one, as in: ﴿We will seize him by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock﴾ (96:15–16). Alternatively, it may be in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), with the implied verb "I praise" (amdah), since specification comes from both a noun in the apparent form (ism zahir) and a pronoun of the third person (damir al-gha'ib).

His saying ﴿and we are submitting to Him﴾ is a nominal clause (jumla ismiyya) in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun in "we worship" (na'budu), or it is conjoined to the clause "we worship." It was expressed as a nominal clause to convey the stability and permanence of the attribute for them, after the verbal clause it is conjoined to had conveyed the meaning of renewal and continuity.

[p. 735]

﴿That is a community that has passed away. For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾ The preceding verses, from His saying ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord﴾ (Q 2:124), were followed by this verse because those verses contained praise of Abraham and his descendants, an honouring of their status, and an implicit reproach to those among their descendants who did not follow in their footsteps. It is as if the deluded might take from this a pretext for themselves, saying: "Even if we fall short, we have a path to our salvation through the virtue of our forefathers." So this verse was revealed to establish that reward comes through deeds, not through reliance (on ancestry).

The demonstrative *tilka* ("that") refers to Abraham and his descendants, in view of their being a group, and in view of the reference to them with a feminine noun, *ummah* ("community"), which is its wording.

The meaning of *ummah* was explained a moment ago, at His saying ﴿And of our descendants, a Muslim community for You﴾ (Q 2:128). His saying *qad khalat* ("has passed away") is an attribute of *ummah*. The meaning of *khalat* is "passed away." The root sense of *khalaa* is "emptiness," so the original sense of *khalat* is "the place became empty of them." The emptiness is then attributed to the people of the place, by way of the rational metaphor (*al-majaz al-'aqli*) for the sake of emphasis. The statement here is a metaphor (*kinaya*) for the fact that others do not benefit from their righteous deeds. Otherwise, the fact that they have passed away is something that needs no informing. For this reason, His saying ﴿For it is what it earned﴾ up to the end of the verse is a detailed substitution (*badal mufassal*) from the general statement (*badal mufassal min mujmal*) "has passed away."

The address is directed to the Jews, meaning: the righteousness of your forefathers will not benefit you if you do not follow their way. So His saying ﴿For it is what it earned﴾ is a preface to His saying ﴿and for you is what you have earned﴾, since the latter is the intended purpose of the speech. What is meant by *ma kasabat* and *ma kasabtum* is the reward of deeds, as is shown by the expression *laha* and *lakum* ("for it" and "for you"). You may also take the statement as belonging to the type of *ihtibak* (interlocking) and specification, meaning: *laha ma kasabat wa 'alaykum ma kasabtum*, i.e., its sin. From this verse and similar ones, al-Ash'ari derived the expression of the servant's action as *kasb* ("acquisition").

The fronting of the two predicates before the subjects in *laha ma kasabat* and *lakum ma kasabtum* serves to restrict the subject to the predicate, meaning: what the community earned does not pass beyond it to others, and what you earned does not pass beyond you. This is a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*), to reverse the belief of the addressees, for in their delusion they suppose that the virtues their predecessors possessed would remove the sins they themselves committed, or that their predecessors would bear those sins on their behalf.

His saying ﴿And you will not be questioned about what they used to do﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿For it is what it earned﴾, and it is part of the detailed elaboration of the meaning of *khalat*. If you take ﴿For it is what it earned and for you is what you have earned﴾ as specific to righteous deeds, then His saying ﴿And you will not be questioned﴾ and so on completes the divisions, meaning: and (you will not be questioned) about any sinful deed one has done. For this reason, there he used the expression *kasb*, which is common in (the senses of) storing up and competing, and here he used the expression *'amal* ("doing").

He negated questioning about the deed because it is the least kind of being held accountable for a crime. A person is taken to account for his own crime, so he is questioned about it and punished. A person may also be questioned about another's crime without being punished, just as a people are blamed for the unseemly act of some of them. This is common among the Arabs. Zuhayr said:

*By my life, what a fine clan was it that Husayn ibn Damdam brought down upon them by what did not befit them.*

So negating the very basis of questioning is more forceful and more comprehensive of both matters. If, however, you take His saying ﴿and for you is what you have earned﴾ to mean the blameworthy deeds that encompass them, then His saying ﴿And you will not be questioned﴾ and so on is a safeguard (*ihtiras*) and a completion for establishing the meaning of specification, meaning: each group is specifically bound by its own deed or its consequence, and nothing of that reaches the other, nor is the other questioned about it. That is: you will not be held accountable for the deeds of your predecessors, but you will be held accountable for your own deeds.

[Page 737]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Qur'an 2:135:

﴿They say, "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided."﴾ The apparent meaning is that this is coordinated (ʿatf) with His words ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130]. After He had censured them for turning away from accepting Islam, which comprises the qualities of the ḥanīfiyyah (the upright monotheistic faith of Abraham), He explained the manner of their aversion and the extent of their delusion: they confined guidance to Judaism and Christianity. That is, each group confined guidance to its own religion.

The confinement is derived from the jazm (the apocopate, jussive mood) of ”tahtadū“ (you will be guided) as the answer to the imperative. It is conditional in meaning, so the implied sense of the condition is that whoever is not a Jew, the Jews do not regard as guided, and whoever is not a Christian, the Christians do not regard as guided. In other words, they denied guidance to the follower of the religion of Abraham, and this is the utmost of their delusion.

The waw in ﴿They say﴾ refers to the Jews and the Christians, by the indication of the context of address in His words ﴿Or were you witnesses?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133] and His words ﴿You will have what you earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 134]. The "aw" (or) in His words "or Christians" is a division after a collective statement, because the listener returns each part to its speaker. The jazm of ”tahtadū“ as the answer to the imperative serves to indicate the meaning of the condition, so that by the implied sense of the condition, it is conveyed that if you are on other than Judaism and Christianity, then you are not guided.

* * *

[Page 737]

﴿Say, "Rather, [follow] the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth, and he was not of the polytheists."﴾ The clause "Say" is detached from a conjunction because it occurs in a context of dialogue, answering their statement ﴿Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided﴾ in the manner already mentioned. That is: rather, there is no guidance except by following the religion of Abraham, for when Islam brought it, it nullified what was before it of religions.

"Millata" (religion) is in the accusative by an implied verb of following, because of the context, since "Be Jews" means "follow Judaism." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as a coordination with "Hūdan" (Jews), and the estimate would be: "Rather, we will be the religion of Abraham," that is, the people of his religion. This is like the statement of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim when he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) to embrace Islam: "I am of a religion, or of the people of a religion," meaning Christianity.

The word ḥanīf (upright in faith, one who inclines away from falsehood toward truth) is a form of faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, derived from al-ḥanaf, with a vowel on the middle letter, which means a turning inward in a man's leg. The mother of al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays said, while lulling him with it:

"By God, were it not for the bend in his leg, there would be none like him among the youths of you."

What is intended is an inclination in the path, that the one with a ḥanaf turns in his walk away from the usual road. This was praise for the religion because, on the day the religion of Abraham appeared, people were in a blind error, so the religion of Abraham came inclining away from them, and so it was named ḥanīf. Then ḥanīf became a title of praise by dominance.

The preferred reading is to make "ḥanīfan" (inclining toward truth) a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of "Ibrāhīm." This is among the cases where there is agreement on the validity of a ḥāl coming from a mudāf ilayhi (the genitive noun in an idafa construction). You may also make it a ḥāl of "millah," but faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil agrees with its described noun, unless "millah" is interpreted as "dīn" (religion), following the pattern of His words "Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the doers of good," meaning His goodness. Or the faʿīl is likened to a faʿīl in the sense of a mafʿūl (passive), etc.

This verse indicates that the Islamic religion is from the Islam of Abraham. His words "and he was not of the polytheists" form a clause that is a second circumstantial description of Abraham. It is a precaution lest the polytheists be deceived by His words "Rather, the religion of Abraham," that is: we will not be Jews or Christians, so the polytheists would imagine that nothing remains of the religions except what they hold, because they claim that they are upon the religion of Abraham. Otherwise, this is not praise of him after what has preceded of his virtues. This is in the same manner as His words, exalted is He, ﴿Your companion is not mad﴾ [al-Takwīr: 22]. The author of al-Kashshāf (Zamakhsharī) committed a gross error in this, as will come later.

[Page 738]

﴿Say: We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting.﴾

This is a *badal* (substitution, in apposition) for the phrase "Say: Rather, the religion of Abraham" (al-Baqarah 2:135). It details how this religion is to be practised, after that was stated in summary in His words: ﴿Say: Rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:135). The command to say something is a command to what it includes, since speech has no value unless it corresponds to belief, because a statement is only established for truthfulness and not for falsehood. The purpose of commanding this utterance is to proclaim it and call to it, because of the manifest virtue it contains: the achievement of the merit of all other religions for the people of this religion, and because of the fairness and soundness of intention it reflects. Thus those who desire it will be drawn to it, and the obstinate will be vexed when they hear it. This serves as a safeguard (*iḥtirās*) after His words: ﴿Say: Rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:135). That is: we do not disparage the law of Moses, the law of Jesus, or what the prophets were given, nor do we deny them; rather, we are submitting to God with the religion of Islam, which remained on the foundation of the religion of Abraham, was an elaboration of it, and a completion of God's intent for it, when God willed its completion. Thus the laws that came after Abraham were like the bends of a road along which nations were led, for benefits that suited their conditions and eras after Abraham. This is like a winding path taken by one whose journey has exhausted him: so that he may rest, the traveller who has left the road in the open desert may set down his baggage, sleep, and then be brought back to the main road after a while. Among the connections of this meaning is that it begins with His words ﴿and what was sent down to us﴾ and ends with His words ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, with the mention of what was sent down to the prophets placed between them.

The pronoun is plural so that it includes the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, for they are commanded to say this. Making it a *badal* indicates that what is meant by the command in His words "Say: Rather" is the Prophet and his community.

The pronoun is singular in the two statements in which it refers to the Prophet, because he is especially singled out for directly responding to the Jews and Christians, since he was sent to guide and rebuke them. This is in His words ﴿Say: Rather, the religion of Abraham﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:135) etc., and His later words ﴿Say: Do you argue with us about God?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:139). The plural pronoun in the statement addressed to the community carries a greater specificity regarding the content of what is commanded, in the context of teaching, namely His words ﴿Say: We believe in God﴾ etc., because the Prophet (ﷺ) already knew this beforehand from what the knowledge of the message contains. For this reason, none of these utterances is free of indicating that the community is included together with the Prophet. Here it is evident through the use of all the plural pronouns. As for ﴿Say: Rather, the religion of﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:135) etc., it is because it is a response that follows immediately upon their words ﴿Be Jews﴾ with a plural pronoun, so it is known that he responded to them in the language of the whole group. As for His later words ﴿Say: Do you argue with us﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:139), it is because, after using the singular for "Say", He uses plural pronouns in "Do you argue with us, when our Lord and your Lord..., and our deeds, and we are sincere" etc. So observe the marvels of the arrangement in these verses and the signs of their inimitability.

He put belief in God first, because the truth does not differ with the differences of laws. Then He joined to it belief in what was sent down of laws.

What is meant by "what was sent down to us" is the Qur'an, and by what is joined to it is what was sent down to the prophets and messengers of revelation and what they were given of scriptures. The meaning is that we believe that God sent down those laws. This does not contradict that some of them abrogated others (*nasakh*, abrogation), or that what was sent down to us abrogated all of them in what differs from them. For this reason He put "and what was sent down to us" first, for the sake of emphasis on it. The variation in expression, using the verb "sent down" for some of these laws and "given" for others, is a stylistic variety (*tafannun*) to avoid repeating the same word many times. The reason neither verb was used alone, nor the complements joined without repeating the verbs, is to avoid a succession of complements, since that would be like a succession of genitive constructions in what we see.

The Tribes (al-Asbāṭ) have been mentioned just before.

The clause ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) or a resumptive new sentence (*isti'nāf*), as if it were said: how do you believe in all of them? For belief in the truth is in one of them. This hypothetical question arises from error and fanaticism, where they believe that belief in one messenger is not complete except with disbelief in another, and that the sanctification of one is not complete except by disparaging another. This is a fault found in religions, sects, schools, parties, and morals, which was common among nations and disciples, and Islam uprooted it. Abū 'Alī ibn Sīnā said in *al-Ishārāt*, in reply to those who defended Aristotle in philosophy and belittled Plato and "the First Teacher": "Although he is of great stature, praise of him does not lead us to disparage his masters."

This is a response to the Jews and Christians who believe in their prophets but disbelieve in whoever came after them. The intent is that there should be no distinction among them in belief in some of them. This does not contradict the belief that some of them are more excellent than others.

*Aḥad* (one, anyone) originally derives from *waḥad* with a *wāw*, and its meaning is "singular". It is a dialectal form for *wāḥid* and a shortened form of it. It has also been said that it is an adjectival form (*ṣifa mushabbaha*), so its *wāw* was changed to a hamza for lightness, and then it came to mean a single individual. Sometimes it means "that which is not multiple", and this occurs when it qualifies a referent or a described thing, as in: ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾. Its use in this way is rare in speech, and from it comes the number name *aḥad 'ashar* (eleven). Sometimes it means "an individual of a kind", and this occurs when it is specified by something that indicates a kind, as in: "Take one of the two garments"; and it is feminine as in His words: ﴿so that one of them may remind the other﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:282). This usage is common, and it is close in meaning to the first usage. Sometimes it means "an individual of a kind" but is not specified, rather it is generalised. Its generalisation may be in affirmation, as in His words: ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:6). It may also be generalised in negation, which is the most common use of it, as in His words: ﴿Not one of you would be able to keep him away﴾ (al-Ḥāqqah 69:47), and the saying of the Arabs: "No one says that." This usage conveys generality, as is the case with all indefinite nouns in negation.

From this it becomes clear that *aḥad* is a term whose meaning is "one" in origin, its morphology is single, but the positions of its usage, which branch from its original application, differ, until they become like multiple meanings, and *aḥad* becomes like a synonym. This gathers the scattered, lengthy discussions of the scholars about the word *aḥad*, which al-Qarāfī dealt with at length in his book *al-'Iqd al-Manẓūm fī al-Khuṣūṣ wa al-'Umūm*.

The word *bayna* (between) indicates an omitted element whose estimated form is "and another", because *bayna* requires two or more things.

As for His words ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, the discussion of it is the same as that of its counterpart mentioned just before, at His words: ﴿one God, and to Him we are submitting﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:133).

This is an interjected statement placed between His saying ﴿Say: "We believe in God"﴾ (2:136) and His saying ﴿the baptism of God﴾ (2:138). The *fa'* (then) indicates a consequence (*tafri'*) drawn from His saying ﴿Say: "We believe in God"﴾ (2:136). The *fa'* appearing within an interjected statement is common in speech, though some grammarians have doubted it. The "saying" here is meant as a public declaration, that is, "Proclaim your religion and openly call to it." Then, if those who said ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ (2:135) follow you, their faith is guidance. Before that they were not upon guidance, contrary to their claim that they were upon it, as in their saying ﴿Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided﴾ (2:135). The implication (*mafhum*) of the conditional clause shows that they are not upon guidance so long as they do not believe in Islam.

[Page 741]

The conditional is introduced here with the particle *in* (if), which carries the sense of doubt about the realisation of its condition, signalling that their faith is not expected.

The *ba'* in ﴿with the like of what you believed in﴾ indicates association (*mulabasah*) and is not the *ba'* of transitivity (*ta'diyah*). The meaning is: faith similar to your faith. Thus "likeness" means equality in creed and similarity in it with regard to the adherents of the creed. It is not a similarity in which multiplicity of religions is taken into account, since the context rejects that. It has been said that the word *mithl* (like) is superfluous; it has been said that the *ba'* indicates instrument or means; and it has been said that the *ba'* is superfluous. All these views are far-fetched.

His saying ﴿And if they turn away, then they are only in dissension﴾ means: it has become clear that they are neither seekers of guidance nor of truth, since there is no clearer proof than your calling them, and no fairer argument than this one.

*Al-shiqaq* (dissension) is intense opposition. It derives from *al-shaqq* (with a fatha on the shin), which means splitting and separating a body. The word *fi* (in) is used to indicate that dissension has taken firm hold of them, as though it were an enveloping container around them. The use of *in* (if) here, although their turning away is what is expected of them, is merely for harmony (*mushakalah*) with His saying ﴿if they believe﴾. His saying ﴿So God will suffice you against them﴾ is made a consequence of His saying ﴿then they are only in dissension﴾, to strengthen the Prophet ﷺ. Informing him that these people are in dissension, given their known numbers and the strength of their supporters, could cause the listener distress. So God promised him that He would suffice him against the evil resulting from their turning away.

The *sin* (sa-) is a particle that restricts the imperfect verb to the future. It is thus specific to entering upon the imperfect, and is like the particle *sawfa*. The more correct view is that there is no difference between the two in anything other than the time of futurity. It has been said that *sawfa* has a wider scope, and this is well known among the majority of scholars, who say *sawwafahu* when someone delays fulfilling a matter with another. I think there is no escape from distinguishing between *sin* and *sawfa* in futurity, so that the placement of one rather than the other in eloquent speech has a particular effect. Moreover, when either of them comes in the context of a promise, it lessens the promise. Among examples is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He said: "Peace be upon you; I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord"﴾ (19:47). Thus the *sin* here serves to affirm God's promise to His Messenger ﷺ that He will suffice him against the harm of their dissension.

The meaning of their being sufficed is the sufficing of their evil and their dissension, for they were people of zealotry for their religion, and they were supported by followers and helpers, especially the Christians among them. The sufficing of the Prophet is a sufficing of his community, because he did not come for anything that benefits only himself.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: that is, He hears their harm spoken, and knows their inner thoughts. That is, be assured that God is sufficient for you against what you fear of their evil and harm through their numbers. In His saying ﴿So God will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ there is both a promise and a warning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 138:

﴿The dyeing of Allah. And who is better than Allah at dyeing? And we are worshippers of Him.﴾

This is connected to the statement commanded in "Say: We believe in Allah," and what lies between them is an interjection (i'tiraD), as you know. The meaning is: "We believe in Allah and in what was sent down to us and what was sent down to the prophets before, with the faith of Allah's dyeing (ṣibghat Allah)."

Ṣibgha, with a kasra on the ṣād, originally is ṣibgh without the feminine marker. It is the thing with which something is dyed, on the pattern fi'l, indicating the sense of the object (maf'ūl), like dhibh (slaughtered), qishr (peel), kisr (broken piece), and filq (split piece). Its attachment to the feminine marker is for the sense of a single unit, like qishra (a piece of peel), kasra (a fragment), and filqa (a split piece).

So al-ṣibgha is the specific dye prepared to be dyed with. Its being in the accusative is either as an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq) substituting for its verb, meaning "We have dyed the dyeing of Allah," just as "the promise of Allah, Allah does not break His promise" is in the accusative after His words ﴿He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [al-Rum: 5], with the implied sense "they promised them victory." Or it is a substitute (badal) for the phrase "the religion of Abraham," meaning the religion which Allah made our emblem, like the dye among the Jews and Christians. Or it is in the accusative as a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun indicated by the verb "we believe in Allah," the implied meaning being "we believe with a belief of Allah's dyeing." This is the view that suits the use of ṣibgha in the figure of speech called mushākala (assimilation). What al-Kashshāf's author claimed, that it leads to the dislocation of the structure, is an exaggeration not to be heeded in eloquent speech, because the coherence of meanings and context repels such dislocation. Indeed, are interjections and their complements anything but a kind of separation, by which words are dislocated without affecting the meanings? The author of al-Kashshāf, following Sibawayh, took it as a verbal noun describing the manner, like al-jilsa (the way of sitting) and al-mishya (the way of walking), and they made its accusative the absolute object emphasizing itself, meaning for a thing which is itself, that is, the concept of the emphasized and the emphasizing are identical; thus it emphasizes "we believed," because faith and the dyeing are mutually implicated, in the manner of the accusative of "the promise of Allah" in His words ﴿The promise of Allah; Allah does not break His promise﴾ [al-Rum: 6], as an emphasis on the content of the sentence before it, which is His words ﴿On that day the believers will rejoice﴾ [al-Rum: 4] ﴿in the victory of Allah, He gives victory to whom He wills﴾ [al-Rum: 5]. This view contains two evident strains.

Here ṣibgha is the name of the water with which the Jews bathe as a sign of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. Its origin among them is the washing whose obligation was prescribed in the Torah for the priest when he wished to offer a sacrifice of atonement for sin, on behalf of himself or his household. The washing which the priest also performs on the Day of Atonement, for the sins of the children of Israel every year, is likewise. Among the Christians, ṣibgha originally refers to purification in the river Jordan, a washing established by the Prophet Yahya ibn Zakariyya (John the Baptist) for whoever repents of sins. Yahya would admonish some people to repent, and when they repented they came to him, and he would order them to wash in the river Jordan as a symbol of spiritual purification. They called this ma'mūdhīt, with a dhāl marked with a dot and a tā' at the end, and also said mamū'dhītā with an alif after the tā'. It is a word of the Aramaic language meaning "purity." The Arabs arabicized it, saying ma'mūdiyya with an unmarked dāl, a feminine hā' at the end, and its yā' lightened. When 'Isā ibn Maryam was baptized with the water of the ma'mūdiyya, Allah sent down to him the revelation of the message, and he called the Jews to what Allah had revealed to him. The Jews' disbelief in what 'Isā brought arose, and Yahya had believed in him; so discord arose between the Jews and Yahya and 'Isā, and the Jews rejected baptism. 'Isā had baptized the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) who believed in him, so baptism became established in the practice of the Christians for anyone who enters the Christian religion as an adult. Constantine, Caesar of the Romans, was baptized when he entered the Christian religion. As for those born to Christians, they baptize them on the seventh day after their birth.

The use of the name ṣibgha for the ma'mūdiyya may be one of the Qur'an's innovations, or the Christian Arabs may have called that washing ṣibgha. I have not found anything from the pre-Islamic speech that establishes this. The apparent words of al-Rāghib indicate that the usage is ancient among the Christians, for he said: "When a child was born to the Christians, they would dip him after the seventh day in the water of the ma'mūdiyya, claiming that this is their ṣibgha."

As for the reason for calling the ma'mūdiyya ṣibgha, it is obscure, since the water of the ma'mūdiyya has no colour that would make the smearing with it the root of ṣ-b-gh. In the Encyclopaedia of Islam, the word originates from the Hebrew ṣ-b-' (to immerse). This implies that when it was arabicized, they replaced the unmarked ʿayn with a marked ghayn, perhaps because the root ṣ-b-gh with an unmarked ʿayn is rare in its derivatives. Whatever the case, the use of ṣibgha for the water of the ma'mūdiyya, or for washing with it, is a metaphor based on a comparison whose aspect is imaginative (takhyīlī), since they imagined that baptism endows the one baptized with the quality of Christianity and colours him with its hue, as dye colours a dyed garment. Close to this is the use of ṣibgh for the customs and character of a people. They recited, for one of the kings of Hamdan:

"Every people has its dye, and the dye of Hamdan is the best of dyes;
we have dyed our sons upon this, so how honourable is our dye among dyes."

In their churches the Christians have placed small basins containing water which they claim is mixed with remnants of the water that was poured on 'Isā when Yahya baptized him, and that what dripped from it was collected and poured into much water. From that water, measures are taken which are considered blessed, because they are never free of a portion of the water that dripped from the washing of 'Isā at his baptism, as is stated at the beginning of the four Gospels.

So His words ﴿the dyeing of Allah﴾ are a response to the Jews and Christians together. As for the Jews, because the dyeing originated among them; as for the Christians, because it is a continuing practice among them. And since baptism was prescribed for them, owing to the predominance of the influence of sensible things over their beliefs, it was answered to them that the dye of Islam is the belief and the action indicated by His words ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 136] up to His words ﴿and we are Muslims to Him﴾ [al-Baqara: 136]. That is: if your faith is obtained by the dye of the priest, then our faith is by the dyeing and colouring of Allah, that is, His shaping of faith in the natural disposition (fitra) together with His guiding to it. So the use of ṣibgha for faith is a metaphor whose relation is resemblance, a hidden resemblance made attractive by the intention of mushākala. Mushākala is among the rhetorical embellishments (muḥassinat badī'iyya), and it returns to metaphor; the intention of mushākala is what prompts the metaphor. The scholars called it mushākala only because the aspect of the comparison is hidden, so they neglected to call it metaphor and named it mushākala. It is really the bringing of a metaphor for the sake of matching one word with another that occurs with it. If the word whose match is intended is stated, it is mushākala; we may describe it as actual mushākala (mushākala taḥqīqiyya), as in the words of Ibn al-Raq'amaq:

"They said: Propose something, and we will find you its cooking;
I said: Cook for me a robe and a shirt."

He used "cooking" for sewing, to match his words "we will find you its cooking." If the word is not stated but understood from the context, it is called implied mushākala (mushākala taqdīriyya), as in the words of Abu Tammam:

"Who will convey to all the tribes of Ya'rub
that I built the neighbour before the dwelling?"

He used "building" for choosing and selecting, because it matched the building of the dwelling implied in the known phrase "before the dwelling." His words, Allah's "the dyeing of Allah," belong to this category. The implied matching in the verse is more precise than that in Abu Tammam's line, and it is based on what is known of the customs of the Christians and Jews, as shown by His words ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqara: 135], including what that entails of baptism.

The interrogative in His words ﴿And who is better than Allah at dyeing?﴾ is denial, and its meaning is: none is better than Allah in the matter of His dyeing. So ṣibgha is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), a specification of relation transferred from a second subject (mubtada') which is to be understood after "who" in His words ﴿And who is better﴾. The implied meaning is: "And whose dyeing is better than Allah's," that is, than the dyeing of Allah. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr al-Muhit: "How little what the grammarians mentioned about the specification transferred from the subject."

This transfer in the specification may bring a wondrous brevity, for two words are dropped without ambiguity. Since the superlative quality was attributed to "who," it is permissible for the comparative "min" to be placed before the divine name, by supposing an omitted genitive, because that transfer made what is attached to ṣibgha the thing judged to lack the superlative, so it is known that the one compared against is the omitted genitive, that is, "And who is better than the dyeing of Allah?"

The clause "and we are worshippers of Him" is coordinated with "we believed." And the placement of the prepositional phrase "to Him" before its governing verb in "worshippers of Him" conveys a restriction of specification against the Christians, who were dyed with baptism, yet they worshipped the Messiah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 139:

﴿Say: Do you dispute with us concerning Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds, and we are sincere to Him alone.﴾ This is a resumption (isti'naf) of His saying, "﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 136], as has preceded there. "Do you dispute with us" is an address to the People of the Book, because it is a reply to their previous statement, and by the evidence of His later saying, "﴿Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians?﴾" [al-Baqarah: 140]. The interrogation is for astonishment and reproach. The meaning of "dispute concerning Allah" is arguing about His affairs, by way of implication (dalalat al-iqtida'), since there is no dispute about the Essence as such. What is meant is the matter that moved the People of the Book to dispute with the believers concerning it, namely what the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) contained: that Allah abrogated (naskh) the law of the Jews and Christians, that He preferred him and preferred his community. Their disputation goes back to envy and the belief that they are exclusively entitled to the favour and honour of Allah, exalted is He.

Page 746

Therefore His saying, "﴿And He is our Lord and your Lord﴾," has a bearing in reinforcing the denial, i.e., your audacity has reached the point that you dispute with us about nullifying the call of Islam without any proof other than your claim that Allah has singled you out for excellence, although Allah is our Lord just as He is your Lord. So why does He not bestow upon us what He bestowed upon you?

Thus the clause "and He is our Lord and your Lord" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: how can you dispute with us in this well-known state, which admits no doubt? By this clause the subject of the dispute is clarified. Likewise the clause "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds," which is coordinated with the circumstantial clause, climbing higher in refuting their disputation: after stating that lordship qualifies one for His bounty just as it qualified them, it ascends to make the basis of Allah's good pleasure toward His servants their deeds. So if He has honoured you for the sake of righteous deeds, perhaps He has honoured us for the sake of the righteousness of our deeds. So come, look at your deeds and look at our deeds, and you will find our state closer to righteousness than yours.

Al-Baydawi said: "It is as though he obliged them, on every doctrine they adopt, to be silenced and rebuked. For the honour of prophethood is either a bounty from Allah upon whomever He wills, in which case all are equal in it, or it is the outpouring of a right upon those who are prepared for it through persistence in obedience. Just as you have deeds which perhaps Allah takes into account in bestowing them, so we also have deeds."

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in "For us are our deeds" is for exclusivity, i.e., our deeds are ours and not your deeds, so do not dispute with us that you are better than us. The coordination with "﴿and for you are your deeds﴾" is a safeguard to repel the assumption that the Muslims might be sharers with the addressees in their deeds, and that "for us are our deeds" would indicate the exclusivity of the speakers to what they did together with the sharing in the deeds of others. This is the same as the coordination of His saying, exalted is He, "﴿and for me is my religion﴾" [al-Kafirun: 6] upon His saying "﴿for you is your religion﴾" [al-Kafirun: 6]. All of this is from the composed speech (al-kalam al-musannaf), like His saying, exalted is He, "﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance, or in manifest error﴾" [Saba: 24]. The clause "and we are sincere to Him alone" is another coordination upon the circumstantial clause, and it is a third ascent to show that the Muslims are more entitled to the outpouring of good. For though they share with the others in lordship and in the capacity for the performance of righteous deeds, the Muslims have made their religion sincere to Allah, while their opponents have mixed the worship of Allah with the worship of others. That is: why should we not be closer to Allah's good pleasure than you?

The nominal sentence conveys continuity of sincerity, as has preceded in His saying, "﴿and we are Muslims to Him﴾" [al-Baqarah: 136].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 140:

Page 747
﴿Or do they say, "Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians." Say, "Do you know better, or does God?" And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God? God is not unaware of what you do.﴾
Am (أم) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), meaning "bal" (rather), and it marks a shift (idrab) from one topic to another. An interrogative is implied within it, and that interrogative is for rebuke and denunciation. This is because of the depth of their ignorance of the history of their religious laws. They claimed that Abraham and his sons were upon Judaism or upon Christianity, as His saying, Exalted is He, "Say, ﴿Do you know better, or does God?﴾" indicates. It is also indicated by other verses, such as ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 67], and His saying ﴿People of the Book, why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Will you not reason?﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 65]. When a nation is immersed in ignorance, its beliefs become mere delusion, held without reflection, and it holds together beliefs that contradict each other and cannot be reconciled with evidence. The Prophet (ﷺ) found on the day of the Conquest, in the Ka'bah, a picture of Abraham seeking decision by arrows in the Ka'bah. He recited His saying, ﴿Abraham was not...﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 67] up to His saying ﴿nor was he of the polytheists﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], and said, "By God, he never sought decision by them at all." And concerning the People of the Book He said, ﴿The Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him. Will you not reason?﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 65], thereby charging them with lack of reason.

Ibn Kathir and Hafs from 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read with the second person (ta' al-khitab), on the basis that am is connected (muttasilah) and equivalent (mu'addilah) to His saying ﴿Do you dispute with us concerning God?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 139], so that His saying ﴿Say, "Do you know better, or does God?"﴾ is a second command following His saying ﴿Say, "Do you dispute with us..."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 139]. But this reading is not necessarily the only sound one, since considering the shift (iltifat) provides an escape from that.

The meaning of ﴿Say, "Do you know better, or does God?"﴾ is an estimation (taqdir): God has informed us that Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian. This is like His saying in Surah Ali 'Imran: ﴿People of the Book, why do you argue about Abraham...﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 65]. It is derived from the affirmation in His saying ﴿Do you know better, or does God?﴾ that He informed them of a matter their common people were ignorant of and their elite had concealed. For this reason He said, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God?﴾ It points to the elite of the rabbis and monks, who left their common people drifting in erroneous, deluded and misguided beliefs while they remained silent, not objecting to them, seeking to please them and to win their affection. This is a matter which, when it persists long among a nation, it becomes accustomed to it and mistakes its ignorance for knowledge, so that reform later fails to take hold among them, because they see the reformers as having brought what the earlier generations did not bring, and so they say, "We found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following in their footsteps."

Page 748
* * *
﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God? God is not unaware of what you do.﴾
This is part of the speech reported by His saying ﴿Say, "Do you know better, or does God?"﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say that to them as a reminder of the covenant that is in their books, in the hope that they would reconsider and re-examine themselves if they were wavering, or would return to the truth if they were deliberately being stubborn. The "min" in His saying ﴿from God﴾ is initial (ibtida'iyyah), meaning a testimony he has which reached from the side of God through His messengers.
