The waw is conjunctive, joining the sentence "And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony" to the sentence "Do you know better, or does God?" This rhetorical interrogative is a metonymy (kinayah) for the Muslims not being deceived by their claim that Abraham and his sons were Jews or Christians, and it is not an argument against them. His saying ﴿God is not unaware of what you do﴾ is the remainder of the speech, and it is a warning, because one who is capable and not unaware has no obstacle preventing him from acting in accordance with his knowledge. Similar examples have already occurred in several places.

﴿That is a nation that has passed away. For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾ This is a repetition (tikrar) of its counterpart that came just before, in order to firmly fix its meaning in the minds of the listeners, out of concern for what it contains, since it is a meaning whose hearing had not preceded for the addressees, so they were not satisfied with it after only one occurrence. Similar repetition occurs in the speech of the Arabs. Labid said:

So the two of them contended over a long-flowing shade that floats like the smoke of a kindled fire whose blaze is ignited,

Its smoke mixed with the new growth of arfaj (a kind of shrub), like the smoke of a bright fire whose fuel is high in the air. ∗∗∗

For when he likened the scattered dust to a blazing fire, and then digressed to describe the fire, saying that the north wind blew upon it, increased its smoke, and kindled it with fresh arfaj because of the abundance of its smoke, he repeated the simile a second time, because it is strange and novel.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 142 (part 1 of 3):

Page 5
Surat al-Baqarah

﴿The foolish among the people will say, "What has turned them away from their qiblah, which they had been facing?" Say, "To Allah belong the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path."﴾

The placement of this verse among the verses that follow it has been obscure, because its apparent meaning is that it is a report about a matter that will occur in the future, and that the qiblah mentioned in it is the qiblah that existed at the beginning of the Hijrah in Madinah, namely facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and that the turning away from it is its abrogation (naskh) by facing the Ka'bah. Thus the matter would be that the criticism of the critics concerning this change should be anticipated after the occurrence of the abrogation, that is, after the verses abrogating the facing of Bayt al-Maqdis, because of the well-known habit of theirs of watching for opportunities to criticise the conduct of the Muslims. For the surah was revealed in sequence, and the basic principle is that the recitation should follow the order of revelation within a single surah, except for what is established as having been revealed later but recited earlier.

The apparent meaning is that the qiblah intended by "the changed qiblah" is the abrogated qiblah, which is facing Bayt al-Maqdis, I mean to the east, and it is the qiblah of the Jews. None of the exegetes and authors of the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) has satisfied the thirst on this point, and the connection between it and the verses before it is not clear, so some exegetes had to strain to show it.

What my understanding has settled upon is that the connection of this verse's placement here is a wonderful connection, namely that the verses before it repeatedly commend Abraham, his creed (millah), and the Ka'bah, and that whoever turns away from them has made himself foolish. So this became a source for the polytheists to say: "Why did Muhammad and his followers turn away from their qiblah, which they had in Makkah, that is, facing the Ka'bah, although he says that he is upon the creed of Abraham and refuses to follow Judaism and Christianity? How then did he abandon Abraham's qiblah and face Bayt al-Maqdis?" And because the allusion to this purpose has been repeated in the preceding verses by His saying: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115], and His saying: ﴿Neither the Jews nor the Christians will be pleased with you until you follow their creed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 120], as we mentioned there. Allah knew this from them, so He informed His Messenger of their words and placed it in this remarkable position, namely that He put it after the verses that stir this up and before the verses that were revealed to him concerning the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis and the command to face the direction of the Ka'bah in prayer,

Page 6

so that the Qur'an in which is the command to face the Ka'bah would not be revealed after the statement of the polytheists, lest they boast with their noses in the air, saying: "Muhammad changed his qiblah because of our objection to him." Thus the placement of this verse here had the best firmness and the strongest connection, and by this the reason for its revelation before the verse of abrogation becomes clear, which is His saying: ﴿We have seen the turning of your face towards the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144] and what follows; for the statement of the polytheists, or the expectation of it, existed before the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis and arose from the emphasis on the creed of Abraham and the Ka'bah.

So by "the foolish" is meant the polytheists, and this is indicated by His specifying them with the words ﴿among the people﴾. It is known in the terminology of the Qur'an revealed in Makkah that the word "people" (al-nas) is intended to mean the polytheists, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It does not appear that the intended meaning is the Jews or the People of the Book, for if that were so it would have been appropriate to say "they will say" with a pronoun, since their mention had not ceased to be close to the preceding verses up to His saying: ﴿and you will not be asked﴾ [al-Baqarah: 141], and so on.

What supports this is what al-Fakhr (al-Razi) related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and al-Hasan that the intended meaning of "the foolish" is the polytheists. al-Qurtubi mentioned that this is the saying of al-Zajjaj. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the hypocrites, and their description with this was previously mentioned at the beginning of the surah, so the aim would be the hypocrites who conceal polytheism, and what moves them to this statement is the very same thing that moves the polytheists. It has been narrated from al-Suddi that "the foolish" here are the hypocrites.

As for those who interpreted "the foolish" as the Jews, they fell into perplexity about the placement of this verse, because it is evident that this statement arose from the change of the qiblah to Bayt al-Maqdis, and that event had been reported before the hearing of the verse of abrogation of the qiblah, since the basic principle is that the recitation follows the order of revelation. How then would the foolish say this statement before any cause for it had occurred? For they only criticise the turning away from facing Bayt al-Maqdis because it is their mosque and their qiblah according to the view of many scholars. For this reason the proponents of this view affirmed decisively that this verse was revealed after the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis, and they related this from Mujahid. al-Bukhari related in the Book of Prayer, through the chain of 'Abdullah ibn Raja', from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', the hadith of the change of the qiblah, and in it occurs: "The foolish, who are the Jews, said: 'What has turned them away from their qiblah, which they had been facing? Say, to Allah belong the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path.'" He related it also in the Book of Faith through the chain of 'Amr ibn Khalid, from Zuhayr, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', without this addition, but instead of it he said: "The Jews had been pleased that he prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis and the People of the Book; when he turned his face towards the House, they denied that." He related it in the Book of Tafsir through the chain of Abu Nu'aym, from Zuhayr, without either of these two additions. The apparent view is that the first addition was inserted by Isra'il from Abu Ishaq, and the second addition was inserted by 'Amr ibn Khalid, because Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related the hadith of al-Bara' from Abu Ishaq through chains other than that of Isra'il, and it did not contain either of the two additions. So they were compelled to interpret the particle of the future in His saying ﴿will say﴾ as meaning certainty only; that is, "the foolish have said what has turned them away."

The reason this verse is separated from what precedes it without a conjunction is the difference of its purpose from the purpose of the preceding verses. So it is a pure resumption (isti'naf), not an answer to an assumed question.

The better view is to keep the sin (sa-) on its meaning of the future, since there is no need to turn it to the meaning of the past, and you know the reason for reporting it before its occurrence from them. al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: The benefit of reporting it before its occurrence is that knowledge of it before it occurs is further from confusion when it does occur, and that a ready answer before the need for it is more decisive against the opponent and more effective in repelling his clamour. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the placement of the future in the position of the past, to indicate their continuity in it. al-Fakhr said: this is the preference of al-Qaffal.

It seems that what led them to this is that they look at the fact that this statement occurred after the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis and that the verse was revealed after that; and this is a forced reading which should not be relied upon. The reporting of their future statements is not rare in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿So they will say, "Who will restore us?"﴾ [al-Isra': 51], and ﴿So they will shake their heads at you﴾ [al-Isra': 51]. And if what moved them to this is the establishment that they said this statement before the revelation of this verse, and its spread, then interpreting the future as past has a sound basis, and it gives support to what we have set forth in the explanation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115] and His saying ﴿Neither the Jews nor the Christians will be pleased with you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 120].

"Al-Sufaha'" (the foolish) is the plural of safih, which is an adjectival form (sifah mushabbahah) from safuha with a damma on the fa', when foolishness has become a disposition for him. The discussion of foolishness was earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Who turns away from the creed of Abraham except one who makes foolish his soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130]. The benefit of describing them as being "from the people," although this is known, is to draw attention to their reaching the utmost limit of foolishness, such that no foolish persons are found among the people apart from these; so when the human species is divided into categories, these would be the category of the foolish. Thus it is understood that there is no fool other than them, as an exaggeration. The meaning is that everyone from whom this statement issues is foolish, whether the speaker is the Jews or the polytheists of Makkah.

Page 8

The plural pronoun in His saying ﴿what has turned them away﴾ refers to something known from the context, not mentioned in the wording, as a quotation of the words of the foolish; and by the pronoun, or by what is expressed by it in their speech, they mean that it refers to the Muslims.

The verb ﴿walla-hum﴾ originally derives from the doubled form walla, meaning to draw near and be close; so its basic usage is to be transitive to one object by means of doubling, and it is said: wallahu min kadha, meaning he brought him near to it; and wallahu 'an kadha, meaning he turned him away from it. From it is His saying here: ﴿what has turned them away from their qiblah﴾. Its usage became widespread in speech, so they often omitted the preposition that makes it transitive to a second complement, and thereby made it transitive to a second object extensively, so they said: walla fulanan wajhahu, for example, without saying walla fulanun wajhahu min fulanin or 'an fulanin. It came to resemble verbs like kasa and a'ta, and for this reason they did not mind placing either of the two objects before the other. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 15]; the original is: "do not turn the backs away from them," so "the backs" is the agent in meaning, for if it were put in the nominative it would be said: "his back turned to the unbelievers." From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We shall give him what he has turned to﴾ [al-Nisa': 115], meaning we shall make him a wali (protector) of what he has turned to, that is, close to it, that is, attached to it. This is the clarification of the derivations of this verb.

The clause ﴿what has turned them away﴾ etc. is the content of the saying. So all the plural pronouns refer to a known antecedent from the context, and they are the Muslims; this admits of nothing else, lest the pronouns be scattered and the apparent sense of the reporting of the sayings be contradicted.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿what has turned them away﴾ is used to imply a rebuke of error and confusion of intellect.

The intended meaning of "qiblah" in His saying "from their qiblah" is the direction towards which they turn their faces during prayer, as indicated by the context and by the reports on the occasion of revelation of these verses.

The qiblah, in the original form, is a noun on the pattern fi'lah with a kasra on the fa' and a sukun on the 'ayn, which is the pattern of a verbal noun denoting the manner of the act of facing, that is, turning. It was derived irregularly by dropping the sin and the ta', and then it was applied to the thing that the one facing faces, metaphorically, and this is what is meant here, because turning away does not occur from the manner. Hassan said in lamenting Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him:

Was he not the first to pray towards your qiblah?

In my view the more apparent is that qiblah is a noun of the object on the pattern fi'l, like dhibh and tihn, and its feminine form is due to considering the direction, as they say: "he has no qiblah or dibrah in this matter," meaning no direction.

The attribution of the qiblah to the pronoun of the Muslims serves to indicate its greater specificity to them, since no other nations faced it, for the polytheists were not among those who prayed, and the People of the Book did not face it in their prayers,

Page 9

and this supports taking "the foolish" to mean the polytheists; for if the Jews were intended, it would have said "from our qiblah," since they would not be content to attribute that qiblah to the Muslims. And whoever interprets "the foolish" as the Jews and attributes to them the facing of Bayt al-Maqdis takes the attribution to the least connection, since the Muslims faced that qiblah for a period of a year and some months, so it became a qiblah for them.

The plural pronoun in His saying ﴿what has turned them away﴾ refers to a known antecedent from the context, not mentioned explicitly, as a quotation of the words of the foolish; and by the pronoun, or by its equivalent in their speech, they mean its reference to the Muslims.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 142 (part 2 of 3):

His saying ﴿which they used to follow﴾ means that they were constant in it. Here "upon" (ʿalā) expresses figurative firmness (al-tamakkun al-majazi), meaning the intensity of constancy, like His saying ﴿those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. In it there is an added implication of denial and wonder: how did they turn away from it after they had persisted in it? Their facing it was not a mere coincidence, for they had faced the Kaaba for thirteen years before the Hijrah.

Know that the Jews face Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and this facing is not part of the origin of their religion, because Bayt al-Maqdis was built after Musa (peace be upon him); Sulayman (peace be upon him) built it. You will not find in the five books of the Torah any mention of facing a specific direction in the worship of God, the prayer, or the supplication. However, Sulayman (peace be upon him) is the one who established facing Bayt al-Maqdis. In the first Book of Kings: when Sulayman had completed the building of Bayt al-Maqdis, he gathered the elders of Israel and their multitude, stood before the altar in Bayt al-Maqdis, spread out his hands, and supplicated God with a supplication in which he said: "If the people of Israel are defeated before the enemy, then return and confess and pray toward this house, then bring them back to the land which You gave to their fathers. And if the people go out to fight the enemy and pray to the Lord toward the city which You have chosen and the house which I have built for Your name, then hear their prayer and their supplication, etc." He mentioned after that that God appeared to Sulayman and said to him: "I have heard your prayer and your supplication which you made before Me." This does not indicate that facing Bayt al-Maqdis is a condition of prayer in the religion of the Jews. Its utmost implication is that turning toward Bayt al-Maqdis in prayer and supplication is a virtuous practice. Perhaps the Children of Israel adopted it, especially after their departure from Bayt al-Maqdis, or perhaps their prophets who existed after their departure commanded them to do so by revelation from God.

Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: the Jews used to think that the Messenger's agreement with them regarding the qiblah might lead him to become entirely in agreement with them. The words of Ibn al-ʿArabi in Ahkam al-Qur'an proceeded on the definite judgment that the Jews used to face Bayt al-Maqdis, based on the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, but this has not been established from the religion of the Jews, as you have learned.

[p. 10]

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) mentioned from Abu Muslim what implies that the Jews used to face the direction of the west and the Christians the east. You have learned just now that the Jews did not have a specific direction in their prayer which they faced, and that in their supplication they sought blessing by turning toward the region of Bayt al-Maqdis, depending on the varying location of its direction from the lands in which they were. So there is no specific direction for them among the directions of the rising and setting of the sun and what lies between them. When this became a custom among them, they supposed it to be part of the religion, and they wondered at the Muslims' opposition in that matter.

As for the Christians, there was no alteration in their Gospel of what the Jews had regarding the matter of facing in prayer, nor any specification of a specific direction. However, when they saw the Romans making the doors of their temples face the rising of the sun, so that the rays of the sun upon its rising entered through the temple door onto the idol, which was the owner of the temple placed at the far end of the temple, they reversed that. They made the doors of the churches face west, and thus the altar was to the west and the worshippers facing east. Al-Khafaji mentioned that Paul (Bulus) was the one who commanded them with this. This was the condition of the Christians at the time the verse was revealed. Then the Christians, from the Middle Ages until now, became broader and abandoned facing a specific direction, so their churches are of different orientations, and likewise the multiple altars within a single church.

As for facing the Kaaba in the hanifiyyah (the pure monotheistic religion), the apparent meaning is that when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) built the Kaaba, he faced it during supplication and during prayer, because he built it for prayer around it, for its interior cannot accommodate the masses of people. And if its building was for prayer around it, then it was the first qiblah placed for the worshipper to face, and by this it became famous among the Arabs. This is indicated by the saying of Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl:

"I take refuge in what Ibrahim took refuge in, facing the Kaaba while standing."

As for his turning toward its direction from a land far from it, there is no evidence that this occurred. Therefore, the command to adhere to facing in prayer is among the distinctive features of this sharia and among the meanings of the perfection of the religion through it, as we will clarify.

This verse has indicated that the Muslims used to face one direction and then turned to another direction, and the one to which the Muslims turned was none other than the direction of the Kaaba. Thus it indicates that they used to face Bayt al-Maqdis, and the narrations have come with this. The sound hadiths on this are three. The first and most authentic of them is the hadith of the Muwatta, from Ibn Dinar, from Ibn ʿUmar: "While the people were in the Subh prayer at Quba', there came to them a messenger who said: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) has had revelation sent down to him tonight, and he has been commanded to face the Kaaba, so face it.' Their faces had been toward Syria, so they turned around toward the Kaaba." It was also transmitted by al-Bukhari through the chain of Malik, and by Muslim through the chain of Malik, through the chain of ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Muslim, and through the chain of Musa ibn ʿUqbah. In it: the revelation of the verse of changing the qiblah occurred before the Subh prayer, and it was not during the course of the prayer, and he prayed Subh facing the Kaaba. This hadith is the origin of the chapter and it is the decisive word (fasl al-khitab).

The second: the hadith of Muslim from Anas ibn Malik, in which: "A man from Banu Salamah passed by them while they were bowing in the Fajr prayer, and they had prayed one rak'ah. He called out: 'Verily the qiblah has been changed.' So they turned as they were, toward the qiblah."

The third: the hadith of al-Bukhari and Muslim, with the wording of al-Bukhari in the Book of Tafsir, from al-Bara' ibn ʿAazib, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen months or seventeen months, and the Messenger of God loved to be directed toward the Kaaba. So God the Exalted revealed: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], and he turned toward the Kaaba. Then he said: a man prayed with the Prophet, then went out after he had prayed and passed by a people of the Ansar in the 'Asr prayer, praying facing Bayt al-Maqdis. He said: 'He testifies that he prayed with the Messenger of God and that he turned toward the Kaaba,' so the people turned until they faced the Kaaba."

The mention of the Subh prayer in the two narrations of Ibn ʿUmar and Anas ibn Malik, and the mention of the ʿAsr prayer in the narration of al-Bara', are each understood as relating to a specific place. There are other reports that contradict these which have no sound chain; al-Qurtubi mentioned them.

The changing of the qiblah occurred in Rajab of the second year after the Hijrah, two months before Badr. It was said that it was on Tuesday, in the middle of Sha'ban of that year.

They differed over whether his (ﷺ) facing Bayt al-Maqdis was before the Hijrah or after it. The majority hold that when prayer was prescribed for him in Makkah, he used to face the Kaaba, and when he came to Madinah he faced Bayt al-Maqdis, to win over the Jews. This was said by some of them, and it is weak. It was said that he used to face Bayt al-Maqdis while he was in a place where the Kaaba was in front of him to the east, so he would be facing both the Kaaba and Bayt al-Maqdis together. This view has not been authenticated.

They differed over whether facing Bayt al-Maqdis was by a command from God. Ibn ʿAbbas and the majority said: God made it obligatory upon him by revelation, then abrogated it (naskh) by facing the Kaaba, and their evidence is His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you were upon﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], etc. Al-Tabari said: he had the choice between the Kaaba and Bayt al-Maqdis, and he chose Bayt al-Maqdis to win over the Jews. Al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, and Abu al-ʿAliyah said: that was from his own ijtihad (independent reasoning) (ﷺ). According to this view, His saying ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144] indicates that he exercised ijtihad and saw fit to follow the qiblah of the two religions that came before him, while still desiring that God would command him to face the Kaaba. When the qiblah was changed, the foolish ones said, and they were the Jews or the hypocrites according to the differing of the narrations mentioned earlier. It was also said they were the disbelievers of Quraysh, who said: "Muhammad longed for his homeland, and soon he will return to your religion." This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and attributed to al-Bara' ibn ʿAazib, Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan. Al-Qurtubi related that the first of the Muslims to pray facing the Kaaba was Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, but in this report there is weakness.

His saying ﴿Say: To God belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ is a decisive answer. Its meaning is that all directions are equal in that they are locations for some exalted created things. Directions belong to God, following the things in them which are His possession, and no direction deserves to be faced or turned toward by its own intrinsic merit. The mention of "the east and the west" is intended to generalize the directions, as previously mentioned at His saying ﴿And to God belong the east and the west﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115]. It is also possible that what is meant by the east and the west is a metonymy for the whole earth, because people's convention is to divide the earth into two directions, eastern and western, according to the rising and setting of the sun. The intended meaning is that no particular direction has a special closeness to God the Exalted, since He is exalted above direction. His command to face some directions is for a wisdom He intends, such as seeking blessing (al-tayammun) or remembrance (al-tadhakkur). So there is nothing strange in turning toward one direction rather than another, according to what God the Exalted commands. Thus His saying ﴿To God belong the east and the west﴾ is an indication of the validity of turning toward the Kaaba, and His saying ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ is an indication of the reason for preferring turning toward the Kaaba over turning toward other than it. This is because His saying ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ is an implicit hint that what God commanded the Muslims is guidance, not the qiblah of the Jews. However, this implicit hint is delivered in a manner of fair speech, insofar as there is in His saying "whom He wills" a generality which the context clarifies: the one guided is from two groups who were in one state, namely the group whom He by whose hand is guidance commanded to shift from the state in which the other group shared with them to a state specific to them. Thus this verse, in this meaning, indicates the preference of one of the two meanings of a directed speech over the verse ﴿And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24].

He took the path of turning away and rebuke in this answer to them, because their denial was out of obstinacy, not out of seeking the truth. They were therefore answered with something that does not remove their confusion, and the wisdom of changing the qiblah did not become clear to them, nor did the Kaaba's worthiness to be faced. That is what the believers know.

[p. 13]

So when we follow the view of those exegetes who ascribed to the Jews facing the direction of the west and to the Christians facing the direction of the east, then on their interpretation we may say that the mention of east and west is an allusion to the qibla of the Christians and the qibla of the Jews. The answer would then be a turning away from preferring the qibla of the Muslims, since it is of no benefit here. Or His saying ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ is an allusion to the qibla of Islam. The "straight path" here means the means of good and what leads to it, as mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha: 6]. This includes every guidance to good, and among it is guidance to facing the best direction. Thus the clause ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the Name of Majesty (Allah), and it is not appropriate to make it a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾, because the meaning of the clause ﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾ does not clearly include the meaning of the clause ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾. For the implication of the first is that the whole earth belongs to Allah, so directions are not superior to one another, and the implication of the second is that guidance is in the hand of Allah.

The scholars of Islam agreed that facing the Ka'ba, that is, turning toward it, is a condition for the validity of the obligatory and voluntary prayer, except in cases of necessity in the obligatory prayer, such as fighting, or of the sick person who has no one to turn him toward the direction of the qibla, or of a concession in the voluntary prayer for the traveler when he is riding an animal or in a ship that does not stay steady. As for the one who is in the Masjid al-Haram, it is obligatory for him to face the very structure of the Ka'ba from one of its sides. Whoever is in Mecca at a place from which he can see the Ka'ba must turn toward the side of the Ka'ba that he sees. When the row extends along one of the sides of the Ka'ba, it is obligatory upon those in the row who are not facing a corner of the Ka'ba to turn so that they pray in rows encircling the Ka'ba, one row behind another, by turning around. As for the one from whose sight the very structure of the Ka'ba is hidden, he must make ijtihad (independent judgment) by seeking to face its direction. Some scholars said: the worshipper should seek to face the direction in which he coincides with the very structure of the Ka'ba, such that if a line were drawn between him and the Ka'ba, his face would be opposite its wall. This is difficult, and its realization is hard except through the observation of astronomical science. This is expressed as facing the structure (istiqbal al-'ayn) and facing the bearing (istiqbal al-samt). This is the view of Ibn al-Qassar, and it was chosen by one of the teachers of Abu al-Tayyib 'Abd al-Mun'im al-Kindi. The Malikis transmitted it from al-Shafi'i. Among the scholars is one who said: the worshipper should seek to face the direction of the nearest point between him and the Ka'ba, such that if he walked straight he would reach around the Ka'ba. This is expressed as facing the direction (istiqbal al-jiha), that is, the direction of the Ka'ba. This is the view of most Malikis, and it was chosen by al-Abhari and al-Baji, and it is the view of Abu Hanifa and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. It is of the ease and the removal of hardship.

Whoever is in Medina takes as a guide the place where the Prophet ﷺ prayed in his mosque, because Allah permitted His Messenger to pray in it. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik that "Jubayr is the one who set up the qibla of the Prophet's ﷺ mosque."

Al-Mazari explained the meaning of muhadhat (coinciding): that a part of the surface of the face of the one praying and a part of the bearing of the Ka'ba are the two endpoints of a straight line. This is possible when the row of worshippers is like a straight line joining the endpoints of two threads spreading apart that emerge from the center to the circumference in its direction, because every point of it is a passage for something coming out from the center to the circumference. End of quote. Izz al-Din ibn 'Abd al-Salam considered this statement unlikely, because burdening a distant person with facing the very point of the House is beyond what can be borne, and because of their consensus on the validity of the prayer of those in a row a hundred cubits long, while the breadth of the House is five cubits, so part of this row is clearly outside the outline of the House. Al-Qarafi agreed with him, then answered that the House, for those facing it, is like the center of a circle for its circumference, and the lines extending from a center to its circumference widen as they get farther from it, especially at a distance.

When the rows are lengthened, there is no fault upon them, because it is only obligatory for them to be turned toward the direction that they call the qibla of the prayer.

Whoever errs in the qibla or forgets to face it until he finishes his prayer is not required to repeat his prayer according to Malik, Abu Hanifa and Ahmad. However, Malik recommended for him to repeat it as long as the time has not run out, while Abu Hanifa and Ahmad did not hold this. This is based on the view that the obligation of the responsible person is to make ijtihad in facing the direction. As for al-Shafi'i, he obligated him to repeat it always, based on his view that the obligation of the responsible person is to hit the bearing of the Ka'ba.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And thus We have made you a median nation, that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you.﴾

This sentence is an interjection (i'tiraD) between the sentence ﴿The foolish among the people will say...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142] and the sentence ﴿We did not make the qiblah which you used to face...﴾, and the wa' is an interjectory wa' (waw al-i'tiraD), which is of the same category as the resumptive wa' (waw al-isti'naf). The preceding verse, when it indicated that those who were guided to the straight path are the Muslims, and that this is a favour upon them, was appropriate for it to digress to mention another virtue for them, which is better than what preceded it, namely the virtue of the Muslims being just (*'udul*) and choice (*khiyar*),

صفحة ١٥
so that they may bear witness over the nations, because the verses that come after it concern the matter of the qiblah, and this verse is not connected to the matter of the qiblah.

His saying "thus" (*kadhalika*) is composed of the kaf of comparison (*kaf al-tashbih*) and the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishara*), so it is necessary to determine what is being pointed to and what is the object of comparison (*al-mushabbah bihi*). The author of al-Kashshaf said: i.e., like that wondrous act of making (*al-ja'l al-'ajib*), We made you a median nation. Its commentators differed in explaining his words and clarifying his intent:

al-Baydawi said: the demonstrative refers to what is understood (*al-mafhum*) from the saying of the Exalted, ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142], i.e., just as We made you a median nation, or just as We made your qiblah the most excellent qiblah, We made you a median nation. End of quote. That is, His saying ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142] indicates that the guided ones are the Muslims, and that the thing to which they were guided is facing the Ka'bah at the time when the foolish said "what turned them away," as we have previously stated. This makes the kaf remain on the meaning of comparison, and he did not turn to al-Kashshaf's description of the making as wondrous, as though he saw that the demonstrative noun does not necessarily require more than pointing, and although it is the demonstrative for the distant, it is often used without intending distance. But this is open to consideration. The thing pointed to in this view is a meaning that preceded in the earlier discourse, so the demonstrative is then directed to a previously mentioned matter established in knowledge, and it proceeds in line with the ways of demonstratives. The commentators of al-Kashshaf took the kaf to be other than an apparent comparison. As for al-Tibi and al-Qutb, they said: the kaf in it is a noun meaning "like" (*mithl*), placed in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) of *ja'alnakum*; i.e., "like the wondrous making We made you." So it is not a comparison, but an illustration of a state (*tamthil li-halah*), and the thing pointed to is what is understood from the content of the saying "He guides," which is the matter of wondrous import, i.e., complete guidance. The reason for using the demonstrative of distance is to alert to the magnification of the thing pointed to, which is what he meant in al-Kashshaf by the "wondrous making." So the magnification here is for the novelty and strangeness of the matter. Then al-Qutb put forward speech with which he undermined the opening of his own speech.

As for al-Qazwini, author of al-Kashf, and al-Taftazani, they explained it by saying that the kaf is an inserted particle, like an extra one (*za'ida*), which does not indicate illustration or comparison. Thus the demonstrative noun in this case takes the place of an absolute object of *ja'alnakum*, as if it were said "that making, We made you," so he turned away from the verbal noun (*masdar*) to its demonstrative noun, which stands in for it, to convey the strangeness of this making by the sign of distance that is required in the demonstrative for the distance of rank. The comparison in this view is intended for emphasis, by implying that if the one making the comparison wished to compare this in its strangeness, he would find nothing for it except to compare it with itself, and this is close to the saying of al-Nabigha: "And foolishness is like its name."

So the kaf is neither an extra particle nor for comparison, but it is close to the extra, and the demonstrative then refers to what will be mentioned after the demonstrative noun. The speech of al-Kashshaf is clearer in this interpretation, and it indicates this by its explicit statement in its parallels, when he said in His saying ﴿Thus We caused them to inherit it, the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 59]: the kaf is in the accusative in the sense of "like," i.e., like that expulsion We expelled them and made them inherit it.

Know that what led the author of al-Kashshaf to this interpretation is that the use of the demonstrative in this and similar cases does not consistently allow considering a thing pointed to from what preceded in the speech. Do you not see that it is not valid to consider a pointed-to thing in this verse and in the verse in Surat al-Shu'ara'? But the author of al-Kashshaf himself departed from this in His saying in Surat al-An'am ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy﴾ [al-An'am: 112], so he said: as We left between you and your enemies, thus We did with those before you of the prophets and their enemies. End of quote. What he said in this verse is a good direction, but the scholars have not thoroughly examined it. My own verification is that the original sense of "thus" (*kadhalika*) is to indicate the comparison of one thing with another, where the object of comparison is apparent and pointed to, or as good as apparent by claim. The object of comparison that is pointed to may be mentioned, as in His saying ﴿And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing﴾ [Hud: 102], which points to His saying ﴿We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves, and their gods that they invoked besides Allah did not avail them...﴾ [Hud: 101], and like the saying of al-Nabigha:

"I found trust, it did not betray it; thus was Nuh, who did not betray."

The object of comparison that is pointed to may be understood from the context, so it is possible to consider it a comparison, and it is possible to consider it an absolute object, as in the saying of Abu Tammam:

"Thus let the matter be grave and let the affair be heavy, for there is no excuse for an eye whose tears have not flowed."

al-Tibrizi said in his commentary: the demonstrative is for magnification and awe, and it is at the beginning of the qasidah, nothing preceded it that could be compared to it, so the consideration of comparison is set aside and it is used in the implication of the meaning of comparison. End of quote. He means that the poet pointed to the great event, which is the death of Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Tusi, and similar is the saying of al-Asadi in the Hamasah poets lamenting his brother:

"Thus time goes on, and knowledge fades away in it, and the trace is effaced."

صفحة ١٧

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation﴾, according to what al-Baydawi interpreted it by, is of this category.

It may also be intended to exalt goodness, so it is made as if it were something the speaker wants to compare, then he finds nothing but to compare it with itself, and in this there is a cutting off of consideration of comparison in reality. Similar is the saying of one of the poets of Fazarah in the chapter on Adab in the Hamasah:

"Thus I was trained, until there became part of my nature that I saw the criterion of character is adab."

That is, I was trained in this hidden, wondrous adab. From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"Thus is their tent, and for every people, when adversity touches them, there is a tent."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation﴾ is of this category according to the commentators of al-Kashshaf, and this is the truth. More clear than it in this meaning is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And thus We tested some of them by means of others﴾ [al-An'am: 53], for no thing was mentioned before other than what Allah the Exalted named a trial, taking it from the verb *fatanna*.

The demonstrative in this interpretation, its pointed-to thing is derived from a statement that comes after the demonstrative noun, as you have just learned, for the making derived from ﴿ja'alnakum﴾; and placing the pointed-to thing after the demonstrative is an eloquent usage in the context of arousing curiosity, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He said: This is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Or it is derived from a statement preceding the demonstrative noun, as in al-Baydawi's view, when he made the pointed-to thing the guidance derived from His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142], and perhaps he saw the necessity of the pointed-to thing preceding.

The *wasat* (median): it is a noun for a place lying between places that surround it, or for a thing lying between things surrounding it, and it is not, by custom, closer to some of them than to others. Since reaching it does not occur except after breaking through what surrounds it, the meaning of protection and honour was taken into it by nature, like the middle of a valley, which herders and animals cannot reach except after eating what is on its sides, so abundant pasture and grass remain there; and by convention, like the middle of a kingdom, which is made the seat of its capital, and the middle of a city, which is made the site of its citadel, because a middle place is not easily reached by an enemy; and like the middle of a necklace, where the most precious pearl is. For this reason, the meanings of preciousness, honour and choice became by convention part of the meaning of *wasat*, so they applied it to the precious choice by metonymy (*kinayah*). Zuhayr said:

"They are a median, whose judgment the people are content with, when one of the nights of difficulty descends upon a dilemma."

And the Exalted said, ﴿The best of them said: Did I not tell you, why do you not glorify Allah?﴾ [al-Qalam: 28].

It is said that *awsat al-qabilah* means its noblest members. As for applying *wasat* to a quality that falls as a just balance between two blameworthy traits, where there is excess and deficiency in both, such as courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between miserliness and extravagance, and justice between mercy and harshness, that is a metaphor by likening an imagined thing to a perceived thing. For this reason the hadith "The best of matters is their median" has been related, though its chain is weak, and these two usages have become widespread until they became two customary literal meanings.

So *wasat* in this verse has been explained as "choice" on the basis of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110], and it has been explained as "just" (*'udul*). The second interpretation was related by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: hasan sahih. Combining the two interpretations is the correct view, as we have mentioned in the ninth introduction.

The nation is described as *wasatan* in the masculine form, because it is a fixed (*jamid*) noun, and by its fixity it is common to masculine and feminine, like describing with a verbal noun in its fixity and its indication of description, unlike saying: "I saw these two Zaydayn," for that is a description with a noun that agrees (in the sense of being purely demonstrative), since it does not indicate a quality but is a pure pointing that does not suggest connection in essence. The pronoun of addressees here is intended to refer to the assembly of Muslims, because it is consequent upon being guided to facing the Ka'bah, so it includes everyone who prayed toward it. And because His saying ﴿that you may be witnesses﴾ has been explained in a sound hadith as the testimony of the whole nation over the nations, the pronoun is not restricted to those present on the day the verse was revealed.

The verse is a praise of the Muslims, because Allah has stored up for them favour and made them a median by what He prepared for them of its causes in explaining the Shari'ah, an explanation that made the minds of its followers safe from being deceived by the misguidances that were current among the nations. Fakhr al-Din said: it is possible that they are "median" in the sense that they are moderate in religion between the excessive and the deficient, the extremist and the negligent, because they did not exaggerate as the Christians exaggerated, making the Messiah the son of Allah, nor fall short as the Jews fell short, altering the books and treating the messengers lightly. The scholars of usul al-fiqh have used this verse as evidence that the consensus (*ijma'*) of the scholars of the Ummah, that is the mujtahids, is a legal proof in what they agree upon, and in explaining this argument there are several methods:

The first: Fakhr al-Din said: Allah informed of the justice and excellence of the Ummah, so if they committed a forbidden act they would not have been characterised by excellence, and once that is established, it is necessary that their agreement be a proof. End of quote. That is, because the collective of mujtahids are just, setting aside the possibility that the attribute of justice is absent in some of them individually. This is refuted by the fact that error does not contradict justice or excellence, so the verse does not indicate their immunity from error in what they agree upon.

صفحة ١٩

This refutation is firm. It was answered that complete justice, which is the balance between the two extremes of excess and deficiency, entails immunity from all of them falling into error in statements, acts, and beliefs.

The second method: al-Baydawi said: If there were falsehood in what they agreed upon, their justice would be impaired. End of quote. He means that the verse requires complete justice from the collective of the Ummah, so if their agreement were upon a false matter, their justice would be impaired, that is, it would be deficient, and that does not fit the praise upon them in this verse. This returns to the first method.

The third approach: some scholars said that the address is to the Companions, and that they do not agree upon an error. So the verse is an argument for ijma' (scholarly consensus) in general. It is objected that the justice ('adalah) of the Companions does not preclude error in ijma' (scholarly consensus) reached through ijtihad (independent legal reasoning). Their consensus may come from ijtihad. As for their consensus on matters that are transmitted (naql), it falls under what we will mention below.

In my view, the verse clearly states that the attribute mentioned in it is a praise of the whole community (ummah), not of its scholars specifically. Therefore there is no point in using it as evidence for the authority of ijma', which is a state of some of the community, not of all of it. The correct view is that the verse indicates the authority of the consensus of the whole community in matters whose basis is transmission (naql) of the Shari'ah. This is what is expressed by tawatur (mass transmission) and by what is known of the religion by necessity (ma 'ulima min al-din bi-al-darurah), which is the agreement of the Muslims on attributing a statement, an action, or a description to the Prophet (ﷺ), of what is legislated as a foundation or a general explanation, such as the number of prayers and units (raka'at), the manner of prayer and of hajj, and the transmission of the Qur'an. This belongs to the states of establishing the Shari'ah. By it the ambiguous matters were explained and the Shari'ah was founded. This is what the scholars referred to when they said that one who denies what is agreed upon in it is a disbeliever. It is also the matter in which Abu Bakr al-Baqillani required agreement of the common people, while others required the number needed for tawatur. It is what many early usulis (jurists of legal theory) describe as taking precedence over all other proofs.

As for the verse being evidence for the authority of the ijma' of mujtahidun (qualified jurists) who reach their view through reflection and ijtihad, this cannot be derived from the verse except by saying that the verse may be cited as supporting evidence for it. When it informs that God the Exalted made this community a middle nation (wasat), and we know that the wasat is the excellent, just one, standing between two extremes of excess and deficiency, we know that God the Exalted perfected the intellects of this community through what their intellects are raised upon: habituation to sound beliefs, avoidance of the foolish fantasies into which the intellects of other nations sank, and habituation to receiving the Shari'ah through the channels of trustworthy transmitters, and establishing its rulings through reasoning, by istinbat (derivation) for the scholars and by understanding for the common people. If that is so, it follows from the meaning of the verse that the intellects of the individuals of this community are sound intellects, and this is the meaning of its being a middle nation. Then this uprightness varies according to what suits each class of the community and each individual. Since the attribute mentioned applies to the whole community, we say: this whole does not fall into error, neither deliberately nor by mistake. As for deliberate error, it contradicts justice ('adalah). As for mistaken error, it contradicts the natural constitution of upright judgment. So if error is possible for its individuals, it is not possible for all its scholars to converge upon error, by reasoning. Both matters have occurred to earlier nations, and they agreed upon error by following the opinion of one of them, either because their revealed laws did not warn them against that, or because they misinterpreted them. Then the common people take a share of this infallibility in what is specific to it, which is only the transmitted part (al-juz' al-naqli). With this the argument is ordered.

His saying ﴿لِتَكُونُوا شُهَداءَ﴾ (that you may be witnesses) is the cause (illah) for their being made a middle nation. All the acts of God the Exalted are tied to wisdoms and ends, by His knowledge and wisdom. This is by will and choice, not like the emanation of an effect from its cause, as some philosophers say, nor by obligation and compulsion, as the expressions of the Mu'tazilah seem to imply, although their intention in them was good. They meant that this is obligatory for God the Exalted Himself because of the perfection of His wisdom.

The word ﴿النّاسِ﴾ (the people) is general, and what is meant by it is the past and present nations. This witnessing is both worldly and otherworldly. As for the worldly witnessing, it is this community's judgment upon the past and present nations, by vindicating those believers among them who believed in the messengers sent in every age, and by condemning the disbelievers among them who rejected their messengers and the stubborn ones who clung to their creeds after the coming of the abrogating law (nasikh) and the appearance of the truth. This is a great historical and religious judgment. When the community is raised upon it, it is raised upon the habit of presenting all events to the standard of correct criticism.

As for the otherworldly witnessing, it is what al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Noah will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to him: Did you convey? He will say: Yes, my Lord. Then his community will be asked: Did he convey to you? They will say: No warner came to us. Then He will say: Who are your witnesses? He will say: Muhammad and his community. So you will be brought, and you will bear witness." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾, he said: "just," ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾. Here his saying "then he recited" shows that this witnessing is part of the meaning of the verse, not that it is the entire meaning of the verse. The apparent cause (ta'lil) is the first witnessing, because it is what branches from "We have made you a middle nation." As for the coming of the witnessing of the Hereafter in accordance with it, that is because of what we have known: the states of the Hereafter follow the states of this world. God the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124]. ﴿He will say: My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, while I was seeing?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125]. ﴿He will say: Thus came to you Our verses, and you forgot them; and thus today you are forgotten﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126].

Among the things that complete the meaning of witnessing over the people in this world is the obligation upon us to call the nations to Islam, so that this takes the place of the Messenger's call to them, until the witnessing is complete for the believers among them against those who turn away.

Witnessing over nations is both for them and against them. But the verse restricted it by using the preposition ﴿عَلَى﴾ (over/against), indicating that the greater and more important part of this community's witnessing is its witnessing against those who turn away, because the believers are already vouched for by their faith. Thus the use of ﴿عَلَى﴾ is a warning to the nations not to be in a position where witness is borne against them, and an honouring of the Muslims with the state of their being safe from the stain of being among those against whom witness is borne, and with the state of their being ennobled by this distinction, which is to make those who oppose them stand condemned by the consequence of their testimony.

His saying ﴿ويَكُونَ الرَّسُولُ عَلَيْكم شَهِيدًا﴾ (and the Messenger may be a witness over you) is coordinated with the cause (ma'tuf 'ala al-'illah) and is not a second cause, because it is not intended in itself. Rather it completes the first witnessing, because our being made a middle nation requires that we have no need of witnessing for us and no witnessing against us. As for the worldly witnessing, the Messenger's witnessing over us in it is his witnessing in his own person over his contemporaries, and the witnessing of his Shari'ah over those who came after him, either through their fulfilment of what his Shari'ah made obligatory upon them, or through the opposite. As for the otherworldly witnessing, it is what was narrated in the hadith mentioned above, of the Messenger's witnessing to the truthfulness of the community in what it bore witness to. It is also what was narrated in the other hadith in al-Muwatta' and the Sahihs (the authentic collections): "Some people will be driven away from my Pool, and I will say: My Lord, my community! It will be said: You do not know what they innovated after you; they altered and changed. Then I will say: Away, away with whoever altered after me."

The transitive use of the witnessing of the Messenger over the community with the particle ﴿عَلَى﴾ is for the sake of agreement (musha-kalah) with his previous saying ﴿لِتَكُونُوا شُهَداءَ عَلى النّاسِ﴾ (that you may be witnesses over the people). Otherwise it is a witnessing for the community. It was also said that the word shahid (witness) is used in both places with the implied sense of raqib (watcher) and muhaymin (guardian), as in al-Kashshaf.

This verse indicates the honouring and ennobling of witnessing, to the point that the All-Knowing, Who knows everything, makes clear that He does not judge except after it has been established. It is derived from the verse that the witness is a witness by what knowledge he has acquired, even if the one he testifies against has not witnessed it himself, and that he testifies on the basis of knowledge acquired by hearing and by decisive proofs, even if he did not see with his eyes or hear with his ears. And that certification (tazkiyah) is a great foundation of testimony, that the one who certifies must be more excellent and more just than the one certified, that the one certified does not need certification, and that the community does not bear witness against the Prophet (ﷺ). For this reason he used to say in the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Have I not conveyed? They say: Yes. He says: O God, bear witness." So God is made the witness of his conveyance. This is among the most subtle points.

The placing of the prepositional phrase ﴿عَلَيْكم﴾ before its governing verb is, I think, only for the purpose of emphasis (al-ihtimam), honouring the matter of this community, so that it bears witness over the nations and the messengers, while only its own messenger bears witness over it. It may also be that its placement is so that the word with which the verse ends falls at the place of pausing (waqf) as a word having a long vowel (harf madd) before the last letter, since the elongation is more suitable for pausing. This is one of the marvels of the eloquence of the Qur'an. It was also said that the fronting of the prepositional phrase conveys the restriction of the agent to the object (qasr al-fa'il 'ala al-maf'ul), but this is strained, and the like of it is not usual in their speech.

* * *

﴿وما جَعَلْنا القِبْلَةَ الَّتِي كُنْتَ عَلَيْها إلّا لِنَعْلَمَ مَن يَتَّبِعُ الرَّسُولَ مِمَّنْ يَنْقَلِبُ عَلى عَقِبَيْهِ وإنْ كانَتْ لَكَبِيرَةً إلّا عَلى الَّذِينَ هَدى اللَّهُ﴾ (And We did not make the qiblah which you were facing except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels; and indeed it was a great matter except for those whom God guided.)

The conjunction wa (and) is coordinated with the sentence ﴿سَيَقُولُ السُّفَهاءُ مِنَ النّاسِ﴾ (The foolish among the people will say) [al-Baqarah: 142], and with what is connected to it of the answer in His saying ﴿قُلْ لِلَّهِ المَشْرِقُ والمَغْرِبُ﴾ (Say: To God belong the east and the west) [al-Baqarah: 142]. It is intended to explain the wisdom of the legislation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis, then the change of that to the legislation of facing the Ka'bah. Between the two sentences, from His saying ﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْناكم أُمَّةً وسَطًا﴾ (And thus We made you a middle nation) to its end, is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD).

The verb ja'ala (made, appointed) here is the making of legislation, as is shown by its object being a matter of worship, not of creation. Its object is the word al-qiblah (the direction of prayer). For this reason the verb ja'ala here is transitive to one object, because it means shara'na (We legislated). These verses were revealed after the command to face the Ka'bah. So the intended meaning is Bayt al-Maqdis. He turned away from naming the subject by its name to using the relative pronoun, in imitation of the speech of those who were refuted when they said ﴿ما ولّاهم عَنْ قِبْلَتِهِمُ الَّتِي كانُوا عَلَيْها﴾ (What turned them from their qiblah which they had been facing?) [al-Baqarah: 142], together with an allusion to the explanation of the wisdom indicated by His saying ﴿إلّا لِنَعْلَمَ﴾ (except that We might know), meaning: We did not make that a qiblah while intending to abrogate it, but We obliged you to it for a time, except that We might know, and so on.

The exception in His saying ﴿إلّا لِنَعْلَمَ﴾ is an exception from causes and circumstances. That is: We did not make that for one reason and in one state, except that We might make manifest who was sincere in faith in both states: the state of the legislation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis, and the state of the change of facing to the Ka'bah. 'Abd al-Hakim reported that some Arabs apostatised from Islam when the Messenger of God faced Bayt al-Maqdis, out of zealous partisanship for the qiblah of the Arabs. And the Jews had found pretexts for themselves in outwardly professing Islam, as we explained at His saying ﴿وإذا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قالُوا آمَنّا﴾ (And when they meet those who believe, they say: We believe) [al-Baqarah: 14]. So they were hypocrites, interpreting for themselves that praying with him was an act of worship to God the Exalted, and an addition to their own prayers which they kept when they were alone with their devils. Yet their prayer with the Muslims did not include anything that contradicted the glorification of their rites, since they were facing Bayt al-Maqdis. When the qiblah was changed, the manner of prayer became contrary to the glorification of their rites, because it meant turning their backs to what must be faced. Thus they had no room left for interpretation, and it became clear who remained in Islam and the hypocrites turned away from the prayer.

Making God's knowledge of who follows the Messenger and who turns back on his heels the cause of these two legislations requires that what the legislation implies should occur in future time, as the force of the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil) requires, and the supposition of an (an) after the lam. An is a particle of the future, even though God knows that, and that knowledge is essential to Him, not something that arises or renews. But what is meant by knowledge here is the knowledge of its occurrence, which is the relation of His knowledge to the occurrence of the thing which He knew from eternity would occur. This is a specific relation, and it is occurrent, because it is like the immediate relation of will and power, although the theologians neglected to count it among the relations of knowledge.

You may also take His saying ﴿لِنَعْلَمَ مَن يَتَّبِعُ الرَّسُولَ﴾ (that We might know who follows the Messenger) as a kinayah (metonymy) for: that everyone who did not know would know by it, in the manner of symbolic metonymy, so the speaker mentions his own knowledge while meaning the knowledge of people. Just as Iyas ibn Qubaysah al-Ta'i said:

I shall begin with the verse of poetry, "wa-aqdamtu wal-Khatti yakhtiru baynana li-a'lama man juba'uha min shuja'iha" ("I advanced while the spear swayed between us, that I might know which of its cowards are distinguished from its brave"). It is said that he wished to make manifest who among them is a coward and who is brave; so I know it, and people know it. The Qur'an came in this verse and its likes in this style. You may also take it as a metaphor (kinaya) for the reward of the one who follows and the one who turns back, each according to what suits him. You may also take "na'lama" as a figure (majaz) meaning "to be distinguished" (tahayyuz), so that it becomes manifest to the people, by the indicator of the word "man" called "man al-fasliyya" (the separating "man"), as Ibn Malik and Ibn Hisham named it. In reality it is among the branches of the meanings of the initial "man" (man al-ibtida'iyya), as the author of al-Mughni inclined to conclude. And this objection which they mention should not trouble you: how can the newly-occurring making (ja'l) be a cause for the occurrence of eternal knowledge? It becomes clear to you that it returns to a figurative (kinai) meaning.

Al-inqilab (turning back) is returning to the place from which one came; it is said "inqalaba ila al-dar" (he turned back to the house). His saying ﴿'ala 'aqibayh﴾ ("on his heels") is an intensification of emphasis in returning to what was behind him, because the 'aqibayn are the backs of the two shins; i.e., he turned back on the path of his heels. Here it is a figurative metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya) for apostasy from Islam, returning to the earlier disbelief. "Man" is a relative pronoun, and it is the object of "na'lamu"; knowledge here means recognition, and its verb transitively takes one object.

His saying ﴿wa-in kanat la-kabira illa 'ala alladhina hada Allah﴾ ("and indeed it was a great thing, except for those whom Allah guided") is coordinated (ataf) upon the sentence ﴿wa-ma ja'alna al-qibla allati kunta 'alayha﴾ ("and We did not make the qibla which you were upon..."). The connection is evident, because the sentence ﴿wa-in kanat﴾ stands in the position of a cause for the sentence "na'lama man yattabi'u al-rasul," for it indicates following and turning back only because it is a great matter with no leniency in it, so that the believer of pure faith is distinguished from the mixed. The feminine pronoun refers to the event or to the qibla, in view of its change.

"In" is a lightened (mukhaffafa) form of the heavy "inna." "Al-kabira" here means "the severe, the one that embarrasses the souls." The Arabs say: "kabura 'alayhi kadhā" when it is heavy upon him in his self, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿wa-in kana kabura 'alayka i'radhuhum﴾ (Al-An'am: 35).

* * *

﴿Wa-ma kana Allahu li-yudi'a imanakum inna Allaha bi-al-nasi la-ra'ufun rahim﴾

The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "li-na'lama," meaning: that We may make manifest who follows the Messenger and who turns back on his heels, while We are not wasting your faith. Mention of the Name of Majesty (al-jalala) is an explicit noun in the place of the pronoun, for magnification.

Al-Bukhari related from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: "Men had died while upon the qibla before it was changed; we did not know what to say about them. So Allah, Exalted, revealed ﴿wa-ma kana Allahu li-yudi'a imanakum﴾." In his saying "qutilu" (were killed) there is a difficulty, that there had been no fighting before the change of the qibla; we shall clarify that. Al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the Prophet was turned toward the Ka'ba, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what about our brothers who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis?' So Allah revealed: 'wa-ma kana Allahu li-yudi'a imanakum' (the verse)." He said: "This is a hadith hasan sahih."

Idaa'a (waste) is the destruction of a thing and the nullification of its effects. "Iman" is interpreted in its apparent sense, and it has also been interpreted as prayer, transmitted by al-Qurtubi from Malik. The verb "yudi'u" is connected to "iman" by supposing an omitted noun. If "iman" is interpreted in its apparent sense, the estimate is: "to waste the due of your faith, when the whisperings of Satan did not shake it at facing toward a qibla you did not love." If "iman" is interpreted as prayer, the estimate is: "Allah would not waste the merit of your prayers or their reward." In applying the name "iman" to prayer there is an honouring of prayer, because it is the greatest of the pillars of faith. From Malik: "Indeed I recall with this the saying of the Murji'a: 'Prayer is not part of faith.'"

The meaning of the hadith of al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi is that the Muslims used to think that the abrogation of a ruling makes the abrogated void, so the effects of acting upon it are not established; therefore they feared for the prayers of their brothers who died before the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis, such as As'ad ibn Zurara ibn Ma'rur and Abu Umama. The questioners supposed that it would be obligatory upon them to make up what they had prayed before the abrogation. For this reason their question was answered with what includes them and includes those who died earlier. He said "imanakum" and did not say "imanahum," according to the form of the question.

The closing with His saying ﴿inna Allaha bi-al-nasi la-ra'ufun rahim﴾ is an emphasis on the non-waste of their faith, a favour, and a teaching that an abrogated ruling only cancels action in the future, not in the past.

"Al-Ra'uf al-Rahim" are two attributive adjectives (sifat mushabbaha); the first is derived from "al-ra'fa" and the second from "al-rahma." "Al-ra'fa" is explained as "rahma" in the general usage of the majority of the lexicographers, and al-Zajjaj followed it. But the research scholars among the lexicographers restricted "al-ra'fa" to the meaning of a particular mercy. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "Al-ra'fa is more than al-rahma," that is, stronger; it is a strong mercy, and this is the meaning of al-Jawhari's saying: "Al-ra'fa is the strongest mercy." In al-Mujmal he said: "Al-ra'fa is more specific than al-rahma and hardly occurs in dislike, whereas al-rahma occurs in dislike for the sake of benefit." Al-Qaffal derived from this: "The difference between al-ra'fa and al-rahma is that al-ra'fa is an intensification of a particular mercy, namely the removal of harm and the averting of injury, like His saying ﴿wa-la ta'khudhkum bihima ra'fatun fi dini Allah﴾ (An-Nur: 2). As for al-rahma, it is a comprehensive name in which that meaning enters, and in which bestowal and beneficence enter." This is the best of what has been said about it; al-Fakhr and 'Abd al-Hakim preferred it, and perhaps he was pointing to the fact that between al-ra'fa and al-rahma there is general and specific relation, absolutely. Whatever the meaning of al-ra'fa, the combining of "ra'uf" and "rahim" in the verse gives the confirmation of the signification of one by the signification of the other, either by equality or by addition.

As for the view which takes the research scholars' explanation of the meanings of al-ra'fa and al-rahma, the combining of the two attributes serves to indicate that He, Exalted, shows strong mercy to one who deserves it, and shows mercy in general without that.

The meaning of al-rahma was given earlier in Surat al-Fatiha. The placing of "ra'uf" first is so that "rahim" falls as the closing word (fasila), making it more suitable to the closing rhymes of this surah, since their closings are built on a long vowelled letter followed by a quiescent consonant. The attributive "ra'uf" has its quiescent letter relying on the hamza, and the hamza resembles the vowel letters, so its pronunciation is not fully firm upon the tongue; and the letter fa', because it comes out from the inside of the lower lip and the tips of the incisors, resembles the soft letter, so the quiescence of pause does not settle firmly upon it.

The placing of "bi-al-nas" before its governed element, which is "ra'uf rahim," serves to alert to His care for them, waking them so that they may give thanks, together with observing the closing rhyme. The majority read "la-ra'ufun" with a quiescent waw followed by a hamza; Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it without a waw, with the hamza vowelled by damma, on the pattern of "'adud," and this is a dialect against analogy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 144 (part 1 of 3):

﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, so We will surely turn you to a qibla that will please you. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.﴾

This is a resumptive new sentence (istinaf ibtida'i, a sentence that begins a new topic) and a preparation for the legislation of facing the Ka'bah (qibla, the direction of prayer) and the abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another) of facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). This is the purpose of the discourse that opened with His words ﴿The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from the qibla they used to face?"﴾ (al-Baqarah: 142). Before this, God had prepared the ground and readied people to await it, in various ways, beginning with His words ﴿To God belong the east and the west﴾ (al-Baqarah: 115), then His words ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 120), then His words ﴿And when We made the House﴾ (al-Baqarah: 125), then His words ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ (al-Baqarah: 142). In the speech of the Arabs, qad (a particle) indicates confirmation (tahqiq). Do you not see that the scholars of rhetoric (ahl al-ma'ani) compared hal (in interrogation) with qad (in declarative statements), and said that for this reason hal is used to seek assent (talab al-tasdiq), while the particle qad confirms the action; so it stands with the verb in the position of inna with nouns. This is why al-Khalil said: "It is a reply to people who are awaiting news; if they were not awaiting it, one would not say qad fa'ala kadha (he has indeed done such-and-such)." End of quotation. Since God's knowledge of this is something the Prophet (ﷺ) does not doubt, so that the report would need confirmation, the report, together with its emphasis, is used for its implication (lazim) by way of metonymy (kinayah, indirect expression), to remove any impatience on his part, and to reassure him, because the Prophet was eager for its occurrence; and this implies a promise of its occurrence. Thus two successive metonymies result.

[Page 27]

The present tense is used with qad to indicate recurrence (tajaddud), and the intended meaning is the recurrence of its implication, so that it serves as emphasis for that implication, which is the promise. For this reason, qad when it precedes the present tense has come to be understood as expressing frequency, like rubba (perhaps/often) in rubba yaf'alu (he sometimes does). 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras said:

"I often leave the opponent pale at the fingertips, as if his garments were dyed with firsad (a red dye)."

The fuller explanation of this will come when discussing His words ﴿We know well that what they say grieves you﴾ (al-An'am: 33) in Surat al-An'am. The verb taqallub is the intransitive form (mutawa'ah) of qallabahu, meaning he turned it, and it is equivalent to qalabahu with the light form. Thus the meaning of taqlib al-wajh (turning of the face) is looking about (iltifat), that is, turning it from its original direction. Here it means repeatedly moving it toward the sky. Some have derived from the shift to the form tafa'ul, which indicates frequency, that this turning was repeated; but there is room for disagreement, since it may be due to the eagerness and intensity of this turning, so the form tafa'ul expresses the intensity of the manner. They said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would sense by inspiration that God would turn him toward Makkah, so he kept turning his face toward the sky, and it was said that he was waiting for Gabriel to descend with this. In my view, if this were the case, it would necessarily follow that the turning of his face occurred at the time when the revelation of the verse was about to descend, for otherwise he would not have been awaiting Gabriel. This shows that this turning was not repeated from him.

The fa' in ﴿so We will surely turn you﴾ is the fa' of consequence (ta'qib), to emphasize the promise with explicitness after the preparation for it through the allusion in His words ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face﴾. The word tawliyah (turning) has already been discussed at His words ﴿What has turned them away from their qibla which they used to face﴾ (al-Baqarah: 142). So the meaning of ﴿We will surely turn you to a qibla﴾ is: We will direct you toward a qibla that will please you.

Qibla is in the accusative (nasb) by extension (tawassu'), in the position of the second object; its original form is: "We will turn you from a qibla," and likewise His words ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾.

The meaning is that the turning of his face toward the Ka'bah will take place immediately following this promise. This promise includes two emphatic particles and a particle of immediacy, and that is the utmost of gentleness and kindness.

He expressed it with ﴿that will please you﴾ to indicate that his inclination toward the Ka'bah is an inclination of intending good, based on the fact that the Ka'bah is the most worthy of God's houses to indicate tawhid (monotheism), as has already been mentioned. Therefore it is the most worthy of being faced, over Bayt al-Maqdis.

[Page 28]

Also, because in facing it there is an indication of the independence of this religion from the religion of the People of the Book. Since riḍa (pleasure) implies love arising from understanding, it was chosen in this context instead of "tuhibbuha" (you love it) or "tahwaha" (you desire it), or similar words, because the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ) is too exalted for his inclination to attach itself to something that is not a superior interest after the expiry of the temporary interest that was the reason for the legislation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis. Do you not see that when the matter of their qibla came, after it was abrogated, it came with His words ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 145), and so on.

His words ﴿So turn your face﴾ are a consequence (tafri') of the promise and a hastening toward it. The meaning is: turn your face during the prayer. This is understood from the context of the discourse, which deals with the disputation with the foolish about the direction of prayer.

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the command is directed to him in view of what it contains of satisfying his desire. He will follow it with associating the community with him in the command, in His words ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾.

Al-shatr, with a fatha on the shin and a sukun on the ta', means the direction and side. Qatadah explained it as "facing" (tilqa'), and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read it that way. Al-Jubba'i and 'Abd al-Jabbar explained al-shatr here as the middle of a thing, because shatr is applied to half of a thing; when it is added to the mosque, and the mosque is a place, it implies that its half refers to half its measure and area, which is its middle. They also made shatr al-Masjid al-Haram a metonymy for the Ka'bah, because it lies within the Sacred Mosque at the middle of its area on all sides, approximately. 'Abd al-Jabbar said: "What indicates that what we have mentioned is intended are two points.
