First, if the one praying stands in a place where he faces the mosque but not the Ka'bah, his prayer is not valid. Second, if we do not interpret shatr as we have mentioned, there would be no benefit in mentioning shatr, since it would suffice to say: 'So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque.' And the obligation would be to face the Sacred Mosque, not specifically the Ka'bah."

If you say: What is the benefit of His words ﴿We will surely turn you to a qibla that will please you﴾ before His words ﴿So turn your face﴾? Why did He not say: "In the sky, so turn your face..."? I say: its benefit is to show concern for the desire of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and that it is something to be cared for, as the description of the qibla by the clause "that will please you" indicates.

The meaning of nuwalliyannaka is: We will direct you. In the notion of directing there is a figurative nearness, because wallā, when transitive by itself, if it does not mean actual nearness, then it means connection to it, and from it come al-wala' (allegiance) and al-wali (protector/ally). It is apparent that its transitivity to a second object is by ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: he turned his face to such-and-such, and then they transitivize it to a third object with the particle 'an,

[Page 29]

so they say: "He turned from such-and-such," and they treat it as intransitive with regard to the other two objects. So they supply: he turned his face toward the direction of such-and-such, turned away from such-and-such, meaning the one that was facing him before. With the variation of these usages the meanings differ, as has been mentioned.

So al-qibla here is a noun for the place that the one praying faces, and it is either derived from the noun of form (ism al-hay'ah) or from the noun of the object (ism al-maf'ul), as has been mentioned.

Al-Masjid al-Haram refers to the mosque known among Muslims. Al-Haram: the thing made an attribute of the mosque, is the forbidden, that is, what is protected by prohibition of reverence and sanctity, for the root of prohibition (tahrim) indicates avoidance of a thing, so avoidance is understood in every context according to what suits it.

It became common among the Arabs to describe Makkah as al-Balad al-Haram (the Sacred City), meaning protected from tyrants, oppressors and aggressors. It is described as al-Muharram in His words, relating the words of Abraham: ﴿near Your Sacred House﴾ (Ibrahim: 37), meaning the honored and respected. The sanctuary (Haram) was also named, as He said: ﴿Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary?﴾ (al-Qasas: 57). Thus describing the Ka'bah as the Sacred House and the sanctuary of Makkah as the Haram are ancient and widespread descriptions among the Arabs. As for the name al-Masjid al-Haram, it is one of the Qur'anic titles, made a proper name for the sacred precinct surrounding the Ka'bah, which is the place of circumambulation (tawaf) and seclusion (i'tikaf). It was not known as "the mosque" in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah), because they did not have a prayer with prostration, and the mosque is the place of prostration. So the name al-Masjid al-Haram became a proper name by dominance for the enclosed area surrounding the Ka'bah, which has gates, among them Bab al-Safa and Bab Bani Shaybah. When this name was applied to what surrounds the Ka'bah, Muslims and others did not hesitate about what was meant by it. So al-Masjid al-Haram is among the Islamic names before the Hijrah, and its mention occurs in Surat al-Isra', which is Meccan.

The majority hold that what is meant here by al-Masjid al-Haram is the Ka'bah, because of the widely transmitted authentic reports that the qibla was turned to the Ka'bah, and that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) "was commanded to face the Ka'bah," and that he prayed toward the Ka'bah on the day of the Conquest and said: "This is the qibla." Ibn al-'Arabi said, mentioning the Masjid al-Haram: "What is meant by it is the House, because the Arabs express the House by what is adjacent to it or what it includes." And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "The House is a qibla for the people of the mosque, the mosque is a qibla for the people of the sanctuary, and the sanctuary is a qibla for the people of the east and the west." Al-Fakhr said: "This is the view of Malik." I say: this is not known from Malik in the books of his school.

Shatr al-Masjid is in the accusative as the second object of walli, and it is not accusative as a place adverb (zarf).

[Page 30]

His words ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ are an explicit statement generalizing the ruling of facing the Ka'bah to all Muslims, through the generality of the pronouns in kuntum (you are) and wujuhakum (your faces), because they occur within the context of the generality of the conditional particles bi-haythu-ma (wherever) and hina-ma (whenever), in order to generalize the regions of the earth, lest it be thought that His words ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ are specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). For His words ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ are an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), though the situation required that it be addressed to him specifically, because it is a consequence of His words ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾, so that it would be good news to him, and so that he would know that his community is like him, because the basic principle of Islamic legislation is that it applies to both the Messenger and his community, unless a proof indicates the specification of one of them. When it was feared that this ruling might be understood as specific to him, or that a single turning would suffice, or that facing only some directions, such as Madinah or Makkah, would suffice, the generalization was intended for the responsible persons (mukallafun) and for all lands. For this reason the conjunction with waw was used, although it would have sufficed to say: "and turn your faces toward it." So something was added that indicates the generalization of places, explicitly and emphatically, because of the generality implied by the annexation of shatr to the pronoun of "al-Masjid al-Haram," since shatr is an indefinite noun that resembles the plural in indicating many individuals, so its annexation was like the annexation of plurals. It also emphasizes the indication of the legislative command toward repetition, to draw attention to the importance of this ruling. So it was as if it had been conveyed twice in relation to those responsible and their circumstances: the first being general, and the second detailed.

This passage is evidence for the obligation of this facing (*istiqbal*, facing the qiblah). It has great wisdom. The purpose of prayer is worship and submission to God, Exalted is He, and submission grows in proportion to the presence of the One worshipped in the heart. From this come its good effects: the servant's sincerity toward his Lord and his devotion to worship, which is the foundation of obedience and avoidance of what is forbidden. For this reason the sound hadith says: "Ihsan (excellence in worship) is that you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you." Since God, Exalted is He, is beyond being encompassed by the senses, whoever seeks to bring His greatness to mind must take for himself a reminder of Him from something that has a special connection to Him. Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi) said: God created in man a rational faculty that perceives abstract and intelligible realities, and an imaginative faculty that operates in the world of bodies. The rational faculty rarely separates from the accompaniment of the imaginative faculty. So when a person wishes to bring to mind an abstract intelligible matter, he must set for it a sensory image that he can perceive, so that this image helps him grasp those intelligible meanings. And since a weak servant, when he arrives at the assembly of a great king, must necessarily face him with his face, extol him at length with his tongue, and serve him, facing the qiblah in prayer is like being in the presence of the King. The Qur'an and the glorifications are like praise of Him, and bowing and prostration are like service. End of quote.

[Page 31]

When the presence of the desired Essence cannot be brought to mind through the senses, then it is brought to mind through something that has a direct connection to it, such as dwellings, or through an intermediary, such as lightning and breeze and the like, or through resemblance, such as the gazelle for lovers. Poets have long been enamored of the traces of the beloved, such as the ruins in the line "Halt, let us weep for the memory of a beloved and a dwelling," and their sayings about lightning and wind. Malik ibn al-Rayb said:

"Desire called me, from my beloved folk and neighbors, at Dhu al-Tayyisayn, so I turned back looking."

God, Exalted is He, is beyond being encompassed by the senses, so the means of bringing His Essence to mind is to bring to mind what gives greater indication of Him, Exalted is He.

Undoubtedly, the creatures most worthy of being made a means for bringing the Creator to mind in the heart of His servant are those whose existence was for the sake of indicating God's oneness, His transcendence, and His attribution with the attributes of perfection, while being free of anything that could suggest they are the object of worship. These are the mosques that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) built, and he kept them free of anything that might suggest it was the object of worship. He did not give them any name other than God's name. He built the Ka'bah as the first house, and he built a mosque in the place of the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa), and he built other mosques whose mention occurs in the Torah under the title "altars." The Sabians, after Nuh (Noah), built temples to glorify idols and to magnify their standing in souls, and they attributed them to the names of men such as Wadd and Suwa', or to the names of the stars. Al-Mas'udi, in Muruj al-Dhahab (Meadows of Gold), mentioned several temples that were set up among past nations for this purpose, among them the temple of Sandusaba in the land of India, and the temple of Masina in the direction of al-Raqqah, which the Sabians built before Ibrahim, and Azar, the father of Ibrahim, was one of its custodians. It is also said that 'Ad built temples among them, including Jilliq, the temple of the land of al-Sham (Syria).

When a believer in God faces any of the houses that were set up to counter the people of polytheism and to indicate God's oneness and glorify Him, this is bringing the Creator to mind through what is most closely attributed to Him. However, these houses, despite their number, differ only by the sincerity of intention in building them, by whether they were built for that purpose, and by the precedence of some over others in this aim. If you wish, you may make all these three meanings one meaning, namely precedence, because the earlier one has distinction over the later one by being the one whose founder laid its foundation for the later one's foundation. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Surely a mosque founded upon piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:108]. And concerning the Mosque of Harm He said: ﴿Do not stand in it ever﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:108], meaning because it was founded with the intention of dividing the believers. And He said: ﴿Surely the first house appointed for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:96]. So He made it a guidance for people because it is the first house. Therefore the houses built after it, such as the House of the Holy Place (Bayt al-Maqdis), are traces of guidance that their builders were guided to through the first house.

Some scholars have said: the Ka'bah is the first temple erected for worship. There is an issue with this that will come under His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Surely the first house appointed for mankind is that at Bakkah﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:96], in Surah Al 'Imran. There is no doubt that the first temple erected for affirming God's oneness and transcendence, announcing that, and nullifying association (shirk) is the Ka'bah, which Ibrahim built, the first who argued with the idolaters with proofs, and the first who opposed idolatry with the strength of his hand, making the idols into pieces. Then he built that great temple to perpetuate the remembrance and oneness of God, so that everyone who comes would know that the reason for its building was the nullification of idol worship. Ages have passed over this house, and seeing it has become a reminder of God, Exalted is He. Thus it has the distinction of being first, and then the distinction that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) built it with his own hand and the hand of his son Isma'il without anyone's help. So for this meaning it is more deeply rooted in indicating both God's oneness and prophethood, and these are the two poles of the faith of believers, and in this attribute no one else shares with it.

Then the pilgrimage to it was established to renew this remembrance and to spread it among other nations. Therefore it is undoubtedly most worthy of being faced by one who wishes to bring to mind the majesty of true Lordship. The houses of God were not built, like the Farthest Mosque, until many centuries after it. So it was the qiblah of the Muslims.

We mentioned earlier that the condition of facing a specific direction was not among the rulings of previous laws. How could it be, when the Farthest Mosque was built after Musa (Moses) by more than four hundred years? The most that facing it after Sulayman's supplication (du'a') meant was facing it for the purpose of ensuring that supplication and prayer would be accepted, not because it was a condition. Furthermore, the choice of that temple as a direction, even if it was a supplication, is the supplication of a prophet, which can only come from divine inspiration. So perhaps the wisdom behind it at that time was that God intended to populate the holy land, as He promised Ibrahim and promised Musa. He wanted to increase the attachment of the Children of Israel's hearts to it, so He made clear to them the facing of the faithful temple that His prophet Sulayman had built there, so that this sanctuary would move their souls to be eager to keep those lands in their hands.

It is also possible that God had prescribed for them facing it after that through the tongues of prophets after Sulayman, but this is far-fetched, because their prophets did not bring anything beyond the law of Musa, and they came only to strengthen it. So God's prescribing that Muslims face a specific direction in their prayers is a perfection of the meaning of humility in the prayer of Islam. It is one of the perfections that God reserved for this law, so that the completion of the religion would honor its bearer (ﷺ) and his community, if the first possibility is correct. If the second is correct, then the command to face it is for us, so that our prayer would not be weaker in bringing God's majesty to mind than the prayer of others.

For this reason our scholars agreed that facing a specific direction coincided with the legislation of prayer in Islam. If the Prophet's (ﷺ) facing the direction of the Ka'bah was by his own ijtihad (independent reasoning), its reason is that it is the mosque that the People of the Two Books (Jews and Christians) venerated, and that was not mixed with association, and no idols were set up in it. So this was the closest evidence for facing its direction for one who wishes to bring to mind the oneness of God, Exalted is He. If facing the House of the Holy Place was by revelation from God, Exalted is He, then perhaps its wisdom was to win over the hearts of the People of the Two Books, and so that it would become clear afterward to the Prophet and the Muslims who among the People of the Book followed them truthfully, and who followed them hypocritically. For the latter may follow Islam outwardly and face their former qiblah in their prayers, and see no harm to themselves in that. But when the qiblah was changed, they feared for their intention of turning away from it, so they revealed what they had been concealing of disbelief, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah that you were upon except that We might know who follows the Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143], and so on.

Perhaps the turning away from the command to face the Ka'bah in the early days of Islam was to break the arrogance of Quraysh's obstinacy and their attacks on Islam. For if he had faced Makkah, they would have held their noses high and said, "This is our town, and we are its people." Facing it would have been a yearning for it and a regret over emigrating from it. As His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:114], and His saying ﴿To God belong the East and the West﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:115], may be an allusion to this, as we have mentioned. Accordingly, the change of the qiblah to the Ka'bah afterward was good news to the Prophet (ﷺ) that the affair of Quraysh was about to decline, and that the battle of Badr would be the decisive division between the Muslims and them. Then God commanded changing the qiblah to the House that is more deserving of that, and to its direction, for the one far from it.

* * *

﴿And surely those who were given the Book know that it is the truth from their Lord, and God is not heedless of what they do﴾

This is an interjection between the clause ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ and the clause ﴿And from wherever you go out, turn your face﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:149], and so on.

The more evident view is that by ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ are meant the rabbis of the Jews and the rabbis of the Christians, as was narrated from al-Suddi, as the expression about them with the relative clause ﴿were given the Book﴾ indicates, rather than saying "the People of the Book."

The meaning of their knowing that it is the truth is that their knowledge of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), according to the good news about him in their books, entails that what he brought is true.

The more evident view also is that by ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ are meant those who have remained upon disbelief, so that the place of His saying ﴿And surely those who were given the Book know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾ becomes clear. For the report about them that they know it is the truth, with its double emphasis, implies that the apparent state of them, when they denied facing the Ka'bah, was that they denied it because they believed it was false, and that the Muslims thought they believed that. And so the place of His saying ﴿And God is not heedless of what they do﴾ becomes clear, which is a threat of punishment.

The definite article in His saying ﴿that it is the truth﴾ indicates restriction (qasr), meaning: they know that facing the Ka'bah is the truth and not other than it, following their knowledge of the abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one) of their law by the law of Islam. It was also said that they found in their books that their qiblah would be annulled. Perhaps this is derived from the warnings of their prophets, such as Irmiya (Jeremiah) and Ishiya (Isaiah), which announced the ruin of the House of the Holy Place, since facing it would then become facing a thing that no longer exists.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 144 (part 3 of 3):

As for His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what they do﴾, the majority (al-Jumhur) read it with the ya' of the third person (ghayba), the pronoun referring to "those who were given the Book" (lilladhina utu al-kitab), meaning: He is not unaware of their deeds done in defiance of what they knew. Thus what is meant by "what they do" is this act and similar acts of stubbornness (mukabara), obstinacy (i'nad) and foolishness (safah). This statement is a kinaya (metonymy) for a warning (wa'id) of recompense for their evil conduct, because the saying of one who is capable, "I am not unaware of the criminal," is a clear indication of his punishment, since nothing prevents the capable one from requiting except lack of knowledge. Therefore it is a warning to them. Their warning, in the rhetorical context (al-maqam al-khitabi), implies a promise (wa'd) to the Muslims, because it indicates their great rank, for the warning was only attached to their opposition to the believers. Thus it is inevitable that a reward will follow for the believers for obeying the change of the qibla. Also, the One who is not unaware of the deeds of those people is not unaware of the deeds of these people either, so He will recompense each according to what he deserves.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Rawh from Ya'qub read it with the ta' of address (khitab). Thus it is a kinaya for a promise to the Muslims for their obedience in facing the Ka'ba, and it implies a warning to the disbelievers, the reverse of what the previous reading implies. On both readings, it is a general concluding statement (tadhyil ijmali) so that each party takes its share from it, and it is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraid) between the sentence ﴿And indeed those who were given the Book﴾ and the sentence ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145].

In His saying ﴿la-ya'lamuna﴾ and His saying ﴿'amma ya'malun﴾ there is a complete paronomasia (jinas tamm muharraf) according to the reading of the majority, and an incomplete paronomasia (jinas naqis mudari') according to the reading of Ibn 'Amir and those who agree with him.

[p. 36]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on surah 2, verse 145:

﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla (direction of prayer), nor are you one who follows their qibla, nor do some of them follow the qibla of others. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿And if you were to bring﴾ is a conjunction (*'atf*) with His words ﴿And indeed those who were given the Book surely know﴾ [2:144]. The connection is that they know and yet do not know. When it was stated that they know it to be the truth, in the manner previously explained, this implied a rebuke that they are obstinate. It was therefore fitting to affirm, by negating any hope of their following the qibla, that the listener should not suppose they might be expected to follow it because they know its rightness. For this reason the sentence negating their following is emphasised with an oath, with the *lam* that prepares for an oath (*al-lam al-muwatta'a*), and with a conditional clause framed in the most extreme form that is customarily possible.

The intended meaning of ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ [2:144] is the same as the intended meaning in His words ﴿And indeed those who were given the Book surely know﴾ [2:144], as stated earlier. What their rabbis do serves as an example for their common people. So if their rabbis do not follow the qibla of Islam, then their common people are even less likely to follow it.

The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun here serves to make public their blame, so that this sentence explicitly targets them. As is customary with the apparent noun used in place of the pronoun, the purpose is to increase attention and fix the matter firmly in the mind.

The intended meaning of ﴿every sign﴾ is many signs in abundance. By "sign" is meant the proof and evidence that facing the Ka'ba is the qibla of the *hanifiyya* (the pure monotheistic religion of Abraham).

The use of the word "every" (*kull*) to mean a large quantity is common in Arabic speech. Imru' al-Qays said:

*Fa-yalaka min laylin ka-anna nujūmahu*
*bi-kulli mughāri al-fatli shuddat bi-yadhbuli*

[Page 37 follows.]

Oh, what a night this is! As if its stars were tied with every twisted rope bound with the Yadhbul fibre.

Its origin is a metaphor, in which many individuals of a thing are made to resemble the totality of all its individuals. Then this usage became so frequent that it equalled literal usage, and so it became one of the meanings of *kull* that does not require a context or a consideration of the comparison of a large number of individuals of a class to the generality of all its individuals. This is so much so that it occurs where there cannot be a generality of individuals, as in His words here ﴿every sign﴾, for signs cannot be conceived as having a number that can be encompassed. Similar is His words, exalted is He, ﴿Then eat from all the fruits﴾ [16:69], and ﴿Indeed those against whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾ [10:96], ﴿Even if every sign should come to them﴾ [10:97]. Al-Nabigha said:

*Bihā kullu dhayyālin wa khansā'a tar'awī*
*ilā kulli rajjāfin mina al-ramli fārid*

In it is every ... and a female ... grazing toward every ... of the sand-dunes, solitary.

This usage is repeated three times in the words of 'Antara:

*Jādat 'alayhi kullu bikrin ḥurratin*
*fa-taraknna kulla qarāratin ka-al-dirhami*

Every pure, noble virgin poured upon him, leaving every hollow like a dirham.

*Saḥḥan wa tiskāban fa-kullu 'ashiyyatin*
*yajrī ilayhā al-mā'u lam yataṣarrami*

In a steady flow and a pouring, so every evening the water runs toward it without ceasing.

The author of *al-Qamus* said under the root *k-l-l*: "The use of *kull* to mean *ba'ḍ* (some) is an opposite (*ḍidd*)," thereby affirming a departure from the meaning of encompassing. But he was rash in saying "to mean *ba'ḍ*"; the more correct formulation would have been "to mean *kathīr*" (many).

The meaning is this: their denial of the rightness of the Ka'ba as the direction of prayer is not due to any doubt that a proof could remove. Rather, it is obstinacy and stubbornness. Therefore there is no benefit in extended argument against them.

The attribution of "qibla" to the pronoun of the Messenger is because it is more specific to him, being the qibla of his sacred law, and because he requested it in the language of his situation.

The singular "qibla" in His words ﴿nor are you one who follows their qibla﴾, though there are two qiblas, is explained as follows: if each of the People of the Book had a specific qibla, then there are more than one. If they had no specific qibla and were free to face any direction, then the singular expresses the sense of distribution, because if one follows the qibla of one of the two groups, one is not following the qibla of the other.

The purpose of His words ﴿they would not follow your qibla﴾ is to display their obstinacy, thereby despairing of their faith. The purpose of His words ﴿nor are you one who follows their qibla﴾ is to exonerate the Prophet and to imply to them despair of the believer returning to facing Bayt al-Maqdis (the Temple Mount in Jerusalem). In His words ﴿nor do some of them follow the qibla of others﴾ there is a comfort for the Prophet, that this is their habit and disposition regarding disagreement. Long ago some of them disagreed with others about their qibla, to the extent that the Christians opposed the qibla of the Jews, even though the law of the Jews is the root of Christianity.

The clause ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿nor are you one who follows their qibla﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*). The benefit of this conjunction, after informing that their qibla will not be followed, is to increase the emphasis on the command to face the Ka'ba, and to warn against negligence in this matter, to the extent that it is supposed, by way of hypothesis, that if he were to follow the desires of the People of the Book in this, such and such would follow. For this reason the particle is *la-in* ("if indeed"), because it has connotations of doubt, and the condition is assumed to occur.

His words ﴿from the knowledge﴾ explain ﴿what has come to you﴾, meaning "after that which has come to you," and that which has come is knowledge. He made what was sent down to him to be knowledge in its entirety, in an exaggerated manner.

The *ahwā'* (desires) is the plural of *hawā*, which is an intense love that demands the attainment of the beloved thing even if it brings harm to the one who attains it. For this reason the word *hawā* came to be used predominantly for a love that neither right guidance nor reason requires. Hence it was applied to passionate love (*'ishq*). Its use in the Qur'an also became common for the creed of error, and for this reason the scholars of Islam called the people of deviant creeds "People of Desires" (*ahl al-ahwā'*).

This warning has been emphasised by the combination of the condition and its consequence with several reinforcements. Al-Zamakhshari (author of *al-Kashshaf*) alluded to them, and the author of *al-Kashf* detailed them to ten:

1. The oath indicated by the *lam*.
2. The *lam* that prepares for the oath, because it increases the oath's emphasis.
3. The particle of emphasis in the consequent clause.
4. The *lam* of inception in its predicate.
5. The nominal form of the sentence.
6. Making the conditional particle the one that indicates doubt, namely *in*, which implies that even the smallest part of following their desires is sufficient for wrongdoing.
7. The use of *idhan*, which indicates consequence, since it reinforces the binding of the consequent to the condition.
8. The summary followed by detail in His words ﴿from the knowledge that has come to you﴾, which indicates concern, and concern about the restraining factor leads to establishing the punishment for the committing of the act, since the excuse is cut off. It also makes what was sent down to him to be knowledge itself.

The definite article in *al-zālimīn* (the wrongdoers) indicates that they are among those known for this quality, which is a disposition for them.

It is not hidden that everything that leads to establishing the link between the consequent and the condition, or to establishing its cause, or to establishing the occurrence of the consequent, or to magnifying some of its connected elements, all of this reinforces the intended purpose for which the condition is brought.

The expression "knowledge" here refers to revelation and divine certainty. It is a declaration of the elevated status of knowledge and a drawing of the minds of this community to it, because its word is frequently repeated in their ears.

His words ﴿surely among the wrongdoers﴾ are a stronger indication of attributing wrongdoing than "you are indeed a wrongdoer." This was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾ [2:67].

By "wrongdoers" is meant those who wrong themselves. Wrongdoing has degrees, all of which fall under this description. The listener understands that every kind of following their desires is reduced to a kind of wronging of oneself, until it culminates in their erroneous creeds, and their wronging of themselves then ends in disbelief, which casts one into everlasting punishment.

Someone may say that something close to this sentence was mentioned earlier, at His words ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God is the guidance. And if you were to follow their desires after what has come to you of knowledge, you would have no protector or helper from God﴾ [2:120]. There He used the relative pronoun *alladhī* and here He used the relative *mā*; there He said *ba'd* after *min ba'd* here; there He made the consequence of the condition the absence of a protector and helper, and here the consequence is being among the wrongdoers. The author of *Durrat al-Tanzil wa Ghurrat al-Ta'wil* raised this question and tried to present distinctive features distinguishing between what the two verses differ in, but he did not provide a satisfying answer. What his speech suggests is that we should say: although *alladhī* and *mā* both are relative pronouns, *mā* is the origin of relative pronouns. Since the knowledge that came to the Prophet ﷺ in the purpose of the first verse was the knowledge connected with the root of the religion of Islam, the falsity of the religion of the Jews and the religion of the Christians after abrogation, and the proving of the obstinacy of both groups regarding the validity of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ, all of this beginning from His words ﴿And they say: God has taken a son, glory be to Him﴾ [2:116] to His words ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God is the guidance﴾ [2:120], then the knowledge that came in that context was the clearest and most ancient knowledge, and it was fitting that it be expressed with the explicit relative pronoun in definiteness.

As for the second verse that we are concerned with, it relates to the nullification of the qibla of the Jews and the Christians, because it is preceded by an explanation of this beginning from His words ﴿The foolish among the people will say: What has turned them away from the qibla that they were on?﴾ [2:142]. That is a derivative legislative matter. So the warning that comes after it is a warning against following the two groups in the matter of the qibla, and that is not of the same importance as the warning against following their religion as a whole. Therefore the knowledge that came to the Prophet about the matter of their qibla did not have the same importance as the knowledge that came to him about the falsity of the roots of their religion. For this reason, in defining it, the relative pronoun *mā* was used, which is attached to the definites, though originally it is an indefinite qualified noun that was transferred to the relative function.

The reason *min* was introduced in this second verse before *ba'd* in His words ﴿after what has come to you of knowledge﴾ is that this verse occurs after the first verse in a single surah, and there is no great separation between them. So the knowledge that came to him in it, from His words ﴿that they follow your qibla﴾, is a particular part of the general knowledge that came concerning the nullification of their entire religion. It was therefore fitting that its being a particular part be indicated by the use of the partitive, *min* of origin (*min al-ibtidā'iyya*).

[Page 39 ends.]

Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their own sons, but a group of them knowingly conceal the truth.

This is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) placed between the phrase ﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Book every sign...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145] and the phrase ﴿For each there is a direction he faces...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 148]. It is a digression (istiṭrād) occasioned by the mention of the People of the Book's attacks on the Islamic qibla. Their attack was born of obstinacy while they knew that the Islamic qibla is the truth, as indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed, those who were given the Book know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]. So He digresses to state that their attack on the Islamic qibla is nothing but part of their overall attack on Islam and on the Prophet (ﷺ). The evidence that this is a digression is His saying after it, ﴿For each there is a direction he faces﴾ [al-Baqarah: 148], for the discourse has returned to the topic of facing the qibla.

The object pronoun in ﴿yaʿrifūnahu﴾ (they recognize it) does not refer to the change of the qibla, for if it did, the sentence would be a repetition of the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, those who were given the Book know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]. Rather, it refers either to the Messenger, even though no explicitly suitable antecedent has preceded the third-person pronoun, yet he is known from the previous discourse, and his address has been repeated in it through His sayings ﴿We did not make the qibla which you used to face except...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will like﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], and ﴿So turn your face toward...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]. Thus, the use of the pronoun in the third person is an iltifāt (shift of grammatical person), and it is according to an implied omitted noun, meaning: they recognize his truthfulness. Or the pronoun may refer to the truth in His earlier saying ﴿they conceal the truth﴾, so that it includes the Messenger's message and all that he brought. Or it may refer to the knowledge in His saying ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145].

The simile in His saying ﴿as they recognize their own sons﴾ is a simile of clarity and certainty of recognition, for a man's recognition of his close relations is a recognition that admits no confusion, as Zuhayr said:

"They, and the valley of ar-Rass, are like the hand to the mouth,"

as a comparison for the clear intensity of closeness.

He specified sons because fathers are strongly attached to them, so the father gazes at them often and thus their features are firmly fixed in his recognition. Therefore, the recognition of this truth is established among all of their scholars.

He chose ﴿yaʿrifūn﴾ rather than saying ﴿yaʿlamūnahu﴾ (they know it), because recognition (maʿrifa) generally relates to essences and perceptible things. Allah the Exalted said ﴿You recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 24], and Zuhayr said:

"Only with difficulty did I recognize the abode after I had misjudged it."

One says "ʿaraftu fulānan" (I recognized so-and-so), but one does not say "ʿaraftu ʿilma fulān" (I recognized the knowledge of so-and-so), unless one means that his knowledge has become as if witnessed before you. For this reason the verb ʿirfān (recognition) is not transitive to two objects as the verbs of supposition and knowledge are. For this reason Allah is described by the attribute of knowledge, so it is said "al-ʿAlīm" (the All-Knowing), and He is not described by the attribute of recognition, so one does not say "Allah recognizes such-and-such." Thus the meaning is: they recognize the attributes of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his signs mentioned in their books, and they recognize the truth as one recognizes a thing that is witnessed.

By His saying ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾ is meant the rabbis of the Jews and the Christians. For this reason they are characterized as those who were given the Book, that is, they knew the knowledge of the Torah and the knowledge of the Gospel.

His saying ﴿Indeed, a group of them knowingly conceal the truth﴾ is a specification of some of those who were given the Book with obstinacy regarding the matter of the qibla and regarding other matters which the Prophet (ﷺ) brought. It is also a censure of them, for they conceal the truth while they know it. These are the majority of those who were given the Book, before Ibn Ṣūrīyā and Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. Then there remained another group who knew the truth and declared it, namely those among the Jews who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) before ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, and among the Christians such as Tamīm al-Dārī and Ṣuhayb.

As for those who do not know the truth, let alone conceal it, they are not considered in this context, and they are not included in His saying ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾, nor does His saying ﴿they recognize it as they recognize their own sons﴾ include them.

The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.

This is a tadhyil (a concluding phrase that generalizes the preceding statement) to the sentence ﴿And indeed, a party of them conceal the truth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. It is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose implied sense is: "This is the truth." Omitting the subject in such a case follows the established usage of omitting the subject when what indicates it has already been mentioned, like the phrase after mentioning the abodes, "a desolate, abandoned campsite" (rabʿun qawā'), and after mentioning the one being praised, "a youth" (fatan), and similar cases, as the author of al-Miftah (Sakkaki, Miftah al-'Ulum) pointed out.

His saying ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾ is a prohibition against being among those who doubt in this matter, and this is the intended meaning here.

The definite article in al-haqq (the truth) is the definite article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), as in His saying "All praise is due to Allah" and the saying "Generosity belongs to the Arabs." This definiteness applied to both parts of the sentence, the stated and the implied, conveys a restriction of the reality to what they conceal, and this is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb): that is, not what they display of denial, and it makes clear that this is contrary to the truth.

Al-imtira' (doubting) is an iftiʿal form derived from al-mira' (dispute/doubt), and the iftiʿal here is not for reflexive effect (muṭāwaʿa). The verbal noun al-mirya has no simple base verb known for it; rather, it is always in the iftiʿal form. The intended purpose of addressing the Prophet ﷺ in His saying ﴿And if you were to follow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145] and His saying ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾ is to warn the community. This is the Qur'an's habit in every important warning, so that the address to the Prophet carries such a warning, he being the closest of creation to Allah, and the most deserving of His honor. It is evidence that whoever falls into such a thing among the community, the word of punishment has become due against him, and he has no door to salvation. It is also permissible that the address in His saying ﴿from your Lord﴾ and His saying ﴿so do not be﴾ is an address to an unspecified individual, to anyone who is fit for this address.

**[Page 42]**

It is a continuation (*'atf*) on the clause ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their own sons﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. It is therefore part of the interjected statement (*i'tiraḍ*). Alternatively, it is a continuation on the clause ﴿Even if you brought those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145], taking into account the sentences that were begun anew (*istu'nifa*) after it. This is because, after the Messenger ﷺ was taught what to answer to their statement ﴿What turned them away from their qiblah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142], and after he explained to the Muslims the excellence of their qiblah, that they were upon the truth, and despaired them of hoping for the People of the Book to acknowledge the validity of facing the Ka'bah, this was concluded (*dhuyyila*) with this concluding statement (*tadhyil*), which gathers together lofty meanings. It closes the discussion with the Jews about the matter of the qiblah, as is said in address: "Leave this," or "Turn away from this." The meaning is that for every group there is a direction of understanding and fear of God when seeking to reach the truth.

This statement is addressed to the Muslims, i.e., leave off disputing with the People of the Book over the matter of the qiblah, and do not let their opposition concern you, for the opposition of an opponent does not harm the right of one who is right.

In it there is a redirection of the Muslims to be concerned with the higher objectives and to attend to the reform of their community. Its meaning is similar to the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in God and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], to the end of the verse. For this reason He followed it with His saying ﴿so race to [all that is] good﴾. Thus His saying ﴿wherever you are﴾ carries the sense of a reason (*ta'lil*) for the command to race toward good. Thus the arrangement of the verse according to this style is like the arrangement of sermons: by mentioning an introduction, an objective, an explanation of it, a reason, and a concluding statement.

**[Page 43]**

*Kull* (every) is a noun that denotes encompassment and totality. It is indefinite, and it becomes specified by what is added to it. When the added-to noun is omitted, a nunation (*tanwin*) is substituted for it on *kullin*, and this is called the nunation of substitution (*tanwin al-'iwaḍ*), because it indicates the noun that was added to, and so it is a substitute for it.

The omission of what *kull* is added to here is due to the context indicating it. The estimated omitted word is *ummah* (community), because the whole discussion concerns the differing of the communities over the matter of the qiblah. This omitted added-to noun is estimated by what the statement itself indicates by its wording, as in His saying: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and the believers—all of them believe in God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285]. Or it is estimated by what the meaning of the preceding statement indicates, without a word preceding it, as in His saying: ﴿And for each We have made heirs (*mawali*)﴾ [al-Nisa: 33] in Surah al-Nisa. Of this type is what is in this verse, because the discussion concerns the disagreement of the Jews, the Christians, and the Muslims over the direction of prayer. So the estimate is: "And for each of the Muslims, the Jews, and the Christians there is a direction." A parallel to this has already passed at His saying: ﴿Each is devoutly obedient to Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116].

*Wijhah* (direction) is in its literal sense the place toward which one turns. It is on the pattern *fi'lah*, the feminine of *fi'l* in the sense of *maf'ul*, like *dhibh* (slaughtered). Because it is a noun of place, the *waw* which is the first radical of the word was not dropped when the feminine *ta'* was attached, since dropping the *waw* in such a form occurs only in *fi'lah* in the sense of the verbal noun (*maṣdar*).

*Wijhah* is metaphorically borrowed for what a person is concerned with among affairs, by likening it to the place toward which one turns, a comparison of an intelligible thing to a perceptible thing. The word ﴿*wijhah*﴾ in the verse is suitable for both the literal and the figurative meaning, so the expression with it is a directed statement (*kalam muwajjah*), and it is among the beauties of style. Close to it is His saying: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48].

**[Page 44]**

The pronoun in *huwa* refers to the omitted added-to noun of *kullin*.

The first object of *muwalliha* is omitted, since the estimate is: "He turns it (himself) toward it" or "He turns its face (*wajhahu*)" in the manner we explained at His saying: ﴿What turned them away from their qiblah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142]. The meaning is: he faces it and remains attached to it.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *muwalliha* with a *ya'* after the *lam*. Ibn 'Amir read *muwalla-ha* (هو مُوَلّاها) with an *alif* after the *lam*, in the passive form (*sighat ma lam yusamma fa'iluh*), meaning: it is turned toward it by one who turns it, and this one is its religion and its outlook.

Some exegetes held that the intended meaning of *wijhah* is the qiblah, so "race (you) to good," which is facing the Ka'bah. It was also said that the meaning is: for every community there is a qiblah, so there is no way for you to be gathered upon one qiblah; so hold fast to your qiblah, which is the qiblah of Abraham, for you are upon the good. It was also said: the meaning is the structure (*haykal*) of a qiblah, so there is no way for you to be gathered upon one qiblah; so hold fast to your qiblah, which is the qiblah of Abraham, for you are upon the good. It was also said: the meaning is that for every people there is a qiblah, so their opposition does not harm you; leave them, and race to the good, toward the Ka'bah. It was also said: the meaning is that for every group among the Muslims there is a direction of the Ka'bah which they will face. The meanings of the Qur'an are to be taken in the most comprehensive and inclusive of the aspects.

His saying ﴿so race to [all that is] good﴾ is a derivation (*tafri'*) of the command from what preceded it, i.e., since the objectives have multiplied.

Thus competition (*munafasah*) occurs in encountering the truth.

*Al-istibaq* is of the form *ifti'al*, and what is meant by it is precedence (*sabq*). Its proper construction is with *li* (to), but it has been extended so that it is transitive by itself, as in His saying: ﴿And they both raced to the door﴾ [Yusuf: 25]. Or the verb *istabiqu* is taken to include the sense of *ightanimu* (seize the opportunity).

So what is meant by racing here is the figurative sense, namely eagerness to encounter good and to increase in it. ﴿*Al-khayrat*﴾ is the plural of *khayr* in an irregular pattern, as they said *suradiqat* and *hammamat*.

What is intended is the generality of all goods, for hastening toward good is praiseworthy. Among that is hastening to repentance, fearing the destroyer of pleasures and the sudden arrival of loss. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And hasten toward forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]; ﴿And the forerunners, the forerunners﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10]; ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 11]; ﴿in gardens of bliss﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 12]. Among that is the excellence of the foremost early ones among the Emigrants and the Helpers. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest; those are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought﴾ [al-Hadid: 10]. And Moses said: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84].

His saying ﴿wherever you are, God will bring you all together﴾ is a clause carrying the sense of a reason for the command to race toward good. For this reason it was separated (*fussilat*) [from what precedes it], because a reason is not joined by a conjunction, since it stands in the position of the object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). The meaning is: "Race toward good, so that you may be with those whom God brings together for the good companionship, because God brings all people together, both their good and their bad."

**[Page 45 is not marked; continuing]**

*Kana* here is complete (*tammah*), meaning: wherever you are found, from among the places of good and the places of evil. *Al-iti'a* (bringing) with a thing is to bring it, and it is a metaphor for its necessary concomitant. Among its uses is its employment for nearness and obedience.

Humayd ibn Thawr said, praising 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan:

*"God brought me to you, the One who illumined guidance,*
*and light and Islam are a guide for you."*

He meant: He subjected me to you (*sakhkharani ilayk*). In the hadith: "O God, guide Daws and bring them (*wa'ti bi-ha*)," i.e., guide them and bring them near to Islam. It is used of the capability to do a thing and of knowledge of it, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, if it is the weight of a mustard seed and is within a rock or in the heavens or the earth, God will bring it forth﴾ [Luqman: 16].

Other views concerning the interpretation of ﴿wherever you are﴾ come according to the views on the interpretation of ﴿for each there is a direction﴾, namely that the meaning is: God accepts your deeds in racing toward good, for that is what matters, not facing directions. The meaning is: you are only facing what reminds you of God, so strive in His pleasure through good deeds; God knows that from every place. Or it is a warning (*tarhib*), i.e., in whatever direction God brings you, He will reward and punish. Or it is an exhortation to hasten to righteous action, i.e., you are returning to God from every place, so hasten to obedience before it is lost by death. And other aspects besides these.

His saying ﴿indeed God is over all things competent﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) that fits all the meanings mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 149–150:

﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed, it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it, so that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who commit injustice. So do not fear them, but fear Me, and so that I may complete My favor upon you and that you may be guided.﴾ The phrase ﴿And from wherever you set out﴾ is joined to ﴿turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ as a ruling joined to a ruling of the same kind, to inform that facing the Ka'bah in the obligatory prayer is not to be neglected in its observance, even in a state of excuse such as travel. So the meaning is: from wherever you set out, from every place you set out from, while traveling, because travel is the occasion of hardship in finding the direction of the Ka'bah, so someone might imagine that facing it falls away from him. Along with his saying ﴿and indeed, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, the majority of this verse carries greater emphasis on the matter of the qiblah, reinforcing his saying in the previous verse ﴿the truth from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 147].

His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is an additional warning against negligence in the matter of the qiblah.

His saying after it, ﴿And from wherever you set out﴾, is a conjunction to the sentence before it, and the wording of the earlier sentence is repeated so that the causal clause with his saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾ may be built upon it. His saying ﴿and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ is a conjunction to his saying ﴿And from wherever you set out﴾ and what follows.

The purpose is the generalization of this ruling in travel for the Muslims, lest it be imagined that it is restricted to the Prophet ﷺ.

From the repetition of most of the words there results an emphasis of the ruling, so that his saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾ follows from it.

The command to face the Ka'bah has been repeated three times for the Prophet, and the command for the Muslims to face the Ka'bah has been repeated twice.

The phrase ﴿it is the truth﴾ has been repeated three times, and the generalization of directions has been repeated three times. The aim of all of this is to draw attention to the matter of facing the Ka'bah and to warn against any slackness in it, establishing the truth in the hearts of the Muslims and adding a response to those who deny it, by way of emphasis. [This is] from the addition of ﴿And from wherever you set out﴾, and from interjected sentences, to increase the attention given to the ruling of facing: namely the sentence ﴿And indeed, those who were given the Scripture know it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144] and following verses, and the sentence ﴿And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, and the sentence ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾ and following verses. In this is a manifestation of the greater rightfulness of the Ka'bah in this regard, because one who is upon the truth is not increased by the denial of deniers except in firmness, and firmness calls for repeating the speech that indicates what one is firm upon, since repetition indicates the certainty of the meaning of the speech.

In the course of this has been mentioned, from the explanation of the benefits of this change and what surrounds it, that which dispels the slight weariness arising from hearing repetition. So he mentioned his saying ﴿And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord, and Allah is not unaware﴾ etc., and he mentioned his saying ﴿so that people will have no argument﴾ etc.

The pronoun in ﴿And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord﴾ refers to the content of the sentence, which is the ruling of the change; so it refers to what is taken from the context. Thus the pronoun here is like the pronoun in his saying ﴿those whom We gave the Scripture recognize it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. The majority read ﴿ta'malūn﴾ (ﷻ) with a feminine-second-person ta (i.e., addressing) — "what you do" — while Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' of the third person.

His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾ is the cause for his saying "fa-wallū" (so turn), which indicates the demand for the act and its compliance; that is, "I prescribed that for you so that We might refute the argument of the nations against you." The usual form of giving a reason for imperative expressions is that the reason is for the demand in terms of carrying out the required act.

For the meaning of the demand's form is the performance of the act or its abandonment, not the informing that the one commanding is commanding; otherwise compliance would not be obligatory for the commander, and the mere hearing of the demand would suffice. But that is not the intended meaning.

The definite article in "an-nās" (the people) is for comprehensiveness, including the polytheists of Makkah, for among their doubts is that they would say: "We do not follow this religion, since it is not the creed of Ibrahim, for it faced the qiblah of the Jews and Christians and the People of the Book." And the argument is that they would say: "Muhammad followed us and faced our qiblah, so how does he call us to follow him?"

And for all people other than you there is an argument against you, meaning: so that this religion would differ in its direction from every religion that preceded it, so that no adherents of any religion among the religions would claim that Islam borrowed from it.

There is no doubt that the manifestation of the direction occurs in a matter visible to everyone, because perceiving the difference in rulings, legal objectives and the spiritual perfections by which Islam excels over others is not grasped by everyone; rather, none knows it except those given knowledge. On this basis, his saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾ refers to his saying ﴿And indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144] and his saying ﴿those whom We gave the Scripture recognize it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146].

Various other meanings have been stated for "the argument of the people," which I consider far-fetched.

The "ḥujjah" in the speech of the Arabs is what is intended to establish the opponent's position, such that he finds no escape from it; for this reason one says of the one who overcame his opponent with his argument: "qad ḥajjahu" (he has overcome him with argument). As for "al-iḥtijāj," it is the arguer's bringing what he supposes to be an argument, even if it is a sophism; he says "iḥtajja," and one says "ḥājja" when he brings what he supposes to be an argument. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]. So "ḥujjah" is not used in its literal sense except for a proof and evidence that is decisive and silences the opponent; its application to a doubt is figurative, because it is presented in the form of an argument. From this is His saying: ﴿Their argument is invalid with their Lord﴾ [al-Shura: 16]. This is the jurisprudence of the language, as indicated by al-Kashshaf. As for what opposes it from the speech of some lexicographers, it is a confusion between the literal and figurative application, and they only intended to escape the difficulty of the exception, which was problematic for them because the excepted item is ruled by the opposite of the ruling of the item from which it is excepted, according to the overwhelming majority of the people of the language and the scholars, except for a disagreement that is not considered in the science of usul. Thus this exception implies that those who committed injustice have an argument against you. So the author of al-Kashshaf answered that he only applied the term "ḥujjah" to it because of its resemblance to the argument in their context of it, placing it in the manner of proof; that is, the exception of those who committed injustice implies that they bring an argument, i.e., something resembling an argument. So the particle "illā" requires the implicit presence of the word "ḥujjah" used in its figurative meaning. The use of a word in its literal and figurative senses is not a novelty, especially with the use of a word differing from the first. Moreover, the exception may be considered disjunctive, meaning: "But those who committed injustice will create disturbance against you, so do not fear them."

His saying ﴿and so that I may complete My favor upon you﴾ is a second reason for his saying ﴿so turn your faces toward it﴾, conjoined to his saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾ on the basis of the consideration we explained just now, namely that it is the reason for compliance. The meaning is: I commanded you with that so that I may complete My favor upon you by fulfilling the causes of that completion, among which: that your qiblah be toward the most excellent house built for Allah the Exalted. It is well known that the completion of the favor is by complying with what we were commanded, and the sum of that is uprightness, and by it is entry into Paradise. That is, the ultimate end of completing the favor upon us is entry into Paradise. This was not in the explanation of this verse, but it is among the totality of its meaning. So "completion" here means giving a thing in full from the outset, not completing it after it had been deficient; it is close to his saying, "fa-atammahunna" (so he fulfilled them), i.e., complied with them perfectly, and the intent is not that he did some of them and then did others. So the meaning of the verse: "and that My favor may be a complete favor in every state."

His saying ﴿and that you may be guided﴾ is conjoined to "and so that I may complete"; that is, I commanded you with that in hope of your compliance, so that guidance to the truth may come about from you.

The particle "la'alla" in His saying ﴿and that you may be guided﴾ is used figuratively for the necessary meaning of hope, which is the nearness and expectation of that. The meaning of making that nearness a cause is that their facing the Ka'bah indicates that they will be upright in all their affairs, because beginnings point to ends; it is like His saying ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], as we previously mentioned. And Habib said:

"When you see the crescent's growth, you are certain that it will become a full moon."
