Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 151:

﴿As We have sent among you a messenger from yourselves, reciting to you Our verses, purifying you, teaching you the Book and the wisdom, and teaching you what you did not know.﴾

This is a comparison for the two causes mentioned in His words ﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾ and His words ﴿so that you may be guided﴾. That is: this is among My favours upon you, like the favour of sending Muhammad (ﷺ). The sending is made the thing compared-to because it is earlier and more evident in establishing what is compared; that is, the beginnings indicate the ends. This is like His words in the hadith, "as You blessed Abraham" (kama sallayta 'ala Ibrahim). The word "messenger" (rasul) is indefinite for glorification, and so that the attributes apply to him, each of which is a particular favour. The address in His words "among you" and what follows is to the believers from the Muhajirun (Emigrants) and the Ansar (Helpers), as a reminder to them of Allah's favour upon them in that He sent to them a messenger from among them and of their own people, because that is stronger in facilitating their guidance. This is in the manner of Abraham's supplication: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. Allah has also bestowed favour upon the believers in general, from the Arabs and others, by His words ﴿Allah certainly conferred favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164], that is, from their human kind, because that is more reassuring to them than if their messenger were from the angels. He, exalted is He, said ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am: 9].

For this reason the particle "fi" (in) is attached to the verb "arsalna" (We sent), and the particle "ila" (to) is not attached to it, as in His words ﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger as a witness over you﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15], because that is a context of argument, while this is a context of favour; so it is fitting to mention what completes the favour, which is that He made their messenger among them and from them, that is, he is present among their people and he is an Arab like them. The Muslims at that time were the Arabs, that is, those who speak the Arabic language. So the Arab nation at that time spoke one tongue, whether the 'Adnanis or the Qahtanis, and those who followed them from the allies and clients, like Salman al-Farisi, Bilal al-Habashi, and 'Abd Allah ibn Salam the Israelite, since the favour of the messengership lies in conveying and making understood. The messenger speaks to them in their tongue, so they understand all his purposes, perceive the inimitability of the Qur'an, and attain the distinction of conveying this religion to the nations. This distinction is attained by everyone who knows the Arabic tongue, like most of the Islamic nations. Thus the conveying of Islam was through a complete nation, so its transmission is mass-transmitted (mutawatir) and its spread is easy and swift.

The rasul (messenger) is the mursal (one who is sent); it is fa'ul in the sense of maf'ul, like dhalul. Its discussion, from the aspect of the correspondence of its described referent, will come later at His words ﴿So go, both of you, for indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 16] in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

His words ﴿reciting to you Our verses﴾ mean reading the Qur'an to you. He called it "verses" first in consideration of each speech in it being a miracle, and called it "Book" second in consideration of its being a Book of law. A similar usage was mentioned just before, at His words ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and the wisdom﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129].

He used the expression "yatlu" (recites) because the revelation of the Qur'an is continuous, and the Prophet's recitation of it is successive, and with each recitation knowledge of the miracle is attained by the listeners.

His words "wa yuzakkikum" (and purifies you), etc.: tazkiyah is the purification of the soul; it is derived from zakah, which is growth. This is because in the original creation of souls there are perfections and purities that are obstructed by impurities arising from error or misguidance; so the refinement and straightening of souls increases in them that good which Allah has deposited in them. He, exalted is He, said ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 5] ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Tin: 6]. And in the hadith: "I was sent to perfect good character." So guidance to righteousness and perfection is a growth of the good that Allah has deposited in souls by nature.

His words ﴿and teaching you the Book and the wisdom﴾ mean teaching you the law (shari'ah). Here "the Book" is the Qur'an in consideration of its being a book of legislation, not in consideration of its being a miracle. "And teaching you" means teaching you the foundations of virtues. "Wisdom" is the teachings that prevent falling into error and corruption. Its counterpart was mentioned in the supplication of Abraham, and it will also come later at His words ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269] in this surah.

The clause "wa yuzakkikum" is placed before the clause "wa yu'allimukumu al-kitab wa al-hikmah" here, the reverse of what is in the previous verse in the report of Abraham's words ﴿reciting to them Your verses and teaching them the Book and the wisdom and purifying them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. This is because the context here is one of favour upon the Muslims, so he placed first what conveys the benefit obtained from the recitation of the verses to them, which is the benefit of purifying their souls, showing concern for it and stirring it up through eagerness to attain its means, and hastening the good news of it. As for Abraham's supplication, the clauses were arranged according to the order in which what they contain occurs in reality, along with the variety that this difference brings.

His words ﴿and teaching you what you did not know﴾ are a generalization for everything that is neither law nor wisdom: knowledge of the conditions of nations, the conditions of the governance of states, the conditions of the Hereafter, and other things.

He repeated the words "wa yu'allimukum" (and teaching you), although omitting it by conjunction would have been valid, to make explicit the difference, lest it be thought that "ma lam takunu ta'lamun" is the Book and the wisdom; and to make explicit that "ma lam takunu" is an object (maf'ul), not a subject (mubtada'), so that the hearer does not await a predicate for it and lose his understanding in that anticipation. Know that when the conjunctive particle is used together with the repetition of its governing verb, the conjoined element acts as governed by the same kind of thing; so it becomes a conjunction of clauses, but the conjunctive particle in that case resembles an emphasis of the meaning of the governing verb.

[Page 51]

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 2, verse 152:

﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you. And give thanks to Me, and do not be ungrateful to Me.﴾

The *fa'* (ف) here is *li-l-tafri'* (indicating consequence), conjoining the command to remember God and to give thanks for God's favors with the favors mentioned earlier. That is: since I have bestowed these blessings upon you, I command you to remember Me. His words ﴿fa-dhkurūnī adhkurkum﴾ are two verbs derived from *al-dhikr* (ذِكْر, with a kasra on the *dhāl*) and from *al-dhukr* (ذُكْر, with a damma on the *dhāl*). Both are commanded, because we are commanded to remember God Most High at the moment of undertaking actions, so that we may recall His commands and prohibitions. God, Most High, said: ﴿And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember God and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 135]. It is also reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: "Better than remembering God with the tongue is remembering God at the time of His command and His prohibition." We are also commanded to mention the name of God Most High with our tongues, in phrases that express His praise and glorification, the call to obey Him, and the like.

In the *ḥadīth qudsī* there is: "If he mentions Me in a gathering, I mention him in a gathering better than it." The word *dhikr* in His words ﴿adhkurkum﴾ can carry both meanings. It is necessary to supply an elided element in His words ﴿fa-dhkurūnī﴾ according to both interpretations, because *dhikr* does not attach to God's essence. The supplied meaning is: "Remember My greatness, My attributes, My praise, and what follows from them of command and prohibition," or "Remember My blessings and My praiseworthy qualities." This supplying is by *dalālat al-iqtiḍā'* (implication demanded by the sense of the speech). As for ﴿adhkurkum﴾, it is figurative (*majāz*), meaning: "I will treat you in the manner of one who is not forgotten, by increasing blessings, victory, and care in this world, and by reward and elevation of ranks in the Hereafter." Or it means: "I will create in the highest realm and on earth what people understand as your excellence and My good pleasure with you," like His words ﴿You are the best nation﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 110], and "your good end in the Hereafter." This is because *dhikr* in its two literal senses is impossible for God Most High. Furthermore, its transitivity to the object (*ta'diyatuhu li-l-maf'ūl*) is also by way of *dalālat al-iqtiḍā'*, since what is meant is not remembering the essences of persons, nor mentioning their names, but rather remembering what benefits them when it reaches them, and mentioning their virtues.

His words ﴿wa-shkurū lī﴾ are a command to give thanks, which is more general than remembrance in one respect, or absolutely so. Its transitivity to the object with the *lām* is the more eloquent form, and this *lām* is called *lām al-tablīgh* (the *lām* of conveying) and *lām al-tabyīn* (the *lām* of clarification), as they say *naṣaha lahu* and *naṣahahu* (he advised him). It is like His words ﴿So let them be destroyed﴾ [Muḥammad: 8] (*fa-ta'san lahum*), and like the verse of al-Nābigha:

*I gave thanks to you for the blessings, and I exerted myself in praise, and I left off the reproach of ʿUbayd ibn ʿĀmir.*

His words ﴿wa-lā takfurūn﴾ are a prohibition against ingratitude (*kufrān*) for the blessing. Ingratitude has degrees, the highest of which is denying the blessing and rejecting it, then intending to conceal it, then remaining silent about giving thanks for it out of heedlessness. This last is the weakest of the degrees, and one may neglect it without ill intent, yet it is still a shortcoming.

Ibn ʿArafa said: The conjunction of His words ﴿wa-lā takfurūn﴾ is not evidence that a command to something is not a prohibition of its opposite. That is because the command to give thanks is unrestricted, meaning that the command does not indicate repetition, so it has no generality, and it is satisfied by giving thanks one day. But when He said ﴿wa-lā takfurūn﴾, it conveyed the prohibition of ingratitude permanently. End of quotation. He means: because the verb in the context of prohibition is general, like the verb in the context of negation, since prohibition is the brother of negation.

This passage consists of interpolated clauses (*i'tiraḍ*) placed between the verse "And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it" [2:150] and what is connected to it, and between that verse and "It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west" [2:177], because that verse came as a completion to repel the criticisms concerning the change of the qibla. Therefore it is most closely connected to "so that people will have no argument against you" [2:150], which is connected to "And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it" [2:150].

It is a lengthy interpolation, begun to prepare the Muslims for what they were fit for of supporting God's religion, as thanks to Him for the blessings enumerated in the preceding verses: His making them a justly balanced community (*ummah wasaṭ*) and witnesses over the people; His favouring them by turning them to face the most excellent place; His confirming them that they were upon the truth in this; His command to them to disregard the wrongdoers and not to fear them; His giving them good news that He had completed His blessing upon them and guided them; His bestowing favour upon them by sending among them a messenger from themselves; and His guiding them to comply with great rulings such as gratitude (*shukr*) and remembrance (*dhikr*). Indeed, gratitude and remembrance prepare the souls for great deeds. For all of this, He commanded them here to seek help through patience (*ṣabr*) and prayer (*ṣalāh*), and alerted them that these two are an aid to the soul for great deeds. So it was fitting that this be followed by them. Also, the statement "so that people will have no argument against you" [2:150] implies that there are people who are stationed to create disturbance and doubt for them and to plot against them, so they were commanded to seek help against them through patience and prayer.

All of these are coherent and their transitions are harmonious, except the verse "Indeed, aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God" [2:158] up to "...Appreciative and Knowing" [2:158]. Its placement will be explained later.

The discourse opens with the address (*nidā'*) because it conveys the notice of an important, great matter. The custom with great news that overwhelms the listener is that something be presented before it that prepares the soul to accept it, so that it may be at ease with it before it suddenly confronts it.

In opening this address with seeking help through patience, there is an announcement that it will be followed by a call to a great action and severe trial. This is preparation for jihad, and perhaps it is a preparation for the Battle of Badr al-Kubra. The beginning of the military expeditions (*maghāzī*) was shortly before the time of the change of the qibla, since the change of the qibla occurred in Rajab or Sha'ban of the second year of the Hijrah. The expeditions of Buwat, al-'Ushayrah, and the first Badr occurred in Rabi' and Jumada of the second year, and there was no fighting in them. The great Badr occurred in Ramadan of the second year, so it was about two months after the change of the qibla.

It has already been mentioned in the commentary on His saying "And God would not have caused your faith to be lost" [2:143] that what occurred in the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, in the statement of a narrator that some people were killed before the change of the qibla, is a mistake by one of the narrators from al-Bara'. The first killing in the way of God occurred at the Battle of Badr, which was about two months after the change of the qibla. The more correct version is what is in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the Prophet was turned toward the Ka'bah, they said, 'O Messenger of God, what about our brothers who died while they were praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis?'" – the hadith – and he did not say "those who were killed."

So the correct approach to the interpretation of this verse is that it is a preparation for the Muslims to be patient through the hardships of war, and an endearing of martyrdom (*shahādah*) to them.

For this reason, the present tense was used in His saying "for those who are killed in the way of God" [2:154], which indicates a future matter. They are those who were killed in the Battle of Badr shortly after the revelation of this verse.

The discussion of the parallel of this verse was already presented at His saying "And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult, except for the humble" [2:45], and the verse. However, we say here that God Most High said to the Children of Israel, "and indeed it is difficult," knowing their weakness of resolve regarding great deeds, and He said there, "except for the humble" [2:45]. He did not mention the like of this here. In this there is an indication that for the Muslims, what is difficult for others may be made easy, and that they are the humble ones whom God excepted there. Here He added, "Indeed, God is with the patient" [2:153], so He gave them good news that they are among those who comply with this command and are counted in the company of the patient.

His saying "Indeed, God is with the patient" [2:153] is a concluding clause (*tadhyīl*) with the meaning of a causal explanation, i.e., be patient so that God will be with you, for He is with the patient.

His saying "And do not say of those who are killed in the way of God, 'They are dead.' Rather, they are alive" [2:154].

He connected the prohibition to the command before it, because of the relevance of the mention of fighting, in which killing in the way of God is to be expected. When they were commanded to be patient, they understood that death in the way of God is the strongest thing they would have to endure. However, He alerted them, along with that, that patience turns into gratitude when the martyr sees his honour after martyrdom, and when his people are certain of his destiny of eternal life. So His saying "do not say" is a prohibition against a saying that arises from belief, because a person says only what he believes. The meaning is: "do not believe." Apparently this is a completion of His saying "And God would not have caused your faith to be lost" [2:143], as was mentioned in the hadith of al-Bara', for he said: "Some people were killed before the change of the qibla," so His saying "And God would not have caused your faith to be lost" [2:143] was followed by the statement that the virtue of their martyrdom is not diminished.

The word "dead" (*amwāt*) is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject; i.e., "Do not say, they are dead."

"Bal" (rather) is for the retractive transition (*iḍrāb ibṭālī*), cancelling the content of what was forbidden to be said. The implied meaning is: "Rather, they are alive." The meaning is not "Rather, say, they are alive," because the intent is to inform the addressees of this great news. So "alive" (*aḥyā'*) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and it is a resumed statement after the retractive "bal."

He said "but you do not perceive" [2:154] to indicate that this is a life that is not bodily or material, but rather a spiritual life. However, it exceeds the general life of souls, for all souls have a life, which is non-dissolution and the capacity for embodiment at the Resurrection, along with some awareness that they are heading to bliss or to Hellfire. As for the life of those who were killed in the way of God, it is a life that includes perceptions of the enjoyment of the pleasures of Paradise and the higher worlds, and complete unveilings. For this reason, a hadith reports: "Indeed, the spirits of the martyrs are placed in the crops of green birds that graze on the fruit of Paradise and drink from its water."

The wisdom in this is that the connection of pleasures to spirits depends upon the mediation of the bodily senses. So when the spirit separated from the body, it was given a body suited to Paradise, so that it would be a means to its bliss.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 155–157:

﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and a loss of wealth, lives and fruits.﴾

He joined "And We will surely test you" to His saying ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153], as a conjunction of the purpose (al-maqsid) to the preface (al-muqaddimah), as we pointed out earlier. You may also make His saying "And We will surely test you" a conjunction to His saying ﴿and so that I may complete My favour upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150] and what follows, to inform the Muslims that the completion of the favour and the station of honour with Allah do not prevent them from being struck by worldly calamities linked to their causes. These calamities are a manifestation of their steadfastness in faith, of their love for Allah the Exalted, and of their submission to His decree. Thereby they attain the joy of their souls in what befalls them, seeking Allah's pleasure, and they increase in elevation and purification through it. They also grow in certainty that their adherence to this religion was not for the attainment of worldly portions, and that a reward accrues to them from it. Therefore, after it comes ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾. He placed His saying ﴿O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153] and the verse following it between these two conjoined statements, so that it would be advice for remedying the two matters: the completion of the favour and the guidance, and the testing. Then there was repeated upon it what makes the whole a report, by His saying ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾.

The word "something" (shay') was used to make the frightening news lighter, and to point to the difference between this testing and the hunger and fear that Allah imposed upon some nations as punishment, as in His saying ﴿So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear, for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 112]. Therefore here He used the word "something," while there He used what indicates close enveloping and possession, namely that He borrowed for it the garment that is necessary for the one who wears it. This is because the word "shay'" (something) is among the highest and most general nouns of kind (asma' al-ajnas). When it is annexed to a noun of kind, or is specified by it, it becomes known that the speaker added the word "shay'" before the name of that kind only for the purpose of diminishing, because the restriction to the name of the kind that the speaker mentioned after it would, had the speaker wished, have served the same function without it. So the speaker mentions the word "shay'" only with the intention of indicating that the indefiniteness of the noun of kind is neither for magnification nor for diversification, and so the indication of belittlement remains. This is like the saying of al-Sarri addressing Abu Ishaq al-Sabi:

*So, a little of the blood of the grape-cluster, I will make in place of my blood.*

Thus Allah's saying ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ is a deviation from saying "with fear and hunger." As for when the word "shay'" is mentioned with other than a noun of kind, as when it is followed by an adjective, or not followed by one, or annexed to something other than a noun of kind, it then indicates pure diversification, as in the saying of Quhayt al-'Ijli:

*So do not hope—may you spurn the curse—for her, and her being withheld from you is by something within reach.*

Al-Marzuqi and others explained that the meaning of "bi-shay'" here is one of the meanings of the preposition: overpowering, exchange, ransom, or the like. And the specification of this word may be omitted when the context indicates it, as in His saying ﴿Then if anything is remitted to him by his brother﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]; it is the blood-money according to some exegeses, or it is pardon according to another interpretation. Similarly is the saying of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a:

*And one who fills his eyes with the beauty of another's [wife], when the fair ones like dolls go toward the Jamra.*

That is, with the beauty of a woman other than his own wife.

And the saying of Abu Hayya al-Numayri:

*When a day and a night make demands upon a man, there is a something that demands unceasingly.*

That is, something of time. And from this is His saying ﴿Their wealth and their children will not avail them at all against Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10], meaning, of availing.

And it seems that the observance of these two usages of the word "shay'" is what led Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir in *Dala'il al-I'jaz* to rule on the fine effect of the word "shay'" in the verse of Ibn Abi Rabi'a and the verse of Abu Hayya al-Numayri, and on its paucity and diminution in the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

*Were the revolving sphere to hate its motion, something would hold it back from turning.*

This is because in Abu al-Tayyib's verse the meaning of diminution is not connected to it, as is evident, nor is the meaning of diversification, because the benefit of diversification is slight here, since no one is unaware that whatever obstructs the sphere must be something.

By "fear and hunger" and what is conjoined with them, the intended meanings are their obvious ones: what befell the Muslims of scarcity and of the gathering of the polytheists against them after the Hijrah, as occurred on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), when they came upon them from above them and from below them, and when ﴿the eyes swerved and the hearts reached the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10]. As for hunger, it is as it befell them from the scarcity of provisions in some of the military expeditions (ghazawat). The loss of wealth is what arises from little care for their palm groves when they went out to raid. The loss of lives occurs through few births, due to their distance from their women, as al-Nabigha said:

*Fissures of the 'Ilafiyyat between their [women's] thighs, and the chaste women are absent during their purity periods.*

And as al-A'sha said, praising Hawdhah ibn 'Ali, lord of al-Yamamah, for the abundance of his raids:

*Is it every year that you undertake a raid, tightening your resolve to its farthest reach?*
*Bequeathing wealth, and in glory there is elevation, for what was lost in it of your women's menstrual periods.*

Likewise, the loss of lives includes martyrdom in the way of Allah, and what befalls them during that and after it of calamities that return to these matters.

Discussion of wealth comes at His saying ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188] in this surah, and at His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve—their wealth will not avail them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10] in Surah Al 'Imran.

* * *

﴿And give good tidings to the patient, who, when disaster strikes them, say, "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return." Those upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and those are the rightly guided.﴾

The clause ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ is conjoined to "And We will surely test you," and the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), because he is among those included in His saying "And We will surely test you." It is a conjunction of an imperative (insha') to a report (khabar), and there is no pronoun in it according to whoever has mastered the styles of the Arabs and has seen in their speech the frequency of conjoining a report to an imperative and the reverse.

The content of the clause, which is the attainment of blessings, mercy and guidance for the patient, has been conveyed by way of good tidings through the tongue of the Messenger, in honour of his station and to increase the believers' attachment to him, such that their goods come through him. Therefore it is one of the subtleties of the Qur'an that the attribution of trial is made to Allah without an intermediary, while the attribution of the good tidings of the coming good is made from Allah to the Messenger.

The discussion of patience (sabr) and its virtues has passed at His saying ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45].

The description of the patient as ﴿those who, when disaster strikes them, say﴾, etc., is to indicate that their patience is the most perfect patience, since it is patience accompanied by insight into the command of Allah the Exalted. At the moment of calamity they know that they belong to Allah the Exalted, who disposes of them as He wills, so they do not panic at what comes to them; and they know that they will return to Him, and He will reward them for it. Thus "saying" here means the statement that corresponds to belief, since speech was only set for truthfulness, and that statement is considered only if it is an expression of what is in the heart. Whoever says these words without belief in them has no virtue; he is like one who shouts at what does not hear. Allah taught them this comprehensive formula to be their motto at the time of calamity, because belief is strengthened by explicit declaration, as the soul's apprehension of non-sensory realities is weak and needs reinforcement by something sensory. Also, in their explicit declaration of this there is an announcement of this belief and a teaching of it to people. The discussion of "disaster" (musibah) comes at His saying ﴿But if disaster strikes you, he says, "Allah has bestowed favour upon me"﴾ [al-Nisa': 72] in Surah al-Nisa'.

The emphasis with "inna" (indeed) in their saying "Indeed we belong to Allah" is because the context is one of concern, and because it places the one afflicted in the position of one who denies that he is Allah's possession and servant, since the disaster makes him forget that and its terror comes between him and his right judgment. The "lam" in it is for ownership.

The use of the demonstrative in His saying ﴿Those upon them are blessings from their Lord﴾ is to draw attention to the fact that what is referred to is the one described by all the preceding attributes that came before the demonstrative, and that the ruling that comes after the demonstrative is consequent upon those attributes, like ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. This is an explanation of the reward for their patience. The word "ṣalawat" (blessings) here is used metaphorically for purifications and forgiveness, and that is why mercy is conjoined to it, though mercy itself is among the meanings of prayer (salah) used metaphorically, as in His saying ﴿Indeed Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56].

The literal meaning of prayer (salah) in the speech of the Arabs is utterances that reveal a love of good for someone. For this reason its most well-known meaning is supplication (du'a'), and this has passed at His saying ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. Because of this, the attribution of this verb to One from whom good is sought alone becomes necessarily a metaphor in its implied meaning, which is the occurrence of good. So when prayer is attributed to Allah, or annexed to Him, it indicates mercy and the bringing of what is beneficial, whether mercy, forgiveness or purification.

His saying ﴿and those are the rightly guided﴾ is an explanation of the excellence of their attribute, since they have been guided to what is the right of every knowing servant. Thus calamities did not unsettle them, nor did they become a barrier to them from realizing the station of patience, because they know that life is never free of troubles. As for those who were not guided, they make calamities a cause for their objecting against Allah, or for their disbelief in Him, or for saying what is unfitting, or for doubt about the soundness of the Islam they are upon. They say: "If this were the religion pleasing to Allah, no punishment or calamity would have befallen us." This is the condition of the people of misguidance, whose matter Allah warned us of in His saying ﴿And if a good thing befalls them, they say, "This is ours"; and if an evil thing befalls them, they attribute it to Moses and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131]. He also said about the hypocrites ﴿And if an evil thing befalls them, they say, "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [al-Nisa': 78]. The decisive word is that the recompense for deeds appears in the Hereafter, while the calamities of this world are caused by worldly causes, arising when their cause arises. Allah may make the cause of a calamity a punishment for His servant in this world for bad conduct or the like, to lighten for him the punishment of the Hereafter. It may also be for raising the ranks of the soul. It has states and subtleties that none knows except Allah the Exalted, and the servant may come to know some of them when he watches over his soul and takes account of it. For Allah the Exalted, in both states, there is gentleness and a striking that the effect of one of them appears to those who know Him.

﴿And give good tidings to the patient, who, when disaster strikes them, say, "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return." Those upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and those are the rightly guided.﴾

The clause ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ is conjoined to "And We will surely test you," and the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), because he is among those included in His saying "And We will surely test you." It is a conjunction of an imperative (insha') to a report (khabar), and there is no pronoun in it according to whoever has mastered the styles of the Arabs and has seen in their speech the frequency of conjoining a report to an imperative and the reverse.

The content of the clause, which is the attainment of blessings, mercy and guidance for the patient, has been conveyed by way of good tidings through the tongue of the Messenger, in honour of his station and to increase the believers' attachment to him, such that their goods come through him. Therefore it is one of the subtleties of the Qur'an that the attribution of trial is made to Allah without an intermediary, while the attribution of the good tidings of the coming good is made from Allah to the Messenger.

The discussion of patience (sabr) and its virtues has passed at His saying ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45].

The description of the patient as ﴿those who, when disaster strikes them, say﴾, etc., is to indicate that their patience is the most perfect patience, since it is patience accompanied by insight into the command of Allah the Exalted. At the moment of calamity they know that they belong to Allah the Exalted, who disposes of them as He wills, so they do not panic at what comes to them; and they know that they will return to Him, and He will reward them for it. Thus "saying" here means the statement that corresponds to belief, since speech was only set for truthfulness, and that statement is considered only if it is an expression of what is in the heart. Whoever says these words without belief in them has no virtue; he is like one who shouts at what does not hear. Allah taught them this comprehensive formula to be their motto at the time of calamity, because belief is strengthened by explicit declaration, as the soul's apprehension of non-sensory realities is weak and needs reinforcement by something sensory. Also, in their explicit declaration of this there is an announcement of this belief and a teaching of it to people. The discussion of "disaster" (musibah) comes at His saying ﴿But if disaster strikes you, he says, "Allah has bestowed favour upon me"﴾ [al-Nisa': 72] in Surah al-Nisa'.

The emphasis with "inna" (indeed) in their saying "Indeed we belong to Allah" is because the context is one of concern, and because it places the one afflicted in the position of one who denies that he is Allah's possession and servant, since the disaster makes him forget that and its terror comes between him and his right judgment. The "lam" in it is for ownership.

The use of the demonstrative in His saying ﴿Those upon them are blessings from their Lord﴾ is to draw attention to the fact that what is referred to is the one described by all the preceding attributes that came before the demonstrative, and that the ruling that comes after the demonstrative is consequent upon those attributes, like ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. This is an explanation of the reward for their patience. The word "ṣalawat" (blessings) here is used metaphorically for purifications and forgiveness, and that is why mercy is conjoined to it, though mercy itself is among the meanings of prayer (salah) used metaphorically, as in His saying ﴿Indeed Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56].

The literal meaning of prayer (salah) in the speech of the Arabs is utterances that reveal a love of good for someone. For this reason its most well-known meaning is supplication (du'a'), and this has passed at His saying ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. Because of this, the attribution of this verb to One from whom good is sought alone becomes necessarily a metaphor in its implied meaning, which is the occurrence of good. So when prayer is attributed to Allah, or annexed to Him, it indicates mercy and the bringing of what is beneficial, whether mercy, forgiveness or purification.

His saying ﴿and those are the rightly guided﴾ is an explanation of the excellence of their attribute, since they have been guided to what is the right of every knowing servant. Thus calamities did not unsettle them, nor did they become a barrier to them from realizing the station of patience, because they know that life is never free of troubles. As for those who were not guided, they make calamities a cause for their objecting against Allah, or for their disbelief in Him, or for saying what is unfitting, or for doubt about the soundness of the Islam they are upon. They say: "If this were the religion pleasing to Allah, no punishment or calamity would have befallen us." This is the condition of the people of misguidance, whose matter Allah warned us of in His saying ﴿And if a good thing befalls them, they say, "This is ours"; and if an evil thing befalls them, they attribute it to Moses and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131]. He also said about the hypocrites ﴿And if an evil thing befalls them, they say, "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [al-Nisa': 78]. The decisive word is that the recompense for deeds appears in the Hereafter, while the calamities of this world are caused by worldly causes, arising when their cause arises. Allah may make the cause of a calamity a punishment for His servant in this world for bad conduct or the like, to lighten for him the punishment of the Hereafter. It may also be for raising the ranks of the soul. It has states and subtleties that none knows except Allah the Exalted, and the servant may come to know some of them when he watches over his soul and takes account of it. For Allah the Exalted, in both states, there is gentleness and a striking that the effect of one of them appears to those who know Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 158 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever makes the Hajj to the House or performs 'Umrah, there is no blame upon him for going around between them. And whoever volunteers good, then indeed Allah is Appreciative and Knowing.﴾

This statement came as an interjection within the argument with the People of the Book and the polytheists concerning the qibla. It was revealed because of hesitation and confusion among the Muslims regarding the sa'y (running/walking) between as-Safa and al-Marwah, and that was in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada'), as came in the hadith of 'A'ishah that follows. This verse was revealed after the verses before it and after the verses that we read after it, because the Hajj had not yet been made obligatory. It is among the verses that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to attach to some surahs that had been revealed a while before its revelation. The connection between it and what precedes it is that turning away from the sa'y between as-Safa and al-Marwah resembles the action of those whom He described as "the foolish ones" (al-sufaha') concerning the qibla, and denying the turning away from facing Bayt al-Maqdis. Therefore the position of this verse, after it has been attached to this place, is the position of an interjection within an interjection.

The sa'y between as-Safa and al-Marwah had been among the rites of the Hajj since the time of Ibrahim ('alayhi al-salam), as a reminder of Allah's blessing upon Hajar and her son Isma'il, when Allah rescued him from thirst, as in the hadith of al-Bukhari in the Book of the Beginning of Creation, from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ: "When Hajar, the mother of Isma'il, was left by Ibrahim in the place of Makkah with her son, who was a suckling infant, and he left for her a bag of dates and a waterskin containing water. When the water in the waterskin ran out, she became thirsty and her son became thirsty too, and she began to look at him writhing. So she set off, out of distaste for watching him, and she found as-Safa the nearest mountain adjoining her, so she stood upon it, then faced the valley, looking to see whether she could see anyone, but she saw no one. So she descended from as-Safa and came to al-Marwah and stood upon it and looked to see whether she could see anyone, but she saw no one. She did this seven times." Ibn 'Abbas said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "For this reason the people run between them." Then she heard a sound and said to herself, "Sh!" Then she listened again and said, "You have made me hear; if you have any help..." Then behold, there was the angel at the place of Zamzam, and he dug with his heel until the water appeared. So she drank and nursed her child."

It is possible that Ibrahim ran between as-Safa and al-Marwah in remembrance of gratitude for the blessing, and commanded Isma'il to do so. It is also possible that Isma'il attached it to the acts of the Hajj, or that those who came from his descendants did so, and so it became firmly established among the symbols for the Quraysh without doubt.

In the pre-Islamic period, around the Ka'bah there were two stones which were among the idols that 'Amr ibn Luhayy brought to Makkah, and the Arabs worshipped them. One of them was called Isaf and the other was called Na'ilah. One of them was placed near the wall of the Ka'bah and the other was placed near Zamzam. Then they moved the one near the Ka'bah to the direction of Zamzam, and the Arabs used to sacrifice for them both. When 'Abd al-Muttalib renewed the digging of Zamzam, after Jurhum had buried it when they left Makkah, and he built the sigayat Zamzam (the water-drinking station), he moved those two idols: he placed Isaf upon as-Safa and Na'ilah upon al-Marwah. After that the polytheists made small idols and figures between the two mountains on the path of the sa'y. So the Arabs who came after that imagined that the sa'y between as-Safa and al-Marwah was a circumambulation around the two idols. The Aws, the Khazraj and Ghassan worshipped Manat, which was an idol at al-Mushallal near Qudayd, so they would not run between as-Safa and al-Marwah out of scruple at circumambulating other than their idol. In al-Bukhari, in what he suspended from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from 'A'ishah, she said: "Some men from the Ansar, among those who used to assume ihlal for Manat, said: 'O Prophet of Allah, we used not to circumambulate between as-Safa and al-Marwah, out of glorification of Manat.'"

So when Makkah was conquered, the idols were removed, circumambulation of the House was permitted, the Muslims performed Hajj with Abu Bakr, and the Quraysh ran between as-Safa and al-Marwah, the Ansar became scrupulous about running between as-Safa and al-Marwah. A group of them asked the Prophet ﷺ: "Is there any blame upon us if we circumambulate between as-Safa and al-Marwah?" So Allah revealed this verse.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated in the Muwatta' from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "I said to 'A'ishah, while I was then young: 'Do you see the word of Allah, the Exalted, "Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever makes the Hajj to the House or performs 'Umrah, there is no blame upon him for going around between them," so there is nothing upon a man if he does not circumambulate between them?' 'A'ishah said: 'Never! If it were as you say, it would have been: "There is no blame upon him for not going around between them." Rather, this verse was revealed concerning the Ansar, who used to assume ihlal for Manat, and Manat was opposite Qudayd, and they were scrupulous about circumambulating between as-Safa and al-Marwah. So when Islam came, they asked the Messenger of Allah about that, and Allah revealed: "Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah..." the verse.'"

In al-Bukhari, from Anas: "We used to consider them to be from the affairs of the Jahiliyyah. When Islam came, we refrained from them, so Allah revealed: 'Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah...'" In it there is also the statement of Ma'mar mentioned earlier, that they used not to circumambulate between as-Safa and al-Marwah in the Jahiliyyah, out of glorification of Manat.

The emphasis of the sentence with inna (indeed) is because the addressees were hesitant about whether they are among the symbols of Allah, and they were more inclined to believe that the sa'y between them is among the practices of the Jahiliyyah. In the Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: their question was in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage. With all of this it becomes clear that this verse was revealed years after the revelation of the verse about the change of the qibla, and its placement in this position is for the sake of connection with the verses that address the confusion of the groups regarding the qibla and the rites.

As-Safa and al-Marwah are two names for two mountains facing each other. As for as-Safa, it is the top end of the mountain of Abu Qubays, and as for al-Marwah, it is a peak at the end of the mountain of Qu'ayqi'an. As-Safa was named so because its stones are from al-Safa, which is the smooth, hard rock. Al-Marwah was named Marwah because its stones are from al-Marw, which are the white, soft stones that produce fire, and with which one slaughters, because their flint produces pieces with sharp edges; and they are struck against stones from as-Safa and then crack. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"Until I am, for the calamities, a Marwah, struck at the Safa of al-Mushaqqar every day, it splinters."

It seems that Allah, the Exalted, showed kindness to the people of Makkah by providing them with a mountain of Marwah, for benefit in striking fire and in their slaughtering, and He placed opposite it as-Safa, for benefit in their building.

As-Safa and al-Marwah are near the Masjid al-Haram, and the distance between them is seven hundred and seventy cubits. The path of the sa'y between them passes alongside the wall of the Masjid al-Haram. As-Safa is near a gate called Bab as-Safa among the gates of the Masjid al-Haram, and the one performing the sa'y ascends to as-Safa and al-Marwah by something like a staircase. Al-Sha'a'ir is the plural of sha'irah, with fatha on the shin, and sh'arah with kasra on the shin, meaning a sign, derived from sha'ara, when one knows and perceives. It is a fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ulah, i.e., marked by it. From this is their saying: "The camel was marked (ush'ira)" when a mark was made on its hump indicating that it was prepared as a sacrificial offering.

So the sha'a'ir are whatever has been made a sign of the performance of an act of the Hajj or 'Umrah, and they are the honored places, such as the miqat points where ihram takes place, among them the Ka'bah, the Masjid al-Haram, the Maqam, as-Safa and al-Marwah, 'Arafat, al-Mash'ar al-Haram at Muzdalifah, Mina, and the jamarat.

The meaning of describing as-Safa and al-Marwah as among the symbols of Allah is that Allah made them two markers upon a place of worship, like the naming of the miqats of the Hajj as miqats. Their description with this is a clear statement that the sa'y between them is an act of worship, since no act of worship is connected to them, having been made markers of it, other than the sa'y between them. Their attribution to Allah is either because they are two markers of His worship, or because He made them so.

His saying ﴿So whoever makes the Hajj to the House﴾ is a consequence of their being among the symbols of Allah, and that the sa'y between them in the Hajj and 'Umrah is among the rites. So what took place in them of the doings of the Jahiliyyah should not cause him doubt, because a sacred thing does not lose its sanctity by what surrounds it of bad accidents. For this reason He drew attention with His saying "there is no blame upon him" to negate what had stirred in their souls after Islam, as in the hadith of 'Urwah from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.

Al-junah (blame), with a damma on the jim, is sin, derived from janaha, when one inclines, because sin inclines a person away from the path of good. They considered in it the inclination away from good, the reverse of their consideration in hanaf, that it is an inclination away from evil toward good.

Al-hajj: in the linguistic sense it is a name for intention, and in custom, the intention to the Sacred House in Makkah for the worship of Allah the Exalted there, by circumambulation, standing at 'Arafat, and ihram. For this reason it became, by unrestricted use, a customary reality in this meaning, generically, by dominance, like a proper noun by dominance. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "They (Hajj and 'Umrah) in meanings are like al-najm (the star) and al-bayt (the house) in entities, so there is no need to mention a genitive complement except in a context of attention to specification. For this reason it occurs in the Qur'an unattached to an annexation, as in ﴿The Hajj is well-known months﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], up to His saying
﴿nor is there disputing during the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], and it occurs annexed in His saying ﴿And for Allah is the pilgrimage to the House upon mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], because it is a station of the beginning of legislation, so it is a station of explanation and elaboration." The verb hajja in the sense of qasada (to intend) has not ceased to be used in the sense of intending in the speech of the Arabs, so mentioning the object was for the increase of clarity.

As for the correctness of your saying "Hajja fulan" (so-and-so performed Hajj), and His saying ﷺ "Indeed Allah has prescribed upon you the Hajj, so perform it" without mention of the object, that is an ellipsis relying on the context. So the dominance of the use of the verb for intending the House is less than the dominance of the use of the noun hajj for that intention.

Al-'umrah: a name for visiting the Sacred House at a time other than the time of Hajj, or at its time without attending 'Arafat. So 'umrah in relation to Hajj is like the solitary prayer in relation to congregational prayer. It is in the form of a noun, the dominant proper noun for visiting the Ka'bah, and its verb became dominant for that visit following the dominance of the noun, so it equaled it in that. For this reason the object was not mentioned here, and it was not heard.

Dominance in every case does not prevent the other usage occasionally.

The negation of blame for one who goes around between as-Safa and al-Marwah does not indicate more than that it is not forbidden. So it is compatible with what is permissible and recommended, and obligatory and a pillar, because what is permitted is compatible with all the things mentioned, so establishing its ruling requires another proof. For this reason 'A'ishah said to 'Urwah: "If it were as you say, it would have said: 'There is no blame upon him for not going around between them.'" Ibn al-'Arabi said in Ahkam al-Qur'an: "The statement of one who says 'There is no blame upon you to do it' is a permission for the act, and his statement 'There is no blame upon you not to do it' is a permission for leaving the act. So this expression did not come to permit leaving the circumambulation, nor is there in it any proof for it. It came only to convey the permissibility of circumambulation for one who had been scrupulous about it in the Jahiliyyah, or for one who used to circumambulate in the Jahiliyyah with the intention of the idols that were there." End of quotation.

His meaning is that "There is no blame upon you to do it" is a text negating sin from the doer, and it is compatible with permissibility, recommendation, and obligation, so it is ambiguous regarding any one of them. Unlike "There is no blame upon you not to do it," which is a text negating the sin of omission, and it is compatible with the prohibition of the act and its disliked status, so it is ambiguous regarding one of them. Yes, the undertaking to inform of the negation of sin from the doer of something which appears to be a thing that is likely to be forbidden, this is the custom of the use of speech. So your saying "There is no blame upon you in doing such-and-such" is apparent in permissibility, in the sense that both sides are equal, not recommendation or obligation, since no one intends an obligatory duty, a requirement, or a recommended act

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 158 (part 2 of 2):

He says concerning it, "There is no sin upon you for doing it." On account of this, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr understood from the verse that performing the sa'y (the ritual running between al-Safa and al-Marwa) is not obligatory. He was indeed correct in understanding from the standpoint of the usage of the language, since he was a man of the tongue. However, there was a cause that prompted the expression of negating sin from the one who performs the sa'y, namely the belief of many Muslims that there was sin in doing so. Thus the factor prompting the negation of sin from the one who performs the sa'y became confronting the belief with what indicates its opposite, together with knowledge that the possibility of intending mere permissibility, in the sense of the equality of the two options, is excluded, by what is known from the commands of the Shari'a that came after the revelation of the verse or preceded it. For this reason 'Urwa said in what he narrated, "And I was at that time young in age," meaning that he had no knowledge of the Sunnah and the occasions of revelation. His intention by his youth was not ignorance of the language, because in grasping its meanings the young and the old are equal. For this same reason 'A'isha said to him, "Evil is what you said, nephew," intending to censure his statement from the standpoint of what it led him to, namely a misunderstanding of the purpose of the Qur'an had he persisted in that understanding, in keeping with their custom of frankness in speaking the truth. Thus the apparent meaning of the verse, according to what is customary, became interpreted by knowledge of the cause for addressing the negation of sin from those who circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwa.

So the sin negated in the verse is a sin that accrued to running between al-Safa and al-Marwa due to the placing of the idols Isaf and Na'ila upon them, and not to the act of running itself. When its cause ceased, the sin ceased, as in His saying, ﴿There is no sin upon them if they make peace between themselves with a settlement, and settlement is best﴾ [al-Nisa: 128]. He negated sin from reconciliation and affirmed that it is good. So the sin negated from settlement is what preceded it of causes of discord and aversion. Similar to this is His saying, ﴿But whoever fears from a testator deviation or sin and makes reconciliation among them, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqara: 182], although reconciliation among them is encouraged. What is meant is that there is no sin upon him concerning what was diminished from the right of one of the two parties, and that is an accidental sin.

The verse indicates the obligation of running between al-Safa and al-Marwa by describing them as among the symbols (sha'a'ir) of Allah. Because of this the legal schools differed regarding the ruling on the sa'y. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, in the more well-known of the two narrations from him, held that it is an obligatory pillar (fard) of the Hajj, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and the majority. Its basis is that it is one of the acts of the Hajj, and the Prophet ﷺ gave it great attention and hastened to perform it, as in the hadith of the Two Sahihs and the Muwatta'. Since his act wavered between being a Sunna and being obligatory (fard), Malik said that it is a fard of qada' which entered the realm of caution. Also, it is an act involving the whole body that is specific to the Hajj and has no obligatory counterpart, so it is analogized to standing at 'Arafa, the Tawaf al-Ifada and the ihram. This is unlike the two rak'as of the tawaf, for those are a prayer and not specific to the Hajj; and unlike abstaining from wearing sewn garments, for that is an abstention; and unlike stoning the jamarat, for that is an act performed by a limb, namely the hand. My phrase "has no obligatory counterpart" excludes the Tawaf al-Qudum, for although it is an act involving the whole body, it has an obligatory counterpart, which is the Ifada, so that makes it unnecessary to make it obligatory. Also, His saying in the hadith: "Run, for Allah has prescribed for you the sa'y," and the command is apparent in indicating obligation. The basic principle is that fard and wajib are synonymous according to us, except in the Hajj, where wajib is less than fard; but the obligation indicated by the command is equal to fard.

Abu Hanifa held that it is a wajib which is compensated by a sacrifice (damm). The Hanafis argued for this by saying that it has not been established by a definitive (qat'i) proof in its indication, so it is not a fard but a wajib, because the verse is definitive only in its text, while the hadith is speculative (zanni) in both respects. The answer is that the combined apparent meaning of the saying and the act indicates fardiyya; otherwise, standing at 'Arafa has no proof of its being fard, and likewise the ihram, so where would this category called fard by them be established? A group of the early scholars held that it is a sunna.

His saying, ﴿And whoever volunteers good, then indeed Allah is Grateful, Knowing﴾, is a concluding statement (tadhyil) appended to what the verse conveyed of encouragement toward running between al-Safa and al-Marwa, by the import of His saying ﴿among the symbols of Allah﴾. The purpose of this concluding statement is to bring a universal ruling concerning all good deeds, whether obligatory and voluntary or voluntary alone. So the intended meaning of "good" is not specifically the sa'y, because "khayran" is an indefinite noun in the context of a conditional, and therefore it is general. For this reason the clause was connected with the conjunction "wa" rather than "fa", lest the good be restricted to the circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwa. This is unlike His saying in the verse on fasting, ﴿And for those who are able to do it, there is a ransom of feeding a needy person. Whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾ [al-Baqara: 184], because there what was intended was to clarify that fasting, despite the permission to break it, is better than abandoning it, or that adding to the feeding of one poor person is better than limiting oneself to it, as will come.

The verb "tatawwa'a" is used in the sense of performing an act of obedience and undertaking it with effort, and it is also used as the intransitive form of "taw'a'ahu," meaning he made him obedient, so it indicates the meaning of voluntary giving (tabarru') predominantly, because voluntary giving is an addition to obedience. On both readings, the accusative of "khayran" is by removal of the preposition, meaning "volunteers with good," or by implying in "tatawwa'a" the meaning of "fa'ala" or "ata."

Since the clause is a concluding statement, it does not indicate that the sa'y is among the voluntary acts, meaning among the recommended ones, because it serves to convey a universal ruling after mention of a great legislation. Furthermore, "tatawwa'a" is not fixed to mean "tabarra'a," but may bear the meaning of "ata bi-ta'a" (performed an act of obedience) or "takallafa ta'a" (undertook an act of obedience).

Al-Jumhur read "man tatawwa'a" in the past tense, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read "yatTawwa'" in the present tense with the ya' of the third person and the jazm on the 'ayn.

"Man" here is conditional, as evidenced by the fa' in its response. His saying ﴿then indeed Allah is Grateful, Knowing﴾ is the indication of the response, since the implied meaning is: whoever volunteers good will be rewarded for it, because Allah is Grateful, meaning He does not waste the reward of a doer of good, Knowing, meaning nothing of his goodness is hidden from Him. He mentioned the two attributes because withholding reward for goodness happens only through denial of the virtue or ignorance of it, so these two are negated by His saying "Grateful, Knowing." In my view, the more apparent is that "Grateful" here is a metaphor of the representational kind (isti'ara tamthiliyya): the affair of Allah regarding the reward of the servant for obedience is likened to the state of one who is grateful to someone who has bestowed a favor upon him. The benefit of this comparison is to depict the hastening and certainty of the reward, because the condition of one who is benefited is to hasten to thank his benefactor.

﴿Indeed, those who conceal the clear proofs and the guidance that We sent down, after We made it clear to the people in the Book, those—Allah curses them, and the cursers curse them.﴾ ﴿Except those who repent, amend, and make clear; those—I accept their repentance, and I am the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

A return to the subject from its original course, from which it was separated by the digression concerning the legislation of the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwa, as you have recently learned. The exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning the scholars of the Jews, for their concealment of the signs of the truthfulness of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), his attributes, and the attributes of his religion, which are present in the Torah, and for their concealment of the verse of stoning (al-rajm). This requires that the relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul) be for a specific reference (al-'ahd), since the relative pronoun for what follows it is definite by the article (al-ma'rifa bi-l-lam), and according to this there is no generality here. However, I am of the view that the relative pronoun here is for the category (lil-jins), so it is like the definite article of comprehensiveness (lam al-istighraq), and it therefore covers all cases, and it is one of the general (al-'amm) terms that came on a specific occasion (sabab khass), and it is not restricted by its occasion. Rather, it encompasses the individuals of its occasion with a primary encompassing that is stronger than its indication of the rest of the individuals that are suitable to be indicated by it, because the indication of the general term upon the form of the occasion is definite (qat'iyya), while its indication of other things included in the concept of the general term is probabilistic (zanniyya). Thus, the placement of this verse after the one before it is because what preceded it was among the varied Qur'anic modes that present diverse forms, concerning the mention of what the Jews opposed the call of the Prophet (ﷺ) with, and their likening of themselves in this to the condition of their predecessors in opposing the call of their prophets before them, up to His exalted saying ﴿Do you hope that they will believe for you, when a party of them used to hear the words of Allah?﴾ [al-Baqara: 75]

[Page 66]

up to His saying ﴿When there came to them a messenger from Allah confirming what was with them, a party of those given the Book threw away the Book of Allah behind their backs﴾ [al-Baqara: 101], and the verse; and what their likes among the Christians and the polytheists opposed the Islamic call with. Then this led to a rebuke of the polytheists for their scant fidelity to the injunctions of Abraham, whom they boast of being descended from, and that they are the custodians of his House. So He said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them?﴾ [al-Baqara: 114] and the verses that follow. Thus He honored Abraham, the Ka'ba, facing it in prayer, and its rites. Interwoven with this was a refutation of what proceeded from the Jews of denying the facing of the Ka'ba, up to His saying ﴿Indeed, a party of them conceal the truth while they know﴾ [al-Baqara: 146], meaning their scholars. Then He followed this with completing the virtues of the Ka'ba and its rites. When all of that was complete, He turned the discourse to the detailed explanation of what He had charged them with in summary in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, a party of them﴾, so He said ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down...﴾ etc. This is a method in rhetoric, which is giving the intended purpose its right, shortening the digressions and interruptions that occurred within it, and then returning to what it is important to return to, after a detailed account of a digression or interruption that intervened in the intended purpose.

So the sentence ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ etc. is a resumptive statement, from which the listener understands the detailed account of what was previously stated in summary. The emphasis with "inna" is merely for attention to this report.

Al-katm and al-kitman mean not informing about something that should be informed of, whether a heard or seen event. Among this is concealing a secret, which is information that you tell another and command him to conceal, so he does not inform anyone else of it.

He expressed "yaktumuna" with the present tense to indicate that they are currently concealing the clear proofs and the guidance. Had it been expressed in the past tense, the listener would have supposed that what was meant were people who had passed away, whereas the intent is to establish proof against those present.

The ruling on those who passed and those who will come is known by the indication of the implication of the discourse (lahn al-khitab), since they are equal in this. What is meant by "what We sent down" is what the Torah contained of indications and guidance, and what is meant by "the Book" is the Torah.

Al-bayyinat is the plural of bayyina, which is proof. This includes what is among the foundations of the Shari'a, that which is an indication of many rulings, and it includes the evidences guiding to the divine attributes, the conditions of the messengers, and the taking of the covenant from them to follow every messenger who came with signs of truthfulness, especially the messenger who would be sent among the brothers of Israel, who are the Arabs, among whom his mission appeared and from whom it spread. Al-huda is that by which guidance is achieved, that is, the direction to the path of good, so it includes the verses of rulings by which the people's welfare is achieved in themselves and their welfare in their society.

[Page 67]

Concealment occurs by abandoning memorization, teaching and instruction. It also occurs by removing it from the Book altogether, and this is its apparent meaning. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and you conceal much﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 15]. It occurs through remote interpretations far from the intent of the Lawgiver, because concealing the meaning is a form of concealing it. The omission of the object of "yaktumuna", which indicates what is concealed from, is for generality, meaning they conceal that from everyone, so that it may be forgotten and lost.

His saying "min ba'di" is related to "yaktumuna". He mentioned this adverbial phrase to increase the reprehensibility of the state of concealment, because they concealed the clear proofs and guidance while there was no excuse for that. For if they had concealed what had not been made clear to them, they would have had some excuse to say "we concealed it because its meaning was not evident." So how much more so when it has been made clear and manifest in the Torah.

The lam in His saying "lin-nas" is the lam of causation, meaning: We made it clear in the Book for the sake of the people, that is, We intended its announcement and dissemination, that is, We made it manifest. In this there is additional censure of them for what they did of concealment, for it is both concealment of the truth and deprivation from it, and it is an aggression against its rightful recipient for whose sake it was made. Thus their action is misguidance and injustice.

The definiteness in "an-nas" is for comprehensiveness, because Allah sent down the laws for the guidance of all people, and this is a customary comprehensiveness, that is, the people for whom the law was prescribed.

His saying "ula'ika" is a demonstrative referring to "those who conceal." He placed the demonstrative between the subject of "inna" and its predicate to draw attention to the fact that the ruling that follows applies to them deservedly, because of those attributes mentioned before it, such that those attributes made them as if they were present before the listener, so they were pointed to, and in reality it is a pointer to their attributes. Therefore, the demonstrative indicates that those attributes are the cause of the ruling, and it is an allusion to the cause, in the manner of ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5].

The demonstrative of the distant was chosen so that it would more strongly rouse the listener to reflect upon them and turn attention to them, or because a demonstrative in this form is the most frequently used in their speech.

Two allusions to the reason for the consequence of the curse upon concealment have come together in the verse: the allusion by the relative clause to the reason for the ruling, that is, its cause and occasion, and the allusion by the demonstrative to draw attention to their deserving of that. So the emphasis of the allusion to the causation served in place of an explicit statement of the cause.

[Page 68]

Al-la'n (curse) is distance from mercy together with humiliation and wrath. Its effect appears in the Hereafter through deprivation of Paradise and punishment in Hell. As for the people's cursing of them, it is their supplication that Allah distance them from His mercy in the manner mentioned. The present tense verb was chosen to indicate renewal, with the knowledge that He also cursed them in the past, since every listener knows that there is no reason to restrict their curse to the future time.

The same applies to His saying ﴿and the cursers curse them﴾. He repeated the verb "yal'anuhum" while the conjunction letter obviates its repetition, because the meaning of "al-la'inun" differs: the curse from Allah is distance from mercy, and the curse from humans is supplication against them. This is the reverse of what occurred in ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56], because the verified view is that the blessings of Allah and the angels are one and the same, which is good mention.

The definiteness in "al-la'inun" is for comprehensiveness, and it is a customary comprehensiveness, meaning every curser curses them. What is meant by "al-la'inun" are the religiously committed who reject wrongdoing and its perpetrators, and who become angry for the sake of Allah, exalted is He, and who become aware of the concealment of these people. So they curse them by specification if they become aware of their specific identity, and if they do not become aware of their specific identity, they curse them by the general category, that is, whenever they curse everyone who concealed the verses of the Book, whenever they recite the Torah. Allah had taken the covenant from the Children of Israel that they would make the Torah clear and not conceal it, as He said: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those given the Book: you must make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187].

The mention of the curse upon neglecting the covenant of Allah has come in the Torah many times, the most famous of which is the covenant that Moses took from the Children of Israel at Horeb, as found in the Book of Exodus, chapter 24. And the covenant he took from them in Moab, in which is the curse upon whoever abandons it, which is in the Book of Deuteronomy, chapter 28 and chapter 29, and from it: "You stand this day all of you before the LORD your God... that you may enter into the covenant of the LORD your God, and into his oath, lest there should be among you this day a man... And it shall come to pass, when he heareth the words of this curse, that he bless himself in his heart... then the anger of the LORD and his jealousy shall smoke against that man, and all the curses that are written in this book shall lie upon him, and the LORD shall blot out his name from under heaven, and the LORD shall separate him unto evil out of all the tribes of Israel, according to all the curses of the covenant that are written in this book of the law."

And in chapter thirty: "And it shall come to pass, when all these things are come upon thee, the blessing and the curse, which I have set before thee..."

[Page 69]

And in it: "I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing." So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the cursers curse them﴾ is a reminder to them of the curse recorded in the Torah, for the Torah is constantly recited among them. Whenever the readers read this statement, the curse upon those it is addressed to is renewed. Those who concealed what was sent down of the clear proofs and guidance also read the Torah, and when they read the curse upon the concealers, they have cursed themselves with their own tongues. As for those who curse the criminals and wrongdoers other than the concealers of what was sent down of the clear proofs and guidance, they are not included in this generality. By this, the comprehensiveness derived from defining "al-la'inun" with the lam is customary comprehensiveness.

Know that the lam of customary comprehensiveness is intermediate between the lam of nature (lam al-haqiqa) and the lam of true comprehensiveness (lam al-istighraq al-haqiqi).

He turned to the definite form even though it is like the indefinite, for emphasis on its actualization, to the extent that it becomes as if it were known, because the indefinite is unknown. Or the definiteness may be for specific reference (al-'ahd), that is, those whom the prophets cursed, who had enjoined the announcement of the covenant and that they should not conceal it.

Since the relative clause of "those who conceal" contains an allusion, as we have stated, every person who does an act of the kind of the content of the relative clause, other than those people, is deserving of what the demonstrative and its predicate contain. For among the purposes of the Qur'an in mentioning past narratives is that Muslims should take lessons from them in good and evil. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that every fault for which Allah blamed the People of the Book is one from which Muslims are warned against the like of. For this reason Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), when the people said "Abu Hurayra narrates too much from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," said: "Were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, I would not have narrated to you a single hadith after the people said 'Abu Hurayra narrates too much.' ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of the clear proofs and guidance﴾..." the verse, and he then related the hadith.

[Page 70]

He is also forbidden, by way of analogy (*qiyas*) indicated by the reason (*'illa*), to spread among the people what would cause them to fall into delusions, by teaching them something when he does not know how to apply it (*tanzil*) or how to interpret it (*ta'wil*). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Speak to the people in terms they can understand. Would you like Allah and His Messenger to be called liars?" The same applies to anything that is known to be something people do not know how to deal with properly.

[Page 70 continues]

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, al-Hajjaj said to Anas ibn Malik: "Tell me about the severest punishment the Prophet ever inflicted."
