Ibn 'Arafa said in his commentary: It is not permissible for the scholar to mention to a wrongdoer an interpretation or a concession (*rukhsa*) by which he will extend himself into corruption. An example of this is one who mentions to a wrongdoer what al-Ghazali said in the *Ihya'* that if the treasury (*bayt al-mal*) is weak and the ruler is compelled to raise what will equip the armies of the Muslims to repel harm from them, then there is no harm in imposing a tithe or other levy on the people to maintain the army and fill the shortfall. Ibn 'Arafa said: Mentioning this injustice is among the things that cause grave harm to the people.

The sultan of Cordoba, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya al-Dakhil, asked Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi about a day on which a man had deliberately broken his fast during Ramadan, having been overcome by desire to have intercourse with one of his concubines on that day. Yahya ruled that he must fast sixty days. The jurists were present and did not dare to oppose Yahya. When they left, they asked him: "Why did you specify for him one of the optional expiations?" He said: "If we opened this door for him, he would have intercourse every day and then free a slave or feed people. So I obliged him to the most difficult option, so that he would not repeat it." End of quotation. I say: by concealing from him the two expiations between which he had a choice, he applied the principle of preventing the corruption of boldness against the sanctity of the obligation of fasting.

Thus, when the scholar is singled out personally to convey knowledge or to explain the Sharia, it is obligatory upon him to explain it, like those whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent to convey his letters or to call their peoples. If he is not singled out personally, then his situation is one of two kinds. Either what he knows is something the community needs to learn from him specifically, such that he alone holds this knowledge in a region or a city, so that it would be impossible for people to seek it from anyone else, or it would be so difficult that if he did not teach it to them they would go astray, such as tawhid and the foundations of belief. In this case, it is obligatory upon him to explain it as a specific, individual obligation (*wajib muta'ayyan*), if he is the only one with this knowledge in his era or region, or if he is the most proficient in it. Al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah related from Abu Sa'id that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Verily the people are followers of you, and there will be men who come to you seeking to understand or to learn. When they come to you, then enjoin good upon them."

If others of his peers share this knowledge with him, then its obligation falls upon all who know it as a collective obligation (*kifaya*). The other kind is that what he teaches consists of the details of the rulings and their benefits that serve the people or a group among them. Then, whether individually or collectively according to the two situations mentioned above, it is obligatory upon him to explain what the need calls for. Among what is considered a case where the need calls for explanation is that a group of people is designated for him so that he may teach them. In that case, it is obligatory upon him to teach them what he sees as beneficial to their knowledge, and as within their capacity to understand and to apply properly. For this reason, when people sit with the scholar in order to learn, it is obligatory for him to present to them the knowledge they are able to receive and comprehend. From this it becomes clear that concealment has many degrees, and the highest of them is what this verse includes. The remaining degrees are derived by analogy.

This also applies to the scholar's answers to the questions put to him. If he is the only one who has the answer, or if he has been designated to answer, as in the case of one who is appointed to issue fatwas in some regions, then he must explain it when he knows that the questioner needs it. The two previously mentioned positions regarding individual and collective obligation apply to whether he is the only one with this knowledge or has been designated to answer, and to when he is not the only one.

Outside of this, he has the choice to answer or to refrain.

By this, the interpretation becomes clear of the hadith related by the authors of the Four Sunan, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is asked about a matter of knowledge and conceals it, Allah will bridle him with a bridle of fire on the Day of Resurrection." Its general application, regarding persons and circumstances, is thus restricted by specifications indicated by the evidences, to which we have alluded in summary. Al-Qurtubi mentioned from Sahnun that the hadith refers to a witness who conceals his testimony.

The responsibility for the scholar to place himself in the rank appropriate to him among these stated ranks lies with his own judgment of himself in this matter, and with what he finds to be the safeguard of his religion and his honor.

The responsibility for knowing the circumstances of the seekers and the questioners lies with him, so that he may treat them in the forms that are required of him, according to what he discerns of their conditions and of the circumstances surrounding them. If the matter remains unclear to him, whether regarding his own state or the state of his questioner, then he should consult the people of knowledge and sound judgment in religion.

It is necessary not to overlook the wisdom of the conjunction in the words of the Exalted, "and the guidance" (*wa al-huda*), so that this serves as a governing principle for what concealment leads to.

His saying ﴿except those who repent﴾ is an exception from those who conceal, meaning they will not be struck by the curse. It is a true exception (*istithna' haqiqi*), in the accusative case, [and it is] a complete sentence on its own, following from ﴿those who conceal what We have sent down﴾, and so on. Among the conditions of repentance is that they correct what they have corrupted, which is by manifesting what they concealed and making it clear to the people.

[Page 71]

Therefore their confession alone, or in private, is not sufficient. Repentance here is faith in Muhammad (ﷺ), since it is a turning back from their concealment of the testimony to him that is found in their books. The use of "repentance" to mean faith after disbelief is very common, because faith is the repentance of the disbeliever from his disbelief. The phrase "and corrected and made clear" was added after this because the condition of every repentance is that the penitent makes up, as far as possible, for what he has lost through the very act he repents from.

Perhaps the conjunction of "and made clear" to "corrected" is an explanatory conjunction (*'atf tafsir*).

His saying ﴿then those, I will accept their repentance﴾ is a new sentence, not for explanation but for a new benefit. Since He has made an exception of those who repent, the statement is complete, and the listener knows that those among the concealers who repent will not be cursed by Allah or by those who curse. The demonstrative pronoun, used as the subject, represents the subtle point mentioned earlier.

The sentence is joined with the particle *fa* (then) to indicate something added beyond what the exception conveys, namely that their repentance is followed by Allah's good pleasure with them.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Ibn Mas'ud, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah is more pleased with the repentance of His servant than a man who stopped at a place of peril, with his riding animal carrying his food and drink. He placed his head down and slept a sleep, then woke up and his riding animal had gone, until the heat and thirst intensified upon him, and whatever Allah willed. He said: 'I will return to my place,' so he returned and slept a sleep, then raised his head, and there was his riding animal beside him."

Thus in the verse there is a wonderful arrangement, whose underlying sense is: "Except those who repent, the curse is removed from them, so I accept their repentance," that is, I am pleased with them. The placement of the demonstrative in the middle adds the indication of cause, and this is a wonderful conciseness.

﴿Indeed, those who conceal the clear proofs and the guidance that We sent down, after We made it clear to the people in the Book, those—Allah curses them, and the cursers curse them.﴾ ﴿Except those who repent, amend, and make clear; those—I accept their repentance, and I am the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

A return to the subject from its original course, from which it was separated by the digression concerning the legislation of the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwa, as you have recently learned. The exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning the scholars of the Jews, for their concealment of the signs of the truthfulness of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), his attributes, and the attributes of his religion, which are present in the Torah, and for their concealment of the verse of stoning (al-rajm). This requires that the relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul) be for a specific reference (al-'ahd), since the relative pronoun for what follows it is definite by the article (al-ma'rifa bi-l-lam), and according to this there is no generality here. However, I am of the view that the relative pronoun here is for the category (lil-jins), so it is like the definite article of comprehensiveness (lam al-istighraq), and it therefore covers all cases, and it is one of the general (al-'amm) terms that came on a specific occasion (sabab khass), and it is not restricted by its occasion. Rather, it encompasses the individuals of its occasion with a primary encompassing that is stronger than its indication of the rest of the individuals that are suitable to be indicated by it, because the indication of the general term upon the form of the occasion is definite (qat'iyya), while its indication of other things included in the concept of the general term is probabilistic (zanniyya). Thus, the placement of this verse after the one before it is because what preceded it was among the varied Qur'anic modes that present diverse forms, concerning the mention of what the Jews opposed the call of the Prophet (ﷺ) with, and their likening of themselves in this to the condition of their predecessors in opposing the call of their prophets before them, up to His exalted saying ﴿Do you hope that they will believe for you, when a party of them used to hear the words of Allah?﴾ [al-Baqara: 75]

[Page 66]

up to His saying ﴿When there came to them a messenger from Allah confirming what was with them, a party of those given the Book threw away the Book of Allah behind their backs﴾ [al-Baqara: 101], and the verse; and what their likes among the Christians and the polytheists opposed the Islamic call with. Then this led to a rebuke of the polytheists for their scant fidelity to the injunctions of Abraham, whom they boast of being descended from, and that they are the custodians of his House. So He said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them?﴾ [al-Baqara: 114] and the verses that follow. Thus He honored Abraham, the Ka'ba, facing it in prayer, and its rites. Interwoven with this was a refutation of what proceeded from the Jews of denying the facing of the Ka'ba, up to His saying ﴿Indeed, a party of them conceal the truth while they know﴾ [al-Baqara: 146], meaning their scholars. Then He followed this with completing the virtues of the Ka'ba and its rites. When all of that was complete, He turned the discourse to the detailed explanation of what He had charged them with in summary in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, a party of them﴾, so He said ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down...﴾ etc. This is a method in rhetoric, which is giving the intended purpose its right, shortening the digressions and interruptions that occurred within it, and then returning to what it is important to return to, after a detailed account of a digression or interruption that intervened in the intended purpose.

So the sentence ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ etc. is a resumptive statement, from which the listener understands the detailed account of what was previously stated in summary. The emphasis with "inna" is merely for attention to this report.

Al-katm and al-kitman mean not informing about something that should be informed of, whether a heard or seen event. Among this is concealing a secret, which is information that you tell another and command him to conceal, so he does not inform anyone else of it.

He expressed "yaktumuna" with the present tense to indicate that they are currently concealing the clear proofs and the guidance. Had it been expressed in the past tense, the listener would have supposed that what was meant were people who had passed away, whereas the intent is to establish proof against those present.

The ruling on those who passed and those who will come is known by the indication of the implication of the discourse (lahn al-khitab), since they are equal in this. What is meant by "what We sent down" is what the Torah contained of indications and guidance, and what is meant by "the Book" is the Torah.

Al-bayyinat is the plural of bayyina, which is proof. This includes what is among the foundations of the Shari'a, that which is an indication of many rulings, and it includes the evidences guiding to the divine attributes, the conditions of the messengers, and the taking of the covenant from them to follow every messenger who came with signs of truthfulness, especially the messenger who would be sent among the brothers of Israel, who are the Arabs, among whom his mission appeared and from whom it spread. Al-huda is that by which guidance is achieved, that is, the direction to the path of good, so it includes the verses of rulings by which the people's welfare is achieved in themselves and their welfare in their society.

[Page 67]

Concealment occurs by abandoning memorization, teaching and instruction. It also occurs by removing it from the Book altogether, and this is its apparent meaning. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and you conceal much﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 15]. It occurs through remote interpretations far from the intent of the Lawgiver, because concealing the meaning is a form of concealing it. The omission of the object of "yaktumuna", which indicates what is concealed from, is for generality, meaning they conceal that from everyone, so that it may be forgotten and lost.

His saying "min ba'di" is related to "yaktumuna". He mentioned this adverbial phrase to increase the reprehensibility of the state of concealment, because they concealed the clear proofs and guidance while there was no excuse for that. For if they had concealed what had not been made clear to them, they would have had some excuse to say "we concealed it because its meaning was not evident." So how much more so when it has been made clear and manifest in the Torah.

The lam in His saying "lin-nas" is the lam of causation, meaning: We made it clear in the Book for the sake of the people, that is, We intended its announcement and dissemination, that is, We made it manifest. In this there is additional censure of them for what they did of concealment, for it is both concealment of the truth and deprivation from it, and it is an aggression against its rightful recipient for whose sake it was made. Thus their action is misguidance and injustice.

The definiteness in "an-nas" is for comprehensiveness, because Allah sent down the laws for the guidance of all people, and this is a customary comprehensiveness, that is, the people for whom the law was prescribed.

His saying "ula'ika" is a demonstrative referring to "those who conceal." He placed the demonstrative between the subject of "inna" and its predicate to draw attention to the fact that the ruling that follows applies to them deservedly, because of those attributes mentioned before it, such that those attributes made them as if they were present before the listener, so they were pointed to, and in reality it is a pointer to their attributes. Therefore, the demonstrative indicates that those attributes are the cause of the ruling, and it is an allusion to the cause, in the manner of ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5].

The demonstrative of the distant was chosen so that it would more strongly rouse the listener to reflect upon them and turn attention to them, or because a demonstrative in this form is the most frequently used in their speech.

Two allusions to the reason for the consequence of the curse upon concealment have come together in the verse: the allusion by the relative clause to the reason for the ruling, that is, its cause and occasion, and the allusion by the demonstrative to draw attention to their deserving of that. So the emphasis of the allusion to the causation served in place of an explicit statement of the cause.

[Page 68]

Al-la'n (curse) is distance from mercy together with humiliation and wrath. Its effect appears in the Hereafter through deprivation of Paradise and punishment in Hell. As for the people's cursing of them, it is their supplication that Allah distance them from His mercy in the manner mentioned. The present tense verb was chosen to indicate renewal, with the knowledge that He also cursed them in the past, since every listener knows that there is no reason to restrict their curse to the future time.

The same applies to His saying ﴿and the cursers curse them﴾. He repeated the verb "yal'anuhum" while the conjunction letter obviates its repetition, because the meaning of "al-la'inun" differs: the curse from Allah is distance from mercy, and the curse from humans is supplication against them. This is the reverse of what occurred in ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56], because the verified view is that the blessings of Allah and the angels are one and the same, which is good mention.

The definiteness in "al-la'inun" is for comprehensiveness, and it is a customary comprehensiveness, meaning every curser curses them. What is meant by "al-la'inun" are the religiously committed who reject wrongdoing and its perpetrators, and who become angry for the sake of Allah, exalted is He, and who become aware of the concealment of these people. So they curse them by specification if they become aware of their specific identity, and if they do not become aware of their specific identity, they curse them by the general category, that is, whenever they curse everyone who concealed the verses of the Book, whenever they recite the Torah. Allah had taken the covenant from the Children of Israel that they would make the Torah clear and not conceal it, as He said: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those given the Book: you must make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187].

The mention of the curse upon neglecting the covenant of Allah has come in the Torah many times, the most famous of which is the covenant that Moses took from the Children of Israel at Horeb, as found in the Book of Exodus, chapter 24. And the covenant he took from them in Moab, in which is the curse upon whoever abandons it, which is in the Book of Deuteronomy, chapter 28 and chapter 29, and from it: "You stand this day all of you before the LORD your God... that you may enter into the covenant of the LORD your God, and into his oath, lest there should be among you this day a man... And it shall come to pass, when he heareth the words of this curse, that he bless himself in his heart... then the anger of the LORD and his jealousy shall smoke against that man, and all the curses that are written in this book shall lie upon him, and the LORD shall blot out his name from under heaven, and the LORD shall separate him unto evil out of all the tribes of Israel, according to all the curses of the covenant that are written in this book of the law."

And in chapter thirty: "And it shall come to pass, when all these things are come upon thee, the blessing and the curse, which I have set before thee..."

[Page 69]

And in it: "I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing." So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the cursers curse them﴾ is a reminder to them of the curse recorded in the Torah, for the Torah is constantly recited among them. Whenever the readers read this statement, the curse upon those it is addressed to is renewed. Those who concealed what was sent down of the clear proofs and guidance also read the Torah, and when they read the curse upon the concealers, they have cursed themselves with their own tongues. As for those who curse the criminals and wrongdoers other than the concealers of what was sent down of the clear proofs and guidance, they are not included in this generality. By this, the comprehensiveness derived from defining "al-la'inun" with the lam is customary comprehensiveness.

Know that the lam of customary comprehensiveness is intermediate between the lam of nature (lam al-haqiqa) and the lam of true comprehensiveness (lam al-istighraq al-haqiqi).

He turned to the definite form even though it is like the indefinite, for emphasis on its actualization, to the extent that it becomes as if it were known, because the indefinite is unknown. Or the definiteness may be for specific reference (al-'ahd), that is, those whom the prophets cursed, who had enjoined the announcement of the covenant and that they should not conceal it.

Since the relative clause of "those who conceal" contains an allusion, as we have stated, every person who does an act of the kind of the content of the relative clause, other than those people, is deserving of what the demonstrative and its predicate contain. For among the purposes of the Qur'an in mentioning past narratives is that Muslims should take lessons from them in good and evil. Since He has made an exception of those who repent, the statement is complete, and the listener knows that those among the concealers who repent will not be cursed by Allah or by those who curse. The demonstrative pronoun, used as the subject, represents the subtle point mentioned earlier.

The sentence is joined with the particle *fa* (then) to indicate something added beyond what the exception conveys, namely that their repentance is followed by Allah's good pleasure with them.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Ibn Mas'ud, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah is more pleased with the repentance of His servant than a man who stopped at a place of peril, with his riding animal carrying his food and drink. He placed his head down and slept a sleep, then woke up and his riding animal had gone, until the heat and thirst intensified upon him, and whatever Allah willed. He said: 'I will return to my place,' so he returned and slept a sleep, then raised his head, and there was his riding animal beside him."

Thus in the verse there is a wonderful arrangement, whose underlying sense is: "Except those who repent, the curse is removed from them, so I accept their repentance," that is, I am pleased with them. The placement of the demonstrative in the middle adds the indication of cause, and this is a wonderful conciseness.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 161–162:**

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, all together.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic) to convey the state of another group that shares with the one before it in deserving the curse of Allah and of those who curse, and this is a second curse.

This group is the polytheists (mushrikun), for disbelief (kufr) is often used in the Qur'an to mean polytheism. Allah says: ﴿And do not hold on to the ties with disbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]. This is because the polytheists were previously mentioned alongside the People of the Book. Allah says: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists do not wish that any good be sent down upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105], up to the verse. And: ﴿Those who do not know said, "Why does Allah not speak to us or a sign come to us?" Likewise said those before them, similar to their saying. Their hearts are alike﴾ [al-Baqarah: 118]. So when the discourse was resumed with a statement about the curse upon the People of the Book who conceal (the truth), this was followed by a statement about the punishment of the polytheists as well. The discussion of the resumptive sentence here is therefore like the discussion of the resumptive sentence in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ [al-Baqarah: 159], as to whether it is explanatory (bayani) or merely independent.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "Those who disbelieved" is general, and it includes those who conceal and others. The sentence is a tadhyil (a concluding sentence that generalizes what precedes it), meaning that because it generalizes the ruling after it had been attached to some individuals only. In al-Kashshaf (by al-Zamakhshari), however, the intended meaning of "those who disbelieved" is specifically those who conceal and die upon that, and that He mentioned their curse while they were alive and then cursed them again after death. This is far from the meaning of the verse, because repeating "and disbelieved" serves no purpose, since it could be dispensed with by saying: "And those who died while they were disbelievers." Moreover, this is already implied by the preceding sentence along with its exception. The curse's effect does not appear until after death, so there is no sense in making it two curses. Also, its being followed by His saying: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163] indicates that the intended meaning here is the polytheists, so that the reason for the transition becomes clear.

He said "and mankind, all together" here because the polytheists are cursed by the People of the Book and by all the religious people who affirm the oneness of the Creator. This is unlike those who conceal what was sent down of the clear proofs, for they are cursed by Allah and by the righteous among the people of their own religion, as was mentioned earlier, and they are cursed by the angels. The generality of "mankind" is customary (urfi), that is, it refers to those who are among the people of monotheism (tawhid).

His saying "abiding therein" is an explicit statement of the necessary implication of the lasting curse. The pronoun returns to Hell (jahannam), since it is known from the context, like His saying: ﴿until it (the sun) was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32], and ﴿No! When it (the soul) reaches the collarbones﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 26]. It is also permissible for the pronoun to return to the curse, meaning its effect and its necessary consequence.

His saying ﴿the punishment will not be lightened for them﴾ means: because their disbelief is great, it prevents them from many good things, unlike the disbelief of the People of the Book.

Al-Inzar means al-imhal (granting respite). One says: nazarahu nazratan, meaning he granted him respite. The apparent meaning is that they will not be given respite in the descent of punishment upon them in this world, which is the punishment of killing, since nothing is accepted from them except Islam, not the jizyah (poll tax), unlike the People of the Book. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15], and ﴿On the day We will strike with the greatest striking; indeed, We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16]. That striking is the striking of the Day of Badr.

Some have said that "yunzarun" here is from seeing with the eye (nazar al-'ayn), and it is transitive by itself as it is also transitive with ila (to). That is, Allah will not look at them on the Day of Resurrection, and this is a kinaya (metonymy) for anger and contempt.

The nominal sentence is used here because it indicates permanence and stability, unlike His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah curses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 159]. The intended meaning there is renewal, so that they may not despair of repentance.

﴿And your God is one God; there is no god but Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 161).

The connection is that, after mentioning what awaits them for associating partners with God, namely the curse and eternal abiding in the Fire, He explained that what they disbelieved in and associated with Him is one God. This coordination also strengthens the view I have adopted, that those who disbelieve here refers to the polytheists, because the People of the Book believe in one God.

The address with the plural *kaf* (you) is addressed to everyone who can be addressed at the time of the revelation of the verse or after it, from every reader and hearer of the Qur'an. The pronoun is therefore general, but its primary intended reference is the polytheists, because they were ignorant that the god (*ilah*) can only be one.

In the language of the Arabs, *ilah* (god) means the one who is worshipped (*al-ma'bud*), and for this reason they had many gods, and the word *ilah* was applied to every idol they worshipped. This usage arose from error about the reality of divinity, because worshipping one who can neither benefit himself nor his worshipper is vain and a mistake. Therefore the description of God as "one" here is because He, in reality, is the one truly worthy of worship. The application of *ilah* to the one truly worthy of worship is not a transfer of meaning in the language of Islam; rather, it is an affirmation of the truth.

What occurs in the Qur'an of applying the plural of "gods" to their idols is in the context of refuting their claim, such as ﴿Why then did those whom they had taken as gods besides God, as offerings, not help them? Rather, they strayed from them. That was their falsehood and what they used to invent﴾ (al-Ahqaf: 28). The indicator is the plural form, and for this reason the Qur'an never applies *ilah* in the singular to a worshipped one who has no right to be worshipped. With this you will be spared from exhausting your mind with the far-fetched interpretations that some exegetes engaged in regarding the meaning of ﴿And your God is one God﴾.

The statement about "your God" with *ilah* ("a god") is a repetition so that the description "one" can follow it. The intended meaning is "your God is one," but the word *ilah* was placed between the subject (*mubtada'*) and the predicate (*khabar*) to establish the meaning of divinity in the one spoken of, just as you say, "the scholar of Madinah is an outstanding scholar." It also makes what was originally a predicate take the position of a qualifier (*na't*), which indicates that it is a fixed attribute of the described, because the original function of a qualifier is to be a fixed attribute, while the original function of a predicate is to be a temporary attribute. This is a usage followed in eloquent speech, namely that a noun or verb is repeated after being mentioned so that a description or complement may be built upon it, as in His saying ﴿a single god﴾, and His saying ﴿When they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ (al-Furqan: 72). This was discussed earlier at His saying, may He be exalted, . . . .

The indefiniteness (*tankir*) in *ilah* is for classification (*nau'iyyah*), because what is intended by it is to establish the meaning of divinity, and not for singularity, because singularity is derived from the word "one." This differs from the view of the author of *al-Miftah* regarding His saying ﴿He is only one God﴾ (al-An'am: 19), for he made the indefiniteness in *ilah* indicate singularity and made its explanation by "one" a clarification of unity. The reason is that moving to singularity as the intended meaning of indefiniteness is a path that an eloquent speaker would not choose when he has an alternative.

His saying "there is no god but Him" affirms the meaning of unity and explicitly states it, to remove the possibility that the intended meaning is perfection, as in the expression used for exaggeration, "he is unique in himself" (*nasij wahdih*), or that the intended meaning is the god of the Muslims alone, as the polytheists imagined. Do you not see the saying of Abu Sufyan: "We have al-'Uzza, and you have no 'Uzza"?

The clause "there is no god but Him" conveys unity, because it negates the reality of divinity from anyone other than God, may He be exalted. The predicate of *la* (no) is omitted, and what indicates it is the negation contained in *la*, because every hearer knows that the intended meaning is the negation of this reality. The estimated form is therefore: "there is no god but Him." Scholars of grammar (*nuhat*) were perplexed about estimating the predicate in this phrase, because estimating it as "existing" (*mawjud*) suggests that there may be a god other than Him existing at the time of speaking this sentence. I answer that the intended meaning is the refutation of the existence of any god other than God, in response to those who claimed gods existing now. As for the non-existence of a god in the future, it is known, because kinds that have not been found are not expected to come into existence afterward, since those who affirm gods attribute eternity to them, so an increase in their number is not imagined. It is attributed to al-Zamakhshari that there is no estimated predicate here, and that the original form of "there is no god but He" is "He is a god," so he placed *ilah* first and delayed *huwa* for the sake of restriction by *illa*. They mention that he wrote a treatise on this. This is an artificial construction. The truth, in my view, is that estimated elements have no conceptual implications, so the estimation "there is no god existing" is not equivalent to uttering "there is no god existing." Rather, the estimation serves to reveal the meanings of the speech and bring understanding closer. Otherwise, when the negating *la* negates an indefinite noun, it indicates the negation of the genus, that is, the negation of the realization of the reality. The meaning of "there is no god" is therefore the negation of divinity except God, that is, except for God.

His saying "the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful" are two descriptions of the Pronoun, that is, the One who bestows great blessings and subtle ones. They are two descriptions of praise, and in them there is an allusion to the proof of divinity and of His singularity in it, because the One who blesses is the one worthy of worship, and others do not bestow blessings. The two attributes do not indicate restriction in themselves, but they serve as an implicit reference here, because the speech is directed toward nullifying the divinity of others. Thus the attributes mentioned, which necessitate divinity, carry the meaning of restricting it to Him, may He be exalted. In combining the two attributes "the Most Merciful" and "the Especially Merciful" is what was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Fatihah. Moreover, mentioning the attribute "the Most Merciful" provokes the polytheists, for they refused to describe God as "the Most Merciful," as God related about them when He said ﴿They said, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ (al-Furqan: 60).

Know that His saying "but Him" is an exception from the negated god, meaning that the genus of god is negated except this one individual. In such contexts, the predicate of *la* is often omitted, because the generic negation (*la al-tabri'ah*) is itself sufficient to negate the genus, so the benefit is already obtained from it, and the predicate is not needed except when it is intended to restrict the negation to a state, such as "there is no man in the house except [who is] not..." However, because they disliked leaving the form of a noun and a particle without a predicate, they mentioned a predicate with the noun of *la*. Do you not see that when they found something that could take the place of the predicate in form, they omitted the predicate with *la*, such as the exception in "there is no god but God," and the repetition in the saying: "There is no kinship today nor friendship." Abu Hayyan has far-fetched constructions here.

His saying ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ is an addition in refuting the polytheists, because they said ﴿And what is the Most Merciful?﴾ (al-Furqan: 60).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 164 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of the night and the day, the ships that run upon the sea with that which benefits people, the water that Allah sends down from the sky, giving life thereby to the earth after its death and scattering in it creatures of every kind, the turning of the winds, and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth, are signs for a people who reason.﴾

The position of this verse after the preceding one is the position of the proof after the claim. This is because Allah, exalted is He, declared that the God is one God, with no god besides Him. This is a matter that many people are bound to reject, so it was fitting to establish a proof for the one who is not convinced. Thus He brought these clear indications, which leave the observer no choice but to accept them.

As for *inna* (indeed) here, it serves merely to emphasize the news and draw attention to it. It is also possible that they (the people addressed) were treated as one who denies that there are signs in that for a people who reason, because they did not act in accordance with what those signs indicate.

*Inna* here does not signal a causal explanation of the sentence before it. This is because the condition for that is that the content of the following sentence be suitable to explain the content of the preceding one, such that the position would be that of the conjunctive *fa'* (so). In that case, the occurrence of *inna* suffices in place of the conjunctive *fa'*, as mentioned by Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir (al-Jurjani) in *Dala'il al-I'jaz* (The Proofs of Inimitability). We have expanded upon this matter at the words of the Exalted, ﴿Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you ask for﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61].

The purpose of this verse is to establish the indications of Allah's existence and His oneness. For this reason it is mentioned right after the mention of oneness, because once oneness is established by them, existence is established by necessity.

The verse is suitable as a refutation of the disbelievers of Quraysh, both their materialists (*dahriyy*) and their idolaters (*mushrik*). The idolaters are the primary intended audience. In this verse Allah has affirmed indications that are all clear, drawn from various kinds of created things. Yet despite their clarity, they contain secrets that people vary in grasping, so that each category of rational beings may take from them the measure of proof according to the degree of their intelligence and knowledge.

The word *khalq* (creation) here is a verbal noun, and it was chosen because it encompasses everything in the creatures of the heavens and the earth that contains a lesson. There is also a lesson in the collective form itself, in the formation of the heavens and the earth and the order that unites them. Just as every created thing among them or in them is a sign and a lesson, so too is the whole of their creation. Perhaps the verse alludes to what is termed in *'ilm al-hay'a* (astronomy/cosmology) the solar system, which is the orderly system governing the relations of the earth with the wandering planets, termed here "the heavens."

*Al-samawat* (the heavens) is the plural of *sama'* (sky). When *sama'* is used in the singular, it refers to the lofty atmosphere above us, which appears as if it were a blue dome, the vast expanse in which the stars float. This is the meaning in such words of the Exalted as ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest sky with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5], ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest sky with an adornment of the stars﴾ [al-Saffat: 6], and ﴿And He sent down from the sky water﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22].

When it is used in the plural, it refers to great celestial bodies possessing a particular order, like the earth. These are the great known planets, and those that became known later and those that will become known: Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Sun, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Perhaps these are the seven heavens and the Great Throne. The secret of using the plural *samawat* here, and the singular for *al-ard* (the earth), is that the earth is a single world, whereas its plural in some verses refers to its layers or the divisions of its surface.

The meaning is that in the creation of the totality of the heavens together with the earth there are signs. For this reason *khalq* is given in the singular, and the earth is joined as a conjunct to the heavens, so that the genitive (*al-mudaf*) governs both of them.

The sign in this creation, for a people who reason, is a great sign for whoever knows the secrets of this order and the principles of gravitation (*al-jadhibiyya*) which Allah, exalted is He, placed in the motion of this whole system of planets in a manner that is free from defect or rupture: ﴿The sun is not permitted to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each is floating in an orbit﴾ [Ya Sin: 40]. The greatest of those secrets is their formation in the shape of a sphere. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: 'Umar ibn al-Husam used to read the *Kitab al-Majisti* (the Almagest) to 'Umar al-Abhari. One of the jurists said to them one day: "What are you reading?" Al-Abhari said: "I am explaining His words, exalted is He, ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it?﴾ [Qaf: 6]. I am explaining how it was built." Al-Abhari spoke truly, for whoever plunges deeper into the seas of creation is more knowledgeable of the majesty and greatness of Allah, exalted is He. End of quotation.

I say: Among the wonders of this creation is that Allah, exalted is He, made some of it supply the others with what each needs, so that nothing is diminished from the supplier, because another supplies it with what replaces what it lost. Thus we find existing things interacting: the sea supplies the atmosphere with moisture, from which the water that falls as rain comes, and yet it does not decrease over the long ages, because every river and valley supplies it.

This is a sign for one whose intellect is below this rank, who perceives from the whole of this creation a wondrous spectacle in the rising and setting of the sun, and the appearance and disappearance of the stars in the atmosphere.

As for reflection on what is in them of created things, and what surrounds them of existing things, such as the fixed stars and meteors, and what is on the earth of mountains, seas, rivers, and animals, that belongs to the branches of that collective cosmic structure.

His words ﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾ are a reminder of another great sign, one that is not hidden from any of the intelligent: the alternation of the night and the day, that is, the alternation of the two states of the earth in light and darkness, and what is beneficial to people in the light, and what is beneficial to them in the darkness, through the attainment of their rest and the restoration of their strength, which has been worn down by labor.

In this is a sign for the elite among the intelligent, who know the causes of the alternation of night and day on the earth, and that it is a result of the earth's rotation around the sun each day. For this reason the sign was placed in their alternation, and this implies that each of them is a sign.

*Al-ikhtilaf* (alternation) is a reflexive form derived from *al-khalf*, which means that one thing comes in place of another thing and succeeds it in its position. *Al-khilfa*, with a kasra on the kha', means successor. Zuhayr said:

"Among them the wild cattle and the gazelles walk in succession."

The alternation is attributed to each of the night and the day because each one succeeds the other, so that from each there arise benefits that are the opposite of the benefits of the other, such that if either one lasted, the benefit would turn into harm. ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Allah could bring you light? Will you not then listen?﴾ [al-Qasas: 71] ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Allah could bring you a night in which you rest? Will you not then see?﴾ [al-Qasas: 72].

The alternation also has another meaning that is also intended, which is their difference in length and shortness. At one time they are equal, and at another one exceeds the other. This occurs according to the times of the seasons and according to the places on the earth in the lengths and breadths of the countries, as is established in the science of astronomy. This too is one of the places of lesson, for it is a trace of the wondrous craftsmanship in the shape of the earth and its size with respect to the nearness and distance of the sun.

Thus in the choice of the expression "alternation" here there is a wondrous secret, so that the phrase is suitable for both lessons.

*Al-layl* (the night) is the name for the extent of darkness and blackness that covers an amount of half the sphere of the earth, which is not facing the sun. When the disk of the sun is hidden from half of the earthly sphere by the spherical opposition, the rays of the sun contract from that amount of the earthly sphere, so the light begins to weaken and the original darkness returns, which only the rays of the sun had removed. The contraction of light is gradual, from the time the disk of the sun sets from facing the horizon, beginning at the time of sunset, then the time of the red twilight, then the white twilight, until the blackness becomes complete at the time of 'isha' (night prayer), when the disk of the sun has moved far from the horizon from which its setting began. And whenever the disk of the sun approaches the other horizon, it bestows light from its rays, beginning from the time of dawn, to the brightening of the sky, to the sunrise, to the forenoon, at which point the light of the sun's rays directed toward that half of the sphere becomes complete, gradually.

That light is what is called *al-nahar* (the day). It is the complete light, spread over the surface of the earthly sphere, even though the sphere may be illuminated by the moon during most of its nights with incomplete illumination, and by the light of some stars with a faint illumination that is hardly considered.

This, then, is what is meant by the alternation of the night and the day, that is, their succession and the succeeding of one by the other. Among the eloquence of the science of the Qur'an is that it named this "alternation," a name suited to the succession of accidents (*a'rad*) upon substance (*jawhar*), because it is a thing not inherent in essence. What is inherent in the essence does not alternate. Thus it indicated that the night and the day are not essences, but are accidents, contrary to the belief of the ignorant nations that the night is a black body, as the ancient Egyptians depicted it on some statues, and as Imru' al-Qays said of the night:

"I said to it, when it stretched out its back and let down its rear, and leaned heavily with its chest."

And the Exalted said in Surat al-Shams: ﴿By the day when it displays it, and by the night when it covers it﴾ [al-Shams: 3].

His words *wa al-fulk* (and the ships) are a conjunct to *khalq* and *ikhtilaf*, so it is governed by *fi* (in), meaning: and in the ships. Describing them with the relative clause "which run" is to give the reason for the conjunction, meaning that their being conjoined to the creation of the heavens and the earth is because they are a sign in that they run upon the sea, and a blessing in that they run with what benefits people. As for their running upon the sea, it contains two signs. One is the sign of the creation of the sea in which the ships run, a wondrous and great creation, since it is water covering most of the earthly sphere, together with the creatures in it and the chemical salts and minerals placed in its water so that it does not rot. Rather, on the contrary, it releases to the air beneficial components for the living things on the earth. The second is the sign of the ships' movement in it, for it is water on which walking is naturally impossible. Thus the running of ships is a sign of the inspiration of Allah, exalted is He, to human beings to contemplate this wondrous subjugation by which they were able to traverse the sea as they walk on the earth. The making of ships is among the oldest inventions of mankind; Allah, exalted is He, inspired it to Nuh (peace be upon him) in the earliest ages of humanity.

Then Allah, exalted is He, subjected to the ships the periodic winds, which are winds that blow in the morning toward one direction and in the evening toward another, along the coasts. They arise from the heating of the sun's rays in the middle of the day on the air over the land, so that the air becomes light, and then air comes from the direction of the sea to replace that land air that has risen. Thus a gentle wind arises from the direction of the sea. The opposite occurs after sunset, when a wind comes from the land toward the sea. This wind is beneficial to fishermen and merchants, and it is more regular in some locations than in others.

He also subjected to the ships seasonal winds, which blow in one direction during some months of the year and in the opposite direction during other months. They arise from the direction of the heat of the sun's rays on the places lying between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn on the earthly sphere, when the sun moves from the equator toward the Tropic of Cancer and toward the Tropic of Capricorn. Thus this wind occurs twice a year. It is abundant on the shores of Yemen and Hadramawt and in the Indian Ocean, and is called the trade wind.

As for its being a blessing, it is because in the subjugation there is benefit for trade, travel, warfare, and other things. For this reason He said "with that which benefits people," aiming at generality together with brevity.

The fulk (ships) here is necessarily a plural, because the lesson lies in its multiplicity. The singular and the plural have the same form, so the broken plural (taksir) is a matter of convention. The original singular is fulk, with two dammas, like 'unuq (neck). It was pluralised to fulk, like 'urb (Arabs), 'ujm (non-Arabs) and usd (lions). The singular was then lightened by sukun (vowelling the middle radical with a sukun), because a sukun on the middle radical with a damma on the first radical is a derivative of the form with a damma on the middle radical, and the purpose was lightness, as al-Radi explained. Thus the singular and the plural became identical in pronunciation. It was also said that the singular is fatha on the first radical and sukun on the lam, while the plural is damma on both, as in asad and usud (lion, lions) and khashab and khushub (wood, pieces of wood), after which the lam was given sukun for lightness. The eloquent usage for both the singular and the plural is damma on the fa' with sukun on the lam. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And make the ship﴾ [Hud: 37], ﴿the laden ship﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 119], ﴿and the ship that runs in the sea﴾, and ﴿and the ship runs upon the sea by His command﴾ [al-Hajj: 65], and ﴿until, when you are in the ship and they sail﴾ [Yunus: 22]. Furthermore, the original singular is masculine, as God, exalted is He, says: ﴿the laden ship﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 119]. It may be feminine if it is interpreted as meaning "the vessel." God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And He said: Embark therein﴾ [Hud: 41] and ﴿while it runs with them﴾ [Hud: 42], all of which come after His saying ﴿and he was making the ship﴾ [Hud: 38].

It seems that this is what Ibn al-Hajib relied upon, since he counted the word fulk among the words that are feminine without a ta' or an alif. He said in his poem:
"And the fulk runs, and it is in the Qur'an [feminine]"

This is because the criterion is its usage as feminine, even if its femininity is by interpretation. It has been said that for the singular alone it is permissible to have damma on the lam together with damma on the fa', and this was read so in an irregular (shadh) reading, but the view is weak. Al-Kawashi said: "It is with damma on the lam also, for both the singular and the plural." This is rejected, since the lexicographers did not state it, and there is no need for it. He probably said it by analogy with the sukun form.

In God's bestowal of favour through the running of the ships on the sea there is evidence for the permissibility of sailing the sea without necessity, such as sailing for jihad, pilgrimage and trade. Malik in al-Muwatta' related, and the compilers of the Sahihs followed him, the hadith of Umm Haram bint Milhan in the chapter on encouragement to jihad, the second chapter of al-Muwatta', from Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he went to Quba', would enter upon Umm Haram bint Milhan, and she would feed him. She was married to 'Ubada ibn al-Samit. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon her one day and slept, then woke up laughing. She said: 'I said: What makes you laugh?' He said: 'Some people of my community were shown to me as warriors in the way of Allah, sailing the middle of this sea like kings on thrones.' I said: 'Ask Allah to make me one of them.' So he prayed for her." The hadith continues.

[Page 82]

In the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'We sail the sea and carry with us only a little water.'" The hadith continues. Based on this, what is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, that he wrote to 'Amr ibn al-'As that he should not carry the army of the Muslims on the sea, is interpreted as caution and avoidance of recklessness. I think he intended by it the fear that the reinforcements of the Muslims in their campaigns would be delayed, because ships may arrive late if the winds do not assist them, the winds moving contrary to what the ships desire. Also, carrying a large number on the ships of that age is a likely cause of drowning, and the number of Muslims at that time was small in comparison to the enemy, so it is not appropriate to expose them to danger. This is from considering the public interest in specific circumstances, so it is not used as evidence for general rulings for people.

When 'Umar died, Mu'awiya asked 'Uthman's permission, and he permitted him to sail. So he sailed for the campaign of Cyprus, then for the campaign of Constantinople. In the campaign of Cyprus the interpretation of the Prophet's (ﷺ) vision in the hadith of Umm Haram became manifest. It has been said that when 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz assumed the caliphate he forbade sailing, and then the people sailed after him. It is related from Malik that he disliked a woman's travel on the sea for the pilgrimage and jihad. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "The hadith of Umm Haram refutes this report, but his companions interpreted it as meaning that he disliked it out of fear that women would see the nakedness of men, since it is difficult to avoid that. So his companions restricted it to the ships of the people of the Hijaz, because they are small and narrow and people crowd in them, and the route from Medina to Mecca by land is possible and easy. As for large ships, like the ships of the people of Basra, in which concealment is possible and crowding is less, there is no harm in a woman travelling on them according to Malik."

﴿and what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾ is coordinated with the nouns that precede it. It is brought as a relative pronoun so that a clause is coordinated with a clause, and the sentence thus retains the purpose of lesson and blessing. The first clause, "what Allah sends down from the sky of water," is a reminder of the lesson, because the clause evokes the situation in a way that words like "rain" and "downpour" do not. The attribution of the sending down to Allah is because He is the one who created the causes of the descent of water by His making things at the creation of this world according to a firm order.

The singular sama' (sky) is the atmosphere and air surrounding the earth, as was mentioned just before, and it is what all listeners see.

[Page 83]

The aspect of the lesson is that the nature of water which waters the earth is to spring forth from it. So making water descend upon it from its opposite, the sky, is a wondrous lesson. In the verse there is also a scientific lesson for those who come from the people of natural science. The making of water descend from the sky indicates that water vapour turns into water in the atmospheric sphere when it meets the zamharirī layer (the very cold layer), and this layer becomes frigid when the heat of the sun's rays decreases. Perhaps in some of the heavenly bodies, especially the moon, there are cold airs by which frost occurs in the high atmosphere, so it has an effect in producing coldness in the upper atmosphere, and therefore the sending down of water is attributed to them metaphorically (majaz 'aqli). It may be supported by a narrated hadith: that "rain descends from a sea beneath the Throne," meaning that the element of wetness forms there and reaches the neighbouring regions until a little of it reaches our atmosphere. When the earth meets it, water forms from their union. God has said: ﴿and He sends down from the sky mountains in which is...﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. Perhaps these are the mountains of the moon's sphere. It is established in astronomy that the moon's day lasts fifteen days and its night is likewise, so a great change occurs in it from intense heat to intense cold. When the period of intense cold is the period of its facing the earth, it produces the element of coldness in the earth's atmosphere.

God's saying ﴿So He gives life by it to the earth﴾ is coordinated with the clause by fa' (then), because the earth's life follows swiftly upon the descent of water. Both the act and the fa' are a place of lesson and a place of blessing. "Life" is used for the movement of the growing powers in the earth, which is the power of plants, metaphorically, because life in its true sense is the manifestation of growing powers in animals, so the earth is compared to it.

If we take life as literal in the manifestation of the powers of growth, and we take plants as described by life and death literally, then His saying "He gives life by it to the earth" is a metaphor in the attribution (majaz 'aqli), and what is intended is giving life to what the earth is meant for, which is vegetation.

In the juxtaposition of "sky" and "earth," and of "gives life" and "death," there are two antitheses (tibaq).

God's saying ﴿and He spread therein from every creature (dabba)﴾ is coordinated either to "sent down," so it is a second relative clause, and with regard to what was coordinated before it to the clause, a third clause; or it is coordinated to "gives life," so it is a second coordinated item to the clause. In either case it is a sign and a separate blessing. If you make it coordinated to the clause, then "min" in "min kulli dabba" is explanatory (bayaniyya), and it is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), a settled adverbial. If you make it coordinated to what was coordinated to the clause, which is "gives life," then "min" in "min kulli dabba" is partitive (tab'idiyya), and it is a loose adverbial (zarf laghw), meaning: He made to multiply therein, in number, from every kind of the kinds of creatures, in the sense that every kind of creature spreads many of all its kinds. So the indefinite in "dabba" is for generalisation, meaning: from all the kinds, not restricted to one kind over another.

The original meaning of "al-batth" (spreading) is to scatter what was hidden, and from it come "batth al-shakwa" (to disclose a complaint) and "batth al-sirr" (to reveal a secret), that is, to make it manifest. The Bedouin woman said: "I have revealed to you my concealed matters and fed you my condiment." In the hadith of Umm Zar': "The sixth said: 'He does not put his hand in to know the batth,'" meaning he does not search for the secret of his wife so that she would divulge it to him. She likened the search to inserting the hand to extract what is hidden. Then it was used metaphorically for the spreading of a thing after it had been latent, as in this verse. It was also used for general dispersal. Al-Hamasi said:
"Why did they not prepare me for one like me, when they lost each other, while in the earth there are scattered a viper and a scorpion?"

The spreading of creatures, if its being coordinated to the verb "sent down," is the creation of kinds of creatures on the earth, and so it is expressed by "spreading" to depict that wondrous and abundant creation. So the meaning is: "And He created and spread therein from every creature."

If "and spread" is coordinated to "gives life," then the spreading of creatures is their dispersal in pastures after having been emaciated and crouching, and the dispersal of their offspring by birth. All of this is dispersal and spreading, which Labid described with his saying:
"Provided with the springs of the stars, and the thunder-cloud's pouring rain has watered it, its generous and abundant downpour."
"The tops of the eryngo grew, and the gazelles and ostriches brought forth their young between the two sandy hills."

The verse is more concise than the two verses of Labid and fuller in meaning. God's saying ﴿and what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾ is more concise than the first verse, and His saying ﴿So He gives life by it to the earth after its death﴾ is more concise than his saying "the tops of the eryngo grew," more general, and more skilful in its metaphor of life. His saying ﴿and He spread therein from every creature﴾ is more concise than his saying "and they brought forth their young..." while being more general, since it is not restricted to gazelles and ostriches.

"Dabba" is whatever crawls upon the face of the earth. The word "kull" (every) indicates that the intended meaning is all the kinds, so the possibility that "dabba" means specifically those with four legs is excluded.

God's saying ﴿So He gives life by it to the earth after its death, and He spread therein from every creature﴾ has gathered the principles of the science of natural history, namely the three generations: minerals, plants and animals, in addition to what is in the rest of the verse, before and after, of scientific indications relating to the science of astronomy, the science of physics, physical geography and the science of atmospheric events.

[Page 85]

God's saying ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾ is coordinated to what follows "fi" (in), and it is among the signs of the existence of the Creator and the greatness of His power, because the blowing of the wind and its stillness are a sign, and the variation of its directions is a sign. Were it not for the Wise Maker who deposited the secrets of creation, the wind would not have blown or been still, and its directions would not have varied, but would have continued from one direction only. This is the place of lesson. In the turning of the winds there is also a place of blessing, namely that its blowing is sometimes needed by people in a place for cooling from heat, or for bringing weapons, or for driving away insects such as locusts and the like, or for bringing benefits such as birds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 164 (part 3 of 3):

The people of Makkah may need the winds to change their directions, so that a cold wind comes after a hot one, or a moist wind after a dry one, or so that a wind blows toward the coast and the people of the ships return from their voyages or from fishing. All of this is a place of blessing, and it is what all people observe. For the people of knowledge ('ilm), there is also a more wondrous place of lesson ('ibrah) and blessing in this. The cause of the variation of the winds is that God surrounded the terrestrial sphere with air that He created along with it. Living beings breathe by means of it. It encompasses the whole sphere, its sea and its land, is attached to its surface, and occupies above its surface a height at which living beings could not survive if they ascended to its top. God created it composed of two gases, nitrogen (al-nitrujin) and oxygen (al-uksujin), and in it there is another accidental component, which is a portion of the water vapour that rises to it from the evaporation of the seas and the moisture of the earth by the rays of the sun. This vapour is a fine gas that is not seen. This air is receptive to heat and cold through the proximity of something hot or cold. Its heat comes from the rays of the sun and from the rising of the earth's heat when the sun warms it. Its cold comes from the weakness of the sun's heat and from the cold of the ice rising from the zamharir (the frigid upper atmosphere), which increases with the height of the atmosphere, as has been explained earlier.

Since heat by its nature expands the parts of things, and so they become rarefied through that expansion, as is established in chemistry (al-kimya'), and cold is the opposite, when there is air in a hot region, such as the desert, and air in a cold region, such as a frozen place, a difference in density arises between the two airs. The light one, which is the hot one, rises upward, and the dense one descends downward. As the light air rises, it leaves a void which the dense air fills, seeking balance. Thus a movement arises that is called wind (rih). If the movement is gentle, because the difference between the two airs is slight, the movement is called a breeze (nasim). If the movement intensifies and speeds up, it is a whirlwind (zawba'a).

[Page 86]

So "wind" is the genus of this movement, and the breeze, the whirlwind and the storm (za'za'a) are its species.

Among the benefits of these winds is their assistance in forming clouds and moving them from one place to another, and in purifying the atmospheric sphere of the harmful germs that settle in it. These two matters are a place of lesson and blessing for the people of knowledge.

The expression "variation" (tasrif) was chosen here rather than words such as "alteration" (tabdil) or "difference" (ikhtilaf), because it is the word whose meaning suits describing the state of the winds. Tasrif is a form of the verb with the intensive pattern (tafil) from the root ṣ-r-f, for emphasis. You have already learned that the origin of wind is the turning of some air toward one place while other air is turned into the place that the first one vacated. So it is permissible to read it as: "and the variation of the winds by God the Exalted." The attribution of the variation to the winds, although the winds came into being through that variation, is then the attribution of a name to what has come about at the time of the attribution, as in His saying ﴿wa-yal'anuhumu al-la'inun﴾ (and those who curse will curse them) (al-Baqarah: 159). This is a kind of majaz (figurative usage) of the first type. Alternatively, one may take tasrif in the sense of change (taghyir), that is, the alteration of a wind from one direction to another. In that case the literal meaning remains, but the scientific inimitability (i'jaz 'ilmi) is lost, and the choice of the word tasrif rather than taghyir would be because it is lighter.

The plural "winds" (al-riyah) is used here because the variation requires multiplicity, since whenever the direction of a wind changes, it has become a wind other than the one that preceded it. The majority of readers (al-jumhur) read al-riyah in the plural, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read al-rih in the singular, intending the genus. A definite noun denoting a genus gives generality whether it is singular or plural, so both readings are equivalent. It has been said that the plural form riyah is used more often for winds of good, and the singular rih more often for winds of evil. They relied on what they transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), that when he saw the wind he would say: "O God, make them winds (riyahan), not a wind (rihan)." This is a distinction of predominance (taf-riqat aghlabiyya), and otherwise the singular has been used in place of the plural and the reverse in the reading of many reciters. The hadith is not authentically established. On the basis of the distinction, the best explanation for it is that the wind that benefits people comes gently and its waves are interspersed with gaps, so no harm results from it. Because of the gaps between its gusts, it is put in the plural. As for the violent wind, it leaves no gap for people, so it is made a single wind. This is taken from the words of al-Qurtubi.

Riyah is the plural of rih. The word rih is of the form fi'l, with the first consonant vowelled with kasra and its middle radical originally waw, which became ya' because of the kasra, as is shown by their plural arwah. As for their plural riyah, the change of the waw to ya' in it is like its change in the singular, because of the kasra, as they say diymah and diyam, and hilah and hiyal, both of which derive from the waw-type roots.

[Page 87]

His saying ﴿wal-sahabi al-musakhkhar﴾ (and the clouds made subservient) is coordinated (ma'tuf) either with ﴿tasrifi al-riyah﴾ (the variation of the winds) or with al-riyah. The sense would then be: "and the variation of the subservient clouds," that is, moving them from one place to another.

This is both a lesson ('ibrah) and a favour (minnah). The lesson lies in their coming into being after they were not, in their being made subservient, and in their being in the open air. The favour lies in all of that. Their formation is a favour, their being made subservient and moved from one place to another is a favour, and their being between the sky and the earth is a favour, because rain falls from them onto the earth from a height, which allows the water to penetrate into the ground. And if they were at the surface of the earth, people would suffocate. This is what appears to everyone. There is also a lesson and a favour in this for the people of knowledge. Their formation is a lesson for them, since it forms from the rising of the vapours of the seas and the moisture of the earth, which the rays of the sun evaporate. For this reason, the air is never free of water vapour, as we have said. However, water vapour is transparent and gaseous. When it comes into contact with a cold surface, it becomes heavy and condenses, becoming mist, dew or clouds. It condenses because the particles of vapour gather together, and so the air's capacity to carry them diminishes. Then, when their gathering is complete, they fall as rain. Because the vapour that rises into the atmosphere comes mostly from the sea, since the sea covers the largest part of the terrestrial sphere, the clouds most often form over the seas. People used to think that all rain came from sea water, and that the trunks (kharatim) of the clouds hang down to the waves of the sea, draw water from it, and then descend as rain. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

May it give drink to Umm 'Amr every last night,
Dark cloud-trunks, whose water is pouring down.
They drank from the water of the sea, then rose up,
Among green seas, whose roar is heard.

Al-Badi' al-Asturlabi said:

I present to your noble assembly, though what I give
Is only what I have gained of your bounties:
Like the sea that the clouds rain upon, which
Has no merit over it, since the water is its own.

Were it not for the winds making the clouds subservient, moving them from place to place, rain would fall only into the seas.

The place of favour in this lies in their formation, so that they carry water to give life to the earth, in their being made subservient so that they may move, and in their being between the sky and the earth. They are made subservient between sky and earth until the water in the atmosphere is complete, and the cloud grows heavy and rain falls when the air no longer has the capacity to bear it. God the Exalted said: ﴿wa-yunshi'u al-sahaba al-thiqal﴾ (and He brings into being the heavy clouds) (al-Ra'd: 12).

His saying the Exalted, ﴿la-ayatin li-qawmin ya'qilun﴾ (surely there are signs for a people who use their reason), means: indications (dala'il). The discussion of the word "sign" (ayah) and the plural "signs" (ayat) has already been presented.

[Page 88]

The plural ayat is used because everything mentioned, the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is coordinated with it, consists of signs.

If the intent is to infer from them the existence of God alone, they are clear indications, and this is a refutation of the dahriyyun (materialists who deny a Creator) among the Arabs. Their mention after ﴿alladhina kafaru wa-matu wa-hum kuffar﴾ (those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers) (al-Baqarah: 161), where those meant are the polytheists, completes the category of the sects of the Arabs. Then His saying after that ﴿wa-min al-nasi man yattakhidhu min duni Allahi andadan﴾ (and among people are those who take other than God as equals) (al-Baqarah: 165) returns to the polytheists. This interpretation goes back to inferring the existence of the Maker from the world, which is a well-known argument in the books of kalam (scholastic theology). If, however, the intent is to infer from these indications the oneness of God, which entails His existence, and this is the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿li-qawmin ya'qilun﴾ (for a people who use their reason), since inferring the existence of the Maker from these indications and their like does not indicate perfection of intellect, unlike arguing from them for the oneness of God. Also, it was mentioned after His saying ﴿wa-ilahukum ilahun wahid la ilaha illa Hu﴾ (your God is one God; there is no god but He) (al-Baqarah: 163). And also because the mass of the Arabs were polytheists, not atheistic dahriyyun who deny God (al-mu'attilun).

The sufficiency of these indications in refuting the polytheists lies in the fact that they did not claim that the idols had power to create, as His saying indicates: ﴿afaman yakhluqu kaman la yakhluqu afala tadhakkarun﴾ (Is He who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then remember?) (al-Nahl: 17). If the intent is to infer from these effects the oneness of God against the nations that affirm that the gods share in creation, such as the Magians of Persia and the polytheists of the Greeks, then the way these signs indicate the oneness is that this wondrous order in the things mentioned, that arrangement in their formation, their interaction, their passing and returning, and their set times, all of it is a proof that they have a wise Maker, characterized by perfect knowledge, power, wisdom, and the attributes that divinity requires. Undoubtedly, the God described with these attributes must be one, since the polytheists acknowledged that the laws of creation and the governance of the world are the act of God the Exalted. They did not claim that their associates had created anything. For this reason God the Exalted said: ﴿afaman yakhluqu kaman la yakhluqu afala tadhakkarun﴾ (Is He who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then remember?) (al-Nahl: 17). In Surah al-Naml, He mentioned inference from some of what is here to show that there is no god with God. So the aim is to remind them that true divinity is absent from their associates. As for the scholarly method of inference, it is through the demonstrative proof known in kalam as the proof of mutual exclusion (burhan al-tamana'). It will come at His saying ﴿law kana fihima alihatun illa Allahu lafasadata﴾ (Had there been in them gods other than God, both would have been corrupted) (al-Anbiya': 22) in Surah al-Anbiya'.

The qawm (people) are a group of men, and the term is also applied to a man's tribe, as 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib said:

Had my people's spears made me speak...

[Page 89]

It is also applied to a nation (ummah). The phrase "a people who use their reason" was used instead of "those who use their reason" or "the reasonable," because applying the attribute to the word qawm implies that this attribute is a disposition (sajiyyah) among them, and one of the completers of their peoplehood. For tribes and nations have characteristics that distinguish them and by which they are known, as God the Exalted said: ﴿wa-ma hum minkum wa-lakinnahum qawmun yafraqun﴾ (They are not of you, but they are a people who are fearful) (al-Tawbah: 56). This recurs in many places in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. The meaning is: in that are signs for those whose disposition is reason. This is an allusion that those who did not benefit from these signs do not have firm minds, and reason is not an established faculty (malakah) in them. This was repeated in Surah Yunus.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 165 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals (rivals) whom they love as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah.﴾

This is coordinated (*'atf*) with ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth…﴾ (al-Baqarah: 164) and what follows it, because that verse contained the statement that a people who use their reason reasoned from the creation of the heavens and the earth, and what is conjoined to it, that Allah is One, and so they affirmed His oneness. It is therefore appropriate to conjoin to it the condition of those who were not guided by this, and who took partners for themselves despite the presence of these clear proofs. Those who took others besides Allah are the ones spoken of just before, in His words, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers…﴾ (al-Baqarah: 161), and the verses that follow.

His words "from the people" (*min al-nas*) are a fronted predicate (*khabar muqaddam*). We have already mentioned the reason for predicating it and the benefit of fronting it at His words, ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 8). Its coordination with the mention of the proofs of divine oneness, the fronting of the predicate, and the fact that the predicate is "from the people," indicate that it expresses astonishment at their condition.

The word *man* in His words "those who take" (*man yattakhidh*) refers to a group, not a single individual, as shown by the return of the pronoun in His words, ﴿whom they love as they love Allah﴾.

By "equals" (*al-andad*) is meant equals in divinity and worship. The discussion of *nidd* (with a kasra on the nun) has already passed at His words, ﴿So do not set up equals to Allah while you know﴾ (al-Baqarah: 22). His words "besides Allah" (*min dun Allah*) mean "alongside Allah," because *dun* indicates a barrier in the sense of "behind."
