So when they say, "he took it *dun Allah*," the meaning is that he singled it out and turned away from Allah. When they say, "he took it *min dun Allah*," the meaning is that he made it a kind of barrier between himself and Allah, that is, he associated it with Allah, because association (*shirk*) entails turning away from Allah during the times one is occupied with worshipping that partner.

[p. 90]

His words "besides Allah" (*min dun Allah*) are a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *yattakhidh*. His words "they love them" (*yuhibbunahum*) are a comprehensive apposition (*badal ishtimal*) of *yattakhidh*, because taking (*ittikhadh*) includes love and worship. It is also permissible for it to be a descriptive clause (*sifa*) of *man*. It is permissible too for it to be a descriptive clause of *andadan*, but this is weak, because it creates ambiguity in the pronouns, since it could be understood that the lovers are the equals, who love those who took them. The more evident reading is that it is a circumstantial clause of *man*, to make their condition in this taking appear reprehensible: the taking of equals that they set up alongside Allah in love and in belief concerning them.

By "equals" here, and in their other occurrences in the Qur'an, is meant the idols, not the leaders, as has been said. The pronoun of the plural of rational beings in His words "they love them" refers back to them, because once they believed in the divinity of the idols, the idols became deserving of the pronoun for rational beings. Moreover, this usage is attested in Arabic even without this interpretation. The love (*mahabba*) here is used in its literal meaning, which is the inclination of the soul toward what it finds beautiful, through seeing, hearing, or the attainment of a benefit, whether real or imagined. This is because love is not confined to the soul's inclination toward visible things, contrary to some lexicographers. The inclination toward a good character (*khuluq*, with a damma on the kha') and toward a good deed and perfection is a love more intense than love for the beauties of the essence. Thus these meanings share the name "love" in view of what is present in the soul, regardless of the cause of its presence.

The truth is that love relates to the remembrance of a person, to the benefit that comes from him, and to his good reputation, even if one has not seen him. Thus we love Allah for the attributes of perfection we know of Him, and for the blessing, grace, and mercy that reach us from Him. We love His Messenger for the perfection we know of him, for what has reached us through him, and for the eagerness we know he has for our guidance and our salvation. We love our forefathers, we love our predecessors among the scholars of Islam, and we love the wise and the reformers of the earlier and later generations. And how well Abu Madyan expressed this meaning:

*"How many a lover has loved without having seen, and the love of a youth through hearing is a higher rank."*

The opposite of all this is hatred.

Some people claimed that attributing love to Allah is a metonymy (*majaz mursal*) for obedience and veneration, by the relation of necessity, because the obedience of a lover to the beloved is a customary consequence of it. Al-Ja'di said:

*"Had your love been true, you would have obeyed Him; indeed, the lover is obedient to the one he loves."*

Or it is a metonymy by ellipsis, the estimated sense being: "they love the reward of Allah or His blessing," because love does not attach to the essence of Allah, either because it is one of the types of will, and will attaches only to what is possible, which is the view of some theologians, or because it is the seeking of what is agreeable, and pleasure is not attained except through perceptible things. Both proofs are plainly weak, as al-Fakhr (al-Razi) has explained. Based on this preference among the uses of the word "love" here, the comparison refers to equality in intensity.

[p. 91]

Some have made love for Allah a metonymy, and also made love in His words "they love them" a metonymy, and this is the approach taken in the *Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari's commentary). Its basis is that the original principle in comparing one noun to a similar one is to compare an individual of the reality to another individual of it. But you have learned that this is not definitively required.

His words "as the love of Allah" indicate the equality of the two loves, because the basic principle of comparison is equality. The addition of "love" to the Name of Majesty (*ism al-jalala*) is an addition to the object, so it has the status of a passive verb (the object is made the subject). Thus the omitted agent is omitted here for the sake of generality, that is: whatever way you estimate the love of any lover for Allah, the love of these people for their equals is equal to that love. The reason for this generality is that the conditions of the polytheists vary. Some of them worship the equals, whether idols, jinn, or stars, while acknowledging the existence of Allah and placing the equals on a par with Him, calling them partners or children of Allah. Others assign to Allah the supreme divinity and make the equals intercessors before Him. Others restrict themselves to worshipping the equals and forget Allah. He said: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves﴾ (al-Hashr: 19). Among these were the Sabians of the Arabs, who worshipped the stars. Yet there are also lovers of Allah apart from these and from some of them. Thus the love of these for their equals is equal to the love of the lovers of Allah for Him, in the sense of its being equally vivid in the minds of the lovers on both sides. So one may estimate: "they love them as one ought to love Allah," or "they love them as the monotheists love Allah," or "they love them as they love Allah." Some exegetes have followed each of these forms of estimation. The truth is that the estimated element is the common measure, which is what we estimated at the beginning of the discussion.

Know that the intent is to deny that they love the equals at all, not to deny that they equal them with the love of Allah. The qualification with the likeness of the love of Allah was added to make it ugly, and as a call to the lowliness of the minds of its holders. It also serves to awaken the eyes of most polytheists, who claimed that the idols were their intercessors, as their accounts on this are repeated frequently in the Qur'an. They were alerted that they equated the love of the follower with the love of the one followed, and the love of the created with the love of the Creator, so that perhaps they would awaken. When they begin to examine what the idols deserve of love, and seek the causes of love, they find it missing, just as Abraham (peace be upon him) said: ﴿O my father, why do you worship what neither hears nor sees, and does not avail you in anything?﴾ (Maryam: 42), together with the added reason for denunciation in this situation.

[p. 92]

His words "but those who believe are stronger in love for Allah" mean: stronger in love for Allah than the love of the people of equals for their equals, despite the firmness they show in it, and stronger than the love of some of them for Allah among those who acknowledge Allah alongside the equals. This is because the love of all these lovers, however firm they are in their beloveds, is a love detached from proof, and it does not reach the level of those whose belief is sincere and supported by demonstration. Also, their belief in their gods is for immediate purposes, such as fulfilling needs and removing afflictions. By contrast, the love of believers for Allah is love for His essence and for His being worthy of love, and then there follow purposes, the greatest of which are the far purposes of raising ranks and purifying the soul.

The intent is to disparage the polytheists even in their belief in their gods, for they often turned away from them when they did not find in them what they hoped for.

Thus the locus of equality between the two loves, indicated by the comparison, differs from the locus of preference indicated by the comparative form here. This is because equality looks to the intensity of love at the moment it arises, while preference looks to the firmness of love and its not departing. This is taken from the *Kashshaf*, and is stated explicitly in al-Baydawi's commentary, with additional refinement. This makes you independent of the many possibilities and far-fetched interpretations that arose here for some exegetes and some commentators on the *Kashshaf*.

It is narrated that Imru' al-Qays, when he wanted to fight the Banu Asad after they killed his father Hujr, their king, passed by Dhu al-Khalasa, the idol that was at Tabala between Makkah and Yemen. He sought the decision by the arrows that were beside the idol, and the arrow of prohibition came out three times. So he broke those arrows, threw them at the face of the idol, cursed it, and recited:

*"Had you been, O Dhu al-Khalasa, avenged, like me, and had your buried elder been like me, you would not have forbidden the killing of enemies, falsely."*

Then he marched against the Banu Asad and defeated them.

It is also narrated that a man of the Banu Malkan came to Sa'd, the idol on the coast of Jeddah, and he had camels with him. His camels bolted when they saw the idol. The Malkani became angry at the idol and struck it with a stone, saying:

*"We came to Sa'd so that he might gather our scattered unity, but Sa'd scattered us, so we are not of Sa'd."*

*"Is Sa'd anything but a rock in a desert of the earth, which calls to neither error nor guidance?"*

[p. 93]

The comparative form (*ism al-tafdil*) was introduced here through the word *ashadd* (more intense). Al-Taftazani said: "He preferred *ashadd hubban* over *ahabb* because *ahabb* became common for preferring one beloved over another. You say: 'he is more beloved to me.' And in the Qur'an: ﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your clan, the wealth you have acquired, the trade you fear will decline, and the dwellings you are pleased with are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger…﴾ (al-Tawbah: 24)."

He means that the verb *ahabba* is the common usage, and the verb *hubba* is rare. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding confusion, they restricted each in usage to particular places. They said *ahabba* (in the sense of "to love") and "he is loving" (*muhibb*) and "more intense in love" (*ashadd hubban*). They said *habib* from *habba*, and *ahabb ilayya min habba*, also.

* * *

﴿And if only you could see those who did wrong when they see the punishment, that all power belongs to Allah, and that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

This is coordinated with His words ﴿And among the people are those who take…﴾. This is because, since that statement explained the reprehensible error of their taking equals to Allah despite the manifest proofs of His oneness, so that "and among the people" indicated astonishment at their condition, as we have mentioned, and since the enormity of their conduct was increased by their taking equals to Allah and loving them as they love Him, it was fitting to shift from that to the outcome of this conduct. He mentioned their end from this action and described the awfulness of their condition in the Hereafter, just as He had disparaged their condition in this world.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 165 (part 2 of 2):

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read ﴿ولو ترى﴾ with a feminine (taʾ) prefix. Here the address is to an unspecified person and encompasses everyone who hears this address, because their state has reached the utmost extreme of horror and evil, so that even if people were present, it would be apparent to all of them. It is also possible that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ. In both readings, ﴿الذين ظلموا﴾ is the object of ﺗﺮى. ﴿إذ﴾ is a temporal adverb. The seeing (ruʾya) is visual in both the first and second readings, because in both places it relates to things that are seen, and because that is the proper meaning. However, the time of the two seeings differs. The meaning is: "If you could see them now, when they see the punishment on the Day of Resurrection," i.e., "If you could see their state now."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿يرى الذين ظلموا﴾ with a yaʾ prefix. Then ﴿الذين ظلموا﴾ is the subject of ﻳﺮى, and the meaning is again: "If they could see now." The object of ﻳﺮى is omitted because the context indicates it, and its implied object is: "If they could see their punishment," or "If they could see themselves." Alternatively, ﴿إذ﴾ is a noun other than an adverb, meaning: "If they were to look at that time now," so that it is a badal ishtimal (inclusive apposition, a substitute that includes its referent in meaning) for ﴿الذين ظلموا﴾.

﴿الذين ظلموا﴾ refers to those who took rivals (andad) besides God. This is an use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun (al-ʾiẓhar fi maqam al-ʾiḍmar), so that it encompasses these polytheists and others. Their taking of rivals is called wrongdoing (ẓulm) because it is a transgression against several rights. They transgressed against the right of God Most High, which is that He be made One, and they transgressed against those whom they made rivals to God among rational beings, such as the angels and ʿIsa. They also transgressed against those such as Wadd, Suwaʿ, Yaghuth, Yaʿuq and Nasr. It is narrated in the Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas that they were righteous men of the people of Nuh; when they died, their people made images of them and then worshipped them. Likewise, al-Lat, of whom the Arabs claim that he was a man who kneaded sawiq (a flour porridge) for the pilgrims, and that his original name was al-Lattu with a shaddah on the taʾ. Thus they wronged them, because they were the cause of a terror that befalls them from questioning on the Day of Resurrection, as God Most High said: ﴿And when God says, "O ʿIsa son of Maryam, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?'"﴾ And He said: ﴿And on the Day when He gathers them all, then says to the angels, "Did these worship you?"﴾ [Saba': 40], and He said: ﴿And on the Day when He gathers them and what they worship besides God, then He says, "Did you lead these My servants astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 17].

They wronged themselves in this by exposing themselves to mockery in this world and to punishment in the Hereafter. They also wronged their descendants and their people who follow them in this error, so that the centuries and generations pass upon it. For this reason, the object of ﻇﻠﻤﻮا is omitted, for the purpose of generality. You may also take ﻇﻠﻤﻮا to mean "associated partners" (ashraku), as is common in the Qur'an. God Most High said, concerning Luqman: ﴿Indeed, associating partners with God is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. On this reading, the verb is treated as intransitive, because it has become like a title.

The sentence ﴿والذين آمنوا أشد حبا لله﴾ is a parenthetical clause (muʿtarida). Its purpose is to honor those who believed, indicating that their love for God has become stronger than the love of those who worshipped the rivals. This is like the saying of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab to the Prophet ﷺ: "You are dearer to me than my own self which is between my two sides."

The construction "wa-law tara" and similar ones, such as "law raʾayta," are among the expressions that have become like proverbs, and so they were constructed in abbreviated form. Such expressions occur frequently in the Qur'an.

The answer (jawab) of ﻟﻮ is omitted for the purpose of magnification and to emphasize the terror of the matter, so that the mind may roam in every possible direction in imagining it. Similar examples are: ﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾ [al-Anʿam: 93], ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ [al-Anʿam: 27], and ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains could be moved﴾ [al-Raʿd: 31]. Al-Marzuqi said, commenting on the verse of al-Shamaydhar al-Harithi:

"It has distressed me what war has caused between us, sons of our paternal uncles, were it a matter near at hand."

The omission of the answer in such places is more eloquent and more indicative of the intended meaning, as evidenced by the fact that when a master says to his servant, "If I come to you," and then falls silent, there crowd upon the servant such threatening thoughts that would not crowd upon him if he had explicitly specified a particular kind of punishment. The estimated answer, according to the reading of Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, is: "You would see a great matter," and according to the reading of the majority: "They would see a great matter."

Concerning His words "that the power": the majority read it with a fatha on the hamza of "anna," and it is a badal ishtimal from "al-ʿadhab" (the punishment) or from "alladhina zalamu," because that punishment is part of their conditions. The separation between the substituted noun and its substitute does not harm, because the substitute is long. It is also possible that there is an omitted lam of causation, so that the estimate is: "Because the power belongs to God entirely," and the causation is by the content of the estimated answer, i.e., "You would see what is terrifying, because it is the punishment of God, and power belongs to God entirely."

The word "jamiʿan" (entirely) is used to mean abundance, so the power of anyone else is as nothing. This is like the use of words of abundance to mean power, and words of paucity to mean weakness, as in the verse of Taʾabbata Sharran:

"Rarely complaining to the afflicted one who befalls him, much love, scattered in dwellings and paths."

He meant: intense passion.

Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿إن القوة﴾ (with a kasra on the hamza of "inna") as a resumption of explanation (istiʾnaf bayani, a resumed sentence that answers an implied question), as if a questioner had said: "What do I see, and what is this terror?" So it is said: "Indeed the power..." It is not correct for it to be causal here in the way that could replace the fa' (the particle of consequence), as in the verse of Bashshar:

"Indeed that success lies in early rising."

This is because that usage occurs in positions where what precedes it needs a cause, so that the causal particle is explicit in that meaning.

Ibn 'Amir alone read ﴿إذ يُرَوْنَ العذاب﴾ with a damma on the yaʾ, meaning: when God shows them the punishment, in the sense of His words: ﴿Thus God shows them their deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167]. "Jamiʿan" is in the accusative as an emphasis (tawkid) of "al-quwwa" (the power), meaning: the whole of the category of power belongs to God. This is an intensification, indicating that the power of others is not taken into account. Thus the meaning of "jamiʿ" here is the same as that of the particle of total inclusion (lam al-istighraq) in His words: "All praise is for God."

Law has come in such a construction with a present-tense conditional verb. It has been stated among the majority of grammarians that "law" is for the past tense conditional, and that the present-tense verb, when it is the conditional after it, is turned to the meaning of the past when one wishes to evoke a past state. When the present verb after it is specifically about the future, the majority interpret it as past in all its positions, and they strain themselves in many of them, as happened to the author of al-Miftah. Al-Mubarrad and some of the Kufans held that "law" is a particle with the meaning of "in" (if), for mere conditionality, not for the impossibility of the condition. Ibn Malik, in al-Tashil and al-Khulasa, held that this is permissible but rare, meaning relative rarity in relation to the occurrence of the past tense. Otherwise it occurs in the Qur'an and in eloquent Arabic.

[Page 96]

The truth is that the impossibility which "law" indicates is of varying degrees, and it returns to the fact that its condition and its answer are assumed hypothetically, and the occurrence of the condition is not intended. Sometimes it is possible to occur, and sometimes it is impossible. For this reason, it is better to express it by non-occurrence (intifaʾ) rather than impossibility (imtinaʾ), because impossibility suggests that it cannot occur, whereas non-occurrence is more general. The fact that the verb after it is past or present is not for the purpose of measuring the degree of impossibility, but for different purposes that vary according to the implications of the two verbs in their positions within conditionals and other contexts. Often one intends to link a condition with "law" in the future, as in the verse of Tawba:

"Even if our echoes were to meet after our death, and between our two graves of earth a desert plain,
the echo of my voice would remain, even if I were a decayed bone, responding to the echo of Layla's voice, rejoicing and delighted."

This is explicit about the future, and this verse is similar to it.

[Page 97]

Qur'an 2:166–167 (Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, part 1 of 2)

﴿When those who were followed will disown those who followed, and they will see the punishment, and their means will be cut off from them.﴾ ﴿And those who followed will say: "If only we had another return, we would disown them as they have disowned us." Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them, and they will not be ones who exit the Fire.﴾

"Idh" (when) is an adverbial of time that stands in apposition of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*, a substitution in which the second term includes the first) for the adverbial of time in "idh yaraw al-'adhab" (when they see the punishment). That is, if you were to see them in these two states, at the moment of seeing the punishment, which is a dreadful state, it includes the state of their taking [others as equals] and disowning one another, which is a shameful state. Both occur at one time.

The verb after "idh" here is in the past tense, although its meaning is future, because it will occur in the Hereafter. This is to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence. If you hold that "idh" does not go beyond being an adverb of the past, according to the view of the majority of grammarians, then it is used in the sense of confirmation, like the past verb that accompanies it, and so it serves to reinforce the sense of following. If, however, you hold that it may be an adverb of the future, which is the more correct view, and which al-Tashil attributes to some grammarians, then there are many examples of this in the Qur'an. Allah says: ﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:152), where "idh tahussunahum" is the thing promised. And He says: ﴿But they will soon know﴾ (Ghafir 40:70), ﴿when the shackles are around their necks﴾ (Ghafir 40:71). In that case, the figurative usage lies in the verb "tabarra'a" alone.

[Page 98]

*Tabarru'* (disowning) is the act of seeking *bara'a* (freedom from something), which is distancing oneself from a matter whose nearness is harmful. For this reason it is said: *tabarra'a* when each one distances the other from a consequence that is certain or expected.

"Alladhina ittubi'u" (those who were followed), in the passive voice, refers to those who misled the polytheists and set up for them the idols (*ansab*), such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy. The phrase "ittubi'u" implies that they were calling people to follow them. This is supported by His words after it: ﴿so we would disown them as they disowned us﴾, meaning: We will requite them for their breaking of promises.

The meaning of their disowning them is their disavowal of the promises of benefit in the Hereafter which they had made to them in this world, and of intercession on their behalf, and their turning them away from joining them when they rushed to them.

The clause "wa ra'aw al-'adhab" (and they see the punishment) is a circumstantial clause: that is, they disown them at the time of seeing the punishment. The meaning of their seeing it is that they saw its causes and knew that it was prepared for those who misled people. So they began to distance themselves from their followers, lest the punishment of those who misled should be due upon them. It is also possible that "seeing the punishment" is a metaphor for experiencing the torment, as in His words: "the punishment will touch them." The placement of the circumstantial clause here is very fitting, and it serves in place of the new sentence (*isti'naf*) that the context requires, because the listener would wonder about the cause of this disowning, since it is strange. Therefore it is said: "they saw the punishment." When the aim was to depict the state and to magnify the horror, one turned away from a new sentence to a circumstantial clause, fulfilling the right of magnification, and dispensing with the new sentence through the circumstantial clause, since their position is close. It cannot be coordinated with the clause "tabarra'a," because its meaning would then become a repetition of the meaning of the clause "If only you could see those who did wrong when they see the punishment" [2:165]. It would thus become merely an emphasis of it, and what we have mentioned of its particular features would be lost. The pronoun in "ra'aw" is an ambiguous pronoun referring to both groups: those who followed and those who were followed.

The clause "wa taqatta'at bihim al-asbab" (and their means were cut off from them) is coordinated with the clause "tabarra'a," meaning: and when their means were cut off from them. The pronoun in the genitive refers to both groups.

*Taqatu'* (being cut off) is a strong severance, because its root is the reflexive form of *qatta'ahu* with the doubled letter, which is the intensive of *qata'a* without the doubling.

*Asbab* is the plural of *sabab*, which is the rope that is stretched out for one to climb upon a palm tree or a roof. His words "wa taqatta'at bihim al-asbab" are a figurative representation (*tamthiliyyah*): it likens their condition at the disappointment of their hopes, when they did not find the bliss for which they had toiled all their lives, and which they had believed had come at its appointed time, but instead found punishment in its place, to the state of one who climbs a palm tree to pick the fruit for which he has toiled all year long, and then the rope is cut as he climbs, so he falls and perishes. Likewise, all of them at that time knew that there was no salvation for them, and so their state is like that of one who falls from a height with no hope of safety.

[Page 99]

This figurative representation is remarkable, because the likened condition comprises seven things, each of which is fit to be a likeness of one of the things contained within the likening image. They are: the likening of the polytheist in his worship of idols and his following of their religion to the one who climbs, by the common factor of striving; the likening of worship and the acceptance of the gods of it to the connecting rope; the likening of bliss and reward to the fruit at the top of the palm tree, since one can reach it only after a long time, which is the duration of life; the likening of life to the palm tree in height; the likening of being deprived of reaching bliss to the cutting of the rope; the likening of disappointment to distance from the fruit; and the likening of falling into punishment to the destructive fall. It is rare in figurative representations that the parts of the compound likeness are fit to be independent likenesses. What occurs in this respect is in few things, such as the verse of Bashshar, who is regarded as an example of excellence:

*As if the dust of the battle above our heads,
and our swords, were a night whose stars are falling.*

There are not more than three likenesses in this verse.

The preposition "ba" in "bihim" expresses accompaniment (*mulabasah*): that is, the means were cut off while being connected to them, meaning that they fell. This meaning is the locus of the likeness, because if the rope were cut without being connected to the climber, there would be no harm in it, since he would hold on to the palm tree and seek another means by which to descend. For this reason he did not say "wa taqatta'at asbabuhum" or something similar. Whoever says that "ba" here means "'an" (from), or expresses causality, or transitivity, has strayed far from eloquence. It is with this "ba" that the meaning of the figurative representation of one climbing the palm tree with a rope is established. This meaning is lost in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*The means of love and longing were cut off
on the evening we passed Hama and Shayzar.*

His words "wa qala alladhina ittaba'u" (and those who followed said) are more apparent in the place where a pronoun would be expected, because the two pronouns of the third person preceding it refer to the totality of both groups. Moreover, the relative clause "alladhina ittaba'u" includes an indication of provoking the anger of those who were followed and stirring up their regret, and this is a psychological punishment which doubles the physical punishment. His words point to this: ﴿Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them﴾.

The "law" (if only) in His words "law anna lana karratan" (if only we had another return) is used to express wishing (*tamanni*). This is a common usage of the particle "law," whose original function is conditional, its condition and its answer being omitted, and it was borrowed for expressing wishing through the relation of necessity, because a thing that is difficult to attain is often wished for. The verbal noun takes the place of the condition and answer. The sense of the sentence is: If a return were established for us, we would disown them. The accusative "ma kana" stands as the answer, as the answer of the wish. This usage became so widespread that it became one of the meanings of "law," and it is a common usage. Its origin is a compound metonymy (*majaz mursal murakkab*), and in this verse it is strengthened by the accusative of the answer.

[Page 100]

*Karrah* (return) is the coming back to a place in which the one returning had been; it is one instance of the verb *karr*. For this reason it is used in the Qur'an for the return to this world, because it is a return to a previous place. The complement of the word *karrah* is omitted here because it is evident.

The "ka" in "kama tabarra'u" (as they disowned) is a particle of comparison, used here in the sense of requital, because it is the nature of a requital to resemble the act being requited. Allah says: ﴿And the requital for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (al-Shura 42:40). This "ka" is close to the "ka" of causation, or is its origin. The clearest instance of the meaning of requital outside the Qur'an is the verse of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

*I shake with it in the assembly of the tribe its side,
as he shook my side with the noble she-camels of the stallion.*

The distinction between this "ka" and the "ka" of causation is that if what follows it is of the same kind as the thing compared, as in the verse and in the verse of Abu Kabir, it is taken to mean requital. If, however, what follows it is of a different kind, and what follows the "ka" is the motive for the comparison, it is taken to mean causation, as in His words: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:198).

The meaning is that they wished to return to this world after they had come to know the truth, and their wrongdoing had been revealed to them. Then the leaders would call them to their religion, and they would not respond, in order to quench their rage against their leaders who had forsaken them, and so that the leaders would suffer disappointment and humiliation, just as the leaders had disappointed them in the Hereafter.

If you ask: When they return, they will all return knowing the truth, so the leaders will not call them to the worship of idols, so that they would then refuse their call? I say: The door of wishing is wide. The followers wished to return to this world knowing the truth, while the leaders would return to their former misguidance. It may also be said that the followers accuse their leaders of having misled them knowingly, since the followers, who are usually deluded by their ignorance, know that the leaders knew. So if they all returned to this world, the leaders would return to misleading as they had before, with knowledge, on the basis that what they saw on the Day of Resurrection had not frightened them, because they had been certain of the final destination from before. And the followers would return knowing the deception of the leaders, so they would not obey them.

The clause "kadhalika yurihim Allahu a'malahum hasaratin 'alayhim" (Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them) is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) and a summation (*fadhlakah*) for the story of the leaders disowning their followers.

The demonstrative in His words "kadhalika yurihimu Allah" (thus Allah shows them) refers to the showing that is derived from "yurihim," in the style of His words: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:143).

[Page 101]

The meaning is that Allah shows them the consequences of their deeds with a showing like this one, since there can be no showing of their deeds that is more striking than this. This is an instance of likening a thing to itself with a difference of consideration, as if it were intended that He show them their deeds in a shameful manner, and no state more shameful than this was found. This is like predicating the subject by its own word, as in "my poetry is my poetry," or by its synonym, as in "foolishness is like its name." Its details were mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:143).

The showing here is visual, and for this reason "hasaratin 'alayhim" (regrets for them) is a circumstantial clause describing "a'malahum" (their deeds). The meaning of "yurihimu Allahu a'malahum" is: He shows them what are the consequences of their deeds, because deeds are not perceived by sight, since they have passed away, so they do not sense them.

*Hasrah* (regret) is grief accompanied by remorse and anguish. Its verb is of the pattern of *fariha* (to rejoice). Its derivation is from *hasr*, which means uncovering, because uncovering the reality is the cause of remorse over what has passed through the lack of caution about it.

His words "wa ma hum bikharijina mina al-nar" (and they will not be ones who exit the Fire) are a circumstantial clause or a parenthetical statement at the end of the speech, intended as a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) for the content of "kadhalika yurihimu Allahu a'malahum hasaratin 'alayhim." This is because if they are not going to exit the Fire, it becomes clear that their wish to return to this world, and the disappointment that befalls them at the hands of their leaders, serves no purpose except to inflict the pain of regrets upon them. Otherwise, they remain in the Fire in any case.

The verse departs from the verbal sentence, which would be "wa ma yakhrujuna" (and they do not exit), to the nominal sentence, in order to indicate that this ruling is established and is among their attributes. The fronting of the predicated subject here carries no particular nuance, except that it is the default in such expressions with a nominal sentence, since this structure cannot be achieved otherwise. Thus the fronting does not indicate exclusivity, for the reason you have known. Moreover, fronting the subject before a derived predicate does not, according to the majority of the scholars of rhetoric, indicate exclusivity. Exclusivity is posited only in fronting before a verbal predicate. For this reason the author of *al-Kashshaf*, following Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir, stated explicitly that the position of the pronoun here is like its position in the verse of al-Mu'adhdhal al-Bakri:

*They spread the felt for every swift and sturdy one,
and every sleek fast horse that outstrips the rest.*

Its indication is of the strength of their command over what is attributed to them, not of exclusivity. End of quote.

The author of *al-Miftah* claimed that fronting the subject before a derived predicate may indicate exclusivity.

Like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And you are not against us a mighty one﴾ [Hud: 91], ﴿And I am not one to drive away those who have believed﴾ [Hud: 29], and ﴿And you are not over them a guardian﴾ [al-An'am: 107]. The correct view is that placing the subject (al-musnad ilayhi) before the predicate that is a derived noun (al-musnad al-mushtaqq) does not, in itself, convey restriction (al-takhsis). Restriction may be understood from some of its uses through contextual indicators (al-qara'in), but there is nothing in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they are not going to come out of the Fire﴾ that conveys restriction or calls for it.

[Page 97]

Qur'an 2:166–167 (Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, part 1 of 2)

﴿When those who were followed will disown those who followed, and they will see the punishment, and their means will be cut off from them.﴾ ﴿And those who followed will say: "If only we had another return, we would disown them as they have disowned us." Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them, and they will not be ones who exit the Fire.﴾

"Idh" (when) is an adverbial of time that stands in apposition of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*, a substitution in which the second term includes the first) for the adverbial of time in "idh yaraw al-'adhab" (when they see the punishment). That is, if you were to see them in these two states, at the moment of seeing the punishment, which is a dreadful state, it includes the state of their taking [others as equals] and disowning one another, which is a shameful state. Both occur at one time.

The verb after "idh" here is in the past tense, although its meaning is future, because it will occur in the Hereafter. This is to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence. If you hold that "idh" does not go beyond being an adverb of the past, according to the view of the majority of grammarians, then it is used in the sense of confirmation, like the past verb that accompanies it, and so it serves to reinforce the sense of following. If, however, you hold that it may be an adverb of the future, which is the more correct view, and which al-Tashil attributes to some grammarians, then there are many examples of this in the Qur'an. Allah says: ﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:152), where "idh tahussunahum" is the thing promised. And He says: ﴿But they will soon know﴾ (Ghafir 40:70), ﴿when the shackles are around their necks﴾ (Ghafir 40:71). In that case, the figurative usage lies in the verb "tabarra'a" alone.

[Page 98]

*Tabarru'* (disowning) is the act of seeking *bara'a* (freedom from something), which is distancing oneself from a matter whose nearness is harmful. For this reason it is said: *tabarra'a* when each one distances the other from a consequence that is certain or expected.

"Alladhina ittubi'u" (those who were followed), in the passive voice, refers to those who misled the polytheists and set up for them the idols (*ansab*), such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy. The phrase "ittubi'u" implies that they were calling people to follow them. This is supported by His words after it: ﴿so we would disown them as they disowned us﴾, meaning: We will requite them for their breaking of promises.

The meaning of their disowning them is their disavowal of the promises of benefit in the Hereafter which they had made to them in this world, and of intercession on their behalf, and their turning them away from joining them when they rushed to them.

The clause "wa ra'aw al-'adhab" (and they see the punishment) is a circumstantial clause: that is, they disown them at the time of seeing the punishment. The meaning of their seeing it is that they saw its causes and knew that it was prepared for those who misled people. So they began to distance themselves from their followers, lest the punishment of those who misled should be due upon them. It is also possible that "seeing the punishment" is a metaphor for experiencing the torment, as in His words: "the punishment will touch them." The placement of the circumstantial clause here is very fitting, and it serves in place of the new sentence (*isti'naf*) that the context requires, because the listener would wonder about the cause of this disowning, since it is strange. Therefore it is said: "they saw the punishment." When the aim was to depict the state and to magnify the horror, one turned away from a new sentence to a circumstantial clause, fulfilling the right of magnification, and dispensing with the new sentence through the circumstantial clause, since their position is close. It cannot be coordinated with the clause "tabarra'a," because its meaning would then become a repetition of the meaning of the clause "If only you could see those who did wrong when they see the punishment" [2:165]. It would thus become merely an emphasis of it, and what we have mentioned of its particular features would be lost. The pronoun in "ra'aw" is an ambiguous pronoun referring to both groups: those who followed and those who were followed.

The clause "wa taqatta'at bihim al-asbab" (and their means were cut off from them) is coordinated with the clause "tabarra'a," meaning: and when their means were cut off from them. The pronoun in the genitive refers to both groups.

*Taqatu'* (being cut off) is a strong severance, because its root is the reflexive form of *qatta'ahu* with the doubled letter, which is the intensive of *qata'a* without the doubling.

*Asbab* is the plural of *sabab*, which is the rope that is stretched out for one to climb upon a palm tree or a roof. His words "wa taqatta'at bihim al-asbab" are a figurative representation (*tamthiliyyah*): it likens their condition at the disappointment of their hopes, when they did not find the bliss for which they had toiled all their lives, and which they had believed had come at its appointed time, but instead found punishment in its place, to the state of one who climbs a palm tree to pick the fruit for which he has toiled all year long, and then the rope is cut as he climbs, so he falls and perishes. Likewise, all of them at that time knew that there was no salvation for them, and so their state is like that of one who falls from a height with no hope of safety.

[Page 99]

This figurative representation is remarkable, because the likened condition comprises seven things, each of which is fit to be a likeness of one of the things contained within the likening image. They are: the likening of the polytheist in his worship of idols and his following of their religion to the one who climbs, by the common factor of striving; the likening of worship and the acceptance of the gods of it to the connecting rope; the likening of bliss and reward to the fruit at the top of the palm tree, since one can reach it only after a long time, which is the duration of life; the likening of life to the palm tree in height; the likening of being deprived of reaching bliss to the cutting of the rope; the likening of disappointment to distance from the fruit; and the likening of falling into punishment to the destructive fall. It is rare in figurative representations that the parts of the compound likeness are fit to be independent likenesses. What occurs in this respect is in few things, such as the verse of Bashshar, who is regarded as an example of excellence:

*As if the dust of the battle above our heads,
and our swords, were a night whose stars are falling.*

There are not more than three likenesses in this verse.

The preposition "ba" in "bihim" expresses accompaniment (*mulabasah*): that is, the means were cut off while being connected to them, meaning that they fell. This meaning is the locus of the likeness, because if the rope were cut without being connected to the climber, there would be no harm in it, since he would hold on to the palm tree and seek another means by which to descend. For this reason he did not say "wa taqatta'at asbabuhum" or something similar. Whoever says that "ba" here means "'an" (from), or expresses causality, or transitivity, has strayed far from eloquence. It is with this "ba" that the meaning of the figurative representation of one climbing the palm tree with a rope is established. This meaning is lost in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*The means of love and longing were cut off
on the evening we passed Hama and Shayzar.*

His words "wa qala alladhina ittaba'u" (and those who followed said) are more apparent in the place where a pronoun would be expected, because the two pronouns of the third person preceding it refer to the totality of both groups. Moreover, the relative clause "alladhina ittaba'u" includes an indication of provoking the anger of those who were followed and stirring up their regret, and this is a psychological punishment which doubles the physical punishment. His words point to this: ﴿Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them﴾.

The "law" (if only) in His words "law anna lana karratan" (if only we had another return) is used to express wishing (*tamanni*). This is a common usage of the particle "law," whose original function is conditional, its condition and its answer being omitted, and it was borrowed for expressing wishing through the relation of necessity, because a thing that is difficult to attain is often wished for. The verbal noun takes the place of the condition and answer. The sense of the sentence is: If a return were established for us, we would disown them. The accusative "ma kana" stands as the answer, as the answer of the wish. This usage became so widespread that it became one of the meanings of "law," and it is a common usage. Its origin is a compound metonymy (*majaz mursal murakkab*), and in this verse it is strengthened by the accusative of the answer.

[Page 100]

*Karrah* (return) is the coming back to a place in which the one returning had been; it is one instance of the verb *karr*. For this reason it is used in the Qur'an for the return to this world, because it is a return to a previous place. The complement of the word *karrah* is omitted here because it is evident.

The "ka" in "kama tabarra'u" (as they disowned) is a particle of comparison, used here in the sense of requital, because it is the nature of a requital to resemble the act being requited. Allah says: ﴿And the requital for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (al-Shura 42:40). This "ka" is close to the "ka" of causation, or is its origin. The clearest instance of the meaning of requital outside the Qur'an is the verse of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

*I shake with it in the assembly of the tribe its side,
as he shook my side with the noble she-camels of the stallion.*

﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality, and to say about Allah what you do not know.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), serving as a conclusion to the disfiguring of the states of the people of polytheism, in both the roots and the branches of their religion. The discourse on this began with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 161], up to the end of the verse. He mentioned their disbelief in summary, then refuted it with His saying: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163], and argued for its refutation with His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] and the verses that follow. Then He described their disbelief with His saying: ﴿And among the people are those who take other than Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], and described their state and their regret on the Day of Resurrection. Here He describes some of the evils of the religion of the people of polytheism concerning what they forbade for themselves from what Allah had brought forth for them from the earth. The appropriateness of mentioning it here is that it comes after what was contained in the argument for Allah's oneness and the bestowal of His favour upon them, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] up to His saying: ﴿and what Allah sends down from the sky of water, by which He gives life to the earth after its death, and disperses therein every kind of moving creature﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]. It is thus a preparation and a summary of what follows of the legislation of Islam concerning foods and other matters, which will come from His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172].

Thus the address "O mankind" (yā ayyuhā al-nās) is directed to the polytheists, as is the usual manner of the Qur'an's address with "O mankind."

The imperative in His saying ﴿eat of what is on the earth﴾ is used in the sense of reproach for abandoning that, and it is neither obligatory nor merely permissive, since the disbelievers are not addressed with the branches of the Sharia. Thus His saying "eat" is a preparation for what follows it: (﴿and do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾).

His saying "lawful and good" (ḥalālan ṭayyiban) is an oblique rebuke for their folly in what they burdened themselves with, forbidding for themselves good blessings, fabricating against Allah. It also contains an allusion to the reason for its permissibility in Islam, and an instruction to the Muslims regarding the attributes of actions which are the criterion of lawfulness and unlawfulness.

The intended purpose is the refutation of what they invented of forbidding the eating of the baḥīra, the sā'iba, the waṣīla, and the ḥāmī, and what Allah related of them in Surat al-An'am in His saying: ﴿And they say, "These are cattle and crops, forbidden; none may eat of them except whom we wish," by their claim﴾ [al-An'am: 138] and the verses that follow.

It was said that it was revealed concerning Thaqīf, the Banū 'Āmir ibn Ṣa'ṣa'a, Khuza'a and the Banū Mudlij, who forbade for themselves from the cattle, that is, from what is mentioned in Surat al-An'am.

The "min" (from) in His saying "of what is on the earth" is partitive (li-l-tab'īd), and the partitiveness refers to the eaten thing being a part of every kind, and not to the eaten thing being some kinds without others, because that would defeat the purpose of the verse. So "what is on the earth" is general, and the description "lawful and good" specifies it, so the forbidden things whose prohibition is established by the Book or the Sunna are excluded.

His saying "lawful and good" is two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl) of the relative "mā." The first is to explain the legal ruling, and the second to explain its cause, because the good is by nature something souls seek out to benefit from. So when goodness is established, lawfulness is established, because Allah is gentle with His servants and has not forbidden them what contains their pure or predominant benefit.

The meaning of "good" here is what sound and upright perception accepts, free of aberration, from souls that desire what is agreeable, perfect, or preponderant, such that its consumption does not bring bodily or spiritual harm. The meaning of "good" linguistically will come at His saying: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4] in Surat al-Ma'idah.

In this description there is a great meaning alluding to the principle of lawful and unlawful. For this reason our scholars said: the ruling on things about which the Sharia has stated nothing is that the basis of harms is prohibition and the basis of benefits is permissibility. This is with regard to the thing itself, regardless of its accidents, such as the attachment of another's right to it which necessitates its prohibition, since prohibition in that case is a ruling for the accident and not for the thing accidented.

"Good" has been interpreted here as what the Sharia permits, but this is far-fetched, because it leads to repetition, and because it requires using a term in a meaning not customary among them.

His saying "and do not follow the footsteps of Satan": the pronoun refers without doubt to the people, and they are the polytheists who are constantly engaged in what is forbidden. As for the believers, their share of it is warning and admonition.

Following footsteps is a figurative expression (tamthīliyya). Its origin is that a traveller who sees the traces of the footsteps of travellers follows that path, knowing that the one before him only walked on it because it leads to the goal. So he likened the follower who has no guide except the one he follows, while he thinks the path leads to the goal, to one who follows the footsteps of travellers. This figure became so common that they say: "He follows the footsteps of so-and-so," meaning he imitates him and obeys him.

"Khuṭuwāt" (footsteps), with a ḍamma and then a sukūn, is the plural of khuṭwa, like ghurfa and qubḍa, with the first letter vowelled with ḍamma, in the sense of the thing stepped, grasped, or held. So it means the distance between the two feet when a walker walks, as he steps it. As for khaṭwa with a fatḥa on the kha', it is one instance of the verbal noun of khaṭw, and it is also used for the thing stepped, by the usage of the verbal noun for the object.

The majority read "khuṭuwāt" with ḍamma then sukūn, on the basis of the sound plural. Ibn 'Āmir, Qunbul from Ibn Kathīr, and Ḥafṣ from 'Āṣim read it with ḍamma on the kha' and ṭā' by ittibā' (vowel assimilation). Ittibā' is equal to sukūn in lightness on the tongue.

Imitating Satan is letting the soul act upon what he whispers to it of human thoughts. Satans are existent perceptible beings who have a connection with human souls, perhaps like the connection of gravity with the celestial bodies and of magnetism with iron. When an orientation occurs from one of the two to the other, through causes not known, evil thoughts arise in the soul. If the responsible person lets his soul follow them and does not restrain them with his will and resolve, he realises them in his action; if he holds it back and turns it away from that, he overcomes them. For this reason Allah placed in us intellect, will, and power, and completed that for us with the religious guidance, as help and protection against responding to them, lest the satanic thoughts mislead us so that we see as good what is not good. For this reason the hadith says: "Whoever intends an evil deed but does not do it, Allah records it with Him as one complete good deed," because when he intends it, that is when the satanic power dominated him, and when he turns away from it, that is when the will for good prevailed over it. The same applies to good thoughts, which arise from angelic orientations. When the two callers contend in our souls, we need, in overcoming, to seek help from our intellects, our opinions, our power, and God Almighty's guidance to us. That is what al-Ash'arī called "kasb" (acquisition), and upon it reward and punishment are based.

The lam in "al-shayṭān" is for the genus (li-l-jins), and it may be for specific reference (li-l-'ahd), with the intended meaning being Iblīs, who is the origin of the satans and their commander. Everything arising from the whispering of the satans goes back to him, because he is the one who took the first steps.

His saying: "Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy." The particle "inna" here is for mere emphasis of the report, because the enmity between Satan and humans is known and established among believers and polytheists alike. They used to throw pebbles at the jamarāt during the Hajj, believing they were stoning Satan. Or "inna" is for emphasis, by treating one who is not doubtful about the ruling as if he were doubtful or denying, since they, by following satanic suggestions, are like one who denies his enmity. As 'Abda said:

"Indeed, those you see as your brothers,
their hearts' rage is healed only when you are struck down."

Whatever the case, "inna" here conveys the meaning of causation and linkage in such a context, and does the work of "fa" (so), which is its function after commands and prohibitions, as stated in Dalā'il al-I'jāz. Similar is Bashshār's saying:

"Go early, my two companions, before the midday heat,
indeed success lies in going early."

This has been mentioned before.

He was an enemy because the element of his creation is different from the element of human creation, so his contact with a human produces what is contrary to what suits him. The Qur'an often depicts Satan in the form of an enemy who lies in wait for us, to stir the motive of opposition in our souls, so that we do not become deceived when we find evil thoughts within ourselves and think they arose in us only because they are beneficial to us, since they were generated from our own souls. For this same reason the soul is also depicted for us in the form of an enemy in such situations.

The meaning of "mubīn" (clear): manifest in enmity, from abāna, which is in the sense of bāna (to be evident), not from abāna whose hamza is causative meaning "to make clear." Because Satan does not make his enmity manifest to us; rather he dresses his whispering in the garb of sincere advice or of bringing what is agreeable. For this reason Allah named him a protector: ﴿Whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss﴾ [al-Nisa': 119]. However, Allah has exposed him, so no Muslim is deceived by his deceptions, even while following his footsteps: he knows they are his harmful whisperings, but his desire overcomes him, his resolve is weak, and his religious commitment is thin.

His saying: "He only commands you to evil and immorality" is an explanatory resumption (istinā'f bayānī) of His saying "Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy," and it amounts to being a cause of the cause, since the listener asks about the establishment of enmity given that there was no prior knowledge and given the distance between us and him. So it is said: "He only commands you," that is, because he commands you only to evil, and so on; that is, he makes attractive to you what harms you, because his enmity is a hidden matter which we know from the traces of his actions.

The "command" in the verse is a metaphor for whispering and beautifying, since no one hears command forms from Satan. You may also take the clause "He only commands you" as a figure (tamthīl), by likening his state and theirs in beautification and whispering, and in their receiving of what he whispers to them, to the state of the commander and the commanded. The word "yaʾmuru" (commands) is then used in its literal sense, indicating, together with the mention of the symbol, that they have no will and do not control their own affairs. In this there is added reproach of their state and a stirring up of enmity between Satan and them.

"Al-sū'" (evil) is harm, from sā'ahu sū'an. The verbal noun is with fatḥa on the sīn, while al-sū' with ḍamma on the sīn is a noun used for the verbal noun.

"Al-faḥshā'" (immorality) is a noun derived from faḥuša, when something exceeds the known limit in one's action or speech. In Arabic usage it has been specialised for what exceeds the bounds of propriety and whose denunciation is great, because the whisperings of the soul lead either to harm, such as drinking wine or killing that leads to vengeance, or to shame and disgrace, such as fornication and lying. So the conjunction here is a conjunction of two things different in concept and essence without doubt, by the testimony of language, even if they are identical in the legal ruling, since both fall under the description of the forbidden or the major sin. As for their coinciding together in some sins, such as theft, no attention is paid to it, like other universals that coincide.

His saying: "and to say about Allah what you do not know" refers to what the polytheists and the people of error invented of the rites of worship, and of attributing to the religion of Allah things which Allah did not command. He singled it out for conjunction, although it is part of evil and immorality, because it includes the greatest of the major sins, which is polytheism and fabrication against Allah.

The object of *ta'lamun* is omitted; it is a pronoun referring back to *ma*, and it is the connecting pronoun of the relative clause. The meaning of *ma la ta'lamun* ("what you do not know") is: you do not know that it comes from God. This is shown by the context of His words *'ala Allah* ("against God"), meaning: you do not know that it pleases Him and that He commands it. The way to know God's pleasure and command is to refer to revelation and to what branches from it, namely analogical reasoning (*qiyas*) and the evidences of the Law (*adillat al-shari'a*) that are derived from its sources by induction.

For this reason the usul scholars (*al-Usuliyyun*, the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence, *usul al-fiqh*) said: a qualified jurist (*al-mujtahid*) may say, concerning what his independent reasoning has led him to by way of analogy, "This is the religion of God," but he may not say, "God said this." This is because the mujtahid has acquired a definitive premise drawn by induction from the Law, upon which there is a consensus (*ijma'*), namely that he must act upon what his reasoning has led him to, by acting on it in giving legal opinions (*fatwa*), in judgment (*qada'*), and in his own personal conduct. So when he issues a legal opinion on it and reports it, he has said "against God" only what he knows pleases God, according to what he is obligated to do on the basis of probable judgment (*zann*).

﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality, and to say about Allah what you do not know.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), serving as a conclusion to the disfiguring of the states of the people of polytheism, in both the roots and the branches of their religion. The discourse on this began with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 161], up to the end of the verse. He mentioned their disbelief in summary, then refuted it with His saying: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163], and argued for its refutation with His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] and the verses that follow. Then He described their disbelief with His saying: ﴿And among the people are those who take other than Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], and described their state and their regret on the Day of Resurrection. Here He describes some of the evils of the religion of the people of polytheism concerning what they forbade for themselves from what Allah had brought forth for them from the earth. The appropriateness of mentioning it here is that it comes after what was contained in the argument for Allah's oneness and the bestowal of His favour upon them, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] up to His saying: ﴿and what Allah sends down from the sky of water, by which He gives life to the earth after its death, and disperses therein every kind of moving creature﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]. It is thus a preparation and a summary of what follows of the legislation of Islam concerning foods and other matters, which will come from His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172].

Thus the address "O mankind" (yā ayyuhā al-nās) is directed to the polytheists, as is the usual manner of the Qur'an's address with "O mankind."

The imperative in His saying ﴿eat of what is on the earth﴾ is used in the sense of reproach for abandoning that, and it is neither obligatory nor merely permissive, since the disbelievers are not addressed with the branches of the Sharia. Thus His saying "eat" is a preparation for what follows it: (﴿and do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾).

His saying "lawful and good" (ḥalālan ṭayyiban) is an oblique rebuke for their folly in what they burdened themselves with, forbidding for themselves good blessings, fabricating against Allah. It also contains an allusion to the reason for its permissibility in Islam, and an instruction to the Muslims regarding the attributes of actions which are the criterion of lawfulness and unlawfulness.

The intended purpose is the refutation of what they invented of forbidding the eating of the baḥīra, the sā'iba, the waṣīla, and the ḥāmī, and what Allah related of them in Surat al-An'am in His saying: ﴿And they say, "These are cattle and crops, forbidden; none may eat of them except whom we wish," by their claim﴾ [al-An'am: 138] and the verses that follow.

It was said that it was revealed concerning Thaqīf, the Banū 'Āmir ibn Ṣa'ṣa'a, Khuza'a and the Banū Mudlij, who forbade for themselves from the cattle, that is, from what is mentioned in Surat al-An'am.

The "min" (from) in His saying "of what is on the earth" is partitive (li-l-tab'īd), and the partitiveness refers to the eaten thing being a part of every kind, and not to the eaten thing being some kinds without others, because that would defeat the purpose of the verse. So "what is on the earth" is general, and the description "lawful and good" specifies it, so the forbidden things whose prohibition is established by the Book or the Sunna are excluded.

His saying "lawful and good" is two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl) of the relative "mā." The first is to explain the legal ruling, and the second to explain its cause, because the good is by nature something souls seek out to benefit from. So when goodness is established, lawfulness is established, because Allah is gentle with His servants and has not forbidden them what contains their pure or predominant benefit.

The meaning of "good" here is what sound and upright perception accepts, free of aberration, from souls that desire what is agreeable, perfect, or preponderant, such that its consumption does not bring bodily or spiritual harm. The meaning of "good" linguistically will come at His saying: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4] in Surat al-Ma'idah.

In this description there is a great meaning alluding to the principle of lawful and unlawful. For this reason our scholars said: the ruling on things about which the Sharia has stated nothing is that the basis of harms is prohibition and the basis of benefits is permissibility. This is with regard to the thing itself, regardless of its accidents, such as the attachment of another's right to it which necessitates its prohibition, since prohibition in that case is a ruling for the accident and not for the thing accidented.

"Good" has been interpreted here as what the Sharia permits, but this is far-fetched, because it leads to repetition, and because it requires using a term in a meaning not customary among them.

His saying "and do not follow the footsteps of Satan": the pronoun refers without doubt to the people, and they are the polytheists who are constantly engaged in what is forbidden. As for the believers, their share of it is warning and admonition.

Following footsteps is a figurative expression (tamthīliyya). Its origin is that a traveller who sees the traces of the footsteps of travellers follows that path, knowing that the one before him only walked on it because it leads to the goal. So he likened the follower who has no guide except the one he follows, while he thinks the path leads to the goal, to one who follows the footsteps of travellers. This figure became so common that they say: "He follows the footsteps of so-and-so," meaning he imitates him and obeys him.

"Khuṭuwāt" (footsteps), with a ḍamma and then a sukūn, is the plural of khuṭwa, like ghurfa and qubḍa, with the first letter vowelled with ḍamma, in the sense of the thing stepped, grasped, or held. So it means the distance between the two feet when a walker walks, as he steps it. As for khaṭwa with a fatḥa on the kha', it is one instance of the verbal noun of khaṭw, and it is also used for the thing stepped, by the usage of the verbal noun for the object.

The majority read "khuṭuwāt" with ḍamma then sukūn, on the basis of the sound plural. Ibn 'Āmir, Qunbul from Ibn Kathīr, and Ḥafṣ from 'Āṣim read it with ḍamma on the kha' and ṭā' by ittibā' (vowel assimilation). Ittibā' is equal to sukūn in lightness on the tongue.

Imitating Satan is letting the soul act upon what he whispers to it of human thoughts. Satans are existent perceptible beings who have a connection with human souls, perhaps like the connection of gravity with the celestial bodies and of magnetism with iron. When an orientation occurs from one of the two to the other, through causes not known, evil thoughts arise in the soul. If the responsible person lets his soul follow them and does not restrain them with his will and resolve, he realises them in his action; if he holds it back and turns it away from that, he overcomes them. For this reason Allah placed in us intellect, will, and power, and completed that for us with the religious guidance, as help and protection against responding to them, lest the satanic thoughts mislead us so that we see as good what is not good. For this reason the hadith says: "Whoever intends an evil deed but does not do it, Allah records it with Him as one complete good deed," because when he intends it, that is when the satanic power dominated him, and when he turns away from it, that is when the will for good prevailed over it. The same applies to good thoughts, which arise from angelic orientations. When the two callers contend in our souls, we need, in overcoming, to seek help from our intellects, our opinions, our power, and God Almighty's guidance to us. That is what al-Ash'arī called "kasb" (acquisition), and upon it reward and punishment are based.

The lam in "al-shayṭān" is for the genus (li-l-jins), and it may be for specific reference (li-l-'ahd), with the intended meaning being Iblīs, who is the origin of the satans and their commander. Everything arising from the whispering of the satans goes back to him, because he is the one who took the first steps.

His saying: "Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy." The particle "inna" here is for mere emphasis of the report, because the enmity between Satan and humans is known and established among believers and polytheists alike. They used to throw pebbles at the jamarāt during the Hajj, believing they were stoning Satan. Or "inna" is for emphasis, by treating one who is not doubtful about the ruling as if he were doubtful or denying, since they, by following satanic suggestions, are like one who denies his enmity. As 'Abda said:

"Indeed, those you see as your brothers,
their hearts' rage is healed only when you are struck down."

[Page 106]

﴿When it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers doing." Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾

In my view, the best reading is that it is coordinated (ʿatf) with His saying: ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168]. The address in that verse is directed mainly at the polytheists, since they are the ones who followed Satan's command to evil and immorality, and especially to say about Allah what they do not know. The Muslims are free of all of that.

In this coordinated verse there is an added intensification of the condition of the people of polytheism. After affirming that they followed the steps of Satan in what they forbade themselves of the good things, it follows with mention of their turning away from the one who calls them to follow what Allah has sent down. They clung to not opposing what they found their fathers upon, and they turned away from being called to anything else, without reflection or contemplation.

"Rather" (bal) here is a particle of cancellation (iḍrāb ibṭāl), meaning they set aside the Messenger's saying, "Follow what Allah has sent down," with a turning away that has no proof except that it contradicts what they found their fathers upon.

In the pronoun in "to them" (lahum) there is a shift (iltifāt) from the address in His saying: ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168].

What is meant by "what they found their fathers upon" is what they found them upon of matters of polytheism, as they said: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23]. "Community" (ummah) means religion (millah), and the greatest of that is the worship of idols.

His saying, "Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided," is a statement from another direction, answering their saying, "We will follow what we found our fathers upon." When the speaker related their saying, he answered it with a question intended for rejection and then for amazement. So the interrogative particle (hamzah) is used for denial by implication (kināyah) and for amazement by allusion (īmāʾ). By denial is meant rejection and correction, not denial in the sense of negation.

The word "even though" (law) is a conditional particle, and its answer is omitted, indicated by the preceding speech; its estimated form is: "they would have followed them." What is being questioned is the connection between the condition and its answer. The interrogative particle came to mean rejection because it is known that what is questioned is answered affirmatively, by the circumstantial indications of the one reported about and the one asking.

This construction is among the most wondrous of Arabic constructions and the highest in concision. "Law" in such a usage is called conjunctive (waṣliyyah), and likewise "in" (inna) when it occupies the place of "law." The scholars differ about the meaning of the conjunction "waw" and the conditional particle in such a usage, in three opinions:

[Page 107]

The first opinion: it is circumstantial (ḥāl). This was the view of Ibn Jinnī, al-Marzūqī and the author of al-Kashshāf. Ibn Jinnī said in his commentary on the Ḥamāsah, on the verse of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib:

"Beauty is not in a loincloth, know this, even if you wrap yourself in a mantle."

And similar to it is the verse in the Kitāb:

"Return to Herat, even though its inhabited parts have become ruined."

That is because the "waw" and what follows it are in the accusative position governed by what precedes them, just as in the verse "even if you wrap yourself in a mantle" the "waw" and what follows are in the accusative position governed by what precedes them. Close to this is: "I visit you desiring me, and I do good to you thanking me," where "desiring" and "thanking" are in the accusative of circumstance governed by what precedes them, and they carry the meaning of a condition, while what precedes them takes the place of the omitted answer. Do you not see that its meaning is: if you desire me, I visit you, and if you thank me, I do good to you? I once asked Abū ʿAlī about the verse "Return to Herat, even though its inhabited parts have become ruined," how the "waw" is placed here. I pointed to what we are dealing with in that matter, and he appeared to be evasive in answering, not from incapacity, praise be to Allah, but from reluctance to burden himself with it, so I left it alone. Al-Marzūqī said there: "His saying, 'even if you wrap yourself in a mantle,' is in the place of circumstance, as if he said: your beauty is not in a loincloth with a mantle upon it. Circumstance may contain the meaning of a condition, just as a condition may contain the meaning of circumstance. The first is like your saying: 'I will do it whatever state it is in,' that is, if it is this or if it is that. The second is like the verse in the Kitāb: 'Return to Herat, even though its inhabited parts have become ruined,' because the 'waw' there is in the place of circumstance, as it is in the verse of ʿAmr, and in it there is the word of the condition and its meaning, and what precedes it takes the place of the answer. Its estimate: if its inhabited parts are ruined, then return to it; and even if you wrap yourself in a mantle over a loincloth, beauty is not in that." End of quotation.

The author of al-Kashshāf said: in this verse and in its parallel in Sūrat al-Māʾidah, the "waw" is circumstantial.

[Page 108]

Then the apparent sense of the words of Ibn Jinnī and al-Marzūqī is that the circumstance in such a usage is from the clause mentioned before the "waw." This is what al-Bayḍāwī set aside here and ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm preferred. The author of al-Kashshāf held that the circumstance is from an omitted clause, estimated as: "Would they follow them even though their fathers were such?" Given the reading of the "waw" as circumstantial "waw," the interrogative particle in His saying, "Even though their fathers were such?" is not displaced from its place, as is its usual case with the conjunctive "waw," "fa," and "thumma" and "bal." Rather the particle enters upon the circumstantial clause, because the locus of denial is that state. For this reason the author of al-Kashshāf said in Sūrat al-Māʾidah: "The 'waw' is the 'waw' of circumstance, and the interrogative denial particle has entered upon it." Here and in al-Māʾidah he estimated an omitted element which is what the interrogative particle governs, indicated by what precedes it. So here he estimated it: "Would they follow their fathers?" and in al-Māʾidah he estimated: "Do we suppose that they are so?" This is a difference in his opinion. Whoever does not estimate an omitted element makes the interrogative particle enter upon the circumstantial clause.

The second opinion: the "waw" is coordinating (ʿaṭf), coordinating with the preceding clause. This was said by al-Bayḍāwī, and I do not know of any predecessor for it, but it is very plausible. That is, they said: "Rather, we will follow, even if their fathers were such." On this reading, the coordinated clause is sometimes part of the reporter's speech, as in this verse, meaning they say it in every state, "even if their fathers were such," and this is coordination of two speakers' speech by way of instruction (ʿaṭf al-talqīn), as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿He said: "And of my offspring?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. Sometimes it is from the speech of the original speaker, as in the verse of the Ḥamāsah and the verse of the Kitāb. Sometimes it is from the speech of the reporter, as an instruction to the one reported and an estimate of it as his own speech, like the verse of Ruʾbah:

"The cousins said: O Salma, even if he is poor, destitute, they said, even if."

It was also said that it is coordination with an omitted clause, and al-Raḍī attributed this to al-Jarmī. They estimated the clause as a conditional clause different from the stated condition. The estimate: "They follow them if they understand and are guided, and even if they did not understand and were not guided." The same estimate applies to its parallels among the examples.
