This indicates that the Muslims have realised the meaning of piety (birr), and it contains an implicit contrast that the People of the Book have not realised it, because they did not believe in some of the angels and some of the prophets, because they deprived many people of their rights, did not fulfil the covenant, and did not endure patiently. It also contains an implicit contrast with the polytheists, since they did not believe in the Last Day, the prophets, and the Book, plundered the orphans' wealth, did not establish prayer, and did not give zakat.

The accusative of (al-sabirin), though it is in apposition to nominatives, is in the accusative of specification (al-ikhtisas), according to the familiar usage of the Arabs in the apposition of attributes, where the speaker has the choice between agreeing in case with the word it follows and breaking off (al-qat'). This was stated by al-Radi. Breaking off occurs either by putting in the accusative what should be nominative or genitive, or by putting in the nominative what is the opposite, so that the speaker's intention of breaking off becomes evident when the case differs; for one cannot know that the speaker intended breaking off except by the difference in case. As for the accusative, it is by supposing a verb of praise or blame according to the context, and the most apparent is to suppose the verb "I specify" (akhussu), because it conveys praise for the praised and blame for the blamed.

By putting (al-sabirin) here in the accusative two benefits are obtained. The first is general to every break-off of attributes. It is related from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi that when many attributes are mentioned in the context of praise or blame, it is better to vary their case and not make them all follow what they describe, because this is one of the places of elaboration (itnab). When the case of the attributes is varied, the intended meaning becomes more complete, because when the case differs the speech becomes like kinds of speech and varieties of exposition.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "It is put in the accusative in praise, and this is a wide topic, which Sibawayh has divided into examples and evidences." I say: Sibawayh said, in the chapter on what is put in the accusative for glorification and praise: "If you wish, you may make it an attribute, following the first; and if you wish, you may break off and begin it, like the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ up to His saying: 'and the patient'. And if al-sabirin were put in the nominative as a continuation of the beginning of the speech, it would be good; and if you began it and put it in the nominative as a beginning, it would be good. The parallel of this accusative is the saying of al-Khirniq:

Let not my people be far away, those who are
the poison of enemies and the bane of the struck
the descending ones in every battlefield,
and the good ones at the knots of the waistcloths,

with the accusative of "al-nazilin." Then he said: Al-Khalil held that the accusative of this is because you did not intend to inform people or those you address of something they did not know, but they already knew of it what you know; so you made it praise and glorification. Its accusative is by a verb, as if he said: 'I mention the people of that and I mention those who establish,' but it is a verb whose overt form is not used." I say: This view is supported by the fact that its like recurs in parallel verses in Surah al-Nisa': ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾ [al-Nisa': 162], in coordination with ﴿but those firm in knowledge﴾ [al-Nisa': 162]; and in Surah al-Ma'idah, "wal-sabi'un," in coordination with ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62].

The second benefit of putting al-sabirin in the accusative by supposing "I specify" or "I praise" is to draw attention to the distinction of the patient ones and the excellence of their attribute, which is patience.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "One should not give heed to what they claim, that it is a grammatical error in the script of the Mushaf. Perhaps someone who has not studied the book and does not know the ways of the Arabs and their freedom in the accusative of specification may give heed to it." I say: Its recurrence as mentioned, and the closeness of the words, safeguard it from being an error or a slip, and it lies between two words whose cases differ.

It is related from al-Kisa'i that its accusative is in coordination with the objects of "atā" (gave), meaning: "and gave wealth to the patient ones," that is, the poor who abstain from asking when adversity and harm befall them, and the patient ones in time of battle, who do not find what to spend for the expedition and desire to fight, because they are a burden on the Muslims. God said: ﴿Nor [is there blame] upon those who came to you that you might mount them, and you said, "I find not anything to mount you on," and they turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears out of grief that they could not find anything to spend﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92]. It is also related from some commentators that the accusative of "wal-sabirin" was a mistake by the scribes of the Mushafs, and that it was among what 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, intended. It is reported of him that after reading the Mushaf they had written, he said: "I find in it a lahn (error), which the Arabs will set right with their tongues." This is a fabrication against 'Uthman. Even if it were sound, he would have meant by lahn what is in the orthography of the Mushafs of signs, like writing the alif in the form of the ya' as a sign of imalah (inclination), and lahn was not used to mean error. Ya'qub read "wal-sabirun" with the nominative, in coordination with "wal-mufun" (and those who fulfil).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 178 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿O you who believe, retaliation (qisas) is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female.﴾

The address ﴿O you who believe﴾ is repeated because this is a category of legislation for rulings of great importance to the welfare of the Islamic community and the establishment of its order and security, at the time when the Muslims, after the Hijra, had become a community with its own independence and its own city. These verses were among the first revealed at Medina in the year of the Hijra, as the exegetes mention regarding the occasion of their revelation, in the explanation of God's words that follow it: ﴿And fight in the way of God those who fight you﴾ [al-Baqara: 190], and so on.

These are consecutive rulings for reforming the conditions of individuals and of society. The rulings on retaliation were given first, because the greatest of disorders in conditions is the disruption of the preservation of the lives of the community. The Arabs had been extreme in neglecting this principle, as anyone with knowledge of their history, customs and conditions knows. Their excess in this matter reached the point of nearly perishing, had it continued and had God not rescued them in it with the blessing of Islam.

[Page 135]

They would raid one another to seize the livestock, slaves and women of the other. The one raided would defend himself, and souls would perish on both sides. Then from this arose the pursuit of blood-feuds (tha'rat), so that everyone who had a slain relative would strive to kill the killer of his kinsman. If he could not do so, he would kill another in his place, someone equal to him, or a number of people whom he considered not to be comparable to him. They called this "takayul fi al-dam" (the measuring out of blood), meaning that the blood of a nobleman was measured against many bloods. Sometimes they estimated it at two, ten or a hundred. The matter continued thus, growing excessively until it became mutual destruction. Zuhayr said:

*You two reconciled 'Abs and Dhubyan after they had destroyed one another and crushed between them the perfume of Manshim.*

The matter would pass from one tribe to another through alliance, lineage, pacts and support, until enmities became widespread. They then abandoned one another and some tribes sought help against others. The Persians and the Romans found an opening to divide them, so they ruled over them and subjugated them. The allusion to this, God knows best, is in His words: ﴿And remember God's favour upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became by His favour brothers; and you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire and He saved you from it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103]. That is: you were enemies because of raids and wars, so He united you through the word of Islam. You were on the verge of ruin, so He rescued you from it. Here He gave the example of swift destruction that leaves nothing, by the pit of the Fire. One standing on its edge has between himself and destruction only the smallest movement.

The meaning of (kutiba 'alaykum) ("it is prescribed for you") is that it is a binding right for the community, from which there is no escape. The pronoun in ﴿'alaykum﴾ refers to the community as a whole, to those who hold the right of retaliation. It does not mean that retaliation is obligatory upon every individual, because the guardian of the blood has the right to pardon the killer, as God says: ﴿But whoever is granted some pardon by his brother, let there be the following in kindness﴾. The original sense of kitaba is inscribing letters on stone, parchment or cloth. Since such inscription is meant to secure what is written and to ensure its lasting remembrance, the word "kutiba" was applied to the meaning: "was established and confirmed", that is: it is the right of the family of the slain.

Qisas is the name for compensating a right of injury, or a right of debt upon someone, with its like from the one who owes it, in fairness and justice. Thus qisas is applied to the punishment of the offender with the like of what he committed, and to the settling of accounts by a creditor regarding what a debtor owes him, so that the debt is discharged. All its usages indicate equivalence and reciprocity in rights and obligations that are subject to dispute.

It is on the pattern of fi'al, which is the verbal noun of fa'ala from qassa, meaning "to cut". From it comes the saying "a bird with clipped wings" (ta'ir maqsus al-janah), and from it the scissors (miqass) are named after the instrument of cutting, that is, cutting. Qussat al-sha'r (a lock of hair), with a dammed qaf, is what is cut from it. It is so called because it operates between two mutual rights between two sides. One says "qassa fulan fulanan" when a person deducts a portion of a debt owed to him from another person's obligation, so that the other owes him an amount that is due to him. Thus reciprocity is likened to cutting, because it cuts off the dispute that has arisen before it. For this reason the retaliatory killing (qawd), which is the enabling of the guardian of the slain to kill the killer of his master, is called qisas. God says: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 179]. The punishment of one who wounds another deliberately and unjustly is also called qisas, by his being wounded in the same way that he wounded the other. God says: ﴿And wounds are subject to retaliation﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45]. They also call the treatment of an aggressor with the like of his offence qisas: ﴿And the sacred violations are subject to retaliation﴾ [al-Baqara: 194]. Thus the essence of qisas includes the essence of compensation and equivalence.

So God's words ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ carry the meaning of requital for killing by killing for the killer. They also carry the meaning of equivalence and parity in that requital, by means of something that is like a compensation for it and its equal. They also carry the meaning that no one other than the killer is killed, of those who had no share in the killing of the slain. Thus the words ﴿kutiba 'alaykum﴾ establish the right of accountability among believers regarding the slain, so that the right of a slain person is not lost in vain, and no one other than the killer is killed in vain. This is a repudiation of what they practised in the Jahiliyya: neglecting the blood of a lowly person when a nobleman killed him, and neglecting the right of the weak when a strong man killed him whose people were feared. It also repudiates their arbitrariness in seeking the killing of someone other than the killer: when someone killed a nobleman, they sought to kill a nobleman like him. They would not kill the killer unless he was a bawa' (equal) to the slain, that is, a peer in nobility and glory. They regarded the value of blood as varying according to the variation in lordliness and nobility, and they called this variation takayul, from kayl (measure). The daughter of Bahdal ibn Qaraqa al-Ta'i said, urging her kin to kill a man who had killed her father, and mentioning that she would not be content with killing him as the substitute unless Islam had abolished the measuring of blood:

*Is there not among the Banu Hisn, son of Karihah, from the people, those who seek vengeance, the fierce ones? They kill by force a man who was not his peer; but there is no measuring out of blood.*

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The blood of the Muslims is equal." 

By this verse, the legislation of qisas for intentional killing is established. The wisdom behind this is to deter the people of aggression from undertaking the killing of souls, when they know that their punishment is death. Life is the most precious thing to a human being by nature, so no punishment equals death in deterrence and restraint. Among its wisdom is also the reassurance of the families of the slain that the judiciary will take vengeance for them upon those who transgressed against their slain. God says: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority, but let him not commit excess in killing; indeed, he is supported﴾ [al-Isra': 33]. That is, lest the heirs of the slain take it upon themselves to avenge their master's killer personally, because that leads to the form of war between two groups, in which the destruction of souls becomes abundant, as was mentioned earlier in the discussion of the beginning of the verse. It will come under God's words: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 179].

[Page 137]

The first blood for which retaliation was carried out in Islam was the blood of a man from Hudhayl, whom a man from Banu Layth had killed. The Prophet (ﷺ) enacted retaliation for him while he was travelling to the conquest of al-Ta'if, at a place called Bahrat al-Rughba' on the road to al-Ta'if, and that was in the eighth year after the Hijra.

The "fi" in God's words ﴿fi al-qatla﴾ ("regarding the slain") is for the figurative sense of location. Retaliation does not occur within the slain themselves, so an elided genitive (mudaf) must be understood. Its omission here is to include all the affairs of the slain and all the meanings of qisas, so this is brevity and generality.

The plural of (al-qatla) ("the slain") is according to the plurality of those addressed, that is, "in your slain". The definite article in "al-qatla" is the definite article of genus. A qatil (slain) is one whom another person from among people kills. Killing (qatl) is a human act of causing another human to die, so a dead person is not a slain without the act of an agent.

The clause ﴿the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾ explains and details the clause ﴿retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾. The "ba'" in "bi-al-hurr" and what follows it is connected to an omitted element indicated by the meaning of qisas. The implied sense is: the free man is subject to retaliation or is killed for the free man, and so on. The implicative meaning (mafhum) of the restriction, together with the descriptive sense of "the free", "the slave" and "the female", requires that a free man be killed only for a free man and not for anyone else, that a slave be killed only for a slave and not for anyone else, and that a female be killed only for a female and not for anyone else. The scholars of Islam have agreed that this implicative meaning is not applied uniformly. They differed, however, over the extent to which it is applied according to the differing textual evidence from the Book and the Sunna, and over the intended meaning of this verse and the interpretation of its sense. In the Muwatta', Malik said: "The best I have heard concerning this verse is that God's words ﴿the free for the free and the slave for the slave﴾ refer to males, and His words ﴿and the female for the female﴾ mean that retaliation applies among females just as it applies among males. A free woman is killed for a free woman just as a free man is killed for a free man, a female slave is killed for a female slave just as a male slave is killed for a male slave, retaliation applies among women just as it applies among men, and retaliation also applies between men and women."

That is: the female was specified by mention although she is included in the generality of "the free for the free" and "the slave for the slave", lest it be supposed that the masculine form in "al-hurr" and "al-'abd" is intended only for males.

Al-Qurtubi said, on behalf of a group: the verse came explaining the ruling for each kind when it kills its own kind. It therefore states the ruling of a free man who kills a free man, of a slave who kills a slave, and of a female who kills a female, without addressing the case of one kind killing the other. Thus the verse is muhkam (definitive) and contains an ijmal (ambiguity) that is clarified by God's words: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the soul is for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45], and so on, end of quotation.

On this reading, the restriction serves to show that there is no preference among the individuals of a kind, and it has no implicative meaning beyond that regarding differences between kinds, either affirmatively or negatively. Al-Sha'bi said: it was revealed concerning a people who said: "We will certainly kill the free man for the slave and the male for the female." This occurred in a fight between two clans of the Ansar. But this report is not established, and in any case it does not suffice to determine the meaning of the verse. On these two interpretations, the general implicative meaning of the restriction is not relied upon, because the condition for relying upon it is that no cause for mentioning the restriction appears except to exclude its opposite. When another cause apart from exclusion appears, the argument from the implicative meaning is void. In that case, the verse gives no indication that a free man may not be killed for a slave, or a female for a male, nor the reverse. The evidence for equality between the female and the male, and for non-equality between the slave and the free man according to those who deny their equality, is derived from other proofs.

Third: it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that this was a ruling at the beginning of Islam, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of al-Ma'ida: ﴿that the soul is for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45]. It is quoted in al-Kashshaf from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Nakha'i, al-Thawri and Abu Hanifa. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi rejected this, on the grounds that the verse of al-Ma'ida is a narration about the Children of Israel, so how can it abrogate a ruling that was established in the Islamic law? That is, even on the view that the law of those before us is law for us, its application is confined to what has not come in our law with a contrary provision.

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Ahkam, on behalf of the Hanafis: God's words ﴿in the slain﴾ are the end of the statement, and His words ﴿the free for the free﴾ come after that. The generality of equality has been established by His words ﴿retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾, because "al-qatla" is general, and the specificity of the latter part of the verse does not nullify the generality of its first part. For this reason they said: a free man is killed for a slave. I say: it is objected to this that there would be no benefit in the detailing if it were not intended, and that the discourse is to be understood by its final parts, so the specific qualifies the general without doubt. There is no escape from regarding it as a detailing, unless they say that this is like an illustrative example. What is reported from the Hanafis in al-Kashshaf is what we mentioned just now.

[p. 139]

After these interpretations, a question still remains about the reason for singling out the female after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The free for the free, and the slave for the slave﴾, and whether the female falls outside being either a free woman or a slave woman, once it has become clear that what is meant by "the free" and "the slave" is the two genders (genera). The form of the masculine plural in it is not meant to exclude women from among them, since the definite article (*al*), once it makes the noun a generic noun (*ism jins*), makes the ruling apply to the genus, and whatever feminine form it has is nullified, just as whatever plural form it has is nullified.

Because of this difficulty, I asked the eminent scholar, al-Jadd al-Wazir, may Allah have mercy on him, about the reason for this antithetical structure, which implies that no category is to be subjected to retaliation except for killing a counterpart of the same attribute. He left me a sheet in his own handwriting, containing the following: "The apparent meaning, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that the verse, meaning the verse of Surah al-Ma'idah, was revealed to inform about the ruling concerning the Children of Israel, as a consolation and a preparation for the ruling of the Islamic Sharia. For this reason, it included attaching the ruling to the word *nafs* (soul), which encompasses male and female, free and slave, young and old, and it did not include a ruling for slaves or for females. It began with His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. The second verse, meaning the verse of Surah al-Baqarah, began with His saying: (﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you﴾), and attached the ruling therein to freedom, which encompasses all categories. Then it mentioned the ruling for slaves and females, in response to those who claim that retaliation is not carried out for them, and it specified the female with the female, to indicate that her blood is protected. This is because, if retaliation is carried out for her against a female but not against a male, her blood would be protected in one respect and unprotected in another. This is from the subtlety of the communication, in that the ruling includes its evidence. As for his saying:

*He prescribed killing and fighting for us,*
*and for the coquettes, dragging of trains,*

this is a pre-Islamic ruling." End of quotation. He means that the verse was intended only to nullify what was the practice of the pre-Islamic era, namely abandoning retaliation out of pride of lineage or out of indifference. So it aimed at equality through His saying: ﴿The free for the free and the slave for the slave﴾, meaning that a noble free man has no superiority over a lowly free man, nor do the slaves of masters have superiority over the slaves of commoners. And by mentioning the female, it aimed to nullify what the pre-Islamic era practiced, namely not regarding the crime of a female as counting, and treating her as not held accountable for her crimes. By his saying "a pre-Islamic ruling," he meant that it does not follow the rulings of Islam, because the verse is by Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah, who was an Islamic poet from the early period of the Umayyad state.

If you say: the proper wording would have been not to say "for the female," since it implies that a female is not killed for a male, even though the Muslims have reached a consensus (*ijma'*, scholarly agreement) that a woman is subjected to retaliation for a man. I say: it is apparent that the qualification came out in the manner of the usual case, since the common custom is that a female kills only a female, as men and women do not usually fight one another. Thus the mention of "for the female" is given in consideration of what is usual, like the form of the description "grazing" in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "In grazing sheep there is zakat." The conclusion is that the verse yields no sound meaning free of difficulty except the meaning of intending equality among the categories, for the purpose of nullifying the customs of the pre-Islamic era.

[p. 140]

Since it has been established that the verse has no indication either for negating retaliation between the differing categories, or for affirming it, because every other interpretation is refuted on another ground, it is determined that His saying: ﴿The free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾ means, beyond any doubt, the equality of the individuals of each category with one another, without preference among individuals. Then, the evidences of the scholars regarding the equalizing of retaliation between some categories with others, the male with the female, and regarding its absence, such as the non-equalizing of free persons with slaves according to those who do not equate the two categories, in contrast to Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, and Dawud, are evidences other than this qualification in the apparent wording of the verse. As for Abu Hanifah, he took by the generality of His saying "the slain" and did not establish a specifier for it, and he excepted from it only retaliation between a Muslim and a non-Muslim combatant (*harbi*), and this exception is not disputed. Its basis is that the combatant's blood is not protected. As for the covenanted non-Muslim (*mu'ahad*), there are differing opinions regarding the ruling on a Muslim killing him. As for al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, they negated retaliation from a Muslim for a *dhimmi* (protected non-Muslim) or a covenanted person, and they took by the hadith: "A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever." Malik and al-Layth said: there is no retaliation from a Muslim who kills a *dhimmi* or a covenanted person in a case of aggression, but they affirmed retaliation from him if he kills by treachery (*ghilah*).

As for retaliation between the free and the slave in the cutting off of limbs, it is not among the matters connected to this verse, and it will come under His saying, exalted is He: (﴿And wounds, retaliation﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]) in Surah al-'Uqud. Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad negated retaliation from the free for the slave, relying on the practice of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the silence of the Companions, and on narrated reports, and by analogy with the absence of retaliation from a free person for injuring a slave's limbs, since the soul is more deserving of protection. Retaliation from the slave for his killing of a free person is established according to both of them by implication (*fahwa*), and retaliation from the male for killing a female is established by the implicit meaning of the discourse (*lahn al-khitab*).

* * *

﴿Then whoever is pardoned something by his brother, let there be the following up with good conduct and payment to him with kindness. That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy.﴾

The *fa'* (then) is for the sequencing of the report; that is, for mere verbal sequence, not to indicate that what the sentence conjoined with it contains occurs as a result of what preceded it. The intended meaning is to explain that the guardian's taking of retaliation, derived from the forms of ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you concerning the slain﴾, is not obligatory upon him, but is merely a right belonging to him, lest it be imagined from His saying (﴿is prescribed for you﴾) that taking it is obligatory on the guardian of the slain. The mention of this after the mention of the right of retaliation is intended to hint that the better course for people is to accept reconciliation, in order to preserve the bonds of Islamic brotherhood.

Al-Azhari said: "This is a difficult verse, and they have explained it in a manner that brought it close to the understanding of the people of their age." Then al-Azhari proceeded to explain it with what revealed no meaning and removed no difficulty. The commentators have many approaches to the interpretation of its words. Al-Qurtubi mentioned five of them, and al-Kashshaf mentioned another interpretation, and al-Tibi mentioned two interpretations that return to the interpretation of al-Kashshaf. All of them agree that its purpose is to encourage reconciliation regarding bloodshed. We should not lead the minds of the reader along scattered paths. The decisive statement is that what "whoever" (*man*) refers to in His saying ﴿whoever is pardoned﴾ is the guardian of the slain, and what is meant by "his brother" is the killer. He is described as a brother to remind of brotherhood in Islam and to soften the soul of the guardian of the slain, for if he regards the killer as his brother, it is part of manliness that he not be content with retaliation from him, since it is as if he were content with the killing of his brother. Indeed, some of the Arabs said, when his brother had killed his son intentionally, and he was brought forward so that retaliation might be taken from him, he threw down the sword and said:

*I say to the self, in consolation and solace,*
*one of my hands struck me, and it did not intend it.*
*Both are a replacement for the loss of the other:*
*this one is my brother when I call him, and that one is my son.*

The referent of "something" (*shay'*) is the compensation for reconciliation. The word *shay'* is a noun extremely indefinite, indicating the kind of thing that the context of the speech allows. The excellence of the placement of the word *shay'* has already been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155]. The meaning of ﴿is pardoned something by his brother﴾ is that he was given the pardon, that is, what is easy for the killer of the compensation of reconciliation. Among the meanings of *'afw* (pardon) is what is easy of wealth that does not burden its giver, and *'afw* was interpreted with this meaning in His saying: (﴿Take what is easy﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]). The choice of this verb is because it indicates regard for facility and generosity, which are part of the character of Islam. This is an emphasis on the encouragement indicated by His saying (*min akhihi*, "from his brother"). The expression of the compensation for blood by *shay'* is because the compensation varies: sometimes property of gold or silver is offered to the guardian of the blood, sometimes camels or goods are offered, or a settlement of bloods between two tribes; for the compensation in intentional killing is not fixed, as it is in the blood-money for accidental killing.

*Ittiba'* (following up) and *ada'* (payment) are two verbal nouns that stand in place of two verbs. The estimated sense is: "let him follow up with following up, and let him pay with payment." He turned away from putting them in the accusative of the absolute object to the nominative, to convey the sense of permanence and the affirmation achieved by a nominal sentence. This is like His turning to the nominative in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿He said, "Peace"﴾ [Hud: 69]) after His saying: (﴿They said, "Peace"﴾ [Hud: 69]). The development of the verbal noun, whose origin is an absolute object, to its being in the nominative, has already been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He: (﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2]). So the structure of the sentence is: following up is occurring from the one who was pardoned something by his brother, and payment is occurring from his brother to him.

[p. 142]

In this there is an exhortation to the one who was pardoned to accept what was granted to him, and an exhortation to his brother to pay what he offered with kindness.

*Ittiba'* is used in the sense of acceptance and contentment; that is, let him be content with what was granted to him, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "And if one of you is referred to a wealthy person for payment, let him follow up."

The pronoun understood in "*ittiba'*" refers to "whoever is pardoned," and the pronoun understood in "*ada'*" refers to "his brother." The meaning: let him be content with what was offered to him of the easy reconciliation, and let the one offering the reconciliation pay what he offered without delay or shortfall. The pronoun governed by *li* (to) and the pronoun governed by *ila* (to) both refer to ﴿whoever is pardoned﴾.

The aim of the verse is to encourage contentment with taking a compensation for the blood of the slain in place of retaliation, in order to change what the people of the pre-Islamic era used to take shame in, namely accepting reconciliation for intentional killing, and considering it a sale of the blood of their clients, as Murrah al-Faqʻasi said:

*So do not take a blood-price from the people, for I*
*see that shame remains while the blood-wealth is lost.*

Another poet said, describing a people who did not accept reconciliation from him for a slain man:

*Had a living one accepted money as ransom,*
*we would have driven to them a gift of wealth, overflowing.*
*But a people whose brother was struck refused the*
*shame's contentment, and chose blood over milk.*

All of this concerns pardon for intentional killing. As for accidental killing, its ruling is blood-money from the killer's *'aqilah* (paternal kin who bear the blood-money), and it will come in Surah al-Nisa'.

The use of the description "brother" for one who shares the same religion of Islam establishes a principle that the Qur'an brought, by which agreement in creed is made like agreement in lineage of brotherhood. Indeed, agreement in religion is a psychological bond, and agreement in lineage is a bodily bond, and the spirit is more noble than the body.

Ibn 'Abbas argued with this verse against the Kharijites, that sin does not remove faith, because Allah called the killer a brother of the guardian of the blood, and that is brotherhood in Islam while the killer is disobedient.

As for His saying (﴿with good conduct﴾), *al-ma'ruf* (the known good) is that which souls are familiar with and find beautiful. It is what souls are gladdened by, do not shrink from, and do not reject. Its opposite is called *munkar* (the reprehensible). It will come at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind, enjoining the good and forbidding the reprehensible﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110] in Surah Al 'Imran.

[p. 143]

The *ba'* in His saying (﴿with good conduct﴾) is for accompaniment; that is, following up accompanied by the good: contentment, acceptance, and good manner in demanding if delay occurs, and acceptance of installments if the killer asks for them.

*Ada'* is paying and delivering the right, and what is meant by it is giving the reconciliation property. He mentioned its complement, which is His saying (*ilayhi*, "to him"), which indicates arrival at him and reaching him, to point out delivering the reconciliation property to the slain, by taking it to him and not requiring him to come himself to receive it or to send someone to collect it. In this there is an indication that he should not delay him. This is further confirmed by His saying (﴿with kindness﴾), that is, without anger, without harsh speech, or without rudeness in dealing.

[p. 144]

His saying, ﴿That is a lightening from your Lord﴾, refers to the ruling just mentioned, which is accepting the pardon, graciously making the payment, and turning away from retaliation (qisas, the law of equal retribution). It is a lightening from God upon people, and so it is mercy from Him, that is, a result of His mercy, since lightening a ruling is a result of mercy. Taking retaliation is justice, and taking the pardon is mercy.

Since the legislation of retaliation was sufficient to achieve the purpose of the Shari'a (divine law) in prescribing retaliation, namely deterring people from killing souls and securing the rights of the slain by giving the choice to the guardian, the permission to pardon, if both parties agree to it, was a mercy from God toward both sides. Justice comes first, and mercy follows it.

It has been said that the verse alludes to what existed in the Israelite law: the prescription of retaliation for deliberate killing, without pardon and without blood money (diyah, compensation paid to the victim's family). Many exegetes have mentioned this, and it is in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also the apparent meaning of what is in the Book of Exodus, Chapter 3: ("Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall surely be put to death. But the one who did not intend it, but God caused it to come into his hand, I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee. And if a man acts presumptuously against his neighbor to kill him by treachery, you shall take him from My altar to die.") Al-Qurtubi said that the ruling of the Gospel is absolute pardon. The apparent meaning is that this is not established in the Shari'a of Jesus, because God related of him only that he said ﴿and to make lawful for you part of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 50]. Perhaps it is something the scholars of Christianity derived from his command to pardon and forgive. But this is a ruling from which the laws of God are exempt, because it leads to the disruption of the order of the world. How different is the state of one who commits murder in Islam, who expects retaliation and places his life in the hand of the guardian of the slain man's blood, not knowing whether he will accept reconciliation or refuse it, from the state of one who is confident that there is no retaliation against him, for that would embolden him to kill his enemy and opponent.

* * *

[p. 144]

﴿Whoever transgresses after that, for him is a painful punishment﴾

This is a derivation from the ruling on pardon, because pardon requires thanking God for having saved him through the legislation permitting pardon, and for having made the guardian willing to pardon. And among thanks is that he not return to the crime again. If he returns, then ﴿for him is a painful punishment﴾. The majority of scholars interpreted the painful punishment as the punishment of the Hereafter, and the intent is to intensify the punishment upon him, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And whoever returns, God will take retribution from him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. Then he has, under their ruling on pardon and blood money, what the killer has at the outset according to them. Some interpreted it as the punishment of this world, namely killing. They said: if the one pardoned returns to killing a second time, then he must be killed, and the ruler does not allow the guardian to pardon him. They transmitted this from Qatadah, Ikrimah and al-Suddi, and Abu Dawud narrated it from Samurah ibn Jundab, from the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also reported from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz that it is left to the discretion of the imam (ruler). What is derived from their statements here, whether the punishment is that of the Hereafter or that of this world, is that repetition of the crime necessitates severity. This is evident from the objectives of the Lawgiver, because the crime may become a habit for him, and his return to killing a soul indicates his contempt for souls, so people must be relieved of him. Qatadah and those with him had this in view. However, this does not prevent the ruling of pardon if the guardian agrees to it, because the right is his. How excellent is the statement of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz in delegating it to the imam to consider whether this killer has become one who takes souls. If he is pardoned, it is fitting that the punishment be made harsher upon him than a hundred lashes and a year's imprisonment, even if they did not say this. For God's mention of this ruling after mentioning mercy is evidence that this offender is not deserving, on this occasion, of further mercy. This is a subtle point of jurisprudence requiring careful consideration. A man in the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) used to kill, then pay the blood money, then the guardian of the blood would betray him and kill him. Close to this is the story of Husayn ibn Damdam, to which Zuhayr alluded in his saying:

By my life, the tribe was excellent, yet Husayn ibn Damdam brought upon them what does not befit them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 179:

﴿And in retaliation (qisas) there is life for you, O people of understanding, that you may become righteous.﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to these great rulings, by which he reassured the souls of both parties, the guardians of the blood and the slayers, regarding their acceptance of the rulings of retaliation. So he explained that in retaliation there is life. The indefiniteness in (ḥayah, "life") is for magnification, as indicated by the context; that is: in retaliation there is life for you, that is, for your souls. For in it there is the deterrence of people from killing souls. Were the ruling of retaliation neglected, people would not be deterred, because the most dreaded of the calamities that human souls guard against is death. If the killer knew that he would be safe from death, he would proceed to kill, treating punishments lightly, as Sa'd ibn Nashib said when he shed blood and fled, and the governor of Basra punished him by demolishing his house there:

"I will wash the shame from me with the sword, bringing upon myself the decree of God, whatever it brings upon me.

And I will forget my house, and make its demolition a screen for my honor against the remaining blame.

And my inherited wealth will seem small in my eyes when my right hand turns to attaining what I sought."

Had the matter been left to taking vengeance as it was in the Jahiliyyah, they would have excessed in killing and the matter would have continued in a chain, as has been mentioned before. So in the legislation of retaliation there is great life on both sides. The encouragement to take compensation for reconciliation and to pardon does not contradict the wisdom of retaliation, because the deterrence is achieved by giving the guardian the choice of accepting the blood-money (diyah), so the one harboring intent to kill rarely feels secure in the guardian's pardon, and this is sufficient for deterrence.

In His saying, "O people of understanding," there is an alert, by the particle of address, to reflect upon the wisdom of retaliation. For this reason, the description was expressed by way of the idafah (construct), indicating that they are people of complete intellects, because the wisdom of retaliation is grasped only by people of sound reasoning, since at first glance it seems like a punishment equal to the crime. For in retaliation there is a second loss, but upon reflection it is life, not loss, for the two reasons mentioned earlier.

And He said: ("that you may become righteous") to complete the cause; that is, to bring you close to being mindful, so that you do not exceed the bounds of justice and fairness in taking vengeance. "La'alla" (perhaps/that) expresses hope, and here it is either an imagery (tamthil) or a subsidiary metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah), as was mentioned earlier at His saying, "O mankind, worship your Lord" [al-Baqarah: 21] up to His saying, "that you may become righteous" [al-Baqarah: 21], at the beginning of the surah.

His saying, "in retaliation there is life," is one of the comprehensive expressions (jawami' al-kalim), surpassing what was circulating among the Arabs as a proverb: "Killing is the preventer of killing." Al-Sakkaki explained it in Miftah al-'Ulum, and those who came after him among the scholars of rhetoric (ma'ani) appended to it. We add to them that the word qisas has indicated the nullification of blood-feuding by reciprocal killing, and the nullification of killing one of the killer's tribe when they fail to seize the killer; and their comprehensive saying does not convey this.

[Page 146]

(﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches any of you, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest to parents and relatives according to what is fair. This is a duty upon the God-conscious.﴾)

This is an independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) to explain the ruling concerning property after the death of its owner. No prior legislation on this matter had preceded it, and it does not open with "O you who have believed," because bequest (wasiyyah) was already known before Islam. Its legislation was therefore not the introduction of something unfamiliar, and it does not require additional attention to receive the ruling. The occasion for mentioning it is that it changed what they had been doing at the beginning of Islam, from the remnants of pre-Islamic customs regarding the property of the dead. They often deprived a close relative of inheritance on the assumption that he wished for his relative's death so as to inherit from him, and sometimes they preferred some relatives over others. Since this leads to enmities, and through enmity the social order is disrupted by sowing hostility among relatives, as Tarafah said:

"The wrong done by kin is harder to bear for a man
than the stroke of a polished Indian sword."

Changing this practice to a state of justice was among the most important objectives of Islam, as we explained in detail earlier in the verse ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178].

As for the reason it is mentioned after the ruling on retaliation, it is the continuation of the mention of the death of the victim and the death of the killer by retaliation.

The discussion of (كُتِبَ) (kutiba, "prescribed") was given in the previous verse. It is apparent in indicating obligation, close to explicit in it. Its being unmarked for feminine gender, although its subject is feminine in form, is due to two justifications for omitting the feminine marker: that the feminine is not real (ghayr haqiqi), and that a separator intervenes between it and the verb. Al-Shaykh al-Radi claimed that the combination of these two justifications makes the omission of the feminine marker preferable, but this claim is open to objection.

The meaning of the presence of death (huduru al-mawt) is the presence of its causes and signs, which indicate that the death imagined by people has arrived in the presence of the sick person or the like, to make him dead. Ta'abbata Sharran said:

"And Death is abashed, looking on."

The presence of a thing means its arrival and descent, and it is the opposite of absence. So the use of (hadara, "to be present") here is not of the type of using the verb to mean being near to the act, as in: "The prayer has been established," nor in the sense of intending the act, as in ﴿When you rise to prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], ﴿When you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98]. Rather, it is

[Page 147]

a metaphorical attribution to death, because it is the presence of its causes. As for the presence itself, it is used metaphorically for approaching and appearing. Furthermore, the use of "death" to refer to its causes is widespread. Ruwaysh ibn Kathir al-Ta'i said:

"Say to them: hasten to pardon, and seek a word that will clear you,
for I am Death."

Al-khayr (the good) means wealth, and it is said: much of it. The majority of scholars hold that bequest is legislated concerning property, whether little or much. It is related from 'Ali, 'A'ishah, and Ibn 'Abbas that bequest is obligatory only for much property.

It was the custom of the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah that if the deceased had a son or sons who were male, they monopolized all his property. If he had no male son, his property was monopolized by the nearest male relative: a father, an uncle, or a paternal cousin, the closest first and then the next closest. The owner of the property sometimes bequeathed part of his property or all of it to some of his children, relatives, or friends. When the Muslims settled in the abode of emigration (Dar al-Hijrah) and became united in their community, God legislated for them the sharing of some relatives in their property, namely those whom they had been neglecting in inheritance, such as daughters, sisters, and parents when sons were present. For this reason the sons are not mentioned in this verse.

He expressed the verb (taraka, "leaves") in the past tense while meaning the future, i.e., "if he leaves," to draw attention to the nearness of the future to the past when it is about to become past. The meaning is: "if he is about to leave wealth" or "if he is close to leaving wealth," as they have interpreted it in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 9] in Surat al-Nisa', and His words: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe. Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 96-97] in Surat Yunus; that is, "until they come close to seeing the punishment."

Al-wasiyyah (bequest) is fa'ilah from awsa, so it is what is bequeathed (al-mu'sa biha). Thus the omission and the transitive form occurred so that the pattern fa'ilah could be formed in the sense of maf'ulah, because the pattern fa'ilah is not formed from an intransitive verb.

Bequest is the command to do or to abstain from doing something that benefits the one commanded or the commander, in the absence of the commander during his life or after his death. Its use became widespread for a command to do something that is suitable after the death of the one who bequeathes. In the hadith of al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah, he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) admonished us with an admonition by which hearts trembled and eyes overflowed. We said: 'O Messenger of God, it is as if this were the admonition of one bidding farewell, so counsel us,'" and so on.

The definiteness in al-wasiyyah is the definiteness of the genus; that is: "What is known to you as bequest is prescribed for you, to parents and relatives." Thus His words "to the parents" (lil-walidayn) are connected to the bequest as its complement, because the verbal noun (ism al-masdar) operates like the infinitive, and it does not need to be interpreted with "that" (an) and a verb. Al-wasiyyah is the nominative substitute for the subject of the verb (kutiba), and (idha) is an adverbial clause.

[Page 148]

Al-ma'ruf (what is known/fair) is the act that minds accept and souls do not reject. It is the thing that is loved and approved. It was named ma'ruf because, through its frequent circulation and familiarity, it became known among people. Its opposite is called al-munkar (the reprehensible), and it will come under His words: ﴿You enjoin what is fair and forbid what is reprehensible﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110] in Surat Al 'Imran.

What is meant by al-ma'ruf here is justice that involves no harm, and from which no envy arises among relatives. The testator considers who is more deserving of being bequeathed to, by reason of the strength of kinship or the intensity of need. If he does this, people will approve of his act and will not blame him. Among what is fair in bequest is that it not be for the purpose of harming an heir, a spouse, or a relative. This will come under His words: ﴿But whoever fears from a testator deviation or sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 182]. The preposition (bi) in (bil-ma'ruf) indicates accompaniment, and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of al-wasiyyah.

His words "bil-ma'ruf" include both the determination of what is bequeathed and the distinguishing of who is to receive it, and this is left to the judgment of the testator. He is entrusted with choosing who is worthy of preference in giving, as His words indicate: ﴿upon the God-conscious﴾.

His word (haqqan, "a right/duty") is an infinitive emphasizing (kutiba), because it has the same meaning. And (ʿala al-muttaqin, "upon the God-conscious") is a qualifier; that is: "a right being upon the God-conscious." You may also make it an object of (haqqan), and there is no obstacle to an emphatic infinitive governing something, and that does not remove it from being emphatic with what exceeds the meaning of its verb, because emphasis is achieved by repeating the meaning of the verb. Yes, if that object imposes a restriction that makes it a type or a number, then at that point it leaves the category of emphasis.

This right was specified for the God-conscious as an encouragement to accept it willingly, because what is characteristic of the God-conscious is a precious matter. So the verse contains no evidence that this obligation applies to the God-conscious only, excluding other sinners. Rather, its meaning is that this ruling is part of piety, and that neglecting it is disobedience. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The God-conscious were singled out for mention as an honor to their rank, so that people might compete to attain it."

Parents and relatives were singled out because they are the ones most likely to be forgotten by the testator, since they used to bequeath to the sons or to the chiefs of the tribe.

Parents were mentioned first to indicate that they have the greater claim to be given priority in bequest. People sometimes bequeathed to favor some of their children over others, or bequeathed how their property should be divided among their children. Among the most famous bequests in this regard is the bequest of Nizar ibn Ma'd ibn 'Adnan, who bequeathed to his son Mudar the red (ruby/red camel?) [al-Hamra'], to his son Rabi'ah the horse,

[Page 149]

to his son Anmar the donkey, and to his son Iyad the servant, and he made the division in this matter the responsibility of al-Afa al-Jurhumi. It has been said that the Arabs used to bequeath to distant persons in pursuit of glory, and would leave close relatives in poverty. This may also be due to enmity and hatred.

This verse is explicit in establishing the obligation of bequest, because His words "﴿prescribed for you﴾" are explicit in that. The majority of scholars hold that the ruling of the obligation to bequeath to parents and relatives was established by it. The obligation was timed with the moment of the presence of death, and the time of the anticipation of death is added to it. It did not specify the quantity to be bequeathed. The Sunnah has encouraged preparing a bequest from the time of health, by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No right of a man who has property in which he would bequeath should pass two nights without his bequest being written and kept with him." That is, because death may come upon him suddenly.

The verse implies that the determination of the amount to be bequeathed is left to what the testator sees fit, and it commanded him to justice by His words "﴿according to what is fair﴾." Thus the ruling of bequest was established in the early days of Islam for relatives other than sons, in addition to what the sons receive. Then the verses of inheritance in Surat al-Nisa' abrogated this verse with a general abrogation (naskh mujmal), explaining the inheritance of each specific relative. So his right no longer depended on the deceased's bequest to him; rather his right became fixed and specified, whether the deceased was pleased or not. Thus the establishment of the ruling on bequest at the beginning was a preparation (istinas) for the legislation of the fixed shares of inheritance. For this reason God Exalted began the verses of the shares with His words: ﴿God enjoins you concerning your children﴾ [al-Nisa': 11], making it His own bequest, may He be glorified, to nullify the favor that the testator had (of giving as he willed).

With the fixed shares, the obligation of bequest that this verse required was abrogated, and bequest remained recommended (mandub), based on the principle that when an obligation is abrogated, the recommendation remains. This is the view of the majority of scholars among the people of reasoning: al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Jabir ibn Zayd. In al-Bukhari, in the commentary on Surat al-Nisa', it is related "from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah who said: The Prophet and Abu Bakr visited me on foot among Banu Salamah, and the Prophet found me unconscious. He asked for water, performed ablution with it, then sprinkled it on me, and I regained consciousness. I said: 'O Messenger of God, what do you command me to do with my property?' Then God revealed: ﴿God enjoins you concerning your children﴾ [al-Nisa': 11], and the verse." End of quotation. This shows that the last stage of the legislation of bequests was the question of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah. In al-Bukhari also, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Property belonged to the child, and bequest was to the parents. Then God abrogated from that what He willed," and so on.

It has been said that the legislation of bequest was abrogated and it became forbidden. This was said by Ibrahim ibn Khuthaym, and it is an anomalous view (shudhudh).

[Page 150]

Contrary to what is well known in the Sunnah, unless one means by it that it became prohibited for the heir. It has also been said that the verse is muhkam (not abrogated), and that its intended meaning from the outset was bequest to someone other than an heir, from among the parents and close relatives, such as disbelieving parents, slaves, and relatives who have no share of inheritance. This was the view of al-Dahhak, al-Hasan in one narration, and Tawus, and al-Tabari chose it. The more correct view, however, is the first.

Then, those who hold that the ruling of bequest remained after abrogation are of two kinds. Some said it remained obligatory for the close relatives who do not inherit. This is the view of al-Hasan, Tawus, al-Dahhak, and al-Tabari, because they said: it is not abrogated. Among those who said it is abrogated, Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq, Muslim ibn Yasar, and al-Ala' ibn Ziyad also held this. Others said it remained recommended (mandub) for close relatives and others. This is the view of the majority, except that if one's relatives are in need and he does not bequeath to them, then "what he did is evil" (fa-bi'sa ma sana'a), yet the bequest is not void. It has also been said that it is restricted to kinship: if he bequeaths to others, the bequest is void and is returned to his relatives. This was stated by Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Sha'bi, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, and al-Hasan al-Basri.

What is held by those whose opinions are relied upon is that a bequest to a non-heir, when one does not fear through leaving it the loss of anyone's right owed by the testator, is desirable, and that it lies between obligation and emphasized Sunnah, based on the hadith: "It is not lawful for a man who believes in Allah and the Last Day, who has property regarding which he wishes to make a bequest, to spend two nights without his bequest being written at his head." If this hadith was said by the Prophet ﷺ after the prescription of the obligatory shares, then it is so; but if it was before that, it was an explanation of the verse of bequest and an incitement to it. The Muslims have continued to regard bequest of property as a legal right. In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of Talhah ibn Musarrif, who said: I asked 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, "Did the Prophet make a bequest?" He said, "No." I said, "How then was bequest prescribed for people, if he did not bequeath?" He said, "He bequeathed the Book of Allah." End of quote. It means that since the Prophet ﷺ did not leave an inheritance, likewise he did not bequeath his property; rather he bequeathed what returns benefit to the Muslims, by holding fast to the Book of Islam. It was also the custom of Muslims to say to a sick person, when death was feared for him, "Make your bequest."

The scholars of Islam have agreed that a bequest is not to be made to an heir, due to what the compilers of the Sunan narrated on the authority of 'Umar ibn Kharijah, and what Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated on the authority of Abu Umamah, both saying: I heard the Prophet say: "Indeed Allah has given every rightful person his right; so there is no bequest to an heir." This was at the Farewell Pilgrimage. Thus it specified the generality of "parents" and the generality of "close relatives," and this specification is abrogation, because it occurred after acting upon the general text. Although it is a report of solitary transmission (khabar ahad), it has been treated as among the mutawatir, because the whole community heard it and the scholars of the Ummah received it with acceptance.

Page 151

The majority hold that a bequest exceeding one-third is void, based on the well-known hadith: on the authority of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, that he fell ill and the Prophet ﷺ visited him, and he asked his permission to bequeath all his property, and he forbade him, until he said to him: "One-third, and one-third is much. Indeed, if you leave your heirs wealthy, that is better than leaving them dependent, begging from people." Abu Hanifa said: if the testator has no heirs, even only an 'asaba (agnatic relatives), other than the public treasury (bayt al-mal), it is permissible for the testator to bequeath all his property, and this is upheld, taking as evidence the indication of the reason in his words: "Indeed, if you leave your heirs wealthy, that is better..." etc. He said: the public treasury is a collector, not an 'asaba. It was also narrated from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh. It has been disputed whether it is valid for an heir if the rest of the heirs permit it. The position of the scholars of the major cities is that if an heir permits it, it stands. This is all. The Muslims have agreed that Allah the Exalted determined the manner of dividing the estate of the deceased by the verse of inheritance, and that the verse of bequest mentioned here has, after that, ceased to have its apparent meaning intended. Thus those who hold that it is muhkam say: the bequest remains for non-heirs, and the bequest to an heir is only in what exceeds his share of inheritance; so there is no abrogation between the two verses.

Those who hold abrogation say, among them: those who see that bequest remained obligatory for non-heirs say that the verse of inheritance abrogated the option regarding the beneficiary and the unrestricted quantity bequeathed. Among those who see that its obligation has been abrogated and it became recommended, they say: the verse of inheritance abrogated this entire verse, so the bequest prescribed by this verse became abrogated by the verse of inheritance, by consensus that the verse of inheritance abrogated the generality of "parents and close relatives" who are heirs, and abrogated the unrestrictedness in the wording of bequest; and specification after acting upon the general, and restriction after acting upon the unrestricted, both were abrogated. Although the wording of the verse of inheritance does not indicate what contradicts the verse of bequest, since it allows that inheritance may come after the giving of bequests or in the absence of a bequest, indeed its apparent sense is that, due to His words: ﴿after bequest﴾ [an-Nisa: 11]. And although the two hadiths reported on this are solitary reports, unfit to abrogate the Qur'an according to those who do not hold that the Qur'an is abrogated by solitary reports, a new ruling for bequest has nonetheless been established, namely recommendation or obligation, depending on the difference regarding non-heirs and regarding one-third, by the evidence of consensus resting on the hadiths and the practice of the Companions. Since a new ruling for bequest has been established, it is a ruling not derived from the abrogated verse, but rather a ruling resting on consensus. This is the statement of the principle of the scholars' deduction in this matter, and in it is what removes from the inquirer many difficulties raised by the exegetes and jurists in explaining how abrogation occurs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 181:

[152]
﴿So whoever alters it after he has heard it, indeed its sin is upon those who alter it. Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾

The pronouns that appear in (baddalahu) [alteredit], (sami'ahu) [heard it], (ithmuhu) [its sin] and (yubaddiluna-hu) [they alter it] refer to the statement or speech that the testator utters, which is indicated by the word al-wasiyyah (the bequest). This is confirmed by what is indicated by his saying (sami'ahu), since speech is what is heard. It has also been said that they refer to the act of bequeathing (al-iesa') understood from his saying (al-wasiyyah), that is, just as the pronoun refers to a verbal noun derived from the verb, as in the verse ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8]. You may also make the pronoun refer to al-ma'ruf (what is fair), and the meaning would be: whoever alters the bequest that was made in accordance with what is fair, because the sin lies in altering what is fair, as evidenced by His later saying: ﴿But whoever fears from a testator an error or sin and brings about reconciliation among them, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 182].

By "alteration" (al-tabdil) here is meant annulment (al-ibtal) or diminution (al-naqs). The referent of "whoever alters it" is the one in whose hand lies the execution of the bequest, from among the close heirs such as the sons, and from among the witnesses to it, whether by the testator's call for witness or by their presence at the place of the bequest, as in the bequest during travel mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿We will not exchange it for any price, even if it were [to] a near relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed, we would then be among the sinful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106]. Thus "tabdil" is used in its figurative sense, since the literal meaning of tabdil is placing one thing in the place of another, and annulment entails bringing the opposite of what was annulled. The restriction of the alteration by the temporal clause "after he has heard it" is a justification for the threat; that is, because he altered what he heard and knew to be true. Otherwise, alteration is not conceivable except regarding something known and heard, since souls are not directed toward the unknown.

The restriction in His saying (﴿fa-innama ithmuhu﴾) is relative (idafi), to negate sin from the testator. Otherwise, his sin too would fall upon the one who takes what the testator did not grant him, knowingly, if the executor of the bequest or the judge shows him favoritism, for a ruling does not make lawful what is unlawful. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever I decide in his favor concerning the right of his brother, I am merely cutting for him a piece of Fire." The sin is negated from the testator because he has cleared himself when he bequeathed in accordance with what is fair, so there is no burden upon him for the opposition of people after him to what he bequeathed, since ﴿no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Najm: 38] and ﴿that man will have only what he strove for﴾ [al-Najm: 39].

The purpose of this restriction is to refute the excuse of some people for abandoning the bequest, on the pretext of fear that those entrusted with its execution will not carry it out. That is: so upon you is the bequest. The obligation of execution is binding upon the one overseeing the bequest; if he alters it, then upon him is its sin. His saying ﴿indeed its sin is upon those who alter it﴾ indicates that this alteration is prohibited by the Law, and that rulers should restrain the hand of whoever attempts this alteration, since sin does not establish a legal ruling.

[153]
His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾ is a threat to the one who alters it, because nothing is hidden from Allah, even if people devise tricks to annul rights by various stratagems and commit injustice in all kinds of oppression. Allah hears the testator's bequest and knows the deed of the one who alters it. And since He is Hearing and Knowing, and He is capable, there is no barrier between Him and requiting the one who alters it. The emphasis by "inna" looks to the alterer's judicial state in His saying ﴿whoever alters it﴾, because in his undertaking of the alteration he is like one who denies that Allah is Knowing, so the ruling is emphasized for him, treating him in the position of one who denies.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 182:

﴿Then whoever fears from a testator partiality or sin and makes reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This is a derivative (tafri') upon the ruling that preceded it, which is the prohibition of altering (al-tabdil). Just as the command to uphold justice in bequest (al-wasiyyah) is followed by a warning against the one who alters it, so too the warning against the alterer is followed by a permission to make an alteration that is among what is good (al-ma'ruf). This is the alteration of a bequest that contains injustice and unfairness, carried out by way of reconciliation between the beneficiaries and the one who has suffered unfairness from that bequest. This occurs when the testator left out someone who was deserving of being named as a beneficiary, or allotted to someone a share less than what he deserved and so wronged him. This is because the verse of bequest (ayat al-wasiyyah) restricted the division of the deceased's estate to the carrying out of his bequest and made that matter entrusted to his trustworthiness (amanah) according to what is good (al-ma'ruf). Thus, when someone fears a clear unfairness and deviates from what is good, the rulers (wulat al-umur) are commanded to effect reconciliation.

The meaning of (khafa, "fears") here is suspicion and expectation (al-zann wa al-tawaqqu'), because the supposition of something disliked is a kind of fear (khawf). So the word "fear" is applied to its concomitant, which is suspicion and expectation, indicating that what the one who expects it anticipates is of the category of what is disliked. The indicator (al-qarinah) is that partiality (al-janaf) and sin (al-ithm) do not frighten anyone, especially one who is not among the people of the bequest, namely the reconciler between its people. Among the application of "fear" in this sense is the verse of Abu Mihjan al-Thaqafi:

"I fear, when I die, that I will not taste it"

That is: I suspect and know something disliked. For this reason he said before it:

"Its roots will water my bones after my death."

The word janaf means injustice (al-hayf), inclination (al-mayl) and oppression (al-jawr), and its verb follows the pattern of fariha.

Ithm means disobedience (al-ma'siyah). Thus what is meant by janaf here is the preference of one who does not deserve preference over others among the relatives, when he is equal to them or more entitled. This includes what was done without intention, yet in reality it is an injustice to the right. What is meant by ithm is that the testator intended by it to deprive one who deserves, or to prefer another over him.

Page 154

Reconciliation (al-islah) is making a thing sound (salih). It is said: aslahahu, meaning he made it sound. For this reason it is applied to intervening between two disputants with mutual consent, because it makes them sound after they had become corrupt. It is said: aslaha baynahum, with the verb being construed with the meaning of "entered" (tadmin). The pronoun governed by bayn in the verse refers to the testator and the beneficiaries, which are the two notions implied by the word (musin), since it requires beneficiaries. The meaning of ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾ is that no blame attaches to him for altering the bequest, because it is an alteration toward what is good.

The meaning is: whoever finds in the testator's bequest harm to some of his relatives, such as by depriving one of them of his bequest, or by giving precedence to one who is more distant in lineage, or by appointing a wealthy one of his relatives as executor while leaving aside their poor, and then strives to reconcile this and asks the testator to change his bequest, there is no sin upon him in that, because he has striven for reconciliation among them. Or a dispute arises among the relatives after the testator's death because he favored some of them over others. For this reason it is followed by ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. In this there is an emphasis on safeguarding the execution of the bequests of testators, to the point that altering their injustice requires permission from Allah the Exalted, along with an explicit statement that such a person is forgiven.

The majority (al-jumhur) read ﴿mūṣin﴾ as the active participle of "awsa." Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read (muwassin) with a fatha on the waw and a shaddah on the sad, as the active participle of the doubled form "wassa."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 183 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ ﴿for a limited number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]

The ruling on fasting (sawm) is one of the great rulings that Allah Most High has legislated for the community. It is among the acts of worship aimed at purifying the soul and disciplining it, and in it lies the wellbeing of individuals, one by one, since society is formed from them. The sentence is separated from what precedes it in order to move to a different purpose, and it opens with ﴿O you who have believed﴾ because the address carries a display of concern for what will be said after it.

The discussion of the meaning of ﴿has been prescribed for you﴾ and its indication of obligation has already passed, at His saying: ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is the bequest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], and so on.

Fasting (al-siyam), also called al-sawm, is, in the technical usage of the Sharia, the name for abstaining from all eating, all drinking, and sexual relations for a period fixed by the Sharia, with the intention of obeying Allah's command, or for the purpose of drawing near to Allah through a vow made for that purpose.

Page 155

Al-siyam is a noun transferred from the verbal noun of the form fa'āl, its middle radical being a waw that was changed to a ya' because of the kasra on the first radical of the word. The regular verbal noun is al-sawm, and both verbal nouns occur in the Qur'an. Thus, in the lexical language, al-siyam is not used in its literal sense except for abstaining from all food and drink, and in Islam abstaining from sexual relations has been added to it. So if someone abstains from some kinds of food or from some women, it is not fasting, as al-'Arji said:

"If you wish, I will forbid women other than you, and if you wish, I will not taste cool water or sweet water."

The word siyam has other figurative usages, such as its application to holding horses back from running, in the words of al-Nabigha:

"Some horses are held in fasting, and others are not fasting, under the dust, while others chew their bits."

It was also applied to a wild ass abstaining from drinking water, and Labid, describing the wild ass and his she-ass after the end of winter, when the asses do not drink water because they are satisfied with the moist pasture, said:

"Until, when they had completed six months of Jumada, a portion, their fasting lengthened, and so did hers."

The apparent view is that the term sawm in the lexical language is literal for abstaining from eating and drinking with the intention of drawing near to Allah, for the Arabs knew fasting in the Jahiliyya from the Jews, in their fasting on the day of 'Ashura', as we shall mention.

As for the statement of the jurists that sawm in the lexical language means abstaining in general, and that its application to abstaining from the two desires is a technical Sharia usage, this is not sound, because it contradicts the statements of the lexicographers, as in al-Asas and elsewhere. As for the application of sawm to abstaining from speech in His saying, quoting the mother of 'Isa: ﴿So say, "Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being"﴾ [Maryam: 26], it is not an application of sawm to abstaining from speech, but the meaning is that fasting was followed by abstaining from speech in its perfect and excellent form.

Thus the definite article in al-siyam in the verse is the mental (ʿahd dhihni) definite article; that is, ﴿has been prescribed for you﴾ refers to the known kind of fasting. The Arabs knew fasting, for it is reported in the two Sahihs from 'A'isha who said: The day of 'Ashura' was a day that the Quraysh used to fast in the Jahiliyya, and in some narrations her words are: "And the Messenger of Allah used to fast it." And from Ibn 'Abbas: "When the Messenger of Allah emigrated to Medina, he found the Jews fasting on the day of 'Ashura'. He said: 'What is this?' They said: 'A day on which Allah saved Musa, so we fast it.' The Messenger of Allah said: 'We have more right to Musa than you,' and he fasted it and ordered its fasting." So the meaning of his question is a question about the purpose of the Jews in fasting it, not an inquiry into the origin of their fasting. In the hadith of 'A'isha: "When Ramadan was revealed, Ramadan became the obligatory fast, and the Messenger of Allah said: 'Whoever wishes may fast the day of 'Ashura', and whoever wishes may not fast it.'" So fasting the day of 'Ashura' became obligatory by the Sunna, and then that was abrogated by the Qur'an.

Page 156

Thus the thing commanded is a known fast, to which were added, in its legally valid manner, the specifications of the limits of its states and times by His saying: ﴿So now, have relations with them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], up to His saying: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], and His saying: ﴿the month of Ramadan﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], the verse, and His saying: ﴿And whoever is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. By this it becomes clear that in His saying ﴿fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ there is a general statement whose details came in the verses after it.

Thus in the fasting of Islam there occurred what differs from the fasting of the Jews and the Christians in the specifications of the essence of fasting and its manner, and our fasting was not entirely identical to theirs. So His saying ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ is a comparison in the basic obligation of the essence of fasting in its modes, and comparison is satisfied with some aspects of resemblance, namely the aspect of resemblance intended in the purpose. The aim of this comparison is not to refer, regarding the nature of fasting, to what it was among the earlier nations, but it contains three purposes:
