The first: attention to this act of worship and the highlighting of it, for Allah legislated it before Islam for those who were before the Muslims, and legislated it for the Muslims, and that requires the continuity of its benefit and the abundance of its reward, and the stirring of the aspirations of the Muslims to receive this act of worship, lest those before them be distinguished by it.

The Muslims used to compete in acts of worship, as in the hadith: "Some companions of the Messenger of Allah said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the people of wealth have taken the rewards: they pray as we pray, fast as we fast, and give charity from the surplus of their wealth'," the hadith; and they love to be preferred over the People of the Book, and to cut off the boasting of the People of the Book over them, claiming that they are people of a Sharia. Allah Most High said: ﴿Lest you say: "The Book was only sent down upon two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study"﴾ [al-An'am: 156] ﴿or you say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them." But there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord, and guidance and mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 157].

There is no doubt that they rejoice in the matter of fasting, and their fasting, which they observed on the day of 'Ashura', was only following the Jews in it, so they were looking forward to Allah singling them out with a fresh fast. This is the benefit of the comparison for the ambitious among the Muslims, since Allah joined them to the righteous nations in the laws that bring the good of this world and the Hereafter. Allah Most High said: ﴿And for this let those who compete compete﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 26].

The second purpose: in the comparison with the earlier ones there is an easing for those obligated with this act of worship, so that they do not find this fasting burdensome; for in following others there is an example in hardships. This benefit is for one who may consider fasting too great from among the polytheists, so that its presence in Islam prevents him from faith, and for one who finds it burdensome from those recently converted to Islam. This implicit meaning was confirmed by His saying after it: ﴿for a limited number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184].

Page 157

The third purpose: stirring up resolve to carry out this obligation, so that they do not fall short in accepting this duty, but rather take it with a strength that surpasses what the earlier nations performed it with.

It occurred to Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi in al-'Arida that he said: "Among Malik's statements about the manner of our fasting is that it was like the fasting of those before us, and that is the meaning of His saying: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾." There is discussion in this, which we will address when interpreting His saying: ﴿Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

This verse therefore legislated the obligation of fasting Ramadan, because the verb "kutiba" (was prescribed) indicates obligation. The beginning of the revelation of Surat al-Baqara was at the start of the Hijra, as has passed. So the fasting of 'Ashura' preceded it by a year, then Ramadan was made obligatory in the year that followed. In the Sahih: "The Prophet ﷺ fasted nine Ramadans," so there is no doubt that he fasted the first Ramadan in the second year of the Hijra. The fasting of 'Ashura' was thus obligatory for only one year, namely the beginning of the second year of the Hijra.

The intended meaning of ﴿those before you﴾ is those who were before the Muslims among the people of the revealed laws, namely the People of the Book, meaning the Jews, because they are the ones the addressees know and whose apparent affairs they know, and they were in contact with them in Medina. The Jews had a fast that God imposed on them, which is the fast of the tenth day of the seventh month of their year, which is the month called by them Tishri. The fast begins from sunset of the ninth day until sunset of the tenth day, and it is the Day of Atonement for sins, which they call Kippur. Then their rabbis legislated fasting four other days, namely the first days of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months of their year, in memory of the events of Jerusalem; and the fast of the day of Purim in memory of their deliverance from the wrath of the Persian king Ahasuerus in the event of Esther. Among them is voluntary fasting. In a hadith: "The most beloved fasting to Allah is the fasting of Dawud: he fasted one day and broke his fast one day." As for the Christians, their law contains no text legislating fasting beyond what is in the Torah, so they followed the Jews' fasting. In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn 'Abbas: "They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the Jews glorify the day of 'Ashura'," and so on. Then their monks legislated a fast of forty days, following al-Masih, since he fasted forty days before his mission. Among them vowing to fast at repentance and other occasions is legislated, except that they expand in the manner of fasting; for them it is abstaining from strong foods and drinks, or it is taking one meal a day, which may be followed by a light snack.

His saying ﴿so that you may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183] is an explanation of the wisdom of fasting and that for which it was legislated. It is in the sense of a purpose clause (maf'ul li-ajlihi) for "kutiba." "La'alla" is either used figuratively with the meaning of "kay" (in order that), as a subsidiary metaphor, or it is an illustrative figure in which the matter of Allah, in His will in legislating fasting for piety, is compared to the situation of one who hopes for something from another. Legal piety is refraining from sins. Fasting was made to bring about refraining from sins because sins are of two kinds: one kind is effectively prevented by reflection, such as wine, gambling, theft, and usurpation, whose avoidance is achieved by promise for avoiding it, threat for committing it, and admonition through the conditions of others. Another kind arises from natural motives, such as matters arising from anger and from natural desire, which may be hard to abandon by reflection alone. So fasting was made a means of guarding against them, because it moderates the natural faculties which are the motive for those sins, so that the Muslim may rise through it from the depths of immersion in matter to the zenith of the spiritual world. It is thus a means to training in angelic qualities and to shaking off the dust of animal impurities.

In the authentic hadith: "Fasting is a shield" (junna), meaning a protection. Since the object of "junna" is omitted, it is restricted to what suits it among the desirable kinds of protection: in fasting there is protection from falling into sins, protection from falling into the punishment of the Hereafter, and protection from diseases and ailments arising from excess in the enjoyment of pleasures.

His saying ﴿for a limited number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184] is an adverbial complement of time for "fasting," like your saying: "The going out is on Friday." It does not harm that there is a separation between "fasting" and "days," namely His saying "as it was prescribed" through "that you may become righteous," because on close examination the separation was not by a foreign element, since the state and the purpose clause derived from "la'alla" are all completions of the governing element of the adverbial complement, which is "fasting," and completions of the governor of that are the governor itself, "kutiba." The governor of a governor is a governor of that thing. Separation by a foreign element is permitted when the governed element is a time adverb, because of their latitude with adverbs. This is the preferred view of al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari, and al-Radi. The root of this question is avoiding the scattering of speech by disturbing its known order, avoiding a complexity that harms eloquence.

**[Page 159]**

The prevailing condition of nations in their jahiliyya (the age of ignorance before Islam), and especially of the Arabs, was to indulge excessively in worldly pleasures: foods, intoxicants, the diversions of women, and ease. All of this supplies the bodily and blood-related strengths in the bodies, so the animal faculties in a human being become strong, namely the appetitive faculty (al-quwwa al-shahwiyya) and the irascible faculty (al-quwwa al-ghadabiyya). They then overpower the rational faculty (al-quwwa al-ʿaqila). Therefore the sacred laws (al-sharāʾiʿ) brought the legislation of fasting (al-ṣiyām), because it accomplishes the refinement of those faculties, for it restrains a person from excessive consumption of the things that stimulate their excess. Its result is the moderation of those faculties at specified times, which are the likely times for their being satisfied until other times.

Fasting (al-ṣawm), meaning reducing the intake of food below the amount that reaches satiety, or abstaining from some kinds of food, is an ancient principle among the principles of piety (al-taqwā) held by the adherents of the religions (al-milliyyūn) and by the Illuminationist sages (al-ḥukamāʾ al-ishrāqiyyūn). The Illuminationist wisdom (ḥikmat al-ishrāq) is founded on purifying the soul (tazkiyat al-nafs) by removing the impurities of animality from it to the extent possible. This is based on the premise that the human being has two faculties: one is spiritual (rūḥāniyya), diffused in its depths from the inner senses; the other is animal (ḥayawāniyya), diffused in its depths from all the bodily organs. Since food replaces for the body what it loses of its animal strength, through a loss that arises from the natural functioning of the principal organs and others, it is inevitable that increasing food beyond the amount needed provides the body with animal strength beyond its need, while decreasing it restricts that strength until it reaches the amount without which the preservation of life is impossible. The predominance of the manifestation of one of the two faculties is in proportion to the diminishing of the manifestation of the other. Therefore they found that weakening the animal faculty reduces its operation, so the spiritual faculty dominates the body. The matter progresses gradually until the person in this state becomes closer to the spirits and the abstractions than to the animal, such that he has no share of animality except the life of the body that preserves the spirit within it. For this reason it is necessary to moderate the degree of this reduction in a manner that does not lead to the dissolution of life, because that would defeat the purpose of purifying the soul and preparing it for the otherworldly realms. Thus this balancing and weighting between the two faculties is the origin of the legitimacy of fasting in the religions, and its placement within the wisdom of illumination. In its form, the sacred laws differ in a manner suited to the particular conditions of those to whom they are addressed, such that the purpose of both lives is not lost. Undoubtedly, the best form for achieving this aim of fasting is the form that Islam brought.

It has been said in *Hayākil al-Nūr* (The Temples of Light): The rational souls, being of the essence of the dominion (al-malakūt), are only distracted from their world by the bodily faculties and their preoccupations. When the soul becomes strong through spiritual virtues, and the authority of the bodily faculties weakens through reducing food and increasing vigil, the soul sometimes escapes to the world of holiness (ʿālam al-quds), connects with its Holy Father, and receives knowledge from Him. Among fasting is the abstention of the Brahmins (al-barāhima) from eating the flesh of animals, and their restricting themselves to plants **[Page 160]** or milk. The sages of the Greeks (ḥukamāʾ al-yūnān) used to train themselves to reduce food gradually until they became accustomed to abstaining for consecutive days. They agreed that the reduction of food should be gradual, in a manner that does not threaten the integrity of the body's health. (One method is) that the wise person weighs his satiety from food using twigs of fig wood, fresh, and then does not renew them; he weighs each day's food with them, not exceeding their weight. He continues in this way until they become so dry that they cannot dry any further, and that is then the weight of each day's food.

In *Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq* of al-Suhrawardī: "Before beginning to read this book, one should train oneself for forty days, abstaining from the flesh of animals, reducing food, and devoting oneself to contemplating the light of God." End of quotation.

Since it is impossible for the human physical body, being a repository of animal life, to strip itself of its animality, it is equally impossible for it to cut itself off entirely from supplying its animality with what it desires. Therefore, for the pursuit of its soul's elevation, it is necessary to progress through the attainable degrees of refining its animality and freeing it from excessive immersion in it, to the extent possible. For this reason fasting is among the most important preliminaries to this aim, because it contains two great qualities: moderation in supplying the animal faculties, and training in patience by turning them back from their impulses. Since reaching the complete extent of this is impossible, as you know, the masters of psychic wisdom (asāṭīn al-ḥikma al-nafsāniyya) sought to reduce it. Some of them treated reduction by lessening the quantities, and this is the fasting of the sages. Others attempted it by cutting the times of enjoying them, and this is the fasting of the religions, which is more effective in reaching the goal and more evident in the faculty of patience. By this, a person acquires a habituation to abandoning his desires, so he becomes qualified to adorn himself with perfection, for what stands between him and perfections and virtues is weakness in enduring turning away from his whims and desires.

*"If a man does not abandon a food he loves,*
*and does not restrain a misguided heart wherever it heads,*
*then he will soon acquire for himself, through time, a disgrace*
*which, when such things are mentioned, fills the mouth."*

If you say: if the legislative purpose of fasting is the training of the soul in abandoning desires, and arousing awareness of the pain of hunger suffered by the needy, and feeling the equality between the affluent and the comfortable and the poor in the basic pleasures of food, drink and diversion between the two groups, then why did the divine religions differ in the manner of fasting? And why did the Islamic religion adhere to one form of it, and not leave that to the Muslim to adopt whatever he sees suitable for training his soul in achieving the intended purposes?

I say: It is the nature of good instruction to fix for the learner rules and methods that lead him to the desired fruit of the knowledge he practices. The teacher of physical exercise fixes for the learner forms of movements with his limbs and the development of his stature: standing upright, bowing, and squatting. Some of these produce the strength of his muscles, some produce the balance of the blood circulation, and some produce the functions of his arteries. These are forms that the people of that discipline have determined, and through which they have brought near the attainment of the desired fruit. If that were left to the seekers, long periods of time would be lost in experiments, and the forms would multiply according to the multiplicity of the seekers' understandings and choices. This falls under His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God intends ease for you, and He does not intend hardship for you﴾ (2:185).

By "days" in His saying: ﴿numbered days﴾ (2:184), the majority of the exegetes mean the month of Ramadan. He expressed Ramadan by "days," which is a plural of paucity (jamʿ qilla), and described them as "numbered" (maʿdūdāt), which is also a plural of paucity; this is to make the matter light for those obligated. "Numbered" is a metaphor for fewness, because a small thing is counted; therefore they say: "The abundant is not counted." For this reason, the feminine plural form was chosen for the adjective, following the plural in alif and tāʾ, although its coming in the broken plural (jamʿ taksīr), which has the feminine tāʾ marker, is more common. Abū Ḥayyān, commenting on His saying, exalted is He, that comes after it: ﴿of other days﴾ (2:185), said: "An adjective of a plural that does not denote rational beings is sometimes treated as a feminine singular, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except for numbered days﴾ (2:80), and sometimes it is treated as the plural of the feminine, as in: ﴿numbered days﴾ (2:184). So *maʿdūdāt* is the plural of *maʿdūda*, and you do not say *yawm maʿdūda*. Both usages are eloquent. It appears that it was left here for the sake of verification, because the proper way for an adjective applied to a masculine plural, when they make it feminine, is for it to be a feminine singular, since the plural has been interpreted as the group (al-jamāʿa), and the group is a singular word. This is the common usage. However, when they wish to draw attention to the great number of that plural, they apply its adjective to the form of the feminine plural, so that it carries the meaning of groups, and that the plural dissolves into many groups. For this reason I see that *maʿdūdāt* is more than *maʿdūda*." For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days﴾ (2:80), because they minimize them through delusion or deception. He said here "*maʿdūdāt*" because they are thirty days. And in the following verse He said: ﴿The pilgrimage is in known months﴾ (2:197). This is similar to His saying regarding the plural of *jamal* (camel) as *jimālāt*, according to one of the two interpretations, and it is more common than *jimāl*.

It is also reported from al-Māzinī that the plural of what does not denote rational beings, most of it comes with the form of the feminine singular: you say "*al-judhūʿ inkasarat*" (the trunks broke), while the few of it come with the form of the plural: you say "*al-ajdhāʿ inkasarat*" (the trunks broke). End of quotation. This is not evident.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of "the days" is other than Ramadan. Rather, they are days whose fasting became obligatory upon the Muslims when fasting was prescribed by His saying: ﴿numbered days﴾ (2:184). Then their fasting was abrogated (nusikha, naskh meaning abrogation) by the fasting of Ramadan. These days are the Day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, and three days of every month, which are the "white days" (ayyām al-bīḍ): the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth. This view was held by Muʿādh, Qatāda and ʿAṭāʾ. Of the fasting prescribed for the Muslims before Ramadan, only the fasting of the Day of ʿĀshūrāʾ is established, as in the *Ṣaḥīḥ*, and it was obligatory by the Sunnah. It is mentioned that fasting on ʿĀshūrāʾ and the white days was obligatory upon the Prophet ﷺ, but this is not established by a reliable narration (riwāya). Therefore it cannot be correct that they are the intended meaning of the verse, neither linguistically nor by transmitted report. Moreover, all of that was abrogated by the fasting of Ramadan, as indicated by the hadith of the questioner who said: "I will not add to this, nor reduce from it." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "He has succeeded if he is truthful."

[Page 162 continues from the previous part]

﴿So whoever among you is sick or on a journey, then [the fast is owed as] a number of other days.﴾

This is a continuation of the firm rule (*'azima*) by the concession (*rukhsa*), so the *fa'* (then) indicates sequence in the narrative, not derivation. Mentioning it here, before the rest of the provisions for fasting, is a way of quickly reassuring the listeners, lest they assume that fasting is obligatory for them in every circumstance.

The sick person is one in whom sickness is present, and sickness is the deviation of the temperament from its natural balance, such that fever, pain, or weakness arises in the body.

The jurists differ over defining the sickness that permits breaking the fast. As for a severe sickness in which the sick person cannot fast at all, to the point of fearing death or its approach, there is no disagreement among them that it permits breaking the fast; indeed, it makes breaking the fast obligatory. As for sickness below that level, they differ over its extent. The verifying jurists (*muhaqqiqun*) held that it is the sickness which, with fasting, produces hardship beyond the ordinary hardship of hunger and thirst that a healthy person experiences, such that it causes him pains or debilitating weakness, or causes dormant diseases to return to him, or increases his deviation toward the state of sickness, or it is feared that the sickness will prolong because of it. This is the position of Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, with variations among them in wording. The most just of these formulations is what is reported from Malik, because God stated sickness without restricting it, and we know that He permitted breaking the fast only because that sickness has an effect on the fasting person. The principle that clarifies this is the statement of al-Qarafi in the Fourteenth Distinction, where he said: hardships are of two kinds. One kind is light, and the act of worship is not separate from it, such as performing ablution and bathing in cold weather, and fasting, and risking oneself in jihad. The other kind is that from which the act of worship is separate, and this has several types: one type has no effect on the act of worship, such as the pain of a finger, for fasting does not increase the pain of a finger, and this is not to be heeded. Another type has a strong effect along with the act of worship, such as fear for the self, the limbs, or the benefits, and this requires the suspension of that act of worship. And another type is close to this and requires what this requires.

Ibn Sirin, 'Ata', and al-Bukhari held that sickness, which is pain and illness, permits breaking the fast even if fasting does not increase it in severity or intensity, because God, exalted is He, made sickness a cause for breaking the fast, just as He made travel a cause for breaking the fast, without any necessity compelling breaking the fast as in travel. They mean that the effective cause is the likelihood of additional hardship in most cases. It is said that someone entered upon Ibn Sirin during the daytime of Ramadan while he was eating, and when he finished he said: "My finger has caused me pain, so I broke the fast." And from al-Bukhari it is reported that he said: "I fell ill with a mild illness in Nishapur during Ramadan, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh visited me with a group of his companions. He said to me: 'You have broken the fast, O Abu 'Abd Allah?' I said: 'Yes.' 'Abdan informed us, from Ibn al-Mubarak, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata': 'From what sickness may I break the fast?' He said: 'From whatever sickness it may be, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So whoever among you is sick﴾.'" It is also said: if the sick person is unable to pray standing, he breaks the fast. This is a particular case that serves as an example and is not a condition. It is attributed to al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i, and its weakness is not hidden, for where is standing in prayer compared with breaking the fast in fasting? In this disagreement there is room for examination in determining the extent of deviation and sickness that justify the fasting person breaking his fast. The jurist must therefore encompass all of this, and we acknowledge through it the hardship that befalls the traveler and the menstruating woman.

As for His saying: ﴿or on a journey﴾, that is: or he was in the state of travel. The basic meaning of *'ala* (on) is elevation, then it was used metaphorically to mean being established in a state, as was mentioned previously in His saying: ﴿upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. Then it became common in Arabic speech to say: "So-and-so is on a journey," meaning he is traveling, so that the expression is explicit about one who is actually engaged in it, because the active participle may refer to the future. Thus they do not say "on a journey" of one who only intends to travel. As for the statement of ... :

"What of the veiled full moon, if only it would journey?
Indeed the one tormented by his passion is on a journey."

He meant that he is on the brink of death, and this is an error of the later (*muwallad*) Arabic writers. God, exalted is He, by this expression used for actually engaging in an act, indicated that the traveler does not break his fast until he has begun to proceed on the journey, not merely by intention. This matter is disputed. From Anas ibn Malik it is reported that he wished to travel during Ramadan, his mount was saddled, he put on his traveling clothes, and the sun was close to setting. He called for food, ate from it, then mounted, and said: "This is the Sunnah." It was narrated by al-Daraqutni, and it is the opinion of al-Hasan al-Basri. A group said: if he began the day as a resident and then traveled afterward, he does not break the fast for that day. This is the view of al-Zuhri, Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa, and Abu Thawr. If he breaks the fast, he owes making up the day but not an expiation (*kaffara*). Some Malikis went further and said: he owes the expiation. This is the view of Ibn Kinana and al-Makhzumi. It is strange that Ibn al-'Arabi chose it. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "This is nothing, because God permitted him to break the fast by the explicit text of the Book." Abu 'Umar was right. Ahmad, Ishaq and al-Sha'bi said: he breaks the fast if he travels after dawn. They narrated this from Ibn 'Umar, and it is the correct view, supported by the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in the Sahihayn of al-Bukhari and Muslim: "The Messenger of God ﷺ left Medina for Mecca and fasted until he reached 'Usfan. Then he called for water, raised it to his hands so that he could show it, and broke the fast until he entered Mecca." Al-Qurtubi said: "This is an explicit text on the matter, so whatever contradicts it falls away."

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿then [the fast is owed as] a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and He did not say: "then fasting of other days," in order to explicitly state the obligation of fasting a number of days equal to the days on which one broke the fast due to sickness or travel, since a number can only be equal to a similar quantity.

The *min* (from) is partitive if "days" is taken more generally than the days of the count, that is, from the days of time or of the year. Or *min* may be the specifier of *'idda* (a number), meaning a number which consists of days, like His saying: ﴿with five thousand of the angels﴾ [Al 'Imran: 125]. He described the days with *ukhar*, which is the plural of *ukhra*, taking into account the feminine form of the plural, since every plural is feminine. This has been mentioned previously in His saying just before: ﴿days numbered﴾. Abu Hayyan said: the plural form was chosen for the adjective rather than saying *ukhra*, lest it be assumed that it is an adjective of *'idda*. There is room for examination here, for this assumption does not cause confusion, since the number of days is itself days, so there is no need to be concerned with dispelling this assumption. The apparent reason for avoiding *ukhra* is to preserve the plural form in the noun described, together with seeking lightness of pronunciation.

The word *ukhar* is prohibited from *sarf* (declension) in Arabic speech. The majority of grammarians explained its prohibition from declension according to their principles as due to two features: descriptiveness (*wasfiyya*) and *'adl* (deviation from the original form). As for descriptiveness, it is evident. As for *'adl*, they said: since it is the plural of *akhar*, whose singular is in the form of the comparative (*ism al-tafdil*), and it is not defined by the article *al-*, it should by rule remain singular and masculine, following the patterns of its origin, which is the comparative when stripped of the definite article and of attachment to a definite noun. When the Arabs used it agreeing with its described noun in the dual and the plural, we know that they deviated from its original form. Deviation from the original form causes difficulty on the tongue, since it is not customary in usage, so they lightened it by prohibiting its declension. It seems they did not do this for its dual and plural with *alif* and *nun*, due to the rarity of their occurrence. There is more to be said about this.

The verse does not explain the manner of making up the fast of Ramadan. It stated absolutely ﴿a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], so it does not explain whether they must be consecutive or may be separated, nor whether one must hasten to make them up or may delay them, nor whether an expiation is obligatory for deliberately breaking the fast on some of the days of making up. Consideration of these three matters is contested. The evidence for holding to the absolute wording is that there is nothing that restricts it, just as one relies on a general ruling when no specifier appears. And the evidence that the basic principle in making up worship is that it should be in the form of the worship being made up.

As for the ruling on consecutiveness of the days of making up, al-Daraqutni narrated with an authentic chain from 'A'isha that she said: "It was revealed as: ﴿a number of other days, consecutive﴾, then the word 'consecutive' was dropped," meaning it was abrogated (*nusikha*). This is the view of the four imams. Among the Companions, Abu Hurayra, Abu 'Ubayda, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and Ibn 'Abbas held it. That is a concession from God, and in order to draw attention to it, He stated it absolutely as ﴿of other days﴾ and did not restrict it by consecutiveness, as He did in the expiation for *zihar* and in the expiation for accidental killing.

For this reason the majority disregarded the application of the rule that making up worship follows the form of what is made up, and they did not restrict the absolute verse on making up the fast with what the verses on the expiation for *zihar* and the expiation for accidental killing were restricted by.

In the Muwatta' it is reported from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "Whoever breaks the fast of Ramadan due to sickness or travel makes up the fast of Ramadan consecutively." Al-Baji said in al-Muntaqa: "It may be that he meant obligation, and it may be that he meant recommendation."

As for hastening to make up the fast, there is nothing in the Book or the Sunnah that requires it. His saying here: ﴿then [the fast is owed as] a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185] is intended as a command to make up, and the basic form of a command does not require immediacy. The Sunnah has established that making up Ramadan does not require immediacy but is flexible until the month of Sha'ban in the year following the month in which one broke the fast. In the Sahih it is reported from 'A'isha that she said: "I would have to make up days of Ramadan, and I could not make them up except in Sha'ban." This is clearly evident that immediacy is not required, and on this the majority of scholars agreed. Dawud al-Zahiri alone differed and said: making up Ramadan is prescribed beginning on the second day of Shawwal that follows it.

As for one who deliberately breaks the fast on one of the days of making up Ramadan, the majority hold that he owes no expiation, because the expiation was prescribed to protect the sanctity of the month of Ramadan, and the days of making up have no sanctity. Qatada said that he owes the expiation, on the basis that making up an act of worship is equivalent to its original.

* * *

[Page 166]

﴿And for those who are able to fast [but with difficulty], a ransom of feeding a poor person﴾

This is a coordination with His saying: ﴿fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183]. The coordinated item is part of what it is coordinated with, so in meaning it is like an apposition of a part. That is: it is prescribed upon those who are able to fast a ransom; for those who are able to fast are some of those addressed by His saying: ﴿fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183].

The one who is able (*mutiq*) is one who has the capacity to do the act, that is, it was within his power to do it. The *taqa* (capacity) is the closest of the degrees of power to the rank of inability, and for this reason they say of what exceeds capacity: "This is what cannot be endured." Al-Farra' explained it as *jahd* (with a fatha on the jim), which is hardship. In some transmissions of the Sahih of al-Bukhari from Ibn 'Abbas, he recited: (﴿and for those who are made to endure it, but they cannot endure it﴾), and it is, as I believe, an explanation. Similar readings have been reported from him. It is also said that *taqa* means power in general.

So, according to the interpretation of *itaqa* as hardship, the verse intends a concession for those for whom the hardship of fasting is severe, in breaking the fast and in the ransom.

Those who are elderly and infirm are also named, along with the nursing woman and the pregnant woman. These groups break the fast and feed a poor person for each day they break it. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, al-Hasan al-Basri and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and it is the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Then whoever among them is able to make up the fast makes it up, and whoever is not able to make it up does not make it up, like the elderly person. Abu Hanifa agreed on breaking the fast, except that he held the fidyah (ransom) to apply only to the elderly person, because he does not make up the fast, unlike the pregnant and nursing woman. The root of the disagreement is whether the Almighty's words ﴿And for those who are able to do it, there is a fidyah﴾ are for the sake of breaking the fast or for the sake of the lapse of the obligation to make up the fast. The verse allows both, but the first is more apparent. The practice of the early generations supports this: Anas ibn Malik, when he became elderly and reached one hundred and ten years, would break the fast and feed a needy person bread and meat for each day.

On the interpretation of tawaqqah (ability) as capacity, the verse indicates that one who is capable of fasting may substitute it with feeding. Since this ruling is not permanent by consensus, those who held this interpretation said that the verse then contained a ruling that involved latitude and concession, and then consensus was formed on its abrogation. The scholars of abrogation (ahl al-nasikh wa al-mansukh) mention that this was prescribed at the beginning of Islam when fasting was hard on them, and then it was abrogated by the Almighty's words ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and in al-Bukhari from Ibn 'Umar and Salamah ibn al-Akwa', who said: it was abrogated by the verse of the month of Ramadan. Then he narrated, via Ibn Abi Layla, who said: The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) told us: Ramadan descended, and it was hard on them, so whoever fed a poor person each day left the fast, and whoever was able to fast was permitted to do so in that way. Then ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾ abrogated it. Many reports on this are narrated from the Successors. This is the closer one to the Lawgiver's customary practice in gradually legislating obligations that involve hardship for people by changing their habits, just as he proceeded gradually in legislating the prohibition of wine. We attach to the elderly, the nursing woman and the pregnant woman everyone who suffers hardship or fears harm similar to theirs. This varies with differences in temperaments and with differences in the seasons of fasting, whether moderate, or severe cold or heat, and with differences in the work a fasting person does to earn a living, such as the goldsmith, the blacksmith, the bath attendant, agricultural labour, carrying the post, carrying loads, paving roads, and the wet nurse.

The fidyah has been interpreted as feeding in two ways: either by the annexation of the specified to its explanation, as Nafi', Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Ja'far recited (fidyatu ta'ami masakin), with fidyah annexed to ta'am; and the rest recited it with tanwin on "fidyatun" and "ta'amu" as a substitute (badal) for "fidyatun."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far recited (masakina) in the plural form, the plural of miskin, and the rest recited it in the singular. The consensus is that what is obligatory is feeding one miskin. The plural reading is based on considering the plurality of "those who are able," by the matching of plural with plural, like: "the people rode their animals." The singular reading considers what is obligatory upon each individual breaker of the fast.

Feeding is what satisfies, customarily, from the food eaten in the country. The jurists of Madinah estimated it as one mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), of wheat, barley or dates.
* * *

﴿So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾

This is a consequence of the Almighty's words ﴿And for those who are able to do it, there is a fidyah﴾ and so on. Tatawwu' means striving to be willing, not compelled; that is, he complied voluntarily from his own self. Khayr is the verbal noun of khara, when it becomes good and noble, and it is in the accusative either because tatawwa' is construed with the meaning of "came," or khayran is an adjective of an elided verbal noun, meaning: a good volunteering. Without doubt, the good here is what is volunteered, which is the addition to the matter the discourse is concerned with, namely feeding, undoubtedly. That feeding is not obligatory, so it may be that the meaning is: whoever adds to feeding one poor person, it is better; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Or it may be: whoever intends feeding together with fasting, as said by Ibn Shihab. And from Mujahid: whoever adds to feeding beyond the mudd. This is far-fetched, since the mudd is not explicitly mentioned in the verse. Anas ibn Malik fed bread and meat for each day he broke the fast when he became elderly.

The second khayr in His words ﴿it is better for him﴾ may be a verbal noun like the first, and the meaning is another good, that is, the good of the Hereafter. It may also be a comparative: that is, volunteering with the addition is better than leaving it, and the comparative element has been omitted because it is evident.

* * *

﴿And that you fast is better for you, if you know﴾

The apparent reference is to the Almighty's words ﴿And for those who are able to do it, there is a fidyah﴾. If those words were revealed concerning the permission to break the fast for the capable, then "And that you fast" is an encouragement to fasting and making it agreeable. If they were revealed concerning its permission for the one with hardship, such as the elderly, the same applies. It may also refer back to His words ﴿And whoever is ill﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185] and what follows, in which case it is a preference of fasting over breaking it. However, this is disputed among the imams regarding travel, and the position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is that fasting is better than breaking it. As for illness, there is a distinction according to the severity of the illness.

His words ﴿if you know﴾ are a concluding phrase (tadhyil): that is, you know the benefits of fasting, on the reference to His words ﴿And for those who are able to do it﴾ if by them are meant the capable; that is, if you know the benefits of fasting in this world and its reward in the next, or if you know its reward according to the other possibilities.

The word "if" (in) is used in the condition because their knowledge of both matters is not, by nature, certain, since the two benefits are hidden.

[Page 169]

You already know that these verses complete the preceding verses and that there is no abrogation (naskh) within this passage. So His saying ﴿shahru Ramadan﴾ ("the month of Ramadan") is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose implied form is "hiya" ("it is"). The meaning is: "The countable days are the month of Ramadan." The sentence is resumed in explanatory fashion (istinaf bayani), because His saying ﴿ayyaman ma'dudat﴾ ("for a number of days") [al-Baqarah: 184] raises the listener's question about specifying these days. This is supported by the reading of Mujahid, "shahran" with the accusative case, as a substitute (badal) for "ayyaman," a substitution of detail (badal tafsil).

The omission of the subject follows the usual manner of speech: when a passage precedes it that details and clarifies the circumstances of the subject, they omit its pronoun. If you allow that this statement abrogates the beginning of the verse, then it is not correct to take the implied form as "hiya shahru Ramadan." It is then necessarily the case that "shahru Ramadan" is the subject, whose predicate is His saying ﴿faman shahida minkum al-shahra falyasumhu﴾ ("So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast"). The predicate being joined with "fa" (then) in this case is an observance of the subject's qualification by a relative clause (mawsul), which resembles a conditional, and the like of this occurs much in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. Alternatively, it is the addition of "fa" to the predicate, as in the verse:

"And a speaker said: 'Khawlan, so marry their young women.'"

Sibawayh recited it. Both of these readings are weak.

The month (shahr) is one of twelve parts into which the year is divided. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, the day He created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. The month begins from the appearance of the crescent until its disappearance (al-mihaq), then the crescent appears again. It is derived from shuhrah (fame), because the crescent appears to them and they make it known (yushhiruna) so that the people may see it, and thus the month is established among them.

Ramadan is a proper noun ('alam) and is not a transferred noun (manqul), since no verbal noun on the pattern fa'lan from ramida (with the vowel of the mim being kasr), meaning "to be scorched," has been heard; for the pattern fa'lan indicates agitation, and there is no meaning for that here. It has been said that it is transferred from a verbal noun. Ramadan is the proper name of the ninth month of the months of the Arabic lunar year, which begins with Muharram. The Arabs used to begin the months of the year with Muharram, because the end of the year for them was the completion of the Hajj and the period of returning to their regions. Do you not see that Labid made Jumada al-Akhirah, which is the end of the winter season, the sixth month when he said:

"Until, when they had stripped away six Jumadas, a portion, its fasting became long, and so did hers."

Ramadan is not declined (mamnu' min al-sarf) because of being a proper noun and the addition of the alif and nun, since it is derived from al-ramda', which is the heat. This is because Ramadan is the first of the months of heat, according to what occurred of intercalation (nasi') in the year among the Arabs, when the year was divided into six seasons, each season consisting of two months. The first season is autumn (al-kharif), and its two months are Muharram and Safar. The second is spring (rabi' al-awwal), which is the time of the ripening of fruits and the appearance of fresh dates and dried dates, and its two months are the month of Rabi' al-Awwal and the month of Rabi' al-Thani, with "al-awwal" and "al-thani" being adjectives of a month. Do you not see that the Arabs say: "the fresh dates of the two months of Rabi'"? The third is winter (al-shita'), and its two months are Jumada al-Ula and Jumada al-Thaniyah. Hatim said:

"On a night of Jumada, with dews,
the dog cannot see the tent-ropes in its darkness.
The dog does not bark in it even once
until it wraps its tail around its snout."

The fourth is the second spring (al-rabi' al-thani), and "al-thani" is an adjective of spring. This is the time of the appearance of blossoms and truffles, and its two months are Rajab and Sha'ban, and it is the season of milk and rain. al-Nabigha, mentioning the raids of al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith, said:

"They had a spring raid which they feared
when the tribes stirred the water of the sky."

They named it "the second" because it comes after the first spring in the reckoning of the year. al-Nabigha said:

"If Abu Qabus dies, there will die
the spring of al-Thani and the sacred land."

In another narration it is related as "rabi' al-nas" (spring of the people). They named each of the two springs "rabi'" because it is a time of abundance. The fifth season is summer (al-sayf), which is the beginning of heat, and its two months are Ramadan and Shawwal, because in it the she-camels raise their tails, driving away flies. The sixth is the peak of summer (al-qayz), and its two months are Dhu al-Qa'dah and Dhu al-Hijjah. Some tribes divide the year into four, each season having three months: spring (al-rabi'), whose months are Rajab, Sha'ban and Ramadan; summer (al-sayf), whose months are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and Dhu al-Hijjah; autumn (al-kharif), whose months are Muharram, Safar and Rabi' al-Awwal; and winter (al-shita'), whose months are the month of Rabi' al-Thani, with "al-awwal" and "al-thani" being two adjectives of a month and not of spring, and Jumada al-Ula and Jumada al-Thaniyah.

Since the months of the Arabs were lunar, and the lunar year is less than the days of the solar year, by which the seasons come, it falls short by eleven days and a fraction. They wished that the Hajj would fall at the time of the completion of harvesting the crops and fruits, and at the time of safety from cold and extreme heat. So they made an intercalation (kabs) of the months by adding a month to the year after every three years. This is what is referred to as al-nasi'.

All the names of the months are proper nouns (a'lam) except for the month of Rabi' al-Awwal and the month of Rabi' al-Thani. Therefore it was necessary to mention the word "month" (shahr) with them, and then to describe it with "al-awwal" and "al-thani," because its meaning is "the first month of the spring season," that is, the first. So "al-awwal" and "al-thani" are two adjectives of a month. As for the other months, it is permissible to mention the word "month" in an idafah (construct), by the construction of a generic noun with its singular, like "shajar al-arak" (a tree of arak) and "madinat Baghdad" (the city of Baghdad). This is what the speech of Sibawayh and the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqin) indicates. Whoever says that Ramadan is not said except with the idafah of "month" to it, on the basis that Ramadan is a verbal noun, has forced himself into a stretched argument for its being prevented from declension, claiming that it became a proper noun by the idafah of "month" to it, so that part of the proper noun is prevented from declension, just as Hurayrah is prevented in Abu Hurayrah. He has indeed burdened himself with an excess and contradicted what has been related from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward," with Ramadan in the accusative. This misconception has only come to them from the terminology of the chancery books, as in Adab al-Katib.

The month was attributed to Ramadan in this verse, although the brevity sought for them would require not mentioning it, either because it is the more common in their eloquent speech, or to indicate the encompassing of all its days by fasting. For if he had said "Ramadan," it would have been apparent but not explicit, especially with the preceding mention of "ayyaman" (days), so the listeners would imagine that these are days of Ramadan.

So the meaning is that the portion known as the month of Ramadan of the Arabic lunar year is the one made a time (zarf) for the performance of the obligation of fasting prescribed in the religion. Whenever the specified time of the year called the month of Ramadan arrives, it becomes obligatory upon the Muslims to perform the obligation of fasting in it. Since its arrival recurs every year, the obligation of fasting recurs every year, for the fast was not tied to one specific month. Also, what is attributed to the month of qualities confirms that what is meant by it is the periods named by it throughout the age.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿alladhi unzila fihi al-Qur'an﴾ ("in which the Qur'an was sent down") is that the addressees know that the descent of the Qur'an occurred in the month of Ramadan, because the usual case with the relative clause (silat al-mawsul) is that the listener knows its being specific to the one to whom the relative pronoun applies. Also, such a religious event should not be hidden from them. So the speech is a reminder of this great virtue. It is also permissible that it is an announcement of this virtue, and the speech is arranged in the manner of description by the relative pronoun, to alert that the described is specific to the content of this clause, such that it is made a path to knowing him. We do not accept that the addressee must know that the bearer of the clause is characterized by its content in defining by relativity; rather, that is a predominant purpose, as the survey of their speech shows. And the intention is not to inform about the month of Ramadan that the Qur'an was sent down in it, because the structure of the sentence does not permit taking it as a predicate, since the expression "shahr Ramadan" is a predicate and is not the subject. The meaning of the sending down of the Qur'an is the beginning of its sending down upon the Prophet (ﷺ), for in it is the beginning of the descent in the forty-first year of the Elephant. So he expressed the sending down of its first part by the name of its whole, because that quantity sent down is destined to have its completion joined to it, as occurred in many verses, like His saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾ [al-An'am: 92], although that was before the completion of its descent. So it includes everything that is added to it afterwards. His saying ﴿those who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4] has already preceded. The meaning of ﴿unzila fihi al-Qur'an﴾ is "it was sent down in its like," because the month in which the Qur'an was sent down had passed before the descent of the verse of fasting by several years. For the fasting of Ramadan was prescribed in the second year of the Hijrah, so between the prescription of fasting and the month in which the Qur'an was actually sent down there are several years. So by the context it is necessary that what is meant is "it was sent down in its like," that is, in its counterpart from another year.

God has given the specified times a consideration resembling the consideration of a single thing renewed. This consideration is only for reminding of the great days, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remind them of the days of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim: 5]. So God has bestowed upon the times that were accompanied by a great matter of excellence a continuous favor, as an honouring of their being a reminder of a great matter. Perhaps this is the reason God made the sacrificial offering (al-hady) in the Hajj a practice, because in a time like that God tested Ibrahim by slaughtering his son Isma'il, and Ibrahim's resolve and obedience to his Lord were manifested. From this the scholars derived the glorifying of the day that coincides with the birthday of the Prophet (ﷺ). It follows from this the honouring of the descendants of the Messenger of Allah and the sons of the righteous, and the honouring of those in authority over the legal affairs who stand in the place of the Prophet (ﷺ) in their works, from the rulers, judges and imams.

This indicates that what God, exalted is He, intends from the Ummah is the fasting of thirty consecutive days, with a fixed beginning and end, uniform for all Muslims.

Since this is what is intended, it was timed to a specific lunar month, for the ease of fixing its beginning and end by sighting the crescent and by estimation. The month of Ramadan was chosen from among the months, because the Qur'an was honoured by being sent down in it. Since the sending down of the Qur'an was for the purpose of purifying the Ummah and guiding it, it was fitting that what purifies the souls and brings them near to the angelic state should occur in it. In my opinion, the more probable view is that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to fast the days of his seclusion (tahannuth) in the cave of Hira before the revelation came to him, as an inspiration from God, exalted is He, and as an instruction in a remnant of the Hanifiyyah religion. So when revelation was sent down to him in the month of Ramadan, God commanded the Islamic Ummah to fast in that month. Ibn Ishaq related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I stayed in seclusion at Hira during the month of Ramadan." Ibn Sa'd said: the revelation came while he was in the cave of Hira on Monday, seventeen nights having passed of Ramadan.

His saying ﴿hudan lilnas wa bayyinatin mina al-huda﴾ ("a guidance for the people and clear proofs of guidance") are two circumstantial clauses (hal) of the Qur'an, indicating by them the aspect of the preference of the month because of what was sent down in it of guidance and the criterion.

By the first "guidance" is meant what is in the Qur'an of direction toward the general and particular interests which do not contradict the general interest. By "clear proofs of guidance" is meant what is in the Qur'an of argumentation for the hidden guidance which many people deny, such as the proofs of monotheism (tawhid), the truthfulness of the Messenger, and other Qur'anic arguments. "Al-furqan" is a verbal noun of faraqa, and it has become widespread in the sense of distinguishing between truth and falsehood; that is, the proclamation of the distinction between the truth that came to them from God and the falsehood in which they were before Islam. So the meaning of the first "guidance" is a kind of guidance other than the meaning of the second guidance, and therefore there is no repetition.

* * *

﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it; and whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾, which is an explanation (bayan) of His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183], as already mentioned. So this is a return to the explanation after the interruption caused by what He placed after His saying ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183], namely reassurance (istinas) and an emphasis on the excellence of fasting and what is hoped for from its effect on the souls of those who fast, in piety, and what Allah has surrounded His obligation upon the community with of facilitation (taysir) when a hardship of fasting arises.

The pronoun in ﴿minkum﴾ ("of you") refers to those who believed, like the pronouns before it. That is: everyone who is present for the month should fast it. The verb (shahida) may mean "to be present (hadara)", as one says: "So-and-so witnessed Badr, witnessed Uhud, witnessed al-'Aqaba, or witnessed all the battles with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ", i.e., was present at them. Then "the month" is in the accusative as an adverb of time for the verb shahida; i.e., he was present during the month, that is, he was not travelling. This is what suits His saying after it: ﴿and whoever is ill or on a journey﴾, etc.

That is: whoever is present during the month, let him fast all of it. It is understood that whoever is present for part of it fasts the days of his presence. It is also possible that shahida means "to know" (ya'lam), as in His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. Then the accusative of "the month" is as a direct object with an elided noun: he knows of the arrival of the month. Shahida here does not mean "to see (ra'a)", because one does not say shahida meaning ra'a; rather one says shahada. Nor does "the month" here mean its crescent (hilal), on the basis that "the month" is applied to the crescent, as they report from al-Zajjaj, and in al-Asas he recited the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"So he became the one with the clearest sight, who needs no more, he sees the month before the people, while he is emaciated."

That is: he sees the crescent of the month. This is because the crescent cannot validly be the object of the verb shahida meaning "to be present". Whoever understands the verse this way has erred manifestly, and it leads to the conclusion that the obligation to fast of each individual of the community depends on his seeing the crescent of Ramadan; so whoever does not see the crescent is not obliged to fast, and this is false. For this reason, the verse does not explicitly state the means of establishing the month; the Sunnah has explained it, through the hadith: "Do not fast until you see the crescent, and do not break your fast until you see it; but if it is obscured from you, then estimate for it." The meaning of "estimating for it" has various interpretations, which are not part of the tafsir of the verse.

Al-Jumhur recited "al-Qur'an" with an open hamza after the silent ra', and after the hamza an alif. Ibn Kathir recited it with an open ra' followed by an alif, transferring the vowel of the hamza onto the silent ra' for the sake of lightening.

As for His saying: ﴿and whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number﴾: they said, regarding the reason for repeating it although its counterpart appeared earlier in His saying: ﴿so whoever of you is ill﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], that since fasting Ramadan was obligatory with a choice between it and the redemption (fidyah) by feeding, by the first verse, which is ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183] etc., and the obligation had dropped for the sick and the traveller by its text, then when the ruling of that verse was abrogated by His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan﴾ etc., and fasting became obligatory specifically, it was feared that people would think that all of what was in the first verse of concession had been abrogated, so fasting would be obligatory even upon the sick and the traveller. Therefore it was repeated in this abrogating verse, explicitly affirming the continuation of that concession, and the concession of feeding was abrogated with ability, residence and health only. This is based on the view that this verse abrogates the one before it. If we proceed on the view that the two were revealed at one time, then the reason for repeating this ruling is this place, which is fitting with His saying ﴿and whoever is ill﴾, because it came after the specifying of the days of fasting. As for what preceded in the first verse, it is an early informing of the concession, out of gentleness toward the listeners; or its repetition is to remove the suspicion that the first was abrogated by His saying ﴿so whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, if "witnessed" means "ascertained and knew", together with an added emphasis on the ruling of the concession and to increase the clarification of the meaning of His saying ﴿so whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾.

* * *

﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), serving as the cause (illah) of His saying ﴿and whoever is ill﴾ etc., by which He explains the wisdom of the concession; that is: He legislated for you the making-up (qada') because He intends for you ease at the time of hardship.

His saying ﴿and does not intend for you hardship﴾ is a negation of the opposite of ease. These two clauses could have been replaced by a clause of restriction (qasr), such as: "He intends for you only ease", but He turned away from the restrictive clause to two clauses of affirmation and negation, because the primary intended meaning is the affirmative clause, to serve as the reason for the concession, and the negative clause came after it as an emphasis of it. It is also possible that His saying ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ is the cause for everything preceding it from His saying ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183] up to here, so it is an indication that the legislation of fasting, although it appears in the form of hardship and difficulty, contains within it benefits showing that Allah intended by it ease, that is, the facilitation of attaining the training of the soul by a sound method, free from the exhausting of the followers of some other religions of their own souls.

Al-Jumhur recited "al-yusr" and "al-'usr" with a silent sin in both, while Abu Ja'far recited them with a damma on the sin, a damma of assimilation (ittiba').

* * *

﴿and that you complete the period, and that you glorify Allah for having guided you, and perhaps you will be thankful﴾

This is a conjunction (atf) on the clause ﴿Allah intends for you ease﴾ etc., since it is in the position of the cause as you know; for the whole of these four clauses is a cause for what precedes them, from His saying ﴿so whoever of you witnesses the month﴾ up to His saying ﴿then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184].

The lam in His saying "(wa li-tukabbiru)" is called "like the superfluous (shibh al-za'idah)", and it is the lam that frequently occurs after the verb of will (irada) and the verb of command (amr), that is, the root amara, the two of which have as their object "an" (that) the verbal particle with its verb. The object should normally be governed directly by the verb of will and the verb of command without a preposition, but the use of governing it with lam became common in speech, as in His saying: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾ [al-Saff: 8]. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: its origin is "yuridun an yutfi'u", and from it is His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-Zumar: 12]. The verb after the lam is in the subjunctive, with "an" either explicit or implied.

The meaning: Allah intends that you complete the period and that you glorify Allah. The completion of the period is achieved by making up the days that the one obligated to fast has broken, so that he brings the number of the days of the month of Ramadan complete, for in that number there is a wisdom that must be preserved; so by the making-up the wisdom of legislation is achieved, and by the concession of breaking the fast for the one with a valid excuse the mercy of relief is achieved.

Al-Jumhur recited "(wa li-tukmilu)" with a silent kaf and a lightened mim, the imperfect of akmala. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim and Ya'qub, recited it with an open kaf and a doubled mim, the imperfect of kammala.

His saying ﴿and that you glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ is a conjunction on His saying ﴿and that you complete the period﴾. This includes a causal sense, which is a cause in meaning but not including a wisdom; yet it includes the purpose of Allah's will, namely that they glorify Him.

Takbir (glorifying) is the form "taf'il", meant to express attribution and description; that is: that you attribute to Allah greatness. The attribution here is by spoken word, and the greatness here is a moral greatness, not a physical one; it is majesty, glory, and transcendence above all deficiencies. That is: that you describe Allah with greatness, and this is by saying: "Allahu akbar" (Allah is greater). Thus the form "taf'il" here is derived from a verb coined from a saying one utters, like their saying: basmala, hamdala, and hallala (from bismillah, alhamdulillah, la ilaha illa Allah), as was mentioned when discussing the basmala. That is: that you say: "Allahu akbar", and this is a sentence indicating that Allah is greater than every great one in reality, such as sages, kings, lords and leaders, and greater than every great one in belief, such as false gods. The affirmation of greater-ness to Allah in the phrase "Allahu akbar" is a metonymy (kinayah) for His unity in divinity, because superlative implies the deficiency of all others, and a deficient being does not deserve divinity, since the reality of divinity does not admit any deficiency. For this reason, takbir was legislated in prayer to nullify what they used to draw near to their idols by, and likewise takbir was legislated at the end of fasting by this verse. Therefore the Sunnah established that Muslims glorify Allah when going out to the Eid prayer, and the imam glorifies Allah in the Eid sermon.

صفحة ١٧٧

In the wording of the takbir at the end of fasting there is a splendid particularity: the polytheists used to draw near to their gods by eating and smearing themselves with blood, so for the Muslim's saying "Allahu akbar" there is an indication that Allah is worshipped by fasting, and that He is far above the ferocity of idols.

His saying ﴿and perhaps you will be thankful﴾ is another cause, and it is more general than the content of the clause ﴿and that you glorify Allah for having guided you﴾, for glorification includes gratitude, and gratitude is more general, since it occurs through statements in which there is glorification of Allah the Exalted, and occurs through acts of nearness such as charity during the days of fasting and the days of breaking the fast, and among the manifestations of gratitude is wearing the best clothes on the day of Fitr.

The verse indicates the command to glorify Allah, since it made it among what Allah intends; it is not detailed in the wording of the takbir, and it is general regarding the time of the takbir and its number. The sunnah, both verbal and practical, has explained this, with differences among the jurists regarding the circumstances.

As for the wording of the takbir, the apparent meaning of the verse is that it is any statement containing the words "Allahu akbar". The well-known position in the Sunnah is that one repeats "Allahu akbar" three times, and by this Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i held. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: if one wishes, he may add tahlil (la ilaha illa Allah) and tahmid (alhamdulillah) to the takbir, and it is good, and he does not omit "Allahu akbar". If he wants to add to the takbir, he says the takbir twice, then says: "La ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, wa lillahi al-hamd." This is the view of Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas. Ahmad said: it is broad. Abu Hanifa said: nothing other than three takbirs suffices.

As for its time: the takbir of Fitr begins from the moment the one praying leaves his house toward the place of prayer; likewise the imam and whoever goes out with him. When he reaches the place of prayer, he stops the takbir. It is recommended at the start of each of the two rak'ahs of the Eid prayer to open the first with seven takbirs and the second with six. This is the most correct of what is established in the reports, and what the people of Madina practised from the time of the Prophet ﷺ and after him, and what the majority of the scholars of the regions accepted. There is much disagreement on this, and there is no benefit in lengthening the discussion by mentioning it; the matter is broad. Then the imam glorifies in the Eid sermon after the prayer, and those praying glorify with him when he glorifies, and they listen to the sermon except during the takbir.

Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr and al-Shafi'i said: people glorify from the moment the crescent of Fitr is sighted until the end of the Eid prayer, then the takbir stops. All of this is for Fitr, and it is the subject of the verse we are concerned with explaining.

صفحة ١٧٨

As for Adha, what is mentioned for Fitr is supplemented with the takbir after the obligatory prayers, from the Zuhr prayer on the day of Adha until the Subh prayer on its fourth day. Its detail will come in the tafsir of His saying: ﴿and remember Allah during numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 186:

﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the one who calls upon Me when he calls. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me that they may be guided.﴾

The sentence is conjoined to the preceding conjoined sentences, meaning: "that you may complete the prescribed period," ﴿and that you may glorify Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Then the address turned to the Prophet ﷺ alone, because he is in a position of conveying the message, and so He said: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me﴾, i.e., the servants with whom the discourse was concerned. The apparent expectation would have been: ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful to Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and "and call upon Me, and I will respond to you." However, He deviated from this so that within that there would be achieved the magnification of the status of the Prophet ﷺ in that the Muslims ask him about the command of Allah the Exalted, and an indication to the answer of those who might have asked the Prophet ﷺ about the manner of supplication, whether it should be aloud or silent. And so that the arrangement of the verse would signal that Allah the Exalted, after commanding them with what is due to Him from them, honored them, and said: If they ask about their right upon Me, then indeed I am near to them, I respond to their supplication. This good news was made contingent on the supposition of their asking, as an indication that they would have this thought in their souls after hearing the command to complete, to glorify, and to be grateful: "Is there a reward for us for that?" And that they might refrain from asking the Prophet ﷺ about that out of courtesy toward Allah the Exalted. Therefore Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And when he asks you﴾), explicitly stating that this will occur in the future.

The use of such a conditional with the root of asking is for the purpose of emphasizing what will be mentioned after it, a usage well known among eloquent speakers. 'Alqamah said:

"If you ask me about women, indeed I am knowledgeable about the ailments of women, a physician."

Scholars open important issues in their books with the phrase "If you say" (fa-in qult), which is the terminology of al-Kashshaf. This is supported by the omission of the word "Say" (qul) from the answer, which was mentioned in places of questioning in the Qur'an, such as ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: they are measurements of time﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189], and ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: reform for them is best﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220], together with what this wondrous arrangement contains of increasing the presentation of speech in the form of a universal ruling, since it came with a general judgment in the context of a condition, saying: (﴿My servants ask you﴾) and saying: ﴿I respond to the invocation of the one who calls﴾. Had it been said: "and let them call upon Me, so I will respond to them," it would have been a particular judgment specific to them. Thus the connection of the verse to the verses before it, its correspondence to them, and its linkage with them has become clear, without there being any interposed parenthetical sentence.

It has been said that it is a parenthetical sentence joined by the conjunction "and" between the rulings of fasting, to indicate that Allah the Exalted rewards them for their deeds and that He is aware of their conditions. It has been said that He mentioned supplication here after mentioning gratitude, to indicate that supplication must be preceded by praise.

The servants who were attributed to the pronoun of Majesty (Allah) are the believers, because the verses as a whole are explaining the rulings of fasting, its requirements and its reward, and it is one of the symbols of the Muslims. Likewise, the terminology of the Qur'an is generally in mentioning "servants" attributed to the pronoun of Majesty. As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿Did you lead astray these, My servants?﴾ [al-Furqan: 17], meaning the polytheists, the context requires it, as it is in a setting of reproaching them for their enslavement to idols.

He said the Exalted: ﴿indeed I am near﴾ and did not say: "Say to them, indeed I am near," for brevity, since it is evident from His saying: ﴿When My servants ask you concerning Me﴾, and as an alert that the asking is supposed but has not actually occurred from them. In this there is a Qur'anic subtlety, namely the implication that Allah the Exalted Himself took charge of answering their question, since He omitted in the wording what would indicate the mediation of the Prophet ﷺ, as an alert to the intense nearness of the servant to his Lord in the station of supplication.

Emphasis with ﴿inna﴾ was needed because the information is strange, namely that He, the Exalted, is near while they do not see Him.

﴿Ujību﴾ (I respond) is the second predicate of ﴿inna﴾, and it is the intended purpose of the information preceding it, which paves the way for it to make its acceptance easier.

The first-person ya' was dropped from the word ﴿da'ani﴾ in the reading of Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, because dropping it in pause is the dialect of the majority of the Arabs apart from the people of the Hijaz, and among them it is not dropped in continuous speech, since the original is its presence, and because the orthography is built upon the state of pausing. Ibn Kathir, Hisham and Ya'qub affirmed the ya' in both continuous speech and pause. Ibn Dhakwan and 'Asim read with dropping the ya' in both continuous speech and pause, and this is the dialect of Hudhayl. It has already been mentioned that if the word were in final position as a verse-end, dropping would be agreed upon, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And fear Me alone﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40] in this surah.

In this verse there is an indication that the one who fasts is hoped to have his supplication answered, and that the supplications during the month of Ramadan are hoped to be granted, and to the legislated nature of supplication at the end of each day of Ramadan.

The verse indicates that the answering of the caller's supplication is a bounty from Allah upon His servants. However, this does not necessitate an obligation to answer every invocation from everyone and at every time, because a report does not imply generality. It cannot be said that it falls within the scope of a condition and therefore implies necessary correlation, because the condition here is the linking of the answer to the asking, and it is not a linking of supplication to response, since He did not say: "If they call upon Me, I will respond to them."

His saying: ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾ is a consequence of (﴿Ujību﴾), meaning: since I respond to the invocation of the caller, then let them respond to My commands. "Istajaba" and "ajaba" have one meaning. The original meaning of "ajaba" and "istajaba" is turning toward the one who calls with coming, or a statement indicating readiness to attend, such as "Here I am" (labbayka). Then it was used figuratively, in a well-known metaphor, for the realization of what the seeker requests, because when its realization cuts off his request, it is as if he has answered his call.

So it is permissible that the intended meaning of "response" is obeying Allah's command, so that "and let them believe in Me" is a distinct conjunction, the intended purpose of the first command being the act and of the second being persistence. It is also permissible that "response" is meant to include responding to the call to faith, so the mention of "and let them believe" is a specific conjunction over a general one, for the sake of emphasizing it.

His saying: (﴿perhaps they will be guided﴾) has been discussed before in similar contexts. Guidance (rushd) is reaching the truth, and its verb follows the patterns of "nasara," "fariha," and "daraba," and the most common is the first.

[Page 180]

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 2, verse 187 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It has been made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to approach your wives. They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them. God knows that you were betraying yourselves, so He turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you. So now, lie with them, and seek what God has prescribed for you.﴾

This is a transition, within the rulings of fasting, to an explanation of acts performed during some parts of Ramadan that might be thought to conflict with the worship of fasting. Because of this transition, the sentence is disconnected from the preceding sentences.

The reports concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse contain confused and unclear statements. Abu Dawud related from Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "When one of the Muslims slept after praying the 'Isha' prayer, and stayed awake after it, he would neither eat nor lie with his wife after that. 'Umar came, wanting his wife, and she said, 'I have already slept.' He thought she was pretending, so he lay with her."

Al-Bukhari related from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib

[Page 181]

that Qays ibn Sirma came to his dwelling after sunset wanting his food. His wife said to him, "Wait until we warm something for you." He fell asleep. When his wife came and found him asleep, she said, "Woe to you!" He remained in that state, and when midday came he fainted from hunger.

In the Book of Tafsir of the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, from the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, he said: "When the fasting of Ramadan was revealed, they did not approach women throughout Ramadan. Some men were betraying themselves, so God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿God knows that you were betraying yourselves﴾," to the end of the verse. Ka'b ibn Malik experienced something similar to what 'Umar experienced, and this verse was revealed on account of those incidents. It has been said that abstaining from eating and from intercourse after sleep, or after the 'Isha' prayer, was a legislated ruling by the Sunnah, and then it was abrogated (naskh, abrogation). This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun). Abu Muslim al-Isfahani denied that this was an abrogation of something established in our law, and said: "It is an abrogation of what was in the law of the Christians."

Fasting was prescribed only as abstention during the day, not during the night. So I do not think that the verse is an originating of permissibility; rather, it is an informing about the permissibility that was already established in the basic timing of fasting by day. Its purpose is to nullify something that some Muslims had imagined, namely that eating during the night was limited to two times: the time of breaking the fast (iftar) and the time of the pre-dawn meal (suhur). They took the time of iftar to be the period between Maghrib and 'Isha', because they used to sleep right after the 'Isha' prayer and its performance. So when they prayed 'Isha', they would eat only the suhur meal. They were also in the matter of intercourse as they were in the matter of food. When they became accustomed to making sleep the start of the nightly abstention, they thought that if sleep occurred at other than its usual time, it would also prevent eating and intercourse until the time of suhur.
