They also thought that during the time of suhur only eating was permitted, not intercourse, since they considered it sinful to enter the morning in a state of major ritual impurity (janaba) during Ramadan. In *Sahih Muslim* it is reported that Abu Hurayra used to hold this view, meaning after the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Perhaps this spread to them from the People of the Book, as is suggested by what Muhammad ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) related through the chain of al-Suddi. Perhaps they committed themselves to this and did not ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it. Perhaps this did not last beyond part of the month of Ramadan in the year in which fasting of Ramadan was legislated. Thus these various and closely related incidents occurred.

Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned in *al-'Arida*, from Ibn al-Qasim, from Malik: "In the early days of Islam, whoever slept before eating would not eat anything during the night. Then God revealed ﴿So now, lie with them﴾, and they ate after that." His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿God knows﴾ is evidence that the Qur'an was revealed with this ruling

[Page 182]

for the sake of further clarification, since God knew what some Muslims had constrained upon themselves, and revealed it to His Messenger (ﷺ). This indicates that the Muslims did not spread this matter, nor inform the Messenger of God about it. For this reason, we do not find in the narrations of al-Bukhari and al-Nasa'i that people mentioned this to the Messenger of God, except in the hadith of Qays ibn Sirma in Abu Dawud, and perhaps it is one of the narrator's additions.

As for whether this was legislated and then abrogated, I do not think so. For it is not the nature of the religion that prescribed fasting, at first, as one day in the year, and then gradually raised it to a whole month, with a choice between it and feeding the poor, in order to lighten the burden on the Muslims, to then obligate it to be observed night and day, permitting breaking the fast only for a few hours of the night.

The "night of the fast" (laylat al-siyam) means the night that is followed by the fasting of the day after it. This follows the Arab usage of attributing the night to the day that follows it, except for the night of 'Arafa, where what is meant is the night after the day of 'Arafa.

Al-Rafath (the word used for "approach") in *al-Asas* and *al-Lisan*: its literal meaning is speech with women concerning the matters of enjoyment of them, and then it was applied to intercourse as a metonym (kinaya). It has been said that it is a literal term for both, and this is the apparent view. Its being followed by "to" (ila) is so that the intended meaning becomes definite, which is consummation. The saying ﴿They are a garment for you﴾ is a resumed sentence, serving as the cause (illah) of what precedes it, meaning: it has been made lawful because of the difficulty of avoiding that.

That is because if fasting were imposed on people during the night, which is the time of lying down, then abstaining from approaching women at that time would be a great hardship and severe difficulty, which does not exist in abstaining from them during the day, since during the day one can resort to keeping away from the woman. So His saying ﴿They are a garment for you﴾ is a metaphor (isti'ara), based on the shared element of the intensity of closeness at that time. This is a metaphor that the Qur'an revived, because the Arabs had considered it in their saying: "The thing wore the thing (labisa al-shay' al-shay')" when it adhered to it. But they made it, specifically in the form of the *mufa'ala* pattern, into a conventional literal usage. Then the Qur'an came and revived it and made it an original, new metaphor after it had been a subordinate, forgotten one. Close to this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"So loosen my garments from yours, and they will come off."

The word ﴿betraying﴾ (takhtanun): al-Raghib said: *al-ikhtiyan* means seeking to commit betrayal (khiyana), in the sense that it is an *iftial* form from *al-khawn*, and its original form is *takhtawinun*, so the *waw* became an *alif* because of its vowel and the opening of what precedes it. The betrayal of oneself is a figurative expression for burdening it with what it was not charged with, as if this were a deception of it, since it makes it imagine that hardship is prescribed for it when it is not. It is also a figurative expression for deceiving it into indulging in what you see as forbidden to you, so you advance at times and withdraw at other times, like one who attempts betrayal. This is comparable to His saying: ﴿They seek to deceive God﴾ [2:9].

The meaning here is that you compel them to betrayal, or attribute it to them. It has been said that *ikhtiyan* is stronger than *khiyana*, like *iktisab* and *kasb*, as in *al-Kashshaf*. I say: this is a usage, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ [4:107].

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So now, lie with them﴾: the imperative here is for permissibility. The meaning of His saying "So now" (fa-al-an) is not an indication that intercourse was legislated at that moment. Rather its meaning is: "So now the ruling has become clear, so lie with them, and do not betray yourselves." *Ibtigha'* means seeking. "What God has prescribed" means what He has made lawful of intercourse with women outside the time of fasting, or it means: seek what God has decreed for you of offspring, as an encouragement for people to lie with women, that offspring may come into being from that, and that is for multiplying the community and the continuation of the species on earth.

* * *

﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, at dawn. Then complete the fast until night. And do not lie with them while you are secluded in the mosques.﴾

This is conjoined to "lie with them." The "thread" (khayt) is a strand of flax, wool, or other material, with which garments are sewn together by tightening it with a needle or an awl. It is said *kha:ta al-thawb* and *khayyata-hu* (he sewed the garment).

In the report about the graves of the Banu Umayya, they found Mu'awiya, may God be pleased with him, in his grave as a thread. Here the "thread" is intended to mean the ray that extends in the darkness and the blackness alongside it. Abu Du'ad, one of the poets of the pre-Islamic era, said:

"When the dusk-dark was lit for us, and a thread of the dawn appeared and shone."

His saying: ﴿at dawn﴾: the "min" here is for the beginning (ibtida'iyya), meaning: the ray arising from dawn. It has also been said that it is explanatory (bayaniyya), and it has been said that it is partitive (tab'idiyya). Likewise Abu Du'ad's words "of the dawn," because the thread is common in the strand with which one sews, so it is the indicator of one of the two meanings of the homonym. Al-Zamakhshari, in *al-Kashshaf*, made it an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh). Perhaps he did not find established for himself that it was well known in this meaning except in some speech, such as the verse and Abu Du'ad's line. But in my view, the Qur'an used it only because it is an explicit text for the meaning intended in the classical language, without intending a simile, since it is not a clear simile.

[Page 184]

The end point is marked by "until" (hatta), and by "becomes distinct" (yatabayyan), to indicate that abstention occurs when the dawn becomes clear to the observer, which is the true dawn (al-fajr al-sadiq). Then His saying, exalted is He, ﴿until it becomes distinct﴾ defines the end of the time of breaking the fast by explicit statement. It is known beyond doubt from it that it is the beginning of the time of fasting, since in the period of Ramadan there is only fasting and breaking the fast, and the end of one of them is the beginning of the other. So His saying ﴿Then complete the fast until night﴾ is an explanation of the end of the time of fasting. For this reason He said, exalted is He, "Then complete" and did not say "Then fast," because they were already fasting before.

"Until night" (ila al-layl) is an end point for which "ila" was chosen, to indicate hastening the breaking of the fast at the setting of the sun, because "ila" extends the end point with it, unlike "hatta." So the intention here is the coincidence of completing the fast with the night.

Know that "then" (thumma) in the conjunction of sentences indicates a delay in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi). It shows concern for specifying the time of breaking the fast, because that is like good news for them. We do not pay attention to the view of Abu Ja'far al-Khabbaz al-Samarqandi, one of the early Hanafis, who argued from "then" in this verse for the validity of delaying the intention (niyya) until after dawn, supporting the position of Abu Hanifa that it is permissible to delay the intention until the late forenoon.

On the basis that "then" indicates delay, and that completing the fast requires its beginning, it is as if He said: "Then, after distinguishing the two threads of dawn, fast, or complete the fast until night." So the meaning "fast" results after a delay from the time of dawn. This, despite its artificiality and its resort to the weak indication of implication, is a heedlessness of the meaning of "then" as indicating delay in the conjunction of sentences.

Moreover, a story has been related about the understanding of some Companions of this verse and about its revelation in separate parts. Al-Bukhari and Muslim related from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: "When ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾ was revealed, I took a black cord and a white cord and placed them under my pillow. I kept looking at night, but the white did not become distinct to me from the black. So I went in the morning to the Messenger of God and mentioned that to him. He said: 'Your pillow must be wide.'" In another narration: "You have a wide neck, and that is only the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the day."

They also related from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: "The verse ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾ was revealed, and ﴿from the dawn﴾ had not yet been revealed. So when some men wanted to fast, one of them would tie a white thread and a black thread to his leg, and would keep eating until he could distinguish them. Then God revealed afterwards ﴿from the dawn﴾." It is evident from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd that something similar to what 'Adi ibn Hatim did had been done by others long before him, since 'Adi embraced Islam in the ninth or tenth year, and fasting of Ramadan was prescribed

[Page 185]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Baqarah 2:187 (part 2 of 2):

...the year two [AH], and it is not reasonable that the Muslims would remain for seven or eight years in this kind of error. Therefore the place of the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd is that what it describes occurred at the beginning of the period in which fasting was prescribed. As for the import of the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim, it is that 'Adi fell into the same error into which those before him had fallen. Indeed, what is in Muslim, from 'Abd Allah ibn Idris, from Husayn, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Adi, is that he said: "When there was revealed ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread [at dawn]﴾, etc.", and so he mentioned the verse in its complete form. It is therefore necessary that the import of the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd be that this was practised by some people in the obligatory fast before the obligation of Ramadan, that is, the fast of 'Ashura' or the fast of a vow, and in voluntary fasting. Then, when the verse on the obligation of Ramadan was revealed, and in it ﴿from the dawn﴾, they knew that what they had been doing was an error. Then a similar thing happened to 'Adi ibn Hatim.

As for the hadith of Sahl, there is no doubt about the soundness of its chain, except that it is possible that his statement in it, "and there was not revealed ﴿from the dawn﴾", and his statement, "then Allah revealed after that ﴿from the dawn﴾", were narrated by meaning, so that its narrator came with unsettled and unclear expressions. For it occurs in the two Sahihs only through the narration of Sa'id ibn Abi Maryam, from Abu Ghassan, from Abu Hazim, from Sahl ibn Sa'd, and the narrator said: "then He revealed afterwards, or after that, (from the dawn)." The clearer wording would have been: "then Allah revealed afterwards ﴿And eat and drink﴾ up to His saying: (﴿from the dawn﴾)."

In any case, there is in this nothing of the delay of clarification, because the meaning of "thread" in the verse is apparent to the Arabs. Expressing it with it is therefore of the category of the apparent (zahir), not of the category of the ambiguous (mujmal). The failure of some of them to understand the intended meaning does not undermine the apparentness of the apparent. Those who were confused about the meaning of the white thread and the black thread understood the most well-known meanings of "thread," and they thought that His saying "from the dawn" is connected to the verb "becomes distinct," with "min" being causal, i.e., its becoming distinct is due to the light of dawn. So they did what they did. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Adi ibn Hatim: "Indeed your pillow is wide, or indeed you have a wide nape," as a metaphor for lack of perceptiveness. This is a directed metaphor, from the comprehensive utterances of his, peace be upon him.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And do not touch them while you are secluded in the mosques﴾ is a conjunction with His saying "﴿touch them﴾", with the aim that the one in seclusion be proper. They agreed that it does not occur except in the mosque, by this verse. They differed regarding the description of the mosque: it was said that it must be the congregational mosque, and it was said that any mosque is sufficient, and this is the verified view, and it is the position of Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on them. Its rulings are in the books of jurisprudence, and they are not part of the purpose of this commentator.

* * *

﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them. Thus does Allah make His verses clear to the people that they may fear Allah.﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) with a warning against violating what was legislated regarding the rulings of fasting.

The reference is to what preceded, and describing it as "limits" makes clear that what is indicated is the delimitations contained in the preceding discourse, which are in His saying: ﴿until the thread becomes distinct to you﴾, and His saying: ﴿until the night﴾, and ﴿while you are secluded﴾, from every element of delimitation whose transgression leads to disobedience. Thus it does not occur to the mind that the rulings of permissibility are included in the reference, such as: "It has been made lawful for you," and such as: ﴿So now, touch them﴾.

Limits (hudud) are boundaries, barriers, and the ends of things beyond which, when a person passes, he enters into something else. Rulings are likened to limits because crossing them moves one from permissibility to prohibition. In the hadith: "He set limits, so do not transgress them." A further explanation of this will come in His saying: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229].

His saying: ﴿so do not approach them﴾ is a prohibition against approaching them, which leads to going beyond them, by way of metaphor, because nearness to a limit generally entails the intention to cross it, as He said: ﴿and do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ [al-An'am: 152]. For this reason He said in another place: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], as will come there. In the sense of the verse is the hadith: "Whoever grazes around the sanctuary is near to falling into it."

As for His saying: ﴿Thus does Allah make His verses clear to the people﴾, its discussion has already preceded in His saying: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. That is: just as He clarified the rulings of fasting, so He clarifies His verses for the people, that is, all His verses for all people. The purpose is that this is Allah's way of making His rulings evident, lest anything of them be obscure to people. His saying "that they may fear Allah" means: it is intended that they guard against falling into violation, because if Allah had not made the rulings clear to them they would not have been guided to the path of compliance; or it means that they would be engaged in complete compliance and in performing the commanded acts in their proper manner, so that the quality of legal piety (taqwa shar'iyya) would be realized for them, since if Allah had not made it clear to them they would have performed acts of worship not complete in what Allah intended from them. And although they would be excused in the absence of clarification and would not be held accountable for the sin of negligence, yet they would not attain the quality of piety, that is, the fullness of hitting the mark of Allah's intention. So "that they may fear Allah" here is treated as an intransitive verb with no object stated, like: ﴿Are those who know equal [to those who do not know]?﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]. On the first interpretation, its object is omitted due to the context.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 188 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And do not consume one another's wealth wrongfully, nor send it down to the judges so that you may consume a portion of the wealth of people sinfully, while you know.﴾

This is the conjunction (ʿatf) of one sentence upon another. The connection is that His saying, ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], is a warning against daring to violate the fast by breaking it without permission. Breaking the fast without permission is a form of unlawful eating, so another unlawful kind of eating is conjoined to it, namely consuming wealth wrongfully. The parallel (mushakala) strengthened the connection. This is among the ordinances enacted to correct what had become corrupt in their affairs during the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance). For this reason it was conjoined to its counterparts. It is, moreover, a foundational and great legislation concerning wealth in Islam.

Consuming wealth wrongfully was a well-known practice of the people of the Jahiliyyah. Indeed, it was most of their financial dealings. Their acquisition of wealth came through raiding, through gambling (maysir), through the strong seizing the wealth of the weak, through guardians consuming the wealth of orphans, through deception (ghurur) and gambling (muqamara), through usury (muraba) and the like.

All of this is from the wrongful, which does not come from the good pleasure of the soul. "Eating" (al-akl) in its literal sense is putting food into the stomach through the mouth. Here it means taking with the intent of benefiting, without returning it. This is because such taking resembles eating in all its aspects. For this reason the word "eating" is not applied to burning another's property, nor is it applied to a loan (qard) or a deposit (wadiʿa). The "eating" here is not a metaphor of the figurative kind (istiʿara tamthiliyya), since there is no resemblance between the state of one who takes another's property for himself with the intent of not returning it and the state of eating, as is clear.

"Wealth" (al-amwal) is the plural of māl. We define it as: that by which the sustaining of the livelihood of individual people is achieved in obtaining the necessities, the needs, and the embellishments, according to the level of their civilization, when it is acquired through effort (kadh). Therefore air is not considered wealth, nor the rainwater, the water of the valleys and seas, nor is dust wealth, nor the caves of mountains and the shade of trees. Water drawn from wells is considered wealth, as is the dust of quarries, grass and firewood, and what a person hews out for himself from a mountain.

[p. 188]

Wealth is of three types:

The first type is that by which that sustaining is achieved in itself, without depending on anything else. This includes foodstuffs such as grains, fruits, and animals for eating, and for benefiting from their wool, hair, milk, and hides, and for riding. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He made for you from the hides of cattle houses which you find light [to carry] on the day you travel and the day you camp, and from their wool, fur, and hair, furnishings and provision for a time﴾ [al-Nahl: 80], and He said: ﴿That you may ride upon them and from them you eat﴾ [Ghafir: 79]. The Arabs have called camels "māl," as Zuhayr said:

*Healthy wealth [camels], those appearing at Makhram*

ʿUmar said: "Were it not for the wealth which I bear upon [i.e., spend] in the way of Allah, I would not have defended a single span of their lands for them." This type is the highest and most enduring kind of wealth, because its benefit is obtained through it without depending on the circumstances of those dealing with it or on the conventions of those who organize markets. Its owner benefits from it in times of peace and in times of war, in times of trust and in times of fear, when people are pleased with him and when they are not, and when people are in need and when they are not. In a hadith: "The son of Adam says, 'My wealth, my wealth,' but your wealth is only what you have eaten and so it is spent, or what you have given and so it has enriched [you]." So the restriction here (al-hasr) is for perfection in consideration, in respect of material benefit and incidental benefit.

The second type: that by which that sustaining is achieved together with what completes it, of that whose benefit depends upon it, such as land for planting and for building upon it, fire for cooking and melting, water for irrigating trees, and the tools of crafts for making things out of firewood, wool, and the like. This type is below the second type [i.e., below the first type, as the text states], because it depends on things which may be in the hands of people who withhold them, and perhaps obstacles of war, fear, or the difficulty of the road may prevent acquiring them.

The third type: that by which the sustaining is achieved through its exchange value, from what humans have agreed upon as an equivalent for what is intended to be obtained of things. This is what is expressed by "specie" (naqd) or "currency" (ʿumla). The majority of human convention regarding this type has been on the two metals, gold and silver. Some people have agreed to deal in copper, cowrie shells, and beads. The later people have agreed to deal in white iron and paper money, namely the paper notes of the well-known banks, which are instruments of obligation from the bank to pay the amount stated on the note issued by it. This [type of money] is not valid except in times of peace and security, and yet it is of closely similar units. As for the notes that governments circulate in monetary amounts, the subjects of those governments deal with them.

What I said in the definition, "acquired through effort (kadh)," I meant by it that its nature is that it is acquired through a striving that involves hardship.

[p. 189]

For this reason I expressed it by "kadh," to indicate that wealth is conditioned to be acquired (muktasaban), and acquisition (iktisab) has three ways:

The first way: taking from the earth. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He is the One who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29], and He said: ﴿He is the One who made the earth docile for you, so walk in its slopes and eat of His provision﴾ [al-Mulk: 15]. This includes firewood, grass, land and sea game, the fruit of desert trees, and honey. This may be without competition, and it may be with competition, in which case acquiring it is by precedence, such as dwelling in mountains and gathering truffles (kamʾa).

The second way: derivation (istintaj), which is through birth (of livestock), planting, grafting, milking, and through crafts, such as making iron, vessels, clothing, and weapons.

The third way: taking from the hand of another in what one has no need for, either by exchange (taʿamul), namely that a person gives what exceeds his need of what another needs, and takes from another what exceeds that other's need of what he himself needs; or by giving that which people have made a sign that its owner is worthy of receiving with it what is equal in measure to it, such as a dinar or a dirham in exchange for an item valued in them; or by force and dominance, such as fighting over lands and over waters.

"Al-batil" is the active participle of "batala," meaning it went away in loss and ruin, i.e., without a valid reason (wajh). There is no doubt that the valid reason is what satisfies the owner of the property, I mean the compensation in sales and the love of praise in gifts.

The pronouns in such as ﴿And do not consume your wealth﴾ up to the end of the verse are general to all Muslims. The verb "do not consume" (wa la taʾkulu) falls within the scope of the prohibition, so it is general. Thus it conveys a prohibition addressed to all Muslims against every kind of consumption, and concerning all wealth. So here we have two pluralities: the plurality of those who consume and the plurality of the wealth consumed. When two plurals are juxtaposed in Arabic speech, it may be that each individual of the one plurality is paired with each individual of the other plurality distributively, as in "the people rode their animals" (rakiba al-qawmu dawabbahum), and His saying: ﴿And take your precaution﴾ [al-Nisa: 102], ﴿Protect yourselves﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. It may also be like that, but in the sense that each individual is paired with another individual, not with himself, as in His saying: ﴿And do not defame one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], and His saying: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61]. And it may be the pairing of each individual with all the individuals, as in His saying: ﴿And protect them from evil deeds﴾ [Ghafir: 9]. The determination in this is by the contextual indicators (qara'in).

It is known that these two pluralities here are of the second kind, i.e., that some of them do not consume the wealth of others

[p. 190]

wrongfully, by the indicator of His saying "among yourselves" (baynakum), because "between" (bayna) requires a middle position between two sides. So it is understood that the two sides are the consumer and the one from whom it is consumed, and the wealth is between them. Hence the consumer must be other than the one consumed from, for otherwise there would be no benefit in His saying "among yourselves."

The meaning of consuming it wrongfully is consuming it without a valid reason. This consumption has degrees:

The first degree: what all the hearers know to be explicitly wrongful, such as usurpation (ghasb), theft (sariqa), and trickery (hila).

The second degree: what the Law (al-shar') has attached to the wrongful and clarified that it is from the wrongful, though it had been hidden from them. This is like usury (riba), for they said: ﴿Trade is only like usury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]; and like the bribing of judges; and like selling fruit before it has ripened. In a hadith: "Do you see, if Allah withholds the fruit, by what will one of you take the wealth of his brother?" Hadiths on this are many. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: they are fifty hadiths.

The third degree: what scholars have derived from these, so that the description of wrongfulness is realized in it through reflection (nazar). This is a field for ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) in determining the meaning of wrongfulness, and the scholars regarding it are between expansive and restrictive positions, such as Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab among the Malikis. Its detail is in jurisprudence (fiqh).

It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning the case of ʿAbdan al-Hadrami and Imru al-Qays al-Kindi, who disputed before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over a piece of land, and so this verse was revealed. The story is mentioned in Sahih Muslim, but it does not mention that this verse was revealed concerning the two of them. Rather, Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned that.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And send it down to the judges﴾ is a conjunction upon "consume" (taʾkulu). That is: do not send your wealth down to the judges so that through that you may reach the consumption of wealth wrongfully.

He singled out this particular case for prohibition after mentioning what encompasses it, namely consuming wealth wrongfully, because this case is extremely abominable and comprises many prohibited acts. It also serves to indicate that the giver of a bribe is sinful, even though he has not consumed wealth himself but rather has caused another to consume it. It is also permitted that the particle "wa" be for accompaniment (ma'iyya), with "tudlu" in the subjunctive governed by an implied "an" after it in the answer to the prohibition. The prohibition would then be against the combination of the two matters: that is, do not consume them among yourselves while sending them down to the judges so that you may consume. This leads to the conclusion that what is prohibited in this verse is specifically bribery, so the purpose is to give special attention to prohibiting this type of wrongful consumption of wealth.

Idla' (sending down) originally means lowering the bucket into the well. Here it is a metaphor for seeking means and for paying.

[p. 191]

So the meaning according to the first possibility is: do not pay your wealth to the judges so that you may consume with it a portion of the wealth of people sinfully. Thus sending it down with it means paying it as a bribe to the judges so that they will rule in favor of the payer with the wealth of another. This is therefore a prohibition of bribery, of judgment by other than the truth, and of the one in whose favor the judgment is made consuming wealth wrongfully because of a judgment that is wrongful.

The meaning according to the second possibility is: do not consume your wealth wrongfully in a situation where disputes over wealth are presented before the judges, so that you seek through the judgment of the judges to reach the consumption of wealth wrongfully, when you cannot consume it by force. It seems that what led them to adopt this possibility is considering the story mentioned as the occasion of revelation. It is not hidden that restricting oneself to that story has no basis in the interpretation of the verse, because even if its chain is sound, the reading of the verse as prohibiting bribery for the sake of consuming wealth would be evidence for the prohibition of consuming wealth without bribery, by the indication of refining the cause (tanqih al-manat).

According to what we have chosen, the verse indicates the prohibition of consuming wealth wrongfully, the prohibition of bribing judges so that they consume wealth wrongfully, that the judge's ruling does not change the nature of wrongful consumption of wealth, and the prohibition of injustice in judgment through wrongful ruling even without bribery. This is because the prohibition of bribery was only for what it contains of altering the truth. Undoubtedly these matters are among the most important things Islam undertook to establish, changing what they had been upon in the Jahiliyyah. For they used to regard as lawful the wealth of those who could not prevent their wealth from being consumed, so they would consume the wealth of the weak. Ṣannan al-Yashkuri said:

*Even if it were a donkey's watering-trough, you would not drink from it*
*except with the permission of another donkey, forever.*

*But it is the trough of one who destroyed his brethren,*
*the doubts of fate, so he became the sole remnant of the land.*

Regarding the bribing of judges (irshā' al-ḥukkām), the people of the Jāhiliyyah (the pre-Islamic era) used to offer bribes (rishā) to judges. When ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl and ʿAlqama ibn ʿUlātha sought arbitration (tanāfur) before Haram ibn Quṭba al-Fazārī, each of them offered a hundred camels on condition that he would rule in his favour over the other. He did not decide in favour of either of them, but instead judged between them that they were like the two knees of a dark-skinned stallion camel, which are equal in striking the ground. Al-Aʿshā said about this, in some verses:

"You made him your arbiter, and he judged between you,
a radiant one, like the shining full moon.
He does not accept a bribe in his judgment,
nor does he care for the loss of the losing party."

It is said that the first of the judges of the Jāhiliyyah to take a bribe was Ḍamra ibn Ḍamra al-Nahshalī, who received a hundred camels paid by ʿAbbād ibn Anf al-Kalb in an arbitration between him and Maʿbad ibn Faḍla al-Faqʿasī, so that he would rule against him (li-yunaffirahu ʿalayhi), and he did so. It is also said that the first to take a bribe in Islam was Yarfaʾ, the slave of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, whom al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba bribed so that he would give him priority in gaining admission to ʿUmar. This is because Yarfaʾ, being the intermediary in granting people permission to enter, and the right being to give precedence in admission to the one who arrived first, since no one other than him was compelled to give precedence, giving precedence to someone other than the earlier one was a transgression upon the right of the earlier one and thus was oppression; and paying money to obtain it was a bribe. I do not think this is true except from the lies of the people of desires, to belittle the justice of some of the Companions. But if it is authentic (and I do not think it is), then al-Mughīra did not see any harm in it, since the harm inflicted upon another is not counted; or perhaps he saw it as a kindness and did not intend to give precedence, so Yarfaʾ did it out of honouring him for the sake of his gift. As for Yarfaʾ, perhaps he did not grasp the subtle detail of this ruling.

The prohibition of bribery is established by Allah the Exalted through the explicit text of this verse, because if it is given in order to judge unjustly, then it is consuming wealth falsely, and it is not the consuming of wealth falsely in itself; therefore it is joined to the first prohibition, since the judge is the one who delivers the wealth, not the one who consumes it. If it is given in order to judge rightly, then it is consuming wealth falsely, because judging rightly is obligatory. Like it is every payment the judge takes for judging from the litigants, except when nothing is allotted to him from the public treasury (bayt al-māl) and he has no wealth of his own; then they have permitted him to take a specified amount for judging, equally for both litigants.

The indication of this verse that the judge's ruling does not change the prohibition on consuming wealth is from His saying: ﴿and send it forward to the judges so that you may consume a portion of the people's wealth sinfully﴾. So the wealth that one consumes through the medium of a ruling is made sinful, and this is explicit that a judgment does not make lawful what is unlawful, and is not enforced except outwardly. This is something without doubt, were it not for a disagreement that arose on the question. Abū Ḥanīfa differed from the majority of jurists, saying that the judge's ruling makes the unlawful lawful and is enforced both inwardly and outwardly if it concerns a matter of permissibility or prohibition and the one in whose favour it is given claims it on a specific ground; that is, the ruling was based on a contract or its annulment, was grounded in the testimony of witnesses, and the thing judged was something that can validly be initiated. This is what most of the jurists of his school have reported from him, and some of them restrict it to marriage. He argued for this by what is narrated: that a man proposed to a woman who was beneath him, and she refused his proposal, so he sued her before ʿAlī, claiming that she had married him, and he produced two false witnesses, and ʿAlī ruled on the basis of their testimony. When the ruling was passed against her, the woman said: "If it must be so, then marry me to him." ʿAlī said to her: "Your two witnesses have married you." But this evidence, even granting the soundness of its chain, amounts to no more than being the view of a Companion, and it does not oppose established legal principles nor the transmitted hadiths, such as the hadith: "Whoever I rule for him against the right of his brother, let him not take it, for I am only cutting for him a piece of fire." Moreover, its interpretation is clear: ʿAlī suspected that she intended, by concluding the contract after the ruling, to show weakness in the judgment and to publicly deny the one in whose favour it was given; and perhaps if she were asked to conclude the contract she would refuse, and the ruling would be left hanging.

It is apparent that Abū Ḥanīfa's intention was that the judgment, in matters that may be valid or invalid by the law, of whatever does not involve the right of a servant (of Allah), is that the judge's ruling for its validity takes the place of completing its conditions, as a facility for people. The weakness of this is not hidden, and for this reason none of his companions followed him in it.

His saying (﴿and you know﴾) is an emphatic circumstantial clause, because one who sends wealth to the judges in order to consume the people's wealth is certainly aware of what he is doing. So the purpose of this clause is to denounce and make the matter appear grave, declaring that consuming wealth in this manner is among those who consume the people's wealth knowingly and deliberately, so their crime is greater.

[p. 194]

This is an interjection between the rulings of the laws that relate to the regulation of society, prompted by the question that had arisen. Al-Wahidi narrates that it was revealed because a Jew asked an Ansari about the crescent moons (al-ahilla) and their states, how they grow until they become full moons (badr) and then wane until they disappear. The Ansari then asked the Messenger of God ﷺ, and this verse was revealed. It appears that its revelation was several years after the verses prescribing fasting, because the verse ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs﴾ is connected to it. It will come that this verse was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyya or the year of the Qada' 'Umra.

The reason for placing it in this position is the fixing of the time of fasting by the arrival of the month of Ramadan. So it was appropriate to mention the appointed times (mawaqit) in order to establish the system of the Islamic community in the most complete manner. Among the perfection of a system is the regulation of times. It also appears that this verse was revealed after the prescription of the Hajj, that is, after the conquest of Mecca, because of His Exalted saying: ﴿Say: they are appointed times for the people and for the Hajj﴾.

The verse begins with ﴿They ask you﴾ because there was an actual question about the matter of the crescent moons. All the verses that open with ﴿They ask you﴾ contain rulings about which a question was asked, so their place in the Qur'an is with verses suited to them that were revealed at their time or were linked to them. It is narrated that the one who asked about this was Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'laba ibn Ghanama al-Ansari, and they said: "What is the matter with the crescent, that it appears thin, then increases until it becomes full, then continues to decrease until it returns as it began?" Al-Iraqi said: "I have not found a chain of transmission (isnad) for this cause."

He used the plural pronoun in His saying ﴿They ask you﴾, although what is narrated is that the one who asked was two men, because what is asked about concerns all the listeners during the legislation of rulings. Also, part of the complete regulation is that the subject asked about should have spread among the people, and many of them should have looked forward to knowing it, whether those who asked verbally or those who asked themselves. He mentioned the benefits of the creation of the crescents in this context to point out that God made for the Hajj a time of the months that does not accept alteration. This is a preparation for nullifying what was in the Jahiliyya of the intercalation (nasi') in the sacred months of the Hajj in some years.

The question (su'al) is one person's request from another for giving something or for information about a matter. If it is a request for giving, the verb of asking is transitive by itself (without a preposition). If it is a request for information, the verb is made transitive by the particle ʿan (about) or what takes its place. In this surah there are verses opening with ﴿They ask you﴾, seven verses not far from each other. Four of them are not joined by a conjunction, and the last three are joined by it. As for those not opening with a conjunction, there is no need to clarify their being unconnected, because they are in the introduction of new rulings, with no comparison between them and the content of the sentences before them, so they deserve separation without a conjunction, and they require nothing except suitability to their positions.

As for the last three sentences that open with a conjunction, each of them contains rulings that have a stronger connection with the content of what precedes them, so the question reported in them is of the kind that arises from the preceding ones. Hence they deserve to be joined by the conjunction, as will become clear in their places.

The question about the crescents does not concern their essences, since essences are not asked about except concerning their states. So here there is an implied omission; that is, about the states of the crescents. If we assume that the question was about the crescents themselves, it is not granted. It may be about the wisdom (hikma) or about the cause (sabab). If it is about the wisdom, the answer ﴿Say: they are appointed times for the people﴾ follows the question. This is the view of the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari). Perhaps the purpose of the question then is to confirm that the legal intent of them agrees with what they had agreed upon, because that they are appointed times is not hidden enough to need asking about, since it is well known to them. So it is necessary that the purpose of their question, if it occurred, was to establish agreement with the legal purpose.

If the question is about the cause, the answer ﴿Say: they are appointed times﴾ [p. 195] does not correspond to the question. It is then a turning of speech away from the expected sense, directing the questioner to something other than what he sought, to alert him that what he was turned to is the important thing for him. For they were at the beginning of a new legislation, and the one asked was the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him. The important thing for them was to ask him about what benefits them in the welfare of their worldly life and their hereafter, and that is knowing that the crescents determine the terms of transactions and acts of worship, such as the Hajj, fasting and the waiting period (iddah). Therefore he turned them away from explaining what they asked about to explaining another benefit. Especially since the Messenger did not come explaining the causes of the differences in the states of the heavenly bodies, and the questioners did not have the basic principles of the science of the cosmos (hay'a) that would prepare them to understand what they wished to know by mere verbal explanation. Rather, that requires teaching them preliminaries for that knowledge. Moreover, if the bearer of the law had addressed its explanation, he would have explained things of the realities of knowledge that were not known to them and that their minds would not accept at that time, and that would have been a pretext for the polytheists and hypocrites to slander him by denying him. For they had hastened to deny what they had not perceived the outward aspects of, such as their saying: ﴿Shall we point you to a man who will inform you that when you are completely torn apart, you will be in a new creation? Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?﴾ [Saba': 7-8], and their saying: ﴿We have not heard of this in the last religion; this is only a fabrication﴾ [Sad: 7].

Accordingly, this answer with His saying ﴿They are appointed times for the people and for the Hajj﴾ is a turning of the speech away from the expected sense, like the saying of the poet, which I recited in al-Miftah, though he did not attribute it, and I did not find its speaker, nor did I see it elsewhere:

She came complaining of me, that I fell short in providing hospitality, while the guests had seen that they were heading toward my dwelling.
So when I heard her words, I said to her: "They are the guests; be earnest in their hospitality and hurry."

To this view the author of al-Miftah (al-Sakkaki) inclined, and it seems he based it on the fact that they are not suspected of asking about the wisdom in the creation of the crescents, because of their being evident. He also based it on the fact that what is reported in the story of Mu'adh and Tha'laba suggests that they asked about the cause, when they said: "What is the matter with the crescent, that it appears thin..." etc.

The word al-ahilla is the plural of hilal (crescent). The hilal is the moon at the beginning of its facing the sun in every lunar month, on the first and second night, and it is said also the third. Whoever said up to seven nights meant the Hijaz, because it resembles the crescent. The word hilal is also applied to the moon on the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh nights, because it is at the size of the crescent at the beginning of the month. The crescent was named hilal because when people see it they raise their voices in announcing it, calling to one another about it. And hall and ahall both mean raising the voice, as has been mentioned in His saying: ﴿that over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾ [al-Baqara: 173].

[p. 196]

His saying ﴿appointed times for the people﴾ means: appointed times for what is timed of their deeds. So the lam is for causation, that is, for the benefit of people, and it is by way of an elided genitive (muḍāf), that is, for the deeds of people. The deeds timed by the crescents were not mentioned, so that the speech would include every deed that needs timing. He coordinated the Hajj with "the people", with the omitted element taken into account, by conjunction of the particular with the general, for the sake of emphasis on it. The Hajj's need for timing is necessary, for if it were not timed, people would come to the Hajj at different times, and the purpose of their gathering would not be achieved, and they would not find what they need during their travels and their stay in Mecca and its markets. This is unlike prayer, which is not timed by the crescents. And unlike fasting, whose timing by the crescent is supplementary to it, because it is an act of worship confined to the self; if an individual performed it, the legal purpose would be achieved. But the uniformity of time was legislated in it, so that it would be lighter for those charged, since difficulty becomes lighter with togetherness, and so that their condition during that period would be uniform, so that no one would burden another with the difference in times of eating, sleeping and the like.

The word mawaqit is the plural of miqat. The miqat is of the pattern of the noun of instrument from waqqata (to time), and the Arabs used it for "time". Likewise the month (shahr) was named for being derived from fame (shuhra), because whoever sees the crescent of the month makes it famous among people.

The Arabs called a specified time miqat, as if it were an intensive form, though it is the same as time. It is said: the miqat is more specific than the time, because it is a time in which some deed is determined. I say: according to this, its formation in the pattern of the noun of instrument is in consideration that that specified deed is a means for fixing the time, so it is as if it were an instrument for regulating and restricting it to the Hajj and not the 'Umra, because the 'Umra has no fixed time, so the crescents have no benefit for performing it.

The mention of the Hajj in this verse, which is among the first revealed at Medina, while the Muslims were not able to perform the Hajj because the polytheists were preventing them, is an indication that the obligation of the Hajj is established, but the polytheists stood between the Muslims and it. It will come at His saying: ﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97] in the surah of Al 'Imran, and at His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ [al-Baqara: 197] in this surah.

* * *

[p. 197]

﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears God. So enter houses by their doors, and fear God that you may succeed.﴾

It is joined to ﴿They ask you﴾, and is not joined to the sentence ﴿They are appointed times﴾, because it was not among what they asked about, so that it would be spoken by the answerer. The connection of this sentence to the preceding one is that the cause of its revelation was consecutive with or accompanying the cause of the revelation of the preceding verse, and that the content of both sentences was a matter of doubt and difficulty for them, of the kind that it is proper to ask about. So when they entered the state of ihram for the Hajj or 'Umra from their lands, they made among the rulings of ihram that the muhrim should not enter his house by its door, or enter under a roof that stands between him and the sky. When the muhrims wished to take something from their houses, they climbed onto the roofs of the houses, or made a breach in the backs of the houses if they were of the people of settled dwellings (madar). If they were of the people of tents, they entered behind the tent. The Ansar adhered to this practice. As for the Hums, they did not do this. The Hums is the plural of Ahmas, and the Ahmas is one who is strict in the matter of religion and does not deviate from it. They are: Quraysh, Kinana, Khuza'a, Thaqif, Judham, the Banu Nasr ibn Mu'awiya, Mudlij, 'Adwan, 'Adal, and the Banu al-Harith ibn 'Abd Manaf, and the Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'a. All of them are from the inhabitants of Mecca and its sanctuary, except the Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'a, for they were Hums because their mother was Qurashi.

The meaning of negating righteousness from this is: negation that it is prescribed or from the Hanifiyya (the primordial monotheistic faith of Abraham). It was not prescribed, because it is excess in the acts of the Hajj. For although the Hajj includes acts that return to abandoning the comfort of the body, such as abandoning sewn clothing and abandoning covering the head, the purpose of its prescription was not to burden people, but to show detachment and abandon comfort. For this reason the Hums did not do that, because they were closer to the religion of Abraham. So the negation in His saying ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ is the negation of the genus of righteousness from this act, unlike His earlier saying: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces﴾ [al-Baqara: 177]. The indicator here is His saying ﴿and enter houses by their doors﴾, and there He did not say: "face whatever direction you wish." The purpose of the two verses is to show great righteousness, which is what is mentioned after the particle of exception (istidrak) in the two verses, regardless of what negated righteousness from it. This is the point of resemblance and difference between the two verses.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 189 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Wahidi narrates in Asbab al-Nuzul (the Occasions of Revelation) that the Prophet (ﷺ) assumed the state of ihram (ihlal) from Madinah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and that he entered a house. One of the Ansar, said to be named Qutbah ibn 'Amir, and it is also said Rifa'ah ibn Tabut,
[page 198]
had entered that house through its door, emulating the Messenger of Allah. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Why did you enter while you are in ihram?" The Ansari said to him: "You entered, so I entered following your entry." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "I am from the Ahmas." The Ansari said to him: "I too, my religion is upon your religion; I am content with your guidance." Then the verse was revealed. The apparent meaning of these reports is that the Messenger forbade those who were not of the Hums from abandoning what they used to do, until the verse was revealed to abolish it. In the tafsir of Ibn Jarir and Ibn 'Atiyyah, on the authority of al-Suddi, there is something that contradicts this, namely: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered through a door while he was in ihram, and with him was a man from the people of the Hijaz." The man stopped and said: "I am from the Ahmas," so the Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "And I am from the Ahmas," and then the verse was revealed. This report implies that the Prophet announced the abolition of entering houses from their backs, and that the Hums were the ones who used to enter houses from their backs. I say: the sound report on this matter is what al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated, on the authority of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: "The Ansar, when they performed Hajj and came back, would not enter through the doors of their houses, but from their backs. A man came and entered through its door, and it was as if he was reproached for that, so this verse was revealed." The report of al-Suddi is an error, and there is nothing in the Sahih that implies the Messenger of Allah commanded this, nor is it to be supposed that this came from him; and the context of the verse rejects it.

As for His saying: ﴿But righteousness is in one who fears Allah﴾, the discussion of it is like the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

And (ittaqa, "fears") is a verb treated as intransitive, since what is meant by it is one who is characterized by legal piety (taqwa shar'iyyah), through carrying out the commanded acts and avoiding the forbidden ones.

The genitive of ﴿that you come﴾ (bi-an ta'tu) is with the extra preposition bi- for emphasizing the negation with laysa. The requirement of emphasizing the negation is that they used to hold, strongly, that this negated thing was part of righteousness; therefore the state of affairs required that the negation of this assumption be emphasized.

As for His saying: ﴿And come to houses from their doors﴾, it is conjoined to the clause ﴿nor is righteousness﴾, a conjunction of an imperative to a declarative that has the sense of an imperative, since His saying ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] carries the sense of a prohibition against that, so it is like conjoining a command to a prohibition.

This verse must have been revealed in the fifth year, when the Prophet (ﷺ) resolved to set out for 'Umrah in Dhu al-Qa'dah of the fifth year after the Hijrah, and the apparent meaning is that the Messenger of Allah intended to perform Hajj
[page 199]
with the Muslims if the polytheists did not prevent him; so it is possible that it was revealed in Dhu al-Qa'dah or shortly before it.

Al-Jumhur read (al-biyut) in both places in the verse with a kasrah on the ba', contrary to the pattern of the plural of fa'l as fu'ul; it is a kasrah for the sake of the adjacency of the yaa' after a damma, for lightness, as they read (ʿiyun). Abu 'Amr, Warsh on the authority of Nafi', Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on the ba', on the original pattern of the plural form, without regard to some heaviness, since it does not reach the degree of heaviness that requires changing the vowel. Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Awasim: "What I choose for myself, when I recite, is that I pronounce with kasrah the letters attributed to Qalun, except the hamzah; I leave it altogether except where it changes the meaning or confuses it, and I do not give kasrah to the ba' of (buyut) nor to the 'ayn of ('uyun)." He extended this, with some of which there is room for scrutiny. This is his own preference, by preferring some of the well-known readings over others.

The disagreement of the readers over the accusative of (al-birr) in His saying ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], and over the shaddah on the nun of (lakinna) in His saying ﴿But righteousness﴾, has already been mentioned.

As for His saying: ﴿And fear Allah that you may succeed﴾, meaning: that you may attain your goal of righteousness; for righteousness lies in following the Law, so do not do anything except what contains the pleasure of Allah, and do not follow the footsteps of the innovators who added to the Hajj what is not from the Law of Ibrahim. Various interpretations and other possibilities have been mentioned for the verse, all of them far-fetched. It has been said that His saying ﴿and it is not righteousness﴾ is a parable God struck for what they used to do of the nasi' (intercalation); this was said by Abu Muslim, and it is far-fetched literally, figuratively and in meaning, because the verses are addressed to the Muslims, who were the ones who asked about the crescents, while the nasi' is one of the conditions of the people of the Jahiliyyah; and because it leads to an unrefined metaphor. It has also been said that it is a parable struck for their asking someone who does not know about the crescents, and He commanded them to delegate knowledge to Allah; this is very far-fetched, since the answer had already come before. It has been said that they used to vow, when their objective was difficult for them, not to enter their houses through their doors, and so they were forbidden from that; this is far-fetched in meaning, because the address is with the Muslims, who do not do that, and in chain, since no one has narrated that this was the occasion of revelation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 190:

﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.﴾

The clause (wa-qatilu) is conjoined to the clause ﴿It is not righteousness...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189] and so on, and this is a digression (istitrad) prompted by the preparation of the Prophet (ﷺ) for the 'Umrat al-Qada' in the sixth year, and by the Muslims' apprehension of the treachery of the polytheists regarding the covenant. This fighting was anticipated, with the aim of defense, as indicated by His saying: ﴿those who fight you﴾. This verse is the first verse revealed concerning fighting. It is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq that the first verse revealed concerning the command to fight was His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39], in Surat al-Hajj. Ibn al-'Arabi preferred this view on the grounds that that surah is Meccan while the verse in Surat al-Baqarah is Medinan. It is established in the Sahih that "the Messenger of Allah sent 'Uthman ibn 'Affan to the people of Makkah," and then it was rumoured that they had killed him, so the people pledged allegiance to the Messenger (ﷺ) to death in fighting the enemy. Then the matter was clarified, and 'Uthman's safety was confirmed.

The revelation of these verses immediately after the verses that refer to entering the state of ihram for 'Umrah, which we see were revealed concerning the journey to al-Hudaybiyah, indicates that the polytheists had intended to bar the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, but then they desisted from this when they saw the Muslims' readiness to fight them. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191] is guidance to the Muslims with what was beneficial for them on that day. Do you not see that when the verses speaking of fighting had ended, the discourse returned to the purpose from which it had digressed, namely His saying: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], and so on? Moreover, at the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah a truce was struck between the Muslims and the polytheists, under which neither party would fight the other. The Muslims, in the year of 'Umrat al-Qada', feared that the polytheists would betray them when they arrived in their land, and would not keep their word to them, and would therefore bar them from the 'Umrah. So they were commanded to fight them if they did that.

This is a permission for fighting in defense, to repel the enemy's assault. Then after it was revealed the verse of "Bara'ah" (Repentance): ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], abrogating the implicit meaning (mafhum) of this verse according to those who hold that the abrogation of an implicit meaning is valid and that addition to the text is not abrogation. It also abrogates it according to those who hold that addition to the text is abrogation and do not hold that the implicit meaning is abrogated. Although it was revealed for a specific cause, it is general in every situation in which the polytheists initiate fighting against the Muslims, because the cause does not restrict the ruling. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and Mujahid that this verse is muhkam (not abrogated), because the intended meaning of "those who fight you" is those who are prepared to fight you; that is: do not fight the elderly, the women and the children. The restriction serves to exclude a group of combatants, not to exclude those who merely hold back. It was also said: the intended meaning is all the disbelievers, for they are on the verge of fighting. This is mentioned in the Kashshaf; that is, the verb "they fight you" is used to mean engaging in the act or being prepared for it, as previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿if he leaves behind good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180].

The mufa'alah (reciprocal form) "muqatalah" means that the act occurs from two sides. Since its act, which is killing, cannot occur from both sides, for when one of the two sides is killed it cannot kill, the mufa'alah in this root has come to mean the mufa'alah of the causes of killing, that is, warfare (al-muharabah). So His saying "(wa-qatilu)" means "and wage war." Qital is war in all its forms: assault, blocking roads, siege, raiding, and seizing lands or fortresses.

When the mufa'alah is attributed to one of its two agents, the intended meaning is that he is the one who initiates the act. For this reason He said, exalted is He: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾, making the agent of the mufa'alah the Muslims; then He said: ﴿those who fight you﴾, making its agent the pronoun referring to their enemy. Therefore it follows that the intended meaning is: repel those who initiate against you.

By "initiation" (mubada'ah) is meant the indications of intent to fight, such that the Muslims clearly perceive that the enemies have come out to fight them; it does not mean waiting until they strike and attack, because at that stage the Muslims may lose the opportunity to remedy the situation. This ruling is certainly general as to persons, and the generality of persons necessarily entails the generality of circumstances, places and times according to the view of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqin); or it is absolute in circumstances, times and places. For this reason He said, exalted is He, after that: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you therein﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], specifying or restricting it to some places.

His saying "(wa-la ta'tadu)" means: do not initiate fighting. His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors﴾ is a warning against aggression. That entails peaceful dealing with the enemy, sparing them, and granting them respite until they come to believe. It was also said: he meant "and do not transgress in fighting if you fight," and so the transgression was explained in many ways, all returning to exceeding the rules of war. Transgression (i'tida') is initiating injustice. It was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 191–192 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And kill them wherever you encounter them, and expel them from where they expelled you; and fitnah is worse than killing.﴾

This is a command to kill whoever among them is found, even if he is not in the field of battle. For after He had commanded them to fight those who fight against them, He generalized the places and locales, increasing the situations of killing and explicitly extending it to all places. The importance of this aim impels that one not rely solely on the generality of persons to imply the generality of places, so that the Muslims are authorized to do so: every place in which the enemy alights is a place of fighting. The meaning is: "And kill them wherever you encounter them, if they fight against you."

The sentence is conjoined to the one before it, although it complements it, in that what it contains is a specific killing other than the killing of battle itself; thus there arises the difference that requires conjunction. For this reason it says here "and kill them" and does not say "and fight them," as in the verse before it, to draw attention to the killing of the warrior even if, at the time he is found, he is not directly engaged in fighting, and that whoever goes out as a warrior is a killer, even if he has not killed.

"Thaqiftumuhum" (ثَقِفْتُمُوهم) means "you meet them in a meeting of war"; its verb is of the pattern of "fariha" (فَرِحَ). Al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) explained it as "to find oneself in a state of subjugation and dominance."

His saying "and expel them from where they expelled you" means: it becomes lawful for you then to expel them from Makkah, from which they expelled you. In this there is a threat to the polytheists and a promise of the conquest of Makkah. This encounter is for this glad tiding in the souls of the believers, so that they strive toward it until they attain it, and they attained it after two years. In it there is also a promise from Allah Most High to them of victory, as He said: ﴿Indeed Allah fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27], to the end of the verse.

His saying "and fitnah is worse than killing" is a concluding statement (tadhyil), and the "al-" (ألْ) in "al-fitnah" is for the genus, indicating comprehensiveness in the rhetorical context. It is a proof for the Muslims and a removal of blame from them in fighting in Makkah if they are compelled to it.

Fitnah (الفِتْنَةُ) is the instilling of fear and the disruption of the order of life. It has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿...until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102], as an allusion to what the believers encountered in Makkah of harm through insult, beating and mockery, until its end was expulsion from homes and property. The polytheists were therefore already liable for their earlier conduct, so when they broke the covenant they deserved to be held accountable for what had passed, in matters where the truce had prevented their being held accountable for it. Fitnah was worse than killing because its harm is repeated, unlike the pain of a single killing. It is also meant as the anticipated fitnah, on the basis of the expectation that they would bar them from the House or treacherously attack them if they alighted in Makkah. For this reason the Muslims stipulated in the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah that they would enter the following year with swords in their sheaths. The purpose of this is to declare the Muslims' excuse in fighting the polytheists and to cast hatred of the polytheists into their hearts, so that they would be ready to fight them and to take vengeance upon them with constricted and enraged breasts.

The meaning of fitnah is not limited to the specific expulsion from homes, because the concluding statement must be more general than the statement it concludes.

* * *

﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein; but if they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The sentence is conjoined to the sentence "And kill them wherever you encounter them," which conveyed the command to pursue the fighters with killing wherever they alight, whether they were engaged in fighting the Muslims, or in a state of movement, watching, or the like; because the conditions of the warrior cannot be restricted, and there is no leisure to examine his intentions or to judge his purposes, since he may hasten to assassinate his enemy while he is hesitating and reflecting. So He singled out the place near the Sacred Mosque from the generality of places encompassed by His saying "wherever you encounter them." That is: if you encounter them near the Sacred Mosque without their being engaged with you in battle, then do not kill them. The aim of this is the preservation of the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque, which Allah made sacred by His saying: ﴿In it are clear signs, the station of Abraham; and whoever enters it is safe﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. The verse therefore requires the prohibition of the Muslims from fighting the polytheists near the Sacred Mosque, and it indicates their prohibition from killing anyone among the polytheists without fighting near the Sacred Mosque, by the indication of the implication of the address (lahn al-khitab) or its implicit import (fahwa al-khitab).

The prohibition is made conditional by His saying: ﴿until they fight you therein; but if they fight you, then kill them﴾, meaning: if they fight you near the Mosque, then kill them near the Sacred Mosque; because they violated the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque, and if the treatment of them in kind were abandoned, that would be a pretext for the defeat of the Muslims.

If they fight the Muslims near the Sacred Mosque, the command for the Muslims to fight them returns to what it was before this prohibition; so it becomes obligatory upon the Muslims to fight them near the Sacred Mosque and to kill whomever of them they overtake, in the same manner.

In His saying (fa-qtuluhum) ("then kill them") there is an indication of permission to kill them at that time, even without being engaged with them in battle; because they cannot be secured against using the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque as a means to defeat the Muslims.

For this reason the expression came with His saying "fa-qtuluhum," because it encompasses killing without fighting and killing with fighting.

Thus His saying "But if they fight you" means: near the Sacred Mosque, then kill them there; that is, kill whomever you overtake of them at the time of warfare, and let the Sacred Mosque not prevent you from pursuing their traces, lest they take the Sacred Mosque as a refuge to which they retreat when they are defeated.

Many exegetes were perplexed about the coherence of these verses, from His saying "And fight in the way of Allah" [al-Baqarah: 190] to His saying here "Such is the recompense of the disbelievers," until some of them resorted to claiming the abrogation of some of them by others, asserting that verses revealed close together abrogated one another. This is despite the principle that verses adjacent to one another within the same surah were revealed in that sequence, and despite the coordinating particles in these verses, which prevent the claim that some of them were revealed independently of what preceded them. There is nothing here that compels a claim of abrogation. Among the exegetes is one who confined himself to explaining the lexical vocabulary and rhetorical structures, and turned away from stating the meanings arising from the totality of these verses. Allah has indeed permitted the Muslims to fight and to kill the fighter near the Sacred Mosque, and He did not heed what He had made sacred of this Mosque; because its sanctity is the sanctity of its attribution to Allah Most High. When the fighting of the disbelievers near it is a fighting to prevent people from it and an opposition to His religion, they have become no longer respectful of it; and for this reason He commanded us to fight them there, in support of the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque.

The majority read: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾, all three with an alif after the qaf. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "And do not kill them until they kill you; but if they kill you" without an alif after the qaf. Al-A'mash said to Hamzah: "Do you see how, with this reading, a man can be a killer after he has become one killed?" Hamzah replied: "When one of the Arabs among them is killed, they say, 'We have been killed.'" He meant that the speech is by the omission of a modifier from the object, as in the verse:

"Tamim was angered that 'Amir was slain on the day of al-Nisar, so they were pacified at al-Saylam."

The meaning is: "Do not kill any of them until they kill some of you; but if they kill some of you, then kill whomever of them you are able to." Likewise, the attribution of "qatalu" (they killed) to the pronoun of the group of polytheists means that some of them killed some of the Muslims; for the Arabs attribute the act of some of a tribe, a religious community or a sect to a pronoun or an apparent noun that denotes all of them, as here, as in the expression: "Banu Asad have killed us."

This reading requires that the prohibited thing be killing, so it encompasses killing by the clash of war and killing without a battle.

The verse has indicated by its explicit text the permissibility of killing the warrior who fights within the Sacred Precinct, or who seizes control of it; because seizing control is fighting. There is consensus that if an enemy seized Makkah and said, "I will not fight you, and I will prevent you from the pilgrimage, and I will not leave Makkah," it would be obligatory to fight him even if he did not initiate the fighting. Al-Qurtubi transmitted this from Ibn Khuwayz Mindad of the Malikis of Iraq. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: "As for His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾, it is possible that it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193]."

The scholars differed regarding its indication of the permissibility of killing the disbelieving warrior who takes refuge in the Sacred Precinct without there being fighting, and likewise the offender who takes refuge in the Sacred Precinct fleeing from retaliation (qisas) and punishment. Malik held the permissibility of that, and argued for it that His saying: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], to the end of the verse, abrogated this verse; this is the view of Qatadah and Muqatil, based on the lateness of its revelation relative to the time of acting upon this verse, and a general ruling that comes later than the time of action abrogates a specific ruling by consensus. He also argued by the hadith transmitted in the Muwatta' from Anas ibn Malik: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Makkah in the year of the Conquest with the helmet on his head; when he took it off, Abu Barzah came and said: 'Ibn Khatal is clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Kill him.'" This Ibn Khatal is 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn Khatal al-Taymi, who was among those who had embraced Islam and then disbelieved after his Islam, and whose habit was to revile the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Islam. So the Prophet (ﷺ) declared his blood forfeit on the day of the Conquest; when he learned of that, he sought refuge in the curtains of the Ka'bah, and the Prophet (ﷺ) then commanded his killing. Thus the killing of Ibn Khatal was a killing by legal punishment (hadd), not a killing of war; because the Prophet (ﷺ) had already removed the helmet from his head, and the hour in which Allah had made Makkah lawful to him had passed.

And by analogy: the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque is firmly established in the Sacred Law; so when Allah permitted the killing of whoever fights in the Sacred Mosque, we know that the reason is that fighting in it is a challenge to its sanctity and a making light of it; likewise the seeking of refuge in it by the offender. Al-Shafi'i held a view like this, but al-Shafi'i said: if a criminal Muslim takes refuge in the Sacred Mosque, he is constricted until he comes out; if he does not come out, it is permissible to kill him. Abu Hanifah said: a disbelieving person who takes refuge in the Sacred Precinct is not killed, except if he fights in it, by the text of this verse; and it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) in his view. This is also the view of Tawus and Mujahid.

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Ahkam: "I was present in Bayt al-Maqdis, at the madrasa of Abu 'Uqbah al-Hanafi, and al-Qadi al-Zinjani was giving us the lesson on Friday. While we were thus, a man entered wearing tattered garments, greeted with the greeting of the scholars and took a seat at the front of the assembly. Al-Qadi al-Zinjani said: 'Who is the master?' He said: 'A man of the seekers of knowledge from Saghan, whom the highwaymen despoiled yesterday; and my intention is this holy Sanctuary.' Al-Qadi al-Zinjani said: 'Ask him about the custom of hastening to ask questions of the scholars.' The lot fell on the question of the disbeliever who takes refuge in the Sanctuary, whether he is killed or not. He answered that he is not killed. He was asked for the evidence, and he said: His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾. If it is read as '(And do not kill them)', then the verse is an explicit text; and if it is read as '(And do not fight them)', then it is an indication; for when He forbids fighting, which is the cause of killing, it is a clear proof of the prohibition."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 191–192 (part 2 of 2):

...concerning killing. Al-Zinjani objected to him, defending Malik and al-Shafi'i, although he did not hold their school as is customary, and said: "This verse is abrogated by His saying, ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]." Al-Saghani said: "This does not befit the office of the judge, for the verse you have objected with is general regarding places, while the one I have argued with is specific, and it is not permissible for anyone to say that the general abrogates the specific." Al-Zinjani was thereby left speechless, and this is from the wonderful speech. End of quote.

The answer to this is that a general text that comes later than acting upon the specific text is abrogating (nasikh). The hadith of Ibn Khatal indicates that the verse in Bara'ah (al-Tawbah) abrogates the verse of al-Baqarah. As for the view of the Hanafis and some of the Malikis, that the killing of Ibn Khatal took place on the day in which Allah made Makkah lawful for him, this is refuted by the fact that that time ended with the conquest (al-Fath).
