It is established in that hadith that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) removed his helmet (al-mighfar) at that time, and that is a sign of the end of the hour of battle.

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Ahkam: "A disbeliever who does not fight and does not commit any offence, and takes refuge in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), will not be killed." He means that he will not be killed with the killing demanded by the verse ﴿and kill them wherever you overtake them﴾, and this is among what is covered by His saying, ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾.

As for His saying, ﴿Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾, the demonstrative refers to the killing derived from His saying, "kill them" (fa-qtuluhum), meaning: such killing is their recompense, in the manner of what preceded in His saying, ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The rhetorical point of the demonstrative is to terrify them; that is, the recompense of the polytheists is no less than killing, and there is no benefit in sparing them. This is a threat to them. Thus His saying "such" (kadhalika) is a predicate placed first for emphasis. The demonstrative does not refer to ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190], because fighting is not a recompense, since there is no retribution in it; rather, fighting is a matter of alternation, a day for one side and a day for the other.

As for His saying, ﴿But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: if they desist from fighting you, then do not kill them, because Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. Forgiveness should therefore be the practice of the believers. His saying, ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, is the answer to the condition, and it is a wonderful brevity, since every listener knows that the attribution of forgiveness and mercy to Allah does not follow from desisting. Thus it is understood that it is an alert to the obligation of forgiving them if they desist, with admonition, and a confirmation of the elided element. This is from the brevity of ellipsis.

Al-intiha' (desisting) is originally the reflexive form (mutawi') of "nahá" (he forbade). It is said: "nahahu fa-intaha" (he forbade him, so he desisted). Then its usage was widened, and it was applied to refraining from an action or from a resolve, because al-nahy is the demand to abandon an act, whether the demand comes after the act has been undertaken or before it. Al-Nabighah said:

"Indeed I forbade the Banu Dhubyan from Uqur
and from their pasturing in every season of barrenness."

That is: from falling into that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 191–192 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And kill them wherever you encounter them, and expel them from where they expelled you; and fitnah is worse than killing.﴾

This is a command to kill whoever among them is found, even if he is not in the field of battle. For after He had commanded them to fight those who fight against them, He generalized the places and locales, increasing the situations of killing and explicitly extending it to all places. The importance of this aim impels that one not rely solely on the generality of persons to imply the generality of places, so that the Muslims are authorized to do so: every place in which the enemy alights is a place of fighting. The meaning is: "And kill them wherever you encounter them, if they fight against you."

The sentence is conjoined to the one before it, although it complements it, in that what it contains is a specific killing other than the killing of battle itself; thus there arises the difference that requires conjunction. For this reason it says here "and kill them" and does not say "and fight them," as in the verse before it, to draw attention to the killing of the warrior even if, at the time he is found, he is not directly engaged in fighting, and that whoever goes out as a warrior is a killer, even if he has not killed.

"Thaqiftumuhum" (ثَقِفْتُمُوهم) means "you meet them in a meeting of war"; its verb is of the pattern of "fariha" (فَرِحَ). Al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) explained it as "to find oneself in a state of subjugation and dominance."

His saying "and expel them from where they expelled you" means: it becomes lawful for you then to expel them from Makkah, from which they expelled you. In this there is a threat to the polytheists and a promise of the conquest of Makkah. This encounter is for this glad tiding in the souls of the believers, so that they strive toward it until they attain it, and they attained it after two years. In it there is also a promise from Allah Most High to them of victory, as He said: ﴿Indeed Allah fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27], to the end of the verse.

His saying "and fitnah is worse than killing" is a concluding statement (tadhyil), and the "al-" (ألْ) in "al-fitnah" is for the genus, indicating comprehensiveness in the rhetorical context. It is a proof for the Muslims and a removal of blame from them in fighting in Makkah if they are compelled to it.

Fitnah (الفِتْنَةُ) is the instilling of fear and the disruption of the order of life. It has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿...until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102], as an allusion to what the believers encountered in Makkah of harm through insult, beating and mockery, until its end was expulsion from homes and property. The polytheists were therefore already liable for their earlier conduct, so when they broke the covenant they deserved to be held accountable for what had passed, in matters where the truce had prevented their being held accountable for it. Fitnah was worse than killing because its harm is repeated, unlike the pain of a single killing. It is also meant as the anticipated fitnah, on the basis of the expectation that they would bar them from the House or treacherously attack them if they alighted in Makkah. For this reason the Muslims stipulated in the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah that they would enter the following year with swords in their sheaths. The purpose of this is to declare the Muslims' excuse in fighting the polytheists and to cast hatred of the polytheists into their hearts, so that they would be ready to fight them and to take vengeance upon them with constricted and enraged breasts.

The meaning of fitnah is not limited to the specific expulsion from homes, because the concluding statement must be more general than the statement it concludes.

* * *

﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein; but if they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The sentence is conjoined to the sentence "And kill them wherever you encounter them," which conveyed the command to pursue the fighters with killing wherever they alight, whether they were engaged in fighting the Muslims, or in a state of movement, watching, or the like; because the conditions of the warrior cannot be restricted, and there is no leisure to examine his intentions or to judge his purposes, since he may hasten to assassinate his enemy while he is hesitating and reflecting. So He singled out the place near the Sacred Mosque from the generality of places encompassed by His saying "wherever you encounter them." That is: if you encounter them near the Sacred Mosque without their being engaged with you in battle, then do not kill them. The aim of this is the preservation of the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque, which Allah made sacred by His saying: ﴿In it are clear signs, the station of Abraham; and whoever enters it is safe﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. The verse therefore requires the prohibition of the Muslims from fighting the polytheists near the Sacred Mosque, and it indicates their prohibition from killing anyone among the polytheists without fighting near the Sacred Mosque, by the indication of the implication of the address (lahn al-khitab) or its implicit import (fahwa al-khitab).

The prohibition is made conditional by His saying: ﴿until they fight you therein; but if they fight you, then kill them﴾, meaning: if they fight you near the Mosque, then kill them near the Sacred Mosque; because they violated the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque, and if the treatment of them in kind were abandoned, that would be a pretext for the defeat of the Muslims.

If they fight the Muslims near the Sacred Mosque, the command for the Muslims to fight them returns to what it was before this prohibition; so it becomes obligatory upon the Muslims to fight them near the Sacred Mosque and to kill whomever of them they overtake, in the same manner.

In His saying (fa-qtuluhum) ("then kill them") there is an indication of permission to kill them at that time, even without being engaged with them in battle; because they cannot be secured against using the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque as a means to defeat the Muslims.

For this reason the expression came with His saying "fa-qtuluhum," because it encompasses killing without fighting and killing with fighting.

Thus His saying "But if they fight you" means: near the Sacred Mosque, then kill them there; that is, kill whomever you overtake of them at the time of warfare, and let the Sacred Mosque not prevent you from pursuing their traces, lest they take the Sacred Mosque as a refuge to which they retreat when they are defeated.

Many exegetes were perplexed about the coherence of these verses, from His saying "And fight in the way of Allah" [al-Baqarah: 190] to His saying here "Such is the recompense of the disbelievers," until some of them resorted to claiming the abrogation of some of them by others, asserting that verses revealed close together abrogated one another. This is despite the principle that verses adjacent to one another within the same surah were revealed in that sequence, and despite the coordinating particles in these verses, which prevent the claim that some of them were revealed independently of what preceded them. There is nothing here that compels a claim of abrogation. Among the exegetes is one who confined himself to explaining the lexical vocabulary and rhetorical structures, and turned away from stating the meanings arising from the totality of these verses. Allah has indeed permitted the Muslims to fight and to kill the fighter near the Sacred Mosque, and He did not heed what He had made sacred of this Mosque; because its sanctity is the sanctity of its attribution to Allah Most High. When the fighting of the disbelievers near it is a fighting to prevent people from it and an opposition to His religion, they have become no longer respectful of it; and for this reason He commanded us to fight them there, in support of the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque.

The majority read: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾, all three with an alif after the qaf. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "And do not kill them until they kill you; but if they kill you" without an alif after the qaf. Al-A'mash said to Hamzah: "Do you see how, with this reading, a man can be a killer after he has become one killed?" Hamzah replied: "When one of the Arabs among them is killed, they say, 'We have been killed.'" He meant that the speech is by the omission of a modifier from the object, as in the verse:

"Tamim was angered that 'Amir was slain on the day of al-Nisar, so they were pacified at al-Saylam."

The meaning is: "Do not kill any of them until they kill some of you; but if they kill some of you, then kill whomever of them you are able to." Likewise, the attribution of "qatalu" (they killed) to the pronoun of the group of polytheists means that some of them killed some of the Muslims; for the Arabs attribute the act of some of a tribe, a religious community or a sect to a pronoun or an apparent noun that denotes all of them, as here, as in the expression: "Banu Asad have killed us."

This reading requires that the prohibited thing be killing, so it encompasses killing by the clash of war and killing without a battle.

The verse has indicated by its explicit text the permissibility of killing the warrior who fights within the Sacred Precinct, or who seizes control of it; because seizing control is fighting. There is consensus that if an enemy seized Makkah and said, "I will not fight you, and I will prevent you from the pilgrimage, and I will not leave Makkah," it would be obligatory to fight him even if he did not initiate the fighting. Al-Qurtubi transmitted this from Ibn Khuwayz Mindad of the Malikis of Iraq. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: "As for His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾, it is possible that it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193]."

The scholars differed regarding its indication of the permissibility of killing the disbelieving warrior who takes refuge in the Sacred Precinct without there being fighting, and likewise the offender who takes refuge in the Sacred Precinct fleeing from retaliation (qisas) and punishment. Malik held the permissibility of that, and argued for it that His saying: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], to the end of the verse, abrogated this verse; this is the view of Qatadah and Muqatil, based on the lateness of its revelation relative to the time of acting upon this verse, and a general ruling that comes later than the time of action abrogates a specific ruling by consensus. He also argued by the hadith transmitted in the Muwatta' from Anas ibn Malik: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Makkah in the year of the Conquest with the helmet on his head; when he took it off, Abu Barzah came and said: 'Ibn Khatal is clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Kill him.'" This Ibn Khatal is 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn Khatal al-Taymi, who was among those who had embraced Islam and then disbelieved after his Islam, and whose habit was to revile the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Islam. So the Prophet (ﷺ) declared his blood forfeit on the day of the Conquest; when he learned of that, he sought refuge in the curtains of the Ka'bah, and the Prophet (ﷺ) then commanded his killing. Thus the killing of Ibn Khatal was a killing by legal punishment (hadd), not a killing of war; because the Prophet (ﷺ) had already removed the helmet from his head, and the hour in which Allah had made Makkah lawful to him had passed.

And by analogy: the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque is firmly established in the Sacred Law; so when Allah permitted the killing of whoever fights in the Sacred Mosque, we know that the reason is that fighting in it is a challenge to its sanctity and a making light of it; likewise the seeking of refuge in it by the offender. Al-Shafi'i held a view like this, but al-Shafi'i said: if a criminal Muslim takes refuge in the Sacred Mosque, he is constricted until he comes out; if he does not come out, it is permissible to kill him. Abu Hanifah said: a disbelieving person who takes refuge in the Sacred Precinct is not killed, except if he fights in it, by the text of this verse; and it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) in his view. This is also the view of Tawus and Mujahid.

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Ahkam: "I was present in Bayt al-Maqdis, at the madrasa of Abu 'Uqbah al-Hanafi, and al-Qadi al-Zinjani was giving us the lesson on Friday. While we were thus, a man entered wearing tattered garments, greeted with the greeting of the scholars and took a seat at the front of the assembly. Al-Qadi al-Zinjani said: 'Who is the master?' He said: 'A man of the seekers of knowledge from Saghan, whom the highwaymen despoiled yesterday; and my intention is this holy Sanctuary.' Al-Qadi al-Zinjani said: 'Ask him about the custom of hastening to ask questions of the scholars.' The lot fell on the question of the disbeliever who takes refuge in the Sanctuary, whether he is killed or not. He answered that he is not killed. He was asked for the evidence, and he said: His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾. If it is read as '(And do not kill them)', then the verse is an explicit text; and if it is read as '(And do not fight them)', then it is an indication; for when He forbids fighting, which is the cause of killing, it is a clear proof of the prohibition."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 193:

﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah. But if they cease, then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers.﴾

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190]. The apparent requirement would be that this clause not be coordinated, since it explains what was left general in the end-point of the command to fight the polytheists. But it was coordinated because of the separation that occurred between it and the explanatory clause. . .

The clauses preceding, from his saying ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191] up to here, constitute a detailed explanation of the clause ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190], because the generality of ﴿those who fight you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190] gives rise to possibilities regarding circumstances, times and places. The explanation of the circumstances of places has now ended, and the discourse has moved to specifying the circumstances by the end-point ﴿until there is no fitnah﴾.

So when fitnah ends, that is the end-point of fighting; that is, if they break the covenant and violate the protection during the period in which there is an agreement between you to abstain from fighting, then you are free from their covenant. Therefore you may fight them ﴿until there is no fitnah﴾ other than it thereafter, with which they test you, and ﴿until they enter Islam﴾. All of this is conditioned by the earlier condition in his saying ﴿But if they fight you, then kill them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191]. The repetition of the verb (wa-qatilūhum) is so that the end-point may be built upon it with his saying ﴿until there is no fitnah﴾, and by that end-point the difference between it and ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190] was achieved, and it is on account of this that its coordination upon a like clause became permissible. So "ḥattā" in his saying ﴿ḥattā lā takūna﴾ is either made to mean "ilā" (until) as an end-point, or is made to mean the causal "kay" (so that). These two are mutually implicating, because when fighting was limited by this, it became determined that the end-point is the purpose; and whenever the end-point is not perceptible, the meaning of causation arises from (ḥattā), for causation is a notional end-point, as in his exalted saying ﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217].

In any case, the present verb after (ḥattā) is in the subjunctive by "an" (that) implied, to indicate the consequence of the end-point.

The word fitnah was mentioned shortly before, and what is meant by it here is what is meant there. Since it occurs here in a negative context, it encompasses all forms of fitnah. Therefore what is mentioned here equals what is mentioned in his saying ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191]. The repetition of fitnah indefinitely here does not indicate difference, as is common among the grammarians, that when a definite noun is repeated as an indefinite it is other than the first; because its occurrence in a negative context gives generality, encompassing all individual instances of fitnah, equal to fitnah defined by the article of comprehensiveness, except that it is comprehensiveness by customary usage, specified by the context. Thus it is restricted by three restrictions through the context; that is: until there is no fitnah from them against the Muslims in the matter of religion. Otherwise, fitnahs did occur among the Muslims themselves, as in the hadith "Then there will be a fitnah that will not leave a house of the Arabs without entering it."

The non-existence of fitnah is realized in one of two matters: either the polytheists enter Islam and their fitnah ceases through it, or they are all killed and fitnah ends by the annihilation of those who cause it.

It may be supposed that fitnah ends by the Muslims' ascendancy over them and the polytheists becoming weak before the strength of the Muslims, such that they fear their might. However, since fitnah arose from their rigidity in their religion and polytheism, it was not one that vanishes when they are weak; for the readiness to uphold the creed proceeds even from the weak, as it proceeded from the Jews on more than one occasion in Medina, such as the story of the poisoned sheep, and their killing of ʿAbd Allah ibn Sahl al-Ḥārithī in Khaybar. Therefore the intent here is none other than one of two matters: either their entry into Islam or their annihilation by killing. Both matters have occurred among the polytheists: a group embraced Islam, and a group was killed at Badr and other campaigns. For this reason our scholars said: the jizyah is not accepted from the polytheists of the Arabs. And for this reason some exegetes interpreted fitnah here as shirk, an interpretation according to the intended meaning and not according to the signification of the word.

His saying ﴿and religion is for Allah﴾ is coordinated upon ﴿lā takūna fitnah﴾, so it is an object of the implied "an" after (ḥattā), meaning: and until religion is for Allah; that is, until there is no religion there except for Allah; that is, alone.

Thus the definiteness in "al-dīn" is definiteness of the genus, because "dīn" is among the names of abstract things that have no individuals outside, so its definiteness does not admit the meaning of comprehensiveness.

The lām attached to the divine name is the lām of exclusivity; that is, until the genus of religion is exclusive to Allah the Exalted, in the manner established in his saying "al-ḥamdu lillāh" (All praise is for Allah). This amounts to the meaning of comprehensiveness, but it is not identical with it, since in such a case one does not consider individuals. The meaning: and the religion of those you fight shall be purely for Allah, with no share of association in it.

The purpose of this is the purification of the lands of the Arabs from the religion of shirk and the general spread of Islam among them, because Allah chose them to be the heart of Islam and the source of its spring, and the heart is not fit when its elements are mixed.

Al-Bukhari transmitted from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar a fine report, saying: Two men came to Ibn ʿUmar during the fitnah of Ibn al-Zubayr and said: "The people have done what you see, and you are the son of ʿUmar and companion of the Prophet ﷺ; what prevents you from going out?" He said: "What prevents me is that Allah has forbidden the blood of my brother." They said: "Did not Allah the Exalted say: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah﴾?" Ibn ʿUmar said: "We fought alongside the Messenger of Allah until there was no fitnah and religion was for Allah, while you want to fight until there is fitnah and religion is for other than Allah." Ibn ʿUmar said: "Islam was few, so a man would be tested in his religion: either they killed him or they tortured him, until Islam multiplied and there was no fitnah."

Another explanation regarding the like of this verse will come in surah al-Anfal.

His saying ﴿But if they cease, then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾: that is, if they cease from breaking the truce, or if they cease from polytheism by believing, then there is no aggression against them. This is an explicit statement of the concept of his saying ﴿who fight you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190], and it was needed because the qualifier is distant due to the length of the speech, and because the context requires explicit mention of the more important of the two end-points of fighting, lest it be imagined that the last part of the speech abrogated the first and obligated fighting the polytheists in every state.

His saying ﴿then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾ stands in place of the answer of the condition, because it is the reason for the omitted answer. The meaning: if they cease from fighting you and do not advance upon it, then do not seize them with suspicion nor begin fighting them, because they are not wrongdoers; and since there is no aggression except against wrongdoers, this is a wondrous figure of speech.

"ʿUdwān" here is either the verbal noun of ʿadā in the sense of leaping upon and fighting, that is, there is no assault against them; or the verbal noun of ʿadā in the sense of wronging, like iʿtadā, in which case calling it "ʿudwān" is by mushakalah (correspondence) to his saying ﴿against the wrongdoers﴾, just as the recompense of an evil deed is called an evil deed; and this mushakalah is notional.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 194:

page 210
﴿The sacred month is for the sacred month, and violations of sanctity are subject to retaliation. So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is with the righteous.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustan'afa) separated from what precedes it, because it is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani). When He stated the generality of places and excluded from them the Sacred Mosque in a particular situation, the listener was inclined to ask about what is similar to the sacred precincts, namely the sacred times, i.e., the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum), in which fighting is expected to be prohibited.

If this is a legislation revealed without a specific occasion, then it is a completion and a detailed clarification of what the need calls for in explaining at this important juncture. If it was revealed upon a cause, as has been said: when the Muslims in the year of the Qada' (the Qada' Umrah) set out for Makkah in Dhu al-Qa'dah of the seventh year as pilgrims for 'umrah, they feared that the polytheists would not honor their entry into Makkah, or that they would betray them and attack them before entering Makkah while they were in a sacred month; if they defended themselves, they would violate the sanctity of the month. So this verse was revealed. Or, according to what is narrated from al-Hasan, the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ when he performed the 'Umrat al-Qada': "Did you forbid fighting in the sacred month, O Muhammad?" He said: "Yes." Then they intended to fight him, and this verse was revealed. That is: if they make lawful fighting you in the sacred month, then fight them; that is, Allah has permitted them defensive fighting.

Thus the application of "the month" here is by ellipsis of a modifier (hadhf mudaf), whose estimate is clear from the context and from its description as sacred. The estimate is "the sanctity of the sacred month," and the repetition of the word "month" in this sense is not intended to indicate plurality; rather the repetition is by virtue of the difference in the aspect of violating its sanctity. That is: their violation of its sanctity permits you to violate its sanctity.

It has also been said: the meaning of His saying ﴿The sacred month is for the sacred month﴾ is that the Quraysh had barred them from the House in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, in the sixth year, and Allah facilitated for them the return in the year of the Qada', in the seventh year, so He said to them: this month in which you entered is a substitute for that in which you were barred. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi, meaning that it is of the kind of their saying: "A day for a day, and war is alternating (sijal)."

The ba' in His saying ﴿for the sacred month﴾ is for compensation, like their saying: "A sa' for a sa'." There are not two months; rather the intended meaning is the violation of sanctity by them and by you, and these are two violations.

page 211
The definiteness of "the month" here in both places may be the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), and this is the more apparent, because it conveys a general ruling and includes every particular month of the sacred months, on the assumption that the intended month is the month of the Qada' 'Umrah. It may also be the definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd) if the intended month is the month of the Qada' 'Umrah. The sacred months are four: three consecutive ones, namely Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram, whose sanctity is due to the Hajj occurring in them going, returning and performing; and one single separate month, which is Rajab. In the Jahiliyyah it was the month of 'Umrah, and all of Mudar prohibited it, and for this reason it is called "Rajab of Mudar." It was alluded to in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Of them four are sacred﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36].

The meaning of their being "retaliation" (qisas) is: equal in recompense and redress. Whoever violates them by an offense is punished with the recompense of his offense. That is because Allah made the sanctity of the sacred months for the purpose of security; so when someone wants to make that a pretext for betraying security or harming it, the other party has the right to defend himself, because the sanctity of people takes precedence over the sanctity of times. This includes the sanctity of place, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191]. The reporting of the sanctities with the word "retaliation" (qisas) is a reporting by the verbal noun for emphasis.

His saying ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him﴾ is a consequence of His saying ﴿and violations of sanctity are subject to retaliation﴾ and a result of it. This is the sense of al-Kashshaf's statement that it is a summation (fadhlaka). The recompense for transgression is called "transgression" by way of mushakalah (rhetorical correspondence), in the manner mentioned just before in His saying: ﴿There is no hostility except against the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193].

His saying ﴿in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ includes equivalence in measure and in circumstances, such as its being in the sacred month or the sacred land.

His saying ﴿And fear Allah﴾ is a command to be mindful of Allah in retaliation; that is, that one not exceed the limit, because the nature of the one who avenges is that it arises from anger, so it is prone to excess.

His saying ﴿And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾: opening the speech with the word "know" (i'lam) is a notice of concern with what is about to be said, since your saying to the addressee "know" announces the importance of what will be conveyed to him. The full discussion of this will come at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And know that Allah comes between a man and his heart﴾ [al-Anfal: 24] in Surat al-Anfal. The "withness" (ma'iyya) here is a metaphor for assistance by victory and protection. It may also be that the meaning is: fear Allah regarding His sanctities outside the circumstances of necessity; ﴿and know that Allah is with the righteous﴾, so He places them in the locus of His care.

[Page 213]

This sentence is coordinated with the sentence ﴿Fight in the way of God﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:190] and what follows it. When they were commanded to fight their enemy, and the enemy had far greater military equipment, He roused them to prepare by spending their wealth in the way of God. Therefore, those addressed by the command to spend are all Muslims, not only the fighters.

The need for this command, even though the readiness for war is innate in human nature, is to alert the Muslims, for they may fall short of reaching the utmost preparation against a strong enemy. Their hearts are filled with faith in God and trust in Him, and their ears are filled with God's promise of victory to them. Finally, with His saying ﴿Know that God is with the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:194], they were alerted that God's guarantee to them of support and victory does not remove from them the obligation to take the known means of preparation. So they should not suppose that they are not commanded to exert their utmost effort in the means of victory, which are causes that God, exalted is He, has linked to their effects according to the wisdom required by the order He established regarding causes and their effects. Seeking the effects without their causes is an error and a lack of proper conduct toward the Creator of causes and their effects, lest they become like those who said to Moses ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we will remain sitting here﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:24]. So if the Muslims exert their utmost effort, and neglect nothing, and then become perplexed in some matter after that, God is their helper and supporter in what they have no power to achieve. God indeed gave them victory at Badr when they were humble, since they were then the entire body of Muslims, and they had neglected nothing. As for those peoples who squander the wealth of the Muslims on their desires and let opportunities slip during times of security, so that they make no preparation for anything, and then afterward ask God for victory and triumph, those are a deluded people. For this reason God gives their enemies power over them because of their neglect, though perhaps He will make up for them in the course of that by His kindness in what pertains to preserving the religion.

Spending has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:3].

[Page 213 continues]

"Sabil Allah" (the way of God) means His path. When "the path" is attributed to something, it is attributed to that which leads to it. Since it is known that people do not reach God Himself, it is necessarily the case that "the path" means the deed that leads to God's good pleasure and reward. So it is a figurative usage in the wording and a figurative usage in the attribution. The expression "sabil Allah" has become dominant in the technical usage of the Law for jihad, meaning fighting to defend His religion and to exalt His word. The particle "fi" (in) here expresses location, because spending takes the form of giving equipment, horses, and provisions, and all of that is contained within jihad in a figurative sense. The "fi" here is not used to express causation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ is the coordination of one purpose with another. The command to spend in the way of God is followed by a prohibition against actions that have harmful consequences, in order to convey counsel and guidance, lest their certainty of God's support drive them to neglect the means of protection against the enemy's victory. Therefore, the prohibition against casting oneself into destruction comprises the meaning of the command to spend and of other matters of warfare and the preservation of lives. For this reason the sentence contains the meaning of a concluding generalization (tadhyil). It is coordinated with the preceding and not separated from it, because it is another purpose among the purposes of guidance.

"Al-ilqa'" (casting) is throwing something from the hand. It transitively takes one direct object by itself, and the thing thrown toward is introduced by "ila" (to), and the place into which it is thrown is introduced by "fi" (in).

The apparent reading is that "al-aydi" (hands) is the object, since no other object is mentioned. And the "ba'" (with) is extra, serving to emphasize the connection of the verb to its object, as they say of one who submits (a'ṭā bi-yadihi), meaning "he gave his hand," because one who surrenders in war and the like binds his hands. So the addition of "ba'" is like its addition in His saying ﴿shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree﴾ [Maryam 19:25] and the verse of al-Nabigha:

"May good be yours, if the earth covers you, one..."

The meaning is: do not give destruction your hands, so that it seizes you as one who is bound. He made destruction like one who seizes and captures, a metaphor based on the common element of encompassing the one who casts himself. It is also permissible to make "hand" in this context a figurative expression for the self (dhat) by the relation of part to whole, since the hand is the most important part of the self in this sense. This applies to both matters, like the verse of Labid:

"Until, when she cast a hand into an unbeliever..."

meaning: until the sun cast itself (into the west). It has also been said that the "ba'" is causal, and "al-aydi" is used in the sense of the self as a metonymy (kinaya) for choice, and the object is omitted; that is: do not cast yourselves into destruction by your own choice.

"Al-Tahlukah" (destruction), with a "ḍamma" on the lām, is a verbal noun (ism masdar) meaning destruction. It is a verbal noun and not a regular infinitive because the pattern tafʿulah with a ḍamma on the ʿayn is not known among infinitives; the infinitive pattern is tafʿilah with a kasra on the ʿayn. But it is the infinitive of a verb with a doubled middle radical and a weak final radical, like zakkā and ghaṭṭā, or with a final hamza, like jazza'a and hayya'a. Sibawayh reports that it has two parallels among derived nouns: al-tuḍurrah and al-tusurrah, with a ḍamma on the ʿayn, from aḍarra and asarra, meaning harm and joy. Among fixed nouns there are al-tanḍubah and al-tatfulah: the first is the name of a tree, and the second is the young of the fox. In Taj al-ʿArus it is reported that al-Khalil read it as "al-tahlikah" with a kasra on the lām. I do not think al-Khalil read it that way, for this is not transmitted from any of the readers, either in the well-known or the irregular readings. If this report is sound, perhaps al-Khalil pronounced it as an example, and whoever transmitted it from him did not record it with precise accuracy, for al-Khalil is too exalted to recite the Qur'an with a reading that is not transmitted.

The meaning of the prohibition against casting oneself into destruction with one's own hands is the prohibition against causing the destruction of the self or of a people, when the destruction is certain, without any intended benefit being gained from it.

He coordinated this with the command to spend, to indicate the reason for the legislation of spending and the cause of the command to it. For abandoning spending in the way of God and going out without equipment is casting oneself with one's hands into destruction, as it has been said:

"Like one who runs into the battle without a weapon..."

For this reason spending became obligatory. Also, the belief that faith in God and the support of His religion are sufficient to defeat the enemies is an incorrect belief, because it is like one who throws himself into destruction and says, "God will save me." So this prohibition conveys both meanings together, and this is among the most excellent forms of concision.

In al-Bukhari, it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and a group of the Successors (tabiʿun) regarding the meaning of ﴿do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾: do not abandon spending in the way of God and fear poverty, even if it is only an arrow or a pair of shears; go and bring it.

It has been said regarding the interpretation of ﴿do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ that there are several sayings. The first: that "spend" is a command to spend on one's dependents, and "destruction" is extravagance in it or extreme stinginess. This was narrated by al-Bukhari from Hudhayfah. But this is far-fetched because of His saying ﴿in the way of God﴾, and because applying the word "destruction" to extravagance is remote, and to stinginess is even more remote.

[Page 214]

The second: that it is spending on the poor, that is, charity, and "destruction" is withholding. This is far-fetched because of the lack of fit in the coordination, and because "destruction" is not applied to withholding.

The third: spending in jihad, and casting oneself into destruction is going out without provisions.

The fourth: casting oneself with one's hands into destruction is surrendering in war; that is, do not surrender to captivity.

The fifth: that it is preoccupation with setting one's wealth in order, away from jihad and from spending on it.

At-Tirmidhi reported from Aslam Abu ʿImran, who said: "We were in the city of the Romans, Constantinople, and they brought out to us a great line of Romans, and from the Muslims there came out a similar number to them. A man from the Muslims charged at a line of the Romans until he penetrated into them. The people shouted and said, 'Glory be to God! He throws himself with his own hands into destruction!' Then Abu Ayyub al-Ansari stood up and said, 'O people, you interpret this verse with this interpretation, but it was revealed about us, the company of the Helpers, when God exalted Islam and its supporters became numerous. Some of us said to one another in private, without the Messenger of God knowing, that our wealth had been lost, and God had exalted Islam and its supporters had become numerous, so if we stayed with our wealth and set right what had been lost of it... Then God revealed to His Prophet, responding to what we had said: ﴿And spend in the way of God, and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. So the destruction was remaining at home over our wealth and setting it right, and abandoning the raid.'" End of quotation. The verse can bear all the acceptable meanings.

The occurrence of the verb "tulqū" (you cast) in the context of a prohibition requires the generality of every casting with one's hand into destruction; that is, every cause of destruction deliberately brought about. So it is forbidden and prohibited, unless there is a factor that removes that prohibition, which is when preserving something takes precedence over the preservation of the self, while the preservation of that thing is certain to be achieved through casting oneself into destruction, or the preservation of part of it is achieved by that means.

Therefore, neglecting preparation for jihad is absolutely forbidden, because it is casting oneself with one's hand into destruction, and casting the community and the religion into destruction by destroying the lives of the Muslims. The scholars have differed regarding such a report as that transmitted by al-Tirmidhi from Abu Ayyub, namely one man breaking into the enemy's line. Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, among the Successors, ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun, Ibn Khuwayz Mandad among the Malikis, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, the companion of Abu Hanifa, said: there is no harm in this if he has strength, and if he acts with a sincere intention for God, exalted is He, and with hope of salvation or of inflicting harm on the enemy, or with the aim of emboldening the Muslims against them. This happened from some Muslims on the day of Uhud in the sight of the Prophet (ﷺ). But if it is not like that, it is part of casting oneself into destruction.

[Page 216]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do good﴾. Ihsan (good conduct) is doing what is beneficial and agreeable. So if one does a beneficial act that is painful, he is not a doer of good. Thus you would not say, when you strike a man to discipline him, "I have done good to him," nor when you indulge him in harmful pleasures, "I have done good to him." Likewise, if one does a harmful act that is agreeable, he is not called a doer of good.

Omitting the object of "ahsinu" (do good) indicates that good conduct is required in every state, and this is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the authentic hadith: "Indeed God has prescribed good conduct for everything."

In the command to good conduct after mentioning the command to retaliate against the aggressor, to spend in the way of God, and the prohibition against casting oneself with one's hands into destruction, there is an indication that all these circumstances are accompanied by good conduct and surrounded by it. In retaliation, good conduct consists in stopping at the limits, moderation in retaliating, and contentment with what achieves the desired benefit. In jihad in the way of God, good conduct consists in kindness to the captive and the defeated, in preserving the property and homes of the defeated from destruction and burning. The Arabs say: "You have power, so be lenient." And caution against casting oneself with one's hands into destruction is good conduct.

His saying: ﴿Indeed God loves the good-doers﴾ is a concluding generalization (tadhyil) encouraging good conduct, because God's love for His servant is the ultimate goal people seek, since God's love for the servant is the cause of righteousness and good in this world and the next. The "al-" (the) here is for the customary generalization, and what is meant is the good-doers among the believers.

[p. 217]

This is a return to the discussion of 'Umrah. It is coordinated (*'atf*) with His words, ﴿And righteousness is not that you enter houses from their backs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189], and so on. What lies between them is a digression (*istitrad*) or a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*). Moreover, the coordination of rulings with one another for the sake of relevance (*munasabah*) is a Qur'anic method. Therefore you may consider this sentence coordinated with the one before it in the manner of one story coordinated with another.

There is no disagreement that this verse was revealed at al-Ḥudaybiyah in the sixth year, when the polytheists barred the Muslims from the House. This is as will come in the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah. The Muslims had intended 'Umrah, and this was before the Hajj was made obligatory.

[p. 217 continues]

The primary purpose of the speech is 'Umrah. The Hajj is mentioned by way of incidental inclusion (*idmaj*), as good news that they would soon be able to perform the Hajj. This is one of the miracles of the Qur'an.

*Al-itmam* (completion) is finishing a thing and attending to what remains of it until it covers all of it.

A command of this kind, which concerns the description of an act, occurs in their speech in two ways. The first, which is the more common, is that the desired object is the attainment of a specific attribute for the act to which the attribute is attached, as with *al-itmam* in His words, ﴿And complete the Hajj﴾, meaning: perfect it if you have begun it. Likewise His words, ﴿Then complete the fast until night﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], according to what we have chosen, and His words, ﴿Then complete for them their treaty﴾ [al-Tawbah: 4]. A similar example is your saying to one who is walking slowly: "Hasten the walk." The second is that the command concerns the description of the act, meaning the attainment of the act itself in that manner from the very first moment, like His words, ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150]. This is like your saying: "Speed up the walk and call Fulan for me," addressed to someone who has not yet begun walking. You are commanding him to produce a swift walk from the very first moment. A parallel is their saying: "Widen the mouth of the well," and their saying: "Widen the sleeve of the robe and narrow its collar," meaning: bring it into being in that state from the start. This is a type of expression that is neither a metonymy (*kinayah*) nor a metaphor (*majaz*), but it is a command to a combination of two things, which is less common. For the normal case is that the object demanded by a command in its primary form is the event from which the verb's root derives.

The verse admits both usages. If it is the first, then it is a command to complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah, in the sense that they should not be a Hajj and 'Umrah mixed with turmoil, sedition and disorder. Or it is a command to complete both and not to turn back from them after entering the state of ihram by them, and not to be deterred from them by the enmity of the enemy. If it is the second, then it is a command to perform them whole, that is, fulfilling what has been prescribed in them.

The first meaning is more evident and more fitting to the verses before it. It seems that this exhortation indicates that the most important purpose of the Hajj and 'Umrah here is the first performance (*al-ṣarūrah*) of the Hajj, and likewise of the 'Umrah according to the view that it is obligatory.

The *lām* in *al-Ḥajj* and *al-'Umrah* is for the definition of the genus. Both are well-known acts of worship among those addressed, distinguished from the rest of the genera. The Hajj is visiting the Ka'bah at a specific season, at one specific time, for a group, and it includes standing at 'Arafat. The 'Umrah is visiting the Ka'bah outside a specific season, and it is for each individual person specifically. The root meaning of *al-Hajj*, with the ḥāʾ either open or with kasra, is the repetition of intention toward a thing or the multitude of those who intend it. From Ibn al-Sikkit: "Al-Ḥajj is the abundance of coming and going. It is said: The people of so-and-so repeatedly went to him," meaning they frequented him. In *al-Asās*: "So-and-so is repeatedly sought by the caravans," meaning he is sought. Thus he made it indicate intention by a group, as in the words of al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di, whose name was al-Rabi':

"And I witnessed from 'Awf many gatherings
That make pilgrimage to the abuse of al-Zibriqan the saffron-dyed."

The Hajj is among the most renowned acts of worship among the Arabs, and it is something they inherited from the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, as God related in His words, ﴿And proclaim to the people the Hajj﴾ [al-Hajj: 27], and so on. It has even been said that the Arabs were the earliest nation known to have the custom of the Hajj. They believed that visiting the Ka'bah was an effort toward God, the Exalted. Al-Nabighah said describing the pilgrims and their mounts:

"Upon them are dishevelled ones intent on their Lord,
So they are like the tips of the bent palm-branch, humbled."

They used to strip themselves of sewn garments at the state of ihram, not touch perfume, not approach women, and not hunt. The Hajj was circumambulation of the House, running between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, standing at 'Arafat, and sacrificing at Minā.

Some Arabs perhaps did not eat *aqt* (dried curd) or ghee during the period of the Hajj, because these were the food of the affluent. They did not shelter under a roof. Some would perform the Hajj naked of garments, some would not shelter from the sun, and some would perform the Hajj in silence without speaking. They did not drink wine during the months of the Hajj. They had rites and rulings in the Hajj, which we have mentioned in the history of the Arabs. The nations contemporary with the Arabs had many pilgrimages, and the most renowned of these nations in this were the Jews. They used to make pilgrimage to the place where the Ark of the Covenant was, that is, the Temple of Jerusalem, which is al-Masjid al-Aqsa, three times a year, in order to sacrifice there, since offerings are valid only there. One of these times was the feast of Passover.

The Christians undertook many visits as pilgrimage, the most renowned being their visits to the birthplaces of 'Isa, peace be upon him, and the visit to Jerusalem. Likewise the visit to the tomb of Mar Bolus (Paul) and the tomb of Mar Butrus (Peter) at Rome. Among the Christian pilgrimages that many people do not know, and which is the oldest of their pilgrimages, is that before Islam they used to make pilgrimage to the city of Asqalan on the Syrian coastal lands. It is presumed that those who initiated its pilgrimage were the Christians of Syria, from the Ghassanids, aiming to divert people away from visiting the Ka'bah. Suhaym, the slave of Bani al-Hisḥas, who was among the *mukhaḍramūn*, mentioned this in his words describing wild animals swept away by a torrent:

"As if the wild animals in it were of Asqalan
Met in the horn of Hajj, poisoned."

[p. 219]

That is, poison struck them and killed them. The linguists have mentioned this. The Egyptians and the Chaldeans had pilgrimages to the lands sacred to them. The Greeks had many visits to sacred sites, such as Olympia and the Temple of Zeus. The Hindus have many pilgrimages.

The purpose of this verse is the completion of the 'Umrah for which they had set out, and mentioning the Hajj along with it is incidental inclusion, because the Hajj had not yet become obligatory on that day, since the Hajj was in the hands of the polytheists. Mentioning it therefore carries good news that it will soon come under the control of the Muslims.

As for 'Umrah, it is derived from *al-ta'mir*, which is occupying a place, the opposite of leaving it empty. But in this form it is used only for visiting the Ka'bah outside the months of the Hajj, and it was known among the Arabs. They used to set its appointed time as anything other than the months of Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram and Safar. They would say: "When the sore on the camel's back has healed, the traces have faded, and Safar has passed, the 'Umrah is lawful for whoever performs it." Perhaps they set this so that the 'Umrah would come after returning from the Hajj and after giving the mounts rest.

The Mudar tribe agreed to make Rajab the month of 'Umrah, and for this reason Mudar sanctified it, so it was named Rajab of Mudar. The rest of the Arabs followed them, so that the traveler for 'Umrah would be safe from his enemy. For this reason they called Rajab "the month with spears unsheathed," and they regarded 'Umrah during the months of the Hajj as an act of wickedness.

His words "for God" (*lillāh*) mean: for the sake of God and for His worship. From the time of the Jahiliyyah the Arabs did not intend the Hajj except for God, nor the 'Umrah except for Him, because the Ka'bah is the House of God and His sanctuary. So the restriction here with "for God" alludes to the fact that the Hajj and 'Umrah are not for the sake of the polytheists, even though they had some benefit from them, and they were the custodians of the Sanctuary, and they were the ones who prevented the Muslims from it. This is so that the Muslims would not become weary of the Hajj in which they had met the harm of the polytheists. So it was said to them that this does not turn them away from the desire for Hajj and 'Umrah, because you perform the Hajj only for God and not for the sake of the polytheists. Also, a good and desirable thing, when something disliked surrounds it, should not become a reason to turn away from it; rather, that accidental obstacle must be removed. Among the ways of removing it is fighting, which is alluded to in the preceding verses.

It is also possible that the restriction with "for God" is to purify the intention from what used to mix with the intentions of people in the Jahiliyyah of drawing near to idols. When the polytheists placed Hubal upon the Ka'bah, and placed Isaf and Na'ilah upon al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, they had associated idols with God, the Exalted, in their circumambulation and their running.

It may be that the purpose of this restriction is both benefits.

[p. 220]

According to Malik and Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on them both, there is no proof in this verse for the obligation of the Hajj or of the 'Umrah. But the evidence for the ruling on the Hajj and 'Umrah according to both of them is other than this verse. Accordingly, the meaning of the verse for both of them is the obligation of these two acts of worship upon whoever has entered the state of ihram for them. As for Malik, he counted them among the acts of worship that become obligatory by beginning them, and they are, according to us, seven acts of worship: prayer, fasting, *i'tikāf*, Hajj, 'Umrah, circumambulation, and completion. As for Abu Hanifah, he made all voluntary acts (*nawāfil*) obligatory upon beginning them.

Whoever does not regard voluntary acts as obligatory by beginning them, and does not regard 'Umrah as obligatory, makes the ruling on completing them the same as the ruling on the beginning itself. Then the command to complete in the verse is used in the common element of demand, relying on the indicators (*qarā'in*). Among these are those who read *wa-al-'Umrah* with a *ḍammah*, so that it would not be included in what the command to complete covers, on the basis that the command implies obligation, so it would be restricted to the Hajj.

The Shafi'iyyah took it as evidence for the obligation of 'Umrah like the Hajj. The line of reasoning for them is that God commanded its completion. Either the command to complete means performing them whole, that is, fulfilling the conditions and pillars, so completion means completing the legal meaning according to one of the two earlier usages. They said: since there is no speech here about beginning, so that completion would be commanded. Also, it is supported by the reading *wa-aqīmū al-ḥajj* (and establish the Hajj). Or the intended meaning of completion here is reaching the end of the act of worship, which entails the command to begin, because completion depends on beginning, and what a required act cannot be completed without is itself required. So the command to complete is an implicit reference (*kināyah*) to a command to perform the act.

The truth is that taking the command in this matter as a command to the essence of the act and not to its attribute is a rare usage, as you have come to know. The reading *wa-aqīmū* (and establish), because of its irregularity, does not compel interpretation, nor does it stand in the position of a single-transmission report (*khabar al-āḥād*) when its chain of transmission is not sound back to the one to whom it is attributed. As for the first possibility, the figurative use of completion for the obligation of the act is a departure from the apparent meaning, while the wording is suitable to be taken in its apparent sense, namely to indicate the meaning: "When you begin, then complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah." This is implication (*dalālat al-iqtiḍā'*), and it is literal and a wonderful brevity. This is what the context indicates, as we have said earlier, because they had intended the 'Umrah. Moreover, the obligation of a means by the obligation of what it leads to requires that the thing explicitly stated as obligatory be the goal itself. So how can the Shafi'iyyah claim that "complete" here means the obligation of beginning, because what the obligatory act cannot be completed without is itself obligatory, as al-'Isam pointed out?

[p. 221]

Therefore the truth is that the verse is not evidence for the ruling on 'Umrah. The scholars have differed on its ruling. Malik and Abu Hanifah held that it is a sunnah. Malik said: "I do not know of anyone who permitted abandoning it." This is also the position of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Ibn Mas'ud among the Companions, and al-Nakha'i among the Successors.

Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ibn al-Jahm from the Malikis held that both (i.e., 'Umrah and Hajj in the sense of obligatory) are obligatory, and this was also the view of 'Umar, Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas among the Companions, and of 'Ata', Tawus, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Burda, Masruq and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh.

Our evidence is the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, is 'Umrah obligatory like Hajj? He said: No, but if you perform it, it is better." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it. Also, if an act of worship like this were obligatory, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have commanded it, and an obligation cannot be established by weak patchworks of reports. It is also related from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to say: "Were it not for scrupulousness, and that I did not hear anything from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, I would have said: 'Umrah is obligatory." End of quote. The point of argument is his saying "I did not hear," etc. Also, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And for Allah is the pilgrimage to the House upon mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], and He did not mention 'Umrah. Also, there cannot be two obligatory acts of worship of the same kind.

Also, the nature of an obligatory act of worship is that it be time-bound. Our companions also argued with the hadith "Islam is built upon five," and the hadith of Gabriel about faith and Islam, in which 'Umrah is not mentioned, and the hadith of the Bedouin who said: "I will not add to it or subtract from it," and he (ﷺ) said: "He has succeeded if he is truthful," and 'Umrah is not mentioned. The Shafi'is did not argue with more than this verse, since 'Umrah is mentioned in it alongside Hajj; and with the view of some Companions; and with caution.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab argued with this verse against prohibiting Tamattu', which is performing 'Umrah, then exiting the state of ihram from it during the period of Hajj, then performing Hajj in the same period before returning to his land. In al-Bukhari, he narrated the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me to a people in Yemen. I came to him while he was at al-Batha' in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, and he said: 'With what did you enter ihram?' I said: 'I entered ihram as the Prophet entered ihram.' He said: 'You did well. Do you have a sacrificial animal with you?' I said: 'No.' So he commanded me, and I circumambulated the House and between al-Safa and al-Marwah, then he commanded me and I exited ihram, and I came to a woman from my people who combed my hair or washed my head. Then I entered ihram for Hajj, and I was giving legal opinions to the people accordingly until the caliphate of 'Umar. I mentioned it to him, and he said: 'If we take the Book of Allah, it commands us to completion, for He said: "And complete the Hajj and 'Umrah for Allah." And if we take the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he did not exit ihram until the sacrificial animal reached its place of sacrifice.'" 'Umar meant, and Allah knows best, that Abu Musa entered ihram in the manner of the Prophet's entry, while the Prophet was in ihram for Hajj and 'Umrah together, so he was a Qarin, and the Qarin is bound to Hajj, so it is not permissible to exit ihram during the course of his Hajj. He held to the Messenger's action that he was a Qarin and did not exit ihram. This is based on the principle of not specifying the mutawatir (widely transmitted) by the ahad (solitary reports), as in his (i.e., 'Umar's) view regarding the hadith of Fatima bint Qays concerning maintenance.

His saying: ﴿But if you are held back, then what is available of the offering﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "complete" (atimmu), and the fa' is for the sequencing of mention (al-tafri' al-dhikri), for when He commanded the completion of Hajj and 'Umrah, He mentioned the ruling for what prevents that completion.

Especially Hajj, because its time generally passes after the impediment is removed, unlike 'Umrah. Al-ihsar (being held back) in the speech of the Arabs means the prevention of a person from doing something. It is said: ahsarahu, meaning a barrier prevented him. He the Exalted said: ﴿For the poor who are restricted in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273], meaning poverty prevented them from traveling for jihad. Ibn Mayyada said:
"The abandonment of Layla is not that she has become distant from you, nor that business has held you back."
This is a hamzated verb which the hamza does not render transitive, because it is synonymous with hasarahu. Similar are sadda and asadda. This is the view of the verifying scholars among the linguists. However, the use of the hamzated "ahsara" became common for prevention arising from other than an enemy, and the use of the unaugmented "hasara" became common for prevention by an enemy. He said: ﴿And seize them and besiege them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. So it is literally used for both meanings, but usage favored one of them, as al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf. Among the linguists some said: "ahsara" is literal for prevention by non-enemy, and "hasara" is literal for prevention by enemy; this is the view of al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj. Among the linguists some reversed this, and it is Ibn Faris, but it is very anomalous.

The condition came with the particle "in" because the content of the condition is disagreeable to them, so He conveyed the speech to them as conveying a report whose occurrence is doubtful. The intent is to make them aware that the polytheists would prevent them from 'Umrah. The jurists differed about the intended meaning of ihsar in this verse, in line with the difference regarding its lexical or usage meaning. My own view is that the ihsar here is used to cover prevention by an enemy or by other than an enemy, by the indication of His saying after it: ﴿But when you are secure﴾, for it is a clear and strong indication that what is intended is safety from fear of an enemy. This generality also serves the requirement of brevity in gathering the rulings of ihsar and then distinguishing them, as I will explain at His saying: ﴿But when you are secure﴾. It seems that this is what Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, held. Therefore, in the Muwatta' he did not argue for the ruling of ihsar by other than an enemy with this verse, but argued with the Sunnah. The majority of his companions said: it means the prevention arising from illness and the like, not the prevention by an enemy, based on the premise that using ihsar for this prevention is more common in the language.

Also, this verse made a sacrificial offering obligatory upon the one held back, and the Sunnah did not come with the legislation of the offering for one held back by an enemy, i.e., the legislation of the offering on account of ihsar. As for one who drove the offering with him, his rite is upon him, not on account of ihsar. Therefore Malik held the offering obligatory upon one held back by illness, childbirth, or a break, from every obstacle that prevents him from standing at the Station with the people, along with the obligation of tawaf and sa'y when the obstacle is removed, and the obligation of making up the Hajj in the following year, because of what is in the Muwatta' from the hadith of Ma'bad ibn Hizabah al-Makhzumi, that he was thrown down on part of the road to Makkah while in ihram, and he asked Ibn 'Umar, Ibn al-Zubayr and Marwan ibn al-Hakam, and all of them ordered him to seek treatment and offer ransom; then when he recovered, he performed 'Umrah and exited ihram, and then he must perform Hajj in the following year. And 'Umar ibn al-Khattab commanded this to Abu Ayyub and Habbar ibn al-Aswad when they missed the standing at 'Arafat. This differs from the siege by an enemy. In the Muwatta' he argued that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not command any of his Companions or those with him to make up anything or to return for anything. Our companions explained this by the distinction: the obstacle in illness and the like is from the pilgrim's own person, therefore he is required to complete; but in the case of the enemy's siege, the obstacle is external. The more apparent in argument is that the verse, though it may apply to every prevention, is more apparent in prevention other than by an enemy, and its apparentness has been confirmed by the Sunnah. Al-Shafi'i said: there is no making up in either case, and this is the apparent meaning of the verse, limiting to the offering. This is limiting to the mafhum (implied meaning) of the verse and opposing what is established by the Sunnah. Abu Hanifa said: every prevention, whether by an enemy or by illness, entails the obligation of making up and the offering, and there is no obligation of tawaf or sa'y after the excuse is removed; rather, if he slaughters his offering he exits ihram, and the making up is upon him.

It is not required of him what the hadith of al-Hudaybiyah implies, because if the verse was revealed after it, its generality abrogated the specific of the hadith, and if it was revealed before it, then it is an ahad report which, in his view, does not specify the Qur'an. Moreover, the hadith of al-Hudaybiyah is mutawatir, because those who witnessed the Prophet (ﷺ) that day exceed the number required for tawatur, and it was not transmitted from them that (the making up), although it is among matters whose transmission is strongly motivated.

Al-Shafi'i said: what is meant here is prevention by an enemy, by the indication of His saying: ﴿But when you are secure﴾. Also, it was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, which was a siege by an enemy; therefore he made the offering obligatory upon the one held back. As for one held back by an enemy, it is by the explicit text of the verse; and as for others, it is by analogy to it.

Accordingly: if his excuse is removed, then he must perform tawaf around the House and sa'y. He did not say that making up is obligatory for him, since it is not in the verse nor in the hadith.

His saying: ﴿then what is available of the offering﴾ is the answer of the condition, and it contains one of the two pillars of the predication, namely the subject (musnad ilayhi) without the predicate (musnad), so there must be an estimated element indicated by His saying: ﴿of the offering﴾. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "then upon you." The more apparent is to estimate an imperative verb: i.e., "then offer what is available of the offering." Both estimates indicate the obligation of the offering.

Its obligation in Hajj is clear, and in 'Umrah likewise, since it is among what must be completed after entering ihram, by the consensus of the majority.

"Istaysara" here means "yasura" (to be easy), so the sin and ta' are for emphasis, like "istasba'a 'alayhi" meaning "sa'uba" (to be difficult). That is: whatever is possible of the offering, by the possibility of obtaining it and the possibility of sending it. So "istaysara" here is meant to include all aspects of ease.

The hady (offering) is the name of the animal brought near to Allah in Hajj; it is a verbal noun from ahda. It is also said that it is the plural of hadiyya, as jadiyy al-sarj was pluralized as jadiy. If it is a name, then "min" is explanatory (bayaniyya), and if it is a plural, then "min" is partitive (tab'idiyya). The least that is known to them as hady is a sheep, and therefore Allah did not specify it here. If the one who intends Hajj or 'Umrah had driven this offering with him and then was held back, then sending it is obligatory if possible; and if he did not drive it with him, then it is upon him to send it, according to the disagreement about its ruling, whether obligatory or not. The purpose of this is to achieve some of the benefits of Hajj to the extent possible; so when the rites have passed, what benefits the poor of Makkah and its surroundings is not lost.

His saying: ﴿And do not shave your heads﴾ up to the end of the verse is a clarification of the continuance of the state of ihram until the offering reaches its place. He specified the prohibition of shaving rather than other prohibitions of ihram, such as perfume, as a preparation for His saying: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head﴾. The continuance of the ruling of ihram in the remainder is known by the indication of analogy and context; this is among the implications of the structures, and it is not a metaphor for exiting ihram, because the connection is not clear.

The purpose of this is to achieve as much as possible of the states of the rites, which is preserving the disheveledness that is intended in the rites.

Al-mahill, with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the ha', is the place of alighting or its time; it is said: halla bi-l-makan yahillu (with kasra on the ha') meaning the thing's station. What is intended here is its arrival point, which is its slaughter for the poor. It is said that "mahilluhu" is the place of slaughtering offerings, which is Mina; the first is the view of Malik.

His saying: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head﴾ up to the end of the verse: what is intended is an illness that requires shaving, whether the illness is in the body or in the head. His saying: ﴿or has an ailment of the head﴾ is a metonym for severe filth and lice, out of dislike for explicitly mentioning lice. The word "min" is for origin, i.e., an ailment arising from his head.

In al-Bukhari, from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, who said: "I was brought to the Prophet while lice were falling on my face. He said: 'I did not think the hardship had reached you to this extent. Do you not find a sheep?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'Fast three days, or feed six poor people, half a sa' of food for each poor person, and shave your head.' So this verse was revealed concerning me specifically, and it is general for you." End of quote. Among the subtleties of the Qur'an is leaving explicit mention of what is despised in words.

His saying: ﴿then a ransom of fasting﴾ has an elided subject for its being evident, i.e., "upon him," and the meaning: "let him shave his head, and upon him is a ransom." The indicator of the elided element is His saying: ﴿And do not shave your heads﴾. Allah has summarized the ransom and its quantity, and the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah explained it. The word "nusuk" (with two dammas or a sukun on the sin, with the nun having three vowels) means worship, and it is also applied to the slaughtered animal whose purpose is devotion; this is what is meant here. It is derived from nasaka (like nasara and karuma), when one worships and slaughters for Allah; and the worshipper is called nasik. Its most common application is to the slaughtered animal brought near to a deity. In the hadith: "And the other is a day you eat from your nusuk," meaning the sacrifice.

* * *

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 196 (part 3 of 4):

﴿So when you are secure, whoever enjoys [the benefit of] 'umrah until hajj shall [offer] what is feasible of sacrificial animals; and whoever does not find [any], then a fast of three days during hajj and seven when you return. Those are ten complete. That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque.﴾

The fa' here is for coordination (al-'atf) with "if you are prevented" (uhsirtum), if what is meant by security is the removal of the prior obstruction. It may be that this verse was revealed after hajj had been prescribed, because it mentions tamattu' and the fasting of the one who enjoys tamattu' if he does not find a sacrificial animal: three days during the period of hajj and seven when he returns to his homeland. That can only occur after they have become able to perform hajj. The fa' here serves merely as a sequential link in the narration (al-ta'qib al-dhikri).

The particle idha is used because the condition (fi'l al-shart) is something desired. Amn (security) is the opposite of fear, and it also means safety from everything feared. Amina, like fariha, yields amnan, amanan, amnan, amanatan, and imnan (with a kasra on the hamza). It is intransitive with respect to that from which one is safe, so it takes "min," as in: amintu min al-'aduww (I was safe from the enemy). It is transitive with respect to the one made safe, as in: amintu fulanan (I made so-and-so safe from me) when you make him secure from you. The more evident view is that security as the opposite of fear from the enemy, when its object is not stated, is treated as intransitive. The Qur'an says: ﴿Then deliver him to his place of safety﴾ [al-Tawbah: 6]. If no object is mentioned, it is considered intransitive, and this indicates the absence of fear of fighting. It was discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126].

Page 226

This indicates that the obstruction mentioned earlier is meant to include the prevention by an enemy, and for this reason it is said: "if you are secure." This is supported by the fact that these verses were revealed concerning the 'umrah of al-Hudaybiyah, as already mentioned. Therefore there is no implied contrary meaning (mafhum) to the condition here, because it came on account of a specific event. The verse thus establishes the ruling for 'umrah, since it is not performed except with security. This is because the Muslims came in the year of the 'umrah of qada' as performers of 'umrah, intending, if they were enabled, to perform hajj. The ruling for the sick and similar persons, when the impediment is removed, is known by analogy to the ruling for one who was in fear.

His saying ﴿fa-man tamatta'a﴾ is the response (jawab) of "idha," and the implied meaning is: "So when you are secure after the obstruction and the time of hajj has passed you, and it is possible for you to perform 'umrah, then perform 'umrah and wait until the following year, and seize the good of 'umrah. Whoever enjoys 'umrah [in this way], upon him is a sacrificial animal in place of the hajj sacrifice." The apparent meaning is that the beginning of the verse refers to the obstruction in which the one prevented can perform neither hajj nor 'umrah, and that His saying ﴿fa-idha amintum﴾ refers to the attainment of security together with the possibility of performing 'umrah, after the time of hajj has passed. That is, the time has passed for him but the place of hajj has not passed for him. It is known that whoever becomes secure while there remains enough time for him to perform hajj must perform hajj.

The meaning of ﴿tamatta'a bil-'umrati ila al-hajj﴾ is that he benefited from 'umrah immediately. Benefiting from it may mean benefiting from its reward, or by the dropping of its obligation, if it is said to be obligatory, since he has performed it during the journey of hajj. Or it may mean benefiting by exiting the state of ihram from it and then re-entering ihram for hajj, so that he is spared the burden of ihram for a long period. This is a concession from God Most High, since He permitted 'umrah during the period of hajj, after this had been forbidden in the Age of Ignorance, when they regarded 'umrah in the months of hajj as among the greatest wickedness.

The ba' in His saying "bil-'umrah" is connected to the verb "tamatta'a." His saying "ila al-hajj" is related to an omitted element indicated by the meaning of "ila": "waiting until the time of hajj" or "reaching up to the time of hajj," that is, its days, which are the first ten of Dhu al-Hijjah. It is understood from the word "ila" that between 'umrah and hajj there is a period in which the one performing 'umrah is not in ihram. This is the release (ihlal) between 'umrah and hajj in tamattu' and qiran. Upon him is what is feasible of sacrificial animals because of the release between the two ihrams. This applies where he did not offer [the sacrifice] at the time of the obstruction, as I see it, and God knows best.

The verse uses the word tamattu' in its linguistic sense, that is, benefiting, and it points to what the Muslims named tamattu' and qiran. It is one of the laws of Islam by which the law of the Age of Ignorance was abolished. The term tamattu' includes both, but it specifically restricts tamattu' to the pilgrim who enters ihram for 'umrah in the months of hajj, then releases from it, then performs hajj in the same year before returning to his homeland. It restricts qiran to joining hajj and 'umrah in one ihram, beginning with 'umrah, then releasing from it, and it is permissible for him to add hajj to 'umrah.
