God legislated all of this as a concession to people and as an abolition of what the Age of Ignorance practised, namely the prohibition of 'umrah in the months of hajj. God made the sacrifice obligatory as compensation for the hardship he would bear in returning to Makkah to perform 'umrah, as they used to do in the Age of Ignorance. For this reason it was named tamattu'.

The early scholars (al-salaf) differed concerning tamattu' and its description. The majority hold it to be permissible, and that one releases from the 'umrah he entered into in the months of hajj, then enters ihram again for hajj in that same year. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan did not regard tamattu' as valid and forbade it during his caliphate. Perhaps he interpreted this verse in the same way that Ibn al-Zubayr interpreted it, as will come shortly. 'Ali and 'Imran ibn Husayn opposed him. In al-Bukhari, from 'Imran ibn Husayn: "We performed tamattu' during the time of the Prophet, and the Qur'an was revealed. Then a man among us said with his own opinion what he wished," meaning 'Uthman. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab did not regard the qarin, who enters ihram for both 'umrah and hajj together and completes the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah, as permitted to release from his ihram until he releases from the ihram of hajj. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said to him: "I came from Yemen and found the Messenger of God in Makkah in ihram," that is, in the Year of Farewell. He said to me: "With what did you enter ihram?" I said: "I entered ihram with the same ihram as the Prophet." He said to me: "Do you have a sacrifice with you?" I said: "No." So he commanded me, and I performed tawaf and sa'y, then I released, washed my head, and a woman from 'Abd al-Qays combed my hair. When Abu Musa related this to 'Umar, 'Umar said: "If we follow the Book of God, it commands us to complete [the rites], and if we follow the Sunnah of His Messenger, he did not release until the sacrifice reached its place of slaughter." The majority of the Companions and jurists disagree with the opinion of 'Umar and act upon the report of Abu Musa and the hadith of 'Ali: "The Messenger of God ﷺ said: Had I not had the sacrifice with me, I would have released." Some people attribute to 'Umar the view that tamattu' is not permissible, but this is a mistake. Rather, 'Umar's view was that release from 'umrah in tamattu' is not permitted until one releases from hajj, and this is the meaning of his saying: "He did not release until the sacrifice reached its place of slaughter." Perhaps he regarded release for one already engaged in the intention of hajj as contradicting that intention, which he expressed as "completion." Perhaps he did not regard a single report (ahad) as specifying what is mass-transmitted (mutawatir) from the Book or the Sunnah, because the Prophet's action here is mass-transmitted, since many of his Companions witnessed it and transmitted his hajj, and that he entered ihram for both together.

Yes, Abu Bakr and 'Umar held that ifrad in hajj was better than tamattu' and qiran, and Malik followed this. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan related from him that he preferred one of two conflicting hadiths by the practice of the two shaykhs. 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, may God be pleased with him, held that tamattu' is specific to one who is obstructed, if he is able to reach the House after the standing at 'Arafah has passed him, so he makes his hajj an 'umrah and performs hajj in the following year. He interpreted His saying "ila al-hajj" to mean "until the time of the following year's hajj." The majority say: "ila al-hajj" means "until the days of hajj."

His saying "fa-man lam yajid fa-siyam thalathati ayyam" (etc.) is joined to "fa-man tamatta'a," because "fa-man tamatta'a" together with its response, "fa-ma istaysara," implicitly contains the meaning "whoever performs tamattu' while finding the sacrifice," so "fa-man lam yajid" is coordinated with it.

God made fasting a substitute for the sacrifice, as an addition to the concession and mercy. For this reason He legislated the fast in separate parts, making it ten days: three of them during the days of hajj and seven after returning from hajj.

His saying "fi al-hajj" means during its months, if he was able to perform 'umrah before the period of hajj ended. If he did not reach hajj and performed 'umrah, that is another case which the verse does not address.

His saying "tilka 'asharatun kamilah" is the summation of the calculation (fadhlakat al-hisab), that is, its totalling. When a calculator mentions two or more numbers and wishes to sum them, he says: "fa-dhalika" (that is, the counted total) "is so-and-so." This expression was coined into a word by contraction (nahṭ), like basmala (saying bismillah) and hawqala (saying la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah). So the letters of fadhlaka are gathered from the letters of fa-dhalika, as al-A'sha said:

Three in the morning are enough for me, and six when evening overtakes me.
So that is nine in the day, my satisfaction; but drinking beyond satiety is an illness.

The word fadhlaka is a later coinage (muwallada) not heard from the speech of the Arabs. The term fadhlaka became dominant for the summary of the total of numbers, even if the spoken phrase did not use the word "dhalika," as we say of His saying "tilka 'asharatun kamilah" that it is a fadhlaka, although the word in the statement is "tilka," not "dhalika." Similar is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

Three and two, so that is five, and a sixth inclining toward the kiss.

That is, toward smelling and kissing.

There are several views concerning the need for fadhlaka in the verse. It has been said that it is merely emphasis, as one says "I wrote with my hand," meaning that it came in the manner of what occurs in the poetry of al-A'sha, that is, in an Arabic style, and serves only to fix the ruling in the mind twice. For this reason the author of al-Kashshaf, when he mentioned a similar case, said: "like the Arabs' saying: two kinds of knowledge are better than one kind of knowledge."

It is related from al-Mubarrad that it is for emphasis to repel the assumption that something remained of what must be fasted. Al-Zajjaj said: Someone might suppose that what is meant is a choice between fasting three days during hajj or seven days when he returns to his land in place of the three. This is removed by the clear meaning of His saying "tilka 'asharah." Al-Zamakhshari followed him, saying: the waw may come for permissiveness (ibahah), as in your saying: "he sat with al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin," so fadhlakta is to negate the assumption of permissiveness. He means by permissiveness that it is for the choice which permits combining and is not fixed.

Both statements need an explanation of the source of the assumption of the meaning of choice, so I say: although this meaning goes against the original usage of waw, to the extent that Ibn Hisham claimed that waw does not come for it and that choice is derived from the form of the imperative, nevertheless it may be assumed because God mentioned two numbers in two different conditions and made the smaller number for the more difficult condition and the larger for the easier. Therefore there arose the assumption that God required only the fasting of three days, and that seven is a concession for one who wishes a choice. God therefore clarified what removes this assumption. Indeed the indication is that God's intention is the obligation of fasting ten days, and that dividing it is only a concession and mercy from Him, the Glorified. Thus the benefit of drawing attention to the divine mercy is achieved.

A parallel is His saying: ﴿We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was complete forty nights﴾ [al-A'raf: 142], since it indicates that He intended from Moses forty nights of intimate communion, but He conveyed it to him distributed for ease.

I have been asked about the wisdom of the days being ten. I answered that it perhaps arose from combining seven and three, because they are two blessed numbers. But the benefit of distribution is evident, and the wisdom of the distribution being into two unequal numbers rather than equal ones is evident: because of the difference between the state of being occupied with hajj, in which there is hardship, and the state of settling at home.

The benefit of making part of the fast within the period of hajj is making part of the worship occur at its cause. The benefit of the distribution into three and seven is that both are blessed numbers by which religious and judicial matters have been regulated.

[Page 230]

As for the phrase "kamilah" (complete), it conveys an exhortation to fast all the days without missing any of them, and it also highlights that fast as a path to perfection for the one who observes it. Thus "perfection" (al-kamal) is used in both its literal and figurative senses.

His saying, ﴿That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾, refers to the nearest thing mentioned in the discourse, which is the sacrificial offering of tamattu' (the pilgrim who combines 'umrah and hajj, hadi al-tamattu') or its substitute, which is fasting. The meaning is that the offering is required of the one who comes from outside Makkah, so that he does not have to make the journey again for 'umrah. As for the Makkan, he gains no benefit from being spared the repeated journey, so he is not required to offer a sacrifice. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority. Accordingly, for them, the people of Makkah have no sacrificial offering for tamattu' or qiran (combining hajj and 'umrah in one ihram), because there is no hardship for them in repeating the 'umrah. Abu Hanifa said: the reference (of "that") is to everything that the preceding discourse includes before the demonstrative, namely tamattu' with 'umrah together with hajj and the obligation of the offering. Accordingly, he does not hold that tamattu' and qiran are for the people of Makkah. This is a valid line of reasoning.

The "present at the Sacred Mosque" (hadiri al-Masjid al-Haram) are the people of the city of Makkah and those who live adjacent to it. Scholars differed over the definition of "adjacent." Malik said: those connected to Makkah, which extends from Dhi Tuwa, a few miles from Makkah. Al-Shafi'i said: whoever is at a distance of qasr (the distance at which one shortens the prayer). Ibn Habib attributed this to Malik, but the shaykhs of the school considered this an error.

'Ata' said: the present at the Sacred Mosque are the people of Makkah and the people of 'Arafah, Marr, 'Urannah, Dajnan and al-Raji'. al-Zuhri said: the people of Makkah and whoever is at a distance of a day's journey or so. Ibn Zayd said: the people of Makkah, Dhi Tuwa, Fajj, and what is near them.

Tawus said: the present at the Sacred Mosque are everyone who is within the Haram. Abu Hanifa said: they are those who are within the miqat (the boundaries where pilgrims must enter ihram), whether they are Makkans or others, whether they dwell within the Haram or outside it in the Hill (al-Hill).

* * *

﴿And fear Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾

This is a charge to piety after the explanation of the rulings, which are not free of hardship, to warn against being careless about them. Thus the command to piety is general, and the inclusion of hajj within it is part of that generality, and it is the most fitting of its particulars, because the discourse concerns it.

His saying, ﴿and know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾, begins with "wa'lamu" (and know), in order to give emphasis to the information. He did not limit himself to saying, ﴿And fear Allah; indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. Had he limited himself to that, the desired knowledge would have been attained, since knowledge is obtained from information. But since he intended to affirm the information, he opened with the command to know, because it has the sense of affirming the information, as if he were saying: do not doubt this. It conveys the meaning of "inna" (indeed). This was previously mentioned at His saying, ﴿And fear Allah and know that Allah is with the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 197 (part 1 of 2):

Page 231
﴿The Hajj is in well-known months. So whoever undertakes the Hajj in them, there shall be no sexual relations, no transgression, and no disputing during the Hajj.﴾

This is an independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) to inform the reader of the detailed rites of the Hajj. In my view, these verses were revealed after the verse in Surah Al 'Imran: ﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by everyone able to make the journey to it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. That verse enjoined the Hajj in general terms, while this verse explains its acts. This is a clarification delayed after what is clarified (bayan mu'akhkhar 'an al-mubayyan), and delaying clarification until the time of need occurs more than once. It appears, then, that this verse was revealed in the year nine, in preparation for the Hajj of the Muslims with Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Between the revelation of this verse and the revelation of the verse ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196] there was about three years. Thus it is, in my view, among the verses which the Messenger (peace be upon him) was commanded to place in this position in this surah, to combine the acts of the Hajj with the acts of the 'Umrah.

It is an injunction concerning the obligations and sunan of the Hajj, and concerning what must be observed in its performance, and it mentions what Allah intended to enjoin regarding its pillars and rites.

The care of Allah Most High for this great act of worship is evident, for He set out its details and circumstances, together with altering what the people of the Jahiliyyah had introduced into it.

He described the months as "well-known" (ma'lumat), referring to what was already known to the Arabs. They were inherited from the law of Ibrahim, and extend from the beginning of Shawwal to the end of the days of Muharram. Some of them are among the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum), because they made sacred a month and some days before the day of Hajj, and made sacred after it the remainder of Dhu al-Hijjah and all of Muharram, so that the sacred months would be a sufficient period for the pilgrims to return to their homelands. As for Rajab, Mudar alone made it sacred, because it is the month of 'Umrah.

So His saying ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ means: during months, because of His following words ﴿So whoever undertakes the Hajj in them﴾. You may also estimate: the period of the Hajj is months, as the Arabs say: "The fresh dates are two months of spring (rabi')."

The purpose of His saying ﴿The Hajj is in months﴾ may be that it is a preface to His saying ﴿there shall be no sexual relations, no transgression﴾, making the period of abstaining from sexual relations, transgression and disputing easier, since abstaining from these is difficult for people. For this reason the period was described with the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah). This is like what Malik narrated in the Muwatta': 'A'ishah said to 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr: "O son of my sister, it is only ten nights; if anything troubles your soul, leave it," meaning eating the flesh of game.

It may also be a confirmation of what they had in the Jahiliyyah regarding fixing the months of Hajj. It is like His saying ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. It was also said that the purpose is to state the time of the Hajj, but I am not satisfied with this.

The months intended are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and Dhu al-Hijjah, and no others. They differed as to whether the whole of Dhu al-Hijjah is a month, or only its first ten days, or only nine days of it, or thirteen days of it. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, al-Zuhri, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr and it is a narration of Ibn al-Mundhir from Malik held the first view. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, Abu Hanifah and it is a narration of Ibn Habib from Malik held the second view.

al-Shafi'i held the third view, and the fourth view is the position of the Maliki school, mentioned by Ibn al-Hajib in al-Mukhtasar without attribution.

The application of the plural "months" to two months and part of months, according to the proponents of the third and fourth views, is explained either by applying the plural to two, or by the Arabs' consideration of entering into a month or year as completing it, as they said: "son of two years" for one who has entered the second year. The fruit of this disagreement appears in one who performed some acts of the Hajj which may validly be delayed, such as the Tawaf al-Ziyarah after the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah. Whoever holds that he performed it within the days of Hajj does not consider a sacrifice (dam) obligatory upon him, and whoever holds otherwise holds otherwise.

They also differed concerning entering into ihram for Hajj before the months of Hajj begin. Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: it is not valid, and it counts for him as 'Umrah, like one who enters into prayer before its time. He is obliged to renew the ihram from the miqat at the beginning of the months of Hajj. al-Shafi'i argued with His saying ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾. Ahmad said: it is valid but disliked. Malik, Abu Hanifah and al-Nakha'i said: it is permissible to enter ihram for Hajj and 'Umrah at any time of the year, except that Malik disliked 'Umrah in the remainder of Dhu al-Hijjah, because 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to forbid it and would strike its doer with the whip. Malik's evidence in this is what has passed of the Sunnah. al-Nakha'i argued with His saying ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: they are times for people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189], since He made all the new moons times for the Hajj without specifying. This argument is weak, for the verse does not generalize all new moons to the timing of Hajj; rather the context is that all new moons are suitable for timing in general, with distribution in detail, so each act is timed by the appearance of the new moon that corresponds to it, according to what other evidences from the Book and the Sunnah clarify.

Page 233
Since the verse admits several interpretations regarding the mention of the months of Hajj, I do not see that the scholars have any proof in it for fixing the time of Hajj.

His saying ﴿So whoever undertakes the Hajj in them﴾ is a branching from this preface, explaining that Hajj takes place in them and explaining its most important rulings.

The meaning of (faradha) is "intended and resolved." The intention of Hajj is the resolve to perform it, which is the ihram. For Malik and Abu Hanifah, the intention must be accompanied by one of the utterances of Hajj, which is the talbiyah, or by one of its acts, such as driving the sacrificial animal. For al-Shafi'i, Hajj is entered by intention alone, even if not accompanied by an utterance or act, and this is the preferred view, because intention in acts of worship is not required to be accompanied by a part of the acts of worship. There is no disagreement that the Sunnah is to accompany the ihram with ghusl, the talbiyah, and the mounting of the riding animal once the rider is settled on it.

The pronoun in (fihinna) refers to the months, because it is a plural of non-rational beings, which takes the feminine form.

His saying ﴿there shall be no sexual relations, no transgression, and no disputing during the Hajj﴾ is the answer (jawab) of the conditional "man". The link between the conditional clause and the answer is the pronoun implied in ﴿fala rafatha﴾ which returns to (man), since the estimate is "fala yarfuth" (he shall not commit sexual relations).

He negated sexual relations, transgression and disputing by the negation of the genus, for emphasis in prohibiting them and keeping them far from the pilgrim, to the point that they are treated as though the pilgrim had prohibited them and refrained; thus their genera are negated. Similar examples are many in the Qur'an, such as His saying ﴿And divorced women shall wait﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]. This is of the kind of tamthil (figurative representation), in that the state of the one commanded at the time of the command is likened to the state resulting after he has complied, so that he is as if he complied and did what was commanded, and thus he is described as having done it. This is as al-Zamakhshari established in the Kashshaf regarding His saying ﴿And divorced women shall wait﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], where the compound expression indicating the form that is compared is used for the form compared.

The majority read the three words negated by "la" with a fatha at their ends, taking (la) as a negation of the genus explicitly. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "rafathun" and "fusuqun" with a damma, taking (la) as the sister of "laysa", a negation of the genus without explicitness. They read ﴿wa la jidala﴾ with a fatha on the lam, taking (la) as a negation of the genus explicitly, and as the coordination of one sentence upon another. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr that he said: the nominative means: "there shall be no sexual relations and no transgression," meaning that the predicate of (la) is omitted, and the two verbal nouns stand in place of their verbs, and they were put in the nominative to express permanence, like the nominative in "al-hamdu lillah." Then the speech is complete, and he began the negation anew, saying ﴿wa la jidala fi al-hajj﴾ with "fi al-hajj" as the predicate of (la). According to both readings, the statement is a report used in the sense of prohibition.

Page 234
Rafath: idle speech and obscenity in speech. This is what Abu 'Ubaydah said, citing the verse of al-'Ajjaj:
"And many a flock of pilgrims, restraining themselves from idle talk and the obscenity of speech."
Its verb is in the patterns naṣara, fariha and karuma. What is meant here is the euphemism for intercourse with women.

I reckon that the euphemism with this word rather than another is intended to combine the two meanings, the explicit and the figurative. In the Jahiliyyah they used to avoid it. al-Nabighah said:
"May my Lord greet you; for we are not permitted the play of women, and the religion has resolved [on that]."
He means by "the religion" the Hajj. They explained his words "the play of women" as flirtation.

This is a report intended as an emphatic prohibition, and it implies that intercourse during Hajj is forbidden and invalidates the Hajj. The Sunnah has clearly explained this. Entering ihram prevents intercourse until release by the tawaf al-ifadah, and this covers the whole period of ihram. If forgetfulness occurs, Malik said it invalidates the Hajj, and he must repeat his Hajj if the standing at 'Arafah has not passed; otherwise he makes it up in the following year. This is in view of the fact that the occurrence of sensual pleasure is inconsistent with the detachment of Hajj and the asceticism required in it, regardless of whether it was deliberate or forgotten. al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, and Dawud al-Zahiri said: the Hajj is not invalidated, but a sacrifice (hady) is due. As for courting women and speaking about lawful intercourse, it is a means that should be blocked, because it diverts the heart from devotion to the remembrance of Allah in Hajj.

Reciting old poetry containing mention of flirtation is not included in rafath, since its aim is not to produce rafath. Ibn 'Abbas once urged on his mount, while in ihram, with a verse containing a word from rafath, and his companion Husayn ibn Qays said to him: "Do you commit rafath while in ihram?" He said: "Rafath is what is said in the presence of women," i.e., the act that is in the presence of women, i.e., intercourse.

Fusuq is well known, and its discussion has been given more than once before. It has been said that what is meant here is the prohibition of sacrificing to idols, a view narrated from Malik, and it seems he said this because it relates to abolishing what they practised in the Jahiliyyah. However, the apparent meaning is that fusuq covers all sin. All the mufassirun have remained silent on the ruling for committing sin during the state of ihram.

Joining fusuq with rafath, which invalidates the Hajj, implies that committing sin during the period of ihram invalidates the Hajj in the same way. I have not seen any jurist who held that fusuq invalidates the Hajj, nor that it does not invalidate it, except Ibn Hazm, who said in al-Muhalla: the Zahiri position is that all sins invalidate the Hajj, and what

Page 235
appears is that minor sins do not invalidate the Hajj, but deliberately committing major sins does invalidate it, and it is more fitting to invalidate it than intercourse with women, which is a lawful pleasure. And Allah knows best.

Jidal is the verbal noun of jadalahu, meaning he contended with him in fierce contention. I have already expounded on it at His saying ﴿And do not dispute on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 107] in Surah al-Nisa', since its explanation escaped us here.

The meaning of jidal here has been disputed. It was said: it is insulting and anger. It was also said: it is the dispute of the Arabs over their differing about the standing place, since some of them would stand at 'Arafah and some would stand at Jam', and this is narrated from Malik.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 197 (part 2 of 2):

The scholars agreed that studying knowledge and debating about it are not among the forbidden disputation (jidal) that is prohibited. I heard from our teacher, the eminent scholar al-Wazir, that when al-Zamakhshari completed his tafsir, al-Kashshaf, he placed it in the Ka'bah during the season of Hajj, intending that the scholars who attend the season might read it, and he said: "Whoever wishes to dispute anything, let him do so." They claimed that some of the people of knowledge objected to him, saying: "How did you interpret His words, exalted is He: ﴿There shall be no disputing during the Hajj﴾?" and that he was struck dumb by it. I think, if this account is authentic, that al-Zamakhshari turned away from answering him, because he saw that the man did not distinguish between the disputation forbidden during Hajj and disputation about knowledge. They agreed that arguing in order to reject what is wrong and to establish the limits of the religion is not among what is forbidden. What is forbidden is that which leads to anger and mutual abuse and violates the sanctity of Hajj. Because of the detailed variations in the states of disputation, the verse is general regarding the kinds of disputation that invalidate Hajj, so the explanation of that is referred to other evidences.

As for His words: ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾, it follows the prohibition of forbidden acts in order to encourage the attainment of the opposites of those forbidden acts. It is as if He said: "Do not do what you have been forbidden, and do good; whatever good you do, Allah knows it." The knowledge of Allah is mentioned in its general sense, but its necessary consequence is intended, which is recompense for what is known, by way of kinaya (metonymy). So it is conjoined to His words: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity﴾, and so on.

* * *

﴿And take provision, for the best provision is taqwa (God-consciousness). So fear Me, O people of understanding﴾

This is conjoined to the clause ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾, in view of the kinaya in it concerning encouragement to do good. The meaning is: "Increase in doing good."

Tazawwud (taking provision) is preparing provision, which is the food that a traveller carries. It is a verb of the form tafa''ala derived from a solid noun, zad (provision), as one says ta'ammama (he wore a turban) and taqammasa (he put on a shirt), meaning: he made that his companion.

[Page 236]

Accordingly, tazawwud is used metaphorically for increasing in doing good in preparation for the Day of Recompense. It is likened to a traveller preparing provision for his journey, based on the use of the terms "journey" and "departure" for death. Al-A'sha said in his qasidah, which he composed in praise of the Prophet (ﷺ) and in which he mentioned some of what the Prophet called to, drawing upon this verse and others:

If you set out without provision of piety, and you meet after death one who has provided himself,
You will regret that you were not like him, and that you did not prepare what he had prepared.

Thus His words ﴿for the best provision is taqwa﴾ serve as a tadhyil (concluding statement): that is, taqwa is better than provision for the journey, so be keener upon it.

It is also permissible that tazawwud be used, together with that, in its literal meaning, by way of using the word in both its haqiqa (literal) and majaz (figurative) senses. Then it is a command to prepare provision for the journey of Hajj, as an allusion to a people from Yemen who used to come to Hajj without any provision and would say, "We rely upon Allah," so they became a burden upon people by begging insistently.

His words ﴿for the best provision﴾ and so on indicate an emphasis on the command to take provision, drawing attention to the fact that it is a part of taqwa, because it preserves dignity and honour.

His words ﴿and fear Me﴾ serve as an emphasis of His words ﴿for the best provision is taqwa﴾. He added only His words ﴿O people of understanding﴾, which indicate that taqwa is something that people of intellect desire.

Albab is the plural of lubb, which means intellect. The lubb of anything is its pure essence. Its verb is labuba, yalubbu, with the vowel of the lam being damma. They said: in the speech of the Arabs there is no form fa'ula, yaf'ulu (with damma on the ‘ayn) in the past and present tenses of a doubled verb except this verb. Sibawayh related it from Yunus, and Tha'lab said: "I do not know a parallel to it."

Thus His words ﴿for the best provision is taqwa﴾ serve as a tadhyil: that is, taqwa is better than provision for the journey, so be keener upon it. The placement of His words ﴿So fear Me, O people of understanding﴾, on the assumption that tazawwud is meant in both its literal and figurative senses, is to convey the command to taqwa, which is the provision of the Hereafter, in connection with the command to take provision, because worldly taqwa is attained by preserving one's honour.

[Page 237]

Taqwa is the verbal noun of ittaqa, meaning to beware of something. Its origin is taqiya, and they changed its ya' into waw to distinguish between the noun and the adjective. The adjective with ya' is like the feminine form taqya, as in khazya and sadya. It has been used in the Shari'ah for caution against the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, by following His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. It was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿a guidance for those who are mindful of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

This is a clause interposed between two connected statements, prompted by the prohibition on certain acts during the Hajj that defeat its purpose. It moves on to permit what they used to avoid during the Hajj, namely trade, by showing that it does not defeat the lawful purpose. This refutes the practice of the polytheists, who considered trade forbidden to one in the state of ihram for Hajj.

﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾. Here "bounty" (fadl) means wealth, and "seeking bounty" means trade for the sake of profit, as in His saying: ﴿and others who travel through the land seeking of God's bounty﴾ (al-Muzzammil 73:20).

The people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) used to hold buying and selling forbidden once they left the market of Dhu al-Majaz for Makkah. Al-Nabighah said:

"Nearly did my saddle and saddle-cloth unseat me at Dhu al-Majaz, and I had not perceived the sound of a nagging voice, a Himyarite woman's voice, when they had departed, saying: 'Is there among your travelers one who will buy butter?'
I said to her as she hastened beneath her necklace: 'Do not let it destroy you; indeed, buying has ceased.'"

That is, buying had come to an end and was forbidden.

From Ibn 'Abbas: "'Ukaz, Majannah and Dhu al-Majaz were markets in the Jahiliyyah, so they considered it sinful to trade during the seasons, and so this was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ during the season of the Hajj." End of quotation. That is, Ibn 'Abbas recited it with the addition "during the season of the Hajj."

The market of 'Ukaz used to open at the beginning of Dhu al-Qa'dah and last twenty days. In it precious goods were sold, tribes boasted, and poets competed. It was the greatest market of the Arabs. Its location was between Nakhlah and al-Ta'if. From 'Ukaz they would go on to Majannah, then to Dhu al-Majaz. It is presumed that they spent the rest of the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah between these two markets, because al-Nabighah mentioned that he stayed at Dhu al-Majaz for four nights, and that he left Dhu al-Majaz for Makkah. He said, describing his mount:

[p. 238]

"She spent three nights, then one more, at Dhu al-Majaz, watching over a camp-site of ..."

Then he mentioned that he set out from there as a pilgrim, saying:

"Nearly did my saddle and saddle-cloth unseat me..."

* * *

﴿Then when you pour forth from 'Arafat, remember God at the Sacred Mash'ar﴾. The fa' is conjunctive, linking to His saying ﴿so there shall be no lewd speech nor wickedness﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:197) and what follows. The command is conjoined to the prohibition. His saying "when you pour forth" (idha afadtum) is a condition for the intended matter, which is ﴿remember God﴾.

Ifadah (pouring forth, a rapid departure) here means leaving swiftly. Its root is from fada al-ma' (the water overflowed) when it increased over what contained it, so it issued forth and flowed. For this reason they called the drawing of arrows in the game of maysir (gambling with arrows) ifadah, and the one who draws them mufid (one who pours forth), because he brings out the arrows from the quiver with force and speed, without choosing or feeling to see which arrow comes out. They also called the departure from 'Arafat ifadah, because they depart at one time, and they are a great number, so their departure has intensity. The word ifadah is used in this verse for departure from 'Arafat and departure from Muzdalifah.

The Arabs used to call the departure from 'Arafat daf' (pushing), and they called the departure from Muzdalifah ifadah. Both usages are figurative, because daf' is driving a body away with force. Part of the eloquence of the Qur'an is its use of ifadah for both departures, because "afada" carries a close resemblance in meaning of abundance without intensity.

Moreover, avoiding "daf'tum" (you pushed) guards against the hearers' supposing that the journey involves some people pushing others, since they used to make noise, commotion and rapid movement in their pushing. So the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that in the Farewell Pilgrimage and said: "Righteousness is not in hastening (al-ida'), so when you pour forth, upon you is tranquility and dignity."

'Arafat is the name of a valley, also called a basin (batn). It is a wide watercourse into which the waters of surrounding mountains flow, known as the mountains of 'Arafah in the singular. 'Arafat has become a proper name for that valley in the plural form with alif and ta'. It is also called 'Arafah in the singular form. Al-Farra' said: "The people's saying 'the Day of 'Arafah' is a later (muwallad) usage, not purely Arabic." Most scholars disagreed with him and said: "It is said 'Arafat and 'Arafah." It has come in numerous hadiths: "the Day of 'Arafah." Some lexicographers said: "One does not say 'the Day of 'Arafat."

In the middle of the valley of 'Arafah is a small hill, on which some of those who stand at 'Arafah stand, and on which the preacher delivers the sermon to the people on the ninth of Dhu al-Hijjah at midday. The Prophet (ﷺ) stood upon it mounted on the Day of 'Arafah. On the top of that hill a marker has been built at the spot where the Prophet (ﷺ) stood, and the imams stand at it on the Day of 'Arafah.

It is not known why the place is named 'Arafat or 'Arafah, nor whether it is a transferred (manqul) proper noun or an originally proper one (murtajal). What al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah chose is that it is an original proper noun. What appears is that one of the two names is the original and the other is a later development upon it: the original is 'Arafat from ancient Arabic, and 'Arafah is a lightened form that became common in speech. It is also possible that the original is 'Arafah and that 'Arafat is an extension (ishba') from the dialect of some tribes.

The mention of ('Arafat) by name in the Qur'an points to the fact that standing at 'Arafah is a pillar (rukn) of the Hajj. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Hajj is 'Arafah."

The place was named 'Arafat, which is in the pattern of the plural with alif and ta', so they treated it as a plural with alif and ta', and they did not prevent it from taking tanwin (nunation), despite its being a proper noun.

The feminine plural is not prevented from taking tanwin, because the plural removes the definiteness (ilmiyyah) found in the singular, since the plural implies "things named such-and-such." So what is pluralized was only pluralized after the intention of making it indefinite. The feminine ending that prevents tanwin together with proper-noun status or adjectival status is the ending with ta' marbutah (the feminine ending spelled with a ha').

Mentioning the ifadah from 'Arafat requires that standing at it has already taken place, since there is no ifadah except after arriving there. Mentioning 'Arafat by name is an honouring (tanwih) of it, indicating that standing there is a pillar. Among the rites, none is mentioned by name except 'Arafah, al-Safa and al-Marwah. This indicates that these are among the pillars, contrary to Abu Hanifah regarding al-Safa and al-Marwah. The pillar of ihram is derived from His saying: ﴿whoever imposes the obligation of the Hajj therein﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:197). As for the tawaf al-ifadah (the circumambulation of pouring forth), it is established by the Sunnah and by the consensus of the jurists.

"Min" (from) is for starting point (ibtida'iyyah).

The meaning is: when you pour forth, departing from 'Arafat towards Muzdalifah.

The explicit mention of the name 'Arafat in this verse is to refute the Quraysh, for they used to stand in the Jahiliyyah at Jam', which is Muzdalifah, because they were of the Hums (a group of tribes who placed themselves under special sanctity and claimed that standing could only take place within the sanctuary). They held that standing could not occur outside the Haram. Since Muzdalifah is within the Haram, they used to stand there and would not be content to stand at 'Arafah, because 'Arafah is outside the Haram (in the area of ordinary territory), as will come. For this reason God Most High did not mention Muzdalifah by name in the second ifadah, but said: ﴿from where the people pour forth﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:199), because Muzdalifah is the place from which people pour forth after the ifadah from 'Arafat. That is a reference to what they already know.

[p. 240]

"Al-Mash'ar" is a name derived from al-shu'ur, meaning knowledge, or from al-shi'ar, meaning sign, because a sign like a minaret was erected there from the time of the Jahiliyyah. Perhaps they did so because they departed from 'Arafat at the end of the evening, and the darkness after sunset overtook them, and they were large groups, so they feared they might lose the way and time would become constrained for them.

He described al-Mash'ar with the description "al-Haram" (the sacred) because it is from the land of the Haram, unlike 'Arafat.

Al-Mash'ar al-Haram is Muzdalifah. It was called Muzdalifah because it drew near (izdalafat) from Mina, meaning it came close, because they spend the night there intending to reach Mina at dawn.

Muzdalifah is also called Jam', because all the pilgrims gather there in standing, the Hums and others, from the time of the Jahiliyyah. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"He spent the night at Jam', then set out toward Mina, and in the morning he was returning, seeking to mix with the sahl (watered drink)."

As for one who says that it is called Jam' because it combines the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers there, he has overlooked the fact that the name existed before Islam.

Muzdalifah is also called Quzah, with a kasrah... [meaning: with a damma on the qaf and a fatha on the zay, not taking tanwin], by the name of a mountain peak among the mountains at the edge of Muzdalifah. It is called al-Miqdah, because the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah used to kindle fires on it. It was the standing place of the Quraysh in the Jahiliyyah, and the imam's standing place in Muzdalifah is at Quzah.

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related that when the Prophet (ﷺ) entered the morning at Jam', he came to Quzah, stood on it, and said: "This is Quzah, and it is the standing place, and all of Jam' is standing place." The Maliki school holds that spending the night is a Sunnah, while staying there for a portion of the night is obligatory.

'Alqamah, a group of the Successors, and al-Awza'i held that standing at Muzdalifah is a pillar of the Hajj, so whoever misses it has invalidated his Hajj, holding to the apparent command in His saying: ﴿remember God﴾.

[p. 241]

The Arabs in the Jahiliyyah did not pour forth from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah until one of the "Banu Safwah" permitted them to. They are the sons of al-Ghawth ibn Murr ibn Udd ibn Tabikhah ibn Ilyas ibn Mudar, and his mother was of Jurhum. Al-Ghawth was given the title Safwah because his mother could not bear children, so she vowed that if she bore a male she would dedicate him to the service of the Ka'bah. She then bore al-Ghawth. They used to tie a ribbon of wool (sufah) to the hair of the boy vowed to serve the Ka'bah, and this was called al-Rabit (the bond). Al-Ghawth managed the affairs of the Ka'bah together with his maternal relatives from Jurhum. When Qusayy ibn Kilab took control of the Ka'bah, he gave the permission (al-ijazah) to al-Ghawth, and then it remained among his descendants until they died out. It was also said that those who gave the sons of al-Ghawth the right to permit the pilgrims were the kings of Kindah. The one who gave permission for them from 'Arafah would say:

"O God, I am a follower of the followers' tradition;
if there is any sin, it is upon Qudha'ah."

Because Qudha'ah used to make the sacred months lawful.

When the sons of Safwah died out, the permission passed to the Banu Sa'd ibn Zayd Manat ibn Tamim, and they inherited it through nepotism (al-qu'dud), so it remained among the family of Safwan from them. When Islam came, it was in the hands of Kirb ibn Safwan. Aws ibn Maghra' said:

"People will not cease, as long as they perform the Hajj, to make their standing known,
until it is said: 'Permit the family of Safwan!'"

* * *

﴿And remember Him as He has guided you, though before that you were indeed among the astray﴾. The waw is conjunctive, linking to His saying: ﴿remember God at the Sacred Mash'ar﴾. The conjunction implies that the remembrance commanded here is other than the remembrance commanded in His saying: ﴿remember God at the Sacred Mash'ar﴾. So this is a general command to remember after a specific command to remember, and it has the meaning of a concluding summary (tadhyil) after the command to remember at the Sacred Mash'ar.

It is also possible that what is meant by this sentence is His saying ﴿as He has guided you﴾, so its position is that of a concluding summary. The apparent expectation was that it should not be conjoined but separated, yet it was conjoined with the waw, due to its difference from the preceding sentence in what it contains of the reason for remembrance and the explanation of its cause. This difference is weak, but it justifies the conjunction, as in the verse of al-Harith ibn Hammam al-Shaybani:

"O son of Zayyabah, if you meet me, do not meet me among the grazing herd..."
"And you meet me, a swift chestnut horse rushes with me, its gait forward like a rider."

The second clause "you meet me" is in the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) for "do not meet me among the grazing herd", because its meaning is "do not meet me as a herder of camels", and that negation implies that he is a horseman, since a man cannot be free of one of two states. So the apparent expectation was to separate the clause "you meet me, a swift chestnut horse rushes with me", but he conjoined it for some difference.

His saying ﴿as He has guided you﴾ is a simile of the remembrance to guidance, and "ma" is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyyah).

The meaning of the comparison in such a case is similarity in equivalence; that is, mention Him with a remembrance equal to His guidance to you, which conveys the sense of recompense and reciprocation. For this reason they say that the kaf in mithlihi (مِثْلِهِ) is for causation (lil-ta'lil). The distinction between it and the kaf of recompense (kaf al-mujazah) has already been mentioned at His Most High's words: ﴿So we will disassociate ourselves from them, as they have disassociated themselves from us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167]. This usage is frequent in the kaf that is accompanied by (ma), however it may be; and it has been said that this is specific to the kafah "ma" (the ma that restricts the kaf). The truth is that it occurs both with the kaf accompanied by "ma" and in other cases.

The pronoun in (min qablihi) refers back to the guidance understood from the verbal "ma" (مَا المَصْدَرِيَّةُ), and (in) is a lightened form of the heavy "inna" (إنَّ).

The intended meaning is their misguidance in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) through the worship of idols, the alteration of the rites, and other things besides that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 199:

﴿Then press on from where the people press on, and seek forgiveness from God. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

What the majority of exegetes hold is that "thumma" (then) is for the sequence of narration, moving to a further report, and that the "ifada" (pressing on) commanded here is the very same ifada mentioned in God's words: ﴿So when you press on from ʿArafat﴾ [al-Baqara: 198], and that the conjunction with "thumma" is a return to speaking about that ifada.

So the intended object of the command is the complement of "afidu" (press on), namely His words: ﴿from where the people press on﴾, referring to ʿArafat. This entails the command to stand at ʿArafat and not elsewhere, nullifying the practice of the Quraysh, who used to stand on the day of the Greater Pilgrimage at Quzah, called Jamʿ, and at al-Mashʿar al-Haram, which is part of Muzdalifa. The rest of the Arabs and others stood at ʿArafat, so "the people" in the majority of their sense refers to those other than Quraysh.

On the authority of ʿAʾisha, she said: "The Quraysh and those who followed their religion used to stand on the Day of ʿArafa at Muzdalifa, and they were called al-Hums. The rest of the Arabs stood at ʿArafa. When Islam came, God commanded His Prophet to go to ʿArafat, stand there, and then press on from it. That is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then press on from where the people press on﴾." End of quotation.

صفحة ٢٤٣
Thus the addressees of "afidu" are all Muslims, and "the people" (al-nas) means people in general, that is, other than Quraysh and those of the Hums who used to press on from Muzdalifa, namely Quraysh, their descendants, Kinana and their allies.

Al-Tabari narrated from Ibn Abi Najih, who said: "The Quraysh — I do not know whether before the Elephant or after it — innovated the matter of the Hums by opinion. They said: 'We are the custodians of the House and the residents of Mecca, so no one among the Arabs has a right like ours or a standing like ours. Do not glorify anything of the non-sacred territory as you glorify the Sanctuary,' meaning because ʿArafa is part of the non-sacred territory. For if you did that, the Arabs would belittle your sanctuary and say: 'They have glorified part of the non-sacred territory just as they glorified part of the Sanctuary.' Therefore they abandoned standing at ʿArafa and pressing on from it. Kinana and Khuza'a had joined them in this." End of quotation. That is, they would press on only once, by waiting for the pilgrims to come down from ʿArafat to Muzdalifa, so all the people would gather at Muzdalifa. Perhaps this is the reason Muzdalifa was called Jamʿ, because the Hums and others gathered there in the pressing on. Thus the verse rejects the Quraysh's restriction of standing to Muzdalifa alone.

It has also been said that what is meant by ﴿then press on﴾ is the pressing on from Muzdalifa to Mina, so "thumma" would indicate sequence and order in time; that is, after you mention God at al-Mashʿar al-Haram, which is from the ancient sunna since the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, as it is said, and the Arabs in the Jahiliyya followed it. The authority to grant passage in it belonged to Khuza'a, then after them it passed to Banu ʿAdwan of Qays ʿAylan. The last of them to hold this authority was Abu Sayyara ʿUmayla ibn al-Aʿzal, who granted passage to the people for forty years until Mecca was conquered, and the authority was then abolished and the people followed the amir of the pilgrimage. In the Jahiliyya they would leave Muzdalifa on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijja after the sun rose over Thabir, the highest mountain near Mina. The one who granted passage would stand shortly before sunrise facing the qibla and supplicate with a supplication in which he said: "O God, make hatred between our camels, make love between our women, place wealth in our generous ones. O God, be a protector for us against those we fear. Fulfil your covenants, honour your neighbour, and feed your guest." If the sunrise drew near, he would say: "Shine, Thabir, so that we may raid." Abu Sayyara would ride a black donkey, and when the sun rose he would set off with them, and the people followed him. Their rhymester said of that:

Leave the way clear for Abu Sayyara, and for his clients, the Banu Fazara,
Until he grants passage to his donkey safely, while facing the qibla, calling upon his protector.

That is, he calls upon God, Exalted, with His words: "O God, be a protector for us against those we fear."

صفحة ٢٤٤
So His words ﴿from where the people press on﴾ mean: from the place from which all the people press on, which is Muzdalifa.
He expressed it thus because all the Arabs gather at Muzdalifa. Were it not for the hadith that came, this interpretation would be more evident, so that the verse would mention the two pressings explicitly, and to match His words after it: ﴿Then when you have completed your rites﴾ [al-Baqara: 200].

His words ﴿and seek forgiveness from God﴾ are coordinated with ﴿press on from where the people press on﴾: He commanded them to seek forgiveness just as He commanded them to remember God at al-Mashʿar al-Haram. In it there is an indirect rebuke of the Quraysh for their abandonment of standing at ʿArafa.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 200–202 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when you have completed your rites (manasik), remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance. Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share in the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 199], because that departure is the movement from Muzdalifah to Mina, or because it necessitates that. Mina is the place of stoning the pillars (rami al-jimar), and the verse points to stoning the Jamrat al-'Aqabah on the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah. It commands that they remember Allah at the stoning, then the sacrifice (al-hady) after that. With that the Hajj is complete and its rites are fulfilled.

The scholars have agreed that the pilgrim does not stone on the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) except the Jamrat al-'Aqabah, from sunrise until midday (al-zawal), then he sacrifices after that, then he goes to the Ka'bah and performs the Tawaf al-Ifadah. With that the Hajj is complete and everything becomes lawful for the pilgrim except sexual relations with women.

Al-manasik is the plural of manSak (mansak), derived from nasaka nasakan (from the pattern nasara), meaning to worship. It has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And show us our rites (manasikana)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128]. Here it is either a mimi verbal noun or a noun of place. The first is more appropriate to His saying "qadaytum" (you have completed), so that we do not need to supply an elided noun, i.e., "the acts of worship of your rites."

All read (manasikakum) with the two kaf's separated (fakk al-kafayn), but al-Susi from Abu 'Amr read it with their assimilation (idgham), which is the great assimilation (al-idgham al-kabir).

[Page 245]

His saying: ﴿fadhkuru Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198] repeats the command to remembrance after having commanded it together with seeking forgiveness, as an exhortation to it, and as a nullification of what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah of occupying themselves with idle talk and boasting, for that leads to disputation and contention. The aim is that the pilgrim be immersed in worship in deed, speech and belief.

His saying: ﴿kadhikrikum abaa'akum﴾ is an explanation of the quality of the remembrance. The prepositional phrase is an adjective (na't) to an elided verbal noun, i.e., "a remembrance like your remembrance," etc., pointing to what they used to do during the days of Mina of boasting about lineages and the glories of their days. They would stand between the mosque of Mina, i.e., its location, which is the Masjid al-Khayf, and the mountain, i.e., the mountain of Mina whose beginning is the 'Aqabah where the jamrah is stoned, and they would do that.

In the Tafsir of Ibn Jarir, on the authority of al-Suddi: a man would stand and say, "O Allah, my father was great in tent-size, great in serving-bowl, abundant in wealth, so give me the like of what You gave him." He would mention no one but his father. He mentioned sayings similar to this.

The intended meaning is to liken the remembrance of Allah to the remembrance of their fathers in frequency and repetition, and in filling free times with it. There is nothing in it that indicates combining the remembrance of Allah with the remembrance of fathers.

His saying: ﴿aw ashadda dhikran﴾ — "aw" here is either for the sake of the original (asl) or for choice (takhyir). Since the item conjoined by "aw" in such a context is more fitting to the content of the verb governing the item conjoined to, "aw" conveys a meaning of ascending gradation. The intended meaning is that they remember Allah much. It was first likened to the remembrance of their fathers, by way of allusion that they occupy themselves in those rites with a remembrance that benefits nothing, and that it is more fitting for them to replace it with the remembrance of Allah. So this is an allusion to nullifying the remembrance of fathers through boasting.

For this reason Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and Ibn Jinni said: "aw" in such a case is for transitional idrab (al-idrab al-intiqali, a shift from one statement to another), and they denied the condition that a negation or its equivalent must precede it, and the condition of repeating the governing element.

On this interpretation His saying is explained: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or they increase﴾ [al-Saffat: 147]. On this basis, the purpose of the first comparison is to show that Allah is deserving of remembrance there just like their fathers, then He clarified that the remembrance of Allah is more intense, because He is more deserving of being remembered.

"Ashadda" is either conjoined to an elided verbal noun in the accusative, governed as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) after His saying "kadhikrikum abaa'akum," the meaning being: "remember Allah with a remembrance like your remembrance of your fathers," so the fatha at the end of "ashadda" is the fatha of the accusative, its accusative being by conjunction to the elided verbal noun indicated by His saying "kadhikrikum." The estimate being: "a remembrance like your remembrance of your fathers." On this aspect, the accusative of "dhikran" appears to be a specification (tamyiz) of "ashadda," and since "ashadda" is a description of the elided "dhikr," the result is that the specification becomes a specification of a thing by its synonym, which contradicts the purpose of specification that is to remove ambiguity. Yet such a thing occurs in eloquent speech, though rarely, a rarity that does not detract from eloquence, relying on the difference in form of the two synonymous words, with the specification then giving emphasis to the specified, as Sibawayh related that they say: "He is the most stingy of people man (ashanna al-nas rajulan)," and "they two are the best of people two (khayru al-nasithnayn)." This is what al-Zajjaj followed in his Tafsir. I say: close to it is the use of the specification of "ni'ma" as emphasis in the verse of Jarir:

"Provide the like of your father's provision among us, for the best provision is your father's provision, provided."

It is also possible that the accusative of "ashadda" is a circumstantial (hal) from "dhikran" which follows it, and that the original of "ashadda" is an adjective to it, the arrangement of speech being: "aw dhikran ashadda," then the adjective was placed first and became a circumstantial. The motive for placing the adjective first is then concern with the attribute of being "ashadda," and to allow the prolonging of the letter of the verse-ending when pausing upon it, and to separate as much as possible the repeated words for remembrance, which occur three times.

Or "ashadda" is conjoined to "dhikran," the one in the genitive by the kaf in His saying "kadhikrikum." Nor does what is said about the impermissibility of conjoining to a genitive without repeating the preposition prevent this, because that is not agreed upon among the imams of grammar. The Kufans do not prohibit it, and some later scholars agreed with them, such as Ibn Malik, and upon it is the reading of Hamzah ("wa-ttaqu Allah alladhi tasa'alna bihi wa-l-arham" [al-Nisa': 1]) with the genitive of "al-arham." Al-Zamakhshari permitted here and in His saying: "like the fear of Allah or greater fear" [al-Nisa': 77] in Surat al-Nisa' that the conjunction be to the genitive governed by a particle without repeating the preposition. Some grammarians permitted it when the genitive is by annexation (idafah) and not by a particle, as Ibn al-Hajib said in Idah al-Mufassal. On this, the fatha of "ashadda" substitutes for the kasra, because "ashadda" is prohibited from declension. On this aspect, the accusative of "dhikran" is a specification in the manner previously mentioned in the first aspect from Sibawayh and al-Zajjaj.

Al-Zamakhshari has two other explanations of the i'rab of "aw ashadda dhikran," in which there is artificiality (ta'assuf) that prompted him to them in fleeing from the synonymity of specification and specified. Ibn Jinni, following his shaykh Abu 'Ali, has another explanation, which prompted him to it, similar to what prompted al-Zamakhshari, and his explanation is even more artificial. Ibn al-Munir mentioned it from him in al-Intisaf, and al-Zamakhshari followed it in his Tafsir of the verse in Surat al-Nisa'.

This verse is among the strange usages of Arabic, and its counterpart is the verse of Surat al-Nisa'. Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa said in his Tafsir:

[Page 247]

"This is a lengthy and intricate issue. I have not seen anyone among the shaykhs who understood it except Ibn 'Abd al-Salam and Ibn al-Hubab, and al-Tibi did not fall short in it, and he is the one who uncovered the veil over it here and in His saying in Surat al-Nisa': 'They fear people as they fear Allah or with greater fear' [al-Nisa': 77]. His discourse on that verse is what led the Tunisians to copy it, for I was with Ibn 'Abd al-Salam when the Wasil came with al-Tibi's book, and I said to him: 'Let us look at what he said about "ashadda khashyatan" [al-Nisa': 77],' and we examined it and found in it an addition to what the people had said, so the shaykh at that time urged copying it." End.

His saying: ﴿fa-min al-nas man yaqulu﴾ etc. The listeners knew that remembrance includes supplication (du'a'), because it is from the remembrance of Allah, and especially at the places and times where supplications are answered, since those who go to those sites, in their various states, intend only blessing and hope. So there was in the speech an implied element, as if it were said: "Remember Allah as you remember your fathers or with greater remembrance, and call upon Him." Then the detail of those who supplicate is intended, to draw attention to the difference among those whom those rites gather. The general remembrance is not specified in detail as supplication, because remembrance that is not supplication occurs only in one way, namely glorifying Allah and praising Him, so there is no need to detail it in a way that points to what is not praiseworthy. The division into the two groups covers all people, both Muslims and polytheists, because the verse was revealed before the prohibition of Hajj for the polytheists by the verse of "Bara'ah" [al-Tawbah]. Therefore it is determined that the intended by "for whom there is no share in the Hereafter" are the polytheists, because the Muslims do not neglect supplication for the good of the Hereafter, however heedless they become. So the aim of the verse is an allusion to censuring the state of the polytheists, for they do not believe in the life to come.

His saying: "(atina)" leaves out the second object, the verb being treated as if it were intransitive to a second object, since the purpose does not depend on specifying it; i.e., "give us a gift in this world," or the object is estimated as "bounty" (in'am), "reward" (ja'izah), or it is elided, indicated by the qualifier "hasanah" later on; i.e., "give us in this world a good (hasanah)."

"Khalaq," with a fatha on the kha', means a portion of good and something precious, derived from "khala'qah," which is worthiness. One says "khalaqa bi-l-shay'" (with a damma on the lam) when he is worthy of it. Since the meaning of worthiness implies the preciousness of that by which one is worthy, what is derived from its synonym indicates preciousness, whether it is restricted by the genitive as here or left unrestricted as in his saying, peace be upon him: "Only one who has no khalaq wears these," i.e., in good, and the saying of al-Bu'ayth ibn Huraith:

"Nor, though brought near one day, will I sell my khalaq or my religion for the pursuit of love."

[Page 248]

The clause "wa-ma lahu fi al-akhirati min khalaq" is conjoined to the clause "man yaqulu," so it is initial like it. The purpose is God Most High's information about this group of people that they have no share in the Hereafter, because the intended by this group are the disbelievers. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: their custom in the Jahiliyyah was to supplicate only for worldly benefits, since they did not know the Hereafter.

It is possible that the waw is circumstantial, and the meaning: one who says that while having no share in the Hereafter, and perhaps the circumstantial is for wonderment.

"Hasanah" originally is an adjective to a deed or trait, so the qualified noun is elided and the adjective is treated as a noun, like their treating "khayr" as a noun although its origin is a thing qualified by goodness, and like treating "salihah" as a noun in the verse of al-Hutay'ah:

"How is the satire, while there continually comes to me from the family of La'm, in the absence of the sight, a righteous one (salihah)?"

"Hasanah" occurs in the context of supplication, so it conveys generality, because supplication is intended to be general, like al-Hariri's saying: "O people of this abode, may you be spared harm."

This is customary generality, according to what each petitioner suits from the two goods.

He added in the supplication "wa-qina 'adhab al-nar" because attaining the good in the Hereafter may come after some punishment, so it was intended to state explicitly in the supplication the request for protection from the Fire.

His saying: ﴿ulaika lahum nasibun mimma kasabu﴾ refers to the second group. "Nasib" is the share given to someone in good or evil, whether little or much. Its measure is the form fa'il. I do not know the origin of its derivation; perhaps they, when they assigned a share to someone, set it up and it became visible and prominent. This is the apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari in al-Asas and al-Raghib in Mufradat al-Qur'an. Or it is a noun that came in this form without intending from it the meaning of an agent or an object. The application of "nasib" to the undivided share in their saying "nasib al-shafi'" (the shuf'ah-claimant's share) is a metonymy by the first sense.

Know that in the Arabic language, in the root (k-f-l) *kafala*, it is not said "this is the *nasib* (share) of so-and-so" unless an equal share has been prepared for someone else. When it is a single share, one does not say *nasib*. This is a rare usage. I have not seen it in anyone else except that al-Fakhr (al-Razi) transmitted something similar from Ibn al-Muzaffar, in his commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿There will be for him a share (*kifl*) of it﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 85], in Surat al-Nisa. It also occurs in the words of al-Zajjaj and Ibn 'Atiyya in their commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿And they assign to God a share (*nasiban*) of the produce and livestock that He created﴾ [al-An'am: 136]. Al-Zajjaj said: The sense of the sentence is: "They assigned to God a share, and to their associates a share." Ibn 'Atiyya said: The statement "they made a share of such-and-such" implies that another share remains which is not included in the ruling of the first. End of quotation.

[Page 249]

This is a promise from God Most High to answer the supplications of the Muslims who supplicate in those blessed standing places. However, He promised to answer some of what they asked for, according to what their circumstances and God's wisdom require, and provided that it does not lead to general corruption, which God Most High does not approve. Therefore *nasib* is indefinite (*nakkara*) so that it applies to both the little and the much. As for granting all of it, when it happens, it is stronger and better. The verb *kasabu* (they earned/gained) here means "they sought," because *kasaba* can mean "sought what one desires."

It is also permissible that *al-kasb* here means "work/action," and the *nasib* is the share of reward, so *min* would be initial (*ibtida'iyya*, indicating origin/source).

The demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*) refers to the people who say: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good﴾. The use of the demonstrative serves to draw attention to the fact that their being characterized by what follows the demonstrative is something they deserved because of the report about them of what precedes the demonstrative; that is, God answered them because of their belief in the Hereafter. From this it is understood that the supplication of the disbelievers is in error.

His words: ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾ are a concluding statement (*tadhyil*), intended to confirm the promise of the answer being granted and to add good news for the people of that standing place, because the answer to supplication in it comes quickly. Thus it is known that "reckoning" here is applied to taking account of the deed and its recompense.

Reckoning (*hisab*) originally means counting. Then it was applied to counting things for which recompense or settlement is intended, so *hisab* came to be used for fulfilling a right. It is said: *hasabahu*, i.e., rewarded him or gave him his due. From this, the Day of Resurrection is called the Day of Reckoning. God Most High said: ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 113], and He said: ﴿A recompense from your Lord, a gift in accordance (*hisaban*)﴾ [al-Naba: 36], i.e., in correspondence with their deeds. Here too it is meant as fulfilling the promise and delivering what was promised. So the good news of the swift attainment of their desire is derived in a general way, because their being answered is part of God's reckoning of His servants according to what He promised them, and so it enters into that generality.

The meaning is: So when you have completed your rites, O Muslims, then do not cease to remember God by glorifying and praising Him, and by turning to Him in supplication to obtain the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter. Do not occupy yourselves with boasting, [Page 250] for the remembrance of God is better than your remembrance of your fathers, as you used to mention them after completing the rites before Islam, and as the polytheists mention them now.

And do not be like those who supplicate only for the good of this world and do not reflect on the life of the Hereafter, because they deny life after death. For if you ask Him, He will give you a share of what you ask for in this world and in the Hereafter, and God hastens the answering of your supplication.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 200–202 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when you have completed your rites (manasik), remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance. Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share in the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 199], because that departure is the movement from Muzdalifah to Mina, or because it necessitates that. Mina is the place of stoning the pillars (rami al-jimar), and the verse points to stoning the Jamrat al-'Aqabah on the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah. It commands that they remember Allah at the stoning, then the sacrifice (al-hady) after that. With that the Hajj is complete and its rites are fulfilled.

The scholars have agreed that the pilgrim does not stone on the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) except the Jamrat al-'Aqabah, from sunrise until midday (al-zawal), then he sacrifices after that, then he goes to the Ka'bah and performs the Tawaf al-Ifadah. With that the Hajj is complete and everything becomes lawful for the pilgrim except sexual relations with women.

Al-manasik is the plural of manSak (mansak), derived from nasaka nasakan (from the pattern nasara), meaning to worship. It has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And show us our rites (manasikana)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128]. Here it is either a mimi verbal noun or a noun of place. The first is more appropriate to His saying "qadaytum" (you have completed), so that we do not need to supply an elided noun, i.e., "the acts of worship of your rites."

All read (manasikakum) with the two kaf's separated (fakk al-kafayn), but al-Susi from Abu 'Amr read it with their assimilation (idgham), which is the great assimilation (al-idgham al-kabir).

[Page 245]

His saying: ﴿fadhkuru Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198] repeats the command to remembrance after having commanded it together with seeking forgiveness, as an exhortation to it, and as a nullification of what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah of occupying themselves with idle talk and boasting, for that leads to disputation and contention. The aim is that the pilgrim be immersed in worship in deed, speech and belief.

His saying: ﴿kadhikrikum abaa'akum﴾ is an explanation of the quality of the remembrance. The prepositional phrase is an adjective (na't) to an elided verbal noun, i.e., "a remembrance like your remembrance," etc., pointing to what they used to do during the days of Mina of boasting about lineages and the glories of their days. They would stand between the mosque of Mina, i.e., its location, which is the Masjid al-Khayf, and the mountain, i.e., the mountain of Mina whose beginning is the 'Aqabah where the jamrah is stoned, and they would do that.

In the Tafsir of Ibn Jarir, on the authority of al-Suddi: a man would stand and say, "O Allah, my father was great in tent-size, great in serving-bowl, abundant in wealth, so give me the like of what You gave him." He would mention no one but his father. He mentioned sayings similar to this.

The intended meaning is to liken the remembrance of Allah to the remembrance of their fathers in frequency and repetition, and in filling free times with it. There is nothing in it that indicates combining the remembrance of Allah with the remembrance of fathers.

His saying: ﴿aw ashadda dhikran﴾ — "aw" here is either for the sake of the original (asl) or for choice (takhyir). Since the item conjoined by "aw" in such a context is more fitting to the content of the verb governing the item conjoined to, "aw" conveys a meaning of ascending gradation. The intended meaning is that they remember Allah much. It was first likened to the remembrance of their fathers, by way of allusion that they occupy themselves in those rites with a remembrance that benefits nothing, and that it is more fitting for them to replace it with the remembrance of Allah. So this is an allusion to nullifying the remembrance of fathers through boasting.

For this reason Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and Ibn Jinni said: "aw" in such a case is for transitional idrab (al-idrab al-intiqali, a shift from one statement to another), and they denied the condition that a negation or its equivalent must precede it, and the condition of repeating the governing element.

On this interpretation His saying is explained: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or they increase﴾ [al-Saffat: 147]. On this basis, the purpose of the first comparison is to show that Allah is deserving of remembrance there just like their fathers, then He clarified that the remembrance of Allah is more intense, because He is more deserving of being remembered.

"Ashadda" is either conjoined to an elided verbal noun in the accusative, governed as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) after His saying "kadhikrikum abaa'akum," the meaning being: "remember Allah with a remembrance like your remembrance of your fathers," so the fatha at the end of "ashadda" is the fatha of the accusative, its accusative being by conjunction to the elided verbal noun indicated by His saying "kadhikrikum." The estimate being: "a remembrance like your remembrance of your fathers." On this aspect, the accusative of "dhikran" appears to be a specification (tamyiz) of "ashadda," and since "ashadda" is a description of the elided "dhikr," the result is that the specification becomes a specification of a thing by its synonym, which contradicts the purpose of specification that is to remove ambiguity. Yet such a thing occurs in eloquent speech, though rarely, a rarity that does not detract from eloquence, relying on the difference in form of the two synonymous words, with the specification then giving emphasis to the specified, as Sibawayh related that they say: "He is the most stingy of people man (ashanna al-nas rajulan)," and "they two are the best of people two (khayru al-nasithnayn)." This is what al-Zajjaj followed in his Tafsir. I say: close to it is the use of the specification of "ni'ma" as emphasis in the verse of Jarir:

"Provide the like of your father's provision among us, for the best provision is your father's provision, provided."

It is also possible that the accusative of "ashadda" is a circumstantial (hal) from "dhikran" which follows it, and that the original of "ashadda" is an adjective to it, the arrangement of speech being: "aw dhikran ashadda," then the adjective was placed first and became a circumstantial. The motive for placing the adjective first is then concern with the attribute of being "ashadda," and to allow the prolonging of the letter of the verse-ending when pausing upon it, and to separate as much as possible the repeated words for remembrance, which occur three times.

Or "ashadda" is conjoined to "dhikran," the one in the genitive by the kaf in His saying "kadhikrikum." Nor does what is said about the impermissibility of conjoining to a genitive without repeating the preposition prevent this, because that is not agreed upon among the imams of grammar. The Kufans do not prohibit it, and some later scholars agreed with them, such as Ibn Malik, and upon it is the reading of Hamzah ("wa-ttaqu Allah alladhi tasa'alna bihi wa-l-arham" [al-Nisa': 1]) with the genitive of "al-arham." Al-Zamakhshari permitted here and in His saying: "like the fear of Allah or greater fear" [al-Nisa': 77] in Surat al-Nisa' that the conjunction be to the genitive governed by a particle without repeating the preposition. Some grammarians permitted it when the genitive is by annexation (idafah) and not by a particle, as Ibn al-Hajib said in Idah al-Mufassal. On this, the fatha of "ashadda" substitutes for the kasra, because "ashadda" is prohibited from declension. On this aspect, the accusative of "dhikran" is a specification in the manner previously mentioned in the first aspect from Sibawayh and al-Zajjaj.

Al-Zamakhshari has two other explanations of the i'rab of "aw ashadda dhikran," in which there is artificiality (ta'assuf) that prompted him to them in fleeing from the synonymity of specification and specified. Ibn Jinni, following his shaykh Abu 'Ali, has another explanation, which prompted him to it, similar to what prompted al-Zamakhshari, and his explanation is even more artificial. Ibn al-Munir mentioned it from him in al-Intisaf, and al-Zamakhshari followed it in his Tafsir of the verse in Surat al-Nisa'.

This verse is among the strange usages of Arabic, and its counterpart is the verse of Surat al-Nisa'. Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa said in his Tafsir:

[Page 247]

"This is a lengthy and intricate issue. I have not seen anyone among the shaykhs who understood it except Ibn 'Abd al-Salam and Ibn al-Hubab, and al-Tibi did not fall short in it, and he is the one who uncovered the veil over it here and in His saying in Surat al-Nisa': 'They fear people as they fear Allah or with greater fear' [al-Nisa': 77]. His discourse on that verse is what led the Tunisians to copy it, for I was with Ibn 'Abd al-Salam when the Wasil came with al-Tibi's book, and I said to him: 'Let us look at what he said about "ashadda khashyatan" [al-Nisa': 77],' and we examined it and found in it an addition to what the people had said, so the shaykh at that time urged copying it." End.

His saying: ﴿fa-min al-nas man yaqulu﴾ etc. The listeners knew that remembrance includes supplication (du'a'), because it is from the remembrance of Allah, and especially at the places and times where supplications are answered, since those who go to those sites, in their various states, intend only blessing and hope.
