So there was in the speech an implied element, as if it were said: "Remember Allah as you remember your fathers or with greater remembrance, and call upon Him." Then the detail of those who supplicate is intended, to draw attention to the difference among those whom those rites gather. The general remembrance is not specified in detail as supplication, because remembrance that is not supplication occurs only in one way, namely glorifying Allah and praising Him, so there is no need to detail it in a way that points to what is not praiseworthy. The division into the two groups covers all people, both Muslims and polytheists, because the verse was revealed before the prohibition of Hajj for the polytheists by the verse of "Bara'ah" [al-Tawbah]. Therefore it is determined that the intended by "for whom there is no share in the Hereafter" are the polytheists, because the Muslims do not neglect supplication for the good of the Hereafter, however heedless they become. So the aim of the verse is an allusion to censuring the state of the polytheists, for they do not believe in the life to come.

His saying: "(atina)" leaves out the second object, the verb being treated as if it were intransitive to a second object, since the purpose does not depend on specifying it; i.e., "give us a gift in this world," or the object is estimated as "bounty" (in'am), "reward" (ja'izah), or it is elided, indicated by the qualifier "hasanah" later on; i.e., "give us in this world a good (hasanah)."

"Khalaq," with a fatha on the kha', means a portion of good and something precious, derived from "khala'qah," which is worthiness. One says "khalaqa bi-l-shay'" (with a damma on the lam) when he is worthy of it. Since the meaning of worthiness implies the preciousness of that by which one is worthy, what is derived from its synonym indicates preciousness, whether it is restricted by the genitive as here or left unrestricted as in his saying, peace be upon him: "Only one who has no khalaq wears these," i.e., in good, and the saying of al-Bu'ayth ibn Huraith:

"Nor, though brought near one day, will I sell my khalaq or my religion for the pursuit of love."

[Page 248]

The clause "wa-ma lahu fi al-akhirati min khalaq" is conjoined to the clause "man yaqulu," so it is initial like it. The purpose is God Most High's information about this group of people that they have no share in the Hereafter, because the intended by this group are the disbelievers. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: their custom in the Jahiliyyah was to supplicate only for worldly benefits, since they did not know the Hereafter.

It is possible that the waw is circumstantial, and the meaning: one who says that while having no share in the Hereafter, and perhaps the circumstantial is for wonderment.

"Hasanah" originally is an adjective to a deed or trait, so the qualified noun is elided and the adjective is treated as a noun, like their treating "khayr" as a noun although its origin is a thing qualified by goodness, and like treating "salihah" as a noun in the verse of al-Hutay'ah:

"How is the satire, while there continually comes to me from the family of La'm, in the absence of the sight, a righteous one (salihah)?"

"Hasanah" occurs in the context of supplication, so it conveys generality, because supplication is intended to be general, like al-Hariri's saying: "O people of this abode, may you be spared harm."

This is customary generality, according to what each petitioner suits from the two goods.

He added in the supplication "wa-qina 'adhab al-nar" because attaining the good in the Hereafter may come after some punishment, so it was intended to state explicitly in the supplication the request for protection from the Fire.

His saying: ﴿ulaika lahum nasibun mimma kasabu﴾ refers to the second group. "Nasib" is the share given to someone in good or evil, whether little or much. Its measure is the form fa'il. I do not know the origin of its derivation; perhaps they, when they assigned a share to someone, set it up and it became visible and prominent. This is the apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari in al-Asas and al-Raghib in Mufradat al-Qur'an. Or it is a noun that came in this form without intending from it the meaning of an agent or an object. The application of "nasib" to the undivided share in their saying "nasib al-shafi'" (the shuf'ah-claimant's share) is a metonymy by the first sense.

Know that in the Arabic language, in the root (k-f-l) *kafala*, it is not said "this is the *nasib* (share) of so-and-so" unless an equal share has been prepared for someone else. When it is a single share, one does not say *nasib*. This is a rare usage. I have not seen it in anyone else except that al-Fakhr (al-Razi) transmitted something similar from Ibn al-Muzaffar, in his commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿There will be for him a share (*kifl*) of it﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 85], in Surat al-Nisa. It also occurs in the words of al-Zajjaj and Ibn 'Atiyya in their commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿And they assign to God a share (*nasiban*) of the produce and livestock that He created﴾ [al-An'am: 136]. Al-Zajjaj said: The sense of the sentence is: "They assigned to God a share, and to their associates a share." Ibn 'Atiyya said: The statement "they made a share of such-and-such" implies that another share remains which is not included in the ruling of the first. End of quotation.

[Page 249]

This is a promise from God Most High to answer the supplications of the Muslims who supplicate in those blessed standing places. However, He promised to answer some of what they asked for, according to what their circumstances and God's wisdom require, and provided that it does not lead to general corruption, which God Most High does not approve. Therefore *nasib* is indefinite (*nakkara*) so that it applies to both the little and the much. As for granting all of it, when it happens, it is stronger and better. The verb *kasabu* (they earned/gained) here means "they sought," because *kasaba* can mean "sought what one desires."

It is also permissible that *al-kasb* here means "work/action," and the *nasib* is the share of reward, so *min* would be initial (*ibtida'iyya*, indicating origin/source).

The demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*) refers to the people who say: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good﴾. The use of the demonstrative serves to draw attention to the fact that their being characterized by what follows the demonstrative is something they deserved because of the report about them of what precedes the demonstrative; that is, God answered them because of their belief in the Hereafter. From this it is understood that the supplication of the disbelievers is in error.

His words: ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾ are a concluding statement (*tadhyil*), intended to confirm the promise of the answer being granted and to add good news for the people of that standing place, because the answer to supplication in it comes quickly. Thus it is known that "reckoning" here is applied to taking account of the deed and its recompense.

Reckoning (*hisab*) originally means counting. Then it was applied to counting things for which recompense or settlement is intended, so *hisab* came to be used for fulfilling a right. It is said: *hasabahu*, i.e., rewarded him or gave him his due. From this, the Day of Resurrection is called the Day of Reckoning. God Most High said: ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 113], and He said: ﴿A recompense from your Lord, a gift in accordance (*hisaban*)﴾ [al-Naba: 36], i.e., in correspondence with their deeds. Here too it is meant as fulfilling the promise and delivering what was promised. So the good news of the swift attainment of their desire is derived in a general way, because their being answered is part of God's reckoning of His servants according to what He promised them, and so it enters into that generality.

The meaning is: So when you have completed your rites, O Muslims, then do not cease to remember God by glorifying and praising Him, and by turning to Him in supplication to obtain the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter. Do not occupy yourselves with boasting, [Page 250] for the remembrance of God is better than your remembrance of your fathers, as you used to mention them after completing the rites before Islam, and as the polytheists mention them now.

And do not be like those who supplicate only for the good of this world and do not reflect on the life of the Hereafter, because they deny life after death. For if you ask Him, He will give you a share of what you ask for in this world and in the Hereafter, and God hastens the answering of your supplication.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 200–202 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when you have completed your rites (manasik), remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance. Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share in the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 199], because that departure is the movement from Muzdalifah to Mina, or because it necessitates that. With that the Hajj is complete and everything becomes lawful for the pilgrim except sexual relations with women.

This is what al-Zajjaj followed in his Tafsir. I say: close to it is the use of the specification of "ni'ma" as emphasis in the verse of Jarir:

"Provide the like of your father's provision among us, for the best provision is your father's provision, provided."

It is also possible that the accusative of "ashadda" is a circumstantial (hal) from "dhikran" which follows it, and that the original of "ashadda" is an adjective to it, the arrangement of speech being: "aw dhikran ashadda," then the adjective was placed first and became a circumstantial. The motive for placing the adjective first is then concern with the attribute of being "ashadda," and to allow the prolonging of the letter of the verse-ending when pausing upon it, and to separate as much as possible the repeated words for remembrance, which occur three times.

Or "ashadda" is conjoined to "dhikran," the one in the genitive by the kaf in His saying "kadhikrikum." Nor does what is said about the impermissibility of conjoining to a genitive without repeating the preposition prevent this, because that is not agreed upon among the imams of grammar. The Kufans do not prohibit it, and some later scholars agreed with them, such as Ibn Malik, and upon it is the reading of Hamzah ("wa-ttaqu Allah alladhi tasa'alna bihi wa-l-arham" [al-Nisa': 1]) with the genitive of "al-arham." Al-Zamakhshari permitted here and in His saying: "like the fear of Allah or greater fear" [al-Nisa': 77] in Surat al-Nisa' that the conjunction be to the genitive governed by a particle without repeating the preposition. Some grammarians permitted it when the genitive is by annexation (idafah) and not by a particle, as Ibn al-Hajib said in Idah al-Mufassal. On this, the fatha of "ashadda" substitutes for the kasra, because "ashadda" is prohibited from declension. On this aspect, the accusative of "dhikran" is a specification in the manner previously mentioned in the first aspect from Sibawayh and al-Zajjaj.

Al-Zamakhshari has two other explanations of the i'rab of "aw ashadda dhikran," in which there is artificiality (ta'assuf) that prompted him to them in fleeing from the synonymity of specification and specified. Ibn Jinni, following his shaykh Abu 'Ali, has another explanation, which prompted him to it, similar to what prompted al-Zamakhshari, and his explanation is even more artificial. Ibn al-Munir mentioned it from him in al-Intisaf, and al-Zamakhshari followed it in his Tafsir of the verse in Surat al-Nisa'.

This verse is among the strange usages of Arabic, and its counterpart is the verse of Surat al-Nisa'. Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa said in his Tafsir:

[Page 247]

"This is a lengthy and intricate issue. I have not seen anyone among the shaykhs who understood it except Ibn 'Abd al-Salam and Ibn al-Hubab, and al-Tibi did not fall short in it, and he is the one who uncovered the veil over it here and in His saying in Surat al-Nisa': 'They fear people as they fear Allah or with greater fear' [al-Nisa': 77]. His discourse on that verse is what led the Tunisians to copy it, for I was with Ibn 'Abd al-Salam when the Wasil came with al-Tibi's book, and I said to him: 'Let us look at what he said about "ashadda khashyatan" [al-Nisa': 77],' and we examined it and found in it an addition to what the people had said, so the shaykh at that time urged copying it." End.

His saying: ﴿fa-min al-nas man yaqulu﴾ etc. The listeners knew that remembrance includes supplication (du'a'), because it is from the remembrance of Allah, and especially at the places and times where supplications are answered, since those who go to those sites, in their various states, intend only blessing and hope. So there was in the speech an implied element, as if it were said: "Remember Allah as you remember your fathers or with greater remembrance, and call upon Him." Then the detail of those who supplicate is intended, to draw attention to the difference among those whom those rites gather. The general remembrance is not specified in detail as supplication, because remembrance that is not supplication occurs only in one way, namely glorifying Allah and praising Him, so there is no need to detail it in a way that points to what is not praiseworthy. The division into the two groups covers all people, both Muslims and polytheists, because the verse was revealed before the prohibition of Hajj for the polytheists by the verse of "Bara'ah" [al-Tawbah]. Therefore it is determined that the intended by "for whom there is no share in the Hereafter" are the polytheists, because the Muslims do not neglect supplication for the good of the Hereafter, however heedless they become. So the aim of the verse is an allusion to censuring the state of the polytheists, for they do not believe in the life to come.

His saying: "(atina)" leaves out the second object, the verb being treated as if it were intransitive to a second object, since the purpose does not depend on specifying it; i.e., "give us a gift in this world," or the object is estimated as "bounty" (in'am), "reward" (ja'izah), or it is elided, indicated by the qualifier "hasanah" later on; i.e., "give us in this world a good (hasanah)."

"Khalaq," with a fatha on the kha', means a portion of good and something precious, derived from "khala'qah," which is worthiness. One says "khalaqa bi-l-shay'" (with a damma on the lam) when he is worthy of it. Since the meaning of worthiness implies the preciousness of that by which one is worthy, what is derived from its synonym indicates preciousness, whether it is restricted by the genitive as here or left unrestricted as in his saying, peace be upon him: "Only one who has no khalaq wears these," i.e., in good, and the saying of al-Bu'ayth ibn Huraith:

"Nor, though brought near one day, will I sell my khalaq or my religion for the pursuit of love."

[Page 248]

The clause "wa-ma lahu fi al-akhirati min khalaq" is conjoined to the clause "man yaqulu," so it is initial like it. The purpose is God Most High's information about this group of people that they have no share in the Hereafter, because the intended by this group are the disbelievers. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: their custom in the Jahiliyyah was to supplicate only for worldly benefits, since they did not know the Hereafter.

It is possible that the waw is circumstantial, and the meaning: one who says that while having no share in the Hereafter, and perhaps the circumstantial is for wonderment.

"Hasanah" originally is an adjective to a deed or trait, so the qualified noun is elided and the adjective is treated as a noun, like their treating "khayr" as a noun although its origin is a thing qualified by goodness, and like treating "salihah" as a noun in the verse of al-Hutay'ah:

"How is the satire, while there continually comes to me from the family of La'm, in the absence of the sight, a righteous one (salihah)?"

"Hasanah" occurs in the context of supplication, so it conveys generality, because supplication is intended to be general, like al-Hariri's saying: "O people of this abode, may you be spared harm."

This is customary generality, according to what each petitioner suits from the two goods.

He added in the supplication "wa-qina 'adhab al-nar" because attaining the good in the Hereafter may come after some punishment, so it was intended to state explicitly in the supplication the request for protection from the Fire.

His saying: ﴿ulaika lahum nasibun mimma kasabu﴾ refers to the second group. "Nasib" is the share given to someone in good or evil, whether little or much. Its measure is the form fa'il. I do not know the origin of its derivation; perhaps they, when they assigned a share to someone, set it up and it became visible and prominent. This is the apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari in al-Asas and al-Raghib in Mufradat al-Qur'an. Or it is a noun that came in this form without intending from it the meaning of an agent or an object. The application of "nasib" to the undivided share in their saying "nasib al-shafi'" (the shuf'ah-claimant's share) is a metonymy by the first sense.

Know that in the Arabic language, in the root (k-f-l) *kafala*, it is not said "this is the *nasib* (share) of so-and-so" unless an equal share has been prepared for someone else. When it is a single share, one does not say *nasib*. This is a rare usage. I have not seen it in anyone else except that al-Fakhr (al-Razi) transmitted something similar from Ibn al-Muzaffar, in his commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿There will be for him a share (*kifl*) of it﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 85], in Surat al-Nisa. It also occurs in the words of al-Zajjaj and Ibn 'Atiyya in their commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿And they assign to God a share (*nasiban*) of the produce and livestock that He created﴾ [al-An'am: 136]. Al-Zajjaj said: The sense of the sentence is: "They assigned to God a share, and to their associates a share." Ibn 'Atiyya said: The statement "they made a share of such-and-such" implies that another share remains which is not included in the ruling of the first. End of quotation.

[Page 249]

This is a promise from God Most High to answer the supplications of the Muslims who supplicate in those blessed standing places. However, He promised to answer some of what they asked for, according to what their circumstances and God's wisdom require, and provided that it does not lead to general corruption, which God Most High does not approve. Therefore *nasib* is indefinite (*nakkara*) so that it applies to both the little and the much. As for granting all of it, when it happens, it is stronger and better. The verb *kasabu* (they earned/gained) here means "they sought," because *kasaba* can mean "sought what one desires."

It is also permissible that *al-kasb* here means "work/action," and the *nasib* is the share of reward, so *min* would be initial (*ibtida'iyya*, indicating origin/source).

The demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*) refers to the people who say: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good﴾. The use of the demonstrative serves to draw attention to the fact that their being characterized by what follows the demonstrative is something they deserved because of the report about them of what precedes the demonstrative; that is, God answered them because of their belief in the Hereafter. From this it is understood that the supplication of the disbelievers is in error.

His words: ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾ are a concluding statement (*tadhyil*), intended to confirm the promise of the answer being granted and to add good news for the people of that standing place, because the answer to supplication in it comes quickly. Thus it is known that "reckoning" here is applied to taking account of the deed and its recompense.

Reckoning (*hisab*) originally means counting. Then it was applied to counting things for which recompense or settlement is intended, so *hisab* came to be used for fulfilling a right. It is said: *hasabahu*, i.e., rewarded him or gave him his due. From this, the Day of Resurrection is called the Day of Reckoning. God Most High said: ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 113], and He said: ﴿A recompense from your Lord, a gift in accordance (*hisaban*)﴾ [al-Naba: 36], i.e., in correspondence with their deeds. Here too it is meant as fulfilling the promise and delivering what was promised. So the good news of the swift attainment of their desire is derived in a general way, because their being answered is part of God's reckoning of His servants according to what He promised them, and so it enters into that generality.

The meaning is: So when you have completed your rites, O Muslims, then do not cease to remember God by glorifying and praising Him, and by turning to Him in supplication to obtain the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter. Do not occupy yourselves with boasting, [Page 250] for the remembrance of God is better than your remembrance of your fathers, as you used to mention them after completing the rites before Islam, and as the polytheists mention them now.

And do not be like those who supplicate only for the good of this world and do not reflect on the life of the Hereafter, because they deny life after death. For if you ask Him, He will give you a share of what you ask for in this world and in the Hereafter, and God hastens the answering of your supplication.

﴿And remember Allah during the numbered days. Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him, for those who fear Allah. And fear Allah, and know that you will be gathered to Him.﴾

It is coordinated (ma'tuf) with ﴿So remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200], and what lies between them is a digression (i'tiraḍ). The repetition of the verb "remember" (udhkurū) is for the sake of building upon it the attachment of the prepositional phrase, namely His words ﴿during numbered days﴾, because its referent, ﴿So remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200], is distant. This is because the intention is to restrict the remembrance by its quality and then to restrict it by its time and place.

So the second remembrance is the very same as the first remembrance, and its coordination with it considers the difference brought about by the time attached to it.

The "numbered days" are the days of Mina, which are three days after the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). People stay in Mina during them, and they are called the days of tashrīq (the days of drying meat), because people dry the meat during them, and tashrīq means drying. Or it is because the sacrificial animals are not slaughtered during them until the sun rises (tushriq).

They knew that their stay in Mina after the Day of Sacrifice, after the ṭawāf al-ifāḍa (the circumambulation of return), was three days, so they knew that these were what is meant here by "the numbered days." Accordingly, the majority of jurists said: "The numbered days are the days of Mina, which are after the tenth day." This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Jabir ibn Zayd and Malik. They are other than the "known days" (al-ayyām al-ma'lūmāt) mentioned in His words, exalted is He, ﴿that they may mention the name of Allah on known days﴾ in the chapter of al-Ḥajj.

The "known days" are the three days of sacrifice (ayyām al-naḥr): the tenth day and the two days after it.

The "numbered days" are the days of Mina after the Day of Sacrifice. So the tenth day is among the "known days," not among the "numbered days,"

[p. 262]
and the two days after it are among both the "known days" and the "numbered days," and the fourth day is among the "numbered days" only. They argued for this with His words, exalted is He, ﴿and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the livestock of the grazing animals﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 28], because there is no sacrifice or slaughter on the fourth day by consensus. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: there is no difference between the "known days" and the "numbered days," and they are the Day of Sacrifice and the two days after it. So the fourth day, according to them, is neither "known" nor "numbered." It is reported from al-Shafi'i that the "known days" are from the first of Dhu al-Hijjah until the Day of Sacrifice, and what comes after that is "numbered." This is also a narration from Abu Hanifa.

The verse indicates the requirement of remembering Allah, exalted is He, during the days of stoning the pillars (ramy al-jimār), and this is the remembrance at the time of stoning and at the time of slaughtering the sacrificial animals.

The believers were commanded to remember Allah during these days because the people of the Jahiliyyah used to occupy them with boasting and flirting with women. Al-'Araji said:

"We do not meet except during three nights of Mina, until the departure of the crowd separates us."

And 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

"There appeared to me from her a wrist, when she stoned the pillars, and a hand dyed with henna, adorned with fingertips.

"By Allah, I do not know, though I am knowledgeable, whether I stoned the pillars on the seventh or on the eighth."

This is because they used to see that the pilgrimage had ended with the end of the tenth day, after they had refrained from their pleasures for a long period, so they would return to them. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, commanded them to remember Him during these days, and the remembrance of Allah during them is His remembrance at the stoning of the pillars.

The three numbered days involve stoning the three pillars each day after the decline of the sun (zawāl). One begins with the pillar that is next to the mosque of Mina with seven pebbles, then the other two pillars are stoned, each with the same, and one says "Allahu akbar" with each pebble. The last is the Jamrat al-'Aqaba. Regarding the rulings on stoning, its time, reversing the beginning by starting with the pillar of the mosque of Mina, and spending the night outside Mina, there are differences among the jurists.

The verse indicates that staying in Mina during the numbered days is obligatory. So it is not permissible for the pilgrim to spend those nights anywhere except Mina. Whoever does not spend the night in Mina has neglected an obligation and must offer a sacrifice (hady). Spending the night outside Mina is permitted only for those whose tasks require being away from Mina. The Prophet ﷺ permitted

[p. 263]
al-'Abbas to spend the night in Makkah because he was in charge of the watering of Zamzam, and he permitted the herders of camels to spend the nights away because of their need to graze the camels in distant pastures away from Mina. All of this is after they have stoned the Jamrat al-'Aqaba on the Day of Sacrifice and return the next day to stone the pillars. He also permitted the herders to stone at night. And Allah, in this verse, permitted the one who hastens to his homeland to leave off staying in Mina for the last two of the numbered days.

His words ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ are a verbal consequence (tafrī' lafẓī) of the permission for the concession of abandoning the presence in some days of Mina for one whose return to his homeland hurries him. The particle fa' is used to indicate the sequence of mentioning the concession after mentioning the original command (al-'azīmah), as a mercy from Him, exalted is He, toward His servants.

The two verbs "ta'ajjala" and "ta'akhkhara" indicate hastening and delaying in staying in the place that the phrase "the numbered days" implies. So what is meant by hastening is not lingering, which is departing from Mina, and what is meant by delaying is remaining in Mina until the day when all the pilgrims depart. It is possible that the form ta'ajjala and ta'akhkhara means the reflexive form (muṭāwa'a) of 'ajjalahu and akhkharahu, because the form tafa''ala comes for the reflexive, as if he hastened himself so he hastened, and he delayed it so it was delayed. Then the two verbs are intransitive, and there is no need to posit objects for them. But the one hastened from and the one delayed to are understood from the phrase "the numbered days," meaning the hastening of departure and the delaying of departure. It is also possible that the form tafa''ala in both verbs indicates effort (takalluf) of the act, as if he was compelled to hurry or to delay, and then the object is omitted because it is clear, meaning: whoever hastens the departure, and whoever delays it.

So His words ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ are clear in meaning regarding the negation of sin from him. But His words ﴿and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾ raise a problem, because negating sin implies the possibility that it might occur, so that delaying until the fourth day would become a concession, though it is in fact the original obligation. This suspicion is answered by what is reported: the people of the Jahiliyyah were of two groups. One group permitted hastening, and another group permitted delaying until the fourth day. So the verse came to widen the scope in both matters. Or the meaning of negating sin in both becomes a metaphor (kināyah) for choice between the two matters, though delaying is more excellent. There is no objection in speech to choosing between two matters even if one of them is more excellent, just as the traveler is given the choice between fasting and breaking the fast, even though fasting is more excellent.

In my view, the reason for mentioning ﴿and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾ is that when Allah commanded remembrance during the days of Mina, and the abandonment of what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, namely occupying those days with vanities, as has preceded, and then said after that ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, it was feared that one might suppose hastening the departure was better, as a way of avoiding speech that is not fitting. So this was repelled by His words ﴿and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾. When this supposition is negated, the listener knows that the one who delays has been granted the excellence of staying in those blessed places and sharing in them through the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. For this reason He followed it with His words ﴿for those who fear Allah﴾, meaning: for those who fear Allah in their delay, so that they do not engage in obscenity or sin during the days of Mina. Otherwise, delaying there for one who does not fear Allah is a sin. So the phrase is connected to what the negation particle "lā" indicates of negation, or it is the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: that is for those who fear Allah. Without this, there appears no clear reason for the addition of ﴿for those who fear Allah﴾, even if the commentators have strained to explain it in ways the soul does not incline to accept.

His words ﴿And fear Allah﴾ are an exhortation to piety, placed at the end of the explanation of the principal rulings of the pilgrimage. It is coordinated with ﴿And remember Allah﴾ and is a digression between ﴿and whoever delays﴾ and ﴿And among the people is one whose speech may impress you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204], etc.

The state of those addressed with the rulings of the pilgrimage is brought to mind in the state of their pilgrimage, because the opening of these verses was His words ﴿Whoever undertakes the pilgrimage therein, there shall be no obscenity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], etc. When they were concluded with His words ﴿And remember Allah during the numbered days﴾, which are the last days of the pilgrimage, and reference was made thereby to dispersal and returning to homelands with His words ﴿Whoever hastens in two days﴾, etc., He followed that with His words, exalted is He, ﴿And fear Allah﴾, a comprehensive injunction to those returning from the pilgrimage to watch over the fear of Allah in all their conditions and places, and not to confine their piety to the duration of the pilgrimage, as the Jahiliyyah used to do, for when the pilgrimage ended they would return fighting, raiding and causing corruption. This is also what many sinning Muslims do at the end of Ramadan.

His words ﴿And know that you will be gathered to Him﴾ are an encouragement to piety and a warning against its opposite, because whoever knows this strives for what brings the pleasure of the One to whom they will return, and avoids His displeasure.

So the command in "i'lamū" (know) is for reminder, because that is known to them, and it was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿and know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

Ḥashr (gathering) means assembling after dispersal. Therefore His words "tuḥsharūn" (you will be gathered) suit the two states: the dispersal of the pilgrims after the end of the pilgrimage, and the gathering of the individuals of each group back to their land afterward.

The word "tuḥsharūn" was chosen here rather than "taṣīrūn" (you will arrive) or "turja'ūn" (you will be returned), because "tuḥsharūn" is more comprehensive: it indicates arriving and returning, together with indicating that they will arrive gathered together, all of them, as they were gathered at the time their condition was brought to mind in this address, which is the gathering of the pilgrimage. Also, people after the pilgrimage are gathered to their homes, so He reminded them of the great gathering. Thus the word "tuḥsharūn" is more fitting to the context in many respects. The Arabs

[p. 265]
used to disperse on the fourth day of Mina, then return to Makkah to visit the House for the farewell circumambulation (ṭawāf al-wadā'), then depart, and each group returns to its homeland. Imru' al-Qays, describing the dispersal on the fourth day of the sacrifice, which is the day of al-Muḥaṣṣab in Mina, said:

"By Allah, the eyes of one who saw a dispersal more scattering and more distant than the parting at al-Muḥaṣṣab!

On the morning they departed, one traveled along the valley of Nakhlah, and another among them went longing for Najd Kabkab."

And Kuthayyir said:

"When we had fulfilled from Mina every need, and the one who wipes the corners has wiped,

And our saddles were tightened on the swift camels, and the one who departs in the morning, who is returning, did not look back,

We took up the ends of conversations among us, and the valleys flowed with the necks of the mounts."

The meaning is: let your remembrance of Allah and your supplication be during your days of staying in Mina, which are the three numbered days following the day of Eid al-Adha. Stay in Mina during those days. So whoever is driven by need to hasten back to his homeland, there is no sin upon him in leaving two days of the days of Mina, namely the twelfth and the thirteenth of Dhu al-Hijjah.

[p. 266]

It is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, grammatical coordination) with the clause ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾ [2:200], and so on. This is because He mentioned there the state of the open polytheists, who have no share in the Hereafter, and set against them the mention of the believers who desire good in this world and the Hereafter. Here He moves to the state of another group, who have no share in the Hereafter but pretend that they desire it, while their state is contrasted with the state of the sincere believers who prefer the Hereafter and the eternal life over the life of this world. These are the ones mentioned in His words ﴿And among the people is one who sells his soul seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [2:207].

*Min* (مِن, "among/some of") here means "some of," as in His words ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾ [2:8]. Thus it is valid to apply it to a group or to a specific individual. The relative pronoun *man* (مَنِ, "he who") is likewise valid for a group or an individual.

*Al-ijāb* (الإعجاب, "being impressed/pleased") is the producing of *ʿujb* (العُجْب) in the soul. *Al-ʿajab* (العَجَب, "wonder/astonishment") is an emotion that arises in the soul upon witnessing something unfamiliar whose cause is hidden. Since the nature of what has a hidden cause is that the soul desires it, *ʿajab* comes to imply approval. One says, "The thing impressed me" (*aʿjabanī al-shayʾ*), meaning it caused me to find it admirable. Al-Kawashī said: It is said in the sense of approval, "*aʿjabanī kadhā*" (this pleased me), and in the sense of disapproval, "*ʿajibtu min kadhā*" (I marvelled at this). So His words *yuʿjibuka* mean: his speech is pleasing to you.

By "speech" here is meant what it indicates of his state in faith and in sincere counsel to the Muslims, because that is what concerns the Messenger and pleases him. The intended meaning is not the quality of his speech in eloquence and rhetoric, since there is no purpose in that here, because the intended matter is what contradicts his words ﴿and he is the most contentious of adversaries﴾ and what follows.

The address may be either to the Prophet (ﷺ). That is: among the people is one who shows you what pleases you of speech, namely faith, love of good, and turning away from the disbelievers. In this case "min" refers to the hypocrites, most of whom were Jews, and among them were polytheists of Yathrib. This is my preferred view. Or it refers to a particular group of hypocrites. It has been said that what is meant is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafī, whose name was Ubayy, and who was a client (*mawlā*) of the Banū Zuhra of Quraysh, who were the maternal kin of the Prophet (ﷺ). He used to show love for the Prophet (ﷺ). He did not join the polytheists at the Battle of Badr, but withdrew (*khanasa*, "slipped away") from going out with them to Badr. He had three hundred men from the Banū Zuhra, his allies, and he prevented them from joining the polytheists. It was said that he used to show Islam while being a hypocrite. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It is not established that he ever embraced Islam; rather he used to show affection for the Messenger. After the Battle of Badr ended, it was said that he burned a field of crops belonging to the Muslims and killed their donkeys, and so this verse was revealed concerning him. It was also revealed concerning him: ﴿And do not obey every vile oath-swearer, a backbiter, going about with slander﴾ [68:10], and: ﴿Woe to every slanderer, defamer﴾ [104:1]. It has also been said that there was enmity between him and his people, the Thaqīf, and he attacked them by night, burned their crops and killed their livestock, and so the verse was revealed concerning him. On this view, the rebuke is because he betrayed and corrupted them.

It is also possible that the address is to an unspecified person, so that it applies to every addressee, as a warning to the Muslims against the stratagems of the hypocrites being effective upon them, and an alert to them to investigate the conditions of people, which is necessary.

The adverbial phrase in His words ﴿in the life of this world﴾ may be connected to *yuʿjibuka* (pleases you). In that case, the group of people intended are the hypocrites who show the words of Islam and desire for it, in the manner of His words ﴿and when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [2:14]. That is: your pleasure with their words does not go beyond occurring in this world, for in the Hereafter you will find them in a state that will not please you. So this is a preparation for His words at the end of the verse ﴿so Hell is sufficient for him﴾. The sense of "in" (*fī*) derived here is a real (*ḥaqīqiyya*, literal) sense of time/place.

It may also be connected to the word *qawlihi* (his speech), i.e., his speech concerning matters of this world, such as praiseworthy fidelity in oaths with the Muslims and affection for the Prophet, and he says nothing about matters of religion. So this is an alert that he does not profess Islam openly. The intended person here is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

The particle *fī* in this sense is for figurative (*majāziyya*) location, meaning *ʿan* (about), and the implied sense is "his speech about the life of this world."

The meaning of ﴿he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ is that he combines the good of his speech and the apparent display of affection with calling Allah to witness that what is in his heart corresponds with what is in his utterance. The meaning of calling Allah to witness is his swearing that Allah knows he is truthful.

The phrase "what is in his heart" conveyed the sense of correspondence with his words because, when he called Allah to witness while speaking sweet words, it became necessary that he was claiming his heart matched his tongue. He said, ﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you﴾ [9:62].

The meaning of ﴿and he is the most contentious of adversaries﴾ is that he is intensely hostile, i.e., enmity. It is derived from *laddahu yaladduhu* (with the vowel of the *lām* in the past tense being *fatḥa*), because it is of the pattern *faʿila*. One says: "You (are) contentious, O Zayd," with a *kasra* on the *dāl*, when he disputes. So he is *lādd* and *laddūd*. Thus *al-laddad* is intensity of dispute, and *al-alladd* is one who is very contentious. Al-Ḥamāsī, Rabīʿa ibn Maqrūm, said:

*And the most rancorous of those who hold a grudge against me, as if the heat of his chest were boiling in a cauldron.*

So *alladd* is an adjective of the attributive form (*ṣifa mushabbaha*), not an elative (*ism tafḍīl*). Do you not see that its feminine form came in the pattern *faʿlāʾ* and they said *laddāʾ*, and its plural came in the pattern *fuʿl*? He said: ﴿and to warn thereby a people who are *lud*﴾ [19:97]. At this point the idiom of its being attached to *khiṣām* (contention) presents a difficulty, because its meaning becomes "most intense contention in respect of contention." Al-Zamakhsharī in *al-Kashshāf* said: Either the attribution is for intensification, so that "contention" is made into the most contentious, i.e., its contention is treated as a person who has contention, so the two become separate things, and the attribution is valid according to the path of rational metaphor (*al-majāz al-ʿaqlī*), as if it were said: "His contention is most intense contention," as they say: "His madness went mad" and "His fortune had fortune." Or the attribution is in the sense of *fī*, meaning: he is most intense in contention, i.e., in the state of contention. Some said that a deleted subject is to be assumed after "he is," so that the sense is: "He is, his contention is the most contentious contention." This assumption is not valid, because contention is not described as "most contentious." So it must be interpreted as having been made like an opponent, and in that case interpretation without assuming any deletion is preferable. It was also said that *khiṣām* here is the plural of *khaṣm* (opponent), like *ṣaʿb* and *ṣiʿāb*, and is not a verbal noun. In that case the attribution is clear, i.e., he is the most contentious of people who dispute.

His words ﴿and when he turns away, he strives in the land﴾: *idhā* is an adverb of time that includes the sense of a conditional.

*Tawallā* may be derived from *al-tawliya*, which is turning away and departing. One says *walla* and *tawallā*, and His words have already been mentioned ﴿what turned them away from their qibla﴾ [2:142], i.e., when he departs from you he strives in the land to corrupt.

The object of *tawallā* is deleted, its intended sense being "he turned away from you." The implied address follows the two aforementioned possibilities.

It may also be derived from *al-wilāya* (governance). One says *waliya al-balad* and *tawallāhu*, i.e., when he becomes a governor, that is, when he assumes leadership and heads the people, he strives in the land with corruption. Al-Akhnas was the leader of his clients, who were the Banū Zuhra.

His words ﴿he strives in the land to corrupt in it﴾: *al-saʿy* (striving) is literally brisk walking, as He said: ﴿and a man came from the farthest part of the city, striving﴾ [28:20]. *Al-saʿy* is also used for work and earning, as He said: ﴿and whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due striving﴾ [17:19]. Imruʾ al-Qays said:

*"If what I strive for were for the lowest livelihood…"* (the two verses).

It is also used for mediation among people to reconcile their relations or to lessen harm. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm said:

*"And among us before him was Kulayb the mediator, so what excellence remains except that we have been given charge of it?"*

Labīd said:

*"And they are the intermediaries when the clan is in dire straits…"* (the verse).

It is also used for eagerness and exerting determination to achieve something, as He said concerning Pharaoh: ﴿Then he turned his back, striving﴾ [79:22]. So it is possible that it is here in the first and fourth senses: he went about in the land raiding and plundering to corrupt in it.

This would indicate what al-Akhnas did to the crops of some Muslims, because that indicates his disbelief and his lying in his affection for the Prophet (ﷺ), since if his affection were sincere he would not have harmed his followers.

Or it indicates what he did to the crops of the Thaqīf, according to the view of some exegetes that al-Akhnas attacked the Thaqīf by night, while there was enmity between him and them, though they were his own people. So he raided them with those of the Banū Zuhra who were with him, burned their crops and killed their livestock.

Because his action against a people, even if they were disbelievers at that time, does not concern the Muslims with their harm, and because he did not do it in support of Islam, nor was he in a state of war with them, his act reveals a corruption of disposition that does not match what he shows of goodness and gentleness of speech. [p. 269] For it is the nature of a person's character to be consistent and to show what is within. Allah does not approve of harming His servants, even if they are disbelievers, with harm that does not lead to their benefit, because he did not attack them in order to bring them to faith, but to corrupt and destroy. For this reason He said: ﴿and Allah does not love corruption﴾.

His words ﴿in the land﴾ are an emphasis on the meaning of *saʿā* (strove), to remove the suspicion of figurative usage, that *al-saʿy* might mean work and earning. So it was intended to specify that this striving is walking through the land for corruption, which is raiding and plundering not for the elevation of the word of Allah. For this reason He said after it: ﴿to corrupt in it﴾. The *lām* is then for causation, because corruption is the intended aim of this striver.

It is also possible that *saʿā* is a metaphor for intention and planning, i.e., he plotted a scheme, because devising corruption and employing a stratagem to achieve it, together with displaying sincere counsel in speech, is a scheme. In that case *li-yufsida* is the object of the verb *saʿā*, and the sense is: he intended corruption in the land and planned it. The *lām* would then be the *lām* of communication (*tabligh*), as already mentioned in His words ﴿Allah intends ease for you﴾ [2:185] up to ﴿and that you complete the period﴾ [2:185]. So the *lām* is similar to the superfluous *lām*, and what follows the *lām* of the verb (with the implied *an*, "that") is the object, as in His words ﴿They want to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾ [61:8], and in the verse of Juzʾ ibn Kulayb al-Faqʿasī:

*"Ibn Kūz sought, and foolishness is like its name, to hunt from us when we spent winter nights."*

The implied sense is: he sought to hunt from us. Al-Marzūqī said: He used the verb with *lām* because *tabaghghā* is like *arāda* (to want). So just as God, Mighty and Majestic, said ﴿They want to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾ [61:8], and the meaning is "they want to extinguish the light of Allah," so too he said "*tabaghghā li-yastāda*," i.e., he sought to hunt from us. End of quote.

I say: This usage occurs in every place where the object of a verb is the reason for the verb while also being the direct object. So the eloquent speaker employs it together with the *lām* of cause, relying on the fact that its being an object is known from the implied *an* (the verbal *an*).

His words *fī al-arḍ* (in the land) are connected with *saʿā*, to indicate that his striving is in a matter of the affairs of the people of your land. In this way the repetition of *fīhā* (in it) in His words ﴿to corrupt in it﴾ becomes an explanation of the general *fī al-arḍ* together with emphasis.

His words ﴿and He destroys the crops and the offspring﴾, with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* (*yuhlika*), i.e., He destroys it.

*Al-ḥarth* (crops) here means the crops, and *al-nasl* means the young of animals, derived from *nasl al-ṣūf*, meaning the wool when it falls off and separates. [p. 270] In my view, destroying the crops and the offspring is a metonymy (*kināya*) for the disruption of what sustains people's conditions. They were a people of crops and livestock, so the intention is not these two specifically, but the loss of what sustains people. This is in the manner of a proverb. It has been said that the crops and the offspring here refer to what al-Akhnas ibn Shariq did. In any case, the verse indicates that whoever causes such things, explicitly or implicitly, deserves punishment in the Hereafter, and for this reason He followed it with the concluding clause ﴿and Allah does not love corruption﴾, as a warning and rebuke.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 204–206 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of the negation of love (al-mahabba) is the negation of being pleased with corruption (al-fasad). Otherwise, love, which is an emotional state of the soul and a natural inclination arising from approval, is impossible for God Most High, so its negation is not valid as such. Rather, what is meant is its necessary consequence, which is contentment (al-rida) according to us, and will (al-irada) according to the Mu'tazilah. This question is based on the question of the creation of acts (khalq al-af'al).

There is no doubt that the implied meaning is: if He is not pleased with something, He will punish its doer, since nothing prevents Him from doing so. God has called that corruption, even if the crops and tilled land belong to the polytheists, because the destruction of the good things of the earth is a calamity upon all people. Fighting occurs only through the destruction of things that are instruments of destruction and causes of aggression.

Corruption (al-fasad) is the opposite of righteousness (al-salah). The meaning of corruption is the destruction of what is beneficial to people, either purely beneficial or predominantly beneficial. Thus, destroying milk, for example, is destroying a purely beneficial thing, and destroying firewood out of fear of burning is destroying a predominantly beneficial thing. By "predominance" is meant the predominance of its use among people, not the predominance of the quantity of benefit over the quantity of harm. Thus, destroying poisonous medicines is corruption, even if their use as medicine is rare, because destruction by them is treated as nonexistent given the restraint in people's minds against destroying by them; so their harm is guarded against through caution in their circulation and through the trustworthiness of those to whom they are entrusted. As for destroying less beneficial things, it is not corruption, such as destroying intoxicants; much less the destruction of what has no benefit at all, such as destroying snakes, scorpions, mice, and rabid dogs.

Corruption is not beloved to God because, in corruption as we have explained it, there is a nullification of what God created in this world for the wisdom of the benefit of people. The Wise does not love the nullification of what wisdom requires. Thus, fighting the enemy is the destruction of a predominant harm, and for this reason fighting is restricted to what achieves the destruction of harm without excess. For this reason he forbade burning dwellings in war and cutting down trees, except when the commander of the army judges that leaving some of them would increase the enemy's strength, prolong the fighting, and it is feared for the Muslim army that it might turn into defeat. This returns to the principle: "Necessity is measured by its extent."

His saying ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes him to sin﴾: that is, when a preacher admonishes him with what calls for reminding him of God's fear, he becomes angry at that. Originally, "al-akhdh" (taking) means grasping a thing with the hand, and it is used figuratively in the well-known sense of seizing. God said, ﴿And seize them and besiege them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and in the sense of subjugation, like "And We seized them with adversity."

It is also used for receiving, as in ﴿God took the covenant of the prophets﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81], and from this one says "so-and-so was held to account by so-and-so's words." In the sense of enveloping and encompassing one says, "fever seized him" and "the cry seized them." From this is His saying here, ﴿pride seized him﴾, that is, the pride of ignorance (al-jahiliyyah) enveloped him.

Pride (al-'izza) is a trait by which its possessor believes that no one else can overpower him and that his speech cannot be opposed, because of his standing among his people and his pride in their strength. Al-Samaw'al said:

"We deny, if we wish, the words of people, and they do not deny our words when we speak."

From it comes "izza" in the sense of strength and dominance, and it is mostly prevalent among the Arabs because of the large number of a tribe, though courage may make up for numbers. Among their proverbs: "Honor belongs only to the numerous." They also said: "We will not be defeated for lack of numbers." Al-Samaw'al said:

"Our being few did not harm us, and our neighbor is honored, while the neighbor of the many is humbled."

From it comes the description "al-'Aziz" as will come in His saying, ﴿Know that God is Mighty, Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209].

The "al" in "al-'izza" is for specificity, meaning the well-known pride of the people of ignorance, which prevents its possessor from accepting blame or being changed. Since pride implies the sense of protection, "pride seizing him" is a metaphor for his not listening to the advice of counselors.

His saying "bil-ithm" (with sin): the "ba'" here is for accompaniment, meaning pride accompanied by sin and wrongdoing seized him. The qualifier is a precaution, since there is a pride that is praiseworthy, as God said, ﴿And honor belongs to God, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. That is, it prevented him from accepting admonition and kept him an ally of the sin he had become accustomed to, not restraining himself from it, and these two go together.

His saying ﴿So Hell is enough for him﴾ is a consequence of this state. The root of "hasb" is sufficiency, as will come at His saying, ﴿And they say, "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173] in Al 'Imran.

Since the sufficiency of a thing ought to be according to its measure and what satisfies it, as Abu al-Tayyib said:

"Ambitions come according to the measure of people of resolve."

He applied "hasb" to recompense, as here.

"Jahannam" is a proper name for the abode of punishment, fired with flame. It is a diptote. Some grammarians said it is because of definiteness and feminine gender, since the Arabs treated it like place names. Others said it is because of definiteness and being non-Arabic, and this is the view of most: it came from a non-Arabic language, and therefore there is no need to search for its derivation. Whoever considered it Arabic claimed that it derives from "jahm," which means dislike. Some claimed its pattern is "fa'anl" with two added nuns, its original being "fa'nal" with one nun, which was doubled. It was also said its pattern is "fa'alal" with repetition of its first radical, which is the nun, to join it to quinqueliterals. Whoever said: its origin is Persian, "kahnam," which was Arabized as "jahannam."

It was also said its origin is Hebrew, "kihinam" with kasra on the kaf and kasra on the ha, which was Arabized. And whoever said that the pattern "fa'anal" does not exist has no weight, because there exist "dawna" (the name of a valley in the upper region) and "hafanka" (a name for the weak), which is written with an unpointed ha, an open fa, a sakin nun, a kaf and an alif; these two are rare, so Jahannam would be rare. As for the Arabs' saying "rakiyyat Jahannam," meaning deep of bottom, it is no proof, because it arises from comparing the well to Jahannam, since they describe Jahannam as a deep well filled with fire. Waraqa ibn Nawfal or Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said, lamenting Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, and both were among those who abandoned idol worship in the Jahiliyyah:

"You were guided and you prospered, son of 'Amr, when you avoided a dark furnace of fire."

The description of Jahannam has come in the Hadith in a similar manner, and God named it in His Book in many places "fire," and made "its fuel people and stones" [al-Baqarah: 24]. This has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿Then fear the Fire whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24].

His saying ﴿And how wretched is the resting place﴾: that is, Jahannam. "Mihad" is what is spread out, that is, prepared for one who sleeps. God called Jahannam "mihad" in mockery, because the sinners are cast into it and it meets their sides and backs.

It is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, grammatical coordination) with the clause ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾ [2:200], and so on. This is because He mentioned there the state of the open polytheists, who have no share in the Hereafter, and set against them the mention of the believers who desire good in this world and the Hereafter. Here He moves to the state of another group, who have no share in the Hereafter but pretend that they desire it, while their state is contrasted with the state of the sincere believers who prefer the Hereafter and the eternal life over the life of this world. These are the ones mentioned in His words ﴿And among the people is one who sells his soul seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [2:207].

*Min* (مِن, "among/some of") here means "some of," as in His words ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾ [2:8]. Thus it is valid to apply it to a group or to a specific individual. The relative pronoun *man* (مَنِ, "he who") is likewise valid for a group or an individual.

*Al-ijāb* (الإعجاب, "being impressed/pleased") is the producing of *ʿujb* (العُجْب) in the soul. *Al-ʿajab* (العَجَب, "wonder/astonishment") is an emotion that arises in the soul upon witnessing something unfamiliar whose cause is hidden. Since the nature of what has a hidden cause is that the soul desires it, *ʿajab* comes to imply approval. One says, "The thing impressed me" (*aʿjabanī al-shayʾ*), meaning it caused me to find it admirable. Al-Kawashī said: It is said in the sense of approval, "*aʿjabanī kadhā*" (this pleased me), and in the sense of disapproval, "*ʿajibtu min kadhā*" (I marvelled at this). So His words *yuʿjibuka* mean: his speech is pleasing to you.

By "speech" here is meant what it indicates of his state in faith and in sincere counsel to the Muslims, because that is what concerns the Messenger and pleases him. The intended meaning is not the quality of his speech in eloquence and rhetoric, since there is no purpose in that here, because the intended matter is what contradicts his words ﴿and he is the most contentious of adversaries﴾ and what follows.

The address may be either to the Prophet (ﷺ). That is: among the people is one who shows you what pleases you of speech, namely faith, love of good, and turning away from the disbelievers. This would indicate what al-Akhnas did to the crops of some Muslims, because that indicates his disbelief and his lying in his affection for the Prophet (ﷺ), since if his affection were sincere he would not have harmed his followers.

Or it indicates what he did to the crops of the Thaqīf, according to the view of some exegetes that al-Akhnas attacked the Thaqīf by night, while there was enmity between him and them, though they were his own people. So he raided them with those of the Banū Zuhra who were with him, burned their crops and killed their livestock.

Because his action against a people, even if they were disbelievers at that time, does not concern the Muslims with their harm, and because he did not do it in support of Islam, nor was he in a state of war with them, his act reveals a corruption of disposition that does not match what he shows of goodness and gentleness of speech. [p. 269] For it is the nature of a person's character to be consistent and to show what is within. Allah does not approve of harming His servants, even if they are disbelievers, with harm that does not lead to their benefit, because he did not attack them in order to bring them to faith, but to corrupt and destroy. For this reason He said: ﴿and Allah does not love corruption﴾.

His words ﴿in the land﴾ are an emphasis on the meaning of *saʿā* (strove), to remove the suspicion of figurative usage, that *al-saʿy* might mean work and earning. So it was intended to specify that this striving is walking through the land for corruption, which is raiding and plundering not for the elevation of the word of Allah. For this reason He said after it: ﴿to corrupt in it﴾. The *lām* is then for causation, because corruption is the intended aim of this striver.

It is also possible that *saʿā* is a metaphor for intention and planning, i.e., he plotted a scheme, because devising corruption and employing a stratagem to achieve it, together with displaying sincere counsel in speech, is a scheme. In that case *li-yufsida* is the object of the verb *saʿā*, and the sense is: he intended corruption in the land and planned it. The *lām* would then be the *lām* of communication (*tabligh*), as already mentioned in His words ﴿Allah intends ease for you﴾ [2:185] up to ﴿and that you complete the period﴾ [2:185]. *"Ibn Kūz sought, and foolishness is like its name, to hunt from us when we spent winter nights."*

The implied sense is: he sought to hunt from us. Al-Marzūqī said: He used the verb with *lām* because *tabaghghā* is like *arāda* (to want). End of quote.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 204–206 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of the negation of love (al-mahabba) is the negation of being pleased with corruption (al-fasad). Otherwise, love, which is an emotional state of the soul and a natural inclination arising from approval, is impossible for God Most High, so its negation is not valid as such. Rather, what is meant is its necessary consequence, which is contentment (al-rida) according to us, and will (al-irada) according to the Mu'tazilah. This question is based on the question of the creation of acts (khalq al-af'al).

There is no doubt that the implied meaning is: if He is not pleased with something, He will punish its doer, since nothing prevents Him from doing so. God has called that corruption, even if the crops and tilled land belong to the polytheists, because the destruction of the good things of the earth is a calamity upon all people. Fighting occurs only through the destruction of things that are instruments of destruction and causes of aggression.

Corruption (al-fasad) is the opposite of righteousness (al-salah). The meaning of corruption is the destruction of what is beneficial to people, either purely beneficial or predominantly beneficial. Thus, destroying milk, for example, is destroying a purely beneficial thing, and destroying firewood out of fear of burning is destroying a predominantly beneficial thing. By "predominance" is meant the predominance of its use among people, not the predominance of the quantity of benefit over the quantity of harm. Thus, destroying poisonous medicines is corruption, even if their use as medicine is rare, because destruction by them is treated as nonexistent given the restraint in people's minds against destroying by them; so their harm is guarded against through caution in their circulation and through the trustworthiness of those to whom they are entrusted. As for destroying less beneficial things, it is not corruption, such as destroying intoxicants; much less the destruction of what has no benefit at all, such as destroying snakes, scorpions, mice, and rabid dogs.

Corruption is not beloved to God because, in corruption as we have explained it, there is a nullification of what God created in this world for the wisdom of the benefit of people. The Wise does not love the nullification of what wisdom requires. Thus, fighting the enemy is the destruction of a predominant harm, and for this reason fighting is restricted to what achieves the destruction of harm without excess. For this reason he forbade burning dwellings in war and cutting down trees, except when the commander of the army judges that leaving some of them would increase the enemy's strength, prolong the fighting, and it is feared for the Muslim army that it might turn into defeat. This returns to the principle: "Necessity is measured by its extent."

Page 271

His saying ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes him to sin﴾: that is, when a preacher admonishes him with what calls for reminding him of God's fear, he becomes angry at that. Originally, "al-akhdh" (taking) means grasping a thing with the hand, and it is used figuratively in the well-known sense of seizing. God said, ﴿And seize them and besiege them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and in the sense of subjugation, like "And We seized them with adversity."

It is also used for receiving, as in ﴿God took the covenant of the prophets﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81], and from this one says "so-and-so was held to account by so-and-so's words." In the sense of enveloping and encompassing one says, "fever seized him" and "the cry seized them." From this is His saying here, ﴿pride seized him﴾, that is, the pride of ignorance (al-jahiliyyah) enveloped him.

Pride (al-'izza) is a trait by which its possessor believes that no one else can overpower him and that his speech cannot be opposed, because of his standing among his people and his pride in their strength. Al-Samaw'al said:

"We deny, if we wish, the words of people, and they do not deny our words when we speak."

From it comes "izza" in the sense of strength and dominance, and it is mostly prevalent among the Arabs because of the large number of a tribe, though courage may make up for numbers. Among their proverbs: "Honor belongs only to the numerous." They also said: "We will not be defeated for lack of numbers." Al-Samaw'al said:

"Our being few did not harm us, and our neighbor is honored, while the neighbor of the many is humbled."

From it comes the description "al-'Aziz" as will come in His saying, ﴿Know that God is Mighty, Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209].

The "al" in "al-'izza" is for specificity, meaning the well-known pride of the people of ignorance, which prevents its possessor from accepting blame or being changed. Since pride implies the sense of protection, "pride seizing him" is a metaphor for his not listening to the advice of counselors.

His saying "bil-ithm" (with sin): the "ba'" here is for accompaniment, meaning pride accompanied by sin and wrongdoing seized him. The qualifier is a precaution, since there is a pride that is praiseworthy, as God said, ﴿And honor belongs to God, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. That is, it prevented him from accepting admonition and kept him an ally of the sin he had become accustomed to, not restraining himself from it, and these two go together.

His saying ﴿So Hell is enough for him﴾ is a consequence of this state. The root of "hasb" is sufficiency, as will come at His saying, ﴿And they say, "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173] in Al 'Imran.

Since the sufficiency of a thing ought to be according to its measure and what satisfies it, as Abu al-Tayyib said:

"Ambitions come according to the measure of people of resolve."

He applied "hasb" to recompense, as here.

"Jahannam" is a proper name for the abode of punishment, fired with flame. It is a diptote. Some grammarians said it is because of definiteness and feminine gender, since the Arabs treated it like place names. Others said it is because of definiteness and being non-Arabic, and this is the view of most: it came from a non-Arabic language, and therefore there is no need to search for its derivation. Whoever considered it Arabic claimed that it derives from "jahm," which means dislike. Some claimed its pattern is "fa'anl" with two added nuns, its original being "fa'nal" with one nun, which was doubled. It was also said its pattern is "fa'alal" with repetition of its first radical, which is the nun, to join it to quinqueliterals. Whoever said: its origin is Persian, "kahnam," which was Arabized as "jahannam."

It was also said its origin is Hebrew, "kihinam" with kasra on the kaf and kasra on the ha, which was Arabized. And whoever said that the pattern "fa'anal" does not exist has no weight, because there exist "dawna" (the name of a valley in the upper region) and "hafanka" (a name for the weak), which is written with an unpointed ha, an open fa, a sakin nun, a kaf and an alif; these two are rare, so Jahannam would be rare. As for the Arabs' saying "rakiyyat Jahannam," meaning deep of bottom, it is no proof, because it arises from comparing the well to Jahannam, since they describe Jahannam as a deep well filled with fire. Waraqa ibn Nawfal or Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said, lamenting Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, and both were among those who abandoned idol worship in the Jahiliyyah:

"You were guided and you prospered, son of 'Amr, when you avoided a dark furnace of fire."

The description of Jahannam has come in the Hadith in a similar manner, and God named it in His Book in many places "fire," and made "its fuel people and stones" [al-Baqarah: 24]. This has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿Then fear the Fire whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24].

His saying ﴿And how wretched is the resting place﴾: that is, Jahannam. "Mihad" is what is spread out, that is, prepared for one who sleeps. God called Jahannam "mihad" in mockery, because the sinners are cast into it and it meets their sides and backs.

[p. 266]

It is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, grammatical coordination) with the clause ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾ [2:200], and so on. This is because He mentioned there the state of the open polytheists, who have no share in the Hereafter, and set against them the mention of the believers who desire good in this world and the Hereafter. Here He moves to the state of another group, who have no share in the Hereafter but pretend that they desire it, while their state is contrasted with the state of the sincere believers who prefer the Hereafter and the eternal life over the life of this world. These are the ones mentioned in His words ﴿And among the people is one who sells his soul seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [2:207].

*Min* (مِن, "among/some of") here means "some of," as in His words ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾ [2:8]. Thus it is valid to apply it to a group or to a specific individual. The relative pronoun *man* (مَنِ, "he who") is likewise valid for a group or an individual.

*Al-ijāb* (الإعجاب, "being impressed/pleased") is the producing of *ʿujb* (العُجْب) in the soul. *Al-ʿajab* (العَجَب, "wonder/astonishment") is an emotion that arises in the soul upon witnessing something unfamiliar whose cause is hidden. Since the nature of what has a hidden cause is that the soul desires it, *ʿajab* comes to imply approval. One says, "The thing impressed me" (*aʿjabanī al-shayʾ*), meaning it caused me to find it admirable. Al-Kawashī said: It is said in the sense of approval, "*aʿjabanī kadhā*" (this pleased me), and in the sense of disapproval, "*ʿajibtu min kadhā*" (I marvelled at this). So His words *yuʿjibuka* mean: his speech is pleasing to you.

By "speech" here is meant what it indicates of his state in faith and in sincere counsel to the Muslims, because that is what concerns the Messenger and pleases him. The intended meaning is not the quality of his speech in eloquence and rhetoric, since there is no purpose in that here, because the intended matter is what contradicts his words ﴿and he is the most contentious of adversaries﴾ and what follows.

The address may be either to the Prophet (ﷺ). That is: among the people is one who shows you what pleases you of speech, namely faith, love of good, and turning away from the disbelievers. In this case "min" refers to the hypocrites, most of whom were Jews, and among them were polytheists of Yathrib. This is my preferred view. Or it refers to a particular group of hypocrites. It has been said that what is meant is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafī, whose name was Ubayy, and who was a client (*mawlā*) of the Banū Zuhra of Quraysh, who were the maternal kin of the Prophet (ﷺ). He used to show love for the Prophet (ﷺ). He did not join the polytheists at the Battle of Badr, but withdrew (*khanasa*, "slipped away") from going out with them to Badr. He had three hundred men from the Banū Zuhra, his allies, and he prevented them from joining the polytheists. It was said that he used to show Islam while being a hypocrite. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It is not established that he ever embraced Islam; rather he used to show affection for the Messenger. On this view, the rebuke is because he betrayed and corrupted them.

It is also possible that the address is to an unspecified person, so that it applies to every addressee, as a warning to the Muslims against the stratagems of the hypocrites being effective upon them, and an alert to them to investigate the conditions of people, which is necessary.

The adverbial phrase in His words ﴿in the life of this world﴾ may be connected to *yuʿjibuka* (pleases you). In that case, the group of people intended are the hypocrites who show the words of Islam and desire for it, in the manner of His words ﴿and when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [2:14]. That is: your pleasure with their words does not go beyond occurring in this world, for in the Hereafter you will find them in a state that will not please you. So this is a preparation for His words at the end of the verse ﴿so Hell is sufficient for him﴾. The sense of "in" (*fī*) derived here is a real (*ḥaqīqiyya*, literal) sense of time/place.

It may also be connected to the word *qawlihi* (his speech), i.e., his speech concerning matters of this world, such as praiseworthy fidelity in oaths with the Muslims and affection for the Prophet, and he says nothing about matters of religion. So this is an alert that he does not profess Islam openly. The intended person here is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

The particle *fī* in this sense is for figurative (*majāziyya*) location, meaning *ʿan* (about), and the implied sense is "his speech about the life of this world."

The meaning of ﴿he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ is that he combines the good of his speech and the apparent display of affection with calling Allah to witness that what is in his heart corresponds with what is in his utterance. The meaning of calling Allah to witness is his swearing that Allah knows he is truthful.

The phrase "what is in his heart" conveyed the sense of correspondence with his words because, when he called Allah to witness while speaking sweet words, it became necessary that he was claiming his heart matched his tongue. He said, ﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you﴾ [9:62].

The meaning of ﴿and he is the most contentious of adversaries﴾ is that he is intensely hostile, i.e., enmity. It is derived from *laddahu yaladduhu* (with the vowel of the *lām* in the past tense being *fatḥa*), because it is of the pattern *faʿila*. One says: "You (are) contentious, O Zayd," with a *kasra* on the *dāl*, when he disputes. So he is *lādd* and *laddūd*. Thus *al-laddad* is intensity of dispute, and *al-alladd* is one who is very contentious. Al-Ḥamāsī, Rabīʿa ibn Maqrūm, said:

*And the most rancorous of those who hold a grudge against me, as if the heat of his chest were boiling in a cauldron.*

So *alladd* is an adjective of the attributive form (*ṣifa mushabbaha*), not an elative (*ism tafḍīl*). Do you not see that its feminine form came in the pattern *faʿlāʾ* and they said *laddāʾ*, and its plural came in the pattern *fuʿl*? He said: ﴿and to warn thereby a people who are *lud*﴾ [19:97]. By "predominance" is meant the predominance of its use among people, not the predominance of the quantity of benefit over the quantity of harm. Thus, destroying poisonous medicines is corruption, even if their use as medicine is rare, because destruction by them is treated as nonexistent given the restraint in people's minds against destroying by them; so their harm is guarded against through caution in their circulation and through the trustworthiness of those to whom they are entrusted. As for destroying less beneficial things, it is not corruption, such as destroying intoxicants; much less the destruction of what has no benefit at all, such as destroying snakes, scorpions, mice, and rabid dogs.

Corruption is not beloved to God because, in corruption as we have explained it, there is a nullification of what God created in this world for the wisdom of the benefit of people. The Wise does not love the nullification of what wisdom requires. Thus, fighting the enemy is the destruction of a predominant harm, and for this reason fighting is restricted to what achieves the destruction of harm without excess. For this reason he forbade burning dwellings in war and cutting down trees, except when the commander of the army judges that leaving some of them would increase the enemy's strength, prolong the fighting, and it is feared for the Muslim army that it might turn into defeat. This returns to the principle: "Necessity is measured by its extent."

Page 271

His saying ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes him to sin﴾: that is, when a preacher admonishes him with what calls for reminding him of God's fear, he becomes angry at that. Originally, "al-akhdh" (taking) means grasping a thing with the hand, and it is used figuratively in the well-known sense of seizing. God said, ﴿And seize them and besiege them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and in the sense of subjugation, like "And We seized them with adversity."

It is also used for receiving, as in ﴿God took the covenant of the prophets﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81], and from this one says "so-and-so was held to account by so-and-so's words." In the sense of enveloping and encompassing one says, "fever seized him" and "the cry seized them." From this is His saying here, ﴿pride seized him﴾, that is, the pride of ignorance (al-jahiliyyah) enveloped him.
