Pride (al-'izza) is a trait by which its possessor believes that no one else can overpower him and that his speech cannot be opposed, because of his standing among his people and his pride in their strength. Al-Samaw'al said:

"We deny, if we wish, the words of people, and they do not deny our words when we speak."

From it comes "izza" in the sense of strength and dominance, and it is mostly prevalent among the Arabs because of the large number of a tribe, though courage may make up for numbers. Among their proverbs: "Honor belongs only to the numerous." They also said: "We will not be defeated for lack of numbers." Al-Samaw'al said:

"Our being few did not harm us, and our neighbor is honored, while the neighbor of the many is humbled."

From it comes the description "al-'Aziz" as will come in His saying, ﴿Know that God is Mighty, Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209].

The "al" in "al-'izza" is for specificity, meaning the well-known pride of the people of ignorance, which prevents its possessor from accepting blame or being changed. Since pride implies the sense of protection, "pride seizing him" is a metaphor for his not listening to the advice of counselors.

His saying "bil-ithm" (with sin): the "ba'" here is for accompaniment, meaning pride accompanied by sin and wrongdoing seized him. The qualifier is a precaution, since there is a pride that is praiseworthy, as God said, ﴿And honor belongs to God, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. That is, it prevented him from accepting admonition and kept him an ally of the sin he had become accustomed to, not restraining himself from it, and these two go together.

His saying ﴿So Hell is enough for him﴾ is a consequence of this state. The root of "hasb" is sufficiency, as will come at His saying, ﴿And they say, "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173] in Al 'Imran.

Since the sufficiency of a thing ought to be according to its measure and what satisfies it, as Abu al-Tayyib said:

"Ambitions come according to the measure of people of resolve."

He applied "hasb" to recompense, as here.

"Jahannam" is a proper name for the abode of punishment, fired with flame. It is a diptote. Some grammarians said it is because of definiteness and feminine gender, since the Arabs treated it like place names. Others said it is because of definiteness and being non-Arabic, and this is the view of most: it came from a non-Arabic language, and therefore there is no need to search for its derivation. Whoever considered it Arabic claimed that it derives from "jahm," which means dislike. Some claimed its pattern is "fa'anl" with two added nuns, its original being "fa'nal" with one nun, which was doubled. It was also said its pattern is "fa'alal" with repetition of its first radical, which is the nun, to join it to quinqueliterals. Whoever said: its origin is Persian, "kahnam," which was Arabized as "jahannam."

It was also said its origin is Hebrew, "kihinam" with kasra on the kaf and kasra on the ha, which was Arabized. And whoever said that the pattern "fa'anal" does not exist has no weight, because there exist "dawna" (the name of a valley in the upper region) and "hafanka" (a name for the weak), which is written with an unpointed ha, an open fa, a sakin nun, a kaf and an alif; these two are rare, so Jahannam would be rare. As for the Arabs' saying "rakiyyat Jahannam," meaning deep of bottom, it is no proof, because it arises from comparing the well to Jahannam, since they describe Jahannam as a deep well filled with fire. Waraqa ibn Nawfal or Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said, lamenting Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, and both were among those who abandoned idol worship in the Jahiliyyah:

"You were guided and you prospered, son of 'Amr, when you avoided a dark furnace of fire."

The description of Jahannam has come in the Hadith in a similar manner, and God named it in His Book in many places "fire," and made "its fuel people and stones" [al-Baqarah: 24]. This has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿Then fear the Fire whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24].

His saying ﴿And how wretched is the resting place﴾: that is, Jahannam. "Mihad" is what is spread out, that is, prepared for one who sleeps. God called Jahannam "mihad" in mockery, because the sinners are cast into it and it meets their sides and backs.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 207:**

﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of God, and God is Kind to the servants.﴾

This is the counterpart (*qasim*) of ﴿And among the people is one whose speech impresses you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204]. Its mention here comes as a digression (*istitrad*), to encompass both categories of people. This is the category whose action is purely for good, reaching its utmost extent: exposing his self, which is the most precious thing to him, to destruction in order to attain what pleases God Most High. The pleasure of God is in people's action for the good that He has commanded them.

[Page 273]

*Yashri* means *yabi'u* (sells), just as *yashtari* means *yabtai'u* (buys). This was already discussed in His words ﴿Do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41].

Here *yashri* is used figuratively (*majaz*) for giving up. The meaning is: among the people is one who gives up his self to destruction seeking the pleasure of God, that is, to be destroyed in the cause of supporting the religion. This is the highest degree of faith, because the self is the most precious thing a person has.

*Mardat Allah* means His pleasure (*ridah*). It is a verbal noun of *radiya 'ala*, on the pattern *maf'alah*, with a *ta'* added by transmission (*sama'*), as in *al-mad'atah* and *al-mas'atah*.

Regarding the occasion of revelation (*asbab al-nuzul*), Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: it was revealed concerning Suhayb ibn Sinan al-Namiri ibn al-Namir ibn Qasit, who was nicknamed "al-Rumi," because the Byzantines (*al-Rum*) had captured him in the pre-Islamic period in the regions of Mosul, and the Banu Kalb bought him, and he became their client (*mawla*). He grew wealthy in Makkah during the pre-Islamic period, and he was among the earliest Muslims. When the Prophet (ﷺ) migrated, Suhayb set out as a migrant, and a group of Quraysh caught up with him in order to seize him. He dismounted from his riding animal, took out his quiver, and he was a skilled archer. He said to them: "You know that I am among the best of you at shooting. By God, you will not reach me until I have shot all that is in my quiver, and then I will strike with my sword as long as anything remains in my hand." They said: "We will not let you leave us rich when you came to us poor. But show us your wealth, and we will leave you alone." They made a covenant with him on this, so he showed them where his wealth was. When he came to the Prophet (ﷺ), the Prophet said to him when he saw him: "The sale has profited, Abu Yahya," and he recited this verse to him. It was also said that the disbelievers of Makkah tortured Suhayb for his Islam, so he ransomed himself from them with his wealth and migrated. It was also said other than this. The most apparent view is that the verse is general, and that Suhayb or someone else is in mind as the first of those it includes.

His words ﴿and God is Kind to the servants﴾ are a concluding phrase (*tadhyil*), meaning: He is Kind to the righteous servants, among whom is the one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of God. Kindness (*ra'fah*) is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for its necessary consequence, which is granting good things, as with mercy (*rahmah*).

The apparent reading is that the definite article in *al-'ibad* (the servants) is a definiteness of comprehensiveness (*ta'rif al-istighraq*), because God is Kind to all His servants, and they vary in this. Among them are those who receive God's kindness in this world and the Hereafter, with variations between the two according to what God's knowledge and wisdom require. And among them are those who receive God's kindness in this world but not in the Hereafter, and they are the polytheists and disbelievers, for among His kindness to them is that He has given them health and provision. It is also possible that the definiteness is a definiteness of reference (*ta'rif al-'ahd*), meaning the servants of this kind, that is, the kind who sells himself seeking the pleasure of God.

It is also possible that the *al-* is a substitute (*'iwad*) for the genitive complement, as in His words ﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 41], meaning "their refuge." When *al-'ibad* is attributed to the Name of Majesty (*ism al-jalalah*, i.e., Allah), it refers to the servants brought near (to God). He Most High said ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], in Surah al-Hijr.

The connection between this concluding phrase and the sentence is that those described have given up their selves to God and made themselves His servants. So God is Kind to them as a person is kind to his servant. If the referent of *man* is general, as is apparent for everyone who gives up his self to God, then the meaning is "God is Kind to them," and the phrase shifts from the pronoun to the noun in order to form this concluding phrase, and to indicate that the cause of the kindness toward them is that they made themselves servants to Him. If the referent of *man* is Suhayb, may God be pleased with him, then the meaning is "God is Kind to the servants among whom is Suhayb." In every case the sentence is a concluding phrase. The connection is that Suhayb was a slave of the Byzantines, then of a group of Quraysh, namely the Banu Kalb, and they did not show him kindness, because he was tortured for God's sake. When he became a servant of God, God was kind to him.

In this verse, from His words ﴿And among the people is one whose speech impresses you in the life of this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204] to His words ﴿Kind to the servants﴾, there are meanings from the meanings of the discipline of souls, their ranks, and their characters. They teach the believers the obligation of discerning realities and inner matters, and not being deceived by outward appearances until after testing and examination. Among people is one who is deceived by the beauty of his outward appearance while inwardly harboring evil, who gives forth from his tongue sweetness of expression while concealing malice and treachery. Al-Ma'arri said:

*And a man may betray the expectation of his clan, even if his appearance and splendor please.*

This condition is also covered by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed, there is magic in eloquence," in one of its two meanings, which contains both, and it is one of the comprehensive utterances (*jawami' al-kalim*). His faith may become so weak that he calls God to witness that what he says is true, while on the contrary he harbors enmity and hatred within himself.

The sign of the inner state appears in a person's conduct. The one who loves corruption and destroys crops and offspring is not a person of good conscience. The one who does not respond to the call of truth when you call him to it, and displays arrogance in wrongdoing, does not desist from his error and does not abandon his blameworthy character. The one who does not hold back his self in supporting the truth shows through his character that he prefers truth and goodness over falsehood and corruption. And whoever does not show kindness, God will not show kindness to him.

[p. 275]

﴿O you who believe, enter into peace (al-silm) completely, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ ﴿But if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) in the manner of a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ), seizing the opportunity to call people to enter into peace (al-silm). Its connection to what precedes it is that the previous verses contained a division of people in relation to religion into ranks. The highest of them is ﴿one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 207], because the self is the most precious thing that can be expended, and the lowest is ﴿one whose speech about the life of this world impresses you, and who calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, while he is the most contentious of opponents﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204], meaning he conceals treachery and corrupts for the people what benefits them all, namely the good things of the earth. This includes that he has transgressed against peaceful people. Therefore, it is fitting that after the people have been summoned to enter into what is called peace, this connection is strengthened or weakened according to the multiplicity of possible meanings of the call to enter into peace.

The address ﴿O you who believe﴾ is an address to the Muslims, according to the Qur'an's customary use of this title, and because the relative construction (al-mawṣūl) functions as a definite noun with the definite article of previous reference (al-'ahd).

Dukhūl (entering) is in its literal sense the penetration of a body into a body or an enclosed place such as a house or a mosque. It is used figuratively, and commonly, for arriving at a wide place, as one says "he entered the lands of Banu Asad." Here it is used metaphorically for following, adhering to, and being deeply engaged in the matter.

As for al-silm, it is read with a fatḥa or kasra on the sīn with the lām sukūn. Nāfi', Ibn Kathīr, al-Kisā'ī and Abū Ja'far read it with fatḥa on the sīn, and the rest of the ten readers read it with kasra on the sīn. It is also said salam with fatḥa on both the sīn and the lām. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace (al-salam), "You are not a believer"﴾ [al-Nisā': 94]. The literal meaning of al-silm is reconciliation and the abandoning of war. 'Abbās ibn Mirdās said:

"Peace: take from it what you are content with, / while war will leave you the gasps of its breath as sorrow."

Examples of this are numerous in their speech. Zuhayr said:

"And you two have said: if we attain peace, wide..."

It is derived from al-salāmah, which is deliverance from pain, harm, or obstinacy. One says "aslama nafsahu li-fulān," meaning he gave himself to him without resistance; and "istaslama" means he sought peace, that is, he abandoned resistance. The Arabs say: "Aslimun am ḥarb?" meaning, "Are you at peace or at war?" All these meanings derive from one another, and therefore the lexicographers affirmed that al-silm, with kasra, fatḥa, or the vowelled form, is used for each of them in the sense in which the others are used.

They said: al-silm, in its three forms, is also applied to the religion of Islam. This is attributed to Ibn 'Abbās, Mujāhid and Qatādah, and they cited the verse of Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Ābis al-Kindī concerning the apostasy of his people:

"I called my clan to peace when / I saw them turning their backs in flight, / So I will not exchange God for another lord, / nor take another religion in place of peace."

This application was mentioned only by the commentators. Al-Rāghib did not mention it in his Mufradāt al-Qur'ān, nor did al-Zamakhsharī in al-Asās, nor the author of Lisān al-'Arab. Al-Fīrūzābādī mentioned it in al-Qāmūs following the exegetes. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned it in al-Kashshāf as a reported opinion regarding the meaning of al-silm here. Therefore, this application is not reliably established. The verse of al-Kindī may bear the meaning of peaceableness, i.e., peaceableness toward the Muslims, and his words "dīnan" would then mean a constant habit, as al-Muthaqqab al-'Abdī said:

"She says, when you have turned her saddle-girth for her: 'Is this his habit forever, and my habit?'"

On the authority of Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā', al-silm with kasra on the sīn is Islam, and al-salm with fatḥa on the sīn is peace (al-musālamah). For this reason he read ﴿enter into al-silm﴾ in this sūrah with kasra on the sīn only, and he read the instances in Sūrat al-Anfāl and Sūrat Muḥammad ﷺ with fatḥa on the sīn. Al-Ṭabarī, in justifying its meaning here as Islam, said that it refers to Islam alone, and not to the two other verses.

Al-Mubarrad rejected this distinction and said: language is not taken in this manner; it is taken by hearing (samā') and not by analogy (qiyās), and whoever makes the distinction needs evidence.

That al-silm is among the names of reconciliation is undisputed among the lexicographers, so it is undoubtedly intended by the verse. That it is applied to Islam, if this is established, it is permissible that it also be intended, and it would be from the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in both its meanings.

So if al-silm is taken to mean peace (al-musālamah), as is required by their being addressed as ﴿O you who believe﴾, which is in effect a title for the Muslims, the meaning is a command to them to enter into peace rather than fighting. And as required by the form of the imperative in "udkhulū," since its literal sense is seeking the accomplishment of an act that was not yet accomplished, or was neglected in part.

What appears to me is that the connection of this verse to what came before it is this: the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190] and the verses that follow are a preparation for fighting the polytheists, because they hindered the Muslims from the House, and because they spread rumors that they had resolved to fight them, and the rumor of the killing of 'Uthmān ibn 'Affān in Makkah when the Messenger of Allah sent him to the Quraysh. He mentioned this and then digressed after it to explain the rules of the Ḥajj and 'Umrah. When the entire right of all that was fulfilled, and what God had commanded to be placed in its proper position among those verses had been joined to it, the command to them is resumed here to be content with the peace and reconciliation which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concluded with the people of Makkah in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyah, because many of the Muslims were grieved by its occurrence, including 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who said: "Are we not upon the truth and our enemy upon falsehood? Then why should we give the humiliation in our religion?" This is related by the people of the Ṣaḥīḥ. So the period between the Muslims' encampment at al-Ḥudaybiyah and the back-and-forth of envoys between them and the Quraysh, and between the occurrence of the peace, is the period of the revelation of the verses from His words ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190] up to here.

Know that if the pronoun in His words ﴿Do they await...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] refers to "among the people is one who impresses you" or "among the people is one who sells himself," as will come, then His words ﴿O you who believe, enter into al-silm﴾ form a parenthetical insertion between the sentence concerned with the return (al-ma'ād) and the sentence concerned with the pronoun.

As for when al-silm is interpreted as Islam, that is, the religion of Islam, then the address ﴿O you who believe﴾ and the command to the believers to enter into Islam is interpreted as a command to increase their firmness in it and to penetrate deeply into it, because it is said: "Faith entered his heart" when it became settled and firmly established. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 14]. And al-Nābighah said:

"Heedlessness refused me, for when I mention her, / a disease stirs in my heart, penetrating within."

This is the apparent meaning. So the command in "udkhulū" means persistence in that. It has also been said: what is intended by "those who believe" are those who displayed faith, so the address is to the hypocrites. Then "those who believe" is interpreted as "those who displayed faith," and it becomes a mockery of them in the manner of His words ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed, indeed you are mad"﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 6]. This would be an address to the hypocrites. But this interpretation is far-fetched, because "those who believe" has become like a title for whoever follows the religion truly, and because the apparent sense in this case would be to attribute to the hypocrites the status of Islam and to demand from them faith, not the reverse, according to the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿The bedouins say, "We believe." Say, "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 14].

It has also been said that what is meant by "those who believe" are those among the Jews who believed, such as 'Abd Allāh ibn Salām. Then "udkhulū" is interpreted as the intensity of engagement, meaning by abandoning what the religion did not bring, because they persisted in the prohibition of the Sabbath, the abandonment of drinking camel's milk, and some of the customs they had grown used to during their Jewish days, if what those who compiled the reports of the occasions of revelation related is correct, that a group of Jewish believers did this.

It is also possible that what is meant by al-silm here is its literal meaning, and that the peace intended is peace among the Muslims: God, exalted is He, commands them, after they have been characterized by faith, that none of them should be at war with another as they were in the days of ignorance, and that they should forget the enmities that existed between their tribes. The connection of this to what came before is that when they were commanded to remember God as they remember their fathers, and they used to recount their vendettas during the season of Ḥajj and boast in a way that might lead to fanaticism, they were commanded after that to enter into peace. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Do not return after me as disbelievers, striking one another's necks." Thus the verse is a completion of the rulings concerned with reforming the conditions of the Arabs that they were in during the days of ignorance, and by it the verse is a foundation for peace being the basis of Islam, namely the removal of mutual slaughter (al-tahārj), as al-Shāṭibī said, that is, mutual killing and what leads to it.

Or the intended meaning of al-silm here is peace with God, exalted is He, in a figurative sense: that is, enter into peace with God, exalted is He, by following His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, just as war is figuratively applied to disobedience in His words ﴿So know that there is war from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279], and in the sacred hadith related by al-Tirmidhī: "Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war upon him."

And "kāffah" is a noun that denotes encompassing all the parts of what it describes. In its form it resembles the form of the active participle feminine from "kaffa," but that is a coincidence in the form of its construction, and there is no sense of restraining in it. There is no need to labor in explaining a connection between the shape of its wording and its intended meaning in speech, since this is of little benefit. It conveys the sense of the words of emphasis that indicate totality and comprehensiveness.

The tā' attached to it is invariably present in all circumstances, whether the thing emphasized is feminine or masculine, singular or plural, as in ﴿And fight the polytheists all together (kāffatan)﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. Most often, "kāffah" in speech is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of a noun preceding it, as here. So "kāffatan" is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "udkhulū," meaning: in the state of your being all together, with none of you excepted.

Ibn Hishām, in Mughnī al-Labīb, in discussing the fifth aspect of the fifth chapter, on the circumstantial qualifier from the agent and from the object, said: when "kāffah" is used in the sense of totality and comprehensiveness, it is only a circumstantial qualifier of what it applies to, and it is only indefinite, and its modified noun is only a rational being. But al-Zajjāj and al-Zamakhsharī permitted making "kāffah" a circumstantial qualifier of al-silm, and al-silm is feminine. In the Indian glosses on al-Mughnī by al-Damāmīnī, it is stated that "kāffah" occurred as a noun for a non-rational thing, not as a circumstantial qualifier but as a construct, in the letter of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb to the family of Kākilah: "I have granted to the family of Kākilah, from the treasury of the Muslims, two hundred mithqāl of pure gold every year."

Know that prohibiting what the Arabs did not use, when the rules permit it, is a restriction on the language. Rather, following the Arabs in their usage is more conducive to eloquence, but it does not oblige one to stop at it without going beyond it. So when it occurs in the Qur'an, it has been established.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 208–209 (part 2 of 2):

His saying ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ is a warning against what would turn them away from entering into peace (silm), which was commanded, by way of a prohibition against opposing what was commanded. Its benefit is to alert [the reader] that what arises from refusing to enter into peace is among the paths of Satan, who is known for not directing toward good. This prohibition is either more specific than the command, together with an explanation of the reason for the command, if by peace is meant other than the branches of Islam, such as an allusion to what crept into the souls of most of them of aversion to giving humiliation to the polytheists in the treaty of Hudaybiyah, as 'Umar said: "Are we not upon the truth and our enemy upon falsehood, so why should we give humiliation in our religion?" And as Sahl ibn Hunayf said on the day of Siffin: "O people, suspect your opinion, for indeed we saw ourselves on the day of Abu Jandal, and if we could have reversed the action of the Messenger of Allah, we would have reversed it, and Allah and His Messenger know best," informing them that what the Messenger of Allah did would only be good. Likewise Abu Bakr said to 'Umar: "He is the Messenger of Allah, and Allah will never waste him," alerting them that what crept into their souls of aversion to the peace was among the whisperings of Satan. Or it is merely to explain the reason for the command to enter into peace, if by peace is meant the branches of Islam. The meaning of ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan; indeed he is to you a clear enemy﴾, and the metaphor it contains, was already discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on earth [that is] lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168], the verse.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ is a consequence of the prohibition, meaning: if you follow the steps of Satan and thus slip, or if you slip and then follow the steps of Satan. By "slipping" is meant opposition to the prohibition.

The root of zalal is zalaq, that is, the instability of the foot and its movement in the place where it was meant to be planted. Here zalal is used metaphorically for the harm resulting from following Satan, by building an allegory upon an allegory: since the state of one who acts upon the whisperings of Satan was likened to the state of one walking in the footprints of another, the harm that befalls him in that walk was likened to the slipping of the foot while walking on a slippery road. From this it is understood that what Satan commands is likewise in the position of a slippery road, by way of metaphor (makniyyah). His saying "you slipped" is a takhyil (imaginative representation), and it is a tamthiliyyah (allegorical representation), so it belongs to the takhyil which was a metaphor, and the metaphor here lies in its whole construction.

Al-bayyinat: the proofs and miracles, and their coming, their appearance and their clarification, because "coming" is the appearance of the one who comes after his absence.

"In" (in) was used in the conditional for the rarity of this slipping occurring among those who believe, or because the speaker does not desire its occurrence, if the address is to one who believed outwardly but not in his heart.

In it there is an indication that what crept into their souls of aversion to the peace is a great slip.

His saying ﴿then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ is the answer to the condition, and ﴿that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ is the object of "know," and the intended meaning is knowledge of its necessary implication, which is punishment.

Al-'Aziz is fa'il from 'azza, when one becomes strong and is not overcome; its origin is from al-'izzah (might). The discussion of it has already passed at His saying ﴿the pride took him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206], and it is its opposite. So knowing that He, exalted is He, is Mighty implies their certainty that He will punish them and will not let them escape, because the mighty one does not spare the one who opposes him.

Al-Hakim may be an active participle from hakama, meaning one of firm judgment, and it may be that He is the one who perfects affairs, so it is from the use of fa'il with the meaning of mufil. Its relevance here is that the one who perfects affairs does not let escape the one deserving punishment, so the statement is a warning; otherwise all people know that Allah is Mighty and Wise.

You may also take His saying "then know" as treating their knowledge as if it were non-existent, because they did not act according to what it requires of hastening to enter the religion, or of abiding by the rulings of the religion, or of resentment toward the peace which the Messenger concluded.

Allah, exalted is He, only said ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾ as an excuse for them. In it there is an indication that it is obligatory upon them to entrust knowledge to Allah, who revealed to His Messenger the concluding of the peace with the polytheists, for He revealed it only for a benefit, and that is not a weakness for the Muslims, because Allah is Mighty and is never weakened before anyone, and because He is Wise, placing affairs in their proper places, and choosing for the Muslims what contains the victory of His religion. You have seen the clear proofs indicating Allah's care for His Messenger, and that He will not disgrace him nor waste his affair; and among those proofs is what they witnessed of victory on the day of Badr.

If by the intended meaning is entering into Islam or persisting upon it, then the meaning of ﴿if you slip﴾ is: being characterized by what contradicts the command to enter into peace. And by "the clear proofs" is meant the miracles which indicate the truthfulness of the Messenger. Al-Fakhr reported from the tafsir of al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar: the verse indicates that punishment for sin does not occur except after clarification, and that punishment occurs after the clear proofs have come, not after the certainty of the mukallaf, because he is not excused for not attaining certainty if the proofs are sufficient.

In al-Kashshaf it is narrated that a reciter recited this verse as "then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful," and a Bedouin heard him and rejected it, saying: "The Wise does not say such a thing; He does not mention forgiveness at the time of slipping, for that is an incitement to it." End of quote. In al-Qurtubi, from the tafsir of al-Naqqash, such a story is attributed to Ka'b al-Ahbar. And al-Tibi mentioned from al-Asma'i who said: "I was reciting: (And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, a punishment from Allah; and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful)," and beside me was a Bedouin, so he said: "Whose speech is this?" I said: "The speech of Allah." He said: "This is not the speech of Allah." So I became alert and recited ﴿and Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38], and he said: "You are right, this is the speech of Allah." I said: "Do you recite the Qur'an?" He said: "No." I said: "How did you know?" He said: "O you, He is Mighty and judges, so He cuts off; had He forgiven and shown mercy, He would not have cut off."

[p. 275]

﴿O you who believe, enter into peace (al-silm) completely, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ ﴿But if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) in the manner of a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ), seizing the opportunity to call people to enter into peace (al-silm). Its connection to what precedes it is that the previous verses contained a division of people in relation to religion into ranks. The highest of them is ﴿one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 207], because the self is the most precious thing that can be expended, and the lowest is ﴿one whose speech about the life of this world impresses you, and who calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, while he is the most contentious of opponents﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204], meaning he conceals treachery and corrupts for the people what benefits them all, namely the good things of the earth. This includes that he has transgressed against peaceful people. Therefore, it is fitting that after the people have been summoned to enter into what is called peace, this connection is strengthened or weakened according to the multiplicity of possible meanings of the call to enter into peace.

The address ﴿O you who believe﴾ is an address to the Muslims, according to the Qur'an's customary use of this title, and because the relative construction (al-mawṣūl) functions as a definite noun with the definite article of previous reference (al-'ahd).

Dukhūl (entering) is in its literal sense the penetration of a body into a body or an enclosed place such as a house or a mosque. It is used figuratively, and commonly, for arriving at a wide place, as one says "he entered the lands of Banu Asad." Here it is used metaphorically for following, adhering to, and being deeply engaged in the matter.

As for al-silm, it is read with a fatḥa or kasra on the sīn with the lām sukūn. Nāfi', Ibn Kathīr, al-Kisā'ī and Abū Ja'far read it with fatḥa on the sīn, and the rest of the ten readers read it with kasra on the sīn. It is also said salam with fatḥa on both the sīn and the lām. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace (al-salam), "You are not a believer"﴾ [al-Nisā': 94]. The literal meaning of al-silm is reconciliation and the abandoning of war. 'Abbās ibn Mirdās said:

"Peace: take from it what you are content with, / while war will leave you the gasps of its breath as sorrow."

Examples of this are numerous in their speech. Zuhayr said:

"And you two have said: if we attain peace, wide..."

It is derived from al-salāmah, which is deliverance from pain, harm, or obstinacy. One says "aslama nafsahu li-fulān," meaning he gave himself to him without resistance; and "istaslama" means he sought peace, that is, he abandoned resistance. The Arabs say: "Aslimun am ḥarb?" meaning, "Are you at peace or at war?" All these meanings derive from one another, and therefore the lexicographers affirmed that al-silm, with kasra, fatḥa, or the vowelled form, is used for each of them in the sense in which the others are used.

They said: al-silm, in its three forms, is also applied to the religion of Islam. This is attributed to Ibn 'Abbās, Mujāhid and Qatādah, and they cited the verse of Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Ābis al-Kindī concerning the apostasy of his people:

"I called my clan to peace when / I saw them turning their backs in flight, / So I will not exchange God for another lord, / nor take another religion in place of peace."

This application was mentioned only by the commentators. Al-Rāghib did not mention it in his Mufradāt al-Qur'ān, nor did al-Zamakhsharī in al-Asās, nor the author of Lisān al-'Arab. Al-Fīrūzābādī mentioned it in al-Qāmūs following the exegetes. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned it in al-Kashshāf as a reported opinion regarding the meaning of al-silm here. Therefore, this application is not reliably established. The verse of al-Kindī may bear the meaning of peaceableness, i.e., peaceableness toward the Muslims, and his words "dīnan" would then mean a constant habit, as al-Muthaqqab al-'Abdī said:

"She says, when you have turned her saddle-girth for her: 'Is this his habit forever, and my habit?'"

On the authority of Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā', al-silm with kasra on the sīn is Islam, and al-salm with fatḥa on the sīn is peace (al-musālamah). For this reason he read ﴿enter into al-silm﴾ in this sūrah with kasra on the sīn only, and he read the instances in Sūrat al-Anfāl and Sūrat Muḥammad ﷺ with fatḥa on the sīn. Al-Ṭabarī, in justifying its meaning here as Islam, said that it refers to Islam alone, and not to the two other verses.

Al-Mubarrad rejected this distinction and said: language is not taken in this manner; it is taken by hearing (samā') and not by analogy (qiyās), and whoever makes the distinction needs evidence.

That al-silm is among the names of reconciliation is undisputed among the lexicographers, so it is undoubtedly intended by the verse. That it is applied to Islam, if this is established, it is permissible that it also be intended, and it would be from the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in both its meanings.

So if al-silm is taken to mean peace (al-musālamah), as is required by their being addressed as ﴿O you who believe﴾, which is in effect a title for the Muslims, the meaning is a command to them to enter into peace rather than fighting. And as required by the form of the imperative in "udkhulū," since its literal sense is seeking the accomplishment of an act that was not yet accomplished, or was neglected in part.

What appears to me is that the connection of this verse to what came before it is this: the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190] and the verses that follow are a preparation for fighting the polytheists, because they hindered the Muslims from the House, and because they spread rumors that they had resolved to fight them, and the rumor of the killing of 'Uthmān ibn 'Affān in Makkah when the Messenger of Allah sent him to the Quraysh. He mentioned this and then digressed after it to explain the rules of the Ḥajj and 'Umrah. When the entire right of all that was fulfilled, and what God had commanded to be placed in its proper position among those verses had been joined to it, the command to them is resumed here to be content with the peace and reconciliation which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concluded with the people of Makkah in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyah, because many of the Muslims were grieved by its occurrence, including 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who said: "Are we not upon the truth and our enemy upon falsehood? Then why should we give the humiliation in our religion?" This is related by the people of the Ṣaḥīḥ. So the period between the Muslims' encampment at al-Ḥudaybiyah and the back-and-forth of envoys between them and the Quraysh, and between the occurrence of the peace, is the period of the revelation of the verses from His words ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190] up to here.

Know that if the pronoun in His words ﴿Do they await...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] refers to "among the people is one who impresses you" or "among the people is one who sells himself," as will come, then His words ﴿O you who believe, enter into al-silm﴾ form a parenthetical insertion between the sentence concerned with the return (al-ma'ād) and the sentence concerned with the pronoun.

As for when al-silm is interpreted as Islam, that is, the religion of Islam, then the address ﴿O you who believe﴾ and the command to the believers to enter into Islam is interpreted as a command to increase their firmness in it and to penetrate deeply into it, because it is said: "Faith entered his heart" when it became settled and firmly established. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 14]. And al-Nābighah said:

"Heedlessness refused me, for when I mention her, / a disease stirs in my heart, penetrating within."

This is the apparent meaning. So the command in "udkhulū" means persistence in that. It has also been said: what is intended by "those who believe" are those who displayed faith, so the address is to the hypocrites. Then "those who believe" is interpreted as "those who displayed faith," and it becomes a mockery of them in the manner of His words ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed, indeed you are mad"﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 6]. This would be an address to the hypocrites. But this interpretation is far-fetched, because "those who believe" has become like a title for whoever follows the religion truly, and because the apparent sense in this case would be to attribute to the hypocrites the status of Islam and to demand from them faith, not the reverse, according to the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿The bedouins say, "We believe." Say, "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 14].

It has also been said that what is meant by "those who believe" are those among the Jews who believed, such as 'Abd Allāh ibn Salām. Then "udkhulū" is interpreted as the intensity of engagement, meaning by abandoning what the religion did not bring, because they persisted in the prohibition of the Sabbath, the abandonment of drinking camel's milk, and some of the customs they had grown used to during their Jewish days, if what those who compiled the reports of the occasions of revelation related is correct, that a group of Jewish believers did this.

It is also possible that what is meant by al-silm here is its literal meaning, and that the peace intended is peace among the Muslims: God, exalted is He, commands them, after they have been characterized by faith, that none of them should be at war with another as they were in the days of ignorance, and that they should forget the enmities that existed between their tribes. The connection of this to what came before is that when they were commanded to remember God as they remember their fathers, and they used to recount their vendettas during the season of Ḥajj and boast in a way that might lead to fanaticism, they were commanded after that to enter into peace. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Do not return after me as disbelievers, striking one another's necks." Thus the verse is a completion of the rulings concerned with reforming the conditions of the Arabs that they were in during the days of ignorance, and by it the verse is a foundation for peace being the basis of Islam, namely the removal of mutual slaughter (al-tahārj), as al-Shāṭibī said, that is, mutual killing and what leads to it.

Or the intended meaning of al-silm here is peace with God, exalted is He, in a figurative sense: that is, enter into peace with God, exalted is He, by following His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, just as war is figuratively applied to disobedience in His words ﴿So know that there is war from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279], and in the sacred hadith related by al-Tirmidhī: "Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war upon him."

And "kāffah" is a noun that denotes encompassing all the parts of what it describes. In its form it resembles the form of the active participle feminine from "kaffa," but that is a coincidence in the form of its construction, and there is no sense of restraining in it. There is no need to labor in explaining a connection between the shape of its wording and its intended meaning in speech, since this is of little benefit. It conveys the sense of the words of emphasis that indicate totality and comprehensiveness.

The tā' attached to it is invariably present in all circumstances, whether the thing emphasized is feminine or masculine, singular or plural, as in ﴿And fight the polytheists all together (kāffatan)﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. Most often, "kāffah" in speech is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of a noun preceding it, as here. So "kāffatan" is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "udkhulū," meaning: in the state of your being all together, with none of you excepted.

Ibn Hishām, in Mughnī al-Labīb, in discussing the fifth aspect of the fifth chapter, on the circumstantial qualifier from the agent and from the object, said: when "kāffah" is used in the sense of totality and comprehensiveness, it is only a circumstantial qualifier of what it applies to, and it is only indefinite, and its modified noun is only a rational being. But al-Zajjāj and al-Zamakhsharī permitted making "kāffah" a circumstantial qualifier of al-silm, and al-silm is feminine. In the Indian glosses on al-Mughnī by al-Damāmīnī, it is stated that "kāffah" occurred as a noun for a non-rational thing, not as a circumstantial qualifier but as a construct, in the letter of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb to the family of Kākilah: "I have granted to the family of Kākilah, from the treasury of the Muslims, two hundred mithqāl of pure gold every year."

Know that prohibiting what the Arabs did not use, when the rules permit it, is a restriction on the language. Rather, following the Arabs in their usage is more conducive to eloquence, but it does not oblige one to stop at it without going beyond it. So when it occurs in the Qur'an, it has been established.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 208–209 (part 2 of 2):

His saying ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ is a warning against what would turn them away from entering into peace (silm), which was commanded, by way of a prohibition against opposing what was commanded. Its benefit is to alert [the reader] that what arises from refusing to enter into peace is among the paths of Satan, who is known for not directing toward good. This prohibition is either more specific than the command, together with an explanation of the reason for the command, if by peace is meant other than the branches of Islam, such as an allusion to what crept into the souls of most of them of aversion to giving humiliation to the polytheists in the treaty of Hudaybiyah, as 'Umar said: "Are we not upon the truth and our enemy upon falsehood, so why should we give humiliation in our religion?" And as Sahl ibn Hunayf said on the day of Siffin: "O people, suspect your opinion, for indeed we saw ourselves on the day of Abu Jandal, and if we could have reversed the action of the Messenger of Allah, we would have reversed it, and Allah and His Messenger know best," informing them that what the Messenger of Allah did would only be good. Likewise Abu Bakr said to 'Umar: "He is the Messenger of Allah, and Allah will never waste him," alerting them that what crept into their souls of aversion to the peace was among the whisperings of Satan. Or it is merely to explain the reason for the command to enter into peace, if by peace is meant the branches of Islam. The meaning of ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan; indeed he is to you a clear enemy﴾, and the metaphor it contains, was already discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on earth [that is] lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168], the verse.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ is a consequence of the prohibition, meaning: if you follow the steps of Satan and thus slip, or if you slip and then follow the steps of Satan. By "slipping" is meant opposition to the prohibition.

The root of zalal is zalaq, that is, the instability of the foot and its movement in the place where it was meant to be planted. Here zalal is used metaphorically for the harm resulting from following Satan, by building an allegory upon an allegory: since the state of one who acts upon the whisperings of Satan was likened to the state of one walking in the footprints of another, the harm that befalls him in that walk was likened to the slipping of the foot while walking on a slippery road. From this it is understood that what Satan commands is likewise in the position of a slippery road, by way of metaphor (makniyyah). His saying "you slipped" is a takhyil (imaginative representation), and it is a tamthiliyyah (allegorical representation), so it belongs to the takhyil which was a metaphor, and the metaphor here lies in its whole construction.

Al-bayyinat: the proofs and miracles, and their coming, their appearance and their clarification, because "coming" is the appearance of the one who comes after his absence.

"In" (in) was used in the conditional for the rarity of this slipping occurring among those who believe, or because the speaker does not desire its occurrence, if the address is to one who believed outwardly but not in his heart.

In it there is an indication that what crept into their souls of aversion to the peace is a great slip.

His saying ﴿then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ is the answer to the condition, and ﴿that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ is the object of "know," and the intended meaning is knowledge of its necessary implication, which is punishment.

Al-'Aziz is fa'il from 'azza, when one becomes strong and is not overcome; its origin is from al-'izzah (might). The discussion of it has already passed at His saying ﴿the pride took him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206], and it is its opposite. So knowing that He, exalted is He, is Mighty implies their certainty that He will punish them and will not let them escape, because the mighty one does not spare the one who opposes him.

Al-Hakim may be an active participle from hakama, meaning one of firm judgment, and it may be that He is the one who perfects affairs, so it is from the use of fa'il with the meaning of mufil. Its relevance here is that the one who perfects affairs does not let escape the one deserving punishment, so the statement is a warning; otherwise all people know that Allah is Mighty and Wise.

You may also take His saying "then know" as treating their knowledge as if it were non-existent, because they did not act according to what it requires of hastening to enter the religion, or of abiding by the rulings of the religion, or of resentment toward the peace which the Messenger concluded.

Allah, exalted is He, only said ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾ as an excuse for them. In it there is an indication that it is obligatory upon them to entrust knowledge to Allah, who revealed to His Messenger the concluding of the peace with the polytheists, for He revealed it only for a benefit, and that is not a weakness for the Muslims, because Allah is Mighty and is never weakened before anyone, and because He is Wise, placing affairs in their proper places, and choosing for the Muslims what contains the victory of His religion. You have seen the clear proofs indicating Allah's care for His Messenger, and that He will not disgrace him nor waste his affair; and among those proofs is what they witnessed of victory on the day of Badr.

If by the intended meaning is entering into Islam or persisting upon it, then the meaning of ﴿if you slip﴾ is: being characterized by what contradicts the command to enter into peace. And by "the clear proofs" is meant the miracles which indicate the truthfulness of the Messenger. Al-Fakhr reported from the tafsir of al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar: the verse indicates that punishment for sin does not occur except after clarification, and that punishment occurs after the clear proofs have come, not after the certainty of the mukallaf, because he is not excused for not attaining certainty if the proofs are sufficient.

In al-Kashshaf it is narrated that a reciter recited this verse as "then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful," and a Bedouin heard him and rejected it, saying: "The Wise does not say such a thing; He does not mention forgiveness at the time of slipping, for that is an incitement to it." End of quote. In al-Qurtubi, from the tafsir of al-Naqqash, such a story is attributed to Ka'b al-Ahbar. And al-Tibi mentioned from al-Asma'i who said: "I was reciting: (And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, a punishment from Allah; and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful)," and beside me was a Bedouin, so he said: "Whose speech is this?" I said: "The speech of Allah." He said: "This is not the speech of Allah." So I became alert and recited ﴿and Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38], and he said: "You are right, this is the speech of Allah." I said: "Do you recite the Qur'an?" He said: "No." I said: "How did you know?" He said: "O you, He is Mighty and judges, so He cuts off; had He forgiven and shown mercy, He would not have cut off."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 210 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, with the angels? The matter would then be decided. And to Allah all matters are returned.﴾

If the pronoun is used in accordance with what is apparent, then the pronoun in "yanzurun" (they await) refers to a previously mentioned referent, which is either ﴿Of mankind is he whose speech about the life of this world pleases you﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:204), or ﴿And of mankind is he who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:207), or both of them together, because both groups await the Day of Recompense. One of the two groups awaits it out of doubt about the threat of punishment, while the other group awaits it with the expectation of the reward of the hopeful.

A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿Do they await anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them? Say: Then wait, I am with you among those who wait﴾ (Yunus 10:102). Their waiting for the days of those who passed away is the waiting of anticipating evil, while the Prophet's waiting along with them is the waiting of affirming his threat.

If the pronoun is used contrary to what is apparent, then it refers to those addressed by His saying, ﴿Enter into peace﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:208) and what follows it, or to those who slipped, which is derived from His saying, ﴿But if you slip﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:209). In that case it is an iltifat (shift) from address to the third person, either merely to renew the listener's energy if it refers to those addressed by His saying, ﴿O you who have believed﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:208), or to add the subtle point of distancing those addressed by His saying, ﴿But if you slip﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:209) from the honour of presence. Al-Qurtubi said: "Do they await" means those who abandon entering into peace. Al-Razi said: the pronoun refers to the Jews, on the basis that they are the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:208), i.e. O you who have believed in Allah and some of His messengers and books according to one of the earlier mentioned interpretations, and on the basis that "al-silm" (peace) is intended to mean Islam. The subtle point of the shift according to this view is the same.

If the pronoun refers to "man yu'jibuka" (whose speech pleases you) or to him and to "man yashri nafsahu" (who sells himself), then the sentence is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because these two strange conditions, of good and of evil, provoke the question of one who asks about the recompense of both groups. So His saying, ﴿Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them﴾ is an answer to that. If the pronoun refers to those who believed, then the sentence ﴿Do they await﴾ is a resumption to incite entering into Islam out of fear of the Day of Recompense or in hope of its reward. If the pronoun refers to those who slipped from His saying, ﴿But if you slip﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:209), then the sentence is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive substitution) of the content of the sentence ﴿Then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:209), because its meaning is: if you slip, then Allah will not let you escape, for He is Mighty and Wise, and non-escape includes the coming of the command of Allah and the angels. If the pronoun refers back to the Jews, then it is a rebuke for them for their obstinacy in refusing to acknowledge the truth of Islam.

In all the possibilities that do not contradict one another, the arrangement of His saying, ﴿Do they await﴾ with the plural pronoun has come as an arrangement that gathers all these meanings together, which is one of the marks of the miraculous nature of this glorious speech, indicating Allah's knowledge of everything.

The particle "hal" conveys both interrogation and confirmation (tahqiq), and this shows that it is set for asking about a matter that one wants to confirm. Therefore the imams of ma'ani (rhetorical meanings) said: "hal" is for seeking the establishment of a judgmental relation (nisba hukmiyya) that becomes known to the questioner. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: the origin of "hal" is that it is a synonym of "qad" in interrogation only, meaning "qad" which is for confirmation, and it acquired the meaning of interrogation from an implied interrogative hamza with it, as is shown by the appearance of the hamza with it in the verse of Zayd al-Khayl:

"Ask the horsemen of Yarbu' about our valour,
Whether they saw us at the slope of the level plain of the hillocks."

He said in al-Mufassal: and from Sibawayh, that "hal" has the meaning of "qad," except that they dropped the alif before it, because it occurs only in interrogation. He means that the interrogative hamza was obligatorily dropped, being dispensed with because "hal" is constantly used in interrogation. No one has said that "hal" comes with the meaning of "qad" free of interrogation, for its occurrences in Arabic speech and in the Qur'an refute that. This was attributed to al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad regarding His saying, ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time from eternity?﴾ (al-Insan 76:1). Perhaps they intended an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical construction. We do not know in Arabic speech of "hal" being combined with the interrogative particle except in this verse, and their argument from it does not stand, because it can be explained as combining two interrogative particles for emphasis, just as a particle is emphasized in some speech, as in the saying of Muslim ibn Ma'bad al-Waliba'i:

"By Allah, there is no cure for what is in me,
Nor for the ailment of theirs, ever."

Here he combined two lam particles of genitive. Whatever the case, "hal" is purely for interrogation in all its positions. This will come in the commentary on His saying, ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time from eternity?﴾ (al-Insan 76:1) in the surah of al-Insan.

The interrogation here is denial beyond doubt, as shown by the exception, so the speech is a statement in the form of a question. "Al-nazar" means waiting and anticipating, and it is said "nazarahu" meaning "tarakkabahu" (awaited him), because one who awaits someone directs his gaze towards his direction to see his figure when it appears. It is not intended here to negate visual sight, i.e. they will not look with their eyes in the Hereafter except at the coming of the command of Allah and the angels, because in reality eyes look at other things. Unless it is meant that their seeing other than that is like nothing because of the severity of the terror of the coming of the command of Allah, in which case it is an ascriptive restriction (qasr idda'i). Or their eyes are deprived of looking at anything else.

This construction is not used for what it was set for, which is denial. Rather it is used either for threat and warning, which is the apparent meaning in accordance with most of the earlier mentioned possibilities regarding the pronoun; or for promise, if the pronoun refers to "man yashri nafsahu" (who sells himself); or for the common element, which is the promise of the manifestation of recompense, if the pronoun refers to both groups; or for mockery (tahakkum), if the intended referent of the pronoun is the hypocrites, the Jews or the polytheists. As for the Jews, they used to say to Musa, ﴿We will not believe you until we see Allah plainly﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:55).

It is possible that this is a report about the Jews, i.e. they will not believe and enter into peace until they see Allah in canopies of clouds, in the manner of His saying, ﴿And even if you brought to those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:145).

As for the polytheists, Allah has related of them, ﴿And they said: We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth﴾ (al-Isra 17:90), up to His saying, ﴿Or you bring Allah and the angels as a guarantee﴾ (al-Isra 17:92). The discussion of this construction and its meaning will come at length when we discuss His saying, ﴿Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds﴾ in surat al-Baqarah.

"Al-zulal" (canopies), with a dhamma then a fatha, is a plural noun of "zullah." The word "zullah" is used for several meanings, and what has become clear to me of its real meaning in the language is that it is a name for something like a raised structure in the air, joined to a wall or resting on pillars, under which one sits to shield from the rays of the sun. It is derived from the noun "zill" (shade), formed on the pattern "fu'lah" in the sense of "maf'ul" (object) or "maf'ul biha" (object of the act), like "qubdah" (a handful, with a dhamma on the qaf) for what is grasped in the hand, and "ghurfah" (a scoop, with a dhamma on the ghayn) for what is scooped by the hand, as in His saying, ﴿except one who takes a handful with his hand﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:249), in the reading of some of the ten readers with a dhamma on the ghayn.

Here it is a metaphor (isti'ara) or a likened thing in an eloquent comparison (tashbih baligh): the great clouds, each cloud of which resembles the canopy of a palace.

"Min al-ghamam" (of clouds) is an explanation of the likened element and it is the indicator (qarina) of the metaphor. Its parallel is His saying, ﴿For them there will be canopies of fire above them and canopies below them﴾ (al-Zumar 39:16).

"Al-ityan" (coming) is the presence of an entity in a place other than where it was previously. The coming was ascribed to Allah in this verse in an affirmative form, so its apparent meaning implies that Allah is described by it. Since coming necessarily involves movement or extension, so as to be located in a place after not having been there, so that coming is valid, and this would imply a body, from which Allah is exalted, the wording must be diverted from its apparent meaning by rational proof. If the speech is a report or mockery, there is no need for interpretation, because their belief in that is refuted by proofs. But if the speech is a threat from Allah, interpretation becomes necessary, because Allah exists in reality but is not described by what belongs to created things, such as movement and extension, as you know. So this must be interpreted according to our view, following the school of al-Ash'ari in interpreting the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses. This interpretation is either in the meaning of "ityan," or in its ascription to Allah, or by implying an omitted noun, either a modifier or an object. To these possibilities return the aspects that the exegetes mentioned.

The first aspect: the earliest generation of the community (Salaf), before the emergence of the doubts of the heretics (malahida), went to affirm the ambiguous attributes without interpretation. So "ityan" is affirmed for Allah, but how it is, is part of the ambiguous, like istiwa' (establishment), nuzul (descent) and ru'yah (seeing). That is, it is a coming that is not like the coming of created things.

As for the way of the later imams of the Ash'aris, to repel the attacks of the heretics, there come several aspects from them. The second aspect: I say it is permissible to interpret Allah's coming as manifestation and attentiveness (al-tajalli wal-i'tina'), if the pronoun refers to "man yashri nafsahu ibtigha'a mardat Allah" (one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah). Or it is a metaphor for the immediate effect of power (ta'alluq al-qudra al-tanjizi) with the manifestation of the recompense, if the pronoun refers to both groups. Or it is a metaphor for annihilation (isti'sal), as one says "atahum al-malik" (the king came upon them) when he punished them. This was said by al-Qurtubi. I say: that applies to every coming ascribed to an avenger, enemy or conqueror, as you say "atahumu al-sabu'" (the beast came upon them) meaning it destroyed them, and "atahumu al-waba'" (the plague came upon them). That is why they say "ata 'alayhi" (came upon him) meaning destroyed him and uprooted him. When that became common, the use of "ityan" spread to its necessary consequence, which is destruction and annihilation. Allah says, ﴿So Allah came to them from where they did not expect﴾ (al-Hashr 59:2), and He says, ﴿So Allah came upon their structure from the foundations﴾ (al-Nahl 16:26). His saying, ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ does not contradict this meaning, because the manifestation of Allah's command and the occurrence of the effect of His power will be enveloped by that, so that the angels may perceive it. The explanation of ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ will come shortly.

The third aspect: the ascription of coming to Allah is a figurative ascription (isnad majazi). What will come to them is the punishment of Allah on the Day of Resurrection or in this world, and His being ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ is an added emphasis of that manifestation and its impact on the observers.

The fourth aspect: there will come to them the speech of Allah that indicates the command, and that speech will be heard from the direction of canopies of clouds, surrounded by the angels.

The fifth aspect: there is an implied noun, so that "ya'tihim amr Allah" (the command of Allah comes to them), i.e. His decree among creation, or "ya'tihim ba's Allah" (the might of Allah comes to them), based on similar instances in the Qur'an: ﴿Or the command of your Lord should come﴾ (al-Nahl 16:33), and His saying, ﴿Then Our might came upon it at night﴾ (al-A'raf 7:4). It is not hidden that the coming in this case must be a metaphor for the manifestation of the command.

The sixth aspect: an implied noun is omitted, its estimate being "ayat Allah" (the signs of Allah) or "bayyinatuhu" (His clear proofs), i.e. the indicators of His power or the indicators of the truthfulness of His messengers. This is made remote by His saying, ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾, unless it returns to the fifth aspect or to the third aspect.

The seventh aspect: there is an implied object indicated by His saying, ﴿Then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:209). The estimate is: that Allah should come to them with the punishment or with His might.

The best is to estimate a general command that includes good and evil, so that the sentence is both a promise and a threat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 210 (part 2 of 2):

I have already discussed, in the commentary on His words ﴿He it is who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are definitive, they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7] in Surat Al 'Imran, what can be drawn from it: that the attributes, rulings, and actions ascribed to God, the Exalted, as they occur in the Book and the Sunnah (the Prophet's normative practice and sayings), fall into four categories. The first category: God is described by it in its literal sense, such as existence and life, but in a manner that differs from what is familiar to us. The second: God is described by a necessary implication of its meaning, which has become so common that the meaning that comes to mind is the appropriate meaning without the implications, such as mercy, anger, good pleasure, and love. The third: it is ambiguous, but its interpretation (ta'wil) is apparent. The fourth: it is ambiguous to a very high degree.

[Page 286]

His words ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ are more problematic than the attribution of coming (ityan) to God, the Exalted, because it implies the notion of place (zarfiyyah), which is impossible for God, the Exalted. Its interpretation may be either that (fi) here means (bi), i.e., (He will come to them with canopies of clouds), which are canopies that carry punishment, such as thunderbolts, a violent wind, or the like, if the punishment is worldly; or ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ comprises that which indicates the command of God, the Exalted, or His punishment, ﴿And if they should see a piece of the sky falling, they would say, "A layered cloud"﴾ [al-Tur: 44]. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to show fear in his face whenever he saw a cloud, lest there be punishment in it. Or the canopies are over His speech, the Exalted; or they are veils over lights that God will make a sign for people on the Day of Resurrection at the beginning of the separation of judgment, whose indication is grasped by the people of the place of standing through direct inner perception (al-inkishaf al-wijdani). In the tafsirs of al-Qurtubi and al-Razi it is said that the verse contains an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and the original sentence is: that God and the angels should come to them in canopies of clouds, so the clouds are a container for the coming of the angels. It is narrated that Ibn Mas'ud recited it in this way. All of these interpretations are based on the view that this is a report about a future matter. As for taking the pronoun in (yanzurun) to refer to the hypocrites among the polytheists or the Jews, with the sentence being mocking, meaning: what are they waiting for in delaying their entry into Islam? They are waiting for nothing but that God should come to them in states they believe in, so that He speaks to them and they enter the religion. For they said to Musa: ﴿We will not believe you until we see God openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55], and they believed that God was in the clouds. Or the intended meaning may be an allusive rebuke directed at the polytheists. Some of the interpretations have already been mentioned together with the interpretation of coming.

The majority of reciters read (wa al-mala'ikatu) in the nominative, as a conjunction with the Name of Majesty (God), and the attribution of coming to the angels is because they are the ones who come with the command of God or His punishment, and they are entrusted with carrying out His decree. So the attribution of coming to them is literal. If the coming attributed to God, the Exalted, is used in a figurative sense, then its use with respect to the angels is in its literal meaning; this is an instance of using a word in both its literal and figurative senses. And if the attribution of coming to God, the Exalted, is a figurative attribution (majaz fi al-isnad, a figure in the predication), then its attribution to the angels through conjunction is literal in the predication, and there is no obstacle to this, because the predicative figure is an expression for the speaker's intention together with a clue. Hamid ibn Thawr said, praising 'Abd al-Malik:

"The One who lit up guidance has brought you to me, ∗∗∗ and light and Islam are a guide over you."

He attributed the coming, with respect to him, to God, which is a literal attribution. Then he attributed it by conjunction to the light and Islam. The attribution of the coming to these two is figurative, because they are the cause of the coming. Do you not see that he said (over you is a guide)?

[Page 287]

Abu Ja'far read (wa al-mala'ikati) with the genitive (al-mala'ikati) as a conjunction with (zulal), meaning (canopies).

As for His words ﴿and the matter is decided﴾: it is either a conjunction with the clause ﴿Do they await...﴾ if that clause is a report about those spoken of, and the past tense verb here is meant in the sense of the future, but it is used in the past form to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence or the imminence of its occurrence. The meaning is: they await nothing but that God should come to them, and the matter will be decided. Or it is a conjunction with the clause ﴿Do they await...﴾ as a threat or a promise, and the verb is likewise in the future sense. The meaning is: they await nothing but the coming of the command of God and the decision of the matter. Or it is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), with the past tense retaining its original sense and "qad" being omitted, whether the clause ﴿Do they await...﴾ is a report, a promise, or a threat; that is, "and then the matter has been decided." Or it is an admonition that, if they are waiting for Muhammad's truthfulness to be confirmed by God and the angels coming to them, then if that happens, the matter will have been decided, that is, the destruction will have been made binding upon them, like His words ﴿And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" If We had sent down an angel, the matter would certainly have been decided, and then they would not be reprieved﴾ [al-An'am: 8]. Qada' (decision) means completion and finishing.

The definite article in (al-amr, the matter) is either for the genus, intended to encompass everything, meaning all matters have been decided; or it is for a known reference, meaning the matter of these people, that is, their punishment; or the matter known to all people, which is the recompense.

His words ﴿and to God all matters are returned﴾ are a concluding statement (tadhyil) that comprehends the meaning of: and the matter has been decided. The basic meaning of return (ruju') is coming back to the place from which the one returning departed, and it is used figuratively for the end and final purpose of a thing and the manifestation of its effect. From this is His words ﴿Surely to God all matters come to their end﴾ [al-Shura: 53].

The verb (raja'a) may be transitive: you say, "I returned Zayd to his town," and its verbal noun is (al-raj'). It may also be intransitive: you say, "Zayd returned to his town," and its verbal noun is (al-ruju'). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read (turja'u) with a dammah on the ta' and a fathah on the jim, as the imperfect of (arja'ahu) or the passive imperfect of (raja'ahu), meaning: it causes the matters to be returned, the one returning them being back to God. The agent is omitted on this reading, either because there is no conventionally determined agent for this returning, or because it is omitted to avoid the apparent contradiction between the Name of Majesty being the agent of returning and being the object governed by the preposition (ila, to). The remaining seven readers read it in the active voice, from (raja'a), whose verbal noun is (al-ruju'), so that (al-umuru) is the subject of (tarji'u, it returns).

[p. 288]

﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them. And whoever substitutes the favour of God after it has come to him, then indeed God is severe in punishment.﴾

This verse, in relation to the preceding one, stands as proof of the meaning of the previous sentence. His saying ﴿Do they await...﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:210], whether it is a report, a threat, a promise, or a mockery, and whatever the referent of the pronoun in it is according to the earlier possibilities, indicates in every case an allusion to groups who are deluded, persistent in disbelief, and who derive little benefit from the clear signs. So it is fitting that this be followed by directing their attention to what reached them of the little benefit the Children of Israel derived from the signs of guidance given to them, despite the scarcity of the effect of the signs upon them in spite of their abundance. For they opposed their messenger, then believed in him with a weak faith, and then altered the religion after that alteration.

On the possibility that the pronoun in "yanzurun" (they await) refers to the People of the Book, namely the Children of Israel, then the shift here from the pronoun to the noun, by saying "Children of Israel," serves to intensify the address and to expose their condition, and the argument against them becomes stronger in that case: they had seen many signs, so it would have been appropriate for them to hasten to believe in the Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, because they are the people most knowledgeable of the conditions of the messengers. In any case, this verse and what follows are parenthetical digressions between the successive legislative topics in this surah.

"Sal" (ask) is the imperative of "sa'ala, yas'alu," its original form being "isal," and the hamzah was dropped for lightness after its vowel was transferred to the consonant before it, by analogy with the transfer of the vowel of a weak letter, because the hamzah resembles a weak letter. When the beginning of the imperfect became vowelled, the connecting hamzah (hamzat al-wasl) was dispensed with. It is also said that "sal" is the imperative of "sa'ala," whose hamzah was changed into an alif, like the imperative of "khafa, yakhafu," which is "khaf." The Arabs use this lightening greatly in "sa'ala," both in the past tense and in the imperative; however, when the imperative follows a waw or a fa', they generally abandon this lightening.

The one commanded to ask is the Messenger, because he is the one whom the Children of Israel are expected to answer when he asks them, since they do not heed the questioning of anyone else. This is because what is meant by the question is a question of affirmation for the purpose of rebuke. The word "su'al" (question) is used for whatever interrogative particles are used for.

The purpose of the affirmation is to show their acknowledgement of their opposition to what the signs require, so rebuke arises from this affirmation. Therefore the aim is not that they explicitly confess, but merely that they have no means to deny.

[p. 289]

By "Children of Israel" is meant those present among the Jews. The pronoun in "ataynahum" (We gave them) refers to them, but what is meant is the giving to their predecessors, because the characteristics established for the ancestors of tribes and nations may validly be attributed to their descendants, since the effects are ascribed to all of them, as is common in the terminology of past nations, among the Arabs and others.

It is also possible that the meaning of their being given the signs is that, when they transmitted the signs of their messengers in their books and became certain of them, it was as if they had been given them directly.

"Kam" (how many) is a noun denoting an indefinite number. It may be interrogative, or it may be informative. When it is informative it indicates a large indefinite number, and for that reason it requires a specifying noun (tamyiz) in the informative use. Here it is interrogative, as its occurrence within the scope of the question indicates, so what is asked about is the number of the signs.

The verb "sa'ala" should by rule take two objects, after the pattern of "kasa" (to clothe), that is, its first object is not originally a subject and predicate, and the clause "kam ataynahum" cannot be its second object, since the interrogation is not what is sought, but is itself the very act of seeking. Hence the verb "sal" is suspended (mu'allaq) from the second object for the sake of the interrogation, and the clause "kam ataynahum" occupies the position of the second object and takes its place.
