Ṣāḥib al-Kashshāf considered it an *iltifat*, on the basis of the preceding words ﴿God guided those who believed to what they differed about﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], and that this would require saying "Or did they suppose," i.e., those who believed. The more apparent view is that when the shift from one theme to another occurred through the digressive *idrab* contained in "am," the discourse became a pure opening, and by this the consideration of a shift from one style to another is reinforced. Thus the *iltifat* here is not a matter to be considered, in verification.

Entering Paradise here means entering it without prior toil and trial. It is the entry of those who have fulfilled every obligation upon them and fallen short in none of it. Otherwise, entry into Paradise is reckoned for every believer, even if adversity and hardship do not reach him, or reach him and he does not bear them patiently. The meaning is that patience in these things and not complaining about them brings forgiveness of sins. Or the intended meaning is that when hardship befalls them, they endure and do not apostatize from the religion. In this sense, entry into Paradise is conditional on patience in the face of hardship and adversity. The occurrence of this condition is a divine custom (*sunnah*) among the followers of the messengers at the first appearance of the religion, and it is among the causes of the increase of the merits of following the messengers. For this reason the Muslims were prepared to receive it before it occurred, out of kindness to them, so that its occurrence would be easier for them.

The Muslims in the early period of Islam suffered hardship and adversity from the harm of the polytheists, were driven from their homes, and bore the bitterness of exile. When they reached Medina, they encountered harm from the Jews to their persons, and harm from the polytheists of Mecca to their relatives and property, which clouded the pure welcome of the Helpers (*Ansar*) toward them. Likewise the Helpers suffered severe constraint in their own homes, and even in their property, to the point that the Helpers would offer the emigrants (*Muhajirun*) that they relinquish to them a share of their wealth.

*Lamma* (not yet) is a sister of *lam* (not) in indicating the negation of the verb, but it is composed of *lam* and the negating *ma*. Therefore it conveys emphasis of negation, because it is composed of two particles of negation. For this reason, negation with it indicates that the hearer was anticipating the occurrence of the verb negated by it, so the negation with it is a negation of imminent occurrence. It also indicates that the occurrence of what is negated by it will be after some time. This usage is supported by induction, and they cited in its support the verse of al-Nabigha:

*Azifa al-tarahhulu ghayra anna rikabana*
*lamma tazul bi-rihalina wa-ka-an qad*

The departure has drawn near, but our riding beasts have not yet moved from their saddles, and [it is as if] it had.

He negated with *lamma* and then said *wa-ka-an qad*, i.e., it is as if it had already moved.

The *waw* is for the circumstantial (*hal*): i.e., did you suppose entering Paradise while the thing you await, namely the touch of hardship and adversity, has not yet befallen you? For you will not enter Paradise in that untroubled manner, free of trial, if you do not bear what is of that kind.

*Ityan* (coming) is a metaphor for occurrence, because a thing that comes into existence after non-existence is treated as if it came from a distant place.

*Mathal* (likeness) means what resembles in form and condition, as already explained in His saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17].

*Alladhina khalaw* (those who passed away) are the nations that went by and perished. The original sense of *khalaw* is: the place became empty of them. This was intensified in ascribing the verb, so the attribute of their place was ascribed to them.

[p. 316]

The *min* in *min qablikum* is attached to *khalaw* merely for clarification, and to show the connection between the two groups.

*Massa* (to touch), in its literal sense, is the contact of one body with another. It is used metaphorically for befalling and reaching something. From this comes *mass al-shaytan* (the touch of the devil), i.e., the harm of the jinn reaching the intellect, and *mass saqar* (the touch of Saqar), i.e., what of its fire reaches one. And *massahu al-faqr wa al-darr* means poverty and harm befell him. Its most common use is for the occurrence of evil, as He said: ﴿When harm touches a man, he calls upon his Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 8]; ﴿When harm touches a man, he calls upon Us﴾ [Yunus: 12]; ﴿When evil touches him, he has abundant supplication﴾ [Fussilat: 51]; ﴿And do not touch them with harm﴾ [al-A'raf: 73]. So the meaning here is: hardship and adversity befell them.

The discussion of *al-ba'sa'* and *al-darra'* has already been presented under His saying ﴿and those patient in hardship and adversity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

His saying *wa-zulzilu* (and they were shaken) means they were disturbed or agitated. What was actually disturbed was the order of their livelihood. He said: ﴿There the believers were tried and shaken with a severe shaking﴾ [al-Ahzab: 11]. *Zalzala* is the violent movement of a body from its place, and from it comes *zilzal al-ard* (earthquake). The form *zulzila* is *fu'lila*, and the doubling in it indicates repetition, as He said: ﴿so they will be thrown down into it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 94]. They also said *lamlama bi-al-makan* when he settled in a place in a manner of residence.

*Hatta* (until) indicates the limit of the touching and the shaking, i.e., the matter reached a point at which the Messenger and those with him say ﴿When will God's help come?﴾

Since the verse informs of a touch that befell those among earlier nations, and warns of the occurrence of its like upon those addressed at the time of revelation, it is permissible for the verb *yaqula* (says) to be understood as the saying of the messenger of a previous nation, i.e., they were shaken until the messenger of the shaken said so; here *al* is for a specific reference (*ahd*). Or it may mean until every messenger to a nation that preceded said so; then *al* is for totality (*istighraq*), and the verb is taken as narrating that astonishing state, so it is put in the nominative after *hatta*, because the verb intended to express a present state is nominative. Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read it in the nominative. It is also permissible to understand the saying as that of the messenger of those addressed, peace be upon him, with *al* here for specific reference. The meaning would be: they were shaken like them until the Messenger said so, and then the verb is in the subjunctive, because the saying had not yet occurred at that time. The rest of the ten readers read it thus. The nominative reading is more appropriate to the apparent context, and the subjunctive reading is more appropriate to the purpose for which the discourse is presented. Both readings achieve both purposes. *Matá* (when) is an interrogative used to express impatience concerning the time of help.

His saying ﴿Surely God's help is near﴾ is a new (*mustanif*) statement, as indicated by its opening with *ala* (surely). It is a glad tiding from God Almighty to the Muslims that help is near, after they had suffered from the calamities mentioned at the beginning of the verse what filled their hearts with terror. Its purpose is to honour this community by ensuring that what touches them does not reach the extent of what touched those before them, and to honour the Messenger ﷺ by sparing him from having to say what the messengers before him said of impatience for God's help, since God's help would come to this community before it was impatiently awaited. This points to the conquest of Mecca.

*[p. 318]*

This is a fresh (ibtida'i) resumptive sentence, answering a question that some of the Muslims put to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Wahidi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the questioner was 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh al-Ansari, who had wealth, and he said: "O Messenger of God, what should I give in charity, and to whom should I spend?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The questioners were the believers, meaning that the question about the details of spending, which they had been commanded to do in general terms more than once, was repeated, and so they asked for clarification of who should receive their spending." The placement of this verse in this position is either because its revelation came right after the verse before it, or because it was deliberately placed here to gather a group of rulings introduced by the phrase "They ask you" (yas'aluna-ka), which are six rulings. It has also been said that it was revealed after the obligation of zakat, so that it explains the recipients of zakat. It was then abrogated (naskh, "abrogation," i.e. superseded) by the verse ﴿Charity is only for the poor and the needy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60] in the Surah of "Bara'ah" (al-Tawbah). It is therefore a specification that excludes parents, close relatives and orphans, even though they are not among the eight categories mentioned in the verse of al-Tawbah.

"Mada" (what) is an interrogative about the one who spends (al-munfiq), with the fatha on the fa' (mādhā, with the fatha). The meaning of the interrogation about the one who spends is a question about the circumstances by which it would be accepted by God. Spending is a well-known reality among humans, and the questioners already knew it in the Jahiliyyah.

In the Jahiliyyah they used to spend on their families, on their drinking companions, and they spent on gambling (maysir, "games of chance"). They would say: "So-and-so completes his maysir-arrows (aysar)," meaning that he pays off, from the wealth of gambling, the shares due from his aysar, and they boasted of squandering wealth.

So in Islam they asked about what among this is considered valid and beyond that. Therefore the answer corresponded to the question when it was answered: ﴿Say: whatever good you spend, it is for parents and close relatives﴾, and so it came with an explanation of the proper recipients of spending. This kind of thing is known through knowledge of its instances. Therefore there is no employment of the "wise approach" (al-uslub al-hakim, i.e. answering a question other than the one asked) in this answer, as has been said, since it is not conceivable that they would ask about the spent wealth in the sense of asking about the type that is spent, whether gold, silver or food, because the purposes of rational people are not connected to asking about this. They know that the aim of spending is to convey benefit to the one who receives it, so it is necessary that the question was about the manner and the recipients of spending. Let it not trouble you in this that the question here used "mā" (what), which is used to ask about the genus and not about accidents (al-'awarid). That is a logical technical term, used to bring closer what they translated of the divisions based on the Greek language, and which al-Sakkaki adopted, because he is preoccupied with the terminology of the logicians; and the Arabic usage does not testify to that.

Al-khayr (good) means wealth, as was previously stated in His words ﴿if he leaves behind wealth (khayran)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180] in the verse of bequest.

"Mā anfaqtum" is a conditional clause, so the verb anfaqtum is intended in the future sense, as the conditional requires. It was expressed in the past tense to show eagerness for the condition to be fulfilled, so it is treated as though it had already occurred and been settled.

The lam in "li-l-wālidayn" (for the parents) indicates ownership, in the sense of entitlement: the one deserving of it is the parents. That is, if you spend, then spend for the parents, or give to the parents. Their identity was previously explained in His words ﴿and gave wealth out of love for it to relatives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], and the verse.

The verse indicates a command to spend on these people and an encouragement to do so. It concerns the spending that is not part of the right of wealth (I mean zakat), nor is it part of the right of the person as a person, like a wife. Rather, this spending is the right of Muslims over one another, for meeting need and for ease. The closest of the Muslims in kinship to the needy among them are most fit to undertake it. Some of it is obligatory, such as the maintenance of poor parents and of young children who have no wealth, until they become able to earn or until the duty of maintenance passes to someone other than the parents. All of this follows the custom of their peers. Among the jurists there is disagreement about defining the kinship that makes spending obligatory.

This verse is therefore not abrogated by the verse of zakat, since there is no contradiction between them such that abrogation would be needed. Nor does the wording of this verse indicate obligation, so as to suppose that it was revealed about obligatory charity before zakat was made obligatory. "Ibn al-sabil" (the wayfarer) is the stranger away from his tribe who passes through on a journey, and he is given what he needs.

His words ﴿And whatever good you do, indeed God is Knowing of it﴾ are a concluding statement (tadhyil). The intended meaning of His words ﴿indeed God is Knowing of it﴾ is a metonymy (kinaya) for the reward for it, since when the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, is obeyed by someone in His command, nothing stands between that person and the reward for it.

The generality of ﴿whatever good you do﴾ includes obligatory and voluntary acts, so it covers expenditures and other things.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 216 (part 1 of 2):

Page 319

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. But it may be that you hate a thing which is good for you, and that you love a thing which is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾

The connection: fighting belongs to the hardship (al-ba'sa', "adversity") mentioned in His words ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise without such as came to those who passed away before you? They were touched by misfortune and adversity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. The nations before us were charged with it: the Children of Israel were charged with fighting the Canaanites along with Musa (peace be upon him), and they were charged with fighting along with Talut, who is Saul, with Dawud (David). Dhu al-Qarnayn was charged with punishing the wrongdoers among the people who were in the west of the earth.

The phrase "kutiba 'alaykum" (it has been prescribed for you) is among the forms of obligation, and it has already been discussed in the verse on bequest. The "al" in "al-qital" (the fighting) is for the genus, and fighting is only against enemies, so it is general in a customary sense, meaning: fighting the enemy of the religion has been prescribed for you.

The address is to the Muslims, and their enemies at that time were the polytheists, because they opposed them in religion and harmed the Messenger and the believers. Thus the fighting commanded is jihad (struggle, here meaning fighting) to raise high the word of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ was not permitted to fight at the beginning of the appearance of Islam. Then he was permitted to do so by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39]. Then the verse on fighting those who initiate fighting against the Muslims was revealed, in His words: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190], as has been mentioned just before.

This verse was revealed concerning the incident of the expedition of 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, as will come, and that was in the seventeenth month after the Hijrah. The verse appears in this surah together with a group of legislations and systems it contains, such as His words: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183], ﴿Retaliation has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178], ﴿It has been prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180].

According to the preferred view, His words ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾ are a report about a ruling that had already preceded, to increase its confirmation, and so that the discourse may move from it to His words ﴿though it is hateful to you﴾ and what follows. Or it is a repetition of the establishment of the obligation of fighting, for further emphasis. Or it is a fresh establishment of the obligation of fighting, if this was the first verse revealed on this meaning, based on the view that His words, exalted is He, ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39] are a permission for fighting and a preparation for it, not an imposition of it.

His words ﴿though it is hateful to you﴾ are a necessary circumstantial clause (hal lazimah), and it may be connected with the conjunction "wa" (and). You may also make it a second sentence coordinated with the sentence ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾. However, since this information was known to the addressees

Page 320

it becomes necessary that the intended meaning of the report is its necessary benefit, namely: "We have prescribed it for you while We know that it is burdensome for you." This view is perhaps preferred by His words after this: ﴿And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾

Al-kurh with a dammah on the kaf means dislike and aversion of the nature toward a thing, and al-kurh with a fatha is, according to the more correct view, the same. It was said that al-kurh with a dammah means hardship and aversion of the nature, while with a fatha it means compulsion, and what comes upon a person from another, such as being forced to do something with harm or hardship. Since both readings are recited here and in His words ﴿His mother carried him with hardship and bore him with hardship﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15], and since there is no meaning of compulsion here or there, it is necessary that it means dislike and the nature's refusal, as the Hamasi al-'Uqayli said:

"By the dislike of our nobles, O family of 'Amr, we set out against you with sharp-edged blades."

They related it with a dammah on the kaf and with a fatha.

Moreover, His words after this, ﴿But it may be that you hate a thing which is good for you﴾, which comes as a concluding summary, is evidence that what precedes it is a verbal noun meaning dislike, so that it is a particular instance of the particulars of "that you hate a thing."

The author of al-Kashshaf strained to interpret the fatha in this verse and the other verse as a metaphor. al-Tibi and al-Taftazani confirmed it with what contains artificiality. Since it is a verbal noun, reporting it is an intensification of the attribute's firmness in the subject reported about, like the saying of al-Khansa':

"It is nothing but advancing and retreating."

That is, it advances and retreats. It was also said that al-kurh is a name for the disliked thing, like al-khubr.

So fighting is hateful to souls, because it comes between the fighter and his tranquillity, his pleasures, his sleep, his food, his family and his home. It compels a person to enmity with one who was his companion, and exposes him to the danger of destruction or the pain of wounds. But in it there is the removal of the humiliation resulting from the domination of men and their subjugation. In the hadith: "Do not wish for encounter with the enemy; but when you meet them, be patient." This is an indication that fighting is among the necessities that people do not love except when leaving it would lead to great harm. Al-'Uqayli said:

"We weep when we kill you, over you, and we kill you as though we did not care."

Page 321

It is known that the dislike of the nature does not contradict receiving the obligation with it willingly, because most obligations are not free of hardship.

Then, if the verse is a report about a legislation that has passed, the clause ﴿and it is hateful﴾ may be a narration of a state that passed, namely the time of the Muslims' small numbers, when imposing fighting was burdensome upon them. Among its rulings was that one of them was required to stand against ten of the polytheist enemies, and that is among the causes of their dislike of fighting. Accordingly, it does not follow that this dislike remained until the time of the revelation of this verse. It is possible that it was revealed concerning the matter of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, when they had disliked the treaty and preferred fighting, because at that time they were a large army. Then it is a reminder to them that Allah knows better their interests: He imposed fighting upon them when they were disliking it, and He imposed the treaty upon them at a time when they loved fighting. So that is omitted because of the context, and the intended purpose is to lead to His words ﴿But it may be that you hate a thing which is good for you﴾, so that their souls may be reassured that the treaty they disliked is good for them, as has been mentioned in the exchange of 'Umar with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and with Abu Bakr. In the verse there is ihtibak (a rhetorical device of omission on both sides): the discourse is about fighting, so the implied structure is: "Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you, and you have been prevented from it, and it is beloved to you; and it may be that you hate fighting, and it is good for you, and it may be that you love it, and it is bad for you." If, however, the verse is a newly established legislation, then the dislike exists at the time of the revelation of the verse, and so it is not revealed concerning the matter of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. The first of the two views is, in my opinion, the more apparent, to fit His words that follow it: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217].

His words ﴿But it may be that you hate a thing which is good for you﴾ are a concluding summary (tadhyil), needed to remove the astonishment arising from His words ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you﴾, because if it is hateful, the mercy of Allah toward His creation would require that He not prescribe it for them. So He concludes with this to remove that.

The clause "wa 'asa" (and it may be) is coordinated with the clause ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾. The clause ﴿and it is good for you﴾ is a circumstantial clause from "shay'an" (a thing), according to the correct view on the coming of a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun. This speech is a gentle kindness from Allah, exalted is He, to His Messenger and the believers. Although He, glorified is He, is independent of explaining and giving reasons, since He commands and is obeyed, nevertheless explaining the wisdom lessens the hardship of the obligation, and it trains the Muslims to receive the Law explained and made easy. It indicates that the wisdom of obligation depends on interests and the averting of harms, and does not depend on the agreement or disagreement of the nature. For the nature may dislike a thing in which is its benefit, and may love a thing in which is its ruin, and that is by considering consequences and ends,

Page 322

for a thing may be pleasant and agreeable, yet its commission leads to destruction; and a thing may be hateful and repugnant, yet in its commission there is righteousness.

The common state of people is heedlessness of consequence and end, or ignorance of them. Therefore the Laws and their bearers among the scholars and the wise would urge people toward actions and abstentions by considering ends and consequences.

If you say: What is the wisdom in making many beneficial things disliked, and many harmful things loved? Why did Allah not make all the beneficial loved and all the harmful disliked, so that souls would be drawn to the beneficial by their choice and would avoid the harmful likewise, and we would be spared the burden of the question of the good and the better that al-Ash'ari disputed with his teacher al-Jubba'i, and over which al-Ash'ari parted from the doctrine of the Mu'tazila? I say: The wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, built the order of the world upon the existence of the beneficial and the harmful, the good and the wicked, among essences, attributes and events. He entrusted to man authority over this world, by virtue of creating man fit for both matters, and He showed him the two paths of good and evil, as we have set forth at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213]. Wisdom required that the beneficial be more than the harmful. Perhaps the existence of harmful things was created by Allah so that they might serve as an instrument for driving some people to follow the beneficial, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿In it is severe might and benefits for mankind﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. He established the order of this world upon the existence of opposites, and made human perfection attained when all the beneficial attributes are present in a person, such that when some beneficial attributes in him are deficient, the rest of his beneficial attributes are diminished or vanish. Allah made perfection rarer than deficiency, so that the ranks of souls might appear in this world, and the extent of human intellects in it, so that people acquire, waste, harm and benefit; thus the harmful increases and the beneficial decreases by what people earn and do. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: The evil and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of evil impresses you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 100].

Just as the perfect and excellent essences became fewer than their opposites, the attributes of perfection became hard to attain, and their rarity and preciousness were enclosed by the difficulty of attaining them for mankind and by the dangers and toils surrounding them. For if they were things toward which souls are drawn easily, people would be equal in them, the ranks of perfection would not appear, and there would be no rivalry among people in acquiring virtues and facing hardships to attain them. Abu al-Tayyib said:

"There is no merit in them for courage and generosity, nor in the patience of the young man, were it not for meeting the peoples."

This is the cause of the difficulty of perfections for souls.

Page 323

Then Allah, exalted is He, made the order of existence in this world through the generation of one thing from between two things, which is what is expressed by pairing (al-izdiwaj). However, this generation occurs in essences by the known manner of generation, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And of all fruits He made in it two mates, two﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3]. As for its occurrence in meanings, it happens only by the attribute arising from between two opposite attributes that are balanced in a soul, whence from their balance a third attribute arises.

Virtues were made to be generated from deficiencies: courage from recklessness and cowardice, generosity from extravagance and miserliness. There is no doubt that a thing generated from two things is less than what it was generated from, for it is less than a third. Not every time two attributes exist does a third attribute come from them; rather, there must be balance and equilibrium between those two opposite attributes, and that is rare to obtain. Undoubtedly, this rarity dictates that souls have little habituation to these attributes, so they are difficult for them because of their little habituation to them.

Beyond that, Allah set for people a system for using beneficial and harmful things in what they were created for, so the responsibility in the form of their use falls upon man. This entire system is a preparation for the ranks of created beings in the eternal world, the world of immortality, which is the Hereafter, as it is said: "This world is the field of the Hereafter." By this the theory of refutation is completed, with which Shaykh al-Ash'ari refuted his teacher al-Jubba'i concerning their principle of the obligation of the good and the better. Thus al-Ash'ari's discussion is a refutation, and what we have said here is an argument by way of support and reversal, moving into demonstration.

The clause ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾ is a concluding summary (tadhyil) for all of the preceding. The two objects of "yaʿlamu" (knows) and "taʿlamūna" (you know) are omitted, but what precedes them indicates them; that is, "And Allah knows the good and the evil, while you do not know them." This is because Allah knows things as they really are, whereas knowledge is confused for people, so they consider what is agreeable to be beneficial and what is repugnant to be harmful.

The purpose of this is to teach the Muslims to receive the command of Allah the Exalted with the belief that it is righteousness and good. And that what the nature of which has not become clear to us, among the actions imposed upon us, we are certain that in it there is an attribute suited to the ruling of the Shariah concerning it; so we seek that attribute as far as possible, perhaps we will attain it, in order to derive rulings from it and to analogize. Under this fall the questions of the methods of establishing the effective cause (ʿillah, the operative cause of a ruling), because Allah the Exalted does not issue His command and prohibition except in accordance with His knowledge.

[Page 324]

The most important details concerning the fighting that was prescribed for the Muslims in the verse before this one are whether the fighting between them and the polytheists happened during the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum). This was a prohibition (mahjar) among the Arabs since ancient times, and Islam did not mention its abolition, because it served public interests. God the Exalted said: ﴿God made the Kaaba, the Sacred House, a means of standing for the people, and the sacred month﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 97]. So the situation prompted a question about whether the sanctity of the sacred month continued in the view of Islam.

Al-Wahidi, in Asbab al-nuzul (occasions of revelation), related from al-Zuhri in a mursal (a report in which a link in the chain is missing) and al-Tabari related from Urwa ibn al-Zubayr in a mursal and in a lengthy form, that this verse was revealed concerning the matter of the sariyya (military expedition) of Abdullah ibn Jahsh. The Prophet (ﷺ) had sent him with eight of his companions to intercept a caravan of Quraysh at Batn Nakhla in Jumada al-Akhira in the second year after the Hijra. The Muslims encountered the caravan, which contained merchandise from al-Ta'if, and Amr ibn al-Hadrami was in charge of it. A man among the Muslims killed Amr, and they captured two of his companions, who were Uthman ibn Abdullah ibn al-Mughira and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, while Nawfal ibn Abdullah ibn al-Mughira fled from them. The Muslims seized booty. That was the first day of Rajab, though they thought it was from Jumada al-Akhira. This weighed heavily on Quraysh, who said: "Muhammad has made the sacred month lawful," and they spread this criticism, and so this verse was revealed. It is said that the Prophet (ﷺ) returned the booty and the two captives to them; and it is said that he returned the two captives and kept the booty.

If this is established, then the revelation of this verse occurred a long time before the revelation of the verse ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqara: 216] and the verse ﴿Fight in the way of God those who fight you﴾ [al-Baqara: 190]. When those two verses were revealed after this one, their placement in the recitation before it was by a specific divine directive (tawqif khass), so that this verse would complete what those two other verses included. This has parallels in many verses with respect to revelation and recitation.

In my view, the more evident position is that this verse was revealed after the verse that precedes it, and that it is a complement and confirmation of the verse ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾ [al-Baqara: 194].

The question mentioned here is the question of the polytheists to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of al-Hudaybiyya: whether fighting may take place in the sacred month, as was previously explained at the words of God the Exalted ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾ [al-Baqara: 194]. This suits His words here ﴿and hindering from the way of God﴾, etc. It is also said that the question was of the polytheists concerning fighting in the sariyya of Abdullah ibn Jahsh.

The sentence is therefore a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), and it responds to the people's question about fighting in the sacred month. Its placement right after the verse ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 216] is evidently appropriate.

The definite article in "al-shahr al-haram" (the sacred month) is the generic definite (ta'rif al-jins), and for this reason the replacement of the indefinite noun in His words ﴿fighting in it﴾ was made well. It is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition), which permits replacing a definite noun with an indefinite one, unlike badal al-ba'd (partitive apposition). Moreover, the qualification of the indefinite noun here by the phrase "in it" makes it equivalent to a definite.

The meaning is to explain the ruling for any of the sacred months and for any fighting. If the question was a denial from the polytheists, then it is evident that the intended meaning is the category of these months; and likewise if it was an inquiry from the Muslims. The fact that the incident that gave rise to the question occurred in a specific month does not require restricting the question to that month, since this would not occur to the questioner. Rather, the intent of the question was about the continuation of this ruling, which was established among them before Islam, and it does not single out one month over another.

The method of apposition was chosen here, whereas the apparent form would have been to say: "They ask you about fighting in the sacred month." The emphasis on the sacred month serves to alert that the question is about the sacred month: will fighting take place in it? Not about fighting: will it take place in the month? Both meanings are close to each other. However, the placement of the sacred month first serves to satisfy the importance of that matter. This is a point regarding the use of explicative apposition ('atf al-bayan) which is beneficial in many contexts. Furthermore, the method of inclusive apposition creates suspense by presenting the general first and then the detail. The indefinite "fighting" is intended to be general, since the subject of the question is not a specific fighting nor fighting in a specific month, but rather this category within this category. "In it" is an adverbial phrase of description (zarf sifa) modifying "fighting," specifying it.

His words ﴿Say: Fighting in it is a great (matter)﴾ repeat the word "fighting" explicitly in a place where a pronoun could have been used, so that the answer is explicit and it is not supposed that the sacred month itself is the great thing. Also so that the answer corresponds to the question in wording. He did not define the word "fighting" a second time with the article, although it was mentioned earlier in the question, because it is sufficient without definition, since the two descriptions are the same in the wording of the question and the wording of the answer, which is the adverbial phrase "in it." The purpose of defining an indefinite noun with the article when it is repeated is only to specify that the intended thing is that first one and not something else, and this has been achieved by the identical description. Al-Taftazani said: "So the subject of the question is the subject of the answer and nothing else, contrary to what has been imagined, based on the claim that when an indefinite noun is repeated as indefinite it becomes other than the first. This is not an inescapable rule; it means that this depends on the contextual indicators."

The answer is legislation (tashri') if the question came from the Muslims, and an acknowledgment and silencing (i'tiraf wa ibkat) if the question was a denial from the polytheists, because they expected that he would answer them by permitting fighting, so that they would incite the Arabs and those in whose hearts there is sickness.

The word "great" (kabir) originally means one large in body among its kind. It is used figuratively for the strong, the numerous, the aged, and the grave. This is a metaphor (isti'ara) based on the comparison of the intelligible to the perceptible: the strong among its kind is compared to the large in body among individuals, because it is familiar that the strong is powerful. Here it means great in sins, by the context, like calling a sin a "major sin" (kabira), and like the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "They are not being punished for something great, yet it is indeed great," in the hadith.

The meaning is that fighting in the sacred months is a great sin. The indefinite noun here is for generality, by the context, since there is no particularity to fighting one people over others, nor to killing in one month over another. This is especially so, since the correspondence of the answer to the question has strengthened the generality, because what is asked about is the ruling of this category, which is fighting within this category, which is the sacred month, without detail. For the most fitting type of fighting to be permissible is our fighting of the polytheists, and yet it is this that was asked about and this that caused hesitation. As for the fighting of Muslims among themselves, its sin is not specific to occurring in the sacred month; and as for the fighting of other nations, it does not come to mind at that time.

The verse is evidence for the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months and a confirmation of the sanctity that those months possess, which God made for them since ancient times, perhaps from the time of Abraham (peace be upon him). The sanctity of a time requires abstaining from sin during its period.

These months are a time for the Hajj and its preliminaries and conclusions, and likewise for the Umra. So if fighting had not been forbidden during them, the Hajj and the Umra would have been disrupted. For this reason Islam maintained them during the time when there were polytheists in the lands of the Arabs, for the benefit of the Muslims and for the benefit of the Hajj. God the Exalted said: ﴿God made the Kaaba, the Sacred House, a means of standing for the people, and the sacred month﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 97], and so on.

The prohibition of fighting in the sacred month was later restricted (khussisa) after this verse and then abrogated (nusikha). As for its restriction, it was by the words of God the Exalted ﴿Do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾ [al-Baqara: 191], up to His words ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and sacred things are subject to retribution﴾ [al-Baqara: 194].

As for its abrogation, it was by the words of God the Exalted ﴿A declaration of immunity from God and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a treaty: go about freely in the land for four months﴾ [al-Tawba: 1], up to His words ﴿When the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]. This explicitly annulled the covenant that the Muslims had made with the polytheists for a truce, which was the covenant made at the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya. It was not a covenant limited to a specific time, nor an unlimited one. Also, the polytheists had broken their oaths, as in the other verse ﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths and resolved to expel the Messenger?﴾ [al-Tawba: 13]. Then God the Exalted set for them a term, which was the end of the sacred months of that year, the year nine after the Hijra, during the pilgrimage of Abu Bakr with the people. This is because that verse [al-Tawba: 1] was revealed in the month of Shawwal, and the polytheists had already departed. So He said to them: ﴿go about freely in the land for four months﴾ [al-Tawba: 2]. He postponed it to the end of Muharram of the tenth year after the Hijra. Then He said ﴿When the sacred months have passed﴾ [al-Tawba: 5], meaning those four months, ﴿kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]. Thus the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months was abrogated, because the word "polytheists" is a plural defined by the definite article of the category, and it is among the forms of generality. The generality of persons necessarily entails the generality of times and places, according to the precise view. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) fought the Thaqif in the month of Dhu al-Qa'da, immediately after the conquest of Mecca, as is recorded in the books of Sahih.

He also sent Abu Amir on a military campaign to Awtas during the sacred month. The Muslims have agreed on the legitimacy of military campaigns in all months of the year, fighting the People of the Book, and they are more deserving of the sanctity of the sacred months than the polytheists are.

If you say: if the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months has been abrogated, then what is the meaning of the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed your blood, your property, and your honour are sacred to you as the sacredness of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours"? For the comparison requires the affirmation of the sanctity of the sacred months. I say: the prohibition of fighting in them follows from their glorification, their sanctity, and their being kept clear of the occurrence of crimes and injustices. Thus a crime committed in them is considered greater than if it were committed in other times.

Unjust fighting is forbidden at all times, while fighting for the sake of right is an act of worship. So the prohibition of fighting in them was abrogated for this reason, and the sanctity of the months remained with respect to the rest of the crimes.

A better explanation is that the verse affirmed the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months for the wisdom of securing the routes of the Hajj and the Umra, since most of the Umra was performed in Rajab. For this reason He said ﴿Fighting therein is a great (matter)﴾. This continued until the Prophet (ﷺ) annulled the Hajj for the polytheists in the year of the pilgrimage of Abu Bakr with the people, since Mecca had come under the control of the Muslims, Quraysh and most of the Arab tribes had entered Islam, and the remainder were prevented from visiting Mecca. This prohibition would have required the cancellation of the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months, because its prohibition therein was for the sake of securing the route of the Hajj and the Umra.

This was rendered moot with respect to the polytheists, and the Hajj remained only for the Muslims, among whom there is no fighting, since unjust fighting is forbidden at all times and the fighting for right occurs at every time unless it is occupied by something preventing it, such as the Hajj. Calling this "abrogation" is a loose usage (tasamuh); it is actually the cessation of the purpose of the ruling. This kind of loose usage in terminology is well known in the speech of the earlier scholars. Then all the polytheists embraced Islam before the Farewell Pilgrimage, and the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned the sanctity of the sacred months in his sermon. By then the application of the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months had ceased, since no polytheist remained who intended the Hajj.

Thus the meaning of the abrogation of the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months is that the need for it had ended, just as the portion of "those whose hearts are to be reconciled" (al-mu'allafa qulubuhum) from the categories of zakat ended by consensus, due to their extinction.

* * *

﴿Hindering from the way of God, disbelief in Him, the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it is greater in the sight of God; and persecution is worse than killing﴾

[Page 329]

It is a rebuke to the polytheists and a disclosure of their wrongdoing, after Ibn ʿAshur had already reproached them by affirming the sanctity of the Sacred Months (al-ashhur al-ḥurum). This indicates that what the expedition's men did, killing a man in that month, was by mistake or by the supposition that the sanctity had lapsed for the purpose of fighting the enemy. The polytheists exaggerated the gravity of this act and denounced it, while they themselves committed what was far more abominable. That is because the prohibition of fighting in the Sacred Month is not due to the months in themselves, since time has no sanctity of its own. Its sanctity arises from God's making it sacred, so its sanctity follows the events that occur within it. The sanctity of the Sacred Months is intended to safeguard the security of the path of the Hajj and the ʿUmrah and their preliminaries and attendant matters during them. Therefore, those who exaggerated the occurrence of fighting in the Sacred Month, and who violated inviolable things in themselves by barring the Muslims, and who disbelieved in God, who made the Kaʿbah sacred and made the Sacred Months sacred for the sake of its pilgrimage, and who expelled the people of the Sanctuary from it and harmed them, are deserving of ridicule and blame. This is because all the things mentioned are forbidden in themselves, not merely as a consequence of something else.

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (may God have mercy on him) said to a man from the people of Iraq who came asking him whether the blood of a gnat, if it fell on a garment, makes it impure. This happened right after the killing of Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī (may God be pleased with them both). He said: "How strange of you, O people of Iraq! You permit the blood of Ḥusayn, yet you ask about the blood of a gnat." It is fitting to quote here the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Are you angered that the two ears of Qutayba were cut off openly, yet you were not angered by the killing of Ibn Khāzim?"

[Page 329 ends; the next portion continues:]

The meaning is that barring from the path of God and what is coordinated with it of the polytheists' acts is greater in sin in the sight of God than the sin of fighting in the Sacred Month.

The "in the sight of God" (ʿinda Allāh) is figurative, namely in the sense of God's knowledge and judgment. The superlative in His saying "greater" (akbar) is a comparison of sin, meaning that each one of those mentioned is greater in sin.

By "barring from the path of God" is meant preventing those who wish to accept Islam from it. A parallel to this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You threaten and bar from the way of God whoever believes in Him﴾ (7:86).

Disbelief in God means associating partners with Him, as far as the polytheists are concerned, and they are the majority of the Arabs. Likewise, it means denying His existence as far as the materialists (ad-dahriyyūn) among them are concerned. The discussion of disbelief (kufr) and its criterion has already preceded at His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them﴾ (2:6), etc.

As for His saying "in Him" (bihi), the bāʾ here is to make the verb "kufr" transitive (muʿaddī), and it is not for location. The pronoun governed by the bāʾ refers to the Name of Majesty (Allāh).

"Disbelief" (kufr) is coordinated with "barring" (ṣadd), meaning: barring from the path of God and disbelief in God are greater than the fighting in the Sacred Month, even if the fighting is great.

"The Sacred Mosque" is coordinated with "the path of God," so it is dependent on "barring" (ṣadda) in accordance with the dependence of the element it is coordinated with.

Know that the apparent sequence of the wording would require that it be said: "Barring from the path of God, disbelief in Him, barring from the Sacred Mosque, and the expulsion of its people from it are greater in the sight of God." But this apparent arrangement was departed from to the form in which the verse came, by placing "and disbelief in Him" first, making it coordinated with "barring" before "barring" had completed what it depends on. "Barring" depends on "the path of God" and on "the Sacred Mosque," for the latter is coordinated with "the path of God," which depends on "barring." The coordination with the dependent element is itself dependent, so it deserves priority over the coordination with the noun on which it depends. This is because what is coordinated with the dependent element is part of the connection of the thing coordinated with, whereas what is coordinated with the noun on which something depends is foreign to the thing coordinated with.

The motive for this order is that the composition of the speech follows a subtler style than the apparent requirement. That style is concern with placing first what is most abominable among their crimes, for disbelief in God is more abominable than barring from the Sacred Mosque. So the order of the composition is by putting first the more important and then the more important. Barring from the path of Islam gathers many wrongs, since it is aggression against people in what they choose for themselves, and a denial of the Messenger of God, and its motive is their defense of their idols: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ (38:5). So disbelief in God is only one pillar of barring from Islam. For this reason, He put first "barring from the path of God," then repeated "disbelief in God" in order to convey, by the implication of correspondence (dalālat al-muṭābaqa), after barring from the path of God had indicated it by implication of inclusion (dalālat al-taḍammun). Then He enumerated against them "barring from the Sacred Mosque," then "the expulsion of its people from it."

It is not valid for "and the Sacred Mosque" to be coordinated with the pronoun in His saying "in Him" (bihi), because there is no sense of disbelief in the Sacred Mosque. Disbelief applies to what is worshipped, to what is a religion, and to what contains a religion. Moreover, they glorify the Sacred Mosque and do not believe in it anything that would justify stretching the use of the word "disbelief" for it in a figurative sense.

His saying "and the expulsion of its people from it" means the expulsion of the Muslims from Mecca, for they were around the Sacred Mosque. Their expulsion involved many wrongs, for the emigrants fell ill during their departure to Medina, and many of them were struck by fever, until it was lifted from Medina through the blessing of the supplication of the Messenger (ﷺ). Moreover, the superiority (of the sin) is related only to the occurrence of fighting in the Sacred Months, not to the killing itself, for the killing has a ruling of its own.

"Ahl" (people, family) means the group that has a greater particular connection to what the word is attached to. Thus "the people of a man" means his clan, "the people of a town" means those who settle in it, and "the people of generosity" means those characterized by it. Here it refers to those settled in Mecca, who are the Muslims. In this there is an allusion that they have a greater right to the Sacred Mosque, for they are the ones who followed the religion of the one who built the Sacred Mosque. He said, may He be exalted: ﴿They were not its guardians. Its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾ (8:34).

His saying "and persecution is greater than killing" is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) brought as a justification for His saying "and the expulsion of its people from it." Since the expulsion of the people of the Sanctuary from it is greater than killing, what was mentioned before it, namely barring from the religion, disbelief in God, and barring from the Sacred Mosque, is greater by implication (dalālat al-faḥwā), because those are greater crimes than the crime of expelling the Muslims from Mecca.

"Fitnah" (persecution, trial) means agitation, causing confusion, and the disruption of life. It is a comprehensive term for the greater harm that befalls one person or a group from others. Here it means what the Muslims suffered from the polytheists by way of calamities in religion, through attacking them with harm by word and deed, preventing them from openly practicing their worship, boycotting them in dealings, mocking them, beating them until they bled, conspiring to kill the Messenger (ﷺ), expelling them from Mecca, depriving them of their wealth and women, and barring them from the House. It is not hidden that the sum of all this is greater than the killing of one of the polytheists' men by the Muslims, namely ʿAmr al-Ḥaḍramī, and their taking of two men from them as captives.

"Akbar" means more great, that is, stronger in forbidden acts, meaning it is greater than the killing that took place in the Sacred Month, which is itself great.

* * *

[Page 330 onward, continuing the discussion:]

﴿They will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they can.﴾

This is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ, interjected statement). What prompted its insertion is the connection with His saying "and persecution is greater than killing," because of the persecution that the polytheists inflict upon the Muslims and because persecution includes fighting, which both sides carried out in turn.

For fighting includes all kinds of harm, and killing is only one state of fighting. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾ (22:39)? Here He called the unbelievers' act against the Muslims "fighting," and He called the Muslims "those who are fought against" with the letter tāʾ vowelled with a fatḥah. In this there is information that the polytheists were intending to raid the Muslims and were preparing for it, but they delayed it after the Hijrah because they were suffering the effects of years of drought. So His saying "they will not cease" (lā yazālūna), though it suggests that their fighting is ongoing, means by it the causes of fighting, which is harm, and the intention of fighting likewise. And if they begin it, they will not desist from it. Moreover, the explicit meaning of "lā yazāl" (they will not cease) indicates that this continues into the future. "Ḥattā" (until) denotes a limit, and here it is a limit of causation (ghāyah taʿlīliyyah). The meaning is that their persecution and fighting continue until their aim is achieved, which is that they turn you back from your religion.

His saying "if they can" (in istaṭāʿū) is an indirect implication that they are not able to turn the Muslims back from their religion. Therefore the position of this condition is that of a precaution against what the limit in His saying "until they turn you back from your religion" might suggest. For this reason the condition was introduced with the particle "in" (if), which indicates that the fulfillment of the condition is expected not to occur.

"Radd" (turning back) means diverting from something and returning to what was before it. It is transitive directly to its object, and it also takes "ilā" (to) and "ʿan" (from) to complete it. Here one of the two complements has been omitted, namely the one that is connected through "ilā" (to), because it is evident that they fight them in order to turn them back from Islam to the polytheism they had been upon. This is because the adherents of every religion, when they believe in its correctness, are eager to bring people into it. He said, may He be exalted: ﴿The Jews and the Christians will never be pleased with you until you follow their religion﴾ (2:120), and He said: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾ (4:89).

The attachment of the condition with "in" (if) indicates that their being able to do this, even with individual Muslims, is an improbable matter because of the strength of the Muslims' faith. Therefore the attempt of the polytheists to turn back even one of the Muslims would be a futile exertion.

* * *

[Page 332 onward:]

﴿Whoever of you apostatizes from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein forever.﴾

This is a second parenthetical clause, or a coordination with the parenthetical clause before it. Its purpose is warning. Because He mentioned the eagerness of the polytheists to turn the Muslims back from Islam and followed it by considering it improbable that this would come from the Muslims, He followed it with a warning against it. The form "yartadid" was used, which is a reflexive form (ṣīghat muṭāwaʿah), indicating that their return from Islam, if it were assumed to occur, would not happen except through an attempt by the polytheists, for whoever has tasted the sweetness of faith does not easily return from it, and whoever has known the truth does not turn back from it except with difficulty. The second object was not considered here, since there is no consideration for the religion to which one returns. Rather, the ruling was tied to apostasy from Islam to any religion. From that day onward, the term "ridda" (apostasy) became a technical legal designation for leaving the religion of Islam, even if this departure involves no return to a religion that this apostate had been upon. His saying "and dies" (fa-yamut) is coordinated with the condition, so it is like a second condition.

The verb "ḥabiṭa" (to be void) belongs to the pattern of "samiʿa" and is transitive with a hamzah. The lexicographers said: its origin is from "al-ḥabaṭ" with a fatḥah on the bāʾ, which is swelling in the bellies of camels from excessive eating, so that they die from it. Its application to the nullification of deeds is a metaphor (tamthīl), because camels eat green plants out of desire for fullness, and it then ends in their death. Thus He likened the state of one who performs good deeds for their benefit in the Hereafter, yet finds no effect of them, to livestock that ate until the bloating struck them. For this reason the deeds were not restricted by the qualifier "righteous," because this metaphor is evident.

The voiding of deeds is the cessation of their effects which were ordained to follow from them by the Sharīʿah. It therefore includes their effects in this world and the reward in the Hereafter. This is the secret of His saying "in this world and the Hereafter."

The effects in this world are what follows from Islam among the distinctive features of Muslims. The first of these is the effects of the testimony of faith: the inviolability of lives, wealth, and honor, the funeral prayer upon him after death, and burial in the graveyards of the Muslims.

Also among them are the effects of acts of worship and the merits of the Muslims through emigration and the brotherhood between the Emigrants and the Helpers, and the bond of Islam (walāʾ al-Islām), and the effects of rights, such as the right of a Muslim in the public treasury (bayt al-māl) and its stipends, the rights of inheritance and marriage, eligibility for offices (al-wilāyāt), and justice, and what God guaranteed to the Muslims, such as His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while he is a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ (16:97).

[Page 333]

Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 217 (part 3 of 3):

As for the effects in the Hereafter, they are deliverance from the Fire because of Islam, and what follows from righteous deeds of reward and bliss.

By "deeds" is meant the deeds through which they draw near to God Most High and hope for their reward, as indicated by the root meaning of the word and by the context of warning. For if the blameworthy deeds were what was nullified, the statement would become an exhortation. The deeds are not mentioned in the Qur'an with "habitat" (حبطت) except without being restricted by "righteous," relying on the context.

His saying ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ is a conjunction with the clause of the recompense for disbelief, since matters are judged by their endings. Two things follow from disbelief: the nullification of the value of previous deeds, and the punishment of eternal abiding in the Fire. Because abiding forever is a second punishment, the demonstrative "those" is repeated in His saying ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire﴾.

In the use of the demonstrative in both places there is an alert that they deserve what is mentioned after the demonstrative because of what was mentioned before it.

Now, He attached the nullification of deeds to the combination of two matters: apostasy and dying upon disbelief. He did not restrict apostasy by dying upon it in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has become worthless, and he is in the Hereafter among the losers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿If you associate, your deeds will surely become worthless, and you will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and His saying ﴿And had they associated, what they used to do would have been worthless for them﴾ [al-An'am: 88]. The scholars have differed concerning the apostate from Islam who repents of his apostasy and returns to Islam. According to Malik and Abu Hanifah, whoever apostatized from among the Muslims and then returned to Islam and repented, his deeds that he did before apostasy do not return to him. If he had vows or oaths, nothing of them is binding on him after his return to Islam. If he had performed Hajj before he apostatized and then returned to Islam, he begins the Hajj anew, and he is not held accountable for what was upon him during the time of apostasy, except what he did in disbelief, for which he is held accountable.

Al-Shafi'i said: when the apostate returns to Islam, all his deeds return to him, what is for him and what is against him.

As for the proof of Malik, Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Our scholars said: God only mentioned dying upon it as a condition here, because He made abiding in the Fire contingent upon it. Whoever dies upon disbelief, God makes him abide in the Fire by this verse. And whoever associates, his deed becomes worthless by the other verse. So these are two verses conveying two different meanings and two different rulings." End of quote. He means that between the two conditions and the two responses here there is a distribution. His saying ﴿then those—their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾ is the response to His saying ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion﴾. And His saying ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ is the response to His saying ﴿and he dies while a disbeliever﴾. Perhaps in the repetition of "and those" there is an announcement that it is a second response. And the release of the other verses from restriction by death upon disbelief is an indication of the intention of this qualifier in this verse.

In this argument there is a setting aside of the principle of applying the unrestricted to the restricted. Perhaps Malik's view in setting this aside is that these are rulings that go back to the foundations of religion, and one does not rely on speculative evidence for them. When the unrestricted evidence is applied to the restricted in the branches of the Sharia, that is because it is speculative evidence, and most evidence for the branches is speculative. But in the foundations of belief, the explicit ruling of each verse is taken. There is room for consideration in this, because some of what was mentioned among the deeds belongs to the Sharia observances of Islam and its branches, such as Hajj.

The argument of al-Shafi'i is the application of applying the unrestricted to the restricted, as mentioned by al-Fakhr and endorsed by Ibn al-Faras from the Malikis.

If you say: the righteous deed done in the Jahiliyyah is confirmed by Islam, for the Messenger of God ﷺ said to Hakim ibn Hizam: "You became Muslim upon what you had already done of good." So is the apostate from Islam in a lesser state than the people of the Jahiliyyah?

The answer is that the state of Jahiliyyah before the coming of Islam was a state empty of the Sharia, so it was among the virtues of Islam to confirm it. Based on this, there is a disagreement concerning the continuation of the ruling of companionship (suhbah) for those who apostatized after the Prophet ﷺ and then returned to Islam, such as Qurrah ibn Hubayrah al-'Amiri, 'Alqamah ibn 'Ulathah, al-Ash'ath ibn Qays, 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn, and 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib. In the commentary of Qadi Zakariyya on the Alfiyyah of al-'Iraqi: "As for including whoever met the Prophet ﷺ as a Muslim, then apostatized, then embraced Islam after the death of the Messenger among the Companions, there is great disagreement." End of quote. Hululu said in the commentary on Jam' al-Jawami': "If a Companion apostatized during the life of the Messenger ﷺ and returned to faith after his death, this falls under the disagreement about apostasy: does it nullify the deed by the act itself, or does it nullify it only with the condition of dying upon it? Because companionship with the Messenger ﷺ is a great virtue. As for accepting his narration after his return to Islam, there is consideration in it."

As for whoever apostatized during the life of the Prophet ﷺ and returned to Islam during his life and kept his company, the virtue of companionship is attained by him, like 'Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh.

If you say: what is the secret in the combination of these two conditions in this verse, while the rest of its parallels are free of the second of the two conditions? I say: those other verses came to magnify the matter of association on the assumption of its occurrence from an unspecified person, as in the verse ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], or its occurrence from one whose occurrence of it is impossible, as in the verse ﴿And had they associated, what they used to do would have been worthless for them﴾ [al-An'am: 88], and the verse ﴿If you associate, your deeds will surely become worthless﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. In them, it is limited to what arises from association after faith: the nullification of deeds, and loss in general terms. As for this verse, it came after mention of the attempt of the polytheists and their treatment to turn the Muslims addressed by the verse back from Islam. So the assumption of the occurrence of association and apostasy from them was closer, given the polytheists' attempt at that by fighting the Muslims. Therefore it mentions in it an additional magnification, which is eternal abiding in the Fire.

This verse was also among the signs of prophethood, for in the year of the apostasy it occurred that those in whose hearts a trace of association remained tried to make the Muslims apostatize and fought them over that. A great group apostatized, and as-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, rose against them with his resolve and certainty and fought them, and those among them who remained alive returned. Had it not been for this verse, they would have despaired of the benefit of returning to Islam, which is the benefit of not abiding forever in the Fire.

The conjunction in His saying "fa-yamut" (and he dies) with the particle fa, which indicates sequence, indicates that death follows apostasy. Everyone knows that most apostates' deaths do not come immediately after apostasy, so the listener then knows that the apostate is punished with death as a legal punishment. Thus the verse becomes evidence for the obligation of killing the apostate. The scholars of the Community have differed on this. The majority said: the apostate is asked to repent for three days and is imprisoned for that purpose; if he repents, his repentance is accepted, and if he does not repent, he is killed as a disbeliever. This is the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, and Malik, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said the same, whether a man or a woman. Abu Hanifah said the same regarding the man, but he did not see killing the female apostate; rather he said she is enslaved. His companions said she is imprisoned until she becomes Muslim. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Tawus, 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Umar, 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn al-Majishun, and al-Shafi'i said: the apostate is killed without being asked to repent. It was also said he is asked to repent for a month. The evidence of all of them is the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "Whoever changes his religion, kill him," and the practice of the Companions: Abu Bakr fought the apostates, and 'Ali burned the Sababiyyah who claimed the divinity of 'Ali. They agreed that the intent of the hadith "whoever changes his religion" is religion, which is Islam. The majority agreed that the word "whoever" includes males and females, except for those who deviated from them, namely Abu Hanifah, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Thawri, 'Ata', and al-Hasan, who said the female apostate is not killed. They relied on the Messenger of God ﷺ's prohibition of killing women and specified by it the generality of "whoever changes his religion." This is a strange argument, because this prohibition is stated in the rulings of jihad, and women by nature do not fight. He also prohibited killing monks and rabbis. Would these say that whoever among monks and rabbis apostatizes after his conversion is not killed?

Malik and Abu Hanifah were strict regarding the apostate by zandaqah, that is, the manifestation of Islam and concealment of disbelief. They said: he is killed, and his repentance is not accepted if he is seized before he comes repentant. Whoever reviles the Prophet ﷺ is killed, and his repentance is not accepted.

Furthermore, know that apostasy in origin is leaving the creed of Islam according to the majority of Muslims. Leaving the creed and abandoning the practices of Islam is the view of the Kharijites and some Mu'tazilites who hold that the perpetrator of a major sin is a disbeliever. The exit of a Muslim from Islam is indicated by his declaring it, by explicit confession or implicitly. The explicit is clear. The implicit is that someone utters a word or does an act that includes that and admits no other interpretation, such that God and His Messenger have stated, or the Muslims have agreed, that it can only proceed from a disbeliever, such as prostrating to an idol, and frequenting churches in the manner of their adherents.

They also included in this the denial of what is known by necessity to have been brought by the Messenger, that is, what knowledge of it is necessary. Ibn Rashid said in al-Fa'iq: "Regarding takfir by denying what is known by necessity, there is disagreement. As for fixing its reality, there are views among the jurists, whose place is the books of fiqh and khilaf."

The wisdom of legislating the killing of the apostate, although the original disbeliever is not killed, is that apostasy is the departure of an individual or a group from the Islamic community. By leaving Islam after entering it, he signals that when he mixed with this religion he found it unsuitable and found what he had been upon before it more righteous. This is an insult to the religion and a belittling of it. It also paves a way for whoever wants to slip out of this religion, and that leads to the dissolution of the community. If no deterrent were set for that, people would not refrain. We find no deterrent like the anticipation of death. Therefore death was made the punishment for the apostate, so that no one enters the religion except with insight, and so that no one leaves it after entering it. This is not compulsion in religion, which is negated by His saying ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256], according to the view that it is not abrogated, because compulsion in religion is compelling people to leave their religions and enter Islam. As for this, it is compulsion to remain in Islam.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 218:

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who emigrated and strove in the way of Allah — those hope for the mercy of Allah. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Al-Fakhr said: Regarding the connection of this verse to what precedes it, there are two views. The first: 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh said, "O Messenger of Allah, suppose there is no punishment upon us for what we did; then do we hope from it for a reward or a recompense?" So this verse was revealed, because 'Abd Allah was a believer, an emigrant, and, by means of this fighting, a striver (mujahid); that is, the three attributes were realized in him.

The second: that when He, exalted is He, made jihad obligatory by His saying, ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216], He followed that with mention of those who undertake it. End of al-Fakhr's words. What appears to me is that the placing of this verse after what precedes it belongs to the category of following a warning with good news, and it is a declaration of the believers' innocence from the possibility of their apostasy, for none of the emigrants apostatized. This sentence is a parenthetical insertion between the verses of legislation.

"Those who emigrated" (alladhina hajaru) are those who left Makkah for Madinah fleeing with their religion. It is derived from al-hajr, which is separation. The form of the verb with the infix (mufa'alah) was used for it to indicate that it was a separation arising from enmity on both sides, so each of the one who moves and the one moved from has forsaken the other and sought his distance. Or the mufa'alah is for intensification, like their saying, "Allah grant you well-being" (ʿafakaʾllah), indicating that he forsook a people with an intense forsaking. ʿAbidah ibn al-Tabib said:

"Indeed she who struck a tent, one who emigrated, in Kufa, the garrison city, the ghoul has ruined her love."

And "jihad" (mujahadah) is a mufa'alah derived from al-jahd, which is hardship, and it is fighting, because it involves the expenditure of effort, like the mufa'alah for intensification. It has been said: because the one who strives joins his effort to another effort in supporting the religion, like al-musa'adah, which is a man joining his forearm (sa'id) to another's forearm for help and strength; so the mufa'alah here has the meaning of joining and repetition. It has also been said: because the striver expends his effort in fighting one who expends his effort likewise in fighting him, so it is a true mufa'alah. And fi here is for causation.

"The way of Allah" (sabil Allah) is that which leads to His pleasure and the establishment of His religion. Jihad and mujahadah are among the Qur'anic and Islamic technical terms. The relative pronoun was repeated to magnify emigration and jihad, as if they were each independent in the realization of hope.

[Page 338]

The demonstrative noun was brought to indicate that their hope for the mercy of Allah is on account of their faith, their emigration, and their jihad; thereby what the relative clause indicates of an allusion to the reason for the predicate's construction is reinforced. It was needed to emphasize this because the two relative clauses, since the Muslims and a group among them were distinguished by them, became like an epithet; for in that day in the language of the Shari'ah the name "those who believed" was applied to the Muslims, just as the name "emigrants" was applied to the Muslims of Quraysh at that time. So the relative pronoun emphasized the intention of indicating the reason for the predicate's construction.

Ar-raja' (hope) is the anticipation of good together with the predominance of the expectation of its occurrence, for although Allah's promise is not broken, out of His bounty and truthfulness, nevertheless the endings are unknown, and the conformity of the deed with what Allah intends may fail due to impediments that the responsible person does not know; and so that they do not rely upon the deed in their reliance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 219 (part 1 of 4):

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: "In both there is great sin and [some] benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit."﴾

This is a resumptive statement (istinaf) that nullifies two practices that were widespread among people in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period): drinking wine and gambling (maysir). This is one of the rulings that the surah explains which concern reforming the conditions in which people lived in the Jahiliyyah. The explanation of these rulings begins with His words, Exalted is He, ﴿O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the murdered﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178] and continues to the end of the surah, apart from the etiquette, deterrents, glad tidings, admonitions, parables and stories that are interspersed among them, in keeping with the Qur'an's habit of varying its styles, to energize those addressed, the listeners, the readers, and whoever is conveyed to. This verse is coherent with all of that.

The askers are Muslims. Al-Wahidi said: It was revealed concerning 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and a group of the Ansar who came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, give us a ruling on wine, for it takes away the intellect and destroys wealth." So this verse was revealed. In al-Kashshaf [of al-Zamakhshari] it says: When this verse was revealed, some people abandoned wine while others continued to drink it. Then after it the verse of al-Ma'idah was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, wine, gambling...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90], and so on.

Drinking wine is a practice deeply rooted in humankind since ancient times. No religious law (shari'ah) has forbidden it, neither the intoxicating amount nor anything less than that. As for what some scholars of Islam mention, namely that intoxication is forbidden in all the religious laws, this is a claim for which they have no evidence. Rather, the evidence to the contrary is abundant. What led them to this view is what they established in usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) that the universal legislative objectives (al-kulliyyat al-tashri'iyyah), namely the preservation of religion, life, intellect, lineage, property and honor, are things on which all the religious laws agree. Although we support this view, its meaning in my opinion is that all the religious laws aimed at preserving these matters in their legislation. As for whether it is a consistently observed principle in religions other than the religion of Islam, I do not think that this is established. Moreover, observance of them has degrees, and there is no need to investigate this further. However, the books of the People of the Book do not contain a prohibition of wine, nor a stipulation of abstaining from drinking it. In the Torah that is in the hands of the Jews, it is said that Noah drank wine until he became intoxicated, and that Lot drank wine until he became intoxicated, an intoxication which, by their claim, led to a shameful matter. The latter is among the falsehoods, because prophethood entails infallibility (ismah). Although the religious laws differ in permitting certain things, there are things that are impossible for the prophets, which would lead to their diminishment in the view of rational people. What must be believed is that the prophets do not commit the act of drinking wine, because those who drink it do so only for pleasure, amusement, and intoxication, and all of these are things from which the prophets are pure.
