Nor do they drink it with the intention of strengthening themselves, since that intention is rare among those who drink it.

In the Book of Leviticus of the Torah: "And God spoke to Aaron, saying: Do not drink wine or strong drink, you and your sons with you, when you enter the Tent of Meeting, lest you die. It is a perpetual statute throughout your generations, and to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean."

The prevalence of drinking wine in the Jahiliyyah is well known to anyone who knows their literature and history. Wine was the mainstay of their livelihood, the peak of their pleasures, the joy of their time, and the entertainment of their hours. Tarafah said:

Were it not for three things that are part of a young man's living and his ardor, I would not care when my reproacher stands up.
Among them is my outrunning the blamers with a sip of dark red wine, which, when mixed with water, foams up.

From Anas ibn Malik: Wine was forbidden, and at that time there was no life that the Arabs found more pleasing than it, and nothing forbidden to them was harder on them than wine. Therefore, Islam came to prohibit it gradually. It permitted its drinking for a period, and the reminder of this favor is sufficient in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapes you take from them intoxicant and good provision﴾ [al-Nahl: 67], according to the interpretation of those who explained "intoxicant" (sakar) as wine. It was also said that sakar is non-intoxicating nabidh (date wine), but the first interpretation is more apparent.

The verse of surah al-Nahl was revealed in Makkah. The people of transmitted reports (ahl al-athar) agree that the prohibition of wine took place in Madinah a few days after the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), that is, at the end of the fourth year or in the fifth year, depending on the disagreement about the year of the Battle of the Confederates.

The correct view is the first. God favored people by allowing them to make intoxicant from the fruits He created for them. Then God did not neglect His mercy toward people, even in guiding them toward their interests, so He brought them this in gradual steps. It was said that this verse of surah al-Baqarah is the first verse that announced the cause of prohibition in wine, and that the reason for its revelation is what has already been mentioned. Thus describing it with its sin and its benefit is an alert for them, since they used to mention only its virtues. This was a preparation for them for the prohibition that would come later. Al-Baghawi said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God has preceded in the prohibition of wine" [i.e., He began preparing its prohibition]. It is said: "I have preceded to you in such and such," meaning I presented it to you. In the tafsir of Ibn Kathir: it paves the way for the absolute prohibition of wine, but it was not explicit; rather it was allusive, that is, it alluded to abstaining from drinking it as a matter of purity.

The majority of exegetes hold that this verse was revealed before the verse of surah al-Nisa' and before the verse of surah al-Ma'idah. This is the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, as Abu Dawud transmitted. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he held that the verse of al-Ma'idah abrogated (nasakha) ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], and abrogated the verse ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾. It is attributed to Ibn 'Umar, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

Some exegetes held that this verse of al-Baqarah established the prohibition of wine, so this verse, in their view, was revealed after the verse of surah al-Nisa': ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]. Since surah al-Baqarah was revealed before surah al-Nisa' and surah al-Ma'idah, it follows according to the view of these people that this verse was revealed after the revelation of surah al-Baqarah, and that it was placed here as an addition to the matters about which their question was recounted.

The meaning of ﴿in both there is great sin﴾ is that in indulging in them, by drinking one and playing the other, there is a great sin. This is the more apparent meaning of the verse, since it describes the sin in it with a great description. Therefore, the verse of surah al-Ma'idah is only an emphasis of the prohibition and an explicit text upon it. This is because the mention in our verse of benefits could be interpreted by those who interpret it as an excuse for drinking. It has been reported in some reports that some people drank wine after the revelation of this verse, and two men prayed while intoxicated and began to utter speech that no one knew what it was. And a man among the Muslims drank wine and began to lament the polytheists killed at Badr. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he came to him in alarm and raised something that was in his hand to strike him. The man said: "I seek refuge in God from the wrath of God and His Messenger," and he swore: "I will never eat it again." So God revealed the prohibition of it in the verse of surah al-Ma'idah.

Al-khamr (wine) is a noun derived from the verbal noun of the verb khamara, khamarahu (from the pattern nasara), meaning he covered it. It was named after the juice of grapes when it ferments, rises, and froths, becoming intoxicating, because it covers the intellect from its natural functioning. This is a metaphorical naming, and it is either a naming by the verbal noun, or it is a noun that came in the form of the verbal noun. It is the name for every intoxicating drink, whether it is grape juice, juice of something else, water in which raisins, dates, or other nabidh (steeped drinks) were soaked and left until it fermented and frothed. Ibn al-Qamus (the author of al-Qamus) favored this view. The truth is that khamr is every intoxicating drink, except that it became dominant for intoxicating grape juice, because they used to compete over it. Other drinks are also called khamr, nabidh and fadikh. Authentic reports indicate that most of the Arabs' drinks on the day wine was prohibited were fadikh (date-based), and that the drinks of the people of Madinah on that day were five, other than grape juice. They were made from dates, raisins, honey, maize, and barley, and some of them were called fadikh, naqi', sukurkah, and bit'.

As for what is reported in some reports from Ibn 'Umar: "The prohibition of wine was revealed when there were five drinks in Madinah, none of which was grape juice," its meaning is that grape juice was not counted among the five because it was rare, and it does not mean that grape juice was not found in Madinah.

Grape juice used to be brought to the Hijaz and Najd from Yemen, al-Ta'if, and Syria. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"And it does not leave the wines of Andarin."

Andarin is a town in the lands of Syria. The disagreement over the meaning of khamr in Arabic usage has led to a disagreement regarding the rulings. All scholars agree that grape wine is forbidden, its large quantity by consensus (ijma') and its small quantity according to the majority of scholars. The one who drinks a large quantity of it is subject to the hadd punishment according to the majority, and there is disagreement regarding a small quantity, as will come in surah al-Ma'idah, God willing. Then they disagreed about what is other than it. The majority said: Every drink whose large amount intoxicates, its small amount is forbidden, and its ruling is the same as the ruling of wine in every respect, taking the name khamr in their view, and by clear analogy (qiyas jali) that the wisdom behind the prohibition is intoxication, which is present in all of them. This is the correct view. Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Sufyan al-Thawri said:

[Page 342]

Grape juice is singled out for those rulings. As for other drinks, only the intoxicating amount of them is forbidden. This is how the opponents transmit it from Abu Hanifah. Scholars in earlier times used to transmit this without qualification, to the point that their transmission may have given the impression that he did not hold that a person who becomes intoxicated from something other than wine is liable for anything. The principle that what is permitted by the law is not restricted to being safe increases this impression, and they sometimes reinforced it with transmitted stories and incidents, such as the saying of Abu Nuwas:

"The Iraqi permitted nabidh and drinking it, and said: Both al-mudamah (wine) and intoxication are forbidden."

But what the Hanafis settled on is that intoxicating drinks are of two kinds. One of them is forbidden to drink, and it is four: khamr, which is raw grape juice when it boils, rises, and froths; tila', with a kasra on the ta' and with a long vowel, which is grape juice boiled until less than two-thirds of it has evaporated, then left until it becomes intoxicating; sakar, with a fatha on the sin and the kaf, which is raw water of ripe dates, meaning water hot poured over ripe dates, which then becomes intoxicating; and naqi', which is raw nabidh of raisins. These four are forbidden, whether little or much, and they are najis in substance. But whoever considers khamr lawful is declared a disbeliever, and the one who drinks a little or a lot of it is subject to the hadd punishment. As for the other three, the one who considers them lawful is not declared a disbeliever, and their drinker is not subject to the hadd punishment unless he becomes intoxicated.

The second kind: intoxicating drinks whose drinking is lawful. These are date and raisin nabidh if it is boiled, even the slightest boiling; mixed nabidh of the two if it is boiled with the slightest boiling; and nabidh of honey, figs, wheat, barley, and maize, whether boiled or not. And mutallath, which is grape juice boiled until two-thirds of it is gone and one-third remains. These four are lawful to drink if it is not intended for amusement and pleasure, but rather for strengthening oneself for worship, or for aiding digestion of food, or for medical treatment. Otherwise it is forbidden. The one who drinks them is not subject to the hadd punishment unless he becomes intoxicated.

[p. 343]

This distinction is based on analogy (qiyas), because these beverages no longer contain the intoxicant that is usual (in wine). As for the prescribed penalty (hadd), there is no basis for distinguishing in it, because if it is attached to intoxication, then all of them are equal in intoxicating, and moreover it would follow that the penalty applies only when intoxication occurs, and there is nothing in the reports that supports anything other than that. If the penalty is for blocking the means (sadd al-dhari'a), then I do not see that the principle of blocking the means extends to punishing the one who commits the means before the thing it leads to occurs. The Hanafis cited, for this distinction, that the Companions drank nabidh, and this is a weaker argument than the one before it, since the Companions were far too pure to drink intoxicants, and they only drank the nabidh before it fermented. The term nabidh is applied to both the sweet and the fermented, so the wording became imprecise. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (al-Shaybani) opposed his own imam in this matter and agreed with the majority (jumhur).

It is perhaps mentioned by some in their argument that khamr is, in its literal sense (haqiqa), the drink of unfermented grape juice, and metaphorical (majaz) in other cases, such as nabidh and cooked drinks. The word khamr has come in the verse, so it is to be understood in its literal sense, and extending it to other things is establishing language by analogy, and this is invalid. This is because the dispute over whether khamr is literally applied to grape wine or to the more general category is a dispute over linguistic naming and application. Setting that aside, how can a mujtahid suppose that God Most High prohibits specifically grape wine and leaves other things that are equal to it in all the attributes that affect rulings? If they say: the attribute mentioned in the Qur'an, we have equated all beverages in it, namely by prohibiting the intoxicating quantity, and the rulings that were established by the Sunna remain for khamr, such as the prohibition of a small amount and the penalty for it or for intoxication, then those are the point under consideration. We reply: this is a begging of the question (musadara), since we argued against them that one cannot suppose of the Lawgiver that he distinguishes in rulings between things that are alike in attributes. Moreover, it has been established in the Sahih, with a firmness that leaves no room for doubt in minds, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Khamr is from grape juice, raisins, dates, wheat, barley and sorghum." Narrated by al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, and it is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud. He also said: "Khamr is from these two trees, the palm and the vine." Narrated by Abu Hurayra, and it is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud. He said: "Every intoxicant is khamr, and every intoxicant is forbidden." Narrated by Ibn 'Umar, in the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi. Anas said: "Khamr was prohibited while we found no drink of grapes except a little, and most of our drink was fadikh (date-wine)." As in the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi.

As for the broadening of the meaning of khamr to what is cooked, this is a distortion of jurisprudence (fiqh) and a defilement of it. What benefit is there in cooking if the intoxication is still present?

God's description of khamr, that in it is "a great sin and benefits," (﴿In both is a great sin and some benefits﴾). Ithm (sin): disobedience to God by doing what is corrupt and does not please God. Al-Raghib indicated that the derivation of ithm carries the meaning of delay from good. Ibn al-'Arabi, in his commentary on Surat al-A'raf, said: ithm is an expression for the blame that comes upon an act, as if he is pointing out that ithm is the opposite of reward. The apparent technical usage (istilah) of the Sharia is that ithm is the act that is blameworthy in the Law, so it is the opposite of an act of devotion (qurba). Thus the meaning of ﴿In both is a great sin﴾ is that from them there results what is sinful, both in the state of rowdiness and in the state of gain and loss, from quarreling.

Describing "great" (kabir) for sin is a metaphor, because sin is not a physical body. So what is meant by "great" is "intense within its kind," as previously mentioned.

The preposition fi (in), which indicates location, was used to convey the intensity of the connection of sin and benefit to them both, because the notion of being "in" is the strongest type of connection. Here it is a metaphorical "in," common in Arabic speech. The "in" is connected to khamr and maysir themselves for emphasis, and what is meant is their habitual use.

The expression by "sin" was chosen to indicate that it returns to the one who drinks it as punishment in this world and the next.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ithmun kabirun﴾ with a single "b" (ba') after the kaf, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it as kathir (with the three-dotted tha'), and this is a metaphor: the attribute of "much" is borrowed for "intense," likening the strength of the quality to the abundance of number.

Al-manafi' (benefits) is the plural of manfa'a, which is a noun on the pattern maf'ala. Its origin may be a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi), meant to convey the strength of benefit, because the mimi verbal noun is more emphatic due to the additional letter in its form. It may also be a noun of place, indicating abundance of what is in it, as in their saying: "masba'a" and "maqbara," meaning that much benefit is in them, of the kind of their saying "maslaha" and "mafsada." So manfa'a is in any case more emphatic than naf'.

The sin that is in khamr arises from what follows from drinking it, sometimes from excess in it and rowdiness, from quarrels that lead to hatred and turning people away from the path of God and from prayer. In it is the loss of reason and exposure to ridicule. In it is the loss of wealth in drinking it, and in spending on companions, to the extent that they sometimes pawned their clothes with the khammarin (tavern-keepers). 'Umara ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi said:

"We are not those who, when they are drunk, drink Umm 'Amr's wine, whose clothes among them are like spoils (of war)—
But we, O Umm 'Amr, our companion is like one who floats, not one who sinks."

'Antara said:

"And when I am drunk, I am one who squanders my wealth, while my honor remains intact and unharmed."

They used to buy khamr at high prices and considered haggling over its price a fault. Labid said:

"I make the price of the cheap wine high, every dark old jar or jug that is broken open and whose seal is removed."

And among its sins is what the later physicians established: that it produces harm in the liver, lungs and heart for those addicted to it, and weakness in offspring. Islam alone among all the religious laws has prohibited it. And because of the harms it does to manliness and dignity, some Arabs prohibited it for themselves in the pre-Islamic period. Among those who prohibited it for himself in the Jahiliyya was Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari, because he once drank until he became drunk, dragged his daughter and seized her garment, and he saw the moon and spoke words. When he was informed of this when he became sober, he swore that he would never taste khamr as long as he lived, and he said:

"I saw khamr as good, but in it are qualities that corrupt the forbearing man,
So by God I will never drink it while healthy, nor will I be cured by it ever while sick,
Nor will I give my life for its price, nor ever call a companion to it,
For khamr exposes its drinkers, and brings upon them a great matter."

In the Amali of al-Qali, the first two verses are attributed to Safwan ibn Umayya. Among others are 'Amir ibn al-Zarib al-'Adwani; 'Afif ibn Ma'di Karib al-Kindi, uncle of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays; Safwan ibn Umayya al-Kinani; Aslum al-Bali; Suwayd ibn 'Adiyy al-Ta'i; and Asad ibn Kurz al-Qasri al-Bajali, who reached Islam and who was called in the Jahiliyya "Lord of Bajila"; 'Uthman ibn 'Affan; Abu Bakr al-Siddiq; 'Abbas ibn Mirdas; 'Uthman ibn Maz'un; Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt; and 'Abd Allah ibn Judan.

As for the benefits, some of them are bodily benefits, which is what it gives of strength to the body of the weak in some states, and what benefits there are in trade, for the trade of al-Ta'if and Yemen was in khamr. In it are benefits of pleasure and joy. Tarafa said:

"Were it not for three things, which are part of the youth's life and your prosperity,
I would not have cared when my reprovers stood up.
Among them is my overcoming the blamers with a drink of dark red wine, which, when mixed with water, froths."

Some of our scholars went so far as to say that the benefits are only financial, fleeing from acknowledging bodily benefits in khamr. This is a denial of what exists. It is strange that some claimed that khamr has bodily benefits, but that these disappeared with its prohibition.

In this verse, maysir is mentioned, coordinated with khamr and reported about them both with unified reports. So whatever is said about what this verse requires, regarding the prohibition of khamr or abstaining from drinking it, is said likewise about maysir. It has become clear that maysir is the companion of khamr in its firm hold on the souls of the Arabs at that time, and it is the greatest pastime they engaged in. They often resorted to it at the time of drinking when they lacked meat for roasting during the drinking of khamr. They would seek by various means to slaughter a camel at that time, and these means could even lead them to attack the camels of others by slaughtering them, as in the story of Hamza, when he slaughtered a she-camel belonging to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib while Hamza was drinking, and his singing slave-girl urged him on with this she-camel, singing:

"Oh Hamza, to the she-camels, the fat old ones,
And they are tethered in the courtyard."

He stood up to them, split open her belly, took out the liver and roasted it, in a famous story. Tarafa said, describing his attack on a camel of his father's herd in a state of drunkenness:

"Then there passed a thick-necked, dignified she-camel, with a fleshy hump, the prized one of an old man like a rough-skinned ostrich.
He says, when he has seen her forelegs and her shanks: 'Do you not see that you have come with one of strength?'
And he said: 'Look, what do you think of a drinker, strongly hostile to us in his transgression, deliberately?'"

So there is no doubt that maysir was easier for them to obtain meat for drinking, and for this reason their speech often paired it with drinking. Sabra ibn 'Amr al-Faq'asi said, mentioning camels:

"We favor our equals with them and humiliate them, and we drink with their prices and gamble."

Labid mentioned khamr, then mentioned maysir in his Mu'allaqa, saying:

"I make the price of the cheap wine high, every dark old jar or jug that is broken open and whose seal is removed."

Then he said:

"And a slaughtered camel of the gamblers, whose death I summoned by arrows that are alike in their bodies."

'Antara mentioned both in one verse, saying, describing the virtues of the opponent he struck down in battle:

"One whose hands are with the arrows when he plays in winter, a tearer of the boundaries of trade, one who is blamed."

Therefore, for this reason, mention of khamr is coupled with mention of maysir in this verse, and for this reason they are linked in the question of the questioners about them, if there was indeed a question.

Maysir is a noun of kind (ism jins) on the pattern maf'il, derived from maysir, which is the opposite of hardship and difficulty, or from yasar (ease, wealth), which is the opposite of poverty. It is as if they formed it on this pattern in consideration of the form of the noun of place from yasara yaysiru. It is a metaphorical place, and they treated that gambling as like the vessel in which there is ease or prosperity, because it leads to comfort of life and the removal of the difficulty of times of scarcity and the harshness of winter. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it is a verbal noun like al-maw'id. In that there is the point that if it were a verbal noun it would have a fatha on its sin, since a verbal noun on the pattern maf'il is only with a fatha on its 'ayn, apart from what is anomalous. They did not mention maysir among the anomalous ones, unless it is answered that the Arabs made this name on the pattern of an anomalous verbal noun so that it would be known that it is now not a verbal noun.

Maysir is a form of gambling that the Arabs had in the Jahiliyya. It is among the ancient gambling that was deeply rooted in antiquity, which belonged to 'Ad before. The first one whose mention of the game of maysir is reported in Arab speech is Luqman ibn 'Ad, and it is said Luqman al-'Adi. Apparently he was a son of 'Ad ibn 'Aws ibn Iram ibn Sam, and he is not Luqman the Wise. The Arabs claim that Luqman was the person who played maysir most, to the extent that they said in a proverb: "More at ease than Luqman." They claim he had eight arrows (aysar) that never left him, and they were among the leaders and nobles of 'Ad. For this reason they compare the people of maysir, when they are of the noble among the people, to the arrows of Luqman. Tarafa ibn al-'Abd said:

"They are the arrows of Luqman, when the winter has made the camels with their hides thin and bare."

He meant an eloquent simile.

[p. 347 ends]

**Description of the maysir:** They would make ten *qidah* (plural of *qidh*, with a kasra on the qaf), which is the arrow smaller than the *nibl* and smaller than the *sahm*. It is a small arrow, like the arrows children play with, and it has no iron head. They called these *al-hizha'* (plural of *hizwa*), which is the small arrow. All of them were made of *qasab al-nab'* (the wood of the nab' tree). These *qidah* are: *al-fadh*, *al-tawam*, *al-raqib*, *al-hils*, *al-nafis*, *al-musbil*, *al-mu'alla*, *al-safih*, *al-mani'*, and *al-wagh*. It was also said that *al-nafis* is the fourth and *al-hils* is the fifth. The first seven have shares (*huzuz*), from one to seven, according to their order, while the last three have no shares and are called *aghfal* (plural of *ghufl*, with a damma on the ghayn and sukun on the fa'), which is the one left unmarked. These marks are lines, from one to seven, like the numerals of Roman reckoning up to four. They marked the marks on the arrows that bear marks, either by scraping the reed (*bi-al-shalt*) or by burning with fire, and the mark is then called *qarma*. These marks are placed at the bottoms of the arrows.

When they wished to gamble, they bought a camel (*jazur*) on credit, payable after the gambling. They divided it into *abda'* (that is, parts): into twenty-eight parts or into ten parts, there being a difference between al-Asma'i and Abu 'Ubayda. The apparent view is that the Arabs had two methods in this, and therefore al-Asma'i and Abu 'Ubayda differed. Then they put those arrows in a leather pouch called the *rababa* (with a kasra on the ra'), which is like the quiver of arrows. It is wide and has a narrow opening that does not allow two or three arrows to come out at once. They entrusted this *rababa* to a man who was called among them the *hurda*, the *darib* and the *mujil*. They would blindfold his eyes with a blindfold, and place on his hands a white cloth, which they called the *mijwal*, which they bound on his hands, or a thin skin which they called the *sulfa* (with a damma on the sin and sukun on the lam). This *hurda* would wrap himself in a garment from which he would put his head out, then kneel on his knees
*[Page 348]*
and place the *rababa* between his hands. Behind him would stand a man called the *raqib* or the *wakil*, who is the trustee over the *hurda* and over the *ayasir*, so that no one would cheat another. He is the one who orders the *hurda* to begin the maysir. They sit, and the *ayasir* around the *hurda* on their knees (*jithiyyan*). Duraid ibn al-Simma said:

*I pushed toward the mujil, while they knelt on their knees,*
*at the rising of every sun.*

Then the *raqib* says to the *hurda*: "Jaljil the arrows", that is, shake them, so he agitates them in the *rababa* so that they become mixed. Then he *yufid* them, that is, he pushes them toward the exit of the arrows from the *rababa* in one single push, upon one name from the *ayasir*. An arrow comes out, and the *wakil* steps forward, takes it and examines it. If it is one of those with shares (*dhawat al-ansiba'*), he hands it to its owner and says to him: "Stand up and withdraw," so he stands and withdraws to one side. Then the *jalajala* is repeated. They have excused that if the first arrow to come out is an *aghfal*, it is not counted as either loss or gain, but is returned to the *rababa*, and the *ihala* is repeated, and so on. Those for whom the *aghfal* arrows came out pay the price of the camel.

As for the description that al-Asma'i gave, that the camel is divided into twenty-eight parts, it is clear that all of the people of the arrows who are winners (*al-qamira*) have a share of the parts of the camel, because the total of the marks on the winning arrows is twenty-eight, and the people of the *qidah* who are losers (*qaddah*) bear the cost of its price.

As for the description that Abu 'Ubayda gave, that the camel is divided into ten *abda'*, this requires that not all of the gamblers are winners, because the gain would be by the measure of ten arrows from those marked on the arrows. In that case, when the parts are exhausted, the distribution ends, and the owners of the *aghfal* arrows bear the price of the camel. Those for whom arrows with shares came out, after those who had taken the camel's parts, receive nothing, since there is no more than one camel in the maysir. Labid said:

*And a camel of the ayasir, I called upon for its destruction,*
*... (the verse)*

And since there is no gain in the maysir except from the meat, not from dirhams or other things. Perhaps each of the two descriptions of al-Asma'i and Abu 'Ubayda was a method of the Arabs in the maysir, according to what the people of the maysir agreed upon. When the sufficient number of participants (*mutayasirun*) is not gathered, some of those present take two or three arrows, and so their gain or loss increases. This is only done by the people of generosity and wealth, because such a person is exposed to a great loss if his arrow does not win. It is said of the one who takes more than one arrow that he is *mutammim al-ayasir* (completer of the ayasir). Al-Nabigha said:

*I complete my ayasir, and I grant them (to others),*
*a double of favors, and I clothe the bowl with the dark-skinned (meat).*
*[Page 349]*

They call this completion *mathna al-ayadi* (double favors), as al-Nabigha said, because by it he intends the repetition of kindness at the time of gain. *Al-ayadi* means the favors. They would give the wage of the *raqib*, the *hurda* and the butcher from the camel's meat. As for the wage of the *raqib*, it is given to him from the first division and the best meat, and they call it *bad'*. As for the *hurda*, he is given meat less than that. As for the butcher, he is given from what remains after the division, of bone or half a bone, and they call it *al-rim*.

Those who attend the maysir without being participants are called *al-a'ran* (plural of *arin*, in the pattern of *katif*), and they attend out of greed for the meat. Whoever does not like the maysir and does not attend it, due to his poverty, is called *al-barim* (with vowelling by movement).

The essential aim of the maysir is the aim of gambling in general, which is gain and amusement. What indicates this is their praising themselves and boasting of giving the winnings of the maysir to the poor, because if this giving were consistent for everyone who plays the maysir, there would be no praise in it. Al-A'sha said:

*They who feed the guest when winter comes,*
*and who make the sustenance dependent on the one who plays the arrows.*

Then their noble men wished to show their disdain for greed for the gambler's wealth, so they began to make the gain go to the poor, the orphans, and whoever visits their courtyard of guests and neighbours. Labid said:

*I call with them for the barren or the one with a young child,*
*whose meat was given to the neighbours, all of them.*

So the guest and the distant neighbour, as if they had descended upon fertile Tabala, its valleys green.

Thus the maysir became among them a mark of the people of generosity, as was mentioned in Labid's verses. 'Antara said, as was mentioned before:

*one whose hands are dexterous with the arrows when winter comes,*
*a breaker of the limits of trade, a bright-faced (man).*

That is, he is light-handed in the maysir, because he played the maysir much in winter for the benefit of the poor. 'Umayr ibn al-Ja'd said:

*a player, when winter comes, and a feeder*
*of meat, not stingy, not stingy-hearted.*

*Al-Kubbunah* (with two dammas) is the one who is contracted, the little known. *Al-'Ulfuf*, like *'usfur*, is the harsh one.

So the benefits of the maysir are particular and general, and they are all worldly. The sin in it is what it causes of enmity and hatred, of wasting time, of habituation to idleness, sloth and frivolity, of turning away from the remembrance of Allah, from the prayer, from deep understanding of the religion, from trade and the like, by which the affairs of civilization are sustained. These are sins which have their harmful effects in the Hereafter. For these considerations, the jurists joined to the maysir every game in which there is gambling, like backgammon (*nard*). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware of these two *ka'batayn*, for they are from the maysir of the non-Arabs," meaning backgammon.
*[Page 350]*
And 'Ali said: "Backgammon and chess are from the maysir." This is the view of the majority of jurists, and of Malik and Abu Hanifa. Al-Shafi'i said: If chess is free of wagering, and the tongue free of arrogance, and the prayer free of forgetfulness, it is not forbidden, and it is outside the maysir, because the maysir is that which requires the giving and taking of wealth, and this is not so. This is a sound view, and the issue is fully discussed in the books of jurisprudence.

"And the people" is meant in its generality, because of the differing benefits. And because the statement came by means of *fi* (in), which indicates location, there is nothing in the speech requiring that every individual among the people benefits from wine and the maysir. Rather, the speech requires that these benefits exist in wine and the maysir for whoever wishes to benefit from them, like His saying: ﴿In it is healing for the people﴾ [al-Nahl: 69].

"The people" does not mean a particular group, since the *al* here is not suitable for the specific reference. If a group were intended, it would not be correct unless it were said: "and the benefits of the drinkers and the gamblers," as He said: ﴿and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers﴾ [Muhammad: 15]. If you say: what is the reason for mentioning the benefits of wine and the maysir when the context of prohibition and preparation for it requires the ignoring of benefits? I say: if the verse was revealed to prohibit wine and the maysir, then the benefit of mentioning the benefits is to explain the wisdom of the legislation, so that Muslims become accustomed to taking note of the causes (*'ilal*) of things, because Allah made this religion a lasting religion and entrusted it to a community from which He wanted to have legislators for different and renewed events. Therefore He pointed out the causes of rulings in more than one place, like His saying: ﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12] and similar. The specification of stating causes for some rulings in some verses is only in places where the causes are hidden. For wine's benefit was well known among them, and they had taken the maysir as a means of benefiting the poor, so it was necessary to explain what harms are in both, to inform them of the wisdom of prohibition. Another benefit is to reassure the obligated ones upon their weaning from their greatest pleasures, reminding them that their Lord wants only their good and not their harm, like His saying ﴿Fighting is prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216] and His saying ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183].

There is also another benefit, which is their excuse for what passed from them, so that they would not become despondent at this prohibition and the denunciation of its harms, like His saying ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves, so He turned to you and pardoned you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

* * *

*[Page 351]*

﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus. Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses, that you may give thought﴾ ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾.

Their question about wine and the maysir came together with their question "what should they spend?", so the verse that contains the answer to their question "what should they spend?" was joined to the verse answering the question about wine and the maysir. For this reason, the style that had preceded in the various verses with the phrase "they ask you" without conjunction was departed from, and this was brought conjoined with *wa* (and) to the one before it.

The structural relation is that the prohibition of wine and the maysir would lead to the expectation of the cessation of great spending which the needy benefited from. So the verse explained to them the true way of spending. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that the questioner about this was Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'laba ibn Ghanama. It was also said that it is a return to the answer to the question of 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who is said to be the one answered by His saying ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: whatever good you spend is for parents﴾ [al-Baqarah: 215], etc. According to this, the answer to his question is distributed across the two places, so that the answer falls in each place in a manner suited to it.

And to show what removes their expectation of the cessation of benefit to the needy, this verse was joined to the one before it with the conjunction *wa*.

**Page 351**

*Al-'afw* (the surplus) is a verbal noun from *'afa*, *ya'fu*, meaning "to increase and grow." God says: ﴿Then We replaced the bad state with the good until they increased﴾ [al-A'raf: 95]. Here it means what exceeds a person's need of wealth, that is, what remains after his own expenditure and the expenditure on his dependents according to the customary standard of people like him. The meaning is that a person is not required to commit sins in order to spend on the needy. Rather, he spends on them from what he has in surplus. This is a command to spend that does not burden the giver, and it is the best form of spending. The purpose of the Sharia in spending is to establish the welfare of the weaker Muslims, and a substantial amount is achieved only through making it general and continuous, so that similar amounts flow at all times. Generality and continuity are achieved only by spending from what exceeds the needs of the spenders. In that case it does not burden them, so none of them abandons it, and none of them neglects it at any time. This is a profound wisdom and a principle of economic civilization. In the hadith: "The best charity is that given out of richness (independence), and begin with those you support." Beginning with those one supports is a form of spending, because if he leaves them in poverty they will need to take from the wealth of the poor. In another hadith: "That you leave your heirs wealthy is better than that you leave them dependent, begging people," meaning stretching out their palms to ask.

**Page 352**

It becomes clear that the one who spends on those he supports reduces the burden on the poor by reducing the number of those who fall among them. For this reason it is narrated in the hadith: "You do not spend an expenditure seeking the Face of God except that you are rewarded for it, even the morsel you place in the mouth of your wife."

For this reason, in this verse, He commanded the spending of *al-'afw*, because the verse addresses all spenders in general. There is therefore no contradiction in a person spending some of his wealth that he himself needs, or all of his wealth, if he is patient in doing so and has no one for whom he is obligated to provide maintenance.

The *alif-lam* in *al-'afw* is for the generic class, known to the listeners. *Al-'afw* is predicated by gradation (*tashkik*), because it depends on determining what the spender needs, and people differ in that. God made the whole surplus to be spent, to encourage spending. This indicates that what is meant by spending here is voluntary spending. For the textual evidences of the Sharia have converged, and the consensus of the scholars (*ijma'*) has been established, that a Muslim is not obligated to spend except for obligatory maintenance and obligatory almsgiving (*zakat*). Zakat may itself come from some of what exceeds the wealth of the wealthy, except for what Abu Dharr deviated on, for he regarded the hoarding of wealth as forbidden and proclaimed this in Syria. Mu'awiya complained about him to Uthman, and Uthman ordered that he be returned from Syria to Medina, and then settled in al-Rabadha at his own request. Uthman strove to close the door of strife. From Qays ibn Sa'd it is narrated that this verse concerns the prescribed zakat. According to his view, the *alif-lam* in *al-'afw* is for a known referent outside the text, namely the growth of wealth determined by the threshold (*nisab*).

Al-Jumhur read ﴿qul al-'afwa﴾ with *al-'afwa* in the accusative, as the object of a verb implied by *madha yunfiqun* ("what they spend"). This reading is based on treating *dha* after *ma* as nullified (not a relative pronoun), so that *ma* the interrogative is the object preceding *yunfiqun*. It is therefore appropriate for the explainer of *ma* in the answer to come in the accusative, like its explanation.

Ibn Kathir, in one of two narrations from him, and Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it in the nominative, as the predicate of an implied subject: "it is the *'afw*." This reading is based on treating *dha* after *ma* as a relative pronoun, meaning: "they ask you about that which they spend." Because in that case it is a relative clause, it is a subject (*mubtada'*), since its relative clause does not govern it, and the interrogative *ma* is a predicate of the relative *ma*. Its explainer in the answer, which is *al-'afw*, came in the nominative like its explained element, so that the answer matches the question in both considerations. Both readings are eloquent Arabic constructions.

His words: ﴿Thus God makes clear to you the signs﴾. That is, thus does God make clear to you the signs by this kind of clarification. The *kaf* (thus) is for comparison, standing in the position of an absolute object clarifying the type of "makes clear." The discussion of the aspects of this demonstration has already been presented in His words: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

**Page 353**

Or the demonstration refers to the clarification in His words: ﴿Say: in both there is great sin﴾, up to His words: *al-'afw*. He joined the demonstrative with the mark of distance to exalt the status of what is pointed to, for its perfection in clarification: it is a clarification of the ruling together with the clarification of its cause, so that the community receives it with contentment, and so that they may attach its analogues to it, and it is a clarification of the principle of spending in a way that does not deviate from any spender. Because the *kaf* is not intended for address, but only for the abstract sense of distance for exaltation, it was not used in accordance with the apparent form of addressing the group. Therefore it did not say "thus for you" in the manner of His words: ﴿God makes clear to you﴾.

The *lam* in *lakum* is for causation and purpose, and it is a favour and an honouring with this virtue, since it implies that clarification in this manner is something particular to this community, so that they may receive the obligations with insight, in the position of an admonition delivered to a person of complete reason, clarified by its consequences, because God willed for this community that its scholars be legislators.

He explained the benefit of this clarification in this manner by His words: ﴿so that you may reflect upon the world and the Hereafter﴾, that is, so that the community may attain reflection and knowledge regarding the affairs of this world and the affairs of the Hereafter. For reflection is related to this world and the Hereafter, so the supposition of an elided noun is necessary by the indication of His words "and the Hereafter," since it has no meaning for reflection to occur on the Day of Resurrection. If it had been limited to clarifying the prohibition, obligation, reward and punishment, it would have been a clarification of reflection on the affairs of the Hereafter only. And if it had been limited to clarifying benefits and harms, by saying: "In both there is benefit and harm," it would have been a clarification of reflection on the affairs of this world only. But the mention of benefits and harms, and of reward and punishment, is a reminder of the welfare of both abodes, and in this there is an emphasis on the importance of setting right the affairs of the community in this world.

It occurred in the words of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, when a man disparaged this world in his presence, that he said to him: "This world is an abode of truth for whoever speaks truly of it, an abode of salvation for whoever understands from it, an abode of richness for whoever provides himself from it, the descent-place of God's revelation, the prayer-place of His angels, and the mosque of His prophets. So who is it that disparages it, when it has announced its parting?" etc.

It is not hidden that what is suited to reflection is the ruling tied to its cause, namely the ruling on wine and gambling, and then what arose from it: His words ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾.

It is permissible that the demonstration in His words "thus" refers to the spending being from the surplus, but this is weak, because that clarification does not show the full extent of favour in a way that makes it a model of the sublime divine clarifications, and so that it is the locus of complete favour, and so that its ultimate aim is reflection on this world and the Hereafter. Nor should it impress you that it is nearer to the demonstrative noun, for attaching oneself to such verbal matters among the subtleties of inimitability is a squandering of minds and a clinging to husks.

His words ﴿so that you may reflect﴾ are the ultimate aim of this clarification and its wisdom, and the discussion of *la'alla* ("so that") has already been presented. His words ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217] are connected to *tatafakkarun* ("you reflect"), not to *yubayyinu* ("He makes clear"), because the clarification occurs in this world only. The meaning: so that there may come to you reflection, that is, knowledge, concerning the affairs of this world and the Hereafter. Anything beyond this is forced.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 220 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: "Setting things right for them is good. And if you mix with them, they are your brothers. God knows the corrupter from the reformer. Had God willed, He would have burdened you. Indeed God is Almighty, All-Wise."﴾

The explanation of how to deal with orphans is conjoined (with *wa*, "and") to the explanation of spending (*infaq*), because both matters are connected to the ruling on prohibiting gambling (*maysir*), or to warning against it. Gambling had been a wide avenue for spending on the needy and on orphans. Labid mentioned feeding orphans after mentioning feeding on the meat of the slaughtered camels of gambling, when he said:

*"And they crown themselves when the winds blow in gusts, with bowls drawn forth, whose orphans are stretched out (as thin, dry hands)."*

That is, they stretch out hands like spear-shafts that are thin and dry, meaning meat-poor hands on bony fingers. So the prohibition of gambling raised the question of closing this avenue of provision for orphans, though it contained great benefit for them. That question provided a fine occasion for moving to the charge concerning orphans and mentioning, in summary, their condition within the broader matter of setting right the conditions they lived under before Islam. This is the reason for conjoining this sentence to the one before it with the conjunction *wa*, since some of these questions are linked to one another, as was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: "The surplus."﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:219).

It has been reported that the one who asked about orphans was 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha. Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas that when the words of God, Mighty and Majestic, were revealed, ﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan except in the best manner﴾ (Al-An'am 6:152), ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ (Al-Nisa' 4:10), and the verses that follow, whoever had an orphan in his care separated the orphan's food from his own food and the orphan's drink from his own drink. He began to set aside some of his food, which was kept for the orphan until he ate it or it spoiled. This became burdensome for them, so it was mentioned to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and God revealed ﴿And they ask you about orphans﴾ and the verse.

[p. 355]

However, Surat al-Nisa' was revealed after Surat al-Baqarah. So perhaps the mention of the verse of al-Nisa' is a mistake by the narrator. What he meant is that when the verses warning against the property of orphans were revealed, like the verse of Surat al-Isra' ﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan except in the best manner﴾ (Al-An'am 6:152), then in al-Tabari's Tafsir, traced back to Ibn 'Abbas: when ﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan except in the best manner﴾ (Al-An'am 6:152) was revealed, they set aside the property of orphans, so they mentioned that to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and ﴿And if you mix with them﴾ was revealed. Or the narrator's meaning is that when people heard the verse of Surat al-Nisa', they avoided looking after orphans, so they were reminded by the verse of al-Baqarah, provided that the one asking about the verse of al-Baqarah was not among those who avoided it at the time the verse of al-Nisa' was revealed. In any case, it is established that attending to the welfare of orphans is among the most important aims of the Sharia in preserving social order. The Arabs in the Jahiliyya, like other nations in a state of simplicity, had property in the hands of the head of the household, so one rarely found wealth in the hands of a child. Most of their wealth came from their own earning, since wealth was concentrated among few people. Most Arabs were either farmers, planters, raiders, or hunters, and all these occupations end with the death of those who practice them. So when the head of a household died and left young children, they could not earn as their fathers had, except the children of the wealthy. For them, wealth consisted of livestock and orchards, since the Arabs were not a people of gold and silver. Livestock cannot be kept without someone to herd it, and it is a perishable asset. Plantations are likewise. The Arabs' wealth did not include ownership of land, since land was useful only to the one who worked it. Moreover, whoever takes charge of an orphan's affairs takes advantage of his weakness, makes his property lawful for himself, and benefits from it personally. The generosity, extravagance, drinking, and gambling of the Arab do not leave him any wealth, however much he had.

This dominance over the appetites of his companions makes them unable to abandon it, and drives them to seek satisfaction of their desires by every means. Therefore, it is inevitable that the orphan among them becomes poor and humiliated. Add to this that the people of the Jahiliyya had deeply rooted arrogance toward the weak and reverence for the strong. When the orphan lacked a helper and one to defend him, he became exposed to humiliation and neglect, and was treated like a slave by his guardian. For all these reasons, the description of "orphan" among them came to be associated with destitution, neglect, and abasement. Through this, the meaning of God's favor upon His Prophet becomes clear, that He protected him during his orphanhood from what befalls orphans, in His words: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾ (Al-Duha 93:6).

When Islam came, it commanded them to set right the condition of orphans in their property and in all their affairs, until it was said that the guardians of orphans had abandoned managing their property and had withdrawn from the orphans and from mixing with them, so this verse was revealed.

Ișlah (*islah*, setting right) is making a thing sound (*salih*), that is, possessing soundness. Salah is the opposite of corruption (*fasad*), and it is a thing's being in a state by which the ultimate purpose for which it is sought is achieved. So the soundness of a man is the issuing of good deeds and words from him,

[p. 356]

and the soundness of fruit is its being in a state where it can be eaten without harm, the soundness of property is its intended growth, and the soundness of a condition is its being in a state where good consequences follow from it.

"Islah lahum" (setting right for them) is the subject of the sentence and its predicate. The *lam* is for causation or for specification (*ikhtisas*). The phrase describes "islah" with "lahum" (for them) rather than in the construct form, saying "islahuhum" (their setting right). This avoids the restriction of the meaning to setting right their persons, because the basic principle of the genitive construction of a verbal noun (*masdar*) is that it refers to the agent or the object, and so it does not carry the meaning of a particle. Also, since the genitive construction is one of the ways of definiteness, it would appear to refer to a known specific setting right, so it was avoided, just as it was avoided in His words: ﴿Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾ (Yusuf 12:59), where He did not say "bi-akhikum" (your brother), so as not to suggest to them that He did not mean a brother known to Him. The intended meaning here is the entire setting right, not only the setting right of their persons. So it includes setting right their persons, which is primary, and this includes setting right their beliefs and morals through sound teaching and Islamic manners and knowledge of the affairs of the world. It includes setting right their temperaments by protecting them from destructive dangers, diseases, and by treating them. It includes averting harm from them by providing for their needs of food, clothing, and shelter according to what is customary for people like them, without stinginess or extravagance. It also includes setting right their property by developing, maintaining, and preserving it.

This expression is beautifully chosen. If it had said "islahuhum" (their setting right), it would have appeared to be restricted to their persons, so the indication of setting right their property would require analogy. If it had said "qul tadbiruhum khayr" (say: their management is good), it would have immediately suggested the management of property, and then its indication of setting right their persons would require the implication of the discourse (*fahwa al-khitab*).

"Khayr" (good) in the verse may be a comparative form (*af'al tafdil*, "better") if the address is to those whom fear of consuming orphans' property has led to withdraw from their affairs and abandon managing their property, on the ground of fear of mismanaging it, as one says:

"Indeed, safety from Salma and her neighbour is that you do not alight in a state within her valley."

So the meaning is: setting right their affairs is better than neglecting them, that is, more rewarding and further from punishment. It is better in achieving your intended purpose from neglecting them, since neglect leads to the sin of wasting, and there is no reward for effort and sincere advice in it. It may also be an attribute opposite to evil, if the address is to changing the conditions they were under before Islam. Then the meaning is: setting right their property and their bodies, and not neglecting them in both matters, as explained above, is good. This is an allusion (*ta'ridh*) that what they used to do in their dealings was not good, but rather evil. So the meaning of the verse according to this reading is

[p. 357]

both legislation and allusion, since allusion can coexist with the primary meaning, because it belongs to the category of metonymy (*kinaya*), and metonymy occurs together with the intended primary meaning.

The clause ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Setting right for them is good.﴾ "Mukhalata" (mixing) is a verbal form of "khalt" (mixing), which means gathering things together in a way that makes it impossible to distinguish some from others in what they are intended for. From it comes mixing water with water, wheat with barley, and mixing people. Also from it: "the one with the throwing-stick and the one with the arrow are mixed together" (i.e., in a confused battle). Here it is a metaphor for close involvement and association. What is meant is whatever goes beyond setting right property and bringing up orphans from a distance, so it includes companionship, partnership, guardianship, and marriage, since all of these are types of mixing.

His words "fa-ikhwanukum" (then they are your brothers) are the answer to the condition, and for this reason it is joined with *fa*, because a nominal clause cannot directly follow a conditional particle. Therefore "ikhwanukum" is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being "fa-hum ikhwanukum" (then they are your brothers). This is the meaning of a highly eloquent comparison (*tashbih baligh*). The brotherhood meant is the brotherhood of Islam, which requires consultation, gentleness, and sincere advice.

Al-Razi transmitted from al-Farra': "If you put it in the accusative, it would be correct, with the estimate: 'fa-ikhwanakum tukhalituna' (then you mix with your brothers)." But this is a clumsy estimate. The presence of *fa* in the answer indicates that the answer is a purely nominal clause. Moreover, the sense of al-Farra's statement should be understood as meaning that such a construction is permissible in Arabic speech, not that it should be recited that way. Perhaps al-Farra' was bold in making the recitation of the Qur'an conform to what is permitted in Arabic speech, without requiring the soundness of the transmitted reading.

The purpose of this clause is to urge mixing with them. Since God made them brothers, it is especially required to mix with them and to take charge of them in this mixing, because when they are brothers, it is obligatory to give them sincere advice, just as one gives it to a brother. In the hadith: "until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself." This implies an allusion to abandoning their former contempt for orphans, their distancing themselves from mixing with them, and their refusal to marry them. God said: ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ (Al-Nisa' 4:127), meaning: you desire not to marry them, because brotherhood implies equality, and so haughtiness is nullified.

His words: ﴿God knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ are a promise and a warning, because the purpose of informing about God's knowledge is to inform about the consequences of that knowledge. This points out that what some Muslims did by avoiding dealing with orphans' property was a scrupulousness with no benefit, because God knows the one who manages with soundness and the one who manages without soundness. It also contains reassurance for the guardians of orphans regarding what they suffer from the dislike of some of their wards and from being restrained from managing their property, and from the hardship they face in that. The greatest aim is to please God, not to please creatures. The Muslims of that time cared only for God's good pleasure, and they used to hold themselves accountable for their intentions.

[p. 358]

In this there is also an indication that it is not in the interest of people to turn away from looking into orphans' property for fear of the tongues of evil and the accusation of sinful suspicion. If people colluded in that to protect their own reputations, the orphans would be lost. This is not the way of Muslims, for there are signs of soundness and corruption, and behind those who manage are judges and rulers of justice who reward the reformer with praise and public commendation, and who punish the corrupter by keeping him away from the orphans and by making him pay compensation for what he destroyed without consideration.

Ibn Malik said in *al-Tas'hil*: "and for separation (*al-fasl*)." He said in its commentary: "By mentioning separation I indicated its use with the second of two opposites, as in ﴿Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ and ﴿until He distinguishes the wicked from the good﴾ [Al 'Imran: 179]." End of quote. This is an elegant meaning that cannot be dispensed with. Al-Zamakhshari also pointed to it in *al-Kashshaf* in his comment on the verse ﴿Do you approach males from among the worlds?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 165] in Surat al-Shu'ara'. He considered it a established interpretation, saying: "Or, do you (people) approach males from among those other than you of the worlds? He means that you, O people of Lut, alone are specialised in this immorality." End of quote. So he took the meaning of *min* to be *min bayn* ("from among"), which can only be sustained by establishing the meaning of separation. This meaning lies between the beginning-sense (*ibtida'iyya*, "from") and the substitution-sense (*badaliyya*, "in place of"), since the object of the preposition cannot be read purely as a starting point nor purely as a substitute. Thus an intermediate meaning arises. Ibn Hisham discussed this in *Mughni al-Labib*, holding that separation results from the verb *yumayyizu* ("distinguishes") and from the verb *ya'lamu* ("knows"). He preferred the view that *min* here is for the starting point, or means *'an* ("from/about").

His words ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have put you in difficulty﴾ are a concluding phrase (*tadhyil*) for what was implied by His words ﴿Reforming them is good﴾, as previously explained. *Al-'anat* is hardship and severe difficulty. The meaning is: had Allah willed, He would have imposed upon you that which involves hardship, namely prohibiting you from mixing with orphans, so that you would find that burdensome and a difficulty for you. This is because a person's avoidance of mixing with his relatives, such as brothers and paternal cousins, and his leaving them, neglects their affairs, and no one cares for them, which is naturally hard for people. Even if they did this out of caution and scrupulousness, not everything a person begins to do can he sustain.

The omission of the object of the verb of will (*maf'ul al-mashi'a*) is because what follows it suffices in its place. This omission is common with the object of the verb of will, so they almost never mention it. Its discussion was already given at His words ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20].

His words ﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾ are a concluding phrase for what the conditional *law* (if) implies of possibility and impossibility of occurrence. That is: indeed Allah is Mighty, Overpowering, Able. So had He willed, He would have imposed hardship upon you, but He is Wise, placing things in their proper places, and therefore He did not impose it upon you.

Page 359

In combining the two attributes there is an indication that Allah's actions proceed according to all that His attributes require. By this, great difficulties regarding what is expressed as *qada'* and *qadar* (divine decree and predestination) are dispelled.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 221 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And do not marry idolatresses until they believe. A believing slave-woman is better than an idolatress, even though she may please you. And do not marry idolaters until they believe. A believing slave is better than an idolater, even though he may please you. Those invite to the Fire, but Allah invites to Paradise and forgiveness by His permission, and He makes clear His signs to the people that they may remember.﴾

The Muslims, at the time this surah was revealed, were still mixing with the polytheists in Madinah, and they were not far from their relatives among the people of Makkah. So it happened that some of them desired to marry polytheist women, or some polytheists desired to marry Muslim women. Allah therefore made the ruling clear for these situations. By His wisdom, He placed this clarification in the most fitting and most beneficial position, which is the position following the ruling on dealing with orphans. For the Muslims at that time had relatives and clients who were still polytheists, and among them were orphans who had lost their fathers at the Battle of Badr and after it. When Allah mentioned the regulation on dealing with orphans, and marriage ties are among the greatest forms of such dealing, the souls turned their attention to the ruling on this kind of marriage with polytheist women and men. So the ruling on this was joined to the ruling on orphans because of this connection.

Al-Wahidi and other exegetes narrated that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi, and it is said Marthad ibn Abi Marthad, whose name was Kannaz ibn Husayn, and he was an ally of the Banu Hashim, to Makkah secretly to bring out a man from among the Muslims. A woman called 'Anaq heard of his coming, and she had been his lover in the Jahiliyyah. She came to him and said: 'Woe to you, O Marthad, will you not be alone with me?' He said: 'Islam has forbidden what was in the Jahiliyyah.' She said: 'Then marry me.' He said: 'Until I ask the permission of the Messenger of Allah.' He came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked his permission, and he forbade him to marry her, because she was a polytheist." So this verse was revealed concerning this incident.

In the speech of the Arabs, nikah (marriage, a technical term meaning the marriage contract) is literally used for the contract of marriage with a woman. Therefore they say: "Fulan married Fulanah" (nakaha fulanun fulanatan), and they say: "Fulanah married Fulan" (nakahat fulanatun fulanan). So it is literally used for the contract, because frequency of use is one of the indications of the literal meaning. As for its use for sexual intercourse, it is a metaphor (kinayah). It has also been said that it is literally used for intercourse and metaphorically for the contract. This was preferred by the jurists of the Shafi'i school, though it is a weak view in linguistics. It has also been said that it is literally used for both, and so it is a homonym (mushtarak), and this is the weakest view.

صفحة ٣٦٠

They said: it does not occur in the Qur'an except with the meaning of the contract. It has been said that there is an exception in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], because the contract alone does not suffice to make the irrevocably divorced woman lawful again until her husband has consummated the marriage with her, as in the hadith of the wife of Rifa'ah. But the more correct view is that this verse also means the contract, and it is the Sunnah that clarified that along with the contract there must be intercourse. This is the apparent meaning. The prohibition in this verse is connected to the contract by consensus.

In the language of the Shari'ah, the mushrik (polytheist) is one who holds to a plurality of gods along with Allah, glory be to Him. The term, wherever it appears in the Qur'an, refers to the polytheists of the Arabs who worshipped other gods along with Allah, exalted is He. In the division of disbelievers, they are contrasted with the People of the Book, who believed in Allah, His messengers and His books, but denied the message of Muhammad ﷺ.

The text of this verse prohibits a Muslim man from marrying a polytheist woman, and prohibits a Muslim woman from being given in marriage to a polytheist man. It is explicit in this. As for a Muslim man marrying a woman of the People of the Book, and a Muslim woman marrying a man of the People of the Book, the verse is silent about it, because the word mushrik is a title (laqab) that has no implied meaning (mafhum) except when it is attached to a described noun, as we shall explain at His words, exalted is He, ﴿better than an idolater﴾. The Qur'an has permitted a Muslim man to marry a woman of the People of the Book in His words ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5] in the surah of al-'Uqud. Therefore the majority of scholars said that it is permissible for a Muslim man to marry a woman of the People of the Book, but not a polytheist or Magian woman, and on this the four Imams, al-Awza'i and al-Thawri agreed. So the marriage of a Muslim woman to a man of the People of the Book remained without an explicit text, and all Muslims prohibited it, either based on their restricting themselves to the context of stating the legislation, or based on evidences from the Sunnah and from analogy, which we shall point to, or from consensus, and this is the more evident view. Some scholars went another way in deriving the jurisprudence of this question, saying: the People of the Book have become polytheists by the saying of the Jews "Uzayr is the son of Allah," and by the saying of the Christians "the Messiah is the son of Allah," and fatherhood of God entails divinity of the Son. This meaning was adopted by 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, for in the Muwatta' it is narrated from him: "I know of no shirk greater than that a woman says her lord is 'Isa." But this path is very weak, because including the People of the Book within the meaning of the polytheists is far from the technical usage of the Shari'ah, and this verse and similar verses were revealed, and this is well known and widespread. Also, if it is established for the Christians in a consistent manner, it is not established for the Jews, because those who said "Uzayr is the son of Allah" are only a small group of the Jews, the followers of Phinehas, as al-Fakhr related. So if this verse prohibits a Muslim from marrying a Jewish or Christian woman, and prohibits any of the Jews and Christians from marrying a Muslim woman, then the verse in surah al-'Uqud has specified the general prohibition by the explicit saying ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], and Allah knew their saying ﴿the Messiah is the son of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30] and the saying of the others, "Uzayr is the son of Allah." Thus the marriage of a Muslim woman to them remains included in the generality of the verse of al-Baqarah. This is a path taken by some Shafi'is. Among the scholars of Islam, there are those who disliked marrying a woman of the People of the Book, and this is the view of Malik in the narration of Ibn Habib, and it is a narration from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he wrote to Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, when he had heard that he had married a Jewish or Christian woman: "Divorce her." Hudhayfah wrote back to him: "Do you claim that she is haram?" 'Umar said: "No, but I fear that they will take up with the immoral women among them."

Some scholars of an aberrant view said that marrying a woman of the People of the Book is prohibited, and they claimed that the verse of al-Ma'idah was abrogated by the verse of al-Baqarah. This is reported from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, and in a weak narration from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: that he separated between Talhah ibn 'Ubaydullah and a Jewish woman he had married, and between Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman and a Christian woman he had married. They said to him: "O Commander of the Believers, shall we divorce, and you not be angry?" He said: "If your divorce were permissible, your marriage would have been permissible. But I will separate you two, in humiliation and disgrace." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is not transmitted with a good chain, and the other report from 'Umar is better supported than it. al-Tabari said: it contradicts what the Ummah has agreed upon, and there is from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab a view contrary to that which is more authentic than it. 'Umar only disliked for them both their marriage out of fear that people would follow their example and thus become averse to Muslim women.

The phrase ﴿until they believe﴾ is a limit (ghayah) for the prohibition: when she believes, the prohibition ends. For this reason, when a polytheist embraces Islam and his wife does not embrace Islam, she is separated from him, unless she embraces Islam immediately after his Islam, without delay.

His words ﴿A believing slave-woman is better than an idolatress﴾ are a warning about the baseness of polytheist women and a caution against marrying them and against being deceived by what a polytheist woman may possess of lineage, beauty or wealth. These are the ways in which a woman may attract, and this is emphasized by His words ﴿even though she may please you﴾. And whoever is unable to marry a free believing woman, then marrying a believing slave-woman is better for him than marrying a free idolatress. Here "slave-woman" means one who is owned, and "idolatress" means the free woman, by the contrast indicated by His words ﴿a believing slave-woman﴾. The speech is directed toward the extreme of exaggeration in preferring the least of one category over the most complete of the other category. So if a believing slave-woman is better than every idolatress, then a believing free woman is better than an idolatress, by the implication of the discourse (dalalat fahwa al-khitab) which the context requires, and because it is evident that there is no sense in preferring a believing slave-woman over an idolatress slave-woman, this is established by implication, which the believing addressees do not doubt. Also, His words ﴿even though she may please you﴾ apply, for admiration is for free women rather than for slave-women.

صفحة ٣٦١

The intended sense of the comparative "better" (khayr) is the superiority in the benefits gained from the two women. For marrying a believing slave-woman has religious benefits, while a free idolatress has worldly benefits, and the meanings of religion are better than the transient goods of this world which contradict religion. So the purpose of it is to explain the wisdom of the prohibition, to put the Muslims at ease.

In the Kashshaf, the word "slave-woman" is taken to mean women in general, because all people are the slave-women and slaves of Allah. This is transmitted from the judge Abu al-Hasan al-Jurjani, as in al-Qurtubi, and this is false both in meaning and in wording. As for the meaning, it would become a repetition of His words ﴿do not marry idolatresses﴾, since people already know that the idolatress is inferior to the believing woman, and it would defeat the purpose of alerting to the nobility of the least of one category over the noblest of the other category. As for the wording, the Arabs never used "slave-woman" to mean women in general, nor "slave" to mean men in general, except when restricted by being attached to the divine name, as in their saying: "O slave of Allah" and "O slave-woman of Allah." That all people are the slave-women and slaves of Allah is a consideration of realities, not of usage, so how could the Qur'an be made to follow it?

The pronoun in ﴿even though she may please you﴾ refers to the idolatress. The "wa" (even) with "law" (lo) is a conjunctive particle to alert to the furthest of the circumstances which are most likely to make the idolatress preferable, so the believing slave-woman is better than her even in that state. The discussion of the position of (law) as a conjunctive particle, the waw preceding it, and the sentence following it has already passed at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything, nor were they guided?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170].

His words ﴿And do not marry idolaters until they believe﴾ are a prohibition on giving a Muslim woman in marriage to a polytheist. If "idolater" is taken in its apparent sense in the language of the Shari'ah, then the verse does not address the ruling on giving a Muslim woman in marriage to a disbelieving People of the Book, so the prohibition of that is by consensus, which is either based on a proof that the Companions received from the Prophet ﷺ and which was transmitted among them through continuous narration, or based on the convergence of the legal evidences, such as His words ﴿Then do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful to them, nor are they lawful to them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], where He attached the prohibition to disbelief, which is more general than polytheism, even if the intended meaning there is the polytheists, and as His words here, exalted is He, ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾, as we shall explain.

His words ﴿until they believe﴾ are a limit for the prohibition, and it is derived from it that if a disbelieving man's wife embraces Islam, the marriage between them is annulled; then if he embraces Islam, he has more right to her as long as she is still within the waiting period ('iddah).

His words ﴿A believing slave is better than an idolater, even though he may please you﴾ are like His words ﴿A believing slave-woman is better than

صفحة ٣٦٣

from the wording "مِن مُشْرِكَةٍ" — that the intended meaning is the slave woman, not the free polytheist, as has already been explained.

His saying ﴿They invite to the Fire﴾ refers to the polytheist women and the polytheist men, since there is no reason to restrict it to the men alone, given that it can refer to all of them. The waw in "يَدْعُونَ" is the waw of the plural of men, its pattern being "يَفْعُونَ", and the masculine is given precedence over the feminine, as is common usage. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) explaining the prohibition against marrying polytheist women and giving women in marriage to polytheist men. The meaning of "the invitation to the Fire" is the invitation to its causes; thus attributing the invitation to them is a literal rational attribution (haqiqah 'aqliyyah), while the word "the Fire" is a figurative metonymy (majaz mursal), used for the causes of entering the Fire, since what they adhere to leads to the Fire without their knowing it. Since the bond of marriage is a bond of association and companionship, He forbade its formation with those who invite to the Fire, lest that invitation affect the soul, for between the spouses there is affection and familiarity that move each to please the other. And since this invitation from the polytheists is intense, because they do not affirm the Oneness of God nor believe in the messengers, the gulf between them and the Muslims in religion is very wide, with nothing common between them on which they agree; so God did not permit intermingling with them through marriage from either side.

As for the People of the Book, what unites them with the Muslims is belief in the existence of God, His sole creation, and belief in the prophets; what separates us from the Christians is their belief in the sonship of Jesus, and what separates us from the Jews is belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and affirmation of Jesus. God therefore permitted the Muslim man to marry a woman of the People of the Book, but did not permit the marriage of a Muslim woman to a man of the People of the Book, out of regard for the strength of the man's influence over his wife. The Muslim believes in the prophets of the People of the Book and in the validity of their religion before abrogation, so it is likely that this will lead her to Islam, since she is weaker than him in that respect. As for the disbeliever, he does not believe in the religion of the Muslim woman or in her messenger, so he is likely to draw her to his religion, for this reason. Our teacher, the Professor Salim Abu Hajib, used to answer with this concerning the reason for permitting marriage to a woman of the People of the Book and forbidding a man of the People of the Book to marry a Muslim woman.

As for His saying ﴿And God invites to Paradise﴾ and the verse continues, meaning that God invites by this religion to Paradise; therefore the invitation of the polytheists is opposed to the invitation of God, and the purpose of this is to denounce their invitation and that it is contrary to the invitation of God.
