The invitation to Paradise and forgiveness is an invitation to their causes, as already explained in His saying ﴿They invite to the Fire﴾. And "forgiveness" here means forgiveness of what they were upon of polytheism.

As for His saying ﴿by His permission﴾, the permission here is either in the sense of command, as is common, so "by His permission" is a settled adverbial clause of circumstance (hal) relating to "Paradise and forgiveness," meaning obtained by His permission, that is, His will and decree, through what He has made clear of their paths.

Some exegetes understood "permission" as facilitation and decree, and the "bi" as an adverbial of place (zarf laghw), and found this qualification not of great benefit, so they interpreted His saying "God invites" as meaning "and the friends of God invite," who are the believers.

The sentence "and He makes clear" (wa-yubayyin) is coordinated with "invites," meaning: He invites to good together with making it clear and explaining it, so that souls receive it with greater acceptance and complete insight. This is like His saying ﴿Thus God makes clear His signs to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], so it carries a sense of an appended conclusion (tadhyil), even though it comes in a form other than its own. And "la'alla" (perhaps) is used in such a context as a figurative expression for a near outcome.

﴿Yet they ask you about menstruation. Say: It is an harm, so keep away from women during menstruation, and do not approach them until they are pure. But when they have purified themselves, go in to them as God has commanded you. Indeed God loves those who turn often (to Him in repentance) and loves those who purify themselves.﴾

This is a continuation of the sentence ﴿And do not marry idolatresses until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. The connection is that the prohibition of marrying idolatresses implies distancing oneself from the practices of the idolaters. The idolaters would not approach their wives when they were menstruating, and they went to extremes in keeping away from them during the period of menstruation. So it was fitting to define what occurs frequently, which is among the matters in which the idolaters differed from others, and about which the Muslims were asking which of the methods (manāhij) was most correct in this respect. It is related that the questioner on this matter was Abu al-Dahdah Thabit ibn al-Dahdah al-Ansari. It is also related that the questioner was Usayd ibn Hudayr, and it is related that he was 'Abbad ibn Bishr. Thus the question took place during the period of the revelation of this surah, and so it was mentioned in it along with the rulings that will be mentioned.

The impetus for the question was that the people of Yathrib had intermingled with the Jews and had adopted their customs in many matters. The Jews kept far away from the menstruating woman with the utmost distance, according to the ruling of the Torah. In the fifteenth chapter of the Book of Leviticus: "If a woman has a discharge, her discharge being blood from her body, she shall be in her impurity seven days, and whoever touches her shall be unclean until evening. Everything upon which she lies during her impurity shall be unclean, and whoever touches her bed shall wash his clothes and bathe in water and shall be unclean until evening. If a man lies with her, and her impurity falls upon him, he shall be unclean seven days." Al-Qurtubi mentioned that the Christians do not abstain from this, but I do not think that is correct, for there is nothing in the Gospel that indicates it. Also, among the tribes of the Arabs there were those among whom a menstruating woman was hated.

[p. 365]

The tribe of Banu Sulayh, the people of the town of al-Hadr, who were of Quda'ah and Christians, if a woman menstruated they would expel her from the city to the outskirts (al-rabḍ) until she became pure, and they did this with Nasrah, daughter of al-Dayzan, king of al-Hadr. So the situation was a cause for the bewilderment of the Muslims about this matter, prompting them to ask about it.

Al-maḥīḍ (menstruation) is the noun for the blood that flows from the womb of the woman at regular times. The word maḥīḍ is on the pattern maf'il, transferred from the verbal nouns in an irregular manner, since the analogy for the verbal noun of such a form is with an open ‘ayn. Al-Zajjaj said: "It is said ḥāḍat ḥaydan wa-maḥāḍan wa-maḥīḍan. The verbal noun in this category is basically maf'al with an open ‘ayn, but maf'il with a kasra on the ‘ayn is good, and the reason for its goodness is that it resembles its imperfect, for the imperfect with a kasra on the ‘ayn is like al-majī' and al-mabīt." In my view, when maḥīḍ became a noun for the flowing blood from the woman, it was turned away from the analogy of its origin as a verbal noun to the pattern of a noun of place, and it was given the pattern of a place to indicate that it had become a noun. Thus they deviated from the patterns of events (al-aḥdāth) to signal transfer, distinguishing between that from which it was transferred and that to which it was transferred. It is also said ḥayḍ, which is the origin of the verbal noun: it is said ḥāḍat al-mar'ah when blood flowed from her, just as it is said ḥāḍa al-sayl when its water overflowed, and from this the pool is called ḥawḍ because it flows; they changed its yā' to wāw. It is not a transfer from the noun of place, since there is no suitable reason for transfer from it. Rather, whoever claimed it has strained for it, being refuted by adherence to the analogy of the noun of place while ignoring what making it a noun involves of widening the use of the rule of derivation.

What is meant by the question about menstruation is the question about approaching women during menstruation, by way of implication (dalālat al-iqtiḍā'). The questioners knew what they were asking about, and the answer is the clearest indication of it.

Al-adhā (harm) is the injury that is not grievous, as indicated by the exception in His saying ﴿They will not harm you except a little hurt﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 111]. The answer begins with what the man does with his menstruating wife. So He made clear to them that menstruation is an harm, so that the prohibition on approaching the woman that follows would be given a reason, and souls would receive it with insight, and the community would be prepared for legislating in similar matters. He expressed it as adhā, pointing to the abolition of what there was of exaggeration in its matter and the matter of the menstruating woman in the law of the Torah. He established that it is an harm in an indefinite form and did not specify its aspect, so it is determined that the harm in a man's intercourse with a menstruating woman is harm to the man, to the woman, and to the child. As for the man's harm, the first of it is filth. Also, this flowing blood comes from the reproductive organ of the woman, and it contains tiny ova from which fetuses are formed after the end of menstruation, and after those ova mix with the man's water. When the reproductive organ of the man is immersed in the blood, something of that blood passes into his penis with what it contains. Sometimes a part of it is trapped in the urethra of the male and turns into putrefaction that causes stubborn diseases, producing pustules and sores, because it is blood that has become corrupt, and living parts enter into it that corrupt the penis with a corruption like the death of a living thing, so it ends in decay.

[p. 366]

As for the woman's harm, it is because the reproductive organ of hers at that time is in the state of preparing to produce reproductive strength, so when it is disturbed, it is a disturbance at the time of its occupation, and thereby illness and weakness enter it. As for the child, when the seed mixes with menstrual blood, the ova begin to form before the time of their suitability for beneficial formation, which comes after drying. The Arabs knew this from experience. Abu Kabir al-Hudhali said:

*And one freed from every dregs of menstruation, and corruption of a nursing mother, and a stubborn disease.*

Ghubbar al-ḥayḍah is the plural of ghubrah, and it is also pluralized as ghubbar, and it means the last of a thing. He means: his mother did not conceive him at the end of the period of menstruation.

The physicians say that the fetus conceived during menstruation comes out leprous, or is afflicted with leprosy afterwards.

His saying ﴿So keep away from women during menstruation﴾ is the derivation of the ruling from the cause. Al-i'tizāl is keeping far away (al-tabā'ud bi-ma'zil), and here it is a metaphor for abstaining from intercourse with them. The noun governed by fī is a omitted time, and the estimate is: "during the time of menstruation." The substitution of the verbal noun for the adverb of time is very common, as they say: "I will come to you at the rising of the star and the arrival of the pilgrims."

Al-nisā' is a collective noun for woman, having no singular from its own form, and what is meant by it here is wives, as the address of i'tazilū (keep away), directed at men, requires; and one keeps away only from one who is in intimate contact.

The use of al-nisā' for wives is common when it is attached to a genitive, as in ﴿O wives of the Prophet﴾, and without an attachment with an indicator, as here. So the meaning is: keep away from your wives, that is, keep away from what is most specific to them, which is intercourse.

His saying ﴿And do not approach them until they are pure﴾ — the prohibition of approaching them came as an emphasis of the command to keep away from them, and an explanation of what is meant by keeping away, and that it is not distancing from wives in bodies as it was among the Jews, but rather non-approach. The apparent requirement was that the sentence ﴿and do not approach them﴾ be separated without a conjunction, since it emphasizes the content of the sentence ﴿So keep away from women during menstruation﴾ and explains the keeping away, and both matters require separation. But the apparent requirement was contravened out of concern for this ruling, so that the prohibition of approaching would be intended in itself and coordinated with the legislations. Intercourse is called qurbān (approaching) with a kasra on the qāf, the verbal noun of qariba with a kasra on the rā', and for this reason the imperfect with an open ‘ayn is used in it, which is the imperfect of qariba like samiʻa, transitive to the object. For intercourse is not expressed except with this, not with qaruba with a damma, which is intransitive; it is said qaruba minhu meaning danā (drew near), and qariba-hu likewise, and its use for intercourse is because there is nearness in it. But they gave preference to qariba with a kasra on the ‘ayn for it, not qaruba with a damma, as a distinction in usage, just as they said ba'uda when its place became distant, and ba'ida for the abstract sense of distance; and for this reason they say in supplication: "lā yab'ad" (may he not be far).

His saying ﴿until they are pure﴾ is a limit (ghāyah) for i'tazilū and for lā taqrabūhunna. Al-ṭuhr with a damma on the ṭā' is a verbal noun meaning cleanness from dirt and filth, and its verb is ṭahura with a damma on the hā'. The reality of al-ṭuhr is purity of the essence, and it is used in the technical language of the Law for the ritual purity (ṭuhr al-ḥadath) that is considered to be attained by the Muslim through a cause. It is said tatahhara when he acquires purity through his own action in reality, as in ﴿They love to purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 108], or metaphorically, as in ﴿Indeed they are people who purify themselves﴾ [al-A'rāf: 82]. It is said iṭṭahhara with a shadda on the ṭā' and on the hā', which is the form tatahhara in which the tā' is assimilated into the ṭā'. He, exalted, said: ﴿And if you are in a state of janābah, then purify yourselves﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 6]. The pattern tafa''ala in this root is for mere intensification of the occurrence of the meaning of the verb, and for this reason the use of one of them in the place of another is an eloquent usage.

The majority read ﴿until they are pure﴾ with the simple verbal form. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, and Abu Bakr from ‘Āṣim and Khalaf read (yaṭṭahhurna) with a shadda on the ṭā' and the hā', both with a fatḥah.

Since it was mentioned that menstruation is an harm, the listener knows that purity here means cleanness from that harm, for the description of a menstruating woman is contrasted with a pure one, and the menstrual periods (al-aqrā') have been called ṭuhr (periods of purity). Tatahhur may be intended as washing with water, as in His saying ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 108], for its interpretation is cleansing oneself with water after relieving oneself. If the first is meant, it indicates the prohibition of approaching until cleanness from the menstrual blood is attained by its drying, and His saying ﴿But when they have purified themselves﴾ after that is a second condition indicating the obligation of another purification, which is washing away that harm with water, because the form tatahhara indicates purification by action. If the second is meant, His saying ﴿when they have purified themselves﴾ is an explicit statement of the implication of the limit, so that He may build upon it His saying ﴿then go in to them﴾. On the second interpretation, the reading (ḥattā yaṭṭahharna) with a shadda on the ṭā' and the hā' came, so that the intended purity is the acquired purity, which is purity by washing. On this reading it is necessary that it be intended with its meaning together with its necessary implication, which is also cleanness from blood, so that washing takes its proper place, by the evidence of His saying before it ﴿So keep away from women during menstruation﴾. By this the two readings come to the same result.

Al-Mubarrad preferred the reading (ḥattā yaṭṭahharna) with a shadda, saying: "The correct view is that the two words have one meaning, and both are intended to mean washing." This is strange to proceed from him, for the difference of two meanings, if it does not result in an initial contradiction, makes the second word convey something new.

[p. 368]

Al-Ṭabarī preferred the reading with the shadda, saying: "Because the community agrees that it is forbidden for a man to approach his wife after the blood has ceased from her until she becomes pure." This is rejected: there is no need to argue from the evidence of consensus, nor to prefer the reading by it, because the wording is sufficient to convey the prohibition of a man's approaching his wife until she is pure, by the evidence of the implication of the condition in His saying ﴿But when they have purified themselves﴾.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on surah 2, verse 222 (part 2 of 2):

The verse indicates that the end point of keeping away from women during menstruation (al-maḥīḍ, the menstrual period) is the attainment of purity (al-ṭuhr). If we take ṭuhr in its linguistic meaning, it is cleanness from blood (al-naqā' min al-dam). However, the word taṭahhur in His words ﴿when they have purified themselves﴾ must be understood in its legal (sharʻī) sense. Thus the combination of the end point and the condition yields the requirement of both cleanness and the ghusl (the full ritual bath). The scholars of the Mālikiyya (the Mālikī school) held this view and compared it to the words of the Exalted: ﴿Test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them maturity of judgment, release their property to them﴾ [al-Nisā': 6]. Understanding ṭuhr in both places in its legal sense, especially on the reading (ḥattā yaṭṭahharna), yields from the concept of the end point and from the emphatic condition the requirement of bathing with water. This necessarily entails the requirement of cleanness ordinarily, since there is no benefit in bathing before that.

As for the requirement of purity from ritual impurity (ṭahārat al-ḥadath, i.e., the state requiring ablution, ḥadath), the jurists of Islam differed about the general meaning of legal purity here. A group said it is washing the site of the harm (maḥall al-adhā) with water, and this makes intercourse permissible. This is what the verse indicates, because legal purity is applied both to the removal of impurity (najāsa) and to the lifting of ritual impurity (raf' al-ḥadath). The menstruating woman is characterized by both matters, but what prevents her husband from approaching her is the harm, and approaching has no connection to ritual impurity. Therefore the intended meaning must be washing away that harm. Even if the two purities are mutually entailed for a Muslim woman, they are not mutually entailed for a non-Muslim woman of the People of the Book (kitābiyya).

The majority, including Mālik and al-Shāfiʻī, said it is the ghusl of major impurity (ghusl al-janāba). It seems they adopted the most complete instance of this term as a precaution, or they referred to the practice of Muslim women, and it is presumed of Muslim women at that time that they did not delay in performing the ghusl which permits them to pray. Therefore there is no proof in their practice against carrying out what is less than that. Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs and ʻIkrima held that purity is the wuḍūʼ (ablution) like the ablution for prayer, that is, together with istinjāʼ (cleansing of the private parts with water). This view is anomalous (shādhdh).

Abū Ḥanīfa and his two companions held a distinction. They said: if the blood stops at the maximum limit of menstruation, which in their view is ten days, it is permissible to approach her before the ghusl, that is, only with washing the site. If the blood stops at the woman's customary period (ʻāda) but before the maximum limit, it is not valid for her husband to approach her unless she has bathed or a prayer time has passed for her. If it stops before her customary period, it is not lawful to approach her, but she bathes and prays as a precaution, and her husband does not approach her until she completes the duration of her waiting period (ʻidda). They justified this by saying that its cessation at the maximum duration is a complete cessation, after which its return is not feared, unlike its cessation at less than that. Therefore its trace must be examined with water or by the passing of a prayer time.

Then they wanted to make this verse evidence for this distinction. ʻAbd al-Ḥakīm al-Siyālkūtī said: "ḥattā yaṭhurna" ("until they are pure") was read with lightening (takhfīf, yaṭhurna) and with doubling (tashdīd, yaṭṭahharna), so the two readings take the place of two verses. Since one of them conflicts with the other, in that the reading with lightening requires ṭuhr to mean cleanness while the other requires it to mean ghusl, the two readings were combined by applying each in a specific state. End of quotation. This evidence is weak, because it is not known that the two readings are counted as two verses so that a conflict is established. Even if we grant it, they were transmitted at the same time, so their unrestricted form is interpreted by their restricted form, by taking ṭuhr in the sense of cleanness as conditioned by ghusl. Even if we grant the abandonment of this restriction, what is the evidence that assigns each reading to one of these two states rather than the other, or rather than other states? This is nothing but a matter of personal opinion (ṣunʻ bi-l-yad). If you say: why did they base their evidence on making the two readings like two verses, and not on the presence of "yaṭhurna" and "yaṭṭahharna" in two places in this verse as we did? I say: it seems the reason is that the two occurrences in the verse are two parts of one verse, so it is not possible to consider a conflict between two parts of one verse. Rather, they are understood as one of them explaining the other or restricting it.

His words ﴿then come to them﴾ (fa-'tūhunna): the command here is for permissibility (al-ibāḥa) without doubt, because it occurs right after the prohibition, like His words ﴿and when you have come out of the state of ihrām, then hunt﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 2]. The expression "coming to" (al-ityān) is used here, and it is well known as a euphemism (kināya) for sexual intercourse (al-waṭ'), to show that the intended meaning of the prohibited "approaching" (al-qurbān) is that allusive sense. Thus he expressed it as "keeping away" (i'tizāl), then followed it with "approaching" (qurbān), then followed it with "coming to" (ityān). With each expression there is a new benefit and a new ruling. This is one of the marvels of concision within elaboration.

His words ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾ (min ḥaythu amarakumu Allāh): "ḥayth" is an ambiguous noun of place, built on a ḍamma, which is always followed by a clause that specifies it, since its ambiguity is removed. The meaning of this adverbial phrase has been difficult for those who undertook the interpretation (ta'wīl) of the Qur'an. I do not see the cause of its difficulty except that the Arabs customarily expressed this meaning by way of allusion and indirection, and its understanding was left to their intelligence and familiar usage. Ibn 'Abbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda and al-Rabīʻ said: meaning, except from where Allah has commanded you to keep away from them during the menstrual period, that is, the front passage (al-qubul). Al-Qurṭubī said: "min" means "fī" (in), and he compared it to the words of the Exalted: ﴿Show me what they have created of the earth﴾ [Fāṭir: 40], and His words ﴿when the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 9]. And from Ibn 'Abbās, Abū Razīn Mas'ūd ibn Mālik, al-Suddī and Qatāda [it is reported] that the meaning is: from the condition that Allah has commanded you, which is purity (al-ṭuhr). So "ḥayth" is a figurative usage for the state or cause, and "min" is for the beginning of causes, so it means causation.

What I think is that His words ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾ mean that the listeners already understood from it that it is a command from Allah which had occurred before. As for "ḥayth", it is a noun of place, and it may be used figuratively for causation. So it is permissible that the intended meaning of Allah's command is His command contained in the end point expressed by "ḥattā" in His words ﴿and do not approach them until they are pure﴾, because the end point of the prohibition ends in permission. So the command is the permission, and "min" is for figurative beginning, and "ḥayth" is used figuratively for causation as an imaginative metaphor (majāz takhyīlī), that is: because Allah commanded you to come to them at the end of the prohibition's limit, by purification.

Or the intended meaning of Allah's command is His command by which He permitted enjoyment of women, namely the marriage contract. Then the particle "min" is for causation and causal relation, and "ḥayth" is borrowed for figurative place, which is the state of permissibility that preceded the prohibition, as if they had been restrained from using the permissibility, or had been forbidden to benefit from it, then they were allowed to use it. Their state is likened to that of one who was detained at a place and then released, so he goes from it wherever he wishes.

On both of these meanings, the verse contains nothing indicating an intention to specify the place of coming to, such that it would be the place of procreation. Both meanings are supported by the concluding sentence, ﴿Indeed Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾. This is a kindness toward the addressees, that the prohibition was for their benefit, so that they might be purified. As for mentioning the repentant, it is an inclusion (idmāj) to honor the matter of repentance when mentioning what indicates compliance with what Allah commanded them, namely keeping away from women during menstruation. That is, repentance is greater in importance than purification, that is, the intention of compliance is greater than the realization of the benefit of purification for you, because repentance is a spiritual purification (taṭahhur rūḥānī) and purification is a bodily purification (taṭahhur juthmānī).

It is also possible that His words ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾ are meant literally: min for beginning and ḥayth literally for place, and the intended place is the place where the harm of menstruation was. It has been said that the sentence ﴿Indeed Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾ is a parenthetical clause (muʻtaraḍa) between the sentence ﴿when they have purified themselves﴾ and the sentence ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 223].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 223 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Your women are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish.﴾

This sentence is a second concluding statement (tadhyil) following the sentence ﴿then come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqara: 222]. Its purpose is to show kindness to the addressees and to put them at ease, by informing them that the prohibition on approaching women during the period of menstruation is a temporary prohibition for their own benefit, and that Allah
[Page 371]
knows that their women are the place of their care and close contact, and that restraining them from them in some circumstances is not an easy matter for them, were it not for the desire to protect them from harm. This is like the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab when he established the protected pasture (hima): "Were it not for the wealth which I carry for the sake of Allah, I would not have protected a single span of their lands. They are indeed their lands." The sentence ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾ is considered an introduction to the sentence ﴿so go to your tilth however you wish﴾, and it carries the sense of giving a reason (ta'lil) for the permission to come to them however they wish. A reason may be placed first. Had the sense of giving a reason been intended, it would have been placed after the sentence ﴿so go to your tilth however you wish﴾. However, it was preferred that it come before the following sentence, because this is the most tightly woven composition, and so that the eloquent fa' (al-fa' al-fasiha, the fa' of eloquent connection) could follow it. The word hars (tilth) is the verbal noun of haratha al-ard, when one tills the land with an implement that cuts the soil so that seed is sown in its furrows or trees are planted. Here it is used in the sense of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), meaning "that which is tilled."

The application of the word hars to the tilled thing and its types is of several kinds. It is applied to land prepared for sowing or planting, as the Most High said: ﴿And they say: these are livestock and tilth set apart﴾ [al-An'am: 138], meaning cultivated land forbidden to people to cultivate. He also said: ﴿and the branded horses and livestock and tilth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14], meaning gardens, orchards and fields. He said: ﴿like the wind in which is a freezing cold that struck the tilth of a people who wronged themselves, so it destroyed it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 117], meaning it destroyed their crops. He said: ﴿So they called to one another in the morning: go early to your tilth if you are going to harvest﴾ [al-Qalam: 21], meaning by it their garden, that is, to harvest the clusters of dates.

The word hars in this verse is meant as that which is tilled, by the indication that it is the object of the verb in ﴿so go to your tilth﴾. It does not mean the verbal noun, because the context rejects that. The comparison of women to tilth is a subtle image, just as offspring is compared to crops in the words of Abu Talib in his proposal of marriage to Khadija for the Prophet (ﷺ): "Praise be to Allah who has made us of the seed of Ibrahim and the crop of Isma'il."

The fa' in ﴿so go to your tilth however you wish﴾ is a fa' fasiha, because what follows is founded on the established fact that women are tilth for them, especially if they had asked about this, either by speech or by the tongue of circumstance.

The word anna is a noun for an indefinite place, which is specified by a sentence that is its complement (mudaf ilayha). Its use has become common figuratively in the sense of "how" (kayfa), by likening the state of a thing to its place, because kayfa is a noun for an indefinite state which is specified by its governing verb, as in "how he wills." In the language of the Arabs it is said that anna may mean mata (when). In this verse, anna is joined to the sentence "you wish," and the wishes are diverse. Therefore many exegetes interpreted anna as used figuratively and explained it as "how you wish." This is the interpretation of the majority, which they supported by what they narrated about the occasion of revelation of the verse, and there are two reports about it: one from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and the other from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Dahhak interpreted it to mean "when you wish." Others interpreted it according to its literal meaning as an indefinite place-noun. Some of them made it an adverb of place, because that is the basic function of place-nouns when nothing in them indicates a meaning other than adverbial sense, and they explained it as "in whatever place of the woman you wish," and this is what is related in Sahih al-Bukhari as an explanation from Ibn 'Umar. Others made it a place-noun that is not an adverb, and they assumed that it is governed by "min" (from), and explained it as "from whatever place or direction you wish," and this returns to the explanation in the sense of "how." Al-Qurtubi attributed these two interpretations to Sibawayh.

What is most evident from the position of the verse, and what the meanings of its words support, is that it is a concluding statement that comes after the prohibition on approaching women during menstruation.

So anna is understood in the sense of "when," and the meaning is: "come to your women when you wish once they have purified themselves." Its parallel is the Most High's words ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 2], after His words ﴿not permitting the hunting of game while you are in ihram﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1].

There is no reason that would move the verse away from this meaning, except that what has spread among the scholars of the early generations and those after them is the plunging into other interpretations of this verse, and the reports they narrated about the occasions of revelation compel us to pursue a full clarification of the various opinions and interpretations, being persuaded by that, because it indicates the disagreement of the jurists about the meanings of the verse. It is indeed a matter worthy of attention, and its circulation on tongues and in pens is burdensome. Al-Bukhari and Muslim related in their Sahihs from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that the Jews said: "If a man comes to his wife from behind (mujhiya), the child will be born squint-eyed (uhwal)." The Muslims asked about this, and then ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾ was revealed, the verse. Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: This clan of the Ansar were idolaters, along with this clan of the Jews, who were People of the Book, and they regarded the Jews as having superiority over them in knowledge, so they followed much of their conduct. Among the practices of the People of the Book was that they would not come to women except in one manner (ʿala harf), and that was the most concealing for the woman. This clan of the Ansar had adopted this practice. This clan of the Quraysh used to "ravage" (yashrahun) their women, that is, they would have intercourse with them while the women were lying on their backs, facing them, facing away, or lying on their backs. When the Emigrants came to Madina, a man of them married a woman of the Ansar, and he went to do that with her, but she rejected it and said: "We were only approached in one manner, so do that, or else keep away from me," until their dispute grew intense (shara amruhuma, that is, the contention intensified). This reached the Prophet, and Allah revealed ﴿so go to your tilth however you wish﴾, that is, whether they were facing forward, facing away, or lying on their backs, meaning in the place of the offspring. The same was related from Umm Salama, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), in al-Tirmidhi. And what al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn 'Abbas: 'Umar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am ruined!" He said: "What has ruined you?" He said: "I turned my saddle last night," meaning that he came to his wife while she was facing away. The Messenger of Allah did not answer him at all, so Allah revealed to His Messenger this verse: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾, the verse.

Al-Bukhari related from Nafi' who said: When Ibn 'Umar recited the Qur'an he would not speak until he had finished it. One day I took the mushaf from him and he recited Surat al-Baqara until he reached ﴿so go to your tilth however you wish﴾. He said: "Do you know about what it was revealed?" I said: "No." He said: "It was revealed about such and such." In another report from Nafi' in al-Bukhari: "He comes to her in..." and he did not add more. In both of his reports he meant coming to women in their rear (adbar), as he explicitly stated in the report of al-Tabari and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh: "It was revealed about coming to women in their rear." Al-Daraqutni related in Gharib Malik and al-Tabari from Nafi' from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar that a man came to his wife in her rear and he felt remorse about it, so Allah revealed ﴿Your women are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish﴾. It has been related that this man was 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar himself. And from 'Ata' ibn Yasar: a man had intercourse with his wife in her rear during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The people denounced him and said: "He has committed sodomy (athfara) upon her," so Allah the Most High revealed ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾.

According to the interpretation of these people, the words of the Most High ﴿Your women are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish﴾ are a comparison of the woman to tilth, that is, to land for tillage. The phrase ﴿so go to your tilth﴾ is used in the sense of: "till in whatever place you wish."

I say: The speech of Allah the Most High has been stated here in general terms and left ambiguous, and it has clarified the ambiguous by means of other ambiguities from another angle, since ﴿Allah has commanded you﴾ admits of meanings other than obligation and legislation. No prior legislation from Allah on this matter is known, as we have already mentioned. Then it was followed by His words ﴿He loves those who repent﴾ [al-Baqara: 222], which perhaps indicates that an act in this matter used to be committed, and Allah calls to refraining from it. And it was followed by His words ﴿and He loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 222], which indicates that an act in this matter may become entangled with things other than purity, and Allah loves purity from it. This is alongside the possibility that the love is in the sense of preference and honour, like ﴿They love that they should purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawba: 108], and the possibility that it means: He dislikes other than that. Then came what is like evidence, namely His words ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾, so they were made tilth on the basis of several aspects of resemblance. It has been said that it was delegated to what is customary. It may also be said that it was made general to women, and therefore the ruling was attached to the essence of women entirely. Then He said ﴿so go to your tilth however you wish﴾, bringing anna, which admits of modes (kayfiyyat) and places (amkina). It is basic for places and occurs for modes. It has also been said that it occurs for times, so it admits of meaning the places of reaching this coming, or the places of arriving at another intended place, or the places of beginning the coming, or the places of settling. Thus all of this has been stated in a wonderful generality, and it has been praised with a fine praise.

The disagreement about the possible meanings of the verse among the views of exegetes and jurists is subject to the scholar's reflection. There are many sayings and various schools of the jurists of the regions, which are fully treated in the books of the rulings of the Qur'an, the books of Sunna, and the compendia of fiqh. We have limited ourselves to the reports that were connected to the verse as an occasion of revelation, and we have left what lies beyond that to the understanding of minds.

* * *

﴿And put forward for yourselves, and fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good tidings to the believers.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) on the sentence ﴿so go to your tilth﴾, or on the sentence ﴿Allah loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 222]. It is the conjunction of a command (insha') upon a statement (khabar), although the sentence conjoined to, even if it is a statement, is intended to convey the command to repent and purify oneself. So this was repeated out of concern for eagerness toward righteous deeds after speaking about fleeting pleasures. The object of qaddimu (put forward) is omitted for brevity, because it is evident, since putting forward here means preparing good deeds, for they are like the baggage which a traveller sends ahead.

His words ﴿for yourselves﴾ are connected to qaddimu, and the lam is of cause, that is, for the sake of yourselves, that is, for their benefit. His words ﴿and fear Allah﴾ are an exhortation to comply with the Law by avoiding transgression, so it includes abstaining from misdeeds and adorning oneself with obligations and acts of devotion. Its meaning is more general than the meaning of the sentence ﴿and put forward for yourselves﴾, and therefore this sentence is a concluding statement.

His words ﴿and know that you will meet Him﴾ combine warning and encouragement, meaning: meet Him with what He is pleased with from you, like His saying: "and found Allah with him." It is conjoined to His words ﴿and fear Allah﴾.

Al-mula'a (meeting) is a form of mufa'ala from al-liqa' (encounter), which is presence before another, intentionally or by coincidence. The root of the word laqiya implies occurring between two things, so by itself it conveys the sense of mufa'ala. Therefore laqiya and laqa' have one meaning. Allah commanded them to know that they will meet Him, although the Muslims already know that, in order to treat their knowledge as if it were absent in this matter, so that their instruction on this known matter is increased in concern and eagerness for it. Moreover, we have seen that beginning the sentence with the word "know" (i'lamu) indicates concern with the statement and calling for attention to it. This is a great point which will be discussed when we reach the words of the Most High ﴿and know that Allah comes between a man and his heart﴾ [al-Anfal: 24] in Surat al-Anfal.

The first three clauses are arranged in the reverse order of the occurrence of their meanings in reality. The apparent sequence would be that the information about meeting God comes first, followed by the command to be mindful of God (taqwa), and then the command to send ahead for themselves. The apparent order was departed from in order to hasten to the command to prepare for the Day of Recompense. It is followed by the command to be mindful of God, to indicate that this is the preparation itself. Then they are reminded that they will meet God, and this comes in the position of a reason (ta'lil).

His words ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ are a sequel to the warning, with good tidings. What is meant is the perfect believers, who rejoice in meeting God, as has come in the hadith: "Whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him." The mention of this good tiding after what preceded is an indication that complying with the rulings mentioned earlier is part of the perfection of faith. The clause ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿and know that you will meet Him﴾, according to the more apparent view, which holds that the clause ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence) not governed (ma'mula) by ﴿Say, it is a harm﴾ [2:222]. If you make the clause "your wives" part of the object of the speech (ma'mul al-qawl), then the clause "and give good tidings" is conjoined to the clause ﴿Say, it is a harm﴾ [2:222], since its occurrence as a direct speech of the verb "say" is not valid, as al-Taftazani preferred.

[p. 376]

﴿Do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths, that you should not be righteous, God-fearing, and make peace between people. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

This sentence is joined by conjunction (ʿaṭf) to the sentence ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223], as a conjunction of legislation to legislation. The connection between the two sentences is that both their contents concern rules of marital conduct, although the content of the first sentence is a prohibition on approaching wives during menstruation, and the content of this sentence is ﴿For those who swear off their wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226]. Thus this preface falls in the position of an interjection (iʿtirāḍ) between the sentence ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223] and the sentence ﴿For those who swear off their wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226]. The method of conjunction was adopted here because it is a prohibition conjoined to a prohibition in His words ﴿And do not approach them until they are purified﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222].

Al-Taftazani said: "The more evident view is that it is conjoined to an implied element, i.e., 'Comply with what I have commanded you, and do not make Allah an obstacle.'" End of quote. There is in this some strain and a lack of showing the connection. Al-Taftazani also allowed that it be conjoined to the previous commands, which are "and advance [good deeds] for yourselves," "and fear Allah," and ﴿and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223]. End of quote. That is, the connection is that when He commanded them to keep in mind the Day of their meeting with Him, He explained to them some aspect of God-consciousness (taqwā) that is subtle in its path and very hidden, namely God-consciousness through respect for the Exalted Name. For God-consciousness is among the acts which, when attached to names, their meaning is attachment to the named referent (musammā) of the name, not to its wording, since verbal rulings apply to the signified referents, except when there is evidence for their attachment to names, such as "I named him Muhammad." So this verse was brought to explain what follows from magnifying the name of Allah and being mindful of it, in the sacredness of His names when one breaks an oath, together with an explanation of what is permitted regarding breaking an oath. Or it was brought to warn against exposing His exalted name to being treated lightly through frequent swearing, so that one is not compelled to break oaths, according to the two interpretations that follow. After all this explanation, what prevents it [from being conjoined to the commands] is that the coming of His words ﴿And fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223] as a concluding clause (tadhyīl) for the preceding rulings prevents considering that a substantial ruling be conjoined to it, because the concluding clause would thereby be lengthened, and the nature of a concluding clause is brevity.

ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm said: "It is conjoined to the sentence 'Say' by the presumption of 'Say': i.e., 'And say: do not make Allah an obstacle.' Or it is conjoined to his words 'and advance,' if his words 'and advance' are taken as part of what is said by 'Say.'"

A group of exegetes related from Ibn Jurayj that it was revealed when Abu Bakr al-Ṣiddīq swore not to spend on his relative Mistaḥ ibn Uthāthah, because he had joined those who spoke of the slander about ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her. Al-Wāḥidī related from al-Kalbī: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah, who swore not to speak to his brother-in-law (khatan) Bashīr ibn al-Nuʿmān, who was married to his sister, nor to enter his house, nor to reconcile between him and his wife. Whichever of these it is, the conjunction particle waw must connect this sentence to something of the speech preceding it.

The attachment of the verb "make" (jaʿl) here to the essence [of Allah] has the sense of attachment to the name. So the implied meaning is: "Do not make the name of Allah [an obstacle]," and it was omitted because of its frequent use in such contexts when there is an indicator, since it is evident that attaching the action to the named referent is not valid, as in the verse of al-Nābighah:

*I swore, and left no doubt for you;*
*and beyond Allah there is no refuge for a man.*

That is: "and beyond the name of Allah there is no refuge for a man for the oath."

[p. 377]

The word ʿurḍah (obstacle, target) is a noun on the pattern fuʿlah, which is a pattern indicating the passive object, like qubḍah (a handful), musknah (a grip), and huzʾah (a mockery). It is derived from ʿaraḍahu, when one places it on its ʿurḍ, i.e., its side. The meaning of "obstruction" here is making a thing a barrier, from the expression ʿaraḍa al-ʿūd ʿalā al-inā' (he placed the stick across the vessel). From this arose the use of ʿurḍah for an intervening barrier. This is a common usage equal to the literal meaning. It was also applied to what many people gather around, as if it blocks them from departing. In al-Kashshāf he cited:

*And do not make me a target for the blamers.*

The verse admits both meanings.

The preposition lām in "for your oaths" (li-aymānikum) is the lām of transitivity, attached to "ʿurḍah" because of the verbal sense it contains: i.e., "do not make the name of Allah exposed to your oaths, so that you swear by it to refrain from righteousness, God-consciousness, and reconciliation, then you say, 'an oath has preceded from us.'" It is also possible that the lām is causal: i.e., "do not make Allah an obstacle because of your oaths issued that you would not be righteous."

The word "aymān" is the plural of yamīn, which means oath. The oath was called yamīn, taken from the yamīn, which is one of the two hands, namely the hand with which a person performs most of his actions. It is derived from yumn, which is blessing, because the right hand makes action easier than the other hand. The oath was called yamīn because the Arabs had a custom: when they made covenants, the two covenanting parties would grasp each other's right hand. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah; the hand of Allah is over their hands﴾ [al-Fatḥ: 10]. So they would say: "He gave his right hand" when confirming a covenant. This became common in their speech. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

*Until I placed my right hand, not disputing it,*
*in the palm of one of stout arms, his word is final.*

Then they abbreviated and said, "an oath came from him" (ṣadarat minhu yamīn), or "he swore an oath" (ḥalafa yaminan). So calling the oath yamīn is naming a thing by the name of its concomitant that is inseparable from it, or naming a thing by the name of its place. Just as they called water "valley" (wādī). The locus in this naming, in this manner, is an imagined locus (maḥall takhyīlī).

Since most of their oaths were in covenants and pledges, in which the covenanting parties place their hands [p. 378] one upon another, the term yamīn became commonly applied to every oath, following the general prevalent circumstances. So yamīn was applied to a person's oath concerning himself alone, without covenant or pledge.

The purpose of an oath returns to the aim of having a person call Allah the Exalted to witness his truthfulness: in a report, a promise, or a conditional. For this reason one says "by Allah" (billāh), meaning: I inform while bound by the calling of Allah as witness, or I promise, or I make a conditional while bound by the calling of Allah as witness to the realization of that. Therefore the oath includes a strong sense of truthfulness, because whoever calls Allah to witness a falsehood has dared against Him and treated Him lightly. Among what indicates that the origin of the oath is calling Allah to witness is His words: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204], as has preceded, and the Arabs' saying "Allah knows" in the context of a strong oath. For this reason the bāʾ (b) was the original particle of oaths, because it indicates attachment in its basic meanings. The wāw and the tāʾ were added to it in the performative oath, but not in the supplicatory oath.

The meaning of the verse, if "ʿurḍah" means a barrier: it is a prohibition to the Muslims from making the name of Allah an intervening immaterial barrier against doing what they swore to abandon of righteousness, God-consciousness, and reconciliation between people. Thus the lām is causal, and it is attached to "do not make," and ﴿that you be righteous﴾ is attached to "ʿurḍah," with the omission of the preposition lām, whose omission is regular with "an" (that). I.e., "And do not make Allah, because you have sworn by Him, an obstacle against the act of righteousness, reconciliation, and God-consciousness." So the verse in this aspect is a prohibition against adhering to an oath when adhering to it prevents a legal good act. It is a prohibition of either prohibition (taḥrīm) or disapproval (tanzīh), according to the ruling of the omitted thing that is to be abandoned. Among its implications is caution at the time of swearing and avoidance of hastiness in oaths, since one should not expose oneself to frequent dispensations.

The Arabs in the pre-Islamic period used to become angry and swear by Allah, by their gods, and by their fathers, to refrain from something, in order to close with the oath the door of retraction or regret.

In al-Kashshāf: a man would swear to abandon good, such as maintaining kinship ties, or reconciling between people, or doing a kindness, and then say, "I fear that I will break my oath," so he would abandon the act of righteousness. Thus the verse came to correct a defect in their conditions.

It has been said that the occasion of its revelation was Abu Bakr's oath that he would not spend on his cousin (ibn khālatihi) Mistaḥ ibn Uthāthah, because he was among those who engaged in the slander. But there is no apparent connection between this view and the position of the verse.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning the oath of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah that he would not speak to his brother-in-law Bashīr ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Anṣārī, who had divorced ʿAbd Allāh's sister and then wished to return to her and reconcile. So ʿAbd Allāh swore that he would not reconcile between them.

As for the case where "ʿurḍah" means the thing exposed to an action for a purpose, the meaning is: "Do not make the name of Allah exposed to being used in your oaths to refrain from righteousness, God-consciousness, and reconciliation between people." Then "oaths" is in its ordinary sense, namely the swearings, and the lām is attached to "ʿurḍah." "That you be righteous" is the object of "oaths," with an implied "not" after "that": "that you not be righteous," like His words ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 176], which is common. Then the verse is a prohibition against swearing by Allah to abandon acts of obedience, because the exaltation of Allah should not be a cause of cutting off what Allah commanded to be done. This prohibition implies that if the oath was made to abandon righteousness, God-consciousness, and reconciliation, there is no blame in that, and that he expiates his oath and does good.

Or its meaning: "Do not make the name of Allah exposed to oaths," as we said, and "that you be righteous" is then an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi), and it is the cause of the prohibition. I.e., "I have only forbidden you so that you may be righteous, God-fearing, and reconciling." In something close to this, Malik said: "It has reached me that it is swearing by Allah in every matter." On this basis the verse is a prohibition against hastening to swear, because frequent swearing exposes the swearer to breaking his oath. Frequent oaths were among the customs of the pre-Islamic period, among the habits arising from anger and the bluster of folly. So Islam forbade that. For this reason they praised themselves for few oaths. Kuthayyir said:

*Few in his oaths, guarding his oath,*
*even if an oath slipped from him, he fulfilled it.*

In the sense of this, the ʿurḍah may be used figuratively for what many gather around, i.e., do not make the name of Allah like a thing exposed to those who seek it. There is nothing in the verse under these aspects that indicates permission to swear by other than Allah, because the prohibition against swearing by other than the name of Allah and His attributes has been established.

His words ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ are a concluding clause (tadhyīl). What is meant by it is knowledge of words and intentions, and what is intended by its implication is a promise of reward for compliance, under all the possibilities, and an excuse for breaking the oath under the first possibility, and a warning against swearing under the second.

The verse has indicated a great meaning: that the exaltation of Allah should not be made a means to suspend what Allah loves of good. For preserving righteousness in an oath returns to exalting the name of Allah the Exalted, and to confirming the testimony of Him concerning the act sworn upon. And although this is a sublime aim for which the swearer who seeks righteousness is thanked, nevertheless using it as a means to cut off good is something Allah the Exalted does not approve of. Thus two matters have come into conflict

[p. 380]

Both are pleasing to God such that when one is achieved, the other is not. God commands us to give precedence to whichever of the two pleasing matters involves glorifying Him by seeking His good pleasure, together with benefiting His creation through righteousness (birr), piety (taqwa) and reform (islah), rather than the matter in which His good pleasure is sought only by glorifying His name. For God, exalted is He, knew that the glorification of His name is already achieved when the one who swore is scrupulous about breaking the oath, so fulfilling the oath (barr al-yamin) is a courtesy (adab) toward the name of God, while performing righteous deeds is a means of pleasing God. Thus God commanded that His good pleasure be given precedence over courtesy toward His name, as it is said: "Compliance (imtithal) takes precedence over courtesy (adab)." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I do not swear to an oath and then see something else as better than it, except that I expiate for my oath and do that which is better." For this very reason, when Job (Ayyub) swore that he would strike his wife one hundred lashes, God commanded him to take a bundle (dighth) of one hundred twigs and strike her with it. God knew that this was not Job's intention; but since God was not pleased with Job striking his wife, He forbade him from that and commanded him to release himself from the oath (tahallul), preserving Job's eagerness for righteousness in his oath and his dislike of letting go of his customary glorification of the name of his Lord. This is one aspect of the release from an oath (tahillah), which God gave as a ruling to His Prophet. Perhaps expiation (kaffarah) had not yet been prescribed. It is among the ease and forbearance of Islam. God has spared us that, for He prescribed for us the release from oaths through expiation; therefore, in Islam it is not valid for the one who swears to do what Job did.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 225:**

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned. And Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*, a sentence that answers an implied question). The previous verse clearly or implicitly forbade rashness in swearing, so the listeners' minds turned to thinking about and inquiring into the ruling on the oath that flows on the tongue. Its connection to what precedes it is evident, especially if you take His words ﴿Do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾ [al-Baqarah: 224] as a prohibition against swearing.

*Mu'akhadha* (being held accountable) is a form (*mufa'alah*) of *akhdh* (taking) in the sense of counting and calling to account. One says *akhadhahu bi-kadha*, meaning he counted it against him in order to reproach him or punish him. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

*Do not hold me accountable for the words of the slanderers, though I have not sinned, even if the accusations against me have multiplied.*

The *mufa'alah* here is for emphasis on the act of taking, since it does not involve the action occurring from both sides.

*Mu'akhadhah* with an oath means the obligation to fulfil it and not to break it. It follows from this that one commits sin if the oath is broken, except what Allah has permitted as its expiation (*kaffarah*), as in the verse of the surah al-'Uqud (al-Ma'idah).

*Lagh* is the verbal noun of *lagha*, when one speaks an erroneous statement. One says *lagha yalghu laghwan* (like *da'a*) and *lagha yalgha laghyan* (like *sa'a*). The Qur'anic usage is with the *waw*. In *al-Lisan* it is said that there is no parallel to it except their saying *asawtuhu aswan* and *asan*, meaning "I set it right." In *al-Kawashi*: *lagha yalghu laghwan* means he spoke falsehood. *Laghw* is also used for worthless speech that is not counted, which is an erroneous statement, and this usage is widespread. Al-Zamakhshari adopted this meaning in *al-Asas* and did not consider it a metaphor. In *al-Kashshaf* he restricted the interpretation to it, and his followers followed him.

The *fi* (in) here expresses metaphorical location, meaning association (*mulabasah*). It is a fixed adverbial phrase, either a qualifier of *laghw* or a circumstantial modifier of it. *Al-Kawashi* also interpreted it this way. The meaning, if *laghw* is taken as a verbal noun (which is the more apparent), is: Allah will not hold you accountable for uttering a worthless utterance that accompanies oaths, meaning He will not hold you accountable for oaths that issue forth in the manner of idle speech, that is, not intended as speech.

If you take *laghw* as a noun meaning worthless, erroneous speech, then its location within the oaths is not valid, because it is part of the oaths. In this case the locative phrase relates to *yu'akhidhukum* (He holds you accountable), and the meaning is: Allah will not hold you accountable for the oaths of your oaths concerning idle speech, meaning He will not hold you accountable among your oaths for the idle oath. *Aymān* is the plural of *yamin*, and *yamin* means swearing and oath-taking, which is mentioning the name of Allah, or some of His attributes, or some of His exalted affairs or rites. The Arabs used to swear by Allah, by the Lord of the Ka'bah, by the sacrificial animal, and by the rites of the Hajj. Their oath was made with one of the three particles of oath: *wa*, *ba'*, and *ta'*. They sometimes mentioned the word *halaftu* or *aqsamtu* (I swore), sometimes swore by the blood of camels, and sometimes said "and the blood." They sometimes put the *lam* before *'amr Allah*, saying *la'amr Allah* ("by the life of Allah"), and they said *'amaraka Allah* ("may Allah preserve you"). I have not seen that they swore by the names of idols. This oath, which is intended to commit to an action or to disclaim a right, is what is meant. Sometimes they swore by things precious to them to emphasize a statement or a commitment, such as their saying *wa-abiki* ("by your father"), *la'amruka* ("by your life"), and *la'amri* ("by my life"). They also swore by their fathers. When Islam came, it forbade swearing by other than Allah.

Among the customs of the Arabs in oaths is that some would swear to commit to an action that the swearer would perform, in order to compel himself to do it and not regret it. This belongs to the category of the vow-oath (*qasam al-nadhr*). When someone wished to show his resolve to do something that was inevitable, and no one had any hope of diverting him from it, he emphasized it with an oath. Bil'a ibn Qays said:

*And a horseman plunged into the thick of death, when he swears to do something disagreeable, he is true to it.*

That is, when he swears to fight, to kill, or something similar among hardships and harms. From this, war was called "disagreeable." Thus their pronouncement of the oath came to signify resolve, and it became common on their tongues for emphasis and similar purposes, until it flowed on the tongue as words that denote meanings flow without intending an oath. Its frequency in speech became countless, so scrupulousness about it increased in Islam. Kuthayyir said:

*He is sparing in his oaths, guarding his oath, and even if an oath slips from him, he is righteous.*

Thus the flowing of oaths on the tongue came to resemble idle speech.

The scholars differed about the meaning of *laghw al-yamin* (idle oath) in this verse. The majority held that *laghw* is the oath that flows on the tongue, which the speaker did not intend as an oath, but which came in the manner of emphasis or alerting, such as the Arabs' saying: "No, by Allah," "Yes, by Allah," or someone saying: "By Allah, I heard a strange statement from so-and-so." Anything other than this is not idle. This is the view of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), narrated from her in the *Muwatta'* and the *Sahihs*. Al-Sha'bi, Abu Qilabah, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, and Abu Salih also held this view, and al-Shafi'i adopted it. The proof for it is that Allah has made *laghw* a counterpart to what the hearts have earned in this verse, and to what the swearer has bound by oath in His words: ﴿But He holds you accountable for what you have bound by oaths﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]. What you have bound by oaths is what the hearts have earned, because what the hearts have earned is clear, so the general (*mujmal*) statement "what you have bound" is interpreted in its light. It is therefore determined that *laghw* is that in which there is no intention to swear, which flows on the tongue without intention. On this basis the negation of accountability means the negation of accountability for sin and for expiation, because the negation of an action is general. So the oath in which there is no intention carries neither sin nor expiation. Other oaths require expiation to exit from sin, by the evidence of the verse of al-Ma'idah, since it explained the accountability in it by His words: ﴿Its expiation is feeding ten needy persons﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]. Therefore expiation applies to the *ghamus* (perjurious oath, sworn to deceive), to the conditional oath (*yamin al-ta'liq*), and to the oath based on supposition which later proves otherwise.

Malik said: The idle oath is that one swears to something he supposes to be so, and then it turns out to be other than his supposition. He said in the *Muwatta'*: "This is the best I have heard concerning this." It is also narrated outside the *Muwatta'* from Abu Hurayrah, and it was held by al-Hasan, Ibrahim, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Makhul, and Ibn Abi Najih.

Its basis from the verse is that Allah made accountability depend upon what the heart has earned in the oath, and accountability occurs only upon breaking the oath, not upon the oath itself, since there is no accountability merely for swearing, especially when one is truthful. So it is determined that what the heart has earned means its earning of breaking the oath, that is, its deliberate intention to break it. That is where accountability lies. Accountability was summarized in this verse and explained in the verse of al-Ma'idah by expiation. Thus the one who swears on supposition, which later proves to be otherwise, has no deliberate intention to break it, so this is idle, and there is no accountability in it, meaning no expiation. As for a man's saying "No, by Allah" or "Yes, by Allah" while lying, according to Malik this is an oath that is not idle, because idleness relates to breaking the oath after believing it true. The one who says "No, by Allah" while lying has not had his breaking of it become apparent to him after the oath; rather he was heedless of being a swearer. When he becomes aware of the oath, the expiation becomes obligatory upon him, because he swore it when he swore it while being one who breaks it.

We made the explanation of *ma kasabat qulubukum* ("what your hearts have earned") to be the earning of breaking the oath, because the context of the verse concerns breaking the oath, since His words ﴿Do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾ [al-Baqarah: 224] are either permission to break it or prohibition of swearing out of fear of breaking it, according to the two previously mentioned interpretations. His words ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable﴾ are an explanation and justification of that, and the ruling of an explanation is the ruling of what it explains, because it specifies it.

A group said: *Laghw* is whatever is not intended as a lie. It therefore includes both categories, whether it is without intention, like those that flow on tongues in "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah," or with intention while believing it true, and then it turns out otherwise. Among those who held this view were Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sha'bi. Abu Hanifah also held it, and he said: There is no expiation or sin for idle oaths.

He argued for this by saying that Allah made *laghw* here a counterpart to what the hearts have earned, and He negated accountability for idle oaths while affirming it for what the heart has earned. Accountability is necessarily for breaking the oath and not for the oath itself. Thus *laghw* is that in which there is no breaking. He did not see a contradiction between the verse of al-Baqarah and the verse of al-Ma'idah requiring that one be interpreted in light of the other. Rather he said: The verse of al-Baqarah made *laghw* a counterpart to what the heart has earned, and it affirmed accountability for what the heart has earned, that is, what the soul resolved upon. Accountability is unrestricted and is understood to refer to its most complete instances, which is the otherworldly punishment. Therefore it is determined that what the hearts have earned refers to the *ghamus*. In the verse of al-Ma'idah he made *laghw* a counterpart to the binding oaths (*al-aymān al-mu'aqqadah*). The binding (*'aqd*) in its original sense is tying, and this is its linguistic meaning. He attributed it to oaths, which indicates that they are oaths involving a conditional commitment. He explained the accountability in them by His words: ﴿Its expiation is feeding﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89], etc. From the two verses it is clear that *laghw* is what stands opposite the *ghamus* and the binding oath, and these are necessarily two categories. The ruling on the *ghamus*, which is swearing with intent to lie, is that it is a sin. The ruling on the binding oath is that it requires expiation. He agreed with Malik regarding the *ghamus* and disagreed with him regarding one of the two categories of *laghw*. This is the realization of his school.

Besides these views there are other opinions on *laghw*, which Ibn 'Atiyyah enumerated up to ten. We will not lengthen the discussion with them.

His words ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 218] are an appended conclusion to the ruling of negating accountability. The reason the attribute of Forgiving is paired with Forbearing here, rather than Merciful, is that this is forgiveness for a fault that falls under shortcoming in good manners toward Allah. Therefore Allah described Himself as Forbearing, because the Forbearing is one who is not provoked by shortcoming directed at him, does not become angry at heedlessness, and accepts excuses.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 226–227:**

﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. If they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

This is a new, independent sentence, introduced to move on to a legislative ruling concerning a matter that men commonly did in the pre-Islamic period (al-Jahiliyya) and in Islam. Among the most notorious oaths that come between righteousness (birr), piety (taqwa), and reform (islah) are men's oaths to abandon their wives. This kind of oath combines all three, because good companionship is a form of righteousness between those who keep company, and Allah has commanded it in His saying: ﴿And live with them in kindness﴾ [al-Nisa: 19]. Therefore, fulfilling it is part of piety. Its continuation is also part of the continuation of reform, and when it is lost, discord arises, which is contrary to piety. In the pre-Islamic period, a man would take an oath of abstention (ila') from his wife for a year or two years, and his oath would not be dissolved except after the passing of that period, and the woman had no say in the matter. On the authority of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: In the pre-Islamic period, a man would not desire the woman, nor would he like to divorce her, lest another man marry her. So he would swear not to approach her, causing harm to the woman, and he would confirm this oath so that he would not return to her if some regret came over him. He said: Then the people of Islam used to do the same, so Allah removed that, and granted the husband a period of time in which to deliberate. This ruling was one of the most important aims in the rulings on oaths, for which He prepared the ground with His saying: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle [to your oaths]﴾ [al-Baqara: 224].

Al-ila' means swearing an oath. The apparent sense of the words of the lexicographers is that it is an oath in general. It is said: *ala yuli ila'an*, *ta'alla yatata'alla ta'alliyan*, and *i'tala ya'tali i'tila'an*. The noun is *al-ulla* and *al-iliyya*, both with a doubled letter. The root is *w-a-w* (hollow), so *al-ulluwa* is of the form *fu'ula*, and *al-iliyya* is of the form *fa'ila*.

Al-Raghib said: *al-ila'* is an oath that implies shortcoming in the thing sworn about, derived from *al-ulluw*, which means shortcoming. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will not spare you corruption﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]; ﴿Let not those of virtue and abundance among you swear not to give﴾ [al-Nur: 22]. In the Sharia, it became a specific oath. From the words of al-Raghib, it is understood that *ila'* is an oath of refraining and abandoning, because shortcoming is not realized without the sense of abandonment. This is what the root derivation from *al-alw* testifies to, and what the usage of the language testifies to, because we find that they do not often mention the negative particle after the verb *alla* and similar verbs, and they mention it often. Al-Mutalammis said:

*I have sworn never to taste the grain of Iraq for all time*

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Let not those of virtue and abundance among you swear not to give﴾ [al-Nur: 22], meaning: "on the condition that they give." And Allah the Exalted said here: ﴿For those who swear off their wives﴾, so He used *min* with it, and there is no need to claim an omission or an implied meaning.

Whatever the case, *al-ila'*, after the revelation of this verse, became a technical (sharʿi) term for this oath with its specific description.

The use of the *lam* in ﴿For those who swear off﴾ is to show that the waiting period was made a concession for them. So the *lam* is for purpose, like in "this is for you." It is also understood from it the sense of choice in it, meaning that the waiting period is not obligatory. Thus the one who has sworn may return within less than the four months. The verb *ila'* is followed by *min*, although its proper construction is with *ʿala*, because here it implies the meaning of distance, so it is followed by the particle suited to the verb of distance, as if he said: "for those who swear off, keeping away from their wives." So *min* here indicates the figurative starting point.

*Al-nisa'* means wives, as has preceded in His saying: ﴿So keep away from women during menstruation﴾ [al-Baqara: 222]. Linking the ila' to the word "women" is of the type of attributing permission, prohibition, and the like to concrete things, like ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa: 23]. This has been discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion﴾ [al-Baqara: 173].

*Al-tarabbus* means waiting for the occurrence of something by one who is not the one awaited. Discussion of it will come at His saying: ﴿Divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqara: 228]. The attribution of *tarabbus* to "four months" is an attribution with the meaning of "in," like His saying: ﴿Rather, it was the scheming of the night﴾ [Saba': 33].

Placing ﴿For those who swear off﴾ before the subject, which is *tarabbus*, is for emphasis on this concession which Allah granted to the spouses, and to create anticipation for the mention of the subject. *Fa'u* means "they returned," that is, they returned to intercourse with women. The object of *fa'u* is omitted because the intended meaning is clear. The "return" (fay'a) happens through expiation for the oath mentioned in Surat al-Ma'ida.

[p. 386]

His saying ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is the answer to the condition, meaning: their breaking of the oath of ila' is forgiven for them, because Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. In it is an announcement that ila' is forbidden, because the matter of their ila', which the Qur'an addresses, is the intention of causing harm to the woman. Ila' may be permissible if it is not intended to cause harm and its duration is not long, such as when it is for the purpose of discipline, or for another purpose that is legally valid, other than the purpose of harm which is legally blameworthy.

The Prophet (ﷺ) made an oath of abstention from his wives for a month. It was said: it was because of an ailment in his leg. It was also said: it was for the sake of disciplining them, because they had experienced from his great forbearance and gentleness what led some of them to excessive presumption, while the rest followed the example of the others, or regarded it as good. And Allah and His Messenger know best the inner realities of affairs.

As for the permissibility of ila' for a benefit, such as fear for a child from *ghayl* (nursing while pregnant), or abstention for the sake of some illnesses in the man or the woman, its permissibility is established from evidences of benefit and the removal of harm. This is achieved, according to some people, only by oath, because of the weakness of resolve among them and their suspicion of themselves regarding slipping into the matter, if they do not bind themselves with an oath.

*'Azm al-talaq* means determination to it, and the firm settling of opinion on it after reflection. This is something that does not come to every one who swears off on his own accord, especially if the predominant intention of the ila' is anger and harm. So His saying: ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾ indicates an omitted condition, which is indicated by His saying: ﴿If they return﴾. So the implied meaning is: "And if they do not return, then divorce has become obligatory upon them." So they are left with the better of the two options: either they return, or they divorce. If they resolve upon divorce, then their divorce has taken effect.
