Allah has set for men in ila' a specific limit, which they must not exceed. So either they return to lying with their wives, or they divorce, and they have no escape other than these two.

Allah has set for the one who swears off a limit and an end. As for the limit, the scholars of Islam agree upon it. They differ regarding one who swears an oath for less than four months. The four Imams hold that it is not ila'. Some scholars, such as Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and Hammad, say it is ila'. There is no practical result of this disagreement, as far as appears, except what follows from an oath made with the intent of harm, such as the judge's disciplining him if his wife brings her matter before the judge, and his ordering him to return.

[p. 387]

As for the end, they also differed regarding what results after the passing of the limit. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: if his wife brings the matter after that, he is held before the judge, and then either he returns, or he divorces on his own, or the judge divorces on his behalf. This was reported from twelve of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Hanifa said: if the period passes and he has not returned, then she has been separated from him. All agree that one who is unable (to have intercourse) suffices by returning through resolve and intention, and by declaring it before the judge, such as the sick, the imprisoned, and the traveler.

The Malikis argued that Allah the Exalted said: ﴿then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾, so this indicates that there is something heard. For attributing the quality of Hearing to Allah means He is Knowing of what is heard, according to the view of the verifying scholars among the theologians, especially since it is coupled with "Knowing." So there is no room left for the possibility of the view of those among the theologians who say that "Hearing" is synonymous with "Knowing," and that what is heard is only the words of the one who swore off, or the words of the judge, not the legal separation.

His saying "Knowing" refers to intention and purpose. The Hanafis said: "Hearing" refers to his oath of ila', which became divorce by the passing of its term, and "Knowing" refers to the intention of the one resolved to abandon return. They seem to mean that the Lawgiver made the formula of ila' a cause of divorce, on condition that the term passes, and Allah is Knowing of the intention of the one resolved not to return. But the view of the Malikis is more correct, because His saying ﴿then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾ is made a consequence of the resolve to divorce, not of the basic ila' itself. Also, setting time limits and their ending is entrusted to the rulers.

The wisdom of the specific deferment of four months has remained hidden from people. It is a limit that Allah the Exalted set, and we have not come to know its wisdom. That period is one third of the year, so perhaps it is due to the fact that such a period is considered a long time, for a third is regarded as the greater part of a divided thing, like one-third of property in a bequest. The Prophet (ﷺ) indicated this to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As concerning fasting all the time. Some scholars tried to explain it by what has been transmitted in a narration from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Ibn Kathir in his tafsir attributed its report to Malik in the Muwatta' from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar. This is not found in the existing transmissions available to us: the transmission of Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi, nor the transmission of Ibn al-Qasim, al-Qa'nabi, Suwayd ibn Sa'id, or Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani, nor the transmission of Yahya ibn Yahya ibn Bukayr al-Tamimi which al-Mahdi ibn Tumart narrates. So these existing transmissions may contain it in another transmission which we have not found. Abu al-Walid al-Baji mentioned this story in his commentary on the Muwatta' called al-Muntaqa, and he did not attribute it to any of the transmissions of the Muwatta': that 'Umar went out one night, walking around Medina to learn the conditions of the people. He passed by a house and heard a woman in it reciting:

*Ah, this night has grown long, and its side has blackened,*
*and sleeplessness troubles me that there is no friend for me to play with.*

*Were it not for fear of Allah, and nothing else,*
*the sides of this bed would have been shaken from here.*

So he sent for her the next day, and she informed him that her husband had been sent out with the army to Iraq. 'Umar summoned women and asked them about the period a woman can endure patience with her husband. They said: two months, and her patience diminishes in three months, and it is exhausted in four months. It was said: he asked his daughter Hafsa. So 'Umar ordered the commanders of the armies not to keep a man in the campaign for more than four months. When they passed, he recalled the fighters and sent out other groups.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 226–227:**

﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. If they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

This is a new, independent sentence, introduced to move on to a legislative ruling concerning a matter that men commonly did in the pre-Islamic period (al-Jahiliyya) and in Islam. Among the most notorious oaths that come between righteousness (birr), piety (taqwa), and reform (islah) are men's oaths to abandon their wives. This kind of oath combines all three, because good companionship is a form of righteousness between those who keep company, and Allah has commanded it in His saying: ﴿And live with them in kindness﴾ [al-Nisa: 19]. Therefore, fulfilling it is part of piety. Its continuation is also part of the continuation of reform, and when it is lost, discord arises, which is contrary to piety. In the pre-Islamic period, a man would take an oath of abstention (ila') from his wife for a year or two years, and his oath would not be dissolved except after the passing of that period, and the woman had no say in the matter. On the authority of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: In the pre-Islamic period, a man would not desire the woman, nor would he like to divorce her, lest another man marry her. So he would swear not to approach her, causing harm to the woman, and he would confirm this oath so that he would not return to her if some regret came over him. He said: Then the people of Islam used to do the same, so Allah removed that, and granted the husband a period of time in which to deliberate. This ruling was one of the most important aims in the rulings on oaths, for which He prepared the ground with His saying: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle [to your oaths]﴾ [al-Baqara: 224].

Al-ila' means swearing an oath. The apparent sense of the words of the lexicographers is that it is an oath in general. It is said: *ala yuli ila'an*, *ta'alla yatata'alla ta'alliyan*, and *i'tala ya'tali i'tila'an*. The noun is *al-ulla* and *al-iliyya*, both with a doubled letter. The root is *w-a-w* (hollow), so *al-ulluwa* is of the form *fu'ula*, and *al-iliyya* is of the form *fa'ila*.

Al-Raghib said: *al-ila'* is an oath that implies shortcoming in the thing sworn about, derived from *al-ulluw*, which means shortcoming. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will not spare you corruption﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]; ﴿Let not those of virtue and abundance among you swear not to give﴾ [al-Nur: 22]. In the Sharia, it became a specific oath. From the words of al-Raghib, it is understood that *ila'* is an oath of refraining and abandoning, because shortcoming is not realized without the sense of abandonment. This is what the root derivation from *al-alw* testifies to, and what the usage of the language testifies to, because we find that they do not often mention the negative particle after the verb *alla* and similar verbs, and they mention it often. Al-Mutalammis said:

*I have sworn never to taste the grain of Iraq for all time*

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Let not those of virtue and abundance among you swear not to give﴾ [al-Nur: 22], meaning: "on the condition that they give." And Allah the Exalted said here: ﴿For those who swear off their wives﴾, so He used *min* with it, and there is no need to claim an omission or an implied meaning.

Whatever the case, *al-ila'*, after the revelation of this verse, became a technical (sharʿi) term for this oath with its specific description.

The use of the *lam* in ﴿For those who swear off﴾ is to show that the waiting period was made a concession for them. So the *lam* is for purpose, like in "this is for you." It is also understood from it the sense of choice in it, meaning that the waiting period is not obligatory. Thus the one who has sworn may return within less than the four months. The verb *ila'* is followed by *min*, although its proper construction is with *ʿala*, because here it implies the meaning of distance, so it is followed by the particle suited to the verb of distance, as if he said: "for those who swear off, keeping away from their wives." So *min* here indicates the figurative starting point.

This has been discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion﴾ [al-Baqara: 173].

[p. 389]

It is an 'atf (conjunction) on the sentence before it, because of the strong connection between them, and because they share the same ruling, which is waiting (tarabbus), since both express waiting for the sake of returning. For this reason he did not place His words ﴿The divorce is twice﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:229] before His words ﴿And divorced women shall wait﴾. These verses came in a coherent and orderly arrangement, following the connections between topics, in keeping with the Qur'an's manner of presenting rulings in an easy style that does not weary the soul and does not take the form of instruction and lesson. I will discuss divorce when He, exalted, says ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:229].

The clause ﴿And divorced women shall wait﴾ is declarative in form, but it is meant as a command. So the report is used to express a directive. This is a metaphor, and it is permissible to treat it as a compound metonymy (majaz mursal murakkab), by using the report to express a necessary meaning of it, namely that the matter is established and will occur. This is the view chosen by al-Taftazani in His words, exalted, ﴿Then is one against whom the word of punishment has come [to be fulfilled]... can you save those who are in the Fire?﴾ [al-Zumar 39:19], where the report is used for the compound constructive meaning, by the relation of necessary connection between the command, for example as here, and compliance with it, so that the one commanded is treated as an agent and reported about accordingly. It is also permissible to treat it as a figurative illustration (majaz tamthili), as al-Zamakhshari chose in this verse when he said: "It is as if they have complied with the command to wait, so He reports about it as already existing." A similar usage is the people's supplication: "May God have mercy on him," expressing confidence in being answered. Al-Taftazani said: "It is the comparison of what is desired to occur with what is certain to have occurred in the past, as in people's saying 'May God have mercy on him,' or in the future or present, as in this verse." I say: this has already been discussed in His words, exalted, ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, nor wickedness, nor disputing during the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:197], where he applied a compound expression indicating the form that is the likened image to the form that is being likened.

The definite article in al-Mutallaqat is the definite article of the genus, and it implies comprehensiveness (istighraq), since it is not suitable for anything else here. It is general in scope regarding divorced women who have menstrual periods, by the indication of His words ﴿shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾, since that cannot be conceived of for others. So the verse is general regarding divorced women who have menstrual periods. This is not a general term that has been specified in this verse, whether by a connected or a separated specifier, nor is it meant in a specific sense. Rather, it is general in regard to the category described by the presumed attribute, which is part of implicative signification (dalalat al-iqtida'). So the verse is general regarding divorced women who have menstrual periods. It is specified for free women, not for slave-women, so it excludes slave-women, according to what is established in the Sunnah: "The waiting period of a slave-woman is two menstrual periods," narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi. It therefore includes the category of divorced women who have menstrual periods, and it has no connection with other divorced women, such as those who are not of menstruating age, those who have passed the age of menstruation, and pregnant women, whose ruling has been explained in Surat al-Talaq. However, the verse's indication excludes divorced women who were divorced before consummation (al-binā') among those who have menstrual periods. They are specified from this generality by His words, exalted, ﴿O you who believe, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, you have no waiting period for them to count﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:49]. So in this respect it is a general term specified by a separate specifier. The Malikis and the Shafi'is said: it is a general term from which the four categories are excluded by separate specifiers, but this is open to question regarding all except the woman divorced before consummation. According to the Hanafis, it is a general term intended in a specific sense by an indicator, namely the indication of the rulings established for those categories. They resorted to this because they regard a separate specifier as an abrogator (nāsikh), and the condition of abrogation is that the abrogated ruling was established. It is not established that waiting by means of menstrual periods was practiced in Islam for all divorced women.

The truth is that the claim that a separate specifier is an abrogator is a principle not worthy of being rooted in theory. This is because the specification of a general term is its appearance with some individual instances excluded from it by evidence. The general terms that come after specific ones are numerous, and in such cases it is impossible to say that the general term abrogates the specific one, because that is clearly false, nor that the specific term abrogates the general one, because the specific term clearly came earlier, and an abrogator does not precede what it abrogates. Furthermore, as long as the general ruling has not been acted upon, specification is not abrogation.

[p. 390]

The phrase ﴿shall wait by themselves﴾ means they remain and wait for the passage of three periods. The phrase "by themselves" is added as an indirect reproach to them, by presenting their condition as that of women who are hasty and eager to remarry. Therefore they were commanded to wait by themselves, meaning they should hold themselves back and not send themselves to men. In al-Kashshaf it is said: "Mention of the selves includes stirring them to wait and an added incitement, because in it there is something they would find shameful, which leads them to wait." Some grammarians claimed that "by themselves" is an emphatic reinforcement of the pronoun of the divorced women, and that the bā' is redundant, and from this came the view that the bā' is redundant in the moral emphasis. This is mentioned by the author of al-Mughni, who rejected it on grammatical grounds, because the proper emphasis of an attached pronoun should come after the separate pronoun or after some other separator, unless one says that the bā' has sufficed as the particle of genitive; and on semantic grounds, because there is no reason for such emphasis, since the listener's mind does not go to the idea that the one commanded is other than the divorced women, who is the subject whose predicate is the pronoun.

The phrase ﴿three periods﴾ is in the accusative as an adverbial complement of time (ẓarf), since the sentence presupposes an omitted noun, meaning "the duration of three periods." When the omitted noun was dropped, the noun it governed took its place in grammatical case.

The word al-qurū' is the plural of qar' (with the qāf vowelized either as fatḥa or ḍamma), and it is a homonym (mushtarak) meaning both menstruation (ḥayḍ) and purity (ṭuhr). Abu 'Ubayda said that it is originally used for the transition from purity to menstruation or from menstruation to purity, so when it is applied to purity or to menstruation it is applied to one of its two ends. al-Raghib followed him. Perhaps both of them meant by this the reason for its application to two opposites. I think that the most famous meaning of qar' among the Arabs is purity (ṭuhr). That is why it occurs in the ḥadīth of 'Umar, that his son 'Abd Allah, when he divorced his wife during menstruation, asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and 'Umar asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about that. His question was only because they did not divorce except in a state of purity, so that the purity in which the divorce occurred would be the beginning of the waiting period. That the purity in which she was divorced is the beginning of the waiting period is the view of all jurists except Ibn Shihab, who said: the purity in which the divorce occurred is disregarded.

Scholars differed about the meaning of al-qurū' in this verse. The view held by the jurists of Medina and the majority of the people of transmitted reports (ahl al-athar) is that qar' means purity. This is the view of 'A'isha, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Umar, and a group of the Companions from among the jurists of Medina, and of Malik, al-Shafi'i in his clearest statement, and Ibn Hanbal. What is meant by it is the purity that lies between two bleedings. 'Ali, 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, and a group said that it is menstruation. From al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, it is the purity from which one transitions to menstruation, which agrees with what Abu 'Ubayda explained, and it does not contradict the majority view that qar' is purity, so there is no basis for counting it as a third opinion.

In my view, the decisive consideration here is combining the two intended purposes of the Lawgiver in the waiting period. The waiting period is intended to establish with certainty that the womb of the divorced woman is clear of the husband's child, and to allow the husband time to possibly return. The clearing of the womb is achieved by one menstruation or one purity, and anything beyond that is an extension of the period for the sake of waiting for the return. A single menstruation has been made a sign of the clearing of the womb in the istibra' (waiting to ascertain the womb is empty) of a slave-woman upon transfer of ownership, in the case of captives, and in other situations, some of which are disputed among the jurists. Therefore it is established that what exceeds a single menstruation is not for the certainty that there is no pregnancy, but because that period includes ease for the divorcing husband and hardship for the divorced woman. Thus the two purposes conflict, and the right of the divorcing husband to wait for a time after the first menstruation has ended and the purity after it has begun has been given precedence. Those who took qurū' to mean purities took account of easing the burden on the woman, while also allowing the husband a respite, and they relied on the report (athar). Those who took qurū' to mean menstruations added a respite for the divorcing husband, because divorce is agreed to occur only in a state of purity, as stated in the ḥadīth of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in the Ṣaḥīḥ, and they agreed that the purity in which the divorce occurred is counted among the three periods.

The word qurū' is in the plural form of multitude (jam' al-kathra), but it is used for three, which is a small number (qilla), as a broad usage, according to their customary practice with plurals, which alternate between the forms. So in the verse the lighter form was preferred, with the absence of ambiguity, since an explicit numeral is required. With the end of the three periods the waiting period ends, and the divorced woman who may be taken back is separated from her husband. This happens when the third purity ends and she enters the fourth menstruation. The majority said: when she sees the first drop of the third menstruation she leaves the waiting period, after it is confirmed that it is menstrual blood.

Among the most strange arguments for the view that qar' means purity is the argument from the feminine form of the number in His words, exalted, ﴿three periods﴾. They said: purity is masculine, so the word "three" was used in the masculine with it; if qar' meant menstruation, and menstruation is feminine, one would say "thalāth qurū'" (feminine). This was related by Ibn al-'Arabi in al-Ahkam from "our scholars," meaning the Malikis, and he did not criticize it. But this argument is not sound, because what is considered regarding masculine and feminine is either the referent, if the masculinity and femininity are real, or else the state of the noun regarding attachment to the verbal feminine marker, or treating the noun according to a presumed feminine, as in the case of the name "well" (bi'r). As for this argument, it confuses the ruling of the word with the ruling of one of its synonyms.

[p. 391]

His words, exalted, ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs﴾ are a report about the negation of permission to conceal, and this implies the notification that their concealment is forbidden and prohibited. So it is a report about the legislation, and it is a notice to them of that. What God has created in their wombs is the blood, and its meaning is concealing the information about it, not concealing its essence, like the saying of al-Nabigha:

"I concealed you by night at al-Jamumayn, staying awake,"

meaning: I concealed you during the time of the night.

The phrase ﴿what God has created in their wombs﴾ is a relative clause, so it is permissible to take it as referring to a known thing, namely what God created of menstruation, by the indication of the context. It is also permissible to take it according to the meaning of a noun defined by the definite article of the genus, so that it includes both menstruation and pregnancy, which is the apparent meaning. This is a general term that came in connection with a particular cause, because the general term occurring in the Qur'an after the mention of some of its instances has been treated by them as the same as a general term that came in connection with a particular cause. As for those who restrict the wording of generality in such a case to the particular thing mentioned before it, then the inclusion of pregnant women would be by analogy, because the ruling was tied to concealing what God created in their wombs. This is the basis of the difference among the commentators. 'Ikrima, al-Zuhri and al-Nakha'i said: what God created in their wombs is menstruation. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Umar said: it is pregnancy. Mujahid said: it is both pregnancy and menstruation, and this is the more apparent view. Qatada said: the custom of women in the Jahiliyya was to conceal pregnancy so that the child would be attributed to the new husband, that is, so that no connection or dispute over the children would remain between the divorced woman and her divorcer, and this verse was revealed about it. This implies that the waiting period did not exist among them. But with the legislation of the waiting period, concealing pregnancy is not conceivable, because pregnancy does not occur except with the cessation of menstruation, and once the period of the menstruations has passed, it becomes clear that the pregnancy is from the new husband.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir, on surah 2, verse 228 (part 2 of 4):

His saying ﴿if they truly believe in God and the Last Day﴾ is a conditional clause used for admonition (al-tahdid) rather than for restriction (al-taqyid). It is used in a sense other than restriction, in the manner of the figurative usage known as al-majaz al-mursal al-tamthili (the figurative usage in which a whole scene or situation stands for its meaning), just as a statement is used to express regret or threat. There is no point in restricting the prohibition of concealment to their being believing women, even though this is the case in reality, because disbelieving women do not comply with the rulings of lawful and unlawful in Islam. The meaning is rather that if they conceal, then they do not believe in God and the Last Day, since concealment is not the conduct of believing women. In this conditional clause the particle in (if) is used, because it is the basic conditional particle, unless there is an intention to affirm that the condition has been realized, in which case idha (when) is used. When the condition is assumed as a supposition, with no intention of affirming or denying it, in is used. There is nothing in in here of the sense of doubt about whether the condition will be realized, and the verified faith of these women is not treated as if it were doubtful, because that does not hold, contrary to what 'Abd al-Hakim affirmed.

[Page 393]

By belief in God and the Last Day is meant complete belief, which is belief in what the religion of Islam brought. Thus the belief of the People of the Book in God and the Last Day is not intended here, since there is no sense in linking the prohibition of concealment in Islam to the establishment of the belief of the People of the Book.

There is no evidence in the verse for accepting the word of women regarding claims of pregnancy and menstruation, as is common on the tongues of many jurists. It is therefore necessary to observe that their statement be plausible. Whenever doubt is raised about their truthfulness, it becomes obligatory to turn to what is verified, and to the statements of physicians and experts. For this reason Malik said: If a woman who has qurū' (menstrual or purity periods) claims that her waiting period (iddah) has ended within a month from the day of divorce, she is not believed, and she is not believed for less than forty-five days, with her oath. 'Abd al-Malik said: fifty days. Ibn al-'Arabi said: she is not believed for less than three months, because that is the usual period in which three qurū' occur. This was the practice in Tunis, as transmitted by Ibn Najy, and the practice in Fez, as transmitted by al-Sijilmasi. The verse also indicates that a divorced woman of the People of the Book is not believed in her claim that her waiting period has ended.

His saying ﴿and their husbands﴾ (bu'ulatuhunna). Bu'ulah is the plural of ba'l, and ba'l is the term for the husband of a woman. The original meaning of ba'l in their speech is "lord" or "master." It is an ancient Semitic word, and the Canaanites, called the Phoenicians, named their deity Ba'l. God said: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l and forsake the best of creators?﴾ [al-Saffat: 125]. It was applied to the husband because he holds authority over the bond of marriage with his wife, and because the husband was regarded as owning the woman and being her master, so he deserved this name. Then, when the system of the family developed from the time of Abraham (peace be upon him) and the laws that came after him, the sense of ownership in marriage began to weaken, and the Arabs applied the word zawj (spouse) to each of the man and the woman who are bound by the marriage tie. This usage is equitable, because zawj is that which makes the single one a pair, so they became equal in the name. The Qur'an used this name in most places, except those in which it recounted the conditions of past nations, such as His saying ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72], and except the places in which it pointed to reminding of the authority the husband has, such as His saying ﴿And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion﴾ [al-Nisa': 128]. This verse is similar, because when He made the right of return (raj'ah) belong to the man, compelling the woman, He reminded the woman that he is her husband from of old. It was said: ba'l means male, and naming the worshipped deity ba'l is because it is a symbol of the strength of masculinity. For this reason the tree that is not watered is called ba'l, and its plural came in the pattern fu'ulah, whose original form is fu'ul, which is the regular plural pattern for fa'l, but the ta' marbutah was added to it to give the sense of collectivity. Similar to this are fuhulah, dhukurah, ku'ubah, and suhulah, the plural of sahl (plain), the opposite of jabal (mountain). The addition of the ta' to such words is by transmission (sama'i), because it does not indicate a meaning other than emphasizing the sense of plurality by indicating a group.

The pronoun in bu'ulatuhunna refers to the divorced women mentioned before it, who are the revocably divorced women, as has been stated before. God named them divorced women (mutallaqat) because their husbands initiated their divorce, and the name bu'ulah was applied to the divorcers. Its outward meaning therefore implies that they are husbands of the divorced women. However, the issuing of divorce by them is an act of dissolving the bond that existed between them. God made the period of the waiting period (iddah) a period of leniency for the divorcers, perhaps regret will arise in them and a desire to return to their wives. This is based on His saying ﴿You do not know; perhaps God will bring about after that some matter﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], that is, the matter of return. This is similar to what the Law instituted in the case of ila' (a vow of abstention from sexual relations with a wife). Thus the divorcers, according to this situation, are in an intermediate state between the state of husbands and the state of strangers. In view of this intermediate state, the name bu'ulah is applied to them here. This is a figurative usage (majaz) whose indication is clear, and its relation is consideration of what was (i'tibar ma kana), like the application of the name yatama (orphans) in His saying ﴿and give the orphans their property﴾ [al-Nisa': 2].

The majority (al-jumhur) have taken it as figurative, because they regarded a woman who has been revocably divorced as a foreign woman to the one who divorced her, by virtue of the divorce itself. But since the divorcer has the right of return as long as the woman is in the waiting period, even without her consent, it became necessary to apply the requirements of both states. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Malik said: It is not permissible for the divorcer to enjoy his revocably divorced wife, nor to enter upon her without permission. If he has intercourse with her without the intention of returning to her, he sins, but there is no hadd (prescribed punishment) upon him because of the doubt involved (shubhah). It is obligatory that she undergo istibra' (a period to establish that the womb is clear) from corrupt water. If she were a fourth wife, he would not be permitted to marry another woman while that waiting period lasts.

Maintenance is due to her only because she is detained to await his return. An objection to their view is that 'Uthman ruled that she inherits from her divorcer if he dies while she is in the waiting period. He ruled so in the case of the wife of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, with the agreement of 'Ali, and it is transmitted in the Muwatta'. The objection is answered by saying that the completion of the waiting period is a condition for the validity of the divorce, and the validity of the divorce is a barrier to inheritance. So as long as the waiting period has not ended, the divorce is hovering between being effective and being void. This becomes doubt concerning the barrier to inheritance, and doubt about a barrier nullifies its effect.

Abu Hanifah and al-Layth ibn Sa'd took bu'ulah in its literal sense. They said: the marital relationship continues between the revocable divorcer and his divorced wife, because God named them husbands (bu'ulah), and they permitted the divorcer to enter upon her. If he has intercourse with her, that is a return (irtija') according to Abu Hanifah. This was held by al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, and Ibn Abi Layla, and it is attributed to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Ibn Sirin, 'Ata', and some of the companions of Malik. I think these scholars hold that the marital relationship remains between the divorcer and his revocably divorced wife.

[Page 395]

(Ahaqq) It was said: it is in the sense of the active participle, with the comparative sense removed. It is used to express the strength of their right, and this is a usage in which the form af'al is employed, as in His saying ﴿and the remembrance of God is greater﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45], especially if no comparative object follows it with the preposition min. It was also said: it is a true comparative, and the object of comparison is omitted. This was pointed out in the Kashshaf, and al-Taftazani established it with the following explanation: the comparison is between two kinds of right that differ according to what they relate to. They are the husband's right to return if he desires it, and the woman's right to refuse return if she rejects it. The meaning becomes: their husbands have a greater right to the return of the divorced women than the divorced women have to refusal. The structure is composed in the manner of concision (al-ijaz).

As for His saying in that (fi dhalika), the demonstrative dhalika refers to the waiting period, in the sense of its duration. That is, the husbands have the right of return during the period of the three qurū', that is, not after that, as is the implication of the restrictive clause. This is the explanation of the meaning of the verse, on the basis that it came to legislate the ruling on return in divorce during the waiting period. In my view, this is not merely a legislation about return. Rather, the verse combines two matters: the ruling on return, and an exhortation to divorcers to return to the divorced women. This is because a couple who separate must have, on one side or both, a desire to return. God informs men that they are more deserving of desiring to return to women, and of overlooking the causes that necessitated the divorce, because the man is the one who is expected to show insight and forbearance, while the woman is one who is prone to anger and refusal.

The meaning of radd (return) was discussed under His saying ﴿until they turn you back from your religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]. Here it means returning to marital cohabitation, which is return (muraja'ah). Calling return "radd" supports the view that divorce has been regarded in the Law as a severing of the bond of marriage. It is therefore a literal usage according to Malik's view. As for Abu Hanifah and those who agree with him, they interpreted the expression radd as follows: the bond during the waiting period is proceeding toward dissolution, and by the end of the waiting period it will be dissolved. So return was called radd, a turning back from this course that the bond had begun to follow. This is a figurative radd.

His saying ﴿if they desire reconciliation﴾ is a conditional clause whose purpose is to urge the desire for reconciliation, and it is not for restriction.

* * *

[Page 396]

﴿And they (the women) have rights similar to those they have, in accordance with what is reasonable, and the men have a degree over them. And God is Mighty and Wise.﴾

It is not permissible for the pronoun in lahunna (for them) to refer to the nearest preceding noun, which is the divorced women, in the sequence of the pronouns before it, because the divorced women no longer have any bond between them and the men, such that they would have rights and obligations. It is therefore required that the pronoun lahunna refer to the wives, the women whom the phrase "by their return" in the preceding text implies, as shown by its contrast with His saying ﴿and the men have a degree over them﴾.

Thus by "the men" in His saying "and the men" is meant the husbands, as if it had been said: and their husbands have a degree over them. When rajul (man) is attached to a woman, as in "rajul of so-and-so woman," it means the husband, just as a wife is called "the woman of so-and-so." God said ﴿and his wife was standing﴾ [Hud: 71], and ﴿except your wife﴾.

It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the women in His saying ﴿for those who take an oath to abstain from their wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226], since ila' against women is an injustice to their rights when there is no cause for it. So this general ruling came in view of that specific cause, for the sake of contextual relevance. The discourse progressed from mention of women who are in the marital bond, when He mentioned their divorce with His saying ﴿and if they resolve upon divorce﴾ [al-Baqarah: 227], to mention of divorced women on that same basis. When He concluded the ruling on divorce with His saying ﴿and their husbands have more right to take them back in that period﴾, those women who were divorced became wives again. So the pronoun returned to them with reference to this new description, which is the description with which the ruling began. Thus there is in the verse a kind of returning the last part to the first part (radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr), in a wonderful style, and the women reverted to the rulings of wives. The relevance is that in ila' against women there is a domineering over them, and a display of what God has given the husband of the right of disposal over the marital bond. So it was fitting that they be reminded that women have rights equal to those of men.

In the verse there is ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two omitted elements mirror each other). The estimated structure is: "And they have over the men a right like what the men have over them." So something is omitted from the first part due to the indication of the latter, and vice versa. The emphasis was on mentioning the rights women have over men and likening them to what men have over women, because the rights of men over women are well known and accepted since the earliest ages of humankind. As for the rights of women, they were not something people paid attention to, or they were neglected and left to the measure of the wife's favour with her husband, until Islam came and established them. The greatest foundation laid for them is what this verse comprises.

[Page 397]

[p. 398]

The fronting of the adverbial phrase (*al-zarf*) serves to draw attention to the predicate, because it is one of the statements that listeners do not expect. It was placed first so that the listeners would attend to the subject. Had it been postponed, and it had been said, "*Wa mithlu alladhi 'alayhinna lahunna bil-ma'ruf*," this effect would have been lost. In this there is a proclamation of women's rights, a making them known, and a raising up of their mention. Such a statement is naturally received with astonishment, which is why it became a focus of attention.

That is because the condition of the woman in relation to the man in the Jahiliyyah, whether she was a wife or otherwise, was a condition mixed between an appearance of honour and rivalry when desired, and an appearance of contempt and little fairness when angered. The first arose from what the Arab was disposed to: an inclination toward women and sincere love. Thus the woman was the object of the man's gaze and the focus of his rivalry, out of desire to obtain her through one of the forms of companionship known among them. The wife was regarded by her husband with consideration and honour. Their poet Murrah ibn Mahkan al-Sa'di said:

*"O mistress of the house, arise, not abased; / Gather to yourself the baggage of the people and the water-skins."*

He called her "mistress of the house" and addressed her with the address of one who is gentle when he commanded her, and he followed the command with his words, "not abased."

As for the second, the man, despite this, sees the wife as made for his service. So when he was angry with her or she defied him, he would often treat her harshly. When their opinions differed, he would compel her to follow him, rightly or wrongly. The custom of the Arabs regarding these two appearances varied according to their differing degrees of civilization and bedouin life, the differing individuals in their shrewdness and coarseness, and the differing conditions of their women in submission, refusal, nobility, and their opposites.

Al-Bukhari narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "We, the tribe of Quraysh, used to dominate women. When we came to the Ansar, we found a people whose women dominated them. So our women began to take on the manners of the Ansar. I shouted at my wife, and she answered me back. I disapproved that she should answer me back. She said: 'Why do you disapprove that I should answer you? By God, the wives of the Prophet answer him back, and one of them may abandon him from the day until the night.' That alarmed me, and I said: 'Whoever among them does that has failed.' Then I gathered my clothes and went down and entered upon Hafsah, and I said to her: 'O Hafsah, does one of you anger the Prophet from the day until the night?' She said: 'Yes.' I said: 'You have failed and lost...'" (the hadith).

In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, from him ('Umar): "In the Jahiliyyah we did not reckon women as anything. When Islam came and God mentioned them, we saw that they had a right over us because of that, without our admitting them into any of our affairs."

It is necessary that this statement be the beginning of the other narration, which is his saying: "We, the tribe of Quraysh, used to dominate women..." to its end. This indicates that the people of Makkah were harsher than the people of Madinah in their treatment of women. I think the reason for this is that the people of Madinah were from the Azd of Yemen, and Yemen is the most ancient of the lands of the Arabs in civilization, so there was in them an extra tenderness. In the hadith: "The people of Yemen have come to you; they are more tender of heart and softer of hearts. Faith is Yemeni and wisdom is Yemeni." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab called that *adab* (good manners), saying: "So our women began to take on the *adab* of the Ansar."

In the Jahiliyyah, when a man died, his *awliya'* (guardians) had a greater right to his wife. If some of them wished, one of them would marry her when she became lawful to him; if they wished, they would marry her to whomever they chose; and if they wished, they would not marry her off, and she would remain among them. They had the greater right to that. Then the verse came: *"O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will"* (4:19).

In the hadith of the Hijrah: "When the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah with his companions, he established brotherhood between the Muhajirun and the Ansar." He established brotherhood between 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf and Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' al-Ansari. Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' offered 'Abd al-Rahman to share his wealth with him, and said to him: "Look at whichever of my two wives you wish, and I will divorce her for you." 'Abd al-Rahman said: "May God bless you in your family and your wealth." (The hadith continues.)

When Islam came with reform, among what it reformed of the conditions of all mankind was the regulation of the rights of the spouses in a manner that left no room for injustice. Even matters whose details may be hidden, it made arbitration their means of resolution. God the Exalted said: *"And if you fear a breach between the two, send an arbiter from his people and an arbiter from her people. If they both desire reconciliation, God will bring them into agreement"* (4:35). Such a thing had no precedent among the laws.

The first proclamation of this justice between the spouses regarding rights was in this mighty verse, so this verse was among the first things revealed in Islam.

The *mathal* (likeness) is originally the equal and the resembling, like *shabah* (similarity) and *mithl* (equivalent). This has been discussed in God's saying: *"Their likeness is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire"* (2:17). A thing may be a likeness to another in all its attributes, or it may be a likeness to it in some of its attributes, and that is the point of resemblance (*wajh al-shabah*). The point of equivalence may be apparent and so needs no explanation, or it may be hidden and so needs explanation. It has become clear here that the meaning of equivalence does not hold in all conditions and rights, whether as kinds, types, or individuals. This is because the requirement of creation, the requirement of the purpose of woman and man, and the requirement of the Shari'ah all entail a difference between many conditions of men and women in the order of civilization and companionship. Therefore every listener certainly knows that equivalence is not in every condition, and it is necessary to direct it to the meaning of equivalence in types of rights, in a general sense, which the details of the Shari'ah explain. So it should not be imagined that when a wife is obliged to keep her husband's house and prepare his food, he is obliged to do the same; just as it should not be imagined that since he is obliged to spend on his wife, the wife is obliged to spend on her husband. Rather, just as she keeps his house and prepares his food, he is obliged to guard the house and to bring her the kneading-trough and the sieve. And just as she nurses his child, he is obliged to provide for her livelihood so that she does not neglect his child, and to look after its upbringing and discipline. And just as she may not take another husband during the period of her marriage, he is obliged to be just between her and another wife, so that she does not feel wronged and becomes like one who was not married to another. On this analogy, when complete equivalence is achieved, it is legislated. So the woman must treat her husband well, as is shown by the ruling set for *nushuz* (rebellion): God the Exalted said: *"And those [wives] from whose rebellion you fear"* (4:34). And upon the man is the like of this: God the Exalted said: *"And live with them in kindness"* (4:19). It is upon her to guard herself against anyone other than her husband, and upon him the like of this with regard to one who is not his wife: *"Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts; that is purer for them"* (24:30). Then He said: *"And say to the believing women that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts..."* (24:31), and: *"And those who guard their private parts"* (23:5), *"except over their spouses"* (23:6). If he has another wife, then that has a different ruling, which falls under His saying: *"And the men have a degree over them"* (2:228). The equivalence is in sending the two arbiters, and the equivalence is in guardianship. So in the hadith: "The man is a shepherd over his household, and the woman is a shepherdess in her husband's house." And the equivalence is in consultation regarding weaning, as God said: *"But if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation"* (2:233), and: *"And confer among yourselves in kindness"* (65:6).

The details of this equivalence, whether in kind or in degree, are taken from the details of the Shari'ah's rulings. Their basis returns to the negation of harm and to the preservation of the Shari'ah's objectives for the community. God's saying *bil-ma'ruf* ("in kindness") hints at this, meaning: they have a right that is accompanied by what is *ma'ruf*, not *munkar* (reprehensible), in keeping with the requirements of the innate nature (*fitrah*), good manners, the public interests, the negation of harm, and following the Law. All of these are the domain of the views of the *mujtahidin* (qualified jurists). I have not seen in the books of the derivative rulings of the schools any arrangement of chapters that gathers the rights of the spouses. In the Sunan of Abu Dawud and the Sunan of Ibn Majah there are two chapters, one on the rights of the husband over the wife and the other on the rights of the wife over the husband, in brief.

In the Jahiliyyah they regarded the man as a *mawla* (guardian) of the woman, so she was in his charge, as they said. They did not spare her in upbringing, care, compassion, kindness, or in choosing her destiny when they wished to marry her off, because of their eagerness to seek suitable matches. Yet, despite this, they did not regard her as having a right to claim an inheritance, or to share in deciding her own destiny, or to demand what was hers from them. God the Exalted alluded to some of these conditions in His saying: *"And what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women, to whom you do not give what was prescribed for them"* (4:127), and: *"Do not prevent them from marrying their husbands"* (2:232). So God set limits for the dealings with women and legislated rulings for them, which this mighty verse declared in general terms, and then the Shari'ah detailed them. Among the subtleties of the Qur'an in drawing attention to this is that it joins the believing women to the believing men when mentioning many rulings or virtues, and joins women to men.

As for His saying *bil-ma'ruf*, the *ba'* is for accompaniment, and what is meant by it is that which sound minds recognize, free from partiality toward desires, customs, or misguided teachings. That is the good, and it is what the Law has brought, by explicit text, analogy, or what the legal objectives or the general public interest require, provided that the Law contains nothing opposing it. The Arabs use *ma'ruf* for what is the opposite of *munkar*. So the meaning is: for women are rights like those that are upon them, accompanied always by what is not reprehensible in the Law or in reason. Under this are great details, drawn from the Shari'ah, which are the domain of the views of the *mujtahidin* in the various ages and regions. So the view of one who holds that a virgin girl is compelled by her father to marry strips her of the equivalence to the son, and so falls under the degree. The view of one who prohibits compelling her and says she may not be married except with her consent grants her the equivalence to the male. The view of one who prohibits a woman from donating more than a third of her property without her husband's permission strips her of equivalence to the man. The view of one who makes her like a man in disposing of her own property grants her equivalence to the man. The view of one who gives the woman the right to choose separation from her husband if he has a defect grants her the equivalence, and the view of one who does not grant her this strips her of this right. Each of them considers that this is either *ma'ruf* or *munkar*. The same applies to everything on which the Muslims agree concerning the rights of the two sexes, and what they disagree about, whether equalizing between man and woman or differentiating: all of this is viewed in terms of realizing God's saying *bil-ma'ruf*, definitively or probably. So be vigilant in this matter, and take the meaning rather than the mere wording.

The religion of Islam is worthy of concern for reforming the condition of women. How could it not be, when she is half of the human species, and the first educator, who pours forth the upbringing that reaches the souls before anything else, who meets minds that evils have not touched and hearts into which the snouts of Satan have not penetrated? If that upbringing is good, sincere, correct, and true, it is the first thing to be imprinted upon those noble essences and the earliest to mingle with those sound natures. She prepares for her likes, from the thoughts of good, a wide abode, and she leaves to others of evils neither honour nor love.

[p. 399]

ودِينُ الإسْلامِ دِينُ تَشْرِيعٍ ونِظامٍ، فَلِذَلِكَ جاءَ بِإصْلاحِ حالِ المَرْأةِ، ورَفْعِ شَأْنِها لِتَتَهَيَّأ الأُمَّةُ الدّاخِلَةُ تَحْتَ حُكْمِ الإسْلامِ، إلى الِارْتِقاءِ وسِيادَةِ العالَمِ. وقَوْلُهُ ﴿ولِلرِّجالِ عَلَيْهِنَّ دَرَجَةٌ﴾ (And the men have a degree over them) إثْباتٌ لِتَفْضِيلِ الأزْواجِ، في حُقُوقٍ كَثِيرَةٍ عَلى نِسائِهِمْ، لِكَيْلا يُظَنَّ أنَّ المُساواةَ المَشْرُوعَةَ بِقَوْلِهِ ﴿ولَهُنَّ مِثْلُ الَّذِي عَلَيْهِنَّ بِالمَعْرُوفِ﴾ (And they have rights similar to those over them, according to what is known) مُطَّرِدَةٌ، ولِزِيادَةِ بَيانِ المُرادِ مِن قَوْلِهِ بِالمَعْرُوفِ، وهَذا التَّفْضِيلُ ثابِتٌ عَلى الإجْمالِ لِكُلِّ رَجُلٍ، ويَظْهَرُ أثَرُ هَذا التَّفْضِيلِ عِنْدَ نُزُولِ المُقْتَضَياتِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ والعادِيَّةِ.

وقَوْلُهُ ولِلرِّجالِ خَبَرٌ عَنْ دَرَجَةٍ، قُدِّمَ لِلِاهْتِمامِ بِما تُفِيدُهُ اللّامُ مِن مَعْنى اسْتِحْقاقِهِمْ تِلْكَ الدَّرَجَةَ، كَما أُشِيرَ إلى ذَلِكَ الِاسْتِحْقاقِ في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى ﴿الرِّجالُ قَوّامُونَ عَلى النِّساءِ بِما فَضَّلَ اللَّهُ بَعْضَهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾ [النساء: ٣٤]. وفي هَذا الِاهْتِمامِ مَقْصِدانِ: أحَدُهُما دَفْعُ تَوَهُّمِ المُساواةِ بَيْنَ الرِّجالِ والنِّساءِ في كُلِّ الحُقُوقِ، تَوَهُّمًا مِن قَوْلِهِ آنِفًا ﴿ولَهُنَّ مِثْلُ الَّذِي عَلَيْهِنَّ بِالمَعْرُوفِ﴾. وثانِيهُما تَحْدِيدُ إيثارِ الرِّجالِ عَلى النِّساءِ بِمِقْدارٍ مَخْصُوصٍ، لِإبْطالِ إيثارِهِمُ المُطْلَقَ، الَّذِي كانَ مُتَّبَعًا في الجاهِلِيَّةِ. والرِّجالُ جَمْعُ رَجُلٍ، وهو الذَّكَرُ البالِغُ مِنَ الآدَمِيِّينَ خاصَّةً، وأمّا قَوْلُهم: امْرَأةٌ رَجُلَةُ الرَّأْيِ، فَهو عَلى التَّشْبِيهِ، أيْ تُشْبِهُ الرَّجُلَ.

والدَّرَجَةُ ما يُرْتَقى عَلَيْهِ في سُلَّمٍ أوْ نَحْوِهِ، وصِيغَتْ بِوَزْنِ فَعَلَةٍ مِن دَرَجَ إذا انْتَقَلَ عَلى بُطْءٍ ومَهْلٍ، يُقالُ: دَرَجَ الصَّبِيُّ إذا ابْتَدَأ في المَشْيِ. وهي هُنا اسْتِعارَةٌ لِلرِّفْعَةِ، المُكَنّى بِها عَنِ الزِّيادَةِ في الفَضِيلَةِ الحُقُوقِيَّةِ، وذَلِكَ أنَّهُ تَقَرَّرَ تَشْبِيهُ المَزِيَّةِ في الفَضْلِ بِالعُلُوِّ والِارْتِفاعِ، فَتَبِعَ ذَلِكَ تَشْبِيهُ الأفْضَلِيَّةِ بِزِيادَةِ الدَّرَجاتِ في سَيْرِ الصّاعِدِ، لِأنَّ بِزِيادَتِها زِيادَةَ الِارْتِفاعِ. ويُسَمُّونَ الدَّرَجَةَ إذا نَزَلَ مِنها النّازِلُ: دَرَكَةً، لِأنَّهُ يُدْرِكُ بِها المَكانَ النّازِلَ إلَيْهِ. والعِبْرَةُ بِالمَقْصِدِ الأوَّلِ، فَإنْ كانَ القَصْدُ مِنَ الدَّرَجَةِ الِارْتِفاعَ كَدَرَجَةِ السُّلَّمِ والعُلُوَّ فَهي دَرَجَةٌ، وإنْ كانَ القَصْدُ النُّزُولَ كَدَرَكِ الدّامُوسِ (the depths of the damus, i.e., the bottom of a well or the sea) فَهي دَرَكَةٌ، ولا عِبْرَةَ بِنُزُولِ الصّاعِدِ، وصُعُودِ النّازِلِ.

وهَذِهِ الدَّرَجَةُ اقْتَضاها ما أوْدَعَهُ اللَّهُ في صِنْفِ الرِّجالِ مِن زِيادَةِ القُوَّةِ العَقْلِيَّةِ والبَدَنِيَّةِ، فَإنَّ الذُّكُورَةَ في الحَيَوانِ تَمامٌ في الخِلْقَةِ، ولِذَلِكَ نَجِدُ صِنْفَ الذَّكَرِ في كُلِّ أنْواعِ الحَيَوانِ أذْكى مِنَ الأُنْثى، وأقْوى جِسْمًا، وعَزْمًا، وعَنْ إرادَتِهِ يَكُونُ الصَّدْرُ، ما لَمْ يَعْرِضْ لِلْخِلْقَةِ عارِضٌ يُوجِبُ انْحِطاطَ بَعْضِ أفْرادِ الصِّنْفِ، وتَفَوُّقَ بَعْضِ أفْرادِ الآخَرِ نادِرًا. فَلِذَلِكَ كانَتِ الأحْكامُ التَّشْرِيعِيَّةُ الإسْلامِيَّةُ جارِيَةً عَلى وفْقِ النُّظُمِ التَّكْوِينِيَّةِ، لِأنَّ واضِعَ الأمْرَيْنِ واحِدٌ.

[صفحة ٤٠٢ / p. 402]

وهَذِهِ الدَّرَجَةُ هي ما فُضِّلَ بِهِ الأزْواجُ عَلى زَوْجاتِهِمْ: مِنَ الإذْنِ بِتَعَدُّدِ الزَّوْجَةِ لِلرَّجُلِ، دُونَ أنْ يُؤْذَنَ بِمِثْلِ ذَلِكَ لِلْأُنْثى، وذَلِكَ اقْتَضاهُ التَّزَيُّدُ في القُوَّةِ الجِسْمِيَّةِ، ووَفْرَةِ عَدَدِ الإناثِ في مَوالِيدِ البَشَرِ. ومِن جَعْلِ الطَّلاقِ بِيَدِ الرَّجُلِ دُونَ المَرْأةِ، والمُراجَعَةِ في العِدَّةِ كَذَلِكَ، وذَلِكَ اقْتَضاهُ التَّزَيُّدُ في القُوَّةِ العَقْلِيَّةِ وصِدْقُ التَّأمُّلِ. وكَذَلِكَ جَعْلُ المَرْجِعِ في اخْتِلافِ الزَّوْجَيْنِ إلى رَأْيِ الزَّوْجِ في شُئُونِ المَنزِلِ، لِأنَّ كُلَّ اجْتِماعٍ يُتَوَقَّعُ حُصُولُ تَعارُضِ المَصالِحِ فِيهِ، يَتَعَيَّنُ أنْ يُجْعَلَ لَهُ قاعِدَةٌ في الِانْفِصالِ، والصَّدْرُ عَنْ رَأْيٍ واحِدٍ مُعَيَّنٍ، مِن ذَلِكَ الجَمْعِ. ولَمّا كانَتِ الزَّوْجِيَّةُ اجْتِماعَ ذاتَيْنِ لَزِمَ جَعْلُ إحْداهُما مَرْجِعًا عِنْدَ الخِلافِ، ورَجَحَ جانِبُ الرَّجُلِ لِأنَّ بِهِ تَأسَّسَتِ العائِلَةُ، ولِأنَّهُ مَظِنَّةُ الصَّوابِ غالِبًا. ولِذَلِكَ إذا لَمْ يُمْكِنِ التَّراجُعُ، واشْتَدَّ بَيْنَ الزَّوْجَيْنِ النِّزاعُ، لَزِمَ تَدَخُّلُ القَضاءِ في شَأْنِهِما، وتَرَتَّبَ عَلى ذَلِكَ بَعْثُ الحَكَمَيْنِ، كَما في آيَةِ ﴿وإنْ خِفْتُمْ شِقاقَ بَيْنِهِما﴾ [النساء: ٣٥].

ويُؤْخَذُ مِنَ الآيَةِ حُكْمُ حُقُوقِ الرِّجالِ غَيْرِ الأزْواجِ، بِلَحْنِ الخِطابِ (lahn al-khitab, implicit meaning derived from the wording of a text)، لِمُساواتِهِمْ لِلْأزْواجِ في صِفَةِ الرُّجُولَةِ، الَّتِي كانَتْ هي العِلَّةَ في ابْتِزازِهِمْ حُقُوقَ النِّساءِ في الجاهِلِيَّةِ. فَلَمّا أسَّسَتِ الآيَةُ حُكْمَ المُساواةِ والتَّفْضِيلِ بَيْنَ الرِّجالِ والنِّساءِ، الأزْواجُ إبْطالًا لِعَمَلِ الجاهِلِيَّةِ، أخَذْنا مِنها حُكْمَ ذَلِكَ بِالنِّسْبَةِ لِلرِّجالِ غَيْرِ الأزْواجِ عَلى النِّساءِ، كالجِهادِ، وذَلِكَ مِمّا اقْتَضَتْهُ القُوَّةُ الجَسَدِيَّةُ، وكَبَعْضِ الوِلاياتِ المُخْتَلَفِ في صِحَّةِ إسْنادِها إلى المَرْأةِ، والتَّفْضِيلِ في بابِ العَدالَةِ، ووِلايَةِ النِّكاحِ، والرِّعايَةِ، وذَلِكَ مِمّا اقْتَضَتْهُ القُوَّةُ الفِكْرِيَّةُ، وضَعْفُها في المَرْأةِ وسُرْعَةُ تَأثُّرِها. وكالتَّفْضِيلِ في الإرْثِ، وذَلِكَ مِمّا اقْتَضَتْهُ رِئاسَةُ العائِلَةِ المُوجِبَةُ لِفَرْطِ الحاجَةِ إلى المالِ، وكالإيجابِ عَلى الرَّجُلِ إنْفاقَ زَوْجِهِ. وإنَّما عُدَّتْ هَذِهِ دَرَجَةً، مَعَ أنَّ لِلنِّساءِ أحْكامًا لا يُشارِكُهُنَّ فِيها الرِّجالُ كالحَضانَةِ، تِلْكَ الأحْكامُ الَّتِي أشارَ إلَيْها قَوْلُهُ تَعالى ﴿لِلرِّجالِ نَصِيبٌ مِمّا اكْتَسَبُوا ولِلنِّساءِ نَصِيبٌ مِمّا اكْتَسَبْنَ﴾ [النساء: ٣٢]، لِأنَّ ما امْتازَ بِهِ الرِّجالُ كانَ مِن قَبِيلِ الفَضائِلِ.

فَأمّا تَأْدِيبُ الرَّجُلِ المَرْأةَ إذا كانا زَوْجَيْنِ، فالظّاهِرُ أنَّهُ شُرِعَتْ فِيهِ تِلْكَ المَراتِبُ رَعْيًا لِأحْوالِ طَبَقاتِ النّاسِ، مَعَ احْتِمالِ أنْ يَكُونَ المُرادُ مِن قَوْلِهِ ﴿واللّاتِي تَخافُونَ نُشُوزَهُنَّ فَعِظُوهُنَّ واهْجُرُوهُنَّ في المَضاجِعِ واضْرِبُوهُنَّ﴾ [النساء: ٣٤] أنَّ ذَلِكَ يُجْرِيهِ وُلاةُ الأُمُورِ، ولَنا فِيهِ نَظَرٌ عِنْدَما نَصِلُ إلَيْهِ إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ تَعالى.

[صفحة ٤٠٣ / p. 403]

وقَوْلُهُ ﴿واللَّهُ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾. العَزِيزُ: القَوِيُّ، لِأنَّ العِزَّةَ في كَلامِ العَرَبِ القُوَّةُ، ﴿لَيُخْرِجَنَّ الأعَزُّ مِنها الأذَلَّ﴾ [المنافقون: ٨]. وقالَ شاعِرُهم:
وإنَّما العِزَّةُ لِلْكاثِرِ
(Indeed, honour belongs to the many.)
والحَكِيمُ: المُتْقِنُ الأُمُورَ في وضْعِها، مِنَ الحِكْمَةِ كَما تَقَدَّمَ.

والكَلامُ تَذْيِيلٌ (tadhyil, a concluding statement that generalizes the preceding meaning) وإقْناعٌ لِلْمُخاطَبِينَ، وذَلِكَ أنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى لَمّا شَرَّعَ حُقُوقَ النِّساءِ، كانَ هَذا التَّشْرِيعُ مَظِنَّةَ المُتَلَقِّي بِفَرْطِ التَّحَرُّجِ مِنَ الرِّجالِ، الَّذِينَ ما اعْتادُوا أنْ يَسْمَعُوا أنَّ لِلنِّساءِ مَعَهم حُظُوظًا غَيْرَ حُظُوظِ الرِّضا، والفَضْلِ، والسَّخاءِ، فَأصْبَحَتْ لَهُنَّ حُقُوقٌ يَأْخُذْنَها مِنَ الرِّجالِ كَرْهًا إنْ أبَوْا، فَكانَ الرِّجالُ بِحَيْثُ يَرَوْنَ في هَذا ثَلْمًا لِعِزَّتِهِمْ، كَما أنْبَأ عَنْهُ حَدِيثُ عُمَرَ بْنِ الخَطّابِ المُتَقَدِّمُ. فَبَيَّنَ اللَّهُ تَعالى أنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ، أيْ قَوِيٌّ لا يُعْجِزُهُ أحَدٌ، ولا يَتَّقِي أحَدًا، وأنَّهُ حَكِيمٌ يَعْلَمُ صَلاحَ النّاسِ، وأنَّ عِزَّتَهُ تُؤَيِّدُ حِكْمَتَهُ، فَيُنَفِّذُ ما اقْتَضَتْهُ الحِكْمَةُ بِالتَّشْرِيعِ، والأمْرَ الواجِبَ امْتِثالُهُ، ويَحْمِلُ النّاسَ عَلى ذَلِكَ وإنْ كَرِهُوا.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Divorce is twice; then either retention in kindness or release with good treatment.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*) introduced to mention the limit of divorce, which the husband holds over his wife. It arises from God's words ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period] if they desire reconciliation﴾ [al-Baqara: 228], and from something that God's words ﴿And the men have a degree over them﴾ [al-Baqara: 228] point to. God declared that women have rights equal to those of men, and He gave men an additional degree. Among these is that they hold the right of divorce, and they hold the right of return (*raj'a*), as in His words ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that﴾ [al-Baqara: 228]. Since the custom of the Arabs in the pre-Islamic period was to leave the end of divorce undefined, as will come shortly, it was fitting that after all of this he should mention the ruling that fixes the limit of divorce, to establish legislation in this matter and to remove what might cling to people's minds or had already clung to them concerning it.

Malik narrated in the chapter on divorce in the *Muwatta'*, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from his father, who said: "A man, when he divorced his wife and then took her back before her waiting period (*'idda*) ended, had the right to do so, even if he divorced her a thousand times. A man then deliberately went to his wife, divorced her, and when she was about to finish her waiting period, took her back; then he divorced her again and said, 'By God, I will never shelter you, nor will you ever be lawfully free [of me].' So God, exalted is He, revealed ﴿Divorce is twice; then either retention in kindness or release with good treatment﴾. From that day the people began to count divorce anew, whether they had divorced or not."

Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated something close to this from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hakim in his *Mustadrak* narrated it through 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, from 'A'isha, who said: "There was no limit to divorce. A man would divorce his wife and then take her back as long as the waiting period had not ended. There was some dispute between a man of the Ansar and his wife, and he said, 'By God, I will not leave you neither as a woman without a husband nor as a married woman.' So he kept divorcing her, and when the waiting period was nearly over he would take her back. He did this repeatedly. So God revealed ﴿Divorce is twice﴾." There are many narrations close to this in meaning. In the *Sunan* of Abu Dawud there is a chapter titled "The abrogation of return after three divorces," and he narrated the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas that a man, when he divorced his wife, had more right to her return, even if he divorced her three times; then this was abrogated (*nusikha*) and ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ was revealed. According to this, the verse is a nullification of what the people of the pre-Islamic period practised, and a limitation of the husbands' rights to return.

The definite article in ﴿the divorce﴾ is the definite article of the genus (*ta'rif al-jins*), as is most apparent with verbal nouns (*masadir*) and in the context of legislation. Legislation intends to explain legal realities, such as His words ﴿And God has made trade lawful﴾ [al-Baqara: 275] and His words ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾ [al-Baqara: 227]. This is the definition to which the author of the *Kashshaf* pointed in his preference. Here, what is intended is the revocable divorce (*talaq raj'i*) that was discussed just before, in His words ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that﴾ [al-Baqara: 228], since it is the original divorce. In the foundations of the Sharia there is no irrevocable divorce (*talaq ba'in*) that is not subject to return by its very nature, except the third pronouncement that falls after two previous ones; that is what makes the separation final. As for other irrevocable divorces established by the Sunna, their finality is due to an extraneous right, such as the wife's right concerning what she gives from her property in khul' divorce, and like the legal right in divorce through mutual imprecation (*li'an*), since the likelihood of good companionship has ceased after the two have invoked the curse upon each other; and like the woman's right, by a judge's ruling granting her divorce to prevent harm to her.

The qualifier "revocable" was omitted because the context indicates it. Thus the sense becomes: "The revocable divorce is twice." Since the verse informs us that divorce is twice, it is understood that the sense is: the husband's right to pronounce revocable divorce is twice. As for the third pronouncement, it is not revocable. This is indicated by His words after mentioning the two: ﴿then either retention in kindness﴾, and His words after it: ﴿And if he divorces her [a third time], she is not lawful to him afterward until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqara: 230], and so on. A similar explanation has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba narrated that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, "Tell me about God's words ﴿Divorce is twice﴾; where is the third?" The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Retention in kindness or release with good treatment." The man's question about the third indicates that the end of the three was a known ruling, either from the Sunna or from the rest of the verse, and he only asked about the reason for the phrase "twice."

Since the purpose is to explain the ruling for the genus of divorce, with respect to its occurrence from its agent, and since it occurs only from husbands, the word *talaq* returns in meaning to *tatliq* (the act of pronouncing divorce), just as *salam* returns to the sense of *taslim* (greeting).

His words ﴿twice﴾ are the dual of *marra* (occurrence). In their usage, *marra* means a single act from its described subject or its related subject. It only occurs qualifying an action, with a description or the like, or with an addition or the like. It may occur singular, dual, or plural, and thereby indicates either the non-repetition of the action, or its repetition once, or its repetition multiple times. God said ﴿We will punish them twice﴾ [al-Tawba: 101]. The Arabs say, "I forbade you more than once, but you did not desist," meaning many times. The word *marra* does not mean one of the things that are individual entities. Do you not see that you say, "I gave you a dirham twice," when you gave him one dirham and then another, and it is not understood that you gave him two dirhams together? This contrasts with your saying, "I gave you two dirhams."

So God's words ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ indicate that the revocable divorce is legislated with the right of repetition up to a limit of two occurrences, one after another and no more. Thus it is not understood by the people of the language that the meaning is "divorce does not occur except as two pronouncements together, neither more nor fewer." Whoever imagined this and needed an interpretation to dispel it has strayed from the established patterns of Arabic usage. Many of those who engaged in tafsir multiplied the possibilities regarding this verse and built rulings upon them, driven by misguided understandings, and then applied them to dialectical methods of argumentation to support the differing schools concerning whether the innovated divorce (*talaq bid'i*) is valid or not. In their prolixity they deviated from the meanings of established usage. Among the scholars of verification (*muhaqqiqun*) there were those who did not miss the meaning, though their expression did not fully convey it, as occurred in the *Kashshaf*.

It is also possible that the definite article in "the divorce" is the definite article of prior reference (*ta'rif al-'ahd*), and the referent is what is derived from God's words ﴿And divorced women shall wait﴾ [al-Baqara: 228] up to His words ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back﴾ [al-Baqara: 228]. In that case it is like the definite article in God's words ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾ [Al 'Imran: 36], which refers to what was derived from His words ﴿Indeed, I have dedicated to You what is in my womb, as a dedicated offering﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35].

His words ﴿then either retention in kindness﴾ form a clause (*jumla*) that is consequent upon the clause ﴿Divorce is twice﴾. The *fa'* (then) indicates sequence only in the mention, not in the occurrence of the ruling. *Imsak* (retention) is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose implied sense is "so the matter is: retention in kindness or release," following the pattern of ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ [Yusuf: 18]. Since both retention and release are possible at each of the two occurrences of divorce, the meaning is: "retention or release at each of the two occurrences." That is, the nature of divorce is that each occurrence of it is followed either by taking back in kindness or by leaving in good treatment, without harm in either case.

Accordingly, *imsak* and *tasrih* are both verbal nouns, intended in their actual reality and as nouns, not as substitutes for verbs. The meaning is that the one who divorces is in control of his own affair. If he desires his wife, then his course is to retain her, that is, to take her back. If he does not desire her, then his course is to leave off taking her back, and she is released. The purpose of this clause is to combine (*idmaj*) the exhortation to good conduct both in the case of taking back and in the case of leaving her, since God prescribed excellence (*ihsan*) in all things, nullifying the practices of the people of the pre-Islamic period. They used to take a woman back after divorcing her and then divorce her again and again, so that she would remain for a long time in a state of abandonment, as harm to her, since divorce for them did not end at a number after which the husband no longer had the right of return. This prepares for what follows in His words ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them﴾ [al-Baqara: 229], and so on.

It is also possible that *imsak* and *tasrih* are verbal nouns made into substitutes for their verbs, following the pattern of the absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) that substitutes for its verb. Their original form is the accusative, but they were shifted from the accusative to the nominative to express the sense of permanence, just as the shift from accusative to nominative occurs in His words ﴿He said, "Peace"﴾ [Maryam: 47]. This has been discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Fatiha. In this case the clause carries the sense of a command by way of substitution for its verb, and it expresses permanence by the nominative form of the two verbal nouns. The implied sense is: "So retain, or release."

It is thus clear that divorce is limited to two occurrences, each of which may be followed either by retention or by release in kindness. This is a broadening for people, so that they may decide after divorce what suits their situation and the situation of their wives. Perhaps regret will overtake them after tasting separation, and they will realize what they may have overlooked at the moment of pronouncing divorce, out of anger or weariness. This accords with God's words ﴿You do not know; perhaps God will bring about after that some matter﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], and His words ﴿And do not retain them to harm them, transgressing; whoever does that has wronged himself. And do not take the verses of God in jest﴾ [al-Baqara: 231]. This is not so that they may take it as a pretext for harming women, as they used to do before Islam.

It has become clear from this that the intended meaning of the clause is retention or release in their absolute sense. As for the restriction of retention to what is known as fair (*ma'ruf*) and of release to excellence (*ihsan*), this is an inclusion (*idmaj*) of another exhortation in both states, an incorporation of guidance within the course of legislation.

He placed retention before release, indicating that it is the more important and the more favoured in the view of the Sharia. Retention, in its literal sense, is the grasping of a hand on something for fear that it will fall or slip away, and here it is a metaphor for the continuation of marital companionship. Release is the opposite of retention in both its literal and figurative meanings. It is used here metaphorically for ending the cause of companionship after divorce, which is the cause of return. Then the metaphor of that ending is extended to separation, so it is a metaphor at two removes.

*Al-ma'ruf* here is what people know in their dealings of the rights that Islam established or that customs established which do not contradict the rulings of Islam.

It is appropriate to retention, because it includes all the rulings of the marital bond, including good companionship and other matters. It is therefore more general than *ihsan*. As for release, it is separation, and its fair conduct is limited to excellence toward the one being separated, through good words and giving her a provision (*mut'a*), as God said ﴿So provide for them and release them with a gracious release﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49]. Husbands used to wrong divorced women, preventing them from their jewelry and their clothing, and they would greatly disparage them. Ibn 'Arafa said in his tafsir: "If you say, why was it not said 'retention in excellence or release in fairness'? I say: their customary answer is that fairness (*ma'ruf*) is lighter than excellence (*ihsan*), since fairness is good companionship and giving the rights of marriage, whereas excellence is not wronging her in what is her right. Excellence requires giving and bestowing property, which is harder on the souls than good companionship. So fairness was paired with retention, which entails the permanence of the marital bond, since its repetition does no harm, and excellence, which is burdensome, was paired with release, which does not recur."

Some people derived from the verse a prohibition on combining the three divorces in a single utterance, on the basis that the meaning of His words "twice" is separation. We will mention that at His words ﴿And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him afterward﴾ [al-Baqara: 230], and so on.
