It is permissible for the waw (و) to be parenthetical (i'tiraḍiyyah), so that it forms an interjected clause (i'tiraḍ) between the two conjoined elements, namely His saying "then retention" (فَإمْساكٌ) and His saying "then if he divorces her" (فَإنْ طَلَّقَها). It is also permissible for it to be conjoined to "or release with kindness" (أوْ تَسْرِيحٌ بِإحْسانٍ), because part of the kindness of release is that the one releasing, who is the divorcer, does not take a compensation (عِوَضًا) in exchange for the divorce. This is the reason for the placement of this interjected clause. It is an elegant variation (تَفَنُّنٌ بَدِيعٌ) in combining legislative provisions with address to the community, so that each individual among them may take from it what pertains to him. The husband refrains from taking the property. The guardian of authority (وَلِيُّ الأمْرِ) rules that it is not binding. The guardian of the wife, or the head of the husband's tribe, intervenes, commands and forbids. It was the custom of the Arabs that these affairs were handled by men of judgment from the relatives of both sides, while the rest of the community is commanded to comply with that. This is the manner of the Qur'an's addresses in legislation, such as His saying ﴿And do not give to the foolish your property﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 5], up to His saying ﴿and provide for them therein﴾ [al-Nisa: 5]. The author of the al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary) pointed to this. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and the author of the al-Kashshaf said: the address in His saying ﴿and it is not lawful for you﴾ is to the husbands, by the indication of His saying "that you take" (أنْ تَأْخُذُوا) and His saying "that you have given them" (آتَيْتُمُوهُنَّ). The address in His saying ﴿but if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ is to the judges, because if it were to the husbands it would have said: "if you fear that you will not keep within the limits" or "that they will not keep within the limits." The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Something like this is not rare in the Qur'an." That is, the referent of each pronoun is clear from the contextual indications. He compared it, in al-Kashshaf, to His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat al-Saff: ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾ [al-Saff: 13], according to the view of the author of al-Kashshaf, since he made it conjoined to ﴿you believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Saff: 11] etc., because it has the meaning of "believe and strive," so that it is conjoined to the general addresses to the community, even though the giving of good tidings is specific to the Messenger ﷺ, since it can only come from him. What is more evident than the comparison of the author of al-Kashshaf is to compare it with His saying, may He be exalted, in what follows: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 232], since the divorcer and the one who prevents are addressed in it, and they are two different parties.

The feminine pronoun in "that you have given them" (آتَيْتُمُوهُنَّ) refers to the divorced women, which is understood from His saying ﴿Divorce is twice﴾, because the genus (الجِنْسُ) requires a number of divorcers and divorced women. The author of al-Kashshaf permitted that the entire address be to the judges, and he interpreted His saying "that you take" (أنْ تَأْخُذُوا) and His saying ﴿of what you have given them﴾ as meaning that the attribution of taking and giving to the judges is because they are the ones who command the taking and giving. Al-Baydawi preferred this view on the basis of its freedom from confusion of pronouns without a rhetorical reason for a shift (التِفاتٌ), but the author of al-Kashshaf and others criticized it, on the grounds that khul' (divorce by compensation initiated by the wife) may occur without litigation. What the husbands had given their wives as dowries was not taken through the hand of a judge, so this view is void. The meaning of "is not lawful" (لا يَحِلُّ) is "is not permitted and is not allowed." The use of ḥill (lawful) and ḥurmah (unlawful) in this meaning and its opposite is ancient in the Arabic language. 'Antara said:

"O ewe, the game of the one for whom she is lawful is forbidden to me; would that she were not forbidden!"

Ka'b said:

"When he grapples with an opponent, it is not lawful for him to leave the opponent unless he is thrown down."

The word "anything" (شَيْئًا) is used because it is an indefinite noun, extremely broad in its generality, as a warning against taking even the smallest amount, unlike if he had said "property" (مالًا) or the like. This placement is among the elegances of the use of the word "thing" (شَيْءٌ), which the Shaykh (al-Jurjani) pointed out in Dala'il al-I'jaz (Proofs of Inimitability). Its explanation has already been presented at His saying ﴿and We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155].

As for His saying "except that they both fear" (إلّا أنْ يَخافا), the majority read it with a fatḥah on the yā' of the third-person, so the verb is attributed to the subject, and the pronoun refers to the two parties to the khul', which is understood from His saying ﴿that you take of what you have given them, anything﴾. Likewise the pronoun in "they both fear that they will not keep within the limits" and the pronoun in ﴿there is no blame upon them both﴾. This verb is attributed to them both rather than to the rest of the community, because they are the two who know their own situation. Ḥamzah, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read it with a ḍammah on the yā' of the third-person, so the verb is in the passive voice, and the pronoun refers to the two parties to the khul'. The subject is omitted, and it is the pronoun of the addressees. The estimate is: "except that you fear for them both that they will not keep within the limits of Allah."

Fear (al-khawf) is the expectation of the occurrence of what the soul dislikes, and it is the opposite of security. It is also applied to its effect, which is striving to please the one feared and obeying his commands, as in His saying ﴿So do not fear them but fear Me, if you are believers﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 175]. Its synonym is khashyah (awe), because failing to keep the limits of Allah is something the believer fears. Fear transitively takes one object, as Allah, the Exalted, says ﴿So do not fear them﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 175].

A poet satirizing a man from Fa'qas who ate his dog, whose name was Ḥabtar, said:

"O Ḥabtar, why did you eat it, by the one whose... If Allah had feared you concerning it, He would have forbidden it to you."

Ibn Jinni, in his commentary on the Ḥamasah, interpreted the verse of al-Aḥwaṣ concerning it in one of two ways:

"So when he moves, he moves over a violent one, whose sudden attacks on his opponents are feared."

The word "upon" (عَلى) is omitted in the verse because it precedes "that" (أنْ), the verbal (مَصْدَرِيَّةٌ) particle.

Some exegetes have said that fear here means supposition, meaning the supposition of something disliked, since fear is not applied except to the occurrence of the supposition of something disliked. This is fear in its original sense. As for establishing the limits of Allah, Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, explained it as the rights of the husband, his obedience and his kindness to him. So if the woman neglects that, she has transgressed the limits of Allah.

[Page 409]

As for His saying ﴿there is no blame upon them both for what she ransoms herself with﴾, it lifts sin from them both, and it indicates that the one who gives up the unlawful is a partner to the taker in the sin. In the hadith on riba al-fadl (excess usury): "The taker and the giver in that are equal." The pronoun in "what she ransoms herself with" refers to the category of khul'. The context has become entirely determined to return the pronoun to it specifically, since the payment of property is from her alone. The apparent generality of His saying "for what she ransoms herself with" is that khul' is then permissible with what exceeds the dowry, and the disagreement on this will come later.

The scholars of the community did not disagree that the meaning of the verse is taking compensation for separation. They disagreed only about this separation: is it a divorce (ṭalāq) or a annulment (faskh)? The majority held that it is a divorce and that it is never anything but irrevocable (bā'in), since if it were not irrevocable, there would be no benefit in giving compensation. This was the view of 'Uthman, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, 'Ata', Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Zuhri, Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Mujahid and Makhul. A group held that it is an annulment, and this was the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, 'Ikrimah, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and everyone who said that khul' does not occur except by the ruling of a judge. The position of al-Shafi'i varied on this: at one time he said it is a divorce, and at another time he said it is not a divorce. Some report from al-Shafi'i that khul' is not a divorce unless he intends divorce by the khul'. The correct view is that it is a divorce, since a valid marital bond has been established. If by annulment they mean that it involves the abolition of the first bond, then all divorce is ultimately a type of annulment. The benefit of this disagreement appears in a khul' that takes place between them after the husband has pronounced two divorces. According to the majority, the khul' divorce counts as a third divorce, so she is not lawful to the one who divorced her by khul' except after another husband. According to Ibn 'Abbas, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq and those who agree with them, it is not counted as a divorce, and they may conclude a new marriage contract.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin and Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan relied on this verse and said: khul' does not occur except by the ruling of a judge, based on His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿but if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾. The majority hold that it is permissible to carry out khul' without litigation, because the address is not explicitly to the judges. It has been authentically reported from 'Umar, 'Uthman and Ibn 'Umar that they regarded it as permissible without a judge's ruling.

The majority also hold that it is permissible to take compensation for divorce, if the woman's soul is content with it and it is not due to harm to her. They agreed that if it is due to harm to them, then it is unlawful for him. Malik said: if the harm is established, the divorce takes effect, and her property is returned to her. Abu Hanifah said: it takes effect, but he is sinful, based on his principle regarding prohibition when what is excluded is outside the essence of what is prohibited. al-Zuhri, al-Nakha'i and Dawud said: it is not permissible except in cases of ill-treatment (nushūz) and discord (shiqāq). The truth is that the verse is explicit in prohibiting taking compensation for divorce, except when there is fear that the marital relationship will fail because the wife does not love her husband. Allah confirmed this ruling when He said ﴿except that they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾, because the implication of the exception is nearly explicit that if they do not fear this, khul' is not lawful. He emphasized it with His saying ﴿but if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame upon them both for what she ransoms herself with﴾, because its implication is that if they do not fear this, the blame remains. Then He confirmed all of that by prohibition, with His saying ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾, then by threat, with His saying ﴿And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah – it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾. All of this was clarified by the judgment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ between Jamilah bint, or the sister of, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and her husband Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, when she said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, neither I nor Thabit..." or "Nothing gathers my head and the head of Thabit," "By Allah, I do not blame him regarding religion or character, but I dislike disbelief in Islam. I cannot bear him out of hatred." So the Prophet ﷺ said to her: "Will you return to him the garden that he gave you as dowry?" She said: "Yes, and I will add to it." In one narration it adds: he said: "As for the excess, no." The majority replied that the verse did not mention His saying ﴿unless they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ as a condition, but rather because it is the usual circumstance of khul'. Do you not see His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And if they are pleased to give you anything of it willingly, then consume it, with satisfaction and ease﴾ [al-Nisa: 4]. Thus the Malikis answered, as in the Ahkam of Ibn al-'Arabi and the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi. In my view, this answer is void and a claim without benefit. As for denying that what is mentioned in this verse is a condition, it is an extreme interpretation and a diversion of speech from its proper meaning. How can it be so, when it indicates, through three explicit statements and two implicit meanings, that: His saying ﴿it is not lawful for you to take from what you have given them anything﴾, where "anything" is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, meaning that it is not lawful to take even the least amount. His saying "unless they both fear" contains an explicit and an implicit meaning. His saying "but if you fear" contains the same. Moreover, the implicit meaning that comes as the usual case is the implicit meaning of the qualifying adjuncts such as the attribute, the circumstantial state and the limit, not what occurs in speech only for the purpose of exclusion, such as the exception and the condition. As for the argument for permissibility from His saying ﴿And if they are pleased to give you anything of it willingly﴾ [al-Nisa: 4], its context concerns the woman's pardon of part of the dowry, since the pronoun in "of it" refers to the dowries, because the beginning of that verse is ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift, and if they are pleased to give you﴾ [al-Nisa: 4]. It is guidance for what arises during the marital bond, which increases affection. There is no contradiction between the two verses. Even if we grant a contradiction, it would be obligatory for the examiner to follow either reconciling the two verses or giving preference (tarjīḥ).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 3 of 3):**

The scholars differed over whether it is permissible for the husband to take more than the bridewealth (ṣadāq) he gave the wife who separates from him. Ṭāwūs, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Awzāʿī, Isḥāq and Aḥmad said: it is not permissible to take more, because God, exalted is He, restricted the matter here by His saying ﴿what you have given them﴾. They argued with the report that the Prophet ﷺ said to Jamīlah, when she said to him, "I will return to him his garden and add to it," "As for the addition, no." This was narrated by al-Dāraquṭnī from Ibn Jurayj.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) said: it is permissible to take more, on account of the generality of His saying ﴿there is no blame on them both for what she gives up therewith﴾. They relied on what al-Dāraquṭnī narrated from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: "His sister was married to a man from the Anṣār, whom she married for a garden. Then a dispute arose between them, and they brought their case before the Messenger of God ﷺ. He said to her, 'Will you return to him his garden and he divorce you?' She said, 'Yes, and I will add to it.' So he said to her, 'Return to him his garden and add to it.'" They also relied on the fact that when Jamīlah said to him, "And I will add to it," he did not object to it.

Mālik said: "It is not among the noble morals (makārim al-akhlāq), and I have not seen anyone of the people of knowledge who disliked it," meaning he did not consider it forbidden. He did not regard as authentic what was reported: "As for the addition, no." The truth is that the verse clearly magnifies the matter of taking a compensation (ʿiwaḍ) for divorce. God permitted it only when the aversion and repugnance come from the woman at the beginning of the marriage, to prevent harm to the husband through the loss of the bridewealth he paid, from which he has gained no benefit. This is because the aversion usually occurs at the beginning of the marriage, not after living together for a long time.

So His saying ﴿what you have given them﴾ clearly indicates that this is the locus of the concession. However, the majority interpreted it to mean that this is the usual case, namely what burdens the husbands, and that it does not nullify the general sense of His saying ﴿what she gives up therewith﴾. Mālik, by his saying "it is not among the noble morals," indicated that he did not consider it something that makes the act corrupt or forbidden, since it does not affect a necessity (ḍarūrī) or a need (ḥājī); rather it belongs to the embellishments (taḥsīnāt). The practice of the Muslims has continued upon its permissibility.

They differed over whether this verse is *muḥkam* (clear, not abrogated) or *mansūkh* (abrogated). The majority hold that it is *muḥkam*. A group said it is abrogated by His saying, in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, ﴿But if you desire to replace one wife with another, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, take not from it anything﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 20]. Al-Qurṭubī attributed this view to Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī, and it is an anomalous (shādh) opinion. The context of the verse in al-Nisāʾ concerns a man who wishes to separate from his wife, and then it becomes unlawful for him to take back money from her. The verse of al-Baqarah differs: it concerns the wife who wishes to separate from her husband out of aversion.

﴿That is the limits of God; so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of God, those are the wrongdoers.﴾

The clause ﴿That is the limits of God; so do not transgress them﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between the clause ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them﴾ with what is connected to it, and the clause that follows from it, which is ﴿Then if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]. The connection of the parenthetical insertion is that the preceding discourse prohibited taking compensation for divorce, except in the case of fear that they would not keep within the limits of God. The limits of God were clarified in the Book and the Sunnah, so this parenthetical clause was added as a clarification, because the prohibition of taking compensation for divorce is among the limits of God.

"The limits of God" is a metaphor (istiʿāra) for the legal commands and prohibitions, by the indication of the verb of "transgressing." The limits were likened to the boundaries (ḥudūd) placed between people's properties, because the legal rulings separate what is lawful from what is unlawful, and truth from falsehood, and they separate what people were upon before Islam from what they are upon after it. "Establishing" (iqāmah), in its literal sense, means manifesting and bringing into existence, as one says, "He set up a boundary for his land." Here it is a metaphor for acting in accordance with the Sharīʿah, following the metaphor of "limits" for the legal rulings. Likewise, the use of "transgression" (iʿtidāʾ), which is going beyond the limit, for violating the ruling of the Sharīʿah, is a metaphor that follows from likening the ruling to the limit.

The clause ﴿And whoever transgresses the limits of God, those are the wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl). The clause ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾ conveys restriction (ḥaṣr), and it is a true restriction (ḥaṣr ḥaqīqī), since there is no wrongdoer except one who transgresses the limits of God. Thus it becomes clear that the state of the one who transgresses the limits of God is restricted to being a wrongdoer.

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾ is intended to specify the one referred to with the most complete specification, namely the one who transgresses the limits of God, out of concern to attach the description of wrongdoers to them.

The verb "transgresses" (yataʿaddā) is used in a sense that opposes the ruling of God, as a *tarshīḥ* (a supporting figure of speech that completes a metaphor). Because the limits were metaphorically applied to God's rulings, this verb, although it is a *tarshīḥ*, is itself metaphorical for violating God's rulings, since violating a command or prohibition resembles going beyond a limit by encroaching upon the property of its owner. A hadith states: "Indeed, every king has a protected domain (ḥimā). Indeed, the protected domain of God is His prohibitions."

[Page 414]

﴿So if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries a husband other than him. Then if he divorces her, there is no blame upon both of them for returning to each other if they think they will keep within the limits of Allah.﴾

This is a consequence derived from His saying ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. What lies between them is in the position of a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraad). Moreover, placing it here gives it an effect on the derivation of this ruling from everything that preceded, because it is known from the whole of that discourse that after the two divorces there is a choice between returning (to the wife) and not returning. So He arranged the ruling on the assumption of return, which is expressed by "keeping" (imsak). The phrase ﴿if he divorces her﴾ indicates, by implication (iqtida'), a presumed element, meaning: "if he returns to her and then divorces her," in order to explain the ruling of the third divorce. The listener was already prepared to receive this ruling from His saying ﴿Divorce is twice﴾, since he knew that this states the last number of revocable divorces, and that what comes after it is final (batt). Therefore the mention of ﴿if he divorces her﴾ is an added clarification and a preparation for His saying ﴿she is not lawful to him thereafter﴾, and so on.

The fa' (then) may be either:
- a conjunctive fa' linking the clause ﴿if he divorces her﴾ to the clause ﴿keeping (fa-imsak)﴾, in view of what it contains, from His saying ﴿keeping﴾, if the intended meaning of keeping is return and of releasing is not returning. That is: "if the divorcer keeps her, i.e., returns to her, and then divorces her, then she is not lawful to him thereafter." This is the apparent meaning.
- or an explanatory fa' (fasiha) clarifying His saying ﴿or releasing with kindness﴾, if the intended meaning of releasing is the initiation of divorce. That is: "if he persists after the return and then releases her, then she is not lawful to him thereafter." Repeating this in this way serves to make the prohibition of return, except after another husband, a consequence of it, explicitly stating what was understood from His saying ﴿Divorce is twice﴾. The word "divorce" is used here rather than "releasing" for clarity and for variety of expression, according to the two previously mentioned readings. Assigning the pronouns to each of them is not difficult. The hidden pronoun refers to the divorcer, understood from ﴿Divorce is twice﴾, and the pronoun in the object position refers to the divorced woman, also understood from "divorce," as was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿unless they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229].

The verse is an explicit statement of the final limit of the right of return. It is either a nullification of what they practised in the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) and a new Islamic legislation, or an abrogation (naskh) of what was established at the beginning of Islam, if what Abu Dawud related in his Sunan is authentic, in the chapter on return after the three divorces, from Ibn 'Abbas: that a man, if he divorced his wife, had more right to take her back, even if he had divorced her three times. Then this was abrogated, and He revealed ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229].

It is by no means permissible to take His saying ﴿So if he divorces her﴾ as a conjunction to the clause ﴿It is not lawful for you to take﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], nor to make the two pronouns refer to what the pronouns in ﴿unless they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229] refer to, nor ﴿there is no blame upon them both﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], because the ruling of His saying "So if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter" cannot correctly be linked to what the ruling of His saying "It is not lawful for you to take" is linked to. This is because it is not valid to make a divorce, after which the woman is not lawful to him, a consequence of the occurrence of khul' (divorce by compensation), since that is not among the rulings of Islam according to anyone's opinion.

[Page 415]

Thus it is strange what occurred in al-Khattabi's commentary on the Sunan of Abu Dawud: that Ibn 'Abbas argued that khul' is a annulment (faskh) by saying that Allah mentioned khul', then followed it with His saying ﴿if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]. He said: "If khul' were a divorce, the divorces would be four." I do not think this is authentically from Ibn 'Abbas, because it does not accord with the established meanings of Arabic usage.

His saying ﴿she is not lawful to him﴾ means: she is forbidden to him. He mentioned His saying ﴿thereafter﴾, meaning: after three divorces, as a record against the divorcer and as an allusion to the reason for the prohibition, which is the divorcer's carelessness regarding his wife and his disregard for the right of companionship, to the extent that he made her a plaything which the impulses of his anger and his foolishness turn over. So when He mentioned to them His saying "thereafter", the divorcers knew that they had not been right in their conditions which they were in during the Jahiliyyah.

What is meant by His saying ﴿until she marries a husband other than him﴾ is that she enters a contract with another husband, because the word nikah (marriage) in the speech of the Arabs has no meaning except the contract between the two spouses. I have not found for them any other usage of it, neither literal nor metaphorical. Whatever its usage in speech, the intended meaning in this verse is the contract, by the evidence of its being attributed to the woman. For the meaning that those who claim it is one of the meanings of nikah by homonymy and metaphor, namely sexual intercourse (masis), is not attributed in the speech of the Arabs to a woman at all. This is a subtle point which they overlooked in this context.

The wisdom of this great legislation is to restrain husbands from making light of their wives' rights and making them plaything in their homes. Thus He made the first divorce a slip, the second a test, and the third a separation, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said in the hadith about Musa and al-Khidr: "The first from Musa was forgetfulness, the second was a condition, and the third was deliberate." For this reason al-Khidr said to him at the third: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78].

Allah has arranged two rulings upon the third divorce: the first is the removal from the husband of the right of return by the mere pronouncement of divorce, and the second is the removal from the woman of the right to agree to return to him except after another husband. He made marriage to a second husband a condition after that, in order to warn husbands against hastening to the third divorce, except after reflection and deliberation, after which no hope remains of good companionship, since they know the prohibition of returning except after another husband. Thus it is a punishment for husbands who make light of women's rights, when this is repeated from them three times, with a penalty that returns to the pain of conscience, because of what is deeply rooted in souls of the intense aversion to a man's wife being joined to another man. The woman's condition is described by the verse of Ibn al-Zubayr:

*"Among people, if your ropes have decayed, there is one who connects; and in the earth, far from the abode of estrangement, there is one who moves away."*

[Page 416]

In al-Tibi it is related that al-Zajjaj said: "Allah only made this because He knew the difficulty of a woman marrying another man after a husband, so He forbade both of them to remarry after the three, lest they hasten or lest they reconsider." The listeners knew that the requirement of marriage to another husband is a training for divorcers. So it did not occur to anyone, unless the intended meaning of nikah in the verse is its literal meaning, which is the contract. However, since the contract is a means to what is sought from it in most cases, namely consummation and what follows it, a contract that is not followed by the contracting husband's intercourse with his wife is not considered valid for the purpose intended from it. The divorcer who pronounced the three does not pay attention to the mere contract of another husband who has not touched the woman. For this reason, when Rifa'ah ibn Samaw'al al-Qurazi divorced his wife Tamima bint Wahb with a divorce which coincided with the other divorces making three, and she married after him 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr al-Qurazi, she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Rifa'ah divorced me and finalised my divorce, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr married me, but with him is only like the fringe of this garment," and she pointed to the fringe of a garment she had. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her: "Do you want to return to Rifa'ah?" She said: "Yes." He said: "No, until you taste his honey (usayla)," and the hadith continues. Her question indicates that she anticipated that the marriage to Ibn al-Zubayr would not be counted as making the marriage lawful after her final divorce, since the intended aim of deterrence and training of the divorcer was not achieved.

Thus the scholars of Islam agreed that the marriage which makes lawful a woman divorced finally (mabtutah) is the entry of the second husband to the woman and his touching her. I do not think their evidence for this is anything except the return to the purpose of the Shari'ah, which every person who understands this eloquent Arabic speech knows. So there is no need for us to drain the buckets of inference by saying that this is from the word nikah meaning in particular in this verse sexual intercourse, or that it is from the hadith of Rifa'ah, so that it would be a restriction of the Book by a single report (khabar al-wahid), or that it is an addition to the text, so that the disagreement arises as to whether it is abrogation or not, and whether abrogating the Book by a single report is permissible or not. All of that is an entry into matters of no benefit in lengthy elaboration. Rather, for us the consensus of the Companions and the people of the language on understanding this purpose from the words of the Qur'an is sufficient, and none deviated from it

[Page 417]

except Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "Mere contract with a second husband makes the finally divorced woman lawful." This is an anomaly that contradicts the purpose, since what benefit is gained from a contract, if it is nothing but hardship for the contracting parties, the guardian, and the witnesses? Unless one makes the ruling dependent on the contract, on account of what usually results after it, so that if what usually results after it does not occur, it is excused, by way of causation through likelihood (ta'lil bil-mazinnah). No known person followed him in this. Al-Nahhas attributed it to Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and I think that is an error and a mistake on his part.

Allah commanded this ruling, arranged upon the occurrence of the third divorce after two preceding divorces. Therefore it is obligatory to comply with it, and its wisdom is known. So there is no doubt that it should be confined to its original case, and its ruling should not be extended to every divorce in which the divorcer expressed the word "three" for emphasis, or for stress, or as a lie, because that is not a divorce after two divorces, and the wisdom of discipline for bad conduct is not realised in it. The one who pronounces three in his first divorce is no different from one who does not pronounce them, in that his first divorce does not become a second. The most that his statement earns is that he is counted among the foolish or the liars, so he is not punished for that by separation from his wife. This ruling continued to be practised during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and part of the caliphate of 'Umar, as reported in the authentic books: the Muwatta' and what follows it, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him). It is also reported in some narrations, the hadith of Ibn 'Umar when he divorced his wife during menstruation, that he divorced her three times in one utterance. And there is the hadith of Rukanah ibn 'Abd Yazid al-Muttalibi, that he divorced his wife three times in one word, so he asked the Prophet (ﷺ), who said to him: "Allah only gave you one," and he ordered him to take her back.

Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, in the third year of his caliphate, saw incidents of divorce with the word "three" in one utterance, and he said: "I see that people have hastened in a matter in which they had been given respite. So if we enforce it upon them," and so he enforced it upon them.

The scholars of Islam differed about what is required of one who pronounces the divorce of three in a single pronouncement which is not the third. The majority (al-Jumhur) said: he is bound by three, following what 'Umar ibn al-Khattab decided, and his decision was supported by the silence of the Companions who did not object to it, so it is a silent consensus (ijma' sukuti). Based on comparing divorce to vows and oaths, the responsible person is bound by what he has committed himself to. There is no dispute that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab decided this and no one objected to it. However, he decided it by his own ijtihad, so it is his opinion, and the opinion of a Companion is not a proof for others. As for what they supported it with, the silence of the Companions, there is no evidence in it, because silent consensus is not a proof according to the leading scholars such as al-Shafi'i, al-Baqillani, al-Ghazali, and Imam al-Razi, especially since it originated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab

[Page 418]

The first part of the passage addresses the ruling's nature as a judicial decision (qada') and deterrent (zajr). It is a judgment within the sphere of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), which no one is obliged to change. However, the judgment is particular (juz'i) and does not necessitate that it be applied uniformly. The ruler's restriction of a permissible matter for the sake of public interest (maslaha) is open to deliberation, and so this is not part of the consensus (ijma') whose opposition is impermissible.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Masʿud, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, Muhammad ibn Ishaq, Hajjaj ibn Artat, Tawus, the Zahiriyya, and a group of Malikis of al-Andalus said so. Among the latter were Muhammad ibn Zinbaʿ, Muhammad ibn Baqi ibn Makhlad, Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Salam al-Khushani, the jurist of his age in Cordoba, Asbagh ibn al-Habbab, one of the jurists of Cordoba, and Ahmad ibn Mughith al-Tulaytuli, the great jurist. Ibn Taymiyya, from the Hanbalis, said that the triple divorce pronounced in a single utterance takes effect only as one pronouncement, and this is the more preponderant view in terms of both reasoning (nazar) and transmitted evidence (athar).

They argued with many proofs, the first and greatest of which is this verse, for God, exalted is He, made divorce twice and then a third time, and He made the prohibition of returning to the wife contingent upon the occurrence of the third pronouncement in fact, not in words. So if a man says to his wife, "You are divorced three times," and that pronouncement is not in fact the third, nor is there a repetition, he has lied in describing it as three, since it is in fact one or a second. How then can he proceed to make her unlawful to him, when God has not made it unlawful for him? Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Is this not like one who says, 'I recited Surat al-Baqara three times,' when he has recited it only once? His statement, 'three times,' would be false."

The second proof is that God, exalted is He, intended by the multiplicity of divorce to provide ease for people, because a spouse does not know the effect of separation from his partner. When a husband divorces his wife, regret appears to him and he cannot endure separation from her, so he chooses to return. If the single pronouncement were made to bar reconciliation merely by the wording, the legislative purpose of establishing the right of return would be nullified. Ibn Rushd al-Hafid said in al-Bidaya: "It seems the majority gave precedence to the ruling of severity in divorce as a means of blocking the pretext (sadd al-dhari'a). But by doing so we nullify the legal concession and the leniency intended by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps God will bring about after that some matter﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]."

The third proof: Ibn Mughith said: God, exalted is He, says: ﴿or a release with kindness﴾ [al-Baqara: 229], and one who pronounces three divorces is not acting with kindness, because in it there is abandonment of God's expansion (tawsiʿa). This may be derived by analogy (qiyas) from a case in the Mudawwana: such as a person's saying, "My wealth is a charity for the poor." Malik said: a third of it suffices.

The fourth proof: they argued with the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas in the two Sahihs: "The triple divorce was in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and the early part of ʿUmar's caliphate, a single pronouncement."

The majority answered this by saying that its transmitter is Tawus, and the rest of Ibn ʿAbbas's companions transmitted from him that he said, [Page 419] "Whoever divorces his wife three times has disobeyed his Lord, and his wife has become irrevocably separated from him." This weakens Tawus's transmission, for Ibn ʿAbbas would not oppose the Companions in favor of his own opinion. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: "Tawus's transmission is a mistake and an error." Even if it is authentic, the meaning is that people used to pronounce one divorce in place of the three pronouncements that people made, and this is the meaning of ʿUmar's statement: "People have hastened in a matter in which they once had deliberation." If this had been in effect during the time of the Messenger and Abu Bakr, ʿUmar would not have said, "They have hastened," nor would he have blamed them for it. This answer is weak. Abu al-Walid al-Baji said: "The transmission from Tawus with this content is sound." I say: As for Ibn ʿAbbas's opposition to what he transmitted, it does not weaken the transmission, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). We take his transmission, and we are not obliged to take his opinion. As for what they interpreted the hadith to mean, that people used to pronounce one divorce in place of the three, this interpretation is incorrect and contradicts the wording of the transmission and ʿUmar's statement: "If we had enforced it upon them." If enforcing it upon them was already established from the time of the Messenger, then the phrase "if we had enforced it upon them" would have no meaning. If its enforcement was not already established, but was not in effect, then the purpose of the argument is achieved.

The fifth proof is what al-Daraqutni transmitted: "Rukana ibn ʿAbd Yazid al-Muttalibi divorced his wife three times in a single utterance, then asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said to him: 'It is only one, or it is only that one, so take her back.'" The supporters of the majority answered this by saying that it is an unsteady (mudtarib) hadith, for it transmits that Rukana divorced, and in another version that Yazid ibn Rukana divorced, and in another version that he divorced his wife three times. Some transmissions add that he divorced her three times and said: "I intended only one," so the Prophet (ﷺ) made him swear an oath to that effect.

This answer is feeble, because whether or not the addition is authentic, the Prophet (ﷺ) judged it as one in a case where the wording was three. No one among the majority holds that it is a matter of equivocation (tawriya). Therefore the hadith is an argument against them without doubt, although its transmission does not reach the level of acceptable soundness.

The sixth proof is what al-Daraqutni transmitted in the account of Ibn ʿUmar divorcing his wife, when the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to take her back until she becomes pure, then menstruates, then becomes pure. In it he added that he divorced her three times. There is no doubt that its meaning is three in one utterance, for if it had been one pronouncement that coincided with the last of three, it would not have been permissible to take her back. The basis of the argument is that when he ordered him to take her back, he counted it against him as only one. This is a very weak proof, because the transmission is weak, and because such an addition is of the kind that the transmitters in the authoritative books would not overlook, such as the Muwatta', Sahih al-Bukhari, and Sahih Muslim. The truth is that only one pronouncement takes effect, and no account is taken of the statement of one who pronounces three.

Muqatil and Dawud al-Zahiri, in one of the reports from him, held that the triple divorce in a single utterance does not take effect as a divorce at all. He argued that the Qur'an mentioned divorce pronounced separately and did not mention the combined form, so it does not apply because it is not mentioned in the Qur'an. If they had argued on the basis that it is forbidden, and what is forbidden is invalid, it would have been closer to the mark, were it not that invalidity does not affect annulments (fusukh). This is an anomalous and false opinion, and the Muslims have agreed on not acting upon it. How could it not take effect as a divorce when the word "divorce" is in it?

Ibn Jubayr, ʿAta', Ibn Dinar, and Jabir ibn Zayd held that the divorce of a virgin (bikr) three times in a single utterance takes effect as one pronouncement, because it occurs before consummation (bina'), unlike the divorce of a woman with whom the marriage has been consummated. It seems the reasoning behind their view is that the sense of "three" in it is a metaphor (kinaya) for irrevocable separation (bayniyya), and a woman divorced before consummation becomes irrevocably separated by a single pronouncement.

The description "another husband" (zawjan ghayrahu) is a warning to husbands against the third pronouncement, for by mentioning the change of husband, the man remembers that his wife will become another's, like the story of the preacher who was admonished by the poet's verse:

"Today her charm and her talk are with you,
but tomorrow her wrist and bracelet will be another's."

He attributed the return (raj'a) to the two separating parties by the form of mufa'ala, because it depends on the wife's consent after the separation. Then he connected that to His statement: ﴿if they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of God﴾ [al-Baqara: 229]. That is, that they will conduct themselves in the future with good companionship; otherwise there is no benefit in renewing the disputes.

"The limits of God" (hudud Allah) are His rulings and laws, and they were likened to limits because the one obligated does not transgress them, so he stops at them.

The literal meaning of hudud is the boundaries between lands and the like, and this was mentioned earlier in His statement: ﴿unless they fear that they will not keep within the limits of God﴾ [al-Baqara: 229]. The "maintaining" (iqama) is a metaphor for guarding the rulings, following the metaphorical extension of "limits" to rulings, as in the saying: "So-and-so has unravelled his thread." As for His statement: ﴿And these are the limits of God; He makes them clear﴾, "making clear" is appropriate to both the literal and figurative meanings, because establishing a dividing boundary involves making it clear to observers.

By "a people who know" is meant those who understand the rulings with an understanding that prepares them to act upon them, and to grasp their benefits, and who do not devise tricks in understanding them.

* * *

﴿And these are the limits of God; He makes them clear to a people who know﴾

The "and" (wa) is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya), and the sentence is interposed between the two sentences, one of which is conjoined to the other. The position of this sentence is like the position of the sentence ﴿These are the limits of God, so do not transgress them﴾ mentioned just before.

[Page 421] The limits of God have been discussed shortly before. Making the limits clear means mentioning them to people in an explicit, detailed, and reasoned manner. His statement "to a people who know" is connected to the verb "He makes them clear." Describing the people as those who know is an explicit way of praising those who perceive the benefits in God's rulings, and it is an allusion to the polytheists who turn away from following Islam.

The insertion of the word "people" (qawm) indicates that the attribute of knowledge is their disposition and innate faculty, as explained previously in the commentary on His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people who reason﴾ [al-Baqara: 164], up to His statement: ﴿are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqara: 164].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 231:

﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, either retain them in kindness or release them in kindness, and do not retain them to harm them so that you transgress. Whoever does that has wronged himself.﴾

This is a conjunction with the clause ﴿If he divorces her, there is no blame upon them both if they return to one another﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]. The verse conjoins one ruling to another and one legislation to another, for the purpose of increasing the admonition to good treatment whether in union or in separation, along with the warning that follows it, which will be explained.

His saying ﴿they reach their term﴾ indicates that the meaning is: when you divorce women with a divorce that has a term (ajal). The word "ajal" here, since it is attached to the pronoun of the divorced women, is understood to be a known term defined by what it is attached to: the term of waiting, which is the 'iddah (waiting period), namely the tarabbus (waiting) mentioned in the previous verse.

"Reaching" (bulugh) of the term means arriving at it. What is meant here is approaching its arrival, according to the consensus of the scholars, because once the term has passed, the choice between retaining and releasing is removed. The word "reach" is sometimes used for approaching and nearing arrival, as an extension, i.e., a metaphor based on the first meaning. In the fifth rule of the eighth chapter of Mughni al-Labib (Ibn Hisham's grammar work), it is stated that the Arabs use the verb to express several matters. The first, which is the most common and familiar, is the occurrence of the act, and this is the basic meaning. The second is its approaching, such as ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term﴾ and ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives, a bequest for their wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 240], meaning they are close to death, since this is the time of bequest.

[p. 422]

The third is its intention, such as ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. The fourth is the ability to do it, such as ﴿a promise upon Us; indeed We are doers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104], meaning capable.

The word "ajal" in the speech of the Arabs refers to the period of time granted to a person for the occurrence of a specific event, and from this is the saying "he set a term for him" and ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾ [al-Qasas: 28].

The term meant here is the end of the period, because his saying "reach" (fa-balagna) indicates an arrival after traveling toward it. The verb "reach" is attributed to the women because they are the ones who await the end of the term in order to come out of the confinement of the 'iddah, although the term applies to men and women together: for the first (the husband) it is a widening of the opportunity for return, and for the latter (the women) it is a definition of their permissibility to marry. The term is attached to the pronoun of the women for this reason.

The discussion of retaining and releasing has passed shortly before. In this interpretation, the ruling is repeated, which was conveyed by His saying ﴿Then retention in kindness or release with good treatment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. To answer this, one cites what al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: the previous verse conveyed the choice between retaining and releasing during the period of the 'iddah, and this verse conveys that choice again at the end of the 'iddah periods, as a reminder of retention and an encouragement to achieve it. This reminder implies a pointer toward encouraging retention, through the reintroduction of the choice after it had already been mentioned. Mentioning release here alongside retention is to show the meaning of choice between two matters, and to use that as a means of pointing to the Shari'ah's desire for retention, by placing it first in mention; for if both matters were not mentioned, the priority which indicates encouragement could not be achieved. In my view, on this interpretation the ruling was repeated in order to build upon it the prohibition of harm and what follows it of warning and admonition. All of this is something that the earlier clauses, which required the interjection, had distanced from being remembered.

His saying ﴿or release them in kindness﴾ restricts release here with "in kindness" (bi-ma'ruf), whereas in his earlier saying ﴿release with good treatment (ihsan)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229] release was restricted by "ihsan," to indicate that the ihsan mentioned there is the very same ma'ruf that is presented for release. Since it was mentioned previously, there is no need here to distinguish between its restriction and the restriction of retention. Or, the restatement of the conditions of retention and release here is in order to build upon it the prohibition of harm, and the one whose harm is feared is in a position far removed from being asked for ihsan, so he is asked for the right, which is the ma'ruf, of which non-harm is a branch, whether in retention or in release, with the harm of each being according to what suits it.

Ibn 'Arafa said: It has been established that ma'ruf is lighter than ihsan. When the command in the other verse came with release of them accompanied by ihsan, it was feared that one might suppose the command to ihsan at their release is obligatory, so he followed it with this to alert that the command is for recommendation, not obligation.

His saying ﴿and do not retain them to harm them﴾ is an explicit statement of the implication of ﴿retain them in kindness﴾, since harm is the opposite of ma'ruf. It seems that the reason for its conjunction, despite it being derived from the command with its opposite, is to disparage by mentioning this opposite, because it is the most common opposite of ma'ruf that husbands who oppose the ruling of retention in kindness intend, together with the emphasis that it contains. Its purpose is to fix the intended meaning in the mind by two paths whose goal is one.

Al-Fakhr said: The reason for conjoining the prohibition to the command by its opposite in the verse is that a command does not require repetition, unlike a prohibition. This distinction between command and prohibition is not accepted, and there is dispute about it in the science of legal theory (usul al-fiqh). But he built it on the premise that the difference between command and prohibition is what the language requires. Furthermore, if we say that ma'ruf in retention, wherever it is realized, negates harm, and wherever ma'ruf is absent, harm is realized, then harm becomes equivalent to the negation of ma'ruf. In that case we may say that the purpose of the conjunction is to emphasize the ruling of retention in kindness by two paths, affirmation and negation, as if it were said: "and do not retain them except in kindness," as in the saying of al-Samaw'al:

Our souls flow along the edges of the swords, and they do not flow except on the swords.

The word "darar" (harm) is a verbal noun of "darra," and the original pattern of this form is to indicate the occurrence of the act from both sides, like "khasama" (to dispute). It is sometimes used to indicate the intensity of the act, like "'afakallah" (may God grant you well-being). The apparent meaning here is that it is used for intensifying harm, as an abhorrence toward one who intends it, describing him as committing an outrage in it. "Darar" is in the accusative, either as a circumstantial accusative (hal) or as an object of purpose.

His saying ﴿so that you transgress﴾ is governed by the preposition "li" (for), and it is not conjoined with "fa" (then), because governance by "li" is the basic form of expressing purpose. He omitted the object of "ta'tadu" (you transgress) so that it includes transgression against them and against the rulings of God the Exalted. Thus the "li" is used in its meanings of purpose and consequence. Transgression against the rulings of God is not a purpose for the Muslims, so it was placed in the position of a purpose, metaphorically, in terms of its occurrence, as a disparagement of the opponents. Thus the letter "li" is used in both its literal and metaphorical sense.

His saying ﴿then he has wronged himself﴾ makes their wronging of their wives a wronging of themselves, because it leads to the disruption of companionship, the disturbance of the state of the household, and the loss of benefits through the commotion of minds in disputes. He also wronged himself by exposing himself to the punishment of God in the Hereafter.

* * *

[p. 424]

﴿And do not take the signs of God in mockery, and remember the favor of God upon you and what He has sent down upon you of the Book and wisdom, by which He instructs you. And fear God and know that God is Knowing of all things.﴾

This prohibition is conjoined to the prohibition in His saying ﴿and do not retain them to harm them so that you transgress﴾, to increase the warning against their conduct in prolonging the 'iddah for the purpose of harm. In this there is mockery of the rulings of God, by which He legislated the right of return, intending the mercy of people; therefore one must beware of making them a mockery. The signs of God are the legislations of return contained in the Qur'an, such as His saying ﴿And divorced women await by themselves three periods﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], up to His saying ﴿And these are the limits of God; He makes them clear to a people who know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230].

"Huzu'" (mockery) with two dammas is the verbal noun of "hazi'a bihi," when one scoffs and plays. Here it is a verbal noun with the meaning of the passive participle, i.e., do not take them as things mocked. Since the addressees are believers, and it is known that they were not among those who mock the signs, it is determined that the mockery intended is its metaphorical meaning, which is contempt and failure to observe, because one who treats an important matter lightly, despite knowing its importance, is counted as mocking and playing with it. This is a warning to people against using the rulings of the Shari'ah to reach what opposes the intent of God and the objectives of His legislation. Among this forbidden maneuvering is what is called "legal stratagems" (hiyal shar'iyyah), in the sense that they operate according to forms that are valid in appearance, according to the requirement of the ruling of the Shari'ah, such as one who gives his wealth to his wife on the night before the year's end in order to escape the obligation of its zakat. Of the attributes furthest from these is the description "Shari'i" (legal).

So the addressees of these verses are warned not to make the ruling of God concerning the 'iddah, whose purpose is to await regret and to remember the goodness of companionship, perhaps the two will bring the divorcer back to retaining his wife, out of eagerness for the continuance of affection and mercy, into something they change and make into a means to increase spite and the worsening of evil and enmity. In the Muwatta' it is related that a man said to Ibn 'Abbas: "I divorced my wife a hundred times." Ibn 'Abbas said to him: "She was separated from you by three, and ninety-seven you took as mockery of the signs of God." He means that he deliberately went to what God had legislated regarding the number of divorces, with the wisdom of anticipating regret the first and second times, and made it a cause of spite and severity, until he believed he had restricted his own return by making it a hundred. Then God the Exalted, after warning them, called them with encouragement, saying:

[p. 425]

﴿And remember the favor of God upon you﴾. He reminded them of what He bestowed upon them after the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance), through Islam, which He called a favor, as He called it in His saying ﴿And remember the favor of God upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became by His favor brothers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103]. Just as He bestowed on you the release from that misguidance, do not return to it by making covenants after Islam. His saying ﴿and what He has sent down upon you of the Book and wisdom﴾ is conjoined to "favor," and the clause ﴿by which He instructs you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal); it is permissible to make it an inceptive (mubtada'), with the clause ﴿He instructs you﴾ as its predicate. "The Book" is the Qur'an. "Wisdom" is the knowledge derived from the Shari'ah, which is the lesson drawn from the conditions of past nations and the understanding of the benefits of the religion and the secrets of the Shari'ah, as God the Exalted said, after He had explained the ruling on wine and gambling: ﴿Thus God makes clear to you the signs, that you may reflect﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. The meaning of the sending down of wisdom is that it was obtained from the signs of the Qur'an, as we have mentioned, and from indications of the causes (illal), and from what is acquired during the practice of the religion; all of this is sent down from God the Exalted by revelation to the Messenger (ﷺ). Whoever interprets "wisdom" as the Sunnah has interpreted it with one of its indications. "Mawi'zah" and "wa'z" mean advice and reminder with what softens hearts and warns the one admonished.

His saying ﴿And fear God and know that God is Knowing of all things﴾ is a reminder of God-consciousness (taqwa) and of observing their knowledge that God is Knowing of all things, treating them, at the time of their opposing the objectives of the Shari'ah by their actions, as one who is ignorant that God is Knowing. For the Knower nothing is hidden, and if He knows their opposition, nothing prevents His punishment from reaching them, because this Knower is also Powerful.

[Page 426]

The purpose of this verse is to address the guardians (awliya') of women, forbidding them to prevent the women from returning to their husbands. This follows the command to those who divorce to retain them honorably (bi-ma'ruf), and the encouragement to do so. God knew that when a woman sees the desire of the man she once lived with and was intimate with, she will quickly match his desire with her own, for a woman is quick to be moved and her heart is responsive. So if an obstacle arises, it comes from the guardians. For this reason God did not mention encouraging women to agree to return to their husbands, and He forbade the guardians from preventing them.

It is known that among the guardians in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period) and its neighboring periods, there was a sense of pride (al-anafah) about their in-laws when discord arose between them and their wards. They sometimes regarded divorce as a slight against the woman's guardians and as a sign of indifference toward them. Zeal (al-hamiyyah) led them to seek revenge against them when they saw remorse and a desire to return on their part. It has been narrated in the Sahih (the authentic collection) that al-Baddah ibn 'Asim al-Ansari divorced his wife Jumayl (diminutive form), and it was also said Jumal, and it was said Jamilah, the daughter of Ma'qil ibn Yasar. When her waiting period ('iddah) ended, he wanted to take her back. Her father Ma'qil ibn Yasar said to him: "You divorced her with a divorce that allowed you to return, then you left her until her waiting period ended. Then when she was proposed to me, you came to me proposing to her along with the other suitors. By God, I will never marry her to you." Then this verse was revealed. Ma'qil said: "I made expiation for my oath and gave her back to him." Al-Wahidi said: It was revealed concerning Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who had a paternal cousin whose husband divorced her and her waiting period ended. Then he came wanting to take her back, and she was willing, but Jabir prevented him from it, and so the verse was revealed.

The meaning of "ajalahunna" (their term) here is the waiting period, and this supports that this is the meaning of its counterpart in the preceding verse. It has been related from al-Shafi'i that the context of the two statements indicates a difference between the two uses of "balagha" (reaching): in the first verse it means approaching the end of the term, while here it means the end of the term having been reached.

So the clause "wa-idha tallaqtumu al-nisa'" (and when you divorce women) is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the verse ﴿وإذا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّساءَ فَبَلَغْنَ أجَلَهُنَّ فَأمْسِكُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231].

The address in "tallaqtum" (you divorced) and "ta'dulūhunna" (you prevent them) should be understood as directed at one single category without a shift in the addressee. Thus it is directed at all Muslims, because each one is suited to either divorcing, if he is a husband, or preventing, if he is a guardian. The indication for this is clear, and it is hardly obscure in their usage. Since the subject of one of the two verbs is not the subject of the other, as divorce cannot come from one who prevents, nor the reverse, each group takes from the address what is appropriate to them. Thus the meaning of "tallaqtum" is "you pronounced divorce," and they are the husbands; and the meaning of "fa-la ta'dulūhunna" is the prohibition against the occurrence of prevention, and they are the guardians of the women. In al-Kashshaf, the address is made to people in general, meaning: if divorce occurs among you and the divorced women reach their term, then let no prevention occur from you. The reason for this interpretation, he says, is: "because if prevention occurs among them while they are content, they are in the position of those who prevent."

"Al-'adl" (prevention) means refusal, confinement, and not allowing movement. From it comes "'addalat al-mar'ah" (the woman had a difficult childbirth) when her delivery is hard, and "'addalat al-dajājah" (the hen was blocked) when her egg is lodged and does not come out. "Mu'adalah" in speech means the meaning being held back so that it does not appear in the words, which is complexity. It became common in Arabic usage regarding a guardian preventing his ward from marriage. In the Shari'ah, it is prevention without a valid reason. Thus a father is not considered a preventer for rejecting one or two suitable matches, but someone other than the father is considered a preventer for rejecting one suitable match.

The attribution of marriage (nikah) to women here is because they are the ones prevented from it. "Azwājahunna" (their husbands) means those who request return after the end of the waiting period. He called them husbands metaphorically, based on what they had been, because of the closeness of that situation, and to indicate that prevention is an injustice, for they were husbands to them before, so they have more right to return to them.

His statement ﴿إذا تَراضَوْا بَيْنَهم بِالمَعْرُوفِ﴾ (when they agree among themselves in an honorable way) is a condition for the prohibition, because when the guardian knows that the spouses do not agree, and sees that the return will lead to corruption and harm, he has the right to prevent his ward, out of sincere counsel for her. In this condition there is a hint of the reason for the prohibition: that the guardian does not have the right to prevent her when the spouses agree to resume living together, since the guardian is not more knowing of her inclination than she is. This is like the well-known proverb: "The two disputants are content, but the judge is not content." The verse also indicates that the guardianship of a woman in marriage is recognized, based on the usual circumstances of that time, because the woman's side is weak, open to being desired, and protected from being humiliated. So it is not fitting to leave her to handle such a matter herself, since that contradicts her dignity and weakness. Men may disregard her rights out of eagerness for their own benefits, while she is too weak to oppose them.

The point of the indication is that God pointed to two rights: the right of the guardian, through the prohibition against prevention, since if the matter were not in his hand, He would not have forbidden him from preventing it. It cannot be said that He forbade the use of something that is not his right, because if that were the case, prohibiting transgression and aggression would have been sufficient, and the expression "ma yakūnu lakum" (what is not for you) or similar would have been used. And the right of the woman, in her consent. For this reason, God attributed the marriage to the pronoun of the women, and did not say: "an tunkihūhunna azwājahunna" (that you marry them to their husbands). This is the position of Malik, al-Shafi'i, and the majority of the jurists of Islam. Abu Hanifah, according to what is well-known from him, was an exception, for he did not stipulate guardianship in marriage. Al-Jassas argued for him that God attributed marriage here to women, but this is a distant argument from Arab usage in their saying "nakahat al-mar'ah" (the woman married), for it means "tazawwajat" (she got married) without specifying the manner of that marriage. There is no disagreement that the woman's consent to the husband is the contract called marriage. The disagreement is only about requiring the guardian to directly conduct it without compulsion, and this attribution of marriage to them does not contradict that. As for the guardianship of compulsion (wilayat al-ijbar), it is not the purpose of this verse, because it addresses the matter of the unmarried women (al-ayama, i.e., women without a spouse), and there is no compulsion over an unmarried woman by the consensus of scholars.

His statement ﴿ذَلِكَ يُوعَظُ بِهِ﴾ (with this you are admonished) is a reference to the ruling of the prohibition against prevention. The use of the singular "kaf" (the "ka" in "dhālika") with the demonstrative, although the addressees are a group, is in consideration of the forgetting of its original form as a second-person address, as it has been used to mean only the distance of what is pointed to. So its singular form in demonstratives is the original, while its plural form in his statement ﴿ذَلِكم أزْكى لَكم﴾ (that is purer for you and more pure) is a renewal of its original form.

The meaning of "azka" and "atharu" is that it is more conducive to honor (al-'irdh) and closer to good. So "azka" indicates growth and abundance. They used to prevent their wards out of zeal and to preserve manliness from anything that carries a trace of humiliation. So God informed them that not preventing is more conducive to honor, because it involves striving to preserve affection between families that have become related by marriage and kinship. If prevention is a refusal to accept injustice, then permitting the women to return is forbearance, pardon, and conciliation of the situation, and that is more beneficial than refusing injustice.

As for his statement "atharu" (more pure), it means "anzah" (more free from defilement), that is, it is more effective in cutting the causes of enmity, rancor, and hatred, unlike prevention, which you intended for cutting off the return to dispute. What harm does a dispute do in a short time that is followed by reconciliation, compared to the harm of lingering rancor, entrenched enmities, and burning hearts?

You may also take "azka" in the first meaning, looking at the affairs of this world, and "atharu" in a meaning that includes safety from sins in the Hereafter, so that "atharu" is the object of comparison, coming in the comparative form to pair it with "azka."

His statement ﴿واللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ وأنْتُمْ لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (God knows and you do not know) is a concluding phrase (tadhyil), and a removal of their astonishment when they received this ruling, since it contradicted their old customs and what they believed to be beneficial, righteous, and a means of preserving their honor. So God taught them that what He commanded and forbade them is the truth, because God knows what is beneficial, while they know only the apparent. The object of "ya'lamu" (knows) is omitted, meaning: God knows what contains the perfection of your purification and cleanliness, and you do not know that.

[Page 429]

﴿And mothers shall suckle their children for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing. And upon the father of the child is their provision and their clothing, according to what is fair. No soul is burdened except according to its capacity. No mother shall be harmed because of her child, nor a father because of his child. And upon the heir is the like of that. But if they both wish weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them. And if you wish to seek a wet-nurse for your children, there is no blame upon you, provided you hand over what you have given, according to what is fair. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

This is a transition from the rulings on divorce and separation (bayunah, the irrevocable severing of the marital bond). When He prohibited preventing (al-'adl, the wali or husband obstructing a divorced woman from remarrying), and some divorced women had children who were still nursing, and it would be difficult for them to remarry while nursing, since that may harm the children and reduce the desire of husbands for them, this situation became a cause of disagreement between fathers and mothers. Therefore it was fitting to address the matter of how to decide between them in this. The matter of nursing is important, because through it the offspring live, and because regulating it is among the most important affairs of family law. Know that extracting the meanings of this verse is among the most complex matters faced by the exegetes (mufassirun).

The clause ﴿And mothers shall suckle﴾ is joined (ma'tuf) to the clause ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 232], and the connection is clear. The word ﴿mothers﴾ is general, since it is a plural definite noun with the article "al-", but here it is intended to mean specifically the divorced mothers, by the context of the preceding verses, namely His saying: ﴿Divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]. For this reason this clause is connected by conjunction, to indicate the unity of the context. So His saying "and the mothers" means "and the mothers among them," i.e., among the divorced women whose information was given in the preceding verses, that is, the divorced women who have children in the age of nursing. The evidence for this specification is that disagreement over the duration of nursing arises between the father and the mother only after separation, and does not arise during the marriage. It is a well-known custom among the Arabs and most nations that mothers nurse their children during the marriage, and they do not refuse to do so except for the reason of seeking to remarry a new husband after the separation from the child's father, since a nursing woman is not desired by husbands, because she is occupied with her nursing child away from her husband in many circumstances.

[Page 430]

The clause ﴿shall suckle﴾ is a declarative form (khabar) intended as legislation and the establishment of a right of entitlement. It does not carry the meaning of a command to mothers or an obligation upon them, because it is mentioned after the rulings concerning divorced women, and because it is followed by His saying ﴿But if you wish to seek﴾, where the pronoun includes both fathers and mothers, by way of dominance of the masculine (taghlib), as will come. So there is no indication in the verse that nursing the child is obligatory upon its mother, but it indicates that this is her right. This was explicitly stated in Surat al-Talaq with His saying ﴿And if you disagree, another woman will nurse for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 6]. Also, He follows it with His saying ﴿And upon the father of the child is their provision and their clothing according to what is fair﴾, and that is the wage of nursing, while a wife in marriage has no maintenance and clothing for the sake of nursing, but for the sake of the marriage.

His saying ﴿their children﴾ states the object explicitly, although it is known, to indicate the mothers' greater right to it and to encourage them to it, because in His saying "their children" there is a reminder to them of the motive of tenderness and compassion. According to this interpretation, which is the apparent meaning of the verse and what the majority of the early scholars (al-salaf) held, the verse is revealed only to explain the nursing of divorced women of their children. So if a divorced woman wishes to nurse her child, she has the better right to it, whether she does so without payment or asks for the wage of her equivalent. For this reason the well-known position of Malik is that if the father finds someone other than the mother to nurse for him without payment, or for less than the usual wage, he is not to be obeyed in that, as we will explain. Among the scholars are those who interpreted "the mothers" in a general sense, whether they are in marriage or after divorce, as in al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi. It appears from the words of Ibn al-Furs in Ahkam al-Qur'an that this is the position of Malik. Ibn Rushd said in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil: the saying of the Exalted ﴿And mothers shall suckle their children﴾ is to be understood in its generality, both for the wife in marriage and for the divorced woman when the father is in difficulty. He did not attribute this to Malik. For this reason Ibn 'Atiyya said: His saying "shall suckle" is a declarative form whose meaning is a command, obligatory for some mothers and recommended and optional for others. al-Baydawi followed him, and in this there is the use of the imperative form for the common element, which is the general demand, and there is no need for it. The apparent position is that the ruling on a mother's nursing her child during marriage is derived from other than this verse. What indicates that the intended mothers are not those in marriage is His saying ﴿And upon the father of the child is their provision﴾ and so on, since those in marriage are entitled to maintenance and clothing by origin.

The word ḥawl (year) in the speech of the Arabs means "year." It is derived from the turning of the cycle of the moon or the sun in its orbit from a fixed starting point until it returns to the same position from which it began, and that period between the starting point and the return is called a ḥawl.

[Page 431]

The Arab year is lunar, and Islam confirmed this. The description of "two years" as "complete" is an emphasis to remove the assumption that the intended meaning is one year and part of a second, because the use of the dual and plural forms for times and ages to refer to part of what is denoted is a common usage among the Arabs. They say: "he is the son of two years," meaning a year and part of the second year, as has passed in His saying "the Hajj is in known months" [al-Baqarah: 197].

His saying ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾. al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: it is an explanation of who the ruling is addressed to, like the saying "hayta laka" (come, for you), where "laka" explains the one to whom it is addressed. That is, this ruling is for whoever wishes to complete the nursing. It is a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, as he indicated, by estimating "this ruling is for whoever wishes." al-Taftazani said: this subject may sometimes be stated explicitly in some constructions, like His saying ﴿That is for whoever fears sin among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. The referent of "man" (whoever) here is the one who is concerned with this, namely the father, the mother, and whoever stands in their place, such as the guardian of the infant and his nurse. The meaning is that this ruling is due to whoever wishes to complete the nursing while the other refuses. If both wish not to complete the nursing, that is known from His saying ﴿But if they both wish weaning﴾ and so on.

God made the nursing two years, out of regard for these being the maximum period in which the child needs nursing when some condition arises that requires extended nursing. As for after the two years, there is nothing in his growth that is suitable for nursing any longer. Since the disagreement of the two parents over the duration of nursing arises only from a difference in judgment about the child's constitutional need for additional nursing, God made the decision rest with the one who calls for the extension, as a precaution for the preservation of the child. The nations, in ages of little experience and the absence of physicians, did not know what could replace nursing for the child, since when they weaned him they gave him food; so the constitutions of some children needed prolonged nursing, because they could not digest food. These are variable conditions. In our age physicians have come to substitute artificial feeding for some infants, yet they all agree that nothing is better for the child than his mother's milk, unless she has some defect, or the milk lacks the components by which the body's parts are nourished. Artificial feeding also requires great caution to keep the milk free from spoilage in its consistency and its container. The lands of the Arabs are very hot for most of the year, and they did not know how to keep their food from spoiling by storage, so weaning children at the year or near it might cause harm to the nursing infants,

[Page 432]

and temperaments also have an effect in this. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the determination by two years applies to the child who remains in his mother's womb for six months.
