If he remains seven months, his nursing is twenty-three months, and so on, with each extra month in the womb reducing one month from the period of nursing, until the total of the period of pregnancy and nursing is thirty months, by His saying ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]. In this opinion there is an inclination toward taking into account the conditions of temperaments, because the more the period in the womb is reduced, the more the period of maturing of his temperament is reduced.

The majority are against this, and hold that the two years are the limit for the nursing of every infant. They took from the verse that the nursing that counts is that which occurs within the two years, and that what is after them is not needed, and therefore a request for it is not granted.

He referred to the father as "the one to whom the child is born" (al-mawlud lahu), indicating that he is the one most worthy of this ruling, because the benefits of the child accrue to him, and the child is attributed to him and proud of him in the tribe, according to the convention of nations. He is therefore the most entitled to supporting him and providing the means of that. Provision (rizq) means maintenance; clothing (kiswa) means garments; and "what is fair" (al-ma'ruf) means what the people of their kind are accustomed to, and what does not ruin the father.

What is meant here by provision and clothing is what the nursing mother takes as a wage for her nursing, of food and clothing, because they used to give nursing women clothing and maintenance, and most of their hiring was like that. Most Arab tribes were not people of gold and silver. Rather they dealt in goods, and hired workers did not desire the dirham or the dinar, but sought the sufficiency of their necessities, which are food and clothing. For this reason God referred the estimation of these two to what is customary among them according to people's ranks and means. He followed this with His saying ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾. The sentences ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾ up to His saying ﴿nor a father because of his child﴾ are parenthetical insertions between the clause ﴿And upon the father of the child﴾ and the clause ﴿And upon the heir﴾. So the placement of the clause ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾ is a justification for His saying "according to what is fair," and the placement of the clause ﴿No mother shall be harmed because of her child﴾ to its end is likewise in the position of justification. It is a parenthetical statement that conveys great principles for legislation and the order of society.

Taklif (burdening, obligation) is on the pattern taf'il, meaning "making someone have hardship," and kulfa is hardship, and takalluf is exposing oneself to what involves hardship. Taklif is also used to mean commanding an act that involves hardship, and this is a new technical usage in the Sharia.

Wus' (capacity), with three vowelings of the waw, means ability. Its root is from "wasi'a al-inā' al-shay'" when the vessel contains the thing and nothing of it remains, and it is the opposite of "daqa 'anhu" (it was too narrow for it). Wus' is what the thing can contain, so it has the meaning of a passive participle (maf'ul). Its origin is metaphorical,

[Page 433]

because al-Zamakhshari in al-Asas mentioned this meaning in the figurative sense. It is as if they likened the soul's bearing of a laborious task to the expansion of a container for what it holds, since they did not need to convey that except when the observer might think it cannot contain it. From here it was used metaphorically for the hardship that reaches the limit of ability.

So if wus is with a kasra on the waw, it is a noun in the sense of a passive participle, like dhibh (what is slaughtered). If it is with a damma, it is a verbal noun like sulh and bur' that has become in meaning a passive participle. If it is with a fatha, it is likewise a verbal noun with the meaning of a passive participle, like khalq and dars. Burdening beyond capacity is negated in the Sharia.

وبُنِيَ فعلُ ﴿تُكَلَّفُ﴾ للنائب (المفعول الذي لم يُسمَّ فاعله) ليُحذَفَ الفاعل، فيُفيد حذفُه عمومَ الفاعلين، كما يُفيد وقوعُ ﴿نَفْسٌ﴾، وهي نكرة في سياق النفي، عمومَ المفعول الأول لفعل ﴿تُكَلَّفُ﴾، وهو الأنفسُ المُكلَّفة. وكما يُفيد حذفُ المستثنى في قوله ﴿إلّا وُسْعَها﴾ عمومَ المفعول الثاني لفعل ﴿تُكَلَّفُ﴾، وهو الأحكامُ المُكلَّفُ بها، أي: لا يُكلِّف أحدٌ نفسًا إلا وُسعَها. وذلك تشريعٌ من الله للأمة بأن ليس لأحدٍ أن يُكلِّف أحدًا إلا بما يستطيعه. وذلك أيضًا وعدٌ من الله بأنه لا يُكلِّف في التشريع الإسلامي إلا بما يُستطاع، في العامّة والخاصّة. فقد قال في آيات خاتمة هذه السورة: ﴿لا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إلّا وُسْعَها﴾ [البقرة: ٢٨٦].

والآية تدل على عدم وقوع التكليف بما لا يُطاق في شريعة الإسلام، وسيأتي تفصيل هذه المسألة عند قوله تعالى ﴿لا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إلّا وُسْعَها﴾ [البقرة: ٢٨٦] في آخر السورة.

وجملة ﴿لا تُضارَّ والِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِها﴾ اعتراضٌ ثانٍ (جملة معترضة بين الأحكام)، ولم تُعطَف على التي قبلها تنبيهًا على أنها مقصودةٌ لذاتها، فإنها تشريعٌ مستقلّ، وليس فيها معنى التعليل الذي في الجملة قبلها، بل هي كالتفريع على جملة ﴿لا تُكَلَّفُ نَفْسٌ إلّا وُسْعَها﴾؛ لأن إدخال الضرر على أحدٍ، بسبب ما هو بَضعةٌ منه، يكاد يخرج عن طاقة الإنسان؛ لأن الضِّرار تضيق عنه الطاقة، وكونُه بسبب مَن يُتَرقَّب منه أن يكون سببَ نفعٍ أشدُّ ألمًا على النفس، فكان ضُرُّه أشدَّ.

ولذلك اختير لفظ ﴿الوالِدَةِ﴾ هنا دون ﴿الأُمِّ﴾، كما تقدّم في قوله ﴿يُرْضِعْنَ أوْلادَهُنَّ﴾. وكذلك القول في ﴿ولا مَوْلُودٌ بِوَلَدِهِ﴾. وهذا الحكم عامٌّ في جميع الأحوال من فراقٍ أو دوامِ عِصمة، فهو كالتذييل (الجملة الختامية المؤكِّدة)، وهو نهيٌ لهما عن أن يُكلِّف أحدُهما الآخرَ ما هو فوق طاقته، ويستغلَّ ما يعلمه من شفقة الآخر على ولده فيفترص ذلك لإحراجه والإشقاق عليه.

[صفحة ٤٣٤]

وفي المُدوَّنة (المدونة الكبرى لسحنون، وهي من كتب المالكية): عن ابن وهب عن الليث عن خالد بن يزيد عن زيد بن أسلم في قوله تعالى ﴿لا تُضارَّ والِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِها﴾ الآية: يقول: ليس لها أن تُلقيَ ولدها عليه ولا يَجد مَن يُرضعه، وليس له أن ينتزع منها ولدها وهي تُحبّ أن تُرضعه. وهو يُؤيّد ما ذكرناه.

وقيل: الباء في قوله ﴿بِوَلَدِها﴾ و﴿بِوَلَدِهِ﴾ باءُ الإلصاق، وهي للتعدية لفعل ﴿تُضارُّ﴾، فيكون مدخولُ الباء مفعولًا في المعنى لفعل ﴿تُضارُّ﴾، وهو مسلوب المفاعلة (أي إن صيغة المفاعلة فيه لا يُقصد بها المشاركة)، مرادٌ منه أصلُ الضرّ، فيصير المعنى: لا تَضُرُّ الوالدةُ ولدَها ولا المولودُ له ولدَه، أي لا يكن أحدُ الأبوين بتعنُّته وتحريجه سببًا في إلحاق الضرر بولده، أي سببًا في إلجاء الآخر، إلا الامتناعَ مما يُعين على إرضاع الأم ولدَها، فيكون في استرضاع غير الأم تعريضُ المولود إلى الضرر، ونحوُ هذا من أنواع التفريط.

وقرأ الجمهور: ﴿لا تُضارَّ﴾ بفتح الراء مشددةً، على أن ﴿لا﴾ حرفُ نهيٍ، و﴿تُضارَّ﴾ مجزومٌ بـ﴿لا﴾ الناهية، والفتحةُ للتخلّص من التقاء الساكنين الذي نشأ عن تسكين الراء الأولى ليتأتّى الإدغام، وتسكينُ الراء الثانية للجزم، وحُرّك بالفتحة لأنها أخفّ الحركات. وقرأ ابنُ كثير وأبو عمرو ﴿لا تُضارُّ﴾ برفع الراء، على أن ﴿لا﴾ حرفُ نفيٍ، والكلامُ خبرٌ في معنى النهي. وكِلتا القراءتين يجوز أن تكون على نيّة بناء الفعل للفاعل: ﴿لا تُضارِرْ﴾ بكسر الراء الأولى، وبنائه للنائب بتقدير فتح الراء الأولى. وقرأه أبو جعفر بسكون الراء مخففةً مع إشباع المدّ، كذا نُقل عنه في كتب القراءات، والظاهر أنه جعله من ﴿ضارَ يَضِيرُ﴾ لا من ﴿ضارَّ﴾ المضاعف. ووقع في الكشّاف أنه قرأ بالسكون مع التشديد على نيّة الوقف، أي إجراءً للوصل مجرى الوقف، ولذلك اغتُفر التقاء الساكنين.

وقوله ﴿وعَلى الوارِثِ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ﴾ معطوفٌ على قوله ﴿وعَلى المَوْلُودِ لَهُ رِزْقُهُنَّ﴾، وليس معطوفًا على جملة ﴿لا تُضارُّ والِدَةٌ﴾؛ لأن جملة ﴿لا تُضارُّ﴾ معترضةٌ، فإنها جاءت على الأسلوب الذي جاءت عليه جملة ﴿لا تُكَلَّفُ نَفْسٌ إلّا وُسْعَها﴾ التي هي معترضةٌ بين الأحكام لا محالة، لوقوعها موقعَ الاستئناف من قوله ﴿بِالمَعْرُوفِ﴾. ولمّا جاءت جملة ﴿لا تُضارُّ﴾ بدون عطف عَلِمْنا أنها استئنافٌ ثانٍ مما قبله، ثم وقع الرجوعُ إلى بيان الأحكام بطريق العطف، ولو كان المرادُ العطفَ على المستأنفات المعترضات لجيء بالجملة الثالثة بطريق الاستئناف.

وحقيقةُ الوارث هو مَن يصير إليه مالُ الميت بعد الموت بحقّ الإرث. والإشارةُ بقوله ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ إلى الحكم المتقدّم، وهو الرزق والكسوة، بقرينة دخول ﴿عَلى﴾ عليه، الدالّةِ على أنه عديلٌ لقوله ﴿وعَلى المَوْلُودِ لَهُ رِزْقُهُنَّ﴾. وجوّز أن يكون ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ إشارةً إلى النهي عن الإضرار المستفاد

[صفحة ٤٣٥]

من قوله ﴿لا تُضارَّ والِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِها﴾ كما سيأتي، وهو بعيدٌ عن الاستعمال؛ لأنه لمّا كان الفاعل محذوفًا، وحكمُ الفعل في سياق النهي كما هو في سياق النفي، عُلم أن جميعَ الإضرار منهيٌّ عنه أيًّا ما كان فاعلُه. على أن الإضرار منهيٌّ عنه، فلا يحسن التعبير عنه بلفظ ﴿عَلى﴾ الذي هو من صيغ الإلزام والإيجاب. على أن ظاهر المَثَل إنما ينصرف لمماثلة الذوات، وهي النفقة والكسوة، لا لمماثلة الحكم، وهو التحريم.

وقد عُلم من تسمية المفروض عليه الإنفاقُ والكسوةُ أن الذي كان ذلك عليه مات، وهذا إيجاز. والمعنى: فإن مات المولودُ له، فعلى وارثه مثلُ ما كان عليه، فإن ﴿عَلى﴾ الواقعةَ بعد حرف العطف هنا ظاهرةٌ في أنها مثلُ ﴿عَلى﴾ التي في المعطوف عليه.

فالظاهر أن المرادَ وارثُ الأب، وتكون ﴿ال﴾ عوضًا عن المضاف، كما هو الشأن في دخول ﴿ال﴾ على اسمٍ غيرِ معهودٍ ولا مقصودٍ جنسُه، وكان ذلك الاسمُ مذكورًا بعد اسمٍ يصلح لأن يُضاف إليه، كما قال تعالى ﴿لَئِنْ لَمْ يَنْتَهِ لَنَسْفَعًا بِالنّاصِيَةِ﴾ [العلق: ١٥]، وكما قال ﴿وأمّا مَن خافَ مَقامَ رَبِّهِ ونَهى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الهَوى فَإنَّ الجَنَّةَ هي المَأْوى﴾ [النازعات: ٤٠]، أي: نهى نفسَه؛ فإن الجنة هي مأواه، وكقول إحدى نساء حديث أم زرع: «زوجي: المَسُّ أرنبٌ، والريحُ ريحُ زرنبٍ». ولم يسمِّه اللهُ تعالى وارثًا إلا لأنه وارثٌ بالفعل، لا مَن يصلح لأن يكون وارثًا على تقدير موتِ غيرِه؛ لأن اسمَ الفاعل إنما يُطلق على الحال ما لم تقم قرينةٌ على خلافه. فما قال ﴿وعَلى الوارِثِ﴾ إلا لأن الكلامَ على الحقّ تعليقٌ بهذا الشخص في تركة الميت، وإلا لقال: وعلى الأقارب أو الأولياء مثلُ ذلك. على أنه يكون كلامًا تأكيدًا حينئذٍ؛ لأن تحريم الإضرار المذكور قبله لم يُذكر له متعلِّقٌ خاصّ؛ فإن فاعل ﴿تُضارَّ﴾ محذوف. والنهيُ دالٌّ على منعِ كلِّ إضرارٍ يحصل للوالدة، فما فائدةُ إعادة تحريم ذلك على الوارث كما قدّمناه آنفًا؟

واتفق علماءُ الإسلام على أن ظاهر الآية غيرُ مرادٍ؛ إذ لا قائل بوجوب نفقة المرضع على وارث الأب، سواءٌ كان إيجابُها على الوارث في المال الموروث، بأن يكون مبدأةً على المواريث، للإجماع على أنه لا يُبدأ إلا بالتجهيز ثم الدَّين ثم الوصية، ولأن الرضيعَ له حظُّه في المال الموروث، وهو إذا صار ذا مالٍ لم تجب نفقتُه على غيره، أم كان إيجابُها على الوارث لو لم يَسَعْها المالُ الموروث، فيكمل من يده. ولذلك طرقوا في هذا باب التأويل، إما تأويلُ معنى الوارث، وإما تأويلُ مرجع الإشارة، وإما كليهما. فقال الجمهور: المرادُ وارثُ الطفل، أي مَن لو مات

[صفحة ٤٣٦]

الطفلُ لورثه هو. رُوي عن عمرَ بن الخطّاب وقتادةَ والسُّدّي والحسنِ ومجاهدٍ وعطاءٍ وإسحاقَ وابنِ أبي ليلى وأبي حنيفةَ وأحمدَ بن حنبل، فيتقرر بالآية أن النفقة واجبةٌ على قرابة الرضيع، وهم بالضرورة قرابةُ أبيه، أي إذا مات أبوه ولم يترك مالًا: تجب نفقةُ الرضيع على الأقارب، على حسب قربهم في الإرث. ويجري ذلك على الخلاف في توريث ذي الرحم المحرَّم. فهؤلاء يرَوْن حقًّا على القرابة إنفاقَ العاجز في مالهم، كما أنهم يرثونه إذا ترك مالًا، فهو من المواساة الواجبة مثلِ الدية. وقال الضحّاك وقبيصةُ بن ذؤيب وبشيرُ بن نصرٍ قاضي عمرَ بن عبد العزيز: المرادُ وارثُ الأب، وأُريد به نفسُ الرضيع. فالمعنى: أنه إذا مات أبوه وترك مالًا، فنفقتُه من إرثه. ويتّجه على هذا أن يُقال: ما وجهُ العدولِ عن التعبير بالولد إلى التعبير بالوارث؟ فنجيب بأنه للإيماء إلى أن الأب إنما وجبت عليه نفقةُ الرضيع لعدم مالٍ للرضيع، فلهذا لمّا اكتسب مالًا وجب عليه في ماله؛ لأن غالبَ أحوال الصغار ألّا تكون لهم أموالٌ مكتسبة سوى الميراث. وهذا تأويلٌ بعيد؛ لأن الآية تكون قد تركت حكمَ مَن لا مالَ له. وقيل: أُريد بالوارث المعنى المجازيّ، وهو الذي يبقى بعد انعدام غيره، كما في قوله تعالى ﴿ونَحْنُ الوارِثُونَ﴾، يعني به أمَّ الرضيع. قاله سفيانُ، فتكون النفقة على الأم. قال التفتازاني في شرح الكشّاف: وهذا قَلِقٌ في هذا المقام، إذ ليس لقولنا: فالنفقةُ على الأب، وعلى مَن بقي من الأب والأم، معنًى يُعتدّ به. يعني أن إرادة الباقي تشمل صورةَ ما إذا كان الباقي الأبَ، ولا معنى لعطفه على نفسه بهذا الاعتبار.

وفي المُدوَّنة عن زيد بن أسلم وربيعةَ: أن الوارث هو وليُّ الرضيع، عليه مثلُ ما على الأب من عدم المضارّة. هذا كلُّه على أن الآية محكمةٌ لا منسوخةٌ، وأن المشارَ إليه بقوله ﴿مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ﴾ هو الرزق والكسوة. وقال جماعةٌ: الإشارة بقوله ﴿مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ﴾ راجعةٌ إلى النهي عن المضارّة. قال ابن عطية: وهو لمالكٍ وجميعِ أصحابه والشعبيِّ والزهريِّ والضحاكِ. اهـ.

وفي المدونة في ترجمة ما جاء فيمن تلزمه النفقة، من كتاب إرخاء الستور، عن ابن القاسم قال مالك: ﴿وعَلى الوارِثِ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ﴾ أي: ألّا يُضارّ. واختاره ابنُ العربي بأنه الأصل. فقال القرطبي: يعني في الرجوع إلى أقرب مذكورٍ. ورجّحه ابنُ عطية بأن الأمة أجمعت على ألّا يُضارّ الوارث. واختلفوا: هل عليه رزقٌ وكسوة؟ اهـ. يعني مَوْرِدَ الآيةِ بما هو مُجمَعٌ على حكمه، ويترك ما فيه الخلاف، وهنالك تأويلٌ بأنها منسوخةٌ. ورواه أسدُ بن الفرات عن ابن القاسم

[صفحة ٤٣٧]

عن مالكٍ قال: وقولُ الله عزّ وجلّ ﴿وعَلى الوارِثِ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ﴾ هو منسوخٌ. فقال النحّاس: وما علمتُ أحدًا من أصحاب مالكٍ بيّن ما الناسخ، والذي يبيّنه أن يكون الناسخ لها عند مالك أنه لمّا أوجب الله للمتوفّى عنها زوجُها نفقةَ حولٍ، والسكنى من مال المتوفّى، ثم نسخ ذلك نسخٌ أيضًا عن الوارث، يريد أن الله لمّا نسخ وجوبَ ذلك في تركة الميت، نسخ كلَّ حقٍّ في التركة بعد الميراث، فيكون الناسخ هو الميراث، فإنه نسخ كلَّ حقٍّ في المال على أولياء الميت.

Here is the translation of the passage:

In my view, the interpretation found in the Mudawwana of Sahnun is far-fetched, for the reason mentioned just above, and what Malik stated in the narration of Asad ibn al-Furat from Ibn al-Qasim is the correct interpretation. The abrogation (naskh) here applies to its apparent meaning, and the abrogating ruling is the consensus of the community (ijma') that no one has a right to the property of the deceased after his preparation for burial (jihaz), the settlement of his debts, and the execution of his bequest, except for the inheritance. By this, it abrogated everything that was commanded to be paid from the property of the deceased, such as the bequest in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest for the parents and relatives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], and the bequest of housing and maintenance for the wife in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who die among you and leave wives - a bequest for their wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 240]. The ruling of this verse was also abrogated with respect to it, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has given every person with a right his right, so there is no bequest to an heir." This applies if the heir in the verse is understood as the heir of the deceased, meaning that this is an obligation upon all the heirs, whoever they are, in the sense that it is the basis of inheritance. If the heir is understood as one who would inherit from the deceased had the deceased left property, that is, his relative, in the sense that it is incumbent upon him to maintain the son of his relative, then that is abrogated by the establishment of the public treasury (bayt al-mal). This is because this verse legislated this ruling at a time of the weakness of the Muslims, to sustain the order of their affairs through the upbringing of the children of their poor, and the most entitled of the Muslims to this were those closest to the child. Just as he would inherit from his relative if he left property and no son, so likewise he was to be held responsible for it by proof, as was the custom of the tribe in the Jahiliyya, in taking in their orphans and paying their blood-money. When Islam became mighty and the community of Muslims had wealth, it became a right upon the collective body of Muslims to undertake the upbringing of the children of their poor. In the authentic hadith: "Whoever leaves behind a burden (kall) or dependents (dayya'), then it is upon me; and whoever leaves property, then it goes to his heir." There is no difference between feeding the poor and nursing him, and it is nothing but maintenance, and the public treasury was established for precisely this.

As for His words ﴿Then if they both desire weaning﴾, it is a conjunction upon His words ﴿Mothers shall nurse their children for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾, because it is a branch of it. The pronoun refers to the mother and the father of the child, who are mentioned in the sentences before this one.

Al-Fisal is weaning from nursing, because the child is separated (fusila) from the breast of its nurse. The phrase ʿan in His words ʿan tarāḍin ("by mutual consent") is connected to aradā, meaning a desire arising from mutual consent, since their desire may be merely formal, or one of them may in reality be compelled to the desire by fear or necessity. His words wa-tashāwurin ("and mutual consultation") is the verbal noun of shāwara, when one seeks counsel. It has been said that mashūra (counsel) is derived from ishāra (indication), because each of the consulting parties indicates what he sees as beneficial; therefore the one seeking counsel says to the one he consults, "What do you advise me?" (bi-māḏā tushīru ʿalayya), as though its origin is that he indicates the matter in which there is benefit. It is derived from the indication by hand, because the wise counselor who plans is like one who points to the right course and guides to it one who has not found it. Then it is followed by ʿalā because it was made to imply the meaning of planning. Al-Raghib said that it is derived from shāra al-ʿasal, meaning when one extracts honey. Whatever its derivation, its meaning is expressing an opinion about an action that the one consulted wishes to undertake. The discussion of it has already been given at His words ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I will make upon the earth a khalifa (successor)"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and the discussion will come again at His words ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾ [Al ʿImran: 159] in Surah Al ʿImran. He coupled consultation with mutual consent to teach the spouses the affairs of managing the household, for consultation reveals what is right, and mutual consent is achieved through it.

By His words ﴿then there is no blame upon them both﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229] he indicated that this is permissible, and that the right of nursing for the two years takes into account the rights of both parents and the right of the nursling. Since this varies with the differing temperaments of nursing infants, he made the disagreement of the parents a sign of the expectation of the child's need for additional nursing, so he gave effect to the word of whichever of them sought the extension, as previously stated. Then when the two parents consult and agree, after that, on weaning, their mutual consent is a sign that they saw in the state of the nursling what makes extension unnecessary, since they cannot be presumed to collude to harm the child, nor is it presumed that the benefit was hidden from them after their consultation, since the condition of their child is not hidden from them.

His words ﴿And if you wish to seek wet-nurses for your children, there is no blame upon you﴾ shift to the situation of nursing the child by someone other than its mother, when it is impossible for the mother to nurse him due to illness, or her remarriage, or if she refuses where she is entitled to refuse, as mentioned in the preceding verse. That is, if you wish to seek nursing for your children, there is no sin in that. The addressee in "you wish" is the two parents, taking into account that there are two parents in the community, and the addressee is not specifically men, as seen in His words previously: ﴿And mothers nurse their children﴾. Thus the hearer knows that this ruling applies specifically to the situation where both parents agree to it due to the mother's excuse, and to the situation of the mother's absence. It is known from His words ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ that the situation of mutual agreement is the primary intent, because the negation of blame implies that it is expected, and that expectation arises only when the mother is present and it is desired to turn the child away from her to another nurse for a recognized reason. They would only desire this where it is certain there is no harm to the child. Had harm to the child been known, it would not be permitted. The Arabs used to seek wet-nurses for their children, especially the people of nobility. In the hadith: "I was given to nurse among the Banu Sa'd."

The istirda' (seeking nursing) originally means requesting the nursing of the child, that is, requesting that someone other than its mother nurse the child. So the sin and the ta' in tastarḍiʿū are for requesting, and its object is elided; its original form is "that you seek wet-nurses (marāḍiʿ) for your children," because the verb is transitive by the sin and ta', which indicate requesting, to the object from which the action is requested, so it transitions only to one object, and what follows is transitive to it by a preposition. The preposition may be dropped due to frequent usage, as it was dropped in istarḍaʿa and istanjaḥa. So the verb is transitive to the genitive-marked noun by elision and attachment. In the hadith: "I was given to nurse among the Banu Sa'd." In the Kashshaf there appears something implying that the sin and ta' entered upon a hamzated verb transitive to one object, so they added transitivity to a second, and its original form is "the woman nursed the child." When you say "istarḍa'tuhā," it becomes transitive to two objects. The reasoning seems to be that we look at the event whose request is intended: if the event is intransitive and the sin and ta' enter upon it, it becomes transitive to one object, such as istanhadtuhu fa-nahada ("I asked him to rise, so he rose"). If it is transitive and the sin and ta' enter upon it, it becomes transitive to two objects, such as istarḍa'tuhā fa-arḍa'at ("I asked her to nurse, so she nursed"). The reliance is on context, since the origin of nursing is not requested either from the child or from the mother. Likewise, "istanjahtu Allah sa'yī" ("I asked God to make my effort succeed"), since from God one requests only the success of the effort, and there is no sense in requesting the success of God. Therefore, regardless of whether the verb is transitive to two objects or to the second by eliding the preposition, we see that there is no sense in the request applying to the verb here at all. Moreover, were it not for this consideration, it would be impossible to request the occurrence of a transitive verb with sin and ta', and it may request its occurrence. Thus what they raised against the Kashshaf, that the letters of augmentation enter only upon the unaugmented form and not the augmented, is refuted by the fact that when letters of augmentation are repeated and serve different meanings, it is permissible to consider some of them entering after others, even if the object they all govern is the bare verb.

His words ﴿And if you wish to seek wet-nurses for your children, there is no blame upon you﴾ indicate that the phrase "they nurse" (yurḍiʿna) does not intend to legislate an obligation of nursing upon mothers; rather, the aim is to define the period of nursing, and the duties of the nursing parent fall upon the father. As for the nursing by mothers, it is left to what people customarily practice. Thus a woman who is under marriage, if women of her standing nurse, her nursing her children is considered among the husband's rights over her within marriage, for custom is like a condition. A divorced woman has no right owed to her husband, so she does not nurse for him except by her own choice, unless some preventing or compelling factor arises in either situation, such as a married woman's inability to nurse due to illness, or the child's refusal of the milk of others when she is divorced, to the point that he is endangered. A woman of standing who does not customarily nurse, when her husband married her knowing that women of her standing do not nurse, has no right of nursing over her. This is the view of Malik, since custom is like a condition. This custom existed before Islam and was established in Islam. It has been stated in the works of the Malikis in the books of legal theory (usul) that Malik particularized the generality of "the mothers" to those other than women of standing, and that the particularizing factor is custom. We used to follow them in this, but now I do not find this correct, nor do I see that Malik intended particularization at all, since the verse is not directed toward imposing nursing, as previously stated.

His words ﴿when you hand over what you gave in accordance with what is customary﴾ mean: when you hand over to the wet-nurses their wages. Thus what is meant by "what you gave" is the payment. The original meaning of "gave" (ataytum) is "delivered," since it is transitive by "ata" meaning "arrived." Since the original form of "idhā" is that it is an adverb of time for the future, implying the meaning of a conditional, it does not fit with the past-tense verb "ataytum."

In the Kashshaf, "ataytum" is interpreted as meaning "you intended to deliver it," like His words ﴿when you rise to prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], following his words "And if you wish to seek wet-nurses," and the meaning is: when you hand over the wages of the wet-nurses in accordance with custom, without excess or delay.

Ibn Kathir read "ataytum" without the hamza of transitivity. The meaning according to this reading is: when you hand over what you brought, that is, what you intended. Coming here is then a metaphor for intending, like His words ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat: 84]. Zuhayr said:

"Whatever good they brought, it was inherited by them from the fathers of their fathers before."

His words ﴿and fear Allah﴾ are a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the warning and an exhortation to observe what Allah has legislated, without trickery or deceit. His words ﴿and know that Allah﴾ are a reminder to them of this; otherwise they already know it. A similar expression has been given earlier.

[Page 441]

﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind shall have them wait for four months and ten days. When they have reached their term, there is no blame on you for what they do with themselves in an honourable manner. And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾

This is a transition to explaining the waiting period of widowhood ('iddat al-wafat), after the discussion of the waiting period of divorce ('iddat al-talaq) and the related rulings on breastfeeding that follow divorce. It is a pursuit of what preserves the affairs of families, so it is the conjunction of one narrative to another. "Yutawaffawna" is in the passive voice. The Arabs kept the passive voice for certain verbs, such as 'uniya (was concerned with) and idturra (was compelled), and this applies to any verb whose agent is known or whose specific agent they did not identify. "Tawaffa" derives from "tawaffahu Allah" (Allah took him in full) or "tawaffahu al-mawt" (death took him in full). Using the verb "tawaffa" in this sense is therefore a metaphor (majaz), by treating the lifespan of the living as a right owed to death, or to the one who creates death. So they said: "Tuwuffiya fulan" (so-and-so was taken in full), as one says "tuwuffiya al-haqq" (the right was discharged), and a parallel is "qubida fulan" (so-and-so was seized) and "qubida al-haqq" (the right was seized). The intended meaning of "tuwuffiya" thus became "mata" (died), just as the intended meaning of "qabada" became the same. This metaphor spread until it became a customary literal meaning (haqiqah 'urfiyyah, a conventional literal meaning). Then Islam came, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah takes the souls﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], and said: ﴿until death takes them in full﴾ [al-Nisa: 15], and said: ﴿Say: The angel of death, who has been entrusted with you, will take you in full﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11]. The agent, which was unknown to them, thus became apparent in contexts of instruction or admonition. The passive form was kept in other uses, for brevity and in keeping with common usage.

His saying ﴿yatarabbasna bi-anfusihinna﴾ (shall wait by themselves) is the predicate (khabar) of "alladhina" (those who). The connection between the subject and the predicate is made by the pronoun in "yatarabbasna", which refers to the wives. This wife is the object of the verb in the clause conjoined to the relative clause. So they are the wives of those who die, because the pronoun stands in place of the noun it refers to, and this noun stands in place of the noun annexed to the pronoun of the subject. This is according to the view of al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i, who held that the connection may be made by a pronoun returning to a noun annexed to something similar to the returning pronoun. The majority (al-jumhur) disagreed with this, as stated in al-Tashil and its commentary. For this reason, they estimated here an ellipsis: "wa-yadharuna azwajan yatarabbasna ba'dahum" (and they leave wives who shall wait after them), just as they say "al-samnu mannani bi-dirham" (ghee is two manns for a dirham), meaning "minhu" (from it). It is also said that the estimate is: "wa-azwaj alladhina yutawaffawna minkum ilakh yatarabbasna" (and the wives of those who die among you, etc., shall wait), on the basis that it is the omission of an annexed noun. This is how al-Kashshaf estimated it, though there is no need for it, as al-Taftazani said. It is also said that the estimate is: "wa-mimma yutla 'alaykum hukmu alladhina yutawaffawna minkum" (and among what is recited to you is the ruling concerning those who die among you). This is reported from Sibawayh, and in that case "yatarabbasna" is a resumed sentence (isti'naf). All of these estimates are useless once the meaning is sound.

[Page 442]

His saying ﴿yatarabbasna bi-anfusihinna﴾ has already been explained at his saying ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228].

The feminine form of the numeral in His saying "'ashran" (ten) is in accordance with the nights (al-layali). The intended meaning is the nights along with their days, since there is no night without a day, nor a day without a night. The Arabs reckon by nights in dating and in appointed terms. They say: "He wrote for seven nights gone in the month of such-and-such." Sometimes they also reckon by days, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So a fast of three days during the Hajj and seven when you return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], and said ﴿for a specified number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. This is because the act of fasting appears in the day, not in the night. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "The Arabs apply the rules of feminine and masculine to the names of days when they are not following a stated word, in both ways." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will whisper among themselves, "You stayed only ten [days]"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 103], ﴿We know best what they say when their most intelligent in judgment says, "You stayed only a day"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 104]. So by "'ashr" He intended the days, yet He stripped it of the sign of masculine numeral, because the day is reckoned together with its night. Allah has made the waiting period of widowhood dependent on the duration in which a foetus visibly moves, in order to safeguard the lineage of the dead. He made the waiting period of divorce that which indicates the clearing of the womb by a probable indication, namely the menstrual periods (al-aqra'), as has already been explained, because the divorcer knows the state of his divorced wife, whether she is in a state of purity or not, and whether he had intercourse with her before the divorce or not. Likewise, conception is not hidden. So if she claims a lineage against him while he is certain of its negation, he has an alternative in li'an (mutual imprecation). But the dead man cannot defend himself. So his waiting period was made a fixed term during which the absence of pregnancy is certain in such a case, namely four months and ten days. For the foetus is a drop (nutfah) for forty days, then a clot ('alaqah) for forty days, then a lump of flesh (mudghah) for forty days, and then the spirit is breathed into it. So the period between the lodging of the drop in the womb and the breathing of the spirit into the foetus is four months. Since the foetus, after the breathing of the spirit into it, grows stronger gradually, the ten nights beyond the four months were prescribed so that the movement of the foetus would be clearly established. When this period has passed, certainty of the absence of pregnancy is obtained, since if there were a pregnancy it would certainly move, and it moves within four months. The ten were added to it as a precaution, because the movements of foetuses differ in strength and weakness, according to the differences in the constitutions of the mothers.

The generality of "alladhina" in its relative clause, and what is connected with it of wives, requires the generality of this ruling concerning widows, whether they are free women or slave women, whether they are pregnant or not pregnant, and whether they have been consummated with or not. As for slave women, the majority of scholars said that their waiting period is half that of free women, by analogy with the halving of the prescribed penalty (hadd) and of divorce, and with the halving of the waiting period of divorce. None held that they are equal to free women in the waiting period of widowhood except al-Asamm, and in one report from Ibn Sirin, except the umm al-walad (the slave mother of a child by her master). A group said that their waiting period is like that of free women. This is the view of Sa'id, al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, al-Awza'i and Ishaq, and it is reported from 'Amr ibn al-'As. Others said otherwise. The consensus of the jurists of Islam on halving the waiting period of widowhood for a slave woman whose husband has died is indeed one of the most perplexing of juristic questions. So we should consider the wisdom of prescribing the waiting period of widowhood, and the wisdom of prescribing halving for one who is owned, in what we state a legal ruling for. By the method of sabr (examining the candidate causes) and taqsim (division), we find that the waiting period of widowhood is either for a wisdom that secures lineage or its absence, or it is for the purpose of mourning the husband. When Islam abrogated (naskh) what the people of the pre-Islamic period (Jahiliyyah) practised regarding mourning for a full year, it left them one third of a year, just as it left the dead the right of bequest of one third of his property. There is no wisdom for it other than these two, since it does not contain the wisdom of the waiting period of divorce, namely waiting for the divorcer's regret. The second reason is not suitable as a justification, because it is not thought that the Shari'ah would confirm the illusions of the people of the Jahiliyyah, leaving from them a bad legacy. Also, it is known from the conduct of Islam that it nullifies exaggeration of the matter of death and the grief over it that was present among the people of the Jahiliyyah. This is known in more than one place in the Shari'ah's provisions. Also, the jurists agreed that the waiting period of a pregnant widow is the delivery of her child. So if the waiting period of a non-pregnant woman were for the purpose of preserving grief, the two would be equal in the waiting period. It is therefore established that the wisdom of the waiting period of widowhood is the establishment of pregnancy or its absence. Let us turn the examination to the slave woman, and we find in her two attributes: humanity (insaniyyah) and slavery (riqq). If we take the method of extracting the effective cause (takhrij al-manat) to these two, we find that the attribute suitable for justifying the waiting period whose wisdom is the establishment of lineage is the attribute of humanity, since pregnancy does not differ in its state according to the different categories of women and their conventional conditions. As for slavery, it is not an attribute suitable to influence this ruling. Rather, some rulings concerning the slave are halved on the basis of a suitability of an embellishing kind (al-munasib al-tahsini), such as halving the prescribed penalty because of the weakness of his manliness, and because theft spread among slaves. So the halving ruling was extended to them in other matters. The halving of the waiting period of a slave woman in divorce, which is in the hadith, is for the cause of desire to take her back, since if a man desirous of her comes after two menstrual periods, she is free to marry. The principle of halving applies also.

So the correct view is that the waiting period of widowhood for a slave woman is like that of a free woman, and there is no report of halving it. The basis of the consensus is analogy in the presence of a distinguishing factor. As for pregnant women, the disagreement concerning them is strong. The majority held that their waiting period on widowhood is the delivery of their child. This is the view of 'Umar, his son, Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman and Abu Hurayrah, and it is the view of Malik. 'Umar said: "If she delivered her child while her husband was still on his bier, and he had not yet been buried, she would be permitted to marry."

[Page 443]

Their proof is the hadith of Subay'ah al-Aslamiyyah, the wife of Sa'd ibn Khawlah, whose husband died while she was pregnant at Makkah in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage. She delivered her child after half a month, as in al-Muwatta', or after forty nights. She mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to her: "You are now free; marry if you wish." They also argued with His saying in the verse of Surat al-Talaq: ﴿And for those with children, their term is that they deliver their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. The generality of "ulat al-ahmal" (those with burdens), together with the later revelation of that surah than Surat al-Baqarah, requires that the generality of what is in Surat al-Baqarah be understood as specified. Ibn Mas'ud's saying points to this: "Whoever wishes, I will curse him (in mubahalah): the short sura of women came after the long one," meaning the sura of "Ya ayyuha al-nabiyy idha tallaqtum" [al-Talaq], after the long one, that is, al-Baqarah. He did not mean the long sura of al-Nisa'.

In my view, the argument of the majority returns to what we have already stated, namely that the wisdom of the waiting period of widowhood is the certainty of preserving lineage. Since the delivery of the child is the clearest indicator of the clearing of the womb, it suffices in place of anything else. Ibn Mas'ud used to say: "Do you impose severity on her and not impose leniency on her?" He meant that if the period of her pregnancy were prolonged, she would not be permitted to marry. It is also reported from 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud that the waiting period of a pregnant woman on widowhood is the longer of the two terms. Sahnun from the Malikis preferred this view. Some commentators said: "In this view there is a combining of the requirements of the two verses." Others said: "In this view there is precaution (ihtiyat)." The second expression is better, because taking the longer of the two terms is not a combining of the two verses in the technical sense of the principles of jurisprudence (usul). The combining of two conflicting texts means that each of them is acted upon in a state, a time, or individuals other than those in which the other is acted upon, such that in the case of combination an action in accordance with both conflicting texts is realized together. For this reason they call combining "implementing both texts" (i'mal al-nassayn). The purpose of the waiting period is to fix the term of waiting and expectation. So when we take the longer of the two terms, we necessarily nullify the requirement of one of the two verses, because we oblige the widow to exceed what one of the two verses set for her, and we do not find any state in which the requirements of both are realized, as is clear. So the better expression is that it be described as precaution. That is, the two verses conflict in a partial general and specific relation (umum wa-khusus wajhi). We have therefore resorted to the case of conflict and acted upon the requirement of this verse at one time and the requirement of the other at another time, preferring one of the two requirements in each place by the preponderant consideration of precaution. This is therefore a preference (tarjih), not a combining. But

[Page 444]

The hadith of Subay'a in the Sahih has refuted this method of preference (tarjih). Likewise, the opening of Surat al-Talaq with His words, ﴿When you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], points to the restriction of the general statement ﴿And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth﴾ [al-Talaq: 4] to pregnant divorced women. It has been said that Ibn 'Abbas returned to the view of the majority (al-Jumhur). This is apparent from the hadith in al-Muwatta' concerning his disagreement with Abu Salama on this matter, and their sending the one who asked Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her, and she informed them of the hadith of Subay'a.

If you ask: how, on this view, does the Shari'a not take into account what is in the nature of women, namely their grief over the death of their husbands? And how is the abrogation of the grief of a full year not followed by a period in which the woman's condition becomes apparent? And how would a pregnant woman be permitted to marry if she gave birth while her husband had not yet been carried from his bed, as occurred in the statement of 'Umar?

I say: The people of the Jahiliyya used to make the mourning (ihdad) of a full year an obligation upon every widow. Widows differ in this grief, and they also differ in their ability to endure waiting, due to the scarcity of means among most women. So they would endure waiting for the year, either willingly or unwillingly. When the Shari'a abolished this, among the illusions of the Jahiliyya that it abolished, it did not concern itself with legislating a ruling for women in this matter, and left it to what arises in their souls and their dispositions, just as it leaves all innate and natural matters to human feeling (wijdan). For it did not specify for people the quantity of food, travel, speech, and the like. Rather, it was concerned with the legal objective (maqsad shar'i), which is the preservation of lineages. Once that right has been fulfilled, women remain free to do with themselves what they wish, within what is recognized (ma'ruf), as He said: ﴿there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves﴾. So if the woman, after the completion of the 'idda ('waiting period'), wishes to confine herself, let her do so.

As for wives who were not consummated with, the 'idda upon them is the 'idda of widowhood ('iddat al-wafat), not the 'idda of divorce, because of the generality of this verse, and because they inherit. The marital bond was established in a legitimate manner, to the extent that it was a cause of inheritance. The non-consummation of the marriage does not negate the possibility that the husband had approached her secretly, since she is lawful to him. Therefore, the 'idda was obligated upon her as a precaution for the preservation of lineage. For this reason Malik said so, although there is room for consideration in it. The widow whose husband did not consummate the marriage may be analogized to the one whom her husband divorced before touching her, concerning whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, you have no 'idda for them to count﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49].

They have mentioned the hadith of Bir'a bint Washiq al-Ashja'iyya, which al-Tirmidhi related from Ma'qil ibn Sinan al-Ashja'i: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) judged concerning Bir'a bint Washiq, when her husband had died and he had not set a dowry for her and had not consummated the marriage, that she has the like of the dowry of her women peers, and upon her is the 'idda, and for her is the inheritance." [p. 446] No one disagreed about the obligation of the 'idda upon her; they differed only about the obligation of the mahr al-mithl (the customary dowry) for her.

His words ﴿when they have reached their term﴾ mean: when the period specified for waiting has ended, i.e., when they have reached that period through their waiting. The extension of the waiting period is described as "reaching" in the common usage in the phrase "he reached the limit" (balagha al-amad). Its origin is the name of "reaching," which is arrival, and it was borrowed for the completion of a period, comparing time to a road that leads to the intended goal. The ajal (term) is a span of time that is made a container for the occurrence of an act at its end or within it at times.

The pronoun in ajalahunna refers to the wives whose husbands have died. The term (ajal) is defined by its attachment to their pronoun rather than by other means of definition, because the attachment of "term" to them indicates that they have completed what was upon them, so do not burden them by adding to it.

The "reaching" is attributed to them, and the "term" is attached to them, to draw attention to the fact that the hardship of this term falls upon them. The meaning of "blame" (junah) here is "constraint," to remove what may remain in people's minds of disapproval of women's haste to marry after the 'idda of widowhood and before the year has passed. The relatives of the deceased husband may feel constrained about this, so Allah negated this constraint, and said ﴿concerning what they do with themselves﴾, as an emphasis against one who feels constrained about the actions of others. It is as if He says: if the woman had a strong attachment to the covenant of her deceased husband, that would be the motive for increasing her waiting by her own will. But if she has no such motive, then why be constrained by what she does with herself? Then Allah clarified this and restricted it by saying "within what is recognized," as a prohibition against women doing what is not recognized in the Shari'a or custom, such as excessive grief that the Shari'a considers reprehensible, or displaying the abandonment of marriage after her husband. It is also an emphasis against those who object to women's haste after the 'idda or after the delivery of the child, as Subay'a did, meaning that such conduct is part of what is recognized.

The implication (mafhum) of the condition in His words ﴿when they have reached their term﴾ indicates that during the term they are forbidden from certain acts concerning themselves, such as marriage, and what precedes it of betrothal and adornment. As for marrying during the 'idda, the Muslims have agreed to prohibit it, and its detailed discussion will come under His words, the Exalted: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you imply of the proposal to women﴾ [al-Baqara: 235].

As for what is other than this, the disagreement is in two matters: in the ihdad, and in staying at home (mulazamat al-bayt). As for ihdad, it is a verbal noun from "ahadat al-mar'a" when she mourns, wears the clothes of grief, and abandons adornment. It is also said "hidad." In Islam, its meaning is the widowed 'idda-observing woman's abandonment of adornment, perfume, dyed clothing except white, and jewelry. It is obligatory by the Sunna. In the Sahih: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn over a dead person for more than three days, except over a husband, for four months and ten days." No one differed in this except al-Hasan al-Basri, who made the ihdad three days only, and this is weak.

The wisdom of ihdad is to block the means of everything that whispers to men: the seeing of the beauty of the woman in 'idda, so that they keep away from the desire to hasten what is not fitting. For this reason the scholars differed about ihdad for a divorced woman. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Rabi'a, and 'Ata' said: there is no ihdad for a divorced woman, following the explicit hadith, and because the divorced woman is watched by her divorcer, who stands between her and whatever she might be lax about, unlike the widow, as we have mentioned. Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sulayman ibn Yasar, and Ibn Sirin said: a woman divorced with a triple divorce mourns, like the widow, because both are in an 'idda in which lineage is protected. The Kitabiyya wife (Jewish or Christian) is like the Muslim woman in this according to Malik, and she is compelled to it; al-Shafi'i, al-Layth, and Abu Thawr said likewise, because the cause is the same. Abu Hanifa, Ashhab, Ibn Nafi', and Ibn Kinana from the Malikis said: there is no ihdad upon her, adhering to the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day," so he described her by faith. This is a weak argument, because the context of a description is not the context of restriction; rather, the context is encouragement to obey the command of the Shari'a.

The Prophet (ﷺ) was strict about the matter of ihdad. In al-Muwatta': "A woman came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'My daughter's husband has died, and her eyes have become sore; may she apply kohl to them?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'No, no,' twice or three times, 'it is only four months and ten days. In the Jahiliyya, one of you would throw a dung-ball at the end of the year.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) permitted Umm Salama, during her ihdad over Abu Salama, to put aloes (sabr) on her eyes [p. 448] at night and wipe it off by day. Umm Salama issued a similar ruling to a mourning woman whose eyes were sore, that she apply kohl of al-Jila' at night and wipe it off by day. All of this is narrated in al-Muwatta'. Malik said: "When there is necessity, the religion of Allah is ease." For this reason they interpreted the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition to the woman who asked him on behalf of her mother, that she should apply kohl, as meaning that he knew from the 'idda-observing woman that she sought a concession, so she sent her mother to ask on her behalf.

As for the widow remaining in her husband's house, it is not derived from this verse, because the waiting (tarabbus) is a waiting in time, not an indication of remaining in a place. In my view, the apparent position is that the majority derived it from His words, the Exalted: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives, a bequest for their wives: provision for a year without expulsion﴾ [al-Baqara: 240]. That ruling was intended only for the protection of the woman in 'idda. When it was abrogated, according to the majority, by this verse, the abrogation applied to the period, which is the year, not to the rest of the ruling. Moreover, the widow in 'idda has a better claim to residence than the divorced woman in 'idda, concerning whom it was said: ﴿Do not expel them from their houses﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], and it was said concerning her: ﴿House them where you dwell﴾ [al-Talaq: 6]. The exegetes and jurists said: the obligation of remaining in the house is established by the Sunna. In al-Muwatta' and the Sahih: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to al-Fur'a bint Malik ibn Sinan al-Khudri, sister of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, when her husband had died: 'Remain in your house until the Book reaches its term.'" This is a well-known hadith, and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan judged by it. In al-Muwatta', 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to turn back widows from al-Bayda', preventing them from performing Hajj. Ibn 'Umar also held this view, and the majority of jurists of Madina, the Hijaz, Iraq, Syria, and Egypt adopted it. No one disagreed on this except 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'isha, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, Abu Hanifa, and Dawud al-Zahiri. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, took out her sister Umm Kulthum when her husband Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah died, to Makka for 'Umra, and she used to issue fatwa permitting leaving the house. Many of the Companions denounced this against her. al-Zuhri said: "The lenient took the view of 'A'isha, and the people of resolve and piety took the view of Ibn 'Umar." All agreed that the woman in 'idda may go out out of necessity, and may go out during the day for her needs, from the time people disperse until the time they quiet down after 'atama (night prayer). She may not spend the night except in the house. The conditions and rulings of this, the existence of a place for the husband or its rent, and the heirs' waiting for the sale of the house until after the 'idda, and the ruling if she doubts pregnancy and the 'idda is prolonged, [p. 449] are expounded in the books of fiqh and differences of opinion, so we have no need for them here.

Among the irregular readings (qira'at shadha) of this verse is what al-Zamakhshari mentions in al-Kashshaf: that 'Ali recited ﴿wa-alladhina yutawaffawna﴾ with a fatha on the ya' (i.e., yatawaffa), as the active form of the verb "tuwuffiya" ("died"), in the sense of "he completed his term," meaning he fulfilled it.

I, although I committed myself not to address irregular readings, mentioned this reading because of an amusing anecdote which contains a point of Arabic grammar. Al-Zamakhshari alluded to it in al-Kashshaf, and al-Sakkaki elaborated it in al-Miftah. It is that 'Ali was accompanying a funeral, and someone said to him, "Who is the one who has died (al-mutawaffi)?" using the form of the active participle, i.e., with a kasra on the fa', asking about the deceased, who would be the passive participle (al-mutawaffa) with a fatha on the fa'. He did not say "so-and-so," but said, "Allah," correcting him and alerting him that it is proper to say "who is the one who has died" using the passive participle form. He did this only because he knew that the questioner had not used the word "mutawaffi" in the manner that would give it majesty and grandeur, which is the manner of the reading attributed to him, i.e., to 'Ali: ﴿wa-alladhina yutawaffawna minkum﴾ with the active form, intending the meaning: "those who complete the term of their lives."

In al-Kashshaf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari) it is related that the incident occurred with Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, and that when 'Ali learned of it, he instructed Abu al-Aswad to compose a book on grammar (*nahw*). He said: "The report contradicts the reading attributed to 'Ali." So he accepted the reading as authentic and doubted the soundness of the report.

From Ibn Jinni: the report was transmitted by Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami from 'Ali. Ibn Jinni said: "This is, in my view, sound, because it is based on the omission of the object: that is, *wa-alladhina yatawaffawna a'marahum* (and those who die leave their lifespans) or *ajalahum* (their appointed terms). The omission of the object is common in the Qur'an and in eloquent speech."

Al-Taftazani said: "It is not meant that *al-mutawaffa* has two meanings: one of them is causing death, and the other is taking full payment and receiving one's due. Rather, its meaning is only taking full payment and receiving one's due. However, in usage its object may be understood as *al-nafs* (the soul), in which case the agent is God Most High or the Angel of Death. This is the common usage. It may also be understood as *muddat al-'umr* (the span of life), in which case the agent is the deceased himself, because he is the one who has completed the span of his life. This is one of the subtle meanings, which only the eloquent notice." When 'Ali recognized from the questioner that he had not noticed this, he did not take his statement to mean that.

[Page 450]

﴿There is no blame upon you for what you imply in proposing to women, or what you conceal within yourselves. Allah knows that you will remember them, but do not make a secret promise to them, except that you say a fitting word. And do not resolve on the tie of marriage until the prescribed term reaches its end.﴾

It is connected (ʿaṭf) to the preceding sentence, so this is one of the rulings related to the waiting period (ʿidda). The verses before it contained rulings on the waiting period of divorce and of widowhood, and that the term of the waiting period is inviolable. Divorced women, once they have reached their prescribed term, may do what they wish with themselves in a proper manner. From this it is understood that if they have not reached that term, it is not permissible. So marrying during the term of the waiting period is forbidden. Since talk about marriage is intended by the speaker to bring about a marriage, and since it was their custom to rush to propose to a woman in her waiting period and to make promises to her, out of eagerness to have her exclusively after the waiting period ends, the Sharia clarified for them the prohibition of this, and permitted something of it. For this reason this statement is connected to what precedes it. The word junāḥ (blame, sin) means sin, and it has already appeared in His words, ﴿so there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾ [al-Baqara: 158].

His words ﴿what you imply (ʿarraḍtum) by it﴾: mā is a relative pronoun, and its referent is a statement (kalām), meaning a statement by which you imply. This is because taʿrīḍ (implication, indirect allusion) is applied to one kind of the meanings derived from speech. He clarified this with His words ﴿in proposing to women﴾, which indicates that what is meant is speech.

The root form fāʿal in ʿarraḍa contains the meaning of making something: like ṣawwara, derived from ʿarḍ (with a damma on the ʿayn), which means side (jānib). That is, he made his speech into a side. The side is the edge, so the speaker turns his speech away from the straight path of meaning toward a side. A parallel to this is their saying jannabahu, meaning he placed him at a side.

So taʿrīḍ (indirect allusion) is that the speaker intends by his speech something other than what the composition signifies by its literal convention, due to a relation between the signified of the speech and the thing intended, together with an indicator that the allusive meaning is intended. Thus it is understood that there must be a relation between the signified of the speech and the thing intended. This relation is either a necessary connection (mulāzama) or a resemblance (mumāthala). An example is what the one who asks a generous man says: "I came to greet you and to look at your face." Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt expressed this kind of intention in his words:

*When a man praises you one day, the praise suffices him from having to imply (ta'arrud) it.*

Page 451

al-Ṭībī counted among it His words: ﴿And when Allah says, "O ʿĪsā son of Maryam, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah'?"﴾ [al-Māʾida: 116].

So the allusive meaning in such cases arises from necessary connection. Likewise the saying of one who says: "The Muslim is the one from whose tongue the Muslims are safe," in the presence of someone known for harming people. The allusive meaning arises from people's knowledge of the resemblance between the condition of the intended person and the situation in which the meaning of the statement was given. Since resemblance is close to necessary connection, because the presence of the like in the mind accompanies the presence of its counterpart, it is correct to say that the allusive meaning, with respect to compound expressions, resembles the metonymic meaning (kināya), with respect to the signification of single words. If you wish, you may say that the allusive meaning is a kind of metonymy by a compound, and it is singled out with the name taʿrīḍ, just as the metonymic meaning is a kind of metonymy by a single word. On this basis, taʿrīḍ is one of the implications of compound expressions. This is what agrees with the position followed by the author of al-Kashshāf in this matter. For him, taʿrīḍ is distinct from kināya in this respect, though it resembles it, and for this reason he needed to point out the difference between them. So the relation between them, in his view, is one of complete difference (tabāyun). As for al-Sakkākī, he made some taʿrīḍ a part of kināya, and this is the more correct view. Thus the relation between them becomes one of partial overlap (ʿumūm wa khuṣūṣ wajhī). al-Ṭībī and al-Taftazānī interpreted the words of al-Kashshāf in this sense, but I do not think it can bear this meaning.

Now that the meaning of taʿrīḍ has become clear to you, and you know the boundary of the distinction between it and explicit speech (taṣrīḥ), the examples of taʿrīḍ and taṣrīḥ are not hidden. However, regarding some of those expressions as transmitted, there is a difficulty that should not be overlooked in the interpretation of this verse.

The one who makes an implicit proposal (muʿarrid bi-l-khiṭba), his implication may be intended for himself, or he may intend it for another through his mediation. Between these two situations there is a difference, and the ruling on the ambiguous cases of taʿrīḍ should take this into account. It has been related that the Prophet ﷺ said to Fāṭima bint Qays, who was in her waiting period after her husband ʿAmr ibn Ḥafṣ divorced her with the third (irrevocable divorce): "Stay at the house of Umm Sharīk, and do not get ahead of me with yourself," meaning, do not act independently in marrying before seeking my permission. In another narration: "When you have finished, inform me." After the end of her waiting period, he proposed her for Usāma ibn Zayd. So this is a statement without a proposal in it, and the intention of consultation in it is clear.

It occurs in the Muwaṭṭaʾ that al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad used to say, regarding His words, ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you imply in proposing to women﴾, that a man may say to a woman who is in her waiting period after her husband's death: "Indeed you are honorable to me, and indeed I am desirous of you."

Page 452

As for "Indeed you are honorable to me," it is close to explicit intention to marry her, though it is not explicit. So if no promise follows from either of them, its ruling is open to interpretation. As for his saying "Indeed I am desirous of you," it is in the position of an explicit proposal, and its ruling is problematic. Ibn al-Ḥājib pointed to its problem with his words: "They said: Like 'Indeed I am desirous of you' are most of these expressions in explicitness, so leaving the like of it is required." It is reported from Muḥammad al-Bāqir that "the Prophet ﷺ implied (ʿarraḍa) to Umm Salama during her waiting period, from the death of Abū Salama," but I do not think what has been related from him is sound.

In the Tafsīr of Ibn ʿArafa: It was said that our shaykh Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Ḥaydara used to say: If the implication comes from only one of the two sides, [it is as stated]. But if the implication comes from both of them, then the apparent position of the school is that it is like an explicit promise.

The word nisāʾ (women) is general, but married women are excluded from it by rational evidence. It is also restricted, regarding women divorced with a revocable divorce, by analogical evidence and by the evidence of consensus (ijmāʿ), because the revocable divorcée has the ruling of the wife by the cancellation of the distinguishing factor. al-Qurṭubī related a consensus on prohibiting the proposal to a revocably divorced woman during her waiting period. Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām related from the school of Mālik the permissibility of implication toward every woman in the waiting period, whether from death or divorce. This contradicts the statement of al-Qurṭubī, and the matter is open to interpretation, because the revocable divorce has two aspects. al-Shāfiʿī permitted implication toward a woman in the waiting period of widowhood, but forbade it in the waiting period of divorce. This is the apparent meaning of what was related in the Muwaṭṭaʾ from al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad.

His words ﴿or what you conceal within yourselves﴾: ikhnān (concealment) means hiding. The purpose of conjoining concealment (ikhnān) to implication (taʿrīḍ) in the negation of blame, despite its being evident that implication cannot occur except from a resolve in the self, is this: the negation of blame from the mere resolve of the self is necessarily understood from the negation of blame from implication. The intended point is to alert that resolve is a matter that cannot be prevented or forbidden. Since this is so, and since it is part of human nature that the one who resolves speaks of what he has resolved upon, because of weakness in patience to keep it hidden, Allah clarified the place of the concession: it is mercy toward people, while preserving the sanctity of the state of the waiting period. He also clarified the reason for this permission: that it returns to the removal of hardship. So in it is the wisdom of this legislation, which had not been explained to them before.

He placed concealment (ikhnān) later in the mention in order to alert that it is more excellent and more preserving of the sanctity of the waiting period. It also alerts that its occurrence is rare, because if he had put it first, the movement from mentioning concealment to mentioning implication would follow the apparent structure of the speech, in that the subsequent item adds a meaning beyond what the preceding statement covers. Then the hearer would not notice this subtle point. When the apparent expectation was departed from, the hearer understands that this departure aims at a purpose, as is the way of the eloquent speaker in departing from what the apparent order demands. He increased this clarification with His words that follow it: ﴿Allah knows that you will remember them﴾, meaning: Allah knows that you cannot keep hidden what is in your selves. So He permitted implication for you as ease for you. Thus by delaying the mention of "or what you conceal," another benefit is obtained, which is to prepare for His words ﴿Allah knows that you will remember them﴾. The arrangement came wondrous and inimitable. Most exegetes neglected to address the benefit of this conjunction. al-Fakhr (al-Rāzī) attempted to explain it with something that does not satisfy the heart. Ibn ʿArafa explained it with something closer than al-Rāzī's explanation, but the soul of an eloquent person is not at rest with it.

His words ﴿but do not make a secret promise to them﴾ are an exception (istidrāk) indicated by the context, meaning: Allah knows that you will remember them explicitly and by implication, since no one with a resolve is free from mentioning what he has resolved upon by one of the two ways. Since mentioning knowledge in such a place is a metonymy for permission, as when you say, "I know that you do such-and-such," meaning, "I will not hold you accountable, for if I were holding you accountable, and I knew your action, I would have seized you." Likewise His words: ﴿Allah knows that you used to betray yourselves, so He turned to you and pardoned you﴾ [al-Baqara: 187]. This is the most apparent explanation of this exception. It was also said: this is an exception to an omitted statement, meaning: so mention them, but do not make a promise to them, that is, do not be explicit and make a promise to them, that is, promise them and have them promise you marriage.

The word sirr (secret) originally means what is opposite to openness (jahr). It was used as a metonymy for intimacy with a woman. al-Aʿshā said:

*Do not approach a neighbor woman, for her secret (sirr) is forbidden to you, so marry or remain forever.*

And Imruʾ al-Qays said:

*Did not Basbāsa of the tribe claim that I have grown old, and that someone like me does not do well at secrets (sirr)?*

The apparent meaning of the word in this verse is its literal sense. So sirran is in the accusative as a description of an absolute object: meaning an explicit promise in secret, that is, do not conceal the promise. This is an emphasis on avoiding a promise of explicit proposal during the waiting period. His words ﴿except that you say a fitting word﴾ are an exception from the absolute object, meaning except a fitting promise, which is the implication mentioned earlier in His words ﴿what you imply by it﴾. The fitting word is one kind of promise, except that it is not explicit. When the prohibition is on promising in secret, the prohibition on promising openly is understood a fortiori. On this reading, the exception in His words ﴿except that you say a fitting word﴾ is a connected exception (muttaṣil), and the fitting word is the permitted one, which is implication. So it is a confirmation of His words ﴿there is no blame upon you for what you imply by it﴾, the verse.

It was also said: the meaning of "secret" here is a metaphor, that is, "do not make them promises of intimacy." He used it as a metaphor for marriage, meaning an explicit promise of marriage. On this reading, "secret" is the direct object of *tuwā'iduhunna* ("you promise them"), and the exception (*istithna'*) is disjunctive (*munqati'*, not included in the preceding category), because speech is not one of the kinds of marriage. Marriage is a contract (*'aqd*) formed by offer (*ījāb*) and acceptance (*qabūl*), whereas speech is a proposal (*khiṭba*), either explicit (*ṣarāḥa*) or allusive (*ta'rīḍ*). This view is remote, because it contains a metaphor upon a metaphor. It was also said other things that are not worth dwelling on.

If you say: the prohibition of an explicit proposal and of a promise, together with the permission of allusion to the same thing, presents an apparent contradiction, since the outcome of explicit and allusive speech is one and the same. When the suitor and the woman in her waiting period already know that he intends to propose and that she agrees, what is the purpose of attaching prohibition and permission to particular wordings and styles, if the meaning conveyed is one? I say: the Lawgiver intended, by this, to guard against hastiness becoming a pretext for falling into what defeats the wisdom of the waiting period (*'idda*). Dwelling on the matter may lead to the motive of the suitor's haste to contract marriage with a woman in her waiting period, with consummation in view, for the stirring of desire brings about lust, and frankness removes the veil of modesty. Natural restraint is the modesty present in a man when he intends to reveal to a woman something of his desire for her. Modesty in a woman is stronger when a man confronts her with this directly, and when she intends to respond to what he asks of her. Allusion is a style of speech which signals, by the dignity of modesty it carries for its speaker, that he restrains himself from advancing to what has been forbidden. His signalling of this modesty increases the modesty with which the woman is naturally endowed, so her soul withdraws from an explicit response, let alone a promise. Thus the curtain of modesty remains drawn between them, and the veil of propriety is not lifted. This is out of honour for the status of the waiting period. For this reason allusion was permitted as a facility for people, while explicit speech was forbidden, to preserve the sanctity of the waiting period.

His saying ﴿And do not determine the tie of marriage﴾: here *al-'azm* means the contracting of the marriage, not mere resolve to contract it. For this reason *'uqdat al-nikāḥ* is in the accusative as the direct object (*maf'ūl bihi*), and the meaning is: do not contract the marriage tie. The word *al-'azm* is taken in the sense of severing and resolving decisively, as al-Nahhas and others said. You may also take it in its well-known meaning: do not resolve upon the tie of marriage. He forbade resolving upon it because, once resolved, what has been resolved upon will occur.

[Page 455]

It was also said: he forbade resolve as an intensification, and the intended meaning is the prohibition of what is resolved upon, like the prohibition of approaching in His saying ﴿These are the limits of God, so do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqara: 187]. On both of these readings, *'uqdat al-nikāḥ* is in the accusative by omission of the preposition (*naz' al-khāfid*), as in their saying *ḍarbat al-ẓahr wa al-baṭn* ("a blow to the back and the belly"). It was also said that *'azama* was used with the sense of *abrama* ("to conclude firmly"), as said by the author of *al-Mughni* in its eighth chapter. The word *al-kitāb* here means "what is written", that is, what is obligatory from God, namely the waiting period mentioned, with the definite article denoting a known reference. *Al-ajal* is the fixed term for a particular action, and what is meant here is the fixed term of the waiting period, completed in full, as indicated by His saying ﴿So when they have reached their term﴾ [al-Baqara: 234] just before.

The verse is explicit in prohibiting marriage during the waiting period, in prohibiting a proposal during the waiting period, and in permitting allusion.

As for marriage, that is, contracting it during the waiting period: if it is concluded and no consummation has taken place during the waiting period, the marriage is annulled by consensus. The jurists differed only over whether the woman remains permanently forbidden to the one who contracted it. The majority hold that it is not permanent, and this is the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab and the transmission of Ibn al-Qasim from Malik in the *Mudawwana*. Ibn al-Jallab transmitted from Malik a report that it is permanent, but nothing like this is known from anyone other than Malik.

As for consummation during the waiting period: there is consensus on annulment, and they differed over whether the prohibition on her for him becomes permanent. Umar ibn al-Khattab, Malik, al-Layth, al-Awza'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said the prohibition on her for him becomes permanent. They have no proof for this except that they based it on the principle that a transaction produces the opposite of the corrupt intended aim, and this is a weak principle. Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri and al-Shafi'i said the marriage is annulled and the prohibition is not permanent, and after the waiting period she is a woman to be proposed to like any other. It has been said that Umar returned to this view, and this is the more sound. The husband owes her the dowry for what he made lawful of her. Ruwaysh al-Thaqafi married Tulayha al-Asadiyya during her waiting period, so Umar separated them and made her dowry a charge on the public treasury (*bayt al-māl*). This reached Ali, who said: May God have mercy on the Commander of the Faithful. What is the matter with the dowry and the treasury? They were both ignorant. The ruler should return them both to the Sunna. It was said to him: "Then what do you say?" He said: She is owed the dowry for what he made lawful of her, they are to be separated, and neither is to be flogged.

The later Maliki jurists approved that when a judge rules to annul the marriage of one who contracted during the waiting period, he should not address in his ruling the question of making the prohibition permanent, because no dispute over it has come before him. He should therefore refrain from touching on it, perhaps they will adopt the view of those who do not hold the prohibition to be permanent.

[Page 456]

As for proposing during the waiting period and promising, it is forbidden to address the woman with them. The same applies to a father addressing his virgin daughter. As for addressing a guardian who is not a compulsory guardian (*mujbar*), it is disliked. If the consummation did not take place during the waiting period but after it, Malik said: they are separated by a single divorce and her prohibition does not become permanent. Ibn Wahb transmitted from him: separation is more beloved to me. Al-Shafi'i said: the proposal is forbidden, and the marriage concluded after the waiting period is valid.

* * *

﴿And know that God knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him. And know that God is All-Forgiving, Forbearing﴾

This is a continuation of the preceding discussion, from His saying ﴿There is no blame on you for what you insinuate of proposing to women﴾ to His saying ﴿until the decreed term reaches its end﴾. The address begins with *i'lamū* ("know") because the intention is to cut off the thoughts of laxity and interpretive evasion in this matter, so that people may carry out what God has prescribed for them with purity of heart, free of every loophole and stratagem. A parallel to this was already given in His saying ﴿And know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqara: 223].

His saying ﴿And know that God is All-Forgiving, Forbearing﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*), meaning: just as He holds you to account for what you conceal of opposition, He forgives you what He promised to pardon, such as allusion, because He is Forbearing towards you. This is evidence that the permission of allusion is a concession, as we have stated, and that the principle of blocking means (*dharī'a*) requires its prohibition, were it not that God knew the hardship of prohibiting it for people, for the reasons we have mentioned. Perhaps the forgiveness mentioned here means overlooking, not forgiveness of sin, since allusion is not a sin. Or it may be intended in a more general sense that encompasses both forgiveness of sin and overlooking of hardships. The nature of a concluding statement is generality.

**[p. 457]**

﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women before you have touched them or specified for them a dower. But provide for them: the wealthy according to his means, and the straitened according to his means, a provision in kindness, a duty upon the doers of good.﴾ ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have specified for them a dower, then half of what you specified, unless they forgo it or the one in whose hand is the marriage tie forgoes it. And that you forgo is nearer to righteousness. And do not forget graciousness between you. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

This is a resumption of legislation to explain the ruling on what follows from divorce: the payment of the entire dower or part of it, its dropping, and the ruling on the provision (mut'ah), together with the indication that divorce before consummation (al-masis) is permitted. The sentence is a fresh, initial resumption (istinaf ibtida'i), and the reason for its placement is clear. When the preceding verses spoke of divorce that entails the waiting period ('iddah), which is divorce of women who have been consummated with, it turned here to divorce that occurs before consummation. This is the divorce referred to in Allah's words, ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49], in Surat al-Ahzab. Along with this, it mentions here the halving of the dower and its waiving. The literal meaning of "junah" (blame) is sin, as previously mentioned in His words, ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158].

The term "junah" is not known to be used in any sense other than sin. For this reason, the majority of exegetes understood it here as the negation of sin in divorce. In the Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari), "junah" is explained as "responsibility." He said, "﴿There is no blame upon you﴾: there is no responsibility upon you for the obligation of the dower." He then said: "The evidence that 'junah' means the responsibility for the dower is His words, ﴿And if you divorce them﴾ up to His words ﴿then half of what you specified﴾. So His words ﴿then half of what you specified﴾ are an affirmation of the negated 'junah' there." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Some people said: 'There is no blame upon you' means: there is no demand for the entire dower."

So we know that the author of the Kashshaf was preceded in this interpretation, though he did not mention this meaning of "junah" in al-Asas, either literally or figuratively.
