Others understood the imperative in this verse as recommendation, which is the view of al-Shafiʿi. Its basis is the interpretation of the apparent sense of His words ﴿for divorced women﴾ by what is indicated by the implication (mafhum) of His words in another verse: ﴿as long as you have not touched them or fixed for them a dowry﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:236).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 242:

﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs, so that you may understand.﴾

Meaning: like this clear explanation, Allah makes His signs clear. Here "the signs" (al-ayat) are the evidences of the Shari'ah (the sacred law). The discussion of its counterpart has already been presented in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 243–244 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death? So Allah said to them, "Die," and then He revived them. Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿And fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

This is a fresh (ibtida'i) resumption (isti'naf) to urge jihad and to remind that fear does not delay the appointed term, and that the coward may meet his death in the very place where he expects safety. It has already been stated that this surah was revealed during the truce of al-Hudaybiyah and that it prepares the way for the conquest of Makkah, so fighting is among its most important aims. The intended point of this discourse is His saying, ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾, and so on.

The discourse returns to His saying, ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. The verses revealed in between, which begin with "They ask you" (yas'alunaka), separate the two discourses.

The placement of ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes﴾ before ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ is the placement of mentioning the proof before what is to be proven. This is one of the methods of rhetoric (khitabah): the proof is presented before the claim it supports, for various purposes. An example is the statement of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) in one of his sermons, when news reached him of the Syrian army's seizure of most of the lands. He began the sermon by saying: "It is nothing but Kufa; I hold it and I spread it out. I have been informed that Busr, who is Ibn Abi Artat, one of the commanders of the Syrian army, has entered Yemen. Indeed, by Allah, I think these people will overcome you, because they are united in their falsehood and you are divided from your truth." So his saying, "It is nothing but Kufa," is placed in the position of the proof for his saying, "I think these people..." and so on.

Also, 'Isa ibn Talhah said when he entered upon 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr after his leg had been amputated: "We did not consider you fit for combat. Praise be to Allah who left us most of you: He left us your hearing, your sight, your tongue, your mind, and one of your two legs." So he put forward his saying, "We did not consider you fit for combat." The purpose of such a construction is attention to and care for the proof before mentioning the claim, or it is intended to hasten compliance.

Know that the construction "Have you not considered such-and-such" (alam tara ila kadha), when the verb of seeing takes as its object something that the listener would not ordinarily have seen, is a statement intended to urge knowledge of what the verb of seeing is directed to. The exegetes agree on this point. For this reason, the interrogative hamzah is used not in its literal sense of asking but in a figurative or metonymic sense, one of the meanings of non-literal interrogation. The address with it is usually directed to an unspecified audience, and sometimes the addressee is assumed or imagined.

We have three ways of explaining how this construction conveys this urging:

The first way: the interrogation is used to express wonder or to make the listener wonder, at the addressee's lack of knowledge of the object of the verb of seeing. The verb of seeing here is cognitive, among the sisters of "thought" (zanna), according to the view of al-Farra', and this is correct, because "ila" (to) and the preposition "li" (for) alternate often in speech. An example is His saying, ﴿And the command is to you﴾ [al-Naml: 33], meaning "for you." They also say "ahmadu Allaha ilayka," just as they say "ahmadu laka Allah." The noun governed by "ila" is in the position of the first object, because a superfluous (za'id) preposition does not require a complement. The clause ﴿and they were thousands﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), taking the place of the second object, because the original status of the second object of verbs of the heart is that it is a circumstantial clause, as if to say: "It was not right for them to leave." Following from His saying, ﴿and they were thousands﴾ is His saying, ﴿So Allah said to them, "Die"﴾. It is therefore a complement of the meaning of the second object. Alternatively, "ila" is considered to be an extension (tajrid) of the figurative use of the verb of seeing to the meaning of knowing, or it is a qarinah (indicator) of this, or the verb of seeing is taken to include the meaning of looking (nazar), so that the claim is made that this matter, which is grasped by the intellect, is as if it were grasped by sight, because it is clear in truth to whoever knows it. Thus the phrase "Have you not considered such-and-such" in His saying is equivalent to two clauses: "Have you not known such-and-such, and looked at it?"

The second way: the interrogation is affirmative (taqriri), since the affirmative interrogation frequently comes with negated verbs, such as ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1] and ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106]. The discussion of the verb of seeing and of the preposition "ila" in this way is similar to what was said about the first way.

The third way: you take the interrogation as a denial (inkari), denying the addressee's lack of knowledge of the object of the verb of seeing, where the seeing is cognitive. The discussion of the preposition "ila" is similar to what was said under the first way. Alternatively, the seeing is visual, and the verb is taken to include the meaning of "look" (tanzur), on the basis that the verb is originally addressed to one who has neglected to look at a visible thing, and the interrogation is a denial, either literally or by treating it as such. Then the construction was transferred to be used for matters that are not visible, and it became like a proverb. Close to this is the verse of al-A'sha:

You see generosity flowing openly upon his face.

The eliciting of urging, in all three ways, is only through the implication (kinayah) of the necessary meaning of the interrogation, because the nature of a matter that is marvelled at, or affirmed, or denied as to its knowledge, is that the motives to know it are abundant, and that itself urges knowledge of it.

Know that this construction has become like a proverb, in that it is habitually used in this style, except that they changed it according to the differences in the forms of address it contains: masculine and feminine, singular and its opposite, as in "alam tara-yi" addressed to a woman, "alam tara-ya" and "alam tara-u" and "alam tara-na" for the dual and the plural. This applies when the construction is addressed about a matter that is not necessarily visible to the addressee, or not visible at all.

It has been disputed who is meant by ﴿those who left their homes﴾. The most apparent view is that they were a people who left their homes fearing their enemies, and so abandoned their dwellings out of cowardice. My indication for this is His saying, ﴿and they were thousands﴾, which is a circumstantial clause and the place of wonder. The large number becomes a matter of wonder only if the intended fear is of the enemy, because the nature of a large group is not to abandon their homes out of fear and panic. The Arabs say of an army that has reached thousands: "It is not defeated for lack of numbers." It was said that they were from the Children of Israel, who disobeyed a prophet of theirs in his call to them to jihad, so they left their homeland fleeing from jihad. This is the most apparent view, and in that case the story is an illustration (tamthil) of the state of those who are cowardly in fighting, by comparison with the state of those who left their homes, through the common quality of cowardice. The state used as the comparison was more evident in the quality of cowardice and more terrible, just as the state of one who hesitates over something is compared to one who puts one foot forward and draws back the other. It cannot be said that this reduces to comparing a thing with its like. This is the most preponderant of the views, because most of the Qur'an's parables concern the states of famous nations, especially the Children of Israel.

It was also said that they were from a group of the Children of Israel from the people of Dawardan, near Wasit, where a plague struck their land, so they went out to a wide valley, and Allah struck them with a deadly disease for eight days, until they swelled and their bodies stank, then He revived them. It was also said that they were from the people of Adhri'at, in the regions of Syria. All the narrations agree that Allah revived them through the supplication of the Prophet Hizqiyal ibn Buzi (Ezekiel). The story is then a metaphor (isti'arah): those who shrink from fighting are compared to those who shrink from the plague, through the common element of fear of death. The ones compared may be a group of Muslims in whom cowardice crept when they were called to jihad in some expedition; or they may be a hypothetical group, supposed to exist before it does, in order to cut off the thoughts that might occur to their hearts.

In the tafsir of Ibn Kathir, on the authority of Ibn Juraij, from 'Ata': that this is a parable and not an actual historical event. This is far-fetched, since the relative pronoun used for them and His saying, ﴿So Allah said to them﴾, make it distant.

The phrase ﴿fearing death﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and its governing verb is ﴿left﴾.

The most apparent view is that they were a people who fled from their enemy despite their large numbers, and vacated the homes for him. Then calamities befell them on their journey, from which they were brought near to destruction, and then they were saved; or they were epidemics and diseases whose symptoms resembled the symptoms of death, such as the disease of sakt (a fit of sudden collapse), from which they then recovered. So in their state they are like the words of the rajaz poet:

One who went out, whom love of greed drove out, fled from death, and fell into death.

What supports that this is a reference to an actual event and not a parable is His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾, and so on. What supports that those spoken of were not from the Children of Israel is His saying, after this, ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Musa?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246]. The verse alludes to the meaning of His saying, ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾ [al-Nisa': 78], and His saying, ﴿Say: "Even if you had been in your houses, those decreed to be killed would have gone out to their places of death."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154].

As for those who said they were a people from the Children of Israel whom Allah revived through the supplication of Hizqiyal, and those who said this is only a parable and not an actual event, the apparent view is that they meant the vision mentioned in the book of Hizqiyal in chapter 37 of it, when he said: "The Spirit of the Lord brought me out and set me down in the middle of a valley full of bones. He led me round among them, and there were very many of them on the surface of the valley, and they were very dry. He said to me, 'Son of man, can these bones live?' I answered, 'Lord GOD, you know.' Then He said to me, 'Prophesy over these bones and say to them, O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD.' So I prophesied as I was commanded, and as I prophesied there was a noise, and behold a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to its bone. And I looked, and behold, there were sinews on them, and flesh came up, and skin covered them over. But there was no breath in them. Then He said to me, 'Prophesy to the breath, prophesy, son of man, and say to the breath, Thus says the Lord GOD: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live.' So I prophesied as He commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army." This is a parable that the prophet gave for the steadfastness of his people and their surrender to their enemies, because after it he said: "These bones are the whole house of Israel. Behold, they say, 'Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost; we are cut off.' Therefore prophesy and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will open your graves and raise you from your graves, O my people, and bring you into the land of Israel. And I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live."

Perhaps this parable, together with the place where this prophet had his vision, which is al-Khabur, near Wasit, is what led some of the storytellers to claim that these people were from the people of Dawardan, since Dawardan may have been in the regions of al-Khabur, where the prophet Hizqiyal saw what he saw.

As for His saying, ﴿So Allah said to them, "Die," then He revived them﴾, the statement about it is either a figurative use in the sense of creation (takwin), with death being literal, meaning that He placed in them the state of death, which is the stopping of the heart and the loss of perception and sensation. The state of the Creator's receiving the effect of His will is borrowed for the state of the one commanded receiving the command. So the compound expression that indicates the state being compared is applied to the state of comparison, by way of illustration (tamthil). Then He revived them by removing that accident, so they knew that they had been struck by something that, had it lasted, would have been a continuous death. This may be one of the rare diseases resembling the disease of sakt.

Or the statement is a figurative reference to the warning of death, with death being literal: meaning that Allah showed them places of destruction from which they smelled the scent of death, then Allah relieved them and revived them.

Or the statement is a literal speech by the revelation of Allah to one of the prophets, with death being figurative death. It is a command of belittlement, as an insult to them, casting them into humiliation and abasement. Then He revived them and established in them the spirit of courage.

The purpose of this is to admonish the Muslims to abandon cowardice, and to show that fear of death does not ward off death. Those who were described by this parable left their homes fearing death, and their fear did not avail them anything. God made them die and then brought them back to life, so that the disposition of courage would become established in them through direct perception.

The point of lesson in the story is that they tasted the death from which they fled, so that they would know that flight does not avail them anything, and that they tasted life after death, so that they would know that death and life are in the hand of God. As the Most High said: ﴿Say: Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or from killing﴾ [al-Ahzab: 16].

The clause ﴿Indeed, God is most bountiful towards mankind﴾ stands in the position of a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿then He brought them back to life﴾. Its purpose is to instil in the souls of the Muslims the disposition of reliance upon God in all their affairs, and that if they give thanks to God for the blessings He has bestowed upon them, He will increase them from His bounty and make easy for them what is difficult.

The clause ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾ and what follows is the primary aim, since what precedes it is a preparation for it, as you know. In the composition (nazm) it has been made conjoined (ma'tufah) to the clause ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes﴾, by way of conjunction ('atf) on the resumptive sentence (isti'naf). Thus it has the status of a new sentence, a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i). Were it not for the long separation between it and the clause ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216], we would say that it is conjoined to it, since the connection of the two purposes attaches it to that clause without a conjunction.

The clause ﴿And know that God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ is an exhortation to fight and a warning against abandoning it, by reminding them of God's comprehensive knowledge of all things known, both their outward and their inward aspects. The attribute "All-Hearing" is mentioned first, though it is more specific than "All-Knowing," out of concern for it here, because most of the circumstances of fighting in the way of God are things that are heard, such as the clamour of the army, the clashing of weapons, and the neighing of horses. Then the attribute "All-Knowing" is mentioned, because it encompasses knowledge of all things known, including what belongs to the inner talk of the soul, such as the disposition of fear and the soul's whispering to sit back from fighting. In this there is an allusion (ta'ridh) to both promise and threat.

The opening of the clause with "And know" serves to alert to what it contains of explicit meaning and allusion. This has already been mentioned shortly before, at His words, Most High: ﴿And fear God, and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223].

The address with it is usually directed to an unspecified audience, and sometimes the addressee is assumed or imagined.

We have three ways of explaining how this construction conveys this urging:

The first way: the interrogation is used to express wonder or to make the listener wonder, at the addressee's lack of knowledge of the object of the verb of seeing. The verb of seeing here is cognitive, among the sisters of "thought" (zanna), according to the view of al-Farra', and this is correct, because "ila" (to) and the preposition "li" (for) alternate often in speech. An example is His saying, ﴿And the command is to you﴾ [al-Naml: 33], meaning "for you." They also say "ahmadu Allaha ilayka," just as they say "ahmadu laka Allah." The noun governed by "ila" is in the position of the first object, because a superfluous (za'id) preposition does not require a complement. The clause ﴿and they were thousands﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), taking the place of the second object, because the original status of the second object of verbs of the heart is that it is a circumstantial clause, as if to say: "It was not right for them to leave." Following from His saying, ﴿and they were thousands﴾ is His saying, ﴿So Allah said to them, "Die"﴾. It is therefore a complement of the meaning of the second object. Alternatively, "ila" is considered to be an extension (tajrid) of the figurative use of the verb of seeing to the meaning of knowing, or it is a qarinah (indicator) of this, or the verb of seeing is taken to include the meaning of looking (nazar), so that the claim is made that this matter, which is grasped by the intellect, is as if it were grasped by sight, because it is clear in truth to whoever knows it. Thus the phrase "Have you not considered such-and-such" in His saying is equivalent to two clauses: "Have you not known such-and-such, and looked at it?"

The second way: the interrogation is affirmative (taqriri), since the affirmative interrogation frequently comes with negated verbs, such as ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1] and ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106]. The discussion of the verb of seeing and of the preposition "ila" in this way is similar to what was said about the first way.

The third way: you take the interrogation as a denial (inkari), denying the addressee's lack of knowledge of the object of the verb of seeing, where the seeing is cognitive. The discussion of the preposition "ila" is similar to what was said under the first way. Alternatively, the seeing is visual, and the verb is taken to include the meaning of "look" (tanzur), on the basis that the verb is originally addressed to one who has neglected to look at a visible thing, and the interrogation is a denial, either literally or by treating it as such. Then the construction was transferred to be used for matters that are not visible, and it became like a proverb. Close to this is the verse of al-A'sha:

You see generosity flowing openly upon his face.

The eliciting of urging, in all three ways, is only through the implication (kinayah) of the necessary meaning of the interrogation, because the nature of a matter that is marvelled at, or affirmed, or denied as to its knowledge, is that the motives to know it are abundant, and that itself urges knowledge of it.

Know that this construction has become like a proverb, in that it is habitually used in this style, except that they changed it according to the differences in the forms of address it contains: masculine and feminine, singular and its opposite, as in "alam tara-yi" addressed to a woman, "alam tara-ya" and "alam tara-u" and "alam tara-na" for the dual and the plural. This applies when the construction is addressed about a matter that is not necessarily visible to the addressee, or not visible at all.

It has been disputed who is meant by ﴿those who left their homes﴾. The most apparent view is that they were a people who left their homes fearing their enemies, and so abandoned their dwellings out of cowardice. My indication for this is His saying, ﴿and they were thousands﴾, which is a circumstantial clause and the place of wonder. The large number becomes a matter of wonder only if the intended fear is of the enemy, because the nature of a large group is not to abandon their homes out of fear and panic. The Arabs say of an army that has reached thousands: "It is not defeated for lack of numbers." It was said that they were from the Children of Israel, who disobeyed a prophet of theirs in his call to them to jihad, so they left their homeland fleeing from jihad. This is the most apparent view, and in that case the story is an illustration (tamthil) of the state of those who are cowardly in fighting, by comparison with the state of those who left their homes, through the common quality of cowardice. The state used as the comparison was more evident in the quality of cowardice and more terrible, just as the state of one who hesitates over something is compared to one who puts one foot forward and draws back the other. It cannot be said that this reduces to comparing a thing with its like. This is the most preponderant of the views, because most of the Qur'an's parables concern the states of famous nations, especially the Children of Israel.

It was also said that they were from a group of the Children of Israel from the people of Dawardan, near Wasit, where a plague struck their land, so they went out to a wide valley, and Allah struck them with a deadly disease for eight days, until they swelled and their bodies stank, then He revived them. It was also said that they were from the people of Adhri'at, in the regions of Syria. All the narrations agree that Allah revived them through the supplication of the Prophet Hizqiyal ibn Buzi (Ezekiel). The story is then a metaphor (isti'arah): those who shrink from fighting are compared to those who shrink from the plague, through the common element of fear of death. The ones compared may be a group of Muslims in whom cowardice crept when they were called to jihad in some expedition; or they may be a hypothetical group, supposed to exist before it does, in order to cut off the thoughts that might occur to their hearts.

In the tafsir of Ibn Kathir, on the authority of Ibn Juraij, from 'Ata': that this is a parable and not an actual historical event. This is far-fetched, since the relative pronoun used for them and His saying, ﴿So Allah said to them﴾, make it distant.

The phrase ﴿fearing death﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and its governing verb is ﴿left﴾.

The most apparent view is that they were a people who fled from their enemy despite their large numbers, and vacated the homes for him. Then calamities befell them on their journey, from which they were brought near to destruction, and then they were saved; or they were epidemics and diseases whose symptoms resembled the symptoms of death, such as the disease of sakt (a fit of sudden collapse), from which they then recovered. So in their state they are like the words of the rajaz poet:

One who went out, whom love of greed drove out, fled from death, and fell into death.

What supports that this is a reference to an actual event and not a parable is His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾, and so on. What supports that those spoken of were not from the Children of Israel is His saying, after this, ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Musa?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246]. The verse alludes to the meaning of His saying, ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾ [al-Nisa': 78], and His saying, ﴿Say: "Even if you had been in your houses, those decreed to be killed would have gone out to their places of death."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154].

As for those who said they were a people from the Children of Israel whom Allah revived through the supplication of Hizqiyal, and those who said this is only a parable and not an actual event, the apparent view is that they meant the vision mentioned in the book of Hizqiyal in chapter 37 of it, when he said: "The Spirit of the Lord brought me out and set me down in the middle of a valley full of bones. He led me round among them, and there were very many of them on the surface of the valley, and they were very dry. He said to me, 'Son of man, can these bones live?' I answered, 'Lord GOD, you know.' Then He said to me, 'Prophesy over these bones and say to them, O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD.' So I prophesied as I was commanded, and as I prophesied there was a noise, and behold a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to its bone. And I looked, and behold, there were sinews on them, and flesh came up, and skin covered them over. But there was no breath in them. Then He said to me, 'Prophesy to the breath, prophesy, son of man, and say to the breath, Thus says the Lord GOD: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live.' So I prophesied as He commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army." This is a parable that the prophet gave for the steadfastness of his people and their surrender to their enemies, because after it he said: "These bones are the whole house of Israel. Behold, they say, 'Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost; we are cut off.' Therefore prophesy and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will open your graves and raise you from your graves, O my people, and bring you into the land of Israel. And I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live."

Perhaps this parable, together with the place where this prophet had his vision, which is al-Khabur, near Wasit, is what led some of the storytellers to claim that these people were from the people of Dawardan, since Dawardan may have been in the regions of al-Khabur, where the prophet Hizqiyal saw what he saw.

As for His saying, ﴿So Allah said to them, "Die," then He revived them﴾, the statement about it is either a figurative use in the sense of creation (takwin), with death being literal, meaning that He placed in them the state of death, which is the stopping of the heart and the loss of perception and sensation. The state of the Creator's receiving the effect of His will is borrowed for the state of the one commanded receiving the command. So the compound expression that indicates the state being compared is applied to the state of comparison, by way of illustration (tamthil). Then He revived them by removing that accident, so they knew that they had been struck by something that, had it lasted, would have been a continuous death. This may be one of the rare diseases resembling the disease of sakt.

Or the statement is a figurative reference to the warning of death, with death being literal: meaning that Allah showed them places of destruction from which they smelled the scent of death, then Allah relieved them and revived them.

Or the statement is a literal speech by the revelation of Allah to one of the prophets, with death being figurative death. It is a command of belittlement, as an insult to them, casting them into humiliation and abasement. Then He revived them and established in them the spirit of courage.

The purpose of this is to admonish the Muslims to abandon cowardice, and to show that fear of death does not ward off death. Those who were described by this parable left their homes fearing death, and their fear did not avail them anything. God made them die and then brought them back to life, so that the disposition of courage would become established in them through direct perception.

The point of lesson in the story is that they tasted the death from which they fled, so that they would know that flight does not avail them anything, and that they tasted life after death, so that they would know that death and life are in the hand of God. As the Most High said: ﴿Say: Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or from killing﴾ [al-Ahzab: 16].

The clause ﴿Indeed, God is most bountiful towards mankind﴾ stands in the position of a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿then He brought them back to life﴾. Its purpose is to instil in the souls of the Muslims the disposition of reliance upon God in all their affairs, and that if they give thanks to God for the blessings He has bestowed upon them, He will increase them from His bounty and make easy for them what is difficult.

The clause ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾ and what follows is the primary aim, since what precedes it is a preparation for it, as you know. In the composition (nazm) it has been made conjoined (ma'tufah) to the clause ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes﴾, by way of conjunction ('atf) on the resumptive sentence (isti'naf). Thus it has the status of a new sentence, a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i). Were it not for the long separation between it and the clause ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216], we would say that it is conjoined to it, since the connection of the two purposes attaches it to that clause without a conjunction.

The clause ﴿And know that God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ is an exhortation to fight and a warning against abandoning it, by reminding them of God's comprehensive knowledge of all things known, both their outward and their inward aspects. The attribute "All-Hearing" is mentioned first, though it is more specific than "All-Knowing," out of concern for it here, because most of the circumstances of fighting in the way of God are things that are heard, such as the clamour of the army, the clashing of weapons, and the neighing of horses. Then the attribute "All-Knowing" is mentioned, because it encompasses knowledge of all things known, including what belongs to the inner talk of the soul, such as the disposition of fear and the soul's whispering to sit back from fighting. In this there is an allusion (ta'ridh) to both promise and threat.

Page 481

The opening of the clause with "And know" serves to alert to what it contains of explicit meaning and allusion. This has already been mentioned shortly before, at His words, Most High: ﴿And fear God, and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 2, Verse 245:**

﴿Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him manifold? And God withholds and extends, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

This is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) placed between the phrase ﴿Have you not seen those who went out from their homes﴾ [2:243] and what follows it, and between the phrase ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel﴾ [2:246] and the verse after it. It is intended as a digression (istitrad) that urges spending for the sake of God in the ways of righteousness, in connection with the exhortation to fighting. Fighting requires the fighter to spend on himself for his equipment and provisions. The verse also urges the well-off to give generously in the way of God, by providing equipment to those who have none and by supporting the needy among the army. It also clarifies the content of the phrase ﴿And know that God is Hearing, Knowing﴾ [2:244]. So this verse has three purposes.

"Qard" (lending) means advancing property or the like on the condition that its equivalent be returned. It is used metaphorically for giving in expectation of a reward, so that this sense includes giving up one's self and body in hope of reward. Thus the verb "yuqriḍu" is used both in its literal and its metaphorical sense.

The interrogative in ﴿Who is it that will lend to God﴾ is used for exhortation and stirring up to attain goodness, as if the questioner does not know who is worthy of and fit for this good. Ṭarafa said:

*When the people say, "Who is a youth?" I think it is I who am meant; I do not grow lax or dull.*

After interrogative nouns, "dhā" may be used with its literal meaning, as when you say, having seen a person you do not know: "Who is that (man dhā)?" If there is nothing in the context of speech that can be pointed to by the question, then the use of "dhā" after the interrogative noun is a figurative indication: the speaker imagines in his mind an unknown, imagined person who has performed an action, and he asks about his identity. This occurs out of concern for the action that has taken place and a desire to know its doer. Because this usage is always accompanied by a verb after the demonstrative, all grammarians, Basran and Kufan alike, said that "dhā" with the interrogative becomes an indefinite relative pronoun (ism mawṣūl) not previously known. They therefore counted it as a relative pronoun. Sibawayh, in his book, set a chapter heading: "Chapter on our treatment of 'dhā' alone as equivalent to 'alladhī'

[Page 482 continues]

and it is not like 'alladhī' except with 'mā' and 'man' in the interrogative, so that 'dhā' is equivalent to 'alladhī' and 'mā' (i.e., or 'man') becomes the interrogative particle. Our treatment of them together with 'mā' (i.e., or 'man') is as a single noun." He illustrated it with God's words ﴿What has your Lord sent down?﴾ [16:30], to which they replied, "Good." The rest of the demonstrative nouns are like the noun "dhā" according to the Kufans. As for the Basrans, they restricted this usage to "dhā." They did not mean that "dhā" with the interrogative becomes a relative pronoun, since it is common in speech for a relative pronoun to follow it, as in this verse, and there is no sense in having two relative pronouns with the same complement. Rather, they meant that it conveys the function of a relative pronoun, so that what follows it, whether a verb or an attribute, has the meaning of the relative clause. They recorded this only because they overlooked the figurative character of using "dhā" in the interrogative, so recording it was of little benefit.

The correct view is that "dhā" in the interrogative does not leave its function as a demonstrative. It is a figurative indication, and the verb that comes after it stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Thus the pattern of God's words ﴿What has your Lord sent down?﴾ [16:24] matches the line of Yazid ibn Rabi'a ibn Mufarrigh addressing his mule:

*You escaped, and this one you carry is free.*

"Iqrāḍ" is the act of lending. "Qard" is an advance (salaf), which is giving something so that its equivalent or like may be returned. Here it is used metaphorically for giving for which a reward is hoped, to emphasize the certainty of receiving compensation and reward. The description of the loan as "ḥasan" (goodly) is because God is not pleased with it unless it is free from the blemishes of showing off and harm, as al-Nabigha said:

*She is not one of the possessors of scorpions...*

It was also said that "qard" here is used in its literal sense, which is an advance. Perhaps it is attributed to the Divine name (God) because the one who lends to people in hope of reward is as if he lent to God Most High, since lending is one of the acts of goodness that God has commanded. In the same meaning is what came in the sacred hadith: God, Mighty and Majestic, says on the Day of Resurrection: "O son of Adam, I asked you for food and you did not feed Me." He says, "O Lord, how could I feed You, when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He says, "Did you not know that My servant so-and-so asked you for food and you did not feed him?" (The hadith continues.) They also narrated that the reward for charity is tenfold, and the reward for a loan is eighteen times its equivalent.

The majority of readers recited ﴿fa-yuḍā'ifahu﴾ with an alif after the ḍād. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub recited it without an alif after the ḍād and with a shadda on the 'ayn.

The vowel of "fa-yuḍā'ifu" in the majority reading is nominative (raf'), as a conjunction following "yuqriḍu," so that it enters the scope of the exhortation and is parallel to the lending in attainment. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Ya'qub recited it with a fatha on the fā', as an answer to the exhortation (jawāb al-taḥḍīḍ). The meaning in both readings is one.

His words ﴿And God withholds and extends﴾: the original sense of "qabḍ" (withholding) is to tighten and hold firmly, and the original sense of "basṭ" (extending) is the opposite of withholding, which is release and sending forth. From this basic meaning several senses have branched out. Among them, "qabḍ" means taking, as in ﴿then a pledge taken into possession﴾ [2:283], and means stinginess, as in ﴿and they withhold their hands﴾ [9:67]. Among them, "basṭ" means giving generously, as in ﴿God extends provision to whom He wills﴾ [13:26], and means generosity, as in ﴿rather His hands are both outstretched﴾ [5:64]. Among His names, Most High, are "al-Qābiḍ" (the Withholder) and "al-Bāsiṭ" (the Extender), in the sense of the one who restricts and the one who gives.

The majority recited ﴿wa-yabsuṭu﴾ with the letter sīn. Nafi', al-Bazzi on the authority of Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far, and Rawh on the authority of Ya'qub recited it with ṣād, and this is a dialectal variant.

It is possible that the intended meaning here is: He withholds gifts and charities, and extends reward and recompense. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: He withholds souls from goodness, and extends souls toward goodness. In this there is an allusion to the promise of widening provision for the one who spends in the way of God, and of narrowing it for the miser. In a hadith: "O God, give the one who spends a replacement, and give the one who withholds destruction." In Ibn 'Atiyya, on the authority of al-Hulwani from Qalun from Nafi', it is reported that he did not mind how he recited "yabsuṭu," whether with sīn or ṣād. That is, because both are dialects, like "al-ṣirāṭ" and "al-sirāṭ." The original is the sīn, but it was changed to ṣād in "baṣaṭahu" and "yabṣuṭu" because of the ṭā' following it. Its point of articulation is far from that of the sīn, because moving from sīn to ṭā' is heavy, unlike ṣād.

His words ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ are a statement used to alert and remind that what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter as reward for spending in the way of God is greater than what they were promised of good in this world. There is also an allusion that the one who withholds and is miserly in spending in the way of God is deprived of much good.

It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, "Abu al-Dahdah came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'Does God want a loan from us?' He said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Dahdah.' He said: 'Show me your hand.' He gave him his hand, and he said: 'I have lent to God a garden in which there are six hundred palm trees.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'How many a bunch of dates, heavy and spreading, and a spacious abode in Paradise for Abu al-Dahdah!'"

[Page 484]

﴿Have you not considered the eminent men of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Raise up for us a king, and we will fight in the way of God"? He said, "Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, refrain from fighting?" They said, "Why should we not fight in the way of God, when we have been driven from our homes and our children?" Yet when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them. And God knows the wrongdoers.﴾

The clause ﴿Have you not considered the eminent men of the Children of Israel﴾ is a second resumptive clause (istinaf) following ﴿Have you not considered those who went forth from their homes﴾ [2:243]. It is brought in as evidence for ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾ [2:190]. It also adds emphasis to how dreadful is the state of one who holds back from fighting after being readied for the way of God. Repetition in a case like this serves further warning and a veiled rebuke. Those commanded to fight in ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾ [2:190] are never free from two kinds of people. Some are beset by thoughts that discourage them from fighting out of love of life. Others are struck by notions that make death easy for them when they witness the troubles of life and the calamities of humiliation. God therefore set forth two examples for these two states. The first is what preceded in ﴿Have you not considered those who were driven from their homes﴾ [2:243], and the second is ﴿Have you not considered the eminent men of the Children of Israel﴾. He placed one first and delayed the other so that exhortation to fight would fall between them. The reason for placing the first is that it condemns the state of those who submitted and considered themselves weak, so that they went forth from their homes despite their numbers. This state is more suitable to be placed before the command to fight and to defend the homeland, because the command after it will necessarily be received well by the listeners. The reason for delaying the second is that it depicts the state of those who knew the benefit of fighting in the way of God, as shown by their words ﴿Why should we not fight﴾, and so on. They asked him, rather than having it imposed on them. When fighting was specified for them, they turned back on their heels. The point of lesson lies in warning against falling into a situation like theirs after beginning to fight, or after it was prescribed for them. So glorious is the eloquence of this speech and the excellence of this style, in its placing first and last. The word ﴿Have you not considered﴾ was preceded by ﴿said﴾ in the verse before this one.

Al-Mala' (the eminent men): the group whose affair is one. It is an collective noun, like al-qawm (people) and al-rahṭ (company). It seems derived from al-mil' (filling a vessel with water or the like), and it indicates consultation, as in their saying tamāla'a al-qawm ("the people agreed") when they agreed on something. The whole matter derives from filling with water, for they used to fill their waterskins and vessels every evening at the watering place. When one filled for another, he had spared him something important, since water is the sustenance of life. So they used this as a figure for cooperation in a beneficial matter on which the sustenance of life depends. The use of the condition of water as an image in such matters includes the saying of ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him): "O God, bring upon Quraysh (Your judgment), for they have severed my kinship and overturned my vessel," as an image of their neglect of his right.

His saying ﴿after Moses﴾ informs that the people of this story were with a prophet after Moses, for the time of Moses did not have kings appointed over the Children of Israel. It seems to indicate that they wasted the benefit of the time when their messenger was among them. They used to say ﴿Go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾ [5:24], and victory with him was more hopeful for them through the blessing of their messenger. The purpose is an indirect warning to the Muslims against disagreement with their messenger.

The indefinite form of ﴿a prophet for them﴾ indicates that the locus of lesson is not the person of the prophet, so there is no need to specify him; rather the intended object is the state of the people. This is the custom of the Qur'an in its stories. This prophet is Samuel, which in Arabic is Shamwīl with the letter shīn. For this reason it did not say "to their prophet," since this prophet was not known to the listeners so as to be identified for them by an annexation.

In his saying (a prophet for them) there is support for the view of the grammarians that the basic form of the annexed construction (iḍāfa) is with the implied preposition lām of genitive. The meaning of ﴿Raise up for us a king﴾ is "appoint for us a king." That is because when there was no king among them at a time of need for a king, the king was as though absent from them, and their condition seemed to call for his presence. So when a person was appointed king for them, it was as though he had been absent from them and then was raised up, that is, sent to them. Or it is borrowed from raising a camel, that is, making it rise to walk.

His saying ﴿Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you﴾, and the verse, is an interrogative of confirmation and warning. His saying ﴿refrain from fighting﴾ is what is asked about with ﴿perhaps﴾ (hal), and it is the expected predicate of ʿasā ("perhaps"), and it is the evidence for the response of the conditional ﴿if fighting is prescribed for you﴾. This is among the most wondrous kinds of concision (ījāz), for it recounts many sentences that occurred in their speech among themselves. He established them in holding the intention not to fight, testing and probing the measure of their resolve. For this reason the interrogative came with negation, saying what conveys the sense of "Would you not fight?" and not saying "Would you fight?" because what is asked about is the more probable side in the mind of the questioner, even if the other side is presumed. When the interrogative leaves its literal meanings for figurative ones, the speaker's need to choose the more probable side becomes emphatic. He anticipated from them not fighting and warned them against not fighting if it was imposed upon them. So the clause ﴿refrain from fighting﴾ has its meaning contested by each of hal, ʿasā, and in; it was given to ʿasā, so it was linked with an (that), and it is evidence for the rest, so for each operator what it requires is assumed. The purpose of this speech is exhortation, because one of high resolve disdains being attributed to negligence. When this is recorded against him before the appearance of its motives, he is on guard against falling into it in the future, just as one who advises another says: "Do this and that, and I do not think you will do it."

Nāfiʿ alone read ʿasītum with a kasra on the sīn, contrary to analogy, and the majority read it with a fatḥa on the sīn. Both are dialectal forms of ʿasā when a pronoun of the speaker or addressee is attached to it. It seems they intended by the kasra to lighten by causing the sukūn of the yā' to be dropped.

His saying ﴿They said, "Why should we not fight in the way of God"﴾: the conjunctive wāw came in the reporting of their words, since their speech contained what indicates they intended their answer to his speech to be linked with the phrase ﴿Raise up for us a king that we may fight in the way of God﴾ by a conjunction that conveys the same. They wanted to emphasize their eagerness in appointing a king who would manage the affairs of fighting, by saying that they deny every thought arising in their souls of discouragement from fighting. So they made the words of their prophet like an intervening speech in the midst of their own speech, which they completed. Thus what their answer achieves is a response to the doubt of their prophet about their steadfastness. The arrangement of their speech thus followed the manner of the words of God Most High, recounting the messengers: ﴿And in God let the believers put their trust. And why should we not put our trust in God, when He has guided us to our ways?﴾ [14:11].

Mā is an interrogative noun meaning "what thing," and the lām is for specification. The interrogative is one of denial and wonder about the words of their prophet ﴿Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, refrain from fighting?﴾, because the nature of what is wondered at is that its cause be asked about. The interrogative noun is in the position of the subject, and lanā is its predicate, and its meaning is "what has come to be for us" or "what has been established for us." So the lām in His saying lanā is the lām of specification, and an is a particle of verbal noun and futurity, and nuqātila is in the subjunctive governed by an. Since the particle of the verbal noun requires that the verb after it be in the sense of a verbal noun, the verbal noun formed from an and its verb is either made genitive by a genitive particle assumed before an, appropriate to the connection of "we do not fight" with the predicate, the assumed sense being "what is ours in not fighting," that is, the cessation of our fighting, or "what is ours for the sake of not fighting," that is, for the sake of the cessation of our fighting. Then the meaning of the speech is their denial that there should be established for them any cause that would move them to abandon fighting, or any cause for the sake of their abandoning fighting; that is, there cannot be that for them.

Or the verbal noun formed from an is made a substitute for the pronoun in lanā, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl), and the assumed sense is "what is ours for our abandoning fighting."

This pattern of construction comes in five forms, such as ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not trust us with Joseph?﴾ [12:11], ﴿And why should I not worship Him who created me?﴾ [36:22], ﴿What is the matter with you, how do you judge?﴾ [37:154], "So what is the matter with you concerning the hypocrites, two groups?" [4:88], and the line "What is it with you and the circling around Najd?" The more usual case is that what follows the interrogative is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), but the grammatical analysis differs while the ultimate meaning is the same.

Mā is the subject and (lanā) is its predicate, and the meaning is "whatever thing was ours." The clause ﴿that we do not fight﴾ is a circumstantial clause and it is a qualifier of the denying interrogative: that is, nothing is established for us in the state of our abandoning fighting. This is like its parallels in your saying "What is it with me that I do not do it?" or "What is it with me that I do it?" So an is a verbal noun particle in the genitive governed by an omitted preposition assumed as fī or lām of genitive, attached to what lanā is attached to.

His saying ﴿and we have been driven from our homes﴾ is a circumstantial clause explaining the reason for the denial: that is, in this state they are the furthest of people from abandoning fighting, because the causes of love of life weaken in a state of harm and turbidity through being expelled from homes and from children.

The conjunction of children to homes is because expulsion is applied both to removing a thing from its place and to removing it from among what accompanies it. There is no need to claim that the wāw is conjunctive with a deleted verb, whose assumed form is "and He removed us from our children."

His saying ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away﴾ and so on is an intervening clause. It is the locus of lesson and admonition, to warn the Muslims against the condition of these people, that they turn away from fighting after the polytheists drove them from their homes and their children, and after they had wished for fighting against their enemies, and God had prescribed it for them. The reference is to what God related of them later with His words ﴿Then when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him﴾ [2:249], and so on.

His saying ﴿And God knows the wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyīl), because their action is a form of wrongdoing: when they sought fighting, they imagined themselves to be lovers of it, and then they backed away from it. Among the finest kinds of refinement is the verse of the rajaz poet:

"He who says no when a request is made of him has not wronged; but the wrongdoer is he who says no after yes."

This verse refers to a great story from the history of the Children of Israel, because of the knowledge and lesson it contains. The Qur'an mentions historical events to teach the community the benefits of what is in history, and chooses for this what belongs to the history of the people of the revealed laws, because it is closest to the purpose for which the Qur'an came. This story is the event of the transfer of the governing system of the Children of Israel from the consultative form, expressed among them as the era of judges, to the monarchical form, expressed as the era of kings. That is because when Moses, peace be upon him, died around 1380 BCE, there succeeded him among the Israelite nation Joshua son of Nun, whom Moses had designated in the last part of his life to succeed him. When the affair of the Children of Israel came to Joshua, he made

[Page 488]

for the Children of Israel: rulers who would govern them and judge among them. He called them judges (qudah), and they were in several cities. Among these rulers were prophets, and there were also prophets who were not rulers. Each tribe of the Children of Israel acted according to what appeared right to them. Among their judges and prophets was Samuel (Samwil) son of al-Qana, of the tribe of Ephraim, judge over all the Children of Israel, and he was beloved among them. When he grew old and advanced in years, wars broke out between the Children of Israel and the Philistines, and the outcome was alternating between them. Then victory went to the Philistines, and they seized some of the villages of the Children of Israel, to the extent that the Ark of the Covenant (tabut al-'ahd), which will be discussed later, was captured by the Philistines, who took it to Ashdod, their land, and it remained in their hands for several months. When the Children of Israel saw the defeat that had befallen them, they thought that the cause of it was Samuel's weakness in managing their affairs, and they thought that the order of the Philistines' affairs was only due to the monarchical system (al-nizam al-malaki). At that time they were expecting an attack from Nahash, king of the Ammonites, against them as well. So Israel gathered, and they sent their leaders (‘urafa') from every city, and they asked Samuel to appoint for them a king who would fight with them in the way of Allah. Samuel was displeased by this, and he warned them of the consequences of rule by kings, saying: "Indeed, the king will take your sons for his service and the service of his horses, and he will make some of you run before his chariots, and he will conscript some of you as ploughmen for his tillage and as workers for his war equipment and the tools of his chariots, and he will make your daughters perfumers, cooks and bakers, and he will select the best of your fields, vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants, and he will make you slaves. Then, if you cry out on that day against your king, Allah will not answer you." They said: "We must have a king so that we may be like the rest of the nations." And he said to them: ﴿Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, refrain from fighting?﴾ They said: ﴿And why should we not fight in the way of Allah, when we have been expelled from our homes and our children?﴾ and so on.

This occurred in the early eleventh century BCE.

His saying ﴿And we have been expelled from our homes and our children﴾ implies that the Philistines took some of the cities of the Children of Israel, and this was stated in general terms in the seventh chapter of the First Book of Samuel. They also took their children captive and released their elderly and their old men. Mention of expulsion from homes and children is an incitement for the Muslim emigrants (muhajirun) to fight the polytheists who expelled them from Makkah and separated them from their wives and from their children, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And what is wrong with you that you do not fight in the way of Allah and for the oppressed among men, women and children?﴾ [al-Nisa': 75].

[Page 489]

﴿And their prophet said to them: Indeed, God has sent Talut (Ṭālūt) as king for you. They said: How can he have kingship over us, when we have a greater right to kingship than he does, and he has not been given abundant wealth? He said: Indeed, God has chosen him over you and increased him in knowledge and physique. God gives His kingship to whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

He repeated the verb in His words ﴿And their prophet said to them﴾ to indicate that this speech is not part of his earlier speech, but is another discourse, later than it. That is because, after he warned them of the consequences of monarchical rule, and warned them against turning away from fighting, he spoke with them in another speech at another time.

The emphasis of the report with *inna* (indeed) signals that this report is of a kind that is received with astonishment and doubt, as their saying ﴿How can he have kingship over us?﴾ indicates.

In the Book of Samuel (Sifr Ṣamū'īl), in chapter nine, it occurs that when the Children of Israel insisted in their request that he appoint a king for them, Samuel prayed to God Most High, and God revealed to him: Grant them whatever they ask. He did so and said to them: Go back to your cities. Then God revealed to him the description of the king whom He would appoint for them. He met a man from Benjamin named Shā'ūl ibn Qays, and he found in him the described attribute, namely that he was the tallest of the people. Samuel anointed him king over Israel, pouring oil on his head and kissing him. After some days he gathered the Children of Israel in the town of al-Muṣaffāh (Mizpah), brought him, and appointed him king over them. This was in the year 1095 BC.

This king is the one named in the verse as Ṭālūt, and he is Shā'ūl. Ṭālūt is his epithet. It is on the pattern of a verbal noun (ism maṣdar) from height (ṭūl), on the pattern *fa'lūt*, like *jabarūt* (power), *malakūt* (dominion), *rahabūt* (awe), *raghabūt* (desire), *raḥamūt* (mercy). From the same pattern is *ṭāghūt* (idolatry/tyranny), whose original form is *ṭaghayūt*, in which a metathesis occurred. Ṭālūt was described with it for emphasis regarding the great height of his stature. Perhaps it was made his epithet in the Qur'an to indicate the attribute by which he was identified to Samuel in the revelation that God sent to him, as mentioned earlier, and to correspond with Jālūt (Goliath), his adversary in war. Or that was an epithet for him among his people before he was given kingship. Only someone of general standing is given such an epithet.

The pattern *fa'lūt* is a rare pattern in Arabic, and it may be from remnants of ancient Semitic Arabic. This is what its diptotic status (its being barred from *tanwīn*) indicates, for the only reasons for its not taking *tanwīn* are proper-name status and foreignness. Al-Rāghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī) definitively stated that it is a foreign name, but it is not mentioned in the lexicographical books for this reason. Perhaps it was treated like a foreign name when it was made a name in Arabic for this foreign person. So its foreignness is incidental, and it is not foreign in origin, because this name is not known in the language of the Hebrews, as with Dāwūd (David) and Shā'ūl. It is possible that its being barred from *tanwīn* is because it becomes, through substitution, similar to the pattern *fā'ūl*, and the pattern *fā'ūl* in proper names is foreign, like Hārūt and Mārūt, Shā'ūl and Dāwūd. For this reason they also barred Qābūs from *tanwīn* and did not consider its derivation from *qabas* (a firebrand). It seems that the Qur'an's avoidance of mentioning him by the name Shā'ūl is due to the heaviness of that word and the lightness of Ṭālūt.

In His words ﴿How can he have kingship over us?﴾, *anná* means "how," and it is an interrogative used for astonishment. They were astonished at making someone like him a king. He was a peasant man from a lowly house, but he was courageous and the tallest of the people. When Samuel chose him for that, God granted him wisdom, and he prophesied many prophecies. Some of Israel accepted him, and some of them rejected him. In the Book of Samuel, those who did not accept him are said to be the sons of Belial (Belīʿāl). The Qur'an mentions that the Children of Israel said, ﴿How can he have kingship over us?﴾, and this is the truth, because they must have assumed that their king would be one of their nobles and commanders. The secret in their prophet choosing this king for them was that he wanted to preserve their consultative condition as much as possible. So he made their king one of their common people rather than their lords, so that his foothold in rule would not be firm, and it would not be feared that he would become harsh in enslaving his nation. For kings at the beginning of the founding of states are closer to goodness, because they have not yet become accustomed to the grandeur of kingship, and have not forgotten their equality with their peers. They keep expecting to be deposed. For this reason, the caliphate (khilāfa) was the sunna of Islam. Hereditary succession became the principle of kingship in Islam: when Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān designated his son Yazīd for the caliphate after him. It is thought that at that time he could not do otherwise, because the partisans of the Banū Umayya were eager for it. Then the rule of inheritance for kingship became the norm in the states of Islam, and it is one of the traditions of states from the most ancient ages of history. It is an evil practice, and for this reason you find that the founders of states are the best of the kings of their dynasties. The leaders of the Children of Israel did not perceive this wisdom because of the shortness of their vision. They looked only at his lack of lineage, and thought that this would prevent his being made king over them. They did not know that what matters is inner qualities, and that richness is the richness of the soul, not abundance of wealth. What good is abundance of wealth if one does not spend it on the public good? The rajaz poet said:

*Enough for me is the aid of the two Khubayb's;
the imam is not a miserly, grasping one.*

Their saying ﴿and we have a greater right to kingship than he does﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥāliyya*), and the pronoun is from the speakers, who are the leaders of the Children of Israel. They made the clause a circumstance to indicate that, when they mentioned their greater right to kingship, they did not need to argue for it, because this matter was established and well known among them, since they were leaders and chieftains, while Shā'ūl was a man of the common people. So this was a declaration from them of their superiority over him. His words ﴿and he has not been given abundant wealth﴾ are conjoined to the circumstantial clause, so it is a second circumstance. This is an objection that they raised, in which they considered him unfit for kingship, namely that he is poor. The duty of a king is to have wealth to meet the calamities of the nation and to spend money on provisions, gifts, and relieving the distressed. How can one who has no wealth be able to be a king? They only said this because of their deficiency in knowing the politics of nations and the system of kingship. They saw the neighboring kings living in luxury and abundance, so they thought that this was among the requirements of kingship.

Therefore their prophet answered them with His words ﴿Indeed, God has chosen him over you﴾, responding to their saying ﴿and we have a greater right to kingship than he does﴾. They based their claim on the choice of the majority, so he answered them that he is more deserving than they are because God chose him. And with His words ﴿and increased him in knowledge and physique﴾, he responded to their saying ﴿and he has not been given abundant wealth﴾, meaning: He increased him over you in knowledge and physique. Thus their prophet informed them that the qualities needed in governing the affairs of the nation return to originality of judgment and bodily strength. For by judgment one is guided to the nation's interests, especially in times of hardship, when consultation is impossible, or when the people of consultation disagree. And by strength one can stand firm in the places of battle, so that his steadfastness becomes the steadfastness of the army's souls. The Prophet placed knowledge before strength in his speech because its effect is greater. Abū al-Ṭayyib (al-Mutanabbī) said:

*Judgment comes before the courage of the brave;
it is the first, and courage is the second place.*

So the knowledge meant here is the knowledge of managing war and governing the nation. It has been said that it is the knowledge of prophecy, but this is not correct, because Ṭālūt was not counted among their prophets.

Their prophet did not answer them concerning their saying ﴿and he has not been given abundant wealth﴾, being content with the indication in his restricting himself to the words ﴿and increased him in knowledge and physique﴾. For through abundance of knowledge and through victory, wealth becomes plentiful for him, because the subjects bring wealth, as Aristotle (Arisṭāṭālīs) said. Also, even if a king is wealthy, his wealth is not enough to maintain the affairs of the kingdom. For this reason it was not a condition for rulers, from the caliph down, that they be wealthy. Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAlī ruled the nation, and they were not people of means. The wealth of the nation is in its treasury, and from it its interests are maintained and the provisions of its rulers.

The *basṭa* (expansiveness) is a noun from *basṭ*, which means breadth and spread. So *basṭa* means abundance and strength of a thing. A discussion of it will come at His words ﴿and He increased you in creation with expansiveness﴾ [al-A'rāf: 69] in Sūrat al-A'rāf.

His words ﴿God gives His kingship to whom He wills﴾ may be from the speech of the Prophet, in which case he has returned them to submission to God's command, after explaining to them some of God's wisdom in that matter. It may also be a concluding remark to the story, from the speech of God Most High, and likewise His words ﴿God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾.

[p. 493]

Their prophet said to them: "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the Ark (al-tabut) will come to you, containing tranquillity (sakina) from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind, carried by the angels. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers." ﴿وقالَ لَهم نَبِيئُهم إنَّ آيَةَ مُلْكِهِ أنْ يَأْتِيَكُمُ التّابُوتُ فِيهِ سَكِينَةٌ مِن رَبِّكم وبَقِيَّةٌ مِمّا تَرَكَ آلُ مُوسى وآلُ هارُونَ تَحْمِلُهُ المَلائِكَةُ إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً لَكم إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾

Their prophet wanted to challenge them with a miracle that would show that God, exalted is He, had chosen Saul (Shaul) as king for them. So He made for them a sign indicating this: that the Ark (tabut) would come to them, meaning the Ark of the Covenant (tabut al-'ahd), after it had been in the hand of the Philistines, as was mentioned earlier. This refers to the account of God facilitating the return of the Ark to the Children of Israel without fighting. The Philistines returned the Ark to the Children of Israel in a story mentioned in the Book of Samuel (Sifr Samu'il). Its summary is that the Ark remained for seven months in the land of Philistia, placed in the house of their idol Dagon (Dagun). The Philistines saw signs: their idol fell on its face, its hands and head were broken, and they were afflicted with hemorrhoids (bawasir) in Ashdod and its borders, and rats were set upon them, spoiling their crops. When they saw this, they consulted their priests (kahana), who advised them, by inspiration from God, to return it to Israel, because the God of Israel had become angry for His Ark. They should return it accompanied by a gift: images of five golden hemorrhoids and images of five golden mice, according to the number of the great cities of the Philistines: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. The Ark would be placed on a new cart pulled by two cows, and with it a chest containing the golden figures. They would release the two cows to go, by inspiration, to the land of Israel. They did so, and the two cows were guided until the Ark and the chest reached the hands of the Levites (al-Lawiyyin) at the borders of Beth Shemesh. This is how it occurs in the Book of Samuel. However, the apparent context of that book indicates that the Ark's return to them was before the appointment of Saul as king, whereas the explicit text of the Qur'an contradicts that. The words of the Book may be interpreted in agreement with this by taking the events as not arranged in the order of their mention, which is common in their book. What appears to me is:

[p. 494 — no, continuing; see below]

صفحة ٤٩٣

That when the Philistines learned that the Israelites had united under a king, they knew that they had only resolved upon this to seek vengeance against their enemies and to rescue the Ark of the Covenant from their hands. So they devised to show the return of the Ark because of signs they had witnessed, supposing that the fierceness of the Children of Israel would decrease if the Ark was returned to them in the manner mentioned above. It is not possible that this terror befell them before the appointment of Saul and the beginning of the emergence of his helpers.

The Ark (al-tabut) is a non-Arabic word that has been Arabicized (mu'arrab), so its pattern is fa'ul (فاعول). This pattern is rare in Arabic nouns, which indicates that whatever is on this pattern is Arabicized, like nաqus (ناقوس, bell) and namus (ناموس, lawgiver/confidant). Al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhsharī) suggested that its pattern is fa'lul (فعلول) with the middle letter vowelled, because of the scarcity of nouns whose first and last radicals are two identical letters, such as salas (سلس) and qalaq (قلق). For this reason al-Jawhari (al-Jawharī) listed it under the root t-w-b (توب), not t-b-t (تبت). The Ark (al-tabut) means an elongated chest. It is the chest that Moses, peace be upon him, was commanded to make. It was made by Bassaliel (Bassalīʾīl), who was inspired in the craft of gold, silver and copper and carpentry of wood. He made it of acacia wood (khashab al-sant), which is a tree of the kind of the qaraz (carob/tanning tree). Its length was two and a half cubits, its width one and a half cubits, and its height one and a half cubits. He overlaid it with gold inside and outside, and made for it a golden crown (iklil). He cast for it four golden rings on its four legs, and made for it two poles of wood overlaid with gold, so that they would enter the rings for carrying the Ark. He made its lid (ghita') of gold, and on the edge of the lid he made an image of two angels of gold, spreading their wings over the lid. God commanded Moses to place in this Ark the two tablets of testimony (lawhay al-shahada) that God had given him, which are the tablets that God mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses, he took up the tablets﴾ [al-A'raf: 154].

Tranquillity (al-sakina) is on the pattern fa'ila (فعيلة), meaning calm and stillness. In the hadith about walking to prayer, "Upon you is tranquillity (al-sakina)" [occurs]. This is because among the blessings of the Ark is that when it was among them in war or peace, their souls were confident of a good outcome. In it were also the books of Moses, peace be upon him, which the hearts of the nation find tranquil upon seeing and whose rulings they accept calmly. So the locative sense (zarfiyya) is figurative (majazi) according to the first interpretation, and literal (haqiqi) according to the second. In the hadith of Usayd ibn Hudayr, the term sakina is applied to something like a cloud that descends from heaven at the recitation of the Qur'an, so perhaps these are angels called by the name sakina.

The remnant (al-baqiyya) originally means what remains of something after most of it has passed. Here it is specified as what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind. These are remnants of traces of the tablets, and of the garments that Moses clothed his brother Aaron with when he appointed him priest (kahin) for the Children of Israel and guardian of matters of religion and rites of worship. It is said: among these is the staff of Moses.

It is possible that "remnant" (baqiyya) is a metaphor for the precious things, because people only guard precious things, so they remain, as al-Nabigha said:

"A remnant of a pot from pots that were heated, for the family of al-Julah, elder after elder."

This meaning has also been given for the verse of Ruwaysh al-Ta'i:

"If you sin, then your remnant comes to me, then no sin of yours escapes my notice."

That is, the group to whom you return in your affairs come to me. Close to this is the use of "talid" (تليد) for the old inherited wealth.

What is meant by "the family of Moses and the family of Aaron" is the people of their households: the descendants of Aaron, for they are the kin (usba) of Moses, since Moses did not leave children. Or what their families left behind is their traces, which reverts to the meaning "what Moses and Aaron and their families left behind." Or it is meant "what Moses and Aaron left behind," and the word "family" (al) is inserted, as in His saying: ﴿Admit the family of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 46].

Aaron is the brother of Moses, peace be upon them both. He is Aaron son of Imran, of the tribe of Levi. He was born before Pharaoh ordered the killing of the infant sons of the Children of Israel, and he was older than Moses. When God spoke to Moses about the mission, He informed him that He would associate his brother Aaron with him, so that he would be like a vizier to him. Revelation was also sent to Aaron. Moses was the greatest messenger, and most of God's revelation to Aaron was through Moses' tongue. God made Aaron the first priest of the Children of Israel when he established for them the service of the Tent of Worship, and He placed the priesthood in his descendants, so they are singled out with rulings that the rest of the nation does not share, among them the prohibition of wine for the priest. Aaron died in the year 1458 or 1457 BC, on Mount Hor, on the borders of the land of Edom, during the wandering period (al-tih), in the third year after the Exodus from Egypt.

His saying ﴿carried by the angels﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the Ark. The word "carrying" (al-hamal) here means transporting, as in His saying: ﴿[You said], "I cannot find anything to carry you upon"﴾ [al-Tawba: 92], because a riding beast carries its rider, and for this it is called a ḥumūla (حمولة, pack/transport animal). In the hadith of the Battle of Khaybar: "The donkeys were their transport animals (ḥumūlatuhum)." And al-Nabigha said:

صفحة ٤٩٥

"The shepherd of the transport animals imagines it to be a bird."

So the meaning of the angels carrying the Ark is that they drove, by God's permission, the two cows that were pulling the cart on which the Ark was placed, to the settlement of the Children of Israel, without the two of them having previously been accustomed to walking in that direction. This is what agrees with what is in the books of the Children of Israel.

His saying ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾ — the demonstrative refers to the whole situation, i.e., the Ark's return from the hands of your enemies to you without fighting; and to what the Ark contains of the relics of Moses, peace be upon him; and to its arrival without a driver and without a previous habituation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 249–250 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then when Talut set out with the troops, he said: "Indeed, Allah will test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who scoops up a handful with his hand." But they drank from it, except a few of them. Then when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him, they said: "We have no power today against Jalut and his troops." Those who were certain that they would meet Allah said: "How many a small company has overcome a large company by Allah's permission! And Allah is with the patient."﴾ ﴿And when they went out to face Jalut and his troops, they said: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make our feet firm, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ ﴿So they routed them by Allah's permission, and Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom and taught him what He willed.﴾ (al-Baqarah: 251)

The particle *fa* (ف) conjoins the clause "lamma fasala Talut" (when Talut set out) to the clause "wa qala lahum nabiyyuhum inna Allaha qad ba'atha lakum" (Qur'an 2:247: "And their prophet said to them, 'Indeed, Allah has sent you Talut as king'"), because the sending of a king for the sake of fighting necessarily entails going out to the fighting for which they had asked for a prophet to be sent. Between the two clauses a great deal has been omitted, which is implied: their acceptance of the kingship, the coming of the Ark (al-tabut), and the mustering of the troops; for all of this is indicated by the clause "Talut set out with the troops."

The meaning of "fasala bi-l-junud" is: he cut off and moved away with them, i.e., they went beyond their dwellings and villages from which they had departed. It is a transitive verb (fi'l muta'addin), because its original sense is the separation of one thing from another; then they made it transitive to the agent, saying *fasala nafsahu* (he separated himself), until it came to mean *infasala* (to separate, to depart). *When you approached the banners of Tayy, and Tayy were in the caves and the ravines,*
