He means that the one who has practiced war repeatedly does not drink, because he does not tire of running and exertion; if he is restrained, it is lighter for him and quicker. Verse 249–250 (part 2 of 2):

The verse, in His saying ﴿so they routed them﴾ and so on, alludes to the victory of the Children of Israel over the Philistines. It was a great victory, through which the Children of Israel succeeded in Palestine and the land of the Amalekites, despite their small numbers. Their historians said: When Ṭālūt (Saul) went out to fight the Philistines, he gathered an army of three thousand men. When they saw the multitude of the Philistines, severe distress overcame them, and most of the army hid in the mountain of Ephraim, in the caves, thickets and wells, and they did not cross the Jordan. Ṭālūt was perplexed, and Ṣamū'īl (Samuel) sought guidance, and he went out to fight. When he crossed the river Jordan, he counted the army with him and found only about six hundred men. Then battles took place in which victory went to the Children of Israel, and those who had been cowardly and hidden in the caves and elsewhere took courage, came out after the Philistines, and seized abundant spoils. In those days, in the books of the Jews, there is no clarification of the length of time between the events, nor any specification of what came earlier or later, and there are unsuitable transitions in the narratives. Dāwūd (David) son of Yassā (Jesse), the Jew, appeared when God revealed to Ṣamū'īl that he should go to the house of Yassā in Bethlehem and anoint the youngest of Yassā's sons to be king over Israel after a time. God guided Dāwūd to Shā'ūl, "Ṭālūt", by a wondrous decree, so he found favour with Shā'ūl. Dāwūd had previously been a shepherd of his father's flock, and he was possessed of courage, vigour, and good bearing, and he had excellence in the use of the sling. One day the Philistines met the army of Ṭālūt, and a chief of the Philistines named Jalyāt (Goliath) came out, as was mentioned earlier. No one was able to face him in single combat, so Dāwūd stepped forward to him and struck him with the sling, and the stone hit his forehead and felled him to the ground. Dāwūd mounted him, drew his sword, and cut off his head, and he took it to Shā'ūl, and the Philistines were routed. Shā'ūl married his daughter named Mīkāl to Dāwūd, and after a time Dāwūd became king in place of Shā'ūl. Then God gave him prophethood, so he became a prophet-king, and He taught him of what He willed.

The mention of Dāwūd will come at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Ibrāhīm against his people﴾ [al-An'ām: 83], in the chapter of al-An'ām.

Dāwūd had previously been a shepherd of his father's flock, and he was possessed of courage, vigour, and good bearing, and he had excellence in the use of the sling. One day the Philistines met the army of Ṭālūt, and a chief of the Philistines named Jalyāt (Goliath) came out, as was mentioned earlier. No one was able to face him in single combat, so Dāwūd stepped forward to him and struck him with the sling, and the stone hit his forehead and felled him to the ground. Dāwūd mounted him, drew his sword, and cut off his head, and he took it to Shā'ūl, and the Philistines were routed. Shā'ūl married his daughter named Mīkāl to Dāwūd, and after a time Dāwūd became king in place of Shā'ūl. Then God gave him prophethood, so he became a prophet-king, and He taught him of what He willed.

The mention of Dāwūd will come at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Ibrāhīm against his people﴾ [al-An'ām: 83], in the chapter of al-An'ām.

(Page 501)

This great verse concludes all the wondrous events which the preceding verses alluded to. Its purpose is to remove from the attentive listener whatever doubt arises in him about seeking the wisdom behind the occurrence of these events and their like in this world. Moreover, the content of this verse is a lesson among the lessons of the created universe, and a wisdom among the wisdoms of history and the systems of civilization, which no one had been guided to before the revelation of this verse and before grasping what it contains. It is joined to the preceding lessons just as His saying (﴿And their Prophet said to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247]) and what follows it of verse-endings were joined. The usual practice in such cases of omitting the conjunction (*'atf*) and adopting the path of *isti'naf* (beginning a new sentence) was set aside here. Nafi', Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read (﴿wa-law la difa'u Allahi al-nas﴾) with the *mufa'ala* form (*difa'*), while the majority (al-Jumhur) read *dafa'* in the simple form.

*Al-difa'* is the verbal noun of *dafa'a*, which here carries the sense of intensification (*mubalagha*) of *daf'*, not the sense of reciprocity (*mufa'ala*). This is like the saying of Musa Jabir al-Hanafi:

*"O people, I desire nothing but to be reluctant at the door of the commander, nor the repelling of the chamberlain."*

Its attribution to God is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), as in His saying ﴿Indeed, God defends those who believe﴾ [al-Hajj: 38], meaning He repels, because the one who actually repels, in common usage, is the one who directly carries out the repelling. It is attributed to God because He is the One who decreed it and decreed its causes. For this reason He said ﴿some of them by means of others﴾, making some of them the cause of the repelling. This is of the same type as: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw﴾ [al-Anfal: 17]. The original meaning of *daf'* is striking with the hand to push something away from a target. The poet said:

*"So I pushed it, and it pushed back."*

It is a defense of the interest of the one who repels. The meaning of the verse is: were it not for the occurrence of some people repelling others by God's creation and His placing within the repeller the power of repelling and its motives, the earth would be corrupted, that is, those upon the earth, and the order of what is upon it would be disrupted. That is because when God Most High created the existing beings upon the earth in their kinds, types, and categories, He created them susceptible to dissolution (*idmihlal*), and He deposited in their individuals laws indicating that God's purpose was their survival until a term He willed. For this reason we find the law of succession (*qanun al-khalafiyya*) pervading all types of existing beings. Every kind has within its individuals the power to produce similar ones, so that these similar ones may be successors to the individuals when they dissolve. This power is what is expressed as procreation in animals, seeding in plants, exudation in minerals, and generation in chemical elements. The presence of this power in all existing beings is the first proof that their Originator willed the survival of the kinds, just as He willed the dissolution of the individuals at appointed terms, due to deficiency or loss of their fitness. From this we know that God, the Creator of these universes, does not love their corruption. We have already explained His saying ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and animals; and God does not like corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205].

Then, God Most High, just as He deposited in all beings perceptions by which they are led, with or without reflection, to what is good for them and their survival, like the infant's movement to suckle the breast and the young of animals' movement to the udders and pastures, then these perceptions expand, and from them branches out everything that brings about the attraction of what is beneficial and suitable, through insight and habituation. This is called the appetitive faculty (*al-quwwa al-shahiya*). He also deposited in all beings perceptions by which they are impelled to defend themselves and to repel assailants, without insight, such as putting the hand between an attacker and the face, and a cow lowering its head upon merely sensing what is charging at it, without reflecting on the superiority of the attacker's strength over the defender's. Then these perceptions expand and branch out into everything that repels harm, from beginning with destroying whoever is expected to harm, to seeking shelter, to taking up weapons, and to resisting the enemy when destruction is expected, even with the last of one's strength. This is the irascible faculty (*al-quwwa al-ghadiba*). For this reason the power of defense increases in intensity as the expectation of dangers grows, even in animals. And what God has placed in all kinds of existing beings of causes of harm against one who intends them evil is the clearest proof that God created them for the willing of their survival. He has compensated man, in place of what He gave to animals, with intellect and thought to devise escape from one who intends him harm, and to inflict harm upon the one who intends it against him before he targets him, which is expressed as preparedness (*al-isti'dad*). Then He, Most High, made for each kind, or each individual, characteristics in which there are benefits for others and for itself, so that each would be eager for the survival of the other. This is a general law. And He made man, through the intellect He deposited in him, the one who dominates the rest of the kinds, and He made for him knowledge of the characteristics that are in the kinds, and of the benefits that are in the individuals of his own kind.

Thus God Most High established the causes of defense as a kind of repelling from God, who repels the one who intends harm by means that the intended victim employs. Were it not for these means which God Most High entrusted to individuals of the kinds, the appetite of the strong would intensify toward destroying the weak, and the boldness of whoever seeks benefit for himself would intensify to the point of seizing benefits he finds in others and taking them from them. The individuals of each kind would exceed in drawing suitable benefit to themselves by depriving others of the suitable benefit that belongs to them. And the one in need, at the time of need, would forget that the survival of the other is also a benefit to him. Thus every possessor of desire would dominate others, and every strong one would dominate his weak counterpart, so that the strong destroys the weak, and the stronger destroys the strong, and individuals perish one after another, and the kinds likewise, until only the strongest individuals of the strongest kinds remain, and that is a small number. Then, when only one remains, he is deprived of many needs that he cannot find in himself, but which he used to find in others: from individuals of his own kind, as the need of human beings for one another, or from other kinds, as the need of man for the cow. Then it goes to waste.

Since the human kind is the one that dominates the rest of the beings of the earth, and is the one in whose individuals all developments and endeavors appear, the verse addressed it specifically, saying ﴿Were it not for God's repelling people, some by means of others, the earth would be corrupted﴾, since God placed in man the appetitive power for his survival and the survival of his kind, and placed in him the irascible power to check the one who excessively pursues benefit for himself. In that is the preservation of the rest of the kinds, because man defends them in their survival against what would harm his benefit.

By this defense the safety of the strong is achieved, which is evident, and also the safety of the weak, because when the strong finds exertion and troubles in seeking benefit, he tires of it and limits himself to what necessity calls for. What results, were it not for defense, would be corruption rather than righteousness, because corruption is often what the appetitive power is impelled toward by what is found in most corrupt things of immediate, short-lived pleasures; for in many souls, or most of them, there is an inclination toward many corruptions; and because the nature of wicked souls is not to regard the harm they inflict on others, unlike righteous souls. Wicked souls are more prone to violating the sanctities of others. And because corrupt deeds are quicker to produce their effects and to spread, so that a little of them overtakes much of what is good. Therefore, undoubtedly, were it not for people repelling one another, such that the righteous among them repel the corrupters, the corruption would quickly spread into their condition, and corruption would engulf their affairs in the briefest time.

The greatest manifestations of this defense are wars. By an unjust war the aggressor seeks to seize the benefits of others, and by a just war the righteous obtains justice from the wrongdoer. For them, factions and calls to truth are formed, and there is the subduing of wrongdoers and the defeat of disbelievers.

Furthermore, the repelling of people from one another restrains the corrupter from attempting corruption, and the very awareness of the corrupter that others are prepared to repel him restrains him from plunging into many corruptions.

As for the meaning of "the corruption of the earth": either it is the corruption of the human community, as indicated by the linking of the repelling to "people," meaning the people of the earth would be corrupted; or it is the corruption of everything that is susceptible to corruption, in which case there is an ellipsis (*ihtibak*) in the verse. The estimated sense is: "Were it not for God's repelling people, some by means of others, and the rest of existing beings, some by means of others, the earth would be corrupted," that is, those upon the earth, and the people would be corrupted.

The verse is given in the mode of bestowing favor (*imtinan*). For this reason He, Most High, said ﴿the earth would be corrupted﴾, because We do not love the corruption of the earth; for in its corruption, in the sense of the corruption of what is upon it, is the disruption of Our order and the loss of the causes of Our felicity. Therefore He followed it with His saying ﴿But God is full of bounty toward the worlds﴾. This is a corrective exception (*istidrak*) from what is implied by "were it not" (*lawla*) concerning the supposition of the absence of defense, because the original of *lawla* is *law* (if) combined with the negating *la* (not): that is, "if the absence of defense were present, the earth would be corrupted." This corrective exception in this verse is the strongest proof that *lawla* is composed of *law* and *la*, since the corrective exception cannot be completed upon His saying ﴿the earth would be corrupted﴾, because the corruption of the earth is not occurring after assuming the existence of defense, if we say that *lawla* is a particle of the impossibility of something because of the existence of something else. He linked the bounty to all the worlds, because this favor is not specific to any one of them.

The reference is to what the past narratives contain and the lessons in them. But the lofty wisdoms lie in His saying: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling people, some by means of others...﴾ [2:251]. He has placed these narratives in the position of something witnessed, because of their clarity and explicitness. They were called "signs" (āyāt) because they are indications of the greatness of Allah's governance and the vastness of His knowledge.

His saying ﴿And indeed you are among the messengers﴾ is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ): to honor his status, to strengthen his heart, and as an allusion to those who deny his message. The emphasis of the sentence with inna is for attention to this report. He said "among the messengers" rather than "and indeed you are the Messenger of Allah," to refute the deniers by reminding them that he was not a novelty among the messengers, that He sent him as He sent those before him, and that there is nothing in his condition that falls short of theirs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 253 (part 1 of 2):

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
﴿These messengers – We preferred some of them over others. Among them are those to whom God spoke, and some He raised in rank by degrees. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit.﴾
The position of this verse is that of a summary (fadhlaka) for what precedes it and an introduction (muqaddima) to what follows. As for the first: when God related the testing of the messengers Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and what befell them with their peoples, and concluded that with His saying: ﴿These are the signs of God which We recite to you in truth﴾ [al-Baqara: 252], He gathered all of that in His saying ﴿These messengers﴾, drawing attention to the lessons contained within all of it. And when He had finished all that, He followed it with His saying ﴿And indeed you are among the messengers﴾ [al-Baqara: 252], reminding that His informing him of the histories of the nations and the messengers is itself a sign of the truth of his mission, since no one like him could have knowledge of that except through the revelation of God to him. In all of this there is a proof against the polytheists and against the People of the Book who denied the mission of Muhammad ﷺ. Thus the position of the demonstrative is like its position in the verse of al-Nabigha:
"The sons of his paternal uncle, Dunya and 'Amr ibn 'Amir – those are a people whose might is not false."
The demonstrative referring to the group of messengers in His saying ﴿And indeed you are among the messengers﴾ [al-Baqara: 252] was used because of what it carries of the indication of presence, so that the group of messengers seems present to the hearer after the mention of the wondrous states of some of them and what followed of their mention in a general manner.
As for the second: when the discourse on fighting and on exhorting to jihad and taking lesson from the fighting of past nations was extended, it was followed by [the statement] that had God willed, people would not have differed concerning the matter of religion after clear proofs had come to them; but they misunderstood, so they denied the clear proofs, and their misunderstanding led them to an extreme of disagreement among themselves, until it led to fighting. Thus the position of the demonstrative according to this consideration is like the position of the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), meaning: it is the story of the messengers and their nations – We preferred some messengers over others, so some nations envied the followers of some messengers; the Jews denied Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, and the Christians denied Muhammad ﷺ.
The demonstrative was joined to the particle of distance (kāf al-bu'd) to express the elevated status of these [messengers], as in His saying ﴿That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqara: 2].
Page 6
The demonstrative is the subject (mubtada') and "the messengers" is the predicate (khabar). "The messengers" is not an apposition (badal), because informing about the group by saying that they are the messengers is more effective in evoking the wondrous group whose matter is amazing and whose report is dazzling. The clause "We preferred" is a circumstantial clause (hal).
The purpose of this verse is to glorify the reputation of the messengers, peace be upon them, and to teach the Muslims that this good community, despite its great standing, God has preferred some of it over others. The causes of preference are known only to God, Exalted, though they return to what took place at their hands of good that benefits mankind and of the support of truth, and what they suffered of harm in that path, and what they were strengthened with of great laws that differ in the guidance of mankind, and in the generality and durability of that guidance. And if the Messenger ﷺ said: "That God guides a man through you is better for you than what the sun rises upon," then how about those through whom God guided nations across successive eras? For this reason Muhammad ﷺ was the most excellent of the messengers. The discourse includes praise of them and consolation for the Messenger, peace be upon him, regarding what he met from his people.
God has singled out some of the messengers from among them with attributes by which the intended one is specified, or by mention of his name. He mentioned three when He said ﴿Among them are those to whom God spoke﴾, and this is Moses, peace be upon him, for his fame for this great trait in the Qur'an. He mentioned Jesus, peace be upon him, and placed between them an allusion to Muhammad ﷺ by his description, in His saying ﴿and some He raised in rank by degrees﴾.
His saying ﴿and some He raised in rank by degrees﴾ necessarily means by "some" here one specific messenger, not a group, and "degrees" are levels of excellence established for that one; for if "some" meant an indefinite group of messengers and "degrees" meant degrees among them, the statement would be a repetition of His saying ﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾. Moreover, if what was meant were "some preferred over some," He would have said: "and raised some of them above others in degrees," as He said in the other verse ﴿and raised some of you above others in degrees﴾ [al-An'am: 165].
Accordingly, the shift from explicitly naming or from the well-known description is for the purpose of avoiding embarrassment toward the Propagator, who is the intended one of this description, namely Muhammad ﷺ. The Arabs use "some" to refer to the self, as in the words of Labid:
"Abandoner of places when I do not inhabit them, or whose death-pang seizes some of the souls."
Page 7
He meant himself.
And [they use it] to refer to the addressee, as in the words of Abu al-Tayyib:
"If some people are a sword for a dynasty, then among people there are trumpets for it and drums."
What determines the intended meaning in all of this is the context, such as the applicability of the predicate or description to one person, as in the words of Tarafa:
"When the people say, 'Who is the youth?' I think it is I who is meant; I did not hesitate and I was not dull."
There has come, in the manner of this verse, His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿And We did not send you as a guardian over them﴾ [al-Isra: 54] ﴿And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth. And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ [al-Isra: 55]) following His saying ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier﴾ [al-Isra: 45], up to His saying ﴿And say to My servants that they should say that which is best﴾ [al-Isra: 53], up to His saying: (﴿And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ [al-Isra: 55]).
This is an announcement that some messengers are more excellent than others in a general manner, without specifying which is superior among the preferred. That is because each group that shares a quality of goodness must necessarily have some of them more excellent than others by virtue of attributes of perfection that some possess beyond the quality they share. In distinguishing the attributes of preference there is obscurity and a possibility of error and of falling into mistake, and this is not easy for minds prone to heedlessness and error. So when the preference has been reported by the Lord of all and the One to whom preference belongs, it is not within the station of people to take it upon themselves to place the messengers in their ranks; it is enough for them to stop at what God informs them of in His Book or upon the tongue of His Messenger.
This is the context of the sound hadith: "Do not prefer among the prophets," meaning by it the prohibition of detailed preference, unlike preference in a general manner, as we say: the messengers are more excellent than the prophets who are not messengers. It is established that Muhammad ﷺ is the most excellent of the messengers, because of what has been manifest of verses about his preference, the preference of the religion he brought, and the preference of the Book revealed to him. These are closely related in indication, by explicit statement and by clarity; yet their multiplicity produces certainty in their combined meanings, in accordance with the principle: "The multiplicity of apparent indications yields certainty." The greatest of them is the verse ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets: whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must support him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81], and so on.

As for the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "None of you should say, 'I am better than Jonah son of Matta'," by "I" he meant himself according to the more likely of the two possibilities. And his saying: "Do not prefer me over Moses" was said before God informed him that he is the most excellent of creation in His sight.
These degrees are many. Among what we have come to know of them: the generality of the message to all of mankind; its permanence throughout time; its being the seal of the messages; the support by the great miracle which is not confused with sorcery and charlatanry; the permanence of that miracle and the possibility for everyone who prepares himself to grasp the miraculous nature of it to witness it; the founding of his law upon the preservation of benefits and the averting of harms, and the bringing of souls to the peak of perfection; the facilitation of the condemnation of his opponents; his being granted possession of their land, homes and wealth within a short time; the transmission of his miracle being made mass-transmitted (mutawatir), so that none but an obstinate person is ignorant of it; and the sight by his community of his noble grave and the possibility for them to draw near to it and find intimacy with it. He has joined what indicates our Prophet ﷺ to what indicates Moses, peace be upon them both, because of the strong resemblance between their two laws, since the law of Moses, peace be upon him, was the most extensive of the laws before it, unlike the law of Jesus, peace be upon him.
God's speaking to Moses is what He revealed to him without the intermediary of Gabriel, by making him hear speech that he was certain proceeded from God's creating, by God creating sounds in the language of Moses that contained the fundamentals of the law. The explanation of this will come at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And God spoke to Moses directly﴾ [al-Nisa: 164] in Surat al-Nisa.
As for His saying: ﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾: "clear proofs" are the manifest, evident miracles; and the Holy Spirit is Gabriel, for "spirit" here means the particular angel, as in His saying ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr: 4].
"Qudus" with a damma on the qaf and a damma on the dal according to the people of the Hijaz, and with its sukun according to Banu Tamim, means purity and holiness. So the idiom "Holy Spirit" is an annexation of the qualified to the qualifier, and for this one says "al-Ruh al-Qudus." It has also been said that "Qudus" is a name of God like "al-Quddus," so the annexation of "spirit" to it is an original annexation, meaning: a spirit from among the angels of God.

The Holy Spirit is Gabriel, as God said: ﴿Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth﴾ [al-Nahl: 102]. In a hadith: "Indeed the Holy Spirit breathed into my heart that no soul will die until it completes its term." And in a hadith the Prophet ﷺ said to Hassan: "Satirize them, and the Holy Spirit is with you."
Jesus was described with these two, although all the other messengers were supported with clear proofs and with the Holy Spirit, in order to refute the Jews who denied his mission and his miracles, and to refute the Christians who exaggerated and claimed his divinity. For this reason his mother's name is mentioned along with him whenever he is mentioned, to point out that the son of man cannot be a god, and that Mary is the servant of God, not a consort; for the Arabs do not mention the names of their women but use kunyas, saying "the mistress of the house," "the family," and the like. They mention women's names only in love poetry, or the names of female slaves.

Then it is permissible that the pronoun annexed in His saying "from after them" refers to the totality of the messengers, meaning: and had God willed, those who fought one another after those messengers, from the nations differing in creed,

It is also possible that the pronoun in "from after them" (min ba'dihim) refers to the messengers, with a distributive sense, meaning: those who came after each one of the messengers. The sense would then be that the community of each messenger differed and fought, a difference and fighting that arose from some of them declaring others to be unbelievers, as happened to the Children of Israel in many eras, when some groups among them reached the point of leaving the religion to the extent of worshipping idols, and as happened to the Christians in eras when their differences reached the point that some declared others to be unbelievers. Thus the Jews fought more than once, in a war that took place between the Kingdom of Judah and the Kingdom of Israel, and the Christians likewise fought as a result of the dispute between the Jacobites (al-Ya'aqiba) and the Melkites (al-Malakiyya) before Islam. The most famous wars of the Christians are the great wars that arose in the sixteenth century of the Christian era between the adherents of Catholicism and the adherents of the doctrine of Luther, the German monk, who called people to reform Christianity and considered the followers of the Catholic Church to be unbelievers for their claim of the divinity of Christ. Because of this, great wars broke out between France, Spain, Germany, England, and other states of Europe.

The aim is to warn the Muslims against falling into the like of what those people fell into. The Prophet (ﷺ) warned against this with a warning reported through multiple chains, in his saying in the Farewell Pilgrimage sermon: "Do not revert after me to disbelief, striking one another's necks." This warns them against what happened in the Wars of Apostasy (Hurub al-Ridda) and the wars of the Kharijites (Khawarij) on the pretext of takfir (declaring others unbelievers). This admonition is among the great proofs of prophethood.

It is related in the Sahih: "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is the killer, but what about the killed?" He said: "Indeed he was eager to kill his brother." This explains part of it by part of it: that it refers to fighting over differences in creed.

In this reading, "the clear signs" means the clear evidences of the Sharia that distinguish the follower of the Sharia from its opponent, and that do not admit misunderstanding and misinterpretation, if their habit had not been stubbornness and rejecting the religion for the sake of worldly gain. The meaning is that Allah willed their fighting and so they fought, and He willed their disagreement and so they disagreed. The "will" here is the will of creation and decree, not the will of approval, because the speech is framed as a wish for an answer and a lament over its impossibility and non-existence, expressed by "law" (lau), like the saying of Tarafa:

"Had my Lord willed, I would have been Qays ibn Khalid,
and had my Lord willed, I would have been 'Amr ibn Mathad."

His saying ﴿but they differed﴾ is an exception (istidrak) to what is implied in the response of "If Allah had willed," which is: "they would not have fought." But he mentioned in the exception the necessary opposite of the response of "law," which is disagreement, because when they disagreed they fought, and had they not disagreed they would not have fought. The necessary opposite was brought in the exception only to indicate the cause of the fighting, so that it becomes clear that the meaning of negating Allah's will for their not fighting is that He created among them the motive of disagreement, and through that motive they disagreed, and the disagreement drove them to its extreme, which is disagreement over creed, so some of them believed and some disbelieved, and so they fought, because the necessary result of this state being fighting is a common customary matter. If the intended meaning is the disagreement of the community of a single messenger, then belief and disbelief in the verse express the error of the adherents of the religion regarding it, to the degree that it leads some of them to disbelief in it. If the intended meaning is the disagreement of the communities of the messengers with one another, as in His saying ﴿The Jews said: the Christians are not upon anything﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:113], then belief and disbelief in the verse are apparent: that is, some of them believed in the final Messenger and followed him, and some of them disbelieved in him and opposed him, so the two groups fought.

Whichever of the two interpretations is meant, His saying ﴿Some of them believed and some of them disbelieved﴾ indicates that disagreement which does not reach the point where some of the disagreeing parties declare others' faith to be disbelief does not drive the disagreeing parties to fight. For in what Allah has established for them of the clear signs of the Sharia there is sufficiency to settle the disagreement among the disputants, provided that stubbornness and desire have not overcome them, or that bad understanding and scarcity of guidance have not overtaken them.

Undoubtedly, Allah the Exalted placed in the natural constitution of minds the difference of inclinations and understandings, and placed in the differences of intelligence and originality of opinion causes for the difference of the principles of sciences and schools of thought. The causes of disagreement are therefore rooted in human natures. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿Had Allah willed, those who came after them would not have fought﴾

Page 12

Then He said: ﴿But they differed,﴾ so the meaning becomes: had Allah willed, they would not have differed. But disagreement is rooted in the innate nature. Nevertheless, Allah has also placed in the minds fundamental principles that are certain (qat'iyya) or probable to a degree close to certainty, by which minds are able to identify the truth from among differing opinions. What turned people away from following it was only the remote interpretations that stubbornness leads them to, or the dislike of appearing defeated, or love of praise from partisans and people of interests, or pursuit of some immediate worldly gain. Had Allah willed, He would not have implanted in the constitution of souls the motives that incline toward these bad thoughts, and they would not have disagreed with a lasting disagreement. But they disagreed in this way, so some of them believed and some of them disbelieved. Therefore there is no excuse for fighting except between two parties: a believer, and a disbeliever in what the other believes. For the anger and zealotry arising from disagreement in religion have long been a cause of fighting. As for disagreement arising among adherents of one religion that does not reach the point of takfir, it should not be a cause of fighting.

For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says to his brother, 'O disbeliever!', then it returns upon one of them." Because if he attributes disbelief to his brother in religion, he has taken up the causes of dividing the Muslims and generating the cause of fighting. So he himself bears the sin of disbelief, since he is the one who causes what follows from disbelief. And because if he regards some aspects of faith as disbelief, he has himself become a disbeliever, since he has made faith into disbelief. The Prophet (peace be upon him) also said: "Do not revert after me to disbelief, striking one another's necks," so he made fighting the emblem of takfir. The Muslims became deaf to this noble advice, and they disagreed to the point of takfir and fighting. The first of this was the disagreement of the Apostasy in the time of Abu Bakr, then the disagreement of the Harurites (al-Haruriyya) in the time of 'Ali, who declared 'Ali an unbeliever for accepting arbitration (tahkim) of the two arbiters. Then the disagreement of the followers of al-Muqanna' in Khurasan, who claimed divinity and took a golden face (veil), who appeared in the year 159 and perished in the year 163. Then the disagreement of the Qaramita with the rest of the Muslims, in which there is a trace of doctrinal disagreement, because they were originally from the Shia, then they went to extremes and became unbelievers, claiming incarnation (hulul), meaning the indwelling of the Lord in creatures. They uprooted the Black Stone from the Ka'ba and took it to their land in Bahrain, and that was from the year 293. The Muslims also disagreed greatly over schools of thought, which at times drew them into great battles. The most numerous of these were the wars of the non-takfiri Kharijites against the rest of the community in the East; the battles of Abu Yazid al-Nakkari the Kharijite in Qayrawan and elsewhere in the year 333; the fighting between the Shia and Ahl al-Sunna in Qayrawan in the year 407; the fighting of the Shafi'is and Hanbalis in Baghdad in the year 475; the fighting between the Shia and Ahl al-Sunna there in the year 445, followed by repeated evil incidents among them until they reconciled in the year 502 and the evil between them ended; and the fighting of the Batiniyya, known as the Isma'iliyya, against Ahl al-Sunna in Saweh and elsewhere from the year 494 to the year 523. Then it turned into political battles, and then they became supporters of Islam in the Crusader wars. And other battles arising from takfir and misguidance. We do not mention other battles of states and parties that gnawed at the bones of Islam and reached every side of it, even the Sacred City.

Page 13

Thus the verse indicates wonder and warning at the conduct of nations in fighting over their differences, since they did not reach, in soundness of intellect or in purity of intentions, the means by which they could avoid fighting. So they are blamed from this aspect. It also indicates that had Allah willed, He would have created them beforehand in a more perfect state than they are in, so that they would be prepared thereby for guidance to the truth and for foresight into consequences before that critical time. Thus the negation of the will relates to the wisdom of creation, while blame and regret relate to shortcoming in carrying out the Sharia. For this reason He said: ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have fought, but Allah does what He wills.﴾ He repeated ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have fought﴾ as emphasis of the first, and as a preparation for His saying ﴿but Allah does what He wills,﴾ so that the reader of the words of Allah the Exalted knows that in the guidance of Allah there is sufficiency for them, if they wished to be guided, just as He created the angels. Allah creates what He wills, but He perfects the state of creation through guidance and direction, and they neglect that.

[Page 14]

The position of this verse is like the position of "Who is it that will loan Allah a good loan" [al-Baqarah: 245], and so on. When He called them to give up their lives in fighting in the way of Allah, saying, "And fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is Hearing, Knowing" [al-Baqarah: 244], He followed this with a call to spend wealth in jihad, saying, "Who is it that will loan Allah a good loan, so that He multiplies it for him many times over" [al-Baqarah: 245], in the same manner as His saying, "And strive with your wealth and your lives in the way of Allah" [al-Tawbah: 41]. This verse serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil) of the verse "Who is it that will loan Allah a good loan," because the wording of this verse shows more clearly the intention of the general spending required in Islam. Thus the meaning of spending here is broader than spending in the way of Allah. For this reason the object and the complement have been omitted, to move on to the command to give obligatory charity (sadaqat) and other forms of giving. Verses will come that detail this.

His saying, "from what We have provided for you," is an exhortation to spend and an assertion of entitlement to it.

His saying, "before there comes a Day," is another exhortation, because it reminds them that there is a time at which deeds come to an end and the making up of what was missed becomes impossible. The Day is the Day of Resurrection. The negation of trade (bay'), friendship (khullah) and intercession (shafa'ah) is a metaphor (kinayah) for the impossibility of making up for what has been lost. A person obtains what he lacks by means of exchange, which is expressed by trade, or by benefiting from others, which happens through friendship, or through the mediation of an intermediary to someone who is not a close friend.

Khullah, with a dammah on the kha', means affection and companionship. It is permissible to pronounce it with a kasrah on the kha', though no one reads it that way. Khullah with a dammah is also used to mean a friend, as a verbal noun (masdar) used for the person, so that the singular and the plural, and the masculine and the feminine, are alike in it. Al-Hamasi said:

Ala abligha khullati Rashidan wa sinwi qadiman idha ma ittasal
(Lo, convey to my friend Rashid, and to my kinsman of old, whenever we are united.)

And Ka'b said:
Akrim biha khullatan... [the rest of the verse].
(How noble a friend she is...)

So it is permissible that khullah here means affection, and the negation of affection in this sense means the negation of its effect, which is protection of a friend, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "And fear a Day when no parent will avail his child, nor will a child avail his parent at all" [Luqman: 33]. It is also permissible that the negation of friendship is a metaphor for the negation of its necessary consequence, which is benefit, as in His saying: "The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit" [al-Shu'ara': 88]. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

Wa qala kullu khalilin kuntu amulahu ∗∗∗ la ulhinannaka inni 'anka mashghul
(Every friend I had hoped for said: "Do not let me distract you, for I am preoccupied with myself.")

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "la bay'un fihi" (no trade therein) and what follows with a nominative ending (raf'), because trade, friendship and intercession are necessarily meant as genera (ajnas), since they are names of abstract meanings that have no individual instances outside the mind. They are therefore generic names, not indefinite nouns (nakirat). For this reason, their negation does not allow the meaning of negating a single instance, so that when the intention is to explicitly state the negation of the genus, there is no need to build the noun on a fathah. This differs from expressions such as "la rajula fi al-dar" (there is no man in the house) and "la ilaha illa Allah" (there is no god but Allah). For this reason, the transmitted report of one of the women in the story of Umm Zar' reads: "My husband is like the night of Tihamah: neither hot nor cold, neither fearful nor weary," with the nominative only, because these are generic names, as in this verse. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read with a fathah to negate the genus explicitly. The two readings are equal in meaning. It is a forced interpretation here to say, as al-Baydawi did, that the reason for the nominative reading is that the negation stands as an answer to a questioner who asks: "Is there trade therein, or friendship, or intercession?"

Shafa'ah (intercession) is mediation in seeking benefit, and striving with one whose pleasure is wanted, to obtain it for one who is under his displeasure, or to remove estrangement or hatred between two parties. It derives from shaf', the opposite of witr (odd). One says: shafa'a, like manaa, when he made a thing into a pair (shaf'); and shafa'a also, like manaa, when he strove to win satisfaction or the like, because the one who is displeased with or deprived of something moves away from the one he is connected to, and so becomes odd (witr). When the intercessor strives to bring benefit and satisfaction, he has restored them to a pair. Thus intercession requires one who is interceded with and one for whom intercession is made. In their custom, no one undertakes it except one who is certain that his intercession will be accepted. One says: "So-and-so interceded with so-and-so on behalf of so-and-so, and he granted his intercession," meaning he accepted his intercession. In a hadith: "They said: 'This one is worthy, if he proposes marriage, to be married to; and if he intercedes, to be interceded for.'"

From this it becomes clear that intercession may be to remove harm and may be to bring benefit. Someone said:

Fa dhaka fata in tatihi fi sani'atin ∗∗∗ ila malihi la tatihi bi-shafi'
(That is a young man: if you come to him with a favor for his wealth, do not come to him with an intercessor.)

Among what came in the decree (manshur) of the caliph al-Qadir billah to the sultan Mahmud ibn Subuktakin al-Ghaznawi: "We have appointed you over the province of Khurasan and given you the title Yamin al-Dawlah, through the intercession (shafa'ah) of Abu Hamid al-Isfara'ini," meaning: through his mediation and his desire.

Thus intercession in common usage requires that the intercessor have standing (idlal) with the one who is interceded with. For this reason Allah, Exalted, negated it here, in the sense of negating that any created being has the right to be an intercessor with Allah on the basis of such standing.

He affirmed it in other verses, such as His saying shortly after: "Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?" [al-Baqarah: 255], and His saying:

[Page 16]
"And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves" [al-Anbiya': 28]. It was also established for the Messenger, peace be upon him, in many hadiths, and it is alluded to in His saying, Exalted is He: "It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station" [al-Isra': 79]. The verse was interpreted in this sense in a sound hadith. For this reason, affirming the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ) is one of the foundations of our creed. The Mu'tazilah denied it, and they are mistaken in denying it and confused in their argument. The matter is set out at length in the books of kalam (speculative theology).

The intercession negated here is intended to be that which the one interceded with cannot refuse. It therefore does not conflict with the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned in the sound hadiths, because that is an honour with which Allah, Exalted, has favoured him and permitted him to exercise, when He says: "Intercede, and your intercession will be accepted." Thus it refers back to His saying, Exalted is He: "Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?" [al-Baqarah: 255], and His saying: "And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves" [al-Anbiya': 28], and His saying: "And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He has permitted" [Saba': 23].

His saying: "And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers" is a construction of restriction (qasr) that arises from His saying: "There is no trade therein, nor friendship, nor intercession." It indicates that this negation is an implicit warning and threat to the polytheists, so He follows it with an increase in severity against them and a rebuke, that they themselves brought this threat and the one threatened by it upon themselves through their obstinacy, and that Allah has not wronged them. This has a stronger effect on the one being punished, because the wronged person finds consolation in the thought that he has been transgressed against. So the restriction is a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb), by treating them as if they believed themselves to be wronged. You may also take it as a real restriction in the sense of a claim, because their wrongdoing, being the greatest wrong, makes them as if wrongdoing is confined to them.

What is meant by the disbelievers, apparently, is the polytheists. This is one of the marvels of the eloquence of the Qur'an, for this sentence is also suitable as a concluding summary of the command to spend in the way of Allah, because that spending was for fighting the polytheists who began hostility against the religion. They are the wrongdoers, not the believers who fight them to protect the religion and defend its territory. Mentioning the disbelievers in the context of the exhortation is a way of clearing the believers of the suspicion that they would abandon spending, since this is not thought of them. Abandoning it and disbelief are mutually implicated. Thus the disbelievers wrong themselves, while the believers do not wrong themselves. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: "Woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakat" [Fussilat: 6–7]. The Qur'an depicts the believers at the highest ranks of faith and contrasts their state with the state of the unbelievers, as severe condemnation and as a way of clearing them. From this verse and others like it, some sects of Islam held that sins nullify faith, as we have already mentioned.

[Page 17]

﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and their preservation does not burden Him. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾

When He mentioned the terror of the Day of Resurrection and described the state of the disbelievers, He resumed (isti'naf) by mentioning the glorification of Allah, the Exalted, and describing His attributes, to refute the disbelief of the disbelievers and to cut off their hope. This is because it contains ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾. This verse was placed as the opening of the verses establishing Divine Oneness (tawhid) and the Resurrection (ba'th). This great verse was deposited here because it is like a barrier (barzakh) between the preceding and following themes.

The Name of the Essence (ism al-dhat) is used here because it is the clearest way of indicating the entity that is singularly designated by this name. The proper noun ('alam) is the most definite of definites (a'raf al-ma'arif), since in indicating its referent it does not need any indicator or aid, unless there is the possibility of multiple names. When this possibility is negated for the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalala), it is undoubtedly the most definite of definites, since it is independent of indicators and aids. Indicators are such things as speaking and addressing, while aids are such things as a prior mention, pointing with the hand, a relative clause, a prior agreement, and an annexation.

The clause ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ is the first predicate of the Name of Majesty. Its purpose is the affirmation of Oneness. The discussion of the indication of ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ on monotheism and the negation of other deities has already preceded at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your God is one God; there is no deity except Him﴾ (2:163).

His saying "the Living" (al-Hayy) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and "the Self-Subsisting" (al-Qayyum) is a second predicate of that omitted subject. The purpose is to affirm life and to nullify the entitlement of the gods of the polytheists to the attribute of divinity, since life is absent from them, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees?﴾ (19:42). This clause is separated from the one before it to indicate its independence, for if it were conjoined it would be like a subordinate. The apparent sense of the words of al-Kashshaf is that this clause explains what the clause ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him﴾ contains, namely that He is the one who sustains the creation [Page 18] by management. That is, because His exclusivity in divinity necessitates that there is no manager other than Him, therefore it is separated. This is contrary to how al-Taftazani construed his statement, for it is not consistent with his expression.

"Al-Hayy" in the speech of the Arabs means one in whom life subsists. Life is an attribute by which perception and action are possible, namely the perfection of existence as commonly known. In created beings it is by the diffusion of the spirit and the steady flow of blood in the arteries. As for the Creator, it approximates the effect of the attribute of life in us; namely, the absence of inertness, together with transcendence above the accidents of created beings. The theologians (mutakallimun) defined it as: an attribute that makes the one in whom it subsists fit for perception and action.

The author of al-Kashshaf interpreted "al-Hayy" as "the Enduring," that is, the One whose life is everlasting such that non-existence does not befall Him. Thus it is used as a metonymy (kinaya) for a necessary meaning of it, because affirming life to Allah, Exalted, in any sense other than this would be only a metaphor or a metonymy. Al-Fakhr said: "What is clear to me is that 'al-Hayy' in its original linguistic sense is not an expression for the soundness of knowledge and power, but an expression for the perfection of a thing within its genus. He, Exalted, said: ﴿So He revived with it the earth after its death﴾ (2:164). The life of trees is their foliage. So the attribute called 'life' in the terminology of the theologians was named so because the perfection of the state of a body is that it is described by it. Therefore the original meaning from the word 'al-Hayy' is its being applied to the most perfect of its states and attributes."

The purpose of describing Allah here as "the Living" is to nullify the belief of the polytheists in the divinity of their idols, which are inanimate. How could the manager of the affairs of creation be inanimate?

"Al-Hayy" is an attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha) derived from ḥayiya. Its original form is ḥayiyun, like ḥadhirun, and the two yā's were merged. It is of the yā'ī type by the agreement of the imams of the language. As for the scribes' writing of the word ḥayawat (life) in the Qur'an with a wāw after the yā', this contradicts the regular rule. It is said that they wrote it according to the dialect of the people of Yemen, for they say ḥayawatun, meaning ḥayatun. It is also said that they wrote it according to the dialect of emphasizing the fatḥa.

"Al-Qayyum" is on the pattern fa'yul from qama yaqumu, and it is an intensive form. Its original form is qayyum. The wāw and the yā' came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the wāw was changed to a yā' and they were merged. Its purpose is intensification in standing, which is used metaphorically and commonly for managing people's affairs. He, Exalted, said: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like any other]?﴾ (13:33). The purpose is to affirm His comprehensive knowledge, the perfection of life, and to nullify the divinity of the idols of the polytheists, [Page 19] because the polytheists acknowledged that the manager of the universe is Allah, Exalted. They only made their gods intercessors, partners, and distributors of the affairs of tribes. The polytheists among the Greeks had assigned to each of their gods kinds of creatures over which it disposes and nations of humans which belong to it and which it cares for.

The clause ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ confirms the content of the clause ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾, and removes the possibility of exaggeration in it. So the clause takes the place of an explanation of "the Living, the Self-Subsisting." For this reason it is separated from the one before it.

"Al-sinna" is on the pattern fi'la, derived from al-wasan, which is the first stage of sleep. The apparent view is that its original form is a noun of state, like all words that come on the pattern fi'la from a root with an initial wāw. They have also said wasana, with a fatḥa on the wāw, in the form of the single instance. Al-sinna is the first stage of sleep. 'Adi ibn al-Riqa' said:

"Drowsy, overcome by slumber, so drowsiness glazed over his eyes, yet he is not asleep."

Sleep is well known. It is a lethargy that afflicts the nerves of the brain due to the fatigue of exerting the nerves and from the rising of bodily vapors resulting from digestion and nervous activity. It intensifies at sunset and the coming of darkness. The brain and the nervous system which the brain governs seek natural rest. So sense gradually fades, bodily movements become heavy, then sense fades completely until the nerves regain their vigor, and then there is wakefulness.

The negation of drowsiness and sleep as overtaking Allah, Exalted, is an affirmation of the perfection of life and the permanence of management, and an affirmation of the perfection of knowledge. This is because drowsiness and sleep resemble death. The life of the sleeper in their state is a weak life, and they prevent management and knowledge of what occurs while they take hold of the senses.

The negation of drowsiness from Allah, Exalted, does not suffice as a negation of sleep from Him, because among living beings some are not afflicted by drowsiness, so when they sleep they sleep deeply. Among people there are those who are overcome by drowsiness at times other than sleep. The Arabs praised themselves for their ability to stay awake. Abu Kabir said:

"So she brought him, alert of heart, wrapped in wakefulness, when the night of the wilderness slept."

The purpose is that Allah's knowledge is not veiled from anything, neither by a weak veil nor a long one, neither by overpowering nor by acquisition. So there is no need for what al-Fakhr and al-Baydawi sought, namely that the precedence of drowsiness over sleep is observed in terms of the order of existence, and that the mention of sleep is a kind of precaution. This meaning was taken up by Bashshar, who fashioned it in a way suited to the craft of poetry, saying:

"And a dark night whose daughters sleep, and whose sons and foster-children, from its length."

He meant by the daughters and sons of the night those who stay awake constantly, and by the foster-children of the night those who are weaker in staying awake, because the foster-child is weaker in relation than the son and daughter.

The clause ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ affirms His exclusivity in divinity, since all existent things are His creation. It is also a reason for His attribute of self-subsistence, because whoever owns all existent things is worthy of being their sustainer and of not neglecting them. For this reason the clause is separated from the one before it.

The lām here denotes ownership. The heavens and the earth mean the totality of the places of existent things. The clause indicates the generality of existent things through the relative pronoun and its relative clause. When His ownership of the totality is established, it is established that no existent thing deviates from His ownership, so the meaning of restriction (hasr) is achieved. But He added emphasis to it by placing the predicate first, that is, [it belongs] to none other, in order to convey a refutation of the categories of polytheists: the Sabians who worship the stars, such as the Syrians and the Greeks, and the polytheists of the Arabs. This is because the mere occurrence of the meaning of restriction through generality does not suffice to indicate the nullification of erroneous beliefs. So this clause conveys the teaching of Oneness through its generality, and conveys the nullification of the beliefs of the people of polytheism through the particular specificity of the restrictive construction (qasr).

The clause ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ confirms the content of the clause ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, because of what the lām of ownership conveys of the all-encompassing extent of His, Exalted, ownership over everything in the heavens and the earth. And what the fronting of the prepositional phrase includes of restricting that ownership to Him, Exalted, is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb). Thus the attribute of divinity is nullified for other than Him by correspondence, and the right to be emboldened before Him and to intercede with Him, which is not rejected, is nullified by implication. This is because being emboldened is characteristic of an equal or one close in rank, and intercession is a form of being emboldened. This is a refutation of the belief of most of the polytheists of the Arabs, because they did not ascribe to their gods and idols complete divinity. Rather they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ (10:18), and they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in position﴾ (39:3). So this implication was emphasized by explicit statement, and for this reason this clause is separated from what precedes it.

The word "dhā" is redundant for emphasis, since there is no specific referent indicated. The Arabs add "dhā" to what the indication conveys of the existence of a specific person to whom the judgment of interrogation relates. When it becomes clear that he does not exist, that is more indicative that there is no aspirant who sets himself up to claim this judgment. The discussion of "man dhā" has already preceded at His saying: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan?﴾ (2:245).

The interrogation in His saying ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him﴾ is used for denial and negation, by the indicator of the exception stated after it: "except by His permission."

Intercession (shafa'a) has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿There is no trade therein, nor friendship, nor intercession﴾ (2:254).

The meaning is that no one intercedes with Him by right and by being emboldened, because all creatures are His possession. But whoever He wills to show honor to, He grants him permission to intercede for whomever He wills to pardon. This is like how dignities are handed over by the great to outstanding students in the processions of examinations. For this reason, in the hadith of intercession it is reported: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'People come to him so that he may speak to his Lord and lighten for them the terror of the place of reckoning. He comes and prostrates beneath the Throne and speaks words that Allah, Exalted, teaches him. Then it is said: O Muhammad, raise your head, ask and you will be given, intercede and your intercession will be accepted.'" So his prostration is a request for permission to speak, and he does not intercede until it is said: "Intercede." His being taught the words is a prelude to the permission.

The clause ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills﴾ is a confirmation and completion of what the combined two clauses ﴿The Living, the Self-Subsisting; neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ contain, and of what the clause ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ contains. This is because the two clauses ﴿The Living, the Self-Subsisting; neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ indicate the generality of His knowledge of what has occurred and come into being of the created realms, but they do not indicate His knowledge of what will be. So He confirmed and completed it with His saying "He knows" and the verse. It is also a reason for the clause ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾. For a question may arise: why are they deprived of intercession except after permission? It is answered: because they do not know who deserves intercession, and appearances may deceive them, while Allah knows who deserves it. He knows what is before them and what is behind them. For these two meanings the clause is separated from what precedes it.

Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 2, Verse 255 (part 2 of 2)

The meaning of "what is before them and what is behind them" is what is known to them of the knowable things, and what is hidden from them or what they have forgotten of them; or what will happen after them and what happened before them. As for His knowledge of what is in their own time, it is more fitting (for Him to know). It was said: "the future is what is before (aydi, lit. hands) and the past is what is behind (khalf)." It was also said the reverse. Both are usages founded on different points of view in depicting what is before and behind. This is because what is before a person is in front of him: he faces it, sees it, and strives to reach it. What is behind him is what is at his back: he has fallen behind it and cut off from it, does not see it, and has passed it without it yet being connected to him. It was also said that these are the affairs of this world and the affairs of the Hereafter, which is a branch of the past and the future. It was said that they are the sensible things and the intelligible things. In any case, the expression is figurative, and what is intended is the comprehensiveness of knowledge of all existents.

The pronoun in "aydihim wa khalfahum" (their hands and what is behind them) refers to "what is in the heavens and what is in the earth," by giving precedence to the rational beings among the created things, because what is meant by "what is before them and what is behind them" includes the conditions of non-rational beings as well. Or it refers specifically to the rational beings from among the general "what is in the heavens and what is in the earth," so that what is meant is what pertains to the conditions of humankind, which is a part (of the whole), in accordance with the pronoun in "wa la yuhituna" (and they do not encompass), because knowledge is among the conditions of rational beings.

The clause ﴿wa la yuhituna bishay'in min 'ilmihi﴾ (and they do not encompass anything of His knowledge) is conjoined to the clause ﴿ya'lamu ma bayna aydihim﴾ (He knows what is before them), because it completes its meaning, as in His saying: ﴿wallahu ya'lamu wa antum la ta'lamun﴾ (Allah knows, and you do not know) [al-Baqarah: 216].

The meaning of "yuhituna" (they encompass) is that they know with complete knowledge. It is a figurative usage, its literal basis being that encompassing a thing requires containing all of its extremities, such that nothing of it escapes, at its beginning or at its end. So the meaning is: they do not know with certain knowledge any of its known things. As for what they claim, it is a guess about the unseen. Thus "knowledge" in His saying ﴿min 'ilmihi﴾ (of His knowledge) means "the general (sum of knowledge)," like "creation" meaning "the created." Its being attributed to the pronoun of the Name of Majesty (Allah) is a specification of it to the innate knowledge (al-'ulum al-ladunniyyah) which Allah has reserved for Himself, and for which Allah, exalted is He, has not set up rational or customary indications. Therefore His saying ﴿illa bima sha'a﴾ (except what He wills) is an alert that He, glorified is He, may inform some of His chosen servants of what is among the special (aspects) of His knowledge, as in His saying: ﴿'Alimu al-ghaybi fa la yuzhiru 'ala ghaybihi ahadan﴾ (He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone) [al-Jinn: 26], ﴿illa mani-rtada min rasulin﴾ (except whom He has approved of messengers) [al-Jinn: 27].

[Page 23]

His saying: ﴿wasi'a kursiyyuhu al-samawati wal-ard﴾ (His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth) is an affirmation of what all of the clauses contain of the greatness, majesty, knowledge, and power of Allah, exalted is He, and a demonstration of the greatness of His creatures, which necessitates the greatness of His affair; or it is to show the vastness of His dominion in the same way, as we will explain. These clauses have come in a sequential and branching order.

The kursi (chair/throne-footstool) is an object upon which one sits, composed of sticks or other things placed like pillars, evenly spaced, with a surface of wood or other material, sized to hold one person sitting. If it exceeds a single seat and is elevated, then it is the 'arsh (throne). What is meant in the verse is not the literal kursi, since it is not fitting for Allah, exalted is He, because that would require spatial confinement. Therefore it is determined that what is meant by it is other than its literal reality.

The majority said: the Kursi is a great creation, and it is attributed to Allah, exalted is He, because of its greatness. It was said: it is the 'Arsh, and this is the statement of al-Hasan. This is the apparent view, because the Kursi is not mentioned in the Qur'an except in this verse, while the 'Arsh is mentioned repeatedly, and the two are never mentioned together. Had the Kursi been other than the 'Arsh, it would have been mentioned with it, just as the heavens were mentioned with the 'Arsh in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿qul man rabbu al-samawati al-sab'i wa rabbu al-'arshi al-'azim﴾ (Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?) [al-Mu'minun: 86].

It was said: the Kursi is other than the 'Arsh. Ibn Zayd said: it is below the 'Arsh. It was narrated on this authority from Abu Dharr that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The Kursi in relation to the 'Arsh is nothing but like a ring of iron thrown down in the middle of a desert of the earth." This is a hadith that is not authenticated. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, al-Suddi, and al-Dahhak said: the Kursi is the place of the two feet of the 'Arsh, i.e., because the one sitting on a throne is elevated above the earth, so a footstool is placed for him so that his legs are not suspended in space if he does not sit cross-legged. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

It was said: the Kursi is a parable for the knowledge of Allah. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, because the scholar sits on a chair (kursi) in order to teach the people. It was said: it is a parable for the dominion of Allah, exalted is He, as they say, "So-and-so is the holder of the chair of Iraq," meaning the dominion of Iraq. Al-Baydawi said: perhaps it is the sphere called among them the "sphere of the zodiacal constellations."

I say: The Qur'an affirmed seven heavens, and did not specify their names in His saying (in Surah Nuh): ﴿alam tarau kayfa khalaqa Allahu sab'a samawatin tiba'an﴾ (Have you not considered how Allah created seven heavens in layers?) [Nuh: 15], ﴿wa ja'ala al-qamara fihinna nuran wa ja'ala al-shamsa sirajan﴾ (and made the moon therein a light and made the sun a lamp) [Nuh: 16]. It is therefore permissible that the heavens are layers of atmospheres, differing in their properties and distinguished by what fills them of elements, and these are the orbs of the stars. And Allah, exalted is He, has said (in Surah al-Mulk): ﴿wa laqad zayyana al-sama'a al-dunya bi-masabih﴾ (And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps) [al-Mulk: 5]. It is also permissible that the heavens are the great planets bound to the solar system, and these are Vulcan, Mercury, and Venus, which are below the sun down to the earth, and Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, which are above the sun in this order of distance; except that in terms of size, the largest of them is Jupiter, then Saturn, then Neptune, then Uranus, then Mars. So if the 'Arsh is the largest of them, then it is Jupiter, and the Kursi, being below it, is Saturn. The remaining seven are those mentioned, and the moon is added to them. If the Kursi is the 'Arsh, there is no need to count the moon, and this is the apparent view. The sun is among the stars, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa ja'ala al-shamsa sirajan﴾ (and made the sun a lamp) [Nuh: 16] is a specification of it by mention, as a favour upon people, in that it is a light for the earth. However, the sun is greater than all of them under every estimate. If the heavens are seven spheres for suns other than this sun, and each sphere has its own system just as this sun has its system, then that is permissible, and glory be to Him whose greatness of power the minds cannot encompass. The meaning according to this is that Allah, exalted is He, has alerted us to the greatness of His power and the vastness of His kingdom by means of what indicates this, while also agreeing with what is in reality. But He did not detail this for us, because detailing it is not the purpose of the argument for His greatness, and because minds cannot reach its understanding, since it depends on sciences and developments which have not yet been completed. "And you will surely know its news after a time" [Sad: 88].

The clause ﴿wa la ya'uduhu hifzuhuma﴾ (and the preserving of both does not burden Him) is conjoined to the clause ﴿wasi'a kursiyyuhu﴾ (His Kursi encompasses), because it is part of its completion, and it contains a pronoun whose referent is in the previous clause. That is: He who brought these worlds into being is not incapable of preserving them.

"Ada-hu" means he made him one with a crookedness (awad), and awad (with a vowel on the first letter) means crookedness. The meaning of "ada-hu" is that it burdened him, because the one who is burdened bends over and becomes crooked.

It is conjoined to it: ﴿wa huwa al-'aliyyu al-'azim﴾ (and He is the Most High, the Most Great), because it is part of its completeness. Height and greatness are used figuratively for nobility of rank and majesty of power.

This verse has great excellence because of what it includes of the foundations of knowing the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, just as Surat al-Ikhlas includes that, and just as the statement of testimony includes it. In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayra: "A visitor came to him at night and took some of the food of the zakat al-fitr. When he seized him, he said to him: 'When you go to your bed, recite the Verse of the Throne; there will always be a guardian from Allah with you, and no devil will come near you until morning.'" The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "He has spoken the truth, though he is a devil." Muslim narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "O Abu al-Mundhir, do you know which verse of the Book of Allah is greatest with you?" I said: "Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting" [al-Baqarah: 255]. He struck me on the chest and said: "By Allah, may knowledge be pleasant to you, O Abu al-Mundhir." Al-Nasa'i narrated: "Whoever recites the Verse of the Throne after every obligatory prayer, nothing will prevent him from entering Paradise except death." There are many excellences in it that have been tested for protection of the self and the home.

[Page 26 begins here]

This is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*: a sentence that answers an implied question) arising from the command to fight in God's way in His words: ﴿And fight in the way of God, and know that God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 244]. The hearer may take it that fighting is for the purpose of bringing the enemy into Islam. So this verse clarifies that there is no compulsion to enter Islam. The discussion of whether it is *muhkam* (fixed in ruling) or *mansukh* (abrogated) will follow.

The placing of this verse after the Throne Verse (*Ayat al-Kursi*) is because the proofs of God's oneness, the greatness of the Creator, and His exemption from the defects of what the nations ascribed to Him, are such as to lead people of intellect to accept this religion, which is clear in its creed and upright in its law, by their own choice without force or compulsion. And their continuance in polytheism is put in question: will they be left to it, or will they be compelled to Islam? So the sentence came as a clarifying resumption.

*Ikrah* (compulsion) means impelling someone to do something disliked. The *hamza* in it is for making (causative), i.e., making him one who dislikes it. This happens only through intimidating him with the occurrence of something more disliked than the act to which he is being called.

*Al-din* (religion) has already been explained at the words ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ [al-Fatihah: 4], and here it means the Law (*al-shar'*).

The definite article in *al-din* is for a known reference, i.e., the religion of Islam.

The negation of compulsion is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition. What is meant is the negation of the causes of compulsion in the judgement of Islam; that is: do not compel anyone to follow Islam by force. The generic negation (*nafy al-jins*) is used to intend explicit generality. This verse is a clear proof of the invalidity of compulsion in religion in all its forms, because the matter of faith proceeds by reasoning, by the capacity to reflect, and by choice. It has been established in the early period of Islam that polytheists were fought to make them accept Islam. In the hadith: "I have been commanded to fight people until they say, 'There is no god but God.' When they say it, they have protected their blood and property from me, except by its right." It is not possible that this verse was revealed before the beginning of fighting altogether. The apparent view is that this verse was revealed after the conquest of Makkah and the subjugation of the lands of the Arabs, since the revelation of a surah may extend over years, as we have mentioned at the beginning of the commentary on Surat al-Fatihah, particularly since it has been said that the last verse revealed was in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿God makes clear to you that you may not go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], etc. So it abrogated the ruling of fighting in order to make disbelievers accept Islam, and it indicated that they should be content to enter under the authority of Islam, which is expressed as the *dhimma* (protected status). The practice of the Prophet (ﷺ) clarified this, when the lands of the Arabs were cleared of polytheism after the conquest of Makkah and after people entered the religion in multitudes when the delegations of the Arabs came after the conquest. When God's purpose was accomplished—rescuing the Arabs from polytheism and returning them to the creed of Ibrahim, cleansing the Ka'bah from the filth of polytheists, preparing a great group to carry this religion and protect its core, the guidance of Islam becoming manifest, and the obstacles that prevented following it from obstinacy being removed—and God secured the land of the Arabs from polytheism, as occurred in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed Satan has despaired of being worshipped in this your land," then all of that having been achieved, God nullified fighting over religion and kept fighting for the extension of His authority. For this reason He said [Surat al-Tawbah: 29]: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in God or the Last Day, and do not forbid what God and His Messenger have forbidden, and do not adopt the religion of truth from among those who were given the Book, until they give the *jizya* (poll tax) willingly while they are humbled﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29].
