On this basis, the verse abrogates what preceded it of verses about fighting, such as His saying: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be stern with them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73].

Furthermore, the verses revealed before it or after it are of three types:

The first: verses that commanded defensive fighting, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], and His saying: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and sacred things in retaliation. So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you, and fear God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194].

[Page 27 begins here]

This is fighting that is not for compelling people to Islam, but rather to repel the harm of the polytheists.

The second type: verses that commanded fighting the polytheists and disbelievers and were not restricted by a limit (*ghayah*). It is possible that their absolute form is restricted by the limit in the verse: ﴿until they give the jizya﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29], so our present verse, ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, does not conflict with it.

The third type: what is restricted by a limit, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah and religion is for God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193]. Then it is necessary that this be abrogated by this verse and by the verse: ﴿until they give the jizya﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29], just as the hadith "I have been commanded to fight people" was abrogated. This is what appears to us as the meaning of the verse, and God knows best.

There are two views among the scholars before us concerning it. The first: Ibn Mas'ud and Sulayman ibn Musa said it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73], for the Prophet (ﷺ) compelled the Arabs to Islam and fought them, and he was not content from them except with it. Perhaps they mean by abrogation the sense of specification (*takhsis*). The argument for its abrogation by the Prophet's (ﷺ) fighting the Arabs to make them accept Islam is countered by the fact that he (ﷺ) took the jizya from all disbelievers, so the way to reconcile them is specification.

The second view: it is fixed in its ruling but it is particular. Al-Sha'bi, Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: it is particular to the People of the Book, for they are not compelled to Islam when they pay the jizya, and only the people of idols are compelled to Islam. Al-Shafi'i inclined to this view, saying: the jizya is taken only from the People of the Book and the Magians. Ibn al-'Arabi said in *al-Ahkam* (*Ahkam al-Qur'an*): On this basis, whoever sees that the acceptance of jizya from a category of people applies the verse to them—meaning, while a group remains in which compulsion is realised.

Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: this verse was revealed concerning the Ansar. In the pre-Islamic period, when a woman among them was *miqlat* (one whose children do not survive), she would vow that if a child lived for her, she would make him a Jew. When Islam came and they embraced it, many of the sons of the Ansar were Jews, so they said: "We will not leave our sons, rather we will compel them to Islam." Then God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾.

[Page 28 begins here]

Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the story of a man from the Ansar called Abu Husayn, of the Banu Salamah ibn 'Awf, who had two sons. Merchants from the Christians of Syria came to Madinah, and they invited the two sons to Christianity, so they became Christians and went out with them. Their father came and complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked that he send someone to bring them back compelled. Then ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ was revealed. Fighting had not been commanded on that day. Then this was abrogated by the verses of fighting. It has also been said: the meaning of the negation of compulsion is the negation of its effect on the Islam of one who embraced it unwillingly, fleeing from the sword, in the sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of the worldly life﴾ [al-Nisa': 94]. This view is an interpretation of the meaning of compulsion and a taking of the negation as informative rather than imperative.

It has also been said: the meaning of "religion" is monotheism and a religion that has a heavenly book, and the negation of compulsion is a prohibition. The meaning is: do not compel the captive women from the People of the Book, for they are people of a religion, and compel the Magians and the polytheist women among them.

His saying, ﴿The right course has become clear from error﴾, comes in the position of a cause for His saying, ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, and for this reason the sentence is separated (without a conjunction).

*Al-rushd* (right course), with a *damma* then a sukun, or with a *fatha* then a *fatha*, means guidance and soundness of judgement. Its opposite is *al-ghayy* and *al-safah* (folly). *Al-ghayy* is misguidance, and its origin is the verbal noun of *ghawa*, the transitive verb; so its origin is *ghawiy*, the *waw* was changed into a *ya*, then both were assimilated. The verb *tabayyana* (became clear) has the sense of *tamayyaza* (became distinguished), and therefore it takes *min* (from). This distinction came about through the call of Islam and its manifestation in an independent land after the Hijrah.

His saying, ﴿So whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut and believes in God has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾ is a consequence (*tafri'*) of His saying, ﴿The right course has become clear from error﴾, since after the distinction nothing remains except disbelief in al-Taghut. In it is an explanation of the absence of compulsion in religion, since from the distinction of right guidance from error there emerges the clear fact that the follower of Islam holds fast to the most trustworthy handhold, and so he is drawn to it by choice.

*Al-Taghut* means the idols and the images. The Muslims call the idol *al-taghiyah*, and in the hadith: "They used to chant the talbiyah for Manat, the *taghiyah*." They make its plural *tawaghit*. I do not think it is other than one of the technical terms of the Qur'an. It derives from *al-tughyan*, which is rising up and exceeding bounds in pride, and it is blameworthy and disliked. The form of *taghut*, in verification, is *taghayut* (*fa'alut*), one of the patterns of verbal nouns like *malakut*, *rahabut* and *rahamut*. A metathesis occurred in it, between its first and third radicals, so it became *fala'ut*, *tayaghut*, so that the *lam* could be changed into an *alif*, and it became *taghut*. Then the sense of the verbal noun was removed from it, and it became a name for a class of things in which this verbal noun inheres. So it became like *malakut* in that it is the name of a class of things in which the sense of the verbal noun inheres, not like *rahamut* and *rahabut* in that they are verbal nouns, its *ta'* being augmentative. It was made a proper name for disbelief and for idols. Its origin is an attributive of the verbal noun, and it is applied to the singular, the plural, the masculine and the feminine, like verbal nouns.

And ﴿and believes in God﴾ is coordinated with the conditional, because abandoning the worship of idols has no merit unless one replaces it with the worship of God, exalted is He.

The meaning of *istamsaka* (grasped) is *tamassaka* (held fast). The *sin* and the *ta'* are for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 43], and His saying: ﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195], and the line of al-Nabighah: "They married the mother of Jabir." For there is no meaning in seeking to hold fast to the most trustworthy handhold after faith; rather, faith itself is the holding fast. *Al-'urwah* (handhold), with a *damma* on the 'ayn, is what is made like a ring at the end of something so that one may grasp the thing by it. So a bucket has an *'urwah* and a jug has an *'urwah*. The *'urwah* may also be in a rope, by tying its end to another part and fastening it so that it becomes like a ring in it. Therefore *al-Kashshaf* (*al-Kashshaf* of al-Zamakhshari) said: "The most trustworthy handhold is from a firm rope."

*Al-wuthqa* (the most trustworthy) means the one firmly fastened. ﴿There is no breaking for it﴾ means: there is no severing. *Al-fasm* is cutting by separating a connection without fragmenting, unlike *al-qasm* with a *qaf*, which is cutting with separation and fragmentation.

Holding fast to the most trustworthy handhold is a figurative image (*tamthil*). The condition of the believer in his steadfastness in faith is likened to the condition of one who holds fast to a firm handhold of a rope, while he is riding a difficult beast or is in a ship in the terror of the sea. It is an intellectual condition likened to a sensory condition. For this reason *al-Kashshaf* said: "This is an image of the known by way of reflection, likened to the observed." It has been made clear in its commentary on Surat Luqman, where it said: "The state of one who puts his trust is likened to the state of one who wants to lower himself from a high cliff, so he takes precaution for himself by holding fast to the most secure handhold of a firm rope whose severing is trusted not to happen." So the meaning is that the believer has steadfast certainty, is free of the agitation of the heart in this world, and is saved from the abysses of falling in the Hereafter, like the condition of one who holds fast to the handhold of a firm rope that does not break.

[Page 30 begins here]

The verse has pointed out that this is a benefit to the believer which benefits him in his worldly life, by his being upon the truth and insight, which is what souls seek. It has pointed out the benefit of that in the Hereafter by His saying: ﴿and God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, which is an allusion to the promise and the reward.

His saying, ﴿Allah is the Protector (walī) of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light, and those who disbelieve, their protectors are the false deities (ṭāghūt), who bring them out of light into darkness. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾, is placed as the reason for His saying ﴿there is no breaking of it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256], because those who disbelieved in the ṭāghūt and believed in Allah have taken Allah the Exalted as their protector, so He becomes their walī. He decrees for them what benefits them, which is warding off doubts from them. By that, their grip on the firmest handhold continues, and they are safe from its breaking. That is: when someone chooses to be a Muslim, Allah increases him in guidance.

The walī is the ḥalīf (ally). He supports his mawlā (the one he is allied with). By "light" is meant the light of proof and truth, and by "darknesses" are meant the darknesses of doubts and suspicion. Allah increases those who are guided in guidance, because their following of Islam facilitates the paths of certainty, so they go deeper into them day after day. Conversely, those who chose disbelief over Islam, their choice indicates a seal placed upon their minds, so they are not guided, and they increase in misguidance day after day. Because of this continual increase in both matters, the present tense is used in ﴿He brings them out﴾ and ﴿they bring them out﴾. With this, the reason for the connection of these verses to the verse ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], then to the verse ﴿or like the one who passed by a town﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259], then to the verse ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260], becomes clear. All of these came to explain the ways in which doubt and doubts are cleared away from the walīs of Allah the Exalted, whose faith is true. There is no need for what is in al-Kashshāf and others, of interpreting "those who believe" and "those who disbelieve" as referring to "those who intended that," and treating the light and darknesses as a figure for faith and disbelief, since you know that the meaning is evident without needing such interpretation (ta'wīl). Nor would this fit well after His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves in the ṭāghūt and believes in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256], and after His saying ﴿and those who disbelieve, their protectors are the ṭāghūt, who bring them out of light into darkness﴾. Rather, it is definitely to be understood as increasing the misguidance of the disbeliever in his disbelief through greater doubt, as in His saying ﴿So their gods, which they called upon besides Allah, did not avail them at all when the command of your Lord came; and they added nothing to them but ruin﴾ [Hūd: 101]. Also, the ṭāghūt were protectors of those who believed before faith, since all of them were polytheists. Likewise is what Fakhr al-Dīn extended on regarding the aspects of argumentation against the Mu'tazila (a theological school, the Mu'tazila) and their argumentation against us.

The clause (yukhrijuhum, "He brings them out") is a second predicate (khabar thānin) regarding the Name of Majesty (Allah). The clause (yukhrijūnahum, "they bring them out") is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a grammatical term for a clause describing the state of the subject or object) referring to the ṭāghūt. The pronoun referring to the ṭāghūt is restored in the plural form used for rational beings, because the action attributed to them is that of rational beings, even though in reality they are the cause of the exit and not the ones who actually bring them out. The discussion of the ṭāghūt has already preceded at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿whoever disbelieves in the ṭāghūt and believes in Allah has grasped the firmest handhold﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256].

[Page 32]

This statement functions as an argument supporting the content of the preceding sentence, or as an example of it. When God mentioned that He brings those who believe out of darkness into light, and that the taghut (false powers) bring those who disbelieve out of light into darkness, He presented three proofs for this. This is the first and the most comprehensive, because it encompasses the misguidance of the disbeliever and the guidance of the believer, so it has the force of an example.

The purpose of this is to portray the state of the polytheists, in their disputation with the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Resurrection, by likening it to the state of the one who argued with Ibrahim (Abraham) about his Lord. What supports this is the choice (takhyir) in the comparison that appears in His saying: ﴿Or like one who passed by a town﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259], and the verse that follows.

The discussion of the construction (ألم تر) has already been covered.

The interrogative in (ألم تر) is figurative, implying wonder (ta'ajjub). Its detailed meaning and origin were already explained at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen those who left their homes?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 243]. This is an argument presented to establish the oneness of God, exalted is He, and to refute the divinity of anyone else, because He alone gives life and causes death, and because He alone created the visible worlds that people see.

The meaning of (حاجّ) is "disputed" (khasama). It is a verb in the pattern of mufa'alah (reciprocal form). In usage, there is no known simple (mujarrad) verb for (حاجّ) indicating the occurrence of dispute, and the root from which it is derived is not known. Strangely, the ḥujjah (proof) in the speech of the Arabs is the evidence that validates a claim, yet (حاجّ) is generally used only in the sense of contention. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And when they dispute in the Fire﴾ [Ghafir: 47], alongside His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64]. The more common usage is that it indicates contention with falsehood. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And his people argued with him. He said: Do you argue with me about God when He has guided me?﴾ [al-An'am: 80], and He says: ﴿And if they argue with you, say: I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20]. The verses on this are numerous. So the meaning of ﴿the one who argued with Ibrahim﴾ is that he contended with him in a false dispute concerning the attributes of God, the Lord of Ibrahim.

The one who argued with Ibrahim was undoubtedly a disbeliever, as shown by His saying: ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾. It has been said that he was Nimrod son of Kan'an son of Kush... [as transmitted in the text: Nimrud ibn Falikh ibn 'Abir ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam ibn Kush ibn Ham ibn Nuh], so he would be the brother of (Ra'u), the grandfather of Ibrahim. What is relied upon is that he was a tyrannical king who ruled in Babylon, and that he is the one who built the city of Babylon and built the tower that is in Babylon. His name is Nimrud, with the unpointed dal (د) at its end, and it is said with the pointed dhal (ذ). The books of the Jews do not address this story, which is found in narrations.

The pronoun attached to (رَبّ) refers to Ibrahim, and the idafah (genitive construction) serves to honor the one it is attached to. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer back to (the one who), and the idafah would then serve to expose his error, like the saying of Ibn Zayyabah:

"I was informed that 'Amr, having buried his head in deep sleep, threatens his maternal uncles."

That is: it is not part of the manliness (muru'ah) of someone to display evil toward the people of his own kin.

His saying: ﴿that God had given him the kingdom﴾ is a causal clause (ta'lil) from which the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil) has been omitted. It explains what (حاجّ) implies of boldness in this great error, which was made easy for him by his vanity and self-admiration. It is therefore a purely causal clause, not a final cause (ghayah) intended by the one who disputes. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) permitted that it be a final causal clause, meaning: he argued for the sake of God having given him the kingdom. In that case the lam is a subordinate metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah) for a meaning that would be expressed by a particle other than lam. What motivates this metaphor is sarcasm (tahakkum), meaning that he placed disbelief in the position of gratitude, as in one of the two interpretations of His saying: ﴿And you make your provision [consist in] denying [it]﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82], that is, in return for your provision. The giving of the kingdom is a metaphor for bestowing favour upon him by making him a king and granting him that authority. The detail of this verb will come at His saying: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Ibrahim﴾ [al-An'am: 83] in Surat al-An'am. It has been said that Nimrod was the first king on earth and the first to place a crown upon his head.

[Page 33]

The clause (إذ قال) is an adverbial complement (zarf) for (حاجّ). This indicates that Ibrahim was the first to call to the Oneness of God and to argue with a clear proof that every sane person can grasp: that the true Lord is the One who gives life and causes death. Every person knows by necessity that he cannot bring the dead back to life. Therefore Ibrahim began his argument by indicating the inability of people to give life to the dead. By "God gives life" he meant that He creates living bodies, human and animal, and this is known by necessity. In placing the argument from the creation of life first, there is an incorporation (idmaj) of the proof of the Resurrection, because the one who argued with Ibrahim was among the worshippers of idols, who deny the Resurrection. This is the point of lesson in the context of the verse, addressed to the ears of the polytheists in the Qur'an. He then followed it with the evidence of causing death, for a person cannot end the life of a living being. In giving life and causing death there is evidence that both are the act of an agent other than human beings. So God is the One who gives life and causes death, and God is the Everlasting, not others, who have no life at all, such as idols, since they cannot grant life to others while they themselves lack it, and not someone who cannot repel death from himself, like this man who argued with Ibrahim.

The clause ﴿He said: I give life and cause death﴾ explains (حاجّ). The implied sense is: he argued with Ibrahim, saying "I give life and cause death," when Ibrahim said to him ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾. He resorted to sophistry out of ignorance or delusion regarding giving life and causing death, claiming that he would summon someone sentenced to death and pardon him, and summon an innocent man and kill him. This is how they transmitted it. It is also possible that his intention was that giving life and causing death are his own acts, because their matter is obscure and no tangible proof stands on it.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read the alif of the pronoun (أنا) with a short vowel, such that it is like an unextended fatha, and that is a particular usage of the alif of (أنا) in Arabic. Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read it in the same way, except when it is followed by a hamzah of cutting (hamzat qat') that is either damma or fatha, as here, and as in His saying: ﴿And I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-An'am: 163]. In that case he reads it with a long extended alif. Regarding the kasra on the hamzah of cutting, there are two transmissions from Qalun on the authority of Nafi', like His saying: ﴿I am but a warner﴾ [al-A'raf: 188]. This is an eloquent dialect.

His saying "He said: Ibrahim..." is a reply, so it is detached from conjunction (fuqti'at 'an al-'atf), following the method of recounting dialogues. Ibrahim turned away from objecting that this is not the giving of life to which he referred, nor the causing of death to which he referred. He left it aside because he knew the stubbornness of his opponent, and moved on to what the opponent could not claim. For this reason he was confounded, that is, he became incapable and found no counter-argument.

[Page 34]

(بُهِتَ) is a verb in the passive voice. It is said: "baha-tahu fa-buhita," meaning he rendered him incapable of answering, so he became incapable; or he surprised him with something he did not know how to repel.

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Rather, it will come upon them suddenly and confound them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 40]. 'Urwah al-'Udhri said:

"It was only that I saw her suddenly, so I was struck dumb, until I could hardly answer."

From this root comes (al-buhtan), which is a monstrous lie that confounds the one who hears it.

His saying: ﴿And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil), which is the essence of the argument in relation to His saying: ﴿God is the ally of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. The guidance of God is negated for the wrongdoing people because wrongdoing is a barrier between its bearer and the willingness to reflect on proofs and to exercise judgment in what is beneficial, since the mind is occupied away from that by its vanity and delusion.

The verse is evidence for the permissibility of argumentation and debate in establishing beliefs, and the Qur'an is full of this. As for what is forbidden of disputation, it is the disputation of obstinacy, partisanship, and promoting falsehood and error.

**[Page 35]**

This is an instance of *takhyir* (the option of choosing between two similes) in the manner of repeating the simile. Its explanation has already been given at the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]. This is because His words, ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], carry the sense of a parable and a comparison, as has been explained. This is what the author of *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari) means by his saying: "It is permissible to interpret it according to the meaning rather than the wording, as if it were said: 'Have you seen the one who argued, or the one who passed by?'" Since the previous verse had established the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted, in divinity, which is the foundation of Islam, this verse follows with the affirmation of resurrection, whose denial is the foundation of the people of polytheism.

Know that the Arabs use both forms for expressing amazement. They say: "Have you not seen such-and-such?" and they say: "Have you seen the like of such-and-such, or: like such-and-such?" It may also be said: "Have you not seen like such-and-such?" because they say: "I have not seen the like of today," whether for good or for evil. In a hadith: "I have never seen a sight like today." Since that is said for good, it is permissible for the interrogative to be applied to it, so you may say: "Have you not seen the like of today, in good or in evil?" Where the verb that is being asked about has been omitted, you may supply it in either of the two ways. The author of *al-Kashshaf* inclined to supplying it as: "Have you seen like the one who...?" because this is the most common form of amazement with the particle of comparison *kaf*.

As for "the one who passed by a town," it has been said that he was Armiya ibn Hilqiya, and it has been said he was 'Uzayr ibn Sharkhiya (Ezra ibn Serayah). The town is Jerusalem according to most opinions. What appears to me is that he was Hizqiyal (Ezekiel) ibn Buzi, the prophet of the Children of Israel, who was a contemporary of Armiya and Daniel, and who was among those whom Nebuchadnezzar took captive to Babylon at the beginning of the sixth century before Christ. This is because, when he saw Nebuchadnezzar's determination to uproot the Jews and his gathering of the relics of the Temple to bring them to Babylon, he gathered the books of the law of Moses, the Ark of the Covenant, and the staff of Moses, and cast them into a well in Jerusalem, fearing that Nebuchadnezzar would burn them. Perhaps he made for himself a sign by which he would recognise them, and made it a secret between himself and the prophets of his time and their heirs from among the prophets. When he was taken out to Babylon, he remained there and wrote a book in visions which he considered revelation, indicating the calamities of the Jews and the deliverance that was hoped for them. The last thing he wrote was in the twenty-fifth year after the captivity of the Jews, and no news of him is known after that, as is recorded in their history. It is thought that he died or was killed.

Among what he wrote: "The Spirit of the Lord carried me out and set me down in the middle of a valley, and it was full of many bones, and He made me pass over them round about. Behold, they were very dry. And He said to me: 'Son of man, can these bones live?' I answered: 'O Lord GOD, You know.' Then He said to me: 'Prophesy over these bones, and say to them: O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD. Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and I will lay sinews upon you, and will bring up flesh upon you, and cover you with skin.' So I prophesied as I was commanded, and the bones came together, each bone to its bone, and I looked, and behold, sinews and flesh came upon them, and the skin covered them above, and breath entered into them, and they lived and stood upon their feet, an exceedingly great army."

Since the visions of the prophets are revelation, there is no doubt that when Allah restored the building of Jerusalem in the time of the prophet Ezra, around 450 years before Christ, He revived the prophet Hizqiyal, peace be upon him, so that he might see the fulfilment of his prophethood. He showed him the reviving of the bones, and showed him a sign in his food, his drink and his donkey. This is a discourse between the Creator and one of His chosen servants by way of a miracle. He made his report a sign to the people of faith, those who are certain of what Allah, the Exalted, informed them of, or to a people whom Allah had informed of that from among His chosen servants, or to the people of the town in which he had lived and who had lost him, when he came to them after a hundred years and those who knew him recognised him by his attributes.

So His words, ﴿passed by a town﴾, refer to his saying: "The Spirit of the Lord carried me out and made me pass over them," and His words, ﴿He said: How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾, refer to his saying: "Can these bones live?" and "I said: O Lord GOD, You know," since his words here indicate his considering their revival unlikely. His words, ﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years﴾ etc., are among the clarifications the Qur'an added to what is in the books of the Jews, since they wrote them after the passing of ages. From this it is inferred that he died around 560 years before Christ, and the restoration of Jerusalem was around 458, so that is roughly a hundred years. His words, ﴿Look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh﴾, are a reminder to him of that prophecy, which is the restoration of the city of Israel.

His words, ﴿and it was fallen down upon its roofs﴾: *al-khawiyah* means empty of inhabitants and buildings. *al-'urush* is the plural of *'arsh*, which means the roof. The adverbial phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The meaning is that it was empty, fallen upon its roof, and that is the worst kind of ruin, because the first thing to fall from a building is the roof, then the walls fall upon those roofs. The town is Jerusalem. He saw it in his sleep in that state, or he saw it when the envoys of Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it. The first is the apparent meaning, because he was among those taken captive with (Jehoiakim), king of Israel, and the destruction did not occur in his time, but occurred in the time of (Zedekiah), his brother, eleven years later.

His words, ﴿How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾, is a question of denial and of considering it unlikely. His words, ﴿So Allah caused him to die﴾, the sequence in it is according to what follows, so it does not necessarily mean that He caused him to die at the time of his saying: "How will Allah bring this to life?" It has been said that he slept, and Allah caused him to die in his sleep.

His words, ﴿then He raised him﴾, mean: He brought him back to life with a special life by which his spirit was returned to his body, because his body had not decayed as the bodies of the other prophets had not. This is a resurrection that breaks the usual custom, and it is other than the resurrection of gathering on the Day of Judgement.

His words, ﴿He said: I have remained a day or part of a day﴾: he believed that on account of a knowledge Allah had placed in him, or because he remembered that he had slept at the beginning of the day and found that the time in which he awoke was the end of the day.

His words, ﴿Look at your food﴾, are a consequence of His words, ﴿You have remained a hundred years﴾. The command to look is a command to take admonition, that is: look at it while it has not changed. It is apparent that the food and drink were with him when he was caused to die, or that they were placed in his grave if he belonged to a community or a land where they place food for the honoured dead, as the ancient Egyptians did, or that he had food with him when he went out, and Allah caused him to die in his sleep, as has been said.

The meaning of ﴿has not changed﴾ is: has not altered. Its root is derived from *al-sanah* (year), because the passing of years necessarily causes change, like the hardening of clay. The *ha'* is original, not a *ha' al-sakt* (a silent pausal *ha'*). They sometimes treat the *ha'* of *sanah* as the *ta'* in derivation, so they say: "So-and-so was struck by a year (*asnata*)," if a year of famine befell him. Matrud al-Khuza'i, or Ibn al-Zib'ara, said:

"'Amr, the one who crumbled the bread (thareed) for his people, a people in Mecca struck by years of drought, gaunt."

His words, ﴿Look at your donkey﴾: his donkey had decayed, so that only its bones remained, and Allah revived it before him. With His words, ﴿Look at your donkey﴾, the state which is the object of consideration was not mentioned, because the mere looking at it is sufficient, for he saw it as bones and then saw it alive. Perhaps it had perished and then remained in that open area where Hizqiyal was, far from habitation. Allah had gathered for him all kinds of revival: He revived his body by breathing the spirit into it without re-creating it; He revived his food by preserving it from change; and He revived his donkey by re-creation. Thus it was a great sign for the people who are certain of this. Perhaps Allah informed some of His chosen servants of that revival, some of the revived.

His words, ﴿and that We may make you a sign for the people﴾, are joined to an implied element indicated by His words, ﴿Look at your food﴾ and ﴿Look at your donkey﴾, for the command to look in them is for taking admonition, since he would certainly look at that. The intended purpose, in considering it as an argument against the improbability that Allah would revive a town after its death, is that the sense of the discourse is: "Look at what has been mentioned; We have made it a sign for you of the resurrection, and We have made you a sign for the people, because they did not see his food, drink and donkey, but they saw his person and recognised him by his attributes." Then He said to him: ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them﴾. The apparent meaning is that the intended bones are the bones of some of the human beings who had perished, or that the bones of the donkey are intended, in which case the *al-* (the definite article) replaces the possessive suffix, so His words, ﴿to the bones﴾, are in the sense of an apposition to "your donkey," except that the implied governing verb has been made explicit.

The majority of the ten readers recited ﴿nunshiruha﴾ with *ra'*, the present tense of *anshara* (the quadrilateral form), meaning to revive. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited ﴿nunshizuha﴾ with *zay*, the present tense of *anshaza*, meaning to raise it up. *al-nashz* means elevation. The intended meaning is their elevation when they become thick through the enveloping of sinew, flesh and blood around them. Thus two meanings arise from the two readings of one word. In the book of Hizqiyal: "The bones came together, each bone to its bone, and I looked, and behold, with sinew and flesh, and it covered them, and the skin was spread over them."

His words, ﴿He said: I know that Allah has power over everything﴾: the majority read *a'lamu* with a hamzah of cutting (*hamzat qat'*), as the present tense of *'alima* (to know), so it is the answer to "the one who passed by a town," in response to Allah's saying to him: ﴿Look at your food﴾, and so on. The present tense is used to indicate what is in this prophet's speech of the renewal of his knowledge of that, because he had known it before, and his knowledge of it was renewed. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with a hamzat wasl (connecting hamzah), as being part of Allah's own speech, and the apparent expectation was that it would be joined by "and" to ﴿Look at your food﴾, but its conjunction was left out because it was made like the conclusion drawn from the argument in His words, ﴿Look at your food and your drink﴾, and so on.

[p. 39 begins below]

This is coordinated with His saying, ﴿Or like one who passed by a town﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:259], so it is a third example for the matter of His saying, ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:257], and a second example for the matter of ﴿Or like one who passed by a town﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:259]. The implied meaning is: "Or he is like Abraham when he said, 'My Lord, show me,' etc." Abraham, out of his intense love to reach the rank of direct witnessing (mu'ayanah) in the proof of resurrection, desired to move from theoretical, demonstrative knowledge ('ilm nazari burhani) to necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-daruri), so he asked Allah to show him the giving of life to the dead through something perceptible.

Here "kayfa" (how) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), stripped of the interrogative sense, as it is in His saying, ﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs as He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:6].

As for His saying, ﴿Have you not believed?﴾, the wawu in it is the wawu of circumstance (wawu al-hal), and the hamzah is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqriri) regarding this state. The operator of the circumstance is an implied verb indicated by His saying, "show me." The implied meaning is: "Shall I show you while you have not believed?" This is a figurative affirmation, intended to draw his mind to dispelling the whisperings of doubt. Therefore His saying, ﴿Yes, but that my heart may be at rest﴾, is a statement issuing from his testing of his certainty and his finding it free from doubt.

His saying, ﴿that my heart may be at rest﴾, means: that my knowledge may be firmly established and verified, and may move from the struggle of thought and reflection to the simplicity of necessity (basatat al-darurah) by the certainty of observation, and the disclosure of the known in a manner that does not need repeated inference or the removal of doubts from the intellect. The reason is that the literal meaning of (yatma'inn) is "to be still, to settle," its verbal noun is (al-itmi'nan), and the noun of the verbal noun is (al-tuma'nina). It is literally used for the stillness of bodies, and its application to the settling of knowledge in the soul and the cessation of the struggle of inference is originally a metaphor, by likening the hesitation and the labour of inference to agitation and movement. This metaphor became so common that it came to equal the literal meaning, as one says: "his mind was at rest" (ṭama'anna bāluhu), and "his heart was at rest" (ṭama'anna qalbuhu).

The more evident view is that (iṭma'anna) is of the measure (if'alalla), and that there is no metathesis (qalb) in it. Thus the hamzah in it is the final radical (lam al-kalimah), and the mim is the middle radical ('ayn al-kalimah). This is the view of Abu 'Amr, and it is the clearer, since there is no reason for metathesis, for the occurrence of the hamzah as a final radical is more common and lighter than its occurrence as a middle radical. Sibawayh, however, held that (iṭma'anna) is metathesized, and its original form is (iṭ'amanna), and it has been heard as (ṭam'anatuhu) and (ṭa'mantuhu). Most usage places the mim before the hamzah. What caused the disagreement is the failure to hear the unaugmented root from it, since (ṭamana) has not been heard.

The heart here is intended to mean knowledge, since the heart does not become agitated at doubt, nor move at the establishment of a proof; rather, that belongs to thought. By (itmi'nan) he meant perceptible knowledge and the expansion of the soul through it. Allah had directed him to a method by which he would see the giving of life to the dead with his own eyes (ra'y al-'ayn).

His saying, ﴿Take four birds﴾: know that (al-tayr) is used for the singular as a synonym of (ṭa'ir) (bird). It is from naming by the verbal noun, and its original form is a description, so its root is unity, and there is no doubt about this usage. This is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Azhari and Qutrub, and there is no basis for hesitation regarding it. It is also used for its plural, and it is a collective noun of (ṭa'ir), like (ṣaḥb) and (ṣāḥib). This is because its original form is a verbal noun, and a verbal noun applies to the singular and the plural.

(Min) has been brought for partitive meaning (li al-tab'iḍ), to indicate that the four are of different kinds. The apparent wisdom of multiplicity and variety is an increase in the certainty that giving life was not easier with some kinds than with others, and therefore the kinds were enumerated. Perhaps the reason for making them four is that they be placed in the four directions: east, west, south and north, lest one suppose that some directions had a greater specialty in the possibility of giving life. It is also permissible that what is meant by "four" is four parts of one bird, so that the definite article (al-) is for prior reference, pointing to a present bird, that is: "take four of its parts, then call them."

[p. 40 begins below]

Running (sa'y) is a kind of walking, not a kind of flying. Thus He made this a sign that they had been returned to a life different from their previous life, lest one suppose that they had not died completely.

The mention of "every mountain" indicates that he was commanded to place each part of the birds upon a mountain, because placing them on mountains strengthens the scattering of those parts, since they were separated by being cut from their bodies and placed in distant and hard-to-reach places.

A mountain (jabal) is a great piece of the earth of stone and soil, raised above the level ground. There are many mountains on the earth with differing heights. Some of them contain dwellings for humans, such as the mountains of Ṭayyi', and some of them are a refuge for people from the enemy, as al-Samaw'al said:

We have a mountain whose dweller is the one he protects; it is unassailable, turning back the gaze, though it is weary.

The meaning of (ṣurhunna) is "bring them near to you," or "incline them to you." It is said (ṣāra-hu yaṣūru-hu) and (ṣāra-hu yaṣīru-hu) with the same meaning. It is an Arabic word according to the most correct view. It has also been said that it is arabicized (mu'arrab). Thus on the authority of 'Ikrimah it is Nabataean; on the authority of Qatadah it is Abyssinian; and on the authority of Wahb it is Roman. The benefit of the command to bring them near is that he would examine their conditions, so that after their giving of life he would know that no part of them had moved from its place.

His saying, ﴿Then place upon every mountain of them a part﴾, is coordinated with an omitted element indicated by His saying "a part," because dividing them into parts occurs only after slaughter. Thus the implied meaning is: "then slaughter them, then place..." etc.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ṣurhunna﴾ with a damma on the ṣād and a sukun on the rā', from (ṣāra-hu yaṣūru-hu). Ḥamzah, Abu Ja'far, Khalaf, and Ruways from Ya'qub read ﴿ṣirhunna﴾ with a kasra on the ṣād, from (ṣāra yaṣīru), which is a dialect form of this verb.

The majority of readers read (juz'an) with a sukun on the zay, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a damma on the zay. Both are dialect forms.

[Page 41]

Returning to the exhortation to spend in the way of Allah. This parable refers back to His words, ﴿O you who believe, spend from what We have provided you﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:254), and it is an explanatory resumption (*istīnāf bayānī*, a clause that answers an implied question in the listener's mind), because His words ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:254), and what follows it, arouse in the hearers an eagerness to learn what the one who spends in the way of Allah will meet on that Day, after the verse was followed by proofs, admonitions and lessons. The hearts of the listeners were prepared to focus on this, so the discussion was extended in a way that suits its importance.

As for His words, ﴿The parable of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾, it is a comparison of the state of their reward and blessing. The relative clause indicates that what is meant is specifically the state of their spending, with the implied meaning "the parable of the spending of those who...". The state of giving the expenditure, its reaching its proper place, and the reward given to them, is compared to the state of a grain that produced seven ears, etc. That is, it was sown in pure soil and good earth, and rain fell on it, so it produced seven ears. All of that is omitted for brevity, since it is evident that a grain does not produce that except in such conditions. This is therefore a comparison of the intellectual to the sensory, and the thing compared to has a known form. The basis of the parable regarding the multiplication was made a grain, because its multiplication comes from itself and not from anything added to it. The comparison of a good deed to seed and of the one who strives to the one who sows has become widespread, and in the proverb: "Many a striver benefits one who sits, and a sower who is not a reaper." Since multiplication is attributed to a unit of origin, the unit of origin here is what Allah rewards for the smallest good deeds, that is, what is recorded as reward for the least good deeds, such as one who intends a good deed but does not perform it. In the good deed of spending in the way of Allah, it becomes seven hundred times.

Al-Wahidi said in *Asbab al-Nuzul* (Occasions of Revelation) and others: this verse was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. That was because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he wished to set out for the Battle of Tabuk, urged the people to spend in the way of Allah. The army at that time was in need of equipment, and it was the Army of Hardship. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf came to him with four thousand, and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan said: "The equipment of whoever has no equipment is upon me." So he equipped the army with a thousand camels, with their saddles and their harnesses. It was also said that he came with a thousand dinars of gold and poured them into the lap of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

[Page 42]

The meaning of His words, ﴿and Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾, is that the multiplication consists of many degrees that none knows except Allah, the Exalted, because it depends on the circumstances of the giver, the circumstances of the recipient, the times and places of that, sincerity, the intention to obey, love of good for people, preferring others over oneself, and other things that surround charity and spending, which have an effect on multiplying the reward. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾.

He repeated His words, ﴿those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾, to show concern for this relative clause. His words, ﴿then they do not follow﴾, came with the conjunction "then" (*thumma*), although the apparent expectation would be "and" (*wa*). Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: to show the disparity between the spending and the abandonment of reminders of favor and harm, and that abandoning them is better than the spending itself. He means that "then" indicates a principal ordering and not a temporal delay, raising the rank of abandoning reminders of favor and harm above the rank of charity, because giving may arise from generosity of soul and love of praise; so the souls have a share in it alongside the share of the recipient. This is unlike abandoning reminders of favor and harm, in which there is no share for the soul of the giver. The occurrence of an important thing, when it is difficult to obtain, is compared to the occurrence of a thing whose time is later. It seems that what led al-Zamakhshari to this is that he saw that the meaning of delay is not intended here, because what is intended is the occurrence of spending and the abandonment of reminders of favor together.

The root meaning of *mann* is bestowal and favor; one says "manna 'alayhi manna" (he bestowed a favor upon him). Then it was applied to counting the favors upon the one favored. From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and do not confer favor, seeking to receive more﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:6). When it is mentioned after charity and giving, it is restricted to the second meaning.

Reminders of favor in spending in the way of Allah occur only through showing superiority over Muslims, and through showing off in spending, and through showing superiority over the fighters whom one equips or carries. Praising the positions of a fighter in jihad or the positions of his people is not among reminders of favor. Al-Huraysh ibn Hilal al-Qurayi, mentioning his horses in the Conquest of Makkah and the Day of Hunayn, said:

They witnessed with the Prophet, marked (for battle), at Hunayn, while their hooves were bleeding,
And they witnessed the battle of Khalid and scraped their hooves upon the Sacred Land.

'Abbas ibn Mirdas, praising the positions of his people at the Battle of Hunayn, said:

Until, when Muhammad the Prophet said: "O Banu Sulaym, you have fulfilled, so return."
We returned, and had it not been for us, their host would have surrounded the Muslims, and they would have seized what they had gathered.

Harm (*adhā*) is that a hypocrite harms the one he has given to, by an injurious word or deed. Al-Nabigha said:

Upon me, for 'Amr, is a favor upon favor, for his father, and it is not with scorpions (i.e., it is not with stings).

The legal purpose, then, is that the spending of the one who spends in the way of Allah be intended for the support of the religion, with no share for the soul in it. That is the highest degree of spending, and it is what is promised with this great reward. Below that there are many levels, whose conditions vary.

[Page 41]

Returning to the exhortation to spend in the way of Allah. This parable refers back to His words, ﴿O you who believe, spend from what We have provided you﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:254), and it is an explanatory resumption (*istīnāf bayānī*, a clause that answers an implied question in the listener's mind), because His words ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:254), and what follows it, arouse in the hearers an eagerness to learn what the one who spends in the way of Allah will meet on that Day, after the verse was followed by proofs, admonitions and lessons. The hearts of the listeners were prepared to focus on this, so the discussion was extended in a way that suits its importance.

As for His words, ﴿The parable of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾, it is a comparison of the state of their reward and blessing. The relative clause indicates that what is meant is specifically the state of their spending, with the implied meaning "the parable of the spending of those who...". The state of giving the expenditure, its reaching its proper place, and the reward given to them, is compared to the state of a grain that produced seven ears, etc. That is, it was sown in pure soil and good earth, and rain fell on it, so it produced seven ears. All of that is omitted for brevity, since it is evident that a grain does not produce that except in such conditions. This is therefore a comparison of the intellectual to the sensory, and the thing compared to has a known form. The basis of the parable regarding the multiplication was made a grain, because its multiplication comes from itself and not from anything added to it. The comparison of a good deed to seed and of the one who strives to the one who sows has become widespread, and in the proverb: "Many a striver benefits one who sits, and a sower who is not a reaper." Since multiplication is attributed to a unit of origin, the unit of origin here is what Allah rewards for the smallest good deeds, that is, what is recorded as reward for the least good deeds, such as one who intends a good deed but does not perform it. In the good deed of spending in the way of Allah, it becomes seven hundred times.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 263–264 (part 1 of 2):

﴿A kind word and forgiveness are better than a charity followed by harm. And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders and harm, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His example is like a smooth rock with a little dust on it; a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾

Having finished with the aim of praising spending in the way of Allah, the discourse moved on to praising another kind of spending, namely spending on needy people, which is sadaqat (charity). No mention of sadaqah had preceded this, but it comes to mind when spending in the way of Allah is mentioned. When Allah described spending in His way with the quality of sincerity toward Him, by His saying ﴿those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah, then do not follow what they have spent with reminders [of their kindness] or harm﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:262), and so on, the discourse, by way of association, extended that quality to spending on the needy. The reason is that al-Mann (reminding) and al-Adha (harm) occur more often in charity, because charity is directed at specific individuals, unlike spending in the way of Allah, where the spender often does not know most of those who receive the expenditure.

Al-Mann toward the one who receives charity is reminding him of the favour, as mentioned just above.

From the passages of al-Zamakhshari in (al-Kalim al-Nawabigh): "The taste of the blessings (al-ala') is sweeter than al-mann, and it is more bitter than the blessings when al-mann is present." The first "al-ala'" means the favours, and the second "al-ala'" is a tree with bitter leaves. The first "al-mann" is a substance resembling honey that falls like dew on some trees of the Sinai desert, and it is the one referred to in His saying, ﴿And We sent down upon you al-mann and al-salwa﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:57). The second "al-mann" is the benefactor's reminding the beneficiary of the favour.

Al-Adha is injury and slight harm to the one who receives the favour. Allah said: ﴿They will not harm you except with a little harm﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:111). What is meant here is the explicit harm from the benefactor to the beneficiary, such as belittling him by saying "I gave you," or behaving arrogantly toward him because of the gift, not to mention reproaching him for his poverty. This is different from the harm that arises from al-mann. Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, in the Book of Zakat in (Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din), pointed out that al-mann has a root and a source, and it is one of the states and qualities of the heart. From it branch out outward states manifested on the tongue and the limbs. The source of harm is two matters: the giver's dislike of giving away his wealth and the great difficulty this is for him, and his seeing himself as better than the poor person. Both arise from ignorance. Dislike of parting with wealth is foolishness, because whoever gives wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and reward has known that what he gains from giving is more noble than what he gave. And his thinking that he is better than the poor person is ignorance of the worth of being free of need, meaning that people's ranks differ by the purification of their souls, not by the accidents of wealth and poverty, which do not arise from degrees of spiritual perfection.

When Allah warned the giver against harming the one who receives charity, it was understood that warning against causing him injury, such as insulting or beating him, is implied by the implication of the address (fahwa al-khitab), because it is more deserving of prohibition.

Allah expanded upon this subject with explanation, encouragement and warning, through various methods and wonderful variations. Thereby He alerted us to the great concern of Islam for spending in the channels of righteousness and assistance.

How could it not be so, when the cohesion of the community depends on its wealth circulating among its members? One of the greatest aims of the Shari'ah is to benefit from common wealth among the members of the community in comprehensive ways that combine safeguarding the general benefit with safeguarding individual feelings. This is achieved by observing justice toward the one who toiled to gather and earn the wealth, and observing kindness toward the one whose effort has fallen short. This aim is among the most noble legislative aims. The degree of correctness or error in this matter has been the measure of the rise and decline of nations. You will not find a law that has appeared, or a caller to good who called people, without their making for the distribution of wealth to members of the community, from what is in the hands of the wealthy, a great place in their legislation or their call. However, they differ in this, between those who approach it and those who fall short, or between those who aspire and those who plan. Yet you will not find a law that hit the target for this purpose and knew how to distinguish between what is recommended in it and what is obligatory, like this blessed Shari'ah. It has dealt with the system of common wealth in a wonderful manner, establishing it on the principle of distributing wealth among the members of the community. This is done by providing for the needy member of the community the sustenance of his need, in ways that do not deprive the one who earns wealth of the benefit of his earnings and of enjoying them before anyone else.

The first thing it began with was securing the confidence of the earner in the safety of his wealth, that someone should not seize it from him. Allah said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:29). The Prophet (ﷺ) said in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed your blood and your wealth are forbidden to you, as the sanctity of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours." A hundred thousand people or more heard this from him, and they transmitted it throughout the horizons of Islam until it reached the level of tawatur (mass-transmission). Therefore, the principle of preserving wealth became one of the general foundations of legislation, which no Muslim can nullify.

This assurance of the safety of wealth was followed by detailed rulings concerning transactions and documentation, such as the legitimacy of the pledge (rahn) in salam (advance sale) and documentation by witnessing, as the verses that follow declare, along with whatever else in the texts of the Shari'ah, whether explicit or derived by inference.

Then the Shari'ah indicated that among its aims is that wealth should not remain circulating in one direction, one family or one tribe of the community, but that the aim is its circulation. This is in His saying, in the verse of fay' (spoils), ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near relatives and the orphans and the needy and the traveller, so that it will not be a dawlah (circulating commodity) among the rich among you﴾ (al-Hashr 59:7). The pronoun in "yakun" refers to "what Allah has restored" in consideration of its being wealth, meaning lest wealth should be a dawlah. Dawlah is what people circulate among themselves of wealth. That is, We legislated its disbursement to those We named, rather than the soldiers having a right to it, so that the poor may receive their portions from it and become wealthy, and it will not be circulated among a group of the rich, as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, when their leaders took the mirba' (one quarter) and the raiders took three quarters, so that all the wealth remained with a special group.

Then the Shari'ah proceeded to take from this wealth in an organized manner. It made from it a compulsory seizure, part of it during the lifetime of the owner and part after his death. As for what is during his lifetime, it is the obligatory charities, among them zakat, which in most cases is one tenth of the owned goods, or half a tenth, or a quarter of a tenth. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained the wisdom of its legislation when he said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal when he sent him to Yemen: "Indeed Allah has enjoined upon them a zakat, taken from their wealthy and returned to their poor." He made the distribution of what is collected from this wealth to establish the interests of the people and to meet the needs of their weak ones. Thus they became people with a right in the wealth of the rich, not humiliated and not threatened with withholding or harshness. He turned to the wealthy and promised them, for this giving, the best of what is promised to the good-doers, by calling it a loan to Allah, the Exalted, and by multiplying its reward, as the verses that we are now explaining have brought.

To this category belongs the taking of the khums (one-fifth) from war booty, even though it is the right of the fighters. He took this from them and said to them: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of spoils, a fifth of it belongs to Allah and to the Messenger﴾ (al-Anfal 8:41), up to His saying: ﴿if you have believed in Allah﴾ (al-Anfal 8:41). Thus He encouraged them to accept this. There is no doubt that He took it away from the hands of those who had acquired it by their swords and spears. Likewise, obligatory maintenance (al-nafaqat al-wajibah) belongs to this category, other than the maintenance of the wife, because it is not regarded as a seizure, since it is in exchange for the cohesion of the family. Nor does the maintenance of children fall under it in the same way, because the motive for it is innate. As for the maintenance of relatives other than children, according to those who make the maintenance of kin obligatory, it is part of obligatory seizure.

Among obligatory seizures are the expiations (kaffarat) for breaking an oath, for breaking the fast of Ramadan, for zihar, for ila', and for the compensation for hunting game. This is the distribution of part of the wealth of the living during his lifetime.

As for the distribution of wealth after the death of its owner, that is by explaining the rules of inheritance (fara'id al-irth) in a manner that admits no addition or reduction. The Arabs used to give their wealth to whomever they loved, whether a stranger or a relative, as we previously explained in His saying: ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:180). Some nations used to make the inheritance go to the eldest.

The distribution of these shares was made in a manner of mercy toward the people who own wealth. Their wealth was given only to the closest of people to them, and its distribution was according to closeness, as is well known in the questions of exclusion (hajb) in the fara'id, and according to need for wealth, such as preferring the male to the female, because he supports others and the female is supported by others. In this area the Shari'ah also turned to the owners of wealth and left them the right to dispose of one third of their wealth, designating whoever should receive it after their death, on condition that he is not an heir, so that they do not use this to make a particular heir a favoured recipient over others.

The Shari'ah also made among the seizures a seizure that is recommended but not obligatory. This comprises kinds of consolation through charities, gifts, presents, bequests, and lending to the needy without usury. There is no seizure of the actual property of the owned goods in the Shari'ah. Seizure does not exceed taking the benefits, with justice and equality.

The phrase ﴿A kind word﴾ and what follows is a resumptive clause (mustanifah istinafan bayaniyyan), and the indefiniteness of ﴿qawlun ma'ruf﴾ is for minimization, meaning: the least kind word is better than a charity followed by harm. Al-ma'ruf is what people recognise, that is, they do not reject it. What is meant by it is a good word, and it is the opposite of harm.

Al-maghfirah (forgiveness) here means overlooking an offence, that is, the giver overlooking the insistence or boorishness of the one asking, such as one who asks and says, "Give me the right of Allah that you have." Or something similar. It may also mean Allah's overlooking of sins because of that charity when it is accompanied by a kind word. In this there is an allusion that harm is about to nullify the reward of charity.

His saying ﴿And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) serving as a reminder of two of Allah's attributes so that the believers may adorn themselves with them. They are: al-ghina' (freedom from need), which relates to His being above returning the gift with what would soothe the giver's stinginess, and al-hilm (forbearance), which relates to His pardon and forgiveness for the rudeness of some of those who ask.

Al-ibtal (invalidation) is making a thing void, that is, removing it so that it is no longer beneficial for what it was intended. The meaning of the nullification of an act is that its legal effect does not follow. Whether the act is obligatory or voluntary, if it is obligatory, its nullification means it is not valid, so that the responsibility of the legally accountable person is not discharged from that obligation. This happens when a pillar or condition of the act is missing. If the act is voluntary, nullification means the loss of reward for the act due to a legal impediment to its reward being credited. This is what is meant here, in harmonising the evidences of the Shari'ah.

His saying ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾: the kaf (like) is a stable adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqarr), which is a circumstantial element (hal) from the pronoun in "tubtilu" (you invalidate). That is: do not be, in following your charities with reminders and harm, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, while he is a disbeliever who does not believe in Allah and the Last Day, and who gives only so that people may see him. This is the giving of the people of the Jahiliyyah.

The relative clause in "like one who spends his wealth" is meant generically; it does not refer to a specific individual or to a single person. The purpose of this comparison is to make the thing compared to appear hideous. What is intended is not an equality in the legal ruling, in harmonising the legal evidences.

[p. 45]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 263–264 (part 2 of 2):

Ri'a' (ostentation) is spelled with two hamzas and is on the pattern *fi'al*, from *ra'a* (to see). It means that a person frequently displays his good deeds to people. The *fi'al* form here indicates intensity and frequency. The first hamza is original, and the last is replaced from a *ya'* that follows the added *alif*. It may also be said *riya'* with a *ya'* after the *ra'*, by replacing the hamza with a *ya'* after a kasra.

The meaning is a comparison between some of the Muslim almsgivers, who give seeking reward but follow their charity with reminders of favor and harm, and the disbelieving hypocrites who spend their wealth seeking nothing from spending but ri'a' and praise, since they do not seek the reward of the Hereafter.

The point of resemblance is that what they give yields no benefit beyond satisfying what is in their hearts of the desire to dominate the weak and satisfying the habit of harming, to which they are accustomed, with no benefit in the Hereafter.

The state of the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, which is the thing compared, is presented as a similitude that extends to those who follow their charity with reminders of favor and harm, through His saying: ﴿So his likeness is like the likeness of a smooth rock﴾, etc. The pronoun in *mathaluhu* ("his likeness") refers to the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people. Since it is a similitude of the state of the thing compared, it is necessarily a similitude of the state of the thing being compared, so the sentence contains three comparisons.

It compares the state of the disbeliever who spends his wealth to be seen by people with the state of a smooth rock upon which there is dust covering it, meaning the observer thinks it is good soil suitable for sowing. The sentence's sense is: upon it is dust suitable for planting. The description of the dust is omitted for brevity, relying on the fact that the dust that people expect the heavy rain to reach is the dust in which they sow. When the planter sows it, and a heavy rain strikes it, and the planter hopes for the growth of his crop, the water sweeps it off the surface of the smooth rock, leaving nothing of it, and its place remains bare and smooth, so the planter's hope is disappointed.

[Page 49]

This is better and more precise than making the meaning a likeness of the disbeliever's spending to dust upon a smooth rock that a heavy rain struck and swept away, with the point of resemblance being rapid disappearance and lack of permanence, as in His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes on which the wind blows violently on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18]. The context of that verse is another context.

You may also take the particle *ka* (like) in His saying ﴿like the one who spends his wealth﴾ as a description of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), which is indicated by the sense of spending contained in the word *sadaqatihim* ("their charities"). An omitted genitive phrase lies between the *ka* and the relative noun. The sense is: spending like the spending of the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people.

In this similitude, the reverse of the similitude for the one who spends his wealth in the way of God is observed, which is a grain that yielded seven hundred grains.

Thus the comparison is a comparison of an intellectual composite to a sensory composite. The point of resemblance is hope in a state that deceives with benefit and then, shortly after, fails to bring its hoper what he hoped for, so his hope is disappointed. This is because believers are not free of hoping for the attainment of reward from their charities, and it often happens that heedlessness overtakes the giver, so he follows his charity with reminders of favor and harm, carried away by evil thoughts.

His saying ﴿they have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾ is placed in a wonderful position in the arrangement of the speech, through which many meanings flow. In its position, it is suitable to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, so that it is included in the state being compared. The pronoun in *kasabu* ("they earned") is treated as a plural pronoun, because the one who spends (*alladhi yunfiqu*) is interpreted as a group (*ta'wil*). It is also suitable to be a circumstantial clause of "the likeness of a smooth rock," with regard to its being a likeness. This is similar to what is permitted in His saying ﴿or like a downpour from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], since its implied sense is: like the likeness of those with a downpour. Therefore its pronoun came in the plural form, observing the sense even though the antecedent word is singular. It is also suitable to be taken as an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*), because the preceding speech raises the question of a questioner about the outcome of the state of the thing compared. It is also suitable to be taken as a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) and summation (*fadhlaka*) of the presentation of the similitude, so it returns to the beginning of His saying ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders of favor and harm﴾ and to the end of the speech.

[Page 50]

It is also suitable to be taken as a circumstantial clause of "smooth rock," meaning: they have no power over anything of what they have earned from it. The relative clause's returning pronoun is omitted, because it is a pronoun in the genitive governed by the preposition with which the relative noun is governed. The sense of "they have no power" is that they cannot retrieve it, nor do they benefit from its reward, so nothing of it remains for them.

It may also be that the sense is: they do not know how to place anything of what they have earned in its proper place, so they spend their wealth for no benefit that returns to them in their lifetimes, based on His saying ﴿And God does not guide the disbelieving people﴾.

The meaning is: so He leaves it bare, so that they do not harvest any crop from it, as in His saying: ﴿So he began to turn his palms over at what he had spent on it﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. The clause ﴿And God does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ is a concluding statement, and the *waw* is parenthetical (*i'tiradiyya*). This concluding statement is brought to warn believers against the infiltration of the states of disbelievers into their deeds, since among their states is reminding those they spend upon of favor and the harm that comes with it.

[p. 44]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 263–264 (part 1 of 2):

﴿A kind word and forgiveness are better than a charity followed by harm. And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders and harm, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His example is like a smooth rock with a little dust on it; a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾

Having finished with the aim of praising spending in the way of Allah, the discourse moved on to praising another kind of spending, namely spending on needy people, which is sadaqat (charity). No mention of sadaqah had preceded this, but it comes to mind when spending in the way of Allah is mentioned. When Allah described spending in His way with the quality of sincerity toward Him, by His saying ﴿those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah, then do not follow what they have spent with reminders [of their kindness] or harm﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:262), and so on, the discourse, by way of association, extended that quality to spending on the needy. The reason is that al-Mann (reminding) and al-Adha (harm) occur more often in charity, because charity is directed at specific individuals, unlike spending in the way of Allah, where the spender often does not know most of those who receive the expenditure.

Al-Mann toward the one who receives charity is reminding him of the favour, as mentioned just above.

From the passages of al-Zamakhshari in (al-Kalim al-Nawabigh): "The taste of the blessings (al-ala') is sweeter than al-mann, and it is more bitter than the blessings when al-mann is present." The first "al-ala'" means the favours, and the second "al-ala'" is a tree with bitter leaves. The first "al-mann" is a substance resembling honey that falls like dew on some trees of the Sinai desert, and it is the one referred to in His saying, ﴿And We sent down upon you al-mann and al-salwa﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:57). The second "al-mann" is the benefactor's reminding the beneficiary of the favour.

Al-Adha is injury and slight harm to the one who receives the favour. Allah said: ﴿They will not harm you except with a little harm﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:111). What is meant here is the explicit harm from the benefactor to the beneficiary, such as belittling him by saying "I gave you," or behaving arrogantly toward him because of the gift, not to mention reproaching him for his poverty. This is different from the harm that arises from al-mann. Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, in the Book of Zakat in (Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din), pointed out that al-mann has a root and a source, and it is one of the states and qualities of the heart. From it branch out outward states manifested on the tongue and the limbs. The source of harm is two matters: the giver's dislike of giving away his wealth and the great difficulty this is for him, and his seeing himself as better than the poor person. Both arise from ignorance. Dislike of parting with wealth is foolishness, because whoever gives wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and reward has known that what he gains from giving is more noble than what he gave. And his thinking that he is better than the poor person is ignorance of the worth of being free of need, meaning that people's ranks differ by the purification of their souls, not by the accidents of wealth and poverty, which do not arise from degrees of spiritual perfection.

When Allah warned the giver against harming the one who receives charity, it was understood that warning against causing him injury, such as insulting or beating him, is implied by the implication of the address (fahwa al-khitab), because it is more deserving of prohibition.

Allah expanded upon this subject with explanation, encouragement and warning, through various methods and wonderful variations. Thereby He alerted us to the great concern of Islam for spending in the channels of righteousness and assistance.

How could it not be so, when the cohesion of the community depends on its wealth circulating among its members? One of the greatest aims of the Shari'ah is to benefit from common wealth among the members of the community in comprehensive ways that combine safeguarding the general benefit with safeguarding individual feelings. This is achieved by observing justice toward the one who toiled to gather and earn the wealth, and observing kindness toward the one whose effort has fallen short. This aim is among the most noble legislative aims. The degree of correctness or error in this matter has been the measure of the rise and decline of nations. You will not find a law that has appeared, or a caller to good who called people, without their making for the distribution of wealth to members of the community, from what is in the hands of the wealthy, a great place in their legislation or their call. However, they differ in this, between those who approach it and those who fall short, or between those who aspire and those who plan. Yet you will not find a law that hit the target for this purpose and knew how to distinguish between what is recommended in it and what is obligatory, like this blessed Shari'ah. It has dealt with the system of common wealth in a wonderful manner, establishing it on the principle of distributing wealth among the members of the community. This is done by providing for the needy member of the community the sustenance of his need, in ways that do not deprive the one who earns wealth of the benefit of his earnings and of enjoying them before anyone else.

The first thing it began with was securing the confidence of the earner in the safety of his wealth, that someone should not seize it from him. Allah said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:29). The Prophet (ﷺ) said in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed your blood and your wealth are forbidden to you, as the sanctity of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours." A hundred thousand people or more heard this from him, and they transmitted it throughout the horizons of Islam until it reached the level of tawatur (mass-transmission). Therefore, the principle of preserving wealth became one of the general foundations of legislation, which no Muslim can nullify.

This assurance of the safety of wealth was followed by detailed rulings concerning transactions and documentation, such as the legitimacy of the pledge (rahn) in salam (advance sale) and documentation by witnessing, as the verses that follow declare, along with whatever else in the texts of the Shari'ah, whether explicit or derived by inference.

Then the Shari'ah indicated that among its aims is that wealth should not remain circulating in one direction, one family or one tribe of the community, but that the aim is its circulation.
