This is in His saying, in the verse of fay' (spoils), ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near relatives and the orphans and the needy and the traveller, so that it will not be a dawlah (circulating commodity) among the rich among you﴾ (al-Hashr 59:7). The pronoun in "yakun" refers to "what Allah has restored" in consideration of its being wealth, meaning lest wealth should be a dawlah. Dawlah is what people circulate among themselves of wealth. That is, We legislated its disbursement to those We named, rather than the soldiers having a right to it, so that the poor may receive their portions from it and become wealthy, and it will not be circulated among a group of the rich, as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, when their leaders took the mirba' (one quarter) and the raiders took three quarters, so that all the wealth remained with a special group.

Then the Shari'ah proceeded to take from this wealth in an organized manner. It made from it a compulsory seizure, part of it during the lifetime of the owner and part after his death. As for what is during his lifetime, it is the obligatory charities, among them zakat, which in most cases is one tenth of the owned goods, or half a tenth, or a quarter of a tenth. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained the wisdom of its legislation when he said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal when he sent him to Yemen: "Indeed Allah has enjoined upon them a zakat, taken from their wealthy and returned to their poor." He made the distribution of what is collected from this wealth to establish the interests of the people and to meet the needs of their weak ones. Thus they became people with a right in the wealth of the rich, not humiliated and not threatened with withholding or harshness. He turned to the wealthy and promised them, for this giving, the best of what is promised to the good-doers, by calling it a loan to Allah, the Exalted, and by multiplying its reward, as the verses that we are now explaining have brought.

To this category belongs the taking of the khums (one-fifth) from war booty, even though it is the right of the fighters. He took this from them and said to them: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of spoils, a fifth of it belongs to Allah and to the Messenger﴾ (al-Anfal 8:41), up to His saying: ﴿if you have believed in Allah﴾ (al-Anfal 8:41). Thus He encouraged them to accept this. There is no doubt that He took it away from the hands of those who had acquired it by their swords and spears. Likewise, obligatory maintenance (al-nafaqat al-wajibah) belongs to this category, other than the maintenance of the wife, because it is not regarded as a seizure, since it is in exchange for the cohesion of the family. Nor does the maintenance of children fall under it in the same way, because the motive for it is innate. As for the maintenance of relatives other than children, according to those who make the maintenance of kin obligatory, it is part of obligatory seizure.

Among obligatory seizures are the expiations (kaffarat) for breaking an oath, for breaking the fast of Ramadan, for zihar, for ila', and for the compensation for hunting game. This is the distribution of part of the wealth of the living during his lifetime.

As for the distribution of wealth after the death of its owner, that is by explaining the rules of inheritance (fara'id al-irth) in a manner that admits no addition or reduction. The Arabs used to give their wealth to whomever they loved, whether a stranger or a relative, as we previously explained in His saying: ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:180). Some nations used to make the inheritance go to the eldest.

The distribution of these shares was made in a manner of mercy toward the people who own wealth. Their wealth was given only to the closest of people to them, and its distribution was according to closeness, as is well known in the questions of exclusion (hajb) in the fara'id, and according to need for wealth, such as preferring the male to the female, because he supports others and the female is supported by others. In this area the Shari'ah also turned to the owners of wealth and left them the right to dispose of one third of their wealth, designating whoever should receive it after their death, on condition that he is not an heir, so that they do not use this to make a particular heir a favoured recipient over others.

The Shari'ah also made among the seizures a seizure that is recommended but not obligatory. This comprises kinds of consolation through charities, gifts, presents, bequests, and lending to the needy without usury. There is no seizure of the actual property of the owned goods in the Shari'ah. Seizure does not exceed taking the benefits, with justice and equality.

The phrase ﴿A kind word﴾ and what follows is a resumptive clause (mustanifah istinafan bayaniyyan), and the indefiniteness of ﴿qawlun ma'ruf﴾ is for minimization, meaning: the least kind word is better than a charity followed by harm. Al-ma'ruf is what people recognise, that is, they do not reject it. What is meant by it is a good word, and it is the opposite of harm.

Al-maghfirah (forgiveness) here means overlooking an offence, that is, the giver overlooking the insistence or boorishness of the one asking, such as one who asks and says, "Give me the right of Allah that you have." Or something similar. It may also mean Allah's overlooking of sins because of that charity when it is accompanied by a kind word. In this there is an allusion that harm is about to nullify the reward of charity.

His saying ﴿And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) serving as a reminder of two of Allah's attributes so that the believers may adorn themselves with them. They are: al-ghina' (freedom from need), which relates to His being above returning the gift with what would soothe the giver's stinginess, and al-hilm (forbearance), which relates to His pardon and forgiveness for the rudeness of some of those who ask.

Al-ibtal (invalidation) is making a thing void, that is, removing it so that it is no longer beneficial for what it was intended. The meaning of the nullification of an act is that its legal effect does not follow. Whether the act is obligatory or voluntary, if it is obligatory, its nullification means it is not valid, so that the responsibility of the legally accountable person is not discharged from that obligation. This happens when a pillar or condition of the act is missing. If the act is voluntary, nullification means the loss of reward for the act due to a legal impediment to its reward being credited. This is what is meant here, in harmonising the evidences of the Shari'ah.

His saying ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾: the kaf (like) is a stable adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqarr), which is a circumstantial element (hal) from the pronoun in "tubtilu" (you invalidate). That is: do not be, in following your charities with reminders and harm, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, while he is a disbeliever who does not believe in Allah and the Last Day, and who gives only so that people may see him. This is the giving of the people of the Jahiliyyah.

The relative clause in "like one who spends his wealth" is meant generically; it does not refer to a specific individual or to a single person. The purpose of this comparison is to make the thing compared to appear hideous. What is intended is not an equality in the legal ruling, in harmonising the legal evidences.

[p. 45]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 263–264 (part 2 of 2):

Ri'a' (ostentation) is spelled with two hamzas and is on the pattern *fi'al*, from *ra'a* (to see). It means that a person frequently displays his good deeds to people. The *fi'al* form here indicates intensity and frequency. The first hamza is original, and the last is replaced from a *ya'* that follows the added *alif*. It may also be said *riya'* with a *ya'* after the *ra'*, by replacing the hamza with a *ya'* after a kasra.

The meaning is a comparison between some of the Muslim almsgivers, who give seeking reward but follow their charity with reminders of favor and harm, and the disbelieving hypocrites who spend their wealth seeking nothing from spending but ri'a' and praise, since they do not seek the reward of the Hereafter.

The point of resemblance is that what they give yields no benefit beyond satisfying what is in their hearts of the desire to dominate the weak and satisfying the habit of harming, to which they are accustomed, with no benefit in the Hereafter.

The state of the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, which is the thing compared, is presented as a similitude that extends to those who follow their charity with reminders of favor and harm, through His saying: ﴿So his likeness is like the likeness of a smooth rock﴾, etc. The pronoun in *mathaluhu* ("his likeness") refers to the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people. Since it is a similitude of the state of the thing compared, it is necessarily a similitude of the state of the thing being compared, so the sentence contains three comparisons.

It compares the state of the disbeliever who spends his wealth to be seen by people with the state of a smooth rock upon which there is dust covering it, meaning the observer thinks it is good soil suitable for sowing. The sentence's sense is: upon it is dust suitable for planting. The description of the dust is omitted for brevity, relying on the fact that the dust that people expect the heavy rain to reach is the dust in which they sow. When the planter sows it, and a heavy rain strikes it, and the planter hopes for the growth of his crop, the water sweeps it off the surface of the smooth rock, leaving nothing of it, and its place remains bare and smooth, so the planter's hope is disappointed.

[Page 49]

This is better and more precise than making the meaning a likeness of the disbeliever's spending to dust upon a smooth rock that a heavy rain struck and swept away, with the point of resemblance being rapid disappearance and lack of permanence, as in His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes on which the wind blows violently on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18]. The context of that verse is another context.

You may also take the particle *ka* (like) in His saying ﴿like the one who spends his wealth﴾ as a description of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), which is indicated by the sense of spending contained in the word *sadaqatihim* ("their charities"). An omitted genitive phrase lies between the *ka* and the relative noun. The sense is: spending like the spending of the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people.

In this similitude, the reverse of the similitude for the one who spends his wealth in the way of God is observed, which is a grain that yielded seven hundred grains.

Thus the comparison is a comparison of an intellectual composite to a sensory composite. The point of resemblance is hope in a state that deceives with benefit and then, shortly after, fails to bring its hoper what he hoped for, so his hope is disappointed. This is because believers are not free of hoping for the attainment of reward from their charities, and it often happens that heedlessness overtakes the giver, so he follows his charity with reminders of favor and harm, carried away by evil thoughts.

His saying ﴿they have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾ is placed in a wonderful position in the arrangement of the speech, through which many meanings flow. In its position, it is suitable to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, so that it is included in the state being compared. The pronoun in *kasabu* ("they earned") is treated as a plural pronoun, because the one who spends (*alladhi yunfiqu*) is interpreted as a group (*ta'wil*). It is also suitable to be a circumstantial clause of "the likeness of a smooth rock," with regard to its being a likeness. This is similar to what is permitted in His saying ﴿or like a downpour from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], since its implied sense is: like the likeness of those with a downpour. Therefore its pronoun came in the plural form, observing the sense even though the antecedent word is singular. It is also suitable to be taken as an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*), because the preceding speech raises the question of a questioner about the outcome of the state of the thing compared. It is also suitable to be taken as a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) and summation (*fadhlaka*) of the presentation of the similitude, so it returns to the beginning of His saying ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders of favor and harm﴾ and to the end of the speech.

[Page 50]

It is also suitable to be taken as a circumstantial clause of "smooth rock," meaning: they have no power over anything of what they have earned from it. The relative clause's returning pronoun is omitted, because it is a pronoun in the genitive governed by the preposition with which the relative noun is governed. The sense of "they have no power" is that they cannot retrieve it, nor do they benefit from its reward, so nothing of it remains for them.

It may also be that the sense is: they do not know how to place anything of what they have earned in its proper place, so they spend their wealth for no benefit that returns to them in their lifetimes, based on His saying ﴿And God does not guide the disbelieving people﴾.

The meaning is: so He leaves it bare, so that they do not harvest any crop from it, as in His saying: ﴿So he began to turn his palms over at what he had spent on it﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. The clause ﴿And God does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ is a concluding statement, and the *waw* is parenthetical (*i'tiradiyya*). This concluding statement is brought to warn believers against the infiltration of the states of disbelievers into their deeds, since among their states is reminding those they spend upon of favor and the harm that comes with it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 265:

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God, and for the firming of their own souls, is like a garden on a height: a heavy rain strikes it, and it yields its produce twofold. And if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain does. And God sees what you do.﴾

The phrase ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God﴾ is coordinated (ʿuṭifa) with ﴿The likeness of one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264]. This is to add further clarification of the gulf between the two ranks, to emphasise the praise of those who spend sincerely, and for variety in the presentation of the likeness (tafannun fi al-tamthil). He had previously illustrated it with a grain that produced seven ears, and he had illustrated it earlier with a simpler image, not very elaborate in its composition, so that the swiftness of the imagined multiplication of reward would be achieved. When he illustrated the state of the one who spends to be seen, with the image that had passed, he then restated the likeness of the one who spends seeking the pleasure of God with something more marvellous in its beauty of imagery. Likenesses delight the listener the more elaborate they are in composition, and the likened-to image includes good states that lend it beauty, so that this beauty passes over to the thing being likened. This is one of the purposes of the simile.

[p. 51]

The phrase ﴿seeking the pleasure of God and for the firming﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), by interpreting the verbal noun as a descriptive adjective. That is, "seeking the pleasure of God and firming from their own souls." It is not appropriate to make both of them accusatives of purpose (maf'ūl lahu, the object of purpose). As for his saying ﴿ibtighāʾ (seeking)﴾, that is because the meaning of ibtighāʾ is the same as the meaning of the particle lām (of purpose), by which the object of purpose is put in the accusative by implying it, since it returns to the meaning: "for the sake of their seeking the pleasure of God." As for his saying ﴿tathbītan (firming)﴾, that is because its ruling is the ruling of what it is coordinated with.

Tathbīt (firming) is the establishing and fixing of a thing. It is a figurative expression that may be for restraining the soul from doubt and hesitation. That is, they prevent their souls from hesitating in spending in the paths of righteousness, and they leave no room for the thoughts of miserliness. This is from the expression "his foot became firm" (thabata qadamuh), meaning he did not waver and did not turn back. The training of the soul to do what is hard for it has an effect on the firmness of deeds, until it becomes accustomed to virtues and they become its constant practice.

Spending wealth is among the greatest things by which obedience becomes firmly rooted in the soul, because wealth is not an easy matter for the soul. In this sense the particle (min) is partitive (tabʿīd), but it is a figurative partitive in terms of states, that is, firming for some of the states of the soul.

The placement of this (min) in the sentence indicates lowering and moderation in the attachment of the verb, such that the verb is not required to govern the whole essence of the object, but is satisfied with part of the object. The intention is to encourage attaining the act and to lead one towards attaining it. The apparent sense of the words of al-Kashshaf implies that he took the partitive in it to be literal.

It is also possible that (tathbītan) is a figurative expression for confirmation (taṣdīq), that is, a confirmation of God's promise and sincerity in the religion, to be opposed to the state of the hypocrites. The carrying out of hard commands is only from confirmation of the one who commands them. That is, they indicate a firming from their own souls.

In this sense, (min) is inceptive (ibtidāʾiyyah), that is, a confirmation issuing from their own souls.

On the first interpretation of tathbīt there is a noble moral meaning, to which al-Fakhr (al-Razi) pointed. It is established in moral wisdom that the repetition of acts is what brings about the acquisition of a virtuous disposition (malakah) in the soul, such that after its acquisition the soul is drawn to perfections by its own choice, and without difficulty or weariness.

[p. 52]

Faith commands charity and acts of righteousness, and the one who performs those commanded acts firms his soul with the morals of faith. On this interpretation, the verse becomes an exhortation to repeat spending.

This spending is likened to a garden on a height, etc. The point of resemblance (wajh al-shabah) is the configuration resulting from the combination of things by which the benefit is multiplied. The likened configuration is the spending surrounded by the seeking of God's pleasure and the confirmation of His promise, which is multiplied many times over, or somewhat less in abundance. The configuration of the likeness is the configuration of a good garden in a good place which receives heavy rain, so its fruit grows and increases and the produce is completed, or which receives a light rain and is therefore less than that.

A garden (jannah) is a place on the earth with many trees, such that whoever is in it is concealed (yujann), that is, covered. Its name is derived from janna, meaning he concealed. The term jannah is most often used in their speech for a place of fruit-bearing trees of various kinds. As for a plot planted only with palm trees, it is called ḥāʾiṭ (an enclosed orchard). The well-known fruit-bearing trees in the lands of the Arabs, other than palms, are the vine, and its fruit is grapes, the most famous fruit in their lands after dates. The predominant trees in the lands of Yemen and al-Ṭāʾif were these, and among their fruits is the pomegranate. If palms are present along with them, it is also called a jannah, as in the verse that follows this one. What indicates that jannah does not mean a palm orchard is the words of the Exalted in Surat al-Anʿam: ﴿It is He who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised, and palm trees and crops﴾ [al-Anʿam: 141], where He coordinates palm trees with gardens, and mentions the trellis (ʿarīsh), which is made for vines. This is what is derived from the words of the linguists.

From the likening of the state of those who spend their wealth in the way of God with a grain and then with a garden, there results a paronomasia of altered diacritics (jinās muṣaḥḥaf).

Al-Rabwah, with a damma or a fatḥa on the rāʾ, is a place of the earth raised above the level of a small hill. The majority of the Ten Readers read "bi-rabwah" with a damma on the rāʾ, while Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim read it with a fatḥa on the rāʾ. The specification of the garden as being on a rabwah is because the trees of elevated ground are better in appearance and purer in fruit. This qualification has two benefits: first, the strength of the point of resemblance, as the phrase "twofold" indicates; and second, the embellishment of the likened-to image, which returns to the embellishment of the likened in the listener's imagination.

[p. 53]

Al-ukl (the produce), with a damma on the hamzah and a sukūn on the kāf, and also with a damma on the kāf. It has been said that every (fuʿl) form in the speech of the Arabs is a lightened form of (fuʿul), like ʿunq, fulk, and ḥumq. In origin it is what is eaten, and it became widespread for the fruits of trees. God said: ﴿two gardens of bitter produce﴾ [Saba: 16], and He said: ﴿it yields its produce every season by the permission of its Lord﴾ [Ibrahim: 25]. Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Abu Jaʿfar and Yaʿqub read ﴿ukluha﴾ with a sukūn on the kāf. Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it with a damma on the kāf.

As for His saying ﴿twofold (ḍiʿfayn)﴾, the dual form here is merely for repetition, like labbayk (at your service), that is, it yielded its produce multiplied, despite its variation.

As for His saying ﴿And if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain does﴾, that is, if a heavy rain does not strike it, a light rain suffices for it, and it yields its produce less than twofold. The meaning is that spending for the sake of seeking God's pleasure has a great reward, and yet this reward varies according to the degree of sincerity in the seeking and the firming, just as the states of the pure gardens vary in the degree of their purity, but they do not disappoint their owner.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 266:

﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, with rivers flowing beneath it, in which he has every kind of fruit, and then old age strikes him while he has weak offspring, and then a fiery whirlwind strikes it and it is burned? Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs, that you may reflect.﴾

This is a clarifying resumptive statement (isti'naf bayani), prompted by the striking, wondrous parable of the one who spends in the way of Allah. It is likened to a grain that produced seven ears, and to a garden on a height, up to the end of what has been described of the two parables. When it was followed by what indicates that this applies only to those who spend in the way of Allah and do not follow what they have spent with reproach or harm, and then was followed by a prohibition against letting their charities be followed by reproach and harm, the listener's soul was made eager to receive a parable depicting their blameworthy state, just as a parable was given for those who were the opposite of that state in a praiseworthy condition.

Allah struck this as a parable to contrast with the parable of spending seeking the pleasure of Allah and affirming (faith). It is the spending of show-off (riya'). The point of resemblance is the occurrence of disappointment and despair at the very time when hope is complete and the produce is about to be gathered. This is the counterpart of His saying ﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265], and so on. He described the garden with the greatest qualities by which gardens are made good and by which their abundant yield is hoped for. Then He described its owner with the utmost attributes of need for the benefit of his garden, in that he has dependents, so he is in need of their support; and that they are weak (du'afa'), meaning young children, since "weak" in the Arabic language means one who is lacking. "Weak" is also applied to the poor, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But if the one upon whom the obligation lies is foolish or weak﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. Abu Khalid al-'Attabi said:

"Children have increased my love for life,
for they are among the weak."

He has been struck by old age, so he has no ability to earn except from that garden. This is among the most extreme states of greed, like the saying of al-A'sha:

"Like the water-basin of the old Iraqi, overflowing."

From the detailing of this state arises the greatest expectation for the fruit of this garden, just as the giver of his charity is in expectation of its reward.

﴿Then a fiery whirlwind struck it﴾, i.e., a severe wind that uproots trees and plants; ﴿in which there is fire﴾, i.e., intense heat, which is called the samum wind. The use of the word "fire" for intense heat is an eloquent metaphor. ﴿So it burned the garden (i.e., its trees)﴾, meaning its branches became dry. This is the sudden arrival of disappointment at the time of hoping for benefit.

The interrogation in His saying "Would any of you like" is an interrogation of denial and warning, as in His saying: ﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12]. The likened state is omitted, namely the state of the one who spends and then follows his spending with reproach and harm.

Al-Bukhari narrated that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab once asked the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "About what do you think this verse was revealed: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines﴾, to the end of the verse?" Some of them said: "Allah knows best." 'Umar became angry and said: "Say we know or we do not know." Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is something in my self about it, O Commander of the Faithful." 'Umar said: "O son of my brother, speak and do not belittle yourself." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was struck as a parable for a deed." 'Umar said: "What deed?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "For a deed." 'Umar said: "You have spoken truly: for a rich man who worked in obedience to Allah, then Allah sent to him a devil when his life had ended, so he committed sins until his deed was burned up."

His saying ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs﴾ is a concluding remark (tadhyil); that is, just as this clarification, in which the intelligible is brought near through the perceptible, Allah has made clear for you as sincere counsel, hoping you will reflect on the consequences so that you are not heedless. The comparison in His saying ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs﴾ is like what is in His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 267:

﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have produced for you from the earth, and do not aim at the bad of it to spend from it, while you would not take it yourselves except by overlooking in it. And know that Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy.﴾

This leads to the intended purpose, which is the command to give charity. It comes after exhortations, encouragement and warnings have been placed before it. This is a rhetorical method in oratory and discourse: sometimes they present the desired matter first and then bring what makes it acceptable to the listeners, and sometimes they present what makes it acceptable before the purpose, as here. This is a departure from the apparent expectation in the arrangement of the sentences. The reason for this is that encouragement to give charity had spread among the people and was repeated in the revelation of the Qur'an, so it became a well-known religious objective. Attention to clarifying it, encouraging its good qualities and warning against its defects was more deserving of explanation. A parallel to this is the words of 'Ali in his sermon which he delivered when Sufyan al-Ghamidi, one of the commanders of the people of Syria, entered the town of al-Anbar, which is among the lands obedient to the caliph 'Ali, and they killed its governor, Hassan ibn Hassan al-Bakri: "As for what follows: whoever abandons jihad out of aversion to it, Allah will clothe him in the garment of humiliation, affliction will envelop him, he will be struck with abasement, he will be marked with disgrace, and he will be denied justice. Indeed, I have called you to fight these people night and day, and I said to you: attack them before they attack you, for by Allah, no people has been attacked in the heart of their homes except that they were humiliated. But you became idle. This is the brother of Ghamid, whose horses have reached al-Anbar..." etc. Consider the word jihad in this sermon: perhaps its original form was qital (fighting), as indicated by his saying after it: "to fight these people." So someone either distorted it deliberately or out of carelessness, and I do not think it came from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

[Page 56]

The command may be for obligation, in which case the verse concerns the obligatory zakat; or for recommendation, in which case it concerns voluntary charity; or it may refer to the common element of the demand, in which case it includes both zakat and voluntary charity. Other evidences clarify the ruling of each. The restriction to "the good things" suits the generalisation of expenditures.

By "the good things" is meant the best of wealth. The word tayyib (good) is applied to what is best of its kind. Kasb (earning) is what a person obtains through his own effort, such as trade, spoils of war (ghanima) and hunting. Tayyib is also applied to wealth acquired by a lawful means that is not mixed with injustice or deceit, and this is what is "good" in the sight of Allah. This is like the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever gives charity from good earnings, and Allah accepts only what is good, the Most Merciful takes it with His right hand..." and the rest of the hadith. In another hadith: "Indeed Allah is good and accepts only what is good." He did not mention "the good things" together with His words "and from what We have produced for you from the earth," being content with its earlier mention in the paired element. It appears that this was not restricted by "the good things," because His words "produced for you" indicate that it is what a person has gained by his work through ploughing, planting and the like, since wealth that is bad is generally obtained through oppressing people, or tricking and deceiving them, and that does not generally apply to the produce extracted from the earth.

By "what is produced from the earth" is meant crops and fruits. Some of it comes out by itself, and some of it is cultivated by its means, such as watering trees and crops, and then Allah produces it through the customary causes He has established. Some exegetes counted minerals (ma'adin) as included in His words "from what We have produced for you from the earth." According to Malik, zakat is due on minerals if they reach the threshold of the nisab, and its rate is one quarter of a tenth (rub' al-'ushr). It is among the obligatory kinds of wealth. According to Abu Hanifa it is not zakat, and for this reason he said: in it is one-fifth (khums). Some counted buried treasure (rikaz) as included in what is produced from the earth, but that it is subject to one-fifth. According to the Malikis it is assimilated in ruling to spoils of war (ghanima). Perhaps what is meant by "what you have earned" is wealth on which zakat is levied from gold, silver and livestock, and by "what is produced from the earth" the grains and fruits on which zakat is levied.

His words "and do not aim at the bad of it to spend from it": the original form of tayammamu is tatayammamu; the taʾ of the present tense was deleted, and tayammama means to intend or purpose.

Khabith (bad) means the one most evil within its category. Therefore it is applied to what is forbidden and to what is repulsive. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and He makes unlawful for them the bad things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. It is the furthest opposite of good, so it is not applied to the inferior except in an intensive sense. The occurrence of the word in the context of prohibition indicates the generality of everything to which the word applies.

[Page 57]

The clause ﴿to spend from it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), and the prepositional phrase "from it" is placed before it to indicate restriction, meaning: do not intend the bad while in the state of not spending except from it. This is because the point of the prohibition is that a man should bring out his charity from the very worst of his wealth. As for giving from the good and the bad together, it is not prohibited, especially in obligatory zakat, since one gives from everything he has of its kind. In the Muwatta' (of Imam Malik), in the chapter on sales, there is a hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent an official over the charities of Khaybar, and he brought him janib dates. He said to him: "Are all the dates of Khaybar like this?" He said: "No, but I exchange two ṣāʿ of jamʿ dates for one ṣāʿ of janib dates." He said to him: "Sell the jamʿ for dirhams, then buy janib with the dirhams." This indicates that charity is taken from every category of its kind, but what is forbidden is that one singles out the charity to be of the inferior kinds. As for livestock, the middling is taken, because diversification is generally impossible, unless their number is large, in which case there is no difficulty in the estimation of the phrase here.

The majority read tayammamu with a single light taʾ both in connection and at the beginning, its original form being tatayammamu. Al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a shadda on the taʾ in connection, considering idgham (assimilation).

His words "and you would not take it yourselves except by overlooking in it" form a circumstantial clause (jumla hāliyya) from the pronoun in "you spend." It may be that the speech is on its apparent sense of information, in which case the circumstantial clause is a reason for their prohibition from spending from bad wealth by legal analogy, analogising spending from it to earning it, an analogy of equality: just as you dislike earning it, so you should dislike giving it. It seems that their dislike of earning it was known to them and firmly established in their souls, and therefore the analogy was based upon it.

It may also be that the speech is used in the sense of a prohibition against taking bad wealth, so the speech turns toward a second purpose, which is the prohibition against taking bad wealth, and the meaning is: do not take it. In both interpretations, it requires the prohibition of taking wealth whose unlawfulness is known to the one who holds it, and its transfer to another does not make it lawful.

Al-ighmad is the closing of the eyelid, and it is used figuratively for its consequence. It is sometimes used for comfort and rest, because one of the consequences of closing the eyes is the rest of the sleeper. Al-A'sha said:

"Upon you is the like of what you prayed, so close your eyes, for the side of a man lies down [to rest]."

[Page 58]

He meant: be at ease.

It is sometimes used for its consequence of not seeing, and it indicates tolerance of a disliked matter, as in the words of al-Tirimmah:

"No people has taken from us vengeance, and among the people of the ... there are men who are content with overlooking."

When they wish to exaggerate in ignoring a disliked matter, they say: he closed his eye over a speck (qadhan), because closing the eyelid while there is a speck in the eye is for the purpose of ease from the movement of the speck. 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Zurara al-Kallai said:

"I closed my eyes over their specks, and I did not listen to any speaker or to what was said."

The exception in His words ﴿except by overlooking in it﴾, on the first reading where the speech is information, is a restriction of the negation. As for the second reading, where the negation is taken in the sense of a prohibition, it is from emphasising a thing by means of something resembling its opposite. The meaning is: "You would not take it unless you overlook the prohibition and pretend not to know it."

His words ﴿and know that Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy﴾ are a concluding statement (tadhyil), meaning: He is free of need of your charities, which do not benefit the poor, or in which there is the easing of what is unlawful; Praiseworthy, meaning: thankful to the one who gives a good charity. He opened it with "know" for the sake of attention to the information, as was mentioned earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and fear Allah and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqara: 223]. Or the addressees who were forbidden to spend from the bad are treated as those who do not know that Allah is Free of need, so they give for His sake what the needy would accept in any case, and they did not know that He praises the one who gives for His sake from good earnings.

Al-Ghaniyy (the Free of need) is the one who does not need what the majority of people generally need. To Allah belongs absolute freedom from need, so nothing is given for His sake, nor in obedience to His command, except the best of what anyone gives to one who is free of need of wealth.

Al-Hamid is among the intensive forms, meaning: one who is greatly praised, because He praises those who do good deeds. It is also possible that what is meant is that He is praised (mahmud), so that hamid is in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), meaning: then adopt this character, because the attributes of Allah the Exalted are perfections, so be people rich in heart, free from stinginess, praised for your charities, and do not give charities that indicate stinginess, nor will you be thanked for them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 268:

Page 59
﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty and commands you to indecency﴾.
This is a resumption (isti'naf) from His saying: ﴿Spend of the good things you have earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267], because Shaytan turns people away from giving the best of their wealth, and incites them to stinginess or to giving the inferior and the foul, and frightens them with poverty if they give some of their property.

The name of Shaytan was placed first as the subject (musnad ilayh), because placing it first signals the blameworthiness and ill omen of the ruling that the speech is leading to, to warn the Muslims against this ruling, as is said in the example from the science of rhetoric (ilm al-ma'ani): "The murderer is in the house of your friend." Also, placing the subject before the verbal predicate reinforces and confirms the ruling.

The meaning of (yaʿiduku) is: he makes it seem appealing to you that it (poverty) will occur in the future if you spend the best of your property. This happens through what he casts into the hearts of those who adopt Shaytanic character traits. The report of an event occurring in the future is called "promise" (wa'd) figuratively, because a promise is a report from the speaker that something will occur in the future. That is why it is said: "So-and-so fulfilled his promise" (anjaza fulanun wa'dahu) or "broke his promise" (akhlafa wa'dahu), and they do not say "fulfilled his report" (anjaza khabarahu); they say "his report was true" (sadaqa khabaruhu) and "his promise was true" (sadaqa wa'dahu). So the promise is more specific than the report, and the words of the leading scholars of the language indicate this. Thus he likened the casting of Shaytan into their souls of the expectation of poverty to a promise from him that it will certainly occur. The point of resemblance is the sense of certainty contained in a promise. The beauty of this figurative usage here is its harmony with His saying: ﴿Allah promises you forgiveness﴾, for that is a real promise.

Then, if "promise" is used for committing to good and evil, as is the statement of the Qamus following Fasih Tha'lab, then in His saying ﴿yaʿiduku al-faqr﴾ there is one figurative usage. But if it is specific to good, as is the statement of al-Zamakhshari in al-Asas, then in His saying ﴿yaʿiduku al-faqr﴾ there are two figurative usages.

Poverty (al-faqr) is the intense need for the necessities of life due to scarcity or loss of what one could exchange for them. It is derived from fiqar al-zahr (the vertebrae of the back), so its origin is the verbal noun of faqarahu, meaning he broke his back. They made the incapable person like one who cannot make even the slightest movement, because the back is the seat of all movements. From this comes their calling a calamity "fa'iqarah" (back-breaking) and "qasimat al-zahr" (back-breaking). It is said: faqr, faqar, fuqr, and fuqur, with a fatha then sukun, with two fathas, with a damma then sukun, and with two dammas. It is said "rajul faqir" (a poor man), and it is said "rajul faqr," using the verbal noun as an adjective.

Page 60
Al-fahsha' is a name for an action or statement of extreme evil, deserving blame either by custom or by law. It is derived from al-fuhsh (with a damma on the fa' and sukun on the ha'), meaning transgressing the limit. Usage has restricted it to transgression in what is ugly; that is, he commands you to an ugly act. This is an escalation in the warning against the Satanic thoughts that call to blameworthy deeds. The intended meaning of al-fahsha' is not stinginess, because the word al-fahsha' is not applied to stinginess, although the stingy person may be called fahish. Applying the word "command" (amr) to the whisperings of Shaytan and the effect of his power on souls is a figurative usage, because "command" in reality belongs to the categories of speech. The definite article in (al-fahsha') is the definite article of the genus.
* * *
﴿And Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty; and Allah is All-Embracing, All-Knowing﴾.
This is a conjunction over the clause ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾, to show the difference between what the whisperings of Shaytan call to and what the commands of Allah the Exalted call to. The promise in it is a reality without doubt. The discussion of placing the divine name before the verbal predicate in His saying ﴿And Allah promises you﴾ follows the same manner as the discussion of placing the name of Shaytan in His saying ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾.

The meaning of "wasi'" (All-Embracing) is that He is vast in bounty. The description "wasi'" is derived from (wasi'a), the transitive form: when one extends with gift and the like. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. The Arabs say: "I cannot (la yasa'uni) do such-and-such," meaning I find no latitude in it. In the hadith of 'Ali describing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "His cheerfulness and character have embraced the people (qad wasi'a al-nas bishruhu wa khuluqahu)," so the meaning here is that he embraced people and the worlds with his giving.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 269:

﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good. And none will be reminded except those of understanding.﴾

This sentence is an interjection and a concluding summary (tadhyil) of what the verses on spending contained of admonitions, etiquette, and the instilling of noble character, which bestows upon those who act by it soundness of intellect and uprightness of action.

The purpose is to alert them to the preciousness of what Allah has admonished them with, and to make them aware that they have become wise through it after having been ignorant in the Jahiliyyah. The meaning is: this is from the wisdom which Allah has given you, for He gives wisdom to whom He wills. This is like His saying: ﴿And He has sent down to you the Book and wisdom, by which He instructs you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231].

Al-Fakhr said: He indicated that the matter for which it is obligatory to prefer the promise of the Most Merciful over the promise of Satan is that the promise of the Most Merciful is preferred by wisdom and intellect, while the promise of Satan is preferred by desire and the senses, insofar as these two command the attainment of immediate pleasure. And there is no doubt that the judgment of wisdom is the true judgment, free from deviation, whereas the judgment of the senses and desire leads to trial and tribulation. Thus the juxtaposition of His saying ﴿and Allah promises you forgiveness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268] with His saying ﴿He gives wisdom﴾ is an indication that what Almighty Allah promises of forgiveness and bounty is part of wisdom, and that all wisdom is from the bestowal of Allah Almighty, and that Allah Almighty gives it to whom He wills.

Wisdom (al-hikmah) is the perfecting of knowledge and the carrying out of action in accordance with that knowledge. Therefore it has been said: wisdom descended upon the tongues of the Arabs, the minds of the Greeks, and the hands of the Chinese. It is derived from al-hukm, which means prevention, because it prevents its possessor from falling into error and misguidance. Allah Almighty said: ﴿A Book whose verses have been made precise﴾ [Hud: 1]. From this root the iron piece in the bridle that is placed in the horse's mouth is called ḥakama.

The one whom Allah Almighty wills to grant wisdom is the one whom He creates prepared for it, through soundness of intellect and balance of faculties, so that he is capable of understanding realities and submits to the truth when it becomes apparent to him, not being prevented from that by desire, partisanship, obstinacy, or arrogance. Then He facilitates for him the means of that, through the presence of callers (to truth) and the safety of the region from tyrants. When to that is added his turning toward Allah, so that He increases his means of facilitation and withholds from him what veils understanding, then facilitation is complete for him. Wisdom has been defined as knowing the realities of things as they are, to the extent that human capacity reaches; that is, such that similar realities are not confused with one another and one does not err regarding causes and reasons.

Wisdom has been divided into various categories with differing subject matters, according to the differences of eras and regions. The beginning of the appearance of the science of wisdom in the East was among the Hindu Brahmins and the Buddhists, and among the people of China, the Buddhists; and in the lands of Persia in the wisdom of Zoroaster; and among the Copts in the wisdom of the priests. Then the wisdom of these eastern nations passed to the Greeks, was refined, corrected, branched out, and divided among them into two parts: practical wisdom and theoretical wisdom.

As for practical wisdom, it concerns what proceeds from human actions, and it is confined to the refinement of the self, the refinement of the household, and the refinement of the nation.

The first is the science of ethics, which is the adorning of oneself with the attributes of divine exaltedness within human capacity, in what proceeds from it of perfection in the human being.

The second: the science of household management (tadbir al-manzil).

The third: the science of civil and legal politics (al-siyasah al-madaniyyah wa al-shar'iyyah).

As for theoretical wisdom, it investigates matters that are known and are not among actions, but are known for the completion of the soundness of understanding and actions. It has three sciences: a science called the lowest, which is the natural science (al-tabi'i); a science called the middle, which is mathematics (al-riyadi); and a science called the highest, which is the divine science (al-ilahi).

Natural science investigates the general matters of generation, properties, existence and corruption; there falls under it the events of the atmosphere, the layers of the earth, plants, animals, and humans; and there fall under it medicine, chemistry, and astronomy.

Mathematics: arithmetic, geometry, astronomy (al-hay'ah), and music; there fall under it algebra, surveying, mechanical devices (al-hiyal al-mutaharrikah, "machines"), and the moving of heavy loads.

As for divine science, it has five divisions: the meanings of existing things; principles and foundations, which are logic and the refutation of corrupt opinions; the proof of the Necessarily Existent and His attributes; the proof of spirits and immaterial beings; and the proof of revelation and prophethood. Abu Nasr al-Farabi and Abu 'Ali Ibn Sina have clarified this.

As for the later philosophers of the West, they restricted wisdom in philosophy to what lies beyond nature, which is called among the Greeks theology (al-ilahiyyat).

The essential part of wisdom in the view of religion consists of four chapters. The first is knowing Allah with the true knowledge of Him, which is the science of correct belief, and which is called among the Greeks the divine science or metaphysics. The second is what proceeds from knowledge of it: the perfection of the human soul, which is the science of ethics. The third: the refinement of the family, which is called among the Greeks the science of household management. The fourth: the straightening of the nation and the reform of its affairs, which is called the science of civil politics; it is included in the rulings of the imamate and the sultanic rulings, and the call of Islam in its roots and branches is not free of a branch of the branches of this wisdom.

Allah has mentioned wisdom in many places in His Book, intending by it what contains the good of souls: prophethood, guidance, and direction. Among the Arabs, wisdom was used for sayings that awaken the soul and counsel toward good, and that report the experiences of happiness and misery, and comprehensive universal principles gathering the totality of good manners. Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book the wisdom and counsels of Luqman in His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman: 12] and what follows. The poets of the Arabs were keen to deposit wisdom in their poetry, namely by delivering proverbs, as Zuhayr did in the verses whose first is:

"I have seen death as the blind camel's wild stumbling..." , and in those which begin with "man" ("whoever") in his Mu'allaqah. There were also in the hands of some rabbis pages containing etiquettes and admonitions, like some of the Comprehensive Book of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and the like, so the Arabs would transmit sayings from them. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in the chapter on modesty in the Book of Good Manners, it is narrated that 'Imran ibn Husayn said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Modesty brings nothing but good." Then Bashir ibn Ka'b al-'Adawi said: It is written in the wisdom (literature): "Indeed, of modesty is dignity, and indeed of modesty is tranquility." 'Imran said to him: I narrate to you from the Messenger of Allah and you narrate to me from your page.

The sage (al-hakim) is one who excels in these sciences or some of them; by his wisdom he guards himself from falling into error and misguidance in proportion to the extent of his wisdom and the matter to which his wisdom relates.

The sciences of wisdom are the totality of what the guidance of the guides from the people of divine revelation has directed to, which is the foundation of the reform of human intellects. Thus the beginning of the appearance of wisdom was in the religions, then there was added to it what the intelligence of people of reason produced of their views branching from the first foundations of guidance. The early sages paved ways of wisdom, and springs of wisdom gushed forth in close eras in which it was mixed with illusions, imaginings, and misguidance, among the Chaldeans, the Egyptians, the Indians, and the Chinese. Then the Greek sages studied it, refined it, and innovated; they distinguished the science of wisdom from other things, sought the truth as far as they could, removed great illusions, and left much. These sciences were confined to two methods: that of Socrates, which is psychological (nafsiyyah), and that of Pythagoras, which is mathematical and rational (riyadiyyah 'aqliyyah); the first was Greek and the second belonged to Greek Italy. From both Plato took, and his followers became known as the Illuminationists (al-Ishraqiyyin). Then his most excellent student, Aristotle (Aristatalis), took from him, refined his method, and broadened the sciences; his followers were called the Peripatetics (al-Mashsha'iyyin). Wisdom has continued from the time of his appearance until this day relying upon his foundations.

﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾: and the one whom Allah wills to give wisdom is the one for whom much good is attained through soundness of judgment and divine guidance, and from the branches of the principles of wisdom that guard against falling into error and misguidance in proportion to deep penetration into its understanding and keeping its essentials in mind. For when we trace the calamities that befall people, we find most of them result from ignorance, misguidance, and corrupt opinion; and conversely, we find what people gain of benefits and agreeable things stems from knowledge and knowing realities. Had we known all realities, we would avoid everything we see causing misery and wretchedness.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿wa-man yu'ta﴾ with a fatha on the taa' in the passive form, so that the pronoun in "yu'ta" is the deputy subject referring back to the relative (man), and it is the connecting pronoun of the relative clause. Ya'qub read ﴿wa-man yu'ti al-hikmah﴾ with a kasra on the taa' in the active form, so the pronoun in the verb "yu'ti" refers to Allah the Exalted; in that case the returning pronoun is a suppressed object pronoun, and the estimate is: "whoever Allah gives it to" (wa-man yu'tihi Allah).

His saying ﴿And none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾ is a concluding summary (tadhyil) alerting that the one whom Allah wills to grant wisdom is the one possessing intellect (lubb), and that remembering wisdom and retaining its guidance is in proportion to the presence of intellect and its strength. Al-lubb in origin is the essence and core of a thing, and it is here applied to the human intellect because it is the most beneficial thing in him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 270:

Page 65
﴿Whatever you spend of expenditure, or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it.﴾
This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the preceding discourse, which was directed toward the command to spend and its accepted qualities, and toward warning against the things that discourage from it, beginning from His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267].

The purpose of this concluding statement is to remind that nothing of the expenditures and their qualities is hidden from Allah. The vow (nadhr) has been incorporated together with expenditure, so the statement was fit to be a concluding statement.

The vow (nadhr) is the binding of oneself, by the form of obligation, to an act of devotion or charity, such as his saying: "It is incumbent upon me to give charity," or "It is incumbent upon me to equip a fighter," or the like. It may be unconditional or conditional upon something. The Arabs knew the vow from the Jahiliyyah. 'Abd al-Muttalib vowed that if he were granted ten sons, he would sacrifice the tenth of them as an offering to the Ka'bah, and his tenth son was 'Abd Allah, the second of the two sacrificed ones (al-dhabihayn), and what an honour that is. Natilah, the wife of 'Abd al-Muttalib, when she lost her son al-'Abbas, who was young, vowed that if she found him she would clothe the Ka'bah with brocade (al-dibaj). She did so, and she was the first to clothe the Ka'bah with brocade. In the hadith of al-Bukhari, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "O Messenger of Allah, I vowed in the Jahiliyyah that I would perform i'tikaf for a night in the Masjid al-Haram." He said: "Fulfil your vow."

In the earlier nations there was the vow, and Allah related of the wife of 'Imran: ﴿Indeed I have vowed to You what is in my womb, dedicated﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35]. The verse indicates its legitimacy in Islam and the hope of its reward, since it is conjoined with what is among the acts of goodness, whether the vow is unconditional or conditional, because the verse is absolute; and because His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ is intended as a promise of reward. In the authentic hadith from 'Umar, his son 'Abd Allah, and Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed the vow does not bring forward anything nor delay anything, nor does it avert anything, and it does not bring to the son of Adam anything that had not been decreed for him, but it is extracted by it from the miser."

Its thrust is encouragement toward the unconditional vow, not the nullification of the benefit of the vow. Allah has praised His servants, saying: ﴿They fulfil the vow﴾ [al-Insan: 7]. In the Muwatta', from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him, and whoever vows to disobey Allah, let him not disobey Him."

The (min) in His saying "min nafaqah" and "min nadhr" is an explanation (bayan) of "ma anfaqtum" and "nadhartum." Since the nature of explanation is to convey a meaning beyond the meaning of what is explained, and the meaning of the explanation here is exactly the meaning of what is explained, it is determined

Page 66
that its intended purpose is to explain the expended and the vowed by means of the indefiniteness of the two genitive objects of "min," indicating the kinds of expenditures and vows. Thereby it confirms the generality that the conditional "ma" conveys: good or evil, in the way of Allah or in the way of the Taghut. Al-Taftazani said: "Such explanation is for emphasising generality and preventing specificity."
And His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ is a metonymy (kinayah) for the recompense for it, because the knowledge of Allah concerning existing things is not doubted by the listeners, so its necessary implication is intended. It is necessary because the Capable One is not prevented from recompense except by lack of knowledge of what the doer of good or evil does.

* * *
﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾
This is a threat set against the promise indicated by His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾. The wrongdoers intended are the openly polytheists and the hypocrites, because if they withhold obligatory charities they have wronged its recipients in their wealth, and wronged themselves by exposing themselves to the consequences of withholding; and if they withhold voluntary charity, they have wronged themselves by depriving themselves of the virtues of charity and its reward in the Hereafter.

"Al-ansar" is the plural of "nasir," and the negation of helpers is a metonymy for the negation of victory and aid in the Hereafter, which is evident, and in this world, because when they were stingy with their help to the poor with their wealth, Allah makes them lack a helper in tight situations, hardens the hearts of His servants against them, and casts hatred upon them among the people.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 271:

﴿If you disclose your charities, they are excellent; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you. And He will remove from you some of your misdeeds. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) arising from His saying: ﴿And whatever expenditure you spend or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 270], since the generality of ﴿expenditure﴾ [al-Baqarah: 270] implies the case of secret charities. So the listener asks himself: is the disclosure of charities considered showing off (riya'), when he had earlier heard His saying: ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264]?

Page 67

Moreover, His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 270] was a decisive statement regarding the consideration of the intentions of those who give charity and the states of what they display of it and what they conceal of their charities. So this resumption removes an assumption which would lead to the suspension of charities and expenditures: that a person would refrain from them when he finds no alternative to making them visible, fearing that showing off would afflict him.

The definite article in His saying "al-sadaqat" (the charities) is the definite article of genus, and it is taken to be general, so it includes all charities, obligatory and voluntary. This suits the position of this verse following the mention of types of expenditure.

The conditional particle "in" (if) is used with both kinds of charity because it is the origin of conditional particles, and there is no reason to depart from the original, since both kinds of charity are pleasing to Allah the Exalted. The preference for secret charity is fulfilled by the explicit statement: ﴿that is better for you﴾.

His saying "fa-ni'imma" (then excellent is it) is originally "fa-ni'ma ma", so the two identical letters were assimilated (idgham), and the 'ain of (ni'ma) was vowelled with kasra because of the meeting of two consonants. The "ma" in such a construction is an indefinite complete (nakirah tammah), meaning extremely vague, whose description is not intended to be specified by anything that particularizes it. Its completeness is in terms of not being followed by a qualifier, not in terms of its meaning being clear; for this reason it is explained as "thing" (shay'). Since it is so, it is necessarily in the position of a specifier (tamyiz) for the hidden subject pronoun of (ni'ma), so the purpose of it is to draw attention to the intention of not specifying; even when the speaker specifies, he specifies only with something like the thing specified.

His saying "hiya" (it) is restricted to praise, i.e., the charities. The listener already knows that these are the disclosed charities, by the indication of the verb of the condition, so the meaning is explained as: "excellent is their disclosure."

Warsh from Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hafs and Ya'qub read "fa-ni'immā" with a kasra on the 'ain and a shadda on the mim of (ni'ma) together with the mim of (ma). Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the 'ain. Qalun from Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a kasra on the nun and an incomplete vowelling of the 'ain (ikhtilas), between kasra and sukun. Abu Ja'far read it with a kasra on the nun and sukun on the 'ain, with the shadda on the mim retained. This was also transmitted from Qalun, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr.

His saying: ﴿And if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾ is a preference of secret charity, because in it there is preservation of the dignity of the poor person, since no one other than the giver is aware of it. In the authentic hadith, among the seven whom Allah shades with His shade, he counted: «a man who gives charity and conceals it until his left hand does not know what his right hand has spent» — meaning despite the great closeness between the right and left hands, since the reckoning of dirhams and the handing over of things is done by the cooperation of both; so if the left hand were a possessor of knowledge, it would not be informed of what the right hand has spent.

In this verse Allah has preferred secret charity over public charity absolutely. If the charities are taken in their generality, as is apparent, treating the word "charities" as the word "expenditure" in the preceding and following verses, then concealing both obligatory and voluntary charity is better. This is the view of the majority of scholars. Al-Kiya al-Tabari reported that this is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Al-Mahdawi reported: concealment was better for both in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, then people's opinions of one another deteriorated, so the scholars considered it good to make obligatory charity public. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this contradicts the reports that concealing charity is better. Therefore the generality of "charities" in the verse is restricted to voluntary charity, and the restricting factor of a generality is consensus (ijma'). Ibn al-'Arabi reported the consensus on this. If "charities" in the verse is meant as other than zakat, then what is meant is more specific than the expenditure mentioned in the verses before and after it, and the preference of concealment is restricted to recommended charities. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: displaying zakat is better, and concealing voluntary charity is better than displaying it; this is also the view of al-Shafi'i.

His saying: ﴿and give them to the poor﴾: the commentators hesitated over the wisdom of mentioning it, given the knowledge that charity is only for the poor, and that disclosed charity is also given to the poor.

Al-'Isam said: it seems the point of mentioning it here is that disclosure is not separate from giving to the poor, because the poor person is manifest in it and distinguished from others, as people know his condition; unlike concealment, so it was made conditional with giving it to the poor, as an urging to investigate the condition of the one to whom one gives charity; i.e., because the eager among non-poor people are shy about approaching public charities, and nothing deters them from approaching secret charities.

Al-Khafaji said: he did not mention the poor with disclosed charity because it is meant as zakat, whose recipients are the poor and others; as for concealed charity, it is voluntary charity whose recipients are the poor alone.

This is weak for two reasons: first, there is no basis for restricting disclosed charity to the obligatory, and no one holds this; rather the disagreement is whether the preference of concealment includes the obligatory or not. Second, voluntary charity is not barred from being spent on other than the poor, such as equipping armies.

Shaykh Ibn 'Ashur, my grandfather, said in a commentary of his on the hadith on the excellence of concealing charity from Sahih Muslim: the conjunction of giving to the poor onto concealment, which was made a condition for excellence in the verse, despite the knowledge that charity is for the poor, indicates that the excellence lies in concealing the condition of the poor and not displaying the upper hand over him; i.e., it is an allusion to the cause, which is preserving the dignity of the poor person, and this is the decisive statement given the absence of any trace of showing off.

His saying: ﴿And We will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾ was read by Nafi', al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf with the nun of majesty and with the jazm (apocopation) of the ra', in conjunction with the position of the answer clause, which is the clause "it is better for you"; so the expiation is made contingent on concealment. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it also with the nun and with the raf' (nominative) of the ra', as a promise for giving charities openly or secretly. Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read it with the ya' (third person) so that its pronoun refers to Allah, and with raf'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 272:

﴿Thou art not responsible for their guidance, but God guides whom He wills.﴾

This is an interjected resumption (isti'naf mu'taridah) placed between His saying ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 271] and His saying ﴿And whatever good you spend is for yourselves﴾. Its connection here is that the preceding verses reveal several categories of people: among them are those who spend their wealth to be seen by people and do not believe in God or the Last Day; among them are those who nullify their charities through reminders and injury; among them are those who aim at the bad part of their wealth to spend from it; and among them are those whom Satan promises poverty and commands indecency. The existence of these groups weighed heavily upon the Prophet (ﷺ), so God followed that by calming the soul of His Messenger and easing his burden, by saying that the guidance of them is not his responsibility, but his responsibility is only the conveying (of the message). So "guidance" here means compulsion to bring about guidance in their hearts; as for guidance in the sense of conveying and directing, it is incumbent upon the Prophet. Similar instances in the Qur'an are numerous. The pronoun thus refers to all those among whom there remains some lack of guidance, the most extreme of them being the polytheists and the hypocrites.

It was also said that the pronoun refers to certain known people. It is narrated that Asma' bint Abi Bakr had a disbelieving mother and a disbelieving grandfather, and Asma' wished, in the year of the 'Umrat al-Qada', to console them with wealth. It is also said that some of the Ansar wished to give charity to their relatives and in-laws among the Banu al-Nadir and Quraiza, so the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the Muslims from giving charity to the disbelievers, in order to compel those disbelievers to enter Islam. Then God the Exalted revealed: ﴿Thou art not responsible for their guidance﴾ and the verses that follow, meaning the guidance of the disbelievers to Islam, i.e., permit the Muslims to give charity to those disbelievers.

Thus the pronoun refers to something known to the addressee, and the revelation of the verse for that reason arises from the revelation of the verses commanding spending and charity, so the preceding verses are the cause of the cause of the revelation of this verse.

The meaning is that it is not incumbent upon you to guide them beyond calling and direction, without guiding them in fact or by compulsion, since there is no guide for one whom God leads astray, and such a thing is not facilitated for guidance.

The address in ﴿Thou art not responsible for their guidance﴾ apparently is addressed to the Messenger according to the first aspect we mentioned regarding the referent of the pronoun (hudahum). It may also be an address to whoever hears it according to the later aspect, if we take into account what they mentioned as the occasion of revelation, i.e., "It is not incumbent upon you, O you who hesitate to give to your relative."

The "upon" (ʿalā) in His saying "ʿalayka" is for metaphorical elevation, i.e., the demand of an act in the manner of obligation. The meaning: that is not obligatory upon the Messenger, so he should not grieve over the non-occurrence of their guidance, because he has discharged the duty of conveying. Or the meaning: that is not obligatory upon you, O those who treat their conversion by depriving them of spending, to the point that you strive toward their guidance by ways of compulsion.

The placement of the adverbial phrase "ʿalayka" before the predicate's subject "hudahum," if it is treated according to what is established in the science of meanings (ʿilm al-maʿani), that fronting of a predicate that should be postponed yields restriction (qasr) of the subject on the predicate, and this is clear without doubt in affirmation, like ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6] and His saying ﴿For it is what it earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. But when it occurs in the context of negation, it is not clear; for if fronting in the form of affirmation yields restriction, it requires that when it is negated, that restriction is negated, because the sentence qualified by restriction in the case of affirmation is a sentence whose relation is restricted by the qualifier of confinement, i.e., by the qualifier of confining its subject to the meaning of its predicate; so when negation enters upon it, it requires negation of the restricted relation, i.e., negation of that confinement, because the nature of negation, when directed at a restricted statement, is to fall upon that qualifier.

However, the scholars of the discipline, when they mentioned examples of fronting the predicate before the subject, equated among them between affirmation, as we mentioned, and negation, like ﴿Neither therein is any intoxication﴾ [al-Saffat: 47]. Al-Zamakhshari gave it as an example in the Kashshaf at His saying: ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], saying: he intended the preference of the wine of Paradise over the wines of this world. And al-Sayyid, in his commentary there, said: it is counted as restriction of the qualified upon the quality; i.e., the intoxication is restricted to non-occurrence in the wine of Paradise, not exceeding it to non-occurrence in what is opposite to it; or the non-existence of intoxication is restricted to occurrence in it, not exceeding it to occurrence in these wines.

I had referred, at His saying ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], to this verse here, so it is incumbent on us to explain the method of restriction by fronting in negation. That restriction, since it is an accidental mode of the construction and not a verbal qualifier such that negation is directed at it, that mode remains accompanied with the negation. So a sentence like ﴿Neither therein is any intoxication﴾ [al-Saffat: 47] yields restriction of intoxication to being absent from the wines of this world, and does not yield negation of the restriction of intoxication to being in the wines of Paradise. To this al-Sayyid pointed in his commentary on the Kashshaf at His saying ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], when he said: In sum, the negative particle is made a part, or a letter, of the predicate or subject. On this basis, the author of the Kashshaf built; he made the reason why the adverbial phrase was not fronted in His saying ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] as it was fronted in His saying ﴿Neither therein is any intoxication﴾ [al-Saffat: 47] that, if it were interpreted otherwise, it would intend that another book has doubt in it, not the Qur'an; and that is not the intended meaning.

Given this established, His saying ﴿Thou art not responsible for their guidance﴾, if it is treated on this pattern, its import would be: their guidance is restricted to the negation of its being upon you, which entails deriving the nullification of the negation of its being upon other than the addressee, i.e., the nullification of the negation of its being upon God. Both of these implications are not intended, since neither the first nor the second is established. Therefore the matter is either that the fronting here is merely for emphasis, like the fronting of "the day of generosity" in the saying of al-Hariri:

"There is no fault in it except that on the day of generosity its division is unjust,"

by negating that their guidance is truly upon the Messenger, as a way of easing the matter for him. As for the indication that this is entrusted to God, it is from His saying ﴿but God guides whom He wills﴾. Or it is that it proceeds contrary to the apparent requirement, by treating the hearers as those who believe that the creation of faith in the disbelievers occurs through God's creation and through compulsion from the created being; so it restricts their guidance to non-occurrence through the compulsion of created beings, not to non-occurrence in its being upon God; and it follows from that that it is upon God, i.e., entrusted to Him.

And His saying ﴿but God guides whom He wills﴾ employs the particle of exception (istidrak) because of what is in the negated statement of the suspicion that their guidance is possible through eagerness or through compulsion. So the focus of the istidrak is the relative clause, namely "whom He wills," i.e., there is no benefit in compelling one whom God has not willed to guide. The implied sense is: but their guidance is in the hand of God, and He guides whom He wills; so when He wills to guide them, He guides them.

* * *

﴿And whatever good you spend is for yourselves, and you do not spend except seeking the Face of God. And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you, and you will not be wronged.﴾

This is conjoined to the sentence ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾ [al-Baqarah: 271], and its placement is to add excellence to all charities, and that since their benefit returns to the giver himself, he should choose for himself what is good, and he should give abundantly from them by rejecting everything that calls to abandoning some of them.

His saying ﴿And you do not spend except seeking the Face of God﴾ is a circumstantial clause, and it is a declarative statement used in the sense of a command, i.e., the benefit of charities is for your own selves only if you spend only seeking the Face of God, not for show, nor out of regard for the state of a Muslim or a disbeliever. This meaning is suitable for both possible meanings in the preceding verse. It is also permissible for it to be conjoined to it if the declarative is in the sense of a prohibition, i.e., "Do not spend except seeking the Face of God." This statement is a declarative used in the sense of a request for the purpose of affirmation and emphasis; for this reason the style is varied from that of what surrounds it: "And whatever good you spend is for yourselves" and "And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you."

His saying ﴿And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you, and you will not be wronged﴾ is conjoined to the preceding one, to explain that the reward of expenditures is according to their measure, and whoever is deprived of reward is the one who strives toward its diminishment. He repeated the verb "you spend" three times in the verse for greater emphasis on its meaning. It was used twice in conditional form when intending to show the necessary connection between spending and reward, and it was used once in negated and exceptive form because it intended the declarative in the sense of the imperative, i.e., the prohibition against spending except for seeking the Face of God.

"And you" is placed before the verbal predicate merely for strengthening and for added alerting that they are not wronged, but they only wrong themselves.

These rulings were made into separate sentences, some independent of others, and were not made into a single sentence whose benefit is restricted by the restrictions of all the sentences. The verb "spend" was repeated in all of them in varied forms, as a repetition for emphasis on its matter, so that each sentence would be independent in its meaning, short in wording and rich in meanings, thus functioning like proverbs that generations pass down.

From the last verses, according to one of the two interpretations, has been derived the permissibility of giving charity to disbelievers, the intended disbelievers being those who mingle with Muslims without harming them, namely the people of covenant, the protected people (dhimmis), and neighbors. The jurists of Islam agreed on the permissibility of giving voluntary charity to disbelievers.
