The wisdom of this is that charity is relief of the distressed, and the disbeliever is among the servants of God, and we have been commanded to show kindness even to animals. In the authentic hadith: they said, "O Messenger of God, is there a reward for us in (caring for) animals?" He said, "In every moist liver there is a reward."

The jurists agreed that obligatory charity, namely zakat, is not given to disbelievers. The wisdom of this is that it was prescribed only to sustain and support Muslims; it is the property of the Islamic community, taken in fixed amounts, and in it lies the sufficiency of the Muslims, unlike what a person gives willingly out of compassion and kindness. They differed regarding the charity of breaking the fast (zakat al-fitr). The majority attached it to obligatory charities, while Abu Hanifa attached it to voluntary charity and therefore permitted giving it to disbelievers. It would have been more fitting to say this about other than zakat al-fitr, for the festival is the festival of Muslims. Perhaps he regarded it as a charity of thanks for the capacity to fast, so the consideration in it was the state of the giver, not the state of the recipient. The view of the majority is more sound, because its prescription is for securing the Muslim poor from begging on the day of their festival, and so that they may be in greater ease on that day than in the rest of the period; and this aspect of wisdom does not appear regarding poor disbelievers.

**[Page 74]**

﴿For the poor who are restrained in the way of God, who cannot travel about the land. The ignorant man thinks them rich because of their restraint; you know them by their marks. They do not ask people with importunity.﴾

"Lil-fuqara'" (for the poor) is connected to the last occurrence of "tunfiqun" (you spend). This connection indicates that its meaning is linked to the similar expressions mentioned earlier, so every expenditure mentioned just before is for the poor, because the sentences support one another.

"Alladhina uhsiru" (who are restrained) means they were confined and kept under watch. It is possible that "sabil Allah" (the way of God) here means jihad. If the verse was revealed about people who were wounded in the way of God and became disabled, then "fi" (in) is causal (sababiyya). "Darb fi al-ard" (travelling about the land) means walking for jihad, based on the context of "in sabil Allah." The meaning is that they deserve to be supported because of the incapacity resulting from jihad. If they were people ready for fighting who needed help, then "fi" is metaphorically locative (zarfiyya majaziyya). If the intended people are the Ahl al-Suffa (the People of the Suffa, poor emigrants who lived in the mosque), who were the poor Emigrants that left their homes and property in Makkah and came to the Abode of Emigration and could not farm or trade, then the meaning of "uhsiru fi sabil Allah" is that they were prevented from their work for the sake of the way of God, which is emigration, so "fi" is for causation (ta'lil). It has been said that the People of the Suffa used to go out on every raid (sariyya) that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent. In that case, the way of God is jihad, and the meaning of "uhsiru" in this sense is "kept under watch," and "fi" remains causal.

The apparent meaning of ﴿they cannot travel about the land﴾ is that they are unable to trade because of their lack of means. "Darb fi al-ard" is a kinaya (metonymy, an expression whose literal meaning implies another) for trade, because it is the habit of the trader to travel to buy and sell, so he strikes the land with his feet or his mount.

**[Page 75]**

The clause ﴿they cannot travel about the land﴾ may be a circumstantial clause (hal), or it may be an explanation (bayan) of the clause "uhsiru."

His saying ﴿the ignorant man thinks them rich﴾ is a circumstantial clause from "the poor," meaning the one ignorant of their state of poverty thinks them rich. "Min" (from/because of) is for the starting point (ibtida'), because restraint is the source of this kindness.

"Ta'affuf" is the effort to maintain chastity (afaf), which is abstaining from what is unbecoming. In Bukhari there is a chapter "Seeking restraint from asking," in which he narrates the hadith of Abu Sa'id: "The Ansar asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and he gave them, then they asked him and he gave them, until what he had was exhausted. He said: 'Whatever good I have, I will not withhold it from you. Whoever seeks restraint, God will keep him restrained. Whoever seeks independence, God will make him independent. Whoever endures patiently, God will grant him patience.'"

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Ya'qub read "yahsibuhum" with a kasra on the sin, and the rest read it with a fatha on the sin. Both are dialects (lughatan).

The meaning of ﴿you know them by their marks﴾ is by the sign of need. The address is to an unspecified person so that it includes every addressee, and it is not to the Messenger, because he knows their state best. The addressee of "ta'rifuhum" (you know them) is the one who sets himself to observe the conditions of the poor, so he is the counterpart of "the ignorant man" in His saying ﴿the ignorant man thinks them rich﴾.

The sentence is an explanation (bayan) of the sentence "the ignorant man thinks them rich." It is as if it was said: "By what means will the charities of the Muslims reach them, if their poverty is hidden, and how can one know about them?" So this is referred to the place where the reflective person is expected to look, like His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern (mutawassimin)﴾ [al-Hijr 15:75].

"Al-sima" is the sign. It is derived from "sam," which is the metathesis (maqlub) of "wasama," so its original form is "wisma," and its pattern is "'ifla," though in form it is "fi'la." This is indicated by their saying "simah," for its origin is "wasmah." They say "siima" with short vowel, "sima'" with long vowel, and "simiya'" with an added ya' after the mim and a long vowel. They say "sawwama" when he made a mark. It seems they transposed the letters of the word in order to reach lightness through these patterns, because transposing the middle radical (ʿayn) of a word is easier than transposing its first radical (fa'). No unmetathesized verb from "sawwama" was heard in their speech, only the doubled verb in their saying "sawwama farasahu" (he marked his horse).

**[Page 76]**

His saying ﴿they do not ask people with importunity﴾ is a second explanation (bayan) of ﴿the ignorant man thinks them rich﴾, explaining the way in which they are thought rich: they do not ask people. The apparent order would have been to place it before the previous phrase, but it was delayed to emphasise what precedes it, namely the exhortation to discern their need, that they are restrained and cannot travel about the land, because that is the purpose of the context of the speech.

You see how the Qur'an left nothing out of the exhortation to deliver charities into the hands of the poor without mentioning it and showing special care for it.

"Ilhaf" is persistence in asking. It is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) specifying the type. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yas'aluna," in the sense of "importunate." Either way, asking qualified by importunity is negated from them, or they are described as being importunate in it. That does not mean that asking itself is negated from them. Yet His saying ﴿the ignorant man thinks them rich because of their restraint﴾ indicates that they do not ask at all. Al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari interpreted it as meaning that both asking and importunity are negated together, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*On a faded track whose landmarks guide no one*

He means the negation of landmarks and of being guided. The indicator of this intended meaning is that they are described as being thought rich because of restraint. A similar example is His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿The wrongdoers have no intimate friend, nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [Ghafir 40:18], meaning there is no intercessor at all, and since there is no intercessor, there is no obedience, so it produces "no intercessor who is obeyed." It is hyperbole in negating the intercessor, because negating it is like negating its concomitant. They counted this as a type of kinaya. Al-Taftazani said: This method is only good when the qualifier that follows the negation is in the position of a necessary concomitant of the negation, because it is the nature of a faded track to have landmarks, and the nature of an intercessor to be obeyed, so negating the concomitant is negating the thing it accompanies by a demonstrative method. Importunity, compared with asking, is not like that; rather, it is not far-fetched that the opposite of importunity, which is gentleness and courtesy, is closer to a concomitant, meaning that the negated thing is constantly accompanying what is negated from them. The author of al-Kashshaf allowed that the meaning could be: if they ask, they ask with a light gentleness without importunity, meaning that their nature is to be restrained, and when they ask, they ask without importunity. This is far-fetched, because separating the sentence from the one before it is evidence that it is an explanation of it. The more apparent is the first interpretation, which al-Kashshaf gave second. Al-Fakhr answered that He described them as restrained, so this made it unnecessary to mention that they do not ask. And it becomes clear that His saying ﴿they do not ask people with importunity﴾ is an allusion against those who press in asking, meaning that there is added benefit in their not asking.

* * *

﴿Whatever good you spend, indeed God knows it.﴾

The exhortation to spending is repeated and mentioned a fourth time. His saying ﴿indeed God knows it﴾ is a kinaya for the reward for it, because knowledge is often used as a metonymy for its effect. Since spending is encouraged by God, and God's knowledge of that is known to the Muslims, it is necessary that the information that He knows it means that He knows the spender's compliance, meaning that He does not waste his reward, since nothing prevents Him from it, given that He knows it, because He is capable of it. By the combination of these four occurrences of exhortation there has been established the great merit of spending: that it benefits the spender, that it is a connection between him and his Lord, that he attains reward from God, and that it is recorded in God's knowledge.

This is a new sentence that conveys the generality of the virtues of spending, after the discussion had been restricted to spending on the poor who were confined in the way of God. The relative pronoun is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿فَلَهم أجْرُهم﴾ ("then for them is their reward") is its predicate (khabar).

The fa' (فاء) is introduced into the predicate of the relative clause to indicate that entitlement to the reward is caused by the spending. Since the subject contains a relative clause (silah) whose purpose is generality and causation, and which signals the reason the predicate is built on the subject, namely (يُنْفِقُونَ) "they spend," it is correct to introduce the fa' into its predicate, just as it enters the response of a conditional. This is because the basic function of the fa' is to indicate causation, and it is only introduced into the response of a conditional for that purpose. "Secret" (al-sirr) means concealment, and "public" (al-'alaniyah) means open display and manifestness. Mention of ﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("with their Lord") serves to magnify the status of the reward.

[Page 78]

His saying ﴿ولا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ ("no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve") corresponds to His saying ﴿وما لِلظّالِمِينَ مِن أنْصارٍ﴾ ("and the wrongdoers have no helpers") (al-Baqarah: 270), since it is a threat to those who withhold charity, given that people abandon them when calamities befall them. This, however, is good news for the spenders regarding a pleasant life in this world, so they do not fear the aggression of aggressors, because God has given them the love of people. Painful calamities do not befall them, except for what no one is spared from, which is customary in its season.

As for the absence of fear and grief for them in the Hereafter, it is already known from His saying ﴿فَلَهم أجْرُهم عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("then for them is their reward with their Lord").

The word (خَوْفٌ) ("fear") is in the nominative in the negation of the genus (nafy al-jins, the grammatical construction negating a whole category). This is because fear is not taken to refer to an individual instance, since fear is one of the abstract meanings that are pure genera with no individual instances, as previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿لا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ ولا خُلَّةٌ﴾ ("there is no trade in it, nor friendship") (al-Baqarah: 254). From this is what occurs in the hadith of Umm Zar': "There is neither heat nor cold, neither fear nor weariness."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 275 (part 1 of 3)**

﴿Those who consume interest do not stand [on the Day of Resurrection] except as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch. That is because they said: "Trade is only like interest." But Allah has permitted trade and forbidden interest. So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed, and his affair is up to Allah. But whoever returns [to it], those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

The Qur'an arranged the most important principles for preserving the wealth of the community within this series of verses. After beginning with the greatest of these principles, which is establishing a fund for the community by which its affairs are sustained, to be taken from the people of wealth in a just manner from what exceeds their sufficiency, He imposed it upon the people: it is taken from their rich and returned to their poor. This applies equally to what is obligatory, which is the zakat (obligatory alms), and to what is voluntary, which is the sadaqa (voluntary charity). He elaborated at length in urging it, in encouraging its reward, and in warning against withholding it, which contained an admonition for whoever takes admonition. Then the discourse turned to nullifying a means that was among the causes by which the wealthy extorted the wealth of the needy who depended on them.

[Page 79]

This means is dealing in interest (riba), which the Prophet ﷺ named "the interest of the Jahiliyya" (pre-Islamic period). It is that the debtor gives the creditor money in excess of the amount of the debt in exchange for postponement. When the term comes due and he has not paid, the excess is added to the debt. They would say: "Either you pay, or you increase [the interest]." This was widespread in the Jahiliyya, as the jurists have said. The apparent meaning is that they would charge interest on the debtor from the time of the loan, and whenever he requested a respite, he would give another interest payment. Some of them may have been lenient in this. 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib was well known for practicing usury in the Jahiliyya. It is also reported in the Farewell Sermon: "Beware, the interest of the Jahiliyya is abolished, and the first interest I abolish is the interest of my uncle 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib."

The phrase ﴿Those who consume interest﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence not grammatically dependent on what precedes). The relative pronoun was used to indicate the reason for the construction of the predicate, which is His saying ﴿do not stand﴾ and what follows.

Consumption (al-akl) in its literal sense is swallowing food. It was then applied to benefiting from a thing and taking it greedily. Its origin is a figure of speech, and then it became a customary usage, so they say "he consumed the people's property." [The Qur'an says] ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans﴾ [4:10] and ﴿Do not consume your property among yourselves﴾ [2:188]. It is not restricted to taking what is false. In the Qur'an [there is] ﴿But if they give you something from it willingly, then consume it with satisfaction and ease﴾ [4:4].

Riba (interest) is a noun on the pattern fi'l, with a kasra on the fa' and a fatha on the 'ayn. Perhaps they lightened it from ribā'  (with a long vowel), so they made it a verbal noun for the verb "rabā al-shay'u yarbū rabwan" (the thing increased), with the ba' sukun according to the regular pattern, as in al-Sihah (the dictionary), and with a damma on the ra' and ba' like 'uluww. Also ribā' with a kasra on the ra' and a long vowel, like al-rima', meaning it increased. [The Qur'an says] ﴿So it does not increase in the sight of Allah﴾ [30:39] and ﴿It stirs and swells﴾ [22:5]. Since it is from the roots with waw, its dual is rabawān, and it is written with an alif. Some Kufan grammarians wrote it with a ya' considering the permissibility of imala (inclining the alif toward ya') because of the kasra on the ra'. Then they made its dual with a ya' also because of the kasra. Al-Zajjaj said: "I have never seen an error more shameful than this. Are they not content with the error in writing, that they erred in the dual as well? How do they read ﴿And what you give in interest so that it may increase among the wealth of people﴾ [30:39] with a fatha on the waw?" He is referring to the reading of 'Asim and al-A'mash, who are both Kufans, and by their reading the people of Kufa recite.

[Page 80]

The word riba is written in the Mushaf wherever it occurs after it [a letter] with a waw followed by an alif, whereas the standard would be an alif. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "It was written this way according to the dialect of those who use tafkhim, meaning they incline the alif toward the waw." Tafkhim is the opposite of imala. This is far-fetched, since tafkhim is not the dialect of Quraysh for the Mushaf to be written in it. Al-Mubarrad said: "It was written this way to distinguish riba from zina (fornication)." This is even more remote, since the context of the discourse leaves no confusion between them in meaning, except in His saying ﴿And do not approach zina﴾ [17:32]. Al-Farra' said: "The Arabs learned writing from the people of al-Hira, who are Nabateans, and they say in riba: ribaw, with a silent waw, so it was written this way." This is the most remote of all.

What I hold is that the Companions wrote it with a waw in order to indicate its root, just as they wrote the alifs that have changed from ya' in the middle of words with ya's over which are alifs. It seems that at the beginning they wanted the orthography to indicate the roots of words, but then they hurried and it was not made consistent in their orthography. For this reason they wrote zakat with a waw, and they wrote salat with a waw, as an indication that its origin is ruku' (bowing) from moving the two sides of the body, not from islat (being burned). The author of al-Kashshaf said: "They wrote an alif after it in imitation of the waw of the plural." In my view, there is no meaning to giving this as a rationale. Rather, they wrote the alif after it as a substitute for placing the alif above the waw, just as they placed an alif above the ya' that had changed from a ya', so that people would not read it as al-rabw.

What is meant by ﴿those who consume interest﴾ here is those who were upon the religion of the Jahiliyya, because this threat and condemnation is only appropriate to be directed at them, since that is among their conditions of disbelief, and they will not refrain from it as long as they remain in disbelief. As for the Muslims, a legislation prohibiting interest had already been established by His saying ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume interest, doubled and redoubled﴾ [3:130] in Surat Al 'Imran, and they do not say ﴿Trade is only like interest.﴾ So Allah made this threat, among the kinds of punishment, specific to the disbelievers, because of what branched from their disbelief, namely the imposition of interest.

All of this preceded [the present verse]: the Qur'an's denunciation of the people of the Jahiliyya for giving interest, and it was among the first things the Qur'an forbade them in Mecca. In Surat al-Rum it came: ﴿And what you give in interest to increase the wealth of people does not increase in the sight of Allah; but what you give in zakat, seeking the Face of Allah, those are the multipliers [of reward]﴾ [30:39].

[Page 81]

This is an address to the polytheists, because the surah is Meccan, and because after the verse comes His saying ﴿Allah is the One who created you, then provided for you, then causes you to die, then gives you life. Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ [30:40].

It is a habit of the Qur'an to mention the conditions of the disbelievers in order to censure them severely and, by implication, to frighten the Muslims so that they will be averse to the conditions of the people of disbelief. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Everything in the Qur'an that censures the conditions of the disbelievers is also meant to warn the Muslims against the like of it in Islam." For this reason Allah said: ﴿And whoever returns, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ and He said: ﴿Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾ [2:276].

Then He turned to address the Muslims, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾ [2:278] and the verses that follow. Perhaps some Muslims had not refrained from dealing in interest, or perhaps some of them had been tempted by the statement of the disbelievers: ﴿Trade is only like interest.﴾ So the verse in Surat Al 'Imran was the beginning of the prohibition, and this verse was the closing of the door to excuses for consuming interest and an explanation of how to make up for what had already been taken.

Interest occurs in two forms. The first is a loan with an increase over what the lender gives. The second is a loan without increase for a fixed term; meaning, when the borrower does not pay the debt at the term, he must add an increase to it, which both parties agree upon at the due date of each term.

His saying ﴿do not stand﴾: the literal meaning of standing (al-qiyam) is rising and standing up independently. It is also used figuratively for improvement of condition and for strength. From this: "the market stood up" (qamat al-suq) and "the war stood up" (qamat al-harb). If the standing negated here is literal standing, then the meaning is: they will not stand ﴿on the day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [83:6] except as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch; that is, except with a standing like the standing of one whom Satan drives to madness. If the standing is figurative, the meaning is either that their eagerness and activity in dealings of interest is like the standing of a madman, as a denunciation of their greed. This is what Ibn 'Atiyya said. It is also possible on this reading that the meaning is a comparison of what amazes people about the stability of their condition, abundance of their wealth, and strength of their commerce, with what appears of the condition of one whom Satan drives to madness, so that you think he is strong and quick in movement, though he owns nothing for himself. On the literal meaning, the verse is a threat to them of beginning their punishment from the time of standing for judgment until they enter the Fire, and this is the apparent meaning and is appropriate to His saying ﴿That is because they said: "Trade is only like interest."﴾ On the figurative meaning, it is a denunciation or a threat of bad condition in this world, of encountering hardships and the bitterness of life, under an image that the beholder thinks is upright.

[Page 82]

The verb takhabbat (to be driven into confusion) is the reflexive (mutawa') of khabatahu: when one strikes him a severe blow and he is thrown into agitation, meaning he moves with severe movement. Since lack of coordination is a necessary consequence of such movement, the word takhabbut was applied to a person's agitation without coordination. Then they often use the reflexive form and make it transitive with an object when they wish to be concise. Instead of saying khabatahu fa-takhabbata ("he struck him so he was agitated"), they say takhabbatahu, just as they say "idtarrahu ila kadha" (he compelled him to such-and-such). So Satan's takhabbut of a person is making him agitated, that is, moving without coordination.

The one whom Satan drives to madness is the madman who is afflicted with epilepsy, so he is thrown into convulsions and falls to the ground when he tries to stand. When the state was compared to the state, the expression was used for the state being compared, with the words set for indicating it in their speech; otherwise the compared state would not be understood, and this was known to them. Al-A'sha describes his she-camel as energetic and swift in its pace, after she had traveled the whole night:

*"She rises in the morning after the weariness of the journey, as if the spirits of the jinn had touched her, and she is possessed (awlaq)."*

The word masss (touch) in its original sense is touching with the hand, as in their saying: "The touch is the touch of a rabbit" (a proverb). When it is used indefinitely, without a known prior touch, it indicates among them the touch of the jinn. They say: "a man is mamsus," meaning a madman. The statement ﴿from the touch﴾ was needed in order to clarify the intended meaning of Satan's takhabbut, so that it would not be thought to be a figurative takhabbut in the sense of whispering (waswasa). The word min (from) is initial (ibtida'iyya, indicating origin) and is necessarily connected to yatakhabbatuhu.

This, according to the Mu'tazila, is in accordance with what the Arab is accustomed to, like His saying: ﴿Its spathe is as if it were the heads of devils﴾ [37:65], and the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"And a sharpened (blade) of blue, like the fangs of ghouls."*

However, this is something observed, and its cause is imagined. The other two are imagined, because they deny the influence of devils except through whispering. In our view, it is also based on their imagination, though epilepsy arises from ailments that afflict the body, like the excess of bile according to the earlier physicians, and the spasm of the nervous system according to the later ones. Yet in our view it is permissible that all of these ailments originate in the first place from satanic influences, for the worlds of the immaterial beings, such as spirits, have not been revealed to us until now, and perhaps they have connections of radiation which are the sources of generation and corruption.

His saying ﴿That is because they said: "Trade is only like interest."﴾ The demonstrative ﴿That﴾ refers to ﴿as one stands﴾, because (ma) is verbal (masdariyya, forming a verbal noun with the following verb) and the ba' is causal.

As for what is quoted of them by the statement ﴿they said: "Trade is only like interest"﴾: if it was a spoken statement, then what is meant is the saying of some of them, or of their propagandists, who were the hypocrites in Medina. They supposed, through their misunderstanding, that the prohibition of interest was a contradiction at the time of permitting trade, with the aim of tempting the Muslims concerning the validity of the rulings of their law. It would be impossible for everyone who consumed interest to have said this statement. If it was a statement of condition, such that everyone who consumes interest would say it if anyone asked him about the reason for his dealing in interest, then it is a metaphor (isti'ara). It is also possible that (they said) is a figure of speech (majaz), because their belief in the equivalence of trade and interest necessitates that someone would say it. So the speech is attributed and what is meant is its necessary implication, which is the belief in it.

[Page 84]

Their saying, ﴿Verily, trade is only like riba﴾, is a restrictive qasr idafi (a restriction aimed at a particular opponent's claim) in response to those who claimed that the two rulings differ, so that riba was prohibited and trade permitted. Since the word "like" (mithl) was used explicitly, it is permissible to say "trade is like riba," just as it is permissible to say "riba is like trade." It cannot be said that the expected wording would have been "Riba is only like trade," since trade was the thing intended to be assimilated to riba, as in the question raised by al-Kashshaf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari), on which he based his view that the statement is a form of hyperbole. For we say: they were not aiming to attach subsidiary cases to principles through analogical reasoning (qiyas). Rather, they were engaged in both riba and trade, so both were equally present in their minds. But when they heard that riba was prohibited while trade remained permitted, trade came to their minds, so they brought it forward in order to establish the permissibility of riba by means of it. Alternatively, they made trade the basis (asl) by way of mockery of Islam for its prohibition of riba, following the method known in the principles of jurisprudence as qiyas al-'aks (converse analogy). This is because converse analogy is resorted to only in the heat of debate, not when a mujtahid (qualified jurist) is deriving rulings for himself.

[Page 85]

By "trade" here they meant commercial sale, not the sale by a needy person of his goods at their original cost.

As for His saying, ﴿But Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba﴾, it is a words of God Most High, a reply both to them and to the Muslims. It is a turning away from disputing with them, since there is no benefit in argument with them, for they said this out of disbelief and hypocrisy, and so they are not among those to whom the rulings of Islam apply. It is also a persuasion for the Muslims that what the disbelievers said is mere doubt (shubhah) with no substance, and that Allah, the All-Knowing, has prohibited this and permitted that. This is nothing but wisdom and considerations of real distinction, which those who reflect would have grasped, so that they would have perceived the difference between trade and riba. This answer does not, however, remove the doubt explicitly, so it is among the matters that God entrusted to the knowledge of the people of learning among the believers. Moreover, mentioning the prohibition of riba immediately after the exhortation to charity (sadaqat) hints at removing the doubt.

Know that the foundation of the doubt of those who said, ﴿Verily, trade is only like riba﴾, is that in commerce there is an increase over the price of goods, for the purpose of the merchant's profit in return for bringing goods and making them available to buyers in cash sales, and then for the waiting for payment in deferred sales. Likewise, if someone lends ten dirhams, for example, on the condition that he returns eleven dirhams, then he has given him this extra dirham in return for preparing his money for the one who borrows it, because the lender has undertaken to lend and has prepared his money for this purpose, and then for waiting for that after the due date.

The removal of this doubt was undertaken by al-Qaffal, who said: If someone sells a garment worth ten for twenty, he has made the garment itself equivalent to twenty. When mutual consent to this equivalence has been reached, the twenty becomes the counter-value (iwad) of the garment in terms of its monetary worth, so the seller takes nothing from the buyer without return. But if he lends ten for twenty, the lender takes the extra ten without any return. It cannot be said that the excess is the counter-value of the delay, because delay is not property or a thing that can be pointed to, so as to make it a counter-value for the extra ten. The basis of this distinction is that it is merely a conventional, relative (i'tibari) convention, so it is a deficient distinction.

In the course of stating the wisdom behind the prohibition of riba, al-Fakhr (al-Razi) pointed to another distinction, which al-Baydawi refined. Its substance is that one who sells something worth ten for eleven has enabled the buyer to benefit from the item, either in itself or by trading in it. Thus the excess is for the sake of that benefit, which is the pressing need or the expectation of marketability and profit. As for the one who gave a dirham for a loan, he has not obtained a benefit greater than the amount of money he took. It cannot be said that he could trade with it and make a profit, because this is an imagined benefit, not certain to be attained, whereas taking the excess is certain in every case.

This distinction is closer to that of al-Qaffal, but it faces the objection that the borrower's benefit from the money is meeting his needs, so it is like the buyer's benefit from the commodity. As for his engaging in trade with the loaned money or with the purchased commodity, this is rare in such cases.

So the correct view for me regarding the distinction between trade and riba is that it rests on the reasoning by presumptive cause (ta'lil bil-maẓinnah), taking into account the difference between the situations of the borrower and the buyer. Borrowing was for meeting the borrower's need to spend on himself and his family, since they considered debt a burden and distress, and the Prophet (ﷺ) sought refuge from it. The situation of the merchant, however, is that of one who is doing a favour. Likewise, the situations of the lender and the seller differ. The situation of one who gives his money to the needy in order to profit from what they pay him in riba increases their distress, since the borrower is presumptively in need; do you not see that he has no money in his hand? The situation of the seller of goods for trade is that of one who undertakes hardship to bring what the people in need require and to prepare it for them when they call for it, while they give him what they have of money. So trade is a dealing between two wealthy parties. Do you not see that each of them gives what he does not need and takes what he needs? The borrower is presumptively poor, while the buyer is presumptively wealthy. For this reason riba was prohibited, because it exploits the need of the poor, and trade was permitted, because it is assistance to one who seeks needs. Thus it becomes clear that lending is a kind of consolation and kindness, and that it is strongly enjoined upon the one who consoles, whether obligatory or recommended. In either case, it is not lawful for the lender to take a wage for performing a kindness. As for one who borrows money in order to trade with it or to expand his business, he is not presumptively in need, so he is not among those deserving the consolation of the Muslims. Therefore the wealthy man is not obliged to lend to him in any circumstance. If he does lend, he has voluntarily done a kindness, and this suffices as a distinction between the two situations.

Al-Fakhr mentioned four reasons for the prohibition of riba. The first is that it involves taking property without a return. This was objected to in light of what preceded regarding the distinction between it and trade, and that distinction is not persuasive.

[Page 86]

The second: engaging in riba prevents people from undertaking the hardships of working to earn a living, because when the owner of wealth becomes accustomed to taking riba, earning a livelihood becomes light for him. If this spreads among people, it leads to the cessation of benefits to creation, since the welfare of the world is not sustained except by trade, crafts, and construction.

The third: it leads to the cessation of kindness among people through lending.

The fourth: the usual case is that the lender is wealthy and the borrower is poor, so if riba were permitted, the wealthy would be able to take the property of the weak.

We have already pointed out in the earlier discussion of the distinction between riba and trade the reason behind its prohibition, and we will elaborate on this at His saying, ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume riba, doubled and multiplied﴾ [Al 'Imran: 130], in Surat Al 'Imran.

This is what the verse addresses: a ruling, namely the permissibility of trade and the prohibition of riba, since it is a statement from God Most High to announce this legislation after the admonition that preceded it.

The article "al-" in each of (al-bay' wa al-riba) (the trade and the riba) is for defining the genus (ta'rif al-jins). Thereby the rulings of two great principles in people's transactions, which they need, are established: one is called trade and the other is called riba. The first is permissible, and its being a complementary need (hajiyy) for the community is recognized. The second is prohibited, and its complementary need has been nullified because of the harm that opposes it.

The apparent meaning of the genus-definition is that God permitted trade in its entirety, so the permission covers all its instances, and that He prohibited riba in its entirety in the same way. Since the meaning of "God has permitted trade" is "He has allowed it," it has the force of an affirmative proposition. It does not therefore necessarily entail comprehensiveness of the genus by the wording alone, and no indicator was present to intend comprehensiveness, as there is in phrases like "Praise belongs to God." Thus it remains open to the permission covering all instances of trade. But since trade may be affected by causes that make it invalid or unlawful, the Law has tracked the causes of its prohibition, so the probability of comprehensiveness regarding it in this verse is set aside.

As for the meaning of His saying, ﴿and He has prohibited riba﴾, it has the force of a negation, because "prohibited" (harrama) means "forbade," so it necessarily entails the comprehensiveness of the genus of riba by its wording, since nothing can happen to it to make it lawful.

Then the scholars of Islam differed over whether the word riba in the verse remains upon its well-known meaning in the language, or whether it has been transferred to a new meaning in the technical usage of the Law.

[Page 87]

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, and Mu'awiyah held that it remains upon its well-known meaning, namely the riba of the pre-Islamic period, that is, an increase in exchange for a delay. Ibn 'Abbas relied on the hadith of Usama: "Riba is only in deferment (nasi'ah)." He did not adopt what was reported to establish riba of excess (riba al-fadl) without deferment. Al-Fakhr said: Perhaps he did not consider the Qur'an to be specified by a single-transmission report (khabar al-ahad), meaning that he applied "God has permitted trade" in its general sense.

As for the majority of scholars, they held that riba was transferred in the usage of the Law to a new meaning, as many hadiths indicate. This is the view adopted by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'A'ishah, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit. Indeed, 'Umar considered that the word riba had been transferred to a new meaning, and that not all its intended scope had been explained, so in his view it resembled what is general and ambiguous (mujmal). Ibn Rushd reported from him in al-Muqaddimat that he said: "Among the last things God sent down to His Messenger was the verse on riba, and the Messenger of God died without explaining it, so leave aside riba and whatever casts doubt." And: "You claim that we know the categories of riba, and that I would prefer to know them over having the like of Egypt and its districts." Ibn Rushd said: 'Umar did not mean that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not explain the verse on riba, but rather he meant, and God knows best, that he did not explicitly cover all the forms of riba by textual statement. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained the meaning of riba in fifty-six hadiths.

In my view, what 'Umar meant is not that the word riba is ambiguous, because he contrasted it with clarification and explanation. Rather, he meant that the realization of its ruling in the many forms of sales was obscure, and the Prophet (ﷺ) had not covered it explicitly, because earlier scholars were not careful in their expressions to match technical meanings. Thus the Hanafis called specifying qualifiers "clarification of change" (bayan taghyir). Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned in al-'Awasim that the people of hadith are liberal in the meaning of clarification (bayan). In al-Fakhr's Tafsir, on the authority of al-Shafi'i, it is stated that His saying, ﴿And God has permitted trade and prohibited riba﴾, is among the ambiguous statements which may not be relied upon as they stand, that is, relying on their two generalities: the generality of trade and the generality of riba. For if what is intended is the genus of trade and the genus of increase, it would require clarification of which trade and which increase. And if what is intended is every trade and every increase, then there is no trade without some increase in it. Thus the beginning of the verse permits all sales, and its end prohibits all of them, so it becomes necessary to return to the Messenger's (peace be upon him) clarification.

What led the majority to regard the word riba as used in a new meaning are hadiths reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), by word or deed, which indicate that riba is explained as more general than the riba of the pre-Islamic period known to them before Islam. Their principal sources are six hadiths.

[Page 88]

The first hadith: the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "Gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, barley for barley, dates for dates, and salt for salt, like for like, hand to hand. Whoever gives more or takes more has committed riba; the taker and the giver in this are equal."

The second hadith is the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit: "Gold for gold, its raw and its minted form; silver for silver, its raw and its minted form; wheat for wheat, measure for measure; barley for barley, measure for measure; dates for dates, measure for measure; and salt for salt, measure for measure. Whoever gives more or asks for more has committed riba. There is no harm in selling gold for silver and silver for gold, with the greater of the two taken hand to hand. As for deferred exchange, it is not permitted." Related by Abu Dawud. In these two hadiths he called it riba.

The third hadith is that of Abu Sa'id: "Bilal came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with Barni dates. He said to him, 'Where is this from?' Bilal said, 'We had inferior dates, and I sold two sa' of them for one sa' so that the Prophet could eat.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Oh! This is the very essence of riba. Do not do that. But if you want to buy dates, sell them first and then buy with the proceeds.'" Here he called the excess riba.

The fourth is the hadith in the Muwatta' and al-Bukhari from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayrah: "Sawad ibn Ghaziyyah came from Khaybar with Janib dates. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, 'Are all the dates of Khaybar like this?' He said, 'O Messenger of Allah, we take one sa' of this for two or three sa'.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Do not do that. Sell the mixed dates for dirhams, then buy Janib dates with the dirhams.'"

The fifth is the hadith of 'A'ishah in Sahih al-Bukhari: "She said: When the verses at the end of Surat al-Baqarah about riba were revealed, the Prophet recited them and then prohibited trade in wine." Its apparent meaning is that the prohibition of trade in wine was an application of the verse forbidding riba, although trade in wine contains no meaning of the riba known among them; it is rather a void (fasid) sale.

The sixth is the hadith of al-Daraqutni (and it was related by Ibn Wahb from Malik): that al-'Aliyah bint Ayna came to Madinah from Kufah, met 'A'ishah, and informed her that she had sold a slave-girl to Zayd ibn Arqam in Kufah for eight hundred dirhams payable at the time of the 'ata' (the stipend). Then Zayd sold the slave-girl, and al-'Aliyah bought her back from him for six hundred in cash. 'A'ishah said to her, "What a wretched thing you bought and what a wretched thing you sold! Tell Zayd that he has nullified his jihad with the Messenger of Allah unless he repents." She said: I said to her, "What do you think if I take only my capital?" She said: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed﴾. So 'A'ishah counted it as riba, and for this reason she recited the verse.

On the basis of these six hadiths, the jurists established three kinds of riba in the technical usage of the Law. The first is riba al-jahiliyyah (the riba of the pre-Islamic period), which is an increase on a debt in return for deferment. The second is riba al-fadl (riba of excess), which is the excess of one of the two exchanged items when selling one kind of the categories mentioned in the hadiths of Abu Sa'id and 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit for the same kind. The third is riba al-nasi'ah (riba of deferment), which is selling one of those categories for the same kind on deferred terms. The Malikis added a fourth type: that which leads to one of these categories through the suspicion of a ruse to circumvent riba. Malik placed it in the Mudawwanah under the heading "sales of deferred terms" (buyu' al-ajal), and Malik's evidence for it is the hadith of al-'Aliyah. Some scholars held that the term riba includes every void sale, taking as their basis the hadith of 'A'ishah concerning the prohibition of trade in wine, and Ibn al-'Arabi inclined to this view.

In my view, the most apparent of these positions is the position of Ibn 'Abbas, and the hadiths about riba al-fadl are to be understood in light of the hadith of Usamah: "Riba is only in deferment (nasi'ah)," so that the two sets of hadiths may be reconciled. The naming of excess as riba in the hadiths of Abu Sa'id and 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit is evidence for what we have said. As for what Malik took into account, namely the nullification of what leads to dealings in riba when it arises from situations of suspicion, that is a sound consideration, whereas going beyond it is excessive caution. It may be derived from some of Malik's statements in the Muwatta' and elsewhere that the absence of suspicion does not invalidate the contract.

There is no proof in the hadith of 'A'ishah concerning Zayd ibn Arqam, because the Muslims at the first stage of Islam were recent in their acquaintance with the riba of the pre-Islamic period, so their situation required blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i').

In the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi: Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan used to hold that the prohibition on selling gold for gold and silver for silver in unequal amounts applied only to minted dinars and minted dirhams, not to raw gold or silver, nor to crafted items. Muslim related from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit that he said: "We fought a campaign while Mu'awiyah was in command of the people, and we took many spoils. Among what we took were gold vessels. Mu'awiyah ordered men to sell them for the people's stipends. The people disputed this. The matter reached 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who stood up and said: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbid selling gold for gold and silver for silver except equal for equal, hand to hand. Whoever gives more or asks for more has committed riba.'" When this reached Mu'awiyah, he stood up to deliver a sermon and said: "Alas, what is the matter with people who narrate hadiths from the Messenger of Allah that we witnessed and accompanied him in, yet we never heard them from him?" 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit said: "We shall certainly narrate what we heard from the Messenger of Allah, even if Mu'awiyah dislikes it."

The apparent meaning is that the verse intended only the riba of the pre-Islamic period, and that other void transactions which involve consuming wealth unjustly are covered by other proofs.

His saying ﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists﴾, etc., is a consequence (tafri') of the threat in His saying ﴿Those who consume riba﴾.

The word "coming" (ja'ahu) here means knowledge and notification, i.e., whoever knows this warning. This is an excuse for one who continued in dealing in riba before the prohibition reached him. Thus the admonition (mawi'zah) refers to this verse and to the verse of Al 'Imran.

Al-intiha' (desisting) is the reflexive form of nahahu, when one restrains him from what is not fitting. It seems to be derived from al-nuha (with a dammah on the nun), which means intellect. The meaning of ﴿for him is what has passed﴾ is that what has already been received of riba wealth is his, not what contract was made earlier but not yet received, as indicated by His later saying: ﴿But if you repent, you shall have your capital (ru'us amwalikum)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279].

As for His saying ﴿and his affair is up to Allah﴾, the commentators have suggested several possibilities: some of them return the pronoun to (man ja'ahu), and some return it to (ma salaf). The more apparent view is that it refers to (man ja'ahu), since that is the intended subject. The meaning of ﴿and his affair is up to Allah﴾ is that the matter of his reward for desisting is left to Allah, the Exalted. This is one of the ambiguities intended to magnify the matter, so the intended sense is a promise, as shown by its being set against the threat in His saying: ﴿But whoever returns—those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾.

The one who returns is described as abiding eternally in the Fire either because the intended meaning is a return to His saying ﴿Trade is only like riba﴾, i.e., he returned to declaring riba lawful, and that is hypocrisy, for many of them found it difficult to abandon dealing in riba, so Allah knew this about them and made their failure to give it up a sign of the falsity of their faith. In this case "abiding eternally" is in its literal sense. Or the intended meaning is a return to dealing in riba, which is what is apparent from its contrast with His saying: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists﴾. "Khulud" (abiding) means a long stay, as in the words of Labid:

"So I stood asking her, and how can we ask
mute, abiding ruins whose speech is not clear."

And from it: "Allah made the kingdom of so-and-so eternal (khallada)."

[Page 91]

The Khawarij, who hold that the one who commits a major sin is a disbeliever, have clung to the apparent meaning of this verse and others like it, just as they clung to similar verses. They overlooked the severity of Allah's threat at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an, when people were recently released from disbelief, and it is necessary to reconcile the proofs of the Book and the Sunnah.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 2, verse 276:**

﴿Allah destroys interest and makes charity grow. And Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner.﴾

This is a *isti'naf* (a resumptive new sentence) that explains the evil outcome of *riba* (usury, interest) in this world, after its outcome in the Hereafter has already been explained. It is an *isti'naf bayani* (an explanatory new sentence) that anticipates the question of someone who asks about the condition of those who do not desist from Allah's admonition. His saying ﴿and makes charity grow﴾ is an *istitrad* (digression) that explains the outcome of charity in this world as well, namely that the one who gives charity gains good in both abodes, just as the usurer incurs evil in both. Thus this is a worldly promise and warning.

*Al-mahq* is like *al-mahw* (erasing), meaning the removal of a thing. From it comes *muhaq al-qamar* (the waning of the moon), the disappearance of its light on the night of *al-sirar* (the last night of the lunar month). The meaning of ﴿Allah destroys interest﴾ is that He destroys what was gained from it in this world. And ﴿makes charity grow﴾ means He multiplies its reward, because charity cannot accept increase except in the sense of increase in its reward. A parallel to this appears in the hadith: "Whoever gives charity from lawful earnings, and Allah accepts only what is good, the Most Merciful receives it with His right hand, and both of His hands are right, and He makes it grow for him just as one of you raises his foal." Since destruction is attached to interest and growth is attached to charities, the contrast implies the omission of two other counterparts, and the meaning is: Allah destroys interest and punishes for it, and makes charity grow and blesses its giver. This is in the manner of *al-ihtiba'* (the rhetorical device of implicit complementary omission).

The clause ﴿and Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾ is a *i'tiradiyya* (parenthetical clause) placed between the rulings on interest. Since the nature of a parenthetical clause is that it is not free of some connection to the context of the speech, the statement that Allah does not love all the disbelievers indicates that interest is among the emblems of the people of disbelief, and that they are the ones who made it permissible, saying, "Trade is only like interest." Thus this is an allusion that the usurer is characterized by the traits of the people of polytheism.

The implication of the construction is that Allah does not love any of the sinful disbelievers, because *kull* (every) is among the forms of generality. It is established to encompass all the individuals of what it is attached to, and it is not established to indicate a collected mass. For this reason they say it is established for the *kull jami'i* (the distributive "all," each individual). As for the collective *kull majmu'i* (the "all" as a whole), *kull* is used for it only metaphorically. So when *kull* is attached to a noun, it encompasses all of its individuals, whether in affirmation or in negation. When negation enters upon *kull*, the meaning is the generality of negation over all the individuals, because negation is a modality that affects the sentence, so the basic principle is that the content of the sentence remains as it is, except that it is qualified by negation instead of affirmation. So when you say, "Kull al-diyar ma dakhaltuhu" (I did not enter every one of the lands), or "Lam adkhul kulla dar" (I did not enter every house), or "Kulla dar lam adkhul" (every house I did not enter), this conveys the negation of your entering any one of the lands, just as its content in affirmation is the establishment of your entering every house. For this reason, the nominative and accusative cases of the word *kull* are equal in meaning in the verse of Abu al-Najm:

*Qad asbahat Umm al-Khiyar tad'i 'alayya dhanban kulluhu lam asna'i*
"Indeed, Umm al-Khiyar has begun to accuse me of a sin, all of which I did not commit."

As Sibawayh said, if it were put in the accusative it would be better, because the accusative does not corrupt the meaning or disturb the metre. *Kull* does not depart from indicating generality except when the speaker uses it in a statement intended to refute a statement in which *kull* occurred explicitly or implicitly. For example, someone says, "Kull al-fuqaha' yuharrimu akl luhum al-siba' " (all jurists forbid eating the flesh of predatory animals). You reply to him, "Ma kull al-'ulama' yuharrimu luhum al-siba'" (not all scholars forbid the flesh of predatory animals), since you intend to refute the universality, and so some remain. Likewise in refuting mistaken beliefs, as in the proverb *ma kullu bayda'a shahmatan* (not every white thing is fat), which is said to refute the belief in that, as Zufar ibn al-Harith al-Kilabi said:

*Wa kunna hasibna kulla bayda'a shahmatan*
"And we had supposed that every white thing was fat."

Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani looked at this last usage and generalized it to the use of *kull* when it occurs within the scope of negation after a negative particle. He elaborated on this in his book *Dala'il al-I'jaz* (The Proofs of Inimitability), and he claimed that the meaning of Abu al-Najm's *rajaz* (verse) changes according to whether *kull* is in the nominative or accusative in his saying "kulluhu lam asna'i." Al-'Allama al-Taftazani critiqued him in a general way, stating that what he said is the majority case, and that it has been violated in some places. I followed al-Taftazani's view and, in my annotation "al-Ijaz 'ala Dala'il al-I'jaz" (The Summary of the Proofs of Inimitability), I explained that the predominant pattern is the reverse, and its conclusion is what I have mentioned here.

*Page 92*

Verse 277:

﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds, and established prayer and paid zakat, will have their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾

This is a parenthetical clause (jumlah mu'taridah) serving to contrast dispraise with praise. The similar verse was explained earlier, shortly before this. The intended implication is an indirect allusion (ta'ridh) that the attributes opposite to these attributes are the attributes of those who do not believe. The relevance becomes even clearer with His saying: "and paid zakat."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verses 278–279:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains of interest, if you should be believers.﴾ ﴿And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger. But if you repent, you may have your principal. You do not wrong [others], nor are you wronged.﴾

His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains of interest﴾ is a transition to legislation after admonition had been presented before it, which prepared the souls for it. If His saying ﴿Allah has permitted trade and forbidden interest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275] is from the speech of those who said ﴿Trade is only like interest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275], then it is evident. If it is from the speech of Allah, the Exalted, then it is legislation that occurred in the context of refutation. So He did not suffice with a legislation that was not intended, and therefore this explicit, intended legislation was needed. All that preceded is a description of the state of the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period of ignorance), and what remained of it at the beginning of Islam, before the prohibition.

They were commanded to fear Allah before the command to leave interest, because the fear of Allah is the root of compliance and abstention, and because leaving interest is among its components; so it is like a command by way of a demonstrative method.

The meaning of ﴿and give up what remains of interest﴾, and so on, is: leave what remains in the liabilities of those with whom you dealt in interest. This is the counterpart of His saying ﴿for him is what has preceded﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]. So what had already been taken into possession before the revelation of this verse is pardoned, and what had not been taken into possession is commanded to be left.

Page 94
It has been said: this verse was revealed addressing Thaqif, the people of al-Ta'if, when they entered Islam after the conquest of Makkah and after the siege of al-Ta'if, under a truce that was concluded between them and 'Attab ibn Usayd, whom the Prophet ﷺ appointed over Makkah after the conquest. The reason was that they had dealings in interest with Quraysh. Thaqif stipulated, before accepting Islam, that every interest owed to them by the people they would take, and every interest owed by them would be void. The Messenger of Allah accepted their condition. Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse addressing them, and they were recent in their acceptance of Islam, so they said: "We have no power against war from Allah and His Messenger."

His saying ﴿if you should be believers﴾ means: if you should be believers truly. This does not contradict His saying "O you who have believed," since its meaning is: O you who have entered into faith. Thus the difficulties that arose are dispelled.

His saying ﴿And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾ means: if you hold fast to the stipulation, then the truce between us is broken; know that war has returned fresh. This is like His saying: "﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58]." The indefiniteness of "war" (harb) is for the purpose of magnifying its matter. For this purpose, the attribution of war was turned away from Allah and replaced by "min" (from), and it was ascribed to Allah because it is by His permission, by way of metaphorical attribution, and to His Messenger because he is the conveyor and the one who carries it out. This is the apparent meaning. If what has been mentioned about its occasion of revelation is sound, then it is an instance of permitting ijtihad (independent reasoning) to the Prophet ﷺ in rulings, since he accepted from Thaqif the settlement according to what they were owed in interest among the people of Makkah, and that was before the revelation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and give up what remains of interest﴾. It is possible that the Prophet ﷺ judged the truce with Thaqif upon their entry into Islam, while leaving them in possession of what was theirs before Quraysh of interest-money fixed in their liabilities before the prohibition, to be in the public interest, since the rule is that what preceded legislation is not annulled, like the confirmation of the marriage contracts of polytheists. Then Allah did not approve him in that, and commanded them to refrain from taking the interest-money after the prohibition, even if the contract was before the prohibition. For this reason He left them with choice regarding their affair in the truce they had concluded.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 2, verse 280:**

﴿And if the debtor is in hardship, then let there be postponement until a time of ease. But that you give [it] as charity is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿatf, grammatical conjunction) with His saying: ﴿Then you shall have your principal sums﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279], because the apparent meaning of the response is that they recover their principal immediately, since the contracts have been annulled. So He coordinated with it another state. The state that is coordinated with is an implied, understood state, because the conditional clause indicates causation, and the basic principle is that the conditioned occurs when the condition occurs. The meaning is: "And if there occurs a debtor in hardship," that is, an insolvent debtor.

In the verse there is evidence that *dhū* (possessor of) may be attached to something that does not convey a noble quality.

*Al-nazira* (with a kasra on the ẓāʾ) means waiting.

*Al-maysura*, with a ḍamma on the sīn in the recitation of Nafiʿ and with a fatḥa in the recitation of the rest (of the reciters), is a noun for ease, which is the opposite of hardship (*ʿusr*, with a ḍamma on the ʿayn). It is on the pattern *mafʿulah*, like *mashriqah*, *mashrubah*, *ma'lakah* and *maqdurah*. Abu ʿAli said: the pattern *mafʿalah* with a fatḥa is more common in their speech.

The clause "*fa-nazira*" is the response of the conditional, and its predicate is omitted, meaning: "then there is postponement for him."

The form is an imperative, and it admits both obligation and recommendation. If by hardship is meant having nothing, that is, the exhaustion of all his wealth, then the demand is for obligation, and what is intended by it is the nullification of the ruling of selling the insolvent and enslaving him for debt when he has no means of repayment. It has been said that this was a ruling in the Jahiliyyah, and it is an ancient ruling among nations; it was part of the law of the Egyptians. The Qur'an alludes to this in His saying, ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ [Yusuf: 76]. The law of the Romans included enslaving the debtor, and I think that the law of the Torah contained something close to this. It is narrated that it existed at the beginning of Islam, but this is not established. If by hardship is meant straitened circumstances and the harm done to the debtor by hastening repayment, then the demand admits of obligation, and some jurists held this view, and it admits of recommendation, and this is the view of Malik and the majority. So whoever does not wish to grant postponement is not obliged to, even if he must sell all his property, because this is a right that can be recovered, and granting postponement is a good deed (*maʿruf*), and a good deed is not obligatory. Nevertheless, the later scholars in Qurtuba (Cordoba) did not compel the debtor to pay immediately, and they would postpone the debt by discretion, lest harm befall him by hastening the sale of what would free him.

The occasion of revelation of the verse concerns debts arising from usurious transactions, but the majority generalized it to all transactions and did not regard the specific cause. Because it nullified the ruling on usury, the principal became a pure debt. Thus what was specified in the verse, the demand for postponement, is a ruling that applies to all debts. Shurayh disagreed and restricted the verse to debts that were based on usury, whose usury was subsequently nullified.

His saying, ﴿But that you give [it] as charity is better for you﴾, means that remitting the debt of the insolvent and easing his situation by making him rich is more excellent. God called it charity because it relieves distress and rescues the afflicted.

Among the ten canonical readers, the majority read *taṣṣaddaqū* with a shadda on the ṣād (*qiraʾah*, recitation), on the basis that its original form was *tataṣaddaqū*. The second tāʾ was changed to ṣād because of their similarity, and it was assimilated into the ṣād. ʿAsim read it with a lightened ṣād, by omitting one of the two tāʾs for lightness.

[Page 96]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 281:

Page 97
﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah, then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾
The phrase "And fear a Day" is placed here as a concluding summation (tadhyil) of these rulings, because it is suitable for instilling fear of committing what has been forbidden and for encouraging the doing of what has been commanded or recommended. In abandoning what is prohibited there is safety from its sins, and in doing what is required there is abundance of its reward. All of this returns to being mindful of that Day, on which safety is sought and the causes of success are multiplied.

In Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas, it is related that this is the last verse revealed. "And from Ibn 'Abbas: it is the last thing revealed. Jibril said: 'O Muhammad, place it at the head of two hundred and eighty verses of al-Baqarah.'" This is the view of the majority, said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Jubayr and Muqatil. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lived after its revelation twenty-one days; it was also said eighty-one days, seven days, nine days, and three hours. It has been said that the last verse is the verse of kalalah, and other views have been stated. The scholar of al-Itqan (al-Suyuti) has thoroughly surveyed these opinions.

The majority recited "turja'ūna" (تُرْجَعُونَ) with a dammah on the tā' and a fathah on the jīm. Ya'qub recited it with a fathah on the tā' and a kasrah on the jīm.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 2, verse 282 (part 1 of 5):**

﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt with one another for a specified term, write it down. Let a scribe write it down between you justly. No scribe should refuse to write as Allah has taught him. So let him write, and let the one who has the obligation dictate, and let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not diminish anything of it. But if the one who has the obligation is foolish, or weak, or unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate justly.﴾

[Page 98]

When the Qur'an gave attention to organizing the affairs of the Muslims concerning their wealth, it began with what sustains the common welfare of them: aiding the poor and relieving the distressed. This was made clear through what contains a lesson for the one who takes heed. Then it linked to this the warning against oppressing those in need of assistance by the oppression of usury (riba), together with the harms present in those transactions. It then turned to explaining financial safeguards (tawaththuqat), namely attestation (al-ishhad) and what takes its place, which is pledge (al-rahn) and trust (al-i'timan). Establishing safeguards in transactions is one of the greatest means of spreading trust among those who deal with one another, and this helps increase transactions and keep the wheel of commerce turning.

The sentence is a fresh, independent beginning (istinaf ibtida'i), and the connection in the transition is evident, following the discussion about the creditors of the people of usury.

Indebtedness (al-tadayun) is among the greatest causes of the circulation of transactions, because one capable of developing wealth may lack capital and so be compelled to borrow in order to display his abilities in trade, industry, or agriculture. Also, the affluent person may find his wealth depleted before him while he still has claims against others, and if he does not incur debt, the order of his finances is disrupted. So Allah the Exalted legislated for people the continuation of the customary indebtedness among them, lest they suppose that the prohibition of usury, and the return of the transacting parties to their principal capital, amounts to the abolition of all indebtedness. He conveyed this legislation by placing it within another complementary legislation, namely securing it through writing and attestation.

The address is directed to the believers, that is, to them collectively, but what is intended is specifically the parties to the debt. The one most particularly addressed is the debtor, because it is incumbent upon him to put his creditor at ease regarding his wealth. Therefore it is incumbent on the borrower to request the writing, even if the creditor does not ask for it. This is derived from what Allah related in Surah al-Qasas concerning Musa and Shu'ayb, when Shu'ayb hired Musa. When they agreed upon the wage and the determination of its term, Musa said ﴿Allah is Witness over what we say﴾ [al-Qasas 28:28]. That was an attestation on his own part to his employer, without Shu'ayb having asked him for it.

The word "tadayun" is a form of mutual action (tafa'ul), and it is used here even though the act proceeds from one side only, namely the lender, because you say "dana minhu" (he borrowed from him) and "fadanahu" (he lent to him). So the reciprocal form is viewed with respect to the addressees, who are the whole community, since within the collective there is a creditor and a debtor, and thus the collective comprises both sides. You may also take the reciprocal form as not in its original sense, as when you say "tadayantu min Zayd" (I borrowed from Zayd).

The qualifier "bi-dayn" (for a debt) is either merely for emphasis (al-itnab), as people say, "I saw him with my own eye and touched him with my own hand," or it is so that it may refer back to the pronoun in His saying ﴿write it down﴾ (fa-uktubuhu). Without mentioning it, one would say "fa-uktubu al-dayn," and the composition would not be as fine. It is also clearer in distinguishing the types of debt into deferred and immediate, as stated in al-Kashshaf.

[Page 99]

Al-Tibi said, on the authority of the author of al-Fara'id: It is possible to suppose that "tadayun" is used metaphorically for a promise, as in the verse of Ru'ba:

*"I lent to Arwa, and debts are paid: she delayed some of them and paid some."*

So He mentioned His saying "bi-dayn" to ward off the suspicion of metaphor. In the speech of the Arabs, "dayn" means a deferred return. Their poet said:

*"She promised us two dirhams' worth of wine and roasted meat, immediate, not deferred."*

His saying ﴿for a specified term﴾ (ila ajal musamma) is a requirement to specify terms for debts, so that they do not fall into disputes and contentions over claims. Thus the legislation on fixing the term is incorporated within the legislation on recording.

The "ajal" is a span of time with a definite end, placed as a container for an act that is not required to be hastened, because the completion of that act is desired at the end of that span or within it.

"Ajal" is a noun, not a verbal noun. The verbal noun is "ta'jil," which is granting a term. Because it carries the sense of extending the time for an action, "ajal" is applied to delay. This has already been discussed in His saying ﴿when they reach their term﴾ and His saying ﴿until the prescribed term reaches its end﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:235].

"Musamma" in its real sense means that which is distinguished by a name that differentiates it from what resembles it in its genus or species. Among these are proper names and common names. Here "musamma" is used figuratively for the determined and bounded. What is intended is to limit it by an end point among the known periods of time among people. So this is likened to specification by assigning a name, with the common factor being definition, since it cannot be distinguished from its like except by that. Hence the term "tasmiya" (naming) is applied to it. From this is the jurists' expression "al-mahr al-musamma" (the named dower). So the meaning is a term specified by its end. Since a debt is only ever for a term, the purpose of describing the debt with this attribute is to describe the term as "musamma," as an incidental inclusion of the command to specify the term.

His saying ﴿for a debt for a specified term﴾ covers every debt, whether from a loan, a sale, or otherwise. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning the salam (advance sale), that is, the sale of fruits and similar fungible goods on the seller's liability for a deferred term, when the seller is one who has a liability. The salam was among the transactions of the people of Madina. The meaning of his statement is that the salam sale was the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of the verse. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that a specific cause does not restrict the generality of the wording.

[Page 100]

Regarding "fa-uktubuhu" (write it down), it is said that the command is for recommendation (istihbab). This is the view of the majority, and of Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad. In that case His saying ﴿but if one of you trusts another﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:283] is a completion of the meaning of recommendation. It is also said that the command is for obligation (wujub). This was said by Ibn Jurayj, al-Sha'bi, Ata', and al-Nakha'i. It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and it is the view of Dawud. Al-Tabari chose it. Perhaps those who hold the obligation of the attestation that comes later, at His saying ﴿and call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾, are the ones who hold the obligation of writing. In that case His saying ﴿but if one of you trusts another﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:283] is a restriction of the generality of the times of obligation, since the command implies repetition, especially when it is conditioned by a stipulation. The earlier scholars, in their expressions, called this "naskh" (abrogation).

The purpose of the command to write is securing rights, cutting off the causes of disputes, organizing the community's transactions, and making it possible to inspect corrupt contracts. The stronger view is that the command is for obligation, since that is the default meaning of a command, and it has been reinforced by these emphasizing factors. Also, His saying ﴿but if one of you trusts another﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:283], to the end of the verse, is a specific concession applying to the situation of mutual trust between the two contracting parties, as will come. The situation of trust is one free from the arising of denial and dispute. Allah the Exalted intended for the community the cutting off of the causes of lawlessness and chaos, so He obligated them to document in situations of contention, lest they be lax at the outset and then lead to dispute in the outcome. It appears to me that in the obligation there is also a removal of hardship from the creditor if he asks his debtor to write, so that the debtor does not regard that as an insult to his trustworthiness. In laws there is a justification for both transacting parties.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The sound view is that it is not obligatory, because a person may waive this right and leave it, by consensus (ijma'). So how could it be obligatory for him to write it? It is merely a recommendation for caution. This is a statement that may appeal at first glance, but it is refuted by the fact that the context of securing a right is not the context of a voluntary gift.

The objective of the Shari'a is to alert the holders of rights, so that they do not become lax and then regret, and it is not intended to nullify the trust some of them place in others. Among its objectives is also to remove the resentment of the debtor from the creditor's securing of his right, when he knows that it is by a command from Allah. And among its objectives is cutting off the causes of dispute.

His saying ﴿write it down﴾ (fa-uktubuhu) includes two situations. The first: the writing is done by the two contracting parties in their own handwriting, or in the handwriting of one of them, which is then handed to the other, if both of them are able to write, because one's ignorance of writing negates his trust in the other's writing.

[Page 101]

The second: the writing is done by a third party who mediates between them. He writes what the two agreed upon, two witnesses attest to it, and it is delivered into the hand of the holder of the right, when they (or one of them) are unable to write. This was the common situation of the Arabs at the time the verse was revealed. Illiteracy was widespread among them, and writing was found in al-Anbar, al-Hira, some regions of Yemen, and among a few who learned it in Makka and Madina.

His saying ﴿let a scribe write it down between you justly﴾ is a command to the two parties to employ a scribe to write between them, because the general state of them was ignorance of writing.

The command verb is directed at the scribe, which is an exaggeration in commanding the contracting parties to seek a scribe. The Arabs often aim at the desired object and place it in the position of a means, as an intensification of its realization. Like their saying in a command, "Let your son be well-mannered," and in a prohibition, "Do not forget what I have enjoined upon you," and "I will not find you doing such and such."

So the object of the command verb is the adverbial phrase "between you" (baynakum). This is not a command to the scribe. As for the command to the scribe, it is His saying ﴿no scribe should refuse to write as Allah has taught him, so let him write﴾.

His saying "bil-'adl" means "with justice" (bil-haqq). The word "'adl" here does not carry the sense of the uprightness by which a witness is described, so that one would say "a man who is 'adl." This is because the presence of the preposition "bi" turns it away from that meaning. A parallel is His later saying ﴿so let his guardian dictate with justice﴾.
