For this reason, the exegetes restricted His saying "fa-uktubuhu" to the case where the writing is done by someone other than the two contracting parties, because that is the usual case, and because it is followed by His saying ﴿let a scribe write it down between you justly﴾, which serves as an explanation of how "fa-uktubuhu" is to be carried out. Nevertheless, if the two contracting parties are able to write, their writing is understood through the implication (lahn al-khitab) or the spirit (fahwa) of the address.

For this reason, the verse was a proof for the majority of scholars regarding the validity of relying on handwriting (al-ihtijaj bil-khatt), since the employment of a scribe benefits only by reading his handwriting.

His saying ﴿no scribe should refuse to write﴾ is a prohibition addressed to whoever is asked to write between the two debtors, forbidding him from refusing when he is called to it. This is another ruling, and it is not an emphasis of His saying ﴿let a scribe write it down between you justly﴾, for you have already learned that this is a ruling addressed to the two contracting parties. This prohibition has been disputed regarding its implication. It was said to be a prohibition of prohibition (nahy tahrim), so whoever is called upon to write between the two debtors is forbidden to refuse. On this view, responding to write is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn). This is the view of al-Rabi', Mujahid, Ata', al-Tabari, and it is the one that should not be deviated from.

It was also said that responding is an individual obligation only when there is one scribe in the place. If there are others, it is a collective obligation (fard kifaya). This is the view of al-Hasan, and its meaning is that it is left to their religious conscience, because if they collude in refusing, they all incur sin. And if it were said that it is a collective obligation upon those in the locale of the two debtors who know how to write, and that it becomes specific upon being designated by the one who seeks the securing of the right, it would be a sound view. The one most entitled to seek the securing of the right is the borrower, as has been mentioned above.

It was also said that the obligation falls upon the scribe only when he is free, as al-Suddi said. It was also said that it is abrogated by His saying ﴿let neither scribe nor witness be harmed﴾. This is the view of al-Dahhak, and it is reported from Ata'. But there is consideration in this, because attending to write between two debtors is not harm, except in rare situations, such as the great distance between the place of the debtors and the place of the scribe. It is reported from al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd that it is abrogated by His saying, after this, ﴿but if one of you trusts another, let the one who is trusted render his trust﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:283]. I will later demonstrate the invalidity of that.

On the basis of this disagreement, there is a dispute over the permissibility of taking a wage for writing between the two debtors, because if it is obligatory, then there is no wage for it, and otherwise a wage is permissible.

Included within indebtedness are all transactions in which securing a right by writing and attestation is sought.

The discussion of the ruling on giving testimony will come at His saying ﴿let neither scribe nor witness be harmed﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 2 of 5):

His saying: ﴿as Allah taught him﴾ means: writing resembling that which Allah taught him to write. By "resemblance" is meant conformity, not mere association. It is like His saying: ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you have believed in﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137]. The kaf (ka, "as") is in the position of an absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), since it is an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, and "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah).

The meaning of "what Allah taught him" is that he writes what he believes, without distorting or equivocating, for Allah taught only the truth, which is what is settled in human nature (fitrah). People turn away from it through desire, so they alter and change, and that alteration is not what Allah taught them. The saying of the Prophet ﷺ points to this: "Consult your own heart, even if the people give you a fatwa."

It is also possible that the kaf is for the correspondence of one thing to its equal and of a recompense to its repayment, meaning: that he should write a writing that matches Allah's teaching him writing, by benefiting people with it in gratitude for Allah's facilitating for him the means of knowledge of it. This gratitude is achieved only by writing what preserves the truth, without falling short or concealing. From this sense of comparison arises the sense of causation, as in His saying: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾ [al-Qasas: 77], and His saying: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198].

On this view, the kaf is either a substitute for the absolute object or an attribute of a deleted object, through interpreting the verbal noun of "that he write" as "the written." "Ma" in this respect is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). In both cases it is connected to "that he write." The author of al-Kashshaf permitted connecting it to "then let him write," which is also a valid reading of the verse.

His saying: ﴿then let him write﴾ is a consequence of His saying: ﴿and let not a scribe refuse﴾, and it is an explicit statement of what the prohibition implies, and a repetition of the command in His saying: "write it down." It thus conveys both the emphasis of the command and the emphasis of the prohibition. It was repeated so that His saying ﴿and let the one who owes the debt dictate﴾ could be linked to it, because the first command was distant from what followed it by the intervening matter. A similar case is His saying, after His saying ﴿and the people of Musa took after him, from their ornaments, a calf, a body﴾ [al-A'raf: 148] and so on: "they took it."

His saying: ﴿let the one who owes the debt dictate﴾. Amalla and amla are two dialects: the first is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad, and the second is the dialect of Tamim. The Qur'an came with both. He said: ﴿let the one who owes dictate﴾, and He said: ﴿it is dictated to him morning and evening﴾ [al-Furqan: 5]. They said: the original is amlal, then the lam was changed to ya' because it is lighter, the reverse of what they did in their saying taqadda al-bazi, whose original is taqaddada.

The meaning of both words is to deliver speech to a listener so that he may write it down from him. Thus the lexicographers in al-Lisan and al-Qamus explained it, and this is a deficiency in the exegesis, which I think arose from limiting their view to this verse, which concerns the purpose of writing. Yet His saying in surah al-Furqan ﴿it is dictated to him morning and evening﴾ [al-Furqan: 5] shows that imla and imlal occur both for the purpose of writing and for the purpose of narration and transmission, as in the verse of al-Furqan, and for the purpose of memorization, as one says "the teacher dictated to the child for memorization," which is the method of teaching memorization to the blind. The precise statement is therefore that these two words are explained as delivering speech so that it may be written down from, or narrated, or memorized. Here "al-haqq" means what is due, that is, what is established for the creditor.

In this command there is a lesson for witnesses, for among them are those who write in deeds of endowment and the like what the one against whom it is witnessed did not dictate to them, except when he had delegated to the witness the task of comprehending what contains the documentation of his right, or had made him acquainted with it before its execution, in the presence of the notary.

The two pronouns in His saying ﴿and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾ and His saying ﴿and let him not diminish anything from it﴾ may refer to the one who owes the debt, since he is the nearest mentioned antecedent of the two pronouns, meaning: let him not reduce the creditor's due in any way at the time of dictation. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. According to this view, it is a command to the debtor to acknowledge the whole debt and not to cheat the creditor. In my view this is remote, since such a charge would be pointless: if the debtor concealed anything or cheated, the creditor would object to him, because both are present at the writing, as in His saying ﴿and let a scribe write between you﴾. The pronouns may also refer to "scribe," on the basis that this prohibition bears more directly on the scribe, who is the one who may overlook part of what was dictated to him.

The pronoun in His saying "from it" refers to the right (al-haqq), which belongs to both contracting parties. So if he diminishes any part of it, he harms one of them without doubt. This is a wonderful concision.

The lexicographers explained al-bakhs as diminution, but it appears that it is more specific than mere nuqs (diminution): it is diminution by concealment. The closest word to its meaning is ghabn (cheating). Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Ahkam, in commenting on surah al-A'raf: "Al-bakhs in the language of the Arabs is diminution by disparagement and devaluation, or deception regarding value, or trickery in exaggerating the measure, or reduction from it, that is, from the heedlessness of the owner of the right." This is the most fitting meaning for the verse, because what is intended is the prohibition of reducing the right out of the heedlessness of its owner, and for this reason the witness, the debtor, or the creditor is forbidden. It will come in surah al-A'raf at His saying: ﴿and do not defraud people of their things﴾ [al-A'raf: 85].

His saying: ﴿But if the one who owes the debt is foolish, or weak﴾. The safih is one whose reason is impaired, and this was explained earlier at His saying: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142].

The da'if is the young child, and this was explained earlier at His saying: ﴿and he has weak offspring﴾ [al-Baqarah: 266].

The one who ﴿cannot dictate﴾ is the incapable, such as one who is mute, blind, and deaf altogether.

The purpose of emphasizing the hidden pronoun in the verb "yumilla" with the explicit pronoun is to prepare for His saying ﴿then let his guardian dictate﴾, lest people suppose that his incapacity removes the obligation of calling witnesses against him for what he borrows. Before Islam, and in its early period, guardians were the elders of the kin. The walī is one who has authority over the foolish, the weak, and whoever cannot dictate, such as the father, the executor, and the tribal leaders. In the hadith of the delegation of Hawazin, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: "Let your leaders raise your matter to me." This was in the early period of Islam and concerned tribal rights.

The meaning of "with justice" is "with right." This is evidence that the acknowledgment of the executor and the one placed in charge is binding regarding the rights of the one under guardianship when its cause is evident. The later jurists did not act on it, to block the means, for fear of collusion to waste the property of the weak.

* * *

﴿And call to witness two witnesses from your men. But if there are not two men, then a man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses, so that if one of them errs, the other may remind her﴾.

This is a conjunction with "then write it" and is other than it, not an explanation of it, for if it were an explanation it would not be joined by the conjunction "and." So the things commanded to the contracting parties are two: the writing and the calling of witnesses to it. The purpose of the writing is to record the form of the contract and its conditions, and to remember them against forgetfulness. For this reason the jurists called it "the mention of the right" (dhikr al-haqq), and it is called a contract ('aqd). Al-Harith ibn Hillizah said:

Fearing injustice and the disputes, and can the desires undo what is in the records?

Allah said: ﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken into possession﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283]. He did not place between the absence of a scribe and the pledge a level, namely witnessing without writing, because His saying ﴿and you do not find a scribe﴾ comes to mean: "and you do not find witnessing." For this reason the scribe may be one of the two witnesses. The Qur'an made a scribe and two witnesses because few combine knowledge of writing with fitness for testimony.

"Istashhidu" means "ashhidu" (call to witness), so the sin and ta' are merely for emphasis. You may also take them as indicating a request, meaning "seek the testimony of two witnesses," and then it is a charge to strive for witnessing, which is the obligation attached to the owner of the right. His saying ﴿and let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾ is then a charge to whomever the owner of the right asks to witness against them, that he not refuse.

Shahadah in its original sense is presence and observation, and what is meant here is a particular presence, namely presence for the purpose of being informed of the debt. This is a well-known usage of shahadah for presence to observe a contract between two contracting parties, or to hear a contract from a single contracting party, as in divorce and endowment. Shahadah is also used for a report that someone gives of an event that occurred, for the purpose of using it as proof against one who denies it. This is the usage in His saying: ﴿Then they did not bring four witnesses﴾ [al-Nur: 4].

The command is directed to seeking the calling of witnesses, because that is within the capacity of the responsible person. The listener understands that the purpose of seeking witnesses is that they be obtained. For this reason, after that, He commanded the one called as witness (mustashhad, with fatha on the ha') to comply, saying: ﴿and let the witnesses not refuse when they are called﴾.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and call to witness two witnesses from your men﴾, it is said that the command is for obligation, which is the view of the majority of the early scholars (al-salaf). It is also said that it is for recommendation, which is the view of the majority of the later jurists: Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad. This will come at His saying: ﴿and call witnesses when you trade﴾.

His saying "from your men," meaning from the men of the Muslims, combines two conditions: that they are men, and that they are among those whom the pronoun includes.

The plural pronoun of the addressees is intended to mean the Muslims, as in His saying at the opening of these rulings: "O you who have believed."

As for a child, the Law did not count him, because of the weakness of his reason in grasping the places of testimony and the openings of suspicion.

The word rajul in its original linguistic sense denotes maleness, which excludes females, and denotes adulthood, which excludes children. The pronoun added to it denotes the attribute of Islam. As for women, their ruling is mentioned after this. As for the disbeliever, the difference of religion requires distance in conditions, dealings, and manners, so it is not possible to comprehend the states of the upright and the doubtful from the two groups. Moreover, intense association was stipulated in the vetting of Muslims. Also, it is known that most people of other religions treat the rights of those who differ from them lightly, and this comes from confusion of rights and ignorance of the obligations of the Islamic religion. The earlier religions did not address respect for the rights of opponents, so their followers thought it permissible to disregard them. Allah has related of them that they said: ﴿There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]. These are the texts of the Torah in many places, which forbid some things or command others and restrict them to the Children of Israel, and permit violating that with the stranger. We have not seen in any religion an explicit equality in rights except the religion of Islam. How then can we rely on the testimony of those who regard Muslims as apostates from the religion of truth, hostile to them, and who accuse their prophet and others besides him? What, then, is to be hoped from these people, that they would speak the truth for them or against them? Christianity follows the rulings of the Torah. Yet the aloofness of the people of religions is a matter that is like a natural disposition. Even Islam, with its command to Muslims to act justly toward the people of protection (ahl al-dhimmah), we do not see from them obedience in what it commands them regarding those people.

**[Page 107 continues]**

There is an allusion to this cause in the Qur'an, in the words ﴿That is because they said, "There is no blame upon us regarding the gentiles"﴾ [3:75]. In al-Bukhari, in the narration of Abu Qilaba in the assembly of Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz, and what has been related "from Sahl ibn Abi Hathma al-Ansari, that a group of his people went to Khaybar and scattered there, and they found one of them slain. They said to those in whose midst the slain man was found, 'You killed our companion.' They said, 'We did not kill him.' So they went to the Prophet ﷺ and complained to him. He said to them, 'Bring a clear proof against the one who killed him.' They said, 'We have no proof.' He said, 'Then let the Jews swear to you fifty oaths.' They said, 'They do not care if they kill us all and then swear.' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked that his blood should be nullified, and he paid its blood-money from the property of the charity (sadaqa). Thus the Prophet ﷺ affirmed the statement of the Ansar about the Jews, that they do not care if they kill all the people and then swear."

If it is asked: how did the Sharia accept the oath of the defendant who is a disbeliever? I answer: it accepted it because it is the furthest that can be done to repel the claim, and the Sharia regarded it as better than dismissing the claim altogether.

For this reason the scholars of Islam agreed that the testimony of People of the Book is not accepted among Muslims, except in the case of a bequest during a journey. They differed concerning calling upon them as witnesses for a bequest during a journey. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Shurayh said that the testimony of non-Muslims is accepted in a bequest during a journey, and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari judged accordingly during his term as judge in Kufa. This is also the view of Ahmad, Sufyan al-Thawri and a group of scholars. But the majority said that the testimony of non-Muslims is not permissible, and they held that what is in the verse of the bequest is abrogated (mansukh, i.e., superseded by a later ruling). This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam, Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i. They differed concerning the testimony of some of them against others before the judge of the Muslims. Abu Hanifa permitted it, considering that there is no suspicion of their being lax with the rights of Muslims. The majority disagreed with him. The correct position is that it is impossible for the judge of the Muslims to know the trustworthiness of some of them toward others and the truthfulness of their reports, as we mentioned just above.

**[Page 108]**

The apparent meaning of the verse is the acceptance of the testimony of a just slave. This is the view of Shurayh, Uthman al-Batti, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr. But from Mujahid: the intended meaning is free men. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i. What appears to me is that the restriction of slaves from the general wording of the verse is by custom ('urf) and by analogy (qiyas). As for custom: the usual usage of the word "man" (rajul) and "men" (rijal) is that when used without qualification it refers only to free men. They say "the men of the tribe" and "the men of the quarter." Mahkan al-Tamimi said:

*O mistress of the house, rise not in humiliation,*
*gather to you the men of the quarter and the strangers.*

As for analogy: slaves are not counted in society, because the state of servitude cuts them off from matters other than the affairs of their owners, so they generally do not keep track of transactions. Also, they are raised without concern for manly honour (muru'a), so the omission of considering a slave's testimony is grounded in the presumption (of unreliability). Yet my mind is not fully at rest with this reasoning.

The number of witnesses was required, and a single just witness was not sufficient, because when testimony is connected to a specific right of a specific person, the witness is suspected of the possibility that the wrongdoer who claims a false right might approach him and induce him to distort the testimony. So a safeguard was needed to remove the suspicion. Islam was made a condition for the witness, and religion is enough as a restraint, and justice (adala) restrains through religion and honour. A second witness was added to make it unlikely that both witnesses would collude in falsehood. Thus this verse establishes that plurality is a condition of testimony as such, unlike narration (riwaya), because there is no suspicion of self-interest in narration, since it is not connected to a specific right. For this reason, if a narrator related a hadith that is evidence in a case in which the narrator himself has a right, his narration would not be accepted. Umar obliged Abu Musa al-Ash'ari to bring a witness with him to confirm that the Messenger of Allah said, "If one of you asks permission three times and is not granted it, let him return," because Abu Musa claimed that when Umar did not grant him permission the third time, he returned. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri then testified for him before a gathering of the Ansar.

The number is two in financial transactions, as here.

His saying ﴿if there are not two men﴾ means: if the witnesses are not two men, i.e., if two men did not attend the transaction but only one man attended. Then ﴿a man and two women﴾ shall testify. So his saying ﴿a man and two women﴾

**[Page 109]**

is the answer (jawab) of the conditional clause. It is part of a sentence whose predicate has been omitted, because what is implied suits the predicative sense better. The evidence for the omitted element is his saying ﴿and call upon [two witnesses]﴾. The omitted element has been understood, so however you estimate it, it is acceptable to you.

In the verse the incomplete verb (kāna) is used, although it was possible to say "if there are not two men" (in ﴿in lam yakun rajulan﴾). This is to avoid the misunderstanding that the testimony of two women is accepted only when two men cannot be found, as some people understood it, though this contradicts the view of the majority, because the purpose of the Lawgiver is to ease matters for those who transact. There is also another aim in it, which is to train them to include women in the affairs of life, since in the pre-Islamic period women did not participate in such affairs. So God made two women stand in place of one man, and He gave the reason for this in His saying ﴿so that if one of the two errs, the other may remind her﴾. This is another safeguard against the distortion of testimony, namely the fear of confusion and forgetfulness, because a woman is by natural disposition more modest than a man, generally speaking. Here "errs" (taḍilla) means "forgets."

His saying ﴿that she errs﴾ (an taḍilla) was read by the majority with a fatha on the hamza of "an," taking it as having had the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil) omitted from it, as is most common in Arabic speech with "an." Causation in this statement is directed toward what needs to be explained in order to persuade those under obligation, since in this sentence we find no ruling that souls might not accept except the substitution of two women for one man. So its reason was stated explicitly. The implied lam before "an" is connected to the omitted predicate in the conditional answer clause, since the sense is: "then a man and two women shall testify," or: "then let a man and two women testify." They read "fa-tudhakkira" in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿an taḍilla﴾. Hamza read it with a kasra on the hamza, taking "in" as a conditional particle and "taḍilla" as the conditional verb, and with a raf' on "tudhakkiru," taking it as the predicate of an omitted subject after the fa', because the fa' indicates that what follows is not jussive. The sense is: "then she reminds her, the other one," in the manner of His saying: ﴿and whoever returns to it, Allah will take retribution from him﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 95].

Since "an taḍilla" has the meaning of "lest one of them err," the cause appears outwardly to be the erring, but this is not so. Rather the cause is what follows from the erring, namely the loss of the matter testified to. So His saying ﴿then one of them reminds the other﴾ is built upon this, because "fa-tudhakkira" is coordinated with "taḍilla" by the fa' of sequence, so it is part of its completion. What matters is the end of the statement, as we mentioned earlier regarding His saying: ﴿Would any of you wish to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines﴾ [al-Baqara: 266]. A similar example, as in al-Kashshaf, is: "I prepared the piece of wood, lest the wall lean and I prop it up; and I prepared the weapon, lest an enemy come and I repel him." In this usage there is a departure from the apparent form, which would be to say: "lest one of them remind the other when she forgets." The author of al-Kashshaf justified it on the ground that it shows the great concern with the matter of reminding, to the point that the speaker gives as cause the things that lead to it for the sake of achieving it. Ibn al-Hajib, in his Amali on this verse in Cairo in the year 616 AH, claimed that it is a feature of the Arabic language that when they mention a cause, and that cause has a cause, they mention the cause of the cause first and make the cause coordinated with it by the fa', so that both meanings are obtained in a single expression. He illustrated it with the example given in al-Kashshaf. The apparent sense of his words is that this is obligatory, and I have not seen it attributed to anyone else.

What I consider is that the reason for this departure in such cases is that a cause is sometimes simple, as when you say, "I did such-and-such out of honour for you," and sometimes compound, consisting of averting harm and securing benefit by that averting. In that case the speaker, in giving the cause, uses an expression that indicates both matters as a single cause, for brevity of speech, as in the verse and in the two examples. This is because the purpose of plurality is the fear of forgetfulness befalling the lone woman, so the testimony of the woman who is the subject of the claim is taken, and the second woman is intended to remind her. This is better than what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned.

In His saying ﴿then one of them reminds the other﴾ there is an explicit noun where a pronoun would be expected, because the apparent form would be: "then the other reminds her." That is because "the one" (iḥdā) and "the other" (ukhrā) are ambiguous descriptive terms that do not specify the particular person intended. Wherever you place them, in the position of subject or object, the meaning remains the same. If a pronoun were used for "the one" as the object, the referent would be clear, whether the explicit "one" (iḥdāhumā) is subject or object. So it should not be supposed that the explicit "iḥdāhumā" being the subject in the verse contradicts its being an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, because if it were replaced by a pronoun, the pronoun would be an object, and the object is other than the subject, as al-Taftazani supposed. This is because what is considered in the consideration of using an explicit noun in place of a pronoun is the possibility of the pronoun while the meaning remains the same, and this is present in the verse, as is not hidden.

Then the reason for the explicit noun here has been a point over which the thoughts of the exegetes have become perplexed, and the earlier scholars did not address it. Al-Taftazani said in his commentary on al-Kashshaf: "Among what should be addressed is the reason for the repetition of the word 'iḥdāhumā'. There is no doubt that it is not from the placement of the explicit in the place of the pronoun, since the one who reminds is not the one who forgets, unless the second 'iḥdāhumā' is taken to be in the position of the object; but that is not permissible because of the fronting of the object in a place where ambiguity would result. It is possible to say 'fa-tudhakkirahā al-ukhrā,' so the substitution must have a reason." Al-Isam said in the margin of al-Baydawi: "The reason for the repetition is that the original structure was: 'an tudhakkira iḥdāhumā al-ukhrā in ḍallat' (that one of them reminds the other if she errs). When 'in ḍallat' was placed first and presented in the form of a cause, the pronoun could not be used, namely because the referent had not preceded it. It could not be said 'an taḍilla al-ukhrā' because it is not good before the mention of 'iḥdāhumā,' since 'al-ukhrā' cannot be a descriptive term except in opposition to a mentioned opposite descriptive term. So 'iḥdāhumā' was substituted for 'al-ukhrā', and the original cause was not altered from its form, because 'an taḍilla iḥdāhumā' had not been placed before it." This is the reason for the explicit noun.

Al-Khafaji said in the margin of the commentary: "They said: the reason is generality (ibhām), because each of the two women may be subject to what the other is subject to, of forgetting and reminding, so the statement took on the sense of generality. That is to say, the explicit form was used lest it be supposed that one of the two women could only be the reminder of the other, and therefore would not be a witness in her own right." The origin of this answer is from Shihab al-Din al-Ghaznawi, a contemporary of al-Khafaji, in response to a question al-Khafaji addressed to him. This was the question:

*O head of the scholars, noble masters,*
*whose generosity spread over all creation,*
*what is the secret of the repetition of "iḥdā" instead of "tudhakkiruhā"*
*in the verse about witnesses in al-Baqara?*
*The apparent state is brevity of the pronoun in place of*
*the repetition of "iḥdāhumā," had he mentioned it.*
*To take "al-iḥdā" as referring to the testimony itself in*
*the first is not acceptable to the knowledgeable.*
*So plunge with your thought to extract its pearl*
*from the sea of your knowledge, then send us its pearls.*

Al-Ghaznawi answered:

*O you whose benefits are spread by knowledge,*
*and whose virtues are famous throughout existence,*
*"an taḍilla iḥdāhumā" – the wording admits of*
*either of them, so it requires the explicit form.*
*Had a pronoun been used, it would have required*
*the specifying of one woman for the ruling, which is a consideration.*
*And as for what you have returned as the solution, it is, as*
*you indicated, not acceptable to one who has examined it.*

**[Page 110]**

[p. 112]

"This is what the dull mind has allowed itself to suppose, and God knows best what it intends in its meaning."

The question and answer have already pointed to a rebuttal of an answer given by Abu al-Qasim al-Maghribi in his tafsir, when he took (one of them, the first) to refer to one of the two testimonies, and took (she errs) to mean that she loses it through forgetting. He also took (one of them, the second) to refer to one of the two women. Since the referent differs, there is no place for an explicit noun in a position where a pronoun would be expected. This is a forced reading and a scattering of the pronouns for which there is no evidence, so the speech of God should be exempted from such an interpretation. This is what al-Ghaznawi meant by his saying: "And whoever you have refuted, the solution..." etc.

What I think is that this explicit noun in place of a pronoun serves a purpose, namely to make the sentence independent in its meaning, so that it does not need another statement containing a referent for a pronoun, had one been used. This makes the sentence fit to function like a proverb. It seems that the intent here is to indicate that both clauses are a reason for the legislation of having more than one woman as a witness. The woman is exposed to forgetfulness and to weakness in retaining what matters to retain, and multiplicity is a likely cause of differing points of deficiency and error. Thus "lest one of them errs" (﴿أن تضل﴾) is the reason for not being satisfied with one, and his saying "so that one of them may remind the other" (﴿فتذكر إحداهما الأخرى﴾) is the reason for calling a second woman as a witness, so that the testimony of the first is not nullified from its origin.

* * *

﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾.

"Let not refuse" (﴿لا يأب﴾) is conjoined to "and call two witnesses" (﴿واستشهدوا شهيدين﴾), because when He commanded the two contracting parties to call two witnesses, He forbade the one whose testimony is sought from refusing, so that the sought aim, which is the calling of witnesses, may be completed.

The command was given in addressing the contracting parties, and the prohibition was given in addressing the witnesses, out of concern for what is liable to neglect. The contracting parties are suspected of neglecting the calling of witnesses, so they were commanded to do it; the witnesses are suspected of refusing, so they were forbidden. Each implies its opposite.

Calling those who are summoned "witnesses" (shuhada') is based on the first, near sense, which is "being about to be" (al-mushārafah). There seems to be a great subtlety in this, namely an indication that by the very fact of being called to bear witness, answering has become obligatory upon them, and so they become witnesses.

The object of "were called" (du'u) is omitted, either because it is evident from His saying before it, "and call two witnesses" (﴿واستشهدوا شهيدين﴾), meaning: when they are called to testimony, that is, to bearing it (al-tahammul). This is the view of Qatadah and al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman, and it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. The prohibition of refusal at the call to testimony is thus implied all the more. The omission of the object may also be for the purpose of generality, meaning: when they are called for bearing and for delivering together. This is said by al-Hasan, and Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: when they are called to delivering only. Perhaps what led him to this is the word "the witnesses" (al-shuhada'), since they are not truly witnesses except after bearing. What weakens this is that God, Exalted, said after this: ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:283], and that is a prohibition against refusing when called to deliver.

What appears is that the omission of the complement of the verb "were called" serves to convey the inclusiveness of what they are called for in the contract: bearing when the intention of testimony arises, and delivering when the need for proof arises. Ibn al-Hajib said: bearing, where it is needed, is a communal obligation (fard kifaya), and delivering, from among the two couriers if they are two, is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn), and it is not permissible to refer it to an oath.

The discussion of what the prohibition here requires is like the discussion of His saying: ﴿And let not a scribe refuse﴾. It appears that bearing becomes obligatory by appointment from the ruler, or by what he appoints. The norm would be that it be an individual obligation, except in case of necessity, in which case the other two contracting parties shift. As for delivering, it is an individual obligation if there is no harm to the witness in his body or property. According to Abu Hanifa, delivering is a communal obligation unless it becomes obligatory on him, namely when no substitute for him is found. It becomes obligatory only under the conditions of the judge's justice, nearness of the place such that the witness can return to his home on the same day, his knowledge that his testimony will be accepted, and the plaintiff's request. In these qualifications there is a reference of testimony to the various juristic efforts (ijtihad) of the witnesses, and this is a door of interpretations that should not be opened.

Al-Qurtubi said: From this verse it is derived that it is permissible for the ruler to appoint witnesses for the people and to assign them their sustenance from the public treasury, so that they have no occupation except bearing people's rights in order to preserve them. I say: The early judges and rulers of Tunis acted well in appointing witnesses who stand ready to give testimony among the people, taken from those whom the judges accept and know to be upright. Such was also the practice in al-Andalus, and this is part of good consideration for the community. This was not followed in the lands of the East; rather they would rely on the well-known uprightness of some jurists and their mastery of conditions and the writing of documents, so the judges would depend on them and entrust to them what arises in new cases, such as writing claims and judgments. It was among what is counted in the biography of some scholars to say: "He was accepted by the judge so-and-so."

[p. 114]

(﴿And do not be weary of writing it, whether small or large, up to its term﴾) is a generalization over the states or the conditions of the debts commanded to be written. "Small" and "large" here are metaphors for the trivial and the grand. Small transactions are more numerous than large ones, and therefore they are forbidden weariness here. Weariness (al-sa'amah) is boredom from the repetition of some act.

The address is primarily to the two debtors, and it entails the address to the scribe, because when the two debtors call upon him to write, it becomes obligatory on him to write.

The prohibition against it is a prohibition against its effect, which is abandoning the writing, because weariness arises in the soul without choice, so it is not forbidden in itself. It is also said that weariness here is a metaphor for laziness and negligence. "Small or large" (﴿صغيرا أو كبيرا﴾) is in the accusative as a state (hal) of the pronoun governed by "write it" (﴿تكتبوه﴾), or by omitting "was" (kana) together with its subject. Placing "small" before "large" here, though the apparent order would be the reverse, is like placing "drowsiness" before "sleep" in His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255]. This is because the intention here is to state explicitly the generality, in order to repel what may occur to the mind in the way of suppositions about little care for the small, which is more frequent, or the belief that writing the large is not obligatory, had the wording been limited to the small.

The clause "up to its term" (﴿إلى أجله﴾) is a state (hal) of the pronoun governed by "write it" (﴿تكتبوه﴾), meaning: the debt's extent is up to its term on which the two have contracted, and the intended sense is that the limit applies to the writing.

* * *

﴿That is more just in the sight of God, more upright for testimony, and nearer to preventing doubt﴾ is a statement of the reason for legislating the command to write: that writing contains greater reliability. It is "more just" (aqsatu), that is, more strictly just, meaning more equitable, because it better preserves the right and is more upright for testimony, that is, more helpful in establishing it, and nearer to removing suspicion and doubt. These are three reasons. From them it is derived that the legislative aim is that testimony concerning rights be clear and evident, far from possibilities and suppositions. The demonstrative refers to everything mentioned before, considered as a single mentioned thing, which is why it is indicated by the demonstrative of the singular.

[p. 115]

In the verse there is evidence that a legal ruling may be justified by several reasons, and this should not be a matter of disagreement.

The derivation of "more just" (aqsatu) is from "aqsata," meaning "to be equitable," and it is quadriliteral. It is not from "qasata," which means "to be unjust." Likewise, the derivation of "more upright" (aqwamu) from "aqama al-shahadah," meaning "to make the testimony manifest," follows the opinion of Sibawayh that the superlative and the exclamatory may be formed from the quadriliteral hamzated verb, whether the hamzah is for transitivity, as in "a'ta" (he gave), or not for transitivity, as in "afrata" (he exceeded). Sahib al-Kashshaf allowed that "aqsatu" be derived from "qasit," meaning "one possessing justice," that is, a form of nisbah. This is problematic, since there is no verb for this pattern. It has also been objected that forming it from a non-derived noun is harder than forming it from a quadriliteral. My answer is that since the nisbah here refers to a verbal noun, it resembles a derived form, because the verbal noun is the root of derivation. As for "aqwamu" being derived from "qama," which is transformed into the pattern fa'ula with a damma on the 'ayn, indicating an innate disposition, from which comes "qawim" as an adjective of quality (sifah mushabbahah).

* * *

﴿Except that it be a present trade that you conduct among yourselves; then there is no blame on you if you do not write it﴾ is an exception from the generality of the states or conditions in His saying "small or large." It is said to be a disjunctive exception (munqati'), because a present trade is not part of debt at all. The implied sense is: except the case of a present trade.

"Present" (hadirah) means immediate, without delay in it, since "present," "prompt," and "immediate" are synonyms, and "debt," "term," and "credit" are synonyms.

His saying "that you conduct among yourselves" (﴿تديرونها بينكم﴾) is an explanation of the clause "that it be a present trade." The explanation in such a case is closer than in the verse of the poet, which Ibn al-A'rabi related in his Nawadir, and al-'Ayni said it is attributed to al-Farazdaq:

"To God I complain of a need in Medina, and another in Syria: how can the two meet?"

Sahib al-Kashshaf made "how can the two meet?" an explanation of "a need and another." Or you may make "that you conduct" a second adjective of "trade," in the sense of explanation. Perhaps the purpose of mentioning it is to indicate the reason for the concession of not writing, because conducting it in hand has made writing unnecessary. It is also said that the exception is connected (muttasil), and that "present trade" means one deferred to a near term, so it is among the debts, and the concession permits leaving writing for it. This is far-fetched.

His saying "then there is no blame on you if you do not write it" (﴿فليس عليكم جناح ألا تكتبوها﴾) states explicitly the implication of the exception, together with the addition of the word "blame," which indicates that this ruling is a concession, because lifting blame implies that writing is preferable and better.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "trade" in the nominative (tijaratun), taking "be" (takuna) as complete. 'Asim read it in the accusative (tijarata), taking "be" as incomplete, with a concealed pronoun in the verb "be" referring to what the predicate of "kana" indicates, meaning: except that the trade be a present trade, as in the verse of 'Amr ibn Shas, which Sibawayh cited:

"Banu Asad, do you know our trial, when a day was a day of many stars and most dreadful?"

Its implied sense: when the day was a day of many stars.

His saying "illa" (except) originally was "in la" (if not), and it was written joined as a single word.

* * *

﴿And call witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾ is legislation for calling witnesses at sale, even without debt, when the sale is not a present trade. This completes the forms of transaction, since it is either a debt, or leads to one, such as sale on credit; or a spot exchange in trade; or a spot exchange not in trade, such as the sale of property or goods not for trade. It is also said that the intended meaning of "when you conclude sales" (tabaya'tum) is trade, so that the concession is for leaving writing while retaining witnessing without writing. This is very far-fetched, because writing was legislated only for the sake of witnessing and reliability.

His saying, exalted be He, "and call witnesses" (﴿وأشهدوا﴾) is a command. It has been said it is for obligation. This is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid, al-Dahhak,

[p. 117]

'Ata', Ibn Jurayj, al-Nakha'i, Jabir ibn Zayd, Dawud al-Zahiri, and al-Tabari. The Prophet (ﷺ) called witnesses to the sale of a slave whom he sold to al-'Addā' ibn Khalid ibn Hawdhah, and he wrote concerning it: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. This is what al-'Addā' ibn Khalid ibn Hawdhah bought from Muhammad, the Messenger of God. He bought from him a slave with no disease, no defect, and no corruption, a sale of a Muslim to a Muslim."

It has also been said that it is for recommendation (nadb). This was the view of some of the early scholars, al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi, and it is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad. They relied on the Sunnah: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) sold and did not call witnesses." This was related by Ibn al-'Arabi. His answer is that this occurred in matters of trust, and the saying of God, exalted be He, will come: ﴿And if one of you trusts another...﴾, and what Ibn 'Atiyyah said regarding the reason for the non-obligation was previously mentioned, and we refuted it at His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So write it﴾.

* * *

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 5 of 5):

﴿Let no scribe or witness be harmed, and if you do, it is indeed wickedness on your part.﴾

This is a prohibition against harm (al-mudarrah). The phrase admits two readings: the scribe and the witness may be the source of the harm, or the one for whom the document is written and the one for whom testimony is given may be the source of the harm. This is because the verb yudarra (be harmed / harm) may be read in the active or the passive voice. Perhaps the choice of this root here is deliberate, because it carries two rulings, so that the statement is directed at both and is understood in both of its senses, since the two meanings do not contradict each other. This is one aspect of its inimitability (i'jaz).

Harm (al-mudarrah) is causing damage, by which the contracting parties place the two witnesses and the scribe in hardship and loss, or in something that leads to testimony. Our jurists have derived from this verse many rulings that branch out from harm. Among them: a witness should not be made to travel a long distance. Among them: his questioning should not be neglected after a long period, which is the period in which forgetfulness is likely. Among them: he should not be questioned in a way that causes him confusion. It is also derived from this that rulers should set aside a portion of the public treasury (bayt al-mal) to cover the expenses of witnesses' travel and lodging outside their own town, and to compensate them for the financial losses they will suffer from neglecting their families because of that travel, in support of establishing justice to the extent of one's capacity and means.

[Page 118]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and if you do, it is indeed wickedness on your part﴾: the object of "you do" (tafalu) is omitted, and it is understood, since it is the harm that is implied by "let no one be harmed," like the phrase "be just, that is nearer [to righteousness]." Wickedness (fusuq) is a grave sin. He, exalted is He, said: "Wretched is the name of wickedness after faith" (49:11).

* * *

﴿And fear God; God teaches you, and God has knowledge of all things.﴾

He commanded taqwa (God-consciousness), because it is the foundation of all good, and through it the abandonment of wickedness is achieved. His saying, ﴿God teaches you﴾, is a reminder of the blessing of Islam, which brought them out of ignorance into knowledge of the Law (al-shari'ah) and the order of the world, and this is the greatest and most beneficial of knowledge. It is also a promise of the continuance of this, because the present tense (al-mudari') is used. Its conjunction with the command to taqwa implies that taqwa is the cause of the outpouring of knowledge. Some have even said that the waw here indicates causation, meaning "so that He may teach you," and some have considered it one of the meanings of waw, but this is not correct.

The explicit mention of the Divine Name (ism al-jalalah) in the three clauses is for the purpose of drawing attention to each clause, so that each is independent in its meaning, not needing another clause that contains the referent of its pronoun. Thus, when the listener hears each one, he gains independent knowledge, and if he does not hear one of them, that does not harm his understanding of the others. A parallel to this explicit repetition is the saying of the poet al-Hamasi:

Baseness is nobler than Wabr and his father,
and baseness is nobler than Wabr and what he begot.
Baseness is an ailment for Wabr, by which they are killed,
they are not killed by any other ailment, ever.

When he intended to disparage the tribe, and whoever begot it, and what it begot, he made explicit the word "baseness" in the three clauses. And since the fourth clause was like an emphasis of the third, he did not make the word "baseness" explicit in it. Moreover, there is another purpose for the explicit mention of the Divine Name, which is to inspire awe. Repetition has places where it is good and places where it is not good. Shaykh ['Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani] said in Dala'il al-I'jaz, in the conclusion in which he mentioned that taste may perceive things whose causes cannot be identified, and that some of the imams may err in interpretation:

[Page 119]

Among that is what is related from al-Sahib [Ibn 'Abbad] that he said: al-Ustadh Ibn al-'Amid used to select from the poetry of Ibn al-Rumi and would dot what he selected. Al-Sahib said: he handed me the qasidah whose opening is:

Is there beneath my ribs an ember that burns
over what has passed, or a sorrow that renews itself?

He said to me: "Consider it carefully." So I considered it, and I found that he had left out the best verse, on which he had not placed dots, namely his saying:

With an ignorance like the ignorance of the sword while the sword is drawn,
and a forbearance like the forbearance of the sword while the sword is sheathed.

I said: "Why did al-Ustadh leave out this verse?" He said: "Perhaps the pen passed over it." Then he met me later and offered an excuse that was worse than leaving it out. He said: "I only left it out because he repeated the sword four times." Al-Sahib said: "If he had not repeated it, the verse would have been spoiled." Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir said: "The matter is as al-Sahib said." Then he said: Abu Ya'qub said: indirect expression and allusion do not work on minds in the way that explicit statement and clarification do. For this reason, the repetition of the word in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended﴾ (al-Isra: 105), and His saying: ﴿Say: He is God, One; God, the Eternal Refuge﴾ (al-Ikhlas: 1), is a function which, were it not there, would not exist.

Al-Raghib said: they have considered repetition in the verse of the poet:

"So what of the date-stone? Its date was cut, the date was cut,"

to the point that it was said: if a camel were set loose upon this verse, it would graze on the date-stones in it. Then he said: the repetition that is considered good is that which occurs in a manner of magnification or belittlement, in successive clauses, each of which is independent in itself. What is considered ugly is repetition in a single clause, or in clauses with the same meaning, where there is no sense of magnification or belittlement. Thus al-Raghib agrees with al-Ustadh Ibn al-'Amid, and 'Abd al-Qahir agrees with al-Sahib Ibn 'Abbad.

Al-Marzuqi said in his commentary on al-Hamasah, regarding the verse of Yahya ibn Ziyad:

When I saw grey hair had appeared in its whiteness
at the parting of my head, I said: "Welcome, grey hair!"

The required form would have been: "I said to it, 'Welcome.'" But they often repeat proper names and common nouns, and the purpose of the repetition is emphasis.

[Page 120]

Know that repetition is not restricted to magnification. Rather, its place is every context in which it is intended to record the attribution of an action to the possessor of the repeated noun, as has already been mentioned in the two verses of al-Hamasah:

"Baseness is nobler than Wabr..."
. . .
etc.

Repetition has also occurred in succession in His saying, exalted is He, in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿And among them is a group who twist their tongues with the Book, that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book; and they say, "It is from God," but it is not from God; and they speak falsehood against God while they know﴾ (Al 'Imran: 78).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 2, verse 283 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe, then [take] pledges in hand.﴾

This is coordinated with His saying: ﴿When you contract a debt for a specified term﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and so on. All that preceded is a ruling for the state of residence and ability. If they are on a journey and are unable to write because there is no one to write and bear witness, then another ruling has been legislated for them, which is the pledge (rahn). This is the last of the anticipated cases in dealings, and it is the state of travel in most cases; what resembles travel in this condition is attached to it.

Al-rihan is the plural of rahn, and it is also pluralized as ruhun, with a damma on the ra' and a damma on the ha'. The majority of the ten readers recited it with a kasra on the ra' and a fatha on the ha'. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited it with a damma on the ra' and a damma on the ha'. Its plural form takes into account the multiplicity of those addressed by this ruling.

Al-rahn here is a noun for the pledged thing, naming the object by the verbal noun, as in al-khalq (the created). The meaning of rahn is that some of the debtor's property is placed in the hand of the creditor as security for his debt. The original meaning of rahn in the speech of the Arabs indicates restraint. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Every soul is a pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 38]. Thus the pledged item is held in the hand of the creditor until he collects his debt. Zuhayr said:

"And she parted from you with a pledge that has no redemption, on the day of farewell, so the pledge has become locked."

Pledging was common among the Arabs; they would pledge in cases of blood-money and compensation until its payment was made. Sometimes they pledged their sons, and sometimes they pledged one of their chieftains. Al-A'sha said, mentioning that Kisra wanted to take hostages from their sons:

"I swore I would not give him from our sons pledges, lest we corrupt them as one who has corrupted [them]."

Page 121

'Abd Allah ibn Hammam al-Salouli said:

"When I feared their claws, I escaped and pledged Malik to them."

From the hadith of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, that he said to 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf: "Pledge your sons to me."

As for the meaning of (fa-rihan): i.e., pledges with which writing is substituted. Describing them as maqbudah (held in hand) is either merely for clarification, since a pledge is not valid unless it is held; or to exclude pledging as security for debts in the state of residence. From the permission to pledge it is derived that it is permissible. Therefore, when the creditor asks for it, it is granted to him. The verse thus indicates that the pledge is a security for debt.

The verse clearly indicates the legitimacy of pledging during travel. As for the legitimacy of pledging during residence, that is because its conditioning here upon the state of travel is not a conditioning in the sense of restriction, but rather a conditioning in the sense of assumption and estimation: if no witness is found during travel. Therefore there is no implied meaning (mafhum) of the condition, since it came to state a particular state, not for exclusion. The implied meanings of restrictions are not considered unless they are stated as exclusion; and for this reason they did not count them when they came out in the manner of the usual case. There is also no implied meaning in the shift from witnessing, since it is known from the verse that the pledge is a known transaction among them; therefore they were referred to it when necessary, in the sense of guidance and alerting.

Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Dawud al-Zahiri took the apparent meaning of the verse, restricting the pledge to the state of travel, even though the Sunnah established that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Companions pledged during residence.

The verse is evidence that taking possession is among the completions of the pledge in the Sharia, and the scholars did not differ on this. They differed only regarding the rulings arising from abandoning possession. Al-Shafi'i said: possession is a condition for the validity of the pledge, based on the apparent meaning of the verse; so if the contract of pledge is not accompanied by possession, the contract is invalid according to him. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, the companion of Abu Hanifa, said: the pledge is not permissible without possession. The later Hanafis disagreed about the implication of this expression. A group said: it is for him a condition for validity, like the statement of al-Shafi'i. Another group said: it is a condition for binding, close to the view of Malik. All agreed that the pledgor may retract after the contract of pledge if delivery has not occurred. Malik held that possession is a condition for binding, because the pledge is a contract that is established by formula, like sale, and possession is among its necessary consequences. Therefore the pledgor is compelled to allow the pledgee to take possession. However, if the pledgor dies or becomes bankrupt before delivery, the pledgee is on par with the other creditors, since he has nothing that gives him priority over the rest of the creditors. The verse supports this, because God made possession a description of the pledge, so it is known that the reality of the pledge is realized without possession. The people of Tunisia suffice, for pledging real estate and property, with pledging the title deeds, and they consider that to be possession in the case of pledging a debt.

In the verse there is clear evidence for the invalidity of benefiting from the pledge, because God, exalted is He, made the pledge a substitute for witnessing in securing the debt, so there is no basis for benefiting from it; and stipulating benefit from the pledge removes it from being a security to the reality of a sale.

* * *

﴿And if some of you trust others, let the one who is entrusted discharge his trust and let him fear Allah, his Lord.﴾

This is a branch from all that preceded of the rulings on debt: i.e., if each of the two parties to the debt trusts the other, that is, if some of you have confidence in the trustworthiness of others, so that he does not demand from him a witness or a pledge. The nominative "some" is the creditor, and the accusative "others" is the debtor, who is the one entrusted.

Amanah is the verbal noun of amanahu, when he makes him secure. Amn is the tranquility of the soul and its safety from what it fears. The term amanah is applied to the thing entrusted, by applying the verbal noun to the object. The genitive construction of "amanatihi" resembles the genitive of a verbal noun to its object. The mention of amanah in the sense of the attribute of the trustworthy will come at His saying: ﴿And I am a sincere trustworthy adviser to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 68] in Surat al-A'raf.

The term amanah is used here both for the debt upon the person and for the pledge, to magnify that right, because the name "amanat" carries awe in souls. This is a warning against failing to fulfill it; for since it is called amanah, failing to discharge it reverts to treachery, since that is its opposite. In a hadith: "Render the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you."

Page 123

Al-ada' (discharge) is handing over and fulfilling, and returning a thing or its equivalent in what is not intended in its specific form. From it comes the discharge of a trust and the discharge of a debt, i.e., not denying it. He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa': 58]. The meaning: if you suppose that you are free from the need of securing your debts because you are trustworthy among one another, then give the trust its due.

From what has preceded at His saying "write it down" you know that the verse ﴿And if some of you trust others, let the one who is entrusted discharge his trust﴾ is regarded as a completion of the demand for writing and witnessing, a demand of recommendation and preference according to those who understood the command in His saying "write it" as meaning recommendation and preference, and they are the majority. The meaning of its being a completion of that demand is that it explains that writing and witnessing between the two debtors are intended for the good conduct between them; so if they see fit to adopt them, that is well; and if they suffice with what they know of trust between them, they may leave them.

This explanation is followed by an exhortation to both parties to the transaction that they discharge the trust and fear Allah.

It was also mentioned earlier that those who said that writing and witnessing for debts was obligatory and then its obligation was abrogated claimed that its abrogator is His saying: ﴿And if some of you trust others﴾, the verse. This is the view of al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jurayj, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman, and it is attributed to Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

The understanding of their statement and that of Abu Sa'id, if it is indeed established from him, is that by abrogation they meant the specification of a general application of circumstances and times, and calling such a thing abrogation is an ancient usage.

As for those who hold that writing and witnessing for debts is a firm (muhkam) ruling, among them al-Tabari, they restricted the verse ﴿And if some of you trust others﴾ to being a completion of the case of the pledge during travel only, as al-Tabari explicitly stated, though he did not give a clear statement on this, but rather left the matter vague and obscure.

Had they said that this verse refers to the case where a pledge cannot be found during travel, meaning: then none remains except that some of you trust others, the sense would be: "If you do not find a pledge and some of you trust others..." to the end, it would have had a basis, and it would be understood from it that if one does not trust him, he should not lend to him. But this was left implicit to encourage people toward mutual aid and characterizing themselves with trustworthiness. All these three groups make this verse restricted to explaining the case of abandoning securing debts.

Closer to my mind than what they said: this verse is an independent legislation that covers all the circumstances related to debts, including witnessing, pledging, and repayment of debt, and those related to transactions. For this very subtle point the trustees were left unspecified with the word "some," so as to include trust from both sides: that from the creditor's side and that from the debtor's side.

The creditor trusts the debtor when he sees no need for witnessing and does not demand that he give a pledge, whether in travel or in residence.

The debtor trusts the creditor when he hands over to him a pledge whose value is far greater than the value of the debt for which it is pledged; and it is usual that pledges are of greater value than the debts for which they are pledged. So He commanded each trusted party to discharge his trust: the debtor's discharge of his trust is by paying the debt without delay or denial; and the creditor's discharge of his trust, when given a pledge exceeding the value of the debt, is to return the pledge and not deny it, not being concerned with the debt, because the pledge is greater than it, and not to diminish anything of the pledge.

The word amanah is used with two meanings: the attribute of the one who is trustworthy, and the thing entrusted.

From this interpretation is derived the nullification of ghalq of the pledge, which is that the pledged thing becomes the property of the creditor if the debt is not paid at maturity. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The pledge is not locked (la yaghlaq al-rahn)." Locking the pledge was one of the practices of the Days of Ignorance. Zuhayr said:

"And she parted from you with a pledge that has no redemption, at the time of farewell, so the pledge has become locked."

The meaning of "if some of you trust others" is that each of the two parties to the transaction says to the other: "We have no need of witnessing, since some of us trust others," lest the purpose I pointed to earlier be defeated, namely removing the suspicion that one of the two debtors may accuse the other.

Page 125

The warning is reinforced by His saying: ﴿and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾. Mentioning the name of Allah in it, although it could have been dispensed with by saying "let him fear his Lord," serves to instill awe into the listener's heart and cultivate reverence.

His saying ﴿alladhi u'tumina﴾: there occurs a ya' which is the madd at the end of "alladhi," and after it come two hamzas, the first of which is a wasliyyah, the hamza of ifti'al, and the second is qat'iyyah and original. The majority read it with a kasra on the dhal of alladhi and with a silent hamza after the kasra of the dhal, because the hamza of wasl fell away in continuous speech, so the hamza remained in its quiescence; since the motive for changing the second hamza into a madd has disappeared, which is the first hamza. In this reading there is correction of the hamza, since there is no reason for alteration.

Warsh from Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Abu Ja'far read it as "alladhi-tumina," with a ya' after the dhal of "alladhi" then a dammed ta'; considering that the original hamza has changed into a waw after the wasliyyah hamza of ifti'al, because the norm is to damm the hamza of wasl, to harmonize with the vowel of the ta' of ifti'al in the passive construction. When the hamza of wasl was dropped in continuous speech, the second hamza remained as a waw after the kasra of the dhal of "alladhi," and then the waw became a ya'. So in this reading there are two changes.

Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it as "alladhi uwtumina," changing the hamza into a waw in conformity with the damma, indicating the hamza by it.

This difference relates to the mode of recitation, so there is no contradiction in it with the orthography of the Mushaf.

* * *

Surah 2, verse 283 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And do not conceal testimony; whoever conceals it, his heart is indeed sinful. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

This is a second injunction to the witnesses, encompassing all testimony in all circumstances. He first commanded that the witness write down [the debt] with justice, then forbade refraining from writing between the two parties to a debt, and followed this with a prohibition on concealing testimony altogether. This general prohibition thus serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil) of the rulings on testimony regarding debts.

Page 126

Know that the words of the Exalted, ﴿and do not conceal testimony﴾, are a prohibition (nahy). According to the majority of the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh), the requirement of a prohibition is to convey repetition, meaning the repeated abstention from doing what is forbidden at every time the act presents itself. Were it not for its conveying repetition, disobedience would not be realized. And the repetition that a prohibition requires is a repetition that encompasses all the times in which a motive to do the forbidden act arises. Therefore, it is an obligation upon whoever has borne testimony concerning a right that he not conceal it when the occasion for its declaration arises: by conveying it to someone who benefits from it, or by ruling according to it whenever the call for relying upon it appears, or, before that, if the witness fears the loss of what is in his knowledge through absence, the onset of forgetfulness, or the occurrence of death, according to what the witness anticipates regarding his retention of the right that is in his knowledge, to the extent of his capacity and effort.

Since you have already learned that Allah informed us that His purpose is the establishment of testimony in its proper form, by His words ﴿and it is more upright for testimony﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and that He exhorted the witness to appear when summoned to bear witness, by His words ﴿and let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], it is thereby known from all of this that there is concern for making testimony manifest, as a means of manifesting the truth. This meaning is supported and further clarified by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Shall I not inform you of the best of witnesses? He who brings his testimony before he is asked for it." Related by Malik in al-Muwatta', and related from him by Muslim and the Four.

This is the interpretation of the verse in which transmission (athar) and reasoning (nazar) concur. However, it is related in the Sahih from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The best of my ummah is the generation in which I was sent, then those who follow them" — he said it twice, and Abu Hurayrah doubted the third — "then there will succeed a people who bear witness before they are asked to bear witness." The hadith...

It is presented in the manner of censure of those whom it describes as bearing witness before being asked to, and that their censure is on account of that attribute. The scholars have differed regarding its intended meaning. 'Iyad said: "Some took it literally, as censure of one who testifies before testimony is requested from him, while the majority holds otherwise, and that this is not disqualifying. They interpreted what is in the hadith as applying to a case where he testified falsely. Otherwise, it has come in the Sahih: 'The best of witnesses is he who brings his testimony before being asked for it.'" I say: Muslim related from Imran ibn Husayn that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed the best of you is my generation, then those who follow them" — he said it twice or thrice — "then there will come after them a people who bear witness but are not asked to bear witness." The hadith...

Page 127

The apparent meaning is that what Abu Hurayrah related and what Imran ibn Husayn related are one hadith, which both heard, and their wording differed in narrating it. Thus Imran ibn Husayn's wording clarifies Abu Hurayrah's wording, that the meaning of his words "before they are asked to bear witness" is "without being asked to bear witness", i.e., without a summoner having summoned them, meaning they bear testimony regarding what they do not know. This is what al-Mazari meant by his words: "and they interpreted what is in the hadith" — i.e., the hadith of Abu Hurayrah — "as applying to a case where he testified falsely." This is a path to reconciling the two narrations, and it reverts to interpreting the general (mujmal) by the specific (mubayyan).

Al-Nawawi said: "Some scholars interpreted it as meaning that censure applies to a witness who gives testimony before being asked, in the case of testimony concerning the rights of people, unlike what concerns the right of Allah." Al-Nawawi said: "This reconciliation is the position of our companions (the Shafi'is)." This approach reverts to applying each of the two hadiths within its own domain, by interpreting each of the two hadiths in a way other than its apparent meaning, lest either one be nullified.

I say: The Shafi'is built on this a ruling that testimony which the witness delivers before being asked is rejected. Al-Ghazali mentioned it in al-Wajiz. What Ibn Marzuq related in his commentary on Khalil's Mukhtasar upon the Wajiz: "Eagerness for testimony by hastening to it before a claim is not accepted; after a claim and before summoning to testify there are two opinions; and if it is not accepted, does he become impugned? There are two opinions."

As for the Malikis, their statements differ.

What 'Iyad and Ibn Marzuq held is that a witness's delivery of his testimony before being asked for it is accepted, based on the hadith of the Muwatta': "The best of witnesses is he who brings his testimony before being asked for it." Al-Baji related from Malik that the meaning of the hadith is that the witness has testimony for a man who does not know of it, so he informs him of it and delivers it to him before the judge. Malik mentioned it in the Muwatta' without appending anything indicating that no action is taken upon it. Ibn Marzuq followed al-Baji in his commentary on Khalil's Mukhtasar, and claimed that nothing in the school contradicts it.

What Ibn al-Hajib, Khalil, and the commentators on their two abridgments held is that the witness's delivery of testimony before it is requested from him is a barrier to its acceptance. Ibn al-Hajib said: "In delivery, where one begins without a request, in what is purely the right of a human being, it is disqualifying." Khalil, listing the barriers to the acceptance of testimony, said: "or he raised [it] before the request, in pure right of a human being."

Likewise Ibn Rashid al-Qafsi in his book (al-Fa'iq fi al-Ahkam wa al-Watha'iq), and al-Nawawi attributed it to Malik in his commentary on Sahih Muslim, on the basis that the foundation is one, namely the application of the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. Perhaps he took the attribution to Malik from the words of Ibn al-Hajib mentioned above.

Ibn Marzuq claimed that Ibn al-Hajib followed Ibn Shas when he said: "If he hastens to it without a request, it is not accepted." And that Ibn Shas took it from the words of al-Ghazali, who said: "What the texts of the school require is that if he raises it before the request, this does not disqualify it; rather, if his act is not recommended, then at the very least it should not be rejected." He strengthened this with the words of al-Baji in his commentary on the hadith: "The best of witnesses is he who brings his testimony before being asked for it."

They took two routes in explaining the matter: one route reverts to reconciling the two hadiths, which is the route of the Shafi'is, and the route of applying the principle of rejecting testimony on the suspicion of eagerness to act upon one's testimony, and that this is a doubt.

His words: ﴿And whoever conceals it, his heart is indeed sinful﴾ are an added warning. Sin (ithm) is wrongdoing and wickedness.

The heart (qalb) is the name for perception, emotional states, and intentions. Sin is attributed to the heart, though the one who sins is the one who conceals, because the heart, i.e., the movements of the intellect, causes the commission of sin. Concealing testimony is a persistent inner resolve in disobedience. A similar usage is His words: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 116], whereas they only bewitched the people by means of appearances and illusions. And the words of al-A'sha:

"So do likewise, as long as you live, when they flee, and advance when the eyes of people are dazed (tafraq)."

because the dazing (faraq) arises from seeing terrors.

His words: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ are a threat, a metaphor for requital in kind, because the capable one is not prevented from calling to account except by ignorance; so when He is Knowing, He sets up the scale of recompense.

[p. 129]

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾

This is a causal clause (ta'lil) and an argument (istidlal) supporting the content of the phrase ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], and supporting what came earlier, such as: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things,﴾ ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do,﴾ ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do,﴾ and ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾ Since that was an allusion to promise and threat, this statement has come as an explicit declaration and an argument for it. The phrase ﴿And whether you show what is in your selves﴾ through to its end is the focal point of the explicit declaration and the actual purpose of the speech. It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the phrase ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283] up to ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283]. The phrase ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is the locus of the argument, and it is an interposed parenthetical (i'tiraD) between the two conjoined phrases, or it is a causal clause for the phrase ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], in view of the intention of threat and promise. The meaning is that you are His servants, so nothing of your action escapes Him, and the recompense for it is due. On this reading, the phrase ﴿And whether you show what is in your selves﴾ is conjoined to the phrase ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ as a phrase conjoined to a phrase, and the meaning is: You are His servants, and He is your Reckoner. A parallel in meaning is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And keep your speech secret or declare it; indeed, He is Knowing of the contents of the breasts. Should not He know who created?﴾ [al-Mulk: 13–14], and the only difference between them is the stylistic arrangement of the speech.

The sense of the argument here is this: people know that Allah is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and the Creator of creation. So if whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, being created by Him, it follows that all of that must be known to Him, since He is the one who forms their inner thoughts and passing impulses. The comprehensiveness of His knowledge of the conditions of His creatures is part of the full meaning of being Creator and Lord, for if anything were hidden from Him, the servant, in the state of his condition being concealed from Allah's knowledge, would be independent of his Creator. Allah's ownership is the most complete type of ownership in reality, like all the attributes established for Allah, exalted is He. They are the attributes in reality, from necessary existence (al-wujud al-wajib) to what the necessary existence requires of the attributes of perfection. Thus His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is a preparation for His saying ﴿Whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it﴾ and so on.

[p. 130]

His saying ﴿And whether you show what is in your selves﴾ is conjoined with the particle waw (and) rather than fa' (then), to indicate that the ruling it contains is intended in itself, and that what precedes it is a preparation for it.
